rows.question: How does the blood urea to creatinine ratio relate to outcomes in patients with heart failure?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: a higher blood urea to creatinine ratio marks patients with heart failure who go on to die sooner, and the signal is strongest in those with preserved ejection fraction (where the gap is roughly threefold); a raised ratio also tracks with worse symptom class and with more early cardiovascular events, but not with acute kidney injury; the ratio separates individual patients poorly, its added value on top of established biomarker testing is unsettled, and the certainty of the underlying evidence was graded very low. Certainty: The link between a higher ratio and worse outcome is a repeated association of low certainty, not an established cause. Scope: applies to adults with heart failure across the ejection fraction range, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the reported risk estimates as pooled figures, since heterogeneity and missing extractable data prevented statistical pooling and the findings were combined descriptively.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

A higher blood urea nitrogen–to–creatinine ratio (BUN/Cr, or urea:creatinine ratio) is consistently associated with worse survival in heart failure — across acute and chronic HF, and independently of eGFR, creatinine, BUN alone, and natriuretic peptides — but its association with HF rehospitalisation is weaker/inconsistent and its discriminative accuracy is modest, so it is best viewed as a risk marker rather than a validated decision tool.

## Evidence

**Meta-analytic estimate.** A systematic review/meta-analysis of 14 studies found that rising BUN/Cr predicted all-cause mortality in HF ([passage text removed]; I² = 90.8%), with the acute HF subgroup at HR 1.79 (1.15–2.79) and non-acute HF at HR 1.51 (1.34–1.71). The same analysis did **not** support prediction of cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.48, 0.91–2.43) or HF hospitalisation (HR 1.28, 0.73–2.24) [journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0303870; PMC11132513; PMID 38805436]. Effect size scaled with threshold: HR 2.08 (1.59–2.73) for cut-offs >25 versus HR 1.52 (1.24–1.87) for cut-offs ≤20 [PMC11132513]. An earlier pooled analysis of 8 studies/4,700 patients found the highest BUN/Cr category carried ~[passage text removed] (pooled HR 1.77, 1.52–2.07) [PMID 33113531].

**Acute HF.** In PROTECT (n = 2,033 AHF) with reference ranges derived from 4,484 general-population subjects (PREVEND), a BUN/Cr above the age- and sex-specific normal range independently predicted 180-day all-cause death (HR 1.86, 1.29–2.66) and death or cardiovascular/renal rehospitalisation (HR 1.37, 1.03–1.82), but not HF rehospitalisation (HR 1.23, 0.81–1.86) — after adjustment including both creatinine and BUN [heart.bmj.com/content/103/6/407; scholars.duke.edu/display/pub1166429]. Median ratio was 15.0 in the general population versus 21.2 in AHF [[passage text removed]]. In the West Tokyo HF registry, a higher discharge BUN/Cr independently predicted post-discharge all-cause death (HR 1.024 per unit, 1.016–1.030), and the effect was modified by haemoconcentration — the risk was attenuated in patients with extreme haemoconcentration (interpreted as reversible renal dysfunction) but persisted in haemodilution, suggesting failed decongestion or diuretic-resistant neurohormonal activation [PMC6989280; [passage text removed]].

**Chronic/ambulatory HF.** In a pooled individual-patient analysis of five trials (PARADIGM-HF, ATMOSPHERE, DAPA-HF, PARAGON-HF, I-PRESERVE; n = 28,820; median BUN/Cr 20.1 in HFpEF and 18.7 in HFrEF), every outcome examined (HF hospitalisation or CV death, its components, all-cause death) was significantly more frequent above the median ratio after adjustment for NT-proBNP and eGFR; the association was stronger in HFpEF than HFrEF (significant interaction) [PMID 38124454; [passage text removed]]. A per-5-unit increase above a ratio of 20 was associated with HR 1.13 (1.10–1.16) for HF hospitalisation [PMC13239929]. In an older chronic-HF cohort, the top BUN/Cr tertile predicted hospitalisation/all-cause death (HR 1.24, 1.02–1.51), persisting after GFR adjustment (HR 1.23, 1.01–1.51), with a linear trend across tertiles [academia.edu/12874726]. Another chronic-HF cohort found ratio ≥19.37 associated with all-cause mortality (HR 1.885, 1.298–2.737), with the effect concentrated in NYHA IV (HR 2.494, 1.502–4.140) and absent in NYHA II [[passage text removed]]. In ambulatory HFrEF after nurse-led GDMT optimisation, a urea:creatinine ratio ≥95 (AUC 0.701) independently predicted mortality (HR 1.85, 1.09–3.14), including in patients with preserved eGFR (HR 4.03, 1.50–10.9) [mdpi.com/2079-9721/13/11/362].

**Beyond mortality — congestion, AKI, and reversible renal dysfunction.** In outpatients with HF and renal dysfunction, BUN/Cr correlated with inferior vena cava diameter, and ratios above ~25.5 identified caval congestion (adjusted OR 2.98) and predicted all-cause death (HR 2.19, 1.21–3.94) [PMID 26037394; academia.edu/102256096]. In decompensated HF, admission BUN/Cr — but not BUN alone — remained associated with in-hospital *improvement* in renal function after adjustment for admission eGFR (OR 1.4, 1.09–1.82), i.e. it flags a high-risk but potentially reversible ("pseudo-renal") phenotype [PMC4067251]. The ratio also predicts worsening kidney function in ambulatory HF [J Card Fail 2015;21:412–418, cited in PMC9764047].

## Mechanism

Creatinine is minimally reabsorbed, whereas roughly half of filtered urea is reabsorbed, and that reabsorption is amplified by RAAS/sympathetic activation and by arginine vasopressin upregulating collecting-duct urea transporters — so the ratio behaves as a surrogate for neurohormonal activation and renal hypoperfusion rather than pure GFR [jlpm.amegroups.org/article/view/3627/html; [passage text removed]; PMC2733524]. This explains why the marker adds information beyond eGFR and why renal impairment carries worse prognosis mainly when BUN/Cr is high: in ESCAPE, BEST and SOLVD, reduced GFR predicted mortality only in patients with higher BUN/Cr (e.g. BEST HR 1.6, 1.2–2.2), not in those with lower BUN/Cr (HR 0.97, 0.64–1.4; interaction p = 0.02) [academia.edu/12874726].

## Caveats

- **Heterogeneity is high** (I² ~91% for the pooled mortality estimate) and no consensus cut-off exists; reported thresholds vary widely across studies [PMC11132513].
- **Discrimination is limited.** A 2026 systematic review of 20 studies concluded elevated BCR is associated with mortality, rehospitalisation and adverse outcomes, but that "[passage text removed]," with several outcomes graded very-low certainty (e.g. 2-year rehospitalisation significant only in HFpEF, OR 1.78, 1.09–2.93) [PMC13239929; PMID 42178985]. This review has itself attracted a published methodological critique [onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/clc.70431].
- **Direction is not universal.** In one prospective AHF cohort (median follow-up 2.8 years, 197 deaths), it was the *bottom* BUN/Cr quartile that had higher adjusted mortality than the top (HR 1.52, 1.03–2.24), even though the accompanying meta-analysis showed the opposite — highlighting confounding by nutrition, muscle mass and liver function [PMID 33113531]. In the general population the relationship is U-shaped, with lowest mortality around a ratio of ~11.4–14.6 [PMC8856064]; I found no HF-specific study establishing a formal U-shape.
- Commentators have noted that many analyses omit well-recognised prognostic covariates and that prospective validation is needed before the ratio joins routine HF risk models [jlpm.amegroups.org/article/view/3627/html].
- I found no evidence that treating or targeting the BUN/Cr ratio (as opposed to observing it) improves outcomes.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** A higher blood urea (BUN)–to‑creatinine ratio is fairly consistently associated with increased all‑cause mortality and recurrent heart‑failure events across acute and chronic HF, but the association is weaker/inconsistent for cardiovascular death and rehospitalization, its discrimination is poor, the certainty of evidence is low, and part of the signal may be attributable to BUN alone.

**Mortality**
- Pooled meta-analysis of 14 studies: rising BCR predicted [passage text removed]; I²=90.8%), in both acute HF (HR 1.79, 1.15–2.79) and non-acute HF (HR 1.51, 1.34–1.71) subgroups, and in patients ≤70 and >70 years. It did **not** support prediction of CVD mortality (HR 1.48, 0.91–2.43) or HF hospitalization (HR 1.28, 0.73–2.24) [S:21d629a9-e3c2-58dc-b128-1697ff203a01][S:61022f5c-16fa-5ad1-bd41-49487b626719].
- In acute HF (≈2000 patients), after defining age- and sex-specific normal ranges from 4484 people without cardiovascular comorbidity, a higher-than-normal ratio was present in about a quarter of AHF patients and predicted 180-day [passage text removed]) and 60-day death or cardiovascular/renal rehospitalisation (HR 1.37, 1.03–1.82), adding information on top of creatinine and BUN themselves [S:b38da28e-a664-5916-8db4-5f9d53190586][S:3b184dd6-1943-5b48-a7bb-dd46a3c91072][S:f684a209-9ec5-55ff-a790-ac6353b486d5].
- Chronic HF with renal injury (n=504): BUN/Scr ≥19.37 was independently associated with all-cause death (HR 1.885, 1.298–2.737), with effect modification by NYHA class and eGFR [S:6954a19e-1965-5278-8f16-a1b81a91f5b6].
- Ambulatory HFrEF (n=337): urea/creatinine ratio ≥95 independently predicted mortality (HR 1.85, 1.09–3.14; AUC 0.701), and notably also among patients with preserved eGFR (HR 4.03, 1.50–10.9) [S:faa406b7-4c67-55cb-8b75-21c0d979a03a].

**Phenotype and shape of the relationship**
- The signal appears strongest in HFpEF: one cohort using a cutoff of 20.4 found aHR 3.28 (2.00–5.38) for 2-year mortality in HFpEF but null results in HFrEF (1.04, 0.66–1.65) and HFmrEF (1.57, 0.99–2.50) [S:00aa3505-b3ca-55f7-a568-e7a636be7084].
- The association may be non-linear: in 1475 MIMIC-III HF patients, restricted cubic splines showed a U-shaped relationship — no significant association below a ratio of 12.5, an apparently protective range 12.5–22, and increased mortality above 22; the highest quartile had the worst in-hospital (18.8%) and long-term (78.3%) mortality and longer stays [S:f5b3146f-e645-5900-b4a5-ca17b7c2fc14][S:85ed65fc-05db-564a-aea2-f8aaa97085c9].

**Morbidity / HF events and AKI**
- In MADIT-II, BUN:SCr >20 [passage text removed]; 2.5-year cumulative probability of a first HF hospitalization was 34% vs 22%, and of a second HF event 82% vs 44% [S:83d11354-8cf8-5934-b0ba-b2d1c24cfe45][S:594533f6-1da2-51bd-a859-855c1fb6af20][S:d7a661b3-42ca-5874-bfca-832b72612d83].
- In ADHF, timing matters: in a 60-patient prospective study, day-3 urea/creatinine ratio predicted AKI and 28-day mortality (AUC 0.736 and 0.718) whereas the admission ratio did not (p=0.578 and 0.305) [S:189bfa54-f943-59d2-93df-f572d4862c84]. A separate ADHF case-control study found mortality and MACE highest in patients with both AKI and a high BUN/Cr [S:3009becf-d4e9-5211-90e3-5921524f7d55].

**Mechanism**
Roughly 40–50% of filtered urea is reabsorbed in the tubules coupled to sodium and water, a process driven by RAAS, sympathetic and vasopressin activity, so the ratio "normalizes" BUN for glomerular function and behaves as an integrated index of renal function plus neurohormonal activation, hypoperfusion/prerenal azotemia and congestion [S:3b184dd6-1943-5b48-a7bb-dd46a3c91072][S:7b9847ef-5794-5ea3-839e-3b9f0378deb2][S:1684a2a2-2bec-5be4-b7fd-3f4c2ae29e64].

**Caveats**
- Reported associations with the ratio have often not been independent of BUN, suggesting BUN may be the true driving variable [S:4fe5676e-18e5-5ee6-aec9-a193ac953e83].
- The most recent systematic review (20 studies) concluded elevated BCR is associated with long-term mortality, especially in HFpEF, but rated overall certainty **very low** because of heterogeneity and inconsistent follow-up, and noted discriminative ability is poor (e.g., sensitivity 56%, specificity 63%, AUC 0.61 in one cohort); it also reported null findings for 2-month rehospitalization, AKI and eGFR [S:58605250-e9d6-5b0c-b035-500f801d8c54][S:792f75ab-de44-55f1-aa7d-66848f7fbaf6][S:00aa3505-b3ca-55f7-a568-e7a636be7084].
- A published letter criticizes that review for reporting single-study best-case estimates (HFpEF HR 3.28; 1-month MACE OR 2.47, CI 1.01–6.01 from 96 patients) as if pooled, and for omitting the null results from the abstract [S:a80fee42-73e7-589b-816d-df9263104f36].

Practical reading: the ratio is a cheap, routinely available risk marker — elevated values (commonly >20, thresholds in studies ranging ~19–25 for BUN/Cr) flag higher-risk HF patients, especially HFpEF and those whose ratio remains high or rises during hospitalization — but the evidence does not support it as a standalone or well-calibrated prognostic tool.

rows.question: Which markers of hypertension-mediated organ damage warrant assessment when stratifying cardiovascular risk in hypertensive patients?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: left ventricular hypertrophy predicts adverse cardiovascular outcomes over and above the hypertension itself; risk rises continuously across the range of left ventricular mass, including below the conventional thresholds for hypertrophy; A concentric pattern of left ventricular remodelling indicates pressure overload and is associated with poor cardiovascular prognosis; microvascular rarefaction may persist after brachial blood pressure has been normalised, so vascular damage is partly dissociated from blood pressure control. Certainty: These are consistent prognostic associations rather than effects of the damage itself being demonstrated. Scope: applies to adults with hypertension undergoing cardiovascular risk stratification, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents regression of ventricular hypertrophy with intensive blood pressure lowering as a definitive and consistent finding.

answers.websearch:
**Conclusion:** Guidelines converge on a core set of HMOD markers spanning heart, kidney, arteries, eye and brain — ECG-/echo-detected left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic/atrial abnormalities, reduced eGFR and albuminuria, arterial stiffness and plaque/coronary calcium, hypertensive retinopathy, and (in selected patients) cerebral small-vessel disease — because their presence confers roughly a 2–3-fold higher cardiovascular risk and reclassifies patients into a higher-risk treatment category ([[passage text removed]); [esc365.escardio.org/journal/92044](https://esc365.escardio.org/journal/92044)).

**Basic assessment recommended in all hypertensive patients**
- **Kidney:** serum creatinine with [passage text removed] (Class I in 2024 ESC, repeated [passage text removed]) ([sphta.org.pe/…/Guia-ESC-2024_.pdf]([passage text removed]); PMC12011322). The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline newly made UACR a test for *all* patients with high BP rather than optional ([acc.org journal scan, Jones et al. 2025]([passage text removed]); [nephjc.com/news/accaha2025-klno3](http://www.nephjc.com/news/accaha2025-klno3)).
- **Heart:** 12-lead ECG in all patients (Class I), assessing LVH and left atrial enlargement, plus AF/prior MI ([sphta.org.pe ESC 2024 PDF]([passage text removed])). An expert consensus review of the 2024 ESC, 2023 ESH, 2025 AHA/ACC and 2020 ISH guidelines confirms ECG, creatinine/eGFR and morning spot-urine ACR as the universal basic panel (PMID 41603527).

**Selected/advanced tests, when results would change management**
- **Echocardiography** — preferred initial advanced test (PMID 41603527); Class I in 2024 ESC when there are ECG abnormalities or cardiac signs/symptoms (PMC12011322). Markers include LV mass indexed to height^2.7 or BSA, concentric remodelling (relative wall thickness), left atrial volume index, and diastolic dysfunction (e′, E/e′) ([cardiologywiki.com/wiki/sources/ht-esc-2024](https://www.cardiologywiki.com/wiki/sources/ht-esc-2024)).
- **Arteries:** carotid or femoral plaque on ultrasound (focal wall thickness ≥1.5 mm) and stenosis; coronary artery calcium score (which can reclassify risk up or down); carotid–femoral pulse wave velocity >[passage text removed]; CAC >100 Agatston units or >75th percentile ([sphta.org.pe ESC 2024 PDF]([passage text removed]); [revespcardiol.org S1885585725000477]([passage text removed])). The ESH set also includes ankle–brachial index <0.9 (PMID 38365947).
- **Cardiac biomarkers:** high-sensitivity troponin and NT-proBNP/BNP ([revespcardiol.org S1885585725000477]([passage text removed]); [sphta.org.pe ESC 2024 PDF]([passage text removed])).
- **Eye:** fundoscopy — Class I in hypertensive emergency, malignant hypertension, or hypertension with diabetes; Class IIb more broadly when likely to change management (PMC12011322). ESH counts advanced retinopathy (haemorrhages, exudates, papilloedema) as HMOD (PMID 38365947).
- **Kidney imaging:** renal ultrasound should be considered in hypertensive patients with CKD (Class IIa) (PMC12011322).
- **Brain:** cerebral small-vessel disease (white matter hyperintensities, lacunar/silent infarcts, microbleeds) is a recognised HMOD manifestation, detectable by CT/MRI in selected patients in specialised care (PMID 41603527; PMID 42316921). Note that silent cerebrovascular lesions may be more prevalent than cardiac or renal subclinical damage and can occur without other organ damage (PMC3151514) — but I found no strong formal guideline recommendation for routine brain imaging, so this remains selective rather than routine.

**How these markers are used in stratification:** ESC 2024 treats documented HMOD as an automatic high-risk qualifier (alongside established CVD, moderate/severe CKD, diabetes, familial hypercholesterolaemia) that triggers treatment at elevated BP without needing SCORE2 ([sphta.org.pe ESC 2024 PDF]([passage text removed]); [reference.medscape.com/cc1/p10/…]([passage text removed])). For borderline 10-year risk (5% to <10%), CAC, carotid/femoral plaque, hs-troponin/BNP or PWV may be measured to refine risk (Class IIb, B), and HMOD screening is preferred in adults <40 years where SCORE2 is not validated (Class IIb) ([stroke-manual.com ESC 2024 PDF]([passage text removed]); PMC12011322). ESH defines HMOD for staging as increased large-artery stiffness, non-obstructive plaque, LVH, CKD G1–G2/A2 or G3, ABI <0.9, or advanced retinopathy (PMID 38365947). Regression of LV mass and reduction in albuminuria are also treatment targets associated with improved prognosis beyond BP lowering itself (PMID 42316921).

**Answer:** HMOD assessment should cover five target domains — heart, kidney, large/small vessels, brain, and retina — with a tiered "basic" panel (12‑lead ECG, serum creatinine/eGFR, urine albumin‑to‑creatinine ratio) in every hypertensive patient and extended testing (echocardiography, carotid ultrasound, pulse wave velocity, ankle‑brachial index, fundoscopy, brain MRI) when clinically indicated, because these markers reclassify risk independently of office blood pressure. [S:32a1ba4b-7faa-54e6-9beb-dee4e436b198][S:ac06707d-6b56-57df-8d0a-06443cde223f]

**Why it matters for stratification.** HMOD is the mechanistic link between elevated pressure and major cardiovascular/renal events, is frequently subclinical at diagnosis, and its detection both refines risk estimation and triggers treatment intensification. [S:679ffb56-ee7e-5e23-9e91-8859c4e987e7][S:8c653d93-6455-5bd3-b6cb-2caa4702718b] [passage text removed], event likelihood at modestly elevated BP equals or exceeds that of stage 2 hypertension without HMOD — which is why patients with stage 1 hypertension plus HMOD are moved into higher treatment-priority groups. [S:32a1ba4b-7faa-54e6-9beb-dee4e436b198] Screening is emphasised particularly in apparently low–moderate risk individuals, those with 10‑year risk <10%, or those under 40 where SCORE2 does not apply. [S:ac06707d-6b56-57df-8d0a-06443cde223f]

**Cardiac**
- **ECG LVH** — first-choice test given availability and low cost; recommended in all hypertensive patients. [S:bac1f566-db20-5653-a8cd-c6ba6a11e686][S:0dac4094-39f7-5192-a4fd-dbe421fd8787] In hypertensives with echocardiographic LVH followed 15 years, positive Lewis, Lyon‑Sokolow, Cornell voltage and Cornell product predicted worse outcome, with Cornell product the strongest predictor. [S:9a1fec7f-02d0-5bf0-85c0-8b1b08b548c9] ECG is specific but insensitive, so a normal ECG does not exclude LVH. [S:2515c89d-6d35-54ac-b304-e97c9f4713a7]
- **Echocardiography** — more sensitive than ECG; should assess LV mass and wall thickness, systolic and diastolic function, left atrial size, and aortic dilatation/valves. [S:3c46a97f-d360-5d56-bb55-7f68dabf2f2a][S:ae7e5419-65f5-5a33-b5e3-3e1315fc45d3] LVH, abnormal LV geometry, and systolic/diastolic dysfunction are associated with increased morbidity, mortality and MACE. [S:58f726d7-38ad-553a-9127-2110c6ea949b] Left atrial enlargement is an independent correlate of cardiovascular morbidity/mortality and atrial fibrillation, and impaired global longitudinal strain is associated with MACE even in asymptomatic hypertensive heart disease; ESH notes speckle‑tracking echocardiography detects early subclinical LV systolic dysfunction. [S:c55a8a7e-dcef-5175-ab09-14bacd8f64ef][S:ac06707d-6b56-57df-8d0a-06443cde223f]

**Renal**
- **UACR** — [passage text removed] a strong independent predictor of cardiovascular death, with risk rising continuously with ACR even in the high‑normal range. [S:b5fb1cdc-da17-5263-b81d-110489b7b206]
- **Serum creatinine/eGFR** — reflects cumulative glomerulosclerosis and tubulointerstitial fibrosis; eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² markedly increases cardiovascular risk and should be monitored serially. [S:b5fb1cdc-da17-5263-b81d-110489b7b206][S:ae7e5419-65f5-5a33-b5e3-3e1315fc45d3]

**Vascular**
- **Carotid–femoral PWV** for arterial stiffness (>10 m/s indicating significantly increased stiffness); cfPWV >10 m/s is itself regarded as HMOD, with the aorta as the target organ. [S:ae7e5419-65f5-5a33-b5e3-3e1315fc45d3][S:08bb09c1-a1cf-5226-b488-f69f2196ddf7] Increased cfPWV is independently associated with LVH and albuminuria even in pre‑hypertension. [S:69e67eab-6f32-51b7-9ca9-6a7d3fbf2727]
- **Carotid ultrasound (cIMT and plaque)** and **ABI <0.9** indicate atherosclerosis and raise cardiovascular risk. [S:ae7e5419-65f5-5a33-b5e3-3e1315fc45d3][S:32a1ba4b-7faa-54e6-9beb-dee4e436b198] Carotid plaque is a stronger risk indicator than cIMT alone. [S:536defaf-698e-5c3f-b649-1fafcb3584b9] Coronary artery calcium score has been proposed as an additional atherosclerotic HMOD measure for better stratification, and may be considered at intermediate risk. [S:60883152-92c1-5b10-8f58-1735262d35cc][S:0dac4094-39f7-5192-a4fd-dbe421fd8787]

**Cerebral**
- Brain MRI for cerebral small vessel disease (white matter hyperintensities, lacunar infarcts, microbleeds, enlarged perivascular spaces) should be considered when CSVD is suspected, especially with unexplained cognitive symptoms or transient neurological events. [S:32a1ba4b-7faa-54e6-9beb-dee4e436b198][S:383691f9-3d67-5ab9-b918-75d1755974b1] White matter lesions in asymptomatic hypertensives are [passage text removed] and are prognostic for stroke, cognitive impairment, dementia and death. [S:bb8153d6-a1c8-5283-95ce-bee42627255b]

**Retinal**
- Fundoscopy for hypertensive retinopathy is indicated when severe hypertension is suspected or other target-organ involvement is present; guidelines restrict it largely to prognostication (notably haemorrhages/exudates of grades 3–4) rather than universal screening. [S:32a1ba4b-7faa-54e6-9beb-dee4e436b198][S:1e6c1a84-17d3-59a2-8698-3dd0f6d20011] Some frameworks recommend retinal examination in all grade 3 hypertension or diabetes. [S:0dac4094-39f7-5192-a4fd-dbe421fd8787]

**Circulating biomarkers (adjunctive).** Recent ESH guidance advocates NT‑proBNP and high-sensitivity troponin measurement in the chronic setting when assessing HMOD. [S:1c916ce7-a773-5ecc-b262-e7988e808511] Natriuretic peptides are the established traditional plasma marker, but a single biomarker is generally insufficient and a multi‑marker approach is likely needed for early detection. [S:5346d53e-2386-592c-9885-de9bad8b2b04][S:011d3e93-4d28-5293-9938-0a669e629488] One consensus explicitly flags routine NT‑proBNP/hs‑troponin screening in the general hypertensive population as promising but not universally standardised. [S:d187d112-895d-55d7-84f4-2c90f84cb82a]

**Complementary and follow‑up considerations.** ABPM adds prognostic information by detecting white‑coat and masked hypertension and nocturnal non‑dipping, each independently associated with HMOD burden. [S:32a1ba4b-7faa-54e6-9beb-dee4e436b198] Basic screening should be repeated at least annually. [S:6e3a0670-869a-5e38-8bb7-510e1c58e46e] Regression of LV mass and reduction in albuminuria are treatment endpoints linked to improved prognosis beyond BP lowering, supporting serial reassessment. [S:679ffb56-ee7e-5e23-9e91-8859c4e987e7][S:c539ea22-979c-57b2-8bd6-cdcdc552cd54]

**Caveats.** Whether albuminuria mediates cardiovascular progression or merely signals generalised vascular injury is mechanistically unresolved, and reduction in arterial stiffness has not yet been shown in controlled trials to reduce events independently of BP lowering — so PWV is not yet a validated surrogate endpoint. [S:b5fb1cdc-da17-5263-b81d-110489b7b206][S:08bb09c1-a1cf-5226-b488-f69f2196ddf7] Real-world uptake is imperfect: in a Korean registry, adherence to the full basic panel was incomplete and carotid ultrasound and fundoscopy were performed infrequently. [S:1b72fa92-ad82-5ebb-821c-11f56f307e6e] Resource and cost constraints may limit implementation in some settings. [S:43af668e-b57d-5f69-aade-f06f96c267bb]

rows.question: What one-year survival follows heart transplantation from donation after circulatory death donors in recipients with prior cardiac surgery?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: one-year survival after a circulatory-death donor heart transplant is close to nine in ten in recipients with previous conventional cardiac surgery, lower than in recipients without such surgery; the lower survival persisted after propensity score matching on measured risk factors; within the group with previous cardiac surgery, one-year survival was comparable whether the donor heart came after circulatory death or after brain death; the survival penalty is concentrated in recipients whose previous operation combined coronary revascularisation with valve intervention, the subtype with the lowest one-year survival. Certainty: These are consistent associations rather than effects established by direct comparison. Scope: applies to end-stage heart failure treated by heart transplantation from a circulatory-death donor in adults with previous conventional cardiac surgery, excluding those supported by a durable ventricular assist device or with previous congenital heart surgery, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the survival deficit as a reason to withhold circulatory-death donor hearts from recipients with previous cardiac surgery.

answers.websearch:
**Approximately 89–90% one-year survival** — meaningfully lower than DCD recipients without prior cardiac surgery (~96–97%), but essentially identical to prior-cardiac-surgery recipients of brain-dead (DBD) hearts.

**Primary evidence (UNOS registry, DCD recipients stratified by prior conventional cardiac surgery)**
- Among 785 adult isolated DCD heart transplant recipients (1/1/2019–3/31/2024), 233 (29.7%) had prior conventional cardiac surgery; their 1-year survival was 89.6% vs 96.8% in those without (p < 0.001), and inferiority persisted after propensity matching ([passage text removed]) and [passage text removed]). Patients with durable LVADs and congenital cardiac surgery were excluded from this cohort. [PMID 42148782 / PMC13182683 / doi:10.1111/ctr.70569]
- Risk is driven by operative subtype: isolated CABG 93.7%, isolated valve surgery 79.5%, and combined CABG + valve 77.9% versus 96.8% without prior surgery (p < 0.001). Prior-surgery DCD recipients also had more post-transplant [passage text removed]), with comparable length of stay, dialysis, pacemaker, and treated rejection. [PMC13182683]
- Critically, **DCD itself is not the penalty**: among 3,069 recipients with prior conventional cardiac surgery, 1-year survival was 89.6% (DCD, n = 233) vs 89.5% (DBD, n = 2,836; p = 0.985), unchanged after [passage text removed]). [PMC13182683]

**Related sternotomy subgroups**
- Durable MCS/LVAD bridge (a prior-sternotomy population): DCD vs DBD 1-year survival 89.0% vs 90.2% (P = .946). [PMID 42530366]
- Adults with congenital heart disease are the exception where DCD does appear worse: DCD carried higher 90-day graft-failure hazard (HR 2.5, 95% CI 1.23–5.16, p = 0.012) and 3-year hazard (HR 1.83, p = 0.05), though the 1-year hazard was not statistically significant (HR 1.65, 95% CI 0.83–3.33, p = 0.15); prior cardiac surgery was not itself a significant covariate (HR 1.55, 95% CI 0.61–3.9, p = 0.35). [PMC12495479]

**Context:** unselected DCD heart transplant 1-year survival pools at [passage text removed]) in meta-analysis [PMC11811572], so the ~89–90% figure reflects the recipient's reoperative risk rather than the DCD graft.

**Caveats:** the key finding comes from a single registry analysis without exact reported figures for the DCD-prior-surgery group beyond Kaplan–Meier estimates; no randomized data address this subgroup, and I found no source reporting 1-year survival separately by DCD procurement technique (NRP vs DPP) within reoperative recipients.

Isolated CABG (36.0%) and UNOS "other" operations (32.9%) were the most common prior procedures. [S:ec65ca23-a32b-5cd2-9c73-9770dc99c5a8]

**DCD is not the driver of the excess risk.** Among 3,069 recipients with prior conventional cardiac surgery (2,836 DBD, 233 DCD), 1-year survival was essentially identical by donor type (89.6% DCD vs 89.5% DBD, p = 0.985), and remained comparable after [passage text removed]). [S:5dbb1281-cb45-5096-9aab-731d58966331][S:b6dab501-aa13-52af-a99b-bc0d31378465]

**Mechanistic/morbidity context:** DCD recipients with prior cardiac surgery had significantly longer graft ischemic times, higher rates of pretransplant transfusion, and more [passage text removed]), with comparable length of stay, dialysis, pacemaker, and treated acute rejection rates. The authors attribute the vulnerability to redo-sternotomy technical complexity and prolonged ischemia, and suggest refinement of NRP/OCS preservation in this group. [S:eae4df4f-5fc1-55f6-91ba-5edbf69a016c][S:975a2dd3-0420-592d-ab7d-ebc751161f8c]

rows.question: What do changes in urinary albumin to creatinine ratio over time indicate about outcomes in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: a urinary albumin to creatinine ratio that stays high and swings about over repeated measurements marks patients whose risk of cardiovascular death, cardiac arrest or heart failure admission is raised (roughly doubled); a ratio that falls over time does not carry that excess risk, and its apparent link with myocardial infarction rested on few events and was left as exploratory; knowing which pattern a patient follows adds only a small amount to risk assessment on top of the usual clinical variables. Certainty: The link between the albuminuria pattern and later events is a consistent association rather than an established cause. Scope: applies to adults with symptomatic heart failure and preserved ejection fraction undergoing repeated albuminuria measurement, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it recommends treating to bring the albumin to creatinine ratio down as a way of preventing these events, since the patterns were observed rather than assigned and no attempt to change the ratio was tested.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Serial UACR carries prognostic information beyond a single baseline measurement in HFpEF: declining albuminuria tracks with fewer HF hospitalizations and deaths, an unstable/persistently elevated pattern marks the highest risk, and past albuminuria remains prognostic even after it resolves — but UACR has not been validated as a treatment-effect surrogate.

## Falling UACR ↔ better outcomes

In the TOPCAT Americas cohort (n=1,175 with baseline UACR; n=744 with 1-year repeat), each halving of UACR from baseline to the 1-year visit was independently associated with lower risk: [passage text removed] composite endpoint (HR 0.93, p=0.054) and CV mortality (HR 0.91, p=0.064) did not reach significance in adjusted models, and there was no interaction with spironolactone treatment ([PMC6594383]([passage text removed]); [ahajournals.org/CIRCHEARTFAILURE.118.005288]([passage text removed])). Baseline albuminuria was graded in risk (microalbuminuria HR 1.47, macroalbuminuria HR 1.67), driven predominantly by HF hospitalization. Notably, change in UACR correlated with change in systolic BP (p=0.001), suggesting the signal is partly hemodynamic rather than purely structural renal injury ([PMC6594383]([passage text removed])).

## Trajectory *pattern* matters, not just direction

A latent-class analysis of 746 TOPCAT HFpEF participants identified three uACR trajectories — [passage text removed]%) — with primary endpoint rates of 15.02%, 25.20% and 36.08% respectively (p<0.001). In fully adjusted models the fluctuating-high group had [passage text removed]) for the composite and HR 1.91 (1.19–3.06) for HF hospitalization; [passage text removed], 1.33–6.76). Adding trajectory to a clinical model improved discrimination only modestly (C-index 0.758→0.765) ([PMC13475011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13475011); [pubmed 42599016](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42599016)). The authors interpret the fluctuating pattern as reflecting hemodynamic fluctuation and intermittent renal impairment specific to HFpEF, contrasting with diabetic cohorts where "high stable" and "elevated-increasing" patterns dominate risk ([PMC13475011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13475011)).

## Resolution does not fully erase risk

In a 332-patient HFpEF outpatient cohort re-screened at 1 year (250 re-evaluated), 25.2% changed albuminuria category and 10.8% recovered from albuminuria. At ~3 years, the composite of HF hospitalization/all-cause death occurred in 27.1% of those with persistent albuminuria and 22.2% of those who recovered, versus 13.9% of those who developed albuminuria after one year and 8.6% who stayed free of it (p=0.008); 1-year NT-proBNP was lowest in never-albuminuric patients and higher in all other groups (p<0.001). The authors conclude albuminuria at any timepoint is prognostic, including after recovery, and support intermittent re-screening ([PMC11972526]([passage text removed]); [s12933-025-02708-6]([passage text removed])).

## Therapy-induced UACR change: modifiable, but not a validated surrogate

- Spironolactone reduced UACR by 39% overall at 1 year (geometric mean ratio 0.61) and by 76% in macroalbuminuric patients ([PMC6594383]([passage text removed])).
- Finerenone in FINEARTS-HF (HFmrEF/HFpEF, n=6,001) [passage text removed]%) at 6 months with a sustained effect, and reduced new-onset macroalbuminuria by 38% (HR 0.62, 0.53–0.73), yet did not improve the eGFR-based kidney composite (HR 1.33, 0.94–1.89) ([pubmed 39490700](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39490700); [docwirenews summary of McCausland et al.](https://www.docwirenews.com/post/finearts-hf-prespecified-analysis-results-finerenone-and-renal-outcomes)). Larger UACR reductions occurred in higher kidney-risk strata (24%/29%/36%, p_int=0.031), but whether this translates into greater long-term benefit is explicitly unresolved ([acc.org FINEARTS-HF journal scan]([passage text removed])), and CV benefit did not differ by baseline UACR category (p_int=0.48) ([jchf.2025.102778]([passage text removed])).
- In EMPEROR-Pooled (n=9,673, including EMPEROR-Preserved), empagliflozin lowered new macroalbuminuria (HR 0.81, p=0.005) and raised remission from macroalbuminuria (HR 1.31, p=0.009), with no UACR reduction in the overall population; CV/kidney benefit was consistent across baseline UACR categories ([PMC9494272]([passage text removed])).

## Caveats

These are observational/post-hoc analyses; a UACR fall accompanies BP and natriuretic-peptide changes, so it may be a risk marker rather than a causal target ([PMC6594383]([passage text removed]); [PMC11972526]([passage text removed])). Reporting of UACR change as an endpoint has been sparse in major HFpEF trials including EMPEROR-Preserved and PARAGON-HF ([jacc.2022.10.028]([passage text removed])), the trajectory analysis's MI finding rested on few events ([PMC13475011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13475011)), and one recent review notes albuminuria's prognostic value appears more robust in HFrEF/HFmrEF than HFpEF ([PMC12387696]([passage text removed])). I found no trial demonstrating that targeting a UACR reduction improves HFpEF outcomes.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Serial UACR adds prognostic information beyond a single measurement in HFpEF: an unstable/persistently high albuminuria course marks the highest risk of HF hospitalization and cardiovascular events, whereas a fall in UACR (especially treatment-induced) tracks with better outcomes — though having had albuminuria at any point still confers excess risk even if it later normalizes.

## Evidence

**Trajectory patterns (TOPCAT).** In 746 HFpEF patients with ≥3 UACR measurements, latent class trajectory modeling identified [passage text removed]%) patterns; the primary endpoint (CV death, aborted cardiac arrest, or HF hospitalization) [passage text removed]% respectively (p < 0.001) [S:670df299]. In fully adjusted Cox models the fluctuating-high group had elevated risk of [passage text removed] HF [passage text removed]) [S:f5591e88]. Diabetes strongly predicted membership in [passage text removed]) [S:37d3eba0]. Adding trajectory information improved discrimination modestly (C-index 0.758→0.765; 6-year AUC 0.832→0.845) [S:670df299]. No significant associations were found with [passage text removed]; a signal for myocardial infarction in the decreasing group ([passage text removed]) rested on few events and is explicitly exploratory [S:37d3eba0][S:670df299]. Caveats: post hoc analysis of only 746 of 3445 randomized patients, measurement timing not designed for trajectory modeling, small non-stable subgroups, and possible selection bias [S:5979cb8d][S:3e802151].

**Serial albuminuria status (outpatient HFpEF cohort).** In 332 HFpEF patients, baseline albuminuria independently predicted HF hospitalization/all-cause death (aHR [passage text removed]), with the highest risk in those with both diabetes and albuminuria ([passage text removed]) [S:c7fd3358]. Re-testing at one year reclassified 25.2% of patients (10.8% recovered from albuminuria; 22% new albuminuria among those at risk) [S:c7fd3358]. Importantly, from year 1 onward the primary outcome occurred in 27.1% with persistent albuminuria and 22.2% of those who *recovered*, versus 13.9% with new albuminuria and 8.6% who never had albuminuria (p = 0.008) — i.e., albuminuria at any timepoint remained prognostic even after apparent resolution [S:87dfd82a][S:192b63cc]. The authors attribute some recovery to reversible renal venous congestion rather than true risk reversal [S:d45941b1].

**Treatment-related UACR change.** Reviews of TOPCAT report that spironolactone significantly reduced UACR at one year and that a 50% UACR reduction was independently associated with fewer adverse outcomes [S:e0af64bd]; a second review states the reduction in albumin excretion was associated with reduced HF hospitalization and all-cause mortality [S:dc3e87cc]. Magnitude: spironolactone lowered UACR by 39% at one year overall and 76% in those with severely increased albuminuria (placebo-corrected) [S:0ad2de6d]. A caution on interpreting UACR change as a surrogate: sacubitril/valsartan *increases* UACR in HFpEF (PARAMOUNT: 1.9→2.9 mg/mmol vs 2.0→2.0 mg/mmol with valsartan, p = 0.02) while better preserving eGFR [S:e872e466][S:bfed06de], so a rise on ARNI does not carry the same meaning as spontaneous progression.

**Interpretive context.** Albuminuria in HFpEF is thought to reflect systemic microvascular/endothelial dysfunction and inflammation, plus renal venous congestion, rather than isolated renal disease [S:d45941b1][S:db59e4be][S:74dad77f]; UACR has substantial biological variability (which may exceed 20%), so abnormal values require 2–3 confirmatory readings over 3–6 months [S:87333530]. Notably, one acute-HF cohort found microalbuminuria predicted in-hospital mortality in HFrEF/HFmrEF but *not* HFpEF [S:98ce9274], so the signal is not uniformly reproduced.

**Gaps:** no randomized evidence was found showing that lowering UACR *causes* better HFpEF outcomes — all longitudinal findings above are associational, and the trajectory analysis cannot establish mechanism [S:5979cb8d].

rows.question: In Chinese adults admitted with moderate-to-severe valvular heart disease, how does management differ between men and women?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: men were significantly more likely than women to undergo coronary angiography; among patients with atrial fibrillation or flutter, women were more likely than men to receive warfarin; whether women are less likely to receive valve intervention is disputed: one cohort found no difference in the overall intervention rate by sex, while another reports substantially lower odds of intervention in women. Certainty: The treatment findings are consistently described within one cohort, while the difference in access to valve intervention is actively contested. Scope: applies to moderate-to-severe valvular heart disease in adults admitted to tertiary and referral cardiovascular centres in China, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it attributes the pattern of valve intervention by sex to a specific cause such as patient refusal.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

In the nationwide China‑VHD cohort of 13,917 adults hospitalised with moderate‑to‑severe valvular heart disease (VHD), the **overall rate of valve intervention was essentially identical in men and women**; the differences lie in *drug therapy*, in *which procedure* is done (women get more repair, men more replacement), and in *specific valve lesions* (notably aortic regurgitation, where men are treated more aggressively) [[passage text removed]].

## Evidence

**Cohort.** China‑VHD was a nationwide, prospective, multicentre cohort enrolling 13,917 adults with moderate‑to‑severe VHD from April–June 2018 (NCT03484806); 7,621 were men and 6,296 women, with similar median ages (62.42 vs 63.01 years) [[passage text removed]].

**Medical therapy differed systematically by sex** (all p<0.001 unless noted): women received more warfarin (46.00% vs 42.02%), consistent with their heavier rheumatic/mitral burden; men received more aspirin (35.00% vs 25.10%), P2Y receptor inhibitors (23.46% vs 17.63%), beta‑blockers (58.22% vs 51.81%), ACEI/ARB (43.72% vs 35.07%) and diuretics (72.20% vs 70.09%, p=0.006). Digitalis use did not differ (30.99% vs 31.66%, p=0.402) [[passage text removed]].

rows.question: Which characteristics of patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors relate to developing myocarditis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: older age, male sex, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia all mark patients on checkpoint inhibitors as more likely to be flagged with myocarditis; tumour type matters as well, with thymic tumours carrying the highest odds (roughly doubled) and lung cancer a smaller rise, and blocking more than one checkpoint adding further risk; these were suspected rather than confirmed cases, picked up largely through troponin rises that arise for many other reasons. Certainty: These characteristics mark who is more likely to be flagged, and are associations from care as it was delivered rather than established causes. Scope: applies to myocarditis during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy in adults receiving an immune checkpoint inhibitor for cancer, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it lists diabetes among the characteristics carrying extra risk, since it did not hold up once the other characteristics were accounted for.

answers.websearch:
**Conclusion:** The characteristics most consistently linked to ICI myocarditis are treatment with combination checkpoint blockade (anti-CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-1), older age, cardiometabolic comorbidity (diabetes, obesity, hypertension/hyperlipidaemia, pre-existing cardiovascular disease), thymic epithelial tumours (especially thymoma), and concurrent muscular immune-related toxicity — though most evidence is retrospective/pharmacovigilance-based and findings on sex conflict.

**Treatment regimen (strongest signal)**
- In the 8-site international registry, combination ICI was far more common in myocarditis cases than matched controls (34% vs 2%, p<0.001), and current ipilimumab+nivolumab was more frequent in cases (26% vs 8.6%, p=0.02) [[passage text removed]].
- FAERS analysis: concomitant ipilimumab+nivolumab had the highest disproportionality ([passage text removed]) and combination was independently associated with [passage text removed]=0.008) [[passage text removed]].
- A commercial claims cohort found risk "more than doubled" with nivolumab+ipilimumab vs monotherapy, mostly within 100 days of starting treatment [[passage text removed]]. A post-marketing safety database reported 0.27% with combination vs 0.06% with monotherapy (P<0.001) [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11794898].
- In a global real-world cohort of 130,234 ICI-treated patients (0.49% developed myocarditis), ipilimumab remained significant on multivariable analysis ([passage text removed]].

**Age**
- FAERS: age ≥75 years interacting with ICI use, [passage text removed]]. Real-world cohort: age >65, HR 1.34 (1.11–1.63) [same ACR/ASCO abstract]. An integrative review concluded risk is increased in patients older than 64 years [[passage text removed]].

**Metabolic and cardiovascular comorbidity**
- Registry cases had higher prevalence of diabetes (34% vs 13%; OR 3.36, 95% CI 1.37–8.20, p=0.01), higher BMI, and more sleep apnea than controls [[passage text removed]].
- Higher BMI replicated across cohorts (Awadalla; Mahmood 29±8.4 vs 26±6, p=0.02; Zlotoff 28±6.1 vs 26±5.8, p=0.002), and cardiovascular medication use before ICI was identified as a risk marker [[passage text removed]].
- Hypertension (HR 1.31) and hyperlipidaemia (HR 1.34) were independent multivariable predictors in the global real-world cohort [[passage text removed]]; a large real-world study likewise identified pre-existing hypertension and hyperlipidaemia, older age and male sex [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13094356].
- WHO VigiBase case-control (108 cases vs 108 controls): drugs for cardiovascular conditions (proxy for pre-existing CV disease/risk factors) were more strongly associated with myocarditis reports than with other irAEs (p=0.026, Φ=0.214); notably, **no** association was found with pre-existing diabetes (p=0.752) — i.e., the diabetes signal is not consistent [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7700285].
- Age ≥80 with prior acute coronary syndrome and prior heart failure were cumulative predictors in a single-centre cohort (each 1-year age increase: HR 1.07, p=0.02) [[passage text removed]].

**Tumour type**
- Thymic epithelial tumours, particularly thymoma, carry a markedly elevated risk: pharmacovigilance/registry work showed [passage text removed] TET vs other cancers, earlier onset, and more severe disease [[passage text removed]]. A retrospective TET cohort reported myocarditis in 7 of 12 thymoma patients (58.33%) vs a stated ~1.68% in non-TET patients [[passage text removed]]; industry database analysis confirmed higher myocarditis rates with current/prior thymoma [[passage text removed]].
- Lung cancer and melanoma also recur as risk-associated diagnoses (melanoma HR 1.52 in the global cohort; thymoma/thymic carcinoma and lung cancer in the 8,199-patient real-world analysis) [[passage text removed]; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13094356].

**Immune/autoimmune background and other irAEs**
- Anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies (proxy for thymic autoimmunity) were more prevalent in ICI-myocarditis patients than in ICI-treated controls [[passage text removed]].
- A scoping review of 29 studies tabulated autoimmune disease (1.77), Hashimoto's thyroiditis (15.9), development of another irAE (2.08), and ICI-related myositis/dermatitis (4.93) among reported risk estimates for ICI cardiotoxicity [[passage text removed]].
- Concurrent myositis/myasthenia gravis co-occurs frequently, plausibly via shared cardiac–skeletal muscle antigens [[passage text removed]].

**Baseline biomarkers and concomitant drugs**
- Prospective hs-TnT screening of 280 patients: those with baseline hs-TnT >14 ng/L had a higher rate of subsequent irMyocarditis (9.5%) than those with baseline ≤14 ng/L (4.1%), and the authors conclude elevated baseline troponin confers higher risk [[passage text removed]].
- Pharmacovigilance signals link concomitant thiazide/loop diuretic use to ICI myocarditis reporting [[passage text removed]].

**Where evidence conflicts / is weak**
- Sex: FAERS found higher risk in women ([passage text removed]=0.004) [[passage text removed]], whereas case series and large cohorts report male predominance [[passage text removed]; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13094356]; reviews explicitly call the direction conflicting [[passage text removed]].
- One synthesis lists only ICI treatment and combination ICI treatment as "agreed on," with pre-existing autoimmunity, female sex, increased age, thymic tumours, diuretics and pre-existing cardiovascular disease still "unclear" [[passage text removed]]. Genetic/racial predictors and transplant-recipient status remain unsupported by adequate data [[passage text removed]].

Note: features such as reduced LVEF, very high troponin/CK, and concomitant myositis are predictors of **severity/outcome** once myocarditis occurs, not of developing it [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
**Conclusion:** The most consistently supported characteristics are treatment-related (combination checkpoint blockade), demographic (older age, and in most cohorts male sex), cardiometabolic (pre-existing cardiovascular disease, diabetes, higher body weight/BMI, sleep apnoea), pre-existing autoimmunity, certain tumour types (melanoma/lung, and especially thymic epithelial tumours), and co-occurring neuromuscular immune-related toxicity — though several of these (notably sex and diabetes) are inconsistent across data sources.

**Therapy characteristics (best established)**
- Combination ICI is the most established risk factor: risk of myocarditis was ~4.74-fold higher with nivolumab + ipilimumab than nivolumab monotherapy [S:4d0db731][S:214e1fd8], with reported incidences of 0.27% for the combination versus 0.06% for nivolumab alone [S:ae9b7a0b][S:6def6ef0]; nivolumab + relatlimab was reported at 1.7% versus 0.6% for nivolumab alone [S:ce4bc745]. Pharmacovigilance analyses confirm stronger disproportionality signals for combination than monotherapy, with ipilimumab + nivolumab carrying the highest reported risk [S:42964c50][S:6def6ef0]. Risk also varies by agent class, with anti-PD-1 agents contributing the largest share of reports in some analyses [S:6ecfbc58].
- Onset is typically early (median time to onset ~28–30 days, i.e. after the first or second infusion) [S:752b873b][S:214e1fd8][S:ae9b7a0b].

**Demographics**
- Older age: mean/median ages of affected patients are typically in the 65–70 range; age ≥65 years was associated with higher reporting odds ([passage text removed]) in FAERS [S:9c552f06], age ≥75 years emerged as a risk factor in FAERS analyses, and age >80 years in a Mayo Clinic cohort [S:be2b9003][S:840a4009]. Reports cluster in the 65–85-year band [S:fef133b4].
- Sex: most cohorts report male preponderance (67–71%) [S:ce4bc745], and FAERS showed male sex associated with higher reporting odds ([passage text removed]) [S:9c552f06]. However, this is contested — one FAERS study found female sex associated with myocarditis ([passage text removed]) [S:0c605ba8][S:668d5d35], and a VigiBase analysis emphasises heterogeneous findings on sex [S:be2b9003].
- Body weight: risk factors in a FAERS study included body weight ≥75 kg [S:9e421311]; weight 80–100 kg had higher reporting odds than <80 kg ([passage text removed]) [S:9c552f06]; a multicentre registry found higher BMI among myocarditis cases than controls [S:668d5d35].

**Cardiometabolic and cardiac comorbidity**
- Pre-existing cardiovascular disease: in a single-centre registry, patients with ICI myocarditis had [passage text removed] apnoea (33% vs 10%, p = 0.03), and were less often in normal sinus rhythm at baseline [S:fde750f1]. A Mayo Clinic cohort linked history of heart failure and acute coronary syndrome to higher risk [S:840a4009]. A VigiBase matched case-control study found a moderate-sized association between drugs for cardiovascular conditions (proxy for pre-existing CV disease) and myocarditis reporting (p = 0.026, Φ = 0.214) [S:3ac3c0b0]. A retrospective cohort identified hypercholesterolaemia, [passage text removed] as predictors of cardiac irAEs, with hypercholesterolaemia and pre-existing CVD independent in multivariate analysis [S:eeee13d3][S:a23515e0].
- Diabetes, hypertension and smoking are the most frequently cited comorbid risk factors [S:85036ab0]; 34.3% of cases in a multicentre registry had pre-existing diabetes [S:840a4009], and diabetes, sleep apnoea and higher BMI distinguished cases from controls [S:668d5d35]. Counter-evidence: the VigiBase case-control study found no significant association with pre-existing diabetes [S:e7d3693e].
- Traditional atherosclerotic risk factors more broadly (smoking, alcohol, hypertension, diabetes, advanced age, obesity, advanced cancer stage) have been catalogued as patient-specific risk factors [S:3dcd918f].

**Autoimmunity and tumour type**
- Pre-existing autoimmune disease may elevate risk of cardiovascular irAEs [S:85036ab0][S:e6e8909d].
- Melanoma and lung cancer are the most frequent indications among myocarditis reports [S:c1b14c7c], and melanoma/lung patients have been reported to have higher myocarditis rates than other cancers [S:506d424e]. Thymic epithelial tumours — particularly type B thymomas with immature T-cell infiltrates and associated autoimmunity — carry a higher-than-usual risk of severe irAEs including myocarditis [S:15afc36a][S:1c2129d2][S:eee9b140].
- Concurrent anti-cancer modalities (chemotherapy, targeted therapy, radiation) are also implicated [S:c2b64b09][S:d9220287].

**Concurrent toxicity phenotype**
- ICI myocarditis frequently overlaps with myositis and a myasthenia gravis-like syndrome — in one registry 66.7% had MG-like overlap and 50% myositis/rhabdomyolysis [S:fde750f1][S:85036ab0] — so presence of other irAEs raises the probability of myocarditis [S:3f9cca74][S:668d5d35].

**Candidate biomarkers (not yet established risk factors)**
- Rising systemic immune-inflammation index, neutrophil-to-eosinophil ratio, AST/albumin and LDH/albumin ratios relative to baseline were associated with myocarditis incidence and severity [S:44357811]; troponin surveillance detects early myocardial damage [S:f30b5e77][S:8c97614d]. An exploratory blood proteomic signature has been reported as more prevalent in ICI-myocarditis patients [S:a4435be7]. I found no source establishing a validated HLA or germline genetic risk factor specifically for ICI myocarditis.

**Caveat:** much of this evidence is retrospective, case-series or pharmacovigilance-derived, so it reflects reporting associations rather than proven causal risk; combination therapy is the only factor described as "the most established" [S:4d0db731][S:c2b64b09].

rows.question: What is known about the effect of ethanol infusion into the vein of Marshall on achieving durable mitral isthmus block?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: ethanol delivered into the vein of Marshall is associated with durable bidirectional mitral isthmus block being achieved more often than with radiofrequency ablation alone; whether the improvement in block translates into fewer arrhythmia recurrences is disputed, with a randomised trial and pooled analyses reporting less recurrence while one cohort found no significant gain in either block or arrhythmia-free survival; ethanol infusion cannot always be delivered, with reported procedural success between roughly 84% and 92%. Certainty: The gain in block is consistent across the evidence, while the gain in arrhythmia outcomes is actively contested. Scope: applies to persistent atrial fibrillation or mitral isthmus-dependent atrial tachycardia undergoing catheter ablation in adults undergoing catheter ablation in whom mitral isthmus block is intended, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the reduction in arrhythmia recurrence as established for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation as well as for persistent atrial fibrillation.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Vein of Marshall ethanol infusion (VOM-Et/EIVOM) very reliably produces **acute** bidirectional mitral isthmus (MI) block with far less radiofrequency, and most — but not all — studies show it also improves **durability** of that block; however, block is not permanent, with reconnection still found in roughly a third to half of re-mapped patients, characteristically at the mitral annular edge or within the coronary sinus.

## Acute block

- In a two-cohort comparison, acute MI block was achieved in 98.7% (150/152) with adjunctive VOM-Et vs 63.6% (70/110) with RFCA alone, with shorter RF duration (5.00 [3.00–7.00] vs 19.0 [13.6–22.0] min; P<0.001) ([PMID 33197321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33197321)).
- Randomized data: all 45/45 (100%) EIVOM patients achieved MI bidirectional block vs 84.1% (37/44) with RFCA alone ([Zuo et al., 10.1016/j.jacep.2023.11.027](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405500X24000069)).
- Observational series report 94.2% (115/122) acute bidirectional block when VOM-Et was feasible (82% of patients) ([PMID 38040560](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38040560)), and 96% vs 76% with RF alone ([10.3389/fcvm.2024.1253554]([passage text removed])). The original concept paper found block in 100% of patients in whom VOM cannulation was technically feasible ([PMC3419362]([passage text removed])).

## Early (intraprocedural) durability

- In the randomized comparison, MI reconnection after a 30-minute wait occurred in 3/45 EIVOM vs 13/44 RFCA patients ([passage text removed]); final block rates were 97.8% vs 72.7%, and 1-year AF recurrence 17.8% vs 31.8% ([PMID 38658060](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38658060)).
- Even with ethanol, acute block is not synonymous with stable block: in a prospective series combining systematic VoM ethanol with focal pulsed-field ablation, conduction recovered in 9/50 (18%; 95% CI 9.8–30.8) during a 30-minute wait, at a median of 16 minutes (range 8–23), and 6/9 required coronary sinus ablation to restore block ([medRxiv preprint, doi 10.64898/2026.08.28.26361686]([passage text removed]) — not peer reviewed).

## Chronic durability at repeat mapping

- Supportive: among patients undergoing redo procedures, durable MI block was present in 62.9% (22/35) after VOM-Et vs 32.6% (15/46) after RFCA alone (P=0.008); fewer VOM-Et patients needed a repeat procedure at all (23.3% vs 65.7%; P<0.001) ([PMID 33197321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33197321)).
- A three-centre reablation cohort found MI conduction recovery in 46.3% (EIVOM, n=41) vs 80.8% (non-EIVOM, n=50; p=0.002), with absence of EIVOM an independent predictor of recovery ([passage text removed]); LPV isolation durability was *not* improved ([PMC12673498]([passage text removed])).
- Electroanatomical remapping shows the ethanol lesion itself persists (chronic scar median 13.1 cm² vs 12.4 cm² acutely), yet late MI reconnection still occurred in 9/20 patients, localised to the mitral annular edge or the coronary sinus ([PMID 34454885](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34454885)).
- **Discordant evidence:** in 560 non-paroxysmal AF patients, although block was achieved in 97% (171/176) with EIVOM/RF vs 92% (353/384) with RF, reconduction across the MI line at a subsequent session was 58% (25/43) with EIVOM/RF vs 49% (39/80) with RF (p=0.32), and AF/AT recurrence was 37% in both groups ([PMID 34028116](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34028116)). A meta-analysis found the MI reconnection rate significantly lower with EIVoM only after this study was removed in leave-one-out analysis ([passage text removed]) ([PMC11549524]([passage text removed])).

## Why block fails after ethanol (mechanism)

In 231 VOMEI procedures, failures *before* ethanol reflected VOM epicardial connections, epi-endocardial dissociation and pseudo-MI block, whereas recurrences *after* VOMEI were due to incomplete annular endocardial RF and coronary-sinus arrhythmogenesis (CS-mediated perimitral flutter, CS-to-LA and CS ostial re-entry, CS focal activity); CS ablation at the time of VOMEI was associated with reconnection (OR 4.05; P=0.003), as was age (OR 1.06; P=0.011) ([PMID 39269401](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39269401); [Houston Methodist Scholars record]([passage text removed])). Of 36 patients with MI reconnection, endocardial annular RF restored block in 16 (45%) and CS RF was required in 20 (55%).

## Clinical relevance of achieving the block

- VENUS secondary analysis: the benefit of ethanol was confined to patients in whom perimitral block was achieved — primary outcome 54.3% (VOM+CA) vs 37% (CA), P=0.01; with no difference when block was not achieved (34.0% vs 37.0%, P=0.583); interaction P=0.002 ([PMC8254797](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8254797)).
- PROMPT-AF (n=498 randomized, 495 analysed) achieved MI block in 87.4% using an EIVOM-first linear strategy and reported freedom from atrial arrhythmia of 70.7% vs 61.5% with PVI alone ([passage text removed]) ([PMC11574720]([passage text removed])).

## Caveats

Feasibility limits the strategy: ethanol could not be delivered in a proportion of patients in every series (e.g., 82% feasibility in one two-centre cohort, [PMID 38040560](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38040560); VOM not identifiable in 4/55 in the PFA series, [medRxiv]([passage text removed])), and in VENUS the procedure was completed in ~85% ([ACC trial summary]([passage text removed])). Most chronic-durability data come from selected patients returning for reablation, which the authors of the multicentre cohort explicitly flag as a limitation ([PMC12673498]([passage text removed])). No source I found establishes that ethanol makes MI block permanent.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

[passage text removed]) reliably and substantially **increases the rate of acute bidirectional mitral isthmus (MI) block**, and achieving that block appears to be the mechanism by which it improves rhythm outcomes — but the evidence that it produces truly *durable* block is weaker and inconsistent, with reconnection rates at repeat procedures that are numerically but not statistically better than radiofrequency (RF) alone.

## Why the VOM matters mechanistically

The Marshall bundle runs on the epicardial aspect of the MI and forms connections to the left atrium and coronary sinus (CS) musculature that bypass an apparently continuous endocardial line; combined with thick myocardium, epicardial fat, and convective cooling from the CS and circumflex artery, this makes endocardial RF frequently non-transmural [S:db9e8c94-c0a3-5c83-b597-e579c1eb2ab3][S:00ff8bcd-5721-5edf-abc1-0fdd4ad234cd]. With endocardial plus intra-CS RF alone, acute bidirectional block [passage text removed] [S:746e2997-8f1b-50e3-a2cb-f782b96a51bb]. Supporting the causal role of the VOM: among 37 patients with *no* angiographically demonstrable VOM, posterior MI block was achieved in 97.3% versus 65% in matched controls in whom VOM presence was not assessed [S:e4772572-79ac-5c89-85a0-1eb145269d5a].

## Effect on acute block

- Meta-analysis of RCTs: bidirectional MI block was more often achieved with catheter ablation plus EIVOM ([passage text removed], I² = 78%) [S:43639e85-2aaf-5013-9bd9-ef992394978c].
- Broader meta-analysis (2821 patients, 11 studies): MI bidirectional block 85% (95% CI 77–94) with EIVOM vs 73% (61–85) without ([passage text removed]) [S:a376c65b-37aa-5fb1-b226-ae4dcd1f8b81].
- Observational cohort (118 patients): 96% (69/72) vs 76% (35/46), p < 0.01 [S:39ac86e9-6ce0-5c4e-9de8-89b9471f627b].
- As a salvage tool when conventional ablation fails, small series report block in essentially all patients [S:91f2f854-0470-55e7-a85e-e0d9243de40f][S:93aafa76-af92-549b-8b3d-cb25c1276d97].
- Ethanol alone is usually insufficient: in one series EIVOM itself produced block in 7/19 (37%), with the remaining 12 (63%) requiring touch-up endocardial and/or CS RF [S:e22eb29b-a7b7-50bb-9294-79a4762c7670]. Dose matters — block was 92.6% with >4 mL vs 73.1% with ≤4 mL, and >5.75 mL independently predicted block [S:9217f912-da7b-5524-b964-f8f14265f367].

## Durability — the weaker link

- **Head-to-head durability study (560 non-paroxysmal AF patients):** acute block 97% (EIVOM/RF) vs 92% (RF), but at repeat procedures reconduction across the MI line occurred in 25/43 (58%) EIVOM/RF vs 39/80 (49%) RF (p = 0.32); arrhythmia recurrence was identical (37% in both) — the authors concluded EIVOM ensures block but did not reduce reconduction [S:ac89fe78-166a-5b3f-b8b7-27ccf89a8594][S:3d8c0bef-35db-57ee-ac84-edcac389fd98].
- **Meta-analysis:** MI reconnection rate was not significantly reduced ([passage text removed] = 0.14), though leave-one-out sensitivity analysis crossed significance, so the null result is not robust [S:a376c65b-37aa-5fb1-b226-ae4dcd1f8b81][S:2c357d80-6283-5a12-acb8-b4abb9dc2ecf].
- **Another cohort:** reconnection at redo in 2/7 (28.6%) EIVOM vs 18/41 (43.9%) RF (p = 0.439); notably, no perimitral ATs occurred in the EIVOM group vs 7 in the RF group [S:359c3848-80a6-5d99-90df-5ed64d73a526]. Reported MI reconnection rates after first-step EIVOM range 25%–58% [S:b378eccc-4554-50b7-8391-23ce3ca0f2c7]; the Bordeaux group reported 37.1% [S:799b6ce8-a664-5b5e-95fd-6cb68fc59cb8].
- **Where it fails:** residual/recurrent conduction clusters at sites *not* covered by the ethanol lesion — the mitral annulus side of the isthmus and epicardial gaps within the CS/great cardiac vein — suggesting the ethanol effect is partially reversible at lesion borders and that EIVOM-induced low voltage can mask pathways needing meticulous RF [S:b378eccc-4554-50b7-8391-23ce3ca0f2c7][S:db9e8c94-c0a3-5c83-b597-e579c1eb2ab3][S:799b6ce8-a664-5b5e-95fd-6cb68fc59cb8]. In 187 patients, 43.3% still had unblocked MI after EIVOM plus endocardial linear ablation; intra-CS ablation was needed in 77.8% of those, ultimately yielding 95.7% block [S:7d535dad-7d56-5f5e-906b-35da50891901].

## Clinical relevance of achieving the block

A secondary analysis of VENUS showed EIVOM's benefit was confined to [passage text removed] 54.3% vs 37.0%, difference 17.3%, p = 0.01), with no difference when block was not achieved (34.0% vs 37.0%, p = 0.58) [S:af3cd409-051c-50af-951e-426f352e89a5]. Randomized trials using EIVOM within a full lesion set report higher MI block and better outcomes (e.g., Zuo et al.: MI block 93.3% vs 64.9%; PROMPT-AF and Marshall-Plan trials) [S:11a7c4a3-5697-5bec-bdda-ecedbccf163c][S:7428c20e-a783-5305-a7cd-23afdb5dd8ed].

## Context: pulsed field ablation

EIVOM may remain relevant because PFA of the MI shows high *acute* but poor *durable* block — in one prospective series of 236 redo patients (no EIVOM used), acute block was 100%, 14.8% had recovery after the waiting period/adenosine, and remapping at ~3 months showed durable mitral block in only 5.5% [S:75137810-a339-54b6-ba64-91571af140a6]. Epicardial VOM recordings during MI PFA show incomplete electrogram attenuation and pseudoblock patterns, arguing that ethanol may be needed to disrupt VOM epicardial connections [S:b7f7201a-3c00-5acb-9fbf-2cd6f2ff9d67]. No trial has yet directly compared PFA of the lateral MI against EIVOM [S:75137810-a339-54b6-ba64-91571af140a6].

## Safety caveat

Reported EIVOM-related events include small pericardial effusion, pericarditis, and VOM dissection [S:e22eb29b-a7b7-50bb-9294-79a4762c7670]; in RCT meta-analysis major complications did not differ (2.8% vs 3.5%) but overall complications were more frequent with EIVOM ([passage text removed]) [S:e167f71b-8966-546f-9042-e3d29babafb7].
