rows.question: Which imaging modalities establish cardiac sarcoidosis when endomyocardial biopsy is negative or not feasible?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: cardiovascular magnetic resonance is the test to reach for first, because absence of late gadolinium enhancement reduces the possibility of clinically significant disease; magnetic resonance carries the better prognostic information for arrhythmic risk and cardiac mortality; metabolic imaging with fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography answers a different question, showing whether inflammation is currently active and whether it is responding to anti-inflammatory treatment; neither modality alone secures the diagnosis, the highest diagnostic accuracy coming from colocalising focal metabolic uptake with enhancement or with raised native T1. Certainty: These are consistent associations rather than established test characteristics. Scope: applies to suspected cardiac sarcoidosis with negative or unobtainable endomyocardial biopsy in adults with suspected cardiac sarcoidosis, with or without known extracardiac disease, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it states that a normal fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography study excludes cardiac sarcoidosis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement and dedicated cardiac ¹⁸F-FDG PET (± perfusion imaging) are the two modalities that carry the diagnosis when endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) is negative or unfeasible; ⁶⁷Ga citrate scintigraphy is an accepted alternative tracer study, echocardiography contributes supporting criteria, and hybrid FDG-PET/MR is the emerging highest-performing combination.**

**Why imaging must substitute for biopsy.** Unguided EMB has sensitivity of roughly 20% because of patchy, mid-wall disease, rising to 40–50% when guided by FDG-PET, CMR, or voltage mapping; a negative biopsy therefore does not exclude cardiac sarcoidosis (CS) [[passage text removed]].

**Formal diagnostic pathways that use imaging instead of myocardial histology**
- **HRS 2014 clinical ("probable") pathway** — requires histologic extracardiac sarcoidosis plus ≥1 feature, of which three are imaging-based: [passage text removed] compatible pattern, LGE on CMR in a compatible pattern, or positive gallium uptake in a compatible pattern (others being steroid-responsive cardiomyopathy/heart block, unexplained LVEF <40%, unexplained sustained VT, Mobitz II/third-degree AV block), with alternative causes excluded [[passage text removed]].
- **JCS 2016 (the only framework permitting diagnosis with no granuloma anywhere, i.e. isolated CS)** — in patients with negative or no [passage text removed] on ⁶⁷Ga scintigraphy or FDG-PET **plus ≥3 of the other [passage text removed] VT/VF; [passage text removed] dysfunction/LVEF <50% or focal asynergy; myocardial LGE on CMR), with prerequisites that no other organ is involved, whole-body tracer uptake is absent elsewhere, chest CT shows no pulmonary sarcoidosis, and coronary disease and other inflammatory myocardial disease are excluded [[passage text removed]]. In JCS 2016, FDG-PET uptake and CMR LGE were both promoted from lesser status to **major** criteria [[passage text removed] centred on CMR and FDG-PET, prefers biopsy where possible, and advises applying the JCS 2016 criteria when biopsy is negative [[passage text removed]/PMC12589786, [passage text removed]].
- **WASOG 2014** additionally accepts patchy uptake on dedicated cardiac PET or a defect on perfusion scintigraphy/SPECT (with granulomatous inflammation in another organ) [[passage text removed]].

**Comparative performance.** In a meta-analysis of 33 studies (1997 patients, 687 with CS; 17 CMR studies, 26 PET studies), CMR [passage text removed] similar specificity (85% vs 82%, P = .85); in the six head-to-head studies sensitivities were 92% vs 81% and specificities 72% vs 82%. PET sensitivity was higher with quantitative than qualitative reading (93% vs 76%) and CMR sensitivity higher when T2 imaging was included (99% vs 88%) [[passage text removed], S:https://www.scinapse.io/papers/4280601510].

**They are complementary, not interchangeable.** CMR-LGE reflects injury/fibrosis that may be active or burnt-out and has excellent negative predictive value for prognostically significant involvement but cannot separate active from inactive disease; FDG-PET detects active granulomatous inflammation and is used for treatment monitoring [[passage text removed]/PMC11754344]. A meta-analysis of 16 studies/1361 patients found FDG-PET/MRI more sensitive than FDG-PET/CT (0.94 vs 0.77, P = 0.02) with no significant specificity difference (0.79 vs 0.90, P = 0.32) [[passage text removed]]. The EANM/EACVI consensus designates PET/CT as the first-line hybrid approach and notes whole-body FDG-PET also serves to locate the most accessible extracardiac inflammatory lesion for biopsy, which is preferred over EMB [[passage text removed]/PMC11754344]; in one cohort, however, only 1/88 (1%) patients was diagnosed via [passage text removed]].

**Caveats.** Echocardiography and ECG are useful screens but [passage text removed], and no FDG uptake or LGE pattern is pathognomonic — mimics must be actively excluded [[passage text removed]]. FDG-PET specificity is heavily protocol-dependent, with incomplete myocardial suppression driving false positives [S:https://www.cureus.com/articles/413355-[passage text removed]]. Most of these criteria sets [passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

When endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) is negative or not feasible, cardiac sarcoidosis (CS) is established by **cardiovascular [passage text removed])** and/or **dedicated cardiac ¹⁸F-FDG PET (usually with myocardial perfusion imaging)**, interpreted within the HRS 2014 or Japanese Circulation Society (JCS) criteria; ⁶⁷Ga scintigraphy and SPECT perfusion remain criteria-eligible but are largely superseded, and hybrid FDG-PET/CMR gives the highest accuracy. A negative biopsy does not exclude CS.

## Why imaging carries the diagnosis

EMB sensitivity is low because granulomas are patchy — reported at under 25%, and in the 20–30% range without guidance [S:8af04ba1-1a66-5168-8279-0c299abd55c2][S:25fff739-0d96-5684-8c80-920553838457]; a negative biopsy explicitly does not exclude CS [S:c395ac4c-ec6e-59ac-b4cb-c913dab8de08]. Consequently diagnosis "relies heavily on cardiac imaging" [S:83c007bc-9d75-5830-ac53-eb5558221715], and EMB is seldom performed, with multidisciplinary discussion recommended [S:682c0ce5-2578-5689-846c-81e8bbedc760].

## The criteria pathways

- **HRS 2014 "probable CS":** histological extracardiac sarcoidosis plus ≥1 criterion, including LGE on CMR in a consistent pattern, patchy uptake on dedicated cardiac PET, or positive ⁶⁷Ga cardiac uptake — other causes excluded [S:9f55c357-9040-56d8-804a-f3c951489011][S:d3652380-53a0-58bc-8f90-569be980337d]. WASOG adds a perfusion scintigraphy/SPECT defect as a further criterion [S:9f55c357-9040-56d8-804a-f3c951489011].
- **JCS:** myocardial LGE on CMR and abnormally high cardiac uptake on ⁶⁷Ga scintigraphy or ¹⁸F-FDG PET are **major** criteria; SPECT perfusion defects are minor. Critically, **isolated CS can be diagnosed without any biopsy** when ≥3 major criteria plus an abnormal ⁶⁷Ga SPECT or [passage text removed] extracardiac disease [S:d3652380-53a0-58bc-8f90-569be980337d]. The 2017 JCS revision does not mandate tissue confirmation [S:7c3ab85a-244b-5938-9488-7c8328eb8f5c], and JCS/imaging-centric pathways offer "[passage text removed]" [S:1ca0fca9-5da1-53df-82c2-63832b15a113][S:a550adb4-170b-5360-87a5-68c87a00a9f2].

## Modality-specific performance and role

**CMR (LGE ± T1/T2/ECV mapping)** — the diagnostic tool of choice, with high yield against HRS criteria (sensitivity 97%, specificity 100%, AUC 0.984) [S:682c0ce5-2578-5689-846c-81e8bbedc760]; a meta-analysis of eight studies gave 95% sensitivity and 92% specificity [S:25fff739-0d96-5684-8c80-920553838457], and LGE sensitivity/specificity across studies is reported at 78–100% and 76–92% [S:eb3c8b9c-636e-5471-bc51-fafd40d9eca3]. The typical pattern is multifocal patchy mid-myocardial/subepicardial LGE, basal septum and inferolateral/lateral wall, sometimes with RV involvement [S:83c007bc-9d75-5830-ac53-eb5558221715][S:25fff739-0d96-5684-8c80-920553838457]. Limitations: no pathognomonic LGE pattern, overlap with myocarditis and ARVC, gadolinium contraindicated in severe renal disease, and historical device incompatibility (though safety protocols now permit scanning non-conditional devices) [S:f782eb7d-36a2-5847-ad1a-2558788c5bd9][S:3effdc50-b274-5c96-b35a-2c395cd2ac04][S:ea0f27f9-00c9-5a0c-b380-8a35b78fee7a]. CMR oedema imaging is insensitive for inflammation (33% sensitivity, 77% specificity vs FDG-PET in one cohort) [S:8a1b85d3-0d77-5007-9192-7d5262173c5b].

**¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT** — the modality for active inflammation; formally indicated when CMR is unavailable, contraindicated, equivocal or negative despite high clinical suspicion [S:e429be6b-f72e-54d6-ba25-b671ad7106f5][S:3747544a-eda8-568d-8ec4-cf86dcf6e02c]. Pooled sensitivity/specificity 89%/78% [S:d6487806-0905-564c-ae52-4ded241e7e19][S:03915745-7cb8-5347-a892-88f74c53366c]; a later meta-analysis gave 84%/83%, improved by concurrent perfusion imaging [S:d6487806-0905-564c-ae52-4ded241e7e19]. Accuracy is critically dependent on myocardial suppression preparation (prolonged fast, high-fat/low-carbohydrate diet, or heparin) [S:d6487806-0905-564c-ae52-4ded241e7e19][S:682c0ce5-2578-5689-846c-81e8bbedc760]. Combined FDG plus perfusion (⁸²Rb, ¹³N-NH₃, ⁹⁹ᵐTc) stages inflammation versus scar [S:e429be6b-f72e-54d6-ba25-b671ad7106f5][S:ead6c16a-008d-53be-b274-a9c8ec09dcee], and whole-/half-body FDG-PET identifies extracardiac biopsy targets that can convert an "isolated" case into a histologically confirmed one [S:cb79f5f1-53ea-5d7f-89b0-05f012c02b4e][S:844b7ff9-38ad-58f2-aaf7-f9ab1fff91eb].

**CMR + PET are complementary, not interchangeable.** In 107 patients undergoing both, only 66% of those with LGE had abnormal FDG uptake, and combining the two reclassified disease likelihood in nearly half the cohort [S:03915745-7cb8-5347-a892-88f74c53366c]; FDG-PET sensitivity rose [passage text removed] in one retrospective series [S:e429be6b-f72e-54d6-ba25-b671ad7106f5].

**Hybrid FDG-PET/CMR** — highest reported diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.84; 96% specificity, [passage text removed]) versus PET/CT (AUC 0.74) or CMR alone (AUC 0.83), with lower radiation and shorter scan time [S:6384979c-7b53-5fa3-b91c-334af430a088]. In a prospective PET/MRI cohort with T1/T2 mapping, all CS patients had ≥1 abnormality; LGE, T1 and ECV were 100% sensitive while FDG uptake, elevated T2 and FDG–LGE co-localisation were the most specific [S:6c24b568-cc15-5f90-96ec-7955f10c0f90].

**Older nuclear techniques** — ⁶⁷Ga scintigraphy remains in both HRS and JCS criteria but has poor spatial resolution, is falsely negative after corticosteroids, and has been largely replaced by FDG-PET [S:904e51d8-5a26-5973-93c1-ded7b9be7d83][S:87ae060b-2194-565e-9463-b07b92b3c44e][S:68cf58bf-08f1-500d-a62d-e430caa4274e]. Non-coronary SPECT perfusion defects (thallium-201/technetium-99m, with reverse redistribution) are a JCS minor criterion but not part of the HRS algorithm [S:904e51d8-5a26-5973-93c1-ded7b9be7d83][S:5d17f790-2103-529f-b86a-f7d5b7a8e063].

**Echocardiography is a screening tool only** — findings are nonspecific and sensitivity is as low as 14%, so it is unsuitable for establishing the diagnosis, though it is used with ECG to select patients for advanced imaging [S:87ae060b-2194-565e-9463-b07b92b3c44e][S:17534885-069a-5af8-959f-30c38c37b6f0].

## Caveats

No advanced imaging modality can serve as a reference standard in isolation; a multidisciplinary integration of clinical, electrical, structural and tissue-characterisation domains is recommended, with coronary disease and myocarditis actively excluded [S:8a7ffa08-b14d-5bb4-bfa0-f44f159c49ad][S:682c0ce5-2578-5689-846c-81e8bbedc760]. If histology is still wanted, imaging should guide it: electrogram-guided biopsy raised yield to 41% versus the literature 20–25%, with the highest yield when both electrogram and CMR/PET abnormalities were used to target sites [S:2364a8d1-a7df-52af-911a-82f8f54b3085][S:e41f746c-f2df-565d-af51-14151045a645]. ⁶⁸Ga-DOTA somatostatin-receptor PET has been reported to have higher diagnostic accuracy than FDG for CS [S:d6029df9-fe87-574f-bd5b-c5c9a34745fe], but sensitivity and specificity for these tracers are described as currently unknown owing to absent control groups [S:a51a4f18-310b-5beb-abb9-9340efc29d64] — it is not a criteria-based diagnostic modality.

rows.question: How do transcatheter and surgical aortic valve replacement compare over longer follow-up in low surgical risk patients with aortic stenosis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: the early advantage of the transcatheter approach over surgery in low-risk patients does not hold: by seven years the composite of death, stroke and repeat hospital stay is no longer separated, although the early gap was roughly a halving of events; reintervention on the valve moves the other way with longer follow-up, happening more often after the transcatheter procedure and driven mainly by regurgitation rather than by failure of the prosthesis; how this plays out in a bicuspid valve is unsettled, with the only randomised comparison to include such patients underpowered and hinting at harm. Certainty: The differences between the two procedures can be read as caused by which procedure the patient was assigned to receive. Scope: applies to severe aortic stenosis in adults at low surgical risk undergoing aortic valve replacement, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it attributes the early advantage of the transcatheter approach to fewer deaths, since it was driven mainly by fewer repeat hospital stays.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Through 5–7 years, TAVR and SAVR give statistically similar death, stroke, rehospitalization, and health-status outcomes in low-surgical-risk patients, and the early advantage of TAVR at 1 year attenuates over time; the main divergence emerging beyond year 5 is a higher reintervention rate after TAVR with the self-expanding valve, while surgical valves show more severe structural deterioration at 10 years and TAVR consistently shows more paravalvular regurgitation and pacemakers.

## Balloon-expandable valve: PARTNER 3

At 7 years (n=1000 randomized, Sapien 3 vs surgical bioprosthesis), the nonhierarchical primary composite of death, stroke, or rehospitalization occurred in 34.6% vs 37.2% ([passage text removed]), and the hierarchical win-ratio [passage text removed]). Components were death 19.5% vs 16.8%, stroke 8.5% vs 8.1%, and rehospitalization 20.6% vs 23.5%. Mean gradients were 13.1±8.5 vs 12.1±6.3 mm Hg, and bioprosthetic valve failure was 6.9% vs 7.3% ([PMID 41144631](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41144631); NCT02675114; [ACC trial summary]([passage text removed])). The authors note that the initial TAVR advantage in primary-endpoint events diverged only in the first year, with the longer restricted mean event-free survival driven mainly by the rehospitalization difference ([NEJMoa2509766 full text]([passage text removed])). Reintervention was 6.7% vs 6.0% ([cardiovascularbusiness.com]([passage text removed])).

A VARC-3 durability analysis of the implanted cohort (495 TAVR, 453 surgery) found cumulative incidences of stage 2/3 SVD-related bioprosthetic valve dysfunction of 7% vs 8%, all-cause BVF 7% vs 8%, SVD-related BVF 4% vs 5.3%, and reintervention 6% in both arms; the commonest reintervention trigger in both arms was progressive prosthetic stenosis, mostly treated electively ([PMC13294825](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13294825); [ACC journal scan]([passage text removed])). Health status also converged: at 7 years 66% (TAVR) vs 67% (SAVR) were alive with a favorable KCCQ outcome (p=0.695) and 59% vs 62% with an excellent outcome (p=0.404), with earlier recovery after TAVR ([ACC summary of JACC substudy]([passage text removed])).

## Self-expanding valve: Evolut Low Risk

At 5 years (730 TAVR, 684 surgery), [passage text removed]% vs 16.4% (p=0.47), cardiovascular mortality 7.2% vs 9.3%, disabling stroke 3.6% vs 4.0%; hemodynamics favored TAVR (mean gradient 10.7 vs 12.8 mm Hg, p<0.001; effective orifice area 2.1 vs 1.9 cm², p<0.001), and reintervention was 3.3% vs 2.5% (p=0.44) ([JACC 5-year paper]([passage text removed]); [PCRonline summary](https://www.pcronline.com/News/Whats-new-on-PCRonline/2025/ACC/[passage text removed] 6-year update is the key caveat: the primary endpoint remained similar (23.3% vs 20.4%, p=0.43; all-cause mortality 20.9% vs 18.7%), but reintervention was 5.5% vs 3.3% (p=0.07) at 6 years and 9.8% vs 6.0% (subdistribution HR 1.68, p=0.02) using available 7-year data — a signal driven by reintervention for regurgitation. Two of 60 TAVR reinterventions and 4 of 32 surgical reinterventions were followed by death within 30 days/before discharge ([JACC 6-year paper]([passage text removed]); [ACC expert analysis]([passage text removed])).

## Longest randomized follow-up: NOTION, 10 years

In 280 patients (145 TAVI with self-expanding CoreValve, 135 SAVR; mean age 79.1±4.8, mean STS 3.0±1.7%), the composite of death, stroke, or MI was 65.5% in both arms (HR 1.0, 95% CI 0.7–1.3, p=0.90). Severe SVD was lower after TAVI (1.5% vs [passage text removed], p=0.02) and severe bioprosthetic valve dysfunction less frequent (20.5% vs 43.0%, p<0.01), but bioprosthetic valve failure did not differ (9.7% vs 13.[passage text removed], p=0.4). Mild-or-greater paravalvular leak was more common after TAVI (18.0% vs 5.2%), pacemaker implantation far higher ([passage text removed]), and new-onset AF higher after SAVR ([PMC10984572](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10984572); [ACC trial page]([passage text removed])). Interpret cautiously: only ~25% of patients were alive at 10 years (survivorship bias), the TAVI arm used first-generation self-expanding valves, and ~35% of surgical valves were Trifecta ([EuroIntervention durability review]([passage text removed])).

## Pooled evidence

A meta-analysis of 7 trials (n=7785; mean follow-up 5.76±0.073 years) found no difference in death or disabling stroke ([passage text removed]), with higher pacemaker implantation and moderate-to-severe paravalvular leak after TAVR; results were consistent across high-, intermediate-, and low-risk strata ([SCAI EuroPCR 2024 coverage]([passage text removed]); [JSCAI]([passage text removed])).

## Caveats

Durability beyond 10 years is unknown for any contemporary transcatheter platform ([ACC review]([passage text removed])), and the two large low-risk trials have planned 10-year follow-up still pending ([PMC12687276]([passage text removed])). The reintervention divergence appears device-specific so far (present with Evolut, not with Sapien 3), but I found no head-to-head randomized comparison in low-risk patients addressing that difference directly.

**Bottom line:** Through 5 years, the two randomized low-risk trials show broadly equivalent clinical outcomes — the early advantage of TAVR narrows or disappears over time — and out to 10 years (NOTION) major clinical outcomes remain similar; however, pooled trial-level meta-analysis suggests a small late mortality/stroke signal favoring surgery, and device-specific durability/reintervention differences emerge beyond 5 years.

**PARTNER 3 (balloon-expandable SAPIEN 3, mean age 73, mean STS-PROM 1.9%)**
- The large 1-year benefit for the composite of death, stroke, or rehospitalization (8.5% vs 15.1%) was no longer significant at 5 years (22.8% vs 27.2%, p=0.07), with no differences in [passage text removed]%) [S:42d9c475-2dd5-5c42-a48e-9fae037e5543].

- At 5 years the primary [passage text removed] 15.5% (TAVR) vs 16.4% (surgery), p=0.47; all-cause mortality 13.5% vs 14.9%, p=0.39. rows.question: How should cancer therapy related cardiac dysfunction be assessed and managed without interrupting effective cancer treatment?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: cardiac risk is graded before cardiotoxic treatment begins, and biomarker and imaging surveillance is then pitched to that baseline risk rather than applied uniformly; a fall in ejection fraction without symptoms is not on its own a reason to stop effective cancer treatment: cardioprotective medication is started and monitoring tightened while treatment continues; when the dysfunction is symptomatic or marked the drug is held while heart failure treatment is optimised, ischaemia is looked for and ventricular function is reassessed within weeks. Certainty: These are expert recommendations assembled from existing guidance, not a comparison of one management pathway against another. Scope: applies to cancer therapy related cardiac dysfunction in adults receiving potentially cardiotoxic cancer treatment, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it says that adding a cardioprotective agent to reduce heart failure costs cancer control, since response, overall survival and progression-free survival were all unaffected.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: in most cases cardiac dysfunction should be graded (symptomatic vs asymptomatic; mild/moderate/severe) and treated with heart-failure and cardioprotective drugs while cancer therapy continues under intensified imaging/biomarker surveillance and multidisciplinary review — interruption is reserved for symptomatic moderate–severe dysfunction, asymptomatic severe LVEF decline, or immune-checkpoint myocarditis.**

**1. Baseline risk stratification before treatment**
All patients due to receive potentially cardiotoxic therapy should have cardiovascular risk assessment using the HFA-ICOS score, incorporating risk factors, CV history, prior/planned cancer therapy and ECG; higher-risk profiles trigger biomarkers (troponin, natriuretic peptides), imaging, and cardiology referral (https://diagnostics.roche.com/global/en/cardialogue/article/insights-on-2022-esc-cardio-oncology-guidelines.html). Individualised prevention beginning at cancer diagnosis is a Class I recommendation (PMC11288116). An explicit stated goal of the 2022 ESC cardio-oncology guidelines is to "facilitate cancer treatment with minimal unnecessary interruptions" ([passage text removed]), and a guiding principle is that any decision to interrupt be made by multidisciplinary discussion ([passage text removed]).

**2. How to assess**
- Echocardiography and blood biomarkers are the main tools (same ACC key-points source). 3D echocardiographic LVEF plus global longitudinal strain (GLS) is preferred first-line because 2D LVEF has poor reproducibility (~10% day-to-day variability, vs ~6% for 3D and 2.5–4.8% for CMR), and 3D agrees better with CMR (PMC10912891; [passage text removed]-022-00544-3). CMR or MUGA is used when echo is unavailable/technically inadequate, with preference for CMR (ASCO recommendation 5.2.1, https://ascopost.com/issues/april-10-2017/asco-clinical-practice-guideline-on-[passage text removed]).
- Grade severity using the IC-OS/ESC categories: asymptomatic mild = LVEF ≥50% with new relative GLS fall >15% and/or new biomarker rise; moderate = LVEF fall ≥10 points to 40–49% (or smaller fall to 40–49% with GLS/biomarker change); severe = new LVEF <40% (PMC11288116).
- Surveillance cadence: baseline TTE then every 3 months during HER2-targeted therapy and within 12 months of completion, reducing to 6-monthly in the palliative setting after year 1; cTn/NT-proBNP before anti-HER2 therapy is Class I in high/very-high-risk patients (PMC11288116). Anthracycline monitoring is stratified by baseline risk in an integrated biomarker + imaging protocol ([passage text removed]). Frequent imaging plus biomarkers is recommended in all patients who have developed CTRCD (2022 ESC guideline text, [passage text removed]). Practically, a detected LVEF drop should be re-confirmed (with NT-proBNP) within ~3–4 weeks rather than acted on from a single scan ([passage text removed]).

**3. Management that preserves cancer treatment**
- *Asymptomatic mild CTRCD*: continue cancer therapy and start ACEi/ARB and/or beta-blocker if criteria are met; asymptomatic moderate or severe CTRCD warrants interruption ([passage text removed]).
- *Symptomatic CTRCD*: start guideline heart-failure therapy (Class I B); temporary interruption for symptomatic moderate CTRCD with MDT review; discontinuation for symptomatic severe CTRCD (Class I C) (ESC guideline Recommendation Table 24, [passage text removed]).
- *HER2 therapy specifically*: interrupt only for symptomatic moderate-to-severe CTRCD or asymptomatic LVEF <40%; otherwise continue with cardioprotection ([passage text removed]). This "permissive cardiotoxicity" approach is supported by SAFE-HEaRt, in which 30 patients with asymptomatic LVEF 40–49% were treated with beta-blockers and/or ACEi/ARB and 27 (90%) completed HER2-targeted therapy without cardiac events; [passage text removed] follow-up, with no cardiac deaths ([passage text removed]; PMC8207895). In a clinical cohort of 51 patients managed permissively, 47 (92%) completed trastuzumab and 3 (6%) stopped early for severe LV dysfunction/heart failure (https://academic.oup.com/oncolo/article/28/9/e712/7140381). The rationale is that interruption itself carries oncologic cost — that report cites worse overall and disease-free survival with any trastuzumab interruption (adjusted HRs 4.8 and 4.4) — though this is retrospective.
- *Timeliness matters*: in 2,625 anthracycline-treated patients, 98% of cardiotoxicity occurred within the first year and prompt enalapril ± carvedilol/bisoprolol normalised LVEF in 82%, but only 11% recovered fully (PMID 25948538; PMC7093379); in 201 patients no complete LVEF recovery occurred when HF therapy started >6 months after chemotherapy ([passage text removed]). So detect early and treat immediately rather than stop and wait.

**4. Cardioprotection to keep patients on treatment**
- Dexrazoxane (Class IIa B) and liposomal anthracyclines (Class IIa B) should be considered in high/very-high-risk adults when anthracyclines are indicated, and liposomal doxorubicin is also suggested (Class IIb C) for patients who have already developed anthracycline cardiac dysfunction but for whom resuming anthracycline is the best curative option ([passage text removed]). Both preserve antitumour activity while reducing myocardial anthracycline exposure ([passage text removed]).
- Statin: in STOP-CA (300 lymphoma patients), atorvastatin 40 mg/d reduced the primary endpoint (LVEF fall ≥10 points to <55% at 12 months) to 9% vs 22% with placebo (P=.002; OR 2.9, 95% CI 1.4–6.4), with comparable adverse events (PMC10410476; [passage text removed]).
- Neurohormonal blockade triggered by subclinical strain change: in SUCCOUR-MRI, patients with GLS-defined CTRCD randomised to cardioprotection had a smaller 12-month MRI-LVEF decline (−[passage text removed]), but 43% had side-effects attributed to cardioprotection ([passage text removed]).
- SGLT2 inhibitors are promising but evidence is observational: meta-analysed cohorts show lower all-cause mortality (pooled RR 0.52) without a significant reduction in heart-failure incidence (PMC11457630; PMC12010125).

**5. The main exception: ICI myocarditis**
Here the balance flips — ICI is stopped immediately and high-dose corticosteroids started, with ASCO recommending permanent discontinuation after any grade and NCCN after grade ≥2; ESC advises MDT discussion weighing myocarditis severity, cancer stage, alternatives, and de-escalation from dual to single ICI, with rechallenge only case-by-case ([passage text removed]; PMC10330624). Reported recurrence after rechallenge following myocarditis was 37.5% in a pharmacovigilance analysis, based on only 16 cases (same JACC source).

**Honest limits of the evidence**
The parent SUCCOUR trial found no difference in 3-year ΔEF between GLS-guided and EF-guided cardioprotection (−0.03±7.9% vs −0.02±6.5%, p=0.99), so strain-triggered intervention is not proven to change hard outcomes (PMID 36435732). ASCO explicitly states that no recommendation can be made about continuing vs discontinuing cancer therapy in patients with cardiac dysfunction, leaving this to oncologist–cardiologist collaboration (https://ascopost.com/issues/april-10-2017/asco-clinical-practice-guideline-on-[passage text removed]). The permissive-cardiotoxicity trials were small phase I/pilot studies (30 and 20 patients) (https://academic.oup.com/oncolo/article/28/9/e712/7140381), and expert reviews note that evidence for routine baseline/serial troponin and NT-proBNP monitoring is mixed and largely derived from small, low-risk cohorts with surrogate endpoints (PMC11520216).
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

[passage text removed] managed by *risk-stratifying before* therapy, *surveilling with serial imaging plus biomarkers during* therapy, and *grading severity* so that guideline-directed heart-failure drugs are started early — because most mild and moderate asymptomatic CTRCD can be treated *while cancer therapy continues*, with interruption reserved for severe or symptomatic disease and for specific entities such as immune-checkpoint-inhibitor myocarditis. Preserving oncologic treatment intensity is itself an outcome goal: trastuzumab interruption is associated with reduced overall and recurrence-free survival [S:6e3e37b0].

## 1. Baseline risk stratification (before the first cycle)

The 2022 ESC cardio-oncology guideline recommends baseline risk stratification in all patients using the HFA-ICOS tool, which integrates prior cardiovascular disease, cardiac imaging, biomarkers (troponin, natriuretic peptides), patient risk factors and the planned regimen, categorising patients into low, moderate, high and very high risk [S:7636da8d][S:f9e0fa83]. High/very-high-risk patients should be referred to cardio-oncology *before* treatment starts, with a multidisciplinary risk–benefit discussion explicitly framed to "minimize unnecessary interruptions in antineoplastic therapy"; moderate/low-risk patients can be referred at CTRCD onset [S:f1a87769][S:ced298e7]. Baseline work-up: history/exam, ECG, echocardiogram with LVEF and GLS, and troponin/NT-proBNP in high-risk patients [S:ea296b50][S:3b849d5b]. Caveats: the tool is expert-opinion-based, performs better for moderate/severe than mild CTRCD (C statistic 0.78, 95% CI 0.71–0.84 in the largest anthracycline validation), is poorly calibrated for mild events, and requires 16–22 predictors, limiting feasibility outside specialist clinics [S:3c399f6d][S:cb0f2898].

## 2. Surveillance during therapy

**Modality.** Transthoracic echocardiography is first-line; 3D LVEF is preferred (2D Simpson if unavailable), the same technique should be used throughout, and GLS should be measured [S:61effd7a][S:bb525472]. CMR is the reference standard and second-line — for poor acoustic windows, discordant LVEF values, and suspected ICI myocarditis [S:4ae9bfea][S:311175a2]. In head-to-head variability testing, 3D-LVEF, 2D-GLS and CMR-LVEF showed the least overlap with normal temporal variability, with 2D-GLS judged most suitable for individual clinical application [S:52639fbc].

**Thresholds.** A ≥10-point LVEF fall to below the lower limit of normal (<50–53%), confirmed on repeat imaging 2–3 weeks later, defines CTRCD; a >15% relative GLS decline flags subclinical dysfunction before LVEF changes [S:6bf7ebae][S:e90b9e05][S:61effd7a]. Confirmatory repeat imaging matters because echo LVEF measurement variability is substantial (~10%) [S:facac1f0][S:69a6d8d7].

**Frequency (risk-adapted).** Echo every two cycles in high/very-high-risk patients, and after a cumulative doxorubicin-equivalent dose ≥250 mg/m² in lower-risk patients; troponin and natriuretic peptides before every cycle in high/very-high risk and every two cycles in moderate/low risk, then at 3 and 12 months after completion [S:bb525472][S:c59f708c][S:179feabc]. One study found CTRCD frequently developed below 250 mg/m² and before the last anthracycline cycle, arguing for extending two-cycle echo surveillance to moderate-risk patients [S:605fabd6]. For HER2 therapy, ESC recommends troponin/natriuretic peptides at baseline, every 2–3 cycles, [passage text removed] [S:90ccd5e8].

## 3. Severity-graded management — continue where possible

The ESC/IC-OS framework separates symptomatic from asymptomatic CTRCD and grades severity [S:2853eb00]:

- **Mild asymptomatic** (LVEF ≥50% with >15% GLS fall or biomarker rise): continue cancer therapy with closer monitoring; consider ACEi/ARB ± beta-blocker [S:7bc1638d][S:822d9644][S:3b849d5b].
- **Moderate asymptomatic** (LVEF 40–49%): for HER2 therapy, continue with intensified monitoring plus ACEi/ARB and beta-blocker; for anthracyclines, guidelines advise temporary interruption [S:7bc1638d][S:822d9644]. For adjuvant HER2 therapy, discontinuation in asymptomatic patients is not recommended, as benefit outweighs risk provided cardioprotection and close monitoring are in place [S:8a666de2].
- **Severe asymptomatic** (LVEF <40%) or moderate-to-severe symptomatic: interrupt, optimise heart-failure therapy, and re-evaluate for reintroduction by multidisciplinary team once LVEF ≥40% [S:7bc1638d][S:21cd8782].
- **Mild symptomatic:** start heart-failure therapy and decide continuation vs interruption by multidisciplinary consensus [S:21cd8782].

Treatment is guideline-directed HF therapy (ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) titrated to maximally tolerated doses per the 2021 ESC HF guidelines [S:822d9644]. MRAs are considered safe; cardioprotection should continue at least for the duration of cancer treatment [S:69a6d8d7]. Early treatment matters: in an Italian cohort, longer delay in starting cardioprotection meant fewer LVEF responders, with no responders when therapy began >6 months after detection of LVEF <45% [S:d73d3854].

**Prospective evidence that continuation is feasible.** SAFE-HEaRt enrolled 31 patients (30 evaluable) with HER2-positive breast cancer, LVEF 40–49% and no HF symptoms, treated with trastuzumab, pertuzumab or T-DM1 *without interruption* alongside beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors and serial echocardiograms; [passage text removed] end of treatment, 27 patients (90%) completed planned HER2-targeted therapy, 2 had a cardiac event and 1 an asymptomatic LVEF fall to ≤35% [S:2793bfce][S:5f27c192]. Notably, under FDA label rules most of these patients would have required interruption [S:5f27c192]. The SCHOLAR study similarly showed uninterrupted trastuzumab was feasible in mild cardiotoxicity with ACEi/beta-blocker and intensified monitoring, with ~10% risk of moderate-to-severe HF [S:2721c694]. Both are single-arm, so cannot prove net benefit; randomised trials are still needed [S:2721c694].

## 4. Reducing the need to stop: prevention and dose-mitigation

- **Neurohormonal blockade:** consider beta-blockers and/or ACEi/ARB in moderate-to-high-risk patients (elevated troponin, high cumulative anthracycline dose) rather than universally; in HER2 patients, pharmacological prevention produced fewer trastuzumab interruptions than placebo [S:69a6d8d7][S:7feba917]. Meta-analytic effects in unselected patients are modest, and routine prophylaxis in unselected breast cancer patients is not recommended [S:8560ec44].
- **Statins:** STOP-CA (300 lymphoma patients, atorvastatin 40 mg vs placebo) reduced the primary endpoint of ≥10-point LVEF decline to <55% at 12 months (9% vs 22%, p=0.002); PREVENT and SPARE-HF were neutral [S:7ea2feac][S:7c7177d8]. Statins carry a Class IIa ESC recommendation for high/very-high-risk patients [S:405b15dc].
- **Dexrazoxane and liposomal/continuous-infusion anthracyclines:** dexrazoxane reduced heart failure incidence (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.20–0.41 in a Cochrane meta-analysis of 10 studies/1619 patients) and can be used as secondary prevention when anthracyclines are restarted after moderate/severe CTRCD, alongside cumulative-dose minimisation [S:128f5b0c][S:21cd8782][S:822d9644].
- **SGLT2 inhibitors:** observational data in diabetic cancer patients show fewer HF admissions and lower all-cause mortality (pooled RR [passage text removed] in one meta-analysis of four cohorts, n=6708), with no reduction in HF exacerbation in that analysis; dedicated primary-prevention RCTs are ongoing [S:6d2cff01][S:80e9d12b][S:bcad4f83].
- **Non-pharmacological:** risk-factor control, smoking cessation, and aerobic exercise/cardio-oncology rehabilitation before and during anthracycline therapy [S:822d9644][S:69a6d8d7].

## 5. Should surveillance be strain-guided?

Evidence is mixed. The original SUCCOUR trial (331 anthracycline-treated patients with an additional HF risk factor) randomised GLS- versus LVEF-guided initiation of cardioprotection and was neutral for the primary endpoint of LVEF change at 3 years, although more patients received cardioprotection in the GLS arm and among those meeting cardioprotection criteria final [passage text removed]); investigators also raised concern that focusing on GLS could trigger unnecessary changes to cancer therapy [S:f106f79c][S:81db1b06][S:ce9b0e71]. SUCCOUR-MRI then randomised 105 patients with isolated GLS decline (>12% relative) to cardioprotection versus usual care and found a smaller LVEF decrement, higher follow-up LVEF, less 12-month LVEF-CTRCD and GLS improvement [S:81db1b06][S:f9db3a24]. Practically, GLS is best used to trigger *cardioprotection*, not cancer-therapy modification [S:f610d1be].

## 6. Where continuation is not appropriate

ICI-associated myocarditis is the main exception: hold the ICI, start high-dose corticosteroids (ESC/IC-OS: methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg IV daily for ≥3 days, then oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day), and escalate to second-line immunosuppression if refractory [S:24be9aab][S:07bebb09]. NCCN recommends permanent discontinuation for grade 2–4 myocarditis; ASCO calls rechallenge uncertain; ESC/IC-OS defers to case-by-case multidisciplinary discussion [S:24be9aab]. In one case series of 28 steroid-treated patients, rechallenge was performed in six with one myocarditis relapse [S:49814d33]. Severe symptomatic CTRCD generally warrants discontinuation unless an exception is agreed in the multidisciplinary team with a robust cardioprotective strategy and per-cycle monitoring [S:822d9644].

## 7. After treatment

An end-of-treatment assessment is recommended for anyone who developed CTRCD; severe/very severe cases and mild/moderate cases without full recovery should continue guideline-directed therapy indefinitely, whereas mild/[passage text removed] biomarkers may have cardioprotective therapy tapered depending on risk profile and multidisciplinary/patient input [S:8a9c8d60]. Withdrawal data specific to cancer survivors are limited and conflicting; the TRED-HF trial and HF-with-improved-EF data caution against routine withdrawal, and the HER-SAFE trial is recruiting [S:8a9c8d60]. Long-term surveillance is risk-adapted — e.g. echo at 12 months and every 5 years for low/medium risk, versus 6 and 12 months then annually [passage text removed] in high-risk patients [S:a2467f46][S:179feabc].

**Two honest gaps:** neither SAFE-HEaRt nor SCHOLAR was randomised, so the net oncologic-versus-cardiac trade-off of uninterrupted therapy in reduced-LVEF patients is unproven [S:2721c694]; and the optimal duration of cardioprotective therapy remains unknown [S:69a6d8d7].

rows.question: What clinical outcomes follow conduction system pacing versus right ventricular pacing in patients with atrioventricular block?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: conduction system pacing is associated with preservation of left ventricular ejection fraction, with less decline than right ventricular pacing; paced QRS complexes are markedly shorter with conduction system pacing than with right ventricular pacing; whether that translates into fewer heart failure admissions or deaths is disputed within the randomised evidence itself: one trial found no significant difference in heart failure hospitalisation or mortality, a second reduced a composite of pacing-induced cardiomyopathy and resynchronisation upgrade without changing either endpoint individually, and a third reduced heart failure hospitalisation. Certainty: The advantage in ventricular function and activation is consistent, while the effect on admissions and survival is contested within the randomised evidence itself. Scope: applies to atrioventricular block requiring ventricular pacing in adults receiving a pacemaker for atrioventricular block, including those with preserved ventricular function, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the reduction in a composite endpoint as showing that conduction system pacing reduces mortality.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** In AV block, conduction system pacing (CSP — His-bundle or left bundle branch area pacing) consistently reduces pacing-induced cardiomyopathy (PICM), preserves LVEF, and shortens paced QRS versus right ventricular pacing (RVP), and reduces composite endpoints and heart failure hospitalization (HFH); a mortality benefit appears only in observational-weighted pooled data and is not established in randomized evidence. The trade-off is longer procedures and more lead revisions.

**Randomized evidence**
- **CSPACE** (202 patients with AV block without a CRT indication, 1:1 CSP vs RV septal pacing, 2 Australian centres): CSP success 89/101 (88.1%); over mean follow-up 25.2 ± 11.8 months the composite of PICM, CRT upgrade, HFH and death was lower with CSP (7.17 vs 20.69 events/[passage text removed]), driven by less PICM ([passage text removed] no CRT upgrades (HR essentially nil; P=0.043). HFH ([passage text removed]) and all-cause mortality ([passage text removed]) did not differ. Lead revision was more frequent with CSP (8 [7.9%] vs 1 [1.0%]; P=0.017) [PMID 40835365; [passage text removed]]. An accompanying editorial notes PICM incidence of ~30% in the RVsP arm was at the high end versus other AV-block studies, suggesting a population enriched for CRT-benefiting patients [[passage text removed]].
- **Prague CSP** (249 patients; 125 RVP, 124 CSP — 10 His-bundle, 96 LBBAP, 15 deep septal): at 1 year the LVEF decline was smaller with CSP (−2% vs −4%; P=.03) and an LVEF fall ≥10% was less common (5% vs 16%; P=.01), but the composite clinical outcome (4 vs 9; P=.15) and procedural complications (2 vs 9; P=.09) did not differ. Procedure and fluoroscopy times were longer with CSP ([passage text removed]) [PMID 40412596].
- **LBBP-FAVOUR** (160 patients, multicentre China, mean ~36 months): the composite of death, HFH or PICM occurred in 9 LBBP patients (11.6%) vs 25 RVP patients (33.9%), driven by PICM (6.5% vs 18.2%); no significant difference in mortality or HFH alone, with better LVEF, LV dimensions and NYHA class in the LBBP arm [[passage text removed]].

**Pooled randomized data**
- Five RCTs, 985 AV-block patients: composite endpoint [passage text removed]); all-cause mortality not different ([passage text removed]); greater LVEF change (P=0.008) and shorter QRS (P=0.002) with CSP [PMID 42055704, Open Heart 13(1):e003954].
- [passage text removed]): PICM HR 0.30 (95% CI 0.18–0.48; I²=0%), ΔLVEF +[passage text removed]; I²=87%), [passage text removed]–0.48), paced QRS −[passage text removed]); mortality HR 0.57 (95% CI 0.29–1.12; P=0.10) [doi:10.1016/j.amjcard.2026.07.013].

**Observational data (larger, but confounded)**
- Meta-analysis of 19 studies, 5,390 AV-block patients (2,182 CSP; 3,208 RVP): all-cause mortality RR 0.50, HFH RR 0.39, PICM RR 0.36, composite RR 0.44 (all P<0.05); LVEF +2.60%, LVEDD −1.54 mm; no significant difference in cardiovascular death or CRT/BiV upgrade; [passage text removed] not increased. The authors explicitly frame the mortality signal as associative and hypothesis-generating given observational predominance [PMC13317157; BMC Cardiovasc Disord 26:542].
- **Geisinger His-bundle registry** (HBP attempted in 332, RVP 433): primary composite of death, HFH or BiV upgrade 25% vs 32% (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.53–0.94; P=0.02), concentrated in patients with ventricular pacing >20% (25.3% vs 35.6%; HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.46–0.93) and not significant when pacing <20% (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.47–1.30; P=0.34); HFH [passage text removed]); mortality trend only (17.2% vs 21.4%, P=0.06); paced QRS 128±27.7 vs 166±21.8 ms [PMID 29535066].
- **Geisinger-Rush LBBAP registry**: primary composite 10.0% (LBBAP) vs 23.3% (RVP), HR 0.46 (95% CI 0.306–0.695; P<0.001), again driven by patients with pacing burden >20% [PMID 34481985].
- An earlier meta-analysis of 9 de novo pacemaker studies found HBP reduced [passage text removed]) with no significant mortality difference ([passage text removed]) [PMC9622534].

**Interpretation:** benefit is concentrated in patients with high anticipated ventricular pacing burden (>20–40%), and the dominant, reproducible signal is prevention of PICM/LVEF decline rather than mortality reduction. Costs are longer procedure/fluoroscopy time and a higher lead-revision rate. Additional powered trials are ongoing (e.g., LEAP-Block NCT04730921, PROTECT-SYNC NCT05585411, OptimPacing NCT04624763), so long-term hard-outcome evidence remains incomplete.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

In AV block, conduction system pacing (CSP — His-bundle or left bundle branch area pacing) consistently reduces heart failure hospitalisation and preserves/improves left ventricular function versus right ventricular pacing (RVP), with shorter paced QRS and less new-onset atrial fibrillation; a mortality benefit is seen in observational pooled data but is **not** confirmed when only randomised trials are analysed. [S:44d1f3f2-40ba-52be-8980-0e784b15402d][S:58e2ac54-b2b6-5f97-b616-ebb36769c84d]

## Randomised evidence (strongest, but limited)

A systematic review restricted to RCTs pooled five trials in 985 patients with AVB: the composite endpoint favoured CSP (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.31–0.95, p=0.03), heart failure hospitalisation was markedly reduced (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.17–0.54, p<0.0001), but all-cause mortality did not differ (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.36–1.30, p=0.25). Change in LVEF (p=0.008) and paced QRS duration (p=0.002) both favoured CSP. [S:44d1f3f2-40ba-52be-8980-0e784b15402d] The authors explicitly contrast this with earlier, largely observational meta-analyses that reported a mortality reduction, concluding that mortality benefit remains uncertain and that larger, longer RCTs are needed. [S:89b4fe9f-e186-5454-8c7c-e15fdaf1c4cd][S:753d611b-f21a-543e-a002-9b88794f5494]

The Kronborg randomised double-blind crossover trial ([passage text removed], LVEF >40%) found better preserved LVEF with His/para-His pacing versus RV [passage text removed]) and better mechanical synchrony, with no difference in NYHA class, 6-minute walk, quality of life or device-related complications, and a higher capture threshold with HBP. [S:736d1727-863b-5329-9f9d-1578e3462d17][S:431c5811-35bb-5e9d-88c9-158563d0c2cc]

## Observational and pooled mixed-design evidence

- **Mortality + HF:** An updated meta-analysis of 40 studies (8290 patients) found lower HF hospitalisation ([passage text removed]) and lower [passage text removed]) with LBBAP, plus greater LVEF improvement (MD +3.77%), greater LVEDD reduction (MD −2.33 mm), shorter QRS (MD −35.56 ms) and greater NT-proBNP fall, with comparable procedural safety. [S:58e2ac54-b2b6-5f97-b616-ebb36769c84d][S:cc1ee42c-862a-553a-8ec3-47cfb3ae68bc] An earlier pooled analysis of 25 studies (4250 patients) similarly reported lower HFH (RR 0.33), mortality (RR 0.52, over mean follow-up 16.1±8.4 months) and AF (RR 0.43), with no difference in lead-related complications. [S:4fa21436-a760-5443-9d0d-ce7aadbf3e9b][S:1c85f055-49ae-5239-b1e3-0e5c5e8ae2e9]
- **AVB-specific:** In 14 studies (3062 AVB patients with preserved EF), LBBAP reduced HFH ([passage text removed]), shortened QRS (−35.56 ms), raised LVEF (+5.48%) and reduced LVEDD (−3.98 mm), with no difference in implant success, thresholds or complications. [S:35ec3792-3ec7-5d6d-aab6-97e59005d56d]
- **Atrial fibrillation:** Pooling 8 studies (2033 patients), CSP halved new-onset AF (12.2% vs 25.9%; [passage text removed]), a benefit that appeared more pronounced in AVB than in mixed SND/AVB cohorts. [S:e626f63a-0004-507e-a466-4091ce3aea0c][S:19c28e59-3357-53aa-954c-60f7ffd513de]
- **Network comparisons:** For advanced AVB with normal/mildly reduced EF, HBP or BiVP versus RVP gave lower mortality (OR 0.66, 0.51–0.85) and lower HFH (OR 0.61, 0.45–0.82), with EF gain and QRS shortening; ranking favoured HBP. [S:a11c5651-3114-5614-ac1a-b4e68cd50592]
- **Cohorts:** In a five-centre prospective study of AVB patients with LVEF >50%, HF hospitalisation or upgrade to biventricular pacing occurred in 2.6% with LBBAP vs 10.8% with RVP (adjusted HR 0.14, 0.04–0.55), with benefit concentrated in those with pacing burden >40% or baseline LVEF <60%. [S:e038c129-b82e-593e-9a0a-0d31632c7731] A 903-patient AVB cohort found LBBAP independently associated with lower composite death/lead failure/HFH (OR 0.48, 0.28–0.83) and less recurrent unexplained syncope. [S:727319fc-ddf2-5945-a7a1-2c0a8a551d0e] In 738 patients (LBBAP with stylet-driven leads vs RVP), composite outcomes were lower with LBBAP (aHR 0.27 and 0.41), driven mainly by less pacing-induced cardiomyopathy, with no difference in procedural complications. [S:b5bee8a1-2567-51e7-8e5a-156b4a6f791d]

## Trade-offs and caveats

HBP specifically carries higher capture thresholds, longer procedure and fluoroscopy times, and more lead revision than RVP; LBBAP largely overcomes these with higher success rates and more stable thresholds. [S:5223f0c2-33b4-538c-922b-bef8d1541c91][S:ca29958e-40f2-5d16-890a-ddfc07de9b28] Loss of conduction system capture from threshold rise can occur during follow-up. [S:77df1329-1a53-502d-a9ca-ec1612f1e27a] Guideline documents note that most CSP data remain observational with limited long-term lead-survival data [S:bb3be3f7-3157-5353-82e6-a8fd2cc1a928], and a published critique of the largest pooled analysis argues that mixing RCTs with observational studies and heterogeneous follow-up durations may inflate mortality and HFH effect estimates. [S:ca17f669-3058-596e-b7e6-1201bada54b2] Definitive answers await ongoing RCTs including LEAP-Block, PROTECT-SYNC and OptimPacing. [S:620cb48a-e18b-5928-b441-a0ccb25c97b7]

rows.question: What changes occur in peripheral leukocyte and lymphocyte subsets after in situ ischemic postconditioning during thrombectomy?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: patients who received in situ ischemic postconditioning during thrombectomy had a higher helper-to-cytotoxic T-cell ratio than propensity-matched external controls; the same patients had a lower proportion of natural killer cells than the matched controls; total lymphocyte counts were numerically higher in the postconditioning group, but the difference did not reach statistical significance; The proportion of neutrophils in the postconditioning group was lower than in matched controls. Certainty: These immune shifts are preliminary signals rather than confirmed effects. Scope: applies to acute ischemic stroke from large vessel occlusion in adults undergoing mechanical thrombectomy, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it reports that overall infarct volume at seventy-two hours was significantly reduced.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

In the only human study of **in situ (intra-arterial, balloon-based) ischemic postconditioning during thrombectomy** that reports immune data, the changes at 24 h were confined to lymphocyte *composition* rather than total leukocyte counts: the postconditioned group had a **higher helper-T/cytotoxic-T (Th/CTL) ratio and a lower proportion of NK cells**, accompanied by lower IL-6. No grounded data exist for total leukocyte, neutrophil, or NLR changes specific to in situ IPostC.

## Human evidence (in situ IPostC during EVT)

**Jiang et al., *Journal of NeuroInterventional Surgery* 18(8):1757–1764; PMID 40889891; NCT05909982** — a prospective, externally controlled, non-randomized trial of [passage text removed] balloon occlusion / 2 min release at the proximal lesion site after successful thrombectomy) versus contemporaneous thrombectomy-alone controls, with 1:1 propensity-score matching yielding 19 patients per group. Peripheral blood was drawn **24 h post-procedure**, with leukocyte populations assessed and mononuclear subsets characterised by flow cytometry, plus serum inflammatory biomarkers [PMID 40889891]. The immune profile monitored comprised **[passage text removed]-γ [search.proquest.com/openview/d99b725dc30b5151e0fe2dc2cae4d614].

Reported results at 24 h in the IPostC group versus controls:
- **Th/CTL ratio higher**: [passage text removed]) [PMID 40889891]
- **NK cell proportion reduced**: [passage text removed]) [PMID 40889891]
- IL-6 lower: [passage text removed]); deep infarct volume progression less: [passage text removed]) [PMID 40889891]

The authors framed these as "favorable immunomodulatory effects" requiring phase II validation [PMID 40889891]. Important caveats: single 24-h timepoint, non-randomized external control design, and small matched sample. **I found no tool-retrievable data on absolute leukocyte, neutrophil, monocyte or lymphocyte counts, B-cell frequency, or NLR from this trial** — the abstract states leukocyte populations were assessed but reports only the Th/CTL ratio and NK proportion as significant. The related in situ IPostC work from the same programme (a 3+3 dose-escalation trial in 18 AIS patients with M1 occlusion) reported only safety, feasibility and tolerability, not immune endpoints [PMC13097581].

Note that a separate pilot randomized trial of post-recanalization IPostC (STROKEAHA.125.056167) reports reduced infarct growth, but the retrieved text does not describe leukocyte or lymphocyte subset outcomes.

## Preclinical direction of effect (mechanistic context, not human data)

Two studies from the same investigator group support a "shift from brain to blood" pattern:
- In mice, IPostC reduced infiltration of macrophages, CD4 T, CD8 T and B cells into ischemic brain while **attenuating peripheral lymphopenia**: in blood it significantly increased both T-cell subsets and B cells; in spleen it maintained [passage text removed]; bone marrow populations were unaltered [PMC3735351; PMID 23590905].
- By mass cytometry, IPostC **decreased** CD4 T cells, CD4 Tem, cDC and MoDM percentages in ischemic brain at days 1 and 3, while **robustly increasing** [passage text removed] in peripheral blood at days 1 and 3, with signalling changes (e.g. reduced p-STAT1 in CD4 T/CD4 Tem/NK cells; reduced p-EGFR in CD8 T, CD8 Tem and NK cells) [PMC8139206].

Note the human and rodent findings are not fully concordant (rodent blood lymphocyte subsets rose broadly; the human trial showed a CD4-skewed ratio with fewer NK cells), and the rodent work measured different timepoints and compartments.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** In the PROTECT1b exploratory trial, adding in situ ischemic postconditioning (IPostC) to thrombectomy shifted the 24-hour peripheral immune profile toward attenuated post-reperfusion immunodepression/inflammation — a significantly higher Th/CTL ratio and lower NK cell proportion, with only non-significant trends in total lymphocyte counts and other subsets.

**Study design context.** PROTECT1b (NCT05909982) was a prospective, non-randomized, externally controlled study comparing thrombectomy plus [passage text removed] balloon occlusion at the clot site / 2 min release, initiated after antegrade perfusion was restored) with contemporaneous thrombectomy-alone controls drawn from the TRACK-LVO registry; 1:1 propensity score matching yielded 19 patients per group, and peripheral blood was drawn 24 hours post-procedure for leukocyte counts, PBMC flow cytometry, and serum cytokines [S:5df4c899-45d5-5100-9f8e-4f92451ba9f1][S:ccfd22f2-b990-59fe-b365-044696661ac2][S:b51f700f-2a84-5041-95b2-5ca54f1dc0f4].

**Whole-blood leukocyte changes (trend only).** At 24 hours the IPostC group had [passage text removed] neutrophil proportion than controls, but these hematologic differences were not statistically significant: lymphocyte count [passage text removed]; lymphocyte percentage [passage text removed] [S:ea9c63d4-4c72-5515-ba37-4831e86c1bdf][S:94da0014-0a34-59f2-b97c-42c3111340dd]. These trends were the rationale for the targeted flow cytometry/ELISA analyses [S:94da0014-0a34-59f2-b97c-42c3111340dd].

**Lymphocyte subsets by flow cytometry (% of PBMCs, 24 h).**
- Th/CTL ratio significantly increased: [passage text removed] [S:be9e71ed-4915-517a-9192-5b4e69a5864b].
- NK cell proportion significantly decreased: [passage text removed] [S:be9e71ed-4915-517a-9192-5b4e69a5864b].
- No significant differences in total T cells ([passage text removed]), or B cells ([passage text removed]) [S:be9e71ed-4915-517a-9192-5b4e69a5864b].

**Accompanying cytokine changes.** [passage text removed] were all numerically lower with IPostC, but only IL-6 reached significance ([passage text removed]) [S:be9e71ed-4915-517a-9192-5b4e69a5864b]. The authors interpret the overall post-thrombectomy pattern as reduced immune cell counts with elevated proinflammatory markers, an imbalance that IPostC attenuated [S:94da0014-0a34-59f2-b97c-42c3111340dd]. Clinically, the IPostC group had less deep infarct volume progression ([passage text removed]) with no excess adverse events [S:ea38f705-b7cc-5fa4-abcf-5d46458836e9][S:ea9c63d4-4c72-5515-ba37-4831e86c1bdf].

**Preclinical corroboration.** In mouse MCAO, mass cytometry showed IPostC increased peripheral blood [passage text removed] versus MCAO at days 1 and 3, i.e. it attenuated peripheral lymphopenia and systemic immunodepression [S:555f68ae-74ef-50f9-a713-fa2fe9f582ed]; protection was also linked to downregulation of p38 in peripheral CD4 T cells and Tregs [S:c026837d-fb0a-5142-8071-b8fad1b59ea4]. Earlier reviews similarly report that postconditioning reverses stroke-induced reductions in peripheral immune cell numbers and reduces T-cell infiltration into ischemic brain [S:3bbe4731-7617-5010-ae80-f20dbf284600].

**Caveats:** these are exploratory, single-timepoint (24 h) analyses in a small, non-randomized, externally controlled cohort, so the subset findings require phase II validation [S:04741c63-c75b-5f80-b6ec-a59cee050000][S:5df4c899-45d5-5100-9f8e-4f92451ba9f1]. I found no source reporting monocyte, Treg, or neutrophil-subset changes, or later time points, in human in situ IPostC.

rows.question: How does antibody subtype relate to the response to ofatumumab in refractory generalised myasthenia gravis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: in a small retrospective early series, minimal symptom expression was reached by more of the muscle-specific-kinase patients than the acetylcholine-receptor patients, and after a shorter median time; the unadjusted comparison of time to minimal symptom expression did not reach statistical significance; the subtype association appeared only in a model adjusted for age at treatment and attenuated on further adjustment for autoimmune comorbidity; the series was retrospective, uncontrolled and small, with different assays used for the two antibody types and a proactive biomarker-driven dosing intensity, so whether antibody subtype changes the response is left open. Certainty: This is an observation in twenty-one patients rather than a demonstrated subtype difference. Scope: applies to refractory generalised myasthenia gravis in adults treated with anti-CD20 therapy grouped by antibody type, specialist outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it states that memory B-cell counts reliably predict imminent relapse and can be used as a retreatment trigger.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** In refractory generalised MG, antibody subtype appears to modify the response to ofatumumab — MuSK-antibody-positive patients respond faster and more completely than AChR-antibody-positive patients in the only direct comparative study, mirroring the IgG4/plasmablast versus IgG1-IgG3/long-lived-plasma-cell divide — but a second, smaller cohort found no subtype difference, so the evidence is limited and not consistent.

**Direct comparative evidence (21 refractory patients, 13 MuSK+, 8 AChR+; individualised 20 mg subcutaneous induction with B-cell-guided maintenance at CD19+ ≥5 cells/μL)** [PMID 41726319 / PMC12921211; DOI 10.1177/17562864261421717]:
- MuSK-MG reached minimal symptom expression (MG-ADL ≤1) faster (median [passage text removed] more MuSK patients improved by 3 months ([passage text removed]) [PMC12921211].
- QMGS showed a significant antibody × time interaction, with greater reductions in MuSK-MG at month 3 ([passage text removed], p = [passage text removed], p = 0.027), while AChR-MG changed minimally [PMC12921211].
- Titres diverged: MuSK-Ab fell significantly over time (month 6 vs [passage text removed], p = 0.008), whereas AChR-Ab showed no significant change over time [PMC12921211]. An earlier ofatumumab cohort likewise found anti-AChR titre unchanged at 1 and 3 months despite B-cell depletion and clinical improvement [PMC10749496].
- Immunological correlates: baseline BAFF was markedly higher in MuSK-MG (p < 0.001) and declined progressively, whereas AChR-MG showed transient BAFF elevation at month 3 and persistently higher APRIL (month 3 MD 901.06 pg/mL, p = 0.006; month 6 MD 894.32 pg/mL, p = 0.010). BAFF correlated positively with QMGS in MuSK-MG; IgM/IgG correlated with QMGS in both [PMC12921211].
- Non-subtype predictors of earlier MSE were [passage text removed] corticosteroids (p = 0.030); steroid dose fell in both groups without between-group difference. B-cell repopulation trended slower in MuSK-MG (p = 0.053); median time to CD19+ ≥5 cells/μL was 47.70 days (range 17.1–227.4) [PMC12921211].
- The authors' stated mechanism: [passage text removed] IgG4 disease, whereas AChR-MG is germinal-centre-driven IgG1/IgG3 sustained by CD20-negative long-lived plasma cells that escape ofatumumab, hence their conclusion that "[passage text removed]" [PMC12921211]. This matches independent work showing MuSK autoantibodies derive from short-lived plasmablasts replenished by CD20+ memory B cells, while AChR autoantibody production implicates long-lived plasma cells [insight.jci.org/articles/view/94263; PMC8248361], and the analogous rituximab literature (MuSK+ patients all remitted or reached minimal manifestations with >80% titre falls, versus more variable AChR+ responses needing reinfusions) [DOI 10.1212/WNL.0b013e3182407982].

**Contradictory/qualifying evidence:** In a 14-patient refractory gMG cohort (5 MuSK+, 9 AChR+) treated with ofatumumab 20 mg at weeks 0, 1, 2, 4 then every 4–6 months, MG-ADL, QMG and MGC all improved significantly through 12 months with reduced 3-Hz RNS decrement, but there were **no significant differences** between MuSK+ and AChR+ groups at any timepoint or in any muscle-group subscore [PMID 41394139; PMC12695607]. Note the small samples and single-centre retrospective design in both studies.

**Case-level evidence exists for both subtypes:** successful ofatumumab rescue in AChR-antibody-positive refractory gMG, including post-lung-adenocarcinoma resection [PMC13488784; PMID 42615883] and the original refractory MG report [DOI 10.1002/mus.26707], and in refractory MuSK-MG requiring mechanical ventilation, with MuSK titre falling 1:320 → 1:30 [PMID 42358945].

**Caveat:** no randomised trial has stratified ofatumumab response by antibody subtype; all subtype comparisons above are small retrospective cohorts, and the one showing a difference did not reach significance on unadjusted log-rank testing.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** The limited evidence suggests antibody subtype does modify the ofatumumab response — MuSK-antibody-positive (IgG4-mediated) refractory MG tends to respond faster and more completely than AChR-antibody-positive (IgG1/IgG3-mediated) disease — but this is based on one small retrospective comparison, and a second small cohort found no difference between subtypes.

**Direct head-to-head evidence (favours MuSK)**
A single-centre retrospective study of 21 refractory MG patients (13 MuSK+, 8 AChR+) given individualised subcutaneous ofatumumab induction and CD19-guided maintenance found MuSK-MG reached minimal symptom expression sooner (median [passage text removed] had a higher 3-month improvement rate ([passage text removed]) [S:a5b111d5-d770-5011-93cb-4ba9701a7ce0][S:d88ce7d9-6582-54b3-8a2b-fc2911403953]. Despite comparable baseline QMGS, MuSK patients had significantly greater QMGS reductions at month 3 ([passage text removed]), with a significant antibody × time interaction and lower ocular subscores at both timepoints [S:39b96ff5-a05d-59eb-bac7-2d76ee99ffa6][S:b9007e33-5eaa-5a8a-b3c7-c8be5fa1dea7]. Prednisone fell significantly over 6 months overall, but the between-group difference was not significant (p = 0.125), though AChR patients consistently required higher doses [S:b9007e33-5eaa-5a8a-b3c7-c8be5fa1dea7]. Earlier [passage text removed] corticosteroids (p = 0.030); no predictors emerged in the AChR subgroup (n = 8), likely from low power [S:d88ce7d9-6582-54b3-8a2b-fc2911403953][S:39b96ff5-a05d-59eb-bac7-2d76ee99ffa6].

**Mechanistic correlate of the subtype difference**
In the same cohort, MuSK-MG showed synchronised BAFF and APRIL declines, whereas AChR-MG showed transient BAFF elevation with sustained APRIL (BAFF MD at month 3 −111.10 pg/mL, p = 0.024; APRIL MD −901.06 pg/mL at month 3, p = 0.006 and −894.32 at month 6, p = 0.010) [S:39b96ff5-a05d-59eb-bac7-2d76ee99ffa6]. The authors attribute this to divergent immunopathology: MuSK-MG is plasmablast/B-cell-driven (IgG4), while AChR-MG is germinal-centre, T-cell-dependent and sustained by long-lived, ofatumumab-resistant plasma cells that keep consuming APRIL, with a homeostatic BAFF rebound potentially reseeding autoreactive B cells — implying MuSK-MG may suffice with B-cell depletion alone whereas AChR-MG might need dual targeting of the BAFF/APRIL axis [S:7029b18e-8f9b-5358-9241-12529fe2f18a][S:cd4cdd77-76a7-5f94-93a5-8b35d0429424]. BAFF correlated positively with QMGS in MuSK-MG, and IgM/IgG [passage text removed] was 47.7 days [S:d88ce7d9-6582-54b3-8a2b-fc2911403953][S:7029b18e-8f9b-5358-9241-12529fe2f18a]. This mirrors the established rationale for anti-CD20 therapy in IgG4 disease: MuSK IgG4 is largely produced by CD20-positive short-lived plasmablasts, so CD20 depletion removes the relevant producers and their precursors [S:b9355d41-9399-5615-91b1-c9da7c4ec757].

**Contradictory evidence**
A prospective cohort of 14 refractory gMG patients (5 MuSK+, 9 AChR+) treated with ofatumumab 20 mg at weeks 0, 1, 2, 4 then every 4–6 months reported similar clinical benefit in both groups with no significant between-group difference, and no significant baseline differences in age, sex, disease duration or severity [S:df011cde-cdc0-5d07-a2e9-b154383d420b][S:ffac2032-06c7-5fe1-914b-d3a4b997a60f][S:eafe0bd0-fc3e-5e6b-9d2f-24a5f40016dd]. The authors suggest ofatumumab's binding to two discontinuous CD20 epitopes with slower dissociation and stronger complement-dependent cytotoxicity than rituximab may explain efficacy across both subtypes [S:eafe0bd0-fc3e-5e6b-9d2f-24a5f40016dd]. Separately, a cohort of 31 AChR-antibody-positive MG patients showed significant reductions in QMG, MG-QOL15 and MG-ADL at 1 and 3 months with ofatumumab, so AChR-positive patients clearly do respond [S:72b715f9-b069-5d41-9ac0-8e7ca91d8e0c].

**Context from rituximab**
The subtype gradient reported for ofatumumab parallels the well-documented rituximab pattern: better and more durable responses in MuSK-MG than AChR-MG, attributed to IgG4 vs IgG1/IgG3 biology and plasmablast CD20 expression [S:76285799-9962-51dc-849b-22012142fc85][S:61e3a095-0b95-573b-a6a4-0c272bb34a89][S:49020b71-76c8-518f-b3aa-2204fdd9a47b].

**Caveats.** Both ofatumumab datasets are single-centre with very small subgroups (n = 8 and n = 9 AChR+; n = 13 and n = 5 MuSK+), retrospective or uncontrolled, and the primary time-to-MSE log-rank comparison was not significant before age adjustment [S:d88ce7d9-6582-54b3-8a2b-fc2911403953][S:dd245cf5-b03c-5705-85c1-541303345fd1]. No randomised trial of ofatumumab in MG stratified by antibody subtype appeared in my searches; one review notes no MG trials of these second-generation anti-CD20 agents are currently underway [S:b550b937-3c8f-5004-9d4e-eb8b17fe8724]. I found no evidence on ofatumumab response in LRP4-positive or double-seronegative refractory gMG.
