rows.question: What comorbidity burden accumulates in the years following a myasthenia gravis diagnosis in adults?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: cardiovascular conditions, above all hypertension, are the commonest coexisting illnesses already before the diagnosis is made and remain prominent afterwards; in the years after diagnosis the burden shifts, with anaemia, osteoporosis and cataract becoming several times more common than beforehand, a pattern that runs alongside sustained corticosteroid and immunosuppressive use; autoimmune conditions, particularly thyroid and rheumatic disease, run alongside the illness, while psychiatric conditions weigh more heavily on younger than on older patients. Certainty: These are consistent descriptive patterns rather than demonstrated effects of the disease or its treatment. Scope: applies to myasthenia gravis in adults followed from diagnosis in national health registries, population-based settings. An answer is wrong if it states that the post-diagnosis rise was shown to be caused by treatment.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Adults accumulate a broad, largely cardiometabolic, infectious, skeletal, psychiatric, and neoplastic comorbidity load after MG diagnosis, with the steepest accrual in the first year and a substantial share attributable to corticosteroid exposure rather than MG itself.

## Magnitude and pattern of accumulation

**Broad accrual across organ systems.** In a UK CPRD/HES cohort of 1,149 adults followed from first MG diagnosis, most patients had a Charlson Comorbidity Index <1.0 at index, yet during follow-up the commonest comorbidities [passage text removed]%), malignancy ([passage text removed]%) — versus baseline figures of 7.2% for MI, 3.8% for heart failure and 1.1% for dementia (rising to 6.1%) [PMC9082838; BMC Neurol 22:172].

**Faster and more frequent onset than in matched controls.** In the US Veterans Affairs network, 10,632 adults newly diagnosed with MG were matched 1:1 to non-MG controls and followed for a median [passage text removed] (anxiety, autoimmune conditions, cardiovascular disease, depression, diabetes, GERD, glaucoma, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension, infections, malignancy, osteoporosis, sleep disorders, thyroid disorders) MG patients had significantly higher incidence ([passage text removed] (p<0.05) [ispor.org/…/137367]. In a newly diagnosed English cohort (mean follow-up 2.8 years), incidence rates of **all** assessed comorbidities were higher in MG than in matched controls, including dyslipidaemia, autoimmune thyroiditis, obesity, osteoporosis, cardiac arrhythmia, type 1 diabetes and SLE [PMC11949302; pubmed 39973446; [passage text removed]].

**Front-loaded timing.** In 4,925 US adults with newly diagnosed MG, incident comorbidities peaked in the first year after diagnosis (except dyslipidaemia in the 18–49 group); in year 1 among those aged ≥50, cardiovascular disease, infection and type 2 diabetes [passage text removed]% respectively, with lower figures in younger patients [PMC12089002; Neurol Ther 14:1061–1082].

**Infections and malignancy.** In propensity-matched US claims data (5,002 MG vs 20,008 controls, patients with prior malignancy excluded), incidence rates per 1,000 person-years were higher in MG for serious infections (52.81 vs 31.46), opportunistic infections (87.48 vs 57.01), [passage text removed]) and overall malignancy (73.55 vs 50.01) [PMC13437810; 10.1177/22143602251403092]. A population-based Ontario study similarly found crude serious-infection rates roughly doubled (72.5 vs 35.0 per 1,000 person-years) [pubmed 31997519].

**Second autoimmune disease.** In a Danish nationwide case–control study (2,110 cases, 21,100 controls), 5.0% of MG patients versus 2.7% of controls received a new autoimmune diagnosis after the index date ([passage text removed]), concentrated in women and patients ≤50; strongest associations were autoimmune thyroiditis, SLE and pernicious anaemia [PMC12892123; pubmed 41669887].

**Bone and mood.** A Taiwanese population cohort (2,073 MG patients) found a 1.96-fold increased risk of incident osteoporosis (95% CI 1.57–2.44), elevated even in corticosteroid-naïve patients (HR 1.52, 1.11–2.08) and higher in corticosteroid-treated patients (HR 2.37, 1.82–3.07) [10.1212/WNL.0000000000000804]. Fracture data are inconsistent: Ontario incident MG patients had a *lower* adjusted fracture risk (HR 0.74, 0.63–0.88) [pubmed 33554923; 10.3233/JND-200612], UK GPRD found no increase (AHR 1.11, 0.84–1.47) [PMC3557375], while a Korean nationwide cohort reported higher major osteoporotic fracture risk [pubmed 38477782]. For mood, a Taiwanese nationwide cohort found new depressive disorders at 7.60 vs 3.55 per 1,000 person-years (IRR 2.14, 1.22–3.65; adjusted HR 1.94, 1.15–3.27) [PMC6629932].

## How much is treatment-driven

In the VA cohort (mean follow-up 7.8 years), 51.6% of MG patients received corticosteroids versus 21.2% of controls; among MG patients, medium/high annualised cumulative doses significantly raised annualised risk of new-onset diabetes (HR [passage text removed]), plus glaucoma (1.81 at high dose) and depression (1.22 at medium dose); low-dose exposure was not significantly associated [sciencedirect S0022510X2502338X; J Neurol Sci 481:125716]. The authors concluded that while MG itself increases comorbidity risk, [passage text removed] in most cases [[passage text removed]].

## Why it matters

Accumulated comorbidity is not merely additive: in Nordic registry data, MG patients with cancer other than thymoma (HR 1.33, 1.19–1.48), mental and behavioural disorders (1.28, 1.14–1.45) and circulatory disease (1.25, 1.15–1.36) had increased mortality versus MG patients without those conditions, whereas coexisting autoimmune, ophthalmological or musculoskeletal disease did not raise death risk [PMC11420710].

**Caveats:** most of the above are claims/registry analyses subject to coding and detection bias; the VA cohort is older (mean age at diagnosis ~70 years) and predominantly male, limiting generalisability, and the corticosteroid analysis considered only the prior year's dose and did not adjust for non-steroid therapies [ispor.org/…/137367; [passage text removed]]. I found no source giving a single validated summary metric (e.g., mean Charlson increment per year) for post-diagnosis comorbidity accumulation.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Within a few years of diagnosis, adults with MG accumulate a substantially higher-than-expected load of infections, cardiometabolic disease, corticosteroid-related endocrine/bone disease, psychiatric disorders, and malignancy — with incidence peaking in the first year or first few years after diagnosis.

## Timing: front-loaded accrual

In a US claims cohort of adults followed after MG diagnosis, incident comorbidity rates were **highest in the first year post-diagnosis** for nearly all conditions; among patients ≥50 years at diagnosis, cardiovascular disease, infection, and type 2 diabetes [passage text removed]% respectively during year 1, with lower figures [passage text removed] crisis also peaked in year 1 and declined thereafter (26.3% of younger and 21.6% of older patients had an exacerbation) [S:dd80da6f]. In Nordic national registries, prevalence of most comorbidities was higher in the 5 years after diagnosis than the 5 years before, with **anemia and osteoporosis showing three- to six-fold relative increases**; [passage text removed] [S:acf0a4eb][S:b939ec7b].

## Magnitude relative to matched controls

A US cohort of 7,194 newly diagnosed adults vs 35,970 matched controls (mean follow-up 2.84 years) found higher incidence of *new* comorbidities across the board, with rate ratios of 3.98 for systemic infection, 3.51 for infection-related hospitalization, 2.05 for depression, 2.00 for autoimmune disease, 1.99 for type 2 diabetes, 1.84 for osteoporosis, 1.81 for anxiety, 1.73 for obesity, 1.48 for hypertension, and 1.33 for dyslipidemia [S:28aee21b]. In England (CPRD-HES), "any infection" was the most common comorbidity during follow-up (35.8% MG vs 28.0% non-MG), incidence rates of all comorbidities were proportionately higher in MG, 63.5% had ≥1 exacerbation, 3.5% had a myasthenic crisis, and 16.5% died [S:1a80ac65].

## Domain-specific findings

**Infection** is the most consistent signal. A population-based Ontario cohort reported a 39% increased risk of serious infections (adjusted HR 1.39, 95% CI 1.28–1.51) over mean 5.4 years, mainly respiratory [S:3288a58e]; 33.5% of MG patients vs 19% of controls had an infection (72.58 vs 35.02 per 1000 patient-years) [S:a695dd6a]. A US real-world analysis found higher rates of pneumonia, sepsis, UTI, skin, GI, fungal and herpetic infections, [passage text removed]) [S:98ed3484][S:acc4912a].

**Malignancy.** In a matched population-based case–control study, incident malignancy after MG diagnosis was elevated (HR [passage text removed]), highest in the first 3 years, involving respiratory/intrathoracic, non-melanoma skin, urinary tract, soft tissue cancers and myelodysplastic syndrome; immunosuppression did not explain the excess [S:a67ae2f0][S:ed02edac]. US data likewise showed 73.55 vs 50.01 malignancies per 1000 PY [S:98ed3484].

**Treatment-attributable metabolic/bone morbidity.** In a Japanese generalized-MG database study, osteoporosis was the most frequent incident comorbidity (56.4 per 1000 PY), and glucocorticoid use was dose-dependently associated with osteoporosis (HR 3.25, 95% CI 2.67–3.96), diabetes, thrombosis, and hyperlipidemia, with risk apparent even at ≤5 mg/day; fracture showed a consistent association (HR 1.53) [S:a9dbf183]. The Nordic authors attributed the post-diagnosis osteoporosis rise partly to treatment effects, ageing, and improved monitoring [S:7a0beada]. Notably, **serious fracture risk is not uniformly increased**: in the Ontario inception cohort MG patients had a *lower* adjusted fracture risk [passage text removed]) [S:92b33bda][S:a695dd6a] — a discrepancy the authors could not fully explain.

**Psychiatric.** A nationwide retrospective cohort found incident depressive disorders at 7.60 vs 3.55 per 1000 person-years (IRR [passage text removed]), with the excess persisting beyond 1 year of follow-up [S:70be6835]. Nordic data show mental health disorders are relatively more frequent in younger (<65) than older patients with MG [S:acf0a4eb].

**Polypharmacy as a marker.** In a complete national Norwegian cohort, MG patients received more non-MG medications than controls across nearly all drug classes — insulins, thyroid therapy, antidepressants, anti-infectives, lipid-modifying agents and immunomodulators — reflecting broad comorbidity [S:66b959d9][S:10ade820].

## Prognostic consequence

In elderly US Medicare beneficiaries, crude mortality was higher in incident MG than matched [passage text removed]-years), but after adjustment for time-varying Charlson Comorbidity Index the survival difference disappeared (aHR 1.09, 0.87–1.36) — i.e. the excess long-term mortality was largely attributable to accumulated comorbidity; infection-specific mortality was higher in MG (2.0 vs 1.2 per 1000 PY) [S:c022c996].

## Caveats

Much of this evidence is claims/registry-based and cannot fully separate disease effects, immunosuppressive treatment effects, ageing, and surveillance bias; the Nordic and UK authors note that conditions such as hypertension may track age rather than MG itself, and a UK registry cohort found 94.5% of adults with MG had ≥1 comorbidity accumulating with age [S:7b229f35][S:7a0beada]. Follow-up in the largest comparative cohorts is relatively short (means of ~2.8–5.4 years), so beyond-decade trajectories are less well characterized.

rows.question: What does translocator protein positron emission tomography show when lupus with neuropsychiatric involvement is compared with lupus without it?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: peak tracer uptake was significantly higher in patients with neuropsychiatric involvement than in those without, while mean uptake across the region was not; peak uptake correlated with damage index, disability scale and disease activity scores, while mean uptake showed no significant correlation with any of them; peak uptake discriminated the two groups better than mean uptake, but that discrimination was estimated in the same small retrospective sample the models were fitted to and without dynamic modelling of binding kinetics; the tracer marks activated microglia, astrocytes and macrophages together rather than microglia alone, so a raised signal points to a broad inflammatory reaction rather than one cell type. Certainty: This is an early signal in a small sample rather than a validated diagnostic test. Scope: applies to systemic lupus erythematosus with neuropsychiatric involvement in adults undergoing translocator protein positron emission tomography, specialist outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents this imaging as a validated diagnostic test or as having replaced clinical criteria.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** The only direct head-to-head evidence — a retrospective [18F]DPA‑714 TSPO PET/MRI study — shows that in patients with neuropsychiatric SLE, TSPO uptake within brain lesions is *higher* than in SLE patients without neuropsychiatric involvement, and this signal tracks disease severity and has discriminative value.

**Key findings (Huang et al., *Lupus Science & Medicine* 2025;12(2):e001643; PMID 40962360; PMC12443175)**
- Design: retrospective, 19 NPSLE vs 10 non‑NPSLE patients, [18F]DPA‑714 PET/MRI; T2‑weighted MRI lesions used as ROIs and coregistered to PET; ACR classification plus SLICC Model B criteria for NPSLE [PMID 40962360].
- Lesion SUVmax was significantly higher in NPSLE than non‑NPSLE (p<0.01), whereas SUVmean did not differ significantly (p>0.05) [PMID 40962360]. The authors attribute this to SUVmax capturing focal peak inflammation while SUVmean dilutes lesion signal with normal/less-inflamed tissue and lesion heterogeneity [PMC12443175].
- Clinical correlation: SUVmax correlated with SLICC/ACR damage index ([passage text removed]); SUVmean showed no significant correlations [PMID 40962360].
- Diagnostic performance: AUC 0.83 for SUVmax vs 0.68 for SUVmean; the combined model (SUVmax + SUVmean + interaction) reached AUC 0.94; only the SUVmax‑alone logistic model was significant (p=0.01) [PMID 40962360; PMC12443175].
- Lesion topography did not differ between groups (supratentorial predominance in both; no significant difference in lesion location), while SLEDAI, SLICC/ACR and mRS were higher in NPSLE — i.e., the discriminating feature was tracer uptake intensity, not lesion site [PMC12443175].
- Interpretation offered by the authors: greater intralesional TSPO uptake reflects a more prominent microglial/neuroinflammatory response driving neuropsychiatric symptoms, positioning TSPO PET/MR as a candidate objective biomarker to supplement the current symptom‑and‑exclusion diagnosis [PMC12443175].

**Important caveats and contrasting data**
- This is a single small retrospective study with no healthy comparison group and lesion‑restricted (not whole‑brain voxelwise) quantification [PMID 40962360].
- An earlier, differently designed pilot study ([11C]DPA‑713 PET, 10 SLE vs 11 healthy controls) found *no* regional increases in SLE; instead cerebellar and hippocampal TSPO binding was significantly *decreased* versus controls, most markedly in cognitively normal SLE, with "pseudo‑normalization" (relatively higher binding) in the cognitively impaired subgroup — the authors invoked mitochondrial dysfunction plus superimposed glial activation (PMID 27387599; PMC5218990). So the direction of the TSPO signal in SLE depends on the comparator (SLE vs healthy controls versus NPSLE vs non‑NPSLE), tracer, and whether analysis is lesion‑based or region‑based.
- Generic TSPO caveats apply: the rs6971 polymorphism markedly alters second‑generation ligand binding and requires genotyping/stratification, and TSPO is expressed by reactive astrocytes as well as microglia, so it is an indirect neuroinflammation marker (Turku PET Centre methodological summary; PMC5218990; PMID 27387599 discussion of tracer generations).

I found no independent replication cohort comparing NPSLE with non‑NPSLE by TSPO PET, so the 94% AUC figure should be treated as internally derived and unvalidated externally.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** In the one direct head-to-head study available, TSPO PET shows higher tracer uptake in brain lesions of lupus patients with neuropsychiatric involvement (NPSLE) than in lupus patients without it, driven by focal "hotspot" (peak) uptake rather than average lesion uptake — and this signal tracks disease severity and discriminates the two groups reasonably well. [S:dcb5f8d1-8e78-5d34-9a19-ebb974742840]

**The direct comparison ([18F]DPA-714 PET/MRI)**
- Retrospective study of 19 NPSLE and 10 non-NPSLE patients scanned with [18F]DPA-714 PET/MRI; T2-weighted MRI lesions were used as regions of interest and coregistered to PET for cross-modality quantification. [S:f9bfaf2c-8da8-5503-83d3-9abaee0cc284]
- SUVmax in brain lesions was significantly higher in NPSLE than non-NPSLE (p<0.01), whereas SUVmean did not differ significantly (p>0.05). [S:818cd1f0-63bb-5b39-8b2c-b2bbb09204c3]
- SUVmax correlated with clinical severity/activity [passage text removed]; SLEDAI r=0.41, p=0.03); SUVmean showed no significant correlations. [S:ce2e6def-34c2-5805-81a2-8f737b182771]
- Discrimination: AUC 0.83 for SUVmax versus 0.68 for SUVmean; only the SUVmax-alone logistic model was statistically significant (p=0.01), while the model combining SUVmax, SUVmean and their interaction gave the highest AUC (0.94). [S:818cd1f0-63bb-5b39-8b2c-b2bbb09204c3][S:ce2e6def-34c2-5805-81a2-8f737b182771]
- Qualitatively, some patients showed T2 lesions with corresponding high TSPO uptake while others showed T2 lesions without uptake — i.e., PET adds information beyond structural MRI; the authors report spatial overlap between high-TSPO areas and white matter lesions. [S:c98b748c-c053-5b58-9ae4-9e66641871d7][S:8138dc22-9fda-55a7-ad42-fd7fdb8fc0d2]
- The authors interpret the SUVmax/SUVmean dissociation as lesion heterogeneity: focal inflammatory hotspots raise peak uptake, while averaging across the ROI dilutes the signal with normal or less-inflamed tissue. [S:f105e9c7-923a-5eca-8a2f-ecb7c6754225] They describe this as the first in vivo observation of microglial activation in NPSLE lesions. [S:8138dc22-9fda-55a7-ad42-fd7fdb8fc0d2]

**Important caveats and contrary/indirect data**
- An earlier [11C]DPA-713 pilot study (11 healthy controls, 10 SLE) found *no* significant regional increases in SLE overall; instead TSPO binding was significantly *decreased* in cerebellum and hippocampus versus healthy controls, with the decrease most marked in cognitively normal SLE and "pseudo-normalisation" in cognitively impaired SLE because binding was higher in impaired than in cognitively normal patients. [S:91432bd4-3ea6-5adb-8960-ce620a5071c8][S:1b267ced-fd29-5075-95f4-0563229fea4a] Note this compares SLE with/without cognitive impairment against healthy controls, not NPSLE versus non-NPSLE by ACR criteria, and only three impaired patients drove the trend. [S:1b267ced-fd29-5075-95f4-0563229fea4a]
- The PET/MR study is retrospective and single-centre with small groups; the authors themselves call for multicentre, larger studies across NPSLE stages and phenotypes. [S:f105e9c7-923a-5eca-8a2f-ecb7c6754225]
- Interpretive limits of TSPO generally: the signal is not microglia-specific — it also reflects astrocytes, endothelium and cell density rather than activation state, and depends on pathology, disease stage and region. [S:0bcb5f6b-ee22-5050-94bf-7d2a2d9432b0][S:af2daf5e-b4e0-5312-9cbe-4acccddd933d] Second-generation tracers are affected by the rs6971 polymorphism, which must be handled analytically. [S:7edf25ed-3b53-5375-91a6-0a4cc1f53c12]

I found no meta-analysis or replication cohort making this NPSLE-versus-non-NPSLE TSPO comparison, so the higher-uptake finding rests essentially on a single small study.

rows.question: What clinical responses follow CD19 CAR T-cell therapy in refractory myasthenia gravis and other antibody-mediated neurological autoimmune diseases?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: in refractory myasthenia gravis, CD19-directed cell therapy was followed by long-term remission with stable immunoglobulin G concentrations in the two patients reported; in a small single-arm study of RNA-engineered BCMA-directed cells, most of the treated myasthenia patients still showed improvement in activities of daily living, quantitative and composite scores at twelve months; comparable reversals of long-standing disability have been reported in stiff-person spectrum disease and Lambert-Eaton syndrome; refractory antisynthetase myositis and refractory chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy have also responded, with drug-free remission and recovery of unassisted walking reported in the latter. Certainty: The responses are striking but early, and confirmation is still outstanding. Scope: applies to refractory antibody-mediated neurological autoimmune disease in adults who have failed available immunotherapies, specialist cell-therapy centre settings. An answer is wrong if it states the therapy carries no neurological toxicity.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Across small trials and case series, CD19- (and BCMA- or dual-) directed CAR T-cell therapy has produced rapid, deep and often drug-free remissions in refractory myasthenia gravis, stiff-person syndrome and AQP4-IgG NMOSD, with mostly low-grade CRS and no ICANS — but the evidence base is small, largely single-arm, and short-term.

## Myasthenia gravis

**Dual BCMA/CD19 CAR T (phase 1, 18 patients, ChiCTR2200061267).** By day 180 mean changes [passage text removed]; 14/17 (82%) reached minimal manifestation status, [passage text removed] 8 (47%) seroconverted to anti-AChR-negative. Every follow-up patient improved ≥2 points on MG-ADL and ≥3 on QMG, with 15 (88%) improving ≥6 points on MG-ADL. Safety: no dose-limiting toxicity, no ICANS, only grade 1 CRS (39%), transient hematologic grade ≥3 events ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41245531](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41245531); [PMC12615342]([passage text removed])). Patients were refractory to IVIg (67%), FcRn inhibitors (44%) and complement inhibitors (11%) ([institut-myologie.org]([passage text removed])).

**BCMA/CD19 CAR T mechanistic cohort (6 patients).** Five achieved minimal-manifestation, drug-free remission by month 6, sustained through 12 months despite B-cell reconstitution; one flare was associated with [passage text removed] and elevated FCRL5 (doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeb6424; [science.org]([passage text removed]); [rarediseaseadvisor.com]([passage text removed])).

**Fully human CD19 CAR T (miv-cel / KYV-101, KYSA-6 phase 2, n=6).** With a single 1×10⁸ CAR⁺ T-cell dose after cyclophosphamide/fludarabine lymphodepletion, 100% achieved ≥3-point MG-ADL and QMG improvement; mean reductions at 24 weeks were −8.0 (MG-ADL) and −7.7 (QMG), with effects apparent by week 2 and a mean −12-point MGC change at 12 weeks; 5/6 became free of non-steroidal immunosuppressants; no ICANS and no high-grade CRS ([ir.kyvernatx.com press release]([passage text removed]); [checkrare.com]([passage text removed]); [neurologylive.com]([passage text removed])).

**Index case and durability.** The first refractory AChR⁺ gMG patient given CD19 CAR T improved on Besinger and QMG scores with [passage text removed] anti-AChR falling from 2434 to 718 nmol/mL by day 62 (Haghikia et al., Lancet Neurol 2023;22:1104-1105; mechanism reviewed in doi:10.1186/s12974-025-03662-6). A longer-term case series of three treatment-resistant MG patients reported sustained remission for at least 19 months with discontinuation of MG-specific immunotherapy — notably **despite persistently detectable anti-AChR titers**, arguing that clinical remission can decouple from serology ([cell.com/cell-reports-medicine S2666-3791(26)00417-9]([passage text removed])).

**Non-integrating BCMA mRNA CAR T (Descartes-08), for contrast.** In a randomized placebo-controlled phase 2b trial (NCT04146051), 66.7% vs 27.3% achieved ≥5-point MGC improvement at month 3 (P=0.0472); MG-ADL reduction reached −5.5 at month 4 and −4.8 at month 12, QMG −6.0 at month 12, with 33% reaching minimum symptom expression (MG-ADL ≤1) by month 6, sustained to month 12, and no CRS ([nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04171-y]([passage text removed]); [PMC13004676](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13004676)).

## Stiff-person syndrome

The registrational single-arm phase 2 KYSA-8 trial (26 patients, GAD65 or GlyR seropositive, single 1×10⁸ CD19 CAR T dose) met its primary endpoint with a median 46% [passage text removed]); 81% achieved ≥20% improvement, 31% walked at healthy-adult speed (<5 s), and 67% of the 12 baseline walking-aid users no longer needed assistance. All 26 patients remained free of chronic immunotherapy at week 16 and last follow-up (median 6.5 months). Secondary endpoints all improved significantly ([passage text removed], HSS −3.2; all P<0.0001). [passage text removed] in four patients ([medpagetoday.com AAN coverage](https://www.medpagetoday.com/meetingcoverage/aan/120926); [ir.kyvernatx.com]([passage text removed]); [clinicaltrialvanguard.com]([passage text removed])). The precursor case report showed anti-GAD65 falling from 1:3200 to 1:1000 by day +56 and 1:320 at 5 months, with improved stiffness, pain and walking, 40% reduction in GABAergic medication and no further immunotherapy ([doi:10.1007/s00415-024-12642-4]([passage text removed]); [doi:10.1186/s12974-025-03662-6]([passage text removed])).

## NMOSD (AQP4-IgG)

BCMA CAR T (CT103A, NCT04561557, 12 refractory AQP4-IgG⁺ patients): at median 5.5 months, 11/12 (92%) were relapse-free in drug-free remission with all corticosteroids and immunosuppressants discontinued, with improvements in EDSS, ambulation, visual acuity, bladder/bowel function and quality of life; [passage text removed]. CRS was grade 1–2 in all patients with no ICANS or DLT, but grade ≥3 hematologic toxicity was universal and 58% developed infections; one patient had a possible attack at 14 months coinciding with rising AQP4-IgG ([doi:10.1038/s41392-022-01278-3]([passage text removed]); [PMC9810610]([passage text removed]); [PMC12598406]([passage text removed])).

## Other antibody-mediated syndromes (single cases; weaker evidence)

- **Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome:** anti-CD19 CAR T reported effective in a severely affected patient ([cell.com xcrm.2024.101794 supplement]([passage text removed])); two women with concurrent MG and LEMS were also treated ([institut-myologie.org]([passage text removed])).
- **Autoimmune encephalitis:** a refractory anti-DAGLA case (failed steroids, plasma exchange, rituximab) improved on CASE and ICARS scales with antibody clearance and B-cell depletion in blood *and* CSF, but only **partial** remission — the accompanying commentary frames this as inflammation controlled while neurodegeneration continued ([doi:10.1186/s12974-025-03662-6]([passage text removed]); [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42028700](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42028700)). A GAD65 cerebellar ataxia case had only minor improvement, attributed to low baseline disability ([PMC12953506]([passage text removed])).
- **CIDP:** a BCMA-CD19 bispecific case improved on INCAT sensory, INCAT and MRC scores ([passage text removed]; [eurekalert.org](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1048783)), and anti-BCMA CAR T in two refractory patients yielded long-term drug-free remission in one ([cell.com/med S2666-6340(25)00131-X]([passage text removed])). Countervailing signal: CIDP has itself been reported as a delayed non-ICANS neurotoxicity after BCMA CAR T ([PMC12537912]([passage text removed])).
- **Progressive MS** (not classically antibody-mediated): two patients tolerated CD19 CAR T with CSF CAR T expansion and, in one, oligoclonal bands falling from 13 to 6 by day 64 ([neurologylive.com]([passage text removed]); [frontiersin.org 10.3389/fimmu.2025.1604174]([passage text removed])).

## Caveats

A pooled review of the early MG case literature (7 patients across 5 reports) found universal clinical improvement, CAR expansion on days 8–22 and persistence of 28–180 days, but concluded the evidence is uncontrolled and heterogeneous with limited >6-month follow-up, and that CAR T [passage text removed]" pending seven registered trials (>260 participants) reporting 2026–2029 ([ajmc.com]([passage text removed])). One earlier-treated MG patient relapse/durability picture is mixed across the KYV-101 experience, where a relapse was reported in another autoimmune indication ([cgtlive.com]([passage text removed])). I found no controlled trial data for immune-mediated neuropathies or autoimmune encephalitis; those rest on single cases.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Across small case series and early-phase trials, CD19- (and BCMA/CD19 bispecific-) directed CAR T cells produce rapid, deep and often drug-free clinical remissions in refractory antibody-mediated neurological disease — most robustly in myasthenia gravis — with autoantibody titres falling in most but not all responders, and toxicity generally limited to grade 1–2 CRS with little ICANS. All evidence remains small-scale and uncontrolled [S:83603673-387f-5551-aeed-d706f433e493][S:e6e9af8f-4112-579e-afb0-c5becf2139aa].

## Myasthenia gravis

**Prospective trial data (bispecific BCMA/CD19).** In a single-arm phase 1 dose-escalation trial (ChiCTR2200061267) in 18 patients with refractory generalized AChR-antibody-positive MG, mean changes [passage text removed]; 14 (82%) achieved minimal manifestation status, [passage text removed] 8 (47%) seroconverted to AChR-antibody negative [S:39042549-4f10-5c48-8073-cab7fe425593]. Patients were heavily pre-treated (all ≥2 prior immunosuppressants, 50% with prior myasthenic crisis, 44% prior FcRn inhibitor) [S:8914587e-6117-5290-86da-979f16dd3d7d]. Safety: no dose-limiting toxicity, no ICANS, grade 1 CRS in 39%, with transient grade ≥3 haematological toxicities [S:775220fd-0ce0-56b6-980a-0241c245a4e0]. The authors flag prolonged B-cell aplasia and frequent hypogammaglobulinaemia as the main trade-off, though lower respiratory tract infection occurred in 17% and was judged manageable [S:aa86d58c-4edf-564a-870a-c5cde8043823].

**Anti-CD19 (KYV-101) case experience.** In the index refractory AChR-positive case, improvement in arm-holding time and walking distance (gait aid no longer needed) over 60 days accompanied [passage text removed] preserved immunisation-induced IgG titres [S:6d008367-c311-5b67-83bc-3b06923aa042]. At two years, both KYV-101–treated patients had normalised QMG and MG-ADL scores and restored function, notably *despite* persistent or only modestly reduced anti-AChR titres — a dissociation between serology and disease activity; adverse events were mild (one grade 1 CRS), with no neurotoxicity, severe infection or secondary autoimmunity [S:3bbd468a-f640-5e28-8f5d-31176c71046e].

**RNA-engineered BCMA CAR T (Descartes-08, no lymphodepletion).** In 14 adults with generalized MG (AChR, MuSK, LRP4 and seronegative), week-12 mean changes were MG-ADL −6 (95% CI −9 to −3), QMG −7 (−11 to −3), MG composite −14 (−19 to −9) and MG-QoL15r −9 (−15 to −3), with no dose-limiting toxicity, CRS or neurotoxicity [S:2a73d6b6-e8fc-5f4e-9c75-6883dac9f47b]. Two patients stopped IVIg [S:2a73d6b6-e8fc-5f4e-9c75-6883dac9f47b]. In the subsequent phase 2b randomised placebo-controlled trial (31 participants), mean MG composite reduction at 3 months was 5.4 points with roughly two-thirds responding, and benefit persisted ≥12 months in 5 of 7 phase 2a patients [S:0cd3051f-53a9-55e1-826f-1d9b73b63ac5].

A review synthesising five independent case series (7 patients, CD19/BCMA/bispecific) found consistent clinical improvement, peak CAR T expansion at 8–22 days and persistence of 28 to ~180 days, with mainly grade 1–2 CRS and no severe events [S:e6e9af8f-4112-579e-afb0-c5becf2139aa].

## Other antibody-mediated neurological diseases

- **LEMS / MG–LEMS overlap:** two women with concomitant MG and VGCC-positive LEMS had normalisation of both AChR and VGCC antibodies and improved from wheelchair use to normal activities within 2 months (maximum toxicity grade 2 CRS, grade 1 ICANS) [S:6ab567f3-c9fc-58c1-9cc7-3eb061e4086f]. An isolated idiopathic LEMS case showed marked VGCC titre decline with [passage text removed] grade 2 CRS and intermittent neutropenia [S:70f7946d-c083-5f6f-ae27-d2578f1ed3ae].
- **Stiff-person syndrome:** a 69-year-old with 9 years of refractory SPS given KYV-101 had reduced leg stiffness, walking speed increase over 100%, daily walking distance from <50 m to >6 km within 3 months, and 40% benzodiazepine reduction, with only low-grade CRS [S:422d296a-509f-591a-8fcb-b9d1782ae4e2].
- **GAD65 cerebellar ataxia:** a 33-year-old refractory to rituximab and cyclophosphamide had 95% reduction in GAD65 serum titres by day +90, ataxia improvement by day +30, and no progression clinically or radiologically at day +270; toxicity was grade 1 CRS [S:cd465712-273d-52e8-ab7a-1ce67e4c03b1].
- **NMOSD:** in a phase 1 study of anti-BCMA CT103A in 12 AQP4-IgG-seropositive patients, 11 remained relapse-free and drug-free over a median 5.5 months, with declining AQP4 antibodies and improvements in EDSS, vision, ambulation and bladder/bowel function; all had grade 1–2 CRS, and cytopenias/infections were the grade ≥3 events [S:cb4fcdf7-cecf-5f68-84ce-5e2c986e3053][S:e7a07bea-5872-5b33-9e42-1a5ff8bd06b9]. Follow-up was short, limiting interpretation [S:d82a9772-b82f-593e-9546-a8e2a768582e].
- **MOGAD:** a 25-year-old with >6 relapses despite immunotherapy had 1 year of relapse-free disease stability after CD19 CAR T, with MOG antibodies becoming undetectable and vaccination immunity preserved [S:06304bce-1097-5955-a7d3-c54e394775d9].
- **Autoimmune encephalitis (anti-DAGLA):** a 36–37-year-old refractory to steroids, plasma exchange and rituximab improved on CASE and ICARS scores after one CD19 CAR T infusion, with anti-DAGLA antibodies undetectable by day +18 and B-cell depletion in blood *and* CSF; however, he was still bedridden at day +300 (able to eat with support and hold complex conversations), and toxicity comprised grade 1 CRS and a transient coagulation disorder [S:3f2a83c2-f34c-5c5c-a192-5e0eb07ec903][S:bda81d19-17bc-5c60-b89b-dade9c64cead].
- **CIDP / autoimmune neuropathies:** anti-BCMA CAR T produced drug-free remission within 6 months in two refractory CIDP patients, though one relapsed [passage text removed] [S:e8c7e91e-dd51-55e5-835e-f7de8ff93af6]. With CD19 CAR T, a motor-variant CIDP patient improved from INCAT-ODSS 4 to 0 over 300 days with falling neurofilament light, and an anti-NF155 paranodopathy patient regained unassisted walking >200 m with normalised titres by 4 months — both having gone from immobile tetraparesis to independent mobility, with only grade 1 ICANS in one [S:e8c7e91e-dd51-55e5-835e-f7de8ff93af6][S:ed564999-2c48-5e10-b2a4-5bca9d9deb82]. Notably, a third patient did not improve and was subsequently rediagnosed with motor neurone disease [S:ed564999-2c48-5e10-b2a4-5bca9d9deb82]. A bispecific BCMA/CD19-treated CIDP patient recovered from a nadir walking distance <20 m to near-normal function by day +180 with undetectable ganglioside antibodies at 3 months and remained stable off all treatment at 1 year [S:ed564999-2c48-5e10-b2a4-5bca9d9deb82].

## Caveats

Durability beyond ~2 years is unknown, and relapse remains possible once B cells repopulate [S:226b8fb7-6f90-52cb-a5c5-7000db552e86]. A neighbouring autoimmune indication illustrates the relapse problem concretely: a patient with Jo-1 anti-synthetase syndrome relapsed 9 months after CD19 CAR T, failed reinfusion (anti-CAR T cells detected), and required BCMA CAR T to re-induce drug-free remission [S:22b84d80-6906-5b90-bc9d-a6a708dd9b58]. Reviews consistently note that current neurological evidence is restricted to small uncontrolled cohorts pending seven registered trials (>260 patients) reporting 2026–2029, including KYSA-6 (NCT06193889) in refractory generalized MG [S:e6e9af8f-4112-579e-afb0-c5becf2139aa][S:9bd6ecf7-1d54-553b-9dc7-2d2610f5e825].

rows.question: How does concomitant corticosteroid tapering proceed in patients with NMOSD starting satralizumab in routine care?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: once interleukin-6 receptor blockade is started, the oral corticosteroid is the medication clinicians bring down first, and it is stopped altogether in about half of patients over two and a half years; non-steroidal immunosuppressants come down more slowly and unevenly, with azathioprine withdrawn in most patients who were taking it but tacrolimus in fewer than half; reduction follows clinician judgement rather than a standard schedule, and relapse has occurred after corticosteroid withdrawal, so the taper is monitored rather than assumed safe. Certainty: This describes observed practice and its outcomes rather than a tested tapering strategy. Scope: applies to aquaporin-4 antibody-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder in patients starting interleukin-6 receptor blockade in routine care, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it says discontinuations of the biologic were driven by inadequate effect rather than tolerability.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

In routine practice, satralizumab is started as an add-on to ongoing oral glucocorticoids (GCs) and the GC is then tapered gradually over months to years at the treating physician's discretion — typically from ~10–12 mg/day prednisolone equivalent at initiation down to ~2.5–3.5 mg/day by 2–2.5 years, with roughly 40–50% of continuing patients reaching 0 mg/day; there is no protocolised taper schedule, and complete steroid withdrawal is not achieved in everyone.

## Baseline exposure and trajectory of the taper

- Japanese all-case post-marketing surveillance (571 patients, 234 sites): 85.98% were on oral GCs at satralizumab initiation and 48.86% on immunosuppressants. Mean oral GC fell from 12.27 mg/day at baseline to 3.48 mg/day at 30 months; patients on 0 mg/day rose from 13.83% to 38.57%; those on <5 mg/day rose from 18.21% (104/571) to 67.81% (276/407) and <10 mg/day from 36.25% to 92.14%, alongside a Kaplan–Meier relapse-free rate of 85.86% and ARR 0.08/person-year ([PMC12623530]([passage text removed]); [PubMed 40999180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40999180)).
- The taper is front-loaded but incomplete early: at the 6-month interim of the same surveillance, mean dose went from 12.28 ± 10.17 to 8.11 ± 7.30 mg/day, the proportion <10 mg/day rose from 36.14% (206/570) to 59.27% (294/496), and the proportion on ≥10 mg/day fell from ~65% to ~40% (relapse-free rate 94.59%, 95% CI 92.25–96.23) ([PMC11393251]([passage text removed]); [10.1007/s40120-024-00640-7]([passage text removed])). Notably, tapering also occurred in the 85/570 patients who stopped satralizumab (≥10 mg/day fell to ~48% at discontinuation), so dose reduction is not exclusively satralizumab-driven ([d-nb.info/1349426350/34](https://d-nb.info/1349426350/34)).

## Prospective chart-review data (SAkuraBeyond, 25 Japanese sites, UMIN000050027)

- At 26 weeks, GC dose had been reduced in 71.3% of patients who were on oral GC >0 mg at baseline, and was ≤5 mg/day in 33.3%; concomitant immunosuppressants were also tapered — azathioprine and tacrolimus reached [passage text removed] ([PubMed 40203604](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40203604); [S2211034825001269]([passage text removed])).
- At the 2.5-year final analysis (124 patients; 72.6% on oral GC, 16.9% azathioprine, 35.5% tacrolimus at baseline): [passage text removed] off oral GCs entirely and 89.3% were on ≤5 mg/day; mean GC dose fell [passage text removed], with 80.0% and 47.1% off azathioprine and tacrolimus respectively; relapse-free rate 91.8%, ARR 0.03 ([PubMed 41732099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41732099)).

## Other routine-care series

- Japanese hospital claims database (131 satralizumab-treated patients, 93.1% on oral GCs at index): among the [passage text removed]%) were at 0 mg/day without relapse at 360 days; 95.4% were relapse-free ([PubMed 38401202](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38401202); [S2211034824000816]([passage text removed])).
- Retrospective chart review in routine practice: mean daily prednisolone [passage text removed]" ([10.1212/WNL.0000000000212899]([passage text removed]); conclusions: successful GC tapering in routine practice, [PubMed 40902227](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40902227)).

## Reported tapering schedules and timing

- A Japanese case series tapered prednisolone at 1 mg/week from 10 mg/day ([passage text removed] one patient; full discontinuation after 100 weeks in another starting from 30 mg/day), with no relapses; the authors elsewhere describe aligning reduction with 4-weekly injection visits at 1 mg per 4 weeks (≈0.036 mg/day, about 4.5× faster than a previously reported 0.24 mg/30 days) and argue that *timing* of taper initiation matters more than pace ([PMC10024277]([passage text removed])). A follow-up report concludes that starting at 1 mg every 4 weeks beginning 8 weeks after satralizumab introduction appears effective ([10.1111/cen3.70061]([passage text removed])).
- Trial-extension experience (not routine care, but the reference point clinicians use): in the SAkuraSky OLE, 16 of 36 GC-treated patients tapered, from a median 10 (5–25) to 2.75 (0–15) mg/day; 3 stopped steroids entirely and stayed relapse-free, while 2 patients had 3 relapses during tapering — one shortly after a drop from 25 to 10 mg/day ([S2211034822002875]([passage text removed])).

## Caveats

Tapering data in the surveillance study were analysed only for patients who continued satralizumab, since post-discontinuation data were unavailable ([PMC12623530]([passage text removed])). Serious infections were most frequent in the first 6 months and clustered in patients ≥75 years, longer diagnosis-to-treatment interval, ≥3 relapses in 2 years, and EDSS ≥6 ([PubMed 40999180]([passage text removed] group in whom steroid burden reduction is most desirable but relapse risk is highest. The surveillance investigator's own framing is that steroid-free treatment cannot be promised for all patients, though GC reduction is realistic in many ([neurologylive.com]([passage text removed])). Almost all of this real-world evidence is Japanese and predominantly AQP4-IgG-positive; I found no comparable routine-care tapering dataset from North America or Europe in these searches.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** In routine care (evidence is overwhelmingly Japanese), oral glucocorticoids (GC) are tapered gradually and at physician discretion after satralizumab start — typically ~1 mg/day decrements every 4 weeks tied to injection visits — with mean prednisolone doses falling from ~12–14 mg/day at initiation to ~2.5–5 mg/day by 1–2.5 years, roughly half of relapse-free patients reaching 0 mg/day by 2.5 years, and GCs generally reduced before non-steroid immunosuppressants.

**Magnitude and time course**
- SAkuraBeyond, a 25-site Japanese medical chart review of 124 AQP4-IgG+ patients (72.6% on oral GC, 16.9% azathioprine [AZA], 35.5% tacrolimus [TAC] at baseline): by week 130, mean oral GC fell [passage text removed]; 48.8% of relapse-free patients reached 0 mg/day and 89.3% reached ≤5 mg/day. AZA was withdrawn to 0 mg/day in 80.0% and TAC in 47.1% of relapse-free patients receiving them at baseline. Relapse-free rate was 91.8% at week 130 with ARR 0.03 (95% CI 0.02–0.07) versus 0.45 (0.34–0.58) in the preceding 52 weeks [S:53f6bab1-728f-5ec7-9dbd-8ef8d9355fe1][S:a2dff322-13db-5d97-964e-7847b8398caf].
- Japanese post-marketing surveillance (234–243 sites, ~570 patients, 86.0% on GC at baseline): mean GC dose fell from 12.4±10.2 [passage text removed], with the proportion on ≥10 mg/day dropping from 64.1% to 39.9% (relapse-free 94.6%, 95% CI 92.3–96.2) [S:e2901734-e155-5d78-a96e-be4a7684a1b7]; at the 30-month interim, mean dose was 3.5 mg/day, relapse-free rate 85.9%, ARR 0.08/person-year [S:7079afc2-807e-58fc-9258-e03af495dd7c].
- A Japanese claims analysis of 85 patients on ≤15 mg/day GC at satralizumab start found 44/78 (56.4%) had reduced their GC dose without relapse by the last satralizumab prescription, 14/34 (41.2%) reduced immunosuppressant dose, and among 21 patients treated ≥360 days, 6 (28.6%) became steroid-free without relapse [S:ef52b472-0f4c-5f91-9914-bd9e79a23cda][S:e524a23d-5654-50a7-9136-73b82c57f796].

**How the taper is actually operationalised**
- In a Japanese ophthalmology cohort (n=73 satralizumab-treated), prednisolone fell from 13.8±8.6 to 5.3±4.7 mg/day over a mean 10.0±7.0 months (p<0.001); 15 patients discontinued steroids entirely after a mean 8.5±5.8 months from a starting dose of 11.6±8.8 mg, with no relapse after discontinuation. Among 23 patients still on steroids beyond 12 months, doses went from 18.5±7.7 mg/day at initiation to 12.3±4.6 mg/day at 6 months and 8.9±4.0 mg/day at 12 months (both p<0.001) [S:9571f6d6-2168-57be-8953-2da9c51cdfa8][S:f05b95cd-11c0-5554-aa97-4879ce011ef2].
- The same report describes the practical schedule: "[passage text removed]… repeated at intervals of 4 weeks"; the authors caution that because relapse protection may be incomplete early, tapering should start after some period of biologic treatment (or the rate changed around 8 weeks), and should be slower in patients with pre-treatment frequent relapses [S:64c4dd00-676e-56fc-ace4-703b80fb23f7]. A related published rationale for beginning taper 8 weeks after satralizumab start is that serum soluble IL-6 receptor levels plateau around that time; guidance also notes that with combination therapy more aggressive tapering (to ≤10 mg/day by 1 year) is feasible than with steroids alone [S:d1b4eb76-fd6c-5192-adc1-513ff19c1b02].

**Sequencing and heterogeneity**
- SAkuraBeyond investigators explicitly note there was no standardised tapering protocol; reductions were [passage text removed], physicians tended to reduce oral GC before AZA or TAC, and the pattern reflected "[passage text removed]" — the most common stated reasons for starting satralizumab were to reduce GC or immunosuppressant doses [S:c3bb7e6e-6890-517d-9b23-cc51d26dfa20]. Consistent with this, in the SAkuraSky open-label extension each of 16 tapering patients had a unique, physician-tailored pathway (median oral steroid 10 mg → 2.75 mg), most tapering gradually over several years, and one patient had temporary dose increases during taper [S:00749714-1843-5afd-912d-8cbeb4612b24].

**Caveats**
- Relapses can occur during taper: in SAkuraBeyond, several of the nine relapsing patients were still on GC 8–20 mg/day at relapse [S:a2dff322-13db-5d97-964e-7847b8398caf]; and a case report describes a patient tapered by 0.5 mg/month who relapsed about a year after satralizumab initiation [S:6aeccfad-7bac-5847-b0a5-f85a9707ef02]. The authors also caution that long-term monitoring is needed in patients from whom GCs are withdrawn, and that their results may reflect a cautious approach because the cohort was treated immediately after satralizumab launch [S:c3bb7e6e-6890-517d-9b23-cc51d26dfa20].
- Evidence is heavily Japan-centric. Non-Japanese real-world reports I retrieved (US case series of 43 patients, US eculizumab-to-satralizumab switches, German/Austrian NEMOS cohort, Chinese SAILOR/Huashan cohorts) describe relapse and safety outcomes but did not report corticosteroid tapering trajectories in the retrieved text [S:7cf29509-0235-5b8d-aceb-f16fbca59f9d][S:7d2c2217-372e-5a54-ae50-aac5aa61aed7][S:f6a1a99e-b847-5355-8c49-151ddec73303][S:cdad4c9a-4a0b-5725-9d8f-bbe9472b1a4b], so no quantitative taper estimate outside Japan can be given from this evidence.

rows.question: What patient characteristics mark AQP4-IgG NMOSD patients at risk of severe or opportunistic infections during immunosuppression?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: severe or opportunistic infection reaches a substantial minority of patients on long-term immunosuppression and accounts for about a third of deaths; older age at onset, longer time with the disease, a coexisting autoimmune condition and diabetes each mark higher infection risk once the other factors are accounted for; a first severe infection is not a single event: recurrence is common among survivors and carries higher mortality than the first episode, which is what makes continuing an unchanged regimen a decision to weigh. Certainty: These are associations that identify higher-risk patients rather than established causes. Scope: applies to aquaporin-4 antibody-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder on long-term immunosuppression in adults followed for at least a year, specialist outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the number of immunosuppressants or total treatment duration as an independent predictor.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Risk is concentrated in **older patients with longer disease duration, comorbidities (especially diabetes, other autoimmune disease, cancer), accumulated disability with relapse-related bladder dysfunction, and treatment-related immune markers (lymphopenia, low/declining IgG, cumulative anti-CD20 exposure)** — not in serostatus itself.

### Demographic and disease-course characteristics

The most directly relevant study, an Oxford cohort of AQP4-IgG NMOSD, found 49 severe/opportunistic infections [passage text removed]). Nine survivors developed recurrent infections, six of whom died — recurrence itself marks a high-mortality subgroup [PMID 41618998].

A Japanese claims cohort (n = 4231; serious infection rate 5.77/100 person-years) independently confirmed age ≥75 [passage text removed] vs 18–35 years), cancer (HR 1.91), diabetes mellitus (HR 1.43), neurogenic bladder (HR 1.97), urolithiasis (HR 1.97), increasing number of relapses (HR 1.27) and oral glucocorticoid use (>0 to <5 mg/day, HR 1.80) as risks; in secondary models obesity and a lower Barthel Index also emerged, with the lowest Barthel category carrying an eightfold higher risk [PMID 40676373; PMC12450173]. Infections were predominantly urinary (26%) and respiratory (18%), supporting neurogenic bladder/immobility as a mechanistic pathway [PMC12450173].

In satralizumab post-marketing surveillance, factors increasing serious-infection risk were male sex, age ≥75 years, disease duration ≥10 years, and more relapses in the prior 2 years [d-nb.info/1349426350/34].

### Disability and comorbidity

In a 14-year rituximab NMOSD cohort (169 patients), infection risk was independently associated with **higher EDSS** ([passage text removed] [PMC9296048; NXI 10.1212/NXI.0000000000001179]. For COVID-19 specifically, a Turkish NMOSD/MOGAD cohort found advanced age, high disability and comorbid disease predicted severe infection and hospitalisation, with high EDSS the only factor surviving multivariate analysis for hospitalisation [PMC8655726].

### Laboratory and treatment-exposure markers

Among MS/NMOSD patients on anti-CD20 agents, **absolute lymphopenia (<1.0×10⁹/L)** was the independent risk factor for serious infection, with longer B-cell-therapy duration also associated; hypogammaglobulinemia predictors were age ≥50, white race and rituximab (with lower baseline IgG and IgA) [PMID 36917920]. Hypogammaglobulinemia is therefore an imperfect proxy — in a rituximab cohort, hypo-IgG predictors were treatment duration, low annual dose, prior mitoxantrone, baseline hypo-IgG and BMI >25, yet none predicted severe infectious events [PMC9296048]. In an MS rituximab cohort, low IgG and cumulative rituximab dose were independently associated with serious infection, but hypogammaglobulinemia explained at most a minority of the dose-related risk; advanced physical disability was a strong independent factor ([passage text removed]) [10.1212/NXI.0000000000200211].

### Caveats
- The Japanese study found *no* dose-dependent glucocorticoid association and immunosuppressant use was associated with *decreased* risk (HR 0.66), so treatment-exposure signals are confounded by indication [PMC12450173].
- Drug-specific hazards (meningococcal disease with complement inhibitors; TB/HBV screening before satralizumab) are agent characteristics rather than patient characteristics [practicalneurology.com/…/30129; enspryng-hcp.com].
- I found no evidence that AQP4-IgG titre or specific onset phenotype predicts infection risk; searches surfaced these only as relapse/disability predictors.
answers.connect:
## Answer

**Older age (at onset and current), longer disease duration, comorbid autoimmune disease and diabetes mellitus are the best-established patient-level markers of severe/opportunistic infection risk in AQP4-IgG NMOSD on immunosuppression; high disability (neurogenic bladder, high EDSS), cumulative/prolonged immunosuppression exposure, and other comorbidities (cancer, urolithiasis) add further risk.**

### Core evidence: dedicated Oxford AQP4-IgG cohort
In 209 AQP4-IgG NMOSD adults on immunosuppression followed ≥1 year at a UK national service, 49 severe/opportunistic infections (defined as requiring IV therapy or hospitalisation) occurred in 37 patients (18%), and infections accounted [passage text removed] multivariate [passage text removed]) [S:839d42b3-cf1a-50ce-9813-6ecfa8031e1d]. Recurrence marks a particularly ominous group: of survivors, nine developed recurrent infections and six of those died [S:839d42b3-cf1a-50ce-9813-6ecfa8031e1d].

Additional characteristics from the same cohort:
- **Age/immunosenescence:** [passage text removed] [S:18ce9bb4-03a7-5083-8d6f-9f00a5d3e4cc].
- **Disability:** all 10 patients who died as a consequence of severe infection [passage text removed] [S:18ce9bb4-03a7-5083-8d6f-9f00a5d3e4cc].
- **Cumulative treatment exposure:** patients on rituximab [passage text removed] long duration of immunosuppression (oral agents then rituximab); those who died were mostly elderly patients on conventional immunosuppressants [S:1cdc7b32-1388-5da5-b2d4-f0793a34491c].
- **Autoimmune comorbidity** predicted infection *independently of cumulative immunosuppression*, with complement dysregulation proposed (speculatively) as a mechanism; diabetes risk was thought to be compounded by concurrent steroid use [S:18ce9bb4-03a7-5083-8d6f-9f00a5d3e4cc].
- **Spectrum of infections** to screen for: severe pneumonia (16, including COVID-19 and one combined VZV/*Pneumocystis*), urosepsis (10), soft-tissue infection/abscess (6), ocular infection (7 — ophthalmic shingles, orbital cellulitis, toxoplasma chorioretinitis, HSV keratitis, CMV retinitis), fungal infection (3), HSV-2 genital infection (2), sepsis of unknown origin (2), tuberculosis and osteomyelitis [S:22cfb812-d696-5710-8618-369d7feef9e0].

### Corroborating cohorts
- **Japanese claims cohort (n=4231 NMOSD):** serious infection incidence 5.77/100 person-years; risk factors were age ≥75 vs 18–35 ([passage text removed]), diabetes mellitus (HR 1.43), neurogenic bladder (HR 1.97), urolithiasis (HR 1.97), number of NMOSD relapses (HR 1.27) and low daily oral glucocorticoid dose >0–<5 mg vs 0 mg (HR 1.80) [S:ac54d4d4-bb5e-53d8-b00e-1efc044abc89]. Urinary tract was the largest infection site fraction (26.08%), then respiratory (18.32%) [S:8f9fb050-d7da-585a-83cf-703c700f4034].
- **Swedish rituximab cohort:** AQP4-IgG+ patients had a five-fold higher rate of severe infectious events than MOG-IgG+ [passage text removed]), i.e. AQP4 seropositivity itself marks higher risk within rituximab-treated NMOSD [S:fa2fec69-605d-59d1-8b95-1c7a03b2f637]. UTIs and upper respiratory infections predominated; five [passage text removed]+, and neurogenic bladder/bowel dysfunction was proposed as a driver [S:8083f9e8-4d51-55a9-b4a6-dd39318d5aff].
- **Mortality context:** in Liverpool/Oxford national-service AQP4-IgG NMOSD deaths, infection was the leading cause (18 of 31 with known cause), in a group with median EDSS 8 before death and near-universal immunosuppression [S:f40bbcb2-61e6-54e3-8a8c-bbca8cb23489].

### Anti-CD20–specific markers (evidence conflicting)
Reported infection-risk markers with B-cell depletion include prior immunosuppression exposure, hypogammaglobulinaemia before B-cell therapy initiation, and male sex; one rituximab-NMOSD study instead found high EDSS at rituximab initiation and on-treatment relapses (with attendant steroid use) drove infection risk, with no hypogammaglobulinaemia association [S:f8d1365d-71ec-5bdb-8e2e-aaa30526a282]. The Swedish cohort likewise saw no correlation between IgG levels and severe infectious events (OR [passage text removed]) [S:fa2fec69-605d-59d1-8b95-1c7a03b2f637][S:f0957fc1-6fdb-5756-b404-06048bcfd456]. Practice guidance notes secondary antibody deficiency is time- and dose-dependent, that prior immunosuppressant exposure is an additional risk factor, and that patients with low baseline IgG are at particular risk — with serious sinopulmonary infections reported in NMOSD on long-term rituximab, all of whom had prior immunosuppressant exposure [S:17566fe5-e23f-5259-8760-b67e819c58e0][S:3054c0a9-2c5b-54c7-9cad-3620eb424e1d].

### Caveats
The pivotal AQP4-specific dataset is single-centre and retrospective, captured only hospitalised/IV-treated infections (mild and outpatient events excluded), and the authors explicitly note that infection risk with newer targeted agents (eculizumab, satralizumab, inebilizumab, ravulizumab), especially after prior rituximab, remains unassessed [S:2d97dfda-028e-5c3d-b244-5b0ff6229d22][S:f40486df-ed90-5e3e-9917-bb00f826ab39]. Although smoking status and BMI >30 kg/m² were collected in that cohort, I found no tool-retrieved result reporting whether they were significant predictors [S:b611ca9c-00fc-56df-a645-d5d8b0b1fa51].

rows.question: How do serum NfL and GFAP concentrations behave during attacks and remission in NMOSD and MOGAD?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: in aquaporin-4 antibody disease both the axonal and the astrocyte marker rise during attacks and settle again in remission, with z-score cut-offs proposed to separate the two states; in myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease the axonal marker is raised, highest during attacks, fluctuating over the following three months and usually normalising within six; astrocyte-marker data in that disease are inconsistent, some series finding levels stable across relapse and remission without correlation to disability and others finding them raised during relapse and correlated with disability; neither marker rises between attacks, arguing against attack-independent axonal or glial injury. Certainty: The attack-related rise is well supported, while the astrocyte marker in myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease remains genuinely disputed. Scope: applies to aquaporin-4 antibody neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease in patients sampled during attacks and in remission, specialist neurology settings. An answer is wrong if it states that the astrocyte marker runs higher in myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease than in aquaporin-4 antibody disease.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Both markers rise during attacks in both diseases, but with a disease-specific signature: in AQP4-IgG⁺ NMOSD sGFAP rises early and steeply (often to extreme values) and is the better attack marker, whereas in MOGAD sNfL is the informative attack marker and sGFAP moves only marginally; in both diseases, levels fall back toward normal in remission, with only mild residual sGFAP elevation in NMOSD.

## NMOSD (AQP4-IgG⁺)

**Attack.** In a Simoa study, sGFAP was higher after recent relapse than otherwise (median [passage text removed]), and sGFAP was higher in NMOSD than MS ([passage text removed]]. In the N-MOmentum trial, sGFAP jumped from a pre-attack median of 168.4 pg/mL (IQR 128.9–449.7) to 2,160.1 pg/mL (IQR 302.7–9,455.0) at adjudicated attacks (p=0.0015), with elevation (≥170 pg/mL) in 29/37 attack samples (78%) [[passage text removed]]. A Chinese cohort found sGFAP relapse 284.4 vs remission 147.1 pg/mL (p=0.033), while sNfL did not differ significantly (22.6 vs 13.0 pg/mL, p=0.090); values above the 90th percentile (1,822 pg/mL) occurred exclusively in AQP4-ab⁺ patients (up to 67,038.8 [passage text removed]].

**Kinetics differ between the two markers.** In a multicentre retrospective cohort (181 patients, 625 samples), sGFAP z-score [passage text removed] then fell rapidly over ~12 weeks, whereas sNfL rose gradually to [passage text removed] with slower decline over 20 weeks; optimal attack windows were <1 week for sGFAP and 1–[passage text removed] ≥6 months post-attack [[passage text removed]]. Using z-cutoffs of 3.0 (sGFAP) and 2.1 (sNfL), AUCs for attack vs remission were [passage text removed] (0.82–0.91); in validation cohorts sGFAP achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity and sNfL 71%/94% [[passage text removed]].

**Remission.** Longitudinal rituximab-treated cohort: sGFAP rose in *all* clinical attacks, and 19/20 (95%) fell below cutoff within 3 months; sGFAP stayed consistently low between attacks in 17/19 (90%), i.e. subclinical astrocyte damage was rare; sNfL followed a similar but slower pattern [[passage text removed]]. In a cohort studied in sustained remission (median 26 months since last attack), sGFAP was only mildly and non-significantly above healthy controls (109.2 vs 67.7 pg/mL, p=0.07) and sNfL did not differ between groups — yet sGFAP still tracked disability (EDSS SES=1.30, p=0.007) and sGFAP >90 pg/mL predicted shorter time to next attack (adjusted HR 11.6, 95% CI 1.3–105.6, p=0.03) [[passage text removed]]. Similarly, elevated baseline sGFAP tripled attack risk in N-MOmentum (31% vs 12%; HR 3.09, 95% [passage text removed]]. Another cohort showed both sNfL and sGFAP decreasing at 1-year follow-up in NMOSD remission [S:https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34278578].

## MOGAD

**Attack.** In 239 sera from 62 MOGAD patients, sNfL was clearly higher during attacks ([passage text removed] percentile) than remission (0.9, IQR −0.1–1.6; p<0.001), giving 3.5-fold higher odds of attack per z-unit (95% CI 2.3–5.1, p<0.001). sGFAP also differed statistically but remained essentially within the normal range (attack z 0.4, 65.5th percentile vs remission −0.2, 42.1th percentile) [[passage text removed]]. Kinetics: sNfL peaked at z 2.5 [passage text removed]) and reached steady state z 1.3 at 4.7 months; sGFAP peaked at only z 0.9 at 5.3 weeks and settled at z −0.5 at 4.2 months [[passage text removed]]. The sNfL attack signal is phenotype-dependent — lowest in isolated optic neuritis (z 2.1) and highest in cerebral/cerebellar disease (z 3.5) [[passage text removed]].

Another cohort found both markers rising: sNfL relapse 34.1 vs remission 12.5 pg/mL (p=0.049) and sGFAP relapse 187.7 vs remission 108.5 pg/mL (p=0.015) [[passage text removed]]. A plasma study reported pNfL and pGFAP both elevated during MOGAD attacks vs controls (p=0.005 and p=0.018) with no significant remission difference for pGFAP [[passage text removed]].

**Remission.** Longitudinal monitoring showed sNfL significantly elevated in all clinical attacks and falling below or near cutoff within 6 months, with attack-independent neuroaxonal *and* astrocytic injury absent between attacks [[passage text removed]]. sNfL variability was much greater in patients with a recent attack (median 37, [passage text removed]; p=0.006); notably, samples drawn within 2 weeks of symptom onset showed relatively low sNfL that then rose — so very early sampling can be falsely reassuring [[passage text removed]]. In remission, MOGAD sGFAP and sNfL are close to healthy-control values, and sGFAP shows no relationship to disability in MOG-IgG⁺ patients [[passage text removed]].

## Discriminating the two diseases and important caveats

The sGFAP/sNfL ratio is higher in NMOSD during attacks, consistent with astrocyte-predominant injury; the sGFAP/sNfL quotient at relapse separated NMOSD from MS with 73.0% sensitivity and 75.8% specificity [[passage text removed]], and the plasma ratio was higher in NMOSD than MOGAD during attacks (p=0.016) but not in remission [[passage text removed]].

Evidence in MOGAD is genuinely conflicting. One study found only serum tau — not sGFAP or sNfL — rose in MOGAD relapse, while sGFAP ≥128.55 pg/mL indicated relapse [passage text removed]]. A systematic review/meta-analysis concluded that neither serum GFAP nor NfL reliably correlated with disease activity at sampling in MOGAD, with substantial heterogeneity (I²=79% and 89%), although a supplementary analysis did show GFAP significantly elevated at attack vs remission [[passage text removed]]. A separate review found sNfL at onset did not predict relapse risk (relapsing n=15 vs monophasic n=18) and did not distinguish MOGAD from MS or AQP4⁺ NMOSD during attacks [[passage text removed]]. Much of this discordance is attributable to arbitrary attack/remission sampling windows (variably <30 days vs <3 months) [[passage text removed]], and current expert opinion holds that these proposed timing windows and age/BMI-adjusted z-score cutoffs still require external validation before informing clinical management [[passage text removed].0000000000200627].
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

In AQP4‑IgG⁺ NMOSD both markers rise at attack and fall in remission, but sGFAP is the dominant, sharply attack‑locked signal (astrocytopathy), while sNfL rises later, falls more slowly, and tracks disability; in MOGAD the pattern is inverted in emphasis — sNfL rises at attacks and normalises, while sGFAP is only modestly and inconsistently elevated, and neither shows attack‑independent elevation.

## NMOSD

**Attack vs remission.** In a paired cohort, serum NfL and GFAP were both higher at relapse than [passage text removed]), and only GFAP correlated with EDSS (r=0.485, p=0.012) [S:1aedcc25]. In a longitudinal NMOSD cohort, all three measures (NfL, GFAP, GFAP/NfL) were higher at attack, but GFAP discriminated attack from remission best (AUROC 0.876; cut‑off 218.6 pg/mL, sensitivity 94.7%, specificity 74.6%, vs NfL AUROC 0.772) [S:fa57cbc2][S:e43612c6]. Notably, some cross‑sectional data find sNfL does not separate phases significantly (relapse 22.6 vs remission 13.0 pg/mL, p=0.090) whereas sGFAP does (284.4 vs 147.1 pg/mL, p=0.033); extreme sGFAP values (>1,865 pg/mL) occurred exclusively in AQP4‑ab⁺ patients [S:ac3e6513][S:8358a638].

**Time course.** sGFAP peaks within the first week after attack onset and declines over ~12 weeks, whereas sNfL rises gradually, peaks at about five weeks and declines over six months; optimal sampling is week 1 for sGFAP and 1–8 weeks for sNfL, with attack z‑scores of 4.26 (sGFAP) and 2.76 (sNfL) versus 0.99 and 0.81 in remission (both p<0.001) [S:25ab6e7a]. Most patients fall below the sGFAP cut‑off within 3 months of relapse [S:12fb8d54]. In remission, sGFAP declines faster and more completely, while sNfL can stay elevated for months to years, implying continuing secondary neuronal damage [S:58400485].

**Remission-phase behaviour and prediction.** Remission sGFAP carries prognostic information: levels rose already ~1 week before clinical attacks in the N‑MOmentum substudy, elevated baseline sGFAP conferred ~3‑fold higher future attack risk, and sGFAP >90 pg/mL predicted shorter time to next attack (adjusted HR 11.6, 95% CI 1.3–105.6), whereas baseline sNfL was not associated with future attack risk [S:12fb8d54]. Conversely sNfL at attack predicts post‑attack disability worsening and appears the stronger disability biomarker [S:30fccc21]. Longitudinally, patients sampled at a baseline attack showed significant declines in NfL, GFAP and GFAP/NfL by 6–12 months, while patients without a baseline attack showed modest *increases* in NfL and GFAP despite stable EDSS — a possible subclinical signal [S:55d7b458][S:7233e6d3]. In a clinically stable, largely treated cohort, neither marker changed over one year (sGFAP 89.5→89.9 pg/mL, p=0.41; sNfL 21.1→21.7 pg/mL, p=0.67) [S:27e810e7].

## MOGAD

**sNfL.** Longitudinal Simoa sampling showed sNfL significantly elevated at all clinical attacks, falling below or near cut‑off within 6 months, and consistently low between attacks — i.e., no attack‑independent neuroaxonal injury; sGFAP did *not* increase in most attacks and stayed low throughout [S:6096f030]. Z‑score analysis in MOGAD gave sNfL 2.9 during acute activity vs 0.9 in remission (p<0.001), with each one‑unit rise in sNfL z‑score raising the odds of acute activity 2.6‑fold, while sGFAP z‑scores were only 0.4 vs −0.2 [S:0a6e4195]. In MULTIMOGAD (89 adults), baseline sNfL and sGFAP were high at onset and decreased over time (p<0.001 and p=0.027), both associated with EDSS at attacks and lower in optic‑neuritis presentations, and sNfL independently predicted relapse risk (HR 2.06, 1.41–3.01) [S:d4f15df8][S:60ad6500].

**sGFAP — inconsistent.** One cohort found MOGAD relapse vs remission sGFAP 187.7 vs 108.5 pg/mL (p=0.015) and sNfL 34.1 vs 12.5 pg/mL (p=0.049) [S:8358a638][S:ac3e6513], whereas another found both NfL and GFAP comparable between relapse and remission in MOGAD (NfL 10.2 vs 10.9, p=0.836; GFAP 102.5 vs 68.4 pg/mL, p=0.260), with only serum tau rising (0.5 vs 0.2 pg/mL, p=0.027) [S:1aedcc25][S:0e5bb699]. GFAP is generally lower in MOGAD than NMOSD in both phases [S:1aedcc25], and MULTIMOGAD interprets its modest sGFAP rise as bystander/global inflammatory injury rather than primary astrocytopathy [S:2e8ed5dc]. A systematic review/meta‑analysis concluded that within its search window neither NfL nor GFAP reliably correlated with MOGAD disease activity, explicitly flagging heterogeneous sampling timing as a driver of discordance [S:be88b3a8].

## Practical synthesis

- Timing dominates interpretation: sGFAP is informative only close to attack onset, sNfL over a wider 1–8 week window [S:25ab6e7a][S:60590002].
- Near an attack, sGFAP (and the sGFAP/sNfL ratio) is higher in NMOSD than in MOGAD or MS, aiding differential diagnosis [S:b477255b][S:58400485].
- Both markers fall with immunotherapy in AQP4⁺ NMOSD; the treatment effect on NfL in MOGAD is less clear, and MULTIMOGAD found no significant treatment impact on either marker [S:60590002][S:ceec9c4b].
- Plasma data in a mixed cohort suggest relapse-to-remission fold-change is larger in MOGAD for NfL while remission NfL stays higher in NMOSD (5.2 vs 3.6 pg/mL), though this was an exploratory single‑centre analysis [S:3782b45d].
