rows.question: What outcomes follow therapeutic plasma exchange combined with methylprednisolone in children with severe autoimmune encephalitis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: most children still carry substantial functional limitation when they leave hospital, after a median stay of well over a month; only a minority still carry substantial functional limitation at follow-up of a year or more, so recovery unfolds over months rather than weeks; starting the exchange within the first four weeks went with a higher rate of improvement at discharge, which is the clearest available signal on timing; whether adding corticosteroid to the exchange improves on exchange alone is unsettled, since the combination had the highest improvement rate descriptively while the formal comparison across regimens found no difference. Certainty: These are early uncontrolled observations, and the regimen question is left open by the material itself. Scope: applies to severe autoimmune encephalitis in children treated with plasma exchange during the acute admission, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the combination of methylprednisolone with exchange as demonstrated superior to exchange alone.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

In children with severe autoimmune encephalitis, TPE added to IV methylprednisolone is consistently associated with improvement in encephalopathy, seizures and neuropsychiatric symptoms — with better outcomes when started early — but the evidence is entirely retrospective/observational, a substantial minority are left with sequelae, and procedural complications are common though usually mild.

## Direct pediatric cohort evidence

**Combined IVMP + TPE cohort (n=36, Vietnam).** In children with severe AE (most anti-NMDAR, treated with IV methylprednisolone plus TPE; probable antibody-negative cases received TPE alone or with IVMP), TPE improved neuropsychiatric symptoms at discharge, and initiation within 28 days of onset was associated with improvement [S:https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40746120]. [passage text removed] onset to hospitalization [S:https://doi.org/10.1177/08830738251356122]; a subsequent meta-analysis table lists this cohort as 36 patients with a median of 5 TPE sessions, using FFP and/or 5% albumin as replacement [[passage text removed]].

**Steroid/IVIG-pretreated children (n=12, anti-NMDAR).** All received immunoglobulin and high-dose methylprednisolone before PE; 10/12 (83.33%) showed confirmed effectiveness, Glasgow Coma Scale scores differed significantly before vs after PE (P<0.05), CSF/serum NMDAR antibody titers fell, and 15 adverse events (27.78%) occurred, mostly anaphylaxis [[passage text removed]].

**Small series (n=5).** Corticosteroids in all plus 3–7 TPE sessions (median 5, 5% albumin): 4/5 (80%) achieved complete or partial remission, one had persistent neurologic sequelae; no major TPE-related adverse events, but intercurrent infections (pneumonia, UTI, catheter-related bacteremia) in three patients [[passage text removed]].

## Does adding steroids to TPE matter?

**Systematic review of PE in pediatric anti-NMDAR encephalitis.** PE was most often [passage text removed]); it [passage text removed] 54.5% (65/119). Full/substantial recovery at follow-up was higher when PE was combined with steroids (66.7%, 70/105) than when it was not (46.7%, 7/15), and when immunotherapy was given ≤30 days from onset (69.4%, 25/36) vs later (59.2%, 16/27). [passage text removed]] [S:https://www.academia.edu/129058687/International_Consensus_Recommendations_for_the_Treatment_of_Pediatric_NMDAR_Antibody_Encephalitis].

**Individual-patient meta-analysis (1550 NMDARE patients, 46.3% aged ≤18 at onset).** Good functional outcome (mRS 0–2) at 12 months was associated with first-line therapeutic apheresis alone (5.6-fold increased odds), corticosteroids + IVIG (2.7-fold), and corticosteroids + IVIG + apheresis (2.8-fold, P=0.04); PLEX plus steroids gave [passage text removed]), whereas corticosteroids alone was not significant (1.6-fold, P=0.32). Lack of immunotherapy within 30 days of onset was the only first-line approach associated with worse outcome [[passage text removed]]. Consensus recommendations for pediatric NMDARE accordingly advise pulsed IV corticosteroids in all children, with additional IVIG or plasma exchange in severe patients [[passage text removed]].

## Caveats on outcome and safety

- **Sequelae are frequent.** In one pediatric PE series, only 3/8 AE patients sustained improvement; the other 5 had motor difficulties and epilepsy plus learning difficulties [[passage text removed]]. In critically ill children receiving TPE (median 9 days onset-to-TPE, median 7 sessions), 63.6% had favorable neurological outcomes at discharge overall, but outcomes in the autoimmune encephalitis subgroup were variable with most unfavorable at discharge — the authors stress that recovery often continues well beyond hospitalization [[passage text removed]].
- **Complication profile.** Across 53 children (378 procedures) with pediatric neuroimmune disorders, TPE was preceded by corticosteroids and/or IVIG in 83%; [passage text removed], predominantly mild–moderate (nausea, hypotension, catheter issues), severe complications in 11%, no deaths; clinical improvement was documented in 84% [[passage text removed]].
- **Sequencing.** IVIG should follow rather than precede PLEX, since PLEX clears infused immunoglobulin [[passage text removed]]; one protocol allows ≥5 days between rituximab and the next PE cycle and bridges with IV steroids after each cycle [[passage text removed]].

**No randomized trial addresses this combination in children** — the systematic review explicitly notes a paucity of quality data [[passage text removed]], and a pediatric systematic review comparing corticosteroids-then-IVIG vs corticosteroids-then-TPE found results inconclusive for length of stay and no significant difference in relapse risk, with only a suggestion of greater disability improvement with TPE [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

In the only cohort I found that directly addresses this combination, most severely affected children improved by discharge, but the benefit was not statistically distinguishable from other plasma-exchange–containing regimens, and long-term sequelae (seizures, dependency) persisted in a minority.

## Key evidence

**The direct study.** A retrospective case series of 36 Vietnamese children with severe autoimmune encephalitis treated with a therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE)–containing regimen at Children's Hospital No. 2 (Jan 2019–Jun 2022) [S:ac1b9fad]. Median age 7.4 years; all had impaired consciousness, with cognitive impairment in 91.7%, seizures in 86.1% and movement disorders in 86.1% [S:ac1b9fad]. Half (18/36) had anti-NMDAR encephalitis, 38.8% probable antibody-negative AE, plus LGI1 (5.6%) and GABAR (5.6%); patients received a median of 5 TPE sessions over a median 11.5 days [S:3bad3d10].

**Outcomes with IVMP + TPE specifically.** 25 of 36 children were classified as improved at discharge (mRS drop ≥1 point, improved mental status, or reduced seizure frequency/severity) [S:e07596dc, S:fab81ff0]. The IVMP+TPE combination accounted for 19 of the 25 improved versus 7 of the 11 not improved (OR 1.8, P = .448) [S:e07596dc]. The authors state that IVMP+TPE showed the greatest improvement rate of the regimens studied, but explicitly note no significant difference between TPE monotherapy, IVMP+TPE, and IVMP+TPE+IVIG, and that the sample was small [S:8d40d150, S:e07596dc].

**What did predict improvement.** Starting TPE within 28 days of onset was the only significant factor (24/25 improved vs 7/11 not improved; OR 13.7, P = .029) [S:e07596dc]. Antibody subtype, sex, age >6 y, preceding viral infection, mechanical ventilation, number of TPE cycles, and replacement fluid type were not significant [S:e07596dc]. Anti-NMDAR cases had the most favourable outcomes; probable antibody-negative AE fared worse [S:e07596dc, S:06f8ff06].

**Longer-term course.** Median length of stay was 39 days [S:8d40d150]. At ≥1-year follow-up (analysis restricted to patients followed >12 months), 24.2% still had seizures, down from 54.5% requiring antiepileptic drugs at discharge [S:ac1b9fad, S:06f8ff06]. The authors conclude continued follow-up is needed for relapse and seizure management [S:06f8ff06]. Their improvement rate was similar to one prior TPE series (~63.5% improved at end of TPE) but lower than another reporting 94% improvement at 2 months; they attribute limited TPE efficacy partly to intrathecal antibody production behind the blood–brain barrier [S:8d40d150].

**Safety context (not encephalitis-specific).** A Vienna single-centre series of 53 children (378 TPE procedures; AE 19% of diagnoses, TPE preceded by corticosteroids and/or IVIG in 83%) found clinical improvement in 84%, with 42% significantly improved; [passage text removed] but were mostly CTCAE I–II (nausea, hypotension, catheter issues), severe in 11%, with no deaths [S:cf315237]. A 435-child, 1201-procedure series reported complications in 12.7% of procedures, no deaths, and a significantly higher complication rate in anti-NMDAR encephalitis than other diseases [S:b90f99a9].

## Caveats

Evidence is limited to small retrospective, single-centre series with no randomised comparison of IVMP+TPE against IVMP or IVIG alone; the Vietnam cohort used predominantly fresh frozen plasma rather than albumin for cost reasons, and long-term assessment was partly done remotely by video call [S:d0d25f58, S:fab81ff0]. I found no source reporting mortality or relapse rates specifically for the IVMP+TPE subgroup.

rows.question: What burden do repeated NMOSD relapses place on patient disability, quality of life, and caregivers?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: bladder and bowel control problems were more common in patients who had relapsed than in those who had not, and became more common with additional relapses; impact on daily living was high throughout, with over half of patients affected in their ability to work or drive, and significantly more of those with a relapse history not in full-time work and limited in home maintenance; patients who had relapsed required more caregiver support than those who had not, most often from their partner; patient-rated quality of life did not track the physical burden, running counter to trial data in which a single relapse worsens quality of life. Certainty: The burden findings are associations, and the quality-of-life result is in genuine tension with other evidence. Scope: applies to aquaporin-4 antibody-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder in adults under neurologist care with or without relapses since the initial attack, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it states that relapses caused the disability and burden, since the design is cross-sectional and supports associations only.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line
Because NMOSD disability accrues almost entirely in step-wise fashion at the time of attacks, each additional relapse converts into permanent impairment, measurably lower health utility, lost employment, and substantial unpaid caregiving hours — making relapse prevention the principal lever on all three burdens.

## Disability: relapses are the engine of accrual
- In a direct MS-vs-NMOSD comparison, EDSS progression in NMOSD "was almost exclusively seen after clinical attacks," and "[passage text removed] MS patients changed between relapses; NMOSD deterioration was described as irreversible with stepwise accumulation, and NMOSD patients were significantly more disabled [passage text removed] [PMC7431838].
- A decade-long cohort of 281 AQP4-IgG+ patients (mean follow-up 11.3 years, 1,662 EDSS assessments) [passage text removed] and found progression independent of relapse activity to be rare [doi:10.1212/NXI.0000000000200533, reported at [passage text removed]].
- Untreated relapsing NMOSD carries a poor natural history: roughly half of patients [passage text removed] onset, and permanent damage accrues with each attack [[passage text removed]; PMC6397677].
- Repetition matters mechanistically: while a minority are severely disabled by the first attack, "[passage text removed] disability" (EDSS ≥6 or blindness) [cuba.dialogoroche.com — Severity and Unpredictability of NMOSD].

## Quality of life: measurable, durable loss per relapse
- In a pooled analysis of trial data, a **single** relapse produced worse disability scores (mRS at 30 days, p=0.035; EDSS at 90 days, p=0.027) and worse HRQoL on all four instruments [passage text removed]), with EQ-5D-3L VAS scores worse at **all** post-relapse time points; the authors describe the effect as "noticeable and permanent," with 25–50% of relapsing patients crossing clinically meaningful worsening thresholds [Front Neurol 2023;14:1099376 / PMC10126826].
- Because relapse-driven EDSS worsening is what persists, QoL loss tracks it: across SAkuraSky/SAkuraStar (176 patients with paired EDSS and EQ-5D), QoL decreased at each incremental increase in disability, consistently across treatment arms [doi:10.1016/j.msard.2021.103332].
- Real-world UK data quantify the gradient: mean patient EQ-5D-5L utility was 0.54, falling from 0.80 (EDSS ≤4.0) to 0.20 (EDSS 8.0–9.5) [Orphanet J Rare Dis 2022;17:159].
- Beyond motor/visual deficits, residual symptom burden dominates day-to-day QoL — fatigue, pain and depressive symptoms are frequent and impair QoL even in clinically stable patients with low physical disability [PMC9075919]; pain imposes a heavy burden on QoL and healthcare use [PMID 34252701].
- Socioeconomic consequences: in a 193-patient survey, only ~35% were employed, and 63.7% of unemployed respondents reported being disabled [Neurol Neuroimmunol Neuroinflamm [passage text removed]].

## Caregivers
- **Time and work:** among 74 informal carers of NMOSD patients, more than 22% spent over 100 hours per week caring and 40% reported an impact on their employment; care averaged about 15 hours per day, valued at £13,150–£24,560 per 3 months (≈£52,600–£98,240 per year) [Orphanet J Rare Dis 2022;17:159].
- A separate real-world caregiver cohort (n=70) reported mean 40.3 (SD 30.2) caregiving hours/week; 61.4% took time off work, 58.1% had trouble fulfilling work responsibilities, and caregiving interfered with travel/leisure ([passage text removed]%) [AAN 2024 abstract, Patel et al., [passage text removed]].
- **Psychological:** in a mixed-methods study of 31 patients and 22 caregivers, ~45% of caregivers (mean BAI 8.1, SD 9.3) and ~72% of patients reported clinically relevant anxiety; anxiety centred specifically on "the unpredictable nature of subsequent NMOSD attacks," and patient and caregiver anxiety levels were strongly positively correlated (a dyadic burden). Caregivers did not endorse clinically significant depression (mean BDI-II 7.2) [PLOS ONE 2024;19(3):e0300777 / PMC10980246].
- Carer health utility itself was relatively preserved (EQ-5D-5L 0.85; Carer Experience Scale 57.67) [Orphanet J Rare Dis 2022;17:159], and the AAN caregiver cohort likewise showed HRQoL scores suggesting resilience despite substantial reported burden [AAN2024-003642] — so the caregiver signal is strongest for time, work and anxiety rather than global self-rated health.

## System and out-of-pocket cost of repeated relapses (context for the above)
- In US claims data (n=1,363; median 2.0 years follow-up), 47.7% had ≥1 relapse (ARR 0.8, 95% CI 0.7–0.9); mean annualized all-cause spend was $60,599 vs $8,912 in comparators (difference $51,687). Relapse-specific spend averaged $10,070 per patient per year; 35.0% of relapses required hospitalisation (mean 17.5 days, $25,250 per relapse) versus $4,550 for outpatient-managed relapses (mean 15.9 days) [PMC8571448 / PMID 34046846].
- Patients bear part of this directly: in a 103-adult survey, mean out-of-pocket cost was $3,326 per relapse event (for the 52% of events incurring any), indirect costs averaged $1,907 per visit for 26% of visits, and 69% reported lost income from hospital visits [doi via sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211034823000846; [passage text removed]].

## Caveats
Caregiver-specific evidence in NMOSD is thin: the two quantitative sources above are a single-centre UK postal survey (74 carers) and a conference abstract (70 caregivers), plus a 22-caregiver mixed-methods study. I found **no** study that directly correlates *number of relapses* with a validated caregiver-burden score (e.g. Zarit) in NMOSD — the relapse→caregiver link is inferential, via the relapse→EDSS→cost/care-hours gradient documented in [Orphanet J Rare Dis 2022;17:159].
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Repeated NMOSD relapses are the dominant driver of stepwise, largely irreversible disability, and each attack also produces sustained losses in health-related quality of life (HRQoL), unemployment, and substantial cost and caregiving demands — while caregivers themselves show clinically relevant anxiety, role strain, and psychological burden.

## Disability: stepwise, relapse-driven accrual

- Recovery from NMOSD attacks is often poor, driving stepwise accumulation of neurological disability, with a substantial proportion of patients unable to walk without assistance within several years of onset; up to 90% of AQP4+ patients relapse during their disease course [S:62013582-3e43-5a3e-8eba-8984f2face05].
- Disability in NMOSD accrues almost exclusively through attacks: no spontaneous EDSS change independent of attacks was observed, supporting attack frequency/severity as the key outcome [S:b7f5f08f-291e-54b1-8dd2-c42cbdac2d46]. A German claims analysis similarly cites evidence that no EDSS deterioration is detectable during inactive disease periods [S:d196784c-28d2-50c3-809b-6c99ea6e83b4].
- In the CIRCLES North American cohort (n = 505), [passage text removed], 2.03–7.86), self-care (OR 1.90, 1.07–3.38) and composite disability (OR 4.20, 1.71–10.34) — correlates the EDSS did not detect [S:ad1f2c1c-b104-538f-b156-771856c4a2ff]; the authors conclude this reinforces the importance of preventing or minimizing relapses relative to cumulative disability [S:9fb750de-0067-5431-a53d-60d2cbcf0c38].
- Attack severity gates recovery: among patients losing <2 EDSS points at presentation, 82% returned to baseline, versus only half of those losing ≥2 points (p < 0.0009) [S:35ce42e7-f7aa-58ff-8b26-243d4250cdc8]. In late-onset disease, despite comparable annualized attack rates, complete remission after attacks was less frequent ([passage text removed] progression to EDSS 4 was faster ([passage text removed]) [S:65a857b7-6dd4-593b-ab7b-232b1608b20a].

## Quality of life: a single relapse is enough, and effects compound

- A post hoc PREVENT/OLE analysis found that one relapse significantly worsened disability (mRS at 30 days, p=0.035; EDSS at 90 days, p=0.027) and all four HRQoL instruments [passage text removed]), with EQ-5D-3L VAS still worse at every post-relapse timepoint [S:b2552fe4-78b2-534a-81dd-a7bb27d9e4c4]. Between 15% and 50% of relapsing patients met thresholds for clinically meaningful worsening [S:2cce3787-99f8-587e-9b78-6282d6e206da].
- Relapsing patients (n=27) were more likely than non-relapsing patients (n=116) to show clinically meaningful worsening on 4 of 7 instruments; extrapolating to two relapses raised this to 6 of 7, "[passage text removed]" [S:2cce3787-99f8-587e-9b78-6282d6e206da][S:34567200-ecbd-59db-a31e-49bf419b9412]. A related conference analysis extrapolated that after 5 relapses the EQ-5D utility index fell [passage text removed] rose from 4.2 to 5.7 (+35%) — note this is a modelled extrapolation, not observed data [S:ef047205-8142-5cfa-9925-848dda701843].
- Cumulatively, HRQoL correlates with relapse count: a greater number of relapses is associated with poorer HRQoL [S:36122b1d-f8c8-58f1-8c8d-4c99efa13111]. In the German CHANCE NMO study (n=212), the mean EQ-5D index was 0.693, worse than a comparable MS cohort (0.756) despite lower EDSS and younger age, with acute attacks an independent predictor of cost (RC=8,242) and EDSS and need for care independent predictors of both cost and reduced HRQoL [S:76451bba-2314-515d-b0a8-c6567559dda2][S:3f0b2483-ed6e-59fa-8765-83d81b30c096]. Additional relapse-linked QoL burdens include dysautonomic symptoms, which increase [passage text removed]) and independently correlate with all QoL domains [S:71c9f49d-5db3-530c-a700-88b892327b82].

## Socioeconomic and caregiving burden

- Relapse activity is where costs concentrate: German claims data show total cost of care roughly nine-fold higher per active month (€7,632.38) than per inactive month (€834.91) [S:e780d942-e4e1-5541-8b8c-5e9162251e88]; hospitalization cost was >20-fold higher in the 30-day active phase versus inactive phase [S:5c9aaf8c-bd89-5085-96f8-de3517d5e234], and a US analysis found $44,137 versus $1,121 in patients with versus without a relapse [S:0a74699c-698e-59f7-83ac-eabaa28b02e8]. In CHANCE NMO, direct non-medical costs (34% of total) were driven principally by informal care, and indirect costs by lost salary [S:e23b9ee6-9927-555a-a50d-37fc5f244e4d].
- Relapse rate predicts job loss: among 351 Chinese women with NMOSD, 54.1% attributed unemployment to the disease, and higher ARR was an independent risk factor (OR 1.778, p=0.038) alongside severe disability (OR 4.972, p<0.001) [S:99fd4104-0fbd-5fa7-a99c-701195115e56]; internationally, only about one-third of working-age people with NMOSD are in the workforce, with walking aid use, bilateral visual loss, and depressed mood independently associated with unemployment [S:144caab3-4148-5b31-b8af-530dd7c68e76].

## Caregivers

- In a mixed-methods US/Canadian study (31 patients, 22 caregivers), nearly half of caregivers reported clinically relevant anxiety — higher than expected from prior literature — with anxiety centred specifically on "the unpredictable nature of subsequent NMOSD attacks" and disease progression; caregivers also endorsed cognitive fusion and over-controlled coping, though not clinically significant depression [S:c7e88c9e-914a-5c45-b278-1e0ec0f9681b][S:af449b2a-2a9f-588a-bc82-253d84d86563]. Conference figures from the same programme report caregiver anxiety in 45% and cognitive fusion in 50% [S:97028370-8361-5e02-b8cb-49174c780a27].
- Relapses specifically restructure caregiver life: partners described pressure to assume new roles inside and outside the home *during NMOSD relapses*, curtailing hobbies and activities to prioritise the patient's health, plus gender role shift; a fifth of loved ones had mild-to-moderately severe depressive symptoms [S:acfe0e41-cd6d-59b5-9791-9000bab1124d][S:0e361227-e220-5ff1-8ea9-798235ee8fd3].
- Patient and caregiver burden are coupled: anxiety and over-controlled coping were strongly positively correlated across the dyad (anxiety r=.617, p=.005), so neither partner buffers the other; all caregivers relied primarily on over-controlled coping, a style linked to caregiver strain [S:7e3be167-b9cb-5ec9-a37f-80df79322054][S:97028370-8361-5e02-b8cb-49174c780a27].
- Caregiver/family financial burden and caregiver quality of life were formally elicited as patient-relevant value elements in NMOSD, though patients ranked treatment uncertainty, regimen experience and their own financial burden highest [S:57dc9681-9baf-5ccd-8ee4-672e3f26fe21].

## Caveats

The single-relapse HRQoL evidence rests on a small post hoc trial subgroup (27 relapsing patients) and likely underestimates multi-relapse impact, since some relapses occurred on eculizumab, which was ranked as producing less severe relapses [S:17f0c7b2-0930-5ce3-87dd-21c9a8f9afaa]. The multi-relapse figures are extrapolations, not observed longitudinal data [S:34567200-ecbd-59db-a31e-49bf419b9412]. Cost analyses capture direct healthcare costs and acknowledge they underestimate real social care costs and [passage text removed]" [S:3d9e521e-84bc-5a83-af38-0e1748dd0fa4]. I found no study quantifying caregiver hours, caregiver costs, or validated caregiver-burden scale scores (e.g., Zarit) as a function of NMOSD relapse number — that specific link appears unmeasured.

rows.question: How do peripheral immune cells reach the CNS compartment and sustain tissue injury in multiple sclerosis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Peripheral immune cells reach the central nervous system by more than one route: across the blood-brain barrier, across the blood-cerebrospinal-fluid barrier at the choroid plexus, and directly through dura-associated meningeal channels; Cells and immune mediators accumulating in meningeal and perivascular niches are implicated in the subpial demyelination and periventricular tissue damage characteristic of the disease, with the interface regions mattering as well as the parenchyma; High-dose ablative therapy directed at the systemic immune system stops clinical relapses and acute lesion formation, establishing that systemic components underlie them, while the same therapies do not halt the progressive phase once it is established, which indicates that additional mechanisms are involved; Earlier restriction of systemic immune access to the central nervous system is associated with a lower likelihood of later progression, on long-term extension and observational evidence rather than a head-to-head comparison. Certainty: This is a well-supported account of the mechanism, with the treatment-timing element an association rather than a demonstrated comparative effect. Scope: applies to multiple sclerosis in patients across relapsing and progressive disease, specialist neurology settings. An answer is wrong if it claims the animal model mechanisms translate uniformly to patients.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Peripheral leukocytes enter the CNS by a **multi-step, multi-route process** — adhesion-molecule-dependent diapedesis across post-capillary venules, plus entry via the choroid plexus/blood–CSF barrier and the meninges — and then sustain injury by being **locally reactivated behind the barriers**, recruiting and licensing myeloid effectors, and eventually establishing self-perpetuating, CNS-compartmentalized inflammation that continues even when the blood–brain barrier (BBB) is relatively restored.

## 1. Entry route A: the post-capillary venule (the classic BBB route)

Trafficking occurs specifically at post-capillary venules, not capillaries (where nutrient transport occurs) [PMC8902072]. The cascade is canonical: selectin-mediated tethering/rolling via ligands such as PSGL-1, then firm arrest through integrin–CAM pairs — leukocyte VLA-4 (α4β1) binding endothelial VCAM-1, and LFA-1 binding ICAM-1 — followed by transmigration, with ALCAM and PECAM-1 also contributing [PMC9221446; [passage text removed]]. VCAM-1, ICAM-1, ALCAM and PECAM-1 are upregulated on CNS vasculature in both MS and EAE, and VLA-4/LFA-1 are highly expressed on infiltrates within MS lesions [fncel.2023.1101379].

Two lines of evidence anchor this causally:
- **Therapeutic**: natalizumab, an anti-α4 antibody, is among the most effective MS treatments, directly demonstrating VLA-4 dependence of CNS leukocyte entry [fncel.2023.1101379]. In EAE, anti-VLA-4 antibody modulates not only VLA-4 but a broader adhesion-molecule programme, and adhesion-molecule interactions shift across successive disease phases (ICAM-1/LFA-1 peaking at the disease peak) [https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/23/9/4637].
- **Redundancy**: α4 blockade does not close all doors — lymphocyte trafficking can proceed via alternative molecules including PSGL-1 [[passage text removed]], and α4 blockade abolishes Th1 but only partially reduces Th17 spinal cord accumulation, failing to prevent Th17 entry into the cerebrum in an atypical brain-EAE model [fncel.2023.1101379].

**Crossing the endothelium is not sufficient.** Entry is a genuinely two-step process: cells first accumulate in perivascular cuffs/subarachnoid space, then must cross the astrocytic **glia limitans** to reach parenchyma — and clinical signs in EAE begin only at that second step, mediated in part by TNF-induced MMP-2/MMP-9 [PMC8902072]. In the perivascular/subarachnoid space, T cells must re-encounter cognate antigen on border-associated macrophages/APCs; this local reactivation is the prerequisite for parenchymal invasion [PMC8902072]. Healthy CNS lacks MHC II, but blood-derived myeloid cells and B cells in perivascular spaces express it constitutively, and astrocytes/microglia upregulate it under IFN-γ [PMC3679999].

## 2. Entry route B: choroid plexus / blood–CSF barrier, and the meninges

The choroid plexus (ChP) epithelium forms the blood–CSF barrier and gates immune entry into CSF [PMC11634642]. In EAE, CCR6⁺ Th17 entry through the ChP is required for disease initiation [Reboldi et al., cited in fimmu.2023.1233908]. Direct flow-cytometric comparison showed ChP CD45⁺ cells and CD4⁺ T cells increase **before EAE onset** and before their rise in CSF, and remain elevated while brain/spinal cord counts decline in chronic disease — supporting the ChP as an entry site and reservoir; notably, effector Th diapedesis across the blood–CSF barrier in vitro did not require CCR6–CCL20 interaction [PMC10236715 / springermedizin summary]. Imaging supports early ChP involvement: iron-oxide nanoparticles accumulated in choroid plexus and spinal cord meninges in asymptomatic pre-onset EAE mice, before overt inflammation [MDC-Berlin record of the VSOP study]. The meninges are also a permissive port, with constitutively high ICAM-1 and DC presence preceding parenchymal accumulation [[passage text removed]]. For B cells specifically, blocking [passage text removed] each reduced migration (approximately 20%, 40% and 60% respectively), implicating VCAM-1–VLA-4 as dominant for leptomeningeal B-cell recruitment [PMC9221446].

## 3. Barrier failure amplifies entry

BBB breakdown on gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the earliest detectable event in most new MS lesions [PMC3207130]. Post-mortem work localises leakiness to tight junctions, with loss/mislocalisation of claudin-5, occludin and ZO-1 across MS stages, accompanied by fibrinogen leakage [PMC6350359]. Barrier failure is not purely a bystander effect of infiltration: brain microvascular endothelial-like cells differentiated from MS-patient iPSCs show **intrinsic** deficits in junctional integrity, diffusion barrier, efflux pump activity and adhesion-molecule phenotype, partially correctable by Wnt/β-catenin activation [PMC10200307]. In progressive MS, gadolinium enhancement is rare yet fibrin deposition and tight-junction abnormalities persist in cortex and normal-appearing white matter [[passage text removed]]. This is a comprehensive review synthesis area covered by Zierfuss, Larochelle & Prat, *Lancet Neurology* 2024;23(1):95–109 [Semantic Scholar Corpus ID 266200521].

## 4. How injury is then sustained

**T-cell licensing of myeloid effectors.** GM-CSF is the non-redundant T-cell cytokine: autoreactive Th cells lacking GM-CSF fail to initiate neuroinflammation despite making IL-17A or IFN-γ, while GM-CSF from *Ifng⁻/⁻Il17a⁻/⁻* Th cells suffices to induce EAE [https://doi.org/10.1038/ni.2027]; Th17 encephalitogenicity depends on IL-1/IL-23-induced GM-CSF [El-Behi et al., cited in [passage text removed]]. GM-CSF mobilises Ly-6Cʰⁱ monocytes that enter the CNS and acquire DC-like antigen-presenting capacity in situ, and peripheral myeloid cells rather than microglia are the key GM-CSF responders [PMC3535446]. Activated myeloid cells then strip myelin and secrete ROS, nitric oxide, TNF and IL-1β [[passage text removed]].

**Humoral effector arm.** In a subset of patients, active lesions (Lucchinetti pattern II) show immunoglobulin and C9neo (membrane attack [passage text removed], indicating antibody- and complement-mediated demyelination [PMC7035238; PubMed 9546327]. These patterns are stable within a patient over time [PMC4070313].

**Tissue-resident adaptive cells make inflammation self-sustaining.** In chronic progressive MS autopsies, T cells increase from normal-appearing white matter to active/mixed lesions; perivascular T-cell clustering occurred only in progressive cases and correlated with higher proportions of mixed active/inactive lesions and lesion load. CD8⁺ T cells sat mostly perivascularly, but in mixed active/inactive lesions 16.3% were in parenchyma, bearing a Tʀᴍ phenotype (CD69, CD103, CD44, CD49a, PD-1; no S1P1) with markers of homing (CXCR6) and reactivation (Ki-67) [[passage text removed]].

**Meningeal compartmentalisation drives cortical injury.** Ectopic B-cell follicle-like structures — containing proliferating CD20⁺ B cells, plasma cells, CD4⁺/CD8⁺ T cells and CD35⁺ follicular dendritic cell networks — were found in the meninges entering cerebral sulci of 41.4% of SPMS cases and were associated with younger onset, faster disability/death, and more cortical demyelination, microglial activation and neurite loss; all such follicles lay adjacent to large subpial lesions, implicating diffusible pathogenic factors [PubMed 17438020]. In a larger series, follicle-like structures were present in 49/123 SPMS cases (40%), correlating with microglial activation and grey matter demyelination [PubMed 21840891]. Quantitatively, meningeal T- and B-cell (but not myeloid) accumulations were spatially adjacent to subpial lesions and associated with more active/mixed white matter lesions [JCI Insight, insight.jci.org/articles/view/151683], which also notes that subpial lesions occur without major BBB disturbance, sparse parenchymal infiltration and little terminal complement — i.e. a mechanism distinct from classic white matter plaques.

**Chronic active lesions: injury behind a relatively intact barrier.** These "slowly expanding"/smouldering lesions have a hypocellular demyelinated core ringed by iron-laden, chronically activated microglia/macrophages, and represent compartmentalised inflammation behind a relatively intact BBB [[passage text removed]]. Pathologically, iron rims were present in 11 of 24 slowly expanding lesions, iron localised to microglia/macrophages, and rim lesions expanded in vivo over 3.5 years whereas rimless lesions tended to shrink; rims were scarcely seen in remyelinated lesions, suggesting they impair repair [[passage text removed]; PMC5209400]. The lesion **edge**, not the core, carries the microglia/macrophage inflammatory signature that supports ongoing myelin breakdown and axonal injury [fimmu.2026.1901957]. Mechanistically, the inflammation-induced oxidative burst in microglia/macrophages produces reactive oxygen and nitrogen species causing oxidative damage, mitochondrial dysfunction and energy failure ("histotoxic/virtual hypoxia"), amplified by true hypoxia around inflamed vessels — a proposed explanation for watershed-area lesion accumulation [[passage text removed]]. The endpoint is axonal transection, common in MS lesions and the likely correlate of irreversible disability [Trapp et al., *[passage text removed], as cited in practicalneurology.com/.../30127]; the same source notes axons can be attacked directly by CD8⁺ cytotoxic lymphocytes given class I expression on axons.

## Caveats

- The relative contribution of each entry route in **human** MS (versus EAE) remains inferential; ChP-priority evidence is largely from EAE and MRI/nanoparticle studies.
- Whether the ChP mechanisms observed are pathogenic or homeostatic is explicitly unresolved [PMC11634642].
- Meningeal inflammation is **not MS-specific** and also occurs in B-cell lymphoma and TB meningitis [[passage text removed]], so its presence alone does not prove causality.
- Complement findings are heterogeneous: one cohort dominated by long-standing progressive disease found near-universal upstream C1/C3d in active lesions without pattern II C9neo, unlike Lucchinetti's early-MS cohort [[passage text removed]; PMC4070313].
- Slowly expanding lesions on MRI are not yet histopathologically validated as chronic active lesions, unlike paramagnetic rim lesions [medrxiv 2025.12.03.25341192].
- I found no source in this search characterising the quantitative flux of cells through each route in living patients; that gap is real.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Peripheral immune cells enter the CNS by a multistep, adhesion‑molecule–dependent route across the blood–brain barrier (BBB) and via alternative gateways (choroid plexus/blood–CSF barrier and meningeal vessels), must be locally re‑activated at CNS borders before breaching the glia limitans, and then sustain injury through cytokine‑driven myeloid recruitment, cytotoxic and antibody/complement effector mechanisms, and oxidative/mitochondrial damage — a process that becomes self‑sustaining once inflammation is compartmentalized behind a re‑sealed barrier.

## 1. Getting in: the multistep cascade at the BBB

Leukocyte entry proceeds through selectin‑mediated rolling, adhesion, "crawling," and diapedesis, with ICAM‑1/VCAM‑1 on endothelium engaging LFA‑1/VLA‑4 on T cells as the central axis [S:72ec7cc5-8b32-5f7e-8659-49a60c560729][S:9ed33755-02ea-5324-a8ea-7bd0c419c303]. Pharmacological proof of principle is natalizumab, an anti‑α4‑integrin antibody that blocks VLA‑4/VCAM‑1 interaction and markedly reduces CNS lymphocyte numbers, relapses, and lesions; interferon‑β additionally lowers leukocyte MMP9, which facilitates migration across endothelial and extracellular barriers [S:8f74b94c-9838-5b78-becf-cb3a28ff9598][S:47b630d9-ac6c-5e54-9271-ff08a53791e4].

Beyond this canonical pair, several immunoglobulin‑superfamily molecules are upregulated at the MS BBB and on pathogenic subsets:
- **ALCAM (CD166)**, which co‑localizes with leukocyte CD6 in the transmigratory cup, is upregulated in active MS and EAE lesions, and whose blockade restricts CD4⁺ T cell, monocyte and B cell transmigration and attenuates EAE [S:19cc631e-5b46-5e30-b969-7c2e23e17822].
- **MCAM (CD146)**, expressed on BBB endothelium and on activated memory CD4⁺/CD8⁺ cells, promoting adhesion and diapedesis and Th1/Th17 migration [S:45a5be98-0a76-5a60-9436-a3ef89f6dcc2][S:72ec7cc5-8b32-5f7e-8659-49a60c560729].
- **DICAM**, which promotes Th17 migration and is upregulated in active relapsing and progressive MS; blocking antibodies improve EAE [S:72ec7cc5-8b32-5f7e-8659-49a60c560729].
- **JAML**, upregulated on the MS BBB and on patient monocytes and CD8⁺ T cells, forming JAML⁺ transmigratory cups; blocking JAML compromises their migration [S:627fc4e7-ce9b-528b-9528-c0ac050ff285]. Its ligand CAR is also expressed in choroid plexus, implicating JAML at both the BBB and the blood–CSF barrier [S:3a880cfc-3b71-5bb8-91cf-1cd7a9187b86].

## 2. Alternative gateways: choroid plexus and meninges

The choroid plexus is a major entry route: T cells first extravasate through fenestrated choroidal capillaries (shown to be P‑selectin–dependent) into stroma, then must cross the epithelial blood–CSF barrier [S:839410eb-5220-5793-84e6-3f7a785b7fef]. Choroid plexus epithelium constitutively expresses CCL20, and CCR6⁺ Th17 cells use this axis to enter the non‑inflamed CNS; CCR6‑deficient mice are highly resistant to EAE, and wild‑type T cells entering early trigger massive CCR6‑independent recruitment across activated parenchymal vessels — defining distinct ports of entry into non‑inflamed versus inflamed CNS [S:2832f97f-0b58-54eb-b0e2-bbff0cb724a2][S:519f2f7e-6875-5348-bb13-45e5682226d8]. In MS brains the choroid plexus shows abundant HLA‑DR⁺ cells and inflammatory change [S:803d4439-af20-59fb-b22a-ffed55410800], VCAM‑1 is induced in its fenestrated microvasculature [S:519f2f7e-6875-5348-bb13-45e5682226d8], and [passage text removed] EAE [S:065f9f78-f981-54b9-8361-add15fd3b7ec]. Human Th17 cells cross a choroid plexus epithelial model more readily than other Th subsets, though transmigration rates across the epithelium are far lower than across brain endothelium [S:839410eb-5220-5793-84e6-3f7a785b7fef]. **Caveat:** direct in vivo evidence for T cell passage between choroid plexus epithelial cells remains limited and inconsistent across EAE studies, so the plexus may function more as a gateway to CSF than a site of accumulation [S:ea848c92-1326-5df4-973d-f431010118e2]. Meningeal vessels form a distinct blood–meningeal barrier lacking astrocyte endfeet, which may be easier to penetrate [S:78861a8a-6e72-566f-be61-3d82de100f07]; EAE time‑course work found earliest T cell recruitment at meninges and choroid plexus rather than parenchymal vasculature, preceding VCAM‑1 upregulation in deeper tracts [S:127d1246-9c83-5e0a-85bb-ed8d0f791b1e].

## 3. The two‑step barrier: local reactivation and the glia limitans

Crossing the endothelium is not sufficient. Two‑photon imaging in EAE shows disease‑inducing T cells first reach the subarachnoid or perivascular space, where recognition of cognate antigen on border‑associated macrophages drives local reactivation and proliferation — a prerequisite for parenchymal infiltration [S:0f117506-909b-59b6-a182-8585915a9cab][S:2c0fa30a-a20a-58ef-a0a0-132ad5959a11][S:55fc3b07-7676-5a3b-a64d-c58530a78b09]. Reactivation releases TNF‑α/IFN‑γ and IL‑17, which enhance MMP‑2/MMP‑9 activity at the glia limitans; MMP‑2/‑9–deficient mice are completely resistant to clinical EAE despite massive perivascular immune accumulation, because these proteases cleave astrocytic β‑dystroglycan and detach endfeet from the parenchymal basement membrane [S:0f117506-909b-59b6-a182-8585915a9cab]. Reactivation also amplifies trafficking signals on the barriers, recruiting further waves of cells [S:fb880af8-467c-5b46-9fed-4d515977537c].

## 4. Sustaining tissue injury

- **Cytokine amplification loop:** the IL‑23/Th17/GM‑CSF axis is central; GM‑CSF‑deficient mice are resistant to EAE, GM‑CSF is required to recruit inflammatory macrophages, and it acts back on dendritic cells to raise IL‑23, perpetuating chronic inflammation [S:135ce2f6-eebf-566f-a552-d2365ae353b7][S:6aa6dde6-03e1-5d33-b7da-bad0c89ebc99]. IL‑17A downregulates BBB tight‑junction proteins, increasing permeability and further recruitment, impairs oligodendrocyte survival, and can be directly neurotoxic (e.g., granzyme B release onto human neurons) [S:a3061130-7aa5-50e3-b12b-2e9495114d14].
- **Cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells:** CD8⁺ T cells are [passage text removed]:d79e3ebf-3a4c-5880-be2e-4e1331b310ef], produce IFN‑γ/TNF‑α and kill oligodendrocytes and neurons [S:1b6f3091-5f47-54cc-b3f2-20ecf4a291f2]; in a virus‑induced demyelination model, CD8⁺ T cells were the critical mediators of axon injury with perforin as the key effector molecule [S:d1af3959-82ed-51c8-b5a7-2efb8b52cc28].
- **Antibody and complement:** intrathecal IgG synthesis and oligoclonal bands occur in the large majority of patients, clonally expanded B cells accumulate in lesions and CSF, and IgG plus complement deposition is frequent at sites of active demyelination [S:33e217d5-a945-513e-affb-3428891c025d][S:359846e0-a51d-5508-9f3b-a296d123dc65]; consistent co‑localization of complement, antibody and Fcγ receptors in phagocytic macrophages argues that antibody/complement‑mediated myelin phagocytosis is a dominant demyelinating mechanism in established MS [S:91ac7c90-2e54-573b-9fb8-a6999cca9471]. Lassmann notes, however, that demyelination patterns in MS are heterogeneous, implying different mechanisms across patient subgroups [S:df67a1f3-a9bb-5521-a85b-680cce4b80c3].
- **Myeloid oxidative injury:** infiltrated monocyte‑derived macrophages dominate perivascular infiltrates and release ROS, NO and cytokines; ROS also feed back to enhance monocyte adhesion/migration and BBB dysfunction [S:7f352d98-cc89-5431-bdd0-2aeb79da6632]. A greater proportion of monocyte‑derived macrophages than microglia express ROS‑producing enzymes in EAE, and phagocyte ROS injures both myelin and axons, mitigated by ROS/RNS scavengers [S:eab22635-dfd4-526f-842a-bd1b0d439594]. NADPH oxidase subunits and myeloperoxidase are upregulated in active and slowly expanding MS lesions, with oxidized lipids/DNA in oligodendrocytes and transected axons [S:65abf7e5-0309-54a7-8049-9c2a9c958b7a]; peroxynitrite inhibits complex I, whose activity is reduced in chronic MS lesions, creating a mitochondrial injury–energy failure–ionic imbalance cycle [S:9c9df444-af53-5f54-8831-12417c78a241].

## 5. Why injury persists: compartmentalization

With progression, T cells, B cells and plasma cells become trapped behind a closed or repaired BBB, forming follicle‑like meningeal aggregates and large perivascular cuffs associated with active cortical demyelination, slowly expanding white matter lesions, and diffuse normal‑appearing white/grey matter injury [S:4227a86e-79ba-5eaa-9cef-fd9d7346f6c8][S:56ec532e-0c73-587c-9243-d35ec2280f64]. Ectopic B cell follicles are found in a substantial subset of secondary progressive MS, typically adjacent to large subpial lesions, and mark patients with more pronounced cortical demyelination, microglial activation, axonal/neuronal loss, earlier onset and faster progression [S:92fe5255-0aa1-522b-a38b-3d624c99654d][S:a1681480-c5a6-5857-b914-af18575948bd]. In a quantitative postmortem study of 27 progressive MS patients, meningeal T and B cell (but not myeloid) accumulations were spatially adjacent to subpial lesions, larger accumulations tracked with larger subpial lesion area, and higher meningeal inflammation went with a greater proportion of active/mixed white matter lesions [S:f7d46af8-58d5-505e-980b-b836d67f0d2e]. Mechanistically this is attributed to diffusion of cytokines, antibody and complement into cortex driving microglial activation [S:81bae63b-2ed6-5aa0-8f11-6d766701ea32][S:622fff72-d331-5d21-bbe9-5fe5e8152d5b]; leptomeningeal TNF‑α/IFN‑γ overexpression in rats reproduces meningeal inflammation, cortical demyelination and neuronal loss [S:622fff72-d331-5d21-bbe9-5fe5e8152d5b]. Persistence is reinforced by CD8⁺ tissue‑resident memory T cells that dominate MS lesions, show low activation/proliferation, and downregulate S1P receptors — hence escape fingolimod/siponimod and α4‑integrin blockade, which act on recruitment rather than cells already inside [S:4227a86e-79ba-5eaa-9cef-fd9d7346f6c8][S:df67a1f3-a9bb-5521-a85b-680cce4b80c3][S:3a1600d7-19d9-5e93-a7e4-cb070f518a51]. Finally, as inflammation declines with progression, oxidative injury is amplified by age‑ and burden‑related mechanisms including damage‑driven microglial activation, ROS from damaged mitochondria, and iron accumulation liberated in active lesions [S:0c62a2c0-9a4b-5cfe-9103-bc9267bedd4f].

**Uncertainty to flag:** the direct pathological link between cortical lesions and meningeal inflammation remains contested, as some autopsy series find no meningeal follicles or relationship [S:81bae63b-2ed6-5aa0-8f11-6d766701ea32], and whether choroid plexus immune recruitment is beneficial or deleterious in some settings is unresolved [S:ea848c92-1326-5df4-973d-f431010118e2].

rows.question: Which glial activation biomarkers in CSF or serum track astrocyte and microglial involvement in multiple sclerosis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Astrocyte involvement is tracked by glial fibrillary acidic protein and by S100 calcium-binding protein B, which is raised in both cerebrospinal fluid and serum at relapsing-remitting diagnosis and is concentrated in reactive astrocytes within active lesions; Microglial and macrophage activation is tracked by soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2, which is raised in cerebrospinal fluid in this disease; The astrocyte and myeloid markers correlate positively in cerebrospinal fluid, indicating that the two cell types activate in concert; None of these markers is specific to glia or to the central nervous system, between-person variability is wide, and results across studied markers have been inconsistent, so combinations of markers with imaging rather than any single measure are what is being pursued. Certainty: The marker-to-cell-type mapping is reasonably supported but their clinical value remains unproven. Scope: applies to multiple sclerosis in patients sampled in cerebrospinal fluid and serum, specialist neurology settings. An answer is wrong if it presents these markers as validated for routine clinical use.

answers.websearch:
**Conclusion:** The best-supported glial fluid biomarkers in MS are GFAP (astrocytes; CSF and serum), with S100B and SERPINA3 as additional astrocytic candidates, and CHIT1, CHI3L1/YKL-40, sTREM2, sCD163/sCD14 and ferritin as myeloid/microglial markers — GFAP and CHIT1/CHI3L1 having the strongest links to progressive, non-relapsing biology.

**Astrocytic markers**

- **GFAP** is the intermediate-filament protein of astrocytes, released into CSF on astrocyte damage and reaching blood after blood–brain-barrier disruption ([PMC11279275]([passage text removed])). CSF and serum GFAP are higher in progressive than relapsing MS and in controls, and serum GFAP correlates with disease severity and MRI lesion count (10.1038/s41598-018-33158-8). In a multicentre PPMS cohort, serum GFAP correlated with EDSS after age correction, while CHI3L1 and sTREM2 did not (10.3389/fneur.2019.00280). In a two-cohort CSF study, GFAP correlated with slowly expanding lesion (SEL) count (r = 0.33) and SEL T2 volume fraction (r = 0.24) but **not** with acute inflammatory measures, was unaffected by anti-CD20, and predicted long-term confirmed disability progression (HR [passage text removed]) — i.e. it tracks non-relapsing progressive biology (PMID 38466277; JAMA Neurol 81:373–383). Serum GFAP > 65 pg/mL was associated with PIRA in early RRMS (OR [passage text removed]; 10.1007/s00415-024-12389-y), and in fingolimod-treated patients sGFAP Z-scores predicted PIRA (HR 1.64, 95% CI 1.16–2.32) whereas [passage text removed]) (PMID 41237262). Practical caveat: GFAP is strongly age-, sex- and BMI-dependent, so Z-scores/percentiles against healthy-control reference databases are being used, and Simoa and Elecsys values differ ~54% (PMID 41453834).
- **S100B** (astrocytic, also a RAGE ligand) is raised in CSF/serum of relapsing-remitting MS and in active demyelinating lesions, and behaves as a marker of the relapsing phase rather than progression (PMID 26184632; PMID 12076997; [PMC8033985]([passage text removed])).
- **SERPINA3** (reactive-astrocyte-secreted) was elevated in CSF only in primary progressive MS, correlated with [passage text removed]), and was unchanged by ocrelizumab (AAN 2025 abstract AAN2025‑002542).

**Microglial/macrophage markers**

- **CHIT1 (chitotriosidase)**: CSF CHIT1 at diagnostic lumbar puncture predicted faster disability progression, and single-cell/nuclear transcriptomics plus neuropathology localised CHIT1 to a microglial subset enriched in actively demyelinating/active lesions and absent from inactive lesions and normal-appearing white matter (10.1038/s41467-024-49312-y). Earlier work in 143 patients showed CSF CHIT1 reflects early microglial activation and predicts later disease activity (Oldoni et al., Ann Neurol 2020;87:633–645). In progressive MS, CSF CHIT1 correlated with lesion volume, reduced lesional magnetization transfer ratio and altered diffusion in normal-appearing white matter, and fell with natalizumab (10.1016/j.jneuroim.2026 — [KU Copenhagen record](https://researchprofiles.ku.dk/en/publications/[passage text removed]-pat)); CSF CHIT1 also correlated with gadolinium-enhancing lesions (R = 0.33), CSF NfL (R = 0.58) and SEL volume (R = 0.38), and dropped ~41% (RMS) and ~27% (PPMS) at week 52 of ocrelizumab, making it a treatment-responsive myeloid marker (AAN2025‑002542).
- **CHI3L1 / YKL-40** is secreted by monocytes/microglia and activated astrocytes, so it is a mixed glial marker (10.1007/s10072-023-06764-2). Meta-analysis: CSF CHI3L1 higher in MS than controls and than CIS, higher in converting than non-converting CIS, and higher in PPMS and SPMS than RRMS (10.1212/NXI.0000000000001164). CSF YKL-40 and GFAP were independent prognostic markers of disability progression (PMID 25732842), and CHI3L1 independently predicted 1-point EDSS worsening ([passage text removed]; 10.3389/fneur.2019.01008). It is not CNS-specific and findings are not uniform — some cohorts found no link with conversion to SPMS or disability progression ([PMC11674340]([passage text removed])).
- **sTREM2** (shed ectodomain of a microglial/macrophage receptor) is increased in MS CSF, correlates with CSF GFAP, NfL and inflammatory cytokines, and has been linked to EDSS/MS severity, though not consistently across studies ([PMC12569355]([passage text removed]); 10.3389/fimmu.2025.1495529). In the PPMS cohort above, CSF sTREM2 correlated with CSF NfL (ρ = 0.4) and with CHI3L1 (ρ = 0.4) but not with clinical severity (10.3389/fneur.2019.00280). CHI3L1 correlates strongly with CHIT1 (r > 0.5) and modestly with sTREM2 (r ≈ 0.3), indicating these capture partly distinct myeloid states (Oldoni, Ann Neurol 2020;87:633–645).
- **sCD163 and sCD14** (macrophage/microglial activation): the sCD163 CSF/serum ratio is increased in newly diagnosed MS and, added to a panel (CXCL13 ratio, neopterin ratio, CSF NfL, IgG index, serum osteopontin), improved discrimination of MS from symptomatic controls (10.1371/journal.pone.0119681; [PMC4041861](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4041861)).
- **Ferritin** (iron-handling microglia/macrophages) was highest in secondary progressive MS and, unlike S100B, was not tied to relapse timing (PMID 12076997); CSF ferritin and S100B correlated in RRMS (PMID 17893112).

**Framing:** a recent review positions NfL as the acute axonal-damage marker, GFAP as increased in progressive MS and an emerging marker of progression independent of relapses, and CHI3L1 as an emerging marker linked to PIRA and to MRI lesion types including paramagnetic rim lesions ([Lancet Neurol review]([passage text removed])); a consensus on smouldering-associated worsening names GFAP and CHI3L1 as the most promising candidates (10.3390/ijms262411774). None of these are yet validated for routine clinical use, and all reflect glial activation generically rather than a specific pathogenic (damaging vs reparative) glial role (10.3389/fneur.2019.00280).

## Answer

Two astrocyte markers (GFAP, S100B) and a set of myeloid/microglial markers (CHIT1, CHI3L1/YKL-40, sTREM2, sCD163/sCD14, osteopontin) are the fluid biomarkers used to track glial involvement in MS; GFAP and CHIT1/CHI3L1 have the strongest prognostic evidence, and only GFAP is well established in blood.

### Astrocyte markers

**GFAP** — an astrocytic intermediate filament whose release reflects astrogliosis and astrocyte damage; CSF levels are higher in progressive than relapsing MS and correlate with EDSS, making it a supplementary prognostic indicator [S:4ca2e7e2, S:46d27797]. A single-centre CSF study replicated the PMS > RRMS gradient and situates it against a meta-analysis showing CSF GFAP elevated in MS versus healthy controls without a PPMS/SPMS difference [S:05e488b1]. Serum GFAP correlates with its CSF level and with MS disease severity [S:20daebb0], and is not affected by acute inflammatory activity, which is why it is proposed as a marker of non-active progressive pathology [S:44875038]. In a multinational individual-participant analysis, blood GFAP predicted future confirmed disability worsening in progressive MS — particularly SPMS — whereas NfL predicted it only in PPMS [S:2cf41e1b]. In a proteomic/DTI cohort, GFAP was unaffected by DMTs, was the best discriminator of relapsing versus progressive MS, and was the only protein predicting disability progression over 5 years [S:b78c31b9]. The evidence is not uniform: in primary progressive MS, serum GFAP did not predict progression in the absence of relapses/MRI activity [S:724df493], and in one cohort higher GFAP related only to reaching EDSS 3, not to relapse-associated worsening or PIRA except in patients with low NfL [S:d232136d]. In newly diagnosed RRMS, baseline CSF GFAP independently predicted 1-year confirmed disability progression ([passage text removed]), as did CSF CHI3L1 ([passage text removed]) [S:1e41a79f].

**S100B** — astrocyte-derived, also reflecting BBB dysfunction; elevated in CSF at RRMS diagnosis with reactive astrocytes identified as the predominant source in lesions [S:9b37581a], and CSF/blood levels reported to track severity and progression [S:6bb7e816]. But it is less astrocyte-specific than GFAP [S:b9d19469], results are inconsistent (several studies found no MS-vs-control or subtype difference) [S:46d27797], and its sensitivity/specificity are only modest, so its practical role is minor next to GFAP [S:0f1b10b9].

### Microglial/macrophage markers

**CHIT1 (chitotriosidase)** — secreted predominantly by activated microglia and localised to lipid-laden microglia in actively demyelinating lesions [S:0e03d095, S:080fb5b6]. In 143 patients, CSF CHIT1 at diagnostic lumbar puncture predicted reduced lesion tissue integrity (~3 years later, p = 9.6E-04) and disease severity (~5 years later, p = 1.2E-04), distinguished slow from fast disability progression (AUC = 85%), [passage text removed] acted independently of NfL [S:bff20a8a]. Serum CHIT1 was recently linked to imaged glial activation: it [passage text removed] (ρ = 0.27, p = 0.045) and all active lesions (ρ = 0.27, p = 0.048) on [¹¹C]PK11195 TSPO-PET, with a trend to higher levels in progressive versus relapsing MS (30.4 vs 18.8 ng/ml; p = 0.056) [S:8c49af4b].

**CHI3L1/YKL-40** — produced mainly by reactive astrocytes with a microglial/macrophage contribution, so it straddles both compartments [S:5c4aa545, S:fa8a5fbc]. CSF YKL-40 is raised in CIS patients who convert to definite MS (p = 0.00002), correlates with gadolinium-enhancing and T2 lesions, and predicts earlier progression to EDSS 3 (HR 2.78, 95% CI [passage text removed] EDSS 6 (HR 4.57, 95% CI 1.01–20.83; p = 0.05) [S:bbd49f7f]. CSF levels are higher in progressive than relapsing MS and track motor, cognitive and radiological disability [S:63f3a07f], and CHI3L1 is [passage text removed] [S:0bf2b1dc]. It is an independent predictor of progression even after accounting for NfL, supporting combined axonal + glial panels [S:5bb7f90c]. Blood measurement is less reliable: plasma CHI3L1 associated with TSPO-PET glial activation, brain volume loss and EDSS (0.70, 0.12–1.28; p = 0.019) [S:5171e5ba, S:bedcd482], but one newly diagnosed treatment-naïve RRMS cohort found CSF but not serum YKL-40 elevated versus controls [S:c199d46e].

**sTREM2** — shed from microglia by ADAM cleavage and used as a surrogate of microglial activation [S:66043f55, S:a99ca71e]. CSF sTREM2 was increased in RRMS, SPMS and PPMS versus controls and normalised after natalizumab and fell after mitoxantrone [S:276bbb50, S:97a9373f]. It correlates with inflammatory cytokines (IL-8, G-CSF, IL-5) and with CSF GFAP, linking microglial and astrocytic activation [S:a99ca71e, S:8f7bc7ce]. Findings need validation in larger cohorts before it can be considered an established microglial biomarker [S:e6d4ae31].

**sCD163 and sCD14** — myeloid surface proteins released into CSF; [passage text removed] RRMS and PPMS, indicating intrathecal production and macrophage activation in lesions (ROC AUC 0.72) [S:a61b91fc, S:58ae5a51]. Both are proposed as markers of intrathecal microglial/macrophage activation for monitoring activity and treatment response [S:4b1e838b].

**Osteopontin (SPP1)** — released by microglia, macrophages and other cells and reflecting innate immune activation [S:fc6ba2c2]. CSF OPN was increased during [passage text removed]) exacerbations versus other neurological disorders, fell by 3 weeks, and was elevated in PPMS (p = 0.004) in association with disability [S:8ceee843].

### Caveats

- Blood-based microglial markers remain a gap: GFAP (astrocytic) and NfL (axonal) are the two established blood biomarkers in MS, with no validated blood marker of microglial activation [S:5171e5ba].
- Assay sensitivity drives discrepancies — GFAP is now measured by Simoa because ELISA cannot reliably detect it [S:05e488b1]; one study could not detect CSF GFAP by ELISA at all, and its serum ELISA GFAP entered no predictive model [S:5a00fb6b].
- None of these markers is MS-specific: YKL-40 is also raised in CNS infections and neurodegenerative disease [S:5bb7f90c], and sTREM2, CHIT1 and S100B are elevated across ALS, Alzheimer's and brain injury [S:51b0aae8, S:9570c01a, S:bf2d2b7b… see S:bf2dbc7b].

rows.question: What clinical and serological profile do adults with myasthenia gravis show in multi-country observational registry cohorts?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: The enrolled population is predominantly older adults with a slight female majority and, at enrolment, a median disease duration of several years; Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are much the commonest serological group, with muscle-specific kinase antibodies a small minority, and a substantial minority present with purely ocular disease at diagnosis; Most enrolled patients are on immunotherapy, only a small minority need three or more concurrent immunotherapies, and a minority have undergone thymectomy; Composite severity scores are lower at the most recent visit than at the first across serostatus groups, an observation in a treated cohort with no untreated comparator. Certainty: This is a description of an enrolled population rather than a tested relationship. Scope: applies to myasthenia gravis in adults enrolled in multi-country observational registries, specialist outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it states that muscle-specific kinase antibody positive patients had markedly worse recorded outcomes than acetylcholine receptor antibody positive patients.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Across multi-country observational cohorts, adult MG is dominated by AChR-antibody–positive generalised disease with a bimodal age/sex pattern: clinician-entered and patient-reported international registries show a female majority, mean age in the late 40s–50s, ~75–80% AChR+, ~4–7% MuSK+, ~15–30% seronegative, mostly mild-to-moderate MGFA class I–II disease, near-universal immunotherapy exposure and a high burden of thyroid, cardiovascular and psychiatric comorbidity — whereas population-wide Nordic registries, which capture unselected incident cases, are slightly male-predominant with half of cases having very-late onset (≥65 years).

## Evidence

**MGBase (global clinician-entered registry, 8 countries).** From October 2021 to April 2024, 565 patients were enrolled from 16 clinics in 8 countries (Australia 323, South Africa 97, Hungary 65, Greece 34, Kuwait 30, Mexico 12, Croatia 2, Turkey 2), growing to 1225 patients from 15 countries by May 2025 [[passage text removed]]. The cohort is 56% female, mean age 57 (SD 19) years at last visit, median disease duration 5 years (IQR 1.8–10.8) [[passage text removed]]. Serology was recorded in 514/565 (91.0%): 393 (76.5%) AChR+, 35 (6.8%) MuSK+, 5 (1.0%) VGCC+ (consistent with LEMS), and 81 (15.8%) seronegative [[passage text removed]]. Serostatus tracked phenotype: at diagnosis 33.2% of the whole cohort was MGFA class I, but MuSK+ patients clustered in bulbar-predominant class IIb (53.6%) with only 14.3% class I, while seronegative patients were most often class I (43.3%); MuSK+ patients also had the highest mean MG Composite at first visit (10.9, SD 8.8 vs 8.4, SD 8.3 overall), falling to 3.1 (SD 4.5) at last visit [[passage text removed]]. Immunotherapy was used in 87%, ≥3 concurrent immunotherapies in 7%, and thymectomy in 24% [[passage text removed]]. The authors note Australian-led recruitment bias [[passage text removed]].

**MyRealWorld MG (patient-reported digital study, 7–9 countries).** Of 1693 enrolled participants, 69% of 1586 reporting were female, mean age 49.9 years (SD 14.8), with Italy (38.7%) and the USA (33.4%) contributing most; of 1520 reporting MG type, 88.5% were generalised and 11.5% ocular; 68.8% reported being antibody-positive vs 31.2% negative (plus 13.6% tested but unable to recall the result), and among 826 reporting antibody type, 87.8% AChR, 2.4% LRP4, and 62 patients MuSK [[passage text removed]]. Commonest comorbidities among 966 respondents were thyroid problems (37.5%), hypertension (31.4%) and anxiety (28.0%); 52.7% and 43.2% of 889 HADS respondents scored at least mild anxiety and depression respectively; 83.7% of 1412 had received ≥1 routine MG treatment in the prior 12 months and over 30% [passage text removed]/PMC10186408][[passage text removed]]. In the baseline HRQoL analysis ([passage text removed]), self-assessed MGFA distribution [passage text removed] — i.e. most patients in mild-to-moderate generalised classes — and MGFA class strongly predicted every HRQoL domain [[passage text removed]-].

**Nordic population-based registries (Denmark, Finland, Sweden).** In the incident subcohort (n = 1559 / 1797 / 3059), 51–52% were men; median age at diagnosis was 64.9, 64.9 and 67.5 years; 50% (Denmark, Finland) to 55% (Sweden) had very-late-onset MG (≥65 years); men were diagnosed older than women (median 67.4 vs 62.6 years); prevalence was nonetheless higher in women overall, and standardised mortality ratios were modestly elevated (1.32, 1.23, 1.20) with [passage text removed] leading causes of death [[passage text removed]]. In the companion comorbidity/treatment analysis of 8819 people with MG (3159 incident, mean age at diagnosis 59.2–62.5 years, balanced sex distribution), circulatory disease was the most frequent pre-diagnosis comorbidity (19%–29%, largely hypertension 13%–24%); anaemia and osteoporosis prevalence rose three- to six-fold after diagnosis; mental health disorders were commoner in those aged 0–64 than ≥65; acetylcholinesterase inhibitors were the most used first-year treatment in Finland (41%) and Sweden (34%) versus corticosteroids plus non-steroidal immunosuppression in Denmark (33%); by year 5, 40%–47% were on non-steroidal immunosuppression, corticosteroids or both, and only 5%–7% remained treatment-naive [[passage text removed]/PMC13138348].

## Caveats

- The apparent contradiction (female-predominant, younger clinical/patient registries vs male-predominant, elderly population registries) reflects ascertainment: MGBase and MyRealWorld recruit from specialist clinics and advocacy/app channels, while the Nordic cohorts capture all ICD-coded incident cases [[passage text removed]].
- MyRealWorld antibody and MGFA data are patient-reported (including recall of the clinician's classification), which likely inflates the "seronegative"/unknown fraction relative to laboratory-verified registries [[passage text removed]].
- The Nordic registry studies do not report antibody serostatus (claims-based ICD coding), so serological profile in those cohorts is unavailable from these sources.
- LRP4 and other rarer antibodies were captured only in MyRealWorld (2.4% of those reporting a type); MGBase did not report an LRP4 category in the extracted results [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** Across the two largest multi-country observational MG cohorts — the clinician-entered MGBase registry and the patient-entered MyRealWorld-MG study — adults with MG are predominantly female, middle-aged to older, overwhelmingly AChR-antibody positive (~three-quarters) with a small MuSK-positive minority and ~15% seronegative; most are generalised rather than purely ocular, most are on immunotherapy, and a large fraction remains symptomatic with substantial functional/quality-of-life impairment.

**Serological profile (MGBase, 8 countries, 16 clinics, 565 patients enrolled Oct 2021–Apr 2024).** Serology was recorded for 514 (91.0%); of these, 393 (76.5%) had AChR antibodies, 35 (6.8%) MuSK antibodies, 81 (15.8%) were seronegative, and 5 (1.0%) had VGCC antibodies consistent with LEMS [S:88bfff14]. The abstract summarises this as 76% AChR ab+ and 7% MuSK ab+ [S:22165e88]. The authors judged serostatus, thymectomy rates and thymic pathology consistent with prior published cohorts [S:a83a4819].

**Demographic and clinical profile (MGBase).** 56% female; mean age 57 (SD 19) years at last visit; median disease duration 5 years (IQR 1.8–10.8); 33% had ocular MG at diagnosis; immunotherapy in 87%, with 7% on three or more concurrent immunotherapies; thymectomy in 24% [S:22165e88]. MGFA class at diagnosis (recorded for 400 patients) was clustered in the milder-to-moderate range — class I 33.2%, IIb 21.5%, IIIb 19.5%, IIa 10.3% — with a clear serological split: MuSK-positive patients were concentrated in bulbar-predominant class IIb (53.6%) and rarely purely ocular (class I 14.3%), whereas seronegative patients were most often class I (43.3%) [S:88bfff14]. Treatment patterns also differed by serostatus, including high rituximab use in MuSK ab+ patients, more than half of whom were on no current immunotherapy [S:a83a4819]. Enrolment has continued to grow (678 records, 18 clinics, 9 countries as of June 2024) [S:a293a699].

**Patient-reported multi-country cohort (MyRealWorld-MG; digital, prospective, up to 10 countries incl. USA, Japan, Germany, UK, Italy, Spain, Canada, France, Belgium, Denmark)** [S:cf7c4161][S:6c022996]. Baseline for [passage text removed]; MGFA distribution [passage text removed]% / 1.6% for classes I–V; mean MG-ADL rose with MGFA class (2.7, 4.4, 6.3, 8.4 for I–IV), as did loss of utility (EQ-5D-5L 0.817 → 0.530) [S:170cbaea]. In larger analyses, 58.4% of 1,859 respondents had moderate-to-severe MG, with utilities well below general-population comparators (EQ-5D-5L 0.739 vs 0.843; HUI3 0.493 vs 0.746), 34.4% taking sick leave in the past month vs 13.2%, and 34.8% needing caregiver help vs 8.3% [S:a8137d10]. In 2,074 participants, 54.9% [passage text removed] the general-population study) and 69.6%/[passage text removed]/depression [S:290ed28d]. Note this cohort skews younger and more female than physician-based registries [S:0f7e61cf], and thymectomy was reported in only ~12% of one subsample [S:380fd079]; a 1,049-patient working-age subsample was 73.4% women, mostly aged 35–54, mean 8 years since diagnosis [S:e2aa4a0a].

**Corroborating multinational physician-reported surveys.** In the Adelphi MG Disease Specific Programme across the US and five European countries (1,232 patients), MGFA class correlated with ADL impairment but with marked within-class heterogeneity — bulbar symptoms and dyspnoea occurred in some class I–II patients, while [passage text removed] had only mild bulbar symptoms/shortness of breath [S:2df99d71]. In the five-country European DSP (778 patient record forms), mean [passage text removed], mean time from onset to diagnosis 332.4 days, 65.3% were MGFA class II or above at diagnosis, ocular myasthenia was reported in ≥50% at diagnosis and ptosis/ocular symptoms persisted in >50% at survey; 62% of 657 patients on chronic treatment still had moderate-to-severe symptoms, and 22.9% had been hospitalised in the prior 12 months [S:2904a484].

**Caveats.** MGBase serology was missing in ~9% and MGFA class in ~29% of enrollees [S:88bfff14][S:22165e88]; MyRealWorld-MG data are entirely patient-reported (including MGFA class) and community-recruited [S:64cc3c3e][S:cf7c4161]; and the Adelphi analyses did not stratify by autoantibody status [S:3c32aa37]. I found no multi-country registry publication in these searches reporting pooled LRP4-antibody frequencies or pooled thymic histopathology breakdowns, so I cannot give figures for those.
