rows.question: Which clinical features at admission shape short-term prognosis in children with autoimmune encephalitis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: poor short-term outcome is marked at admission by an abnormal brain scan, impaired consciousness, autonomic involvement, fever and a preceding infection, each carrying roughly three- to fourfold higher odds after adjustment; status epilepticus and a raised cerebrospinal fluid cell count separate the outcome groups on their own but do not hold up once the other admission features are accounted for; combining the admission features discriminates better than any single one, though at a level that still leaves substantial misclassification and has not been tested in a separate sample. Certainty: These are associations with outcome rather than established causes, and the accuracy figure is apparent rather than validated. Scope: applies to autoimmune encephalitis in children admitted with acute disease, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it reports a difference in age or sex between the outcome groups.

answers.websearch:
## Answer

**Short-term prognosis in pediatric autoimmune encephalitis (AE) is driven mainly by the severity of the initial neurological presentation — depth of functional impairment (mRS/CASE), impaired consciousness with need for intensive care, seizures/status epilepticus, movement and cognitive dysfunction — plus abnormal baseline brain MRI and very young age; treatment delay is the main modifiable factor.** Individual predictors vary by cohort and most estimates come from small retrospective series with wide confidence intervals.

### Global severity at presentation
- In 73 children with anti-NMDAR encephalitis stratified by 2-month mRS, peak mRS ≥4 (vs ≤3) and abnormal MRI were the only independent predictors of poor short-term outcome ([passage text removed] and [passage text removed]); δ-brush on EEG was significant univariably only ([PMC12597199]([passage text removed])).
- In a 103-patient pediatric antibody-mediated AE cohort, the incompletely recovered group had higher maximum mRS, more fever, more status epilepticus, higher PICU admission rates, and more preceding herpes simplex encephalitis; PICU admission and high maximum mRS also marked children needing second-line immunotherapy ([PMC9304965]([passage text removed]); [10.3389/fped.2022.880693]([passage text removed])).
- The CASE score is valid for grading severity in children with AE and has prognostic utility for later functional independence ([PubMed 36253225](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36253225); reliability/validity confirmed but some items fit children poorly — [10.3389/fimmu.2022.915352]([passage text removed])).

### Specific admission features
- **Cognitive dysfunction**: independently associated with poor 6-month (Liverpool score) outcome in 51 children with anti-NMDAR encephalitis ([passage text removed]) alongside abnormal [passage text removed]); rituximab use was not ([PMC8100243]([passage text removed])). Note the extremely wide CIs.
- **Reduced consciousness, autonomic/respiratory compromise, ICU need**: in 175 Chinese children, poor outcome was associated with decreased consciousness (61.5% vs 19.5%), central hypoventilation (19.2% vs 3.4%), ICU admission (19.2% vs 4.0%), abnormal MRI (76.9% vs 41.6%) and raised CSF protein; CSF WBC and treatment interval were not discriminative ([10.3389/fimmu.2022.889394]([passage text removed])).
- **Intubation/ICU and length of stay**: in a 175-child multicentre cohort, intubation, ICU admission, prolonged length of stay, gastrostomy, and escalation to PLEX/second-line therapy were associated with poor 1-year mRS; abnormal MRI lost significance after adjusting for ICU admission and treatment/improvement timing ([PMC10219134]([passage text removed]); [PubMed 37236807](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37236807)).
- **Seizures/status epilepticus**: in paediatric probable antibody-negative AE, [passage text removed] (OR 4.16, 95% CI 1.16–14.92), despite good mRS/CASE outcomes overall ([snu.elsevierpure.com record](https://snu.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/[passage text removed]-ne-2)).
- **Movement disorder / dyskinesia–dystonia**: dyskinesia/dystonia was independently associated with poor *short-term* functional outcome in antibody-negative severe AE ([passage text removed]), a mixed-age cohort ([10.3389/fimmu.2025.1591771]([passage text removed])).
- **Very young age**: children ≤3 years had more fever and status epilepticus, more MRI abnormality, higher PICU admission, higher maximum and terminal mRS than older children ([PMC9304965]([passage text removed])).

### Baseline MRI as an admission-available prognostic marker
Abnormal MRI *at onset* (not merely at any time) predicted poor outcome (PCPC >1; IRR 3.50, 95% CI 1.31–9.31) in 38 European children, with frontal/frontoparietal T2-FLAIR lesions, hippocampal/thalamic change and atrophy, and failure of age-expected brain growth ([ana.25754 PDF](https://cognitive-neurology.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/ana.25754.pdf)). Frontal and occipital T2 lesions carried the highest odds of poor 1-year outcome ([PMC10219134]([passage text removed])).

### Composite bedside scoring
The NEOS score (ICU admission, treatment delay >4 weeks, lack of improvement at 4 weeks, abnormal MRI, CSF WBC >20/µL) was validated in a 59-patient paediatric-only NMDARE cohort, predicting outcome in the first year and beyond; HSE status and age at onset could complement it ([PMC10032577]([passage text removed])). External validation in Chinese children and a smaller US cohort confirmed the gradient of risk ([10.3389/fimmu.2022.889394]([passage text removed]); [AAN abstract]([passage text removed])). Two of its five items are not admission variables, limiting purely at-admission use.

### Modifiable factor
Earlier immunotherapy is associated with better outcome in children with NMDAR-antibody encephalitis, though the original authors noted this may partly reflect earlier recovery and called for prospective confirmation ([PMC4516400]([passage text removed])).

### Caveats
Short-term mRS understates morbidity: in one cohort 12% of children classed as poor prognosis at 2 months reached mRS ≤2 by 12 months without extra immunotherapy, while 55% had residual cognitive deficits despite functional recovery ([PMC12597199]([passage text removed])); persistent attention/executive/processing-speed deficits are common at 1–2 years ([Springer narrative review]([passage text removed])). No prospectively validated, purely admission-based prognostic model for all-cause paediatric AE was found in these searches.
answers.connect:
**Conclusion:** In children with autoimmune encephalitis (AE), the admission features that most consistently predict worse short-term (discharge to 3–6 month) outcome are markers of encephalopathic severity and multi-domain involvement — impaired consciousness, autonomic dysfunction/dyskinesia, fever and antecedent infection, cognitive impairment, and abnormal brain MRI — rather than antibody subtype.

**Evidence**

- **Largest directly relevant pediatric analysis (96 children, single centre; poor outcome = mRS >2 at discharge):** five features assessed at admission or initial evaluation remained independent predictors after adjustment — abnormal brain MRI ([passage text removed]), disorders of consciousness (OR 4.29, 1.43–12.89), autonomic symptoms (OR 4.09, 1.39–12.02), fever (defined as ≥38 °C at admission; OR 3.69, 1.28–10.51), and preceding infection within 2 weeks of onset (OR 3.03, 1.08–8.48); the model fitted well (Hosmer-Lemeshow P = .458) with no important collinearity [S:0b9acd0e-4d39-58de-bea9-00195bc283ff]. Combined, these five gave an AUC [passage text removed]%), better than any single feature (all AUC <0.70) [S:2db80369-45b3-5a6a-b61b-eb80c04a10d9]. Univariate differences [passage text removed]) outcome groups also included status epilepticus (33.3% vs 61.1%, P = .015), elevated CSF cell count (16.7% vs 38.9%, P = .028) and monotherapy immunotherapy (26.7% vs 52.8%, P = .019), while age, sex, motor/sleep/language/psychiatric symptoms, EEG abnormality and antibody status did not differ [S:83d3c43c-efa4-5025-a2ee-47d653b2146e]; status epilepticus, CSF pleocytosis and monotherapy dropped out on multivariable modelling, suggesting their effect is mediated through the five retained features [S:19485eff-7599-5231-a720-498bc71fdbcb].

- **Anti-NMDAR-specific pediatric cohort (51 children, Hunan; 6-month Liverpool outcome):** cognitive disorder (OR 23.97, 95% [passage text removed]; the confidence intervals are very wide, so the direction is more reliable than the magnitude. Rituximab use was not associated with 6-month outcome [S:10286dba-c388-5b2e-b0a6-e399827b173e][S:5dce941f-2e6e-522a-a6b8-049d2e260549].

- **Independent pediatric AE cohort (102 children, Vietnam; 3-month mRS):** [passage text removed] hospitalisation ([passage text removed]) independently predicted poor outcome; 74.5% achieved mRS ≤2 overall, lowest in the anti-NMDAR subgroup (68.3%) [S:8642892d-af0c-5045-8873-43489ca72920].

- **Severity scales at admission and severe/ICU disease (mixed-age evidence, so extrapolate to children cautiously):** higher CASE score on admission predicted [passage text removed] in a severe AE cohort, with strong correlation to mRS at admission (Spearman 0.68) [S:7399dd3b-da60-5d60-ba29-d02a119e75be]; in an ICU registry, mechanical ventilation (adjusted OR 6.28), tracheostomy, sepsis and autonomic dysfunction (adjusted OR 2.91) predicted worse discharge mRS, whereas antibody type, CSF inflammation and abnormal MRI did not [S:3b111f59-8d15-5df5-905d-3d1ca757b99f]. Central hypoventilation at admission was the only independent risk factor for mechanical ventilation in anti-NMDAR encephalitis ([passage text removed]) [S:960a21a3-39db-5b8b-9ffc-06e8fe71d8c3]. In children with anti-NMDAR encephalitis, autonomic dysfunction accompanied higher peak, discharge and 3-month mRS scores [S:8ce2f372-e4f5-5dc9-9007-583b25e484e1].

**Caveats:** the pediatric evidence is dominated by small single-centre retrospective cohorts with differing outcome scales (mRS, Liverpool) and timepoints; authors of the NEOS validation study explicitly note "dramatic heterogeneity" and "substantial discrepancies" in reported risk factors across centres and call for multicentre work [S:30a1fcae-f7a4-521d-bd54-92c66758bff5], and the 96-child study itself notes it was single-centre with a generally younger population requiring external validation [S:470c4999-cf43-5050-a429-138e13501654]. Treatment-related variables (delay to immunotherapy, monotherapy vs combination) are not admission "clinical features" but consistently modify outcome and confound these associations [S:ca6acbab-e94f-5d63-a774-a921367dd859][S:51ae0a67-88ae-55e6-a0de-bca4ae999479].

rows.question: Which clinical and antibody features distinguish corticosteroid-refractory juvenile myasthenia gravis from corticosteroid-responsive disease?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: acetylcholine receptor antibody positivity marks children less likely to be controlled by corticosteroids alone; isolated ptosis, and ocular-only disease more broadly, marks children more likely to respond to corticosteroids; most corticosteroid-refractory children respond once a nonsteroidal immunosuppressant is added, but the chance of response falls sharply once the first two agents have failed. Certainty: These are associations between baseline features and response group rather than demonstrated determinants. Scope: applies to juvenile myasthenia gravis in children diagnosed before adolescence, specialist outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it credits thymectomy with any of the improvement.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

In the only dedicated pediatric study of this question, corticosteroid-refractory juvenile MG (CRMG) is distinguished chiefly by **AChR-antibody seropositivity**, whereas **pure ptosis (isolated ocular presentation)** marks corticosteroid-responsive disease; secondary evidence adds greater disease severity, thymic hyperplasia, and delayed steroid initiation on the refractory side, and MuSK antibodies as a separate steroid-hard-to-treat phenotype.

## Antibody features

- In a single-centre Chinese cohort of 275 JMG patients (215 corticosteroid-treated, 44.2% refractory), **presence of AChR antibodies was an independent predictor of corticosteroid refractoriness** ([passage text removed], p = 0.033) [PMID 41623245; doi:10.1002/mus.70171].
- Conversely, in a UK paediatric cohort, antibody status was the only significant predictor of drug-free remission, with seronegative patients and those positive only on clustered-AChR cell-based assay (and those with normal repetitive nerve stimulation) most likely to remit — the mirror image of the refractory profile [PMID 32001147; [passage text removed]].
- **MuSK-antibody JMG** forms a distinct hard-to-treat group: predominant bulbar, facial, neck and respiratory involvement, poor response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors requiring immunosuppression [[passage text removed]], and in a French JMG cohort two MuSK-positive children required high corticosteroid doses to maintain control despite rituximab-associated improvement [[passage text removed]]. Note this is case-series-level evidence, not a controlled comparison; MuSK positivity was not identified as a refractoriness predictor in the Chinese CRMG analysis.

## Clinical features

- **Ptosis only was an independent predictor of corticosteroid responsiveness** ([passage text removed]) [PMID 41623245].
- Consistent with this, in 142 paediatric ocular MG cases, "[passage text removed] significantly more often than OMG with other ocular features (P < 0.001) and achieved optimal outcome more often (P = 0.002); patients given glucocorticoid within six months of onset had more optimal outcomes than those treated later (P < 0.001) [PMID 38382246].
- In a large childhood-onset MG cohort (859 patients, 226 prednisone-resistant), reported risk factors for prednisone resistance were **thymic hyperplasia, MGFA class above I, and longer disease duration before starting prednisone**, with prior thymectomy associated with lower risk [PMID 37421800; [passage text removed]]. I read the abstract and a secondary summary only, not the full results tables, so treat the specific factor list as second-hand.
- Thymic hyperplasia also independently predicted **poor response to tacrolimus** in glucocorticoid-resistant childhood MG (OR 3.140, 95% [passage text removed]), while thymoma did not [[passage text removed]].

## Prognostic implication once refractory

65.8% of CRMG children responded to non-steroidal immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, azathioprine, IVIG, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab); 71.0% of those given ≤2 agents responded versus only 14.3% of those requiring subsequent agents [PMID 41623245] — arguing for early switch rather than prolonged steroid escalation.

## Caveat

The pediatric AChR-antibody association is not replicated in adults: in a 126-patient adult refractory-MG cohort, antibody status and thymus histology were *not* significantly associated with refractoriness, whereas younger age (median 33 vs 50.5 years, p = 0.035), early-onset disease (78.6% vs 46.4%, p = 0.023) and male sex (multivariate [passage text removed]) were; refractory patients had more severe exacerbations (64.3% vs 26.8%, p = 0.004) [[passage text removed]]. The JMG findings rest largely on retrospective single-centre Chinese data with predominantly ocular phenotypes, so generalisability is limited.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

The strongest direct evidence comes from a single large Chinese pediatric cohort: corticosteroid-refractory juvenile MG (CRMG) is distinguished mainly by **AChR-antibody seropositivity** (and, on univariate analysis, abnormal repetitive nerve stimulation and generalized rather than ocular disease), whereas **isolated ptosis / pure ocular phenotype** marks corticosteroid-responsive disease. [S:711ebf43][S:267797a1]

## Supporting evidence

**The defining study.** A cross-sectional cohort at Xiangya Hospital, Central South University, analyzed 275 JMG patients diagnosed 2010–2023; 215 received corticosteroids, of whom 44.2% were classified CRMG. [S:711ebf43] Groups were defined by MGFA Post-Intervention Status: CS-responsive = reached CSR, pharmacologic remission, minimal manifestations, or "improved" on corticosteroids without additional immunosuppressants; CRMG = failure to do so. Notably, no patient in this cohort underwent thymectomy, so thymic pathology could not act as a confounder or predictor here. [S:07302809]

**Antibody feature.** AChR-Ab positivity was the only independent serological predictor of refractoriness (OR = 2.78, SE = 0.48, 95% CI 1.09–7.05, p = 0.033) on multivariate logistic regression. [S:84913176][S:711ebf43] This is concordant with an earlier childhood-onset MG cohort from the same center, in which generalized phenotype and AChR-Ab positivity were independent risk factors for poor long-term outcome. [S:f53ad299]

**Clinical features.** On univariate analysis, abnormal RNS and AChR positivity associated with CRMG, while the ocular (OMG) subtype and ptosis-only presentation associated with corticosteroid responsiveness. [S:267797a1] After adjustment, ptosis only remained an independent predictor of corticosteroid responsiveness (OR = 2.13, SE = 0.36, 95% CI 1.05–4.32, p = 0.003). [S:84913176] The authors relate this to prior data that low MGFA class (I–II) predicts corticosteroid response, and recommend pyridostigmine first for OMG with corticosteroids added if it fails. [S:9b8c644e]

**Prognostic corollary (not a baseline feature, but treatment-defining).** Of 76 CRMG patients given add-on immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, azathioprine, IVIG, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab), 65.8% were responders at last follow-up; ~71.0% of those receiving ≤2 agents responded versus only 14.3% of those requiring subsequent agents — i.e., failure of the first two immunosuppressants itself identifies a hard-to-treat subgroup. [S:711ebf43][S:68196b33][S:9b8c644e]

**Complementary predictors in steroid-resistant children.** In a separate Chinese cohort of 149 glucocorticoid-resistant childhood-onset MG patients treated with tacrolimus, 113 (75.8%) responded; multivariate analysis identified **thymic hyperplasia** (vs. normal thymus; OR = 3.140, 95% [passage text removed]) as predicting poorer tacrolimus response, and **exacerbated** rather than **unimproved** pre-intervention status as predicting better response ([passage text removed]) — i.e., children with *acquired* steroid resistance did better than those never responding to steroids. Age at onset, disease duration, MGFA class, QMG/ADL scores, and AChR-Ab titer were not associated. [S:854aaa64][S:586806a2][S:ce4c8e65]

**Antibody subtype and rescue response.** In a single-centre series of 8 girls (ages 8–16) with antibody-positive refractory JMG failing corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants, 6/8 improved on rituximab, with the greatest MG-ADL reduction and steroid-sparing benefit in the three MuSK-positive patients. [S:5d0e43c0] So MuSK positivity in refractory JMG appears to predict rescue-therapy responsiveness rather than intractability.

## Caveats

- There is **no established definition of CRMG**; the cohort above extrapolated from adult refractory-MG criteria (inability to taper without relapse, failure of immunotherapy, or intolerable side effects). [S:33d77566]
- The AChR-antibody signal is not universal: older juvenile MG series found no significant difference in treatment response or decremental response between seropositive and seronegative patients. [S:4d8852e6][S:1652ac89]
- Findings derive predominantly from Chinese/East Asian cohorts, where JMG is far more common and more often ocular than in Western populations, limiting generalizability. [S:33d77566] I found no evidence on LRP4-antibody status, AChR-antibody *titer*, or antibody subtype (binding/blocking/modulating) as discriminators of corticosteroid refractoriness in JMG specifically.

rows.question: Which in vitro models capture microbiota effects on blood-brain barrier integrity for gut-brain axis research?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: barrier integrity is read out as electrical resistance across the cell layer and as leakage of fluorescent tracers, with falling resistance signalling a leakier barrier; complexity is added in steps, from two-dimensional transwell cultures to three-dimensional hydrogel and spheroid constructs that form tighter junctions, and on to multi-organ microfluidic chips linking a microbial compartment to gut, barrier and neural compartments; each step trades physiological realism for experimental control, direct microbe-to-vessel contact only becomes relevant where the gut barrier is severely compromised, and animal work is still required for behavioural and whole-system outcomes. Certainty: This describes established laboratory practice and the recognised limits of each model class. Scope: applies to microbiota-gut-brain axis effects on blood-brain barrier integrity in cultured brain endothelial cells with pericytes, astrocytes and neural cells, co-cultured with microbial compartments, in vitro laboratory settings. An answer is wrong if it claims these findings transfer directly to the human barrier without in vivo work.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** Four tiers of in vitro system are actually used to capture microbiota effects on BBB integrity — (1) 2D Transwell brain endothelial monolayers exposed to defined microbial metabolites, (2) NVU co-/tri-cultures adding astrocytes, pericytes and neural cells, (3) 3D spheroid/organoid and microfluidic BBB chips, and (4) coupled gut–(microbiome)–brain multi-compartment systems that supply real microbial/fermentation-derived inputs rather than purified compounds. A 2026 methodological review of this exact question maps these options and their trade-offs ([PMC12913052]([passage text removed]); DOI 10.1177/0271678X261419964, *Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism* 46:1043–1062).

**1. Transwell BMEC monolayers + defined metabolites (the workhorse).** The review states the most common approach is applying commercially sourced gut microbial metabolites/products to cultured brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs), often with other NVU cells — e.g. LPS and SCFAs as deleterious/protective stimuli, plus TMAO, *p*-cresol glucuronide and secondary bile salts; most models are 2D Transwells with TEER as the integrity readout ([PMC12913052]([passage text removed])). Worked exemplars, all in immortalised human hCMEC/D3:
- Propionate: protective, with NFE2L2/Nrf2 nuclear translocation and reduced rotenone-induced ROS ([PMC5863458](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5863458), *Microbiome* 6:55).
- TMA vs TMAO: hCMEC/D3 grown under polarising conditions on Transwell filters, with 70-kDa FITC-dextran paracellular permeability and TEER; TMA increased permeability, TMAO reduced it via annexin A1, and a U937 monocyte-adhesion assay modelled the immunological barrier ([PMC8626999]([passage text removed]), *Microbiome* 9:235).
- *p*-Cresol glucuronide prevented *P. gingivalis* LPS-induced permeability increase, TEER loss and ZO-1/actin disruption ([PMC9870004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9870004)); *p*-cresol sulfate damaged the barrier via EGFR/ANXA1/STAT3 ([[passage text removed])).
- Paired gut + BBB barrier models screened tryptophan-derived metabolites (indole, indole-3-acetate, indole-3-propionate, tryptamine) ± LPS, showing dose- and cell-type-dependent modulation of both barriers ([PMID 42100498](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42100498), *Neuroscience Applied*).
- Microbiome-derived extracellular vesicles were tracked across Caco-2 and hCMEC/D3 as intestinal and BBB models ([PMC11792502]([passage text removed]) / [10.1128/spectrum.01368-24]([passage text removed])).

**2. NVU co-culture/tri-culture.** Culturing astrocytes on the basolateral filter surface (contact model) gives higher TEER than non-contact co-culture, and adding primary neural progenitor cells improves BMEC ZO-1 staining, TEER and transcriptomic authenticity — relevant because it lets direct neurotoxic/neuroprotective effects of microbial products be read out ([PMC12913052]([passage text removed])).

**3. 3D and chip-based BBB.** Spheroid BBB models scale reproducibly (>3000 spheroids per experiment in one cited study) but have mostly used immortalised human or non-human primary cells; cerebral organoid approaches are discouraged by necrotic-core and long time-course limitations ([PMC12913052]([passage text removed])). A human NVU-on-a-chip with BMECs, astrocytes and microglia showed low apparent permeability and active P-gp efflux exceeding Transwell performance, and gut microbial metabolites applied to it altered brain-side neurotransmitter metabolism ([Lab Chip 2025;25:6504–6516, DOI 10.1039/d5lc00937e]([passage text removed]); [MTBLS13230](https://omicsdi.org/dataset/metabolights_dataset/MTBLS13230)).

**4. Coupled gut–brain / microbiome-integrated platforms.**
- Modular gut–brain-axis-on-a-chip: gut epithelial and brain endothelial modules linked by microfluidic channels, with TEER changes after LPS or butyrate and exosome transport from gut barrier to BBB ([10.1016/j.jiec.2021.06.021]([passage text removed] human gut–brain interaction chip (Caco-2/HUVEC gut layer; hCMEC, HBVP, U87 brain layer) showed butyrate protected against LPS-induced BBB dysfunction by enhancing intestinal epithelial barrier function ([*Biosensors* 2026;16(1):23]([passage text removed]); [PMID 41590276](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41590276)).
- SHIME® (Simulator of the Human Intestinal Microbial Ecosystem) supernatants applied to a Caco-2 intestinal barrier and a BBB co-culture — an integrated SHIME-IB / SHIME-BBB design — revealed discontinuous occludin/claudin-5/ZO-1, reduced *CLDN5* and P-gp, and raised IL-8, without permeability or cytotoxicity changes ([hal-05421671](https://hal.science/hal-05421671v1); *Ecotoxicology and Environmental Safety* 309:119539). This is the clearest example of live-microbiota-conditioned medium rather than purified metabolites.
- MINERVA connects modular microbiota, gut, immune, BBB (endothelial + astrocyte monolayers) and brain chips by microfluidic tubing ([PMID 31998702](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31998702), *Front Bioeng Biotechnol* 2019;7:435; [PMC11503250](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11503250)).
- The gut–liver–cerebral 3XGLB physiomimetic platform links primary human gut and liver MPSs to an iPSC-derived cerebral MPS in circulated medium containing CD4+ Treg/TH17 cells, with SCFAs as the microbiome-derived variable ([PMC7846169]([passage text removed]), *Sci Adv* 7:eabd1707) — note the sources I read describe gut, liver and cerebral compartments, not a dedicated BBB compartment.

**Choosing between them.** Transwell platforms are highly scalable and easy for TEER/permeability but are static and lack cell–cell contact; microfluidic models add flow and stretch at the cost of scalability and PDMS drug absorption; 3D vessel geometries give physiological shear but make TEER and permeability hard to measure ([PMC7178976](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7178976)). hiPSC-derived BMECs address species differences and the weak barrier phenotype of immortalised lines ([PMC7178976](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7178976)).

**Gaps flagged in the literature.** Capillary-associated microglial responses to microbial metabolites at the barrier remain under-researched ([PMC12913052]([passage text removed])), and the same review notes methodological inconsistency across the field as the main obstacle to translation ([PMID 41696786](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41696786)). I found no evidence in these searches for an in vitro platform in which a complex living human microbial community is co-cultured in direct continuity with a BBB compartment and validated against in vivo permeability; current designs interpose either purified metabolites or transferred fermentation supernatants.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Four families of in vitro systems are currently used, in ascending order of physiological complexity: (i) metabolite exposure of brain endothelial monolayers/neurovascular-unit co-cultures in Transwells, (ii) sequentially coupled gut-epithelium → BBB → neural Transwell models, (iii) microfluidic gut–brain-axis-on-chip devices, and (iv) multi-organ "body-on-chip" platforms; direct microbe–endothelium co-culture remains experimental. A recent dedicated review of exactly this question maps the landscape and notes that methodologies remain inconsistent, with no consensus on how best to [passage text removed] [S:88e457eb-f16b-5d11-8d76-8882b2582572].

## 1. Metabolite/product exposure of BBB cultures (the dominant approach)

The most common design applies commercially sourced microbial metabolites to cultured brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs), often with other neurovascular unit cells: LPS to induce barrier damage and SCFAs to induce protection; other tested compounds include TMAO (barrier-enhancing), p-cresol glucuronide (protective against LPS-induced damage), and secondary bile salts (permeability-increasing), with (poly)phenols and indoles emerging [S:71228af2-88ed-55de-8e66-c078cfa2a62b]. The same review flags this as a relatively simplified representation of the axis [S:71228af2-88ed-55de-8e66-c078cfa2a62b].

Readouts and platform choices are standard BBB-field ones: Transwell monoculture, co-culture and tri-culture configurations with pericytes and astrocytes [S:3777064f-a2bd-5a9d-85f3-3b8eae992eb9], with tri-culture giving higher TEER and lower permeability than monolayers [S:d003a9de-c508-52cf-94d5-c7890197b242]. Cell-source trade-offs matter for microbiota work: primary human BMECs are limited by cost, yield, low barrier integrity and donor variability; hCMEC/D3 also has low junctional tightness but is described as well suited to studying brain-endothelial responses to human pathogens and neuroinflammatory stimuli; iPSC-derived BMECs give a renewable, tight barrier but may retain an epithelial-like transcriptomic profile [S:cb48436d-d1f1-530d-8f94-667cab656aba][S:c980b20d-2d1f-511b-8ae6-efddbcd16f6f]. Human cord-blood-derived "brain-like endothelial cells" (BLECs) co-cultured with pericytes are another human option that has been paired with Caco-2 intestinal barriers in the same study design [S:30436cf2-2d30-5219-a83c-88b6d38ed626], and flow in a lab-on-chip increases their barrier and glycocalyx properties [S:3e1945f8-9698-5e30-9aef-8134466e3d17].

## 2. Coupled gut → BBB → neural Transwell models

Modasia et al. used a static three-cell Transwell with gut epithelium (Caco-2) on the apical filter surface, hCMEC/D3 brain endothelium on the basolateral surface, and SH-SY5Y neurons (plus SIM-A9 microglia in a second configuration) in the basolateral compartment, showing that *Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron*-derived extracellular vesicles permeate the gut and BBB barriers sequentially and are then taken up by neural-lineage cells [S:52665f08-0060-5120-bb29-d640cd6feff2]. A related study showed microbiota-released EVs undergo dose-dependent paracellular transport and endocytosis by both Caco-2 and hCMEC/D3 cells [S:e2f03106-32da-5e85-b988-72811eed67eb].

## 3. Gut–brain-axis-on-chip (microfluidic)

- **Modular two-channel gut–BBB chip (Kim et al.):** Caco-2 in one channel, primary human BMECs in the other; LPS lowered TEER and raised FITC permeability in both barriers while butyrate did the reverse, and exosome uptake by BMECs was greater under perfusion than static conditions [S:52665f08-0060-5120-bb29-d640cd6feff2]. Independent descriptions confirm this design and its LPS/butyrate readouts [S:c83cf0a4-34c3-582f-84ac-5af617126b34][S:9b94ec0c-6e9e-59a8-97d9-37c31c9d284c].
- **Decellularised-matrix 3D GBA chip:** a PDMS microfluidic chip supporting 3D multicellular intestinal epithelial barrier and BBB models showed superior barrier function and transporter efflux versus static Transwells, and demonstrated that butyrate protects against gut-derived-LPS-induced BBB dysfunction by enhancing intestinal barrier function [S:2b4ab9d8-6f3c-5ca7-883d-41e1560e81cd].
- **Other chip variants catalogued in the review's Table 2:** a two-chamber device with *E. coli* K-12 in the microbiota chamber, a synthetic PEG-gel barrier of tunable permeability, rat AHPC neurospheres and inbuilt electrochemical serotonin/dopamine sensors (neurotransmitters but not bacteria crossed); and paired gut-chip → brain-chip systems in which *Lactobacillus casei* Hy2782/*L. plantarum* Hy7714 supernatant or exosomes promoted neural differentiation and partly rescued Aβ-impaired neurite growth [S:52665f08-0060-5120-bb29-d640cd6feff2]. A three-channel gut → BBB → brain (and reverse) perfused chip additionally modelled amyloid-β accumulation and α-synuclein fibril delivery, indicating the BBB also transmits damage from CNS to periphery [S:94a0cea3-6edd-59d2-9f7d-45cf5e9f30f0][S:52665f08-0060-5120-bb29-d640cd6feff2].
- **BBB–brain-organoid chips** have been built and shown to maintain barrier integrity (TEER, permeability, claudin-5) with WT and Parkinson's patient organoids, providing a template that could be extended to microbial inputs [S:bb641d89-b05b-5e27-9dd9-91e39ba6fd8f].

## 4. Multi-organ platforms

The MINERVA platform is designed as five serially connected, optically accessible microfluidic organ-chips representing microbiota, gut epithelium, immune system, BBB and brain, with integrated electrodes to measure electrical properties of the gut epithelial and blood–brain barriers; the BBB device seeds endothelial cells and astrocytes on opposite sides of a microporous membrane, and gut microbiota (e.g. from healthy versus Alzheimer's donors) sit in a mucus-mimicking hydrogel whose secretome is carried downstream [S:7c6c91b1-6a2d-58fa-a68a-69980af6824a][S:bb09f6d7-f6d1-5341-bec9-25a665a6e563][S:94a0cea3-6edd-59d2-9f7d-45cf5e9f30f0]. Related "body-on-chip" work notes the technical obstacle of maintaining oxygen gradients for bacterial–host co-culture across serially linked organ compartments [S:9dd5b7a6-1428-50f1-b00d-7f8861a9ffaa].

## 5. Direct microbe–endothelium co-culture and upstream fermentation inputs

Direct co-culture of microbes with neurovascular cells is limited by incompatible gaseous requirements (aerobic BMECs vs anaerobic microbes); the HoxBan system circumvents this by growing anaerobes in solid agar, though direct microbe–NVU contact would physiologically require severe gut-barrier compromise [S:2a45d287-196b-5fd0-8380-833a112f984c]. A complementary strategy is to generate the microbial input in a dynamic fermenter — SHIME/M-SHIME and related colon simulators produce donor-microbiota fermentation supernatants and can be co-cultured with host epithelial, hepatic and immune cells [S:ebc7bf49-2102-5da3-9ca1-4210185fc316][S:ed5212cd-4f42-558c-9832-909df1683732]; such supernatants have been applied to Caco-2/HT29-MTX Transwells with TEER readouts [S:9044b7f1-fdcd-5887-a726-c2600b9be4c6][S:a959615b-b202-5e93-83a9-b82f81d4f08b]. **Caveat:** in the sources retrieved, these fermentation supernatants were applied to intestinal, not BBB, barrier models — I found no source coupling a SHIME-type fermenter directly to a BBB culture.

## Limitations flagged by the sources

Even advanced 3D/microfluidic BBB models differ substantially from in vivo, which uniquely allows longitudinal microbial change across the lifespan and simultaneous multi-organ interrogation [S:550e658e-b8e1-5857-acc4-fc8e872f1e5d]. Several leading gut–microbiome–nervous-system chips (e.g. neuroHuMiX) still lack a BBB compartment altogether, and the review concludes that despite documented [passage text removed] remain relatively unexplored [S:94a0cea3-6edd-59d2-9f7d-45cf5e9f30f0]. Also note the LPS/butyrate chip has been described elsewhere as using murine bEnd.3 or human BMECs, so species and cell-source choices vary between implementations [S:9b94ec0c-6e9e-59a8-97d9-37c31c9d284c].

rows.question: Which second-line immunotherapies are used for refractory autoimmune encephalitis when antibody results remain pending in the ICU?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: when clinical suspicion is high and infection has been reasonably excluded, immunotherapy is started promptly rather than held back while antibody results are awaited; rituximab is the preferred second-line agent for suspected cell-surface-antibody and antibody-negative disease; cyclophosphamide is favoured where a paraneoplastic, intracellular antibody is the concern, and in other refractory disease; interleukin-6 receptor blockade and proteasome inhibition are reached for beyond rituximab in refractory disease but remain under trial evaluation rather than established. Certainty: This reflects settled practice for the sequencing question and unsettled evidence for the newer agents. Scope: applies to autoimmune encephalitis in critically ill adults with suspected or refractory disease, intensive care settings. An answer is wrong if it states that a negative antibody panel excludes autoimmune encephalitis.

answers.websearch:
**Rituximab is the default second-line agent when the antibody result is still unknown, with cyclophosphamide reserved for suspected T-cell–mediated/paraneoplastic disease, and tocilizumab, bortezomib, or (in a NORSE presentation) anakinra as rescue if those fail.**

**1. Rituximab is explicitly the preferred choice under antibody uncertainty.** In the Autoimmune Encephalitis Alliance Clinicians Network survey underpinning the best-practice recommendations, in a clinical scenario with *unknown antibodies*, 80% of responders chose rituximab as the preferred second-line agent versus 10% for cyclophosphamide ([PMID 33649022](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33649022)). The same recommendations advise rituximab for known or highly suspected antibody-mediated autoimmunity and cyclophosphamide for known or highly suspected cell-mediated autoimmunity such as classical paraneoplastic syndromes ([aealliance.org summary](https://aealliance.org/[passage text removed]-acute-symptomatic-and-long-term-management)). Cyclophosphamide is favoured in paraneoplastic disease because [passage text removed], and may double as oncological therapy ([link.springer.com/article/10.1007/S40263-022-00943-Z](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/S40263-022-00943-Z)).

**2. Seronegativity/pending serology does not preclude escalation.** Antibody testing may be inaccessible or take weeks to return, and failure to detect an antibody does not exclude AE ([PMC7122238]([passage text removed])). Delaying immunotherapy until a positive antibody returns is described as impractical and potentially hazardous ([jnnp.bmj.com/content/92/7/757]([passage text removed])). There is evidence for rituximab as second-line therapy in **both seropositive and seronegative** AE, with tolerability and improved outcomes ([PMC7122238]([passage text removed])). Importantly, one ICU-relevant caveat: empiric first-line treatment is appropriate before antibody results in severe cases (status epilepticus, ICU-level care), but all available clinical data should be carefully reconsidered *before* committing to second-line therapy ([Cleveland Clinic]([passage text removed])); the same caution appears as "[passage text removed]," while refractory autoimmune status epilepticus in the ICU is cited as a case requiring prompt aggressive treatment without waiting for antibodies ([ccjm.org/content/88/8/459]([passage text removed])).

**3. Timing of escalation.** Second-line therapy is generally started if there is no clinical/[passage text removed] first-line therapy ([aealliance.org](https://aealliance.org/[passage text removed]-acute-symptomatic-and-long-term-management); [link.springer.com/article/10.1007/S40263-022-00943-Z](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/S40263-022-00943-Z)) — but in the ICU literature second-line agents are considered both after the ~2-week window of anticipated first-line response *and* in severe presentations ([PMC7122238]([passage text removed])). Half of surveyed clinicians would add a second-line agent only after failure of more than one first-line agent, 32% after one, and 15% in all patients ([PMID 33649022](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33649022)).

**4. Regimens reported.** Rituximab 375 mg/m² IV weekly for 4 weeks, or 1 g × 2 doses two weeks apart; cyclophosphamide 750 mg/m² IV monthly for 3–6 months (or 600 mg/m², 5 doses over 8 days) ([Alberta provincial guideline]([passage text removed]); [Cleveland Clinic]([passage text removed])). If PLEX is also being used, timing matters relative to rituximab dosing ([droracle summary of guidance]([passage text removed]) — low-quality source, treat as pointer only).

**5. Third-line/rescue options if second-line fails.** Tocilizumab or bortezomib are suggested when there is no objective or subjective improvement on conventional second-line agents, though the recommendations note only minimal supporting evidence ([aealliance.org](https://aealliance.org/[passage text removed]-acute-symptomatic-and-long-term-management)). In a single-centre retrospective cohort of 91 rituximab-refractory AE patients, the tocilizumab group (n=30) had more frequent favourable mRS (≤2) at 2 months and last follow-up than the additional-rituximab (n=31) or observation (n=30) groups, and 89.5% of those improving by 1 month maintained a long-term favourable [passage text removed] ([PMID 27215218](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27215218)). Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor targeting long-lived plasma cells that resist B-cell depletion, supported only by case reports and small retrospective series ([aealliance.org bortezomib summary]([passage text removed])).

**6. If the ICU phenotype is NORSE/cryptogenic rather than a defined AE syndrome, the second-line menu differs** — anakinra (IL-1RA), tocilizumab (IL-6R), intrathecal dexamethasone, and rituximab, started within the first week if there is no response to first-line steroids/IVIg/PLEX; a review of 28 reports covering 75 NORSE patients found 52 managed with anakinra, 21 with tocilizumab, and 8 with intrathecal dexamethasone ([PMID 38430119](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38430119); [practicalneurology.com]([passage text removed]); [pn.bmj.com/content/21/2/119]([passage text removed])). Rituximab use here can be justified by an elevated IgG index or CSF oligoclonal bands suggesting intrathecal synthesis of an unidentified autoantibody ([practicalneurology.com]([passage text removed])).

**Caveats.** Evidence is almost entirely uncontrolled series; no randomised trials compare second-line agents, and expert consensus explicitly states the evidence does not support any specific second-line agent in cryptogenic NORSE ([link.springer.com/article/10.1007/S40263-022-00943-Z](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/S40263-022-00943-Z); [frontiersin.org/10.3389/fneur.2023.1150496]([passage text removed])). Ongoing trials include ExTINGUISH (inebilizumab, NCT04372615) in NMDAR encephalitis ([link.springer.com/article/10.1007/S40263-022-00943-Z](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/S40263-022-00943-Z)) and COMBAT-NORSE (anakinra vs tocilizumab, NCT07281027) ([smartpatients.com/trials/NCT07281027](https://www.smartpatients.com/trials/NCT07281027)). Infection risk is non-trivial in this population: in an ICU AE cohort, 33% developed severe sepsis/septic shock with organ dysfunction, more than double a German general-ICU comparison rate of 13% ([PMC6278855]([passage text removed])). I found no source giving a validated algorithm specific to "antibody-pending" second-line selection beyond the unknown-antibody survey scenario above.
answers.connect:
## Answer

**Rituximab is the default second-line agent in this scenario, with cyclophosphamide as the main alternative, and IL-6 blockade (tocilizumab/satralizumab) or proteasome inhibition (bortezomib) reserved as escalation/third-line rescue** — and critically, treatment is not delayed for antibody results.

### Treating before antibodies return is the accepted standard
An ICU-focused review states explicitly that [passage text removed]" when clinical suspicion is high and infection has been reasonably excluded, alongside empiric CNS-dose acyclovir and bacterial meningitis coverage until CSF studies return negative [S:fdfc3f4c-b6bf-5b0b-ad5a-4494c8846bd7]. This is not just theory: in one inpatient neurology cohort, antibody panels [passage text removed]), and 14 of 15 empirically treated patients were treated before the panel resulted [S:590f3b22-29dc-5ec6-ad70-cedc7b06d001]. Registry commentary similarly notes that decisions about empiric immunotherapy are usually made days to weeks before antibody results are available [S:c650e6e0-7c9a-51e9-9534-fe87a3563355].

### Escalation timing is compressed in the ICU
Roughly 20%–50% of AE patients respond inadequately to first-line therapy; for ICU patients, escalation is typically considered if there is no improvement or worsening 5–10 days after starting first-line treatment — deliberately shorter than the 2–4 weeks quoted for milder disease, because [passage text removed] [S:047ecf80-a6fb-5b63-9a35-145de631a578].

### The agents

**Rituximab (anti-CD20)** — preferred second line for cell-surface-antibody AE *and* for antibody-negative AE, on efficacy/safety grounds versus cyclophosphamide; typical adult dosing 1000 mg IV repeated at 2 weeks, or 375 mg/m² weekly ×4 [S:047ecf80-a6fb-5b63-9a35-145de631a578][S:fb0345eb-fd5a-5bfd-8415-be953fb69ff3]. ICU-relevant caveats: infusion reactions, delayed neutropenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, infection including HBV/HCV/TB reactivation (screen first), and a therapeutic effect that takes weeks to manifest [S:047ecf80-a6fb-5b63-9a35-145de631a578]. Early escalation to rituximab plus multidisciplinary intensive care was credited with full recovery in an ICU case with poor-prognosis features (extreme delta brush, high CSF titres) [S:a12fa6d7-6bd4-5428-91af-e77eb8b918f1].

**Cyclophosphamide** — the alternative second line, acting on both B and T cells, favoured for paraneoplastic/intracellular-antibody AE and other refractory AE; [passage text removed] [S:fb0345eb-fd5a-5bfd-8415-be953fb69ff3][S:03d27857-cd31-55de-a48d-0a5c0e4a8741]. It is generally less favoured than rituximab because of myelosuppression/infection risk, haemorrhagic cystitis, and infertility [S:6971eea4-82cd-5215-a097-797800a955ce][S:d28f365b-e96f-5c24-96b8-eaa779c10fea]. It crosses the blood–brain barrier and can reduce intrathecal antibody synthesis, and the two agents can be combined in the most severe cases — at the cost of infection/PML risk [S:642cb795-d943-5e79-a172-035a1c534eb0].

**Escalation beyond second line:** tocilizumab and satralizumab (IL-6 receptor), and bortezomib (plasma-cell depletion, effective against plasma cells resistant to anti-CD20), with reported activity in refractory NMDAR and CASPR2 AE; ICU concerns include infection, neutropenia, LFT elevation, herpes zoster reactivation, haematologic toxicity, neuropathy and cardiac dysfunction [S:2471e3a9-743c-5283-8416-bc70fd59a499][S:fb0345eb-fd5a-5bfd-8415-be953fb69ff3]. Bortezomib was studied specifically in patients who remained bedridden and unconscious after first-line, second-line, and tocilizumab therapy [S:7d59a62c-144c-5f01-b639-84940dbe6830]. Inebilizumab (ExTINGUISH, NCT04372615), satralizumab (CIELO, NCT05503264), bortezomib (Generate-Boost, NCT03993262) and rozanolixizumab (LEGIONE) remain investigational [S:fb0345eb-fd5a-5bfd-8415-be953fb69ff3][S:03d27857-cd31-55de-a48d-0a5c0e4a8741].

### If the presentation is refractory status epilepticus / NORSE
Here the pending-antibody problem is handled by mechanism-based choice: published consensus recommends first-line immunotherapy within 72 hours, then ketogenic diet plus second-line immunotherapy within seven days — **rituximab if antibody-mediated disease is strongly suspected or proven, anakinra or tocilizumab for cryptogenic cases** [S:6267ecf9-7654-5792-b5f4-1412532e42d1][S:54a30e8d-bfa3-575c-81aa-50e08f6f1ce2]. Note the diagnostic caution that NORSE is likely over-diagnosed as antibody-negative AE, and escalating immunotherapy is ineffective in non-immune NORSE [S:46c67718-d578-5d93-b5b5-3df74521921a].

### Caveats
There are no consensus guidelines or randomised data establishing the order, dose, or timing of these agents; most evidence is retrospective, case-series-based, and institution-dependent [S:2181230d-1999-560a-8e6f-8c652e720a75][S:5399fba1-2aed-5cc0-beff-7f991b4b369c][S:c88528e7-3e8c-5470-8edc-7e872bd1f44e]. I found no source giving an ICU-specific, antibody-pending randomised comparison of rituximab versus cyclophosphamide. In seronegative AE with high predicted risk of poor outcome, a combination [passage text removed] [S:62604d08-3272-5d52-b30b-50147d538801], and delayed immunotherapy is consistently the key modifiable predictor of poor outcome [S:157a997f-6fbb-589b-acb7-abf652b11bae].

rows.question: In model systems of ischemic stroke, how do microglial phenotype shifts and cytokine release interact during the acute phase?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: in the acute phase after the vessel occludes, microglia activate rapidly and polarise toward a proinflammatory phenotype; those activated microglia release proinflammatory cytokines into the injured tissue, tumour necrosis factor alpha and interleukin-1 beta among them; those cytokines signal through nuclear factor kappa B, which they activate and which in turn drives more of their own production, locking the response into a self-amplifying loop; the same mediators promote apoptosis of vascular endothelial cells and disrupt the blood-brain barrier, so the cytokine response widens the injury rather than only reflecting it. Certainty: This is mechanistic evidence from model systems, consistent in direction but not established in patients. Scope: applies to acute ischaemic stroke in rodent models of cerebral ischaemia-reperfusion and cultured microglia and endothelial cells, preclinical settings.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: in rodent stroke models the relationship is reciprocal and self-amplifying — the acute ischemic cytokine/DAMP milieu instructs microglial phenotype, and the phenotype adopted then determines which cytokines are released, creating feed-forward injury loops (and, in parallel, weaker protective loops) within the first hours to ~3 days; the underlying M1/M2 framing, however, is now known to misrepresent the actual cell states.**

**1. The canonical acute time course, and the loop that drives it.** In 60-min tMCAO, local microglia and recruited macrophages assume an M2-like phenotype early and gradually convert to M1 in peri-infarct regions over 1–14 days of reperfusion; critically, the same study showed *in vitro* that ischemic neurons prime microglia toward M1, and that M1-polarized microglia or M1-conditioned media exacerbate OGD-induced neuronal death while maintaining M2 protects neurons — i.e., injured tissue makes microglia inflammatory, and inflammatory microglial secretions expand the injury ([PMID 22933588](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22933588); [[passage text removed])). Reviews synthesising this and Perego et al. place the M2→M1 switch in the first 2–3 days, with M2 markers detectable from ~12 h, transiently rising at 1–3 days, then declining while M1 markers keep rising through 14 days ([PMC5666817]([passage text removed])). Flow-cytometry data in tMCAO mice agree that CD68 rises from day 1 onward while CD206 rises at day 1 but is no longer elevated by day 7, alongside early IL-10 upregulation ([PMC7457364](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7457364)).

**2. Cytokines are instructive inputs, not just outputs.** Loss of individual anti-inflammatory cytokines re-specifies phenotype and enlarges acute infarcts: IL-4 KO mice show increased M1 and impaired M2 marker expression at 5 and 14 days, with a transient acute (5-day) increase in neuronal tissue loss and long-lasting behavioural deficits, reversible by intracerebroventricular IL-4 ([PMID 26732561](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26732561); [PMC4729613](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4729613)). ST2 (IL-33 receptor) deficiency likewise shifted microglia toward M1, enhanced infarction at 3 days after tMCAO and after distal permanent MCAO, and worsened deficits; IL-33/ST2 engagement potentiated microglial *IL-10*, and IL-33's protection was lost in IL-10 KO mice — a closed cytokine→phenotype→cytokine circuit ([doi 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3233-16.2017](https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3233-16.2017); [PMC5426564]([passage text removed])). Conversely, blocking NF-κB/upregulating PPAR-γ with rhFGF21 suppressed M1 polarization *and* pro-inflammatory cytokine expression together, without affecting IL-10/CD206/IGF-1 ([PMID 32867781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32867781)).

**3. Microglial cytokine output amplifies acute injury through third parties.** Microglia-specific deletion of IL-1β improved acute neurological outcome and reduced neutrophil infiltration and BBB disruption after tMCAO; notably, IL-1α is induced in microglia within hours whereas IL-1β is delayed and confined to a small subset (fewer than 5% of microglia IL-1β⁺ at 24 h post-MCAO), so "the" acute microglial IL-1 signal is isoform- and time-resolved ([biorxiv 2025.12.19.695391]([passage text removed])). Amplification is partly indirect: microglia-derived IL-1α, TNF and C1q are necessary and sufficient to convert astrocytes to the neurotoxic A1 state ([PMID 28099414](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28099414); [PMC5404890](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5404890)), a mechanism explicitly invoked for post-stroke microglia–astrocyte crosstalk ([s13041-025-01244-4]([passage text removed])). Upstream, P2X7 activation drives NLRP3-dependent maturation of IL-1β/IL-18 in microglia, and NLRP3 inhibition reduces infarct and BBB disruption in ischemic mice ([PMC9933144]([passage text removed]); [fneur.2021.620948]([passage text removed].2021.620948/full)).

**4. The interaction is not uniformly detrimental, and depletion studies conflict.** CSF1R/c-Kit blockade with PLX3397 before tMCAO *augmented* [passage text removed] and worsened infarction, with the neuroprotective effect attributed to microglial suppression of astrocyte responses ([PMC5444553]([passage text removed]); [PMC12645133](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133)); the same held in aged mice with PLX5622/AFS98 ([PMID 33221396](https://www.medchemexpress.com/publications/33221396.html)). TNF-KO and myeloid-specific TNF-KO mice develop larger infarcts, implying microglial TNF via TNFR1 can be protective ([dspace.library.uu.nl]([passage text removed])). Against this, genetic depletion of resident microglia (CX3CR1^CreER:R26^iDTR) over the first 3 days *reduced* infarct volume and iNOS⁺ cell density, with iNOS, IL-1β, MCP1 and TNF-α mRNA falling to ~0.4–0.5-fold while Arg1, TGF-β1, IL-10, IL-4 and Ym1 rose 1.8- to 12.8-fold at day 3 ([s12974-021-02127-w]([passage text removed])) — so whether the acute phenotype–cytokine loop is net-injurious depends on depletion method, timing and age.

**5. Interpretive caveat.** scRNA-seq of acute MCAO brain found no separation of microglial subclusters by M1 vs M2 polarization scores at 3 h, 12 h and 3 days, and showed Arg1/Mrc1 (CD206) expressed mainly by macrophages — meaning infiltrating macrophages may have been misread as "M2 microglia" in marker-based studies ([s13073-023-01257-5]([passage text removed]); [PMC12684991]([passage text removed])). Marker co-localisation studies had already hinted at this: after pMCAO, CD68 appeared in both ramified and globular CD11b⁺ cells whereas Ym1 and CD206 were restricted to globular cells, and Ym1⁺ cells sat exclusively in the ischemic core at 24 h while CD68 concentrated in the border zone — mixed, spatially segregated phenotypes rather than two clean populations ([PMID 22152337](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22152337); [PMC3251548](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3251548)).

One gap: I found no source giving a quantitative, causally resolved measurement of how much of the acute cytokine pool is microglia-derived versus astrocyte- or neutrophil-derived at specific acute timepoints, so that apportionment should not be stated.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

In experimental stroke, microglial phenotype and cytokine release form a bidirectional, time-staggered loop rather than a one-way cascade: microglia are the dominant early cytokine source, but the cytokine/damage-signal milieu simultaneously instructs their phenotype — and in the acute window the net microglial contribution is often protective, not purely injurious.

## Microglia as the early cytokine source

Microglia are among the first cells activated after ischemia [S:abd1fb6a-17aa-54d0-9940-bec88abed6c3][S:0474231e-033a-5954-8b3c-9828b62367f9]. Quantitative work in permanent MCAO mice concluded that microglia–macrophages, [passage text removed], with blood-borne macrophages taking over thereafter; TNF mRNA⁺ microglia-like cells were visualized from ~4 h, with no ischemia-induced neuronal TNF upregulation up to 6 h [S:e85ffdcb-cd18-5778-a39e-539042137ec9]. Across rodent models, TNF mRNA rises within 30 min–4 h with peaks between ~3 h (rat) and 10–24 h (mouse) depending on occlusion model, localized to CD11b⁺/Mac-1⁺ GFAP⁻ microglia-macrophages [S:6de6a7b4-f78c-57cb-ba97-3dcf54d23f53]. IL-1β⁺ microglia appear in cortex 6–24 h post-stroke, with mRNA peaking earlier in transient than permanent MCAO — reperfusion timing itself shifts the cytokine curve [S:91b7b8b6-82aa-556b-b3f1-da3eba474f60].

## Phenotype trajectory: acute M2-dominance, delayed M1

Temporal profiling in MCAO shows M2-like (CD206⁺) microglia/macrophages detectable at ~12 h, peaking around days 3–7, then declining, while M1-like (CD16/32⁺, iNOS⁺) cells emerge from days 1–3 and remain elevated through 14 days [S:e60ef797-5810-53b0-bf1b-74fb12f80eb4][S:0474231e-033a-5954-8b3c-9828b62367f9][S:712c8fb1-b531-52a6-9be8-4309d000cb6b]. Thus the acute phase is characterized by early anti-inflammatory/phagocytic polarization that restricts damage and clears debris, followed by an M2→M1 shift in peri-infarct tissue [S:1c75e865-3b3b-5932-8e64-29d59ce6f93d][S:f34bd514-d3eb-56bc-a1c3-ad5300ed90d3]. M2 marker genes (CD206, Arg-1, Ym1/2, IL-10, TGF-β) peak around days 3–5, whereas M1 genes rise continuously from day 3 [S:f34bd514-d3eb-56bc-a1c3-ad5300ed90d3].

## The interaction is bidirectional

**Cytokines instruct phenotype.** The local milieu determines polarization direction (IFN-γ toward M1; TGF-β and IL-10 toward M2), so early-released mediators feed back onto the microglial state [S:db7cb8d5-34d0-57d5-84e9-675379edcc1c]. IL-4-deficient mice show larger infarcts, worse deficits, more M1-polarized microglia/macrophages and more IL-1β and TNF-α, all reversible by IL-4 restoration; i.c.v. IL-4 reduces injury and dampens peri-infarct microglial/astrocytic activation via IL-4/STAT6 [S:42bec58a-910c-5c6d-a469-295ef0ddce02][S:a4530116-2da6-5020-aeaf-f27c7ea5cb92].

**Phenotype determines cytokine output.** M1-like microglia release IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, iNOS and ROS; M2-like cells release IL-10, TGF-β, Arg-1 and BDNF [S:777f8417-e67e-5771-951b-57d85e4884fc][S:abd1fb6a-17aa-54d0-9940-bec88abed6c3].

**Injured neurons close the loop.** Conditioned medium from OGD neurons raised CD16/32 and lowered CD206 on primary microglia, i.e. ischemic neurons directly push microglia toward M1 [S:c621a3b8-50b9-5db7-82d0-f39335d15b93]. Reported neuron-derived drivers include soluble FasL acting via JAK2/STAT3 and NF-κB at 24–72 h post-MCAO, and neuronal exosomes released during ischemia-induced hyperexcitability, whose blockade reversed M1 polarization and lowered brain pro-inflammatory cytokines [S:273dd538-b662-5a90-a065-3f13327458df][S:273dd518-b662-5a90-a065-3f13327458df][S:fc17e78f-cd2f-5818-93e1-60fc06eef132]. Conversely, damaged neurons also release lipocalin-2, IL-4 and VEGF that push microglia toward reparative phenotypes and IL-10 release [S:273dd518-b662-5a90-a065-3f13327458df].

**Cell-intrinsic component.** In pure primary microglial culture, OGD alone triggered rapid gene-expression and cytokine-secretion changes — initially resembling M2, then a mixed pattern — indicating paracrine input from other brain cells is not strictly required for polarization [S:013c0565-d402-5cf3-805c-5fa1a99774fe][S:aecbf96d-8ad0-5ae7-8e65-10fbbd806157].

**Downstream amplification.** Acute M1-skewed cytokine release recruits and activates other compartments: IL-6/TNF-α drive neutrophil recall and BBB breakdown, and M1-derived IL-23 recruits γδ T cells that secrete IL-17 and are pathogenic in ischemia/reperfusion models [S:db7cb8d5-34d0-57d5-84e9-675379edcc1c].

## Important caveats to a simple "M1 = harm" reading

- **TNF form and source matter.** Bone-marrow chimera and conditional-knockout studies indicate microglial-derived TNF is neuroprotective acutely: TNF-KO mice had exacerbated infarcts at 24 h, and myeloid TNF ablation increased lesion volume, whereas mice lacking soluble TNF but retaining membrane TNF had smaller infarcts at 1 and 5 days with reduced TNF, IL-1β, IL-6 and CXCL1 protein and less macrophage infiltration [S:01e7120d-55cd-5218-a18d-ceec384d079e][S:6f1e2ce4-fee3-5514-a3a2-1e89e5d4b1f8][S:371f1b0a-d14a-554a-ba2e-d1338b5d0f27]. The prevailing model is solTNF/TNFR1 injurious, membrane TNF/TNFR2 protective [S:a8c05d53-bfea-5ea2-b535-ca0db56667c7].
- **Removing microglia worsens acute cytokine load.** CSF1R/c-Kit inhibition with PLX3397 before transient MCAO exacerbated deficits and infarction, and augmented inflammatory mediator production, leukocyte infiltration and cell death — largely because microglia normally restrain the ischemia-induced astrocytic inflammatory response [S:68d403f5-4031-5fe6-8942-105eff48ed64][S:208e29e1-9e9f-5f87-b727-cfbd6f64e6f2]. CSF1R inhibition in global ischemia likewise produced a more activated microglial morphology with an enhanced innate immune response and aggravated neurodegeneration [S:dd6399f2-2142-564b-a0f5-2543e1c71e5d]. Direction is context-dependent: in neonatal hypoxia-ischemia, PLX3397 reduced infarction and cytokine/chemokine production [S:e0ef5583-e520-5332-9f7e-aad8e945a595][S:9a8950b7-b03e-5e68-b8dd-7f51d5902077].
- **The M1/M2 frame is an approximation.** Single-cell RNA-seq of MCAO brains identified five microglial subtypes that did not overlap with classical M1/M2 sets, and 14 penumbral subclusters [passage text removed] marker genes; pro- and anti-inflammatory markers can coexist in the same cell, so "multipolarity" rather than dichotomy is the norm [S:472825f4-5543-5a02-9096-272ae727f05f][S:6773231f-27aa-5653-ab31-a0798f5e16f8][S:0d9d4d16-feae-5b30-a198-c62289fb887f].

**Not established from these sources:** the precise quantitative contribution of microglial versus astrocytic/infiltrating-cell cytokines to infarct growth at specific acute time points, and whether the M2→M1 kinetics reported in rodents translate to human acute stroke.

rows.question: What determines clinical outcome in children with NMDA receptor antibody encephalitis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: cerebrospinal fluid antibody titre is the measure that tracks outcome most closely, going with length of hospital stay and with disability from presentation through the first year; initial brain imaging is usually unremarkable and about half of first EEGs are normal, so there is no imaging signature of the disease and normal early studies do not indicate a milder course; no outcome difference was detected between the treatments given or by how quickly they were started, but nearly all children received the same combination, so the comparison could not be made. Certainty: These are things that go together in records reviewed after the fact, not effects of anything on outcome. Scope: applies to children and adolescents diagnosed with NMDA receptor antibody encephalitis, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents cerebrospinal fluid antibody titre as an established test for setting treatment intensity in an individual child.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Outcome in pediatric NMDAR antibody encephalitis is determined chiefly by **how quickly and how aggressively immunotherapy is given**, **initial disease severity (including ICU-level illness and breadth of symptoms)**, **abnormal brain MRI at onset**, **failure to improve early**, and **young age at onset** — with the important caveat that "good" functional (mRS) outcomes conceal frequent persistent cognitive and academic deficits.

## Treatment timing and intensity

- In a pooled literature review of 80 children with first-presentation NMDARE, those who fully recovered (pediatric mRS 0) had been [passage text removed] versus 21 days in those with incomplete recovery [PMC4516400].
- In the large mixed-age observational cohort, immunotherapy and tumour removal produced substantial neurological improvement in 81% of patients over a median 24-month follow-up; second-line immunotherapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide) improved outcome in first-line non-responders and reduced relapses. Within the paediatric subgroup (n=177), 46% failed first-line therapy, and the second-line effect size was comparable to the whole cohort though not statistically significant given the smaller sample [PMC3563251].
- An individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 1550 cases found that **lack of immunotherapy within 30 days of onset was significantly associated with poor 12-month functional outcome**, while first-line apheresis alone, or corticosteroids combined with IVIG (± apheresis), were associated with good outcome; rituximab and long-term IVIG were associated with a non-relapsing course [jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2784410].
- Notably, not all cohorts find a treatment-delay effect, and some report benefit even from late therapy — so delay is a strong but not universal determinant [emjreviews.com/neurology/article/never-too-late-to-treat-nmdar-encephalitis...].

## Disease severity and MRI

- In a European multicentre paediatric cohort (n=38, median onset 12.9 years), **abnormal MRI at first presentation, a presentation with sensorimotor deficits, and treatment delay >4 weeks** were each associated with worse outcome; abnormal initial MRI conferred an incidence rate ratio of 3.50 (95% [passage text removed]) for poor outcome (PCPC >1). The same cohort showed reduced whole-brain, grey matter, hippocampal and basal ganglia volumes and failure of age-expected brain growth [PMID 32314416; [passage text removed]].
- A Chinese cohort of 73 children identified **high peak mRS and cranial MRI abnormality** (especially T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and atrophy) as independent predictors of poor short-term function [doi:10.21037/tp-2025-401].
- A separate South China cohort found **MRI abnormalities and cognitive disorder at presentation** independently associated with poor 6-month outcome; rituximab use was not independently associated with 6-month outcome in that analysis [PMC8100243].
- Decreased consciousness was reported as a risk factor for poor response to initial first-line immunotherapy in children [PMID 40377735].

## Prognostic scores and biomarkers

- The NEOS score (treatment delay >4 weeks, ICU admission, no clinical improvement within 4 weeks, abnormal MRI, CSF WBC >20/µL) — developed in adults — has been **validated in children**, predicting functional status in the first year and beyond (p=0.0014 and p=0.036 at 16 months), and also predicting [passage text removed]) deficits; HSV encephalitis status and age at onset further influenced predictability [PMID 36948591; autoimmune-encephalitis.[passage text removed]...].
- In a French paediatric cohort followed to 2 years (median 39.5 months), higher NEOS score predicted [passage text removed], p<0.001), higher mRS (OR 2.12, 1.34–3.57, p<0.01) and unfavourable recovery (OR 2.00, 1.30–3.06, p=0.015). **Onset before age 5** predicted cognitive impairment (OR 5.69, 1.46–27.7, p=0.02) and unfavourable recovery (OR 6.10, 1.91–27.3, p<0.01). Elevated serum **neurofilament light chain** at onset predicted unfavourable [passage text removed], p=[passage text removed], p=0.012), improving on NEOS alone [PMC12231184; PMID 39715492].

## Age at onset and long-term domain-specific outcome

- In a very long-term paediatric cohort (76 patients; 8 [11%] died; 68 followed mean 7.1 years), three outcome patterns emerged — full recovery (73%), behavioural/school-work deficits (18%), and multidomain deficits (9%). **Younger onset age predicted [passage text removed], p=0.04), and 8 of 23 children with onset under 6 years remained sociofamilially dependent [neurology.org/doi/10.1212/NXI.0000000000200235].
- At ≥2 years after diagnosis in 81 children, 88% had mRS ≤2, yet 45% had cognitive impairment, 70% academic difficulties, and 92% required rehabilitation. **A higher number of symptoms at diagnosis** predicted cognitive impairment (p=0.01) and **abnormal EEG at diagnosis** predicted academic difficulty (p=0.03) [PMID 36196688].
- Korean multicentre data: 79.2% (19/24) had mRS ≤2 at 12 months, but residual CASE-score disability was concentrated in language and memory — supporting use of cognitive-sensitive outcome measures rather than mRS alone [PMID 33046392].
- Broader cognitive-outcome work in NMDARE reports that [passage text removed]].

## Relapse as a separate determinant

Relapses occur in roughly one-fifth of children and are generally milder than the initial event [PMID 31175679]. Not receiving, or delaying, immunotherapy at the first episode raises relapse risk; in the largest relapse cohort, patients who relapsed had received first-line (79% vs 96%, p=0.0001) and second-line (40% vs 72%, p=0.0001) therapy less often and with delay >30 days more often (52% vs 31%, p=0.01), while rituximab given within 60 days of the first episode reduced relapse risk by 60% (HR 0.40, 0.19–0.84, p=0.01) [neurology.org/doi/10.1212/NXI.0000000000200421].

## Caveats

Most of this evidence is retrospective/observational with modest paediatric sample sizes; there are no randomised trials, and international guidance is consensus-based (recommending prompt first-line therapy, corticosteroids first, before antibody results return if alternatives are excluded) [neurology.org/doi/10.1212/NXI.0000000000001052; [passage text removed]]. The role and optimal timing of second-line therapy in children remains incompletely defined, with use rates varying widely across centres [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Outcome in pediatric NMDAR antibody encephalitis is determined chiefly by **acute disease severity, how quickly and how aggressively immunotherapy is given, early treatment response, and the underlying trigger (teratoma vs. post-HSE vs. idiopathic)** — and the outcome you measure matters, because functional (mRS) recovery is usually good while cognitive/fatigue sequelae often persist.

## Severity and baseline markers

The five NEOS variables — ICU admission, no treatment within 4 weeks of onset, [passage text removed], abnormal MRI, and CSF WBC >20 cells/µL — were derived in a mixed-age cohort [S:c23f33fc] and have been validated in a pediatric-only cohort of 59 children (median age 8 years), where the score predicted poor outcome (mRS ≥3) in the first year ([passage text removed] at 16 months), and also predicted deficits in [passage text removed]:f9e1d99b]. Adjusting the cutoffs for children did not improve prediction, but **HSE status and age at disease onset** independently influenced predictability and may define pediatric risk groups [S:f9e1d99b, S:e4ff7cfd].

In a South China cohort of 51 children, cognitive disorder (OR 23.97, 95% [passage text removed] poor 6-month [passage text removed]; rituximab use was not independently associated with outcome, plausibly because of treatment-selection bias [S:10286dba, S:b4a01efb]. In the largest single-centre US pediatric series (103 analysable patients, 2009–2024), **younger children and those with teratomas had a more severe course and worse outcome**, and CSF antibody titre correlated with clinical severity, length of stay, and mRS from presentation through 12-month follow-up, independent of interventions; normal routine CSF and MRI delayed first-line immunotherapy [S:9df22531, S:4e8b629d]. Older pediatric reviews similarly cite younger age, absence [passage text removed] risk factors for worse outcome, with roughly 30% left with residual cognitive/psychiatric disability [S:89a31db9].

## Treatment timing and escalation

In an individual-patient meta-analysis of 1550 NMDARE cases, treatment factors at first event significantly associated with good 12-month functional outcome were first-line therapeutic apheresis alone, corticosteroids plus IVIG, or corticosteroids plus IVIG plus apheresis; **lack of immunotherapy within 30 days of onset was significantly associated with poor outcome**, while rituximab and long-term IVIG were associated with a non-relapsing course [S:f619b714, S:c758ba16]. The same body of work reports [passage text removed], extreme delta brush on EEG, and delayed immunotherapy predict poor functional outcome [S:63090f6a]. International consensus for pediatric NMDARE recommends corticosteroids in all children, added IVIG or plasma exchange in severe cases, second-line therapy (rituximab preferred) considered ~2 weeks after first-line initiation in refractory cases, and treats post-HSE NMDARE like idiopathic disease; total treatment duration is explicitly dictated by severity and clinical course [S:643423ee]. In refractory children, rituximab reduced mRS, though serious infectious adverse events occurred [S:8f4d8131]. Early second-line therapy during the initial attack may also reduce relapse risk in children [S:f6752dc7].

## Which outcome you measure

Functional and cognitive trajectories dissociate. In the Dutch pediatric follow-up study (28 patients identified, 22 assessed, median follow-up 31 months), median Pediatric Cerebral Performance Category was 1 and yet only 64% returned consistently to their previous school level, with significant deficits in sustained attention (z = −2.10, [passage text removed], p = 0.008); fatigue, not cognition, correlated strongly with quality of life (r = 0.82, p < 0.0001) [S:ff6aa5e1, S:94fc94d0]. Long-term cognitive outcome across NMDARE is predicted by [passage text removed] [S:7fc51d0c], with improvement continuing for years [S:4a893310].

## Caveats

Evidence is retrospective and cohort-based, not randomised; several pediatric determinants (male sex, speech disorder, initial mRS, second-line therapy as independent risk factors in a 107-child cohort) come from a source listed as "In Review" and should be treated as provisional [S:c9420f7c]. The prognostic value of MRI is contested — some studies find no correlation with long-term outcome, and dichotomous normal/abnormal scoring may be too crude [S:b393bd83].
