rows.question: What is the long-term neurological course after immune checkpoint inhibitor-related neurological adverse events?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: recovery is only partial: about half of patients improve neurologically by three months, and among those still alive at one year roughly four in ten are left with neurological sequelae; further neurological improvement after the first year is rare and effectively stops after the second, so the deficit present at one year is largely the deficit that remains; recurrence of the neurological event affects a minority of patients, roughly one in seven, and typically occurs within the first year rather than later; sequelae at one year are more likely in patients with paraneoplastic phenotypes and in those who relapse, while a myositis phenotype goes with better recovery. Certainty: These are outcomes counted as they occurred and phenotypes compared after the fact, not effects of any assigned treatment. Scope: applies to neurological immune-related adverse events of immune checkpoint inhibitors in adults treated with checkpoint inhibitors for cancer who develop moderate or severe neurological adverse events, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents rechallenge with the checkpoint inhibitor as established to be safe after one of these events.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Recovery from ICI-related neurological adverse events (n-irAEs) is largely front-loaded: most improvement occurs within the first ~3 months, roughly 40–55% of survivors are left with permanent deficits, late improvement after 1 year is essentially absent, and long-term mortality is high but driven mainly by cancer progression rather than neurotoxicity.

## Trajectory of recovery — a narrow window, then a plateau

In the largest dedicated long-term study (164 patients, median follow-up 13 months, IQR 4–25; 86% CTCAE grade 3–4 at baseline), early neurological recovery by 3 months occurred in 82/164 (50%). Thereafter improvement in CTCAE grade occurred in only [passage text removed] (2%) between 12 and 24 months, and in 0/23 between 24 and 36 months. Among 83 one-year survivors, 33 (40%) had persistent deficits and 35 (42%) were still on immunosuppressive treatment ([PMID 42342405](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42342405); [jitc.bmj.com/content/14/6/e015176]([passage text removed])).

A French two-network cohort (147 patients, grade ≥2, median follow-up 12 months, range 0.5–50) showed the same pattern by mRS: severe disability (mRS 3–5) fell from 108/144 (75.0%) at onset to 33/146 (22.6%) at last visit, but the proportion with minor disability peaked at 6 months (65/116, 56.0%) and did not rise thereafter (56/110, 50.9% at 12 months; 35/86, 40.7% at 18 months) ([PMC10306160]([passage text removed]); [PMID 37389303](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37389303)).

## Frequency and nature of residual deficits

- 53% of patients had long-term neurological sequelae in a PD-1/PD-L1 case series, despite a 74% corticosteroid response rate ([PMID 34651126](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34651126); [PMC8505025]([passage text removed])).
- A systematic review/meta-analysis of 991 reported cases found 77% improved with treatment yet 42% had unresolved sequelae ([PMID 40795646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40795646); [S0305737225001331](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0305737225001331)).
- Deficit types in "chronic inactive" cases: [passage text removed] signs (7%), cognitive impairment (7%) ([PMID 39298719](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39298719); [NXI.0000000000200314]([passage text removed])).

## Course categories: monophasic vs chronic

In an Italian multicentre series of 66 patients, 12 (18%) had a fulminant course (higher risk [passage text removed]). Of 54 non-fulminant patients, 23 (43%) were monophasic and 31 (57%) chronic — 16/31 (52%) chronic *active* (ongoing immunosuppression 69%, relapse on steroid taper 19%, progression 12%) and 15/31 (48%) chronic *inactive* (fixed sequelae without ongoing inflammation). All 16 chronic-active patients were still on immune-active treatment at last evaluation (median follow-up 11 months, IQR 4.8–16.5). Chronic n-irAEs carried higher severe disability at last evaluation, shorter survival and higher mortality (all p<0.01), primarily from cancer progression ([PMID 39298719](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39298719); [NXI.0000000000200314]([passage text removed])).

## Relapses and rechallenge

Relapses occurred in 25/164 (15%) at a median 6.8 months (IQR 3.9–11.8) from onset; ICI rechallenge produced relapse (grade 2) in only 1/21 patients (5%) ([PMID 42342405](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42342405)). Consistently, five patients rechallenged with PD-1 monotherapy had no recurrence ([PMID 34651126](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34651126)).

## Prognostic determinants

- **Worse long-term outcome:** [passage text removed]–44.51 for 1-year sequelae) and relapse within 9 months (OR 11.12, 95% CI 2.13–89.53) ([PMID 42342405](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42342405)); older age (HR [passage text removed] (HR [passage text removed]) reduced the severe-to-minor disability transition ([PMID 37389303](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37389303)).
- **Phenotype matters:** myositis/neuromuscular junction disorders and melanoma increased recovery; myelitis, cerebellar ataxia, sensory neuronopathy and limbic encephalitis were mostly severely disabled at last visit ([PMC10306160]([passage text removed])).

## Mortality

48/147 (32.7%) died over follow-up (median 6 months from onset, range 0–26): cancer progression 35.4%, neurological toxicity 31.2%. Neurotoxicity dominated deaths in the first 3 months (9/14, 64.3%), cancer progression thereafter (16/34, 47.1%) ([PMC10306160]([passage text removed])). Pooled overall mortality was 17.1%, rising to 38% in myasthenia–myositis–myocarditis "Triple M" overlap (respiratory failure 50%, cardiotoxicity 41%) ([PMID 40795646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40795646)).

## Caveats

All the above derive from retrospective referral-centre cohorts with heterogeneous, mostly ≤2-year follow-up; the JITC authors themselves note prior data were limited by small size and short follow-up ([jitc.bmj.com/content/14/6/e015176]([passage text removed])). Quality-of-life data specific to neurological sequelae are sparse — the available HRQoL evidence covers persistent irAEs across all organ systems, showing reduced EQ-5D-5L scores versus patients without persistent irAEs, but the reported chronic events were predominantly non-neurological ([PMID 36198246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36198246)). I found no prospective trial or systematic long-term neurorehabilitation outcome data for n-irAEs.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line: the neurological course plateaus early — recovery is largely determined in the first 3 months, roughly 40% of one-year survivors are left with disabling sequelae, further improvement after 12 months is essentially nil, and relapses (15%) cluster in the first year, mostly triggered by steroid taper/withdrawal.**

**Early plateau, then a fixed deficit.** In a national reference-centre cohort of 164 patients with CTCAE grade ≥2 neurological irAEs (n-irAEs), early neurological recovery at 3 months occurred in 82/164 (50%) [S:89a8a307-f64c-50df-aa9f-4fa5b74fa0aa]. Among the 83 patients alive at 1 year, 50 (60%) were fully asymptomatic while 33 (40%) had sequelae (grade 2 in 10, grade 3 in 23); the commonest were gait impairment (n=21, of whom 15 were wheelchair-bound or needed aids, mostly from cerebellar ataxia or polyradiculoneuropathy) and cognitive impairment (n=9, all in limbic encephalitis or meningoencephalitis) [S:f1d4ef75-26ef-5780-a54f-569bb6fc5385]. Late improvement was rare: CTCAE grade improved in 13/83 ([passage text removed] (2%) between 12 and 24 months, and never (0/23) between 24 and 36 months; sequelae rates and types were similar at 2 and 3 years [S:f1d4ef75-26ef-5780-a54f-569bb6fc5385][S:89a8a307-f64c-50df-aa9f-4fa5b74fa0aa]. Patients without sequelae were far more likely to have recovered early (47/50, 94% vs 11/33, 33%) [S:f1d4ef75-26ef-5780-a54f-569bb6fc5385], and second-line therapy given later did not significantly increase late improvement, arguing for upfront escalation in high-risk phenotypes [S:f1d4ef75-26ef-5780-a54f-569bb6fc5385][S:c3746ce5-837a-5b8a-8fcf-974f8e286f17].

**Disability trajectory and mortality.** In a separate multicentre cohort of 147 patients (median follow-up 12 months), severe disability (mRS 3–5) fell from 108/144 (75.0%) at onset to 33/146 (22.6%) at last visit; the proportion with minor disability rose from 19.4% at onset to 56.0% at 6 months but then declined (50.9% at 12 months, 40.7% at 18 months) as deaths accrued — 48/147 (32.7%) died, from cancer progression (35.4%) or neurological toxicity (31.2%), with neurotoxicity dominating deaths in the first 3 months and cancer progression thereafter [S:9c02999c-dc0b-584d-a12f-36ce3b5b2e6f].

**Phenotype and host factors drive the long-term course.** Myositis/neuromuscular junction disorders and melanoma were associated with higher transition from severe to minor disability, whereas older age and paraneoplastic-like syndromes predicted poorer recovery [S:1c0810cf-310d-522f-a329-7df9ca2c9ddc][S:ab93bad7-4f5e-5b8d-905b-1ea59040f448]. Concordantly, in multivariable analysis 1-year sequelae were more likely [passage text removed]–44.51) and relapse within 9 months (OR 11.12, 95% CI 2.13–89.53) [S:89a8a307-f64c-50df-aa9f-4fa5b74fa0aa]; the authors attribute the poor paraneoplastic prognosis to cytotoxic T-cell–mediated irreversible neuronal loss [S:c3746ce5-837a-5b8a-8fcf-974f8e286f17]. A biopsy cohort of 42 neuromuscular irAEs followed 3–26 months reported good outcome (recovery or ≥2-point mRS drop) in 53.8% [S:419ca883-e26c-5d2a-9ee3-521c862a5989].

**Relapses.** Relapses occurred in 25/164 (15%) at a median 6.8 months (IQR 3.9–11.8) after onset, with 18/24 (75%) within the first year and the latest at 19.3 months; the phenotype was identical to the initial one in 68% [S:964c4f21-3563-5f1e-af4f-08bbcefed868]. Identified triggers were corticosteroid/immunosuppressant withdrawal (9/20) or steroid tapering (8/20) — these relapses occurred significantly earlier (median 4.3 vs 11.8 months, p=0.011) — plus cancer progression, infection and ICI rechallenge [S:964c4f21-3563-5f1e-af4f-08bbcefed868].

**Ongoing treatment and rechallenge.** At 1 year, 35/83 survivors (42%) were still on treatment, predominantly low-dose oral corticosteroids (≤10 mg prednisone in 19/35), with use declining further at 2 and 3 years [S:f1d4ef75-26ef-5780-a54f-569bb6fc5385]. ICI rechallenge caused relapse (grade 2) in only 1/21 patients (5%) [S:89a8a307-f64c-50df-aa9f-4fa5b74fa0aa]; the earlier cohort similarly found ~12% relapse among rechallenged patients [S:7bd26868-d46f-58e9-bc17-676677e08363], though other n-irAE series report higher flare rates (e.g., 6/10, 60%) and guidelines remain cautious [S:30f0d263-6e65-5f6e-8b32-29710b8e19d1][S:b4dc887e-5cc2-50fc-b553-83bed5fb428a]. The authors conclude rechallenge may be safe in fully recovered patients and that prolonged immunosuppression beyond 1 year is likely unnecessary — but this needs prospective confirmation [S:3ab4051d-e7a7-5ad7-a5d2-b5ca2fc37949].

**Chronicity in the wider irAE literature.** In a systematic review of 323 patients with chronic (>12 weeks) non-endocrine irAEs, neurological events were the second most frequent category (19%); irAEs persisted a median of 180 days, >6 months in 52%, with 30% having ongoing symptoms or treatment at reporting [S:9f525be2-9320-590a-98d3-659d643db100]. Onset can also be delayed until after ICI cessation, as in anti-Ma2 limbic encephalitis appearing 3 months after stopping nivolumab with only moderate improvement on immunotherapy [S:77b53212-444f-5008-a49f-57906ad87c0e][S:defd953c-a4a1-55c3-9deb-e9453743c76a].

**Caveats:** the two largest cohorts are retrospective, from referral centres biased toward severe and paraneoplastic presentations, with heterogeneous follow-up [S:ab93bad7-4f5e-5b8d-905b-1ea59040f448][S:3ab4051d-e7a7-5ad7-a5d2-b5ca2fc37949]. I found no prospective long-term or patient-reported quality-of-life data on this question.

rows.question: How does loop diuretic therapy relate to mortality in patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing valve replacement?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Loop diuretic use before valve replacement is associated with roughly twice the long-term mortality of patients not taking one; This mortality signal is not explained by more severe stenosis, which is comparable in treated and untreated patients; Patients on a loop diuretic reach valve replacement with greater congestion and higher filling pressures; The excess mortality is best interpreted as marking an advanced disease stage rather than an established effect of the drug. Certainty: The evidence supports a consistent association rather than a causal effect, and the small number of deaths together with the older, more comorbid and higher-surgical-risk profile of treated patients weakens it further. Scope: applies to severe aortic stenosis treated with aortic valve replacement in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it advises weaning, withholding or stopping loop diuretic therapy around valve replacement as a way to reduce mortality.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Loop diuretic therapy (LDT) in severe aortic stenosis is consistently associated with roughly a doubling of post–valve-replacement mortality, but the evidence indicates it is a **marker of advanced disease stage — congestion, adverse remodeling, comorbidity, frailty — rather than a demonstrated causal driver of death**, since the association attenuates or loses significance on full adjustment.

## Evidence

**Pre-AVR loop diuretic use and long-term mortality (surgical + transcatheter cohort).** In a prospective cohort of consecutive severe AS patients undergoing AVR with invasive catheterization (n = 157 on LDT, median torasemide 10 mg/day; n = 346 not on LDT), 45 deaths (9%) occurred over a median 44 (31–62) months. Patients on pre-AVR LDT had twice the mortality of those not on LDT (HR 2.01, 95% CI 1.17–3.77; p = 0.01), with a dose gradient: high-dose LDT [passage text removed]; p = 0.02) and low-dose LDT [passage text removed]; p = 0.06) versus no LDT; each 5 mg increase in daily torasemide carried HR 1.05 (95% CI 1.01–1.09; p = 0.01) ([PMC12663767]([passage text removed]); [PMID 41316958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41316958)).

**Why: LDT tracks congestion and unfavorable hemodynamics, not stenosis severity.** Despite nearly identical AS severity (indexed AVA [passage text removed] cm²/m²), LDT patients had more advanced biventricular remodeling, higher BNP ([passage text removed]; p < [passage text removed]]; p < 0.001), [passage text removed]; p < 0.001), worse NYHA class, and higher STS and logistic EuroSCORE ([PMC12663767]([passage text removed])).

**The association is not independent.** In multivariable [passage text removed]; the authors interpret LDT as "[passage text removed]" rather than a mediator, noting that LDT+/PAWP+ and LDT+/PAWP− groups had similar torasemide doses but substantially different mortality ([PMC12663767]([passage text removed])). A published correspondence reinforces this, arguing the HR ≈ 2.0 may be overestimated given incomplete adjustment [passage text removed] ([PMC13085121]([passage text removed])).

**TAVI-specific data agree.** In 804 single-center TAVI patients, 48.3% were on pre-TAVI LDT (mean 51.1 mg furosemide equivalents); these patients were frailer with more CKD, prior CABG, PAD, atrial fibrillation/flutter and diabetes, worse LV systolic function, *lower* transvalvular gradients, and higher LV mass index. On propensity-score matching, 1-year death was only borderline higher with LDT ([passage text removed]) ([PMID 32723557](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723557); [ajconline.org S0002-9149(20)30610-X]([passage text removed])).

**Change in dose after AVR carries prognostic information.** In a Danish nationwide study of 4,431 TAVI patients, 49% were on no loop diuretic at TAVI, 21% low, 20% intermediate, 10% high dose. At 1 year, 20% had increased, 23% reduced, and 57% unchanged treatment. Among 1-year survivors, cumulative 5-year death risk was 61.0% (95% CI 56.4–65.3) with increased versus 47.4% (95% CI 44.9–49.9) with reduced/unchanged dose; multivariable Cox [passage text removed]), and [passage text removed]) restricted to those already on diuretics pre-TAVI — adjustment "reduced but not removed" the excess risk ([PMC10019742]([passage text removed]); [PMID 36928217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36928217)).

## Practical reading

LDT status and dose — and especially *escalation* of dose after valve replacement — should be used as a low-cost prognostic flag identifying patients with residual congestion and advanced disease who warrant closer HF surveillance. Nothing in these sources supports withholding loop diuretics to improve survival; no randomized trial of loop diuretic strategy in AS undergoing AVR appeared in my searches, so the causal question remains unanswered.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Loop diuretic therapy (LDT) in severe aortic stenosis is consistently associated with roughly doubled long-term mortality after valve replacement, but the best available evidence indicates it acts as a **marker of advanced disease stage and organ congestion rather than a demonstrated causal driver** of death — the association attenuates to non-significance on multivariable adjustment.

## Supporting evidence

**Pre-AVR loop diuretic use identifies a high-risk, congested phenotype.** In a consecutive single-centre cohort of severe AS patients undergoing TAVR or SAVR (157 on LDT, median daily torasemide 10 [5–15] mg; 346 not on LDT), AS severity was comparable ([passage text removed]) yet LDT patients had more advanced biventricular remodelling, higher BNP ([passage text removed]), higher liver enzymes, a [passage text removed]]), and higher invasive filling pressures (mean RA pressure 8 ± 4 vs 6 ± 3 mmHg; mean PAWP [passage text removed]) [S:ef311312-4cda-57eb-b16c-259c097ee253].

**Mortality signal with a dose–response.** Over median 44 (31–62) months post-AVR, 45 (9%) deaths occurred; LDT patients had twice the mortality (HR 2.01, [passage text removed]). High-dose LDT carried the highest risk ([passage text removed]), low-dose intermediate ([passage text removed]), and each 5 mg/day torasemide increment conferred HR 1.05 (95% CI 1.01–1.09). Combined LDT plus elevated PAWP marked the worst group ([passage text removed]) [S:cb8767b3-097c-52e1-9110-fe857c519d48]. Post-AVR functional capacity was also worse and estimated systolic pulmonary pressure higher (37 ± 11 vs 32 ± 8 mmHg) in LDT patients [S:ef311312-4cda-57eb-b16c-259c097ee253].

**Not independent of risk profile.** In multivariable analysis including non-invasive parameters and established surgical risk scores, [passage text removed]; the authors interpret LDT as a powerful marker of advanced AS and a clinical "red flag" that should trigger thorough evaluation and prompt consideration of AVR, rather than a proven mediator [S:cb8767b3-097c-52e1-9110-fe857c519d48][S:1a1074d1-19e5-59b6-8c62-8138b546b7d1]. The authors themselves note it remains unknown whether the association reflects an adverse drug effect, disease severity, or both [S:85993062-91c4-52ae-ba5b-feabbd3158d7].

**Corroboration from a nationwide TAVI cohort.** Among 4,431 Danish TAVI patients alive at 1 year (2008–2019), 49% were on no loop diuretic at TAVI, 21% low (1–40 mg furosemide-equivalent), 20% intermediate (41–120 mg), 10% high (>120 mg). At 1 year, 20% had increased, 23% reduced and 57% unchanged dosing. Five-year cumulative mortality was 61% (95% CI 56.4–65.3) with increased versus 47% (95% CI 44.9–49.9) with reduced/unchanged treatment; adjusted HR 1.4 (95% CI 1.22–1.52) [S:674c1ebe-4fb8-5202-8581-e8a1a3adb9b2]. Baseline LDT tracked strongly with comorbidity (e.g. heart failure 14.7% in non-users vs 61.7% in high-dose users; chronic kidney disease 6.1% vs 23.7%) [S:2f43094a-407b-5705-b941-869d914f322d], and the authors conclude [passage text removed]," acknowledging that NYHA class, echocardiographic data and the indication for diuretic initiation were unavailable [S:3b490317-e2bf-5052-bb5b-c5d5b45d0c3a].

## Interpretive caveats raised in the literature

Published correspondence stresses confounding by indication: LDT users were older, more symptomatic, with more atrial fibrillation and higher surgical risk scores, and adjustment [passage text removed] post-operative therapy was incomplete, so the ~2-fold HR may be overestimated; neither AS nor HF guidelines regard diuretics as prognosis-modifying [S:ed40a40f-2897-535b-a6e7-5659a61e4f14][S:ca277f4e-07ad-538b-bf8d-677a797376d0]. A second letter notes that many LDT patients still had elevated filling pressures, implying that residual congestion — not diuretic exposure — may drive prognosis, and that more effective decongestion rather than diuretic avoidance is the plausible therapeutic target [S:94fff021-0d55-5c46-af8d-e7300c846430].

**No randomised evidence** addressing whether modifying loop diuretic therapy alters post-AVR survival appeared in the sources retrieved; all data are observational.

rows.question: What is known about echocardiographic assessment of the left atrium when choosing rhythm control in critically ill patients with atrial fibrillation?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Left atrial size, measured as the left atrial volume index, is a central echocardiographic input to the rhythm-versus-rate decision, with a non-dilated left atrium favouring an attempt at rhythm control; A dilated left atrium is associated with longstanding or recurrent atrial fibrillation and steers management towards rate control; Higher left atrial ejection fraction and a higher mitral A wave velocity-time integral measured some hours after cardioversion tracked maintenance of sinus rhythm and fewer recurrences in a single cited septic shock study, a preliminary observation rather than a general rule; Tachycardia limits the mitral A wave velocity-time integral because it fuses the early and late mitral inflow waves. Certainty: These are preliminary observations from a small selected group and should not be read as general facts. Scope: applies to new-onset or unknown-duration atrial fibrillation complicating critical illness in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it states that selecting patients for rhythm control on the basis of left atrial size or function has been shown to improve survival.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Left atrial (LA) assessment — chiefly indexed end‑systolic LA volume (LAVI) before cardioversion, and LA emptying fraction (LA_EF) plus mitral A‑wave velocity–time integral (Avti) after it — is the single most developed echocardiographic input into the rhythm‑versus‑rate decision in critically ill AF, but the evidence base is essentially one group's septic‑shock cohort plus extrapolation from cardiology; LA size does **not** reliably predict cardioversion success in ICU patients as it does in ambulatory patients, and no guideline recommends it.

## Where LA measurement does inform the decision

**A non‑dilated LA supports rhythm control and modifies drug choice.** A recent narrative review proposes an algorithm in which rhythm control is preferred for all patients with a non‑dilated LA (LAVI < 40 mL/m²), no [passage text removed] rationale being immediate improvement in stroke volume and systemic vascular resistance on restoration of sinus rhythm, with consequent vasopressor withdrawal; borderline cases (mild‑to‑moderate LA dilatation) are re‑evaluated after cardioversion ([Balik et al., Intensive Care Med 2025;51:1855–1866, 10.1007/s00134-025-08112-8]([passage text removed]); [PMC12504342]([passage text removed])).

This threshold comes from a randomised trial and its LAVI‑stratified analysis. In 209 septic shock patients with new‑onset supraventricular arrhythmia and LVEF > 35%, propafenone gave faster cardioversion (median 3.7 h vs 7.3 h, p = 0.02) and fewer recurrences (52% vs 76%, p < 0.001) than amiodarone, but sinus rhythm at 24 h did not differ (72.8% vs 67.3%, p = 0.4); patients with a **dilated** LA [passage text removed] vs 18 h to cardioversion, p = 0.05) ([PMID 37698594](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37698594)). In the prespecified LAVI analysis, [passage text removed] 133 patients without LA enlargement, and LAVI < 40 mL/m² was associated with a 1‑year mortality benefit for propafenone ([passage text removed]); conversely, in the 37 patients with LAVI ≥ 40 mL/m², propafenone outcomes were **worse** than [passage text removed]), non‑significant [passage text removed]) ([PMID 38372622](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38372622)).

**Post‑cardioversion LA *function* outperforms pre‑cardioversion LA *size* for predicting durable sinus rhythm.** In the same cohort, cardioversion was achieved in 96% but 134/209 (64.1%) had ≥1 recurrence. At 4 h post‑cardioversion, [passage text removed]) were only *limited* predictors of a single recurrence; LA_EF 44% (36–49) and Avti 8.65 cm (7.13–9.50) were associated with sustained sinus rhythm and fell proportionally with increasing numbers of [passage text removed]). Enlarged LA end‑systolic **diameter** at arrhythmia onset was only a weak predictor of >3 recurrences (p = 0.04), as was [passage text removed]) ([PMID 38759581](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38759581); [J Crit Care 2024;83:154832]([passage text removed])). A separate analysis reported that these Doppler predictors of active LA emptying remain usable despite tachycardia and E/A fusion, so heart‑rate adjustment is not mandatory ([s41598-026-50593-0]([passage text removed])).

## Important caveats

- **The cardiology relationship does not transfer.** In non‑critically ill patients, lower pre‑cardioversion LAVI independently predicts both cardioversion success and 1‑month sinus rhythm maintenance ([PMID 23070632](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23070632)), and a meta‑analysis of 31 studies (2725 patients) found mean LAVI 40.56 mL/m² in sinus‑rhythm maintainers vs 48.69 mL/m² in recurrers (p < 0.001) ([PMC10902144]([passage text removed])). But the ICU review states explicitly that a relationship between LA size and cardioversion success/sinus‑rhythm maintenance **could not be confirmed** in ICU patients, and that [passage text removed] new‑onset AF a moderately dilated LA should not preclude attempting cardioversion ([10.1007/s00134-025-08112-8]([passage text removed])).
- **LA measures do predict arrhythmia burden/occurrence, which is a different question.** LA area was independently associated with new‑onset AF burden in critical illness (OR 1.13 per cm², 1.05–1.21, p = 0.002) ([PMC10994584]([passage text removed])), and in septic shock LA reservoir strain identified new‑onset AF (AUC 0.76 at a 20% threshold; feasibility 94%) ([reviewed in PMC11595645]([passage text removed]), primary study Beyls et al., [passage text removed]). I found no study using LA strain to select rhythm versus rate control in the ICU.
- **Guidelines give no LA‑based recommendation.** The SSAI clinical practice guideline could make no recommendation on first‑line pharmacological agent or on DC cardioversion for haemodynamically unstable ICU patients with new‑onset AF, finding no direct randomised evidence for its PICO questions ([PMID 37289426](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37289426)). The state‑of‑the‑art review likewise lists rate‑versus‑rhythm strategy as a knowledge gap ([Sibley et al., Intensive Care Med 2025;51:904–916, PMID 40323451](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40323451)).
- The ICU review also notes that no cardiology trial has stratified rhythm‑ versus rate‑control strategies by severity of LV diastolic dysfunction — i.e. by how much LV filling depends on atrial contraction — and calls predictors of successful cardioversion in the critically ill a "noticeable knowledge gap" ([PMC12504342]([passage text removed])).

**Bottom line for practice:** LAVI < 40 mL/m² (plus absence of significant valvular disease and preserved-to-moderately-reduced LVEF) identifies a phenotype in which rhythm control, and specifically a class Ic agent, has been associated with faster cardioversion, fewer recurrences and a 1‑year survival signal; a dilated LA argues against propafenone rather than against cardioversion per se; and LA_EF/Avti at 4 h should be used to decide whether to persist with rhythm control. All of this rests on one randomised trial and its secondary analyses, is not guideline‑endorsed, and has not been externally validated.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Left atrial (LA) echocardiography is the most developed tool for triaging rhythm versus rate control in critically ill AF, but the ICU evidence base is thin: proposed cut-offs come largely from single-centre septic-shock work and extrapolated cardiology data, and — importantly — the strong relationship between LA size and cardioversion success seen in cardiology patients has *not* been reproduced in ICU cohorts [S:d9572aa0-e106-5af1-8a60-421b71863b1c][S:ea5df22c-1294-50cd-94a2-92fc61873184].

## Rationale and which measurement to use

LA dilatation reflects the increasing contribution of atrial contraction to filling of a poorly relaxing/non-compliant LV, and enlarged LA size (area or volume) together with LV diastolic dysfunction have repeatedly been identified as independent predictors of new-onset AF in ICU patients [S:6245e040-cdb6-5a12-bf7f-efa514aeab6b]. Biplanar end-systolic LA volume indexed to BSA (LAVI) is preferred over the end-systolic LA diameter (LA_ESD): although LA_ESD should not exceed 45 mm, a value ≥46 mm on TTE poorly predicts recurrent AF in septic shock. Normal LAVI is quoted as <35 mL/m² in sinus rhythm and <40 mL/m² in AF, with the 35 mL/m² cut-off reflecting elevated LV end-diastolic pressure; a large LAVI may indicate longstanding or recurrent AF and steer towards rate control. TOE has not been validated for LA size because the atrium exceeds the 2D field of view [S:7365d758-8682-5371-ba90-e764b15de98f].

## Proposed ICU decision thresholds

A published echocardiography-guided algorithm assigns LAVI <40 mL/m² and LA_ESD <46 mm to rhythm control, and LAVI >48 mL/m² / LA_ESD >46 mm to rate control, alongside post-cardioversion LA function (LAEF >38% and transmitral A-wave velocity–time integral [Avti] >7 cm at 4 h favouring rhythm control; LAEF <20% or Avti <5 cm favouring rate control), plus E/e′, valve status and pulmonary artery pressure [S:74e1f5c9-4982-53f8-acd4-7436632b189d][S:d3788619-d552-5b38-a466-f51a43b938f4]. Rhythm control is preferred in NOAF with a non-excessively dilated LA, no significant valvular disease and high catecholamine requirements, because restored sinus rhythm improves stroke volume and vascular resistance and permits vasopressor weaning; significant LA dilatation, moderate-to-severe valve disease or very high catecholamine doses favour rate control [S:affd8fbd-0def-55aa-958c-6e81c843afe9][S:a09067cd-0cc0-59d8-aa57-1f91d69146d3].

## The key ICU caveat: static LA size performs poorly, function performs better

In the prospective septic-shock sub-study (PRASE), patients had a largely normal-sized LA (median LA_ESD 40 mm, LAVI 31 mL/m²) which did not change with cardioversion; LAEF and Avti at 4 h rose proportionally to fewer recurrences, but as predictors they were only modest (LAEF cut-off 38.4%, AUC 0.69; Avti [passage text removed]) [S:6e2f687d-fb6c-5e04-9b93-16364bb9ea80]. The authors concluded that echocardiographic parameters have *limited* usefulness for predicting sustained sinus rhythm in septic shock, that transmitral A-wave/Avti outperform static 2D LA measurements, and that LAEF is advantageous over end-systolic LAVI because it shifts less with the changing loading conditions typical of critical illness [S:5578fdda-1228-51ff-9e5c-4a656f01ff84][S:9497a237-5097-545a-b6f7-3d58423f5f9c]. Consequently, [passage text removed] [S:d9572aa0-e106-5af1-8a60-421b71863b1c].

## Drug selection and prognosis by LA size

LA size appears to modify antiarrhythmic choice: in the randomised propafenone-versus-amiodarone trial in septic shock, propafenone gave faster cardioversion and fewer recurrences, especially in patients with a *non-dilated* LA, whereas patients with a dilated LA had better rhythm control with amiodarone [S:7c541e09-0613-52a4-859c-7061a1d46440]. The review reports a 12-month survival benefit for propafenone over amiodarone in septic shock patients with NOAF and LAVI <40 mL/m² (OR 0.6, p = 0.01), suggesting LAVI may identify those who benefit prognostically from rhythm control [S:d9572aa0-e106-5af1-8a60-421b71863b1c][S:a09067cd-0cc0-59d8-aa57-1f91d69146d3]. Enlarged LA end-systolic diameter at arrhythmia onset and higher systolic pulmonary artery pressure at 4 h have also been described as predictors of multiple recurrences [S:3e363e4e-7d26-53bd-be68-634b83700afd].

## Electrical versus mechanical sinus rhythm

Restoring sinus rhythm on ECG does not mean restored LA mechanics: recovery may be gradual and not evident until 4–6 h after cardioversion, and up to a month or longer in chronic persistent AF. Patients in ECG sinus rhythm with no A wave on mitral inflow are at high recurrence risk, and long-term rate control is preferred over repeated futile cardioversion attempts [S:9497a237-5097-545a-b6f7-3d58423f5f9c]. Avti's main limitation is tachycardia causing E–A fusion, potentially falsely favouring rhythm control at heart rates ≥85/min, though this was not clinically relevant in septic shock [S:361b0e60-7e47-562e-a72d-9b4bf9a5cd9d]. Restoration of mechanical sinus rhythm with adequate LAEF and Avti is argued to reduce anticoagulation requirements and bleeding risk, but the authors explicitly note ICU data are lacking [S:ea5df22c-1294-50cd-94a2-92fc61873184].

## Supporting (non-ICU) and contextual evidence

Cardiology data underpin the thresholds: severe LA dilatation is associated with [passage text removed], and LA volume predicts incident AF better than linear dimensions [S:680eafd7-85dc-5a78-b33d-58c6f3f4361a]. Pre-cardioversion LAVI predicted AF recurrence after electrical cardioversion (SR group 42.21±12.4 vs AF group 96.08±52.21 mL/m²; cut-off 55 mL/m²) [S:f85f7e27-2977-5df4-94d5-05f3f09a2a05], and a narrative review of DCCV outcome prediction found increased LAVI, LA dilatation, reduced LA appendage flow velocity and reduced atrial strain all associated with failure [S:a3bc3805-2989-5a73-b51c-cc821f8a327f]. Guidelines favour LAVI (>34 mL/m² = enlargement) over AP diameter for this reason [S:74161904-882b-5471-bf85-c3dfa75c50c4].

## Acknowledged gaps

There is an explicit "[passage text removed] AF patients, with scarce ICU data and small single-centre studies; no cardiology trial has stratified rhythm-versus-rate strategy by severity of diastolic dysfunction [S:6245e040-cdb6-5a12-bf7f-efa514aeab6b][S:ea5df22c-1294-50cd-94a2-92fc61873184]. LA strain is limited by absent ICU-specific reference values and ICU image quality [S:affd8fbd-0def-55aa-958c-6e81c843afe9]. The randomised CAFS trial comparing risk, rate and rhythm control in septic shock is ongoing and has not reported outcomes [S:48ad704e-cb4f-53f6-ae13-c3b872ae5b1d]; I found no trial that has randomised critically ill patients to a strategy *stratified by* LA echocardiographic parameters, so the thresholds above remain expert-proposed rather than validated.

rows.question: What is known about bleeding risk with antithrombotic regimens after carotid stenting in patients with atrial fibrillation?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Major bleeding within the first three months did not differ significantly between dual antiplatelet therapy, single antiplatelet plus oral anticoagulation, and triple therapy; Major bleeding was numerically least frequent with dual antiplatelet therapy alone and most frequent with triple therapy, a non-significant trend; Bleeding events were too few and the sample too small to detect real differences, so no regimen can be identified as the safest. Certainty: The evidence is weak and preliminary, with far too few bleeding events to exclude real differences between the regimens. Scope: applies to atherosclerotic carotid stenosis treated with carotid artery stenting with concurrent non-valvular atrial fibrillation in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it recommends dual antiplatelet therapy alone as the preferred regimen or advises withholding oral anticoagulation because bleeding was numerically lowest.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

No randomized trial has tested antithrombotic regimens after carotid artery stenting (CAS) in atrial fibrillation (AF); the evidence is limited to small single-centre cohorts and administrative registries, which consistently signal that **triple therapy (oral anticoagulant + dual antiplatelet therapy) carries the highest bleeding risk**, while anticoagulant + a single antiplatelet — and eventually anticoagulant alone — appear safer without a clear ischaemic penalty. Guidelines extrapolate from the AF-PCI trials rather than from carotid-specific data ([ESVS 2023](https://college-vasculaire.com/storage/page_paragraphe/25/page_paragraphe_fichier/67e86851576838427248711e876e22fd.pdf)).

## Evidence by regimen

**Triple therapy — highest bleeding rates.** In the most-cited comparative cohort (91 of 959 CAS patients with AF; [PMID 35393364](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35393364), [PMC9089259]([passage text removed])), major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding at 30 days occurred in 10/42 (23.8%) on triple therapy versus 1/24 (4%) on DAPT alone (P = .032) and **zero** events in the DOAC + clopidogrel group (P = .007). All four major bleeds and the single intracranial haemorrhage occurred in the triple-therapy arm. Groups were comparably high-risk (median HAS-BLED 4 in all three; median CHA₂DS₂-VASc 5–6), and efficacy endpoints did not differ significantly — there was one stent thrombosis in the DOAC+clopidogrel group and one cardioembolic stroke in the DAPT group. The authors' proposed algorithm is DOAC + clopidogrel for the first month post-CAS, then switching clopidogrel to aspirin ([PMC9089259]([passage text removed])).

**Contradicting/null data.** A larger, more recent retrospective series (1047 CAS patients, 129 with AF; [PMID 41100890](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41100890), [Ovid record](https://www.ovid.com/00134449-202660030-00001)) found **no significant differences** at 3 months: major bleeding 3.2% (1/31) with DAPT, 6.5% (3/46) with single antiplatelet + anticoagulant, 7.7% (4/52) with triple therapy (P = 0.71); ischaemic stroke 6.4%/4.3%/1.9% (P = 0.57) and stent thrombosis 3.2%/6.5%/1.9% (P = 0.32). Note the numerically *lowest* ischaemic event rate was in the triple-therapy arm — illustrating the ischaemia/bleeding trade-off and that these cohorts are underpowered.

**De-escalation (dropping aspirin).** In an edoxaban-based cohort ([PMC13495688]([passage text removed])), stopping aspirin was associated with fewer 12-month bleeding events than continuous dual antithrombotic therapy (8.93% vs 23.44%, P = 0.033), with the difference concentrated after the transition point (6–12 months: 4.69% vs 15.63%, P = 0.047). Embolic events were comparable (14.29% vs 9.38%, P = 0.403), and BARC ≥3 major bleeding did not differ significantly (P = 0.216) — i.e. the reduction was driven largely by less severe bleeding.

**Small DOAC + single antiplatelet series.** A 31-patient study ([PMID 32402723](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32402723)) reported no haemorrhagic or thromboembolic events in the DOAC + single antiplatelet group (n=14), versus a silent subarachnoid haemorrhage and a superior mesenteric artery occlusion among the 17 patients on vitamin K antagonist + DAPT; the authors explicitly note the sample was too small for statistical inference. A separate 32-patient series using abbreviated triple therapy converted to DOAC + a single non-aspirin antiplatelet, guided by platelet-inhibition testing (target PRU <150), reported no haemorrhagic events, stent thromboses, or intracranial haemorrhage within 30 days or at mean 16-month follow-up ([PMC8620833]([passage text removed])).

**Registry data.** In 2116 Taiwanese NVAF patients post-CAS ([Sci Rep 12:1417]([passage text removed]), [PMC8792010]([passage text removed])), groups were antiplatelet only (n=587), anticoagulant only (n=477), dual antiplatelet (n=49), and antiplatelet+anticoagulant combination (n=304). Anticoagulant-containing groups had lower mortality than antiplatelet-only (P = 0.0219), with **no statistically significant differences in major bleeding**, ischaemic stroke, or vascular events; the combination group showed a non-significant trend toward fewer ischaemic strokes but more bleeding. The authors concluded one anticoagulant is sufficient for most such patients.

**Longer-term: drop the antiplatelet.** In 5708 AF patients with carotid artery disease after first ischaemic stroke ([PMID 36692658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36692658), [PMC11266273]([passage text removed])), compared with NOAC alone, major bleeding risk was higher with NOAC + antiplatelet ([passage text removed]), warfarin alone (HR 1.34, 1.12–1.60), and warfarin + antiplatelet (HR 1.66, 1.40–1.96; also mortality HR 1.51, 1.20–1.89), with **no difference in recurrent stroke** between groups. A meta-analysis in AF with cerebral atherosclerosis reached the same conclusion: long-term OAC + antiplatelet did not reduce recurrent ischaemic stroke but substantially increased major bleeding including intracranial haemorrhage ([PMC13243853]([passage text removed])).

## Practical framing

ESVS 2023 recommends aspirin + clopidogrel for ≥4 weeks after stenting in recently symptomatic patients generally, and for AF specifically states that AF-PCI RCTs suggest dual antithrombotic therapy (anticoagulant + single antiplatelet) is superior to triple therapy for bleeding while non-inferior for thromboembolism, offering a "pragmatic algorithm" rather than carotid-specific evidence ([ESVS 2023 PDF](https://college-vasculaire.com/storage/page_paragraphe/25/page_paragraphe_fichier/67e86851576838427248711e876e22fd.pdf)). Left atrial appendage occlusion after CAS has been described as a triple-therapy-avoiding strategy, but only in a four-patient case series ([PMC7341018]([passage text removed])).

**Caveats:** all CAS-specific comparisons are retrospective, non-randomized, and small (largest n=129 AF patients for the three-way comparison); bleeding definitions and follow-up windows differ across studies; and the two direct three-arm comparisons disagree on whether triple therapy's excess bleeding is statistically detectable. Peri-CAS patients carry additional bleeding hazards not present in the PCI trials — recent stroke and hyperperfusion syndrome risk ([PMC9089259]([passage text removed])) — so extrapolation from AF-PCI data is not fully secure. I found no randomized trial addressing this question; the AJNR authors call for one.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Bleeding risk after carotid artery stenting (CAS) in atrial fibrillation (AF) rises with the number of antithrombotic agents — triple therapy (oral anticoagulant + dual antiplatelet) carries the highest hemorrhage rates in the small CAS-specific cohorts, and an anticoagulant + single P2Y12 inhibitor ("dual antithrombotic") is the emerging preferred compromise — but the evidence base is entirely observational, small, and partly inconsistent; no randomized trial exists in this population. [S:7336f3de-3806-591c-b2c1-e8f3ab766d19] [S:bffd04a2-b7b7-545b-9ffa-238079cdc4a4]

## Why the question is unresolved

CAS is often withheld in favor of endarterectomy in AF precisely because stent protection requires dual antiplatelet therapy while AF requires anticoagulation, and [passage text removed] are lacking, so regimens are chosen case-by-case against three competing risks (cardioembolic stroke, coronary ischemia, bleeding). [S:bffd04a2-b7b7-545b-9ffa-238079cdc4a4] [S:327928e1-7128-5ad8-82f3-55ba9ec8895b] Some guidance has explicitly advised endarterectomy over stenting for AF patients with symptomatic high-grade carotid stenosis because stenting adds dual antiplatelet therapy on top of anticoagulation with higher bleeding risk. [S:42410ada-9071-58fb-bbcf-5326094c1acd] Canadian stroke best-practice recommendations similarly advise against routine concomitant antiplatelet plus anticoagulant in AF because of increased bleeding, absent a specific additional indication. [S:c776a227-f241-598c-890e-f4ea0f4e9a48]

## CAS-specific data

**Triple therapy shows the highest bleeding signal.** In a single-center cohort of 91 AF patients after CAS (24 on DOAC+clopidogrel, 42 triple therapy, 25 DAPT; median HAS-BLED 4 in all groups), major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding at 30 days occurred in 23.8% of the triple-therapy group versus 4% with DAPT (P = .032) and no bleeding events in the DOAC+P2Y12 group (P = .007); efficacy endpoints did not differ significantly (one stent thrombosis in the DOAC+clopidogrel group, one cardioembolic stroke with DAPT). The authors concluded triple therapy confers a high bleeding risk and DOAC+P2Y12 inhibitor may offer a good safety profile. [S:https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35393364] [[passage text removed]] A narrative review of carotid/intracranial stent antithrombotics reaches the same reading of that study. [S:5d179682-1632-5a83-bc2c-5269f50b3997]

**A larger, longer cohort found no statistically significant differences.** A retrospective study of CAS in pre-existing AF (2011–2024) comparing DAPT, single antiplatelet + anticoagulation (AA), and triple therapy (TT), with ISTH-defined major bleeding as the primary outcome, found no significant differences in bleeding or ischemic outcomes. [S:7336f3de-3806-591c-b2c1-e8f3ab766d19] [S:3e2f6e7d-aebf-5eb3-ac5d-450051718771] Non-significant trends went in the expected directions: TT had the lowest ischemic event rate (1.9%) but the highest major bleeding (7.7%); DAPT had the lowest major bleeding (3.2%) but the highest ischemic stroke rate (6.4%); the AA group had the highest stent thrombosis rate (6.5%), suggesting a single antiplatelet plus anticoagulation may be insufficient for stent protection. [S:3bbc8924-c29c-5915-8898-05bf2682e896] Within the TT group (n=51), event rates were similar for apixaban-based versus warfarin-based triple therapy. [S:3bbc8924-c29c-5915-8898-05bf2682e896] A related conference abstract reported the same ordering at 3 months — major bleeding 3.2% (DAPT), 5.3% (anticoagulant + antiplatelet), 7.7% (triple), p=0.71; stroke 6.4%, 3.5%, 1.9%, p=0.57 — i.e. underpowered rather than equivalent. [S:05f7b078-6405-5b53-b919-515391707369] The authors attribute discrepancies with the Pardo-Galiana results to differences in technique, stent type, and center-specific antithrombotic protocols. [S:aa3d91d9-fcc2-522b-8162-c2ba6239f28f]

**Aspirin-free dual regimens look safe in small series.** In 32 AF patients on DOACs undergoing CAS with an abbreviated periprocedural triple regimen (DOAC held 48 h with one enoxaparin dose, restarted 12–24 h post-procedure) then discharged on DOAC plus one non-aspirin antiplatelet titrated to PRU <150, there were no intracranial hemorrhages, deaths, embolic strokes, or stent thromboses within 30 days and no new events at ~16 months. [S:03972168-7c1b-5e58-9c97-9801ffa6fd96] In 30 non-valvular AF patients undergoing carotid or vertebral artery stenting transitioned post-procedure to NOAC + P2Y12 inhibitor, there was one hemorrhage (a brainstem hemorrhage in a patient switched from rivaroxaban to dabigatran) and one unexplained embolism, with no stent thrombosis or restenosis at 3 months; the authors advise against switching NOACs in stable patients because of bleeding risk. [S:6e451724-39c8-5c31-840d-2a21c730c99f] [S:fd1cc226-24b8-529a-bab8-b0dff9adbcf7]

**Population-level data.** In 2,116 non-valvular AF patients receiving CAS in the Taiwanese NHIRD (2010–2016), anticoagulant-alone and combined antiplatelet+anticoagulant groups had lower mortality than antiplatelet-alone ([passage text removed]; too few patients stayed on DAPT to match. Notably, about one-third had inconsistent treatment records, reflecting real-world uncertainty in drug selection. [S:ac666e8a-c4ac-5731-9e1e-e62b45bb5536] [S:f136b3fb-6d9d-5576-b00a-6c2d23f5bd4d]

## Context: baseline bleeding after CAS and PCI extrapolation

Even without anticoagulation, hemorrhagic complications after CAS cluster [passage text removed], P<0.0001), with extracranial hemorrhage predominating beyond 30 days. [S:6cf30f5d-58ab-54fd-9bb0-b9e28c7d3c36] Most reasoning is therefore borrowed from AF-PCI trials: WOEST showed any bleeding in 44.4% with triple versus 19.4% with dual therapy at one year [S:a067f4f6-d623-5e67-9acd-dc903a8a22ce]; AUGUSTUS showed major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding in 16.1% with apixaban+P2Y12+aspirin versus 9.0% with apixaban+P2Y12+placebo ([passage text removed]) [S:7b8ad4ee-72ef-5a1f-a5db-9c5c397b3e42]; and network meta-analysis found NOAC+P2Y12 reduced TIMI major bleeding by 47% versus VKA-based triple therapy (OR 0.53; 95% CrI 0.35–0.78) without excess MACE, stroke, or stent thrombosis. [S:d3b3bce5-50e4-5bf8-8431-1ec963e03c4e] The caveat carried into the CAS literature is that aspirin-omitting regimens may increase myocardial infarction and stent thrombosis. [S:327928e1-7128-5ad8-82f3-55ba9ec8895b] [S:939609f0-b812-5f1b-9d2c-f20c72b52152] Neurointerventional guideline updates likewise draw on this cardiac evidence rather than carotid-specific trials. [S:ff969fa5-32ff-529e-8147-2521b30e232e]

## Practice variation

An ESMINT/SNIS survey of 105 participants across 31 countries found 61.9% lack a standardized institutional antithrombotic protocol; dual antithrombotic therapy was preferred over triple [passage text removed]%) by HAS-BLED, 54.3% switch VKA to a NOAC post-CAS, and 69.5% transition to anticoagulant monotherapy at one year — a trend toward DAT driven by hemorrhagic concerns, with randomized trials called for. [S:44c2e493-9f3a-5d30-b02e-c35f38d18a3c]

## Gaps I could not fill from the retrieved evidence

No source provided randomized data, an optimal duration of triple therapy specific to CAS, validated bleeding-risk prediction in this population, or head-to-head comparisons of individual DOACs after CAS.

rows.question: What is known about outcomes after tricuspid transcatheter edge-to-edge repair in the very elderly?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: The very elderly, the oldest patients treated, reach two-year survival after tricuspid edge-to-edge repair comparable to that of the youngest, so older age at intervention is not associated with worse survival; Survival free from heart failure hospitalisation is similar irrespective of age at intervention, including in patients with massive or torrential regurgitation at baseline; Reduction of tricuspid regurgitation is durable in elderly and very elderly patients; Improvement in functional class is of similar degree in older patients as in younger ones. Certainty: The evidence is an observed comparison across age groups in routine practice with no untreated comparison group, so comparable outcomes with advancing age are a consistent pattern rather than proven equivalence or a demonstrated benefit of the procedure. Scope: applies to significant tricuspid regurgitation treated with transcatheter edge-to-edge repair in older adults, including the very elderly, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it states that age can be disregarded in selection so that the procedure should be offered to any very elderly patient irrespective of comorbidity, symptoms, anatomy and expected life expectancy.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: the available evidence — largely observational, with no dedicated randomised data — consistently shows that T-TEER in the very elderly (≥85, including nonagenarians) achieves TR reduction, symptomatic improvement, and survival/heart-failure-hospitalisation outcomes comparable to younger T-TEER patients, so chronological age alone should not disqualify a patient; but absolute event rates remain high and patients >85 with frailty or cognitive impairment are under-represented in trials.**

**Age-stratified registry data (the main direct evidence)**
- The EuroTR registry analysis of age is the largest dedicated dataset: 2,340 T-TEER patients in four age quartiles ([passage text removed]). TR reduction to ≤2+ at discharge was similar across quartiles (77.3%, 82%, 79.5%, 82.8%; p = 0.085), as was TR ≤2+ at follow-up (68.1%, 72.1%, 76.7%, 73.7%; p = 0.135). NYHA improvement was equivalent, and two-year overall survival and survival free from heart-failure hospitalisation did not differ between age groups ([passage text removed]; Novotny, Stolz, Kresoja et al., Clin Res Cardiol 2025).
- In the same study's dedicated very-elderly subanalyses, patients ≥85 and ≥90 years achieved TR ≤2+ in roughly 70–80%, and after T-TEER nearly 60% of those >85 years and almost 70% of those >90 years were NYHA ≤II at follow-up; overall survival in the >85 and >90 groups was comparable to the rest of the cohort. The authors conclude [passage text removed]," while stressing that in nonagenarians symptom and quality-of-life improvement is the most meaningful goal ([passage text removed]). Results were confirmed in a subanalysis restricted to the post-commercial TriClip era (76% of the cohort).
- A German (DGK 2025) registry abstract comparing patients younger and older than 80 concluded that similar reduction of TR severity and heart-failure symptoms is achievable in both groups, though the snippet indicating how octogenarians differed was truncated and I could not read the full text (herzmedizin.de/.../p1807).
- A propensity-weighted analysis specifically of octogenarians undergoing tricuspid TEER exists (Monaco et al., Am J Cardiol 2025; [passage text removed]). The accessible material states there is a scarcity of perioperative data in this group and, per the highlights, [passage text removed] than younger patients; I could not access the full results, so I cannot give its numerical outcomes.

**Context: the pivotal trials and registries are already an elderly population, but not a very elderly one**
- TRILUMINATE Pivotal mean age was 78.1 ± 7.8 years; T-TEER met the primary hierarchical endpoint (win ratio 1.84; P < 0.0001) driven by quality of life, with freedom from all-cause mortality and tricuspid surgery at 12 months of 90.6% (device) vs 89.9% (control; P = 0.82) and comparable heart-failure hospitalisation rates ([passage text removed]) (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39471883; [passage text removed]). So the benefit demonstrated in this age range is symptomatic, not survival.
- Real-world bRIGHT enrolled a mean age of 79 ± 7 years with 80% NYHA III/IV, showing sustained TR reduction (83% moderate or less at 1 year, 80% at 2 years) with 98% freedom from major adverse events and 99% survival at 30 days (structuralheart.abbott/fileadmin/pdf/TriClip_bRIGHT_DataCard_Global_MAT-2402646.pdf). TriCLASP (PASCAL) enrolled patients with a mean age of 80.1 ± 6.0 years, with 30-day cardiovascular mortality of 0.3% and no urgent reinterventions or device embolisations ([passage text removed]).
- Residual risk in these elderly cohorts is substantial regardless of age: a meta-analysis of 10 studies/4,134 patients found pooled 1-year all-cause mortality [passage text removed]), HF hospitalisation 16.9% (8.7–25.1), persistent NYHA III–IV in 30.9% (22.1–39.7), and early residual TR ≥3+ in 19.1%; the pooled mean age was 79 years with 90% atrial fibrillation and 48% chronic kidney disease (annalscts.com/article/view/17557/html; PMC13263422). Notably, in that meta-regression **age was not associated** with 1-year mortality, HF hospitalisation, or persistent NYHA III–IV (age β = 2.03, 95% CI −3.53 to 7.59, P = 0.43), whereas diabetes, COPD, CKD, pacemaker/ICD, higher pulmonary pressures and larger annulus were.
- What does drive outcome is procedural result and disease stage, not age: residual TR ≥3+ independently predicted 2-year mortality ([passage text removed]) in EuroTR (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38812292), and previous cardiac surgery predicted residual TR and higher 2-year [passage text removed]).

**Acknowledged gaps for the very elderly**
- A narrative cardiogeriatric review states explicitly that [passage text removed] that [passage text removed], leaving major knowledge gaps on [passage text removed]; it also notes TRILUMINATE Pivotal excluded lead-associated TR, which is common in older adults (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12774957; [passage text removed]).
- A recent review of TEER in older adults names octogenarians, nonagenarians and [passage text removed] as priority populations for future study, and reports procedural safety remains high with most studies reporting mean ages between 75 and (higher) years ([passage text removed]).
- Supportive geriatric-relevant signals in this population, cited within the EuroTR age paper: physical activity measured by actigraphy [passage text removed] (median age 79), and cognitive function in octogenarians improved in executive function and memory at 3 months ([passage text removed]).

**Caveats:** all very-elderly-specific data are non-randomised and subject to selection of fitter patients; the ≥85/≥90 findings come from supplemental subgroups of one registry with small numbers, and I found no randomised or head-to-head comparison of T-TEER versus medical therapy confined to patients ≥85.

## Bottom line

In the largest dedicated analysis, [passage text removed]) in the very elderly — including nonagenarians — achieves TR reduction, symptomatic improvement, and 2-year survival that are statistically indistinguishable from those in substantially younger patients, so age alone appears to be an inadequate criterion for withholding the procedure. [S:398fa34e-6b40-569e-8187-43c23f9f1a47][S:7ede6b8f-084e-52eb-ac68-f2e7735d33b1]

## Principal evidence: EuroTR age-stratified analysis

The [passage text removed], NCT06307262) analysed 2,340 patients treated with MitraClip/TriClip or PASCAL between 2016 and 2024 at European sites, split into age quartiles from a mean of 69.9 ± 7.2 years (1st quartile, n = 668) to 86.2 ± 2.2 years (4th quartile, n = 561). Secondary TR predominated in every group (83.6%–90.1%). [S:398fa34e-6b40-569e-8187-43c23f9f1a47][S:1b293288-cfbd-56d5-aafa-216d2e822ae6]

- **Procedural efficacy was not worse with age.** TR ≤2+ at discharge: 77.3%, 82%, 79.5%, and 82.8% across quartiles (p = 0.085); residual TR 3+ at discharge was numerically *lowest* in the oldest quartile (13.2% vs 18.6% in the youngest). At latest follow-up, TR ≤2+ was 68.1%, 72.1%, 76.7%, and 73.7% (p = 0.135). [S:398fa34e-6b40-569e-8187-43c23f9f1a47][S:57d40dea-f51e-5952-8f4c-26f3c64351ff]
- **Symptomatic benefit was age-independent.** Baseline NYHA ≥III was 79.8%–86.5% (p = 0.211); at follow-up more than half of every group was NYHA ≤II (57.9%, 67.2%, 58.7%, 56.1%; p = 0.029, with the oldest group similar to the youngest). [S:d64beb32-7621-54b5-8430-1eb85a9b8e06]
- **Survival did not differ.** [passage text removed] heart-failure hospitalisation were comparable across all four age strata, despite an ~16-year age gap between the oldest and youngest quartiles. [S:398fa34e-6b40-569e-8187-43c23f9f1a47][S:95f2871f-812e-515a-8e98-1f973cff0b7c]
- **A plausible explanation is favourable phenotype, not resilience per se.** The oldest patients had preserved LV and RV function and smaller RV and tricuspid annulus dimensions, more atrial fibrillation (94.2% in the 4th quartile), and less pronounced leaflet tenting (tenting height 6.7 ± 3.3 mm vs 7.7 ± 3.6 mm in the youngest) — i.e. an atrial-functional, more repair-favourable substrate. Notably, EuroScore II was higher in the oldest quartile (6.9 ± 5.9 vs 5.6 ± 5.6), yet median TRI-SCORE was 5 in all groups (p = 0.305). [S:95f2871f-812e-515a-8e98-1f973cff0b7c][S:57d40dea-f51e-5952-8f4c-26f3c64351ff]

The authors' explicit conclusion is that T-TEER should not be withheld from nonagenarians in good general condition without comorbidities that would dilute the benefit, and that in this group symptom and quality-of-life improvement is the primary realistic goal. [S:7ede6b8f-084e-52eb-ac68-f2e7735d33b1][S:95f2871f-812e-515a-8e98-1f973cff0b7c]

## Supporting and contextual evidence

- **Real-world registries reinforce feasibility in advanced age.** The bRIGHT post-approval study (mean age 78.9 ± 7.1 years) [passage text removed] marked NYHA/quality-of-life gains "even in elderly patients with torrential TR," with 1-year all-cause mortality of 15.1%; mortality tracked residual TR rather than baseline severity (1-year survival 70.6% with ≥severe residual TR at 30 days vs 91.9% with moderate). [S:982f3967-ba1c-5876-8103-ceeb0a10d73c][S:8238a5d2-bffe-50f3-9551-4f61917c900c]
- **Small single-centre series in the very old.** A UK programme report describes 7 consecutive T-TEER patients aged 79–92 years (mean 84.7), all in NYHA III/IV with prior decompensation, all with atrial fibrillation, treated transfemorally with TriClip or PASCAL. [S:819d5ad9-bb6e-525f-9ca0-8a88874dc64c] A 32-patient Irish series (April 2022–April 2025) reported 91% device implantation, 2-grade TR reduction in 81%, and no procedure-related or in-hospital deaths. [S:41fceca1-5e47-581b-a8ff-c98b949e0560]
- **Risk in older patients is better captured by comorbidity/RV metrics than by age.** In 180 T-TEER patients, TRI-SCORE predicted 30-day and 1-year mortality far better than EuroSCORE II or STS score (AUC 90.3% and 93.1%), with 30-day mortality 0%/1.3%/17.4% across low/intermediate/high-risk groups. [S:13a4da8b-9e05-5160-8bb1-cb1d48472cd5][S:c0a4c708-3879-59d4-9632-0812a9dc741c] In EuroTR, RV dysfunction, RV dilation, and residual TR — not age — were the multivariable predictors of death (e.g. residual TR [passage text removed]). [S:4e9faf4b-d806-57ae-b662-c3773b0d96b0] Frailty carries independent prognostic weight in transcatheter mitral/tricuspid repair (2-year survival 88 ± 5% non-frail vs 62 ± 10% frail; HR 1.54 per SD of the essential frailty toolset). [S:0202f025-c4d2-512c-a3e8-359f39553efe]
- **A futility signal exists at the high-risk extreme.** In pooled/registry data, patients with TRI-SCORE ≥6 had similar survival regardless of treatment modality, [passage text removed]; T-TEER 1-year survival was 89.7% with TRI-SCORE <6 vs 67.6% with ≥6. [S:98e9a475-4480-5cb6-8d38-f57b5140df50][S:998a3a72-e807-5357-b5a5-ca2cd28f7ce0] EuroTR staging work similarly found a mortality benefit versus conservative care only in [passage text removed]), not in early or advanced stages. [S:bcf70800-9d2e-56dd-a5d6-0adc42bb2b84]

## Important limitations of the evidence

- The age-stratified data are **registry-based and non-randomised**, with treatment allocation by local heart teams accounting for comorbidity, anatomy, and life expectancy — so the very elderly who were treated are a selected, favourably phenotyped group, and these data cannot establish that T-TEER improves survival versus medical therapy in this age band. [S:1b293288-cfbd-56d5-aafa-216d2e822ae6]
- The randomised trials that anchor the field (TRILUMINATE Pivotal, mean age 78.0 ± 7.4 years; Tri.Fr, mean age 78 years) enrolled cohorts whose *mean* age is only ~78, showed quality-of-life and symptom benefit without a mortality signal at 1 year, and I found **no published age-subgroup or nonagenarian-specific randomised analysis**. [S:8238a5d2-bffe-50f3-9551-4f61917c900c][S:c476b68c-668e-515f-ba70-d8631d6c6675][S:32b11071-e4c1-59b9-ae27-11886da5e6ba][S:856d96f2-8755-540f-8297-c3eed44c80bd]
- I did not find quantitative age-stratified **safety/complication** data (e.g. single-leaflet detachment or bleeding in patients ≥85 or ≥90); reported T-TEER complication rates are cohort-wide (single-leaflet detachment 2.6–7.0%; TRILUMINATE major bleeding 4.7%). [S:8238a5d2-bffe-50f3-9551-4f61917c900c][S:c476b68c-668e-515f-ba70-d8631d6c6675]
- No source I retrieved reports **KCCQ or objective functional outcomes stratified by age** after T-TEER; the EuroTR symptomatic endpoint was NYHA class only. [S:1b293288-cfbd-56d5-aafa-216d2e822ae6]

rows.question: How does the Naples Prognostic Score relate to mortality in acute coronary syndrome patients undergoing PCI?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: A high Naples Prognostic Score is associated with higher all-cause mortality after percutaneous coronary intervention for acute coronary syndrome, on the order of a two-fold difference between high and low score groups (pooled risk ratio about 0.42 for low versus high); Pooled comparisons of high versus low score groups show no significant difference in death during the index hospital admission; The in-hospital mortality comparison is far less stable than the all-cause mortality result, with heterogeneity between datasets so high that the estimate shifts according to which studies are included. Certainty: The association with all-cause mortality is consistent and quantified but reflects observed differences between patient groups rather than the effect of any assigned treatment, while the in-hospital mortality estimate is too heterogeneous to be relied upon. Scope: applies to acute coronary syndrome treated with percutaneous coronary intervention in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it states that treating the nutritional or inflammatory components of the score lowers the score and thereby reduces death.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** A high Naples Prognostic Score (NPS) at admission is consistently and independently associated with higher mortality in ACS patients treated with PCI — the association is strongest and most reproducible for longer-term all-cause death, whereas its pooled effect on in-hospital death is statistically unstable, and all supporting data are observational and geographically narrow.

**Pooled evidence.** The only meta-analysis on this question included seven observational studies and 13,268 ACS patients undergoing PCI (5,628 low-NPS, 7,640 high-NPS); low NPS was associated with lower [passage text removed]%), lower no-reflow ([passage text removed]), and [passage text removed]), but in-hospital mortality did not differ significantly ([passage text removed]%) (PMID 41459707 / PMC12746426). The in-hospital null result was driven by one study: excluding Saygi et al. reduced heterogeneity to I²=68.2% and made the effect significant ([passage text removed]); the all-cause mortality estimate was robust to leave-one-out analysis (PMC12746426).

**Primary cohorts, long-term mortality.**
- STEMI, primary PCI (n=1,887; median follow-up 15 months; overall mortality 14.6%): [passage text removed] HR [passage text removed]), with improved model fit and calibration — Angiology 74(10):970–980, doi 10.1177/00033197231151559.
- STEMI, primary PCI (n=1,889; median 43 months, IQR 32–78): NPS was independently associated with long-term mortality, improved discrimination when added to a baseline model, and had the greatest contribution in the prediction model on decision-curve analysis — Angiology 75(8):725–733, doi 10.1177/00033197231170982 (PMID 37058422).
- NSTEMI with selective PCI (n=197): 1-year mortality 33.7% (high NPS) vs 8.1% (low NPS), p<0.001; adjusted HR [passage text removed]) — Diagnostics 2025;15(5):640.
- NSTEMI (n=125, mean 60-month follow-up): NPS independently predicted long-term mortality (HR 6.762, 95% CI 1.937–23.602), AUC 0.763 at a cut-off of 2.5 — doi 10.4274/e-cvsi.2025.2051.
- NSTEMI cohort in which 76.5% received PCI: high- vs non-high-risk NPS [passage text removed]) for long-term mortality — PMC12481722 (doi 10.1080/17520363.2025.2548759).

**In-hospital mortality — a dose–response but less consistent signal.** In the largest STEMI cohort (n=3,828 primary PCI), in-hospital mortality rose graded with NPS after adjustment for age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, Killip class, blood pressure, heart rate, LVEF, MI type and no-reflow: [passage text removed] and [passage text removed] vs NPS 0–2 — Coron Artery Dis 2024;35(1):31–37 (PMID 37990558). A 570-patient STEMI series (in-hospital mortality 4.9%) found the Naples score an independent predictor (OR 4.368, 95% CI 2.881–6.625) — [passage text removed]. In NSTE-ACS undergoing PCI, each 1-point increase in the Naples score raised in-hospital mortality odds ([passage text removed], univariable), with performance comparable to a CRP-modified version — Medicina 62(8):1573.

**Contradictory data.** In a single-centre STEMI cohort (n=214, 36 in-hospital deaths), NPS did not differ between survivors and non-survivors and had no significant discrimination (AUC 0.55), while the Ion Shift Index did (AUC 0.70) — PMC12428332 / Diagnostics 2025;15(17):2186.

**Caveats.** All seven pooled studies were conducted in Turkey, all were observational, follow-up ranged from in-hospital to 8 years, and no individual-patient subgroup analysis was possible (PMC12746426). A published commentary further notes that dichotomising continuous components (albumin, NLR) discards gradient risk information and that no clinical action threshold has been defined or tested prospectively (PMID 41622793 / PMC12862230). Broader CAD cohorts (not restricted to ACS-PCI) show a graded association — HR 1.15 per 1-point increase in the fully adjusted model — supporting biological consistency rather than ACS-specific validation (Front Immunol 2025;16:1529779).
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Higher Naples Prognostic Score (NPS) at admission is consistently and independently associated with increased mortality after PCI for ACS — robustly so for long-term/all-cause death, but inconsistently for in-hospital death.

## Pooled evidence

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 studies and 13,268 ACS patients undergoing PCI (5,628 in the low-NPS group) found that low NPS was associated with significantly lower [passage text removed] less no-reflow ([passage text removed]), with higher LVEF in the low-NPS group ([passage text removed]) [S:936a3198-c15e-5f2f-a9db-1e47a58b02f3]. In-hospital mortality did not differ significantly overall ([passage text removed]%), which the authors attribute to only four studies reporting this endpoint and low event rates; a sensitivity analysis excluding one outlier study (which used three-tier NPS categorisation and an earlier study period) reduced heterogeneity to I² = 68.2% and yielded a [passage text removed]) [S:790bf0d8-3be3-5512-aba4-0881fea6a68a].

## Primary studies

- **STEMI, long-term:** In 1,889 STEMI patients treated with primary PCI (median follow-up 43 months), the high-NPS group had higher long-term mortality, NPS was independently associated with mortality, and adding NPS to a baseline model improved prediction, discrimination, and net benefit on decision-curve analysis [S:e47f5aca-e25c-58b1-a832-c5d4d92414b7].
- **STEMI, in-hospital + follow-up:** In 1,887 consecutive primary-PCI STEMI patients (median follow-up 15 months, overall mortality 14.6%), high NPS (3–4 vs 0–2) predicted all-cause mortality (adjusted HR [passage text removed]), and in-hospital respiratory failure, AKI, malignant arrhythmia, and death were all more frequent [S:5a25ad9c-28d7-591e-8942-46718af15652].
- **NSTEMI, 1 year:** Among 197 NSTEMI patients undergoing selective PCI, one-year mortality was 33.7% with NPS 3–4 vs 8.1% with NPS 0–2 (p < 0.001); high NPS was an independent predictor (HR [passage text removed]) [S:ff5fae1b-85f3-5547-b11a-19693e69d60d].
- **Elderly ACS:** In 380 patients ≥75 years (median follow-up 23 months), long-term mortality was higher with high NPS (58% vs 41.1%, p < 0.001), though NPS was *not* associated with in-hospital mortality in that cohort [S:591be665-eae5-54b2-8d21-52c1e0ea1a78].
- **Non-fatal outcomes tracking the same gradient:** high NPS predicted lower discharge LVEF plus higher hospital mortality, shock and no-reflow in 2,280 STEMI patients [S:49f40ff8-5026-50c0-b239-082b2894edea], and independently predicted post-PCI AKI in ACS (OR 4.127; AUC 0.823) [S:63d2cbe8-5185-58bd-a185-3dd774660bbb] and in STEMI [S:3688bd98-ae48-5945-bd8f-7bf566905fb2].

## Caveats

One single-centre STEMI study found NPS *not* predictive of in-hospital mortality, arguing that albumin and cholesterol reflect chronic rather than hyperacute physiology, so NPS may be better suited to subacute/long-term risk; in that cohort only LMR remained an independent predictor of early death [S:8d91dfcb-945f-535d-98d1-d8ed546c7385]. The meta-analysis authors note that none of the included studies directly compared NPS with GRACE or TIMI, so its incremental value over guideline-recommended scores is unquantified [S:6335fa84-463a-55c5-b535-33ef6e2db80b]. A published commentary further criticises dichotomising continuous NPS components, which loses gradient risk information and may inflate heterogeneity [S:2db630c1-8504-5b4a-b045-0a5f469a4835]. The underlying evidence is largely retrospective and single-country/single-centre [S:e47f5aca-e25c-58b1-a832-c5d4d92414b7][S:ff5fae1b-85f3-5547-b11a-19693e69d60d].
