rows.question: Which laboratory biomarkers relate to relapse risk in patients with MOG antibody-associated disease?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Persistent MOG-IgG seropositivity on repeat serum sampling is associated with a relapsing rather than monophasic disease course, with roughly threefold higher odds; A relapsing course is associated with a much lower likelihood of seroreverting to MOG-IgG negative status, so sustained loss of the antibody tracks with a monophasic course; Serum MOG-IgG titre category and cerebrospinal fluid white cell count are supported mainly as markers of an active attack rather than as predictors of long-term course; The link between antibody measures and relapse risk rests on non-experimental data of variable quality with considerable between-study heterogeneity, giving moderate certainty at best. Certainty: These are moderate-strength associations rather than demonstrated causes of relapse, and the supporting data are inconsistent enough to keep the size of the effect approximate. Scope: applies to MOG antibody-associated disease in adults and children, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it advises starting, continuing or stopping long-term immunotherapy on the basis of antibody serostatus or titre alone.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

The best-supported laboratory biomarker of relapse risk in MOGAD is serum MOG-IgG itself — specifically persistence of seropositivity over serial samples, failure/delay of seroreversion, and higher titre — with CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands and CSF pleocytosis as secondary candidates; neurofilament light chain, GFAP and cytokines remain largely investigational and do not reliably predict relapse. [PMC12911599]

## Serum MOG-IgG serostatus over time (strongest evidence)

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 106 studies (≥1710 individuals) found [passage text removed]), a lower likelihood of seroreversion to negative ([passage text removed] versus monophasic patients (median 19 vs 2.5 years, p<0.0001); the authors concluded serial serum MOG-IgG sampling should be used to stratify relapse risk, proposing testing every 3–6 months during the first 12 months of disease. [PMC12911599; jnnp.bmj.com/content/97/2/109] In the same analysis, MOG-IgG titre category discriminated *disease state* rather than future course: clear-positive titre was associated with attack (OR 3.6, 95% CI 2.6–5.0) and negative titre with remission (OR 0.073, 95% CI 0.028–0.19). [PMC12911599]

A multicentre Italian study concluded that [passage text removed] increased relapse risk. [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36460438] A later review citing that study reports an initial remission titre >1:2560 as an independent predictor of relapse ([passage text removed]) and MOG-IgG seroreversion as reducing relapse risk (IRR 0.05, p<0.001). [PMC13102787]

## Titre at onset

Single-centre cohorts report onset titre thresholds as independent relapse predictors: serum MOG titre ≥1:32 was an independent risk factor for 1-year relapse in a nomogram study of 88 adults (p=0.007, model AUC 0.866 training / 0.864 validation) [PMC11911489], and in 108 children a titre ≥1:100 was more frequent in relapsers ([passage text removed]), though it fell short of significance in multivariable analysis (OR 2.891, 95% CI 0.978–8.545, p=0.055). [frontiersin.org/…/fneur.2026.1790844] Persistently positive children relapsed more often than transiently positive children (χ²=4.685, p=0.03). [PMC13102787]

## MOG-IgG epitope specificity (non-P42)

Epitope mapping is an emerging onset-testable marker. In 202 adults, 52 (26%) had non-P42 MOG-IgG with [passage text removed]=0.009), strongest in [passage text removed]=0.038; specificity 95%, PPV 85%), and epitope status was stable over the disease course. [jnnp.bmj.com/content/95/6/544; ovid.com/00005069-202406000-00009] In children (81 MOG-FL–positive sera, 40 non-P42), non-P42 binding [passage text removed]–6.2, p=0.03) after adjustment for phenotype. [mdc-berlin.de/…/mog-antibody-non-p42-epitope…] Note the meta-analysis judged the epitope evidence "mixed," since some studies have not replicated it. [PMC12911599]

## CSF markers

- **CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands:** in pediatric MOGAD, OCB presence was associated with relapsing disease (univariate OR 4.41, 95% CI 1.31–14.8, p=0.016; multivariate OR 3.85, 95% CI 1.09–13.6, p=0.036), independent of sex, onset age and optic neuritis phenotype. [pure.johnshopkins.edu/…/association-of-cerebrospinal-fluidrestricted-oligoclonal-bands-wi] A separate cohort also found higher relapse risk with CSF-OCB, particularly in the first year. [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39812323]
- **CSF pleocytosis:** elevated CSF nucleated cell count (>30 × 10⁶/L) was commoner in relapsing children ([passage text removed]) but not independently significant on multivariable analysis (OR 2.852, 95% CI 0.934–8.709, p=0.066). [frontiersin.org/…/fneur.2026.1790844] CSF WCC was among the most frequently studied candidates in the meta-analysis, which supported it chiefly for diagnosing attacks rather than predicting course. [PMC12911599]
- **CSF MOG-IgG:** no difference in CSF MOG-IgG positivity between relapsing and monophasic children (36.4% vs 34.7%, p=0.865) [frontiersin.org/…/fneur.2026.1790844]; another study was underpowered to show more frequent relapses in CSF MOG-IgG–positive patients (p=0.06). [[passage text removed]]

## Tissue-injury biomarkers (NfL, GFAP) — activity, not relapse prediction

The meta-analysis found neither serum GFAP nor serum NfL correlated significantly with disease activity at sampling, with considerable heterogeneity (I²=79% and 89%). [PMC12911599] A systematic review of sNfL in MOGAD (422 patients) found sNfL higher in MOGAD than controls and higher with brain lesions and during attacks, correlating with attack severity, but onset sNfL was *not* predictive [passage text removed]). [sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S221103482500152X] In one cohort, sNfL was higher in relapse than remission in MOGAD (34.1 vs 12.5 pg/mL, p=0.049), and sGFAP was higher in MOGAD patients who had relapsed within 60 days on univariate but not multivariate analysis (β=1.86, p=0.015). [PMC8008082] Conversely, another cohort found serum tau higher in relapse than remission (0.5 vs 0.2 pg/mL, p=0.027) while NfL and GFAP were comparable. [[passage text removed]] A plasma study reported elevated pNfL and pGFAP associated with increased likelihood of relapse within six months in NMOSD/MOGAD (pNfL AUC 0.906 for recent relapse; pGFAP 0.638), though it does not separate MOGAD-specific estimates in the extract available. [mdpi.com/1648-9144/61/10/1873; PMC12566294] Longitudinal sNfL change correlated with MOG-IgG titre change (rho=0.59, p=0.027) in a small exploratory cohort. [sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211034824003067]

## Cytokines

In a multicentre cohort of 88 MOGAD patients meeting 2023 criteria, higher baseline serum BAFF independently predicted *lower* relapse risk (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.19–0.89, p=0.024; log-rank p=0.038), while baseline BAFF, CXCL10, IL-10 and IL-8 correlated with onset severity. [PMC11702904; iris.unil.ch/…/download] CSF IL-6 and CXCL8 were higher in encephalitic than optic-neuritis pediatric phenotypes, with Th17- and B-cell-related profiles elevated versus non-inflammatory controls — phenotype association, not validated relapse prediction. [[passage text removed]] A review notes IL-6 is the cytokine most consistently associated with disease activity and severity but has low diagnostic specificity. [ovid.com/01787401-202609000-00013]

## Important caveats

Published relapse-prediction scores are driven by clinical, not laboratory, variables: the MOG-AR score comprises immunosuppressive therapy, oral corticosteroid duration, onset age, sex and attack phenotype — no biomarker — and OCB positivity did not differ between its groups (34.44% overall, p=0.766). [PMC11385954; emjreviews.com/neurology/news/…] Some reviews explicitly state relapses are not reliably predicted by antibody titre [frontiersin.org/…/fimmu.2025.1594960], titres may fluctuate independently of attacks, cell-based assays are not internationally standardised, and many persistently seropositive patients never relapse while some relapse after seroreversion. [PMC12911599; frontiersin.org/…/fimmu.2026.1807565] Treatment status at sampling was incompletely reported across the meta-analysed studies and could not be adjusted for. [PMC12911599]
answers.connect:
**Conclusion:** The best-supported laboratory predictor of relapse in MOGAD is longitudinal serum MOG-IgG serostatus (persistent seropositivity and high remission titres raise risk; seroreversion to negative markedly lowers it); MOG-IgG epitope/isoform specificity, CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands, serum NfL and BAFF are promising but less validated, and onset titre, GFAP and blood-cell ratios are inconsistent.

**1. Serial MOG-IgG serostatus — strongest evidence.** A systematic review with individual-participant meta-analysis found persistent seropositivity (≥2 positive results ≥3 months apart) associated with a relapsing course (OR 2.7, 95% CI 1.8–4.0, p<0.0001; 48 studies, 777 participants; GRADE moderate), and relapsing course associated with reduced likelihood of seroreversion (HR 0.19, 0.14–0.26); in a multivariable model adjusting for sex, age and phenotype, persistent seropositivity gave OR 15 (2.2–98, p=0.0059), and the authors support serial [passage text removed] during the first 12 months for risk stratification [S:929631ff-3791-5d76-8dc3-2bbbb50684a3][S:6c21ffc2-586a-54bf-a9ef-29d337f09c57][S:49ae2e04-b31f-5cd2-ac92-ca494b355dbc]. A multicentre quantitative study (102 patients, 354 samples) found remission titres higher in relapsing patients, first-remission titres >1:2560 predicting relapsing course (HR 10.9, 3.4–35.2, p<0.001), and seroconversion to negative associated with a 95% reduction in relapse incidence (IRR 0.05, p<0.001) [S:a82fd514-c9a0-5846-bfb3-485389c2ec36][S:3bcad355-ebcb-58e2-9dc2-e58a3d47bef5]. A prospective cohort similarly concluded persistent MOG-IgG positivity strongly indicates relapse risk while seroconverters did not relapse [S:ee12ab12-3ca6-5c09-a5ec-55ec6f8f0bdf]. In paediatric MOGAD, seroconversion to titre <1:160 within 24 months had high positive predictive value for a monophasic course, with 93% of polyphasic patients still titre-positive at last follow-up versus 70% of monophasic patients becoming negative [S:8453127d-dc54-5f42-9289-c45171af56ac].

**2. Onset titre — conflicting.** A single-centre nomogram identified serum MOG-IgG ≥1:32 at first attack as one of four independent 1-year relapse risk factors (with female sex, cortical encephalitis phenotype, inadequate maintenance therapy; low-risk 18% vs high-risk 61% relapse) [S:295501d0-6148-53ab-9b4b-2434daa6edba][S:5e49da75-efa0-5eec-a9a5-f9613cd038a7]. In 108 children, titre ≥1:100 was more frequent in relapsers ([passage text removed]) but lost significance in multivariable analysis (OR 2.891, 0.978–8.545, p=0.055) [S:93277d24-1dbe-5995-8c03-2734a3d3166a][S:4dc542af-dcc3-57b8-b7eb-e5e69aa2dfba]. Opposing views hold that onset titres do not predict relapse or severity and that titres vary between laboratories [S:1ccdbc66-e972-5634-8723-51ea651eb7e6][S:8453127d-dc54-5f42-9289-c45171af56ac].

**3. Antibody epitope / isoform specificity.** In 202 adults, MOG-IgG not binding the immunodominant proline42 epitope (non-P42, 26% of patients) predicted a relapsing course (HR 1.7, 1.15–2.60, p=0.009; 85% vs 62% relapsing), was stable over time, and was strongest with unilateral optic neuritis at onset (HR 2.5, 1.26–5.0, p=0.01; specificity 95%, PPV 85%); H103/S104 binding carried no risk [S:d4073ee0-f3ca-582b-9edb-4b6e1d4ee642][S:dd325a0f-21e4-5b3c-b5fc-c2a837cbfb36][S:0121e847-f17d-5947-8e65-6cf06b7c6dec]. A conference abstract reports MOGα3-IgG associated with relapse (HR 4.1 derivation, 3.1 national cohort), though not replicated in the UK cohort [S:e7677f95-c320-5284-8482-4a98b113e337][S:45db054e-37ed-5664-9f11-6a4ac4331fb8].

**4. CSF markers.** In the French MOGADOC cohort (190 adults, CSF within 3 months of onset), CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands were present in 16.8% and relapses were more frequent in OCB+ patients (p=0.049), especially in the first year (p=0.007), though OCB+ also flagged MS-like imaging and misdiagnosis risk [S:bc182928-b879-5bf7-a59e-f65ef78c0ba8][S:2cbada1d-1e8b-5416-a721-8b9859a6bfe5]. CSF pleocytosis relates mainly to *current* attack rather than future relapse (CSF leucocytosis ≥5 cells/mL vs normal: OR 3.1, 1.7–5.9, p=0.00044) [S:929631ff-3791-5d76-8dc3-2bbbb50684a3]; in children, CSF cell count >30×10⁶/L was more common in relapsers on univariate analysis ([passage text removed]) but not independently significant [S:93277d24-1dbe-5995-8c03-2734a3d3166a][S:4dc542af-dcc3-57b8-b7eb-e5e69aa2dfba]. CSF MOG-IgG positivity showed no relapse association in that paediatric cohort [S:451a008d-e2fe-5b53-ac8b-84f3549f6535]; paired serum/CSF or CSF-restricted MOG-IgG relates to severity rather than relapse [S:d169ba58-b33e-5046-a284-b5fb3918fcea].

**5. Neuroaxonal/glial markers (sNfL, sGFAP).** In the multicentre MULTIMOGAD study (89 adults, Simoa), sNfL independently predicted relapse risk ([passage text removed]), while sGFAP tracked severity and recovery rather than relapse [S:d4f15df8-1dca-59f9-afdc-f6b68d1611df][S:60ad6500-a7d9-5a3e-8958-c60eaf6ef958]. This is not uniformly reproduced: the relapse-biomarker meta-analysis found NfL and GFAP were the most frequently reported novel markers but did not effectively correlate with disease activity in the reviewed literature [S:49ae2e04-b31f-5cd2-ac92-ca494b355dbc]; a review of soluble biomarkers states that higher onset sNfL does not correlate with increased relapse risk in MOGAD [S:60590002-c6b0-5b3d-acd3-7614518a713a]; and in a small paediatric study onset plasma NfL did not differ between relapsing and non-relapsing patients (MOG-Ab levels were 2.5-fold higher in relapsers but non-significantly, p=0.119) [S:aa59bffd-0fd1-589d-a966-6e06233dd61b].

**6. Cytokines and other blood markers.** In 88 adults with MOGAD, higher baseline serum BAFF predicted a *lower* relapse risk (HR [passage text removed]), while baseline BAFF, CXCL10, IL-10 and IL-8 correlated with onset severity [S:87466ec8-1842-51c4-9eff-f1804bbb0e09]. CSF IL-6 correlated with CSF cell count and poorer recovery, but relapse-free rate did not differ significantly by CSF IL-6 level (log-rank p=0.2406) [S:f33e15d3-7d9b-5c3f-a3b7-1d7ba6c9d45c][S:bbc6b764-a7f4-5ea8-85b4-9daebb5451fc]. Blood-count ratios (NLR, PLR, ELR, neutrophil-to-nonneutrophil ratio) differentiate attack from remission rather than forecasting relapse [S:84dbbe86-a816-5652-a039-501358c90e7b], and a UK cohort found NLR did not predict relapse or disability [S:07a6b6cb-1ec5-54d6-84a5-24b8bd0e32b3]; one single-centre study reported monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio <0.200 at first admission as the only risk factor for recurrence (OR 22.5, 2.552–198.376, p=0.005) [S:23eaba94-cdec-5e9b-8045-0c9e6c7c7e9b], and PLR has been linked to relapse in another report [S:87f2e8cc-0b96-580b-a2cc-b170cd6d2b81]. Reduced T-cell TNFAIP3 expression during relapse versus remission has been proposed as an investigational relapse biomarker [S:0313ee4b-eeb4-515a-8453-528bf0f0a176][S:9c1c7b3d-d0e8-5057-9a3c-b822f7bdc389].

**Caveat:** multiple reviews emphasise that no laboratory marker reliably separates monophasic from relapsing MOGAD; persistent seropositivity does not guarantee relapse and seronegative patients occasionally relapse [S:06a9db95-241c-5789-bf9f-66ac55feabcd][S:d9d594b4-dc6e-53e0-a333-d1508de0f72d][S:ca5f28cd-c902-5a7c-9b88-31003ffc642c], and much of the newer evidence (isoforms, MLR, TNFAIP3) rests on single cohorts or conference abstracts.

rows.question: What is known about interferon beta-1a treatment of multiple sclerosis in children and adolescents?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Reports of children and adolescents treated with injectable interferon beta-1a describe reduced relapse rates during treatment; Registry experience with these formulations suggests treated children may experience outcomes similar to those seen in adult populations; The pegylated formulation was given to far fewer children, and for a shorter median duration, than the intramuscular formulation. Certainty: The underlying evidence is uncontrolled and lacks comparison groups, so the findings are best read as provisional signals rather than as an established treatment effect. Scope: applies to multiple sclerosis treated with interferon beta-1a formulations in children and adolescents, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents interferon beta-1a as the preferred first-line disease-modifying therapy for children and adolescents with multiple sclerosis generally, or as an approved paediatric option.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Interferon beta‑1a has been used off‑label and (in Europe) label‑supported in paediatric MS for over two decades: uncontrolled cohorts consistently show roughly a 70–80% fall in annualised relapse rate with a safety profile similar to adults, but the only randomised trials in which it served as the active comparator (PARADIGMS, TERIKIDS-era CONNECT, and an Italian IFN-vs-glatiramer trial) show it is less effective than fingolimod and dimethyl fumarate on MRI/relapse outcomes, so it is now a lower-efficacy first-line option rather than the standard of care.

## Observational / cohort evidence (safety and relapse reduction)

- **Subcutaneous IFN‑β‑1a, small early cohorts.** Pohl et al. studied tolerability in 51 patients with early‑onset MS: flu‑like symptoms in 65%, asymptomatic leukopenia in 27%, elevated transaminases in 35%; treatment was judged [passage text removed] ([PMID 15753430](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15753430)). Tenembaum and Segura treated 24 children with clinically definite MS at differing doses; after a mean of 44 months it was well tolerated in 22, two had possible serious adverse events, and a significant relapse‑rate reduction was seen at 22 µg [passage text removed], though efficacy could not be inferred from the design ([PMID 16775230](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16775230)).
- **REPLAY, the largest paediatric sc IFN‑β‑1a dataset.** Records of 307 patients who received ≥1 injection before age 18: 168 (54.7%) had ≥1 prespecified medical event, 184 (59.9%) had non‑serious [passage text removed]; commonest laboratory abnormalities were raised ALT (74/195; 37.9%) and AST (59/194; 30.4%). Annualised relapse rate was 1.79 before and 0.47 during treatment, and adult doses (22 and 44 µg three times weekly) were well tolerated ([PMID 23666046](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23666046)). A review notes these data are limited by the retrospective design and absence of a control group ([PMC10951191]([passage text removed])).
- **Intramuscular IFN‑β‑1a (ITEMS, Italy).** In patients treated with 30 µg weekly before age 16, mean annualised relapse rate fell from 1.9 ± 1.1 to 0.4 ± 0.5 after a mean 42.9 ± 19.9 months, with final EDSS 1.3 ± 1.1; adverse events occurred in 35 (67%) — flu‑like 33%, headache 29%, myalgia 21%, fever 11% — most transient ([doi:10.1007/s10072-007-0804-2]([passage text removed])). Very small earlier US series also reported good tolerability of 30 µg IM weekly in children, with no discontinuations for adverse events ([Waubant, Neuropediatrics 2001]([passage text removed])).
- **Tolerability caveats specific to children.** A review of paediatric MS therapeutics reports discontinuation rates for interferon beta in the 30–50% range, flu‑like symptoms in 35–65%, leukopenia 8–27%, and transient transaminase elevation 10–62% ([PMC3916074]([passage text removed])); injection‑site reactions were reported in more than two‑thirds of children on the subcutaneous formulation, with abscess and injection‑site necrosis each in about 6% in the Pohl series ([doi:10.1007/s11940-011-0141-x]([passage text removed])). Breakthrough disease requiring escalation is common — in a six‑centre US cohort of 258 children, 48% switched from their first therapy, 28% for breakthrough disease and 16% for non‑compliance or side effects ([PMC3916074]([passage text removed])).

## Randomised comparator data (where IFN‑β‑1a loses)

- **PARADIGMS (fingolimod vs IM IFN‑β‑1a 30 µg weekly, ages 10–17, n=215, up to 2 years).** Adjusted ARR 0.12 with fingolimod vs 0.67 with IFN‑β‑1a (rate ratio 0.18, 95% CI 0.11–0.30; P<0.001); new/newly enlarged T2 lesions 4.39 vs 9.27 per year (relative difference 53%, P<0.001); relapse‑free at month 24 85.7% vs 38.8%. Adverse events excluding relapses occurred in 88.8% vs 95.3%, but serious adverse events were higher with fingolimod (18/107, 16.8%) than IFN‑β‑1a (7/108, 6.5%) ([PMID 30207920](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30207920); [2minutemedicine summary of the same trial]([passage text removed])). Trial-completion was lower in the IFN arm (88/108, 81.5%) than the fingolimod arm (100/107, 93.5%), and discontinuation was commonly disease-activity related ([PMC6617229]([passage text removed])).
- **CONNECT (dimethyl fumarate vs IFN‑β‑1a, open-label, rater-blinded, n=150, ages 10–17, 96 weeks).** Among trial completers, [passage text removed]) on [passage text removed]) on IFN‑β‑1a were free of new/newly enlarging T2 lesions; 66% vs 52% remained relapse-free, with adjusted ARR [passage text removed]) vs 0.53 (0.33–0.84) — a difference the accompanying commentary described as not significant ([PMC9520348]([passage text removed]); [JAMA Netw Open commentary](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2796815)).
- **IM IFN‑β‑1a vs subcutaneous glatiramer acetate (Phase IIIb, open-label, 30 patients aged 12–17, 96 weeks).** The MRI primary endpoint (proportion free of new/enlarging T2 lesions) was similar in both arms — about one third each — but ARR at week 96 was significantly lower with glatiramer ([passage text removed] with IFN‑β‑1a ([passage text removed]; p=0.018; median rate difference −0.3698, 95% CI −0.6762 to −0.0633); time to first relapse only trended in favour of glatiramer (log-rank p=0.103) ([PMC12488838](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12488838); [PMID 40775552](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40775552)). Roughly one third of the IFN arm and nearly half the glatiramer arm subsequently switched to high-efficacy therapy for partial disease control ([report of the trial]([passage text removed])).

## Regulatory status

Regulators treat the paediatric evidence as safety data only, not efficacy data. The Rebif SmPC states that [passage text removed], and that the paediatric retrospective cohort (children n=52, adolescents n=255) suggests the safety profile at 22 or 44 µg three times weekly in children 2–11 and adolescents 12–17 is similar to adults; it should not be used below 2 years ([Rebif SmPC]([passage text removed]); [EMA variation assessment report EMA/176383/2014]([passage text removed]/rebif-h-c-136-ii-0103-epar-assessment-report-variation_en.pdf)). Rebif is the only one of the platform injectables with an EU marketing authorisation from age 2 years, the others being authorised from age 12 ([HAS assessment]([passage text removed])); consistent with this, it was the most frequently prescribed DMT in a German nationwide paediatric claims analysis ([PMC8504210]([passage text removed])). By contrast, the US label states it is not known whether Rebif is safe and effective in children ([Rebif US consumer safety information]([passage text removed])), and Health Canada has not authorised a paediatric indication ([Canadian product monograph](https://pdf.hres.ca/dpd_pm/00081811.PDF)).

## Gaps

I found no paediatric pharmacokinetic or dose-finding trial data for IFN‑β‑1a (the SmPC explicitly says none exist), and no paediatric-specific data on neutralising-antibody incidence or on long-term effects on growth/puberty in the sources retrieved. Optimal paediatric dosing therefore rests on extrapolated adult doses (22/44 µg sc tiw; 30 µg IM weekly) rather than trial evidence.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** Interferon beta‑1a has been used off‑label (or, in Europe, label‑approved for adolescents) in pediatric MS for decades and is supported only by retrospective/open‑label data showing acceptable tolerability and roughly halved relapse rates — but no placebo‑controlled pediatric trial exists, and the one randomized pediatric trial in which it served as the active comparator (PARADIGMS) showed it was clearly inferior to fingolimod, which has driven a shift away from it.

**Efficacy evidence (observational)**
- The largest dataset is REPLAY: 307 patients given ≥1 injection of subcutaneous IFN β‑1a before age 18; annualized relapse rate fell from 1.79 pre‑treatment to 0.47 on treatment [S:5409c1ad-6870-514b-8e00-f7fb6150a584].
- Earlier Italian and French cohorts: 52–53 children on intramuscular IFN β‑1a had ARR fall from 1.9 to 0.4 over ~42–43 months [S:f4b35cee-2b40-5255-b51b-f9e9944c93ad][S:eb22e0bc-8acf-5acf-8ce6-02486aa7d8b8]; in 197 children on IM/SC IFN β‑1a and SC IFN β‑1b, attack risk was reduced in year 1 (HR 0.31, 95% CI 0.13–0.72) and over 2 years (HR [passage text removed]), with attenuation by 4 years (HR [passage text removed]:f4b35cee-2b40-5255-b51b-f9e9944c93ad].
- Most recent real‑world data (US Network of Pediatric MS Centers registry, 154 patients treated before age 18 with IM IFN β‑1a/Avonex n=130 or peginterferon beta‑1a/Plegridy n=23): after a 3‑month acclimation, probability of remaining relapse‑free over the next year was 68.3% and 69.9%, with ARR 0.50 (95% CI 0.34–0.75) and 0.59 (95% CI 0.12–3.00); probability of no gadolinium‑enhancing lesions at 1 year was 60.5% and 61.7% [S:d0b93e3f-e413-5e94-a048-c4ae537a007a][S:80fff3c6-0427-57ff-84cb-61e08901f2fe]. The authors judged this comparable to adult interferon outcomes, but note small Plegridy numbers, short treatment duration, and that safety/tolerability were not systematically assessed [S:5d90b5f3-929f-54c6-9b29-14f3b63aacb6][S:9932c408-db74-5ef0-a1ab-ea50e0f13915]. Relapse during the first 90 days predicted much shorter subsequent relapse‑free time (median 1.4 vs 3.9 years) [S:80fff3c6-0427-57ff-84cb-61e08901f2fe].

**Safety/tolerability**
- Typical adverse events mirror adults: influenza‑like symptoms, headache, injection‑site reactions, and transaminase elevation [S:037a7241-6cc5-5bda-84f0-da9c309810b1][S:5331cf88-6fcf-5722-99b7-e9cffab644e0]. In REPLAY, 12/307 ([passage text removed]; most common lab abnormalities were raised ALT (74/195; 37.9%) and AST (59/194; 30.4%); no new or unexpected adverse drug reactions were seen, and events were generally nonserious and did not require dose reduction or discontinuation [S:5409c1ad-6870-514b-8e00-f7fb6150a584][S:48ff497e-2a51-5074-8175-4de753513ed1].
- Age comparison: no major difference in medical events between children <12 years and adolescents 12–<18 years [S:48ff497e-2a51-5074-8175-4de753513ed1]; another review reports a similar safety profile in ages 2–11 vs 12–17, with liver enzyme elevation more prominent in the younger group [S:b42396c3-4262-5fc8-be08-d2bf95fe73d5].
- With SC IFN β‑1a, injection‑site abscesses and necrosis were each reported in about 6% of children over a mean 1.8‑year follow‑up [S:b6bf355b-4f84-59e1-b786-6027d25403eb]. Flu‑like symptoms, injection reactions, liver enzyme rises, or perceived lack of efficacy in adolescents can cause non‑adherence [S:5331cf88-6fcf-5722-99b7-e9cffab644e0].

**Dosing**
- Adult doses have generally been used: IM 30 µg once weekly; SC 22 or 44 µg three times weekly [S:eb22e0bc-8acf-5acf-8ce6-02486aa7d8b8][S:5409c1ad-6870-514b-8e00-f7fb6150a584]. IPMSSG/European guidance supports titration, with caution in children under ~10 years — starting at 25–50% of adult dose and escalating [passage text removed] tolerated dose, with liver function and white‑cell monitoring [S:037a7241-6cc5-5bda-84f0-da9c309810b1][S:b6bf355b-4f84-59e1-b786-6027d25403eb][S:5331cf88-6fcf-5722-99b7-e9cffab644e0].

**Regulatory/guideline position**
- Consensus statements (IPMSSG 2012, European 2010, US 2011) listed IM or SC IFN β‑1a, IFN β‑1b, or glatiramer acetate as first‑line pediatric options [S:009e77eb-1d75-5378-8273-d29912df0047]. In Europe, IFN β‑1a products carry pediatric labelling — Avonex from age 12, and Rebif from a younger age (reported as ≥2 years) — making IFN β‑1a the most frequently prescribed DMT in a German nationwide pediatric claims analysis [S:bf38118e-74e6-592b-957a-2e841199ace8][S:fa1e6683-37f2-500a-85df-1806266007a1].

**The key limitation — inferiority to higher‑efficacy therapy**
- PARADIGMS, the first completed RCT in pediatric MS (215 patients aged 10–<18), used IM IFN β‑1a 30 µg weekly as active comparator; fingolimod reduced ARR by 81.9% and new/newly enlarging T2 lesions by 52.6% versus IFN β‑1a [S:e6bc7c5d-b66d-5472-8358-ea85af987b42]. Mean ARR was 0.67 on interferon vs 0.12 on fingolimod, with new T2 lesions reduced 53% and enhancing T1 lesions 66%; overall adverse events occurred in 95% of the interferon arm vs 88% of the fingolimod arm, while serious adverse events were more frequent with fingolimod (17.8% vs 9.3%) [S:2a6d8176-2afe-5d56-971a-2094143ce334].
- Consequently, commentators argue the first‑line-interferon approach "may need to be reconsidered" [S:009e77eb-1d75-5378-8273-d29912df0047], and prescribing has shifted: in Alberta, Canada, injectable DMT dispensing collapsed from 2019 onward, attributed partly to PARADIGMS [S:031e4cca-bf14-5f8c-9529-87723a9b8222]. Interferons nonetheless remain in use, and may be preferred where immunosuppression is a concern (e.g. cytopenias, hypogammaglobulinemia, immune dysregulation) [S:33cedede-3fe9-54aa-8b4a-ecad0a3bd5ba].

**Gaps:** no placebo‑controlled pediatric efficacy trial of IFN β‑1a exists; the pediatric evidence base is retrospective/open‑label with short follow‑up [S:5331cf88-6fcf-5722-99b7-e9cffab644e0][S:009e77eb-1d75-5378-8273-d29912df0047]. A prospective phase 3 pediatric study of peginterferon beta‑1a (NCT03958877) is listed as active/not recruiting [S:https://meddatax.com/clinical-trials/NCT03958877]; I found no published pediatric results for it. I also found no pediatric-specific data on neutralizing antibody incidence with IFN β‑1a.

rows.question: What is known about anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy in stiff-person syndrome spectrum disorder?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: In the first reported treated patient with refractory stiff-person syndrome, anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy was followed by increased mobility and reduced symptomatic medication use; Deep CD19-directed depletion of B-cells and plasmablasts is the proposed rationale, most directly in glycine receptor antibody disease where the antibodies are regarded as directly pathogenic; Cytokine release syndrome and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome remain the principal safety concerns of this therapy; A multicentre phase II trial is currently investigating the safety and efficacy of anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy in this disorder, with safety as its primary focus. Certainty: The clinical evidence rests on a single reported treated patient with no comparison group, so benefit is suggested rather than demonstrated. Scope: applies to stiff-person syndrome spectrum disorder in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it recommends anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy as initial immunotherapy for newly diagnosed disease in place of established first-line treatment.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** [passage text removed]/mivocabtagene autoleucel) has moved from two published compassionate-use case reports of dramatic benefit in refractory SPS to a completed single-arm registrational phase 2 trial (KYSA-8) that met its primary walking endpoint; evidence is still uncontrolled, short-follow-up, and largely conference-reported.

**Rationale.** SPSD is a B-cell/antibody-mediated CNS disorder (anti-GAD65, anti-glycine receptor), and deep CD19-directed B-cell depletion is hypothesised to reach autoreactive B cells in lymphoid tissue and CNS compartments that anti-CD20 antibodies access poorly — relevant because a double-blind placebo-controlled rituximab trial in SPS was negative (doi:10.1002/ana.25002, cited in both case reports) ([trial rationale]([passage text removed]); [NXI e200479]([passage text removed])).

**Index case (Faissner et al., PNAS 2024;121(26):e2403227121, PMID 38885382).** A 69-year-old woman with 9 years of SPS refractory to rituximab and bortezomib received one infusion of KYV-101 (1×10⁸ CAR T cells after fludarabine/cyclophosphamide). Walking speed increased over 100%, self-reported uninterrupted walking distance rose from <[passage text removed] months, and benzodiazepine dose fell by 40%; anti-GAD65 titre declined from 1:3,200 to 1:1,000 (day +56) and 1:320 (day +144); Modified Ashworth score for the right knee fell from 2–3 to 0 from day +14 and pain NRS from 4 to 0. Only low-grade CRS occurred, with no ICANS ([PNAS]([passage text removed]); [PMID 38885382](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885382); [press release]([passage text removed])).

**Second case (Ayzenberg et al., Neurol Neuroimmunol Neuroinflamm 2025;12(6):e200479, PMID 41052399).** A 62-year-old woman with 14 years of anti-GAD-positive SPS plus anti-AChR-positive myasthenia gravis, refractory to IVIg, plasma exchange, steroids, azathioprine and rituximab, received flu 30 mg/m²/cy 300 mg/m² on days −6 to −4 then 1×10⁸ CAR T cells. CAR T expansion peaked at day +19 (468/µL) with prompt peripheral B-cell depletion. Improvement began at month 3: walking 500 m by month 6 and 1 km at month 9; Heightened Sensitivity Scale 4→0; muscle spasm attacks 30/day→10 (months 3–6)→2 (month 9); painDETECT 25→7; anti-GAD 1:320→1:32; anti-AChR became negative; QMG 4→2 by day 20. Toxicity was grade 2 CRS and moderate leukopenia without serious infection, and post-vaccination antibody titres remained stable (attributed to sparing of CD19-negative long-lived plasma cells) ([PMC12514794]([passage text removed]); [neurology.org]([passage text removed])).

**KYSA-8 phase 2 (NCT06588491).** Design: adults 18–75 with seropositive (high-titre GAD65 or glycine-receptor) SPS, inadequate response to ≥1 immunomodulatory therapy and stiffness index ≥2; lymphodepletion then a single 1×10⁸ CAR T-cell dose; co-primary endpoints change in timed 25-foot walk (T25FW) at week 16 and safety; KYV-101 holds FDA RMAT designation for SPS ([WNL.0000000000210669]([passage text removed])). Primary-analysis results presented at AAN 2026 (26 patients, median follow-up 6.5 months): median T25FW improvement of 4.8 seconds, a 45.6% median improvement (p=0.0003); 81% achieved ≥20% improvement; 31% completed the T25FW in under 5 seconds; of 12 patients needing a walking aid at baseline, most no longer did at week 16 (reported as 67% in one account and 63% in the investigator's interview); all 26 remained free of immunomodulatory therapy through last follow-up; among 16 patients reaching week 24 the median gain was 44.4%. Safety: low-grade CRS in 92.3% (grade 1 38.5%, grade 2 53.8%), ICANS in 11.5% (all grade 1), grade 3/4 neutropenia in 15.4% (four patients), and three serious treatment-related adverse events that fully resolved ([EMJ/AAN report]([passage text removed]); [MedPage Today](https://www.medpagetoday.com/meetingcoverage/aan/120926); [checkrare]([passage text removed]); [Kyverna IR]([passage text removed])).

**Caveats.** A dedicated review notes that the index patient retained residual stiffness, plausibly from irreversible neurodegeneration and astrogliosis in long-standing disease, arguing for earlier intervention; open questions include CAR T activity in CSF, the nature of B-cell repopulation, and duration of drug-free remission ([Wickel et al., Ther Adv Neurol Disord 2025;18:17562864251387930, PMID 41230121]([passage text removed]); [CGTlive summary of PNAS discussion]([passage text removed])). KYSA-8 is single-arm and open-label with no control group, and its results are so far available only as conference/company reports, not a peer-reviewed primary publication. I found no published reports of CAR T-cell therapy specifically in glycine-receptor-antibody PERM, although GlyR-seropositive patients were eligible for KYSA-8 and PERM is discussed in the review's scope.

**Bottom line:** CD19-directed CAR T cells (KYV-101/mivocabtagene autoleucel) have moved from a single index case report to a completed registrational single-arm Phase 2 trial (KYSA-8, NCT06588491) in refractory stiff-person syndrome spectrum disorder (SPSD), with consistent gait/mobility gains, falling GAD65 titers, and no high-grade CRS or ICANS reported so far — but no randomized controlled data exist.

**Case-report evidence**
- Index [passage text removed] years of treatment-refractory SPS received one infusion of autologous anti-CD19 KYV-101 and was followed >6 months, with reduced leg stiffness, markedly improved gait, >100% increase in walking speed, daily walking distance rising [passage text removed], and a 40% benzodiazepine reduction; only low-grade cytokine release syndrome occurred [S:422d296a-509f-591a-8fcb-b9d1782ae4e2]. Anti-GAD65 titers fell [passage text removed] by day 56 and to 1:320 at 5 months, indicating depletion of CD19-expressing plasmablasts/short-lived plasma cells; the authors emphasized that a direct pathogenic role of anti-GAD65 remains debated and that CSF antibody measurement would have been more informative [S:efd1df8a-3a3a-5afb-8801-1368c0c98e5f]. Improvement in stiffness itself was only modest, attributed to long disease duration and possible irreversible spinal neuronal loss; no CRS or ICANS ≥ grade 3 occurred [S:1a044dc5-ca30-540d-812b-09583ba5d60c]. Another account of the same patient records diazepam falling [passage text removed] needed, grade 1 CRS and no neurotoxicity [S:500eb161-0e4d-533b-9955-6751e6808808], and deep B-cell depletion [S:7dad6d70-3f88-5296-a342-06d93064c7d8].
- A second compassionate-use case: [passage text removed] plus myasthenia gravis, nearly non-ambulatory, improved to 500 m walking distance by month 6 [passage text removed], experiencing [passage text removed] infection [S:79d7dd1f-7c75-55a5-b3a5-2ea18358934f]. Symptoms were not fully resolved in either case, prompting the hypothesis that earlier treatment — before irreversible damage — may matter [S:fb354977-a0b5-58c8-8dac-f23c3135dc18].
- Related GAD65 spectrum: a CD19 CAR T case in GAD65-antibody cerebellar ataxia has been reported, with the authors noting these two SPS cases as the precedent [S:4cfbec31-b50a-58d1-bfb9-564b33d60c99].

**Mechanistic rationale**
B-cell involvement, intrathecal antibody synthesis, and responsiveness to B-cell-directed therapy (rituximab, plasma exchange, IVIg) underpin the rationale; benefit may come from autoantibody depletion plus broader immune modulation [S:6babd1cd-7995-52be-85fb-2da85bc3b4e9]. CAR T cells reach the CSF in MS patients, which may be relevant given [passage text removed] [S:efd1df8a-3a3a-5afb-8801-1368c0c98e5f]. Rituximab spares CD20-negative tissue-resident B cells/plasma cells, whereas CD19 CAR T achieves bone-marrow-level depletion [S:c749def9-ec2a-5288-8562-a549c90935a3]. Reviews note that lower target-cell burden in neuroimmunological disease may reduce CRS/ICANS risk [S:3e358fe3-1e19-56d0-ac8d-009cc0b58c40].

**Trial-level evidence**
KYSA-8 is an open-label, single-arm Phase 2 study of KYV-101 in refractory seropositive SPS; patients required inadequate response to ≥[passage text removed], received fludarabine/cyclophosphamide lymphodepletion then a single 1×10⁸ CAR T-cell dose, with co-primary endpoints of change in timed 25-foot walk (T25FW) at week 16 and safety; KYV-101 holds FDA RMAT designation for SPS [[passage text removed]]. The trial has completed enrollment of 26 patients at 3 US centers, with lasting benefits announced in topline results [S:edbf3bfb-8c55-553c-86be-3b65cc839af6]. At the week-16 primary analysis (26 dosed patients), median T25FW improvement was 46% (P=0.0003), 81% achieved ≥20% improvement, 31% walked at healthy-adult speed (<5 s), 67% of the 12 baseline walking-aid users no longer needed assistance, and all 26 remained off immunomodulatory therapy at median 6.5 months' follow-up [[passage text removed]]. Secondary endpoints ([passage text removed], HSS −3.2; all p<0.0001) improved, [passage text removed] in four patients, three resolved serious treatment-related events, and exploratory deep transient B-cell depletion with GAD65 antibody reductions; a 153-patient natural-history comparison showed minimal T25FW change on standard care [[passage text removed]]. A BLA for SPS is in preparation [[passage text removed]].

CD20-directed gamma-delta CAR T cells (ADI-001, NCT06375993) are also under investigation including SPS [S:fb354977-a0b5-58c8-8dac-f23c3135dc18]. Key limits: single-arm, unblinded design; short follow-up (patients followed one year) [[passage text removed]]; residual stiffness in long-standing disease; and unresolved questions about B-cell repopulation phenotype and the CD19-negative long-lived plasma-cell niche [S:1a044dc5-ca30-540d-812b-09583ba5d60c]. Note that the detailed KYSA-8 efficacy figures above come from conference-coverage/company sources rather than a peer-reviewed primary publication; full data were slated for a 2026 meeting/publication [[passage text removed]].

rows.question: What distinguishes tumefactive demyelinating lesions with MOG or NMDAR antibodies from those without such antibodies?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: MOG antibody-positive patients showed a more inflammatory cerebrospinal fluid profile, with higher white cell counts, than antibody-negative patients; MOG antibody-positive lesions more often shrank or disappeared on repeat MRI than antibody-negative lesions; NMDAR antibody-positive patients showed higher systemic inflammatory markers than NMDAR antibody-negative patients, possibly reflecting a preceding infection; Comparison of MOG antibody-positive with antibody-negative tumefactive lesions identified no unique clinical or MRI characteristic separating them. Certainty: These are preliminary signals from very small antibody-defined subgroups rather than established discriminators. Scope: applies to tumefactive demyelinating lesions stratified by MOG and NMDAR antibody status in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it asserts that NMDAR antibody positivity here indicates an underlying teratoma that must be resected.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Antibody status shifts the CSF/laboratory profile and the rate of radiological lesion resolution, but not baseline severity, MRI appearance, or prognosis — most tumefactive demyelinating lesions (TDLs) do well on immunotherapy regardless of serology. The clearest discriminators come from one antibody-stratified TDL cohort and a larger MOGAD-vs-MS/AQP4 tumefactive comparison.

## MOG-antibody-positive TDLs

In a retrospective cohort of 30 patients with confirmed TDLs stratified by MOG and NMDAR serology, MOG+ patients had elevated CSF white cell counts and [passage text removed]; the authors concluded these antibodies influence clinical/laboratory characteristics but have limited impact on prognosis ([PMC12496048]([passage text removed]); [PubMed 41048446](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41048446)). Reading the results in detail: MOG+ patients had [passage text removed]) and lower biopsy rates (p<0.001) than MOG−; CSF WCC showed an inflammatory trend (p=0.055 vs MOG−, p=0.036 for Only MOG+ vs double-negative), with **no** difference in oligoclonal band status (p=0.665, p=0.615). MOG+ patients trended toward reduced or disappearing lesion volume (p=0.038), and Only MOG+ patients had lower final mRS than the double-negative group (p=0.045). Cerebellar/brainstem symptoms were the most frequent presentation in MOG+ (47.1% of MOG+, 58.3% of Only MOG+), yet larger lesions were supratentorial, and no imaging differences distinguished the groups ([PMC12496048]([passage text removed])).

The larger, better-powered discriminators come from the Mayo comparison of 108 tumefactive patients (MOGAD=43, AQP4+NMOSD=16, MS=49): tumefactive lesions were more frequent in MOGAD (43/194, 22%) than [passage text removed]); headache (42% vs 20%, p=0.03) and somnolence (28% vs 4%, p=0.003) favoured MOGAD over MS; a [passage text removed] (especially arc pattern), ring enhancement and Baló-like/cystic appearance favoured MS (p≤0.001); oligoclonal bands were far less common in MOGAD (2/37, 5%) than MS (30/43, 70%, p<0.001) with higher median CSF white cell count ([passage text removed]); and lesion resolution was more common in MOGAD ([PMC10065219]([passage text removed]), also indexed as Neurology 2023;100(13):e1418-e1432 via [Continuum reference list]([passage text removed])). Importantly, relapse risk [passage text removed] vs non-tumefactive MOGAD — tumefactive morphology itself did not worsen prognosis ([PMC10065219]([passage text removed])).

## NMDAR-antibody-positive TDLs

In the same 30-patient cohort, NMDAR+ patients showed elevated systemic inflammatory markers versus NMDAR−. On detailed reading, Only NMDAR+ patients had younger onset age ([passage text removed]), higher CSF opening pressure (p=0.043), and were [passage text removed]) than double-negatives; the NMDAR+ vs NMDAR− comparison reproduced the raised intracranial pressure (p=0.029) and treatment tendency (p=0.026) but showed no difference in onset age, inflammatory markers or prognosis, and NMDAR antibodies had **no** effect on CSF WCC ([PMC12496048]([passage text removed])). So the NMDAR signature is raised intracranial pressure and systemic inflammation rather than CSF pleocytosis — the reverse of the MOG pattern.

## Dual-positive (MNOS) TDLs

Four patients were MOG+/NMDAR+; cerebellar and brainstem symptoms were proportionally higher and motor symptoms lower in the antibody-positive groups than double-negatives, but these differences were not statistically significant, and the authors suggest monitoring for NMDAR antibodies in MOG+ TDL patients with cerebellar/brainstem syndromes ([PMC12496048]([passage text removed])). Outside the TDL-specific setting, a meta-analysis of 58 dual-positive cases found relapse in 63.4%, and dual-positives had more mental/behavioural change, involuntary movements, sleep disorder and leptomeningeal lesions and less optic neuritis than MOG+/NMDAR−, and more relapse (OR [passage text removed], subcortical, basal ganglia, brainstem and spinal cord lesions than NMDAR+/MOG− ([PMC8427435]([passage text removed]); [PubMed 34512521](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34512521)).

## Seronegative / idiopathic TDLs

Antibody-negative TDLs are the majority and largely behave as an MS-spectrum or monophasic cryptogenic disease: of 257 TD patients, 71% met 2017 McDonald MS criteria, 5% had MOGAD, none were AQP4+, and 24% were cryptogenic; CSF oligoclonal bands were present in 95/153 (62%) ([PMC10502639]([passage text removed])). In the antibody-stratified cohort, double-negatives had longer disease duration and higher biopsy rates — i.e. they are the group in which biopsy is still driven by diagnostic uncertainty ([PMC12496048]([passage text removed])).

## Pathology

Immunopathological review indicates that type of demyelination, infiltrating cell distribution, [passage text removed] of MS, MOGAD and AQP4+NMOSD origin; MOGAD tumefactive biopsies showed hypercellular lesions with relative axonal preservation, reactive astrocytes, and predominantly MS pattern II demyelination ([PMC8997292]([passage text removed]); [PubMed 35418930](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35418930)). Whether demyelination in NMDAR-antibody disease is a primary process remains unresolved in that review ([Frontiers review]([passage text removed])).

## Caveats

The only study directly answering the MOG-*and*-NMDAR-stratified question has 30 patients across eight serological subgroups, with several findings at borderline significance and no imaging differences detected — it is hypothesis-generating, not definitive. I found no source establishing distinct MRI morphology for NMDAR-antibody TDLs, nor any head-to-head prognostic comparison of NMDAR+ TDLs against seronegative TDLs beyond this cohort.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Antibody status marks distinguishable **laboratory, CSF and lesion-evolution phenotypes** rather than distinct lesion appearances on acute MRI — MOG-positive tumefactive demyelinating lesions (TDLs) behave as an inflammatory, highly reversible variant, NMDAR-positive TDLs as a variant with prominent *systemic* inflammation — yet neither antibody substantially changes prognosis, which is generally favourable [S:bdab9280-71cd-5216-a380-8e5446b250dc][S:ea5f1914-a9fc-5d86-887a-cd7e68cda765].

## Evidence

**Direct antibody-stratified comparison.** A retrospective cohort of 30 TDL patients (Xuanwu Hospital, Beijing, January 2019–December 2024) excluded NMOSD, 2017 McDonald MS and secondary demyelination, then stratified by MOG and NMDAR serostatus in serum and/or CSF [S:0506d71a-86d9-51dc-a60e-dcfc2942385f][S:7f5dde7c-efb7-5378-9c26-bf66f5166a64].

*MOG-positive vs MOG-negative:*
- Cerebellar/brainstem symptoms predominated (47.1% of MOG+; 58.3% of "Only MOG+") [S:d21db005-9fb0-59ba-b8fb-318350e7596a].
- A more inflammatory CSF: CSF white cell count ≥5 in 64.7% vs 16.7% (p=0.029) [S:9bf36a61-764c-587b-9921-edaf00da5580].
- [passage text removed]) and markedly lower biopsy rates (17.6% vs 91.7%, p<0.001) — i.e. serology spared invasive diagnosis [S:d21db005-9fb0-59ba-b8fb-318350e7596a].
- Better lesion evolution: lesions decreased or disappeared on follow-up MRI (p=0.038); "no alterations" in 11.8% of MOG+ vs 54.5% of MOG− [S:9bf36a61-764c-587b-9921-edaf00da5580].
- "Only MOG+" had lower mRS at last follow-up than doubly seronegative patients (p=0.045) [S:9bf36a61-764c-587b-9921-edaf00da5580].

*NMDAR-positive vs seronegative:* younger age at onset (p=0.045), higher serum neutrophil-to-HDL ratio (p=0.048), higher CSF opening pressure (p=0.043; p=0.029 for NMDAR+ vs NMDAR−), and greater likelihood of receiving immunomodulatory treatment (p=0.048). The authors interpret the systemic inflammatory signal as possibly reflecting preceding infection; no tumours were found despite the usual NMDAR–teratoma association [S:9bf36a61-764c-587b-9921-edaf00da5580][S:a078ff23-260b-5f53-bb1e-dd0585ab20ae].

*Dual positivity (MNOS+):* higher prevalence of cerebellar/brainstem syndromes, prompting the recommendation to test for NMDAR antibodies in MOG+ TDL patients with such symptoms [S:a078ff23-260b-5f53-bb1e-dd0585ab20ae].

**What does *not* differ.** No distinct acute clinical or imaging characteristics separated the groups, and multivariable regression in the 25 patients tested for both antibodies found no antibody effect on prognosis; 86.7% achieved a favourable outcome regardless of serostatus, with somnolence (not antibody status) associated with worse outcome [S:a078ff23-260b-5f53-bb1e-dd0585ab20ae][S:d354c8be-7007-5912-af6d-16ee13158446][S:bdab9280-71cd-5216-a380-8e5446b250dc].

**Corroborating imaging/CSF contrasts (MOGAD vs MS/AQP4 tumefactive lesions).** In 108 patients with tumefactive lesions (MOGAD 43, AQP4+NMOSD 16, MS 49), tumefactive lesions were commoner in MOGAD (22%) than AQP4+NMOSD (5%); somnolence and headache were more frequent in MOGAD than MS; [passage text removed] (arc pattern), ring enhancement and Balò-like/cystic appearance favoured MS; oligoclonal bands were far less frequent in MOGAD (5% vs 70%) with higher median CSF cell count (33 vs 6 cells/µL); and T2 lesion resolution occurred in 54% of MOGAD but in none of the MS or AQP4 cases [S:e38effb8-9e3a-5dd7-ac10-8a5774a73999][S:55d7e363-ab46-511f-b366-7182839f3f60]. Descriptively, MOGAD-associated TDLs are reported as poorly demarcated "fluffy" lesions favouring posterior fossa and deep grey matter, versus hemispheric white matter in MS [S:cfe513f1-3b8e-5e34-920a-54b279463b20].

**Seronegative/idiopathic TDLs.** Cases without MOG, AQP4 or neuronal antibodies have been argued to form a separate entity, characterised by white-matter-only tumour-like lesions with open-ring enhancement, no optic nerve or cord involvement, normal CSF without intrathecal IgG synthesis, poor response to IVIg/plasma exchange, and stabilisation only with immunosuppression [S:1624aacc-8982-520e-8d68-bb00258f283b][S:5e57a4b3-2c02-5030-9d5e-6b21d786b85b]. In a series of 19 recurrent-TDL cases, none of the 6 tested were MOG-IgG positive and CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands were present in 5/17 [S:0e847621-2db8-5f51-bd36-b90564cf9860]. Biopsy-based work likewise reports that immunopathological patterns (demyelination type, infiltrating cell composition, astrocyte pathology, complement deposition) can differentiate MS-related from MOG- and AQP4-associated tumefactive lesions, while lacking tissue biomarkers for idiopathic/recurrent TDL [S:dd36027c-1a94-518d-bec9-303bfc560eb7].

## Caveats

The only study directly comparing MOG+/NMDAR+/seronegative TDLs is a single-centre retrospective cohort of 30 patients; subgroups are very small (e.g. 6 doubly seronegative patients), antibody assays came from different institutions over an extended enrolment period, and spinal imaging was often missing [S:ea5f1914-a9fc-5d86-887a-cd7e68cda765]. NMDAR-specific TDL literature is especially thin — the authors note only one prior study describing a "large mass-like lesion" type without in-depth characterisation [S:a078ff23-260b-5f53-bb1e-dd0585ab20ae]. I found no evidence on relapse-risk differences by antibody status beyond the equal monophasic-course rates in this cohort.

rows.question: What do visual evoked potentials contribute to the paraclinical workup of suspected optic neuritis under the 2022 ICON criteria?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Visual evoked potentials detected optic nerve involvement in suspected optic neuritis with high overall diagnostic accuracy in the reported series; Adding visual evoked potentials as a further paraclinical test to the 2022 ICON criteria improved the sensitivity of the criteria in the reported series; An abnormal visual evoked potential is not specific to optic neuritis, since a compressive lesion displacing the optic nerve produced a compatible alteration, so a clear alternative diagnosis from the rest of the workup takes precedence. Certainty: The accuracy estimates remain provisional, derived from a small patient sample scored against an expert reference diagnosis and not yet reproduced independently. Scope: applies to suspected optic neuritis assessed under the 2022 ICON criteria in adults, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it states that a normal visual evoked potential rules out optic neuritis or removes the need for further assessment.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: under the 2022 ICON criteria themselves, VEPs contribute nothing formally — they were deliberately excluded from the list of supporting paraclinical tests (MRI, OCT, antibody/CSF biomarkers) — but validation studies published since show that adding VEPs recovers sensitivity that the criteria lose, mainly by converting "possible" to "definite" optic neuritis (ON).**

**What ICON 2022 actually includes.** The Petzold et al. position paper (Lancet Neurol 2022;21:1120–1134, PMID 36179757) builds possible ON on clinical features alone and definite ON on clinical features plus a positive paraclinical test drawn from brain/orbital/retinal imaging and antibody/protein biomarkers ([ean.org summary]([passage text removed]); [ean.org commentary]([passage text removed])). The operationalised paraclinical items are optic nerve MRI abnormality (enhancement or intrinsic signal increase) and OCT (acute disc swelling or intereye difference >4%/>4 µm mGCIPL or >5%/>5 µm pRNFL) within 3 months, plus AQP4-IgG/MOG-IgG/CSF oligoclonal bands — VEPs are not among them (PMC11537134). VEPs appear only as an optional part of the general ON workup, not as a criterion (edoc.mdc-berlin.de/id/eprint/24591). The stated reason for exclusion: VEPs [passage text removed] ICON expert panel (PMC13100327, citing the ICON paper).

**What VEPs add empirically.**
- In a consecutive cohort of 71 patients with suspected ON who all had VEP, MRI and OCT, VEPs were the most frequently abnormal paraclinical test (65%, 46/71; most often absolute P100 latency prolongation, 59%, 42/71; intereye P100 asymmetry in 6 patients), versus OCT 62% (44/71) and MRI 52% (37/71); reduced P100 amplitude (39%, 28/71) was regarded as non-specific (PMC13100327). [passage text removed]) versus MRI (0.80) and OCT (0.78), with specificity 83.3% — higher than OCT (75%) but lower than MRI (87.5%); false positives were 3 optic nerve–displacing meningiomas and 1 NAION, and biomarkers had the lowest sensitivity (68.1%) (PMC13100327).
- Adding VEPs as a supporting test raised ICON performance from sensitivity 95.7%/specificity 75.0%/accuracy 88.7% to sensitivity 100% (CI 92.5–100.0), NPV 100%, accuracy 91.5% (PMC13100327; doi 10.1177/13524585261424125).
- In a prospective series of 46 patients with a first unilateral subacute ON, original ICON classified 43.5% (20) as definite ON; relaxing the clinical requirement and demanding two abnormal paraclinical tests gave 69.6% (32), and incorporating VEPs gave 84.8% (39), p<0.001, with reclassification occurring mostly from possible to definite and none of the four "not ON" patients being reclassified (doi 10.1007/s00415-026-13972-1).

**Interpretation and caveats.** The gap VEPs fill is the same one identified in the ACON validation, where 42–43% of acute ON patients were classified "not ON" chiefly because RAPD or dyschromatopsia was absent/undocumented — clinical items that ICON does not allow to be substituted by paraclinical tests (PMC11537134; edoc.mdc-berlin.de/id/eprint/24591). Evidence limits: the 71-patient study was retrospective, used expert adjudication as reference standard, and its authors flag incorporation bias (VEP contributed to the reference diagnosis) that may inflate VEP sensitivity, calling for prospective blinded studies (PMC13100327). VEP abnormality is also not disease-specific — compressive and ischaemic optic neuropathies produced false positives in that cohort (PMC13100327). No source I found shows that ICON has been formally revised to include VEPs; both studies are proposals for revision.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Under ICON 2022 itself, VEPs contribute **nothing formally** — they were deliberately excluded from the list of paraclinical tests that upgrade "possible" to "definite" optic neuritis — but validation cohorts published since show VEPs are the single most sensitive paraclinical test in suspected ON and that adding them to the criteria raises sensitivity and negative predictive value to 100% without loss of specificity.

## What ICON 2022 actually specifies

Paraclinical corroboration in ICON 2022 rests on three pillars only: OCT (acute disc swelling, or inter-eye asymmetry of mGCIPL/pRNFL within 3 months), orbital MRI ([passage text removed]), and biomarkers (AQP4-IgG, MOG-IgG, CRMP5-IgG, or CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands) [S:f43e6d79][S:a6bff62b][S:85c81c93]. VEPs were left out because they were judged non-specific by 52% of the Delphi expert panel [S:85c81c93]. (One recent narrative review states ICON 2022 "explicitly recognize[s] VEP as a supportive diagnostic biomarker" [S:0b713511]; this conflicts with the ICON-derived accounts above and with the primary validation literature, and should be treated as an error.)

## What VEPs actually add, empirically

**Head-to-head diagnostic performance (n=71 of 207 consecutively screened suspected-ON patients, all with MRI, OCT and VEP within 30 days of onset):** [passage text removed]), highest [passage text removed]) and [passage text removed]), versus MRI (0.80) and OCT (0.78). VEP specificity was 83.3%, better than OCT (75%) but below MRI (87.5%); biomarkers were the least sensitive (68.1%) but most specific (94.1%) [S:85115acd].

**Effect of adding VEP as a fourth pillar:** ICON 2022 alone gave sensitivity 95.7%, specificity 75.0%, NPV 90.0%, accuracy 88.7%; adding VEP raised sensitivity to 100.0%, NPV to 100%, and accuracy to 91.5%, with specificity unchanged at 75.0% [S:67fda538]. The two patients reclassified had typical histories, very early presentation (3 and 5 days from onset) and mild visual loss — i.e. exactly the situation where structural tests have not yet turned positive [S:67fda538].

**Independent replication:** In a prospective first-episode ON cohort, [passage text removed] for detecting the optic nerve lesion, and 39 of the patients (84.8%) with incomplete clinical core criteria had at least two positive paraclinical tests once VEP was included; the authors concluded their data support including VEP as an ICON paraclinical test [S:15cd0b29][S:be1ae5e1]. In the corresponding full paper, 43.5% (20 patients) met definite ON by original ICON, rising to 69.6% with relaxed clinical criteria plus two abnormal paraclinical tests, and to 84.8% (39 patients) once VEPs were added [[passage text removed]].

**Practical/logistic advantage:** VEP and OCT were obtained closer to the start of acute-phase treatment than MRI (median 0 vs 1 day, p=0.01), which matters because steroids can attenuate enhancement [S:85115acd].

## Caveats on specificity

VEP abnormality localises dysfunction to the visual pathway but does not establish inflammation: false positives in the cohort were three optic-nerve–displacing meningiomas and one non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy [S:85115acd]. This is the concrete expression of the panel's "non-specific" objection, and it is why the authors position VEPs as an *optional* supportive test whose use depends on local availability and workflow rather than a mandatory fourth pillar [S:4a89742a]. Normal VEPs also carry weight in the opposite direction as a red flag for an alternative diagnosis in demyelinating workups more broadly [S:86fd481b].

## Context

Note the divergence between criteria sets: the 2024 McDonald criteria *do* accept VEP (prolonged P100 latency, or inter-ocular latency difference >2.5 SD above the mean) as evidence of a demyelinating optic nerve lesion for dissemination in space [S:920b1fb9], so a clinician following McDonald 2024 and ICON 2022 simultaneously will find VEP admissible for MS staging but not for the ON diagnosis itself.
