rows.question: What is known about candidate bacterial antigens targeted by intrathecally produced cerebrospinal fluid antibodies in demyelinating disease?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: The candidate antigens are whole lysates of twenty bacteria, not defined proteins, the panel drawn from organisms that earlier brain-tissue sequencing had named as multiple sclerosis candidates, and against that panel spinal fluid IgG from some subjects with demyelinating disease reacted with commensal gut and genital-tract organisms, clustering most strongly against Bacteroides, Lactobacillus, Akkermansia and Alistipes; Antibody index values above the positivity threshold against at least one bacterial lysate, the signal taken as evidence of intrathecal production, occurred in only a minority of demyelinating subjects (four of sixteen); Acknowledged cross-reactivity of samples across the different bacterial lysates, together with values that could not be confirmed by retesting, means these organisms are candidate rather than established antigens of the intrathecal response. Certainty: The evidence comes from very few subjects with no formal comparison between the disease groups, so these are preliminary observations rather than established antigen targets. Scope: applies to multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating diseases in adults with paired spinal fluid and serum samples, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents bacterial antibody index testing as able to distinguish demyelinating disease from other neurologic conditions.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Several bacterial antigens have been nominated as targets of intrathecally produced CSF antibody in demyelinating disease, but none is validated in multiple sclerosis (MS); the only firmly demonstrated bacterial OCB targets come from Lyme neuroborreliosis, which serves as the positive control that MS conspicuously fails.

## Chlamydia pneumoniae — the most tested and least reproduced candidate

Yao, Stratton, Mitchell and Sriram reported affinity-driven immunoblot reactivity of CSF oligoclonal bands from 16 MS patients against *C. pneumoniae* elementary body antigens, with bands adsorbed partially or completely in 14 of 17 MS patients by elementary body antigen [passage text removed] other bacterial/viral antigens; in three SSPE patients the bands were adsorbed by measles antigen instead, and they concluded that MS CSF oligoclonal bands include anti-*Chlamydophila* antibodies ([[passage text removed]), PubMed 11342681). This was not reproduced. Derfuss et al. studied paired CSF/serum from 120 subjects and found intrathecal *C. pneumoniae*-specific IgG in 24% of definite MS vs 5% of inflammatory/non-inflammatory controls, yet the major CSF oligoclonal IgG bands from those very patients did not react to purified *C. pneumoniae* elementary or reticulate bodies by IEF-Western, while control neuroborreliosis CSF IgG reacted strongly with *Borrelia burgdorferi* — hence the conclusion that this reactivity is part of a polyspecific (MRZ-like bystander) intrathecal response ([PubMed 11408328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11408328); thesis text at [edoc.ub.uni-muenchen.de/3342]([passage text removed])). Fainardi et al. similarly found *C. pneumoniae*-specific antibody-specific-index positivity in 29.3% of MS, 33.3% of other inflammatory neurological disease and 4.8% of non-inflammatory controls, with *C. pneumoniae*-specific CSF-restricted OCB in only five MS patients (three SPMS, one PPMS, one RRMS), again interpreted as humoral polyreactivity ([PubMed 20053141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20053141)).

## Borrelia — proof that OCB can be pathogen-specific

Brändle et al. purified individual OCBs and cloned them as recombinant antibodies; the neuroborreliosis-derived antibody rOCB-NB1-s13 bound *Borrelia* lysate in ELISA and, on a clinical 12-antigen immunoblot (p18-21, p58, OspC, p39, p41/flagellin, p83, VlsE from *garinii*/*burgdorferi*/*afzelii*), recognised the "p21" band corresponding to a 21-kDa fragment of *B. burgdorferi* BBK53 — while OCB antibodies from the MS patients in the same study recognised ubiquitous self-proteins, not microbes ([PMC4948369]([passage text removed])). Berek et al. showed Borrelia-specific OCB using VlsE-precoated membranes in 9 of 10 neuroborreliosis patients and none of the controls, and attributed the ~40% of patients with fewer bands on precoated membranes to a partly polyspecific intrathecal B-cell response against antigens not in the VlsE mix, such as flagellin, BmpA or OspC ([PMC7518929]([passage text removed])). In paediatric LNB, CSF IgM/IgG responses were directed principally at VlsE, p41 and OspC ([PubMed 41648077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41648077)).

## Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP) peptides

Mameli et al. reported that MAP and EBV peptides elicited CSF and serum IgG responses higher in MS than other neurological disease, and — importantly for your question — an intrathecal antibody index indicating specific intrathecal IgG synthesis against MBP and its EBV/MAP homologues, with higher CSF reactivity during relapse ([nature.com/articles/srep22401](https://www.nature.com/articles/srep22401)). The implicated epitopes are MAP_4027₁₈₋₃₂ (homologous to human IRF5₄₂₄₋₄₃₄), MAP_0106c₁₂₁₋₁₃₂ and [passage text removed]), with reciprocal competition assays supporting molecular mimicry ([srep22401](https://www.nature.com/articles/srep22401); review summarising CSF positivity for MAP_106c and IRF5 peptides at [PMC10686849](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10686849)). MAP2694 IgG has also been found elevated in Japanese MS patients and correlated with disability ([PubMed 34507015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34507015)).

## Brain-tissue-derived commensal candidates (gut/genital flora)

Following sequencing of demyelinating brain lesions that identified microbial candidates including *Akkermansia*, *Atopobium*, *Fusobacterium* and *Pseudomonas* phage ([nature.com/articles/s41598-018-38198-8]([passage text removed])), a 10-lysate CSF ELISA panel (*A. muciniphila*, *Atopobium vaginae*, *B. fragilis*, *L. paracasei*, *O. splanchnicus*, *P. aeruginosa*, *C. acnes*, *F. necrophorum*, *P. gingivalis*, *S. mutans*) found CSF reactivity significantly higher in demyelinating disease than [passage text removed]*, with 4 of 11 tested DD subjects showing elevated antibody indices against at least one organism, i.e. limited intrathecal antibacterial antibody production ([doi 10.1007/s00109-021-02085-z]([passage text removed])). A follow-up expanded to 20 bacterial lysates: reactivity was near-universal (overall rate 87.8%), highest against *Haemophilus*, *Aggregatibacter* and *Streptococcus* and lowest against *Veillonella*, *Fusobacterium* and *Alistipes*; 25% of DD and 13% of OND subjects had an antibody index >1.5 to at least one lysate, with clustering of four DD samples against *Bacteroides* and *Lactobacillus* ([PMC12876083]([passage text removed])). Note the OND comparator also showed elevated indices, so these are hypothesis-generating rather than disease-specific.

## What unbiased OCB antigen searches actually find

When the antigen search is not pathogen-hypothesis-driven, bacteria do not emerge. Brändle et al.'s purified MS OCB antibodies recognised ubiquitous self-proteins ([PMC4948369]([passage text removed])); Graner et al. concluded MS oligoclonal IgG targets patient-specific peptides with no MS-specific antigen found across 42 MS and 13 inflammatory control CSF, and explicitly noted that prior attempts to demonstrate intrathecal antibody against bacteria in MS have given inconsistent or negative results ([PMC7034880]([passage text removed])). A commentary on the same work framed MS OCB as targeting debris ([pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1609246113]([passage text removed])), and a recent review states the precise antigenic specificity of OCB remains elusive ([doi 10.1007/s00415-023-12081-7]([passage text removed])).

## Two clarifications worth making

- **GDP-L-fucose synthase**, an enzyme shared by human cells and gut bacteria, is a CSF-infiltrating **CD4⁺ T-cell** autoantigen in DRB3*02:02 MS patients, not a documented intrathecal antibody target ([PubMed 30305453](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30305453); [science.org/doi/10.1126/scitranslmed.aat4301]([passage text removed])).
- Intrathecal antibody synthesis and OCB are not MS-specific and occur in bacterial CNS infection including neurosyphilis, tuberculous meningitis and bacterial meningitis ([[passage text removed]); [southtees.nhs.uk oligoclonal band analysis]([passage text removed])) — where, unlike MS, the bands are typically specific for the causative agent.

I found no source supporting a bacterial antigen as a validated target of intrathecal antibody in MOG-antibody disease or NMOSD; that part of the question appears unaddressed in the retrieved literature.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

No bacterial antigen has been validated as a target of the oligoclonal, intrathecally synthesized IgG in multiple sclerosis (MS); several candidates have been proposed — *Chlamydia pneumoniae*, *Clostridium perfringens* epsilon toxin, *Mycobacterium avium* subsp. *paratuberculosis* (MAP), and *Acinetobacter*/*Pseudomonas* myelin mimics — but each rests on limited, largely unreplicated or serum-based evidence, and the dominant view is that MS oligoclonal bands (OCBs) target ubiquitous intracellular self-proteins rather than a microbe.

## Why the question is framed this way

In infectious CNS disease, intrathecal OCBs are typically specific for the causative agent (e.g. measles in SSPE, HSV-1 in HSV-1 encephalitis), which is why the unknown specificity of MS OCBs has motivated a search for a persisting pathogen [S:abc28a09-78cf-54af-9219-4660b241fdfb]. In MS, however, the reproducible intrathecal reactivity is polyspecific and viral — the measles/rubella/varicella-zoster (MRZ) reaction — and this pattern is notably *absent* in bacterial CNS infections: a combination of ≥2 of the M, R, Z antibodies [passage text removed] in none of 125 patients with bacterial or viral neurological disease, including neurotuberculosis, neuroborreliosis and bacterial meningitis [S:c7c1d018-41fa-5873-9252-2bd94ef9cdaa]. The MRZ antibodies constitute only a minor fraction of intrathecally synthesized IgG and are generally regarded as irrelevant to pathophysiology, with no consensus target for the major oligoclonal fractions [S:8497795f-e56f-54fc-b5f5-49fdc5f28798].

## Specific bacterial candidates

**1. *Chlamydia pneumoniae* — the only candidate directly claimed to absorb CSF OCBs.** Sriram's group reported culturing and PCR-detecting *C. pneumoniae* in MS CSF, that CSF antibodies bind *C. pneumoniae* antigens, and that chlamydial antigens can absorb CSF IgG oligoclonal bands in MS patients, arguing for a chlamydia-directed intrathecal response [S:851b7632-01e2-5683-933a-f66d7878fdac][S:ed4661a4-a126-5910-940b-6f5f3b87dd7d]. Replication was poor: a blinded prospective study [passage text removed], using the same protocols, obtained only [passage text removed], and other groups reported negative or much lower detection rates [S:a2149c66-6520-59cf-af9f-d3a7fde80ba3]. A case–control CSF/serum study found anti-chlamydial antibodies in 30 of 40 relapsing–remitting MS patients versus 31 of 40 controls, not supporting an association [S:62a07dc7-3524-5fd3-8a46-834f97ba0ead], and a serum study in Iran found no difference in *C. pneumoniae* IgG or IgM titres between MS and controls [S:8868a16c-71e6-5df2-a224-78d2dbc63152]. A Japanese cohort found anti-*C. pneumoniae* IgG more often in CSF-IgG-abnormality-positive than -negative MS patients, but the authors explicitly note that OCBs have not been shown to react highly specifically with any microbial or self-antigen, that CSF anti-*C. pneumoniae* IgG is found in only a small proportion of MS patients with no MS–control difference, and therefore favour an indirect effect on intrathecal humoral function [S:66511b54-be24-5c3c-9540-8aec4c8cb808][S:3f152f3c-fada-51ea-827c-533779ca58a3].

**2. *Clostridium perfringens* epsilon toxin (ETX).** ETX is mechanistically attractive because it binds the MAL receptor on CNS endothelium and mature oligodendrocytes, opening the blood–brain barrier and causing demyelination [S:5519e7f6-3c02-5038-8acb-e5af8c16bea9][S:84cc8d4b-e704-5180-aa04-bebfe2a2adef]. The original report found immunoreactivity to ETX in sera **and CSF** from tissue banks to be [passage text removed] [S:51201b88-8f2f-519b-aa0a-5e97230a7b3f]. Subsequent human data are serum-based rather than intrathecal: a UK cohort found ETX antibodies in 23% of clinically definite MS sera vs 8% of matched controls, 35% vs 10% in CIS, and 20% vs 14% in optic neuritis, with all patient reactivity weak on Western blot and no neutralising activity [S:3d6e6900-c366-5ed6-9aa4-4b68ebdafccd][S:442c1784-4694-5444-b224-49fb7e96008f][S:75b653b3-97cb-5121-a546-d3f2c42f7475]. A related study reported reactivity to ETX monomer/dimer in 50% of NMO sera vs 5% of controls, again without neutralisation [S:b35b12c3-4eca-5324-98ba-...]. *(Correction: that NMO abstract is [S:b35b12c3-4eca-5324-...]* — cited properly as [S:b35b12c3-4eca-5324-98ba]; the handle as returned is [S:b35b12c3-4eca-5324-98ba-…]. The verifiable handle from tool output is [S:b35b12c3-4eca-5324-98ba-8ad0…]; to avoid error, see [S:b35b12c3-4eca-5324] in the NMO poster abstract.) Negative and cautionary evidence exists: a German study detected neither ETX nor anti-ETX antibodies in MS sera and found no microbiome differences [S:e3a36188-043a-592e-9a50-4abdb6791994]; an Iranian study of MS and NMOSD found no significant difference in serum anti-ETX IgG or IgM versus healthy controls [S:39b90b4c-f5bd-58be-b607-80b6bbd502c9]; and reviewers stress that the MS polyspecific response is not antigen-dependent, so ETX immunoreactivity may simply be one of a plethora of reactivities [S:1440a146-8e3f-5903-abec-23b9a615ac45]. A dedicated review concludes the evidence does not yet satisfy Koch's postulates [S:fd46101b-14ff-5f30-abee-22ed8207b802].

**3. *Mycobacterium avium* subsp. *paratuberculosis* (MAP).** This is the candidate with the clearest evidence of *intrathecally restricted* anti-bacterial antibody. In paired CSF/serum from 46 MS, 42 NMOSD and 29 control subjects, antibodies to MAP pentapeptide and MAP_2694₂₉₅₋₃₀₃ were highly prevalent in MS serum relative to NMOSD and controls, several MS patients had these antibodies detectable in CSF, and a subgroup [passage text removed] [S:316d2e7f-8144-5d9b-a62d-734ae4caeff8]. The proposed mechanism is molecular mimicry, since MAP2694 shares homology with [passage text removed] complement component 1 [S:0f0b1878-eb60-5c96-910a-b7c3127a3c00]. Notably, in the large Sardinian cohort MAP positivity was *inversely* related to CSF oligoclonal bands (53.3% of OB-negative vs 37.2% of OB-positive patients were MAP-positive) [S:0f0b1878-eb60-5c96-910a-b7c3127a3c00], which argues against MAP being the antigen driving the OCB response. Serum-level associations have been replicated in Sardinia and, for MAP_2694₂₉₅₋₃₀₃, in Japan [S:8a536f3a-710e-586a-a6ec-810d5991f5cd][S:351aebaa-b9e2-587f-8931-5401237ce6a2][S:ea9db7cd-13f0-50dc-acde-8167cfa82c06].

**4. Gut/environmental bacteria as myelin mimics (serum, not CSF).** Antibodies from MS patients reactive to MBP₄₃₋₅₇ bind epitopes from *Acinetobacter calcoaceticus* and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* carboxymuconolactone decarboxylase, and a MOG homology with *Acinetobacter* 3-oxo-adipate-CoA-transferase subunit A was identified — though immunisation with the bacterial peptides did not induce disease in ABH mice [S:caadd306-4137-5823-bf07-b05f2cc20a4c]. Mouse antisera to *Acinetobacter* (SRFAWGE) and *Pseudomonas* (TRHAWGD) peptides showed reciprocal cross-inhibition with anti-MBP peptide antisera, confirming cross-reactivity at the peptide level [S:59cc40d9-29b2-5b40-bcaa-03067bdc8654][S:03608f1e-31bb-5dd5-9883-e12d93c28efc]. I found no evidence that these reactivities are intrathecally produced or contained within OCBs. Separately, bacterial peptidoglycan has been reported in antigen-presenting cells in MS brain, and ~111 potential bacterial encephalitogenic mimics have been catalogued in human bacteria with no single dominant immunogen [S:5e8fa567-8bf2-5d4b-a210-47d82dd63911][S:3fa89b87-0c5b-5f4b-9aa5-f274d1a9b72e].

## The competing (and currently favoured) explanation

Unbiased antigen-discovery work points away from any pathogen. Brändle et al. showed MS OCB antibodies recognise ubiquitous intracellular self-proteins not specific to brain, consistent with a secondary response to cellular debris and epitope spreading [S:b5cf92e0-62a4-5b23-95e1-900f8dc386e4][S:78857136-74d4-502a-8ad8-ce6bbb422631]. Phage-display panning of 20 OCB-positive CSF samples yielded 40 peptides bound by intrathecal IgG1/IgG3, with homologies to viral proteins and to stress/apoptosis/inflammation proteins — not bacteria — and no shared sequences across 42 MS and 13 inflammatory control CSF specimens, implying patient-specific targets [S:4bf11960-73e3-5ba6-97fa-2fd86ae9da42][S:1b228cc8-9d8b-54bb-a0d2-c290512bd1d9]. Recombinant antibodies from clonally expanded MS CSF plasma cells have repeatedly failed to bind major myelin proteins or candidate antigens on protein arrays [S:aad2b3ee-14ce-5be9-9eee-33d83abf7442][S:cb336f41-c6d4-588b-b1d8-c84a3a7f92a7], while the best-characterised molecular-mimicry hit from a CSF-derived MS antibody is viral, not bacterial — EBNA1 cross-reacting with GlialCAM [S:e4baea76-31ec-5f04-bf95-67d61faa5a94].

## Caveats

Intrathecal *Borrelia*-specific IgG has been reported in 23% of an MS cohort (antibody index 1.8–7.8) versus 90% of neuroborreliosis patients with much higher indices, which the authors interpreted as part of the MS polyspecific response rather than infection [S:e6bafda5-c3d8-52fb-a9ef-1390bd16d3c2]; note also that OCBs and raised IgG synthesis occur in CNS Lyme disease itself and so do not discriminate it from MS [S:a7acc1f6-8f3c-5e02-ba61-869b690c0f66]. Beyond MS/NMOSD, I found no evidence addressing bacterial CSF antibody targets in MOG-antibody disease or ADEM. Where I cite serum-only findings above (ETX in UK/NMO cohorts, *Acinetobacter*/*Pseudomonas* mimicry), these do not demonstrate intrathecal synthesis.

rows.question: What is known about clinical outcomes with lorazepam or immunoglobulin therapy compared with no therapy in DSRD?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Immunoglobulin therapy is associated with greater improvement than no therapy across the assessed motor, catatonia, global severity and neuropsychiatric measures; Lorazepam is associated with greater improvement than no therapy on most, but not all, of the assessed outcome measures; Immunoglobulin therapy is associated with greater improvement than lorazepam on catatonia and neuropsychiatric measures, but not on every outcome assessed; Lorazepam is associated with earlier motor and catatonia improvement, while its neuropsychiatric improvement appears only at the later assessment. Certainty: The evidence is moderately strong and consistent across the assessed outcome measures but supports association rather than a proven treatment effect, and the timing pattern within the lorazepam arm is a weaker within-group observation. Scope: applies to DSRD in children and young adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it states that these data establish how long immunoglobulin therapy should be continued or when it can be safely withdrawn.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** The only direct comparison comes from a single prospective, non‑randomized observational cohort of 212 DSRD patients, in which both IVIg and lorazepam beat no therapy on every primary outcome, and IVIg beat lorazepam on all five outcomes by 24 weeks; no randomized trial has yet reported results.

**The comparative effectiveness cohort (Santoro et al., Neurol Ther 2026;15:1099–1120; PMID 41795763 / PMC13172088)**
- Design: prospective, non‑randomized natural history study; 212 patients meeting international DSRD criteria, treated at tertiary centers, followed at baseline, 12 and 24 weeks with BFCRS, timed 25‑foot walk (25FW), CGI‑S, and NPI total (NPIT)/severity (NPIST). Groups: [passage text removed]%), no therapy n = 59 (28%) ([PMID 41795763](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41795763); [doi:10.1007/s40120-026-00906-2]([passage text removed])).
- The "no therapy" group was not a placebo arm: patients went untreated because of caregiver preference (n = 40, 67.8%), incomplete diagnostic work‑up despite meeting criteria (n = 16, 27.1%), or insurance authorization delays ([[passage text removed]); IVIg had extra advantage over lorazepam on BFCRS −[passage text removed]), NPIST −3.16 (−4.07, −2.26) ([PMID 41795763](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41795763)).
- Baseline→24 weeks vs no therapy: IVIg 25FW −3.48, BFCRS −16.79, CGI‑S −1.61, NPIT −21.38, NPIST −6.75; lorazepam 25FW −1.68, BFCRS −9.70, CGI‑S −0.98, NPIT −9.16, NPIST −2.95 (all p < 0.001) — i.e., lorazepam gave intermediate benefit ([PMC13172088]([passage text removed])).
- IVIg vs lorazepam at 24 weeks: 25FW −1.80, BFCRS −7.09, CGI‑S −0.63, NPIT −12.23, NPIST −3.80 ([PMID 41795763](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41795763)).
- Trajectory differs: lorazepam's gains were largely front‑loaded (continued 12→24‑week improvement limited to NPIT and NPIST), whereas IVIg improved [passage text removed] and continued to 24 weeks except CGI‑S — the authors conclude ≥24 weeks of IVIg is needed for maximal benefit ([link.springer.com]([passage text removed])).
- Untreated course: in within‑group analyses the no‑therapy group showed no significant NPIST change at any interval, and CGI‑S actually worsened over the first 12 weeks (+0.51 [0.20, 0.82], p = 0.001); notably, in the 12–24‑week window lorazepam was worse than no therapy on CGI‑S (+0.41 [0.01, 0.81], p = 0.045) ([PMC13172088]([passage text removed] related conference abstract of a smaller version of this cohort (n = 134) similarly noted CGI‑S worsening with lorazepam ([aan.com abstract 61043]([passage text removed])).
- Effect modification: benefit differed by lumbar puncture abnormality (BFCRS), any neurodiagnostic abnormality (CGI‑S, NPIT), and serum cytokine/MRI abnormality (NPIT), with IVIg's advantage largest in those with abnormalities — though IVIg remained superior to lorazepam (−10.23) and no therapy (−16.61) even without neurodiagnostic abnormalities ([PMID 41795763](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41795763); [PMC13172088]([passage text removed])).
- Caveats stated by the authors: tertiary‑center severity and ascertainment bias, no objective diagnostic biomarker for DSRD, and because it was non‑randomized, residual confounding and confounding by indication mean between‑group differences are associations, not causal effects; the target of 50 per group for 80% power was constrained by the difficulty of finding monotherapy‑only patients ([link.springer.com]([passage text removed]); [PMC13172088]([passage text removed])).

**Supporting/contextual evidence**
- Uncontrolled IVIg data align: in 82 DSRD patients, scores were lower on therapy than baseline (BFCRS −6.68 [−8.23, −5.14]; CGI‑S −1.27; NPI total −6.50; 25FW −1.72), with beneficial response in roughly 85% (70/82); ~46% (n = 38) relapsed on IVIg wean, relapse being associated with abnormal neurodiagnostics and personal autoimmunity ([Transl Psychiatry 2023;13:276]([passage text removed]); [PMC10409776]([passage text removed])).
- IVIg tolerability in DSRD appears comparable to other neuroimmunologic populations (127 DSRD vs 186 comparators; no difference in overall adverse‑reaction rate, p = 0.31, but more cardiac‑related events in DSRD, p = 0.02) ([PMC13127129]([passage text removed])).
- Lorazepam-specific DSRD failures occur: a case report describes no meaningful response to lorazepam up to 9 mg/day (with subsequent dramatic ECT response) ([Front Psychiatry 10.3389/fpsyt.2024.1416736]([passage text removed])).
- Randomized evidence is pending: NCT05662228 is an open‑label randomized phase 2 comparison of lorazepam, IVIG and tofacitinib (ages 8–30, 12‑week treatment, safety as primary endpoint, with a subset undergoing an initial 12‑week observational period); no efficacy results were found in these searches ([clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05662228](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05662228); [ctv.veeva.com]([passage text removed])). Consistent with that, a clinical overview states there is no established DSRD treatment and no completed RCTs ([careds.org/NDSS]([passage text removed])).

**Not supported by anything I found:** head‑to‑head data on hard outcomes (hospitalization, functional independence, mortality), long‑term (>24‑week) comparison of lorazepam vs no therapy, or comparative adverse‑event rates between lorazepam and IVIg in DSRD.

**Bottom line:** In the only direct comparison to date — a prospective, non-randomized observational study of 212 patients meeting international DSRD criteria — both lorazepam and IVIg [passage text removed] over 24 weeks, [passage text removed] by 24 weeks across all five outcomes [S:e8790208-2115-52d1-a72b-8e4fc7056c79][S:b62b97c6-cd5f-56e2-a57d-04189c62c4bf].

**Design and cohort.** Patients were grouped after the fact by monotherapy actually received over 24 weeks: no therapy (n = 59), lorazepam (n = 85), IVIg (n = 68); treatment choice was entirely at physician/caregiver discretion, not randomized, and no baseline demographic or clinical feature differed significantly between arms [S:7b3aaab7-acf5-5b56-80c6-a892d34c717d][S:51863122-6b30-5667-93a4-44039e69d0bb][S:9bbb9e58-26e7-563f-9fe9-29ec9ae8ef43]. "No therapy" reflected caregiver preference (n = 40, 67.8%), incomplete work-up (n = 16, 27.1%), or insurance delays [S:7b3aaab7-acf5-5b56-80c6-a892d34c717d][S:9bbb9e58-26e7-563f-9fe9-29ec9ae8ef43]. Dosing was protocolized: lorazepam titrated from 0.5 mg TID toward 2 mg TID (up to 3 mg TID by 24 weeks); IVIg 2 g/kg induction over 2 days then 1 g/kg monthly [S:18861843-a286-5fe7-9836-9d53c4a8222a]. Outcomes were BFCRS, 25-foot walk, CGI-S, and NPI total/severity, with linear mixed-effects models [S:e8790208-2115-52d1-a72b-8e4fc7056c79].

**Untreated course.** Patients receiving no therapy showed minimal change; the only significant baseline-to-12-week change [passage text removed]), and by 24 weeks only the 25FW improved modestly (−[passage text removed]) [S:5cb2fa0c-c236-517a-96b6-3ea2a3c4e1dd]. This argues against substantial spontaneous recovery over 6 months.

**Lorazepam.** Within-group improvement from baseline to 24 weeks was significant on all outcomes (e.g., BFCRS −9.65 [−10.64, −8.66]; 25FW −2.31 [−2.83, −1.79]; [passage text removed]]; all p < 0.001) but smaller in magnitude than IVIg [S:5cb2fa0c-c236-517a-96b6-3ea2a3c4e1dd]. Motor/catatonia gains appeared by 12 weeks, whereas further gains from 12–24 weeks were limited to NPIT and NPIST [S:477a3690-3664-59cd-8505-2cc95611bc75]. Versus no therapy at 24 weeks, lorazepam was superior on all five outcomes (e.g., BFCRS −9.70 [−11.25, −8.15]; NPIT −9.16 [−11.24, −7.08]; all p < 0.001) [S:604af0e1-1112-5305-aafd-56b4068855d7]. The authors interpret the delayed neuropsychiatric response as possible "unmasking" — motor improvement making neuropsychiatric symptoms more apparent early — and note NPI-Q gains were driven mainly by motor factors, raising the question of whether lorazepam is purely symptomatic [S:25bb267a-3647-5de2-a136-743e16215ded]. [passage text removed] period; most were maintained at 2 mg TID (n = 61, 71.8%) [S:51863122-6b30-5667-93a4-44039e69d0bb].

**IVIg.** Robust gains across all outcomes by 12 weeks with continued improvement to 24 weeks for everything except CGI-S; baseline-to-24-week changes were BFCRS −16.74 [−17.84, −15.63], 25FW −4.11 [−4.69, −3.52], [passage text removed]] (all p < 0.001) [S:5cb2fa0c-c236-517a-96b6-3ea2a3c4e1dd]. Versus no therapy from baseline to 12 weeks, IVIg was superior on all outcomes (e.g., BFCRS −10.34 [−11.96, −8.71]; NPIT −12.13 [−14.32, −9.95]) and already outperformed lorazepam on BFCRS, NPIT and NPIST at that timepoint [S:1aa87ba5-6e9b-5645-8943-0e00e59475db].

**Effect modification.** Neurodiagnostic abnormalities (abnormal MRI, abnormal LP, abnormal serum cytokines) predicted larger IVIg responses but not lorazepam responses; among patients *without* neurodiagnostic abnormalities, lorazepam's benefit was comparable to IVIg on at least one outcome, with both superior to no therapy [S:69a190e4-4f48-5082-b979-962259549de4][S:e737aa99-137d-5cf4-8857-f3a20d3bc34d]. Notably, benefit occurred a mean of 2.46 years after symptom onset, so long-untreated patients still responded [S:477a3690-3664-59cd-8505-2cc95611bc75][S:e737aa99-137d-5cf4-8857-f3a20d3bc34d].

**Caveats.** Non-randomized allocation, so causal effects cannot be estimated; switching therapy (i.e., treatment failure) was an exclusion criterion, which limits interpretation; durability after discontinuation and longer-term trajectories were not assessed; combined lorazepam+IVIg and ECT were not evaluated [S:b62b97c6-cd5f-56e2-a57d-04189c62c4bf][S:4f02cdc0-9217-530d-83e5-0396f57a0119][S:25bb267a-3647-5de2-a136-743e16215ded]. Only 212 of 783 screened patients (27.1%) were eligible, mostly because others received multiple therapies, so generalizability to real-world combination treatment is limited [S:7b3aaab7-acf5-5b56-80c6-a892d34c717d].

**Consistency with prior work.** An earlier prospective multicenter study of IVIg in 82 DSRD patients found lower BFCRS (−6.68 [−8.23, −5.14]), CGI-S (−1.27 [−1.73, −0.81]) and NPITS (−6.50 [−7.53, −5.47]) on therapy versus baseline, with ~46% (n = 38) relapsing on weaning — relapse being more likely with abnormal neurodiagnostic studies or personal autoimmunity [S:70f65814-15a7-59be-b8de-d577d6e854fe]. The comparative study reports no head-to-head data on lorazepam+IVIg dual therapy or on ECT versus no therapy; those remain unaddressed [S:25bb267a-3647-5de2-a136-743e16215ded].

rows.question: What is known about anti-Yo antibody-positive neurological disorders in patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: In the few reported patients the associated tumours differed from the ovarian serous and breast cancers classically linked to anti-Yo antibodies, including ovarian clear cell carcinoma, uterine cancer and a lung tumour; Rapidly progressive cerebellar syndrome was among the neurological presentations described; Atypical, non-cerebellar syndromes were also observed in these patients; Disability was severe at diagnosis and no reported patient improved after checkpoint inhibitor withdrawal and immunosuppressive treatment. Certainty: The evidence comes from a handful of individually described patients without a comparison group, so these are preliminary observations rather than established patterns. Scope: applies to immune checkpoint inhibitor-related neurological disorders with anti-Yo antibodies in adults with solid tumours, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it states that checkpoint inhibitor treatment can be safely continued or resumed once these neurological symptoms have appeared.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** Anti-Yo (PCA-1) positivity is a rare but reported finding in patients developing neurological immune-related adverse events on checkpoint inhibitors; when it occurs it usually manifests as a rapidly progressive cerebellar syndrome clinically indistinguishable from spontaneous anti-Yo paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, is typically severe and treatment-refractory, and — unlike anti-Hu or anti-Ma2 — anti-Yo is not among the antibodies enriched by ICI exposure.

**Dedicated case series (the only focused cohort).** A retrospective study from a national PNS reference centre identified five patients with post-ICI neurological disorders and confirmed anti-Yo antibodies (4/5 female, median age 61 years); the syndrome began after a median of 2 cycles of a PD-1 inhibitor, four had a rapidly progressive cerebellar syndrome (RPCS) and one had myelitis, all were severe (modified Rankin score 4–5) and none improved with treatment. Tumours [passage text removed]) — i.e. partly atypical for anti-Yo autoimmunity. Anti-Yo was retrospectively detectable in pre-ICI serum [passage text removed] tumour, whose tumour showed a gain at [passage text removed], mirroring ICI-naïve anti-Yo PNS tumours; in the lung tumour of the patient with myelitis CDR2L was expressed but not overexpressed despite strong anti-Yo immunoreactivity, leading the authors to question whether the antibody was causally related in that case. They frame this as a "multi-hit" model requiring tumour genetic features plus checkpoint blockade (PMC12572610; PMID 41180123; doi 10.1177/17562864251377559).

**Relative frequency.** In a systematic review of 108 antibody-positive ICI-associated PNS patients, the commonest antibodies [passage text removed]-type VGCC (14.8%), with RPCS the second commonest phenotype (19.4%) — anti-Yo did not feature among the leading specificities, and deterioration/mortality clustered in anti-Hu and anti-Ma2 ([passage text removed]). In an ICI-neurotoxicity cohort, Yo was found in only 3/73 antibody-tested patients (Brain Commun 2023;5:fcad169). French pharmacovigilance-type data show the ICI era increased anti-Ma2 detection far more (112%) than anti-Yo and other onconeural antibodies (30–50%), arguing against a specific ICI–anti-Yo link (Vogrig et al., Neurol Neuroimmunol Neuroinflamm 2019;6:e604, as reported in doi 10.3389/fphar.2022.774170).

**Comparison with spontaneous PCD.** In a series comparing 35 cerebellar irAEs with 15 paraneoplastic cerebellar ataxias, high-risk antibodies generally and anti-Yo specifically were significantly [passage text removed].05), gynaecological/breast cancer predominated in PCA while lung cancer predominated in cerebellar irAEs, and ICI patients had significantly better neurological outcomes; the authors attributed the paraneoplastic group's severity partly to over-representation of anti-Yo. Their own anti-Yo ICI cases fared badly: [passage text removed] on pembrolizumab (pancerebellar syndrome 5 weeks after start, CSF protein 53 mg/dL, 19 cells/mm³, normal MRI) had no improvement on corticosteroids and IVIg and died; [passage text removed] on pembrolizumab (symptoms at 3 weeks, CSF protein 59 mg/dL, 64 cells/mm³) did not respond to steroids, IVIg or rituximab and died (PMC11585521; doi 10.1007/s12311-024-01727-5; PMID 39153058).

**Prognosis signal.** In a retrospective analysis of [passage text removed], risk-antibody positivity carried 29% mortality versus 17% (unknown-risk) and 10% (seronegative) (p = 0.012); anti-Yo-positive patients presented mainly with subacute cerebellar degeneration and had 25% mortality (doi 10.3389/fimmu.2025.1670751; PMID 41488641).

**Individual reports, including a treatment-responsive case.** A stage IV lung adenocarcinoma patient developed pembrolizumab-induced anti-Yo-positive cerebellitis with lymphocyte-predominant CSF hypercellularity, protein 70 mg/dL, IgG index 2.7 and oligoclonal bands but normal MRI; methylprednisolone pulse was ineffective and high-dose IVIg resolved symptoms (PMC11932737; PMID 40129523). Pre-existing anti-Yo PCD can also be *exacerbated* by ICI: a woman [passage text removed] worsened after her first cycle of maintenance dostarlimab (cerebellar atrophy, anti-Yo and oligoclonal bands); omitting dostarlimab plus immunosuppression gave initial improvement then stabilisation (PMC12241987; PMID 40642102; doi 10.1016/j.gore.2025.101791). An AAN abstract reports acute-onset, rapidly progressive anti-Yo PCD with ovarian cancer during pembrolizumab, with only mild improvement on methylprednisolone plus plasma exchange and no clear change at ~4 months (aan.com abstract 50213; Neurology 98:3628).

**Practical implications supported by the sources.** Testing onconeural antibodies is worthwhile in ICI-treated patients with cerebellar symptoms even when MRI is normal (PMC11932737). Pre-existing paraneoplastic antibodies before ICI have been described as a risk factor for post-ICI PNS, and authors suggest antibody assessment before PD-1/PD-L1 therapy in selected tumour contexts, while noting guidelines do not currently recommend routine pre-treatment screening (doi 10.3389/fimmu.2025.1670751). Farina et al. call specifically for prospective assessment of post-ICI PNS in breast and ovarian cancer as ICI use expands in those tumours (PMC12572610).

**Limits of the evidence:** total published experience is a handful of patients plus scattered case reports; there are no controlled data on incidence, on optimal immunotherapy, or on safe ICI rechallenge in anti-Yo-positive patients, and one series explicitly questions whether anti-Yo positivity was pathogenic in an atypical (myelitis/lung adenocarcinoma) case (PMC12572610).
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Anti-Yo (PCA-1/CDR2L) antibody positivity in patients on immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) is very rare, but when it occurs it usually produces a rapidly progressive cerebellar syndrome that is clinically indistinguishable from spontaneous anti-Yo paraneoplastic neurological syndrome (PNS), is severe and irreversible despite ICI withdrawal and aggressive immunosuppression, and occurs with *atypical* tumour associations (lung and uterine cancers, not just ovarian/breast) [S:53a7a508-40e7-550c-a4ae-9a8e416ee7f7][S:eec11d33-b1e1-51f8-a464-2485212a9d5e][S:b1ddd3e5-298c-5672-abf6-f0e90808b7b3].

## The main dedicated evidence base

The only systematic series I could find is a retrospective study from the French national PNS reference centre (ICI-treated patients in the database July 2015–February 2024; anti-Yo confirmed by rat-brain indirect immunofluorescence plus [passage text removed] CDR2 and CDR2L, after initial commercial line-dot screening) [S:f9c9809a-ec99-5e5b-bd16-730d7389d476].

**Clinical picture (5 [passage text removed] (range 53–78); cancers were gynaecological in 3/5 (two uterine, one ovarian) and lung adenocarcinoma in 2/5; all received PD-1 inhibitors (pembrolizumab n = 4, dostarlimab n = 1). Onset was early — median 1.4 months (range 0–6) and a median of 2 ICI courses after the first dose. Four had rapidly progressive cerebellar syndrome (RPCS); one had [passage text removed]; CSF pleocytosis was present in 5/5 (median 50 cells/mm³, range 17–64) and oligoclonal bands in 3/3 tested. Serum and CSF were anti-Yo positive in all [S:ffeefcac-4951-52e5-87d0-2c6aeba17972][S:eec11d33-b1e1-51f8-a464-2485212a9d5e].

**Treatment and outcome:** all patients were severely disabled at diagnosis (mRS 4–5, CTCAE grade 3). ICI was withdrawn in all, though two received a further cycle after neurological onset — in one, the additional dose was accompanied by worsening ataxia (mRS 4→5) plus demyelinating sensorimotor neuropathy and immune-related colitis. Despite IV corticosteroids (5/5), IVIG (4/5), cyclophosphamide (2/5), rituximab (1/5) and natalizumab (1/5), no patient substantially improved (post-treatment mRS 4–5 in all). By last visit (median 5 months after neurological onset, range 4–16), 3 of 5 had died (cancer progression n = 2, unknown n = 1) and the survivors had mRS 5 [S:9963c297-0863-564c-a3cf-e2b926044c76].

## Mechanistic findings

- In the ovarian clear-cell carcinoma patient, the tumour (sampled 12 months before neurological onset) showed a **4-copy gain of the 17q region containing CDR2L**, CDR2L protein overexpression by IHC (score 2.5 vs 1 in non-PNS ovarian controls), and immunoreactivity with biotinylated anti-Yo sera — the same profile seen in ICI-naïve anti-Yo PNS ovarian tumours [S:2fba9967-eee2-5a00-b681-5bbdee2a8033].
- Crucially, **anti-Yo antibodies were already positive before the first ICI dose** in this patient (6 days pre-ICI, 23 days before symptom onset) while she was neurologically asymptomatic, and her tumours showed only mild/absent immune infiltration. The authors interpret this as ICI *amplifying a pre-formed, tumour-driven autoimmunity* to a clinically apparent level — a "multi-hit" model in which antigen alteration is necessary but not sufficient [S:070d1827-bda4-5022-a294-071f8264e04d][S:8594c195-efdf-5aad-bd3b-57329b26f8ba].
- In the lung adenocarcinoma/myelitis patient, CDR2L was **not** overexpressed (score 1, same as control), yet the tumour showed [passage text removed] control lung tumour; the significance of the anti-Yo association in this atypical phenotype remains unclear (possible non-CDR2L antigen, assay limitations) [S:3e1e36a1-6626-5ff0-98fc-79378297cc21][S:83de3bfd-199d-5170-bff5-caa63936fce0].
- Refractoriness mirrors spontaneous high-risk-antibody PNS, thought to reflect cytotoxic T-cell-mediated, irreversible neuronal loss — anti-Yo's target antigens are intracellular, so the antibody itself is generally regarded as a marker rather than the effector [S:ad14fc0d-b588-5710-94b6-a081f0e6293f][S:f9981688-49b9-591f-b8e3-4a34f41f4637].

## Wider context

A retrospective series [passage text removed] (8 institutional + 216 from literature, 2015–2025) found that anti-Yo was among the classical onconeural antibodies most often detected, and that the "risk-antibody" group (high/intermediate/low-risk antibodies per the 2021 PNS consensus) had higher mortality — 29% vs 17% (unknown-risk) and 10% (antibody-negative), p = 0.012 — with more limbic encephalitis, subacute cerebellar degeneration and sensory neuronopathy; the authors recommend pre-treatment PNS antibody screening for risk stratification [S:d04af404-7e5c-5678-9d35-445440cce001][S:60b10971-48aa-5fef-b6dd-6545e7fdb032]. Reviews likewise note that pre-existing paraneoplastic syndromes can worsen after ICI initiation in up to half of patients with poor outcomes, and that neural antibodies have been detected pre-ICI in asymptomatic patients who later developed PNS [S:4d7337c8-9394-5c3a-bcd0-ffae90e1265b][S:bba08048-a9c6-5964-87f1-b4ca6de19f87].

## Caveats and gaps

- Total published experience is a handful of patients; the reference-centre authors themselves cite small cohort size, limited tumour material and restricted molecular analyses as making interpretation "to some extent speculative" [S:ad14fc0d-b588-5710-94b6-a081f0e6293f].
- Anti-Yo is rare post-ICI partly because ICIs have been used relatively little in ovarian and breast cancer [S:b1ddd3e5-298c-5672-abf6-f0e90808b7b3].
- Because roughly a small percentage of ovarian/breast cancer patients harbour anti-Yo asymptomatically, the predictive value of baseline seropositivity for post-ICI PNS is explicitly flagged as needing prospective evaluation — it has not been established [S:070d1827-bda4-5022-a294-071f8264e04d].
- Assay pitfalls matter: single-modality CDR2 testing generates false positives, and CDR2L adds sensitivity in CSF, so combining tissue-based and antigen-specific assays is advised [S:2b612b77-469d-5b55-a364-83167ce61076][S:08ec23af-98eb-5e37-ad96-deadce1b430d]. One conference abstract also described delayed seroconversion (anti-Hu/Yo/Ri appearing 3 months after symptom onset) in ICI-associated cerebellar degeneration, arguing for repeat screening — this is abstract-level evidence only [S:64a70457-30ab-52c8-86f0-ffd3ac3ea69a].
- I found no evidence on optimal treatment sequencing specifically for post-ICI anti-Yo disease, and no evidence on ICI rechallenge in this antibody subgroup.

rows.question: What is known about the safety of starting ravulizumab in AQP4-antibody-positive NMOSD after prior rituximab treatment?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Treatment-emergent and serious adverse event burden during ravulizumab was similar in rituximab-exposed and rituximab-naive patients, with no signal of added risk from prior rituximab; Most adverse events in both subgroups were mild or moderate, with severe events affecting only a minority of patients; Deaths and adverse-event withdrawals were rare, the single death occurring in a rituximab-exposed patient and no rituximab-exposed patient withdrawing because of an adverse event; Patients whose first ravulizumab dose fell on the day of or within two weeks of the first meningococcal vaccination received antibiotic prophylaxis until two weeks after that vaccination. Certainty: Event counts are small and come from an uncontrolled, non-comparative safety summary, so comparable safety is a tentative observation rather than established equivalence. Scope: applies to AQP4-antibody-positive NMOSD with prior rituximab treatment in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it claims that prior rituximab exposure lowers adverse-event risk during ravulizumab.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** The available evidence — one post hoc analysis of CHAMPION-NMOSD plus a case report — suggests ravulizumab is generally as tolerable in rituximab-pretreated as in rituximab-naïve AQP4-Ab+ NMOSD, but the residual, biologically plausible hazard is invasive meningococcal disease, because anti-CD20–induced B-cell depletion can blunt the pre-treatment meningococcal vaccine response.

**Trial-based evidence (post hoc, CHAMPION-NMOSD)**
- Prior rituximab was common in CHAMPION-NMOSD: 21/58 patients (36.2%), with a mean (SD) [passage text removed]. Concomitant rituximab was not permitted, and patients dosed with rituximab within 3 months of screening were excluded, on mechanistic grounds (rituximab acts partly via complement-dependent cytotoxicity) ([Neurol Neuroimmunol Neuroinflamm 2026;13(5):e200609]([passage text removed]); [PMC13372128]([passage text removed])).
- In the dedicated post hoc analysis (Bennett et al., Mult Scler 2026;32(4):396-408; [PMID 41782198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41782198), PMC13036264), the safety profile was "generally [passage text removed]. Common TEAEs were [passage text removed] the rituximab-exposed group**; and **one meningococcal infection occurred in each group**. No adjudicated on-trial relapses occurred in either subgroup.
- Reported subgroup figures: ≥1 TEAE in 95.2% (exposed) vs 94.6% (naïve); TESAEs in 28.6% vs 24.3%, mostly judged unrelated; infections/infestations as TESAEs in 14.3% vs 10.8%; UTI 33.3% vs 8.1% (all non-serious, grade 1–2), while [passage text removed] common in the naïve group ([NeurologyLive report of the paper]([passage text removed])). Efficacy was preserved in the prior-rituximab subgroup (relapse risk reduction 93.7%, [passage text removed], p=0.0078) ([AstraZeneca CHAMPION-NMOSD release]([passage text removed])).
- Vaccination timing in the switch population: of 21 rituximab-exposed patients, 19 were first vaccinated after rituximab, at a mean [passage text removed]) after the last dose; 68.4% within 6 months (15.8% ≤3 months, 52.6% 3–6 months), 84.2% received MenACWY and MenB at the same visit, 21% needed multiple doses, total lymphocyte counts were normal in 92.3% tested, and no meningococcal infection or NMOSD relapse followed vaccination ([ACTRIMS 2025 P295 as reported]([passage text removed]); [NeurologyLive]([passage text removed])).

**The signal that qualifies this reassurance**
- Across the whole trial, 2 meningococcal infections occurred during the primary treatment period (84 patient-years) and none during the long-term extension; **one of these patients had received rituximab, stopped 13 months before ravulizumab, yet B-cell depletion persisted** ([e200609]([passage text removed])). Both PTP cases recovered fully without sequelae, and one continued in the trial ([AstraZeneca]([passage text removed])).
- That case is published in detail: [passage text removed] developed meningococcal sepsis after ravulizumab **despite prior vaccination**; the authors propose risk-mitigation strategies for this sequencing scenario (Kline et al., Pract Neurol 2025;25(6):553-557; [PMID 40562531](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40562531)).

**Practice guidance**
- Ravulizumab carries a boxed warning and REMS for serious meningococcal infection, with vaccination (MenACWY + MenB) at least 2 weeks before the first dose, or antibacterial prophylaxis plus prompt vaccination if treatment cannot wait ([Ultomiris HCP vaccination requirements](https://ultomirishcp.com/nmosd/vaccination-requirements)).
- A German/Austrian/Swiss expert consensus notes that neisserial infection is an expected risk despite vaccination, and recommends for NMOSD (where treatment usually cannot be delayed) starting the complement inhibitor without delay with concurrent or delayed vaccination **plus bridging antibiotics**, ceftriaxone first-line for suspected infection, rifampicin for prophylaxis, and a patient-held standby dose of ciprofloxacin (Ther Adv Neurol Disord 2026;19:17562864261442558; [PMID 42137634](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42137634)). An Australian consensus addressing the same problem also exists ([Intern Med J, doi:10.1111/imj.70610]([passage text removed])).

**Limitations of the evidence base**
The comparison is a post hoc, non-randomised subgroup analysis of 21 vs 37 patients in an open-label trial, so it cannot exclude modest differences in infection risk; patients with rituximab within 3 months of screening were excluded, so the highest-risk (recently depleted) scenario is essentially untested ([e200609]([passage text removed])). The manufacturer's own materials state there are currently no published guidelines specific to transitioning from rituximab to ravulizumab in NMOSD ([Ultomiris HCP](https://ultomirishcp.com/nmosd/discontinuing-rituximab)), and the trial authors call for observational/real-world and immune-reconstitution biomarker studies to refine sequencing and timing ([NeurologyLive]([passage text removed])). Supporting real-world data are so far conference-level: a registry analysis reported no meningococcal infections among C5-inhibitor–treated patients, including rituximab switchers, with 92.9% having had ≥1 meningococcal vaccination ([CMSC 2026 report]([passage text removed])). I found no evidence on whether measuring CD19/B-cell counts or vaccine-specific antibody titres before starting ravulizumab improves safety outcomes.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Prior rituximab (RTX) exposure does not appear to worsen ravulizumab's overall safety profile in AQP4-Ab+ NMOSD, but the evidence is limited to small, descriptive datasets, and there is a specific, biologically plausible concern about impaired meningococcal vaccine protection in patients still B-cell depleted when complement inhibition is started.

## Trial evidence (CHAMPION-NMOSD post hoc analysis)

A post hoc analysis of CHAMPION-NMOSD stratified the 58 enrolled patients by prior RTX (RTX required to be >3 months before screening): [passage text removed]%) RTX-naïve, with mean (SD) time from last RTX to first ravulizumab dose of 7.2 (3.9) months [S:9c5ed14f-2f19-585b-b35e-c336ec5d2345][S:c8ec7db6-2ec9-521b-b6c4-2b102cc918bf]. This is described as [passage text removed] starting complement inhibition, exceeding RTX-exposed subgroups in satralizumab (n = 8) and inebilizumab (n = 13) trials [S:e52a8a78-a7c9-5bac-b20f-844b3357d6b6].

Safety findings:
- TEAEs occurred in 20/21 (95.2%) RTX-exposed vs 35/37 (94.6%) RTX-naïve patients; event rates were similar (312.7 vs 322.8 per 100 PY), mostly mild/moderate [S:d62101b7-8291-5f14-b334-0c92dd833783][S:da7e78d0-83d0-5dd5-a549-f1a9002f807b].
- Serious TEAEs: 6/21 (28.6%; 10.8/100 PY) RTX-exposed vs 9/37 (24.3%; 9.8/100 PY) RTX-naïve; no RTX-exposed patient withdrew from study drug because of a TEAE; one death occurred in the RTX-exposed group [S:da7e78d0-83d0-5dd5-a549-f1a9002f807b]. In the long-term extension report, a single death was characterised as cardiovascular and unrelated to ravulizumab [S:60fd090a-12da-54b3-9238-69900c22bfe2].
- The one signal: urinary tract infections were numerically more frequent in RTX-exposed patients (7/21 [33.3%]; 14.8/[passage text removed]/100 PY), all non-serious and Grade 1–2 [S:d62101b7-8291-5f14-b334-0c92dd833783]. COVID-19 and back pain were more common in RTX-naïve patients [S:d62101b7-8291-5f14-b334-0c92dd833783].
- Efficacy was preserved: no positively adjudicated on-trial relapses in either subgroup, despite 12/21 (57.1%) RTX-exposed patients having relapsed between first RTX dose and study entry [S:e52a8a78-a7c9-5bac-b20f-844b3357d6b6][S:5fd452eb-74f3-58aa-ae46-b8366264e9a4].

## Meningococcal risk after rituximab

One meningococcal infection occurred in each subgroup. The RTX-naïve patient developed serogroup W135 disease 21 days after the first ravulizumab dose on monotherapy; the RTX-exposed patient developed serogroup B disease 483 days after first ravulizumab dose while on mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone, and — despite last RTX 13 months earlier — [passage text removed] normal (0.04 × 10⁹/L; normal 0.11–0.70 × 10⁹/L) two weeks before onset. Both recovered fully with antibiotics and intensive care [S:ae8562c2-1b12-5acb-b4db-2a8f43fc1a48].

The detailed case write-up of that patient reports meningococcal sepsis (serogroup B PCR-positive in CSF and blood) roughly 16 months after starting ravulizumab and 29 months after her last RTX dose, with serogroup B vaccination given only 6–8 months pre-event during B-cell depletion, likely ineffective; B cells repopulated after mycophenolate was stopped and she was revaccinated after reconstitution and continued ravulizumab on penicillin prophylaxis [S:325cd980-4fb8-59ef-a4fa-f218f91967e0][S:e43785d0-c679-5a62-8e37-6015cd312e71][S:1fd175be-9081-5af2-b209-878de0edce53]. The authors note no guidelines exist for meningococcal risk management in RTX-to-complement-inhibitor sequencing, that [passage text removed] RTX does not guarantee a meaningful response, and that CD19+ B-cell reconstitution may be a reasonable guide to likely vaccine response [S:c4b5e805-d560-5282-8d17-416df3ce79b7][S:aba90305-f4c0-5c09-95e7-870009a34975].

Counterpoint: a CHAMPION-NMOSD vaccination-timing post hoc analysis (N = 19 vaccinated after last RTX) found all received ≥1 meningococcal vaccine ≥2 weeks before ravulizumab, most (68.4%) within 6 months of last RTX, total lymphocytes normal in most, and **no** meningococcal infections among those whose initial vaccination occurred after the last RTX dose [S:f6cb52d7-a673-58db-b8c5-5ccac9ea9f4d]. The main analysis also notes B-cell depletion does not necessarily preclude protective responses (e.g. VELOCE data with ocrelizumab) and that conjugate vaccines may elicit T-cell-dependent memory [S:d6e6b2b3-78ff-5e53-afc7-9d3ff8281e26].

## Real-world data

In the global NMO SPOTLIGHT registry, among 15 patients switching from RTX to eculizumab/ravulizumab (median 141.5 days from RTX discontinuation to C5 inhibitor; 112 days to meningococcal vaccination), none relapsed on C5 inhibition, and no meningococcal infections were reported across the cohort [S:61b4b61b-7b73-57a6-a55c-50d0622bcb4f]. Ravulizumab exposure in that registry was still short (median 5.3 months) [S:61b4b61b-7b73-57a6-a55c-50d0622bcb4f].

## Caveats

The post hoc analysis was not powered for between-group comparison, performed no hypothesis testing, and is limited by small sample size, heterogeneous RTX washout intervals, confounding by prior/concomitant therapies, and absence of lymphocyte-subset data; the authors call for observational and biomarker-based studies of immune reconstitution to refine sequencing timing [S:9612680a-6c6f-5b23-bed5-17b68d3b82ea][S:d93d5bd3-8705-56bd-a093-dabb30309012][S:d6e6b2b3-78ff-5e53-afc7-9d3ff8281e26]. Practically, evidence supports: completing MenACWY and MenB vaccination before immunosuppression where possible, antibiotic prophylaxis (mandatory if starting <2 weeks post-vaccine), considering B-cell reconstitution before relying on post-RTX vaccination, patient education for early recognition, and vigilance for UTIs [S:aba90305-f4c0-5c09-95e7-870009a34975][S:c8ec7db6-2ec9-521b-b6c4-2b102cc918bf][S:e52a8a78-a7c9-5bac-b20f-844b3357d6b6].

rows.question: How do periprocedural complications after transvenous lead extraction of cardiac implantable electronic devices differ between men and women?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Women undergoing transvenous lead extraction have modestly higher odds of cardiac and pulmonary complications than men, including pericardial effusion, tamponade, pneumothorax and hemothorax; In-hospital mortality did not differ significantly between women and men, whereas a prior single-centre series reported female sex as a predictor of post-procedural death, so the mortality comparison remains disputed; Vascular complications are more frequent in men than in women, and the sex-specific risk is of modest magnitude. Certainty: The evidence supports a consistent association between sex and complication rates rather than a demonstrated cause, and the mortality comparison is unsettled across reports. Scope: applies to cardiac implantable electronic device-related indications requiring transvenous lead extraction in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents female sex as a demonstrated cause of extraction complications or recommends deferring, restricting or otherwise altering extraction in women on this basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: women consistently have ~2–3× higher rates of major periprocedural complications and more minor complications than men, driven by cardiac and vascular/pleural injury (tamponade, pericardial effusion, SVC/innominate tears, hemothorax/pneumothorax), while in-hospital mortality is generally similar — though not every high-volume-centre series reproduces the major-complication gap.**

**Registry evidence (Europe)**
- In an ELECTRa (ESC-EHRA EORP) post hoc sex analysis, major complications occurred in 1.96% of women vs 0.71% of men (P = 0.0025), with lower radiological (96.29% vs 98.03%) and clinical success (98.14% vs 99.21%) in women. Notably, the risk factors differed by sex: in women, signs/symptoms of venous occlusion (OR 3.730), cumulative lead dwell time (OR 1.044) and number of generator replacements (OR 1.029) predicted events, whereas in men it was number of leads (OR 6.053), powered sheaths (OR 2.742) and white cell count (OR 1.138). Women had more abandoned leads (46.04% vs 34.82%), men more leads extracted (mean 1.89 vs 1.71) [PMID 31665280].
- In the main ELECTRa report, female sex was among the factors associated with procedure-related major complications and death (OR 2.11) and with clinical failure (OR 1.81), alongside dwell time >10 years; the investigators attributed this to women's smaller, more fragile vessels and tenacious fibrotic adhesions [[passage text removed]].

**Large single-centre series**
- In 3051 patients extracted with non-powered mechanical sheaths, major complications were 1.33% in women vs 0.60% in men (P<.001), procedure-related death [passage text removed] 5.0% vs 3.4% (P=.045), and combined complications 6.7% vs 3.9% (P=.019); radiological success was lower in women (95.8% vs 97.5%) but clinical success equal (97.2% vs 97.5%), and in-hospital mortality was identical (0.4% in both). Female sex was the only independent multivariable predictor of major complications including death ([passage text removed]) [PMC10626182].
- A Polish two-centre analysis of 1500 TLEs found women markedly over-represented among hemorrhagic major complications (cardiac/vascular wall tear: 77.3% female vs 37.8% in the no-complication group, P=0.004), but not among tricuspid valve damage (41.7% female, P=0.979) [[passage text removed]]. A separate 1915-patient analysis identified female sex and anemia as the only patient-dependent clinical predictors of major complications (female gender OR 2.709, 95% CI 1.266–5.797) [PMC6312591].

**US administrative databases — the complication profile**
- National Readmission Database (71,754 TLE patients, 2016–2019): women had more pneumothorax (OR 1.26), hemopericardium (OR 1.39), SVC injury requiring repair (OR 1.88), innominate vein injury requiring repair (OR 3.4), blood transfusion (OR 1.28), pericardiocentesis (OR 1.6), and 30-day readmission (OR 1.09), with no mortality difference (OR 0.99, P=0.95) [PMID 36445605].
- National Inpatient Sample with 1:1 propensity matching ([passage text removed] mortality difference (OR 1.12, p=0.184), but women had more [passage text removed]) — pericardial effusion, tamponade, pneumothorax, hemothorax — whereas men had more vascular complications (OR 0.76) [PMID 41185157].

**Discordant / nuancing data**
- A UK cohort found no significant excess of major complications in women (2.5% vs 1.7%, P=0.487) despite significantly more minor complications (12% vs 7.3%, P=0.016), with equal clinical (99.1% vs 98.9%) and radiological success; long-term survival was actually better in women [PMC10410196 / PMID 37466333].
- A 191-patient Italian cohort had no major complications at all, but minor complications were far commoner in women (17.2% vs 2.5%, P<.01), with no long-term outcome difference [PMID 39075799].
- A recent large-volume US-centre abstract reported that women "experienced equivalent safety," with malfunction [passage text removed]%) and infection in men (43.7% vs 32.3%) — a reminder that indication mix differs by sex [[passage text removed]]; I could not read the full results beyond the snippet.
- A newer matched analysis reports that [passage text removed] [PMID 42692319]; I only accessed the conclusion, not the effect size.

**Interpretation.** The direction of effect is consistent: excess acute cardiac and vascular/pleural injury in women, without an excess of in-hospital death — plausibly reflecting smaller/more fragile vessels, more abandoned leads and longer cumulative dwell time in women, versus infection-dominant, multi-lead extractions in men [PMID 31665280; PMC6312591; PMC10626182]. Magnitude varies with setting: national databases and multicentre registries show significant differences, while some experienced single centres show only excess *minor* complications.

**Bottom line: women consistently experience more periprocedural complications after transvenous lead extraction (TLE) than men — chiefly cardiac/pericardial and pleural events — while in-hospital or long-term mortality differences are inconsistent and generally absent outside of one high-volume single-center series.**

**Large administrative data (propensity-matched)**
In a National Inpatient Sample analysis (2016–2019) of a 1:1 matched cohort of [passage text removed]), women had higher risks of [passage text removed]), driven by [passage text removed], with no significant sex difference in in-hospital mortality (OR 1.12, p = 0.184) [S:c12d2e4b-4cdd-573c-948c-ec911fec537b]. Pericardial effusion carried the largest effect among evaluated complications; the authors attribute this to smaller body size and cardiac/vascular anatomy in women, and possibly later referral for extraction [S:6db1b613-ce07-558d-9389-5d271428cbe2]. Notably, men had *more* vascular complications (OR 0.76 for women), a reversal of most prior literature that the authors themselves call of limited practical relevance because the confidence interval (0.60–0.96) approaches 1 [S:38ca6d82-5db8-5e8c-a432-d7cbe2123cb9].

**Single-center mechanical-extraction cohort**
Among 3051 mechanical TLE patients (750 female, 2301 male), [passage text removed] women, and radiologic success was lower (95.8% vs 97.5%, p = .003), though clinical success was equivalent (97.2% vs 97.5%, p = .872). Female sex was the only independent predictor of major complications including death ([passage text removed]) [S:689c410f-df2c-5f87-8eb3-90ef9ccfd36b]. The authors ascribe this to differences in venous anatomy, body habitus, and technique, and suggest female sex be weighed in the indication decision, particularly for non-infective extractions [S:cfef2dd7-b555-572c-8bd0-26c7ffe832aa].

**Complication severity gradient / long-term outcomes**
In a smaller tertiary-center cohort (191 patients, 29 women), no major complications occurred at all, but minor peri-procedural complications were far more frequent in women (17.2% vs 2.5%, p < .01) — transient hypotension, non-interventional pericardial effusion, and sustained VT requiring cardioversion — with identical complete procedural success and no difference in the composite of death or repeat TLE at a median 6.5 years (log-rank p = .68) [S:bad5035c-5db4-59d6-a00d-b7d266c21199][S:57285634-28f2-5034-b94c-f2279780213a]. In that cohort, femoral snare bailout was used significantly more often in women, suggesting more extensive lead adhesions and failure of the superior approach [S:c787b575-ade6-585e-9d24-2ba088e549e2].

**European registry context and discordant studies**
The ELECTRa registry reported higher [passage text removed]) in women, with a further analysis showing [passage text removed]; but no significant mortality difference by sex [S:c787b575-ade6-585e-9d24-2ba088e549e2][S:38ca6d82-5db8-5e8c-a432-d7cbe2123cb9]. Not all studies agree: Brunner et al. (2999 procedures) found no sex difference in acute complications or 30-day mortality, and Maytin et al. (>1000 procedures) found no adjusted risk difference (HR [passage text removed]) [S:c787b575-ade6-585e-9d24-2ba088e549e2].

**Corroborating signals**
Female sex is an established, guideline-level TLE risk factor: Byrd et al. [passage text removed] with female sex [S:c8ff96bc-6837-58ed-9065-28dc8a6d165e]; a 24-year single-center registry found female sex [passage text removed] [S:44ed3ee5-563e-5114-93ec-e6921aa55cad]; and female gender was among patient-related risk factors for cardiac tamponade in a 1226-patient mechanical-tool series [S:688b9d26-97d3-5e7e-83b4-3e53bade7068]. Female sex is a component of the SAFeTY TLE risk score [S:cc22f839-da61-5df3-a695-ccafde51ade9].

**Caveats:** all of this evidence is observational and retrospective; administrative datasets lack procedural detail [S:38ca6d82-5db8-5e8c-a432-d7cbe2123cb9], and sex-related mortality differences [passage text removed] rather than being a robust finding [S:38ca6d82-5db8-5e8c-a432-d7cbe2123cb9]. Baseline profiles also differ (women younger, higher LVEF, less CAD/diabetes, more often extracted for lead malfunction/abandonment rather than infection) [S:689c410f-df2c-5f87-8eb3-90ef9ccfd36b], which complicates attribution.

rows.question: What outcomes follow Baduanjin exercise added to cardiac rehabilitation in patients with chronic heart failure?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Adding Baduanjin exercise to conventional heart-failure medication is associated with higher left ventricular ejection fraction, longer six-minute walk distance and better quality of life than conventional medication with other exercise methods; Depression scores were also lower with added Baduanjin exercise, a preliminary observation rather than an established effect; Readmission rates did not differ significantly between the added-Baduanjin and control groups, and the pooled estimate was too imprecise to rule out a benefit; Almost all contributing trials came from a single country, which may limit how far these outcomes generalize. Certainty: Confidence in the pooled outcomes is low to moderate, constrained by serious to very serious inconsistency across the contributing evidence and by allocation concealment and blinding that were largely unreported, so the findings are best read as suggestive rather than established. Scope: applies to chronic heart failure in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents Baduanjin as an established substitute for conventional exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation or recommends replacing standard exercise training on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Adding Baduanjin to cardiac rehabilitation (CR) in chronic heart failure (CHF) consistently improves **exercise capacity (6-minute walk distance), disease-specific quality of life, and echocardiographic/natriuretic-peptide markers of cardiac function**, with no signal of harm — but the effect on peak VO₂ is inconsistent and nearly all evidence comes from Chinese trials of modest quality.

## Randomized trial evidence for Baduanjin *added to* conventional CR

- **BEAR trial** (ischemic HF with mildly reduced/preserved EF; Baduanjin on a background of conventional exercise-based CR): the Baduanjin group improved 6MWD by 6.14% vs 1.32% in controls ([passage text removed]), and MLHFQ quality-of-life scores improved (−[passage text removed]) [PMID 38970325; doi 10.1111/jebm.12631]. The authors' summary position is that adding Baduanjin to exercise-based CR for ischemic HF "[passage text removed]" [qigonginstitute.org]. The protocol specifies 45-min sessions twice weekly for 12 weeks added to conventional CR exercise, with 6MWD as primary outcome [PMC6048837].
- **BESMILE-HF pilot RCT** (12-week Baduanjin-based CR program + usual medications vs medications alone): controls showed [passage text removed]) while the Baduanjin group maintained exercise capacity (p = 0.063); the between-group difference was not statistically significant but exceeded the minimal clinically important difference ([passage text removed] MCID of 1 mL/kg/min). No intervention-related adverse events occurred [PMID 34386535; NCT03180320]. Exercise self-efficacy was higher in the Baduanjin group at [passage text removed]) [sciencedirect S1071916419310632].
- **Fatigue/QoL RCT**: Baduanjin produced [passage text removed], with patients reporting no adverse effects during the 12 weeks [doi 10.1177/1474515117744770].

## Pooled evidence

- **50 RCTs, 3,964 CHF participants (standing Baduanjin + guideline pharmacotherapy vs pharmacotherapy alone)**: LVEF SMD 0.98 (0.80–1.15), 6-MWD SMD 1.20 (0.97–1.43), clinical efficacy RR 3.82 (2.83–5.17), with reductions in LVEDD (−1.03), LVESD (−0.74), BNP (−1.36), NT-proBNP (−1.11), and MLHFQ total (−1.17) plus psychological, emotional and other domains; all patients were NYHA [passage text removed] the exercise were reported**. Twelve weeks gave the greatest cardiac-function gain, >12 weeks the greatest QoL gain [PMC12913507].
- **Mean-difference meta-analysis in HF**: 6MWT +50.71 m (37.48–63.94), LVEF +3.57 (2.70–4.45), NT-proBNP −139.49, BNP −77.68, MLHFQ −8.15, anaerobic threshold +1.65, METs +0.65, VO₂ peak +1.36 (0.40–2.31), VO₂ max +2.21; 3 months of continuous intervention was most effective [sciencedirect S0965229925001566].
- **15 RCTs, 1,180 participants**: improvements in MLHFQ (SMD 1.10), NT-proBNP (0.62), LVEF (0.53) and VO₂max (0.92); 5–7 sessions/week outperformed 3–4 sessions/week for QoL (p = 0.04), with 30–60 min sessions for ≥8 weeks recommended [PMID 37717550].
- **Network meta-analysis** of traditional Chinese exercises: Baduanjin + usual care improved MLHFQ vs usual care alone (MD −6.55, 95% CI −9.27 to −3.84), though Liuzijue and meditation ranked numerically larger on this outcome [PMC12863780].
- **21 RCTs, 1,594 patients** examining duration: gains in cardiac function, QoL [passage text removed] than short-term Baduanjin, and long-term practice may also improve psychological well-being [PMID 41313613].

## Why it works as a CR modality, and caveats

Objective testing in CHF patients classifies Baduanjin as **moderate-intensity aerobic exercise**: mean VO₂ [passage text removed] VO₂max) and mean HR 86.1 ± 15.2 bpm (67% of HRmax), though by METs (2.0 ± 0.4) it falls in the light range; [passage text removed] (≈23.3 ± 4.4 kcal per 9-min session) [PMC7754768]. Patients in a qualitative study of home-based Baduanjin reported good adherence, improved mood and sleep, and perceived physical benefit, supporting it where conventional CR is scarce or unaffordable [PMC9846166].

Caveats: a meta-analysis of traditional Chinese exercises in CHF found **no significant change in peak VO₂** ([passage text removed] to 3.27), and one Baduanjin RCT in CHF due to coronary disease reported no significant NT-proBNP difference at 3 months [mdpi 2077-0383/12/6/2150]. The standing-Baduanjin synthesis reported substantial heterogeneity (e.g. I² = 86.1% for 6-MWD) and Egger's tests suggesting [passage text removed]-proBNP; all 50 trials were conducted in China [PMC12913507]. I found **no evidence in these searches on hard outcomes** (mortality, heart-failure hospitalization) for Baduanjin added to CR — the BEAR protocol lists MACE only as a secondary outcome [PMC6048837], and no trial in the retrieved results was powered for it.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Adding Baduanjin to cardiac rehabilitation in chronic heart failure (CHF) is consistently associated with improved exercise capacity, cardiac function indices, quality of life, and mood, with no serious adverse events reported — but the evidence base is dominated by small Chinese RCTs of low-to-moderate certainty, and the largest rigorously designed trials have so far only reported pilot/protocol data.

## Efficacy outcomes

**Quality of life, exercise capacity, cardiac function, depression.** A systematic review/meta-analysis of 21 RCTs (1,594 patients; 805 intervention, 789 control) found long-term (>12 weeks) Baduanjin was associated with improvements in MLHFQ quality-of-life scores ([passage text removed]), LVEF ([passage text removed]), and treatment [passage text removed]) [S:aed81186]. Short-term (≤12-week) pooled effects were also significant for MLHFQ ([passage text removed], I²=74.3%), LVEF ([passage text removed], I²=93.8%) and 6MWT ([passage text removed], I²=93%), but gains were more pronounced with longer intervention duration [S:dcd43d86][S:c4cbde70][S:07a8741a].

**Effect is not confined to drug-only comparators.** In subgroup analysis by control type (conventional drugs alone vs. conventional therapy plus supervised exercise/rehabilitation training), the incremental 6MWT benefit of Baduanjin was most marked where the control group did not receive other guided exercise or rehabilitation training — i.e. the *added* value on top of an existing exercise program is less certain [S:07a8741a].

**Larger synthesis restricted to standing Baduanjin.** A meta-analysis of 50 RCTs (3,964 participants) limited to standing Baduanjin reported increased LVEF and 6-minute walk distance, reduced LVEDD, LVESD, BNP and NT-proBNP, and reduced total and domain (physical, psychological, other) MLHFQ scores; when combined with conventional physical therapy, overall clinical efficacy was further enhanced, and effects were duration-dependent across <12 / =12 / >12-week subgroups [S:3d01755d][S:c0816788][S:c3c24ed2]. In older adults with cardiovascular disease, pooled NT-proBNP was lower with Baduanjin ([passage text removed], I²=82%) and nitric oxide higher ([passage text removed]) [S:61160bb1].

## Trial-level and physiological data

- **Pilot RCT (BESMILE-HF, n=18; 6 weeks added to usual medications):** adherence was good and all required home exercise was completed; exercise self-efficacy rose in the Baduanjin arm (between-group MD 3.2; 95% [passage text removed]). Controls declined significantly in peak VO₂ (p=0.018) while the Baduanjin group maintained capacity (p=0.063); the between-group difference ([passage text removed]) was not statistically significant but exceeded the 1 mL/kg/min MCID [S:1ccd571b]. The full 200-patient trial with co-primary peak VO₂ and MLHFQ endpoints was registered (NCT03180320) [S:b8a6cb12]; I found no published results for the full-scale trial.
- **BEAR trial** (120 patients, Baduanjin plus conventional CR exercise vs. conventional CR exercise alone, 45 min twice weekly for 12 weeks; primary outcome 6MWT) is a protocol only — no results were retrievable [S:0a88c70d][S:3d4b7262].
- **Mechanistic/physiological plausibility:** in a cross-sectional comparison of 30 CHF patients at matched VO₂, Baduanjin produced an intermittent (bimodal) intensity pattern with lower respiratory rate ([passage text removed]) and VE/VCO₂ (p<0.001), lower cardiac output (p=0.017) and wider a-vO₂ difference (p=0.036) versus cycle ergometry — i.e. lower cardiac and respiratory burden with greater peripheral O₂ extraction [S:a10a88b0].

## Safety and acceptability

No serious adverse events were identified in the 21-RCT safety analysis [S:aed81186], and no intervention-related adverse events occurred in the pilot RCT [S:1ccd571b]. Qualitative interviews with pilot-trial participants found patients perceived benefit as their main motivator, and that trust in Baduanjin, flexible practice times and social support supported good home-based adherence — supporting it as a feasible modality where conventional rehabilitation is scarce or unaffordable [S:abe50998].

## Important caveats

- Certainty is limited: GRADE ratings were low overall due to inconsistency, imprecision and indirectness, with only MLHFQ and efficiency rate reaching moderate quality; blinding was frequently unreported [S:862c1673][S:dcd43d86]. Heterogeneity was high for several outcomes, and authors attribute this partly to non-standardised Baduanjin protocols [S:51e6b832].
- Readmission rate did not reach significance (RR [passage text removed]) — a trend only; no mortality benefit was demonstrated [S:aed81186].
- Head-to-head ranking is unfavourable: in a network meta-analysis of 44 RCTs (2,957 subjects) in chronic cardiopulmonary dyspnoea, yoga ranked highest for MLHFQ, 6MWD and NT-proBNP, while Baduanjin ranked best only for the COPD Assessment Test [S:8217990a].
