rows.question: What does coronary inflammation measured on routine CT angiography add to risk assessment in non-obstructive coronary artery disease?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Higher coronary inflammation measured as perivascular fat attenuation on routine coronary CT angiography is associated with a higher rate of later cardiovascular events, including in patients whose arteries show only non-obstructive disease; Adding the perivascular attenuation measure to conventional assessment improved identification of high-risk individuals beyond calcium scoring or a standard clinical risk equation; The measure reports inflammatory biological activity in the vessel wall and surrounding fat, information that anatomical quantification of plaque extent alone does not provide. Certainty: The added value rests on observed associations between the imaging measure and later events rather than on any demonstrated causal or treatment effect. Scope: applies to non-obstructive coronary artery disease on coronary CT angiography in adults having clinically indicated coronary imaging, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents a low coronary inflammation value as established grounds for withholding, stopping or de-escalating preventive therapy in patients who otherwise meet treatment criteria.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

CT-derived coronary inflammation (perivascular/pericoronary fat attenuation) adds prognostic information in non-obstructive CAD that is independent of risk factors, calcium score and plaque metrics — and it matters because this population, not the obstructive one, carries most of the absolute event burden. But the size of the incremental gain depends heavily on how the metric is computed, and unadjusted "raw" PCAT attenuation has failed to add value in several cohorts.

## Why the question matters: the event burden sits in non-obstructive CAD

In ORFAN ([passage text removed] across eight UK hospitals, median follow-up 2.7 years), the 32,533 patients (81.1%) *without* obstructive CAD accounted for 2,857 of 4,307 total MACE (66.3%) and 1,118 of 1,754 cardiac deaths (63.7%) ([PMID 38823406](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38823406); full text [PMC11664027]([passage text removed])).

## What inflammation adds

**Independent, graded prognostic signal.** In the ORFAN nested cohort (n=3,393, median follow-up 7.7 years, IQR 6.4–9.1), [passage text removed] of cardiovascular risk factors and of the presence or extent of CAD. The number of inflamed vessels was additive: three vessels in the top versus bottom FAI quartile carried [passage text removed]) for cardiac mortality and HR 12.6 (8.5–18.6) for MACE ([PMID 38823406](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38823406)). Earlier AHA-presented ORFAN data reported that within non-obstructive CAD specifically, high FAI conferred HR 4.77 (3.40–6.69) for MACE and HR 10.49 (5.25–20.95) for cardiac mortality versus low FAI ([tctmd conference report]([passage text removed])).

**Meaningful reclassification.** Versus QRISK3, the AI-Risk classification (FAI Score + plaque metrics + risk factors) significantly reclassified patients over a 10-year horizon — NRI 0.38 (0.23–0.45) and IDI 0.028 (0.014–0.047) for cardiac mortality; NRI 0.27 (0.091–0.32) [passage text removed]) for MACE — and the authors state results were similar in the non-obstructive CAD group, who are typically discharged to primary care ([PMC11664027]([passage text removed])). In a prospective real-world survey of 744 consecutive CCTA patients, availability of AI-Risk [passage text removed]% ([abstract record]([passage text removed]-)).

**Confirmation in dedicated non-obstructive cohorts.** In 1,614 patients with non-obstructive CAD ([passage text removed]), 68 (4.2%) had MACE over a median 28.6 months; PCAT attenuation was an independent predictor (HR 1.060 per unit, [passage text removed]), improved discrimination ([passage text removed] reclassification beyond clinical and CCTA factors, and further stratified risk among patients with high-risk plaque (HR 2.45, 1.09–5.52, p=0.031) ([PMID 39648054](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39648054)). In diabetics with non-obstructive CAD, pericoronary FAI >−73.87 HU independently predicted MACE (HR 5.074, 2.191–11.751) and added to high-risk plaque plus [passage text removed]) ([BMC Med Imaging s12880-025-02146-6]([passage text removed])).

**Risk even without visible disease.** ORFAN investigators concluded that inflammation on routine CCTA captures [passage text removed]" ([ACC summary]([passage text removed])). Sponsor communications about the same Lancet paper quote ~9.5-fold higher cardiac mortality and ~5.5-fold higher MACE risk in the most abnormal FAI-Score group among patients with no/minimal plaque ([press release]([passage text removed])) — treat these as promotional restatements, not peer-reviewed figures.

**Mechanistic coherence with INOCA.** Higher PCAT attenuation associates with impaired PET coronary flow reserve independently of stenosis, plaque extent and high-risk plaque features, and this association was significant in arteries *without* obstructive CAD but not in those with it ([review, ORA/Diagnostics 2024]([passage text removed])).

## Important counter-evidence and caveats

- **Raw PCAT attenuation often adds nothing.** In a long-term cohort, adjusted HRs for PCAT attenuation and MACE were null at every level of analysis: per-patient lesion average 0.970 (0.933–1.008, p=0.121), most obstructive lesion 0.992 (0.961–1.024), highest-PCAT lesion 0.981 (0.946–1.016), and vessel-specific RCA 0.957, LAD 0.989, LCx 0.739 (all p>0.5) ([PMID 39106525](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39106525) / [PMC11441029]([passage text removed])).
- In 1,313 acute chest pain patients (142 MACE, 10.81%, median 38 months), RCA PCAT attenuation was an independent predictor (HR 1.033, p=0.006) but adding it to CAD-RADS did not improve the C-index (0.777 vs 0.760, p=0.129) ([PMC10351906]([passage text removed])).
- The ORFAN authors themselves attribute the difference to processing: FAI Score corrects for scanner/technical variability, local anatomy, age and sex, and "provides stronger prognostic value" than uncorrected PCAT mean attenuation, which is confounded by tube voltage, vendor, kernel and heart rate ([Chan & Antoniades, ORA]([passage text removed]); reconstruction dependence: [PMC12021981]([passage text removed])). Note the two positive ORFAN/CRISP-CT signals rely on a proprietary algorithm ([PMC11441029]([passage text removed])).
- Discrimination from simple patient-level PCAT metrics is modest (mean PCAT [passage text removed]) ([Frontiers Cardiovasc Med 10.3389/fcvm.2026.1863906]([passage text removed])).
- A recent meta-analysis concludes that [passage text removed]," with universal cut-offs discouraged pending standardisation and population-specific thresholds ([QIMS review](https://qims.amegroups.org/article/view/153622/html)); another states further prospective validation and methodological standardisation are needed before routine implementation ([PMID 42659900](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42659900)).

## Practical reading

For a patient with non-obstructive CAD on CCTA, a standardised inflammation metric can move them out of the falsely reassuring "no obstructive disease" bucket — the group where most events actually occur — and is being used to justify statin initiation/intensification and to select candidates for anti-inflammatory therapy. No randomised trial showing that treating on the basis of FAI improves outcomes appeared in my searches; the outcome evidence is observational plus modelled cost-effectiveness.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** Coronary inflammation quantified as perivascular/pericoronary fat attenuation (FAI/PCAT attenuation) on standard CCTA identifies a large group of patients with non-obstructive or no obstructive disease who carry substantial residual risk that stenosis, plaque burden, and clinical risk scores miss — but the evidence is not uniform, and no trial yet shows that acting on it improves outcomes.

**Why this population needs a new marker.** Roughly 80% of patients undergoing CCTA have no obstructive disease, yet this group contributes about two-thirds of major adverse cardiovascular events and just over 60% of cardiac deaths [S:4e402a16]. In ORFAN, [passage text removed] [S:ceee5353]. Non-obstructive CAD itself roughly doubles coronary event risk versus no CAD on CCTA (HR 2.33, 95% CI 1.15–4.69) [S:a63ca513].

**What FAI adds prognostically.** In CRISP-CT (3,912 patients, two cohorts), high FAI around the proximal RCA and LAD predicted all-cause and cardiac mortality after adjustment for risk factors, tube voltage, modified Duke CAD [passage text removed] [S:5fc3c3ef]. Above the −70.1 HU cutoff, cardiac mortality HR was 9.04 (3.35–24.40) in derivation and 5.62 (2.90–10.88) in validation [S:2836610d]. Adding FAI to a state-of-the-art CCTA model raised the AUC for cardiac mortality from 0.913 to 0.962 (derivation) and 0.763 to 0.838 (validation), with significant net reclassification [S:3616d3f5].

**It captures a different biology than plaque morphology.** Among patients without flow-limiting disease, 15% had high-risk plaque and 24% had abnormal FAI, with only 3% overlap [S:e8e21966]. In the CRISP-CT post-hoc analysis, patients with high FAI but *no* high-risk plaque had a 4.9-fold adjusted MACE risk (vs 6.3-fold with both), while among low-FAI patients high-risk plaque conferred no significant excess risk [S:67e8a83e]. Peri-RCA and peri-LAD FAI were each independently associated with cardiac mortality after adjusting for epicardial fat volume and ≥50% stenosis (HR 1.70 and 1.55 per SD) [S:92f719cd].

**Larger and AI-integrated data.** ORFAN comprised 40,091 patients across seven UK hospitals (median follow-up 2.7 years) plus a nested cohort of 3,393 with 7.7 years; [passage text removed] arteries predicted cardiac mortality *with or without* obstructive CAD, the top LAD FAI quartile showed ~20-fold higher cardiac death risk, and an AI model combining inflammation, plaque burden and risk factors reclassified risk beyond clinical scores [S:ceee5353]. Risk rose dose-dependently with the number of inflamed arteries [S:1123beb7]. In real-world use, AI-Risk reclassified 58% of patients versus QRISK3 and 43% versus SCORE, and changed management in 33% — in a cohort where 48% had no CAD and 41% non-obstructive CAD [S:7cc6b7cd]. An independent series reported FAI-based reclassification in 62% of patients [S:f35f2774].

**Complementarity with plaque quantification.** In SCOT-HEART (n=1,697, median 4.7 years), RCA PCAT attenuation predicted MI (HR 1.55, optimum threshold −70.5 HU) while LAD and LCx did not; combining RCA PCAT ≥−70.5 HU with low-attenuation plaque burden >4% gave HR 11.7 versus 4.87 for plaque burden alone [S:c18cc16a].

**Caveats — the signal is not consistent.** In 483 symptomatic patients followed a median 9.5 years, PCAT attenuation did not predict MACE on any analysis (per-patient adjusted HR [passage text removed]), and the authors note prior results have been contradictory, speculating that PCAT attenuation may rise only shortly before events [S:c7dc85ea][S:520aa837][S:53303aa6]. A 2025 review concludes PCAT attenuation has "modest discriminatory potential" for future MI and adds only small independent value beyond risk factors and simple plaque measures [S:5cf9cd32]. Measurements are also sensitive to acquisition: tube voltage and iterative reconstruction significantly alter PCAT attenuation, requiring conversion factors (e.g. 1.267, 1.080, 0.947 for 80, 100, 140 kVp vs 120 kVp) [S:e8e8df2b][S:a8c8a855]; note that proprietary FAI/FAI-Score are adjusted for technical and biological factors, unlike raw mean PCAT attenuation [S:ce335154].

**Additional uses in NOCAD.** FAI was higher in patients without obstructive CAD who had reduced coronary flow reserve, suggesting it may flag microcirculatory dysfunction [S:49292eb6]; elevated pFAI has been reported in MINOCA versus healthy controls [S:1123beb7], and a case report describes FAI localising a spontaneous coronary artery dissection when CCTA showed no stenosis [S:e3fde11d].

**Actionability is unproven.** In CRISP-CT, FAI lost predictive value among patients who started statin and aspirin immediately after CCTA, suggesting the risk is modifiable [S:36ef36a0], and dedicated studies of whether PCAT-guided anti-inflammatory therapy improves outcomes are explicitly called for but not yet done [S:80c17b39]. Commentators agree validation in larger diverse cohorts and outcome trials are needed before clinical integration [S:9c29fb60].

rows.question: How do outcomes after acute coronary syndrome in people with HIV compare with those without HIV?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: One-year mortality after acute coronary syndrome did not differ appreciably between people with and without HIV; New cardiovascular events after acute coronary syndrome, mainly repeat revascularization and recurrent acute coronary syndrome, were numerically more frequent in people with HIV; The hazard comparison for these new cardiovascular events was imprecise and remained compatible with no difference between groups; Pooled results from earlier comparisons point to a modestly higher risk of major adverse cardiac events in people with HIV. Certainty: The evidence is weak and imprecise: too few people with HIV were compared for the comparable outcomes to establish equivalence, and the imprecise event comparison sits alongside pooled results suggesting a small excess. Scope: applies to acute coronary syndrome in adults with and without HIV, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it treats the comparable one-year outcomes as established equivalence and concludes that people with HIV need no additional cardiovascular surveillance or secondary prevention after acute coronary syndrome.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: after ACS, people with HIV (PWH) fare worse — higher all-cause mortality, more recurrent ACS, restenosis and heart-failure readmission — despite presenting roughly a decade younger; the excess is concentrated in those with poorly controlled HIV (low CD4/symptomatic disease), and cardiovascular death per se is not clearly increased.**

**Pooled evidence.** The largest synthesis (15 studies; 9,499 PWH vs 1,531,117 people without HIV) found significantly increased adjusted risks [passage text removed], 1.12–2.97), heart-failure readmission (RR 3.39, 1.73–6.62), and restenosis (RR 2.40, 1.13–5.09), over a pooled mean follow-up of ~16.2 months in PWH; there were no differences in cardiovascular death, target-vessel or target-lesion revascularization ([Haji, JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(5):e2411159]([passage text removed]); [jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2818670](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2818670)). PWH were ~11 years younger (pooled mean age 56.2 vs 67.7 years), more often current smokers, more likely to report illicit drug use, with higher triglycerides and lower HDL; post-discharge statin and β-blocker prescription rates were numerically lower but not statistically significantly so.

**Index hospitalization and short-term outcomes.** In a nationwide US claims cohort, PWH admitted with ACS had higher adjusted inpatient mortality (OR 1.29, 1.15–1.44), 30-day readmission (OR 1.18, 1.09–1.27) and 12-month mortality (OR 1.32, 1.22–1.44), together with reduced filling of cardiac medications at 12 months ([PMID 33226071](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33226071); [natap.org/2020/CROI/croi_220.htm]([passage text removed])).

**HIV control modifies the effect — this is the key nuance.** In Kaiser Permanente Northern California (226 PWH, 86,321 without HIV), ACS recurrence within 3 years did not differ by HIV status (adjusted HR 1.08, 0.76–1.54), but all-cause mortality did (HR 2.52, 1.81–3.52); stratified by CD4, mortality was elevated at <200 cells/µL (HR 5.41, 3.14–9.34) and 201–499 (HR 2.64, 1.66–4.20) but not at ≥500 (HR 0.67, 0.22–2.08; p-trend <0.001) ([PMC6309474]([passage text removed])). Similarly, among AMI patients undergoing PCI in the National Inpatient Sample, symptomatic HIV/AIDS carried a 3.6-fold higher adjusted in-hospital mortality (aOR 3.6, 2.5–5.6) plus more acute kidney failure and cardiogenic shock, whereas asymptomatic HIV did not (aOR 1.0, 0.4–2.4) ([Sci Rep, s41598-024-59920-9]([passage text removed])). A scoping review reached the same conclusion: in-hospital mortality was elevated for symptomatic HIV/AIDS (OR ~2.23–3.03) but not for PWH without an HIV-related illness ([PMC11999250]([passage text removed])).

**Contemporary revascularization data.** In the VA CART program, PWH had worse survival from 6 months post-PCI onward, amounting to a 21% higher 5-year mortality risk (HR 1.21, 1.03–1.42), despite well-controlled HIV and similar procedural metrics ([Parikh, J Am Heart Assoc 2023;12(4):e028082]([passage text removed])). The French prospective PACS-HIV cohort (103 PWH, 195 matched controls, 36 months) found more frequent ACS recurrence in PWH — with HIV the only independent predictor — while the MACCE composite was not significantly different (HR 1.60) ([Boccara, JAHA 2020, PMID 32844734](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32844734); [PMC7660762]([passage text removed])).

**Caveats.** Findings are heterogeneous and not uniformly adverse: a Chinese two-year prospective cohort found HIV [passage text removed], 0.16–2.08) or MACCE (OR 0.65, 0.25–1.67) after adjusting for lesion complexity ([Front Cardiovasc Med 2025;10.3389/fcvm.2025.1702174]([passage text removed])), and a small Finnish register study (35 PWH, 128 without) found comparable 1-year mortality and no statistical difference in new cardiovascular events (HR 1.42, 0.50–3.98) with near-identical high-intensity lipid-lowering prescribing ([doi.org/10.1177/10872914261473689](https://doi.org/10.1177/10872914261473689)). Most pooled data come from high-income countries, and antiretroviral duration/adherence and cardioprotective-drug adherence were generally unavailable.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Outcomes after ACS in people with HIV are broadly similar in the acute/in-hospital phase when HIV is well-controlled, but the longer-term picture is worse — driven mainly by excess recurrent ischaemic events and repeat revascularisation — and outcomes are clearly worse when HIV is advanced/symptomatic (AIDS). Evidence is heterogeneous and mostly from small matched cohorts and administrative databases.

## Presentation differs at baseline

People with HIV present with ACS about a decade younger, predominantly male, and with a very high burden of smoking and illicit drug use; a French matched cohort of ACS patients had a mean age of 49 years and was 94.0% men [S:9b38b4b4-dc6c-562a-8838-bb18773dae3a]. In a South African tertiary-hospital series, HIV-positive patients were younger, more often presented with STEMI and single-vessel disease, yet had *fewer* conventional CAD risk factors — suggesting additional pathogenic mechanisms [S:edaf721b-adf4-5853-9904-891508cf56a9]. This matters for interpretation: crude comparisons are confounded in both directions.

## Recurrent events and repeat revascularisation: worse with HIV

The PACS-HIV study (23 French coronary ICUs; 103 people living with HIV vs 195 matched HIV-negative patients, matched for age, sex and ACS type) found no statistically significant difference in the primary composite MACCE endpoint at 36 months (17.8% vs 15.1%; multivariable [passage text removed]), but recurrent ACS was markedly more frequent with HIV ([passage text removed]), and HIV infection was the only independent predictor of ACS recurrence [S:9b38b4b4-dc6c-562a-8838-bb18773dae3a]. The excess was driven mainly by recurrent unstable angina related to *new* coronary lesions rather than restenosis of treated segments [S:9e78c304-a7e4-578e-b8f3-c4e919c67759]. Notably, secondary prevention was less successful: fewer patients with HIV stopped smoking (47% vs 75%) and their total cholesterol fell less (−22.3 vs −35.0 mg/dL) [S:9b38b4b4-dc6c-562a-8838-bb18773dae3a].

Earlier smaller studies point the same way: after CABG, 30-day outcomes were equal but revascularisation need at a mean 41 months was higher (42% vs 25%) [S:4595d404-d046-54a2-bffc-a8ab6b83f635], and the same group's ACS cohort showed roughly six-fold more recurrent ACS despite similar angiographic disease [S:4f7ab397-e084-5ce5-946d-d83cc1f189d9].

## Mortality: conflicting

- A Swiss nested cohort (133 HIV-positive from the Swiss HIV Cohort Study vs 5,328 HIV-negative from the AMIS registry, first AMI, ~90% on successful ART) found higher 1-year all-cause mortality with HIV (5/133, 3.6% vs 135/5,328, 2.5%; adjusted [passage text removed]), with *no* difference in recurrent AMI (3.0% vs 3.0%; OR 1.16, 0.41–3.27) or cardiovascular rehospitalisation (OR 0.68, 0.42–1.11) [S:85dac302-7c31-5974-977a-5beed6689992][S:8b61bf9f-2b75-5c38-8c12-456c63ee86bc]. The authors caution the small number of events precluded adjusting [passage text removed] [S:bf74eaa3-6415-5a1a-b899-7b1f2638368f].
- A 2017 meta-analysis of 6 comparative studies (2,268 patients, follow-up 1–3.1 years) found no difference in total mortality ([passage text removed]) or cardiac death ([passage text removed]) [S:9e78c304-a7e4-578e-b8f3-c4e919c67759].
- A 2012 meta-analysis (2,442 patients, median 25.5 months) reported a substantial in-hospital death risk (8%) and long-term risks of revascularisation (20%) and MI (9%) among people with HIV admitted for ACS, especially on protease inhibitors — but many included studies lacked an HIV-negative comparator [S:9e78c304-a7e4-578e-b8f3-c4e919c67759].

The PACS-HIV authors explicitly summarise the literature as conflicting: some studies show more recurrent ACS without a mortality difference, one shows higher first-year death, and two show equivalent long-term prognosis [S:9e78c304-a7e4-578e-b8f3-c4e919c67759][S:66de50ce-772d-556f-af9f-9db3d00ee7d2].

## Immune status is the key modifier

In the US National Inpatient Sample (2003–2015; weighted 2,191,129 AMI-PCI cases: 7,140 symptomatic HIV, 4,994 asymptomatic HIV, 2,178,995 HIV-negative), **symptomatic** HIV/AIDS — but not asymptomatic HIV — was associated with more than triple in-hospital mortality (aOR 3.6, 95% CI 2.5–5.2), higher acute kidney injury (aOR 2.6, 1.9–3.4), higher cardiogenic shock (aOR 1.9, 1.3–2.7), longer stay and more procedures; these gaps persisted across 2003–2015 [S:f794b580-6d70-5d3e-a682-bde126cb03d7]. In-hospital mortality in the symptomatic group fell from roughly 8% in 2008 to 4% in 2015, plausibly reflecting newer drug-eluting stents and improved antiretroviral therapy [S:ecbbaf29-a82c-521d-ba5f-73eab04f96e8].

## Care disparities contribute

In a separate NIS analysis of 1,091,759 ACS hospitalisations (0.35%, n=3,783, [passage text removed] were less likely than uninfected patients to undergo catheterisation (OR 0.48, 0.43–0.55), PCI (OR 0.69, 0.59–0.79) or CABG (OR 0.75, 0.61–0.93), whereas asymptomatic HIV showed no difference; drug-eluting stents were used less often in HIV-infected patients regardless of AIDS status [S:941eb19f-2478-5e1c-a20b-da689d589d06][S:e1f20ae1-23b7-5b68-8f4f-e5984ce549f9].

## Stent/restenosis outcomes

Mixed. A 50-vs-50 matched PCI study [passage text removed] (14% vs 16%, p=0.78) at mean 321 days [S:4595d404-d046-54a2-bffc-a8ab6b83f635], and comparative studies generally found no significant difference in restenosis when stenting was used, with new-generation drug-eluting stents not appearing to be a clinical concern [S:66de50ce-772d-556f-af9f-9db3d00ee7d2]. Other small series reported the opposite, including 58.3% severe clinical/angiographic restenosis in 12 HIV-infected patients and lower procedural success (75% vs 85%) in one report [S:2f6871a8-2f3c-52bc-8eae-99473358df5d]; reported 1-year clinical restenosis rates in people with HIV range widely from 9% to 52% [S:66de50ce-772d-556f-af9f-9db3d00ee7d2].

## Caveats

Most comparative studies are small, single-region and matched only on age/sex/ACS type; the administrative-database studies cannot adjust for CD4 count, viral load, ART regimen or stent type [S:5e016959-ba50-5bf8-8667-35ef57ff7341]. I found no large randomised or contemporary (post-2020) prospective comparative outcome trial in this search, so the balance of evidence should be read as observational.

rows.question: Which hypertension subtypes are appropriate candidates for renal denervation in current practice?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Guidelines recommend renal denervation as an adjunct therapy for adults with uncontrolled or resistant hypertension in whom other means have failed or given insufficient blood pressure control; Candidate selection, including the patient's own preference, is settled through a shared decision-making process before the procedure; Against a sham procedure, denervation lowers systolic blood pressure modestly, on the order of 3 to 7 mm Hg, in patients whether or not they continue antihypertensive drugs; Candidacy is not confined to drug-resistant patients, since modest reductions were also seen in treated essential and treatment-naive hypertension, with benefit less consistent at lower drug burden. Certainty: The blood pressure effect rests on blinded sham-controlled comparisons of modest size, while candidacy and the selection process reflect guideline consensus rather than a tested effect. Scope: applies to uncontrolled or resistant hypertension in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents long-term durability of the blood pressure reduction as established by controlled comparison, or recommends the procedure primarily on the strength of a permanent effect.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line
Renal denervation (RDN) is currently appropriate for **primary (essential) hypertension** in two broad phenotypes — **true resistant hypertension** and **uncontrolled hypertension in patients who cannot tolerate or do not wish to take more drugs** — with best evidence in **combined systolic–diastolic hypertension** and preserved renal function; it is **not** for secondary hypertension, and evidence in isolated systolic hypertension (ISH) and stage 1 hypertension is weak.

## 1. True resistant hypertension (the core indication)
All three major guidelines converge here. The ESC/EAPCI clinical consensus statement specifies [passage text removed] m²" ([[passage text removed]); Barbato et al., Eur Heart J 2023;44:1313-30, PMID 36790101). ESH 2023 gives a class II recommendation for RDN as an additional option in true resistant hypertension [passage text removed] ([acc.org cover story]([passage text removed])). ESC 2024 assigns class IIb/B for BP uncontrolled on three drugs including a thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic, in medium-to-high-volume centres ([PMC12666127]([passage text removed])). The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline gives a Class 2b ("may be considered") recommendation for adults with resistant hypertension despite optimal therapy or intolerance to multiple agents ([PMC12995957]([passage text removed])).

## 2. Uncontrolled (non-resistant) hypertension with drug intolerance, non-adherence, or patient preference
The ESC/EAPCI consensus states patients "[passage text removed]," and that RDN is an option for those expressing a preference in shared decision-making ([eurointervention.pcronline.com/...eapci]([passage text removed])). ESC 2024 extends this to patients on fewer than three drugs, particularly with high cardiovascular risk; ESH 2023 covers BP uncontrolled on combination therapy or drug treatment causing [passage text removed] ([recormedical.eu ESH one-pager]([passage text removed])). A guideline-comparison analysis found all three societies converge on **four [passage text removed]**, with only ESC formally endorsing the <3-drug group (IIb/A) ([PMC12993013]([passage text removed]); PMID 41853094). SCAI similarly names resistant hypertension as the primary candidate group, with drug-intolerant/medication-averse uncontrolled patients as secondary, prioritising higher cardiovascular risk ([acc.org]([passage text removed])).

## 3. Haemodynamic phenotype: combined systolic–diastolic > isolated systolic
Pooled SYMPLICITY HTN-3/Global SYMPLICITY Registry data (n=1103; 429 ISH, 674 combined) showed a 6-month office SBP fall of −18.7 ± 23.7 mmHg in combined hypertension vs −10.9 ± 21.7 mmHg in ISH (difference −7.8 mmHg, 95% CI −10.5 to −5.1, P<0.001), and 24-h SBP −8.8 ± 16.2 vs −5.8 ± 15.4 mmHg (P=0.015); combined hypertension and lower baseline pulse pressure were multivariate predictors of response ([PMC5381589](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5381589); PMID 28158510). ISH patients were **excluded from the modern sham-controlled trials**, and while the Global SYMPLICITY Registry and RADIOSOUND suggested comparable efficacy, the consensus treats ISH as an evidence gap ([eurointervention.pcronline.com/...eapci]([passage text removed])). Arterial-stiffness phenotyping may rescue a responsive ISH subgroup: among ISH patients, those in the lowest tertile of invasive pulse wave velocity had BP falls comparable to combined hypertension (12.1 ± 12.6 mmHg, P=0.006) ([PMID 28515119]([passage text removed])). Device labelling does not establish safety/efficacy in ISH ([mdpi.com/2308-3425/13/9/443]([passage text removed])). Practically, the US CMS coverage criterion requires **≥140 mmHg systolic AND >90 mmHg diastolic**, which excludes pure ISH ([CMS NCD 20.40]([passage text removed])) — a limitation flagged repeatedly in public comment ([CMS decision memo]([passage text removed])).

## 4. Subtypes that are NOT candidates
- **Secondary hypertension**: ESC 2024 states RDN is not recommended in secondary hypertension or eGFR <40 mL/min/1.73 m² ([recormedical.eu](https://recormedical.eu/targeted-treatment-selecting-patients-for-renal-denervation)); exclusion of secondary causes is "strongly advised" before RDN ([eurointervention.pcronline.com/...eapci]([passage text removed])). CMS mandates screening at minimum for **primary aldosteronism, obstructive sleep apnoea, [passage text removed] ([CMS decision memo]([passage text removed])). Nuance: an AHA commentary argues a secondary cause does not always preclude RDN — e.g. medically managed bilateral primary aldosteronism or sleep apnoea ([professional.heart.org commentary]([passage text removed])).
- **Pseudo-resistance** must be excluded; ESH defines true resistant hypertension as requiring maximal tolerated triple therapy, uncontrolled out-of-office BP, and exclusion of secondary and pseudo-resistant causes ([hypertasi.gr PDF]([passage text removed])).
- **Anatomical/renal exclusions**: RDN is not advised in kidney transplant recipients, KDIGO G4–G5, fibromuscular dysplasia, single functioning kidney, or haemodialysis ([eurointervention.pcronline.com/...eapci]([passage text removed])); contraindicated in pregnancy and significant renal artery stenosis ([news.medtronic.com](https://news.medtronic.com/Medtronic-announces-2025-American-College-of-Cardiology-American-Heart-Association-updated-hypertension-guidelines-for-renal-denervation-procedure-now-recommended)).
- **Not first-line**: ESC 2024 gives a Class III against RDN as first-line therapy ([PMC12993013]([passage text removed])).
- **Stage 1 hypertension and eGFR <40**: infrequently included in sham-controlled trials, so data are limited ([professional.heart.org commentary]([passage text removed])).

## 5. Cross-cutting requirements regardless of subtype
Diagnosis must be confirmed by ambulatory or serial home BP monitoring, not office readings alone; the AHA scientific statement requires sustained uncontrolled hypertension confirmed by 24-hour ABPM ([Cluett et al., Hypertension 2024;81:e135-e148, PMID 39101202](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39101202)). All guidelines require multidisciplinary evaluation in experienced/medium-to-high-volume centres and mandatory shared decision-making, with patients informed that the expected effect is modest — roughly 4–6 mmHg ambulatory systolic, about equivalent to one antihypertensive drug ([PMC12993013]([passage text removed])). RDN is adjunctive, not curative or a drug substitute ([PMC12995957]([passage text removed])). In the US, Medicare covers RDN only under Coverage with Evidence Development within an approved study, with ≥3 months of guideline-directed therapy and ≥6 months of primary-clinician management (≥3 encounters) before referral ([CMS NCD 20.40]([passage text removed]); [cms.gov CED page]([passage text removed])).

**Not established by the sources retrieved:** whether specific sympathetic-activity biomarkers or renin phenotypes can prospectively select responders — the guideline-comparison paper notes candidate predictors (higher baseline sympathetic activity, preserved renal function, absence of isolated diastolic hypertension) "require prospective validation" ([PMC12993013]([passage text removed])).
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Renal denervation (RDN) is currently indicated for **true resistant primary (essential) hypertension**, and — in most contemporary guidelines — for the broader phenotype of **uncontrolled hypertension at high cardiovascular risk**, including patients intolerant of or non-adherent to drugs. It is *not* for secondary hypertension, pseudoresistance/white-coat hypertension, or advanced CKD, and the isolated-systolic/stiff-artery phenotype responds poorly.

## Subtypes that are appropriate candidates

**1. True resistant hypertension (the core indication).** The 2024 ESC guidelines give RDN a Class IIb, Level B recommendation for uncontrolled BP despite ≥3 antihypertensive drugs including a thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic, performed in medium-to-high-volume centres after shared risk–benefit discussion and multidisciplinary assessment [S:3fdaf8dc-c363-527a-a9ca-937115f43503][S:50ecadc1-4711-5437-9af5-a7fcbd28b398]. The 2023 ESH guidelines give a Class II recommendation conditional on [passage text removed]:c3ca0d16-1291-5c8d-84ed-1c1d9d270903][S:03391efe-16d7-5e7f-aa72-66c2c739b591]. The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline aligns at Class IIb (B-R) for [passage text removed]) uncontrolled [passage text removed] [S:39159648-0c67-5c60-92c1-1d6457b45c1a].

**2. Uncontrolled (non-resistant) hypertension with high CV risk or drug intolerance.** ESC also permits RDN in patients at increased CV risk [passage text removed] (Class IIb, Level A), with the same shared-decision requirements [S:50ecadc1-4711-5437-9af5-a7fcbd28b398][S:a1eea539-a964-5eb9-b69f-6dcd12f3a21a]. ESH extends it to patients in whom pharmacotherapy causes significant side effects and impairs quality of life [S:03391efe-16d7-5e7f-aa72-66c2c739b591]. The FDA indication is broader still — adjunctive BP lowering in hypertension inadequately controlled by lifestyle measures and drugs — which is why expert statements support discussing RDN [passage text removed] [S:99ba8088-4e3d-51b3-83c9-75a334de4395][S:72859fbd-7a0b-5e41-9dea-957547744cfc]. Consensus documents specifically name repeated non-adherence, polypharmacy, multiple end-organ damage, unwillingness to take lifelong drugs, and drug intolerance as selection features [S:a70c341c-e798-58f4-879e-9e41c0f66ca6].

**3. Sympathetically-driven / "conditioned" phenotypes.** The JSH/CVIT/JCS consensus defines the indication as resistant hypertension *or* "conditioned" uncontrolled hypertension, the latter including inability to up-titrate drugs, or high-risk comorbidity attributable to sympathetic overactivity — **orthostatic hypertension, morning hypertension, nocturnal hypertension, sleep apnoea (unable to use CPAP), atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmia, or heart failure** [S:7842c573-8892-567d-b3a0-367d31332d92]. The Taiwan (TSOC/THS) guidelines similarly recommend RDN (Class IIa, level B) in high-CV-risk hypertension [passage text removed] disease, drug intolerance/non-adherence, or features indicative of **neurogenic hypertension** [S:8d98f891-f182-5f3b-885f-a020ef322953]. The Asia RDN Consortium frames the practical target population as [passage text removed], and argues RDN should not be a therapy of last resort [S:08a3c180-8ffe-5887-bd8d-1c6eff167fba].

## Subtypes that are *not* appropriate

- **Secondary hypertension** — explicitly a Class III recommendation in ESC 2024 [S:03391efe-16d7-5e7f-aa72-66c2c739b591][S:50ecadc1-4711-5437-9af5-a7fcbd28b398]. Mechanistically, volume-dependent forms such as primary aldosteronism are characterised by *reduced* sympathetic activity and are unlikely to respond [S:132379cc-6625-5e19-9d82-d60b4c203243]. Screening must exclude primary aldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's, renovascular disease and OSA [S:1b5f95fa-4c84-5104-b0b0-e5020f923d8d][S:23bc2613-bdf3-54ef-b6ce-370bcb3dcc43].
- **Pseudoresistance** — white-coat effect, non-adherence, and suboptimal drug regimens are standard exclusion criteria; in one screening cohort these three forms of pseudoresistance accounted for exclusion of 52.9% of referrals, and only 14.7% of initial referrals were ultimately deemed eligible [S:94b29287-3687-5cdf-bb0d-febafde34c5d][S:8b0b09bd-6f09-5282-b14b-45e9a3f067b6].
- **eGFR <40 mL/min/1.73 m²** — not recommended pending further evidence, since such [passage text removed]:03391efe-16d7-5e7f-aa72-66c2c739b591][S:a1eea539-a964-5eb9-b69f-6dcd12f3a21a][S:49dedfcb-124e-51e4-8ba8-1c8f43fcf11b].
- **Unsuitable renal artery anatomy** — significant stenosis, fibromuscular dysplasia, or vessels below size thresholds; mandatory pre-procedural imaging [S:0ebeedea-53a4-59bc-80c1-04b607568b65][S:1b5f95fa-4c84-5104-b0b0-e5020f923d8d].
- **First-line therapy** — not recommended, given absence of adequately powered outcome trials [S:03391efe-16d7-5e7f-aa72-66c2c739b591][S:50ecadc1-4711-5437-9af5-a7fcbd28b398].

## A phenotype that responds less well

**Isolated systolic hypertension (stiff-artery, typically elderly).** Pooled SYMPLICITY HTN-3 and Global SYMPLICITY Registry data showed less pronounced BP reduction in isolated systolic hypertension than in combined systolic–diastolic hypertension, replicated in a 126-patient bilateral-RDN cohort; the proposed explanation is lower sympathetic contribution and predominant large-artery stiffness [S:080298d9-7b4c-5980-a137-de3f00b3a452][S:3a01e803-a598-599d-a679-969c430a08cd]. Higher aortic stiffness/pulse wave velocity independently predicts poor response, whereas better response occurs with combined versus isolated systolic hypertension [S:18c4bad5-9791-525c-9b33-b1ff042860fc]. One commentary argues the risk–benefit balance may be unfavourable in isolated systolic hypertension and that drug adjustment should be tried first [S:654ed4db-7793-5c86-af7e-b11c764ecff8]. Note this is a *response gradient*, not a formal guideline exclusion — and at least one editorial questions whether the age/ISH signal is fully valid, since older trial participants were already on drugs effective for systolic hypertension [S:bdbbaff8-1679-55a1-98bb-105507c518d9].

## Caveat

Reliable pre-procedural predictors of response remain unestablished beyond arterial stiffness and baseline BP; patient selection is explicitly described as an evolving challenge, and long-term cardiovascular outcome data are still awaited [S:ac80a746-53c7-52f8-af18-6128c742fd69][S:35f12e95-4767-5aba-93e9-830cdd3642fa].

rows.question: What survival outcomes follow post-cardiotomy venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for failure to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: About half of adults supported for failure to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass survived to hospital discharge, with in-hospital death in the remainder; This survival level was in keeping with the roughly 30% to 50% survival reported in earlier postcardiotomy extracorporeal support series; Among survivors, discharge directly home was the minority outcome, most needing rehabilitation or other continuing care, a preliminary observation from a small single-institution series. Certainty: Evidence strength is low, resting on uncontrolled proportions from a small, narrowly sourced group of patients, so the findings describe outcomes rather than demonstrate benefit. Scope: applies to postcardiotomy cardiogenic shock with failure to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents this experience as demonstrating that extracorporeal support improves survival compared with alternative circulatory support strategies.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** Adults placed on VA-ECMO for failure to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) — the single most common post-cardiotomy ECMO indication — have roughly 40% survival to hospital discharge and ~60% in-hospital mortality, but those who reach discharge do well long-term, with about two-thirds alive at 10 years.

**Failure to wean is the dominant indication.** In the PELS-1 multicentre cohort (2058 adults, 34 centres, 16 countries, 2000–2020), failure to wean from CPB was the primary indication in [passage text removed] right ventricular failure (11.9%) ([Mariani et al., J Am Heart Assoc 2023;12:e029609]([passage text removed])). A separate 19-centre registry of 781 patients gave failure to wean 38% and post-weaning heart failure 48% ([Biancari et al., J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg 2020;160:1207](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31864699)); the NICE evidence review of that cohort records failure to wean in 39% (n=788) ([NICE evidence summary](https://www.nice.org.uk/consultations/3070/2/evidence-summary)).

**In-hospital outcomes.** PELS-1 reported in-hospital mortality of 60.5%, stable across the 20-year study period, with age ([passage text removed]) independently associated with death ([JAHA 2023;12:e029609]([passage text removed])). Weaning does not equal survival: in the same cohort the weaning rate was 62.7% but survival to discharge only 39.6% — 36.6% died on ECMO (median support 79 h) and a further 23.1% died after weaning (median support 146 h), chiefly from multiorgan failure (37.2%) and persistent heart failure (36.5%) ([Mariani et al., Ann Thorac Surg 2023;116:1079–1089]([passage text removed])). ELSO registry data concur: weaning 56.4%, survival to discharge 41.7% (2997/7185), with mortality highest after CABG (65.4%), CABG+[passage text removed]%), and lowest after heart transplant (46.0%) ([Kowalewski et al., PMC8217275]([passage text removed]); [NICE summary](https://www.nice.org.uk/consultations/3070/2/evidence-summary)). Meta-analyses give similar or slightly worse figures: weaning 59.5% and hospital survival [passage text removed]) ([Biancari, PMID 29158060](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29158060)); weaning 52.8% and 31.1% discharged alive, with 25.0–56.2% mortality even after successful weaning ([BMC Anesthesiol 2025, PMID 39825250]([passage text removed])); and pooled in-hospital/30-day mortality of 66.6% (95% CI 64.7–68.4) across 2491 patients ([JTCVS 2020;160:1207](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31864699)).

**Timing (the closest proxy for failure-to-wean specifically).** Intraoperative ECMO initiation — which is what failure to wean from CPB entails — carried *lower* in-hospital mortality than ICU initiation despite worse preoperative risk profiles: 57.5% (n=1287) vs 64.5% (n=716), P=.002, with fewer complications and shorter support in survivors; post-discharge long-term survival was similar between groups ([Mariani et al., J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg 2023;166:1670]([passage text removed])). A recent single-centre series found perioperative versus postoperative implantation produced broadly comparable crude weaning and hospital mortality, and explicitly cautions that immortal-time bias favours the postoperative group ([Bratisl Med J, doi 10.1007/s44411-026-00733-9]([passage text removed])).

**Long-term survival.** Among PELS-1 hospital survivors, survival was [passage text removed]) at 1 year, 85.4% (82.5–88.3) at 2 years, 76.4% (72.5–80.5) at 5 years and 65.9% (60.3–72.0) at 10 years; older age, atrial fibrillation, emergency surgery, surgery type, postoperative AKI and septic shock predicted post-discharge death ([JAHA 2023;12:e029609](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37421269)). Counting the whole cohort (deaths included), 5-year survival is far lower — 20% (95% CI 17–23) in women and 24% (21–28) in men ([JTCVS, S0022522324004355]([passage text removed])) — and pooled 1-year survival across studies [passage text removed]) ([Biancari meta-analysis]([passage text removed])).

**Paediatric data are indication-specific.** In 2322 children cannulated explicitly for failure to wean from CPB (ELSO registry), in-hospital mortality was 55%, unchanged over the study period, with 67% weaned; risk rose with noncardiac anomalies (OR 1.78), preoperative arrest (OR 1.67), CPB time >251 min (OR 1.50) and complex procedures (OR 1.43), while age >26 days was protective (OR 0.56) ([PMC7498130]([passage text removed])). A paediatric meta-analysis found pooled survival of [passage text removed]) for CPB weaning failure versus 47.3% for low cardiac output and 37.6% for cardiac arrest, with no significant difference between indications (P=0.19) ([Cho et al., Front Pediatr 2022;10:869283]([passage text removed])).

**Caveats.** Cannulation route matters: central cannulation was associated with higher in-hospital mortality than peripheral (OR 1.54, 95% CI 1.09–2.18) plus more reoperation for bleeding and transfusion ([PMID 31864699](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31864699)). I found no adult study reporting survival stratified *solely* by the failure-to-wean indication versus other post-cardiotomy indications, so adult indication-specific survival must be inferred from intraoperative-initiation subgroups; single-centre protocolised programmes report discharge survival approaching 70%, which is not generalisable ([NewYork-Presbyterian]([passage text removed])).
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Roughly one-third to 40% of adults placed on VA-ECMO for postcardiotomy shock — of whom failure to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is the single commonest indication — survive to hospital discharge; but those who do reach discharge have durable survival, with about two-thirds alive at 10 years [S:ab57d07b-d7c7-5d9d-9d13-976b201a2989][S:5aef65d0-9d6d-5051-9205-ea27a48c98f9][S:adc19b25-3f1c-5986-95d0-0f8a598aa6e5].

## Failure to wean is the dominant indication

In the largest dedicated cohort, the international multicentre PELS-1 registry (34 centres, adults on ECMO for postcardiotomy cardiogenic shock 2000–2020), failure to wean from CPB was the primary indication in 39.7%, ahead of cardiogenic shock (25.2%) and right ventricular failure (11.9%) [S:5aef65d0-9d6d-5051-9205-ea27a48c98f9]. Other reviews likewise identify intraoperative failure to wean as the most common trigger for post-cardiotomy ECMO [S:425dc6ba-949f-5ff4-836b-1fac1bd14fe8][S:29da4e93-7199-56a7-9fb0-8b3b9fcb59cc].

## In-hospital survival

- PELS-1 (n=2058, median age 65): in-hospital mortality 60.5%; independent correlates were age ([passage text removed]). Mortality showed no improvement over the 20-year observation period [S:ab57d07b-d7c7-5d9d-9d13-976b201a2989][S:22b8cb56-de6c-518b-b2dd-ec8d8e01f98c].
- Meta-analysis of 24 retrospective cohorts (1926 patients, 1992–2016): pooled survival to hospital discharge 30.8% (95% CI 0.29–0.34, I²=60%), with advanced age (>70 y) and prolonged ECMO support among the commonly reported adverse prognostic indicators [S:adc19b25-3f1c-5986-95d0-0f8a598aa6e5][S:e2b7eca8-0671-5a23-93a0-852bf16fceba]. A separate pooled analysis of 20 studies (2877 patients) reported survival to discharge of 34% (30–38%) [S:8e6e4bf4-264d-5dbd-88aa-a06ba892af2e].
- Weaning success substantially exceeds survival: a 110-patient postcardiotomy series weaned 67 but discharged 46 [S:35c250c9-1703-5688-97ea-10c4a93e8b4b]; another centre weaned 43.6% with only 25% hospital survival [S:1904ffa8-5296-5493-be26-c1d89677c214]; in the Rastan series of 517 patients, 63.3% weaned but only 24.8% were discharged [S:9cca1538-964f-5a20-829c-3ad862b4ba6b]. Overall, 20–65% of patients weaned from VA-ECMO still die before discharge [S:2ba1c690-7826-500b-8cb5-86b277dc111a].

## Timing: intraoperative (failure-to-wean) versus ICU cannulation

The PELS-1 timing analysis (n=2003) compared ECMO started in the operating theatre (n=1287) with ICU initiation (n=716). Despite worse preoperative risk profiles (lower LVEF, higher EuroSCORE II, more prior cardiac surgery), intraoperatively cannulated patients had *lower* in-hospital mortality (57.5% vs 64.5%, P=.002), fewer complications and reinterventions, and shorter ECMO runs among survivors (median 104 vs 139.7 hours, P<.001); post-discharge long-term survival was equivalent (P=.86) [S:3ffe263b-f787-5b8f-a6e9-1d3adbd14428][S:89f5e2d6-bb41-5e39-beaf-9db77b6265b7]. Notably, the in-hospital mortality gap *widened* when failure-to-wean patients were excluded, indicating that the failure-to-wean subgroup contributes favourably to the intraoperative group's outcome [S:89f5e2d6-bb41-5e39-beaf-9db77b6265b7]. A single-centre series similarly found higher survival when ECMO was started in the operating room after unsuccessful CPB weaning than when started later in the ICU (survival to discharge/transfer 45.2% vs 29.4%) [S:f5b28d0b-df72-565c-859d-5ea38e06d9de].

## Long-term survival after discharge

Among PELS-1 hospital survivors, survival was 89.5% at 1 year, 85.4% at 2 years, 76.4% at 5 years and 65.9% at 10 years; post-discharge mortality was associated with [passage text removed] septic shock [S:ab57d07b-d7c7-5d9d-9d13-976b201a2989][S:22b8cb56-de6c-518b-b2dd-ec8d8e01f98c]. Older single-centre data are less favourable when survival is expressed over the whole cohort: in Rastan's 517 patients cumulative survival was 17.6% at 6 months, 16.5% at 1 year and 13.7% at 5 years [S:9cca1538-964f-5a20-829c-3ad862b4ba6b]; another cohort reported 27.5% discharged alive and 21.7% long-term survival, with health-related quality of life in survivors comparable to coronary disease controls [S:28542350-be42-573b-84d5-0f1d9d00003d].

## Morbidity driving the mortality

Complications are the rate-limiting factor: renal failure requiring replacement therapy and bleeding each affect roughly half of VA-ECMO patients in pooled cardiogenic-shock data [S:a229d5e0-4b75-5382-87c9-3bde5dfbc110]; in a 219-patient postcardiotomy series with 24% 30-day survival, 62% needed reoperation for bleeding, 58% developed acute renal failure and 13% had limb ischaemia [S:fb0abb4a-a5e7-5d0b-8955-0a10dc944044]. Refractory cardiac failure and multiorgan failure are the usual causes of death [S:fb0abb4a-a5e7-5d0b-8955-0a10dc944044]. Failure of lactate clearance and elevated post-ECMO lactate are consistent early prognostic markers [S:bcf2b25e-7cfe-58d5-9d59-940e91f30895][S:a52ae429-259e-5abc-a043-9d57ccd10d77].

## Caveats

Reported survival is highly heterogeneous across centres (older reviews cite ranges of 19–67% and 16–76%), reflecting differing case mix, thresholds for initiation, and publication bias — so a single number should not be quoted as *the* expected outcome [S:fb0abb4a-a5e7-5d0b-8955-0a10dc944044][S:29da4e93-7199-56a7-9fb0-8b3b9fcb59cc]. Higher hospital ECMO volume is associated with lower in-hospital death [S:f4709b98-0ec6-58ca-9c8e-ce1f8a1376d0]. Whether central or peripheral arterial cannulation is superior remains unresolved: an individual-patient-data meta-analysis favoured peripheral cannulation [S:5d0c6f16-27f0-5f80-8013-a7881d55aade], one single-centre study favoured central [S:4653221d-dd8d-5351-a10c-18f4612b4fd6], and a propensity-matched analysis found no difference [S:d14f069b-4ebd-549b-9961-07764656d793]. I found no randomised trial evidence for VA-ECMO in this indication, and no study that reported survival separately for the failure-to-wean subgroup as its primary analysis in adults — the inference above rests on the PELS-1 timing comparison and on cohorts in which failure to wean predominated. Paediatric/congenital figures differ and should not be transposed: generalised postcardiotomy ECMO survival in congenital heart surgery is 40–50% [S:f4109006-b392-50cc-ac3e-fac311e0aab0], though survival for children taken directly from CPB onto ECMO without any stable off-pump interval has been reported as low as 10–30% [S:24c41388-1876-5374-8e7d-8f5d2a185317].

rows.question: What key clinical outcomes follow finerenone therapy in patients with heart failure and left ventricular ejection fraction above 40%?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Finerenone added to standard therapy reduces the composite of cardiovascular death and worsening heart failure events (heart failure hospitalisation or emergency visits) in heart failure with ejection fraction above 40%; The size of that composite effect is modest: about a 16% relative risk reduction, with an absolute risk reduction of only a few percentage points; All heart failure hospitalisations were also reduced, by about 18%, as a secondary endpoint; Cardiovascular mortality taken on its own fell by about 7% and this difference was not statistically significant versus placebo. Certainty: The direction of benefit on the composite endpoint and on heart failure hospitalisations rests on a single large placebo-controlled comparison in which treatment was allocated by chance, with estimates relayed without confidence intervals, while the cardiovascular mortality component on its own did not reach statistical significance. Scope: applies to heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction (ejection fraction above 40%) in adults on standard background therapy, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents finerenone as an established therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, or as demonstrated across the whole ejection fraction range.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

In the pivotal FINEARTS-HF trial (n=6,001; NYHA II–IV, LVEF ≥40%; median follow-up 32 months), finerenone reduced the composite of cardiovascular death and total worsening-heart-failure events by ~16%, an effect driven almost entirely by fewer HF hospitalizations/urgent visits rather than by mortality, with a small symptom benefit and an expected hyperkalemia/hypotension trade-off. [[passage text removed]]

## Efficacy outcomes

- **Primary composite (total worsening HF events + CV death):** 1,083 vs 1,283 events; 14.9 vs 17.7 per 100 patient-years; [passage text removed]]
- **Driver = HF events:** total worsening HF events 842 vs 1,024; RR 0.82 (0.71–0.94), P=0.006. Over median 32 months, 20.8% vs 24.0% had CV death or a first HF hospitalization — absolute risk reduction 3.2%, NNT ~31. [[passage text removed]]
- **Mortality: no significant benefit.** CV death 8.1% vs 8.7% (HR 0.93, 0.78–1.11); all-cause death 16.4% vs 17.4% (HR 0.93, 0.83–1.06). [[passage text removed]]
- **Symptoms/function:** KCCQ total symptom score improved more with finerenone (+8.0 vs +6.4; difference 1.6 points, 95% CI 0.8–2.3; P<0.001), but no difference in NYHA class improvement at 12 months (18.6% vs 18.4%; OR 1.01, 0.88–1.15). [[passage text removed]]
- **Consistency:** benefit was consistent across 17 prespecified subgroups, including LVEF strata (<50% RR 0.84; 50–<60% RR 0.80; ≥60% RR 0.94; P interaction 0.70) and baseline SGLT2-inhibitor use (only ~14% at baseline). [[passage text removed]] Effect also did not differ significantly by baseline eGFR or UACR. [[passage text removed]]
- **Timing signal:** patients randomized during or within 7 days of a worsening-HF event (HR 0.74, 0.57–0.95) or 7 days–3 months after (HR 0.79, 0.64–0.97) appeared to derive greater benefit than those >3 months out or with no prior event (HR 0.99, 0.81–1.21), a hypothesis-generating finding. [[passage text removed]]

## Kidney outcomes

Neutral for eGFR-based endpoints, favorable for albuminuria: [passage text removed] higher with finerenone (75 vs 55 events; HR 1.33, 0.94–1.89); there was an acute eGFR dip of −2.9 mL/min/1.73 m² in the first 3 months but no difference in chronic eGFR slope (+0.2, 95% CI −0.1 to 0.4); UACR fell 30% (25%–34%) at 6 months, with reduced new-onset micro- (HR 0.76) and macroalbuminuria (HR 0.62). [[passage text removed]]

## Safety

- Serum potassium >5.5 mmol/L: 14.3% vs 6.9% (HR 2.16, 1.83–2.56); >6.0 mmol/L: 3.0% vs 1.4%; hyperkalemia hospitalization 0.5% vs 0.2%, with no hyperkalemia-related deaths. [[passage text removed]]
- Conversely, **less hypokalemia** (potassium <3.5 mmol/L: HR 0.46, 0.38–0.56; 4.4% vs 9.7%). [[passage text removed]]
- Systolic BP <100 mm Hg 18.5% vs 12.4%; creatinine ≥3.0 mg/dL 2.0% vs 1.2%; acute kidney injury 3.7% vs 2.1%. Serious adverse events were *lower* with finerenone (38.7% vs 40.5%) and discontinuation rates were similar (20.4% vs 20.6%). [[passage text removed]]

## Context and regulatory status

An individual-patient meta-analysis of RALES, EMPHASIS-HF, TOPCAT and FINEARTS-HF (13,846 patients) confirms the pattern: MRAs reduced CV death or HF hospitalization less in HFmrEF/HFpEF (HR 0.87, 0.79–0.95) than HFrEF (0.66, 0.59–0.73), with HF hospitalization reduced (0.82, 0.74–0.91) but CV death not (0.92, 0.80–1.05). [S:https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/333891] The pooled FINE-HEART analysis across FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD and FINEARTS-HF (18,991 participants) likewise did not meet significance for CV death (HR 0.89, 0.78–1.01). [S:https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-03264-4] On this basis, finerenone is FDA-approved to reduce CV death, HF hospitalization and urgent HF visits in adults with HF and LVEF ≥40%, and has been approved in the EU for the same indication. [[passage text removed]]

**Caveat:** clinical practice interpretation is limited by low baseline SGLT2-inhibitor use in FINEARTS-HF, so the additive benefit of finerenone on contemporary quadruple/HFpEF background therapy remains incompletely defined. [[passage text removed]]

**Bottom line:** In HF with LVEF ≥40% (HFmrEF/HFpEF), finerenone reduces the composite of total worsening HF events and cardiovascular death — driven almost entirely by fewer HF hospitalizations/urgent visits, not by lower cardiovascular mortality — with modest symptom improvement and an excess of hyperkalemia but no signal of harm on hard safety endpoints.

**Primary efficacy (FINEARTS-HF, 6001 patients, LVEF ≥40%, median 32 months)**
- [passage text removed] plus CV death: 16% relative reduction (rate ratio [passage text removed]) [S:f25e7967-15c7-5a36-ae40-b1a3abc80c22][S:b13fcd87-2584-593a-99c9-62e4f5370ab7], corresponding to [passage text removed] [S:f832c54e-d073-54b4-9825-c941253df08d].
- Total worsening HF events: 842 (28.0%) vs 1024 (34.1%); rate ratio 0.82 (0.71–0.94), p=0.006 [S:54f5ddb5-5d7c-569c-94f5-0cfafa556ca7].
- CV death: 242 (8.1%) vs 260 (8.7%), HR 0.93 (0.78–1.11) — not significant [S:54f5ddb5-5d7c-569c-94f5-0cfafa556ca7][S:b13fcd87-2584-593a-99c9-62e4f5370ab7].
- All-cause death: 491 (16.4%) vs 522 (17.4%), HR 0.93 (0.83–1.06) — not significant [S:54f5ddb5-5d7c-569c-94f5-0cfafa556ca7].
- Time-to-first-event sensitivity analysis (first worsening HF event or CV death): 20.8% vs 24.0%, HR 0.84 (0.76–0.94) [S:54f5ddb5-5d7c-569c-94f5-0cfafa556ca7].

**Symptoms/function and kidney outcomes**
- KCCQ overall summary score improved more with finerenone (8.0 ± 0.3 vs 6.4 ± 0.3 points; [passage text removed]–2.3, p<0.001), i.e. a small but statistically significant health-status benefit [S:54f5ddb5-5d7c-569c-94f5-0cfafa556ca7].
- NYHA class improvement at 12 months was not different (18.6% vs 18.4%; OR 1.01, 0.88–1.15) [S:54f5ddb5-5d7c-569c-94f5-0cfafa556ca7].
- The kidney composite (≥50% sustained eGFR decline, eGFR <15, dialysis/transplant) was numerically higher with finerenone: 75 (2.5%) vs 55 (1.8%), HR 1.33 (0.94–1.89) — not significant, in a population with relatively preserved renal function; albuminuria progression was nonetheless reduced [S:54f5ddb5-5d7c-569c-94f5-0cfafa556ca7][S:36e47e8e-8bcf-54fe-8726-725a1d95aa07][S:b569b771-fda2-526e-ac51-b2643411e42c].

**Consistency across subgroups**
- Benefit was consistent across the LVEF spectrum, including LVEF <50%, 50–<60%, and ≥60% (p-interaction 0.70; continuous p-interaction 0.28) [S:9da7d038-cc8b-51d1-aae1-d443632021b9][S:f832c54e-d073-54b4-9825-c941253df08d], and across age, NT-proBNP, renal function, glycemia, atrial fibrillation history, and baseline SGLT2-inhibitor use [S:35629ab2-b3ad-5eec-9265-75753a2caef1].
- SGLT2 inhibitor use did not modify effect (on SGLT2i HR 0.83, 0.60–1.16; not on SGLT2i HR 0.85, 0.74–0.98), supporting additive use [S:76e864d7-cec1-5ee9-86b1-3297e30f0a01][S:ec6d319d-e036-5c75-beab-c87ae23828fe].
- One correspondence reports the largest benefit in patients randomized soon after a worsening-[passage text removed], 0.57–0.95; 7 days–3 months RR 0.79, 0.64–0.97) versus no clear benefit >3 months out or without prior worsening HF (RR 0.99, 0.81–1.21) [S:08971db4-5710-5fe5-9c8c-01d357a5f4d1].

**Safety**
- Investigator-reported hyperkalemia 9.7% vs 4.2% [S:f25e7967-15c7-5a36-ae40-b1a3abc80c22]; serum potassium >5.5 mmol/L 14.3% vs 6.9%, with hyperkalemia-related hospitalization ~0.5% [S:f832c54e-d073-54b4-9825-c941253df08d]. Severe hyperkalemia (K ≥6.0 mmol/L) 3.0% vs 1.4%, with no hyperkalemia-related deaths [S:76e864d7-cec1-5ee9-86b1-3297e30f0a01][S:0336c613-2a6e-520e-ac8e-4a70355ac489].
- Conversely, hypokalemia (<3.5 mmol/L) was less frequent with finerenone (4.4% vs 9.9%) [S:76e864d7-cec1-5ee9-86b1-3297e30f0a01]. Hypotension occurred more often with finerenone than placebo [S:437a8287-7fc1-59ea-8e55-39afcd1631ef].
- Benefit was retained even in patients who developed potassium >5.5 mmol/L when protocol-directed monitoring and dose interruption/re-initiation were applied [S:a66eda78-9c4e-53d5-a6b8-2a958022aa17].

**Caveats.** Pooled FINE-HEART analysis (FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD, FINEARTS-HF; N=18,991) did not show a significant reduction in its primary CV-death endpoint (4.4% vs 5.0%), though all-cause mortality and HF hospitalization were reduced [S:f3bb10a7-0651-5276-9b52-4ca708432be4][S:f592beb6-3acf-580e-91d8-3d7a119cb9e3]. There are no head-to-head trials versus spironolactone or eplerenone, so whether this is a class effect remains unresolved [S:e47507d1-efa0-578e-b3d5-8cbb75a49692], and effects in advanced CKD or high hyperkalemia risk remain unclear [S:95330a12-9360-5ae5-9e8e-ba10104b9b9a]. A reported estimate of [passage text removed] comes from a lifetime-benefit modelling analysis, not directly observed follow-up [S:0336c613-2a6e-520e-ac8e-4a70355ac489].

rows.question: Which pharmacological therapies are currently recommended for patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibition with empagliflozin or dapagliflozin reduces the composite of worsening heart failure and cardiovascular death, a benefit carried by about 21-27% fewer heart failure hospitalisations; Finerenone reduces the composite of total heart failure events and cardiovascular death in patients with ejection fraction of at least 40%; Weekly semaglutide improves the symptom-oriented endpoints of quality of life and body weight in obese patients with preserved ejection fraction; Spironolactone, candesartan and sacubitril/valsartan did not meet their primary endpoints in preserved ejection fraction. Certainty: Both the benefit and the non-benefit claims rest on comparisons in which treatment was allocated by chance rather than chosen, although the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor evidence came from participants spanning preserved together with mildly reduced ejection fraction, leaving the share attributable to preserved ejection fraction alone less securely established. Scope: applies to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents a reduction in death rates with these drug classes as demonstrated in preserved ejection fraction, or recommends them on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Two drug classes now form the core of HFpEF pharmacotherapy — an SGLT2 inhibitor and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (finerenone preferred) — layered on diuretics for congestion and treatment of comorbidities, with incretin-based therapy (semaglutide or tirzepatide) added for patients with obesity. ARNI/ARB remain optional adjuncts, and nitrates/PDE-5 inhibitors are explicitly not recommended.

## 1. SGLT2 inhibitors — the strongest recommendation

Dapagliflozin or empagliflozin carry a Class I, Level A recommendation in HFpEF to reduce HF hospitalization or CV death, based on EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER plus meta-analysis; the guideline text notes the effect was driven by HF hospitalizations, with no significant reduction in CV death ([[passage text removed], Recommendation Table 2]([passage text removed]); [ACC key points]([passage text removed])). Before that update, no disease-modifying therapy had a recommendation in HFpEF at all ([same document]([passage text removed])). The US guideline is slightly weaker: [passage text removed]" — Class 2a, LOE B-R ([2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline]([passage text removed])).

## 2. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists — now a second pillar

- **Trial evidence:** FINEARTS-HF randomized patients with LVEF ≥40% to finerenone (max 20 or 40 mg daily) or placebo added to usual therapy; over a median 32 months the composite of total worsening HF events and CV death fell (rate ratio [passage text removed]), driven by HF events (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.71–0.94, P=0.006) rather than CV death (8.1% vs 8.7%; HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.78–1.11). Hyperkalemia was more frequent with finerenone ([NEJM 2024;391(16):1475-1485, summarized]([passage text removed]); [Bayer](https://www.bayer.com/media/en-us/finerenone-meets-primary-endpoint-[passage text removed])). Benefit was consistent in patients already on an SGLT2 inhibitor ([HFSA]([passage text removed])) and across the EF range including EF ≥60%, where steroidal MRAs had shown attenuated effect; hyperkalemia >5.5 mmol/L occurred in 14.3% vs 6.9% ([PMC12979370]([passage text removed])).
- **Regulatory:** FDA approved finerenone in July 2025 to reduce CV death, HF hospitalization and urgent HF visits in adults with HF and LVEF ≥40% ([Bayer](https://www.bayer.com/media/en-us/us-fda-approves-finerenone-for-new-indication-[passage text removed]); [Optum]([passage text removed])).
- **Guidelines:** the 2026 ESC guideline gives MRAs a Class I recommendation in chronic HF independent of LVEF ([ESC news release]([passage text removed]); [EMJ]([passage text removed])), with foundational medical therapy for HFpEF comprising **MRAs plus SGLT2 inhibitors** ([touchCARDIO]([passage text removed])). The ACC expert consensus decision pathway likewise [passage text removed] for most HFpEF patients, favouring finerenone over spironolactone for its hyperkalemia profile ([JACC [passage text removed], as reported]([passage text removed])). The older 2022 US guideline still lists MRA only as Class 2b ([AHA]([passage text removed])).

## 3. Incretin-based therapy if obesity is present

- **STEP-HFpEF:** 529 patients with HFpEF and BMI ≥30 received semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly or placebo for 52 weeks; KCCQ-CSS rose 16.6 vs 8.7 points (difference 7.8; 95% CI 4.8–10.9; P<0.001), weight changed −13.3% vs −2.6%, 6-minute walk distance +21.5 vs +1.2 m, [passage text removed]–2.15) ([PMID 37622681](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37622681)). The trial was underpowered for clinical events ([ACC trial summary]([passage text removed])).
- **SUMMIT:** 731 patients with EF ≥50% and BMI ≥30 randomized to tirzepatide vs placebo; CV death or worsening HF occurred in 9.9% (36/364) vs 15.3% (56/367), HR [passage text removed]; P=.026) over median 104 weeks ([NEJM 2024, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2410027, as reported]([passage text removed]); [Applied Clinical Trials]([passage text removed])).
- **Recommendations:** ESC 2026 gives semaglutide or tirzepatide a Class IIa recommendation in HFpEF with obesity ([ESC]([passage text removed]); [AJMC]([passage text removed])); the ACC pathway recommends incretin therapy at BMI ≥30 kg/m² ([HCPLive]([passage text removed])).

## 4. Symptom control, comorbidities, and what to avoid

Diuretics as needed carry a Class 1 recommendation for HFpEF, as does titrating antihypertensive therapy to blood-pressure targets; ARNI and ARB are Class 2b; nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors are Class 3 (no benefit) for improving activity or quality of life ([2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA]([passage text removed]); [AHA slide set]([passage text removed])). The ACC pathway adds a systolic BP target of 120–129 mm Hg in HFpEF, favours ARNI/ARB over ACE inhibitors (citing the neutral PEP-CHF result for perindopril), and advises against routine beta-blockers unless another indication such as angina or AF rate control exists ([ACC ECDP summary]([passage text removed]); [ECDP walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HazAsFCjiAI)).

**Caveats:** guideline class assignments differ by vintage and society — the 2022 US guideline predates FINEARTS-HF, SUMMIT and the finerenone approval, so its 2a/2b gradings for SGLT2i and MRA are weaker than current European and consensus-document positions. I found no tool-sourced evidence that any HFpEF therapy has been shown to reduce all-cause or cardiovascular mortality in this population specifically.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Current guideline-recommended pharmacotherapy for HFpEF rests on three pillars — an SGLT2 inhibitor (the only Class I agent), diuretics for congestion, and treatment of comorbidities — with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (now including finerenone), ARNI/ARB as weaker, selective options, and incretin-based therapy emerging for the obesity phenotype.

## SGLT2 inhibitors — strongest recommendation
Empagliflozin and dapagliflozin are the only drugs with a Class I recommendation in HFpEF, based on EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER; the 2023 Focused Update of the ESC heart failure guidelines recommends dapagliflozin or empagliflozin in symptomatic HFmrEF and HFpEF to reduce HF hospitalisation or cardiovascular death (Class I-A) [S:3f92a1b6-210a-5821-b4a3-35a44ab43276][S:cc1f3ed8-16e6-569f-a11b-9535acaf08a5][S:7a545cbf-764e-520c-ac6f-490b7ab0fea8]. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline gives them a Class 2a (Level B-R) recommendation for reducing HF hospitalisation and cardiovascular death, and names only empagliflozin and dapagliflozin [S:f34ad512-f616-5d30-9c78-f0fb22fc8a25][S:8d07ff3e-c011-5ed7-aa5c-7938b9425bb0]. Trial support: empagliflozin reduced CV death or HF hospitalisation ([passage text removed]) and dapagliflozin reduced worsening HF or CV death ([passage text removed]), benefits driven mainly by fewer HF events and independent of diabetes status [S:b4b1f7af-02c1-5d76-99ab-e56274d6fd6e][S:e6d7cb90-1d52-50a4-8a56-50de58d0e13e].

## Diuretics and comorbidity management
A systematic review of HFpEF clinical practice guidelines found unanimity that diuretics (loop diuretics preferred) should be used for fluid retention, and that identification and treatment of aetiologies and comorbidities — AF, valvular disease, hypertension, diabetes, anaemia, sleep apnoea, renal dysfunction — is recommended in all guidelines [S:96c1459a-7ab8-58f2-9378-9ff924f78de4]. Both ESC 2021 and ACC/AHA/HFSA 2022 [passage text removed] [S:5014d470-f7cd-5d54-ae11-9d2e7a3a95d1]; blood pressure control carries a Class 1 recommendation and treatment of AF Class 2a [S:8d07ff3e-c011-5ed7-aa5c-7938b9425bb0].

## Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists
Spironolactone/MRAs carry a Class 2b recommendation in the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline, chiefly to reduce hospitalisations and preferentially at the lower end of the EF spectrum [S:c536c67a-92c1-54a8-91aa-f1ebb39154fb][S:f34ad512-f616-5d30-9c78-f0fb22fc8a25]; the ESC 2023 update added a Class IIb recommendation for MRAs in HFmrEF/HFpEF without endorsing a specific agent [S:7b3c7bc2-adfe-5ab7-ae56-ed019523c1b1]. This area has moved: in FINEARTS-HF (6001 patients, LVEF ≥40%) finerenone reduced total worsening HF events plus CV death ([passage text removed]) [S:08971db4-5710-5fe5-9c8c-01d357a5f4d1][S:941282c0-dd4b-5047-87d6-650ff0fb22d4], with benefit similar with or without background SGLT2 inhibitor [S:7f5a8ef7-b3ce-59a0-aab9-ad56f2bcd289]. The FDA has approved finerenone for HFmrEF and HFpEF [S:129425e2-d665-5971-81a0-1a7288214913], Japanese guidelines give it a Class IIa recommendation [S:00321567-20ef-5632-a2f6-83042ed70198], and updated NICE guidance now advises "consider an MRA and an SGLT-2 inhibitor" for HFpEF, based on FINEARTS-HF and TOPCAT, with monitoring for hyperkalaemia [S:96aedf02-bda6-5ff2-bcc8-7d9ca2078084].

## ARNI / ARB (selective, weak)
The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline gives ARNI and ARB Class 2b recommendations to reduce HF hospitalisation, specifically in patients with LVEF at the lower end of the preserved range, since these trials missed their primary endpoints [S:f34ad512-f616-5d30-9c78-f0fb22fc8a25][S:5014d470-f7cd-5d54-ae11-9d2e7a3a95d1]. ESC guidelines do not formally recommend ARNI or MRA in HFpEF, judging the post-hoc PARAGON-HF and TOPCAT subgroup signals insufficient [S:ddc88cd6-31a4-5247-8f90-4b73a6afcd2b][S:7a545cbf-764e-520c-ac6f-490b7ab0fea8].

## Obesity phenotype: incretin-based therapy
In SUMMIT (731 patients with HFpEF and BMI ≥30), tirzepatide reduced [passage text removed]) [S:30e6042b-f156-5f82-83ec-56a1712cc341][S:059ab469-bbba-50bc-bb74-df80d4ad6f28], and pooled semaglutide data showed a reduction in CV [passage text removed]) [S:30e6042b-f156-5f82-83ec-56a1712cc341]. [passage text removed]:30e6042b-f156-5f82-83ec-56a1712cc341], though one 2025 review notes these findings had not yet entered most guideline recommendations [S:9ceb1128-91c2-5aba-acdd-0593c4e5d2ff].

## What is *not* recommended
No therapy has convincingly reduced mortality in HFpEF; both ESC and ACC/AHA/HFSA acknowledge this, with benefits confined largely to HF hospitalisation [S:5014d470-f7cd-5d54-ae11-9d2e7a3a95d1]. Beta-blockers lack supportive HFpEF evidence — in ELANDD heart-rate control produced no improvement in exercise capacity, and their role remains in question [S:7a545cbf-764e-520c-ac6f-490b7ab0fea8]; earlier NICE guidance found insufficient evidence for ACE inhibitors, ARBs and beta-blockers in this population [S:9b116c7a-6fb2-51dd-8a07-ef968b35b965].
