rows.question: Which cardiovascular magnetic resonance parameters identify acute myocarditis in patients with clinically suspected disease?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Global native T1, global T2 and extracellular volume fraction are each higher in acute myocarditis than in healthy comparison subjects; Extracellular volume fraction separated myocarditis from healthy comparison subjects more sharply than native T1 or T2 alone; The updated two-out-of-two Lake Louise criteria, pairing a T2-based and a T1-based marker, discriminated myocarditis as well as extracellular volume did. Certainty: Support remains preliminary: the group differences look consistent, but the accuracy estimates come from a small sample gathered at a single hospital on one scanner, with thresholds fitted on the same participants in whom they were then evaluated. Scope: applies to clinically suspected acute myocarditis in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents left ventricular ejection fraction or chamber volumes as established markers for identifying acute myocarditis, or recommends relying on them to make or exclude the diagnosis.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

In clinically suspected myocarditis, CMR identifies acute myocarditis by the combination of a **T2-based edema marker plus a T1-based marker of non-ischaemic myocardial injury** (updated/2018 Lake Louise Criteria), with functional and pericardial abnormalities serving only as supportive findings.

## The diagnostic parameters

**Main criteria (both required, "2 out of 2"):** [passage text removed] on [passage text removed] imaging (regional high signal, or global myocardium/skeletal-muscle signal intensity ratio ≥2) — plus at least one T1-based criterion — increased native myocardial T1, [passage text removed]-ischaemic (typically subepicardial/mid-myocardial) distribution [PMID 30545455; [passage text removed]; https://radiopaedia.org/articles/myocarditis; [passage text removed]].

**Supportive (not required) criteria:** pericardial abnormalities indicating inflammation (effusion, pericardial thickening, pericardial LGE/T2 or T1 abnormality) and systolic dysfunction — regional wall-motion abnormality or global hypokinesis [[passage text removed]]. Early gadolinium enhancement (EGE), part of the original 2009 criteria, is no longer required, as its removal does not substantially reduce diagnostic performance [[passage text removed]].

## Performance evidence

- **Criteria as a whole:** the original LLC had pooled sensitivity 78%, specificity 88%, AUC 83% in the meta-analysis cited by the expert panel [[passage text removed]]; another meta-analysis reported pooled sensitivity 74% and specificity 86% for LLC [PMID 30012826]. In a validation cohort the 2018 LLC gave sensitivity [passage text removed] specificity [passage text removed]) versus 72.5% and 96.2% for the original criteria (sensitivity difference p=.031) [PMC7978026]. Against endomyocardial biopsy at 3.0 T, the 2018 LLC achieved AUC 0.91 (sensitivity 95.3%, specificity 86.7%) versus 0.76 for the 2009 LLC [[passage text removed]].
- **Individual parameters:** in the expert-panel synthesis, median AUCs were T1 mapping 89, T2 mapping 80, LGE 83, T2-weighted imaging 73, ECV 74, EGE 73; the best combinations were T1 mapping+LGE (96) and T2 mapping+LGE (90) [[passage text removed]]. A meta-analysis of parametric mapping within the modified LLC found native T1 sensitivity 83%/specificity 86% (AUC 0.91), T2 mapping 81%/86% (AUC 0.89) and ECV 71%/81% (AUC 0.83), with optimal 1.5-T thresholds of 1,021 ms, 52 ms and 28% respectively [PMC12131415]. A separate meta-analysis reported pooled sensitivities of 0.84 (T1), 0.77 (T2) and 0.69 (ECV) with specificities 0.86, 0.83 and 0.77, and noted that specificity of T1 and T2 fell significantly in biopsy-validated cohorts (p<0.01) [PMID 34480832].
- **Thresholds are not transferable:** cut-offs differ by field strength and sequence — e.g. 990 ms for ShMOLLI native T1 at 1.5 T (sensitivity 90%, specificity 91%, accuracy 91%) [[passage text removed]] versus 1,228 ms native T1, 58.5 ms T2 and 31.0% ECV at 3.0 T [[passage text removed]].

## Interpretation caveats

A single positive criterion (T1- or T2-based only) still supports myocardial inflammation in the right clinical context but with reduced specificity; in the validation cohort, T1-only criteria gave AUC 0.85 and T2-only AUC 0.87, not significantly different from the "2 out of 2" approach [[passage text removed]; PMC7978026]. The 2025 ESC guidelines adopt the updated LLC and give a Class I recommendation for CMR in clinically suspected myocarditis, classifying cases as CMR-proven (2/2 criteria), CMR-uncertain (1/2) or CMR-rejected [[passage text removed]; https://cardiac-imaging.org/2025_ESC_myocarditis; [passage text removed]]. Note that some parameters carry prognostic as well as diagnostic weight — LGE is described as the strongest independent predictor of mortality (HR 8.4 all-cause, 12.8 cardiac), and ECV >35% marks adverse outcome [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
## Answer

**Acute myocarditis in clinically suspected disease is identified by the combination of a T2-based marker of myocardial oedema plus a T1-based marker of inflammatory myocardial injury (revised 2018 Lake Louise Criteria), with left ventricular dysfunction and pericardial involvement as supportive findings.**

### The core criteria
- **T2-based (oedema):** regional high T2 signal intensity, a global T2 signal-intensity ratio ≥2.0 versus skeletal muscle on T2-weighted images, or regional/global prolongation of myocardial T2 relaxation time [S:d9517d17].
- **T1-based (injury):** non-ischaemic-pattern late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), or regional/global increase in native myocardial T1 or extracellular volume (ECV) [S:d9517d17][S:41e68d78].
- **Supportive:** pericardial enhancement/high pericardial T1 or T2, pericardial effusion, and regional or global LV systolic dysfunction [S:41e68d78][S:d9517d17][S:93f5de8b].
- One criterion alone can still support the diagnosis in a highly suspicious clinical context, at the cost of specificity [S:d9517d17][S:93f5de8b].
- **Early gadolinium enhancement (hyperaemia)**, part of the original 2009 triad, was dropped: it showed the lowest sensitivity of the three original criteria and its removal did not substantially degrade performance [S:14bdb987][S:fef04927][S:be2490c9].

### Performance
- Revised LLC had higher sensitivity than the original criteria in comparative analysis (88% vs 73%, P = .03) [S:41e68d78]. Original LLC against endomyocardial biopsy: sensitivity 67%, specificity 91%, NPV 69% [S:c210aa28]; a meta-analysis of LLC reported sensitivity 80%, specificity 87% [S:c7a735f8].
- A systematic review of 686 suspected-myocarditis patients and 372 controls found native T1 accuracy 69–99% (sensitivity 64–98%, specificity 87–100%; cut-offs >980 to >1074 ms), T2 accuracy 47–87% (sensitivity 48–94%, specificity 60–92%; cut-offs >54 to >68 ms), and ECV alone only moderate (accuracy 62–76%, sensitivity 47–73%, specificity 76–90%); combining mapping/ECV with LGE raised accuracy to 96% [S:400230ca][S:972a5bd9].
- In a prospective single-centre multiparametric study of 37 suspected cases, optimal thresholds were global native T1 1308.5 ms (AUC 0.879, sensitivity 82%, specificity 79%), [passage text removed]%) and [passage text removed]%); 34/37 (91.9%) met updated LLC (AUC 0.946) [S:fa83a069].
- Native T1 alone can outperform conventional sequences: a threshold >990 ms gave sensitivity 90% and specificity 91%, detected larger areas of involvement than T2-weighted and LGE imaging, and flagged injury where both were negative [S:ebc829ea]. ECV by T1 mapping had the highest AUC (0.85) versus T2-STIR signal ratio (0.58), early enhancement (0.67) and LGE (0.80) in one head-to-head comparison [S:e6ba860e].

### Practical caveats
- **Timing/phase matters.** Against biventricular biopsy (MyoRacer), in acutely symptomatic patients (≤14 days) native T1 performed best (81%), then ECV (75%) and T2 (72%), all superior to LLC; in chronic symptoms only T2 mapping remained acceptable (72%), and 3.0 T performance was lower [S:b1f7978a].
- **Presentation matters.** In biopsy-confirmed myocarditis, sensitivity of both original and updated LLC exceeded 90% with infarct-like presentation but was 55.6% (original) rising to 72.2% (updated) in heart-failure presentation; infarct-like cases had more oedema and more LGE segments, with bright subepicardial inferolateral LGE, versus patchy lower-intensity mid-myocardial LGE in heart failure [S:6745089a][S:27201d9f][S:fef04927].
- **LGE pattern** is typically subepicardial or mid-wall, most often inferior/inferolateral; in one acute cohort LGE was abnormal in 92%, subepicardial in 56%, mid-wall 15%, patchy 25%, transmural 10% [S:5eb1d265][S:6c6c8f3e]. Sub-endocardial/coronary-territory LGE favours infarction, while mid-myocardial and epicardial LGE are the discriminating features for myocarditis [S:e7c2aaab].
- **Specificity limits.** In a real-world consortium-adjudicated cohort, a native T1 cut-off of 1019 ms (AUC 0.835, sensitivity 73.7%, specificity 72.4%) had a 56.6% false-positive rate among patients in whom myocarditis was ultimately excluded, and T1 added no further definitive diagnoses beyond classical LLC [S:4cc0a28b]. Mapping thresholds are scanner- and sequence-dependent and not standardised [S:a86c82ed][S:c0c4e23a]. There is also measurable inter-centre variability in applying LLC [S:7b9cd412].

### Adjunctive parameters (not diagnostic criteria)
Feature-tracking strain adds incremental value: a model combining a T2-map heterogeneity parameter (madSD), LV global circumferential strain and LGE reached AUC 0.93 (sensitivity 97%, specificity 77%) versus 0.79 for LLC [S:8f8c6b49]. Global longitudinal strain correlates with native T1 and oedema markers and carries independent prognostic value beyond LVEF and LGE [S:da1ba6f1][S:35e30ce5][S:0b0cba8c].

rows.question: What is known about the clinical value of AI-derived coronary artery calcium scores for cardiovascular risk prognostication?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: AI-derived coronary artery calcium from chest CT is consistently associated with all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events and obstructive coronary artery disease across varied patient groups and imaging indications; Early prospective and implementation-focused experience links automated calcium reporting embedded in clinical workflows with greater engagement in preventive care; Most included studies report time and labour savings from automated calcium scoring compared with manual Agatston scoring. Certainty: The evidence supports consistent associations with death and cardiovascular events rather than demonstrated benefit, while the workflow engagement and efficiency signals rest on early, methodologically varied, and largely low-strength sources. Scope: applies to cardiovascular risk prognostication using AI-derived coronary artery calcium in adults undergoing non-gated chest CT for cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular indications, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents automated coronary artery calcium scoring as an established, cost-effective component of preventive cardiology that should be switched on as standard of care for every chest CT.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

AI-derived CAC scores from both gated and routine non-gated CT agree closely with expert manual Agatston scoring and carry essentially the same prognostic signal — stratifying all-cause mortality, MI/stroke and MACE independently of traditional risk factors — and notification of AI-detected incidental CAC substantially increases statin prescribing; what is still missing is randomized evidence that this pathway reduces cardiovascular events.

## Prognostic validation in large cohorts

- **Multi-cohort gated + non-gated (n=20,084):** A deep-learning system applied to Framingham Heart Study, NLST, PROMISE and ROMICAT-II produced a score that was a strong, risk-factor-independent predictor of cardiovascular events ([passage text removed]), with Spearman correlation 0.92 against manual scores and substantial agreement across CAC risk groups [Nat Commun 12:715, 2021 — 10.1038/s41467-021-20966-2].
- **Routine ungated CT, real-world (n=5,678 without known ASCVD):** DL-CAC ≥100 vs 0 predicted [passage text removed], 1.45–1.98) after adjustment. Notably, this group had a mean [passage text removed] — an explicit care gap [[passage text removed] — 10.1016/j.jacc.2023.06.040].
- **National health-system scale (VA, NEJM AI):** AI-CAC on nongated scans predicted [passage text removed]%, HR 3.49) and first stroke/MI/death (33.5% vs 63.8%, HR 3.00); gated clinical-report CAC scores gave comparable stratification (22.8% vs 53.4%, HR 3.17). In an 8,052-scan lung-cancer-screening test set, event differences by AI-CAC group were already significant at 11 months. Performance generalized to 48 centers absent from training [10.1056/AIoa2400937].
- **Diabetes:** In 2,241 patients with type 2 diabetes, DL-CACS from non-gated CT was an independent MACE predictor (HR 1.07 per +100) and adding it to the Framingham risk score improved external-validation discrimination (C-index 0.70 vs 0.67, p=0.007) [Cardiovasc Diabetol 24:389, 2025 — 10.1186/s12933-025-02934-y].
- **Oncology populations:** DL CAC from lung-cancer radiotherapy planning CT predicted all-cause mortality and MACE in a proof-of-concept study [JCO Clin Cancer Inform 2022;6:e2100095]; in 913 cancer patients, DL CAC on non-gated chest CT matched manual scoring (total Agatston ICC 0.992; risk-category agreement κ=0.946) [Front Oncol 12:989250, 2022].
- **Beyond the Agatston score:** In MESA (5,830 participants, 1,773 CVD events over 15 years), AI extraction of cardiac chamber volumes plus calcified-plaque characterization from CAC scans gave significantly higher discrimination than the Agatston score alone across 1-, 5-, 10- and 15-year horizons [npj Digit Med 7:309, 2024 — 10.1038/s41746-024-01308-0].

## Measurement accuracy

Externally validated non-gated models calibrated to paired gated scans achieved sensitivity 80–100% and PPV 87–100% for any CAC across four health systems [npj Digit Med 4:88, 2021]; the same algorithm was reported as 82–94% sensitive, 79–100% specific [Circulation 2023;147:703–714]. A commercial tool assessed on 491 non-contrast chest CTs from five hospitals correlated 0.975 with radiologist reference and 0.942 with paired gated report scores [Sci Rep, 10.1038/s41598-025-23183-9]. VA AI-CAC agreed with expert nongated segmentation at ICC 0.96 (κ=0.81 across score bands), with ~89% accuracy for CAC presence [10.1056/AIoa2400937].

## Does it change care?

Two Stanford randomized efforts show the informational value translates into action: NOTIFY-1 (statin prescription 51.2% vs 6.9% at 6 months) [Circulation 2023;147:703–714] and the prospective NOTIFY-PICTURE trial using real-time AI notification (44.0% vs 9.8%) [Circulation, 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.125.078155]; persistence was examined in NOTIFY-EXTEND [JACC Cardiovasc Imaging 2025;18:841]. Both primary outcomes are prescribing, not events — NOTIFY-1's authors state explicitly that whether this reduces ASCVD events remains unanswered.

## Guideline/policy status and caveats

A 2025 AHA scientific statement endorses opportunistic CAC detection [passage text removed] prevention tool, noting ~19 million such scans annually in the US against >17 million guideline-eligible but under-screened individuals [Circulation 2025;152(19):e391–e401 — 10.1161/CIR.0000000000001382]. Limitations to weigh:

- Most non-gated AI-CAC studies are small and retrospective; many evaluate algorithms trained only on gated CT, and motion artifact is a recurring failure mode [Cureus scoping review, cureus.com/articles/410917].
- False positives/negatives arise from non-coronary calcification, motion, very high calcium burden and complex anatomy, plus left-main/LAD vessel misassignment — radiologist oversight is still considered essential in routine practice [PMC13136568].
- Generalizability gaps: the 20,084-patient cohorts were predominantly non-Hispanic white, and CAC-based methods cannot detect non-calcified plaque [Nat Commun 12:715]; the VA model was developed in veterans and may not transfer to general populations [10.1056/AIoa2400937].
- Standardization across scanners, slice thickness and protocols remains unresolved and is a stated prerequisite for longitudinal surveillance use [PMC13070230, PMC11681960].

One further note: a vendor press release describes a new CMS HCPCS code (G0680) for algorithmic CAC/aortic valve calcification analysis on chest CT effective April 2026 [heartlung.ai]. This is an industry source, not peer-reviewed, and I found no independent confirmation within this search.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

AI-derived CAC scores reproduce manual Agatston scoring closely enough to carry essentially the same prognostic signal — they independently predict cardiovascular events, cardiovascular mortality and all-cause mortality across gated and non-gated CT populations — and notification workflows built on them measurably increase statin prescribing; what is still missing is prospective evidence that AI-CAC deployment improves hard clinical outcomes or is cost-effective. [S:21c290b9-3ea7-599b-8897-8fb660e4d3a2][S:13c82115-2c16-57f8-925b-59ef0a553574][S:517c33ea-8a9d-5f14-93fb-97fc694005b7]

## Prognostic performance

The largest single validation applied a deep-learning CAC system to 20,084 individuals across asymptomatic (Framingham Heart Study, NLST) and stable/acute chest pain (PROMISE, ROMICAT-II) cohorts, reporting [passage text removed] independent of risk factors, alongside [passage text removed] [S:21c290b9-3ea7-599b-8897-8fb660e4d3a2]. In NLST (n=14,959; 288 ASCVD deaths; median follow-up 6.7 years), adjusted HRs for ASCVD death versus the very-low-risk group were [passage text removed]) for low, 2.79 (1.70–4.57) for moderate and 3.87 (2.45–6.11) for high AI-CAC risk; comparable gradients were seen in PROMISE (adjusted for Framingham Risk Score, HR 2.95 for high risk) [S:1ee4d23d-d3bf-5e70-a5fd-581ee302bd07]. Test–retest ICC for the automated score was 0.993 versus 0.997 for manual scoring [S:7097dce2-a2e1-5b57-8788-7bf05f42a1b0].

A 2026 scoping review of AI-CAC studies focused on prognostication (not merely algorithm development) found [passage text removed]), and prognostic value beyond traditional risk factors including in asymptomatic and non-cardiac imaging populations [S:8d144438-73ed-53f9-b270-c8efa48b3602][S:13c82115-2c16-57f8-925b-59ef0a553574]. Its tabulated examples span oncology and surgical settings: CVD mortality in lung cancer screening (OR 1.72 for CAC 101–400; 2.62 for >400), post-resection mortality in NSCLC (HR 1.78 for CAC 100–399; 2.37 for ≥400), anthracycline cardiotoxicity in DLBCL (OR 2.59 for CAC 1–100; 5.24 for >100), and a "calcium-omics" radiomics model (HR 3.62 from 39 calcium features for MACE) [S:3631aff3-85ef-52ef-a15f-2c6fdbf3ce2f]. In a separate health-system cohort, DL-derived incidental CAC ≥100 on non-gated chest CT was associated with higher all-cause death (HR [passage text removed]) versus DL-CAC = 0 [S:36f6a537-d964-5d86-be8c-1b1305aca86b], and only 26% of patients with algorithm-detected CAC >100 were on a statin [S:c46ccd49-658a-5824-8214-04cffa3e7c2b].

## Agreement with the reference standard

Automated scores classify patients into the same guideline risk category as expert readers in the large majority of cases: 89% concordance with κ=0.90 and Spearman r=0.90 in one 1,849-scan test set, at ~13 seconds per scan [S:fb056b11-a4d3-5f83-a08c-be174d12fd6c]. On non-gated NLST scans, category agreement was lower (κ=0.72; correct risk group in 78.8%; sensitivity 90%, specificity 94% for CAC presence) [S:91a3d896-d2b0-5de8-941e-638a3d10667d]. On low-dose CT attenuation-correction data, DL CAC scoring showed interscore agreement of 0.986 with manual reading and a 3.6% reclassification rate [S:4246f16c-a474-5872-8ecd-62ada53b5b7c], and automatic LDCT CAC scoring in a PET cohort remained prognostic for MACE (higher event rates in CAC-positive patients, most marked above 400), though detection sensitivity/specificity were 79.3%/80.2%, with 93.2% of missed CAC-positive cases having Agatston scores of only 1–100 [S:f6645d79-c06f-5362-9277-62baf7ac1d50].

## Actionability and downstream care

Notification workflows driven by AI-CAC changed management: statin prescription within 6 months was 51.2% vs 6.9% and 44% vs 9.8% in notification versus usual-care arms, and 87% of patients started on a statin after notification persisted at 18 months [S:3631aff3-85ef-52ef-a15f-2c6fdbf3ce2f]. Notifications also improved downstream lipid testing, LDL-C reduction and CAD evaluation [S:8d144438-73ed-53f9-b270-c8efa48b3602]. The NOTIFY-1 quality-improvement project screened 2,113 patients without known CAD, identifying 424 with CAC, and increased statin prescribing [S:36f6a537-d964-5d86-be8c-1b1305aca86b][S:98379426-b9c7-5487-8ee6-32cdadb573bd]. The rationale is that incidental CAC on non-gated CT is predictive but chronically underreported — reportedly documented in only 44–59% of such scans [S:df2ccfc9-0289-517b-b6b2-821a1494e12d][S:98379426-b9c7-5487-8ee6-32cdadb573bd]. Integrated with SPECT/PET attenuation-correction CT, AI-CAC improved detection of obstructive/haemodynamically significant CAD and reduced false negatives [S:8d144438-73ed-53f9-b270-c8efa48b3602].

## Limitations of the evidence

- Most studies are retrospective and heterogeneous in design, demographics, imaging protocols and outcomes, precluding pooled synthesis; some share overlapping source populations (e.g., NLST), so apparent consistency is not fully independent replication [S:c7feccb2-b485-5b24-aba8-aede80d0225d].
- On an AI translational-maturity framework, most studies remain at stage 1 (initial development/validation), with limited progress to real-world implementation and none addressing long-term model performance monitoring [S:a9de9cfb-c3f5-590e-b075-789d30c7c9f5]; the radiomics studies included were all non-prospective [S:abf5820e-fc3a-592e-ab3b-0a73cb0c436e].
- Health-economic evidence is thin: only a minority of studies quantified economic impact (one estimating US$0.006 per screened patient with automated notification, ≈US$6,485 per million; another placing opportunistic CAC analysis under US$100), and no formal cost-effectiveness analyses were performed [S:abf5820e-fc3a-592e-ab3b-0a73cb0c436e]. CMS reimbursement pathways for AI-detected CAC now exist [S:c7feccb2-b485-5b24-aba8-aede80d0225d].
- Technical failure modes persist: the DL algorithm used for opportunistic screening had a >10% false-positive rate requiring image re-review, and was restricted to non-contrast scans [S:c99c4b5c-ad2d-51b2-b729-13cd90864dd6]. Misclassification from mis-segmentation and pick-up of non-coronary (aortic, annular, valvular) calcium is a recognised source of error [S:d8cff86d-5326-5180-bb23-6d3ebbc1e92e], and single-institution validation limits generalisability claims [S:b32f5512-cc24-5d38-a1ab-903caac0d708].
- Implementation barriers include PACS–EHR interoperability, ownership and actionability of AI findings, follow-up capacity, automation bias and explainability [S:3e65178e-fb38-564e-9624-5048dd6eeb06].
- Whether AI enhancement translates into better treatment adherence or fewer adverse events is described as still unclear, with CAC-guided outcome trials (CorCal, ROBINSCA, CAC PREVENTABLE) pending [S:df2ccfc9-0289-517b-b6b2-821a1494e12d].
- Context on incremental value: in a holistic AI analysis of 10,480 hybrid MPI patients, coronary calcium alone gave an AUC of 0.64 (0.57–0.71) for all-cause mortality versus 0.80 (0.74–0.87) for a combined MPI/CT/stress/clinical model (p<0.001) — i.e., AI-CAC is one contributor, not a standalone predictor [S:d104f41d-d2b6-5754-87dc-5007f35c518a].

I found no source in these searches reporting a randomised trial of AI-CAC deployment with cardiovascular event endpoints; the available randomised evidence is limited to prescribing/process outcomes [S:3631aff3-85ef-52ef-a15f-2c6fdbf3ce2f][S:517c33ea-8a9d-5f14-93fb-97fc694005b7].

rows.question: Which exercise stress parameters stratify risk of major adverse cardiovascular events after a normal exercise SPECT myocardial perfusion study?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: A stress rate pressure product at peak exercise below the conventional threshold of about 25,000 is associated with more cardiac events, independently of the other exercise parameters tested; A low Duke treadmill score is likewise associated with more cardiac events after a normal exercise perfusion study; Neither failure to reach 85% of the age-predicted maximum heart rate nor a low metabolic equivalent level reached independent significance in the same model, a preliminary observation from few events rather than evidence that these parameters carry no prognostic information. Certainty: The risk gradients are moderate-strength observed associations from a single large clinical sample with few events, and the non-significant parameters are underpowered nulls rather than established negatives. Scope: applies to known or suspected coronary artery disease with a normal exercise SPECT myocardial perfusion study in adults able to complete a treadmill or bicycle protocol, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents ischemic exercise ECG changes accompanying a normal perfusion study as an established marker of higher event risk or recommends further testing on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

After a normal exercise SPECT MPI, residual MACE risk is stratified chiefly by **hemodynamic and functional-capacity variables — peak rate–pressure product, exercise capacity (METs/Duke treadmill score), chronotropic response (heart-rate reserve, peak HR), heart-rate recovery, and exercise ST-segment changes** — whereas the conventional "adequacy" criterion of ≥85% age-predicted maximum heart rate performs poorly as a prognostic marker.

## Evidence by parameter

**Peak rate–pressure product (RPP) — the best-supported single parameter.** In a retrospective cohort of patients with normal rest–exercise SPECT MPI (58% male, mean age 59 ± 10 years; 44 primary events over 55 ± 22 months), RPP_stress <25,000 was associated with increased risk of the primary endpoint (HR 2.03, 95% CI 1.08–3.83, p = 0.028), and remained predictive in a multivariable exercise-parameter model ([passage text removed]), while APHR_max <85% was not associated with risk on either univariable or multivariable analysis; Kaplan–Meier curves separated by RPP but not by APHR_max [10.1007/s10554-026-03658-0; PMID 41706385]. Independently, in 266 patients with **known** CAD and normal stress SPECT followed a median 12 years, rate-pressure product at peak stress was an independent predictor of both total mortality and cardiac mortality (alongside age, diabetes, male sex) [PMID 23912382]. In a 15-year follow-up of 233 patients with normal exercise ⁹⁹ᵐTc-sestamibi SPECT, multivariable predictors of MACE included resting rate-pressure product (HR 1.14, 95% CI 1.04–1.25), resting diastolic BP (HR 0.79), peak exercise heart rate (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.71–0.89) and ST-segment changes (HR 2.94, 95% CI 1.44–5.99) [PMC3462309].

**Exercise capacity / Duke treadmill score.** In the same normal-SPECT cohort, METs and DTS were predictive of the primary outcome on univariable Cox analysis, and DTS ≥5 or ≥7 METs portended good prognosis [10.1007/s10554-026-03658-0]. Among patients with a high-risk DTS despite normal exercise-gated MPI, the 2-year non-fatal MI rate was 5.8% versus <1% in low- and moderate-risk DTS groups, and this subgroup had significantly lower METs [PMC6034546]; a separate series found high-risk DTS patients with normal SPECT had lower event rates than those with abnormal SPECT, but not negligible ones [PMID 26037600]. In elderly patients undergoing exercise MPI, lower exercise capacity (<7 METs) predicted mortality, and the normal/abnormal MPI dichotomy did not further stratify those with poor functional capacity [PMC3943782]; achieving ≥10 METs in older adults identified low rates of ischemia and MACE [10.1007/s12350-018-1376-7]. Exercise capacity was also among the predictors of long-term mortality after normal exercise SPECT [PMID 24379127].

**Chronotropic response (heart-rate reserve) rather than the 85% APHR threshold.** In 866 patients undergoing exercise stress MPS, heart-rate reserve <67% (Youden-derived) carried an annualized event rate of [passage text removed]) versus 0.79 (0.54–1.14) for HRR ≥67%, incidence rate ratio 2.18 (1.32–3.61); critically, **among patients with essentially normal perfusion (SDS <5%), annualized event rates were 1.44 with HRR <67% versus 0.74 with HRR ≥67%**, and HRR added to a clinical + MPS model (global χ² 66→82, p < .005) [PMC9553802; 10.1007/s12350-021-02743-2]. Earlier work showed low %HR reserve outperformed the 85%-APMHR criterion for predicting cardiac death [PMID 15261942].

**Heart-rate recovery.** [passage text removed], HRR at 1–3 min predicted MACE independently, with HRR at 3 min strongest (HRR3 ≥35 bpm: adjusted HR 0.119, 95% CI 0.068–0.208; HRR2 ≥34: HR 0.279; HRR1 ≥22: HR 0.472) [PMC10074983]. In broader treadmill cohorts, abnormal HRR plus abnormal chronotropic response predicted death/non-fatal MI even within the **low-risk DTS** stratum ([passage text removed]) [S0002870308003979], and chronotropic incompetence and abnormal HRR each predicted cardiovascular mortality, with relative risk 4.2 when both were abnormal [PMID 17446799].

**Additive/cumulative burden — the integrating concept.** In 892 patients with a normal stress MPI (2015–2017; 82.6% with possible cardiac symptoms), at least one abnormal stress exercise marker was present in 65.1% and ≥3 markers in 9.6%, conferring a stepwise increase in adverse events; per the society summary of this paper, each additional marker was associated with a ~36% relative increase in the rate of all-cause mortality and non-fatal MI [S1071358125001412; PMID 40513979; ASNC news release]. The markers assessed in this literature stream comprise exercise capacity/METs, chronotropic index, heart-rate recovery, hemodynamic gain index, abnormal blood-pressure response, and ST/angina-based DTS [10.1007/s10554-026-03658-0].

## Caveats

- The most directly on-point study (RPP vs APHR_max) was small with few events, used all-cause rather than cardiac death as an endpoint, and could not derive population-specific ROC thresholds — its authors state this explicitly [10.1007/s10554-026-03658-0].
- Hemodynamic gain index and abnormal blood-pressure response were measured in that cohort but I found no tool-sourced result showing either independently stratified MACE after a normal scan; I cannot support a claim either way.
- The HRR-recovery and heart-rate-reserve data come from mixed cohorts undergoing exercise MPS; only the heart-rate-reserve study reported an explicit normal-perfusion (SDS <5%) subgroup analysis [PMC9553802].
- Baseline risk remains low overall: annualized cardiac event rate <1% with 0.28% mortality in the normal-SPECT cohort [10.1007/s10554-026-03658-0], and annualized cardiac mortality ~0.3% at 15 years [PMC3462309] — so these parameters modify a low absolute risk rather than defining a high-risk group.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

After a normal exercise SPECT MPI, risk is stratified mainly by **the hemodynamic burden achieved at peak stress (stress rate–pressure product), exercise capacity measures (Duke treadmill score, METs), and heart-rate response variables (peak/reserve heart rate, heart-rate recovery)** — whereas the conventional "adequate stress" criterion, ≥85% of age-predicted maximum heart rate (APHR_max), does **not** predict events [S:f7561d55][S:c776a58a][S:a806d6ba][S:6abba1c6].

## Primary evidence: dedicated study of stress parameters in normal exercise SPECT

A retrospective cohort of 1,020 patients with normal exercise SPECT MPI (44 primary events) directly compared candidate exercise markers [S:c776a58a]. Prognosis overall was excellent (<1% annualized cardiac event rate; 0.28% mortality) [S:c776a58a]. Patients with events had lower stress rate-pressure product (RPP_stress 25,240 ± 5503 vs 26,758 ± 4969, p = 0.049), lower METs (6.4 ± 2.1 vs 7.1 ± 1.9, p = 0.018), and lower Duke treadmill score (p = 0.011), while %APHR_max did not differ (p = 0.112) and hemodynamic gain index did not differ (1.7 ± 0.7 vs 1.8 ± 0.7, p = 0.741); ECG ischemia criteria were no more frequent in those with events [S:c776a58a].

In multivariable Cox models of exercise parameters [S:f7561d55]:
- **RPP_stress <25,000: [passage text removed].037**
- **DTS <5: HR 2.30 (1.26–4.20), p = 0.007**
- METs <7: HR 1.80 (0.93–3.47), p = 0.082 (not significant)
- APHR_max <85%: HR 1.19 (0.57–2.45), p = 0.644 (not significant)

Combining clinical and exercise risk, RPP_stress <25,000 remained incremental to the Framingham risk score (HR 2.03, 1.08–3.83, p = 0.028) and DTS <5 remained predictive (HR 2.27, 1.24–4.14, p = 0.008), while APHR_max was again non-predictive [S:f7561d55]. RPP became borderline once prior CAD was in the model (HR 1.82, 0.96–3.47, p = 0.066) [S:f7561d55], but stayed predictive [passage text removed], 1.11–4.73, p = 0.025) [S:c776a58a]. Discrimination of individual parameters was modest (AUC 0.59 for RPP_stress at cutpoint <24,896; 0.57 for APHR_max <85.5%) [S:c776a58a]. Clinical covariates that mattered were Framingham risk score and prior CAD (HR 2.60, 1.32–5.14, p = 0.006) [S:f7561d55].

## Corroborating evidence

- **Long-term normal-scan cohort (233 patients, mean follow-up 15.5 ± 4.9 years; annualized MACE 1.8%):** independent multivariable predictors of MACE were age, male sex, diabetes, resting diastolic blood pressure, resting rate–pressure product, [passage text removed] [S:10ae24bd][S:0c74ab2b][S:a806d6ba].
- **Exercise capacity modifies the "warranty period" of a normal scan:** with a normal MPS, achieving ≥10 METs corresponds to cardiac death <0.1%/year; absence of risk factors plus 9 METs to ~0.2%/year annual death, versus ~1.6%/year with ≥2 risk factors (diabetes, smoking, hypertension) and <6 METs [S:6abba1c6].
- **Heart-rate response variables add prognostic information over perfusion data:** in large SPECT cohorts, exercise capacity, percentage heart-rate reserve achieved, and heart-rate recovery were [passage text removed], incremental to SPECT extent/severity [S:f9a9c60b]. In 2,428 patients undergoing exercise testing with thallium SPECT, abnormal heart-rate recovery (≤12 bpm at 1 minute) predicted death after adjustment that included perfusion defects and workload (adjusted RR 2.0, 1.5–2.7) [S:106c350b]; a systematic review likewise lists poor/fair fitness and abnormal heart-rate recovery among independent predictors of all-cause mortality alongside SPECT risk category [S:206c3cad].

## Caveats

The dedicated normal-SPECT comparison is a single retrospective cohort with few events, so hazard ratios are imprecise and the RPP effect is attenuated by prior CAD [S:c776a58a][S:f7561d55]. Evidence for heart-rate recovery and heart-rate reserve comes from mixed cohorts (normal and abnormal scans), not exclusively normal studies [S:f9a9c60b][S:106c350b]; I found no source specifically validating hemodynamic gain index or chronotropic index as predictors within a normal exercise SPECT population — in the one cohort that tested it, HGI did not differ between event and event-free patients [S:c776a58a].

rows.question: In which clinical scenarios do ESC guidelines position cardiovascular magnetic resonance as a first-line diagnostic test?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance is positioned as a first-line, adjudicatory test in scenarios of high diagnostic uncertainty, including myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries, suspected cardiomyopathy, sports participation after myocarditis and complex valvular disease; In chronic coronary syndromes stress perfusion cardiovascular magnetic resonance sits among the frontline functional tests, both for suspected obstructive coronary disease and for angina or ischaemia without obstructive coronary arteries; This positioning reflects a shift from a last-resort problem-solving modality to a frequently recommended investigation, recommendations commonly being Class I or IIa at Level B or C. Certainty: This describes where guidance places the test rather than showing patient benefit; several of these recommendations rest on Level C evidence and no patient outcomes were compared between imaging strategies. Scope: applies to cardiovascular disease requiring diagnostic cardiac imaging in adults, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents magnetic resonance-guided pathways as demonstrated to improve patient outcomes such as mortality or repeat admissions.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

ESC guidelines place CMR as a **first-line (Class I) test in five main settings**: suspected/confirmed cardiomyopathy at initial work-up, MINOCA, suspected myocarditis/pericarditis, suspected AL cardiac amyloidosis, and as one of the initial functional imaging options in suspected chronic coronary syndrome — plus specific arrhythmia and heart-failure scenarios. In valvular disease and most acute coronary scenarios it remains an adjudicatory second-line test. A 2015–2025 mapping review concludes [passage text removed] ESC guidance," identified across 13 ESC guidelines, with recommendations commonly Class I/IIa, Level B/C ([PMC13181430]([passage text removed]); PMID 42145176).

## Scenario-by-scenario evidence

**Suspected cardiomyopathy (initial aetiological work-up).** The 2023 ESC cardiomyopathy guideline recommends contrast-enhanced CMR in all patients with cardiomyopathy at initial evaluation (Class I, Level B), with follow-up CMR every 2–5 years as Class IIa C; contrast CT is positioned as the fallback only when echo is inadequate *and* CMR is contraindicated ([hvt-journal.com/articles/art440](http://www.hvt-journal.com/articles/art440); [mijn.bsl.nl]([passage text removed])). The guideline states for the first time that non-ischaemic scar or fatty replacement on CMR can be the sole clue to a cardiomyopathy diagnosis ([art440](http://www.hvt-journal.com/articles/art440)), and CMR has "a prominent role... [passage text removed])" ([PMC12014885]([passage text removed])).

**MINOCA.** The 2023 ACS guideline: "[passage text removed]" (Class I, Level B). The text calls CMR "[passage text removed]," to be performed as soon as possible after presentation, ideally during the index admission, and states it can identify the cause in up to 87% of such patients ([guideline PDF](https://www.uniklinik-ulm.de/fileadmin/default/09_Sonstige/Klinische-Chemie/Downloads/ESC_Guideline_ACS_2023.pdf)). By contrast, for suspected LV thrombus CMR is only Class IIa C ([europepmc.org/articles/pmc12506753](https://europepmc.org/articles/pmc12506753?pdf=render)).

**Myocarditis and pericarditis.** The 2025 ESC inflammatory myocardial/pericardial syndromes guideline gives CMR a Class I, Level B indication in clinical suspicion of myocarditis and/or pericarditis for non-invasive diagnosis of inflammation, and Class I for diagnosis of suspected myocarditis including oedema, ischaemia and necrosis/fibrosis assessment; follow-up CMR within the first 6 months is also Class I, and for pericarditis CMR is Class I B when diagnosis cannot be made on clinical criteria ([PMC13237535](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13237535); [cardiac-imaging.org/2025_ESC_myocarditis](https://cardiac-imaging.org/2025_ESC_myocarditis)). This is a genuine paradigm shift: CMR can now yield a "CMR-proven" definitive clinical diagnosis using the updated Lake Louise criteria (one T1-based plus one T2-based criterion), paralleling rather than requiring endomyocardial biopsy ([PMC13237535](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13237535); [revespcardiol.org]([passage text removed])).

**Cardio-oncology.** The 2022 ESC cardio-oncology guideline recommends CMR in suspected AL cardiac amyloidosis at Class I, **Level A** — one of only a handful of Level A Class I recommendations in that document — with endomyocardial biopsy relegated to Class IIa C if CMR is non-diagnostic ([guideline PDF](https://www.portailvasculaire.fr/sites/default/files/docs/2022_esc_eha_estro_ic-os_cardio_oncologie_ehj_0.pdf); [acc.org key points]([passage text removed])). CMR is also Class I B to exclude myocarditis and MI in Takotsubo syndrome ([guideline PDF]([passage text removed])). For serial cardiotoxicity monitoring, however, 3D-echo is preferred and CMR is reserved for when TTE is unavailable or non-diagnostic ([cardiologywiki summary]([passage text removed])).

**Chronic coronary syndromes.** The 2024 CCS guideline states that first-line diagnostic testing should be non-invasive anatomical *or* functional imaging, and gives stress CMR perfusion a Class I, Level B recommendation in suspected CCS with moderate-to-high (>15%–85%) pre-test likelihood, to diagnose and quantify ischaemia and/or scar and estimate MACE risk ([guideline PDF](https://api.iscpcardio.org/storage/guidelines/_24_Chr_Coro_Sy_ESC.pdf)). Note the nuance: CCTA is the preferred first-line test to rule out obstructive CAD at low-to-moderate likelihood (Class I A), and PET is preferred for absolute myocardial blood flow, with CMR perfusion offered as an alternative ([same PDF](https://api.iscpcardio.org/storage/guidelines/_24_Chr_Coro_Sy_ESC.pdf); [revespcardiol commentary]([passage text removed])).

**Ventricular arrhythmias / SCD (2022).** CMR is Class I [passage text removed], and Class I in suspected ARVC and suspected HCM; it is Class IIa for newly documented VA with suspected non-coronary structural heart disease and for PVCs/VT atypical for idiopathic origin despite a normal echocardiogram, IIa for DCM work-up/risk stratification, and IIb in relatives of sudden arrhythmic death syndrome decedents ([Europace spotlight, PMC10228619]([passage text removed]); [ARVC recommendation table]([passage text removed])).

**Heart failure (2021).** Two Class I C indications: assessment of myocardial structure and function when echocardiographic acoustic windows are poor, and myocardial tissue characterisation [passage text removed] iron overload/haemochromatosis; LGE to separate ischaemic from non-ischaemic damage in DCM is only Class IIa ([guideline PDF]([passage text removed]); [PMC10364363]([passage text removed])).

**Adult congenital heart disease (2020).** Guideline text designates CMR [passage text removed] (CT as alternative) and the "method of choice" for quantifying ventricular volumes, EF and relative left/right lung blood-flow distribution ([2020 ACHD guideline PDF]([passage text removed])) — a modality-of-choice statement rather than a numbered Class I recommendation.

## Where CMR is explicitly *not* first-line

In the 2021 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, CMR is positioned as the tiebreaker: it "[passage text removed]," and is "useful when echocardiographic evaluation of severe [primary mitral regurgitation] grade is inconclusive" ([PMC9725093]([passage text removed])). Similarly, in HCM, CMR with LGE is Class I B specifically in patients with *inadequate echocardiographic windows* ([PMC10364363]([passage text removed])).

## Caveats

Across all ESC guidelines, 92 CMR-specific recommendations exist, of which 40 (43.5%) are Class I, but most rest on Level C evidence (56/92; 60.9%) and only 2 on Level A ([PMC10364363]([passage text removed]); PMID 37482604). That analysis predates the 2023 cardiomyopathy, 2024 CCS and 2025 myocarditis/pericarditis guidelines, so current Class I counts are higher. Both the guideline-mapping review and Spanish commentary on the 2024 CCS guideline flag limited availability of stress CMR as a barrier to implementing these recommendations ([PMC10364363]([passage text removed]); [revespcardiol.org]([passage text removed])). One discrepancy I could not resolve from the sources retrieved: secondary summaries of the 2025 myocarditis guideline report the 6-month follow-up CMR recommendation as Level C ([PMC13237535](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13237535)) versus Level B ([cardiac-imaging.org](https://cardiac-imaging.org/2025_ESC_myocarditis)); the Class I designation is consistent in both.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

ESC guidelines position CMR as a genuinely first-line (Class I) test in a defined set of scenarios — chiefly suspected MINOCA, suspected/undifferentiated cardiomyopathy, suspected myocarditis and inflammatory myocardial disease, tissue-characterisation questions in heart failure, several cardio-oncology presentations, and quantification of right-heart/great-vessel and regurgitant-lesion burden where echocardiography is inadequate or discordant. A 2015–2025 structured review of 13 ESC guidelines concluded CMR has moved "[passage text removed]," with an "adjudicatory" rather than adjunctive role, most recommendations sitting at Class I/IIa, Level B/C [S:20ca214d-af6e-5b50-a82a-be1206fc2201][S:153fc3af-1462-54a1-ba8d-530db4a1ee43][S:a85afe84-12ec-53df-beea-7f6dd53ee61b].

## Scenarios where CMR is first-line

**1. MINOCA / troponin-positive chest pain with unobstructed coronaries.** The 2020 ESC NSTE-ACS guideline recommends [passage text removed] B) [S:7a597188-71fa-50ea-a6e3-9d468074797a][S:b61eec29-9a3a-5332-bf56-356f56422ed1]; ESC's earlier ACS documents also advised CMR within 2 weeks of symptom onset to maximise diagnostic accuracy for the aetiological cause [S:a6a9e5dd-3b7c-59cb-a8d1-a22754f119e4]. The 2023 unified ACS guideline reinforces CMR in the structured MINOCA evaluation, distinguishing infarction from myocarditis, Takotsubo or other non-ischaemic injury, plus post-infarct prognostic markers (infarct size, microvascular obstruction, intramyocardial haemorrhage, LV thrombus) [S:7886b93a-c1f4-527e-88af-22b644130642].

**2. Suspected cardiomyopathy (baseline phenotyping).** The 2023 ESC cardiomyopathy guideline recommends contrast-enhanced [passage text removed]), with Class IIa for serial follow-up/monitoring [S:2399f812-fd49-5e77-84a4-8091c0287ddf]; it is cited as Class I, Level B for diagnosis and phenotyping, particularly when echocardiography is inconclusive or tissue characterisation is critical [S:659aedaa-43f6-5ec7-9b03-d0b417d06373][S:51259485-b3e0-52bd-a5e5-0e800bd17388]. For the first time these guidelines accept [passage text removed] CMR as the sole diagnostic clue to a cardiomyopathy [S:57f6dc63-4d0d-53fc-946b-17f8dbdf4cbb] — most consequential [passage text removed] converts an indeterminate phenotype into a guideline-defined entity with device implications [S:88d1535c-1e16-589c-bb77-772d7d67e775]. In HCM specifically, CMR with LGE is Class I when echocardiographic windows are inadequate, to confirm the diagnosis [S:77423de6-bf1a-5306-8d4c-cac881a8de8a].

**3. Suspected myocarditis and pericarditis with myocardial involvement.** CMR is recommended for confirmation of myocardial involvement in pericarditis-associated myocarditis (Class I, Level C, 2015 pericardial diseases guideline) [S:a6a9e5dd-3b7c-59cb-a8d1-a22754f119e4][S:d6e76a9d-0b2f-5a2a-b56d-e04b25a4968a]. The 2025 ESC myocarditis/pericarditis guideline recommends CMR in patients with suspected myocarditis who have clinical, biomarker, ECG or echocardiographic abnormalities, applying the updated Lake Louise criteria, with highest sensitivity when performed within the first weeks of symptom onset; endomyocardial biopsy is reserved for severe or specific presentations [S:58c84af0-9aac-5bee-af8f-55c75b5b9512][S:8cdbeba6-7ea6-51ea-995b-a6ea0e6363c9][S:a912cf0f-7d9a-50eb-8a36-414cf48e5fc7]. Note: for pericardial disease generally, CT/CMR are explicitly framed as *second-level* testing (Class I, Level C), so "first-line" does not extend to uncomplicated pericarditis [S:a6a9e5dd-3b7c-59cb-a8d1-a22754f119e4].

**4. Heart failure — poor windows and suspected infiltrative/inflammatory/storage disease.** The 2021 ESC HF guideline gives Class I (Level C) for [passage text removed] echocardiographic acoustic windows, and Class I (Level C) for tissue characterisation in suspected infiltrative disease, Fabry disease, myocarditis, LV non-compaction, amyloid, sarcoidosis and iron overload/haemochromatosis; distinguishing ischaemic from non-ischaemic damage in DCM is Class IIa [S:68a3f52b-7a3c-5a78-b23a-eac06cee7566][S:9ad93201-5699-5988-ab5d-c68ed2c1b4da]. The same guideline names CMR the preferred modality in complex congenital heart disease [S:7c6e77a8-a5dd-5012-9ec8-85173d024190].

**5. Cardio-oncology.** The 2022 guideline carries four Class I CMR recommendations: diagnosis of immune checkpoint inhibitor–associated myocarditis (I, B); exclusion of myocarditis and myocardial infarction in suspected Takotsubo (I, B); confirmation of pericardial disease and exclusion of associated myocarditis (I, C); and suspected AL cardiac amyloidosis (I, A). CMR for routine [passage text removed] is Class IIa — i.e. echocardiography remains first-line for LVEF surveillance [S:bd26da74-7fc8-5dd6-9bae-d8648087a3c6][S:f1d21979-96a7-50c9-9105-7358d045526a].

**6. Chronic coronary syndromes / ANOCA-INOCA.** Stress perfusion CMR is one of the accepted frontline non-invasive functional imaging options for suspected obstructive CAD (the umbrella recommendation "non-invasive functional imaging or coronary CTA as the initial test" is Class I, Level B), with test choice driven by clinical likelihood, local expertise and availability [S:248b3300-bd23-5b09-bcb0-23f76429a7d5]. The 2024 ESC guidance keeps stress CMR alongside other frontline functional tests and raises its profile in ANOCA/INOCA [S:7886b93a-c1f4-527e-88af-22b644130642]. Historically the 2013 stable-CAD guideline listed CMR as a recommended initial test at intermediate pre-test probability (Class I) [S:7dc13449-f719-5b22-9fd9-e8a562f4440a][S:fd46c5ca-d294-55e4-b7d8-464f15f07d81], but the 2019 CCS guideline downgraded CMR for an inconclusive echocardiographic test to Class IIb [S:248b3300-bd23-5b09-bcb0-23f76429a7d5], and coronary CTA is the Class I-A first-line test to exclude significant CAD at low-to-moderate pre-test probability [S:2d145749-0b44-587a-9ae2-ad347e65e47a].

**7. Valvular heart disease — inconclusive or discordant echocardiography, and right-sided lesions.** The 2017 ESC/EACTS guideline directs CMR use when echocardiographic quality is inadequate or results discrepant, to grade regurgitant lesions, ventricular volumes and function, ascending aortic abnormality and fibrosis, and names CMR the *reference method* for RV volumes and function — hence particularly useful in tricuspid regurgitation [S:2db0a70e-9440-56bd-b7f9-46ec5ed8868d]. [passage text removed] echocardiography [passage text removed] regurgitant volume/fraction and reference-standard volumes can define the need to intervene [S:88d1535c-1e16-589c-bb77-772d7d67e775].

**8. Adult congenital heart disease.** CMR's quantitative strengths underpin RV volumes/EF, [passage text removed] — pivotal for timing [passage text removed] and for surveillance of a systemic RV [S:6ea523ae-336d-50eb-881c-a9061e5332f4]. In the 2020 ACHD guideline, extensive RV scarring on CMR is embedded in SCD risk-stratification criteria (Class IIa), and functional imaging including stress CMR is Class I to confirm/exclude ischaemia in coronary anomalies [S:248b3300-bd23-5b09-bcb0-23f76429a7d5].

**9. Aortic disease and pregnancy.** Imaging of the entire aorta by CT or MRI is Class I (Level C) before pregnancy in [passage text removed], and non-contrast MRI is the recommended modality (Class I, Level C) for imaging [passage text removed], arch or descending aorta [S:c6c83ae7-2be9-50fe-bf07-7929f2129d2f][S:9b2e99ce-de46-578b-ae2e-8fea2f314c3d]. The 2014 aortic diseases guideline contained eight Class I CMR-referencing recommendations — the largest Class I count of any ESC guideline surveyed [S:532219a8-2d87-59c9-bd7b-2e3d96df88aa].

**10. Sports cardiology and arrhythmia substrate.** The 2020 sports guideline uses CMR to separate physiological athlete's heart from cardiomyopathy and to inform return-to-play after myocarditis [S:a912cf0f-7d9a-50eb-8a36-414cf48e5fc7]. The 2022 ventricular arrhythmia/SCD guideline is the most CMR-dense document (17 recommendations, 4 Class I), using LGE-CMR for risk refinement in DCM, hypokinetic non-dilated cardiomyopathy, HCM and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, and for substrate delineation before ablation [S:532219a8-2d87-59c9-bd7b-2e3d96df88aa][S:6ea523ae-336d-50eb-881c-a9061e5332f4].

## Where CMR is *not* first-line
Pulmonary hypertension (echocardiography is the Class I first-line screen; RHC is Class I confirmatory; the 2022 guideline contains a single Class IIb CMR recommendation) [S:e7f8a90c-293d-5de1-84a7-2bb9e617157a][S:532219a8-2d87-59c9-bd7b-2e3d96df88aa]; infective endocarditis (no specific CMR recommendation) [S:77423de6-bf1a-5306-8d4c-cac881a8de8a]; routine cancer-therapy LVEF surveillance [S:f1d21979-96a7-50c9-9105-7358d045526a]; and pericarditis work-up beyond myocardial involvement [S:a6a9e5dd-3b7c-59cb-a8d1-a22754f119e4].

**Caveat:** many recommendations remain Level C, and the review authors explicitly call for prospective, management-linked trials to convert CMR metrics into outcome-anchored decision thresholds; access and standardisation remain barriers [S:7886b93a-c1f4-527e-88af-22b644130642][S:153fc3af-1462-54a1-ba8d-530db4a1ee43].

rows.question: How well does photon-counting CT detect obstructive coronary stenosis compared with invasive angiography?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Against invasive angiography at a threshold of more than 50% diameter stenosis, pooled sensitivity is high and similar at patient, vessel and segment level (about 95%); Pooled specificity is lowest when whole patients are classified (about 82%) and rises at the vessel (about 89%) and segment (about 95%) levels; The practical strength of the technique is confident exclusion of obstructive disease, that is a high-confidence rule-out test rather than a stand-alone rule-in test; Between-study heterogeneity across the pooled studies was moderate and most pronounced for specificity. Certainty: Accuracy against the invasive standard is consistently high across the available studies, but the pooled figures come from ten study-level datasets with moderate heterogeneity in specificity, and non-independent vessel- and segment-level data may overestimate their precision. Scope: applies to suspected obstructive coronary artery stenosis in adults undergoing non-invasive coronary imaging, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents photon-counting CT as shown to improve clinical outcomes or cost-effectiveness, or recommends it as a replacement for invasive angiography or as routine surveillance after revascularisation on this basis.

answers.websearch:
**Photon-counting CT (PCCT) coronary angiography detects ≥50% stenosis with high sensitivity (~90–96%) and good-to-high specificity versus invasive coronary angiography (ICA), with the ultra-high-resolution (UHR) mode performing best — especially in heavily calcified vessels — though patient-level specificity remains the weak point.**

**Pooled evidence.** A Bayesian diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis (9 studies, 843 patients) using ICA as reference reported pooled sensitivity 95.9% (95% CrI 90.2–98.7) and specificity 71.2% (54.0–87.4) at patient level; 90.4% (83.7–94.5) and 92.8% (80.1–97.8) at vessel level; and 94.1% (76.4–99.2) and 93.0% (76.3–98.2) at segment level, with all AUCs ≥0.99 (PMID 41410572; doi 10.1148/ryct.250313, Radiology: Cardiothoracic Imaging 2025;7(6):e250313). An independent bivariate random-effects meta-analysis found patient-level pooled sensitivity 94.5%/specificity 81.8%, vessel-level 95.1%/89.2%, and segment-level 95.2%/94.7% (PMID 41672769; doi 10.1136/heartjnl-2025-327108). The pattern is consistent: sensitivity is uniformly high, so PCCT is a strong rule-out test, while per-patient specificity is more modest (false positives persist).

**Key primary studies.**
- *High-risk TAVR cohort (prospective, n=68):* UHR PCCT showed 96% sensitivity (23/24), 84% specificity (37/44), 88% accuracy for stenosis ≥50%, with AUC 0.93 (participant), 0.94 (vessel), 0.92 (segment); accuracy was 88%/91%/95% per participant/vessel/segment for ≥50% and 82%/89%/94% for ≥70% (doi 10.1148/radiol.223305). [passage text removed] participants ([passage text removed]).
- *Head-to-head resolution comparison (n=100, 257 vessels, ICA with 3D QCA; ≥50% stenosis prevalence 70%):* per-vessel AUC was 0.99 (0.98–1.00) for UHR-PCCTA vs 0.94 (0.91–0.98) for standard-resolution, ΔAUC 0.05 (P=0.01); UHR sensitivity/specificity 96%/100% vs SR 87%/88%. In severely calcified vessels performance held (UHR AUC 0.99, SR 0.92), and CAD-RADS agreement with QCA was near-perfect for UHR (κ=0.90) vs substantial for SR (κ=0.63) ([passage text removed]).
- *Protocol optimisation (prospective, 61 patients per arm):* per-segment sensitivity/specificity/accuracy were 92.9%/89.9%/90.5% for standard resolution and 100%/98.6%/98.8% for UHR thin reconstructions (reader 1), with similar values for reader 2 (doi 10.2214/AJR.25.33021).
- *Heavy calcification (Agatston >600):* in the subgroup with Agatston >3000 (n=18), sensitivity 92–100%/specificity 83–100% for >50% stenosis and 88–100%/89–100% for >70%, with κ 0.71–1.00 versus ICA (PMID 41266671; doi 10.1007/s00330-025-12158-z).
- *Stents:* in 44 stents (18 patients), UHR PCCT detected in-stent stenosis ≥50% with 100% sensitivity, 92.3%/87.2% specificity, 100% NPV, but low PPV (62.5%/50%) driven by non-assessable stents (PMID 38177617).

**Clinical consequence.** In a single-centre all-comers comparison (n=7,833), PCCT improved vessel-level specificity (98.0% vs 93.0%), PPV (83.3% vs 63.0%) and accuracy (97.2% vs 92.8%) versus energy-integrating CT with equal sensitivity (90.9% vs 90.7%) and NPV, and was associated with fewer ICA referrals (9.9% vs 13.1%) yet more revascularisation among those referred (43.4% vs 35.5%) (PMID 39466216; [passage text removed]).

**Caveats.** Most primary studies are small, single-centre, and enriched for high-prevalence/high-calcium or TAVR populations referred for clinically indicated ICA, which inflates sensitivity and depresses specificity estimates; the pooled patient-level specificity credible interval was wide (54–87%), and no outcome-based randomised trial of PCCT-guided management versus ICA appeared in my searches.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** Photon-counting CT (PCCT) detects ≥50% coronary stenosis against invasive coronary angiography (ICA) with very high sensitivity (~95%) and good-to-excellent specificity that improves as the unit of analysis narrows — it is an excellent rule-out test and clearly outperforms conventional energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT) on specificity, though a residual false-positive rate persists at the patient level.

**Pooled evidence.** A systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies and 1010 patients (all using a >50% diameter stenosis threshold) reported pooled sensitivity/specificity of 94.5% (95% CI 91.7–96.4) / 81.8% (73.1–88.2) with diagnostic OR 77.2 per patient; 95.1% (91.1–97.3) / 89.2% (83.7–93.1), DOR 159.9 per vessel; and 95.2% (90.8–97.6) / 94.7% (91.7–96.7), DOR 357.4 per segment [S:2c753a1f-1abf-5685-92b2-9a63170c3356]. The authors emphasise that sensitivity consistently exceeded 94% ([passage text removed] ranged 81.8–94.7%, which they attribute to case-mix (stable chest pain vs. heavy calcified burden), UHR vs. standard acquisition, rather than technical instability [S:aee48be3-e3fc-5441-b05f-f2d9ed498150]. Leave-one-out analyses kept estimates within the original CIs, and Deeks' test showed no substantial publication bias [S:fa1182e1-c481-5131-b93c-d076508ffb88][S:460ff65e-cf85-5370-8178-5115acd1cefc].

**Head-to-head vs. conventional CT.** In a prospective study of 143 patients (572 vessels, 2431 segments) with ICA reference, PCD-CT accuracy for ≥50% stenosis was 88.1% (patient), 91.6% (vessel) and 97.7% (segment) vs. 77.9%, 77.8% and 92.4% for EID-CT (p<0.01 all); for ≥70% stenosis, 90.9%/94.6%/98.6% vs. 70.6%/80.9%/94.1% [S:ba104f9d-abe2-530d-82a2-f9b60cbc2b00]. The gain was driven mainly by specificity — e.g. patient-level specificity for ≥70% stenosis was 72.7% (PCD-CT) and 86.9% (UHR subgroup) vs. 28.6% (EID-CT), with vessel-level specificity 94.6%/96.5% vs. 81.5%, while sensitivity remained ≥90% throughout [S:f8f4bafd-fb40-592b-971f-e2ad49159497]. Monte Carlo simulation projected a 14.8% mean reduction in ICA referrals with PCD-CT [S:3528fcd7-7243-5af0-8a71-650464dd0c3f]. A clinical cohort study similarly found lower ICA referral ([passage text removed]), fewer ICAs without revascularisation ([passage text removed]), and higher specificity for stenosis requiring revascularisation (0.81 vs. 0.74; p=0.04) with sensitivity 1.0 in both groups [S:2dfdcfac-f11f-5f27-94a0-dc458760c1ab].

**Hard cases where conventional CT fails.**
- *Severe calcification:* in 62 patients with Agatston >600 (median 2423, up to 7851; 94% pre-TAVR), patient-level sensitivity/specificity/accuracy vs. ICA were 98%/86%/94% and 90%/95%/92% for the two readers at the 50% threshold, and 92%/100%/93% and 93%/94%/94% at 70%; even at Agatston >3000 (n=18) sensitivity was 92–100% and specificity 83–100% for >50% stenosis, with no trend toward worse accuracy at higher calcium scores (p>0.05) [S:6a82082e-5112-56e1-b51b-835ec528f3c0][S:dd397235-9843-554c-a10c-d8ac03d4a9e3].
- *Stents:* in 44 stents/18 patients, UHR PCD-CTA detected ≥50% in-stent stenosis with sensitivity 100% (95% CI 47.8–100), specificity 92.3% and 87.2%, accuracy 93.2% and 88.6%, and NPV 100% for both readers — but PPV was only 62.5% and 50%, in a cohort with just 5 true stenoses [S:a7dc1d98-edc5-595e-a542-bff854f652aa][S:64cab59b-d992-5675-ac58-ca16c2247255].

**Caveats.** The comparative PCD-vs-EID study did not refer patients with <50% stenosis to ICA and performed no quantitative ICA analysis, so patient-level specificity/NPV were not estimable in that design [S:5ea83fa4-14a9-5339-97a0-8b206115a340][S:f8f4bafd-fb40-592b-971f-e2ad49159497]. The stent study was small, single-centre, enriched for TAVI candidates, used visual ICA rather than IVUS/OCT as reference, and did not compare against EID-CT [S:40206578-e370-538c-bba5-d8646b16ace9]. Most evidence derives from a single commercial dual-source PCD-CT platform [S:e0f70e71-6c13-543a-9384-a2199ae46e92], and no randomised outcome trial of a PCCT-first pathway appeared in my searches.

rows.question: How do long-term outcomes after acute coronary syndrome differ among patients presenting with STEMI, NSTEMI and unstable angina?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Among survivors of the first 30 days after acute coronary syndrome, those whose index event was NSTEMI go on to have the highest five-year burden of major adverse cardiovascular events and of death from any cause, exceeding both STEMI and unstable angina; Unstable angina survivors are not a low-risk group, their absolute five-year rates of major adverse cardiovascular events and of death being of a similar order to those seen after STEMI; After adjustment for age and comorbidity, STEMI and NSTEMI carry a higher hazard of major adverse cardiovascular events and of death than unstable angina, in both men and women. Certainty: The comparison rests on a large and complete body of linked outcome data and is consistent in both sexes, but it shows adjusted associations with presentation type rather than demonstrated effects of it. Scope: applies to acute coronary syndrome (STEMI, NSTEMI or unstable angina) after surviving the first 30 days from the index event in adults, population-based settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the outcome differences between acute coronary syndrome presentation types as a causal effect of the presentation type, or asserts that early invasive management or intensified secondary prevention abolishes the difference between subtypes.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

The three subtypes have opposite short- and long-term risk trajectories: STEMI carries the highest early mortality, but from roughly one month onward NSTEMI has the worse trajectory and the highest long-term event burden, while unstable angina (UA) has by far the lowest mortality — though not a low recurrence rate. Much of the NSTEMI excess is attributable to older age and comorbidity rather than the infarct type itself.

## Early vs late reversal (STEMI vs NSTEMI)

- In a large German AMI analysis, 30-day mortality was higher with STEMI (15.8% vs 12.0%), but by 3 years 28.2% of STEMI vs 37.0% of NSTEMI patients had died; landmark analysis gave [passage text removed]) for STEMI in the first month and HR 0.81 (0.80–0.82) thereafter [[passage text removed] — preprint].
- The same crossover was shown in a cardiac catheterisation cohort: "[passage text removed]" [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19506116].
- In an interventional cohort, cumulative 4-year mortality favoured NSTE-ACS because of higher early STEMI death ([passage text removed]), yet in landmark analysis from 6 months to 4 years there was no significant difference ([passage text removed]), with NSTE-ACS trending worse [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4307524].
- At 1 year, differences are often absent: OPERA reported in-hospital mortality [passage text removed] 9.0% (STEMI) vs 11.6% (NSTEMI), log-rank p = 0.09 [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17412730].
- Confounding matters: in the MONICA population registry, crude 10-year death was 19.6% (STEMI) vs 22.8% (non-STEMI, p = 0.11), but after full adjustment the 10-year risk was equivalent (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.83–1.38, p = 0.59), while adjusted 28-day risk remained lower for non-STEMI (OR 0.58, 0.36–0.94) [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7826729]. Similarly, an earlier spectrum analysis found NSTEMI/minor-myocardial-damage patients had worse *unadjusted* survival to 10 years, an excess "associated with more comorbid" conditions [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16644337].

## Three-way comparisons including unstable angina

- TACOS (1,188 consecutive ACS patients, ≥10-year follow-up): 5-year mortality 32.4% (STEMI), 51.3% (NSTEMI), 25.3% (UA); 10-year mortality 52.5%, 69.9%, 41.0% (p < 0.001). Mean survival was 7.3, 5.4 and 7.7 years respectively; NSTEMI patients had the worst outcome throughout follow-up. Deaths were cardiovascular in 73.9%, 72.5% and 57.7% of cases [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078956].
- Western Australian linked population data (73,321 ACS patients; 22.3% STEMI, 43.2% NSTEMI, 34.6% UA): cumulative 5-year MACE was 29.7% after NSTEMI vs 19.4% after STEMI and 19.9% after UA (log-rank p < 0.001) [[passage text removed]; eprints.qut.edu.au/267518]; risk of MACE and death remained high and largely unchanged over the study era among 30-day survivors of all subtypes [scilit.com/publications/e2ffb9f681760f64d1f0a38a4b7f9423].
- Alberta population cohort (31,056 patients: 49.5% NSTEMI, 34.0% STEMI, 16.5% UA): patients with NSTEMI, rather than STEMI or UA, were at highest risk of MACE (death, stroke, recurrent MI), and outcomes worsened incrementally with comorbidity burden [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8248628].
- SCAAR (PCI indications): 1-year mortality was 2.0% stable CAD, 2.2% UA, 4.7% NSTEMI, 9.6% STEMI; between 1 and 6 years the adjusted mortality risk stayed lower for stable CAD and UA than STEMI, with no difference between NSTEMI and STEMI. Recurrent MI at 1 year was 5.5% (UA), 11.0% (NSTEMI), 10.3% (STEMI). The authors attribute the gap — "especially between unstable angina and NSTEMI patients" — to myocardial damage as the key mortality predictor [[passage text removed]].
- A GRACE subset of 19,122 hospital survivors (35% STEMI, 37% NSTEMI, 28% UA) showed lower age- and sex-adjusted 2-year death, recurrent MI, heart failure and unscheduled cardiovascular rehospitalisation in STEMI than NSTEMI [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10748995].
- Contemporary registry data (TIGRIS, stable patients 1–3 years post-MI) confirm continuing divergence: 2-year all-cause death 2.6% (STEMI) vs 4.2% (NSTEMI), CV death 1.5% vs 2.5%, and composite CV death/MI/stroke 3.9% vs 5.6% (all p ≤ 0.001) [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10748995].

## Unstable angina specifically

- Mortality is low but recurrence is not: in a hs-troponin-era UA cohort, the 1-year composite endpoint occurred in 26.2% of patients, driven by new ACS (16.2%) and cardiac rehospitalisation (11.0%), with only 0.5% mortality; the same paper cites SWEDEHEART data in which 14.3% of ACS patients had UA, with all-cause mortality HR 2.06 (0.79–5.39) for UA vs 8.14 (3.63–18.23) for NSTEMI [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12057327]. Reported 1-year MI rates using current hs-cTn-based definitions are 1.4–1.9% with 1-year mortality 0.6–2.2% [[passage text removed]].
- After adjustment, UA prognosis can approach that of stable angina: in a Polish PCI registry, 3-year death/MI/MACE in UA was much lower than NSTEMI (adjusted RR for NSTEMI 1.365, 95% [passage text removed]) and comparable to stable angina [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31821194].
- The boundary is troponin-dependent, not biologically sharp: patients labelled UA who nonetheless have myocardial injury (hs-cTnT >14 ng/L) had similar post-discharge all-cause mortality to NSTEMI patients with modest peak hs-cTnT (15–49 ng/L), lower recurrent MI (HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.29–2.00 favouring UA) and marginally more heart-failure hospitalisation (HR 0.80, 0.64–0.99) over a median 3.0 years [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35063271].

## Mechanistic drivers of the differences

NSTEMI patients are older and carry more chronic heart failure, three-vessel disease, [passage text removed] peripheral arterial disease — comorbidities that drive late death [[passage text removed] — preprint], consistent with the finding that adjustment largely abolishes the late STEMI–NSTEMI gap [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7826729]. Post-ACS heart failure also differs significantly by subtype, with 1-year cumulative incidence differing between all three groups (STEMI vs NSTEMI, STEMI vs UA and NSTEMI vs UA all log-rank p < 0.01) [[passage text removed]].

**Caveats:** the German 3-year data come from a preprint; the UA-vs-NSTEMI contrast is sensitive to troponin assay generation, since progressively more former UA cases are now reclassified as NSTEMI; and several long-term comparisons are unadjusted, which systematically disadvantages NSTEMI. I found no head-to-head randomised evidence comparing long-term outcomes across the three presentations — all evidence above is observational.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Early risk is highest in STEMI, but beyond the first weeks the ordering reverses: NSTEMI survivors have the worst long-term prognosis, unstable angina (UA) the best in adjusted terms — yet UA's absolute late event rate is still high, roughly comparable to STEMI. Most of the NSTEMI excess is explained by older age and comorbidity burden rather than by the infarct type itself.

## The time-dependent crossover

In IMPROVE-IT, STEMI patients had higher mortality only [passage text removed] UA/NSTEMI were higher; the authors note this crossover pattern is consistent with other cohorts where STEMI has higher in-hospital/short-term mortality but cumulative mortality in UA/NSTEMI catches up or surpasses it over longer follow-up [S:6e8383a0-6c65-5767-bb9d-4a36e7500999]. UA/NSTEMI patients remained at higher risk of cardiovascular than non-cardiovascular death long-term, attributed to greater baseline multivessel disease, heart failure, diabetes, CKD and chronic lung disease [S:6e8383a0-6c65-5767-bb9d-4a36e7500999, S:515d7598-d6bf-5300-a89c-7035f870960c].

## Contemporary three-way comparison (all three subtypes)

A population-wide Western Australian linked-data study of 73,321 ACS patients (22.3% STEMI, 43.2% NSTEMI, 34.6% UA; mean ages [passage text removed]) found 30-day case fatality was ordered STEMI > NSTEMI > UA (8.1%, 5.3%, 1.1% in 2002–2007, falling to 6.8%, 3.7%, 0.5% by 2014–2019) [S:634cd9b2-9961-5e70-9d0f-e997a1cb894f, S:523f0195-2b11-5281-bd06-58d598dc4cfc]. Among 30-day survivors, 5-year MACE was 29.7% after NSTEMI versus 19.4% (STEMI) and 19.9% (UA), and 5-year all-cause mortality 29.8% versus 15.9% and 17.2% (log-rank p<0.001) [S:634cd9b2-9961-5e70-9d0f-e997a1cb894f]. Component rates show the NSTEMI excess spans recurrent MI (11.3%), heart failure hospitalisation (12.4%) and CVD death (13.9%), against 8.3%, 6.5% and 7.2% for STEMI and 7.7%, 8.0% and 7.7% for UA; non-fatal stroke was similar across subtypes (~2.4–3.1%) [S:523f0195-2b11-5281-bd06-58d598dc4cfc].

Crucially, after multivariable adjustment the STEMI–NSTEMI gap largely disappeared: both carried an approximately 1.5-fold hazard [passage text removed] relative to UA in both sexes [S:d93b2c14-a845-5256-a7fd-c104c10c6105, S:e455a6d8-0aa4-59c4-8b1b-4beaf840f6b8]. There was no improvement in adjusted long-term risk across nearly two decades for any subtype, and in-hospital PCI or CABG was independently associated with lower 5-year MACE (e.g. CABG HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.52–0.63 overall) [S:d93b2c14-a845-5256-a7fd-c104c10c6105, S:e6b31e59-182c-568e-a61d-4ea1ef46469c].

An Alberta population cohort of 31,056 ACS patients (49.5% NSTEMI, 34.0% STEMI, 16.5% UA) followed 3.0 ± 3.7 years reproduced this ordering: MACE rates 3.58 (NSTEMI), 2.41 (STEMI) and 1.68 (UA) per 10,000 person-years, and mortality 2.23, 1.38 and 0.95 [S:b30c4d51-7886-5852-ad13-1de38048b9ad]. With STEMI as reference, adjusted hazards for MACE were 0.95 (0.90–1.00) for NSTEMI and 0.57 (0.53–0.62) for UA — i.e. once comorbidity was accounted for, NSTEMI resembled STEMI while UA was substantially lower [S:74dcc7ac-c678-557e-a3f9-058d3a2bd2da].

## Unstable angina specifically

Late prognosis of UA in the troponin era is sparsely studied. In the WA cohort UA had 30-day case fatality under 1% but ~20% 5-year MACE and ~16% all-cause mortality, comparable to STEMI survivors, with no temporal improvement; after confounder adjustment UA carried lower risk than NSTEMI or STEMI [S:739d3d47-5eb9-5ff4-becd-13ab9650a03b]. UA patients lack myocardial necrosis and have substantially lower death risk than NSTEMI, and [passage text removed] [S:722be297-061b-5375-9955-225917e192b6]. In a bifurcation-PCI cohort, 2-year MACE did not differ between NSTEMI and UA subgroups of NSTE-ACS [S:3d16709d-319f-51a0-aff8-81d98205dae0], so UA vs NSTEMI separation is not uniform across settings.

## Beyond the first year (stable survivors)

TIGRIS enrolled 8,277 patients 1–3 years after MI with ≥1 additional risk factor and followed them 2 years [S:c5dfe983-d4c4-5b2b-a70f-8d442ab65731]. NSTEMI vs STEMI: unadjusted incidence rate ratio 1.46 (95% CI 1.19–1.80) for CV death/MI/stroke, attenuating to 1.23 (0.99–1.53, p=0.06) after adjustment; all-cause death RR 1.62 (1.26–2.07) unadjusted and 1.34 (1.04–1.73, p=0.02) adjusted. NSTEMI patients also had more hospitalisations, CV hospitalisations and ER visits, while STEMI patients had more cardiologist visits [S:274c2ed4-2853-5427-9792-5b9e4d4f6450].

## Why the difference, and where evidence conflicts

Drivers include older age, more diabetes, CKD, prior MI, multivessel disease, plus lower use of angiography/PCI and guideline-recommended discharge medication in NSTEMI [S:44ae3f2a-1879-5356-82c1-e6035f48a3d6, S:8b870ce2-0e05-5841-ac75-56870512a583, S:e455a6d8-0aa4-59c4-8b1b-4beaf840f6b8]. Registry data suggest 6-month NSTEMI mortality stopped improving after 2010 while STEMI mortality continued to fall [S:f69fd800-2de4-5b7d-8481-a0f9833c605e].

Not all studies agree. A cohort analysing early vs late phases found the adjusted [passage text removed] was no longer significant, with roughly half of late deaths cardiovascular in both groups and similar detailed causes; the authors attribute discrepancies to heterogeneity of the NSTEMI population in the high-sensitivity troponin era (many formerly-UA low-risk patients now labelled NSTEMI) and differing follow-up lengths [S:7f12993d-0549-577d-abaf-2f92507c51e2]. Japanese J-MINUET data, conversely, found worse long-term outcomes for NSTEMI than STEMI, including NSTEMI without CK elevation [S:9ea95db2-3014-5167-86d9-0bd418d9d4cd]. In octogenarians, 1-year mortality was higher in STEMI overall, though among hospital survivors NSTEMI carried increased 1-year mortality [S:44ae3f2a-1879-5356-82c1-e6035f48a3d6].

**Practical implication:** long-term risk after ACS is driven more by age, comorbidity and completeness of revascularisation than by the admission ECG label, and late event rates remain high even after UA — supporting equally intensive long-term secondary prevention and surveillance across all three presentations [S:d93b2c14-a845-5256-a7fd-c104c10c6105, S:739d3d47-5eb9-5ff4-becd-13ab9650a03b].
