rows.question: How do different classes of antihypertensive drug relate to cardiovascular outcomes in patients with HFmrEF or HFpEF?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Benefit on the composite of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalisation is confined to sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists; The other classes examined, including ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers, did not individually show a reduction in that composite endpoint; Across the drug classes, the treatment effect on the composite endpoint and on heart failure hospitalisation did not track the magnitude of achieved systolic blood pressure reduction; Compared with placebo, usual care or another class, active treatment did not reduce all-cause mortality or cardiovascular death, and no single class did so. Certainty: The class-specific benefit rests on comparisons of allocated treatments under controlled assignment, whereas the absence of any relation to the magnitude of blood pressure lowering is an aggregate-level correlation across comparisons, and the mortality findings are formally tested null results. Scope: applies to heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction in older adults with near-normal baseline blood pressure, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it recommends a specific blood pressure target or an intensified blood-pressure-lowering strategy on this basis, or presents the optimal intensity of blood pressure lowering in this population as established.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Across HFmrEF/HFpEF, no antihypertensive class has convincingly reduced mortality; benefits are driven almost entirely by heart-failure hospitalisation, and the size of benefit rises as EF falls toward the HFrEF range — so HFmrEF behaves "HFrEF-like" while EF >60% responds least. The only agents with a positive primary endpoint in this population are SGLT2 inhibitors and the non-steroidal MRA finerenone [[passage text removed]][S:https://www.ccjm.org/content/93/5/273].

## Class by class

**ACE inhibitors and ARBs — neutral.** PEP-CHF (perindopril, LVEF ≥40%) missed its primary endpoint of death or unplanned HF hospitalisation ([passage text removed]/PMC9363838]. CHARM-Preserved (candesartan, LVEF >40%) gave CV death or HF admission in 22% vs 24.3% (HR 0.89, 0.77–1.03), with no mortality difference (11.2% vs 11.3%) and only a trend for HF hospitalisation (15.9% vs 18.3%) [[passage text removed]]. I-PRESERVE (irbesartan) was flat for death or CV hospitalisation (36% vs 37%; HR 0.95, 0.86–1.05) despite lowering BP by ~3.8/2.1 mmHg, with more serious hyperkalaemia [[passage text removed]]. A meta-analysis of five RAAS-blockade trials found no difference in all-cause or CV mortality for ACEi, ARB, MRA or ARNI versus placebo [[passage text removed]].

**ARNI — signal confined to lower EF and women.** PARAGON-HF narrowly missed ([passage text removed]), driven by HF hospitalisation with no effect on CV death (HR 0.95) or all-cause death (HR 0.97) [S:https://www.wikijournalclub.org/wiki/PARAGON-HF][[passage text removed]]. Prespecified subgroups favoured LVEF below the median of 57% (RR 0.78, 0.64–0.98) and women (RR 0.73, 0.59–0.90 vs 1.03 in men; p-interaction 0.017) [S:https://www.wikijournalclub.org/wiki/PARAGON-HF][S:https://scholars.duke.edu/publication/1421922]. Pooled PARAGLIDE-HF/PARAGON-HF analyses showed benefit concentrated at EF ≤60% (RR 0.78, 0.66–0.91 vs 1.09 above; p-interaction 0.021) [[passage text removed]].

**Steroidal MRA (spironolactone) — neutral overall.** TOPCAT (LVEF ≥45%): primary composite [passage text removed]), significant only for HF hospitalisation (12% vs 14.2%; HR 0.83, 0.69–0.99), with hyperkalaemia 18.7% vs 9.1% and doubling of creatinine 10.2% vs 7% [S:https://nerdcat.org/studysummaries/finearts-topcat][[passage text removed]]. The Americas subgroup was positive (HR 0.82, 0.69–0.98), a finding made more credible by undetectable spironolactone metabolites in many Russian participants [S:https://nerdcat.org/studysummaries/finearts-topcat]. The subsequent European SPIRIT-HF trial (730 patients, 80% HFpEF, 20% HFmrEF) was neutral ([passage text removed]) but underpowered after COVID-related under-recruitment, with excess hypotension, hyperkalaemia and renal events; an on-treatment analysis gave rate ratio 0.94 (0.49–1.79) [[passage text removed]]. Pooling SPIRIT-HF with TOPCAT-Americas showed no significant effect [[passage text removed]].

**Non-steroidal MRA (finerenone) — positive.** FINEARTS-HF (n=6001, LVEF ≥40%) reduced total worsening-HF events plus CV death (14.9 vs 17.7 per 100 patient-years; rate ratio 0.84, 0.74–0.95; p=0.007), driven by HF events (RR 0.82) with no CV-death benefit (HR 0.93, 0.78–1.11) and neutral renal composite (HR 1.33, 0.94–1.89); effects were consistent across the LVEF spectrum and irrespective of background SGLT2i [[passage text removed]][S:https://www.ccjm.org/content/93/5/273].

**Beta-blockers — probable benefit in HFmrEF, not in EF ≥50%.** In the individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 11 placebo-controlled trials, among patients in sinus rhythm with LVEF 40–49% mortality was 7.2% vs 12.4% (adjusted HR 0.59, 0.34–1.03) and CV death 4.5% vs 9.2% (HR 0.48, 0.24–0.97); benefit was absent in the small LVEF ≥50% subgroup and in atrial fibrillation [[passage text removed]/PMC5837435][[passage text removed]]. In SENIORS (nebivolol, LVEF >35%) the primary composite HR was 0.86 overall and 0.82 with LVEF ≥35% [[passage text removed]/PMC10724525]. Registry data in HFpEF are mixed: SwedeHF showed lower all-cause mortality (5-year survival 45% vs 42%) but no reduction in the composite with HF hospitalisation (HR 0.98, 0.92–1.04) [[passage text removed]]; other observational work suggests possible harm in HFpEF, and guidelines have moved away from beta-blockers at EF ≥50% except for arrhythmia indications [[passage text removed]].

**Registry evidence in HFmrEF specifically.** In 12,421 SwedeHF HFmrEF patients, propensity-matched RASI/ARNI use was associated with lower CV death/HF hospitalisation (HR 0.90, 0.83–0.98), lower CV death (HR 0.84, 0.76–0.92) but not HF hospitalisation (HR 0.99), and lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.75, 0.69–0.81); beta-blocker use was associated with HR 0.82 (0.75–0.91) for the composite and 0.77 (0.70–0.85) for death [[passage text removed]/PMC10509568][S:https://esc365.escardio.org/journal/2670]. These are observational and subject to confounding by indication.

**Calcium-channel blockers — no evidence of outcome benefit.** In >7,500 older HFpEF patients, CCB use was not associated with death or HF hospitalisation (propensity-adjusted HR 1.02, 0.94–1.11), nor with individual components [[passage text removed]]. There are no outcome RCTs of dihydropyridine CCBs in HFpEF [[passage text removed]].

**Diuretics** are used for congestion/symptoms rather than proven outcome reduction in this population [[passage text removed]]; in HFpEF registry data, post-discharge diuretic use was linked to lower 30-day mortality and HF hospitalisation but this was non-randomised [[passage text removed]].

**Comparator class effects on preventing HF (upstream).** In ALLHAT, versus chlorthalidone, amlodipine had a higher 6-year rate of incident HF ([passage text removed], 1.25–1.52) and lisinopril also higher ([passage text removed], 1.07–1.31), despite no difference in the coronary primary endpoint — relevant to which antihypertensive to choose before HF develops [[passage text removed]].

## Interpretive caveats

- SGLT2 inhibitors, which lower BP modestly, are the comparator benchmark: EMPEROR-Preserved (HR 0.79, 0.69–0.90) and DELIVER ([passage text removed], 0.73–0.92, with CV death HR 0.88, 0.74–1.05) [[passage text removed]][S:https://www.wikijournalclub.org/wiki/DELIVER].
- As LVEF rises, the proportion of deaths that are cardiovascular and of hospitalisations that are HF-related falls, which partly explains attenuated drug effects at high EF [[passage text removed]].
- BP itself relates J-shaped to outcomes in HFpEF, with lowest risk around 120–130 mmHg systolic, so "more BP lowering" is not automatically better [[passage text removed]].
- Guidelines reflect this hierarchy: SGLT2 inhibitors class I in hypertensive symptomatic HFpEF; ARBs and/or MRAs class IIb when BP is above target [[passage text removed]].
- I found no head-to-head randomised outcome trial comparing antihypertensive classes within an HFmrEF/HFpEF population; most class comparisons rest on subgroup or observational data [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

In HFmrEF/HFpEF, outcome benefit tracks the *specific drug class*, not the amount of blood pressure it lowers: SGLT2 inhibitors, MRAs (especially finerenone), ARNI and GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce cardiovascular death/HF hospitalisation, whereas conventional antihypertensives (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, and probably beta-blockers) are neutral, with benefit for the neurohormonal classes concentrated at the lower (HFmrEF) end of the ejection-fraction range.

## Evidence

**BP lowering per se is not the mechanism.** A systematic review/meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials in HFmrEF/HFpEF (39,452 patients) found pharmacological BP lowering reduced the composite of CV death and HF hospitalisation (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.83–0.89), but with significant heterogeneity between classes (p=0.018): benefit was seen with SGLT2i, MRA, ARNI and GLP-1 agonists and **not** with other classes, and meta-regression showed no [passage text removed] effect (slope −0.0125, p=0.304); the same pattern held for HF hospitalisation (RR 0.83, 0.79–0.86; slope −0.0121, p=0.528) [S:6c7411d9]. The eligible drug list explicitly included ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, diuretics, nitrates and alpha-blockers [S:57b5e4e3]. The authors conclude that use of standard antihypertensives outside those four classes "is unlikely to be beneficial" [passage text removed] [S:357ce5f6][S:36f8a169]. Consistently, in EMPEROR-Preserved the benefit of empagliflozin on the primary endpoint and on eGFR slope was not modified by controlled, uncontrolled or resistant hypertension (p for interaction = .92 and .95), suggesting "[passage text removed]" [S:05f64811][S:f540f5ce].

**Class-by-class ranking.** A network meta-analysis of 19 RCTs (20,633 patients with HFpEF/HFmrEF) found no drug class reduced death versus placebo; SGLT2 inhibitors, ARNIs and MRAs significantly reduced HF hospitalisation, with SGLT2 inhibitors the optimal class for that endpoint [S:d9476921][S:3b4e9e93].

**RAS blockade (ACEi/ARB/ARNI).** CHARM-Preserved, PEP-CHF and I-PRESERVE were neutral for mortality and the primary endpoints [S:88004d1a][S:68feae5e]. An older meta-analysis restricted to LVEF ≥40% found no effect of ACE inhibitors (RR 1.10, 0.85–1.43) or ARBs (RR 1.02, 0.93–1.12) on all-cause mortality, and none for pooled RAAS blockade [S:abd1e31e]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed significance (rate ratio 0.87, 0.75–1.01), driven by HF hospitalisations, with greater benefit below the median LVEF of 57% and in women [S:616012eb][S:fdf735c4]. Pooled PARADIGM/PARAGON analyses show a treatment-by-LVEF interaction with benefit attenuating above ~55–57% [S:616012eb][S:fdf735c4].

**Beta-blockers — the most contested class.** A 2018 meta-analysis of trials with LVEF ≥40% reported reductions in all-cause (RR 0.78, 0.65–0.94) and cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.75, 0.60–0.94) with beta-blockers, and no effect of ACEi/ARB/MRA [S:abd1e31e][S:bf4360b9] — but a published critique showed ~64–73% of that pooled weight came from a single 1990s trial enrolling exclusively post-MI HFpEF patients, biasing the estimate [S:0484a128]. Against benefit: in a TOPCAT secondary analysis, beta-blocker use was associated with *more* HF hospitalisations in patients with EF ≥50%, an association absent at EF 45–49% [S:f9044366]; a review notes benefit on hospitalisation/death appears confined to HFmrEF, with no significant benefit in HFpEF and particularly EF >60%, and that Swedish registry data showed lower all-cause mortality but no reduction in the combined mortality/HF-hospitalisation endpoint [S:52d8be4a]. Registry signals are frankly discordant: ACEi/ARB associated with lower mortality in SwedeHF while beta-blocker benefit was limited to those with coronary disease; CHART-2 showed the reverse; OPTIMIZE-HF showed no beta-blocker benefit at LVEF ≥40% [S:97b1de3e][S:1157db4a]. In HFmrEF specifically, a propensity-matched SwedeHF analysis (12,421 patients) found both RASI/ARNI and beta-blockers associated with lower CV mortality/HF hospitalisation (HR 0.90, [passage text removed], 0.74–0.90) and lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.75 and HR 0.79) [S:c61c6b89], and a post-hospitalisation HFmrEF cohort found beta-blocker use associated with ~30% lower 1-year all-cause death and lower CV death but no reduction in hospitalisation [S:96c66ebd].

**MRAs.** TOPCAT missed its primary endpoint (HR 0.89, 0.77–1.04) with a signal in the Americas and at LVEF <55% [S:993eef6d][S:970cbbb3][S:fba9cf61]; FINEARTS-HF showed finerenone reduced CV death plus total worsening HF events by 16% (RR 0.84, 0.74–0.95), driven by worsening-HF events (RR 0.82, 0.71–0.94) [S:1ceae1dc]. Pooled MRA analyses indicate reduced HF hospitalisation without a demonstrated CV mortality benefit, and higher hyperkalaemia risk requiring potassium monitoring [S:fba9cf61][S:7b3c7bc2].

**Calcium channel blockers.** In propensity-matched OPTIMIZE-HF HFpEF patients (810 pairs, EF ≥40%), new CCB prescription had no effect on death or HF hospitalisation (HR 1.03, 0.92–1.14) [S:47615925]; this was consistent for amlodipine and non-amlodipine agents, so CCBs may be used for BP control but should be lower priority than ACEi/ARB/ARNI/MRA [S:5164e9ac]. Non-dihydropyridines are contraindicated/discouraged where EF is reduced [S:5164e9ac][S:6abfc810].

**Diuretics** remain the mainstay for congestion/symptoms rather than an outcome-modifying therapy in this phenotype [S:6ff32b4e].

## Caveats
No RCT has been conducted exclusively in HFmrEF; most evidence is from LVEF >40% trials and post-hoc/subgroup analyses [S:1b28ca80][S:6ff32b4e]. Most trials had short follow-up (median 19 months, range 3–53) [S:357ce5f6], and no randomised trial has directly tested intensive versus less intensive BP targets in HFmrEF/HFpEF [S:36f8a169]. Head-to-head comparisons of SGLT2 inhibitors against other HF classes do not exist [S:3b4e9e93]. Registry findings on beta-blockers are confounded by indication (coronary disease, atrial fibrillation) [S:97b1de3e].

rows.question: What outcomes follow interruption of beta-blocker therapy in patients with prior uncomplicated myocardial infarction?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Interrupting long-term beta-blocker therapy in stable patients years after an uncomplicated myocardial infarction did not prove non-inferior to continuing it for a combined outcome of death, recurrent infarction, stroke or cardiovascular hospitalisation, which occurred modestly more often after interruption (roughly a sixth higher relative risk); Interruption of beta-blocker therapy did not improve patient-reported quality of life compared with continuation; The comparison covered patients with largely preserved left ventricular function who had been taking beta-blockers for years after infarction, with heart failure, a recent cardiac event and other primary beta-blocker indications excluded. Certainty: The event outcome and the quality-of-life outcome both come from a single large comparison of assigned treatment groups, so effect language is supportable for each while resting on one such comparison. Scope: applies to prior uncomplicated myocardial infarction with preserved left ventricular function in adults on long-term beta-blocker therapy, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents continued beta-blocker therapy as demonstrated to prevent deaths or recurrent infarctions, or presents interruption as an established cause of higher mortality, rather than as failing non-inferiority on a combined event outcome.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** In the only two randomized withdrawal trials, stopping a beta-blocker years after an uncomplicated MI with preserved/mildly reduced LVEF did not increase death, reinfarction or stroke, and did not improve quality of life; the French ABYSS trial failed to prove noninferiority because of excess cardiovascular hospitalizations plus a sustained rise in heart rate and blood pressure, whereas the Korean SMART-DECISION trial did meet noninferiority for a harder endpoint.

**ABYSS (interruption vs. continuation, n=3,698; median 2.9 years post-MI, median LVEF 60%, 95% revascularized)**
- Primary composite (death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, or CV hospitalization): 23.8% with interruption vs. 21.1% with continuation; [passage text removed] against a 3-point margin — noninferiority not met [[passage text removed]; S:https://www.wikijournalclub.org/wiki/ABYSS; Silvain et al., N Engl J Med 2024;391:1277-1286, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2404204].
- Hard events were similar: death 4.1% vs 4.0%, MI 2.5% vs 2.4%, stroke 1.0% vs 1.0%; death/MI/stroke 7.2% vs 6.8% ([passage text removed]), and death/MI/stroke/HF hospitalization 8.4% vs 7.6% ([passage text removed]; S:https://www.wikijournalclub.org/wiki/ABYSS; [passage text removed]].
- The difference was driven by CV hospitalization (18.9% vs 16.6%; [passage text removed]), mainly coronary-related admissions (14.2% vs 11.9%), including angina/ischemia (3.6% vs 3.0%) and angiography (7.9% vs 6.3%); HF admissions 1.8% vs 1.2%. No hypothesis testing was performed on these secondary outcomes, so they are not formally significant [S:https://www.wikijournalclub.org/wiki/ABYSS; [passage text removed]].
- Quality of life did not improve: EQ-5D change 0.033 vs 0.032, [passage text removed]].
- Haemodynamic rebound: at 6 months, systolic BP +[passage text removed]), diastolic +3.3 mmHg (2.6–4.0) and resting heart rate +10 bpm (9–11), all P<0.001, sustained through follow-up despite more antihypertensive prescribing; hypertensive patients (43%) had more events than non-hypertensive (25.8% vs 19.2%; [passage text removed]=0.03) [Procopi et al., [passage text removed]].
- Crossover was asymmetric (interruption→continuation 8.6% vs 2.8%), consistent with symptom-driven restarting [S:https://www.wikijournalclub.org/wiki/ABYSS].

**SMART-DECISION (n=2,540, ≥1 year of beta-blocker post-MI, LVEF ≥40%, median 4.7 years from MI)**: discontinuation was noninferior for death/recurrent MI/HF hospitalization — 4-year estimates 7.2% vs 9.0% ([passage text removed]); all-cause death 2.4% vs 3.4%, recurrent MI 2.3% vs 2.6%, HF hospitalization 2.2% vs 2.1%, with no differences in new-onset AF, LV function, quality of life or serious adverse events [Choi et al., N Engl J Med 2026;394:1302-1312, [passage text removed]]. The NEJM authors attribute the discrepancy with ABYSS to design and clinical-context differences, noting that ABYSS's inclusion of CV hospitalization is less suitable for an open-label trial [[passage text removed]].

**Pooled and observational evidence (LVEF >40%, no HF)**: in a systematic review of 10 studies (1 RCT, 9 observational; N=121,114), discontinuation was not associated with increased [passage text removed]) or [passage text removed]), but was associated with more MACE ([passage text removed]), driven by CV hospitalizations — all low-certainty [Thompson et al., JACC Adv 2026;5(6 Pt 2):102840, S:https://ecommons.cornell.edu/entities/publication/71a425d3-7ba6-4e29-9a5c-8c922f622d33; [passage text removed]]. In an Alberta cohort of 4,768 AMI survivors with LVEF ≥50%, stopping within 180 days was not associated with the composite of death/recurrent AMI/revascularization ([passage text removed]), but was associated with more recurrent AMI and repeat revascularization [Chiu et al., JACC Adv 2025;4(6 Pt 1):101814, [passage text removed]].

**Interpretation**: interruption appears not to cost lives or reinfarctions in stable, revascularized patients with preserved LVEF, and does not improve quality of life; the reproducible signal is more symptom/ischemia-driven cardiovascular hospitalization plus loss of heart-rate and blood-pressure control, with hypertensive patients at higher risk — hence guidance to individualize rather than routinely deprescribe [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
**Bottom line: two randomized trials of stopping long-term beta-blockers in stable post-MI patients reached opposite conclusions — ABYSS failed to show that interruption was non-inferior to continuation (driven almost entirely by cardiovascular hospitalizations, plus rises in heart rate and blood pressure and no quality-of-life gain), whereas the later SMART-DECISION trial did meet non-inferiority for hard outcomes.**

**ABYSS (interruption ≥6 months after MI, LVEF ≥40%)**
- Open-label, non-inferiority trial, 3,698 patients at 49 French sites, median 2.9 years from index MI to randomization, median LVEF 60% (≈23% with LVEF 40–50%), median follow-up 3 years [S:08897c5f-29ed-5051-b29e-f9459f3f292a][S:bccda0ac-94bf-58ae-8c85-71651745aeb2].
- Primary composite (death, MI, stroke, CV hospitalization): 23.8% with interruption vs 21.1% with continuation; [passage text removed] — non-inferiority not demonstrated [S:08897c5f-29ed-5051-b29e-f9459f3f292a][S:a450d92b-25b8-5f5c-aeac-c691d683c33e].
- Hard events were similar (death 4.1% vs 4.0%; MI 2.5% vs 2.4%); the difference came from CV hospitalizations (18.9% vs 16.6%) [S:a450d92b-25b8-5f5c-aeac-c691d683c33e], mainly coronary-related admissions for angina/ischemia and angiography [S:ca61988e-45a8-5771-a08b-c259d40a1598][S:8a2fd410-9fb1-50e0-aa1f-935093d9dfad]. Of 816 primary events, 656 (80%) were CV hospitalizations, i.e. a clinician-driven, open-label-susceptible component [S:5d682821-c519-51dc-9f1e-29210eb9b02b]; an independent summary likewise noted stopping "[passage text removed]" [S:6b8ace11-cf7c-55e9-bdb8-8535cf9d8e57].
- Physiological rebound: interruption produced a sustained increase in heart rate (~10 bpm) and systolic/diastolic pressure (3.7/3.9 mmHg), despite added antihypertensives — a plausible mechanism for the excess coronary events [S:8a2fd410-9fb1-50e0-aa1f-935093d9dfad][S:ca61988e-45a8-5771-a08b-c259d40a1598], most marked in patients with prior hypertension [S:ddb4e13a-977f-5701-a91b-d7b4d2b303e1].
- Quality of life (EQ-5D) did not improve after interruption [S:6015bf1c-c640-58d1-b6a5-c8ee9f3001fd][S:08897c5f-29ed-5051-b29e-f9459f3f292a], so the trial did not support routine interruption [S:08897c5f-29ed-5051-b29e-f9459f3f292a].

**SMART-DECISION (discontinuation after ≥1 year, LVEF ≥40%, no HF)**
- 2,540 stable Korean patients randomized; median 4.7 years from index MI, median follow-up 3.1 years [S:https://cardiologynownews.org?p=139814][[passage text removed]].
- Primary composite (death, recurrent MI, HF hospitalization): 7.2% (n=58) with discontinuation vs 9.0% (n=74) with continuation; [passage text removed] non-inferiority (margin 1.4) [[passage text removed]][S:https://www.tctmd.com/news/smart-decision-stopping-beta-blockers-post-mi-safe-stable-patients].
- Secondary outcomes — individual components, new-onset AF, LV function, quality of life, serious adverse events — were similar [[passage text removed]]; an exploratory ABYSS-style composite occurred in 11.0% vs 14.5% [S:https://www.tctmd.com/news/smart-decision-stopping-beta-blockers-post-mi-safe-stable-patients]. Blood pressure and heart rate again rose after discontinuation [[passage text removed]]. Investigators cautioned this is the first trial showing safety of discontinuation and that the population was highly selected [S:https://www.tctmd.com/news/smart-decision-stopping-beta-blockers-post-mi-safe-stable-patients][S:https://cardiologynownews.org?p=139814].

**Observational context (mixed)**
- In a French national healthcare-database cohort of 73,450 optimally treated post-AMI patients without HF, beta-blocker discontinuation after 1 year carried an adjusted HR of 1.17 (95% CI 1.01–1.35) for death or ACS admission and 1.13 (95% CI 0.94–1.36) for all-cause death over ~3.8 years [S:8476548d-fffb-5f62-85f8-0e1d83faa1b3]. Other registry work found discontinuation at 1 year [passage text removed] AMI without HF/LV dysfunction, suggesting waning benefit over time [S:e8d76305-4fba-5b7b-9134-f18895f7558a].

**Interpretation.** Randomized data show no consistent excess of death or reinfarction after interruption in patients with LVEF ≥40% and no HF; the signal of harm in ABYSS was symptom/hospitalization-driven and accompanied by hemodynamic rebound, while SMART-DECISION found discontinuation non-inferior for hard endpoints. Parallel trials of not starting beta-blockers (REDUCE-AMI, REBOOT) likewise show no benefit on death/reinfarction in preserved-EF MI [S:0db06319-5602-5314-bdff-d56fbc67c2f8], and pooled analyses find no reduction in mortality, reinfarction, stroke, MACE or HF admissions [S:b714ada0-987e-5e19-a971-d9fb78cd3363]. Note that abrupt withdrawal after chronic therapy is described as risking a rebound phenomenon with tachycardia, elevated blood pressure and angina [S:8a2fd410-9fb1-50e0-aa1f-935093d9dfad]; the trials do not settle whether tapering mitigates this, and no source I found addresses that directly.

rows.question: How does the CHA2DS2-VASc score relate to in-hospital mortality in patients presenting with acute myocardial infarction?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: A higher CHA2DS2-VASc score at presentation is associated with a higher risk of in-hospital death after acute myocardial infarction; This association persists when other admission characteristics are taken into account, so the score carries prognostic information independent of them; Used as a single bedside threshold, the score separates patients who die in hospital from survivors only modestly. Certainty: The link between higher scores and greater risk rests on associations drawn from routinely collected hospital records rather than on demonstrated causation, and the score's ability to discriminate in-hospital death is only modest. Scope: applies to acute myocardial infarction managed with coronary angiography and percutaneous coronary intervention in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it treats the score as a causal driver of in-hospital death or asserts that lowering its component risk factors during the index admission reduces in-hospital mortality.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Higher CHA₂DS₂-VASc scores are consistently associated with higher in-hospital mortality in acute MI, with a roughly graded (dose–response) relationship, but the score is a repackaging of chronic risk-factor burden rather than acute-phase risk, its discrimination is only modest, and in smaller cohorts the in-hospital signal is often non-significant.

## Evidence for a graded association

**STEMI treated with primary PCI.** In 647 STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI, those with an admission score >2 (n = 126) had significantly higher in-hospital cardiovascular mortality than those with a score ≤2 (n = 521): [passage text removed] likewise 13.4% vs 3.6%, P < .001 ([Bozbay et al., Clin Appl Thromb Hemost, doi:10.1177/1076029616646874]([passage text removed]); [research.bau.edu.tr record](https://research.bau.edu.tr/en/publications/chasub2subdssub2sub-[passage text removed]-2)).

A larger STEMI primary-PCI cohort shows an almost monotonic gradient across the full score range, with in-hospital mortality of 0.7%, 2.2%, 7.9%, 9.7%, 15.2%, 16.7% and 30.8% for scores of 1 through 7 respectively; after adjustment for demographics, smoking, comorbidities, Killip class, anterior MI, stent dimensions and no-reflow, the point estimates remained elevated and rose with score ([PMC6545906]([passage text removed])).

**Independent predictor after multivariable adjustment.** In another STEMI primary-PCI series the score independently predicted all-cause in-hospital mortality (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.17–2.19) alongside no-reflow, thrombus grade and creatinine clearance; a cut-off ≥2 gave 69.7% sensitivity and 64.4% specificity, AUC 0.72 (95% CI 0.62–0.81) ([Medicina 2019;55(2):35]([passage text removed])).

**NSTEMI without AF.** Among 906 NSTEMI patients without AF, the score was independently associated with in-hospital mortality ([passage text removed]) together with SYNTAX score (HR 1.049) and age (HR 1.057); Kaplan–Meier curves split at <4 vs ≥4 separated significantly. The score also correlated with angiographic disease burden (Spearman r = 0.320 with SYNTAX score) ([Akboğa et al., [passage text removed], PMID 34734812 / PMC8575397](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34734812)).

**Broader ACS.** In 2,222 ACS patients the score independently predicted in-hospital mortality (HR 1.393, 95% CI 1.131–1.715, p = 0.002), and mean score rose with SYNTAX tertile (4.24 high, 2.89 intermediate, 2.40 low, p < 0.001) ([Kurtul & Acikgoz, [passage text removed], summarised at H1 Connect](https://archive.connect.h1.co/article/727762424)). A 10-year US National Inpatient Sample analysis of ACS patients with AF undergoing PCI reached the same conclusion — the [passage text removed] and adverse periprocedural events ([Borovac et al., Cardiovasc Revasc Med 2021;29:61-68, PMID 32828675](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32828675)).

## Important caveats

- **Null in-hospital findings exist.** In a 212-patient MI cohort, in-hospital all-cause mortality did not differ by score (8% for ≤3 vs 13% for >3, p = 0.36) even though long-term all-cause mortality did (8% vs 21%, p = 0.009) ([Węgiel et al., Adv Interv Cardiol 2018;14(4):391-398, PMC6309841]([passage text removed])).
- **In diabetic STEMI patients without prior AF**, in-hospital mortality was similar across score groups and the score was *not* a risk factor for in-hospital death, although it independently predicted 12-month death and stroke ([Acta Diabetol, doi:10.1007/s00592-016-0877-6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00592-016-0877-6)).
- **The association is not AF-dependent** — it holds in explicitly AF-free MI populations ([PMID 34734812](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34734812)) — consistent with the score acting as a surrogate for cumulative cardiovascular risk burden rather than thromboembolic risk ([PMC9600317]([passage text removed])).
- **Discrimination is modest and purpose-built scores may do better.** In ACS cohorts the score retained only a modest c-index for MACE, and a dedicated score outperformed it ([Eur J Intern Med, doi:10.1016/j.ejim.2016.09.010 article page]([passage text removed])). Renal-augmented variants performed strongly for STEMI in-hospital death (R2CHA₂DS₂-[passage text removed]) in a model where the unmodified scores did not emerge as independent ([MDPI J Clin Med 2025;14(13):4624]([passage text removed])).
- **Largest AMI registry data speak to long-term, not in-hospital, outcomes.** In 15,681 AMI patients (KORMI), cardiac events rose stepwise across score groups 0–1, 2–3, 4–5 and 6–9, with the score an independent predictor of long-term prognosis (HR 1.414 per scale, p < 0.001); the published abstract reports long-term rather than in-hospital endpoints ([PMID 24972564](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24972564)). Similarly, ACSIS (13,422 patients) reported 1-year mortality up to 6-fold higher for score >5 vs 0–1 (HR 6, 95% CI 4.1–8.8) ([PMID 27707608](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27707608)).

**Bottom line for practice:** the score is a cheap bedside marker that flags a higher-risk AMI phenotype (older, more comorbid, more extensive coronary disease) and tracks in-hospital death in a graded fashion, but it was not designed for this purpose, its accuracy is moderate, and it should supplement — not replace — acute-phase risk tools.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Higher CHA₂DS₂-VASc scores are consistently associated with higher in-hospital mortality and in-hospital MACE after acute MI, even in patients without atrial fibrillation, and in most cohorts the score is an *independent* predictor with moderate-to-good discrimination (AUC ≈0.72–0.83) — but the association is not universal, and it does not clearly outperform GRACE.

## Supporting evidence

**Graded, independent association with in-hospital death**
- In 750 patients hospitalized with a first AMI, in-hospital mortality was 2.8%, median CHA₂DS₂-VASc was 4 in those who died (P < .001), and a score ≥4 remained an independent predictor after adjustment (OR 4.13, 95% CI 1.44–11.83); AUC for in-hospital mortality [passage text removed]), with a cut-off of 4 giving 71.4% sensitivity and 74.3% specificity [S:4cfd9027-32d3-5a3e-a0e3-a10597b33334][S:7a8a96f6-f58b-50a5-b647-c975eb9ab8ad].
- In 647 STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI, in-hospital cardiovascular mortality was 8.7% with score >2 versus 1.9% with score ≤2 (P < .001), and long-term mortality 13.4% vs 3.6% [S:a333ba65-beea-5722-9d7f-360c6a57692e]. The authors attribute this to the score's components (age, female sex, diabetes, hypertension, prior stroke) each being established STEMI mortality predictors [S:8d5ef0c1-9d5b-52fe-9c0f-1afb94ead801].
- In 1331 consecutive primary-PCI STEMI patients (Tehran Heart Center registry), CHA₂DS₂-VASc independently predicted all-cause in-hospital mortality (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.17–2.19), AUC 0.72 (95% CI 0.62–0.81); a cut-off ≥2 gave 69.7% sensitivity / 64.4% specificity [S:6357065c-662c-5ad6-bf32-21b3b8da82fe][S:a12bc1d9-0692-505a-ba4e-664e92fed29d].

**In-hospital composite endpoints including death**
- In STEMI without AF, the score independently predicted in-hospital death or stroke (MACE rate 10%; 2.31, 95% CI 1.37–3.9; P = .0016), alongside Killip class, creatinine, peak CK-MB and no-reflow [S:746611e9-d0ca-5ebe-925b-6317f53d6e61].
- In 746 primary-PCI STEMI patients, risk of in-hospital MACE rose stepwise across score strata versus score 1 (2–3: OR 4.62; 4–5: OR 7.74; >5: OR 11.71), with adjusted OR 1.43 per point; AUC 0.661 overall — significant in men (AUC 0.714) but not women [S:375d5541-afbd-5603-ac6a-f91f4509ce83][S:ffd3b0fa-479e-525c-9edc-73aaa4a307d2].
- A 210-patient STEMI cohort found the score an independent MACE predictor ([passage text removed]), AUC 0.744, cut-off 3.5 — statistically indistinguishable from GRACE (0.827) and TIMI (0.745) [S:3b21b9d3-582a-5748-beb1-edac84282874][S:94dd0b6f-ef92-5a6b-a615-057c8db96d02].

**Plausible mechanism: impaired epicardial/microvascular reperfusion**
Higher scores predicted low initial TIMI flow (adjusted OR 1.502 for score ≥3) and no-reflow, and no-reflow itself was strongly tied to in-hospital death (adjusted OR 8.87) [S:33e1fd40-ae65-5860-a637-2797bb88a9e3][S:7a8a96f6-f58b-50a5-b647-c975eb9ab8ad]; suboptimal reperfusion was likewise independently predicted by the score (OR 1.59) [S:6357065c-662c-5ad6-bf32-21b3b8da82fe].

**Important negative/qualifying data**
- In 857 STEMI patients treated with p-PCI, CHADS₂, CHA₂DS₂-VASc and CHA₂DS₂-VA were higher in decedents on univariate analysis but were *not* independently associated with in-hospital mortality once renal function was accounted for; only the renal-augmented versions were (R₂CHA₂DS₂-[passage text removed]; AUC 0.807) [S:bd696192-3a47-5a66-b341-6b17af92fbd7][S:28e28f0a-60f2-54b6-90e9-da8a293fd44a][S:2d561462-2e20-51a6-8cef-c98f22203937].
- In 472 diabetic STEMI patients without AF, in-hospital mortality did not differ across score groups and the score was not a risk factor for in-hospital death, although it did predict 12-month mortality and stroke [S:9e78b28b-20d6-50ea-ac17-3a4f6c68fd82].
- In a 212-patient MI cohort, in-hospital mortality was numerically higher with score >3 but not statistically significant; the score's prognostic signal was clearer for post-discharge mortality (HR 1.31 per point) [S:f661d373-9775-5e31-abfb-fdfa817c177d][S:f5457d98-134d-5aa9-8e48-266e040ecdee].

**Bottom line:** the relationship is monotonic and robust in direction, with commonly reported cut-offs of >2 to ~4, but effect size and independence vary by population (sex, diabetes, renal function), and where renal function is modelled the plain score's independent contribution can disappear [S:bd696192-3a47-5a66-b341-6b17af92fbd7][S:ffd3b0fa-479e-525c-9edc-73aaa4a307d2].

rows.question: What is known about direct oral anticoagulants versus vitamin K antagonists on clinical outcomes in non-valvular atrial fibrillation?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Direct oral anticoagulant use is associated with a lower risk of recurrent cerebrovascular ischemic events than vitamin K antagonist use; Direct oral anticoagulant use is also associated with a lower risk of major bleeding than vitamin K antagonist use; All-cause mortality did not differ significantly between direct oral anticoagulants and vitamin K antagonists in the pooled comparison. Certainty: Support for the lower ischemic-event and major-bleeding risks is of moderate strength and consistent across combined analyses drawing on both experimentally allocated and routine-care comparisons, so residual confounding cannot be excluded, whereas the mortality comparison was too inconsistent across contributing evidence to be settled. Scope: applies to non-valvular atrial fibrillation requiring long-term oral anticoagulation for stroke prevention in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the ischemic-event advantage as separately demonstrated within specific patient groups such as those anticoagulated around catheter ablation or those with a bioprosthetic heart valve.

answers.websearch:
**In non-valvular AF, DOACs are at least as effective as vitamin K antagonists for preventing stroke/systemic embolism, roughly halve intracranial haemorrhage, and modestly reduce all-cause mortality, at the cost of more gastrointestinal bleeding — with the main exceptions being rheumatic mitral stenosis/mechanical valves and switching in frail elderly VKA-experienced patients.**

**Trial-level evidence (four pivotal RCTs, ~71,000 patients).** The Ruff meta-analysis of [passage text removed] (42,411 on DOAC vs 29,272 on warfarin, median follow-up 1.8–2.8 years) found DOACs [passage text removed]), all-cause mortality (RR 0.90, 0.85–0.95) and intracranial haemorrhage (RR 0.48, 0.39–0.59), but increased GI bleeding (RR 1.25, 1.01–1.55) [NBK174292]. The efficacy gain was driven almost entirely by haemorrhagic [passage text removed], 0.38–0.64), not ischaemic stroke or MI, which did not differ significantly; major bleeding was non-significantly reduced (RR 0.86, 0.73–1.00, P=0.06) [[passage text removed]; https://pace-cme.org/news/meta-analysis-of-large-noac-trials-shows-favourable-riskbenefit-ratio-over-warfarin/2453991]. Bleeding benefit was larger where warfarin control was poor (RR 0.69 in centres with TTR <66% vs 0.93 with TTR ≥66%; p-interaction=0.022) [same ACC source].

**Individual-patient-data confirmation and dose matters.** The COMBINE AF patient-level network meta-analysis (71,683 patients) reproduced this: standard-dose DOAC vs warfarin gave lower stroke/systemic embolism (3.01% vs 3.69%; HR 0.81, 0.74–0.89), death (HR 0.92, 0.87–0.97) and intracranial bleeding (HR 0.45, 0.37–0.56), with no significant difference in major bleeding (HR 0.86, 0.74–1.01). Lower-dose DOACs lost the stroke benefit (HR 1.06, 0.95–1.19) while reducing major bleeding (HR 0.63, 0.45–0.88) [PMC8800560]. Effects were consistent by age and sex, with greater relative benefit in younger patients and in VKA-naïve patients [[passage text removed]].

**Kidney function.** Down to CrCl 25 mL/min there was no value at which standard-dose DOAC was worse than warfarin for bleeding, ICH, stroke/SE or death; benefit for stroke/SE increased as CrCl fell (4.8% HR decrease per 10 mL/min, p-interaction=0.01). Inappropriate dose reduction raised thromboembolism and death without reducing bleeding [PMID 37042255].

**Where VKAs still win.** In rheumatic heart disease–associated AF (INVICTUS, 4,565 patients), rivaroxaban was worse than dose-adjusted VKA for the composite of stroke/systemic embolism/MI/vascular or unknown death (8.21%/yr vs 6.49%/yr; HR 1.25, 1.10–1.41) with no bleeding advantage (HR 0.76, 0.51–1.15) [PMC9988293]. Guidelines correspondingly prefer DOACs over VKAs in AF **except** mechanical valves and moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis [https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/09/17/04/05/2024-esc-guidelines-for-af-esc-2024; [passage text removed]].

**Unresolved: switching stable frail patients.** FRAIL-AF randomised frail patients ≥75 already on a VKA and found switching to a DOAC *increased* major/clinically relevant non-major bleeding (15.3% vs 9.4%; HR 1.69, 1.23–2.32) with no thromboembolic benefit (HR 1.26, 0.60–2.61); the trial was stopped early [[passage text removed]]. A post hoc COMBINE AF analysis of a "FRAIL-AF-like" cohort (n=5,913) found stroke and mortality benefits preserved, with more GI bleeding (HR 1.83, 1.42–2.36) but less ICH (HR 0.29, [passage text removed], 0.23–0.90) [[passage text removed]]. These findings are discordant, and the FRAIL-AF result underpins a guideline caveat favouring continued VKA in such patients [https://www.tctmd.com/news/frail-older-patients-af-may-fare-better-switching-doac].

**Caveats:** the pooled RCT analyses used study-level pooling of mechanistically distinct agents with statistical heterogeneity for bleeding endpoints [https://pace-cme.org/news/meta-analysis-of-large-noac-trials-shows-favourable-riskbenefit-ratio-over-warfarin/2453991], and the pivotal trials excluded significant valve disease [[passage text removed]]. Head-to-head randomised comparisons between individual DOACs do not exist in the sources retrieved.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line: in non-valvular AF, DOACs are at least as effective as vitamin K antagonists for preventing stroke/systemic embolism and clearly safer for intracranial bleeding, with lower mortality but a class-level excess of gastrointestinal bleeding — which is why guidelines now make them first-line, with VKAs retained for mechanical valves, rheumatic mitral disease, and selected frail/stable-VKA patients.**

**Randomised trial evidence.** The four pivotal trials (RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE, ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48) each showed at least non-inferiority for stroke/systemic embolism [S:7c65e60b-5f44-5936-9d4e-8f474b10c31a]. In the pooled analysis of all 71,683 participants (42,411 on a DOAC, 29,272 on warfarin), DOACs reduced stroke or systemic embolism by 19%, driven predominantly by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke, and also reduced intracranial haemorrhage and all-cause mortality (by 10%); overall major bleeding was similar, while gastrointestinal bleeding was increased [S:7c65e60b-5f44-5936-9d4e-8f474b10c31a][S:2fd0d658-aa80-586c-a721-ff5a67a9bcdc]. Independent meta-analyses concur: across 5 studies/51,895 patients, [passage text removed]) and all-cause mortality (RR 0.91, 0.85–0.96) were reduced and haemorrhagic stroke markedly so (RR 0.51, 0.41–0.64) [S:cc64175b-a68e-54d4-828f-8a7844d995e7]; a 12-study/77,011-patient review found [passage text removed]) and 14% mortality reduction (OR 0.86) [S:3cf754dc-9718-5d74-ba61-a85658f43e31]. Notably, the ischaemic-stroke advantage alone is modest — an early 3-trial analysis (50,578 patients) found non-haemorrhagic stroke/SEE similar (RR 0.93, 0.83–1.04) with intracranial bleeding clearly lower (RR 0.46, 0.33–0.65) [S:56688bd5-9f57-54cd-81e0-13e21da0e994].

**Real-world/observational data** point the same way, and often show a major-bleeding benefit not seen in trials. A 2026 systematic review of 11 studies and 814,716 patients reported fewer recurrent cerebrovascular ischaemic events (RR 0.83, 0.78–0.88) and less major bleeding (RR 0.77, 0.71–0.82) with DOACs, with similar mortality [S:c3d79d55-fb6c-5711-b8d5-e077973dddee]. In a French national cohort of 314,184 anticoagulant-naïve NVAF patients with GI-bleeding risk factors, DOACs had lower major bleeding than VKAs across all subgroups (age ≥75, HAS-BLED ≥3, CKD 3–4, polypharmacy) [S:272e8c88-e8b6-58bd-b498-3efaffb689b6]. Not all cohorts are concordant: a 90,773-patient Catalan primary-care study found a protective effect against cerebral bleeding but no difference in stroke or GI bleeding [S:ab84889d-ecfd-5824-b76b-697e0565c408].

**GI bleeding differs by agent.** In trial data versus VKA, dabigatran 150 mg (HR 1.50), rivaroxaban 20 mg (1.42) and edoxaban 60 mg (1.23) increased GI bleeding whereas apixaban 5 mg did not (0.89) [S:ab748c03-dc25-5074-8849-59b33d01288b]. Real-world head-to-head comparisons consistently rank apixaban most favourable and rivaroxaban least favourable for GI bleeding [S:67f66d9b-b2be-519f-bdac-0b8ee46ab775][S:9ae84c92-cdc4-5d1e-bb74-aa5201084c54], and the French cohort found lower major/GI bleeding with apixaban than rivaroxaban across subgroups [S:272e8c88-e8b6-58bd-b498-3efaffb689b6]. The class-level summary is ~19% fewer ischaemic strokes/SEE, 51% fewer haemorrhagic strokes and 10% lower mortality, but ~25% more GI bleeding, possibly excepting apixaban [S:566252d5-a1e2-5804-961b-592265a4efe6].

**Special populations.**
- *Prior stroke/TIA or ICH* (excluded from trials for ICH): observational meta-analysis showed NOACs reduced stroke, systemic embolism, death, major bleeding and ICH after stroke/TIA, and reduced stroke, death and ICH after prior ICH [S:1fb3fa05-8341-5fa1-bcd7-b46c17b21d4b]; a Taiwanese nationwide ICH cohort found lower mortality, ICH and major bleeding with similar ischaemic stroke [S:908afa3f-c89c-5079-9a8e-90ce7a898a30]. RCT data in prior stroke/TIA (20,500 patients) showed ~13.7% relative reduction in stroke/SEE and ~46% in intracranial haemorrhage [S:557222a9-8451-5a42-8c0f-51591addf0f6].
- *CKD*: benefit is preserved in [passage text removed]) per ESC/EACTS [S:8a409e7e-b876-5d39-9de7-2aff6acdad18], but dialysis evidence is thin — AXADIA-AF NET 8 and RENAL-AF found apixaban and VKA similar and were underpowered [S:352fd1a9-736c-5f6a-a962-a4f93726535f]; guidelines allow warfarin or an evidence-based apixaban dose in end-stage disease [S:8a409e7e-b876-5d39-9de7-2aff6acdad18].
- *Frailty/very elderly*: meta-analytic data in ~880,464 frail older patients favour DOACs [S:0a41f2e7-461f-5e5b-baf6-40943f11b084], but the FRAIL-AF randomised trial showed that switching frail patients ≥75 years from stable VKA to a DOAC increased major/clinically relevant non-major bleeding without reducing thromboembolism, and was stopped for futility — hence the ESC recommendation to consider maintaining VKA in such patients [S:8a409e7e-b876-5d39-9de7-2aff6acdad18][S:47b03f4b-72cc-5e6e-bc38-2fa232636404].

**Where VKAs remain superior/preferred.** DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical prosthetic [passage text removed] [S:8026edbd-892f-550d-bada-5460c59bfeac]; RE-ALIGN was stopped early for excess thromboembolic and bleeding events with dabigatran [S:a2eacfbf-cb5e-5293-871d-748f2ba75160], and INVICTUS (4,565 patients with rheumatic mitral valve disease and AF) found rivaroxaban worse than VKA on the composite of stroke/systemic embolism/MI/vascular death (HR 1.25, 1.10–1.41), with more ischaemic stroke and death, despite suboptimal INR control [S:38f7ba71-6fda-5bc0-b61d-215b0c09a610][S:ee75766a-1788-5078-abcb-11afa085974f]. DOACs are acceptable in bioprosthetic valves [S:8026edbd-892f-550d-bada-5460c59bfeac][S:a623547a-09ed-57fe-8d02-80591a035e34], and in NVAF with concomitant native valve disease meta-analysis showed less stroke/SEE and ICH with similar major bleeding [S:4405d749-8309-58f5-963a-dc3a0f6097dc].

**Key caveat.** Comparative benefit depends partly on the quality of warfarin control — effect sizes for stroke, bleeding and mortality varied by time in therapeutic range [S:56688bd5-9f57-54cd-81e0-13e21da0e994], and several DOAC-favouring CKD studies had poor or undisclosed TTR in the warfarin arm [S:60a4c09e-33bd-5c25-8417-2518e85d8cb3]. Also, cross-trial comparisons of individual DOACs are unreliable because of differing trial designs [S:9c718033-4ad1-51b4-8365-0167fa805685], and no head-to-head randomised DOAC comparisons exist [S:8b12ba94-4c34-5663-b700-e52c6eaf945f].

rows.question: What perfusion abnormalities appear on myocardial perfusion scintigraphy in patients with cardiac amyloidosis without obstructive coronary disease?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Abnormal myocardial perfusion findings are common in cardiac amyloidosis, being present in most patients imaged; Stress perfusion defects are the main abnormality, with group average summed stress scores only modestly elevated; A reversible stress-rest difference component is also present, small in average magnitude; As a preliminary observation, these perfusion abnormalities occur despite non-obstructive epicardial arteries, consistent with microvascular rather than obstructive ischaemia. Certainty: The evidence is early and comes from a small group examined without a comparison population, so these are preliminary observations rather than established diagnostic relationships. Scope: applies to cardiac amyloidosis without obstructive coronary disease in adults undergoing myocardial perfusion imaging, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents abnormal perfusion scintigraphy as an established or specific marker of cardiac amyloidosis, or recommends it as a basis for forgoing further evaluation for coronary disease.

answers.websearch:
**Conclusion:** In cardiac amyloidosis with unobstructed coronaries, scintigraphy typically shows reversible ("ischemic") and mixed perfusion defects — often septal — superimposed on a globally reduced, heterogeneous tracer uptake, frequently accompanied by high-risk ancillary features (transient ischemic LV cavity dilation and increased right-ventricular tracer uptake); these reflect coronary microvascular dysfunction rather than epicardial stenosis.

**Frequency and character of defects**

- **Thallium-201 SPECT:** In a retrospective cardiac amyloidosis cohort, abnormal Tl-201 findings occurred in 72.22% of patients, with summed stress score 5.47 ± 6.42 and summed difference score 2.16 ± 2.13 (i.e., a reversible component). Both SSS and SDS [passage text removed]), and posterior wall thickness was the only independent predictor of SSS. Of the eight patients with abnormal scans who underwent angiography, none had physiologically significant coronary lesions [PMID 40990303; doi 10.1177/10815589251384949].
- **99mTc-sestamibi MPS:** Among newly diagnosed amyloidosis patients without preexisting CAD evaluated for symptoms, sestamibi scintigraphy showed [passage text removed] a normal study in 45% (9/20); coronary evaluation revealed nonobstructive lesions or normal coronaries in 75% (18/24), interpreted as microvascular ischemia [PMID 39586273].
- **PET (N-13 ammonia):** In 21 amyloidosis subjects without epicardial CAD, 57% (12/21) had ischemic scans (3 severe); patterns ranged from no ischemia to severe ischemia. A published example shows a **reversible mid- and basal septal defect** with normal CT coronary angiography and coronary flow reserve 1.3, with biopsy showing vascular amyloid obliterating a small vessel lumen. Notably, none of the hypertensive LVH comparators had perfusion defects [doi 10.1016/j.jchf.2014.03.009; PMC4127145].

**High-risk ancillary findings without obstructive CAD**

- Transient cavity dilation of the LV on post-stress images occurred in 76% (16/21) and increased RV tracer uptake in 62% (13/21) of amyloidosis subjects; mean transient dilation ratio 1.18 ± 0.12 versus 1.04 ± 0.18 in LVH (p = 0.03) [doi 10.1016/j.jchf.2014.03.009]. Transient ischemic dilatation — classically a marker of multivessel CAD — has also been reported as a stand-alone presentation in cardiac amyloidosis [PMID 39293709; J Nucl Cardiol 2025;44:102042].

**Global and regional (septal) hypoperfusion pattern**

- In a dual-isotope 99mTc-PYP/201Tl study of ATTR (39 PYP-positive; 35 without a significant Tl defect), thallium heart-to-lung ratio correlated inversely with PYP H/CL and LV mass, and polar-map analysis showed significantly lower septal than lateral %uptake ([passage text removed]; also p = 0.006 in the diffusely hypertrophied subgroup) — i.e., global perfusion reduction with septal-predominant regional heterogeneity despite diffuse hypertrophy; PYP uptake was inversely distributed (higher septally) [PMC11612393].
- A separate dual-isotope series found a **mismatch pattern** (reduced 201Tl uptake where 99mTc-PYP uptake was high, septally) in 13 of 19 PYP-positive patients (68%), and 9 of these 13 had no significant coronary stenosis — attributed to obstructive intramural coronary amyloidosis [doi 10.1186/s41824-025-00255-7].
- A review notes SPECT-MPI perfusion abnormalities in ATTR differ from CAD, that amyloid deposits themselves can cause hypoperfusion and misinterpretation of defects, and that these are not explained by wall thickness alone [PMC12113637].

**Mechanistic corroboration (non-scintigraphic)**

Stress MBF was severely reduced in 93 amyloidosis patients versus three-vessel disease and controls (CA 1.04 ± 0.51 vs 3VD 1.35 ± 0.50 vs unobstructed 2.92 ± 0.52 vs healthy [passage text removed]), with histology showing amyloid infiltration of epicardial arteries and capillary disruption/rarefaction [PMID 38247182]. PET quantification showed markedly increased minimal coronary vascular resistance (111 ± 40 [passage text removed]), reduced stress MBF (0.85 ± 0.29 [passage text removed]; both p < 0.0001) versus hypertensive LVH [PMC6214157]. The CMR literature describes the amyloid perfusion phenotype as diffuse impairment with an endocardial-to-epicardial transmural gradient and base-to-apex gradient [PMC12113637].

**Caveat:** Some of these cohorts are small and single-centre, and a substantial minority of amyloidosis patients have entirely normal perfusion scans (45% in the sestamibi series [PMID 39586273]); I found no large prospective study defining the sensitivity/specificity of scintigraphic defect patterns for amyloidosis itself.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** In cardiac amyloidosis with non-obstructive coronaries, perfusion scintigraphy is frequently abnormal — typically showing globally reduced and regionally heterogeneous tracer uptake with both fixed and partially reversible defects (and occasionally reverse redistribution) — attributable to amyloid-related coronary microvascular dysfunction rather than epicardial stenosis.

**What the scans show**

- **Frequency and semi-quantitative pattern.** In 36 patients with biopsy-/PYP-confirmed cardiac amyloidosis (32 ATTR-CM), abnormal thallium-201 scintigraphy was present in 72.22%, with summed stress score 5.47 ± 6.42 and summed difference score 2.16 ± 2.13 — i.e. mostly modest defect burden with a reversible component in addition to fixed uptake reduction [S:5bf4b516]. Both SSS and SDS [passage text removed]), and posterior wall thickness was the only independent [passage text removed]) [S:5bf4b516].
- **Coronary angiography correlate.** Of the 8 patients with abnormal scans who underwent angiography, none had physiologically significant lesions; the single intermediate lesion (50% mid-LAD) had FFR 0.81 at maximal hyperaemia [S:0ef2b4c0][S:8cee7df2]. Patients with known CAD were excluded a priori [S:6edbebe7].
- **Global reduction plus septal heterogeneity.** In a dual ⁹⁹ᵐTc-PYP/²⁰¹Tl SPECT study of ATTR (39 patients with Perugini grade 2–3 and H/CL >1.3), only 4 had a frank segmental perfusion defect; among the remaining 35, thallium heart/lung ratio correlated inversely with PYP H/CL and with LV mass, and polar-map analysis showed significantly lower mean %uptake in the septum than the lateral wall ([passage text removed]) despite diffuse hypertrophy [S:89cf8c5e]. So the dominant signature is diffuse global hypoperfusion scaling with amyloid burden, with regional (septal-predominant) heterogeneity, rather than a coronary-territory defect.
- **Reverse redistribution.** Amyloidosis is among the conditions in which a reverse-redistribution pattern on thallium/technetium MPI has been reported (defect appearing or worsening on rest/delayed images) [S:366d16ae].
- **Increased ²⁰¹Tl washout.** An earlier small series (5 CA patients vs 12 controls) found significantly increased thallium washout, interpreted as a mixture of viable and necrotic myocardium, and particularly marked in the 4 patients who died within a year [S:f9048d05].
- **Not universal.** In older ¹²³I-MIBG series, *resting* ²⁰¹Tl scans were reported as normal without perfusion defects, producing a perfusion–innervation mismatch [S:16a107e5] — consistent with stress imaging being needed to unmask the abnormality.

**Mechanism and cross-modality corroboration**

Perfusion abnormality is ascribed to amyloid deposition in the interstitium, perivascular space and media of intramyocardial vessels, acting through structural (wall thickening/luminal narrowing), extravascular (perivascular/interstitial compression, reduced diastolic perfusion time) and functional (autonomic and endothelial) mechanisms, with wall thickening causing capillary rarefaction and reduced subendocardial flow [S:ff97c2aa][S:7e538751]. Quantitative modalities show the same physiology: [passage text removed] (1.22 ± 0.70 mL/g/min and 1.62 ± 0.63 vs 3.21 ± 0.64 and 4.17 ± 0.78 in healthy volunteers, p < 0.001), comparable to three-vessel disease, and inversely correlated with ECV, LGE transmurality, NT-proBNP and troponin [S:85e6d5b0]; ¹³N-ammonia PET showed reduced global CFR in ATTR with cardiac involvement ([passage text removed]) in patients presumed free of epicardial CAD [S:b5a16be4], including loss of the normal apical microvascular preservation [S:bb9db794]; and quantitative stress perfusion CMR links lower stress MBF/MPR to higher LV mass and to mortality in AL amyloidosis [S:867b6f0e][S:be852a6d].

**Caveats.** The thallium cohort was small, predominantly A97S hereditary ATTR-CM, had no comparator cardiomyopathy group, and only 8 of 26 patients with abnormal scans were angiographed — so specificity is unestablished, and similar patterns occur with marked LVH from hypertensive heart disease, HCM or aortic stenosis [S:8bffc076]. More broadly, perfusion scintigraphy has had limited clinical use in amyloidosis and the evidence base remains thin [S:f9048d05].

rows.question: What outcomes follow heart transplantation in patients with LMNA-related cardiomyopathy?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Survival at one year and over longer follow-up after heart transplantation for LMNA-related cardiomyopathy did not differ from survival in propensity-matched non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy recipients; Deaths concentrated early after transplantation, most first-year deaths occurring during the index intensive care stay rather than later; Electrical storm in the days before transplantation was associated with higher post-transplant mortality on an unadjusted and imprecise estimate; Neuromuscular and extracardiac involvement was not associated with post-transplant mortality, with no first-year deaths among recipients who had neuromuscular manifestations. Certainty: The evidence is early and imprecise, resting on few patients and few deaths, so it supports associations at best rather than settled effects. Scope: applies to LMNA-related cardiomyopathy treated with heart transplantation in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents electrical storm before transplantation as an established causal determinant of post-transplant death or recommends deferring or withholding transplantation on that basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: heart transplantation in LMNA‑related cardiomyopathy yields survival equivalent to transplantation for other non‑ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy, and neuromuscular involvement does not worsen after surgery — but transplantation performed in the setting of a preceding electrical storm carries a markedly higher mortality.**

**Survival is comparable to matched DCM recipients.** The first dedicated study of post‑transplant outcomes in laminopathy pooled all consecutive LMNA patients transplanted 2003–2024 at three French centres (40 patients, median age 45.4 years, 57.5% male) and compared them with 160 propensity‑score‑matched non‑ischaemic DCM recipients. Post‑transplant survival was 90% at 3 months, 74% at 1 year and 70% at 5 years, statistically indistinguishable from the matched group ([passage text removed]) [PMID 42336625]. The accompanying editorial reports the 5‑year figures as 70% (LMNA) versus 75% (DCM controls), and notes that [passage text removed] [heartjnl-2026-328574]. A single‑institution series of transplantation for Emery‑Dreifuss muscular dystrophy similarly concluded that long-term outcomes were comparable to non‑laminopathy recipients at 1, 2 and 5 years [sudoc.fr/191669660].

**Electrical storm before transplant is the dominant risk factor.** Electrical storm preceded transplantation in one‑third of the LMNA cohort, and was the only variable associated with post‑transplant [passage text removed]) [PMID 42336625]; the editorial reports 1‑year survival of 44% in those transplanted for electrical storm versus 89% in the rest [heartjnl-2026-328574]. This underpins the authors' recommendation to consider transplantation earlier in the disease course, before arrhythmogenic instability develops [PMID 42336625].

**Extracardiac/neuromuscular disease is not a contraindication.** [passage text removed] progress after transplantation [PMID 42336625]. Consistent with this, a family series of 7 recipients with LMNA‑related limb‑girdle muscular dystrophy type 1B had no excess of early or late postoperative complications, no rhabdomyolysis, and no significant change in skeletal muscle symptoms over a mean follow‑up of about 8 years [PMID 19446900; lmnacardiac.org]. In a multi‑institutional US registry analysis comparing 29 muscular dystrophy recipients with 275 matched non‑ischaemic cardiomyopathy recipients, survival was similar [utsouthwestern.elsevierpure.com]; a systematic review confirms that transplant has nonetheless historically been treated as a relative contraindication in inherited muscle disease because of perioperative and graft concerns [PMID 38791328].

**Context — transplantation is frequently needed.** In a Norwegian cohort, 15 of 79 LMNA genotype‑positive patients (19%) underwent transplantation over 7.8 ± 6.3 years, giving a combined death/transplant rate of 24%; two of the six deaths in that cohort occurred after transplantation (intracerebral haemorrhage and infection, one each), and LMNA patients accounted for 6.5% (13/199) of non‑ischaemic DCM transplants [PMID 29095976; PMC5939624]. Other cohorts report transplantation in ~10% of LMNA‑DCM patients with no sudden deaths among those transplanted [10.3389/fgene.2023.1291411], and up to ~9% of DCM transplant recipients carry LMNA variants [PMC7000139].

**Caveats:** the only dedicated outcome study is retrospective with 40 transplanted patients, and the electrical‑storm hazard ratio has a very wide confidence interval [PMID 42336625]. I found no data on genotype‑specific post‑transplant outcomes (e.g. truncating vs missense variants), rejection rates, or allograft vasculopathy specifically in LMNA recipients.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Post‑transplant survival in LMNA‑related cardiomyopathy is equivalent to that of matched non‑LMNA dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) recipients, but a substantial share of these transplants are done as salvage for refractory electrical storm — and that context, not the laminopathy itself or its neuromuscular features, is what drives mortality.

## Evidence

**Survival is comparable to matched DCM controls.** In the first dedicated study of the question — 40 LMNA patients transplanted [passage text removed], median age 45.4 years, 57.5% male, median post‑transplant follow‑up 47.5 months — [passage text removed]% [S:9e00dca4-f4d2-54e3-818f-f9d8b0274a84][S:d534650a-4dc4-5e24-9c8a-9ce1340fff5d][S:f6b14e66-af9a-5320-964d-4d0578d09f58]. Against 160 patients matched 4:1 for sex, age, pre‑transplant circulatory support and transplant year (survival 96.9%, 81.2%, 74.8%), there was no difference (HR 1.01; 95% CI 0.52–1.95; p=0.98), nor in ICU or total hospital length of stay [S:5a40991b-965d-5ec7-b010-3bc1cc0f0d57].

**Graft function and cardiac outcomes.** Median LVEF at 1 year post‑transplant was [passage text removed] management, and none required retransplantation or long‑term circulatory support [S:9e00dca4-f4d2-54e3-818f-f9d8b0274a84].

**Deaths are early and perioperative.** Leading ICU causes of death were multiple organ failure from [passage text removed] [S:9e00dca4-f4d2-54e3-818f-f9d8b0274a84]. The cohort was severely ill pre‑transplant: median LVEF 25%, severe RV dysfunction in 56%, sustained ventricular arrhythmia history in ~50%, 97.4% with a rhythm device, and 25% on VA‑ECMO at transplant [S:d534650a-4dc4-5e24-9c8a-9ce1340fff5d].

**Electrical storm (ES) is the key prognostic driver.** HTx followed ES in one‑third of cases — versus <1% of transplants overall — and ES in the days before HTx was the only factor associated with mortality (HR 8.46; 95% CI 1.66–43.17; p=0.002; OR for 1‑year mortality 10.6, 95% CI 1.66–97.3, p=0.02) [S:f6b14e66-af9a-5320-964d-4d0578d09f58][S:b0800bf5-5895-54d9-a429-d17ae3b5e45d][S:bc44da98-c05e-5543-9f44-6fd80ee90e8e]. Notably, urgent transplantation or isolated cardiogenic shock alone were *not* associated with mortality, and ES patients did not have worse biomarkers of end‑organ dysfunction — suggesting ES marks a distinct frail subset transplanted with little anticipation [S:9431f0ba-5036-5928-a14d-84c54a1ff172][S:bc44da98-c05e-5543-9f44-6fd80ee90e8e]. This matters because VT ablation performs particularly poorly in LMNA disease [S:d6a32ed8-2cce-5427-9820-993992617292][S:7433fba1-aa7c-5fdd-a1a2-447ac60e7c35].

**Extracardiac/neuromuscular outcomes are reassuring.** Nine patients (22.5%) had pre‑transplant neuromuscular involvement (three Emery‑Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, others muscle weakness ± moderate neuropathy); none had lost ambulation or required chronic ventilation [S:d534650a-4dc4-5e24-9c8a-9ce1340fff5d]. None of these patients died in the first year, and on specialist reassessment their extracardiac manifestations were stable with normal CPK; two patients discontinued statins for [passage text removed] weakness [S:bc44da98-c05e-5543-9f44-6fd80ee90e8e][S:a2de7864-0ca9-5935-81cb-492785363850]. The authors conclude moderate neuromuscular involvement should not be a contraindication, while cautioning that no patient had severe neuromuscular disease and systematic pre/post objective neuromuscular testing was lacking, so worsening cannot be formally excluded [S:35012e93-0d94-5fd4-a651-071b0c6364a4][S:a2de7864-0ca9-5935-81cb-492785363850]. A comparable pattern has been described for muscular dystrophy recipients generally, where survival, infection, rejection and vasculopathy matched idiopathic DCM controls [S:7ddef0f9-b3e6-5fde-80dd-606837c89d7f].

**Context — transplant is a common endpoint in this genotype.** Laminopathies account for ~7% of DCM transplant indications and the highest HTx rate among DCM genotypes (19–27%) [S:74af6fce-0a15-5978-9ebe-b6c180eb9588]; in a separate laminopathy series >20% required transplantation, at a median age of 45 years and independently of skeletal muscle involvement [S:882d4a2d-b5d4-5061-8831-08bab7ad611d].

## Caveats
Evidence rests essentially on one retrospective, single‑country cohort of 40 patients; the authors note the DCM control group was heterogeneous, LMNA status may have influenced referral decisions, and limited numbers permitted identification of only one prognostic factor [S:35012e93-0d94-5fd4-a651-071b0c6364a4][S:9431f0ba-5036-5928-a14d-84c54a1ff172]. I found no evidence on LVAD outcomes specifically in LMNA carriers — no device other than VA‑ECMO was used in this cohort [S:9e00dca4-f4d2-54e3-818f-f9d8b0274a84].

rows.question: What does resting heart rate indicate in patients with atrial fibrillation undergoing early rhythm control therapy?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Patients with a resting heart rate at or above 110 beats per minute more often reported severe or disabling atrial fibrillation-related symptoms; Baseline resting heart rate group did not interact with cardiovascular events during follow-up; Early rhythm control reduced cardiovascular events to a similar extent in both heart rate groups, with no interaction detected between the treatment effect and heart rate group. Certainty: Support for the claims is exploratory and hypothesis-generating, since the heart rate groupings arose from pre-existing patient characteristics rather than deliberate assignment and only part of the eligible population contributed data, so the conclusions describe association rather than causation. Scope: applies to recently diagnosed atrial fibrillation still present at the start of treatment in older adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the similar outcomes across heart rate groups as showing that rate control can be withheld or relaxed once rhythm control therapy is started.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** In EAST‑AFNET 4, heart rate during AF is a marker of symptom burden, not of prognosis — a high rate (≥110 bpm) identifies patients [passage text removed], but cardiovascular event rates do not differ by heart rate, and early rhythm control (ERC) reduces events in both high‑ and low‑rate patients.

**Evidence from the dedicated heart‑rate analysis (Koldenhof et al., *Heart*, 2026; [passage text removed])**
- Population: 772 EAST‑AFNET 4 patients who were in AF at baseline with heart rate recorded; mean age 70.8±7.8 years, 305 (40%) women, 385 (50%) randomised to ERC, and 506 (66%) with a heart rate <110 bpm ([research.birmingham.ac.uk]([passage text removed])).
- **Symptoms:** patients with heart rate ≥110 bpm were more often symptomatic ([passage text removed] often severely symptomatic with an EHRA [passage text removed]) ([research.birmingham.ac.uk]([passage text removed])).
- **Prognosis:** the first primary outcome (cardiovascular death, stroke, or hospitalisation [passage text removed]) occurred at 5.1 per 100 person‑years in both strata (116 events with rate <110 bpm; 62 events with rate ≥110 bpm), HR 1.08 (95% CI 0.79–1.48) for ≥110 vs <110 bpm ([research.birmingham.ac.uk]([passage text removed])).
- **Authors' [passage text removed]" (NCT01288352) ([research.rug.nl]([passage text removed]); [PMID 41663267](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41663267)).

**Consistent supporting context**
- Heart rate is not the mechanism by which ERC works: in the mediator analysis of the trial, [passage text removed] ERC's outcome benefit, and ERC gave no reduction in events [passage text removed] (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.65–1.67) ([PMID 36036648](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36036648)). In that analysis's 12‑month data, heart rate was essentially identical between arms (median 62 [IQR 57–71] with ERC vs 64 [57–71] with usual care, p=0.461; ventricular rate in AF 80 vs 81 bpm, p=0.161) ([PMC9584752](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9584752)).

**Caveat:** the ≥110 bpm threshold mirrors the lenient rate‑control target in guidelines (resting heart rate <100–110 bpm for AF patients without heart failure) ([wikijournalclub.org](https://www.wikijournalclub.org/wiki/EAST-AFNET_4)). The analysis is a post‑hoc/secondary look at a baseline single measurement in a subset in AF, so it addresses baseline rate as a prognostic marker rather than the effect of intensifying rate control; I found no EAST‑AFNET 4 evidence on longitudinal rate control targets, and observational data outside this trial (e.g. time‑in‑target‑range analyses) reach different conclusions ([PMC10786089]([passage text removed])).

**Resting heart rate marks symptom severity, not cardiovascular risk, and does not modify the benefit of early rhythm control.** This comes from a prespecified-type subanalysis of the EAST-AFNET 4 trial [S:c997b019-1a90-50c9-a40e-55ef342fdc58].

**What was analysed.** Of 2789 randomised [passage text removed]; after excluding those in sinus rhythm, without an ECG, or without heart-rate data, 772 patients (28%) with baseline heart rate from the ECG at discharge from the randomisation visit were stratified at the guideline threshold of 110 bpm [S:86466d00-476e-5dd9-ab42-d72f503f6d46]. [passage text removed]%) had a heart rate <110 bpm [S:f821a570-4ca9-5e66-b04c-9e0aaa5d21db][[passage text removed] indicates symptom burden.** Patients with a heart rate ≥110 bpm [passage text removed] severe symptoms with an EHRA [passage text removed]) [S:f821a570-4ca9-5e76-b04c-9e0aaa5d21db]; in a mixed model, heart rate ≥110 bpm carried an OR of 1.63 (95% CI 1.04–2.55) for EHRA III/IV [S:24d12206-3b97-52db-a868-acd65b88b282].

**It does not indicate cardiovascular event risk.** The first primary outcome (cardiovascular death, stroke, or hospitalisation for worsening heart failure or acute coronary syndrome) occurred at 5.1 per 100 person-years in both strata (116 vs 62 events), HR [passage text removed]) for ≥110 vs <110 bpm [S:db305cdf-8bcd-516a-9dda-6ad444aa6434][S:f821a570-4ca9-5e76-b04c-9e0aaa5d21db]. Nights spent in hospital per year were also similar (4.72±17.3 vs 4.57±14.6) [S:db305cdf-8bcd-516a-9dda-6ad444aa6434].

**It does not select who benefits from rhythm control.** There was no interaction between heart-rate group [passage text removed] their components, and no difference in the primary safety outcome [S:80591751-8ef1-5182-a718-60bc1ed30e9e]; the authors conclude rhythm control reduced [passage text removed]:78626dd5-f3a9-56ca-908f-1f0b25cacfdf].

**Other signals.** A high heart rate flagged patients who were rate-control naïve or recently started (40% first-diagnosed AF) and, unexpectedly, was more common in paroxysmal AF — plausibly because dosing of negatively chronotropic/dromotropic drugs is constrained by bradycardia during sinus rhythm [S:80591751-8ef1-5182-a718-60bc1ed30e9e][S:ed4f6365-8cc4-51ab-b01e-9dea559aaf60]. It also predicted more intensive rate-control prescribing at discharge: digoxin/[passage text removed]), with no difference in calcium channel blockers (3% vs 6%, p=0.068) [S:24d12206-3b97-52db-a868-acd65b88b282]. Clinical implication drawn by the authors: initiate rate and rhythm control simultaneously in recently diagnosed AF with a high heart rate, for symptom control plus outcome reduction [S:1c384469-db44-5a76-afc4-033f219fc6a6].

**Caveats.** The analysis was not designed to test heart-rate effects, so no causal inference is possible; only patients in AF at baseline were included (enriching for newly diagnosed and persistent AF), no follow-up heart-rate data or drug dosages were available, and intensified rate control during follow-up may have blunted any effect of uncontrolled rate [S:1c384469-db44-5a76-afc4-033f219fc6a6].

**Contrasting evidence outside the early-rhythm-control setting.** In AFFIRM, greater [passage text removed] (<80 bpm) was independently [passage text removed] and all-cause mortality after adjustment, in both rate- and rhythm-control arms [S:fa6e0dcf-7764-596d-af2b-f7b344b5c184] — a longitudinal rate-control metric rather than a single baseline measurement, so it addresses a different question than the EAST-AFNET 4 stratification.
