rows.question: How effectively do CCTA radiomic, structural stress and hemodynamic features identify vulnerable coronary plaques?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: CCTA radiomic features identified all intravascular imaging-labeled vulnerable cases, giving the highest sensitivity but the lowest specificity of the three feature categories; Structural-stress (mechanical) and hemodynamic features were clearly more specific than radiomic features but missed some of the labeled vulnerable cases; Combining at least two of the three feature categories improved classification over any single category, leaving only one misclassified case. Certainty: The findings remain preliminary and internally derived, as classification performance was estimated by leave-one-out resampling within the same small, highly imbalanced patient sample from which the models were built, without external confirmation. Scope: applies to coronary plaque vulnerability defined by intravascular imaging in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents these CCTA-derived features as an established replacement for intravascular imaging or recommends plaque-directed treatment on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

All three feature families discriminate vulnerable/culprit plaques better than conventional CCTA anatomy alone, but each is only moderately accurate in isolation (typically AUC ~0.75–0.85 for radiomics; c-index ~0.79 for hemodynamics), they are complementary rather than redundant, and none has been prospectively validated to a level supporting routine clinical use.

## 1. CCTA radiomics — moderate-to-good, consistently better than conventional CT markers

- A systematic review of CCTA radiomics for plaque vulnerability found all included models reported AUC >0.7 (range 0.72–1), and in the four studies making [passage text removed] vulnerability markers; however, radiomics quality [passage text removed]%, and external validation was largely absent ([mdpi.com/2673-3846/5/4/45](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-3846/5/4/45)).
- The most rigorous study (Chen et al., *Radiology* 2023;307(2):e221693) built a 16-feature radiomic signature (14 textural, 2 geometric) in 225 patients/419 lesions with IVUS-defined high-risk plaque as reference. AUC was [passage text removed]) in training, 0.80 (0.64–0.97) internal test, and 0.77 (0.60–0.94) external test — versus 0.58 (0.54–0.62) for conventional HRP features alone and 0.73 (0.67–0.80) for HRP plus quantitative plaque parameters ([mdpi.com/2673-3846/5/4/45](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-3846/5/4/45); [[passage text removed]); summarised in [re.public.polimi.it/.../2025Corti_reviewCoronary.pdf]([passage text removed])). A key limitation: the signature had a high false-positive rate, with only 12% of high-signature patients experiencing MACE ([re.public.polimi.it]([passage text removed])).
- Against histology, a radiomics ML model using eight features achieved cross-validation AUC 0.900 ± 0.033, falling to 0.754–0.782 in validation versus 0.656 (0.593–0.718) for a conventional CCTA model ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35171348](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35171348); tabulated in [mdpi.com/2673-3846/5/4/45](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-3846/5/4/45)).
- Pericoronary-fat radiomics for OCT-defined thin-cap fibroatheroma is weaker: most individual PCAT features had AUCs in the 0.5–0.69 range, with combined models ~0.77–0.78 ([mdpi.com/2673-3846/5/4/45](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-3846/5/4/45)).

## 2. Structural stress — strong mechanistic and prognostic signal, but mostly derived from invasive imaging

- [passage text removed]; peak PSS is typically ~100–300 kPa and correlates with ACS presentation, rupture and MACE, adding prognostic information beyond imaging alone ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9300846]([passage text removed])).
- In 4,053 VH-IVUS frames from 32 ruptured versus 32 non-ruptured fibroatheromas, ruptured lesions had higher PSS (133 kPa [Q1–Q3 90–191] vs 104 kPa [75–142]; p=0.002) and greater PSS variation (55 vs 43 kPa; p=0.002); PSS >135 kPa predicted rupture in higher-risk regions, and rupture occurred proximal or adjacent to the minimal luminal area in 87.5% ([sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1936878X17305132](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1936878X17305132); [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5725311]([passage text removed])).
- OCT/DSA-based FEA discriminated vulnerable (n=32) from stable (n=71) plaques mainly via maximal stress (151.38±39.75 vs 72.91±26.90 kPa, p<0.05); average stress differed far less (13.96±13.82 vs 12.78±7.50 kPa) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10895097]([passage text removed])).
- In a PROSPECT substudy of 86 non-culprit fibroatheromas, combining ESS, ESS gradient and PSS heterogeneity index with anatomical parameters was associated with most future MACE; notably neither low ESS nor high mean ESS (cut-off 2.7 Pa) was an independent predictor, and TCFA morphology was not significant ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10939719]([passage text removed])). Important caveat: this evidence base is intravascular-imaging-derived, not CCTA-derived.

## 3. CCTA hemodynamics — modest but statistically incremental over anatomy

- EMERALD (72 patients, 66 culprit vs 150 non-culprit lesions with CCTA 1 month–2 years pre-ACS): culprit lesions had [passage text removed] more adverse plaque characteristics ([passage text removed]); on CFD they had lower FFR_CT and higher ΔFFR_CT, wall shear stress and axial plaque stress (all p<0.01). Adding hemodynamics to stenosis+APC raised the c-index from 0.747 to 0.789 (p=0.014), with category-free NRI 0.287 (p=0.047) ([[passage text removed])). Cut-offs defining adverse hemodynamics were FFR_CT ≤0.80, ΔFFR_CT ≥0.06, WSS ≥154.7 dyn/cm², axial plaque stress ≥1,606.6 dyn/cm² ([frontiersin.org/.../fcvm.2021.743538]([passage text removed].2021.743538/full)).
- EMERALD-II (351 patients; 363 culprit vs 2,088 non-culprit lesions) confirmed and extended this with AI-enabled quantitative plaque plus hemodynamic analysis, improving prediction of future ACS lesions to AUC 0.84 versus 0.78 for conventional assessment (p<0.001), independent of the CCTA-to-event interval ([mdpi.com/2075-4418/14/15/1671]([passage text removed]); trial/outcome details [profiles.wustl.edu]([passage text removed]); [acc.org]([passage text removed])). Even the highest-risk combination (stenosis ≥50% + APC ≥2 + plaque burden ≥70% + ΔFFR_CT ≥0.10) identified lesions of which 49% were culprits within 2 years — i.e. positive predictive value remains well below 100% ([acc.org]([passage text removed])).

## 4. Head-to-head and integration (the only direct three-way comparison)

A single-centre study integrating all three on the same CCTA datasets (161 plaques, 46 arteries, 39 patients; vulnerability labelled by intravascular imaging) found: radiomics gave the highest sensitivity (1.00, detecting every vulnerable case) but lowest specificity (0.69); FEA-derived mechanics and CFD-derived hemodynamics gave higher specificity (0.94 and 0.97) with sensitivity 0.86 each. Balanced accuracies were 0.87 (radiomic), 0.89 (mechanical) and 0.92 (hemodynamic); combining any two raised performance to sensitivity 1.00/specificity 0.97 with one misclassification, and the radiomic–mechanical model reached balanced accuracy 0.99 for arteries and 0.98 for patients after material-property data augmentation ([[passage text removed]); [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13290838]([passage text removed]); earlier two-way version: balanced accuracy 0.86 radiomic, 0.89 biomechanical, 0.94 combined, [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39662235](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39662235)). These figures come from leave-one-out cross-validation in 39 patients with only 7 vulnerable cases and no external validation — they should be read as hypothesis-generating.

## Key limitations to weigh

- CCTA's spatial resolution cannot resolve fibrous cap thickness or rupture directly, unlike IVUS/OCT ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8517134]([passage text removed])); expert consensus even advises against CCTA plaque labels implying histology such as "vulnerable" or "lipid-rich" ([acc.org]([passage text removed])).
- Low event rates per plaque mean positive predictive value is poor even for well-discriminating models: conventional high-risk plaque had sensitivity 32.8%, specificity 85.2%, PPV 6.4%, NPV 97.6% for MACE in one large cohort ([cbsmd.cn PDF]([passage text removed])).
- Radiomics lacks pipeline standardisation and multicentre external validation; biomechanical modelling depends on assumed wall material properties and on imaging adequate for CFD (37% of PROSPECT lesions were excluded for insufficient imaging) ([re.public.polimi.it]([passage text removed]); [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10939719]([passage text removed])).
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Each domain achieves moderate-to-good discrimination alone — typically AUCs in the 0.7–0.9 range — with characteristically different error profiles (radiomics is sensitive but non-specific; stress and flow markers are specific but miss some vulnerable lesions), and combining at least two domains consistently outperforms any single one. All of this rests on small, mostly single-centre, retrospective cohorts without external validation.

## Head-to-head evidence within one cohort

The only study to integrate all three explicitly analysed 161 plaques in 46 arteries from 39 patients (7 arteries/7 patients labelled vulnerable by intravascular imaging), extracting CCTA radiomics, finite-element mechanical markers, and transient CFD-derived wall-shear descriptors (TAWSS, OSI, TransWSS, RRT) [S:9834313a][S:0b71f48c]. Radiomics alone reached sensitivity 1.00 but specificity 0.69; mechanics and hemodynamics each reached sensitivity 0.86 with specificity 0.94 and 0.97 respectively [S:9834313a]. Balanced accuracy was highest for hemodynamics (0.92), then mechanics (0.89), then radiomics (0.87); radiomics misclassified 10 non-vulnerable cases while correctly flagging all vulnerable ones [S:925f5068]. Fusing any two domains lifted performance to sensitivity 1.00/specificity 0.97 and balanced accuracy 0.99, with adding the third giving no further gain [S:9834313a][S:e7b67bc0][S:ae84e58f].

## Radiomics

Against histology ex vivo (445 coregistered cross-sections, 30.1% advanced lesions), a radiomics ML model (least angle regression) achieved [passage text removed]) for advanced lesions, versus 0.65 for expert visual attenuation-pattern assessment, 0.55 for low-attenuation area (<30 HU) and 0.53 for mean HU [S:1267b5ec][S:be1892bf][S:b34ae435]. Radiomic features also discriminate napkin-ring-sign plaques, with 20.6% of features outperforming conventional quantitative measures, and spatial-distribution features (GLCM, GLRLM, geometry) beating first-order statistics [S:6a63a981]. Against intravascular reference standards, reported AUCs span roughly 0.80–0.95 (e.g. 0.84 for culprit vs high-stenosis non-culprit plaques in a 35-plaque test set; 0.95 for OCT-defined TCFA in 43 plaques; 0.80 for IVUS-defined vulnerability in 419 plaques; 0.87 in 158 stable angina patients) — note the small test sets behind the highest figures [S:6428d877]. Pericoronary adipose tissue radiomics registered to IVOCT gave AUC 0.78 ± 0.13 (lesion ROI) and 0.77 ± 0.14 (whole vessel) for TCFA, 0.83 ± 0.12 and 0.89 ± 0.09 for microchannels, and [passage text removed] for vessels with both features [S:5dda21fc].

## Structural stress

Mechanistically the strongest signal, but mostly validated on intravascular rather than CCTA geometry. OCT-based finite-element analysis of 10 ruptured vs 10 non-ruptured lesions found peak cap stress [passage text removed] maximal plaque stress [passage text removed]), with AUCs of 0.940 and 0.950 — superior to fibrous cap thickness or macrophage infiltration — and ruptures occurring within ~20° of stress maxima [S:e726e4e4][S:15d70c8c]. In PROSPECT non-culprit lesions, plaque structural stress at the minimal luminal area was higher in MACE lesions (112.1 ± 5.5 vs 90.4 ± 3.3 kPa, p=0.001), and a PSS heterogeneity index further improved identification of MACE lesions among VH-TCFAs ([passage text removed], p=0.01) [S:58ff6ec2].

Translated to CCTA: in 63 culprit vs 146 non-culprit lesions from the EMERALD cohort, a solid-mechanics Cap Vulnerability Index had the highest single-feature AUC (0.752) of 11 candidates, above ΔFFR_CT (0.712), WSS (0.692), diameter stenosis (0.690), low-attenuation plaque (0.669), napkin-ring sign (0.622) and axial plaque stress (0.617); it contributed the largest ΔAUC (0.049) in the combined model and single-handedly matched EMERALD I's best 7-variable model [S:eb0cdf05][S:6c07fc7c][S:962f7c61][S:8b2f4c4c].

## Hemodynamics

In EMERALD (216 lesions, 66 culprit, CCTA 1–24 months pre-ACS), culprit lesions had lower FFR_CT (0.72 vs 0.79), larger ΔFFR_CT (0.17 vs 0.06), [passage text removed]) and higher axial plaque stress (2585.9 vs 1734.7 dyn/cm²); adding adverse hemodynamic characteristics to stenosis, lesion length and plaque features raised the c-index from 0.747 to 0.789 (p=0.014), and lesions with both adverse plaque and hemodynamic features carried [passage text removed]) for being culprit [S:9ed161d9]. WSS, axial plaque stress, pressure gradient and ΔFFR_CT were strongly intercorrelated yet each remained an independent predictor [passage text removed] FFR_CT ≤0.80, and each added significantly to those variables [S:869f1f78]. Mediation analysis indicates hemodynamics acts both directly and indirectly (via plaque vulnerability) on culprit-lesion events [S:e038fee8]. In EMERALD-II, AI-derived quantitative plaque features plus hemodynamics predicted future ACS plaques better than conventional methods (AUC 0.84 vs 0.78, p<0.001) [S:fe04e440].

## Caveats

Conventional visual high-risk-plaque features correlate only modestly with IVUS/OCT-derived vulnerability, which is the gap these quantitative approaches aim to close [S:6a63a981]; the napkin-ring sign itself was ~41% sensitive and 97% specific in one retrospective 895-patient analysis [S:84df1df9]. ML models built on structural or hemodynamic features remain rare, and the integrated results explicitly require validation in larger multicentre datasets [S:0b71f48c]. Simulation outputs are also sensitive to input uncertainty — segmentation, physiological boundary conditions, and assumed wall material properties (the integrated study handled the last by augmenting over 100 material combinations, which raised combined radiomic-mechanical balanced accuracy from 0.94 to 0.99) [S:872ee93f][S:0b71f48c]; unloaded-geometry (zero-pressure) estimation is a further unaddressed source of error [S:ae84e58f].

rows.question: What outcomes follow fluid restriction compared with liberal fluid intake in patients with heart failure?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: All-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalisation did not differ significantly between fluid restriction and liberal fluid intake; Fluid restriction increased thirst distress in most trials that measured it, though findings were not unanimous; Quality of life results were contradictory across the questionnaires used, with no clear overall benefit of fluid restriction; NYHA class and natriuretic peptide levels did not differ between fluid restriction and liberal fluid intake. Certainty: The evidence base is small, heterogeneous and mostly vulnerable to bias, so the absence of differences in death and hospitalisation is suggestive rather than settled, and the symptom and health-status findings point in opposing directions. Scope: applies to chronic and acute heart failure in adults, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents fluid restriction and liberal fluid intake as demonstrated to be equivalent or interchangeable for survival and hospitalisation, or recommends abandoning fluid restriction on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Fluid restriction does not improve survival, hospitalization, congestion, or quality of life compared with liberal intake in heart failure; it reliably lowers fluid intake and increases thirst/thirst distress and worsens adherence, so current evidence and the 2024 ESC HFA consensus favor normal (non-restricted) intake with restriction reserved for selected patients.

## Randomized evidence in chronic HF (FRESH-UP)

The largest trial, FRESH-UP, randomized 504 outpatients with chronic HF (NYHA II–III) to advice for liberal intake versus restriction to ≤1,500 mL/day for 3 months. The primary outcome, KCCQ Overall Summary Score at 3 months, was 74.0 (liberal) vs 72.2 (restriction), adjusted mean difference [passage text removed]) — the primary endpoint was not met, though the point estimate favored liberal intake ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159556](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40159556); doi 10.1038/s41591-025-03628-4). Thirst distress was higher with restriction (TDS-HF 16.9 liberal vs 18.6 restricted, adjusted difference significant at P<0.001), and safety events were low and non-differential: death 1 vs 2, all-cause hospitalization 20 vs 15, HF hospitalization 4 vs 4, IV loop diuretic use 5 vs 7, AKI 3 vs 4 (liberal vs restricted) ([acc.org FRESH-UP summary]([passage text removed])). Achieved separation was modest — about 1,480 mL/day restricted vs 1,760 mL/day liberal — with no differences in death, HF hospitalization, IV diuretic need, or AKI at six months ([acc.org press release]([passage text removed])). Importantly, patients with hyponatremia (Na <130) and eGFR <30 were excluded, so these results do not extend to those groups ([medpagetoday.com/meetingcoverage/acc/114887](https://www.medpagetoday.com/meetingcoverage/acc/114887)).

## Acute decompensated HF

In hospitalized ADHF, aggressive restriction (≤800 mL/day fluid plus ≤800 mg/day sodium) vs an unrestricted hospital diet in 75 patients produced no difference in weight loss (between-group difference 0.25 kg; 95% [passage text removed]) or [passage text removed], significantly worse thirst (5.1 ± 2.9 vs 3.44 ± 2.0), and no difference in 30-day readmissions (11 vs 7 patients; P = 0.41) ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23689381](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23689381); [PMC8747930]([passage text removed])). The authors concluded such restriction is unnecessary during ADHF admission.

## Pooled evidence

A meta-analysis of 4 RCTs (747 patients) restricted to liberal-vs-restricted comparisons found no difference in [passage text removed]), KCCQ-OSS, weight change, or loop diuretic requirement; restriction did lower daily [passage text removed]) and reduced [passage text removed]) ([10.3389/fcvm.2025.1636862]([passage text removed])); a nonsignificant trend toward more AKI with restriction was noted ([the-hospitalist.org article/41031]([passage text removed])). A separate pooled analysis (9 studies, 961 patients) likewise found similar rehospitalization, mortality, thirst, QoL, diuretic dose, and serum sodium, but higher serum creatinine and lower BNP and body weight with restriction ([10.1016/j.ejim.2024.11.xxx — article S0929664624005540]([passage text removed])). A recent narrative/systematic review concluded there is no clear benefit and a signal of harm regarding thirst distress and possibly QoL ([heart.bmj.com/content/112/17/939]([passage text removed])).

**Discordant signal:** an older meta-analysis by Stein et al. reported that fluid restriction *alone* reduced mortality (RR [passage text removed]) and hospitalization (RR [passage text removed]) vs usual care, with no benefit when combined with sodium restriction ([PMC11277838]([passage text removed])); and a 2026 pooled analysis of 9 RCTs (1,271 patients) reported reduced all-cause mortality but not HF rehospitalization with restriction ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41711699](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41711699)). These used usual-care comparators and/or heterogeneous/observational inputs, which is the stated reason RCT-only analyses differ ([PMC12615477]([passage text removed])); I did not retrieve the effect estimates from the 2026 analysis, so its magnitude cannot be quantified here.

## Guidance

The 2024 HFA/ESC clinical consensus statement notes recent data challenge restriction, limits salt to ≤5 g/day, and contemplates [passage text removed], with normal intake generally 1.5–2.5 L/day (15–30 mL/kg/day) ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38606657](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38606657); doi 10.1002/ejhf.3244). ACC/AHA/HFSA reserve fluid restriction for advanced HF with concurrent hyponatremia ([[passage text removed])).

**Evidence gaps:** advanced/NYHA IV HF, hyponatremia, and severe renal impairment remain untested by these trials, and event counts were too low for adequate power on hard outcomes ([acc.org FRESH-UP]([passage text removed])).
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Across randomized trials, fluid restriction reliably lowers fluid intake but does not improve mortality, heart failure hospitalization, congestion relief, NYHA class, or natriuretic peptides compared with liberal intake, while it worsens thirst distress and adherence — so current evidence does not support routine restriction. [S:f9ef7a38-d833-5790-bc35-a8002244cc1a][S:80ad5af6-39f1-576d-8e25-102e19150c21][S:cb4bd28a-32e9-56c6-b82f-ce7bce6bfc49]

## Evidence

**Hard clinical outcomes — no difference.** A 2025 meta-analysis of 4 RCTs (747 patients, 378 randomized to liberal intake) found no significant difference in [passage text removed]) or [passage text removed]), and no differences in acute kidney injury, weight loss, or loop diuretic requirements; restriction did reduce [passage text removed]) [S:f9ef7a38-d833-5790-bc35-a8002244cc1a][S:b126972c-a2a1-5551-9478-cc25076c60ba]. A systematic review of 5 RCTs (769 hospitalized or ambulatory patients) similarly found no mortality or HF-hospitalization differences, and events across all studies combined were identical between groups; the authors caution that small samples preclude definitive conclusions [S:80ad5af6-39f1-576d-8e25-102e19150c21][S:070d9b44-b3f2-5573-9fc7-a96b9c65e7a8].

**Health status/quality of life — no benefit, possibly slightly worse with restriction.** In FRESH-UP (504 outpatients with chronic HF, restriction to 1500 mL/day vs liberal intake, open-label, multicentre), the primary endpoint KCCQ overall summary score at 3 months did not differ, and death, HF hospitalization and loop diuretic changes were also no different [S:03faa7d0-0cb1-5ae5-a699-54da942c1067][S:691d638a-3cde-531c-b570-8386b7203e14][S:00bfee7c-b1e1-5269-a14f-7aced6490520]. In the trial-level data, KCCQ-OSS was numerically higher with liberal intake (72.2 vs 74.0; P=0.056), while clinical, total symptom and physical/social function summary scores were significantly higher with liberal intake (e.g. CSS 74.5 vs 75.9; P=0.032); EQ-5D-5L and NT-proBNP at 3 and 6 months did not differ [S:befab8b8-17d9-58d8-91c7-30022153e439]. The pooled analysis likewise reported a lower KCCQ clinical summary score and lower adherence with restriction [S:f9ef7a38-d833-5790-bc35-a8002244cc1a].

**Thirst and tolerability — worse with restriction.** FRESH-UP showed more thirst distress with restriction (TDS-HF mean 18.6 vs 16.9; p<0.001) [S:befab8b8-17d9-58d8-91c7-30022153e439][S:03faa7d0-0cb1-5ae5-a699-54da942c1067]. In Holst et al.'s 32-week crossover trial (1.5 L/day vs 30 mL/kg/day), [passage text removed] worse during restriction, with no differences in weight, diuretic use, quality of life, 6-minute walk distance or hospitalizations [S:a8977ac3-e216-513f-ae00-f07ec674523b][S:befab8b8-17d9-58d8-91c7-30022153e439]. Restriction is also associated with xerostomia, altered taste, dry skin and itching [S:a8977ac3-e216-513f-ae00-f07ec674523b].

**Acute decompensated HF.** In a single-centre Brazilian trial of 75 patients admitted with acute decompensated HF, aggressive restriction (800 mL fluid, 800 mg sodium daily) did not improve congestion relief, weight loss, or 30-day readmission versus an unrestricted hospital diet; both groups lost more than 4 kg over the first 3 days and the between-group congestion score difference was about half a point and non-significant, while restricted patients were significantly thirstier [S:f7b4340c-2712-5c7d-b05c-aa604b5d764e][S:a5287ab8-9958-538c-9754-d94799315a62].

**Caveats and possible exception.** Evidence is heterogeneous (acute vs chronic HF, 1000–1500 mL/day targets, follow-up from "until clinical stability" to 32 weeks, varied questionnaires), most trials were small and at high risk of bias apart from FRESH-UP, and non-compliant/drop-out patients were often excluded without imputation [S:070d9b44-b3f2-5573-9fc7-a96b9c65e7a8][S:befab8b8-17d9-58d8-91c7-30022153e439]. One trial in hyponatremic HF patients (SALT-HF, 1000 mL/day) reported significantly higher KCCQ follow-up scores with restriction (OSS 72.6 vs 51.0; P=0.038), though without baseline adjustment [S:befab8b8-17d9-58d8-91c7-30022153e439][S:1c2a3284-5627-58f7-aea3-f1b527682ef5]. Reviewers therefore suggest reserving restriction for selected patients — e.g. dilutional hyponatremia, extensive oedema/ascites, or congestion not controlled by diuretics — rather than applying it routinely [S:a7585f8a-bf7c-57fa-a0b0-9d180056490a][S:00bfee7c-b1e1-5269-a14f-7aced6490520][S:691d638a-3cde-531c-b570-8386b7203e14].

rows.question: How does incidentally detected non-ischemic late iodine enhancement on cardiac CT relate to long-term adverse cardiovascular outcomes?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Incidentally detected non-ischemic late iodine enhancement is associated with a higher rate of cardiovascular events, defined as cardiac death or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation, with an adjusted hazard several times that of patients without enhancement but very imprecisely estimated; Deaths recorded during the observation period were almost all non-cardiac, including cancer, with only a single cardiovascular death; The prognostic signal rests on few events in a single retrospective sample observed for about two years, so it is a preliminary observation rather than an established risk estimate. Certainty: The evidence supports an association only, and it is imprecise and early enough that the size of the risk is unsettled. Scope: applies to incidental non-ischemic late iodine enhancement on cardiac CT without obstructive coronary disease in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it turns this imprecise signal into practice policy, recommending routine delayed-phase acquisition on every coronary CT or starting cardiomyopathy or heart-failure therapy on the strength of the enhancement alone.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Incidentally detected non-ischemic late iodine enhancement (LIE) on cardiac CT performed for coronary evaluation is an independent marker of subsequent cardiovascular events (cardiac death and unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization), but the evidence base is a single retrospective cohort with very few events, and it did not independently predict all-cause death.

## Supporting evidence

**Primary evidence (Oguni et al., [passage text removed])**
- Design: retrospective analysis of 465 patients undergoing cardiac CT (CCT) between January 2020 and December 2021, [passage text removed] or after CCT, coronary stenosis, and previous revascularization; 57 had non-ischemic LIE and 408 had no LIE ([[passage text removed])).
- Phenotype: compared with no-LIE patients, non-ischemic LIE was associated with higher high-sensitivity troponin T and BNP, larger LV diastolic diameter, greater LV thickness, and lower LVEF — i.e., it marks a subclinically abnormal myocardium even in the absence of obstructive CAD ([same source]([passage text removed])).
- Follow-up and events: mean follow-up [passage text removed] cohort), of which one was cardiovascular; non-cardiac deaths were predominantly cancer (n=30; 71%) and pneumonia (n=6; 14%). There were 1 [passage text removed] cohort: HF n=3, ACS n=1) ([full text]([passage text removed])).
- Cardiovascular outcome: cumulative incidence of cardiac death/unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization was higher with non-ischemic LIE (log-rank P=0.024); 2 of 57 LIE patients vs 3 of 408 [passage text removed]), and after multivariable adjustment for E/e′ the association persisted ([passage text removed]) ([full text]([passage text removed])).
- Mortality: all-cause mortality was 15.7% with non-ischemic LIE vs 8.1% without (log-rank P=0.031), but in multivariable analysis only sex, age, hs-cTnT and hematocrit remained significant, and **no independent association was seen between non-ischemic LIE and all-cause death** ([PDF]([passage text removed])). The excess in crude mortality is therefore largely non-cardiac (mostly cancer), consistent with confounding by comorbidity.

**Interpretation caveats stated by the authors**: the finding "may have prognostic implications," but "[passage text removed]," and multicentre prospective validation is warranted ([discussion]([passage text removed])).

**Corroborating larger cohort adding ECV (Oguni et al., Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Imaging 2026, doi:10.1093/ehjci/jeag018)**
- 1,207 of 1,305 consecutive patients undergoing CCT (Jan 2020–Sep 2022), followed [passage text removed], stratified into four groups by presence of LIE and elevated ECV. Risk increased stepwise across groups; those with both LIE and elevated ECV had [passage text removed]), with HR 1.84 (95% CI 1.22–2.79) for the composite of all-cause death plus unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization and [passage text removed]) for cardiovascular events ([PubMed 41570084](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41570084); [EACVI summary]([passage text removed])).
- The authors of that paper state that [passage text removed] and represents a strong marker of myocardial disease, and that non-ischaemic LIE appears to confer a stronger prognostic impact than ischaemic LIE ([[passage text removed])).

**Biological plausibility / context**
- Non-ischemic LGE on CMR is the analogous reference finding: approximately 30–45% of dilated cardiomyopathy patients show non-ischemic LGE patterns, associated with heart failure and sudden cardiac death, and non-ischemic LGE can occur with normal LV volumes and LVEF ([Circ J background section]([passage text removed])). Prior work also established that *ischemic* LIE on CCT carries poor prognosis, which motivated the non-ischemic question ([same source]([passage text removed])).

**Measurement limitation relevant to interpretation**: CT is least sensitive precisely for non-ischemic patterns — on photon-counting detector CT iodine maps versus LGE-MRI, per-patient accuracy was 85.2% and per-segment >90%, but "[passage text removed]" ([PMC12559134](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12559134); [PubMed 40310540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40310540)). So incidental non-ischemic LIE identified on CT is likely to represent the more conspicuous, higher-burden end of the fibrosis spectrum, and a negative CT does not exclude non-ischemic fibrosis.

## Bottom line for practice
An incidental non-ischemic LIE pattern in a patient without significant coronary stenosis should be treated as a signal of occult myocardial disease warranting further evaluation (biomarkers, echocardiography, consideration of CMR) rather than dismissed, and it identifies elevated risk of heart-failure hospitalization/cardiac death. However, the confidence intervals in the only dedicated outcome study are extremely wide (1.09–42.2), driven by 5 total events, so the effect magnitude is not reliably estimated; and no evidence supports adding delayed-phase acquisition routinely for screening ([Circ J discussion]([passage text removed])). I found no source addressing whether treatment initiated on the basis of incidental non-ischemic LIE changes outcomes.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Incidentally detected non‑ischemic late iodine enhancement (LIE) on cardiac CT marks a higher‑risk myocardial phenotype and is independently associated with subsequent cardiovascular events (cardiac death/unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization), but the evidence rests on a single small retrospective cohort with very few events, so the effect size is imprecise and the association with all‑cause mortality does not survive adjustment [S:e9a5f70c-2e90-50ad-95ca-31c21e5c7a2b][S:bee39945-a9b1-589f-bbfc-c19be952beb7][S:17f48cc6-ee6a-5d8f-9f6d-f274c306a894].

## Evidence

**Design and prevalence.** A retrospective single‑center cohort (Kumamoto University Hospital) analyzed 465 patients scanned between January 2020 and December 2021 in whom delayed‑phase (equilibrium) imaging was built into the routine coronary CTA protocol; patients with known or subsequently diagnosed non‑ischemic cardiomyopathy, coronary stenosis, prior revascularization, or an ischemic LIE pattern were excluded. Non‑ischemic LIE was found in 57 patients and no LIE in 408 (85.3%) [S:e9a5f70c-2e90-50ad-95ca-31c21e5c7a2b][S:5c5710cc-a863-5d1d-9a42-bb94fd649f25][S:a49f0a3a-97c4-51f2-9536-0b668f6fa9df]. Patterns were exclusively mid‑wall in 28, with junctional (inferior/superior LV–RV) distribution in 23; interobserver (κ=0.791) and intra‑observer (κ=0.853) agreement for detecting non‑ischemic LIE were good [S:5c5710cc-a863-5d1d-9a42-bb94fd649f25][S:b4da44da-7a9a-5e89-98ec-058eee6ce669].

**What it reflects.** Non‑ischemic LIE was associated with higher hs‑cTnT and BNP, larger LV diastolic diameter, greater LV wall thickness, and lower LVEF — interpreted by the authors as an advanced stage of cardiac remodeling, with wall stress, elevated filling pressures, and microvascular ischemia/myocyte necrosis as the proposed mechanism linking it to biomarker elevation [S:e9a5f70c-2e90-50ad-95ca-31c21e5c7a2b][S:f96dae2c-b814-5ae9-934b-ffdf908d316f].

**Outcomes.** Over [passage text removed] (9.0%) died, only one from cardiovascular causes; most deaths were non‑cardiac (cancer, pneumonia, cerebrovascular disease) [S:b4da44da-7a9a-5e89-98ec-058eee6ce669]. All‑cause mortality was 15.7% with non‑ischemic LIE versus 8.1% without (log‑rank P=0.031), but on multivariable analysis only sex, age, hs‑cTnT and hematocrit — not LIE — remained associated with death; post hoc power for the mortality endpoint was 56% [S:bee39945-a9b1-589f-bbfc-c19be952beb7][S:17f48cc6-ee6a-5d8f-9f6d-f274c306a894]. For the composite of cardiac death plus unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization there were only 5 events in the whole cohort (1 cardiac death, 4 admissions: 3 heart failure, 1 acute coronary syndrome); 2 of 57 LIE patients versus 3 of 408 [passage text removed]), with log‑rank P=0.024, and after adjustment [passage text removed] this endpoint ([passage text removed]) [S:17f48cc6-ee6a-5d8f-9f6d-f274c306a894][S:18799935-4eee-5ea6-b480-4f37599aa9d0].

**Interpretation and caveats.** The pattern mirrors CMR data cited by the authors, in which [passage text removed] hospitalization but not sudden cardiac death or all‑cause mortality [S:a49f0a3a-97c4-51f2-9536-0b668f6fa9df]. Key limitations: the extremely wide confidence intervals reflect a handful of events; the authors themselves estimate that ~1,800 patients would be needed for 80% power and call for a prospective study with a composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, non‑fatal MI, heart failure hospitalization and ventricular arrhythmia/ICD therapy [S:8eaec835-a77d-5063-b9c5-72d28d6dba53]. Delayed‑phase imaging also adds radiation (2.4 mSv for the delayed phase in their optimized protocol; ~7.1 mSv median effective dose for the full protocol) and extra contrast (~550 mgI/kg total), and the authors explicitly state it should not be used routinely for screening but reserved for clinically justified indications [S:57c2c635-15f9-5a65-85fd-67fa9f0f7b27][S:9fdc4f14-355e-5810-857d-75abbfdbf4bd][S:0a631f6e-ea04-5f06-b2e5-dc55551b9c0d]. Small junctional LIE patterns in particular may need confirmatory CMR — MRI‑LGE in some of these patients revealed [passage text removed] a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy diagnosis [S:f96dae2c-b814-5ae9-934b-ffdf908d316f].

**Related but distinct evidence.** In other populations, CT‑detected non‑ischemic scar carries adverse implications: in nonischemic cardiomyopathy patients undergoing VT ablation, septal scar on LIE‑CT [passage text removed]) [S:63878ee6-41cc-54c2-a807-ebd260ff14d7], and CT‑derived ECV — a diffuse‑fibrosis correlate of LIE — has been reported as an independent prognostic marker across conditions including dilated cardiomyopathy, amyloidosis and aortic stenosis [S:e70ef808-9490-53dc-9940-a128d5938b54][S:c2ad4935-1e30-55fd-bdbe-a34891575f19]. These are different populations and endpoints and do not directly address incidental detection.

No source in my searches provided truly long‑term (multi‑year) outcome data specific to incidental non‑ischemic LIE; the available follow‑up averages under two years [S:b4da44da-7a9a-5e89-98ec-058eee6ce669].

rows.question: How does sutureless aortic valve replacement differ from TAVI for permanent pacemaker implantation in severe aortic stenosis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Permanent pacemaker implantation rates were statistically comparable between sutureless surgical and transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement in matched high-risk patients; Sutureless valves carry a relevant risk of conduction disturbance attributed to anchoring mechanisms similar to those of self-expanding transcatheter valves; The comparable pacemaker rates come from a small single-centre matched sample with little power for infrequent outcomes and are hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of equivalence. Certainty: The evidence is weak and early, with too little power for infrequent events, so comparable pacemaker rates mean no difference was detected rather than that the approaches are equivalent. Scope: applies to severe aortic stenosis treated with sutureless surgical or transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement in high-risk adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it treats the comparable pacemaker rates as proven equivalence that removes conduction risk from Heart Team discussion or makes post-procedural rhythm monitoring unnecessary after either procedure.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Across observational and propensity-matched comparisons, sutureless AVR (SU-AVR, predominantly Perceval) carries a **modestly lower** need for permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) than TAVI — but the effect is inconsistent, the absolute difference is a few percentage points, and no randomised trial has compared the two, so this is low-certainty evidence. Notably, SU-AVR's pacemaker rate is *higher* than that of conventional sutured SAVR, so it sits between SAVR and TAVI.

## Evidence that SU-AVR has lower PPI than TAVI

- **Propensity-matched meta-analysis (16 PSM studies, 3,258 patients per arm):** SUAVR had [passage text removed]), I²=48%, p=0.04, alongside lower moderate-to-severe paravalvular leak (RR 0.18) and lower 1-, 2- and 5-year mortality ([PMC11607518]([passage text removed]); [imrpress RCM 25/11/391]([passage text removed])).
- **Systematic review/meta-analysis (Minten et al., Sci Rep 15, 34540, 2025):** SU-AVR associated with less PPI (OR 0.659) and far less moderate/severe PVL (OR 0.199), but slightly higher peak and mean transprosthetic gradients and longer hospital stay ([s41598-025-17857-7]([passage text removed])).
- **Largest multi-institutional cohort (2,123 intermediate-risk patients, 824 SU-AVR vs 1,299 TAVI, 2013–2020):** PPI 6.38% with SU-AVR vs 11.8% with TAVI (p=0.002); PVL ≥2 was 0.97% vs 4.84% (p=0.001) ([PMID 37714757](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37714757)).
- **Earlier propensity-matched multicentre study (967 elderly intermediate-risk patients; 291 matched pairs):** PPI 5.5% (sutureless) vs 10.7% (TAVI), p=0.032 ([S0022522320313945]([passage text removed])).
- A 2024 ACC summary of the sutureless-valve literature concludes PPI is *probably higher* after sutureless AVR than conventional SAVR but *lower* than after TAVR ([acc.org key points]([passage text removed])).

## Evidence of no difference

- **Perceval-specific meta-analysis (Ali-Hasan-Al-Saegh et al., 2024):** PPI 7.27% (116/1,595) after SUAVR vs 10.3% (164/1,587) after TAVI — a trend favouring SUAVR that was **not** [passage text removed], I²=57%); at mid-term follow-up 12.9% vs 18.4%, OR 0.66 (0.39–1.09), p=0.1 ([PMC11355092](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11355092)).
- **Earlier meta-analysis of 6 matched studies (741 per arm):** no significant difference in pacemaker need (p=0.86) ([PMC5179463]([passage text removed])).
- **Single-centre PSM cost/outcome study:** PPI 10% (sutureless) vs 9.4% (TAVI), p=0.588 ([thoracickey summary of Santarpino et al.]([passage text removed])).
- **Recent PSM single-centre cohort (197 matched pairs):** PPI [passage text removed]%, p=0.063 — and crucially the *timing* differed: median 2 days after TAVI vs median 190 days after Perceval, so short endpoint windows exaggerate and long follow-up attenuates the difference ([mdpi 1648-9144/62/3/476]([passage text removed])).
- A review of the discussion literature notes three meta-analyses concurred in showing no significant PPI difference, while several large registries (Biancari: 17.3% TAVR vs 9.8% SuAVR) favoured SU-AVR ([S0039606023004932]([passage text removed])).

## Mechanism and why the difference is small

Both devices are **intra-annular** and both rely on slight oversizing for anchoring/PVL prevention, so both can compress the left bundle: in a 501-patient study of patients without pre-existing conduction disease, new complete LBBB at discharge was 23% after su-AVR and 16% after TAVI vs 4% after conventional stented AVR (su-AVR OR 8.5, 95% CI 3.7–19.5; [passage text removed]) — the su-AVR and TAVI prostheses were placed intra-annular whereas the stented prosthesis was supra-annular ([EuroIntervention 2017;12:1660-1666]([passage text removed])). Proposed SU-AVR mechanisms include the annular sealing coil, balloon inflation, nitinol stent profile and decalcification ([imedpub predictors study]([passage text removed])); pre-existing RBBB is a risk factor ([PMC4986555]([passage text removed])). For TAVI, radial force of the stent frame, deep implantation and oversizing drive conduction injury, and rates vary widely by device — with pooled PPI ~17% (range 2–51%) and much higher rates for self-expanding CoreValve than balloon-expandable SAPIEN (37.6% vs 17.3% in a randomised comparison) ([EuroIntervention review]([passage text removed])).

Two practical modifiers:
- **SU-AVR PPI is operator/technique-dependent and falls with experience:** in the SURD-IR registry (>4,500 patients) overall PPI was 8.9%, and within the series the rate fell from 20.6% to 5.6% with avoidance of oversizing and low positioning, careful decalcification and guiding-suture traction ([annalscts 16747]([passage text removed])); a dedicated Perceval series confirmed technical measures (annulus decalcification, precise guiding-suture positioning, release technique) reduce pacemaker rate ([PMID 30684479](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30684479)).
- **TAVI PPI has also declined** with newer delivery systems, greater experience and more restrictive pacing indications ([same EuroIntervention review]([passage text removed])) — so older comparative cohorts may overstate TAVI's disadvantage.

## Caveats

All comparative data are observational; there are no randomised trials of TAVI vs SU-AVR ([ymj-62-885]([passage text removed])). Heterogeneity is substantial (I² 48–57% in the PPI pooled estimates), TAVI arms are typically higher-risk at baseline, TAVI device mix differs across studies, and pacing thresholds are non-standardised. Against conventional SAVR, sutureless valves clearly *increase* PPI (e.g., pooled OR 2.50, 95% CI 1.88–3.33, p<0.00001 for Perceval vs conventional prostheses) ([PMC10284666]([passage text removed])) — a point that should temper any framing of SU-AVR as conduction-sparing.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Sutureless AVR and TAVI share the same mechanism of conduction injury — radial force from a self-expanding stent frame on the membranous septum/conduction axis rather than suture-related trauma [S:a94bf030-32d0-50d8-9634-dd3216cb41c3][S:26067f87-163d-5245-8f05-b68b34ef38bc] — and both carry pacemaker rates well above conventional stented SAVR. In head-to-head propensity-matched comparisons, however, pooled pacemaker rates are **modestly but significantly lower with sutureless AVR than with TAVI**, though the effect is heterogeneous and not seen in every analysis.

## Evidence

**Direct comparative meta-analyses favour sutureless AVR, with caveats**
- A meta-analysis of 16 propensity-matched studies (6,516 patients, 3,258 per arm) found [passage text removed] with sutureless AVR ([passage text removed], I² = 48%, p = 0.04), alongside less moderate-to-severe paravalvular leak and lower 1-, 2- and 5-year mortality [S:34e6549b-ee6f-5290-96b7-24d4052dd4bb].
- A 2025 systematic review of 13 propensity-matched studies reported that across all risk categories, pacemaker implantation and moderate/severe aortic regurgitation [passage text removed] hospital stay were higher [S:5df76134-13f1-5aa8-8b68-dd407a2e70a8]. In the overall pooled analysis the pacemaker odds ratio was 0.659 [S:35385a78-2ac3-5def-b435-408080039f5d]. Crucially, within the intermediate-risk subgroup alone the pacemaker OR was 0.906 (95% CI 0.495–1.659) with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 66.68, p = 0.0038) [S:c6bc141f-d407-5193-a076-4cc07b5764ff], and in high-risk patients the OR was 0.260 (95% CI 0.051–1.328) — non-significant [S:f989451c-4d72-5634-9369-2da9635b783a].
- The direction of effect is inconsistent across individual matched cohorts in that review: e.g. 8.5% vs 12.8% (p < 0.001), 8.8% vs 18.1% (p = 0.011), 3.3% vs 30% (p = 0.01) favouring SU-AVR, but 9.4% vs 2.8% (p = 0.0046) and 7.7% vs 1.9% favouring TAVI [S:0832d5d2-1d3f-531f-80f4-766fb9b14bce].

**Largest single multicentre comparison**
- In 2,123 intermediate-risk patients with isolated aortic stenosis (517 matched pairs, median follow-up 4.3 years), pacemaker implantation was 6.38% with sutureless AVR vs 11.8% with TAVI (p = 0.002); pacemaker implantation was itself an independent predictor of mortality (HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.02–2.20, p = 0.039) [S:9fd82772-132c-5b51-a927-bd80c22da11a][S:3a9472cb-fe17-53ae-9f87-73aa5b3af909].

**Where the difference disappears or reverses**
- A meta-analysis of six matched studies (1,462 patients) found no difference in pacemaker implantation ([passage text removed]); the review notes variability in the TAVI arm is largely driven by device type and technique, with balloon-expandable Sapien valves showing lower pacemaker rates than self-expanding platforms [S:36f9fb2a-e595-56a6-885d-efc08a21dc5b]. Independently, self-expanding TAVI devices carry higher pacemaker rates than balloon-expandable ones (17.4% vs 6.5% for CoreValve/Evolut vs Sapien 3) [S:f57aac3b-62f3-5eb0-ac16-3d93d68ba2cb].
- A single-centre matched analysis of surgical-access (mainly transapical) TAVI vs sutureless/rapid-deployment valves found complete heart block requiring pacing in [passage text removed]) — numerically favouring TAVI [S:50725bda-ddbe-5231-aba9-933ca261f2b8].
- One earlier matched series showed a trend toward higher pacing with sutureless Perceval (10.8% vs 2.7%, p = 0.18), whereas another comparison with CoreValve showed the opposite (25.5% TAVI vs 2% sutureless) [S:8aad75c5-d8de-5997-94a7-b32a19b989b6].

**Shared mechanism and modifiability**
- Both devices injure conduction tissue through radial force on the left ventricular outflow tract/membranous septum, where the His bundle and left bundle branch run [S:f57aac3b-62f3-5eb0-ac16-3d93d68ba2cb][S:26bb68d7-d8f3-51b0-9579-ae25137100a2]. In TAVI, implantation depth, oversizing, baseline RBBB and self-expanding design are established predictors [S:dcfbad78-fdfe-5e65-b3ef-8e9c55291570].
- The same risk factors operate for sutureless valves: oversizing indexed to body surface area independently raises pacemaker rate [S:d6e00606-e057-598b-989b-e3c562e260ac][S:ebc8f44f-d004-5afa-9aa6-e8e2342baa18], as do age, pre-existing AV/bundle branch block and high-pressure balloon expansion [S:ebc8f44f-d004-5afa-9aa6-e8e2342baa18]. Technique refinement (guide sutures at the cusp nadir, avoiding oversizing, gentle post-dilation) lowers rates [S:5e9a290d-c774-54fa-9170-b95da91b459a][S:445901bb-92ce-5d02-89ce-8075ed9fca2d], and a pooled analysis of 9,492 patients gave an overall Perceval pacemaker [passage text removed] rates falling over time — from roughly 11% to 6% in newer cohorts [S:257b6fbe-7ec5-514a-a57b-57477d506338].
- For context on the surgical baseline: sutureless valves have consistently higher pacemaker rates than conventional stented bioprostheses ([passage text removed] in one meta-analysis of 832 vs 3,740 patients) [S:a94bf030-32d0-50d8-9634-dd3216cb41c3][S:bfd19bc7-4a87-5dc1-b914-fd34f7eb6ec6].

## Bottom line for practice

The pacemaker "penalty" is a feature of stent-based anchoring common to both technologies, not a discriminator that cleanly separates them. Pooled data lean toward fewer pacemakers with sutureless AVR (roughly a quarter to a third relative reduction), but the comparison is confounded by TAVI device generation and valve type, sutureless sizing/implant technique, and residual imbalance after propensity matching (TAVI cohorts remained older and higher-risk) [S:f173abf1-9caf-53d2-a07b-c65c730e1449]. No randomised trial comparing TAVI and sutureless AVR exists; all evidence is observational [S:7294ac3e-c1f5-507a-9d05-e370ff82edff].

rows.question: Which patient characteristics relate to the no-reflow phenomenon after percutaneous coronary intervention for acute coronary syndrome?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: The distribution of cardiovascular risk-factor categories differed between patients with and without no-reflow on an unadjusted comparison; No-reflow cases were concentrated in the hypertension, diabetes and smoking risk-factor categories, a preliminary observation resting on very sparse counts; Anterior ST elevation myocardial infarction was over-represented among no-reflow cases without reaching statistical significance. Certainty: Because the evidence comes from a small sample with very few no-reflow events and comparisons unadjusted for confounding, the reported associations should be read as provisional signals rather than established predictors. Scope: applies to acute coronary syndrome treated with percutaneous coronary intervention in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it states that these cardiovascular risk factors are independent predictors of no-reflow after adjustment or that treating them is a proven way of preventing it.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

No-reflow after PCI for ACS clusters around three patient-level domains: **older age and cardiometabolic comorbidity (especially diabetes)**, **worse haemodynamic/clinical severity at presentation (higher Killip class, cardiogenic shock, low LVEF, delayed presentation)**, and **the angiographic/lesion substrate the patient brings to the lab (pre-PCI TIMI flow 0–1, heavy thrombus burden, long lesions, small vessels, degenerated saphenous vein grafts)**. Inflammatory and metabolic laboratory indices add incremental risk.

## Demographics and comorbidity

- A meta-analysis of 27 retrospective and prospective studies in STEMI found increased no-reflow risk with advanced age, male sex, family history of CAD, smoking, diabetes, [passage text removed] CK, higher heart rate, decreased [passage text removed] high thrombus burden. Initial TIMI flow 0–1 (OR 3.83, 95% CI 2.77–5.29) and thrombus score ≥4 (OR 3.69, 95% CI 2.39–5.68) had the greatest impact ([PMC6309153]([passage text removed]); [PMID 30595300](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30595300)).
- **Age** is the most reproducible patient characteristic. In the TOTAL trial angiographic core-lab analysis, no-reflow occurred in 196/1,800 (10.9%); patients were older (64.4 vs 60.8 years) and age per 10-year increment was an independent predictor ([passage text removed]=0.001), alongside [passage text removed]) and direct stenting (OR 0.66) as protective factors; the proportion of women was similar between groups (25.0% vs 22.1%) ([EuroIntervention core-lab analysis of TOTAL]([passage text removed]); [PMID 37382909](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37382909)).
- In HORIZONS-AMI core-lab analysis, independent predictors of final [passage text removed] years), anterior MI (OR 1.65), baseline TIMI flow 0/1 (OR 2.79) [passage text removed]). Patients with TIMI <3 were also more likely to have renal insufficiency, heart failure (Killip 2–4) and LV dysfunction at presentation, and longer symptom-onset-to-balloon and door-to-balloon times; they [passage text removed] ([EuroIntervention 2013;9:220-7]([passage text removed])).
- In a retrospective cohort of 2,925 primary-PCI STEMI patients (no-reflow 18%, 526 patients), independent predictors were [passage text removed]-PCI [passage text removed]; glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor use was associated with reduced risk ([PMC13267993]([passage text removed])).
- A contemporary primary-PCI series found slow-flow/no-reflow [passage text removed], plus diabetes, than with delays >6 hours: diabetes OR 2.32 (1.05–5.11), thrombus burden OR 1.93 (1.34–2.77), symptom-onset-to-balloon per hour OR 1.18 (1.04–1.35) ([PMC12797277]([passage text removed])).

## Presentation severity and procedural substrate

- The externally validated NORPACS score (30,561 Melbourne Interventional Group patients, development; 440,256 BCIS patients, validation; no reflow 4.1% and 9.4%) selected six variables from 33 candidates: **cardiogenic shock, STEMI [passage text removed] TIMI flow <3, and lesion location**. Discrimination was good (C 0.808 development, 0.741 validation); a score ≥8 conferred [passage text removed] ([Circ Cardiovasc Interv, PMID 38487882](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38487882); [full text](https://www.ovid.com/jnls/circinterventions/[passage text removed])).
- **Plaque and thrombus morphology** matter independently of clinical risk factors. In ACS patients studied with IVUS, thrombus formation (OR 4.53, 1.03–20.0) and larger plaque burden (OR 1.79, 1.01–3.23) independently predicted transient no-reflow ([PMID 16377279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16377279)); in a virtual-histology IVUS analysis, percent necrotic-core volume was the only independent predictor after stenting (OR 1.126, 1.045–1.214, p=0.002) ([PMC3155758]([passage text removed])).
- **Saphenous vein graft PCI** is a distinct high-risk setting. In 287 SVG-PCI patients with ACS, independent predictors were degenerated SVG (OR 4.65), thrombus presence (OR 5.65), reduced LVEF (OR 0.927 per unit) and elevated atherogenic index of plasma (OR 3.141); the no-reflow group was older with more [passage text removed] prior stroke ([doi:10.36660/abc.20250162i](https://abccardiol.org/en/[passage text removed])). In NSTE-ACS SVG PCI, congestive heart failure, degenerated SVG, intraluminal thrombus and the triglyceride–glucose index were independent predictors ([doi:10.4274/haseki.galenos.2024.9694]([passage text removed])).

## Laboratory / inflammatory phenotype

- In T2DM patients with STEMI, both the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio and the TyG index were independent predictors; combined high-NLR/high-TyG carried adjusted OR 19.23 (4.35–83.33) versus the reference group, with [passage text removed] independent ([PLOS One, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0345466]([passage text removed])).
- In 578 older STEMI patients, independent predictors were hypertension (OR 2.048), lymphocyte count, platelet count, haemoglobin, multivessel disease (OR 2.237) and systemic immune-inflammation index ≥1814 (OR 3.799); SII had AUC 0.738 ([reported at medicalxpress]([passage text removed])).
- In 1,256 ACS patients undergoing PCI (no-reflow 5.8%, 73 patients), an endothelial stress ratio derived from pre-procedural bloods was the strongest independent predictor (OR 1.48, 1.21–1.82; AUC 0.82), in models that also included Killip class, presentation type, [passage text removed] TIMI flow ([termedia record]([passage text removed])).
- Other reported associations include elevated pre-procedural D-dimer, fibrin monomer, von Willebrand factor, cTnI and NT-proBNP with low free T3 ([Journal of Thoracic Disease]([passage text removed])); plasma calprotectin and LDL-C as independent predictors in ACS ([BMC Cardiovasc Disord, doi:10.1186/s12872-020-01717-5]([passage text removed])); lower haemoglobin (OR 0.747, 0.618–0.888) in 1,200 STEMI patients ([brieflands 107077](https://brieflands.com/journals/mca/articles/107077)); and composite clinical scores such as CHA₂DS₂-VASc ([PMC5913693](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5913693)).

## Caveats

Sex is inconsistent across studies: the meta-analysis reported male sex as a risk factor ([PMC6309153]([passage text removed])), TOTAL found no difference in the proportion of women ([EuroIntervention]([passage text removed])), while a society summary lists female sex among clinical risk factors ([SCAI QI tip]([passage text removed])). Reported no-reflow incidence varies widely (roughly 4% to well over 20% across the cohorts above), largely because definitions and assessment methods differ — inter-rater agreement between operators and core lab in TOTAL was only fair (Cohen's κ 0.29) ([EuroIntervention]([passage text removed])), so predictor effect sizes are not directly comparable between studies. Most of the biomarker studies cited are single-centre and retrospective; only NORPACS among the sources retrieved has been externally validated.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** No-reflow after PCI for ACS is most consistently associated with older age, delayed presentation/long total ischemic time, high angiographic thrombus burden and low pre-procedural TIMI flow, plus diabetes/hyperglycemia, higher Killip class or heart failure at admission, low blood pressure, anemia, renal impairment, and inflammatory/haematological markers — though results across cohorts are heterogeneous and some risk factors are contested.

**Demographics and comorbidity**
- Older age is among the most reproducible patient-level correlates: in a consecutive primary-PCI cohort, no-reflow patients were older, and age >60 years was an independent predictor along with [passage text removed] >360 min [S:9fa51649]; in a 2925-patient STEMI cohort, risk rose with each year of age (OR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01–1.05) [S:05baa83d]. Age was also one of the three most frequent predictors across 16 prediction models [S:d5c7e3b5].
- Diabetes mellitus was independently predictive ([passage text removed]) [S:05baa83d], and diabetes plus peripheral arterial disease were independent correlates in a CHA₂DS₂-VASc–based analysis, in which congestive heart failure, hypertension, and age 65–74 or ≥75 also predicted no-reflow [S:b9ef674d].
- A meta-analysis summarised as reporting [passage text removed] disease, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, delayed reperfusion, higher Killip class, elevated glucose and [passage text removed] as associated with no-reflow [S:47637cc9].

**Clinical presentation and haemodynamics**
- Killip class ≥II at presentation was strongly predictive ([passage text removed]) [S:05baa83d]; Killip ≥2 was independent in another cohort (OR 3.97, 95% CI 1.43–10.99), together with lower LVEF and lower admission eGFR (OR 0.942 per unit, 95% CI 0.917–0.967) [S:fa86eae0]. Acute heart failure at admission independently predicted no-reflow irrespective of thrombus load (OR 3.59, 95% CI 1.09–11.83) [S:affffdcb].
- Systolic BP <100 mmHg was among risk factors in a Chinese STEMI cohort (along with infarct-artery opening time ≥8 h, hs-CRP >18 mg/l, thrombus load, culprit lesion length ≥20 mm) [S:70f073f7], and lower systolic BP was independently correlated in another study [S:b9ef674d].

**Ischemic time**
- Longer symptom-to-door time raised risk (OR 1.14 per 30 min) [S:05baa83d]; reperfusion time ≥6 h was independent alongside admission glucose ≥10 mmol/L and high thrombus burden [S:9c5d3bdc]; mean total ischemic time was roughly double in the no-reflow group versus normal flow (619.0±355.67 vs 321±292.40 min, p=0.002) [S:d9cfed3a].

**Laboratory / biomarker characteristics**
- In a 5122-patient ACS cohort, age, hemoglobin, WBC, glucose and LDL-C were independent predictors, with WBC most predictive (AUC 0.605) — notably younger age and lower hemoglobin here, illustrating inconsistency with other cohorts [S:4bf747b8, S:307b9609].
- Anemia: lower hemoglobin was independently associated with post-procedural low TIMI flow/no-reflow (OR 0.747, 95% CI 0.618–0.888) in 1200 STEMI patients [S:3ca52ee4]; hemoglobin was also lower in no-reflow patients in a geometry study [S:54a6d9a2].
- Inflammatory and thrombotic markers: elevated WBC and thrombus grade were strong independent predictors, with associations also reported for pain duration, maximal ST change, LV function and hs-CRP [S:cf97e6a1]; admission platelet/lymphocyte ratio [S:b98db8db], neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, MPV/PDW and the systemic immune-inflammation index [S:75bff592] have all been linked to no-reflow; admission D-dimer, hypertension, prior ischemic heart disease and CK-MB peak were independent predictors in another study [S:3a7b7d3c]; low admission serum albumin was independent [passage text removed] [S:c50ea4d1]. A nomogram in 3041 AMI patients used NT-proBNP, basophil and neutrophil counts, D-dimer, hemoglobin and RDW (training C-index 0.712) [S:e06b59e6].

**Angiographic/lesion factors (procedure-side, for completeness)**
High thrombus burden (OR 2.89) [passage text removed]) were the strongest angiographic predictors [S:05baa83d]; low initial TIMI flow, [passage text removed] independent in a 100-patient study [S:5c533503]; GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor use was associated with lower no-reflow risk (OR 0.61) [S:05baa83d].

**Caveats**
Reported incidence varies widely (5–50% depending on definition and cohort) [S:cf97e6a1], and findings are not uniform: one prospective ACS cohort in Iraq found no-reflow in 6% and linked it to dyslipidemia, hypertension, diabetes and smoking but *not* to angiographic or procedural variables [S:2335152b, S:f70b0604]; another cohort found no difference in lesion length, vessel diameter, age, sex or ejection fraction [S:47637cc9]. A systematic review of 16 prediction models judged most to be at risk of bias (small samples, missing calibration/validation), with [passage text removed] the most frequent model predictors [S:d5c7e3b5, S:6765f673]; existing scores lack external validation and have only moderate accuracy [S:34464609].

rows.question: In patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, how does left atrial appendage occlusion compare with oral anticoagulation for stroke, major bleeding and procedural safety outcomes?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Left atrial appendage closure met non-inferiority to direct oral anticoagulant therapy for composite endpoints of death, stroke and systemic embolism; closure reduced non-procedural major or clinically relevant bleeding compared with continued oral anticoagulant therapy; in the warfarin-controlled trials, closure showed lower rates of haemorrhagic stroke and cardiovascular mortality than warfarin; closure adds early procedural and device-related hazards, including pericardial effusion, device embolisation, procedure-related stroke and device-related thrombus, seen in a small minority of patients in the more recent trials. Certainty: The composite efficacy and non-procedural bleeding conclusions rest on concurrent, chance-allocated treatment groups in selected patients, supporting causal interpretation, whereas the warfarin-comparison findings for haemorrhagic stroke and cardiovascular mortality and the procedural complication rates are presented as descriptive frequencies without between-group effect estimates. Scope: applies to nonvalvular atrial fibrillation at elevated thromboembolic risk in adults, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents closure as proven superior to oral anticoagulation for stroke prevention, or recommends closure first-line for all patients who tolerate anticoagulation.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Across randomized trials, LAAO is broadly non-inferior to oral anticoagulation for the composite of stroke/systemic embolism/cardiovascular death, clearly reduces long-term non-procedural bleeding and hemorrhagic stroke, but carries a consistent numerical excess of *ischemic* stroke plus an up-front procedural hazard — and in the highest-risk elderly population (CLOSURE-AF) it failed noninferiority outright.

## Thromboembolic efficacy: comparable composite, but a persistent ischemic-stroke signal

- **vs warfarin:** In the 5-year [passage text removed], the composite of stroke/SE/CV-or-unexplained death was similar (HR 0.820; p=0.27), as was [passage text removed]), while ischemic stroke/SE was numerically higher with LAAC (HR 1.71; p=0.080) [jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2017.10.021; pubmed 29103847]. An earlier patient-level pooling with registries found [passage text removed]; HR 0.22; p=0.004) and less CV/unexplained death (HR 0.48; p=0.006) with LAAC [sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0735109715020239].
- **vs DOACs:** PRAGUE-17 (Watchman/Amulet vs 95% apixaban, high stroke *and* bleeding risk) maintained noninferiority at ~4 years ([passage text removed] noninferiority = 0.006; annualized 8.6% vs 11.9%), with no difference in all-stroke/TIA or CV death [[passage text removed]; pubmed 34748929]. OPTION (n=1600 post-ablation) met noninferiority for death/stroke/SE (5.3% vs 5.8% at 36 months) [pubmed 39555822; [passage text removed]]. CHAMPION-AF (n=3000, Watchman FLX vs DOAC, first-line) met noninferiority for CV death/stroke/SE (5.7% vs 4.8%; [passage text removed]), but ischemic stroke or SE was numerically higher with the device (3.2% vs 2.2%; 45 vs 27 ischemic strokes), with hemorrhagic stroke 0.4% in each arm and all-cause mortality 5.0% vs 4.9% [[passage text removed]].
- **Pooled:** A 7-trial meta-analysis (n=7,353; mean CHA₂DS₂-VASc [passage text removed]) found stroke/SE similar ([passage text removed]) and ischemic stroke numerically but not significantly higher ([passage text removed], I²=0%), with the annualized absolute stroke difference not exceeding 0.37%/year in any non-warfarin comparison [jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacep.2026.06.033]. A 4-trial pooling (n=3116) found lower all-cause death (RR 0.78, 0.64–0.95), CV/unexplained death (RR 0.69, 0.51–0.94) and hemorrhagic stroke (RR 0.34, 0.16–0.76) with LAAC [[passage text removed]].

## Bleeding: the consistent advantage — but only *non-procedural* bleeding

- CHAMPION-AF primary safety endpoint (non-procedural ISTH major + [passage text removed] (~45% relative reduction). Including procedural bleeding, 12.8% vs 19.0%. Critically, **procedural + non-procedural ISTH major bleeding alone did not differ (5.9% vs 6.4%, noninferior only)** [[passage text removed]]. Independent commentary notes the bleeding advantage is driven largely by clinically relevant non-major events in an unblinded trial [[passage text removed]].
- OPTION: non-procedural major/CRNM bleeding 8.5% vs 18.1% (superiority, P<0.001); major bleeding including procedural was 3.9% vs 5.0% — noninferior but not superior (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.48–1.24; P=0.28) [[passage text removed]; pubmed 39555822].
- PRAGUE-17: [passage text removed] (0.31–0.97; p=0.039), whereas *all* clinically relevant bleeding was not significantly reduced (sHR 0.75, 0.44–1.27; p=0.28) [[passage text removed]].
- Pooled: non-procedural clinically significant bleeding RR 0.50 (0.39–0.64, I²=0%), ~2–3% absolute annualized reduction (NNT 33–50/year), while **major bleeding overall showed no significant difference** [jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacep.2026.06.033; [passage text removed]].

## Procedural safety

- Contemporary: CHAMPION-AF had procedure-related serious adverse events in 2.3%, pericardial effusion in 0.7%, effective closure (leak ≤3 mm) in 98.6%, and device-related thrombus in 4.8% of imaged patients (1.8% clinically relevant, prompting resumption of anticoagulation; 2 DRT-related strokes) [[passage text removed]]. OPTION implant success was 98.8% [[passage text removed]].
- Pooled across earlier RCTs: procedure-related complications 6.8% (64/933), pericardial effusion 2.7%, device embolization 0.6%, procedure-related stroke 0.6% [escholarship.org/content/qt46j5z59x/qt46j5z59x.pdf].
- Historically, PROTECT AF had a higher primary safety event rate than warfarin (7.4 vs 4.4 [passage text removed]), with pericardial effusion/tamponade constituting ~50% of events; rates fell markedly with operator experience (procedure/device safety events 7.7% in PROTECT AF vs 3.7% in CAP; serious effusion 5.0% vs 2.2%, P=0.019) [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5227183; bostonscientific.com Safety_Manuscript_Reddy_et_al_Circ_Jan_2011.pdf]. Device-related thrombus in pooled PROTECT AF/PREVAIL/CAP/CAP2 occurred in 3.74% and carried a higher stroke/SE rate (7.46 vs 1.78 per 100 patient-years, p<0.001) [[passage text removed]].

## The important discordance

CLOSURE-AF (912 German patients, mean age 78, mean CHA₂DS₂-VASc 5.2, HAS-BLED 3.0) found LAAO **[passage text removed] stroke/SE/major bleeding/CV-or-unexplained death: 16.8 vs 13.3 events per 100 patient-years, adjusted HR [passage text removed]), P for noninferiority = 0.44 (margin HR 1.3) [[passage text removed]; pubmed 41849741; [passage text removed]].

## Interpretation

The trade-off is directional and consistent: LAAO buys freedom from long-term anticoagulant bleeding (especially hemorrhagic stroke and nuisance-to-moderate bleeding) at the cost of a small ischemic-stroke excess and a front-loaded procedural risk. Notably, CHAMPION-AF and OPTION enrolled patients at *low-to-moderate* bleeding risk, so their bleeding-benefit findings do not automatically extend to the high-bleeding-risk group [mdpi.com/2077-0383/15/18/7015], and CLOSURE-AF shows the strategy did not deliver net benefit in elderly patients at high risk of both events. Because CHAMPION-AF was industry-funded with a noninferiority margin criticized as generous (4.8%) against lower-than-expected event rates, and its 5-year ischemic stroke/SE co-primary endpoint is still pending, first-line substitution of LAAO for DOACs in anticoagulation-eligible patients remains unsettled [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** Across randomized trials, LAAO is consistently *non-inferior* to oral anticoagulation for stroke/thromboembolic efficacy endpoints and *superior* for non-procedural bleeding, but it carries an upfront procedural hazard (pericardial effusion/tamponade, device embolization, procedural bleeding, device-related thrombus) and has failed to show net benefit in the highest-risk mixed stroke/bleeding population — so the trade-off is a front-loaded procedural risk in exchange for later bleeding reduction, with no clear ischemic-stroke advantage.

**Stroke / thromboembolism**
- Versus warfarin: PROTECT AF (707 patients, 2:1 randomization) met non-inferiority for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism and cardiovascular death; at 3.8 years mean follow-up the event rate was [passage text removed], driven largely by reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and cardiovascular death rather than ischemic stroke [S:62dceb32-e214-5afc-adaa-65031c24147e][S:1d34c014-439b-5dd3-b89d-ec4a2326924f]. PREVAIL (407 patients) did **not** meet its prespecified non-inferiority margin for the first primary endpoint ([passage text removed]), though it did meet non-inferiority for stroke/systemic embolism occurring >7 days after randomization [S:291d8d79-ded9-590c-a213-c8049f46c86c].
- A patient-level meta-analysis of PROTECT-AF, PREVAIL, CAP and CAP2 found fewer hemorrhagic strokes and fewer cardiac/unexplained deaths with Watchman, but *more* ischemic strokes (P = 0.05); after excluding procedural ischemic strokes the difference disappeared (P = 0.21) [S:fb2ac8e7-1112-5394-bc3c-26bea3df7336][S:9486673d-0478-53f3-98f3-85a72f5ac472].
- Versus DOACs: PRAGUE-17 (~400 patients with high stroke and bleeding risk) showed non-inferiority at median 3.5 years (sHR 0.81, 95% CI 0.56–1.18; P for non-inferiority = 0.006), with stroke/TIA sHR 1.14 (0.56–2.30) [S:6dccbac3-ee98-510f-81be-2d48ef0a8a64].
- OPTION (1,600 post-ablation patients, mean CHA₂DS₂-VASc 3.5) met non-inferiority for death/stroke/systemic embolism at 36 months (5.3% vs 5.8%) [S:a8570696-8504-5d76-992a-7292615d2b9a].
- CHAMPION-AF (Watchman FLX vs NOAC, 3-year follow-up) met non-inferiority for CV death/stroke/systemic embolism (5.7% vs 4.8%), with ischemic stroke or systemic embolism numerically more common in the device [passage text removed]://www.tctmd.com/news/champion-af-win-watchman-flx-caveats].
- Meta-analyses concur that stroke rates are similar: pooled RR 1.15 (95% CI 0.95–1.41) for stroke in LAAC vs DOAC [S:f5bbd137-6cc1-5e5d-8b96-690fa00add66]; across PREVAIL/PROTECT AF/PRAGUE-17, all stroke or SE RR 0.98 (0.65–1.48) with a markedly lower hemorrhagic stroke risk favoring LAAC (RR 0.22, 0.08–0.58) [S:846d53a4-4e53-581e-9d8d-67bd2e658664].

**Major bleeding**
- The bleeding advantage is confined to *non-procedural* bleeding. PRAGUE-17: non-procedural clinically relevant bleeding sHR 0.55 (0.31–0.97), while all clinically relevant bleeding was not significantly different (0.75, 0.44–1.27) [S:6dccbac3-ee98-510f-81be-2d48ef0a8a64]; the curves diverged around 6 months post-procedure [S:3c6a750c-4ead-5fbd-8480-b9a18160b435].
- OPTION met superiority for non–procedure-related major or [passage text removed] (8.5% vs 18.1%) [S:a8570696-8504-5d76-992a-7292615d2b9a].
- CHAMPION-AF: non-procedural bleeding 10.9% vs 19.0% (superiority); including procedural bleeding, 12.8% vs 19.0%; ISTH major bleeding overall was similar (5.9% vs 6.4%, non-inferior) [S:https://www.tctmd.com/news/champion-af-win-watchman-flx-caveats][[passage text removed]].
- Pooled RCT data show no difference in overall major bleeding but [passage text removed] with LAAC (RR 0.53, 0.38–0.74) [S:846d53a4-4e53-581e-9d8d-67bd2e658664].

**Procedural safety**
- Complication rates fell with experience and device iteration: the 7-day procedure-related complication composite was 8.7% in PROTECT AF vs 4.2% in PREVAIL (P = 0.004), with implant success rising from 90.9% to 95.1%; pericardial effusion requiring drainage fell from ~5% to 1.5% [S:3ba4bed9-eb5d-554e-8580-9cd627d38b38][S:291d8d79-ded9-590c-a213-c8049f46c86c].
- PRAGUE-17 reported a periprocedural complication rate of 4.5% including two procedure-associated deaths [S:3c6a750c-4ead-5fbd-8480-b9a18160b435]; the Amulet IDE trial had nearly 10% complications within 90 days [S:edabd95a-d699-5fee-82fd-d9b6045cebff].
- Real-world NCDR LAAO registry data (38,158 Watchman procedures): major in-hospital adverse events 2.16%, pericardial effusion requiring intervention 1.39%, major bleeding 1.25%, stroke 0.17%, death 0.19% [S:412bb347-48c8-5ea6-b8f4-37e0264b2710]. Risk is not uniform — major adverse events occurred in 4.1% of women vs 2.0% of men (49,357 patients), and low operator volume (<15/year) roughly doubled major adverse events [S:edabd95a-d699-5fee-82fd-d9b6045cebff][S:66fa924c-14f7-5dc7-91db-9828c32549f7].
- Device-specific late issues: peri-device leak was detected by TEE in 26% of patients in a 48-study meta-analysis, with leaks >3 mm and >5 mm associated with odds ratios for thromboembolism of 4.14 (2.07–8.27) and 4.44 (2.09–9.43) [S:28772a48-b903-5b05-8c2e-03098057970e]; device-related thrombus is uncommon (pooled ~1.69%) but confers a several-fold increased thromboembolic risk [S:bb3f8688-6bb0-5f35-bf3a-f8586c98417d][S:48a5b55b-7c0a-5a3e-ade6-8b43783167e9].

**Important caveat on the highest-risk population:** CLOSURE-AF randomized 912 patients with AF at high risk of *both* stroke (mean CHA₂DS₂-VASc 5.2) and bleeding (mean HAS-BLED 3.0) to LAAO vs physician-directed best medical care; LAAO was **not** non-inferior for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, major bleeding, or CV/unexplained death (16.8 vs 13.3 events per 100 patient-years; P = 0.44 for non-inferiority), despite 98% implant success and 6% periprocedural complications within 7 days [[passage text removed]].

**Interpretive limits:** the earlier trials enrolled patients *eligible* for anticoagulation and combined competing safety and efficacy events in composite endpoints, leaving them underpowered for individual components [S:3c6a750c-4ead-5fbd-8480-b9a18160b435][S:841be1fa-c075-5db2-a734-4dae2422e20d]. Guidelines still position LAAO primarily for patients at stroke risk [passage text removed] IIb/C; US IIa/B), with a weaker IIb/B recommendation as an OAC alternative based on preference and bleeding risk [S:edfe96ae-6d4b-5613-ad59-d6267303126a]. Mortality signals favoring LAAC in observational/pooled analyses (e.g., all-cause mortality RR 1.87 favoring LAAC over DOAC) come largely from non-randomized data and should be treated cautiously [S:f5bbd137-6cc1-5e5d-8b96-690fa00add66].
