rows.question: What are the updated recommendations for management of secondary mitral regurgitation in the 2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guidelines?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Secondary mitral regurgitation is now separated into atrial and ventricular mechanisms, with distinct diagnostic criteria and separate treatment pathways set out for each; Transcatheter mitral edge-to-edge repair now carries a class I recommendation for selected patients with severe ventricular secondary mitral regurgitation and impaired left ventricular ejection fraction who remain symptomatic despite optimised medical therapy and resynchronisation where indicated; Specific anatomic and clinical criteria identify the patients in whom edge-to-edge repair is expected to further reduce heart failure hospitalisations; For atrial secondary mitral regurgitation, surgery is the first-line option with edge-to-edge repair reserved for high-risk patients. Certainty: The statements report agreed guidance and its stated rationale rather than newly measured effects, so they are firm as practice guidance but carry no independent strength of proof. Scope: applies to secondary mitral regurgitation in adults assessed by a multidisciplinary heart valve team, specialist cardiology settings. An answer is wrong if it recommends transcatheter mitral edge-to-edge repair for every patient with severe ventricular secondary mitral regurgitation irrespective of symptoms, ejection fraction, prior medical optimisation or anatomic and clinical selection.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** The 2025 ESC/EACTS guidelines (doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194) split secondary MR (SMR) into ventricular and atrial phenotypes for the first time, upgrade transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) to Class I, Level A in carefully selected ventricular SMR without significant CAD, and create new Class IIa (surgery) / Class IIb (TEER) recommendations for atrial SMR. [[passage text removed]]

**1. New phenotypic classification.** SMR is now split into atrial SMR (annular dilatation driven by AF or HFpEF) and ventricular SMR (classic functional MR from ischaemic or dilated cardiomyopathy), with explicit echocardiographic and clinical criteria for each, because the two have "contrasting prognostic and therapeutic implications." [[passage text removed]] Atrial SMR criteria include preserved LVEF ≥50% without regional wall motion abnormalities, no/minimal LV dilatation (LVEDD <56 mm in women, <63 mm in [passage text removed]/m²); ventricular SMR is characterised by reduced LVEF with leaflet tethering and secondary annular dilatation. [[passage text removed]] The practical consequence is that every SMR patient should be classified as atrial or ventricular *before* Heart Team discussion. [[passage text removed]]

**2. Ventricular SMR without CAD — TEER Class I A (up from IIa B in 2021).** [passage text removed]] The specified criteria are: anatomy suitable for M-TEER; NYHA ≥[passage text removed] hospitalisation in the previous year or raised natriuretic peptides ([passage text removed]/advanced HF; no CAD requiring revascularisation; no severe aortic/tricuspid valve disease; no hypertrophic, restrictive or infiltrative cardiomyopathy. [[passage text removed]] Patients not fulfilling these optimal criteria, with or without advanced HF, retain a Class IIb, LOE C indication, and isolated surgery for ventricular SMR remains Class IIb C. [[passage text removed]]

*Evidence basis:* extended follow-up of COAPT (5 years), RESHAPE-HF2 and MITRA-FR, plus study-level meta-analysis; the pooled analysis did not show a survival advantage at 24 months versus GDMT but confirmed consistent reductions in HF hospitalisation and improved quality of life. MATTERHORN, comparing TEER with surgery, found TEER non-inferior for efficacy with a better safety profile. [[passage text removed]]

**3. Ventricular SMR with concomitant CAD.** MV surgery is recommended (I B) in severe ventricular SMR undergoing CABG; MV surgery may be considered (IIb B) for moderate SMR undergoing CABG; and PCI followed by TEER after re-assessment of MR may be considered (IIb C) [passage text removed]]

**4. Atrial SMR — new recommendations.** [passage text removed] should be considered (IIa B) in symptomatic patients with severe atrial SMR on optimal medical therapy; TEER may be considered (IIb B) in symptomatic patients not eligible for surgery after optimisation of medical therapy including rhythm control where appropriate. [[passage text removed]] Surgery is favoured here because it can simultaneously address annular dilatation, concomitant tricuspid disease, AF and the left atrial appendage; the IIb TEER recommendation rests on observational data showing good safety and procedural success, with RCTs and longer follow-up still needed. [[passage text removed]]

**5. Practical pathway.** For ventricular SMR the default is GDMT ± CRT, then TEER if anatomy is eligible, [passage text removed]; for atrial SMR: optimise AF/HFpEF, then surgery (annuloplasty + ablation + LAAO) if risk is acceptable, with TEER for high-risk/non-surgical candidates. [[passage text removed]]

**Caveat:** the guidelines themselves note remaining evidence gaps — particularly the absence of randomised data defining [passage text removed]]

**1. New phenotypic classification**
- Atrial SMR criteria: preserved LVEF (≥50%) without regional wall-motion abnormality, no/minimal LV dilatation (LVEDD <56 mm women, <[passage text removed]/m²), typically in the context of AF and/or HFpEF; ventricular SMR is characterised by reduced LVEF, leaflet tethering/restricted motion and secondary annular dilatation [[passage text removed]]. This explicit definition is described as the first in any guideline or consensus document [[passage text removed]], and is one of the guideline's most consequential departures from ACC/AHA 2020, which does not delineate the two forms [S:ec8d2cb7-5bd7-5f36-8fbf-2c0a0f22ab69][S:ddec1b65-a3c0-51ea-8442-66353078593d].

**2. Ventricular SMR without significant CAD — TEER upgraded to Class [passage text removed]), fulfilling specific clinical and echocardiographic criteria" [[passage text removed]]. This is an upgrade from Class IIa B in 2021 [[passage text removed]], driven by 5-year COAPT data, RESHAPE-HF2 and supporting meta-analyses — noting that pooled analysis did not show a 24-month survival advantage, but consistent gains in quality of life and reduced HF hospitalisation [[passage text removed]].

The guideline's Table 7 criteria predicting outcome improvement are: anatomy [passage text removed] hospitalisation in the previous year or raised natriuretic peptides ([passage text removed]/advanced HF; no CAD requiring revascularisation; no severe aortic and/or tricuspid valve disease; no hypertrophic, restrictive or infiltrative cardiomyopathy [[passage text removed]]. Isolated MV surgery for ventricular SMR remains Class IIb C, unchanged, reflecting high surgical risk in this population [[passage text removed]]. However, MV surgery is recommended (Class I B) [passage text removed]]. - Medical/rhythm first: identify and treat underlying causes, manage HFpEF and AF per the relevant guidelines, encourage SGLT2 inhibitors in HFpEF; limited data indicate rhythm control may [passage text removed]].
- **Class IIa B:** MV surgery, plus [passage text removed] on optimal medical therapy [[passage text removed]]. **5. Cross-cutting principles:** SMR decisions remain multidisciplinary Heart Valve Team decisions, with emphasis on multimodality imaging, [passage text removed] Centres [S:99a7b680-a831-52fe-94ea-05e3add354f9][S:7ed6feed-fd50-5f68-af2a-5ab4e6f70590]. rows.question: How does immediate compare with staged complete revascularization for major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with STEMI and multivessel disease?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Immediate and staged complete revascularization of non-culprit lesions produced no significant difference in the composite adverse cardiovascular outcome; All-cause mortality did not differ significantly between the immediate and staged strategies; Recurrent myocardial infarction did not differ significantly between the immediate and staged strategies. Certainty: Confidence in these comparisons is limited and the pooled estimates remain imprecise, with the mortality range still allowing a modestly higher risk under immediate treatment. Scope: applies to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction with multivessel disease in haemodynamically stable adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the similarity of the two timing strategies as established for patients excluded from these comparisons, such as those with cardiogenic shock, prior bypass surgery or complex non-culprit lesions, or recommends immediate revascularization for such patients on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Immediate and staged complete revascularization yield broadly similar hard outcomes (death), but the MACE comparison depends critically on **how long the staged procedure is delayed**: immediate PCI looks superior when staging is deferred weeks after discharge, and looks no better (possibly worse in higher-risk patients) when staging occurs within the index admission.

## Trial-level evidence

**MULTISTARS AMI** (840 hemodynamically stable STEMI patients, 37 European sites; staged arm at 19–45 days, median 37 days): the 1-year composite of [passage text removed] revascularization or HF hospitalization occurred in 8.5% (immediate) vs 16.3% (staged), [passage text removed]), meeting both noninferiority and superiority. The difference was driven by nonfatal MI (2.0% vs 5.3%) and unplanned ischemia-driven revascularization (4.1% vs 9.3%); [passage text removed]%), stroke, and HF hospitalization did not differ, nor did stent thrombosis (1.2% vs 1.4%), AKI (3.6% vs 2.9%) or major bleeding (3.1% vs 4.8%) [[passage text removed]][S:https://www.medpagetoday.com/meetingcoverage/esc/106084].

**BIOVASC** (1,525 ACS patients, ~40% STEMI; staged median 15 days): immediate was noninferior at 1 year (7.6% vs 9.4%, [passage text removed]), superiority not met at 1 year, but superior at 30 days ([passage text removed]]. In the **prespecified STEMI subset (n=608)**, there was no significant 1-year difference in [passage text removed]%, HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.47–1.50), [passage text removed]%), MI (1.7% vs 3.3%), unplanned revascularization (4.1% vs 5.0%) or cerebrovascular events, with only a nonsignificant 30-day trend favoring immediate (3.0% vs [passage text removed]]. At 2 years there was still no significant difference [[passage text removed]].

**OPTION-STEMI** (994 STEMI patients, 14 Korean sites; staged *within* the index admission, median 3 days) is the key discordant trial: noninferiority of immediate was **not** established — 13% vs 11% for death/nonfatal MI/any unplanned revascularization at 1 year, [passage text removed]), p for noninferiority = 0.24. Death was numerically higher with immediate (7.5% vs 5.3%), and there was a significant interaction by Killip class: harm with immediate in patients with heart failure signs (Killip ≥[passage text removed].05) but not without (Killip [passage text removed].41; p interaction = 0.04) [[passage text removed]]. Cardiogenic shock during index hospitalization was reported in 4% vs 2% [S:https://www.pcronline.com/News/Congress-coverages/[passage text removed]-STEMI-MVD].

## Pooled evidence

- An 11-trial, 5,666-patient ACS meta-analysis found lower MACE with immediate (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.66–0.89), with lower reinfarction (RR 0.59) and repeat revascularization (RR 0.62), no difference in all-cause (RR 0.92) or cardiovascular (RR 0.96) mortality. Crucially, the benefit was confined to comparisons against staging at 14–45 days (RR 0.70, 0.56–0.88) and absent when staging occurred <14 days; STEMI subgroup RR 0.81 (0.67–0.97) [[passage text removed]].
- A 10-trial meta-analysis/meta-regression including OPTION-STEMI found lower MACE with immediate in the NSTEMI subgroup **but not** in the STEMI subgroup, and no mortality difference (all-cause death 3.9% vs 3.5%, RR [passage text removed]].
- A 9-trial (4,270 patients) network meta-analysis restricted to STEMI found no pairwise MACE difference (OR [passage text removed]); in the network, only *out-of-hospital* staged PCI carried higher MACE than immediate, driven by ischemia-driven repeat revascularization. Immediate did not increase major bleeding or AKI [[passage text removed]/PMC11935666].
- The most recent STEMI-specific meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis concluded the two strategies give comparable ischemic, safety and mortality outcomes, that information size is insufficient for definitive conclusions, and that certainty of evidence is very low to low [[passage text removed]].

## Caveats and guidance

The MI/revascularization advantage of immediate PCI may be partly ascertainment bias: trials were open-label, periprocedural MI is hard to adjudicate in acute STEMI, and physicians may more readily perform unplanned revascularization in patients whose non-culprit lesions are still untreated [[passage text removed]]. One meta-analysis raised a cardiovascular-death signal with single-stage PCI [[passage text removed]].

Accordingly, the 2023 ESC ACS guidelines give complete revascularization a Class I, Level A recommendation [passage text removed] days, and explicitly formulate **no recommendation favoring immediate over staged**, citing the absence of adequately sized superiority trials [[passage text removed]]. Cardiogenic shock remains an exception where non-culprit PCI should not be done immediately, based on CULPRIT-SHOCK [[passage text removed]]. The OPTION-STEMI investigators' position — limit immediate complete revascularization to stable, low-clinical-risk STEMI patients — is the most defensible synthesis [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

The evidence is discordant and hinges on *when* "staged" means: pooled across randomized trials, immediate and staged complete revascularization produce comparable MACE, but immediate PCI looks superior when staging is deferred by weeks (MULTISTARS AMI) and non-superior — possibly harmful in heart failure — when staging occurs during the index hospitalization (OPTION-STEMI).

## Trial-level evidence

**Favouring immediate (weeks-long deferral):** In MULTISTARS AMI, an international open-label noninferiority trial at 37 European sites, hemodynamically stable STEMI patients with multivessel disease were randomized to immediate multivessel PCI (n=418) or culprit PCI followed by staged multivessel PCI at 19–45 days (n=422). The 1-year composite of death, nonfatal MI, stroke, unplanned ischemia-driven revascularization, or heart-failure hospitalization occurred in 35 patients (8.5%) immediate vs 68 (16.3%) staged (risk ratio 0.52; 95% CI 0.38–0.72; P<0.001 for both noninferiority and superiority), with fewer nonfatal MIs (2.0% vs 5.3%) and unplanned revascularizations (4.1% vs 9.3%); death, stroke, and heart-failure hospitalization appeared similar [S:c9bf71b4-25da-57b1-9627-39c9f6fbc98d]. BIOVASC (ACS, including STEMI; staged within 6 weeks) similarly showed noninferiority of immediate PCI for the composite endpoint, with significant reductions [passage text removed] [S:83b83a68-e5c7-5e76-9ac3-13d97aff9685], and no significant effect on all-cause mortality [S:8dc42b33-8d47-5be7-80b6-dc0f0180bffb].

**Not favouring immediate (same-admission staging):** OPTION-STEMI [passage text removed] at the index procedure vs staged complete revascularization later in the same hospitalization; the 1-year [passage text removed] vs 10.8% with staged, and noninferiority was not demonstrated (p for noninferiority = 0.24) [S:5ed2147c-90cf-5f02-942f-90e0c1713440], with a noninferiority margin of HR 1.42 [S:https://www.pcronline.com/News/Whats-new-on-PCRonline/2025/ESC/OPTION-STEMI-Immediate-vs-staged-complete-revascularisation-during-index-admission-in-patients-with-STEMI-MVD]. A prespecified subgroup of 329/994 patients (33.1%) with Killip II–III heart failure showed significant treatment-by-heart-failure interaction (p=0.043): 22.8% vs 13.3% primary events ([passage text removed]) with immediate PCI, versus no difference in those without heart failure ([passage text removed]].

## Pooled evidence

The most recent meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (4133 STEMI patients) found no significant difference between immediate and staged complete revascularization for [passage text removed]) [S:c711c2c5-3bc3-5bed-9e6b-3e63bb29da69], nor for cardiac mortality, repeat revascularization, stroke, heart-failure hospitalization, or major bleeding [S:cce570b9-eeb2-5042-b8a2-19c4c5c769dc]. Crucially, a significant subgroup interaction by deferral interval (P=0.032) mirrored the trial discordance: immediate PCI trended better than *long*-interval staged PCI ([passage text removed]) but numerically worse than *short*-interval staged PCI ([passage text removed]) [S:c711c2c5-3bc3-5bed-9e6b-3e63bb29da69]. An earlier meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (2023 patients; median time to staged PCI 19 days) likewise found comparable MACE (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.58–1.27), non-procedural MI, death, and cardiovascular death, but a 40% reduction in unplanned revascularization with immediate PCI (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.40–0.89, p=0.01) [S:091ca706-79a0-5ba0-bb8e-ab4f72435685].

## Caveats

- Periprocedural MI is systematically harder to detect when non-culprit PCI is done in the same sitting, potentially biasing MI endpoints in favour of immediate PCI [S:e7995222-7bb1-5a1e-9005-7d4b69c6411f].
- Meta-analyses including non-randomized data have reported *higher* cardiovascular mortality with immediate revascularization (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.09–2.00) with no difference in MI or revascularization [S:32491651-eee8-591f-b102-61f6b4fc340e]; discrepancies across pooled analyses are attributed to differing sample sizes and inclusion of observational studies [S:3b1bf20c-4aec-5d46-b988-f11baead630f].
- Immediate multivessel PCI is not recommended in cardiogenic shock, based on CULPRIT-SHOCK [S:feb94f5d-e5f2-5d48-be3e-c7e2a77cc3d4]; OPTION-STEMI excluded shock patients [[passage text removed]].

**Practical reading:** both strategies are acceptable for hard MACE in hemodynamically stable patients [S:17c26549-215f-5d9c-bb16-1a426246417f, S:091ca706-79a0-5ba0-bb8e-ab4f72435685]; what should be avoided is prolonged deferral of non-culprit PCI, while immediate complete PCI appears best restricted to stable patients without heart-failure signs [S:628fad33-cffe-58d4-936f-693c211b509f].

rows.question: What evidence guides anticoagulation decisions for new-onset atrial fibrillation occurring after cardiac surgery?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation that begins after cardiac surgery is associated with fewer thromboembolic events; The same comparisons show substantially more bleeding in patients given oral anticoagulation; Mortality was not significantly lower with oral anticoagulation than without it in these comparisons; The independent link between post-surgical atrial fibrillation and later stroke is elevated in one large cohort and not significant after adjustment in another. Certainty: The links rest on comparisons in which anticoagulant treatment was not assigned, and the long-term stroke signal disagrees between analyses. Scope: applies to new-onset atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery in adults, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents routine anticoagulation for post-surgical new-onset atrial fibrillation as an established net benefit or recommends it for all such patients on this basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: there is still no completed randomized trial of anticoagulation versus none for post-operative AF (POAF) after cardiac surgery, so decisions rest on observational data, CHA₂DS₂-VASc–based risk stratification, and guidelines that have progressively softened toward individualized, time-limited therapy — with the definitive PACeS trial ongoing.**

**1. The evidence base is observational and of very low certainty.** A systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 observational studies (no randomized trials met eligibility) found anticoagulation associated with lower arterial thromboembolism ([passage text removed]; 6 studies) — absolute risk reductions of 0.8% short-term and 2 events/1000 person-years long-term — but higher bleeding ([passage text removed]), absolute increases of 0.5% and 42 events/1000 person-years; certainty was graded very low, downgraded for risk of bias, indirectness and inconsistency ([PMC9568684]([passage text removed]); [PubMed 36254332](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36254332)). In an STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database–Medicare analysis of 38,936 patients with POAF after isolated CABG (25% discharged on OAC), propensity-matched discharge anticoagulation was associated with *higher* mortality ([passage text removed]) and [passage text removed]), with no difference in ischemic stroke ([passage text removed]), and no apparent benefit in either the CHA₂DS₂-VASc 2–4 or ≥5 subgroup ([PMC9463707]([passage text removed])). A Danish registry cohort found long-term thromboembolic risk in post-CABG POAF was *lower* than in nonvalvular AF (18.3 vs 29.7 events/1000 person-years; adjusted [passage text removed]) and not significantly higher than in CABG patients without POAF ([passage text removed]), though anticoagulation during follow-up was associated with fewer thromboembolic events within the POAF group ([passage text removed]) ([JAMA Cardiology 2018;3:417-424, Butt et al.]([passage text removed])). A Dutch Heart Registry cohort of patients with POAF after isolated CABG reported no survival or thromboembolic advantage from OAC beyond 30 days ([dspace.library.uu.nl]([passage text removed]); [springermedicine.com, ESC 2025]([passage text removed])).

**2. Risk stratification uses CHA₂DS₂-VASc, but recalibrated.** In 6,368 Swedish [passage text removed]* anticoagulated, 1-year ischemic stroke rates [passage text removed]% for CHA₂DS₂-VASc 1, 2 and 3, and ≥2.3% for scores ≥4; the authors concluded OAC should probably be avoided at scores <3, at least over one year ([PMC9238552]([passage text removed]); [PubMed 35574947](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35574947)). A larger analysis of 10,435 POAF patients identified prior ischemic stroke, advancing [passage text removed] predictors, with CHA₂DS₂-VASc and ATRIA showing only moderate discrimination (AUC 0.72 and 0.74) similar to non-surgical AF ([Heart 2025;111:18-26]([passage text removed])).

**3. Guidelines differ and explicitly acknowledge weak evidence.** The 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline gives a Class 2a (B-NR) recommendation to anticoagulate for 60 days after surgery when safe with respect to surgical bleeding, then reassess ([Circulation 2023;148, Joglar et al.]([passage text removed]); [PMC11104284](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11104284)). The 2024 ESC guideline states long-term OAC "should be considered" in POAF [passage text removed] (IIa B) ([2024 ESC AF guidelines PDF](https://www.uninsubria.it/sites/default/files/2024-09/Guidelines%20AF%202024published.pdf)). The STS 2026 POAF guideline downgrades this to a Class IIb recommendation to individualize on overall stroke risk and other OAC indications, framing POAF as distinct from pre-existing AF and noting persistent uncertainty about optimal timing, duration and arrhythmia burden ([Ann Thorac Surg 2026;122:255-277, Chatterjee et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42009116); [sts.org]([passage text removed]); [cardiovascularbusiness.com](https://cardiovascularbusiness.com/topics/clinical/cardiac-surgery/new-sts-guideline-tackles-prevention-afib-after-cardiac-surgery)). A critical appraisal concluded guideline recommendations in this space are not matched by the underlying evidence ([[passage text removed], Chatterjee et al.]([passage text removed])).

**4. The pivotal trial is ongoing.** PACeS (NCT04045665) is a multicenter, open-label, randomized superiority trial of OAC (VKA with INR 2–3 or any approved DOAC) added to background antiplatelet therapy versus antiplatelet alone in new-onset POAF after isolated CABG; randomization within 7 days of the qualifying AF event or by discharge, protocol OAC duration 90 days, primary effectiveness endpoint a composite of death, ischemic stroke, TIA, MI, systemic or venous thromboembolism at 90 days and primary safety endpoint BARC 3 or 5 bleeding, with planned enrollment of ~3,200 ([ctv.veeva.com/NCT04045665]([passage text removed]); [my.clevelandclinic.org]([passage text removed]); [PMC13378743]([passage text removed])). It excludes patients with prior AF, pre-existing OAC indications, planned DAPT, major perioperative complications, and concomitant LAA closure — so its results will not generalize to those groups.

**5. Agent choice and duration.** Comparative data are also non-randomized: a meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (12 studies; 8,587 DOAC vs 8,315 warfarin) found DOACs reduced bleeding ([passage text removed]) without a mortality difference ([Br J Anaesth 2022;129:154-162](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0007091222002483); [PubMed 35729010](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35729010)), and a separate meta-analysis found lower stroke risk with DOACs ([passage text removed]) with similar bleeding and mortality ([PubMed 34111554](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34111554)). The only randomized comparison, NEW-AF (100 patients, rivaroxaban vs warfarin), did not shorten length of stay (7 vs 8 days, P=0.460), recorded no major bleeds, strokes or thromboembolic events in either arm, and found better patient-reported convenience with rivaroxaban ([PubMed 40704706](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40704706)) — a trial far too small to inform efficacy.

**6. Two practical modifiers.** First, POAF frequently recurs undetected after discharge: in SEARCH-AF, 336 cardiac surgical patients at elevated stroke risk in sinus rhythm at randomization had AF/flutter ≥6 minutes detected in 19.6% with 30-day continuous patch monitoring versus 1.7% with usual care, an absolute increase of 17.9% ([PMC8397929]([passage text removed]); [acc.org SEARCH-AF]([passage text removed])) — which is why several sources frame the 2–3-month reassessment as the point to distinguish truly transient POAF from emerging clinical AF ([Front Cardiovasc Med 2023;13:1156626]([passage text removed])). Second, valve surgery carries higher risk: POAF incidence 49.0% in 131,652 valve patients with early stroke 8.0% versus 5.3% (absolute [passage text removed])), and monitoring detected POAF at roughly twice the rate after valve surgery ([passage text removed]) ([Ann Thorac Surg, SEARCH-AF substudy]([passage text removed])).

**What the evidence does not support:** there are no randomized data on optimal duration (the 60-day and 90-day figures come from guideline consensus and the PACeS protocol respectively, not from trial results), no trial-based threshold for AF burden triggering anticoagulation, and essentially no dedicated randomized evidence for valve-surgery POAF, which PACeS excludes.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Anticoagulation for post-cardiac-surgery atrial fibrillation (POAF) rests entirely on **observational data and extrapolation from non-surgical AF** — no completed randomized trial answers the question, so guidelines give only weak (Class IIa) recommendations and decisions are individualized by CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, AF duration/recurrence, and bleeding risk. [S:5143353d-8314-5eca-915e-a2b49168ecf5][S:b38f26cc-e4f6-565a-af8a-7c8a1d38cc7e]

## The evidence base

**1. The risk POAF confers is real but modest.** POAF occurs in roughly 30% of CABG patients and ~44–51% of aortic valve surgery patients, and is associated with increased early and late stroke — in a meta-analysis of over 2 million patients, OR 1.62 for stroke within 30 days and OR 1.37 beyond 30 days, plus increased early and late mortality. [S:b38f26cc-e4f6-565a-af8a-7c8a1d38cc7e][S:430970a9-ffa4-544c-8141-5f97411e2a68][S:865748d5-9357-5793-a0e5-f1423a9062e9] The association is not uniform: in a propensity-matched Asian cohort, POAF raised future AF, heart failure and mortality but *not* TIA/ischemic stroke [S:4c13bff7-c202-5cf0-9477-93fff6c44aa5], and in the Swedish registry POAF after combined SAVR+CABG was not associated with long-term [passage text removed]) though it was after isolated SAVR (aHR 1.32, 1.08–1.59). [S:430970a9-ffa4-544c-8141-5f97411e2a68]

**2. Risk stratification: CHA₂DS₂-VASc works, but the threshold may differ.** In 6,368 Swedish CABG patients with POAF and no OAC (>97% on antiplatelets, 147 strokes in year 1), a CHA₂DS₂-VASc <3 carried a 1-year stroke risk <1%, leading the authors to conclude OAC "should probably be avoided" in that group. [S:6b6078e5-5a5b-5a83-ab34-5443cf4d0660][S:26a8d07e-92b3-5e7e-a46c-cfd3214e0a88] A nationwide cohort found prior ischemic stroke, older age, heart failure and prior MI independently predicted 1-year stroke, with CHA₂DS₂-VASc and ATRIA performing similarly to non-surgical cohorts (ATRIA marginally better). [S:b38f26cc-e4f6-565a-af8a-7c8a1d38cc7e][S:694c0f3c-90b3-51ae-9071-1bd0df76daf6] One review cautions that CHA₂DS₂-VASc was validated in nonsurgical AF and may underestimate short-term postoperative risk. [S:f41b7eb7-a6e5-5955-b9bc-8d5be3f7056d]

**3. Net benefit of OAC is small and offset by bleeding.** A systematic review of 9 observational studies (254,200 POAF patients, 27.3% anticoagulated; no RCTs found) reported lower arterial thromboembolism with OAC (RR 0.83, 0.69–0.99) but markedly more bleeding (RR 3.22, 2.82–3.68); absolute short-term risk reduction in thromboembolism was 0.8% versus a 0.5% absolute increase in bleeding. [S:5143353d-8314-5eca-915e-a2b49168ecf5] A separate meta-analysis of 8 cohorts (15,335 patients, mostly vitamin K antagonists) found only a non-significant mortality signal (HR 0.85, 0.72–1.01) and no difference in thromboembolism (HR 0.68, 0.40–1.15). [S:b523d956-c3e0-5d72-bcc2-a42419b04280] Registry data are conflicting: early OAC after SAVR or SAVR+CABG showed no reduction in death, stroke or thromboembolism [S:b6fe20e8-ef8d-5e0f-a92f-817fe788f622][S:65551065-b625-5ffa-9402-d5211a05e043]; a Danish cohort suggested benefit in anticoagulated POAF patients (aHR 0.55), while another analysis of >38,000 CABG patients found higher mortality (HR 1.16) and major bleeding (HR 1.60) with no stroke reduction regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc. [S:e02c2f20-4102-5729-a852-a15824270871] Timing matters mechanistically: most strokes occur early, when bleeding risk is highest and warfarin least effective. [S:e02c2f20-4102-5729-a852-a15824270871]

**4. Guidelines therefore hedge.** ACC/AHA 2023 considers it reasonable to give OAC for 60 days after cardiac surgery, then reassess (Class IIa, LOE B-NR); ESC 2024 recommends long-term OAC only in POAF patients at elevated thromboembolic risk (Class IIa, LOE B); the 2024 perioperative guideline for noncardiac surgery is Class IIa, LOE C. [S:fb8c74bf-bc60-5bda-a131-296e6b8ced00][S:b32f0dab-a1e9-5134-a750-7301ee0f8219][S:01c522d9-98c9-589c-b4b3-08a462e2bf22] Both major AF guidelines treat POAF as trigger-induced AF and emphasize structured post-discharge rhythm surveillance and stroke-risk reassessment; they explicitly acknowledge no consensus on the AF-duration threshold for anticoagulation. [S:bde7a0d7-6419-5fc3-a990-7b37329ee47c] Older/other documents suggest anticoagulating for POAF >48 h and continuing ~4 weeks after sinus rhythm returns. [S:0473c205-c76a-51c7-8486-62e8c1ccc526][S:2a3523a3-7031-514e-812f-9aebb355b8d5]

**5. Recurrence data increasingly drive the decision.** POAF is not self-limited: recurrence in the first month ranges 30–60%, SEARCH-AF detected recurrent AF >6 minutes in nearly 20% of patients with a wearable ECG patch versus 1.7% with usual care, and pooled loop-recorder recurrence rises from 17.8% (11.9–23.2) at 3 months [passage text removed]. [S:a706a92d-f256-5d54-be73-eb56a43267be][S:75fd5932-52d1-5dc5-847b-ad0dfdc7c705] Detected recurrent AF burden appears prognostically meaningful and is used to select patients for OAC. [S:dea90f2a-2dd4-5f11-9309-472cec9bb382]

**6. Practice is heterogeneous and undertreats high-risk patients.** Fewer than 30% of eligible patients receive OAC at discharge; in the nationwide CABG cohort, discharge OAC did not track individual stroke risk (28.8% vs 27.0% in those with and without prior stroke). [S:f41b7eb7-a6e5-5955-b9bc-8d5be3f7056d][S:694c0f3c-90b3-51ae-9071-1bd0df76daf6] An AF-SCREEN survey found the minimum qualifying AF duration cited by clinicians ranged from 30 seconds to >48 h, with "lack of RCT data" the most common stated concern. [S:fb8c74bf-bc60-5bda-a131-296e6b8ced00]

**7. Agent choice and alternatives.** Direct oral anticoagulant data in this setting are thin — the largest randomized comparison is a 56-patient pilot of apixaban vs warfarin showing no strokes or thromboembolic events in either arm, similar bleeding, and lower total cost with apixaban. [S:6af32a72-ca23-5fff-b4da-96c375f11ba5][S:a7957205-dbef-5abe-8380-ceb4efe6abd0] For patients with AF and CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 undergoing cardiac surgery, LAAOS III showed concomitant left atrial appendage occlusion reduced stroke/systemic embolism (4.8% vs 7.0%, P=0.001) on top of background anticoagulation — but that trial enrolled patients with *pre-existing* AF, not de novo POAF. [S:e2070ec9-46ea-5813-a424-3eb30c5821a9]

## What is still missing

The definitive trial is ongoing: PACES (NCT04045665) is an open-label randomized comparison of OAC plus antiplatelet versus antiplatelet alone after isolated CABG, with a 90-day protocol anticoagulation duration and co-primary thromboembolic and BARC 3/5 bleeding endpoints. [S:1545af30-5d5b-5ab0-81b0-4f3aa0ac0fbc][[passage text removed]] Until it reports, no source I found supports a firm duration threshold or a specific anticoagulant as preferred in this population.

rows.question: Which imaging features indicate a high risk of progression in uncomplicated type B aortic dissection?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: False lumen diameter, baseline aortic diameter and entry tear characteristics show the most consistent independent associations with aortic growth and late intervention; A large false lumen diameter above 22 mm is associated with accelerated aortic growth and aneurysmal degeneration, false lumen diameter being among the strongest such predictors; Partial false lumen thrombosis, true lumen compression and pleural effusion are associated with adverse aortic outcomes but function as context-dependent surrogates of haemodynamic instability rather than independent drivers of progression. Certainty: The evidence is associative: these imaging features track aortic growth and late intervention rather than establishing causation. Scope: applies to uncomplicated type B aortic dissection in adults, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents a single imaging measurement threshold as an established indication that mandates early endovascular repair in uncomplicated disease.

answers.websearch:
**Conclusion:** The imaging features most consistently flagged as high-risk in uncomplicated type B aortic dissection (uTBAD) are a large initial total aortic diameter (>40 mm), a large false lumen (>20–22 mm, or false lumen larger than true lumen), a large (>10 mm) entry tear located on the inner/lesser curvature, partial false lumen thrombosis, radiographic-only malperfusion or true lumen collapse, bloody pleural effusion, and interval aortic growth on serial imaging — with maximum aortic diameter being the only predictor that has survived external validation.

**Guideline-endorsed imaging findings**
- The 2022 ACC/AHA aortic disease guideline lists high-risk imaging findings in uncomplicated acute type B dissection including maximal aortic diameter >40 mm, [passage text removed], and entry tear on the lesser (inner) curvature [[passage text removed]; S:https://www.jtcvs.org/article/S0022-5223(23)00347-1/fulltext]. A companion review enumerates the same set plus an increase in total aortic diameter >5 mm between serial studies and bloody pleural effusion/hemothorax [[passage text removed]]. Under STS/SVS criteria, high risk is [passage text removed]]. Proposed SVS score revisions weight severe bloody pleural effusion, aortic diameter >40 mm, total true lumen collapse, [passage text removed], entry tear >10 mm, and entry tear on the lesser curvature [[passage text removed]]. Presence of high-risk features supports considering endovascular management (Class 2b) [[passage text removed]].

**Supporting primary evidence**
- *Diameter and false lumen size:* [passage text removed] greater than true-lumen diameter independently predicted major adverse events after uncomplicated acute TBAD [[passage text removed]]. A risk score built on initial aortic diameter ≥40 mm, false lumen > true lumen, ulcer-like projection, and age [[passage text removed]]. Subacute false lumen growth ≥2 mm (1–6 months, detected by 3D vascular deformation mapping) was more strongly associated with late adverse events than baseline diameter [[passage text removed]]. ## Answer

High-risk imaging features cluster into five domains: overall aortic size and its change over time, false-lumen size/configuration, false-lumen thrombosis status and flow, entry-tear size and location, and ancillary findings (bloody effusion, imaging-only malperfusion).

**Guideline-endorsed high-risk imaging findings.** The 2022 ACC/AHA aortic disease guideline lists for uncomplicated acute type B dissection: [passage text removed] the [passage text removed] studies, bloody pleural effusion, and imaging-only evidence of malperfusion [S:3daf5bfe-e5a5-5061-8948-f09f484f58ea]. Contemporary reviews reproduce the same list and add radiographic-only malperfusion (e.g., asymmetrical renal perfusion on CTA), [passage text removed] arising from the false lumen, and rapid aortic enlargement [S:32864e36-fd87-5e16-843c-89d7972cbf1b][S:4831812e-6b4b-5e3e-b0a0-07ada7f68329].

In one cohort, [passage text removed], and total aortic diameter >44 mm predicted mortality [S:c0850ed2-9a55-5571-accd-03b6b4a81026]. A single-centre series concluded that late aortic events warranted considering intervention when aortic diameter was ≥40 mm and false-lumen diameter ≥22 mm [S:07e9d125-2cf7-5d2b-aea8-245bc991e6bd]. Rather than an absolute cut-off, the simple relation *false lumen larger than true lumen* on admission CT predicted aortic events and rapid growth in the first 6 months; that study's own ROC cut-offs for false-lumen diameter were lower than the classic 22 mm and it argued FL>TL is more reproducible because it captures both size and configuration [[passage text removed] thrombosis and flow.** Partial thrombosis of the false lumen (versus complete patency) is an independent predictor of post-discharge mortality; in IRAD it was present in about a third of acute type B dissections and independently predicted 3-year death [S:2b3f342f-b0bc-51a5-8dde-8a5331c9a188][S:dc1cb80d-3618-592d-b155-d7c3af1cf2e7]. Growth rate is higher with a partially thrombosed false lumen than with complete thrombosis or patency [S:c0850ed2-9a55-5571-accd-03b6b4a81026]. Conversely, [passage text removed] diameter increase in one series, with markedly higher mean growth in pressurised versus non-flowing false lumens [S:5a56cfef-bf17-5159-b2fc-831094fc36fa].

**Entry-tear geometry.** A primary entry tear at the concavity (inner curve) of the distal arch independently predicted development of complicated type B dissection, and a short distance from the tear to the left subclavian artery was likewise associated with complicated disease; proximal main entry tear >10 mm carried unfavourable outcomes [S:5582ba20-b79b-5897-b4b0-b5a08d0e0a57]. Tear size ≥10 mm or Zone 3 location have been reported as independent predictors of aneurysm formation, and some centres define high risk as intractable pain/hypertension plus aortic diameter >4.0 cm, FL diameter >22 mm, or Zone 3 tear [S:bd19f4de-faf0-582e-8bda-5b5cfad40e98]. On multivariable analysis of medically treated uncomplicated acute type B dissection, an elliptical true lumen and a proximal entry >10 mm on initial CT were associated with aneurysmal change; growth was fastest in the first months and slowed thereafter [S:c52e247c-aa72-58bd-b54c-c8c9ec957da3].

**A wider imaging checklist** (imaging-focused review) adds: single entry tear, false-lumen diameter >2/3 of [passage text removed] after prior type A repair, fusiform dilatation of the proximal descending aorta, helical flow in the false lumen on MRA, number of vessels arising from the false lumen, and increased FDG uptake on PET-CT [S:ccfd195e-bb0d-5ce2-946a-8c4f4781284c]. Vessel-wall inflammation on PET and false-lumen flow patterns remain investigational markers [S:2b3f342f-b0bc-51a5-8dde-8a5331c9a188].

Lower baseline CT thresholds (maximum aortic diameter ≥40 mm, maximum aortic wall thickness ≥10 mm) have also been reported as independent predictors of progression in medically treated type B IMH [S:57b0e267-a2f1-5a28-9d00-b2788cdd8eb1]. Ulcer-like projections (perceptible communication with the aortic lumen, neck >3 mm) carry a worse prognosis than intramural blood pools (connection to a branch vessel, neck <2 mm), which usually do not progress [S:c0dd84b7-b26d-588f-a327-01de546fac1a]. Thresholds for early expansion are not universally standardised and require serial imaging [S:bb8fe403-b548-5dff-89e5-da00030ba807]. rows.question: How does the PRECISE-DAPT score relate to all-cause mortality in patients with acute coronary syndrome?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: A PRECISE-DAPT score at or above the standard high-bleeding-risk threshold is associated with higher all-cause mortality during the index hospitalisation; The same score threshold is also associated with higher all-cause mortality at mid-term follow-up; Discrimination for mid-term mortality was best in ST-elevation myocardial infarction and lower in the other presentations, a preliminary observation from one retrospective series. Certainty: The mortality difference across score strata reflects an observed association rather than established causation, because higher-scoring patients were older and carried more comorbidity, and the discrimination estimates derive from a single sample without external validation. Scope: applies to acute coronary syndrome in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents comparable score performance across discharge antithrombotic regimens as demonstrating that those regimens yield equivalent survival, or recommends choosing between them on that basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: although PRECISE-DAPT was built to estimate out-of-hospital bleeding risk after PCI ([mdcalc.com]([passage text removed])), a consistent body of observational ACS data shows that a higher score is independently associated with higher all-cause mortality — both in hospital and over years of follow-up — with moderate-to-good discrimination.**

**Graded, dose-dependent relationship with long-term death**
- In 552 AMI patients discharged after PCI, Kaplan-Meier curves showed all-cause mortality rising most steeply in the high-score group (≥25), then intermediate (17–24), then low (<17) (P<0.001); after adjustment for comorbidity, coronary lesions, revascularisation and discharge medication, the intermediate and high groups had [passage text removed]) versus the low group. Discrimination for all-cause death was AUC [passage text removed]), better than the WBC, creatinine-clearance and age components individually but not significantly better than haemoglobin alone ([PMC7287192]([passage text removed])).
- In ACS complicated by cardiogenic shock (in-hospital survivors, median follow-up 2.7 years, all-cause death in 197 patients, 67%), the score was positively associated with death: a change from 17 to 38 corresponded to HR [passage text removed]), R²=0.209, time-dependent AUC 0.69 ([PMID 38172314](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38172314)).

**Across ACS subtypes and antithrombotic strategies**
- In 2,953 consecutive ACS patients (mean follow-up 1.9 years), score ≥25 identified markedly higher in-hospital (11.6% vs 1.1%) and mid-term (42.5% vs 10.0%) all-cause mortality (both p<0.0001). Discrimination was best in STEMI (AUC 0.84, 95% CI 0.82–0.87) versus NSTEMI (0.78, 0.76–0.80) and unstable angina (0.75, 0.71–0.79); it was unaffected by revascularisation strategy (AUC 0.803 PCI vs 0.804 CABG) or by discharge antithrombotic regimen (0.78 DAPT, 0.71 dual, 0.72 triple therapy) ([10.1007/s40119-026-00444-w]([passage text removed]); congress abstract: [ehaf784.1958]([passage text removed])).

**In-hospital mortality specifically**
- In NSTEMI (in-hospital death 9.3%, 31 patients), PRECISE-DAPT was an independent predictor of in-hospital all-cause mortality (OR 1.063 per point, [passage text removed]), out-performing the SYNTAX score ([passage text removed]) ([10.1186/s43044-023-00329-6]([passage text removed])).
- In STEMI treated with primary PCI, the score was reported as [passage text removed] ([PMID 30322265](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30322265)), a finding echoed in a later STEMI cohort ([journal.iha.org.ir](https://journal.iha.org.ir/article_193308_de71553dc607b7bf1f290525d9e2e51a.pdf)) and cited as such in subsequent work ([PMC7287192]([passage text removed]); [10.3389/fcvm.2024.1419551]([passage text removed])).

**Comparative / mechanistic context**
- In a 260-patient ACS cohort, score ≥25 carried higher mortality (OR 6.94, 95% CI 3.53–13.62, p=0.001) and this held on Kaplan-Meier analysis irrespective of DAPT score (p<0.001), whereas the ischaemia-oriented DAPT score discriminated neither mortality nor bleeding ([jucvm.galenos.2025.2024-42-114]([passage text removed])). Another cohort reported AUC 0.706 for long-term all-cause mortality, with a >23.5 cut-off giving 72.2% sensitivity and 59.7% specificity ([termedia.pl]([passage text removed])).
- Plausible reasons for the mortality signal: the score's components (age, renal function, haemoglobin, WBC) overlap with established ACS mortality predictors such as those in GRACE ([PMC7287192]([passage text removed]); [researchsquare rs-1589515](https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-1589515/latest.pdf)), and bleeding itself carries mortality risk comparable to or greater than thrombotic events ([EuroIntervention]([passage text removed])).

**Caveats.** The evidence is observational and largely single-centre/retrospective; the score is not a validated mortality model, and its own intended target (bleeding) is predicted only moderately in ACS (c-statistics 0.61 for BARC 2/3/5 and 0.73 for BARC 3/5, with PARIS superior on reclassification and decision-curve metrics in that cohort) ([EuroIntervention]([passage text removed])). I found no randomised or guideline-endorsed evidence that using PRECISE-DAPT to guide therapy reduces mortality.

**In-hospital mortality.** In 1,418 STEMI patients treated with primary PCI, in-hospital all-cause death was 9.4% with a score ≥25 versus 0.9% with a score <25 (P<.001), and the score remained an independent predictor after multivariable adjustment (HR 1.026 per point, [passage text removed]); discrimination for in-hospital death was AUC [passage text removed]), non-inferior to the TIMI risk score (0.79), with a best cutoff of ≥21 (87.5% sensitivity, 67.7% specificity) [S:8f11a966-4d37-57e9-b235-4ef6ca39dabb][S:ae3a6523-02be-5a47-a0e8-1b9482a569cf][S:db583014-82d2-5abd-ae4a-bec5dcd9351f]. Notably, only a minority of deaths were bleeding-related — 12 of 48 deaths were non-cardiac, of which 5 were due to major bleeding — indicating the mortality signal is not merely a bleeding effect [S:ae3a6523-02be-5a47-a0e8-1b9482a569cf]. In NSTEMI, the score was likewise an independent predictor of in-hospital all-cause death (alongside SYNTAX score), whereas other risk scores were not [S:41f730f6-8c62-5809-954b-c46922e2ef42].

In 1,071 ACS patients undergoing PCI followed a [passage text removed]%) and major bleeding (9% vs 4%) were both higher with score ≥25, and the [passage text removed]) as well as MACCE (HR 1.028 per point, 95% CI 1.016–1.039) [S:85b5b94d-9d73-59cd-8fe0-4c69bbc98040][S:2da5b59c-761f-59c0-bbac-5d80b004f18d]. **Why (mechanistic/statistical basis) and caveats.** The score's five components — age, white blood cell count, haemoglobin, creatinine clearance, prior spontaneous bleeding — overlap heavily with variables in established ischaemic/mortality scores such as TIMI, GRACE and PURSUIT, so the score effectively captures general frailty and comorbidity burden rather than bleeding propensity alone [S:2da5b59c-761f-59c0-bbac-5d80b004f18d][S:97e0f8fe-573f-524c-9c65-bb257a63047d]. Consistent with this, high-score patients were over 15 years older with more complex coronary disease, more comorbidity and higher Killip class at admission — i.e. confounding by baseline risk is substantial [S:1f8c9a44-e37c-5755-bc35-a2e73bf6fd71]. More broadly, shared risk factors drive both ischaemic and bleeding events in ACS [S:43940a58-041f-5ac1-a40b-9985b508c93f]. rows.question: Which features in younger patients undergoing mitral valve repair support consideration of prophylactic left atrial appendage exclusion?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Left atrial enlargement and remodeling, together with the risk of residual or recurrent mitral regurgitation, raise projected long-term thromboembolic risk in younger patients whose age-weighted stroke score remains low; Increasingly complex appendage architectures, particularly cauliflower-type morphology, are described as carrying higher embolic risk than the chicken-wing shape; Structural features of the appendage are described as contributing to embolic risk independently of rhythm status; Postoperative and late-onset atrial fibrillation remain frequent after technically successful repair and sustain long-term thromboembolic risk. Certainty: These are descriptive patterns rather than demonstrated effects. Scope: applies to degenerative mitral regurgitation undergoing open mitral valve repair in younger adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents surgical appendage exclusion as an established substitute for long-term anticoagulation should atrial fibrillation be documented later, or recommends withholding anticoagulation on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

The features that support consideration are markers of **structural/atrial disease and long lifetime exposure** rather than a conventional risk score: left atrial enlargement, atrial fibrosis/remodelling, residual or recurrent mitral regurgitation, adverse LAA morphology/flow, and a decades-long horizon in which late AF and cumulative anticoagulation bleeding risk accrue. The direct randomised evidence in non-AF patients is, however, negative, so this remains a case-by-case discussion.

## Supporting evidence

**The explicit argument for young MV-repair patients.** A 2026 perspective by Ibrahimi et al. argues for reconsidering prophylactic surgical LAA exclusion at open mitral repair in younger patients, on the grounds that: CHA₂DS₂-VASc emphasises age and comorbidity and therefore has limited applicability in young patients with low conventional risk profiles; lifelong anticoagulation confers substantial cumulative haemorrhagic burden over decades even when HAS-BLED is low; early repair limits but does not abolish lifetime AF risk, with postoperative and late-onset AF remaining frequent; and residual or recurrent MR promotes progressive atrial dilation and fibrosis, raising [passage text removed]. Their proposed selective framework integrates atrial remodelling, [passage text removed] — i.e. exclusion is offered to *selected young patients with structural atrial disease*, not routinely (Brain & Heart 2026;4(3):025510076, doi:10.36922/BH025510076).

**Late AF is common and persistent after repair, supporting the "lifetime risk" premise.** In David et al.'s long-term leaflet-prolapse repair series, the probability of new AF rose over time to 32.4% at 20 years among patients without preoperative AF; AF patients were anticoagulated and 58 patients had serious haemorrhagic complications, with 11 resulting deaths (JACC, [passage text removed]). Mehta et al. reported de novo AF (>90 days post-op) incidences of 14% at 5 years and 23% at 10 years after mitral surgery, with a clear trend toward increased stroke risk and greater warfarin use (PMID 30248793). This matters more in the young because degenerative repair appears to restore [passage text removed] at any age of operation (PMC7377922).

**Which structural features flag risk.** Left atrial enlargement is a recurrent independent predictor: in a degenerative-MR repair cohort, age, hypertension, left atrial enlargement and interventricular septal thickness were significant risk factors for postoperative AF (PMC12415746); in another mitral surgery cohort, LA diameter enlargement and LAVI were strongly associated with new-onset postoperative AF (PMC10775066), whose authors framed their findings as identifying patients who might benefit from prophylactic LAA amputation or ablation (PMID 38204696). Imaging markers of cardioembolic risk that inform LAA-specific selection include LAA volume >34 cm³, ≥3 lobes, non-chicken-wing (particularly cauliflower) morphology, low emptying velocity (thrombus risk rising at ≤55 cm/s, and <20 cm/s specifically associated with LAA thrombus), plus LA volume, LA strain and LA fibrosis (European guidance PDF on multimodality LA/LAA imaging, saric.us). The ongoing LeAAPS trial operationalises exactly this logic in non-AF surgical patients, enrolling on combinations of CHA₂DS₂-VASc with age, significant left atrial enlargement, or elevated NT-proBNP (NCT05478304; rationale/design PMID 39395566).

**Observational support, and important counter-evidence.** Propensity-matched Medicare data in isolated mitral repair without AF showed reduced 5-year stroke/thromboembolism (6.4% vs 8.3%; HR [passage text removed]) with no 30-day mortality or 5-year survival difference, but more postoperative AF (45% vs 38.4%, P<.01) (PMID 40090461). A single-centre robotic series found an 8-year cumulative stroke/TIA incidence of 2.0% with closure vs 6.3% [passage text removed], P=.02) — but notably *increasing age* was the factor associated with stroke/TIA risk (HR 1.05 per year), and new AF occurred in 31.8% vs 25.2% (PMC11144458). A meta-analysis in MV repair without AF found reduced 5-year thromboembolism (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.46–0.77) and in-hospital stroke (RR 0.43) but increased postoperative AF (RR 1.17) (PMID 42089094).

Against this: in 1,050 sinus-rhythm patients after repair for leaflet prolapse, closure did not reduce TIA/stroke (1.8% vs 2.9% at 5 years, P=0.53) (PMID 36423865); and the randomised OPINION trial (2,118 patients, mean age 56, no AF, CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2, mitral or aortic surgery) found no benefit of surgical LAA occlusion on the 1-year composite of ischaemic stroke, TIA or cardiovascular death (PMID 40888584; ESC 2025 release, escardio.org).

**Bottom line:** in a young repair patient, the defensible triggers for discussing prophylactic exclusion are dilated/fibrotic left atrium, expected residual or recurrent MR, high-risk LAA anatomy or low LAA flow, and an anticipated multi-decade exposure to bleeding if AF later mandates anticoagulation — balanced against a consistently observed increase in early postoperative AF and the absence of randomised benefit to date. Note that guideline Class I surgical LAA occlusion applies to patients *with* AF undergoing non-emergent cardiac surgery (LAAOS III basis; STS 2023 update as summarised at consultqd.clevelandclinic.org), not to prophylaxis in sinus rhythm.

[passage text removed] enables a lifetime-oriented rather than age-weighted risk assessment [S:4a0eaa08-e31c-5cdb-8ebe-31e1bfbcb8c1]. LA fibrosis in MR patients without AF is being formally characterized (ALIVE study) because its clinical implications remain unknown [S:b1b6c531-930f-5da0-bb8d-ff211a8ff3b2].

**2. High-risk LAA anatomy and function.** Structural features of the LAA contribute to embolic risk **independent of rhythm status** [S:4a0eaa08-e31c-5cdb-8ebe-31e1bfbcb8c1]. Non–chicken-wing morphologies (cactus, windsock, cauliflower) carry higher thromboembolic risk than chicken-wing, and patients with non–chicken-wing shape plus extensive trabeculation showed higher stroke risk *regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc score* [S:4502e8f6-56ac-5056-b9fd-822048964a98]; chicken-wing morphology is associated with higher LAA emptying velocity, offering a flow-based mechanism [S:4502e8f6-56ac-5056-b9fd-822048964a98, S:5c8db0ad-3dba-5c0d-91e8-61818f431ec7]. Mitral valve disease with atrial myopathy is itself associated with larger LA and LAA orifices and a higher rate of atypical LAA morphology [S:34fe5da3-002d-57bd-90f8-76fc625a5430].

**3. Residual/recurrent MR and lesion complexity.** In degenerative disease, [passage text removed] residual MR contributes to progressive LA enlargement over time; surgical planning is advised to integrate atrial and ventricular dimensions, remodeling, projected thromboembolic risk, and lesion-specific repair risk when weighing added prophylactic LAA occlusion [S:4a0eaa08-e31c-5cdb-8ebe-31e1bfbcb8c1].

**4. Persistent AF risk despite technically successful early repair.** Early repair limits atrial fibrosis and extreme LA dilation but reduces rather than eliminates lifetime AF risk; postoperative [passage text removed] progresses to persistent AF [S:c64020ea-a400-5d07-a2ec-6f47ad8e25cf]. In 192 patients with no preoperative atrial arrhythmia undergoing repair for degenerative disease, early atrial arrhythmias occurred in 52.1%, and [passage text removed] was 64% (95% CI 55%–72%); early postoperative AF lasting >24 h predicted late AF (HR [passage text removed]) [S:40ce4a79-5c7e-552a-a84c-0eecc703dcf3]. Reported predictors of late AF after repair for prolapse include advanced age, left atrial size >50 mm, more than mild preoperative tricuspid regurgitation, and diabetes [S:b4dcee4d-dcb5-5c37-abd4-75a0651205da]. Preoperative LA volume index and P-wave dispersion/peak-to-peak time were independent predictors of post-repair AF in mitral valve prolapse [S:45b93d26-5730-5b44-9483-93b03d105445]. AF in degenerative MR carries prognostic weight even after repair (10-year post-surgical survival 82% sinus rhythm vs 70% paroxysmal vs 57% persistent AF, p<0.0001, in 2,425 patients) [S:4a0eaa08-e31c-5cdb-8ebe-31e1bfbcb8c1].

**5. Anticipated decades of anticoagulation exposure.** Conventional scores emphasize age and comorbidities and have limited applicability in young low-score patients, while lifelong anticoagulation confers substantial cumulative hemorrhagic burden [S:8e51e670-1251-5a2c-b1fa-0fa8930941b4]; major bleeding risk rises with duration of therapy, arguing for incorporating young age into the risk calculus [S:a9d0c31a-3c45-5970-a570-99cc8c7d25e5]. Anticipated long-term anticoagulation exposure is named as a selection feature [S:9c094eea-f267-52cf-a4ba-01c4487b43bf].

**6. The operative window itself.** Exclusion performed concomitantly with an open procedure allows direct visualization, durable closure, minimal residual leak, and no intracavitary foreign material [S:9c094eea-f267-52cf-a4ba-01c4487b43bf, S:c64020ea-a400-5d07-a2ec-6f47ad8e25cf].

## Countervailing evidence you should weigh

- Randomized proof is confined to AF: LAAOS III enrolled patients **with** AF and CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 and reduced stroke/systemic embolism by 33% (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.53–0.85) [S:aac2166d-144f-52c7-8575-740b37870d80]. The LAAOS III investigators explicitly declined to extend this to non-AF patients without new evidence [S:f50ed9d5-1bdc-55fc-bfce-6c6dcf3c02ab]; the non-AF question awaits LeAAPS (NCT05478304, ~6,500 patients, completion expected 2032) [S:35cd6065-b314-5a55-887a-927b8b8d6d09, S:eab06901-8b8c-5e59-80b8-aee33ecf548b].
- Specifically relevant to *younger* patients: the LAA is a compliant reservoir modulating LA pressure, and this function "could be important" in younger patients, with possible worsening of exercise tolerance; a cohort of 10,633 surgical patients found no association between LAA occlusion and stroke or mortality (adjusted HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.72–[passage text removed]–1.13) with more postoperative AF in the LAAO group [S:f50ed9d5-1bdc-55fc-bfce-6c6dcf3c02ab]; LAA closure has been associated with increased postoperative AF (ATLAS: [passage text removed]) [S:10b03913-406d-525d-92d7-ec9b547b2a5b].
- Exclusion is not a guarantee: in [passage text removed], thromboembolic events still occurred in 12.3% over 3.6±1.3 years, most (10/14) in repair patients, and more often when warfarin was not prescribed at discharge [S:65bd4924-6ad2-50d3-96f4-189c8552d464] — echoed by a correspondent noting the benefit had never been proven in a randomized trial [S:8185c8e4-035c-52ad-ab4e-41083a15735b]. Technique matters: in the original LAAOS, complete occlusion was only 45% with amputation/oversewing and 72% with stapling [S:891cf2c6-f399-52d4-aef2-77785c3130be].

**Net position:** the source advocating this approach frames it as an individualized discussion [passage text removed], and states explicitly that prospective data are needed [S:8e51e670-1251-5a2c-b1fa-0fa8930941b4].

rows.question: What is the prognostic value of baseline extravalvular cardiac damage staging in patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing TAVI?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: All-cause mortality in the year after TAVI is associated with baseline Généreux stage in a stepwise fashion, rising modestly at the borderline stage, roughly doubling at stage 3 (pulmonary vascular or tricuspid damage) and nearly tripling at stage 4 (right ventricular damage) compared with lesser damage; Cardiovascular death follows the same stage gradient, being roughly twofold higher at stage 3, pulmonary vascular or tricuspid damage, and roughly threefold higher at stage 4, right ventricular damage, than with lesser damage; For cardiovascular death the borderline stage did not differ significantly from lesser damage in the pooled comparison, an imprecise preliminary null resting on few contributing studies rather than demonstrated equivalence; Heart failure rehospitalisation is preliminarily observed to be modestly more frequent at stage 3 than with lesser damage. Certainty: The required claims rest on consistently observed associations combined across non-experimental data sources rather than on demonstrated causation, and the borderline-stage estimates remain imprecise, with the all-cause mortality prediction interval extending below no excess risk and the cardiovascular death and rehospitalisation estimates resting on sparse underlying evidence. Scope: applies to severe aortic stenosis treated with transcatheter aortic valve implantation in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents advanced baseline damage stage as a basis for withholding or deferring valve implantation.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Baseline extravalvular cardiac damage stage is a strong, independent, stepwise predictor of mortality after TAVI — roughly a 1.3–1.5-fold increase in death risk per stage increment, with advanced stages (3–4) carrying a 2–4-fold higher risk than early stages — and it also tracks quality-of-life outcomes; however, its incremental discrimination beyond clinical risk scores is modest and it has failed to stratify risk in some real-world cohorts.

## Evidence

**Original derivation (AVR, including TAVI).** In pooled PARTNER 2 patients staged by pre-AVR echocardiography (stage 0 = no extravalvular damage, 1 = LV, 2 = LA/mitral, 3 = pulmonary vasculature/tricuspid, 4 = RV damage), 1-year mortality was 4.4%, 9.2%, 14.4%, 21.3% and 24.5% across stages 0→4 (P trend <0.0001), with HR 1.46 per stage increment (95% CI 1.27–1.67) [PMID 29020232]. Across PARTNER 2 and 3 (n=1,974 with evaluable echoes), 2-year death was 2.5%, 7.1%, 14.6%, 28.2% and 28.2% for stages 0→4, and stage 0 was uncommon (6.8%) while ~half of patients were stage 2 [PMC11979372].

**TAVI-specific registry validation.** In a prospective TAVI registry (n=1,133), 1-year all-cause and cardiovascular mortality rose stepwise: 5.4%/0% (stage 0), 5.3%/1.8% (1), 8.9%/5.9% (2), 17.7%/12.9% (3), 25.8%/19.9% (4) [PMID 33898731; S2352906721000567]. A refined version subdividing stages 3 and 4 (n=1,156) showed 1-year mortality of 3.9% (stage 0–1), 9.6% (2), 14.1% (3), 17.4% ([passage text removed] (severe pulmonary hypertension), 4b (RV dysfunction) and 4c (RV dysfunction + low flow) remained significantly predictive, with a five- to seven-fold increased 1-year mortality risk versus stage 0–1 — notably, low-flow state without RV dysfunction carried risk similar to stage 2 [PMID 34086888; [passage text removed]].

**Meta-analytic estimates.** Pooling 10,466 AVR patients from 9 studies, 1-year mortality was 6.6%, [passage text removed]% for stages 0→4 (HR stage 2: 1.71 [1.32–2.21]; stage 3: 2.79 [2.13–3.64]; stage 4: 3.56 [2.79–4.71]); at 5 years [passage text removed]% (stage 4 HR 3.51 [2.79–4.41]) [PMID 38939639 / [passage text removed]]. A TAVI-restricted systematic review reported 12-month all-cause mortality HRs of 1.61 (1.22–2.12) for borderline stage, 2.06 (1.63–2.60) for stage 3 and 2.77 (2.11–3.64) for stage 4; [passage text removed]]), and rehospitalisation risk was elevated [passage text removed]]) [PMID 41791868; heartjnl-2025-326941].

**Across AS flow-gradient subtypes.** In 2,090 SwissTAVI patients, advanced (stage 3–4) damage predicted 5-year mortality in every subtype: adjusted HR 1.66 (1.34–2.06) high-gradient, 1.49 (1.02–2.16) classical low-flow low-gradient, 1.69 (1.22–2.35) paradoxical low-flow, 1.52 (1.04–2.32) normal-flow low-gradient; advanced damage was most prevalent in classical low-flow low-gradient AS (73.6%) [PMC10687648 / EIJ-D-23-00590].

**Beyond mortality.** In PARTNER 2/3, higher baseline stage was associated with worse KCCQ at baseline and 1 year, and with the composite poor outcome (death, KCCQ-OS <60, or ≥10-point drop) in 10.6%/19.6%/29.0%/44.7%/39.8% of stages 0→4; each one-stage increase raised the odds of a poor outcome by 24% (95% CI 9%–41%; P=0.001) [PMID 36813373; physiciansweekly.com summary of Généreux et al.].

## Caveats

- **Not all damage is fixed, and post-TAVI restaging adds information.** In a real-world TAVI cohort (n=734), stage distribution before TAVI was 4% stage 0, 12% stage 1, 30% stage 2, 31% stage 3, 23% stage 4, and the authors concluded TAVI should ideally precede RV dysfunction, with persistent stage 4 at 6 months conferring continued high mortality risk [PMC12042742]. Post-procedural stage was more strongly associated with 2-year death than baseline stage (HR 2.97 [2.07–4.25] vs HR 1.59 [1.10–2.30] for baseline trend) in another TAVI cohort [[passage text removed]].
- **Discrimination is limited.** In 496 consecutive TAVR patients, the Généreux staging did not significantly stratify 1-year mortality (e.g. stage 4 vs 0–1: HR 1.03 [0.45–2.40]) and its AUC was 0.526 (0.489–0.620), inferior to a strain/RV-coupling-based model (AUC 0.70) — mortality in that elderly cohort was mostly non-cardiac [thevalveclub.com.br/.../Post504_Eco-basico-TVC.pdf]. Adding LV global longitudinal strain (HR 1.384 per stage [1.152–1.663]) [PMID 38999514] or coronary microvascular dysfunction [heart.bmj.com/content/110/8/603] improves stratification over staging alone.
- **Advanced damage should not be read as futility:** in a COMPARE-TAVI substudy, NYHA and 6-minute-walk improvements after TAVI were similar across CD stage groups, though absolute post-TAVI symptom burden and "futility" rates remained higher in stage 3–4 [strapi.merillife.com/.../58_OR_Myval_COMPARE_TAVI_1_sub_study_CD_2025].
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Baseline extravalvular cardiac damage staging (Généreux stages 0–4) is a robust, graded predictor of mortality after TAVI: each stage increment carries roughly a 30–75% relative increase in death risk, and stage 3–4 (right heart/pulmonary involvement) identifies a group with several-fold higher mortality than stage 0–1. Its value is largely additive to conventional surgical risk scores, but it is partly superseded by post-TAVI restaging.

## Evidence

**Stepwise mortality gradient (pooled data).** In a meta-analysis of reconstructed time-to-event data from 16 studies (n = 14,499; 12,282 with symptomatic severe AS undergoing SAVR or TAVR), 1-year mortality rose from 6.6% (stage 0) to [passage text removed]% for stages 1–4; at [passage text removed]%, with stage-0-referenced HRs of 1.30 (1.03–1.64), 1.74 (1.41–2.16), 2.92 (2.35–3.64) and 3.51 (2.79–4.41) [S:f70dff27-e2de-5600-a42d-6ed1c43caada][S:95562fc0-c296-5055-9c79-df1f1e5cb2e3]. Stage distribution is skewed toward established damage (13.3% stage 0, 19% stage 1, 40.4% stage 2, 16.1% stage 3, 11.2% stage 4), and higher stages carry more comorbidity — older age, more NYHA III–IV, CAD, CKD, AF [S:e121bfa7-460e-55f2-b304-fafb62eed296].

**TAVI-specific pooled analysis.** A recent systematic review/meta-analysis restricted to TAVI found a progressive, stage-dependent association of advanced damage with all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality and rehospitalisation, with RVD (stage 4) the strongest signal; meta-regression indicated a *linear* relationship, supporting a continuum rather than discrete categories [S:f046103a-013f-5e96-b9be-fcd8ce8d9353][S:f1e84840-6404-5aea-b849-33fe027f5664]. Importantly, patients in a purpose-created "borderline" stage already had excess mortality and morbidity versus minimal damage, i.e. risk emerges before conventional stage 3–4 thresholds [S:f046103a-013f-5e96-b9be-fcd8ce8d9353][S:bea711f0-8c76-5517-a744-9cd17f3c9a75]. For heart-failure rehospitalisation, pooled RR for stage 3 across six studies was 1.33 (1.12–1.58), risk difference +4.64 percentage points, I² = 8.7% [S:c722f51a-1cf3-56ec-8d68-8f2e48307f4f]. Cardiovascular mortality effects exceeded all-cause effects, suggesting the staging captures disease-specific rather than generic comorbidity risk [S:5b73a2ee-ea91-5234-9a74-fef0617acab8].

**Independent prognostic value in real-world TAVI cohorts.**
- In 734 TAVI patients, baseline staging predicted 2-year mortality (9.4%, 10.6%, 15.5%, 14.5%, 24.7% for stages 0–4; log-rank P = 0.010) and remained independent on multivariable Cox analysis (HR 1.341 per stage, 95% [passage text removed]; and HR 1.316, 1.097–1.577 adjusting for EuroSCORE II and TAVI era) [S:1b7bc6b7-3cf6-55b9-a3f0-83bd11e29144][S:26e982ae-c158-505f-a60c-cc109b574c6b][S:54916d73-cd39-5c2e-9e47-2641f676d3d3]. Notably EuroSCORE II itself was not significant in those models, indicating staging adds information beyond surgical risk scores [S:54916d73-cd39-5c2e-9e47-2641f676d3d3].
- EffecTAVI Registry (n = 262): 1-year mortality 4.3% (stage 0/1), 6.6% (2), 18.6% (3), 21.6% (4), p = 0.008, with cardiac damage independently predictive (HR 1.745, 1.17–2.60, P = 0.006) alongside frailty; secondary endpoints (stroke, MI, pacemaker, rehospitalisation) did not differ [S:9c59a27c-eede-56e9-9280-5e867a12d1ab][S:506e8bcd-2bec-57f6-97ce-71d0f4b6c819].
- A TAVR validation cohort found 2-year all-cause mortality of [passage text removed]% across stages 1–4 (p = 0.023), with stage an independent predictor alongside age, NYHA III/IV, PAD and prior pacemaker [S:63b32cb1-2e5f-5a06-88d5-6f9d7b7f1b33].
- The staging also stratified prognosis in women specifically (baseline P = 0.007) [S:c5a30949-2989-5c25-9d93-50aa819a6ce8].

**What drives the risk — and where baseline staging falls short.** Advanced right-sided/pulmonary damage is the dominant prognostic element; across studies stage 3–4 correlates with far worse mid-to-long-term outcomes than left-sided-only damage [S:474fa05e-8199-5a51-8604-507b447bdd01], and stage-4 RVD often reflects less reversible injury [S:93b44f4d-4661-57d1-aac3-52faeb50c53e]. Baseline staging is also not the whole story:
- **Restaging matters more.** At 6 months post-TAVI, 39.4% improved ≥1 stage, 38.1% were unchanged and 12.7% worsened; once the 6-month stage was entered, baseline staging lost independent significance (HR 0.948, 0.717–1.254, P = 0.710) while follow-up stage remained predictive (HR 1.368 per stage, P = 0.048), and worsening carried HR 3.729 (1.494–9.305) versus improvement [S:11af7a67-4ed5-5660-ac70-939593f89038][S:54916d73-cd39-5c2e-9e47-2641f676d3d3]. Persistent stage-4 RVD at follow-up marked the highest mortality [S:1b7bc6b7-3cf6-55b9-a3f0-83bd11e29144][S:c5a30949-2989-5c25-9d93-50aa819a6ce8].
- **Category granularity is imperfect.** Splitting stage 3 by PASP (Okuno criteria) showed stage 3b (PASP ≥60 mmHg) survival resembled stage 4, whereas stage 3a resembled stage 2 [S:1b7bc6b7-3cf6-55b9-a3f0-83bd11e29144]. Definitions vary between studies (e.g. inclusion/exclusion of atrial fibrillation, TAPSE <17 vs <16 mm), a recognised source of heterogeneity [S:0a54db70-6ff5-5fbf-9c33-ce79e247e5bf][S:b0a80795-a868-5e06-8259-fa41e35f471b][S:5b73a2ee-ea91-5234-9a74-fef0617acab8].
- **Refined systems outperform the conventional one.** A multi-chamber strain-based staging showed [passage text removed] [S:7cc9bde9-414a-5b3e-bbe3-ec7300870944]; LV-GLS integration adds prognostic value [S:5190323c-d375-56c0-8461-c984408e83f7]; and in a small TAVI cohort (n = 90, median 2.9 years) an echo-plus-right-heart-catheterisation staging predicted mortality per stage whereas purely echocardiographic staging did not discriminate [S:0331ca56-ef91-5a01-b9dd-270e975163bd].
- One meta-analysis reported that, on pooled odds-ratio analysis in symptomatic severe AS, only stages 1, 3 and 4 reached significance for all-cause mortality and only stage 4 for cardiovascular mortality — so the per-stage gradient is not uniformly significant in every analytic framework [S:ee203f4e-0eda-5216-8570-3c5aa6e90c4e].

**Clinical implication.** Authors consistently argue for incorporating baseline staging into pre-TAVI evaluation with explicit attention to right ventricular function and pulmonary pressures, and for intervening before stage 3–4 damage develops [S:bea711f0-8c76-5517-a744-9cd17f3c9a75][S:93b44f4d-4661-57d1-aac3-52faeb50c53e][S:0b8e7ee0-11a1-5ded-a0b2-fdc4c665bf58]. The system has been validated in over 30 studies encompassing roughly 40,000 patients [S:61e40548-6fe3-5837-8442-cf4daa21f2e9]. I found no evidence from randomised trials that staging-guided timing of TAVI *improves* outcomes — the data are prognostic/observational, and pooled estimates carry substantial between-study heterogeneity and are mostly from high-income countries [S:bea711f0-8c76-5517-a744-9cd17f3c9a75].
