rows.question: What is the prognostic value of Achilles tendon thickening for MACE after percutaneous coronary intervention in coronary artery disease?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Achilles tendon thickening is associated with a higher cumulative incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events within three years of percutaneous coronary intervention, roughly double the incidence seen in patients without thickening; In patients presenting with acute coronary syndrome the association with three-year events appeared stronger, but it rests on few events and is best read as a preliminary observation rather than an established magnitude; In patients presenting with chronic coronary syndrome, events were numerically more frequent with tendon thickening but the difference did not reach statistical significance. Certainty: The evidence supports an association with later events rather than a causal effect; comparisons were not adjusted for other risk factors and the subgroup estimates are imprecise. Scope: applies to coronary artery disease treated with percutaneous coronary intervention in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the difference in prognostic impact between acute and chronic presentations as a demonstrated effect modification, or recommends on that basis that tendon thickening be disregarded in chronic presentations.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Achilles tendon thickening (ATT) is consistently associated with roughly a 2-fold higher risk of MACE after PCI, independent of LDL-C and of a formal familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) diagnosis — but the evidence base is entirely retrospective, single/limited-centre, and Japanese, so ATT is best regarded as a cheap adjunctive risk marker rather than a validated risk-prediction tool.

## Evidence by cohort

**1-year outcomes (n=406, Heart Vessels 2021).** In 406 consecutive PCI patients, ATT was present in 67 (16.5%); cardiac death was higher with ATT (5.6% vs 0%, p<0.001) even among patients not meeting FH diagnostic criteria, and ATT was independently associated with 1-year MACE (HR 2.09, 95% CI 1.09–4.00, p=0.026) [PMID 32761364].

**3-year outcomes, ACS vs CCS (n=1,362, Circ J 2026;90:1107–1109, CJ-25-0710).** In PCI patients at Chiba University Hospital (June 2016–June 2022), ATT (soft X-ray radiography; ≥8.0 mm men / ≥7.5 mm women per 2022 JAS guidelines) was present in 228/1,362 (16.7%). Three-year MACE (all-cause death, nonfatal MI, and additional components) was 28.4% vs 17.9% (HR 1.99, 95% CI 1.38–2.87, p<0.001). Crucially, the effect was driven by ACS ([passage text removed]), whereas in CCS it was only a non-significant trend ([passage text removed]); the authors attribute this to phase-specific risk and note they did not perform FH-stratified analysis [[passage text removed]; doi:10.1253/circj.CJ-25-0710].

**5-year outcomes (n=887, J Atheroscler Thromb 2023;30:491–501).** Among 887 successful-PCI patients, 241 (27.2%) had ATT; total MACE (CV death, nonfatal MI, or revascularisation for restenosis/progression) was 107/241 (44.4%) vs 166/646 (25.7%), with ATT independently predictive on multivariable Cox modelling (HR 1.887, 95% CI 1.511–2.434, p<0.001). Notably the association persisted in the subgroup with LDL-C <100 mg/dL, and ATT patients achieving LDL-C <70 mg/dL had lower MACE — i.e. the signal is not simply concurrent LDL-C [PMC10164606; PMID 35850983].

**5-year outcomes in the elderly (n=355 aged ≥75, J Cardiol 2023;82:448–454).** With a ≥9 mm cut-off (47 patients, 13.2%), the crude 5-year MACCE difference was not significant (Gray's p=0.10), but CV death/death of unknown cause was (Gray's p=0.034), and multivariable Fine–Gray competing-risk analysis gave HR 1.95 (95% CI 1.12–3.41, p=0.019) for MACCE and [passage text removed]=0.008) for CV death [PMID 37506821].

## Caveats that limit clinical use

- **Event-driver heterogeneity.** In the 887-patient cohort the MACE excess was overwhelmingly repeat revascularisation (restenosis 19.1% vs 11.5%; progression in other vessels 23.7% vs 13.3%) with almost no hard-endpoint difference (cardiac death 1 vs 0; MI 1.2% vs 1.3%), so a large part of the "MACE" signal is angiographically driven [PMC10164606]. The Circ J cohort used a harder composite including all-cause death and stroke.
- **Measurement discordance.** Radiographic and ultrasound ATT do not agree well — a study reported a concordance rate of 83.2% for AT [passage text removed]] — and cut-offs differ by modality (US 6.0/5.5 mm vs X-ray 8.0/7.5 mm under 2022 JAS criteria) [PMC11537786]. Cut-offs also changed over time ([passage text removed] sex-specific values), so cohorts using ≥9 mm are not directly comparable [medRxiv 2023.12.29.23300597].
- **Confounding by FH/cumulative LDL-C.** ATT is an FH diagnostic criterion and plausibly reflects cumulative LDL-C exposure; in FH, ATT trajectory itself stratifies MACE (persistent ATT [passage text removed] vs never-ATT) [[passage text removed]], which raises the question of whether ATT adds information beyond a proper FH work-up and lifetime lipid history.
- **No incremental-discrimination or meta-analytic data found.** My searches returned no meta-analysis of ATT and post-PCI MACE, and none of the retrieved studies reported C-statistic improvement, net reclassification, or calibration when ATT was added to conventional risk models — so the incremental prognostic value over established post-PCI risk factors is unquantified.

**Bottom line:** ATT is a reproducible, inexpensive, non-invasive marker that roughly doubles estimated post-PCI MACE risk across four independent Japanese cohorts spanning 1–5 years, with the strongest and most recent signal in ACS patients; it is reasonable as a prompt to intensify lipid-lowering and to screen for FH, but it is not yet shown to improve risk prediction or to guide therapy in outcome trials.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** Achilles tendon (AT) thickening on soft X-ray is an independent, low-cost predictor of MACE after PCI, roughly doubling risk overall, with the signal concentrated in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients — but the evidence base is limited to a small number of retrospective single-region (Japanese) cohorts, and results depend on the imaging modality used.

**Primary evidence**

1. *Journal of Atherosclerosis and Thrombosis* 2022 (n=887 post-PCI, soft X-ray ATT; thickening defined as >8.0 mm men / >7.5 mm women): 241 patients (27.2%) had AT thickening [S:ed6f92be-6aea-51ea-ba8c-574783820107]. Over up to 5 years, 273 patients (30.8%) had MACE (cardiac death n=1, MI n=9, remainder revascularization), and Kaplan-Meier incidence was significantly higher with AT thickening (P<0.001) [S:c85736dc-fb55-53e6-a866-85baf75ebb61]. In multivariable Cox analysis, AT thickening was independently associated with MACE (HR 1.887, 95% CI 1.511–2.434, P<0.001), alongside LDL-C (HR 1.009) and HDL-C (HR 0.984); BMI, HbA1c, uric acid and statin use lost significance [S:4c6d43f4-2fa6-5887-876d-928c2bde5eda]. Importantly, the excess risk persisted in patients with LDL-C <100 mg/dL, and among patients with AT thickening those achieving LDL-C <70 mg/dL had significantly fewer events — i.e. prognostic information beyond attained LDL-C, with a possible treatment implication [S:4c6d43f4-2fa6-5887-876d-928c2bde5eda]. Baseline differences were modest (higher BMI, LDL-C 100.6 vs 93.6 mg/dL, HbA1c) with similar age, sex, statin/ezetimibe use [S:011e94a1-a216-5ead-8256-1659cde0f529].

2. *Circulation Journal* 2026 (Chiba University, n=1,362 post-PCI, June 2016–June 2022; 2022 JAS cutoffs ≥8.0/≥7.5 mm; primary endpoint 3-year MACE = all-cause death, nonfatal MI, stent thrombosis, stroke, clinically driven target-vessel revascularization) [S:70a3d0c6-e272-5303-87a7-1e1dc86ce608]: ATT prevalence 228 (16.7%), higher in ACS than CCS ([passage text removed]). Three-year MACE was 28.4% with ATT vs 17.9% without (HR 1.99, 95% CI 1.38–2.87, P<0.001); in ACS HR 4.74 (2.02–11.1, P=0.001), in CCS HR 1.63 ([passage text removed]:2a02466b-a661-5e1a-852e-5500918e3aa9]. The authors interpret the ACS signal as reflecting systemic plaque vulnerability/inflammatory burden and argue ATT carries prognostic weight beyond formal FH diagnosis, since not all ATT patients meet FH criteria and acute-phase cholesterol lowering can mask FH [S:52ef6d86-7462-5c2d-8b2d-e4fc1687bfe8]. They position ATT as a simple non-invasive marker of residual risk for phase-specific secondary prevention [S:4bc60bfd-a4f8-5915-a538-9cc7c4f5d980].

**Supporting mechanism / severity link (cross-sectional, not outcome data)**
- ATT correlates with anatomic disease burden: in 87 men with premature ACS, mild xanthoma (ATT ≥8 and <9 mm) was associated with higher SYNTAX score ([passage text removed]; max ATT vs SYNTAX R=0.337, P=0.001), independent of BMI and CRP [S:c1faba6a-527e-5c96-9305-1a70860bfae8].
- Ultrasonographic structural abnormality of the AT was independently associated with higher SYNTAX score in 353 PCI patients even without thickening, while thickness itself correlated only weakly (r=0.167, P=0.02) [S:7946e014-8aa2-57ac-be4e-228639bee177] [S:6cf9da91-dc98-5624-936c-3b3c4be813a5].

**Important caveats**
- Modality matters. In 391 heterozygous FH patients, AT thickening by *ultrasound* predicted MACE (OR 6.67, 95% CI 2.39–18.63 at derived cutoffs; OR 11.76, 1.57–88.56 using 2022 JAS US criteria), whereas AT thickening by *radiography* did not (2017 criteria OR 3.14, 0.88–11.17, P=0.077; 2022 criteria OR 2.48, 0.55–11.10, P=0.236; log-rank P=0.112) [S:ccf1948d-e848-5aa3-86fc-f7b8b7e11189] [S:19a0f5c7-7e30-595c-9554-322c33ed667b] [S:89c917e0-f8c6-58b1-af3f-f0c4db72cf60]. X-ray may overestimate thickness because the skin–tendon boundary is indistinct [S:24f06a90-7027-59f8-a3a5-01e63783bcc1] [S:38e71942-2118-50aa-b57d-393c0aa8fd43].
- Both PCI outcome studies are retrospective; the 887-patient cohort's MACE was dominated by revascularization rather than hard events [S:c85736dc-fb55-53e6-a866-85baf75ebb61], and the Circulation Journal report is a brief analysis whose published effect estimates are unadjusted Kaplan-Meier/Cox hazard ratios without FH-stratified analysis [S:2a02466b-a661-5e1a-852e-5500918e3aa9] [S:52ef6d86-7462-5c2d-8b2d-e4fc1687bfe8]. Statin exposure can reduce xanthoma thickness, potentially attenuating the marker [S:10c9a6c8-e776-549a-9685-c742f2c33c92].
- I found no randomized, non-Japanese, or meta-analytic evidence on ATT and post-PCI MACE, and no data showing that acting on ATT improves outcomes.

rows.question: What patient characteristics relate to mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement for pure native aortic regurgitation?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: A wider ascending aorta is associated with higher 30-day all-cause mortality after transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement for pure native aortic regurgitation; Renal insufficiency is associated with higher 30-day all-cause mortality in these patients; Among the few deaths, those attributed to aortic dissection had a larger mean ascending aortic diameter than the treated group overall, which remains a preliminary observation. Certainty: The size and renal associations are of moderate strength while the pattern among deaths is weak, resting on very few events, and none of it establishes cause. Scope: applies to pure native aortic regurgitation treated with transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement using self-expandable valves in older adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents ascending aortic diameter as a demonstrated cause of early death or treats the registry-derived diameter threshold as a validated, externally confirmed rule for denying transfemoral valve replacement.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Mortality after TAVR for pure native aortic regurgitation (PNAR) tracks with **baseline surgical risk/frailty markers (high STS score, low BMI, low serum albumin), reduced LV systolic function, concomitant ≥moderate mitral regurgitation, renal insufficiency, and aortic root/ascending aorta dilation** — plus procedure-related factors (residual ≥moderate AR, valve embolization/migration, vascular complications, AKI) that are partly a function of the unfavourable anatomy itself.

## Evidence by characteristic

**Surgical risk score, LV function, mitral regurgitation.** In the largest multicentre pure-native-AR TAVR registry (331 patients, mean STS 6.7 ± 6.7%), multivariable analysis identified four independent correlates of 1-year all-cause mortality: [passage text removed]–1.06; p=0.037), LVEF ≤[passage text removed]). One-year all-cause mortality was 46.1% with residual ≥moderate AR vs 21.8% with ≤mild AR (log-rank p=0.001) [[passage text removed]]. Baseline ≥moderate MR also independently predicted 1-year rehospitalization (HR 1.96; 95% CI 1.17–3.28) [same source].

**Low body mass and high STS score (early mortality).** In an international registry of 146 patients (78 with native AR), independent predictors of 30-day mortality were BMI <20 kg/m², STS [passage text removed] [PMID 28521923]. A narrative review of this literature summarises the same 30-day signal set and adds serum albumin <3.3 mg/dL, number of valves implanted, and longer ICU stay, and lists ≥moderate baseline MR, LVEF <45%, STS-PROM >8%, AKI stage ≥2 and moderate/severe post-procedural AR as the 1-year predictors [doi.org/10.15212/CVIA.2023.0033].

**Renal insufficiency and ascending aortic diameter.** In 890 PNAR patients from 72 Chinese centres undergoing self-expandable transfemoral TAVR ([passage text removed] 2.0% and 2.7%), multivariable logistic regression identified ascending aortic diameter (OR 1.103; 95% CI 1.005–[passage text removed]–14.553; p=0.009) as associated with 30-day death; an XGBoost/SHAP analysis flagged ascending aorta as the dominant predictor, with diameter >41.6 mm carrying OR 5.027 (95% CI 2.042–12.696; p=0.0004). [passage text removed] predicted technical success [[passage text removed]].

**Anatomy-driven procedural failure.** In PANTHEON (201 patients, median age 79 years, median STS 5.1%, LVEF 45 ± 14%, 76.2% NYHA III/IV), transcatheter valve embolization or migration occurred in 12.4% and, after propensity adjustment, was associated with 1-year all-cause death ([passage text removed]; p=0.006) and the composite endpoint ([passage text removed]), whereas self-expanding vs balloon-expandable choice was not. Lower LVEF, post-dilation, horizontal aorta (>47°) and larger LV end-diastolic diameter were univariate correlates of embolization/migration [[passage text removed]].

**Characteristics that did *not* predict mortality.** In a study-level meta-regression of on- vs off-label TAVR for AR, coronary heart disease remained an independent predictor of 1-year mortality (coefficient 0.45; 95% CI 0.118–0.782; p=0.026), while atrial fibrillation lost significance after adjustment, and age, mean LVEF, access route, valve [passage text removed] [PMC12542711].

## Caveats

Most of these data are retrospective, registry-based, and confounded by device generation: newer/dedicated devices carry markedly lower mortality (pooled 30-day all-cause mortality 9.5% overall — 6.1% new-generation vs 14.7% early-generation) [PMID 31133516], so apparent patient-level associations in mixed-era cohorts partly reflect device era and residual AR rather than patient phenotype alone. I found no validated PNAR-specific mortality risk score in the sources retrieved.

## Conclusion

Mortality after TAVR for pure native aortic regurgitation (NAVR) tracks mainly with **baseline surgical risk and the degree of pre-existing cardiac damage** — higher STS score, reduced LVEF, concomitant ≥moderate mitral regurgitation, renal insufficiency, low body mass index, aortic root/ascending aortic dilation — plus **procedural failure markers** (residual ≥moderate AR, valve embolization/migration, vascular complications). Valve *type* itself does not appear to drive long-term mortality.

## Baseline clinical characteristics

- In the largest multicenter NAVR cohort (331 patients, 40 centers; mean STS 6.7 ± 6.7), 1-year all-cause and cardiovascular death were 24.1% and 15.6%. On [passage text removed]-1.06; p=0.037), **LVEF ≤45%** (HR 1.78; 1.07-[passage text removed]; 1.29-[passage text removed]; 1.52-5.35; p=0.001) were [passage text removed]].
- In an international registry of 78 NAVR patients, independent predictors of 30-day mortality were **BMI <20 kg/m²**, **STS [passage text removed]].
- In a Chinese national registry of 890 PNAR patients undergoing transfemoral self-expanding TAVR (mean age 73.2 years; in-hospital and 30-day mortality 2.0% and 2.7%), multivariable logistic regression identified **ascending aortic diameter** (OR 1.103; 95% CI 1.005-[passage text removed]-14.553; p=0.009) as associated with 30-day death; machine learning flagged ascending aorta as the key predictor, with diameter >41.6 mm conferring markedly higher 30-day mortality (OR 5.027; 95% CI 2.042-12.696; p=0.0004) [S:902fd383-5d48-582e-8b18-5f7d370dc610][S:9a040918-ef6d-5c49-b9db-0b31973f2796]. [passage text removed] predicted technical (not mortality) failure [S:902fd383-5d48-582e-8b18-5f7d370dc610].
- Over longer follow-up, **baseline STS-PROM score** and **longer ICU stay** were independent predictors of the composite of death, MI, disabling stroke, and heart-failure readmission [[passage text removed]].

## Procedural/anatomic characteristics

- In the PANTHEON project, transcatheter valve embolization or migration (12.4% of patients) was associated, after propensity adjustment, with a roughly fourfold higher 1-year all-cause death ([passage text removed]; p=0.006), whereas self-expanding vs balloon-expandable device choice was not (adjusted HR 0.45; 0.14-1.45); lower LVEF, postdilation, and horizontal aorta (>47°) were associated with embolization/migration on univariate analysis [[passage text removed]].
- A contemporary multicenter international registry (104 high-risk NAVR patients; age 75.8 ± 10.6 years, LVEF 47.1 ± 12.5%, NYHA III/IV in 85.6%, STS 5.7 ± 5.2; technical success 79.8%) found balloon-expandable valve use (adjusted OR 0.46), smaller oversizing (OR 0.78), and lower aortic calcium score (OR 0.68) independently predicted **30-day** MACE, but [passage text removed]) — the authors conclude long-term outcomes are driven by patient risk rather than valve type [S:b4cc1b32-72f5-5424-9b2a-d98dd65fcc85][S:1fd9c845-3faa-54c1-b841-fbbf0e969086][S:42891988-4e98-55e2-9e14-07fb62fe9479][S:f0cb0735-7387-5039-b57c-8dec837b3448].

## Context and caveats

- Meta-analytic pooled 30-day all-cause mortality was 11% (95% CI 7%-16%), 15% with first-generation vs 7% with second-generation valves, and 17% at end of follow-up; authors attribute the excess mortality relative to aortic stenosis cohorts to the high-risk profile of these patients — depressed LVEF, concomitant moderate/severe mitral regurgitation, and dilated aortic diameter [S:3197b0cc-310a-5491-a298-7f9adbd5211c][S:cc3f1564-17f5-5be0-85bc-2951265c6f23][S:2d3cf29a-f3e8-5aad-9df7-e5ec90dfaad0]. Contemporary series report much lower perioperative mortality (pooled [passage text removed]%) [S:b9bb6599-0441-5b82-97e0-aa7d25878d6d], so device era is a major confounder of any characteristic–mortality association.
- **Pulmonary hypertension** identifies a sicker PNAR phenotype (higher STS [passage text removed], more renal dysfunction, higher NT-proBNP, lower LVEF, more moderate-to-severe TR) but in that single-center cohort of 103 patients it was **not** associated with more postoperative adverse events [S:dcd52567-348e-58f9-a425-14fda9526d91][S:58c15cf6-a594-5d11-96ea-bd60e6a53d79].
- I found no NAVR-specific evidence in these searches on sex, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, or frailty as independent mortality predictors; such data exist for aortic stenosis TAVR cohorts [S:2b1fadfe-da22-5253-ac2e-08fc4277a561][S:a653a3e8-356c-5f90-ab80-356ac00b6a1c] but should not be extrapolated. Most NAVR analyses are retrospective, modest in size, and none is randomized.

rows.question: How does sacubitril/valsartan compare with dapagliflozin for patient-reported health status in symptomatic heart failure with ejection fraction below 50%?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Over six months the change in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire overall summary score did not differ significantly between sacubitril/valsartan and dapagliflozin, the small numerical edge for sacubitril/valsartan being well below a clinically meaningful difference; Health status scores improved over six months in both the sacubitril/valsartan and the dapagliflozin group; A composite outcome combining clinical events with health status also showed no significant difference between the two agents; These data neither establish superiority of one agent nor, given an imprecise estimate compatible with anything from no difference to a modest benefit, demonstrate equivalence. Certainty: Confidence is low, because the evidence comes from a single small direct comparison of the two drugs relying on a self-reported outcome assessed without blinding and estimated imprecisely, so it shows only that no difference was detected rather than that the treatments are genuinely similar. Scope: applies to symptomatic heart failure with left ventricular ejection fraction below 50% in ambulatory older adults on background renin-angiotensin system inhibitor and beta-blocker therapy, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the within-group rise in health status as an established drug-attributable effect of the assigned agent.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: the only head-to-head randomised comparison, LAQUA-HF, found no significant difference in patient-reported health status between sacubitril/valsartan and dapagliflozin over 6 months in symptomatic HF with LVEF <50%.**

**The trial**
- LAQUA-HF was a multicentre, open-label, pragmatic, randomised 2×2 factorial trial (Japan, enrolment January 2022–February 2024) in ambulatory patients with symptomatic HF, elevated natriuretic peptides and LVEF <50% despite conventional therapy (RAAS inhibitors, beta-blockers); patients were randomised to sacubitril/valsartan vs dapagliflozin and to torsemide vs furosemide, with change in KCCQ [passage text removed] as the primary endpoint and a hierarchical clinical composite (win ratio) as a prespecified secondary endpoint (PMID 42009572; protocol: BMJ Open 2024;14:e076519, PMC10868297). The protocol notes the eligibility LVEF threshold was widened from ≤45% to <50% in January 2023 after DELIVER (PMC10868297).

**Results**
- Among [passage text removed]% NYHA class II), the adjusted mean difference in KCCQ-OSS change favouring sacubitril/valsartan over dapagliflozin was 2.53 points (95% [passage text removed]) — below the ~5-point threshold generally regarded as clinically important for KCCQ (PMID 42009572; threshold context: PMID 37212600). The torsemide vs furosemide comparison was likewise null ([passage text removed]) (PMID 42009572).
- Hierarchical composite outcomes also showed no difference: [passage text removed]) for sacubitril/valsartan vs dapagliflozin (PMID 42009572).
- The authors concluded there was no evidence of benefit of one agent over the other for health status, and that modest differences cannot be excluded given the sample size and predefined power (PMID 42009572). The trial was powered at 80% to detect a 6-point KCCQ-OSS difference between sacubitril/valsartan and dapagliflozin (two-sided α=0.05) (DOI 10.7326/ANNALS-26-02647-JC).

**Interpretive caveats**
- This is a single, small, open-label trial; before it, comparisons were indirect only — NICE TA679 explicitly stated there were [passage text removed], relying on indirect comparison (nice.org.uk/guidance/ta679), and an indirect network meta-analysis found no significant difference between the two for CV death or HF hospitalisation (esc365.escardio.org/journal/59805).
- Each drug improves KCCQ versus its own comparator in the same EF range: dapagliflozin improved KCCQ-TSS/CSS/OSS at 8 months in DAPA-HF ([passage text removed] vs placebo, P<0.0001), with consistent benefit across the LVEF spectrum in pooled DAPA-HF/DELIVER analyses (DAPA-HF KCCQ analysis summary, gpcardio.org; pooled analysis PDF at dapatrial.org); sacubitril/valsartan improved KCCQ-23 clinical summary score vs enalapril in PARADIGM-HF (−2.99 vs −4.63; between-group difference 1.64 points, 95% CI 0.63–2.65; P=0.001) (entrestohcp.com/hfref/quality-of-life). These are placebo/active-control comparisons in different trials and do not establish superiority of either agent over the other.

I found no other randomised head-to-head data on patient-reported health status for these two drugs in this population; note also one venue ambiguity — search results attribute the LAQUA-HF report inconsistently across sources, so I cite it by PMID only.

**Design.** LAQUA-HF was a physician-initiated, 2×2 factorial, open-label (blinded-endpoint) comparative-effectiveness trial at 13 Japanese tertiary centres, enrolling ambulatory NYHA II–IV patients with LVEF <50% and elevated natriuretic peptides who were already on ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker (± MRA) and a daily loop diuretic but not on an ARNI or SGLT2i; patients were randomised to sacubitril/valsartan vs dapagliflozin and to torsemide vs furosemide, with the primary endpoint being change in KCCQ [passage text removed] [S:e339aa65-1588-5a6d-b521-be133be591fd][S:cf67bb25-8a04-5087-89f2-645bfb084a69]. Patients with systolic BP ≤100 mm Hg, eGFR <30, or K ≥5.4 mEq/L were excluded [S:e339aa65-1588-5a6d-b521-be133be591fd]. The trial was powered (80%) to detect a hypothesised 6-point KCCQ-OSS advantage for sacubitril/valsartan, requiring ~220 patients [S:45b07dbd-8b3f-56f7-b9d4-ac3ff0b2838b].

**Results.** Among [passage text removed]% NYHA II), KCCQ-OSS rose in both arms, with an adjusted mean difference favouring sacubitril/valsartan [passage text removed]) [S:4d5cb833-01af-5d57-ba82-5701b8fe1aae][S:a31d48f9-c975-5fbd-8904-cf68ee385a2c]. The hierarchical composite (death, worsening-HF events, non-improvement in KCCQ-OSS) also showed no difference ([passage text removed]) [S:4d5cb833-01af-5d57-ba82-5701b8fe1aae]. NT-proBNP change differed by −[passage text removed]), and worsening-HF events occurred in 5.9% (sacubitril/valsartan) vs 3.5% (dapagliflozin) [S:a31d48f9-c975-5fbd-8904-cf68ee385a2c]. There was no crossover between the two study drugs and no interaction with the diuretic randomisation; torsemide vs furosemide differed by [passage text removed]) [S:a31d48f9-c975-5fbd-8904-cf68ee385a2c][S:4d5cb833-01af-5d57-ba82-5701b8fe1aae].

**Interpretation and caveats.** The authors explicitly state the point estimate does not establish superiority: the CI spans from no difference to a modest benefit, and secondary outcomes were not powered for equivalence testing [S:b44b0a55-29d1-5d96-a93e-f64a0062a09a][S:62bf304e-6ffa-5aec-9a22-c44a83842361]. Named limitations include an over-optimistic 6-point effect assumption (DAPA-HF showed 2.3–4-point KCCQ-OSS gains vs placebo; PARADIGM-HF ~2 points vs enalapril), open-label design with potential expectation bias for a patient-reported endpoint, a KCCQ baseline measured after run-in with possible ceiling effect, exploratory unadjusted subgroups (no significant interaction by sex or AF), and 6-month follow-up [S:62bf304e-6ffa-5aec-9a22-c44a83842361][S:b44b0a55-29d1-5d96-a93e-f64a0062a09a]. An accompanying editorial adds that the factorial design left the diuretic question underpowered at n=231, that the 4–6-week pre-randomisation dose-adjustment/sequential strategy diverges from current rapid quadruple-therapy consensus, and that enrolment of only stable outpatients limits generalisability — concluding that both drugs can be safely initiated and choice should follow patient phenotype rather than a fixed hierarchy [S:12f0f6c8-2d16-5060-ae36-689f2cd90edb][S:47c2c9c5-20bb-5f11-b629-3af75f71af0f][S:75555fb6-427b-5304-ba44-092ec71e4fe6]. Practically, the trial authors note SGLT2 inhibitors may be better [passage text removed], a group excluded here [S:b44b0a55-29d1-5d96-a93e-f64a0062a09a].

**Context from indirect evidence.** No prior direct comparison existed — the two agents' benefits had only been contrasted across separate placebo/active-controlled trials [S:5079da99-ff55-5d1b-98c0-901e4018e8f4]. Against ACEi/ARB comparators, sacubitril/valsartan yields small but significant KCCQ gains in reduced EF (overall summary [passage text removed]) but not in preserved EF [S:560345f9-01d0-555b-bcb9-bb9606fac5e8]; in HFmrEF/HFpEF the KCCQ-CS gain vs valsartan was 1.13 points (95% CI 0.15–2.11) [S:535c72b6-b54d-5568-be5f-af00262fbd43]. Dapagliflozin's health-status effect vs placebo is of comparable or larger magnitude in some settings [S:cb1e70c9-114c-57cb-a0c0-2411d8b0d1b0]. Both patterns are consistent with LAQUA-HF finding no clear winner.

rows.question: What clinical outcomes follow TAVI compared with clinical surveillance in patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: In asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis at low procedural risk, early TAVI reduced the combined occurrence of death, stroke or unplanned hospitalization compared with clinical surveillance, roughly halving that composite; That advantage was measured on a composite endpoint of death, stroke or unplanned hospitalization rather than on any single component of it; The strategy comparison was open-label, so the size of the observed advantage should be read cautiously. Certainty: Because treatment was allocated rather than chosen, the evidence can support a causal advantage on the composite endpoint, yet unblinded delivery of care and the pooling of dissimilar events within that endpoint leave the magnitude of the benefit uncertain. Scope: applies to asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis in adults at low procedural risk, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents early TAVI as an established survival benefit over clinical surveillance.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

In the only adequately powered randomized trial of this strategy (EARLY TAVR), early TAVI reduced [passage text removed] by about half versus guideline-recommended clinical surveillance — but the benefit was driven overwhelmingly by hospitalization/need for valve replacement, not by a demonstrable mortality reduction.

## Primary evidence: EARLY TAVR

**Design.** 901 patients with asymptomatic severe AS and preserved LVEF at 75 US/Canadian centres were randomized 1:1 to early transfemoral TAVI (balloon-expandable SAPIEN 3/S3 Ultra, n=455) or clinical surveillance (n=446); mean age 75.8 years, mean STS-PROM 1.8%, 83.6% low surgical risk ([NEJMoa2405880](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2405880)). Asymptomatic status was verified by treadmill testing in 90.6% of patients, with the remaining 9.4% adjudicated by physician assessment ([[passage text removed])). Importantly, any aortic-valve intervention in the surveillance arm within 6 months of randomization counted toward the primary endpoint ([pcronline.com EARLY TAVR]([passage text removed])).

**Primary endpoint.** [passage text removed]% (122 patients) with TAVI vs 45.3% (202 patients) with surveillance (HR [passage text removed]) ([NEJMoa2405880](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2405880)). Benefit was consistent across all prespecified subgroups, with a number needed to treat at 2 years of 6 ([scai.org]([passage text removed])).

**Components — where the effect came from.**
- Unplanned CV hospitalization: 20.9% vs 41.7% — the dominant driver ([NEJMoa2405880](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2405880)).
- Death: 8.4% vs 9.2% — no meaningful difference ([NEJMoa2405880](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2405880)).
- Stroke: 4.2% vs 6.7% — a lower rate with TAVI that the investigators themselves called unexpected and requiring confirmation ([acc.org TCT 2024 report]([passage text removed])).

**Crossover — the key interpretive caveat.** 87.0% of the surveillance arm underwent aortic-valve replacement during follow-up ([NEJMoa2405880](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2405880)), 47.2% by 12 months ([ctsnet.org summary]([passage text removed])) and >70% by 2 years, with median time to conversion 11.1 months; roughly 40% of these patients presented with acute, advanced features [passage text removed] oedema, or syncope ([crf.org press release]([passage text removed])). So this is a comparison of *early* versus *deferred* intervention, not intervention versus none.

**Secondary and mechanistic outcomes.** The favourable health-status endpoint (alive with KCCQ ≥75 and no >10-point decline from baseline) at 2 years favoured TAVI: 86.6% vs 68.0%, P<0.001 ([healio.com TCT 2024]([passage text removed])). LV/LA health at 2 years was better with TAVI (48.1% vs 35.9%, P=0.001), whereas change in LVEF, [passage text removed] groups ([crf.org]([passage text removed])). In a cardiac-damage substudy of 538 patients with ≥2-year echo data, 85.6% had baseline cardiac damage; TAVI patients were more likely to improve damage stage ([passage text removed] worsen by [passage text removed]) ([tctmd.com](https://www.tctmd.com/news/early-tavi-improves-prognosis-asymptomatic-no-matter-extent-cardiac-damage)). Benefit was consistent regardless of baseline LV health ([PMID 41128701](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41128701)) and of baseline biomarkers, though relative benefit trended greater at lower NT-proBNP/hs-cTnT ([acc.org trial summary]([passage text removed])).

**Safety.** No apparent difference in procedure-related adverse events between patients treated early and those crossing over from surveillance ([acc.org]([passage text removed] TAVI was not associated with increased stroke or mortality risk ([scai.org]([passage text removed])).

**Longer follow-up.** An early-versus-delayed AVR analysis of the implanted population found a 24-month composite of death, stroke, or HF hospitalization of 6.8% with early TAVI vs 10.6% with delayed AVR (adjusted HR 0.65, P=0.08) — directionally favourable but not statistically significant ([acc.org]([passage text removed]); [S1936879825024811]([passage text removed])). Five-year data presented at New York Valves 2026 reported [passage text removed] HF hospitalization in 15.2% vs 24.2% ([cardiovascularbusiness.com]([passage text removed]-treating-asymptomatic-aortic-stenosis)); the sponsor reports a 5-year Kaplan–Meier HF-hospitalization estimate of 5.3% vs 12% ([treatheartvalvefailure.com]([passage text removed]) — manufacturer material, not peer-reviewed). Independent commentary reads the 5-year data as showing reduced unplanned hospitalization without significant effect on mortality or stroke ([jtd.amegroups.org/article/view/101323]([passage text removed])).

## Corroborating and contrasting trials

A meta-analysis of randomized trials of early AVR vs conservative management in asymptomatic severe AS found reductions in the composite outcome (29.2% vs [passage text removed]), all-cause mortality (10.0% vs 13.7%; RR 0.74, 0.55–0.99), CV hospitalization (14.6% vs 32.5%; RR 0.48, 0.39–0.58) and stroke (4.5% vs 7.2%; RR 0.62, 0.40–0.95), but no significant difference in cardiac-specific mortality; certainty of evidence was rated low, with I²=60% for the composite and a 95% prediction interval spanning 0.18–1.59 ([PMC12533610](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12533610)). A critical review notes that when all four trials are pooled with random effects, early AVR lowers stroke and hospitalization while overall and CV mortality are similar, and that the apparent mortality signal was driven by AVATAR ([[passage text removed])).

EVOLVED, which randomized 224 asymptomatic patients with severe AS *and* mid-wall myocardial fibrosis to early intervention (75% SAVR, 25% TAVI) or conservative care, was neutral for its primary composite [passage text removed] (18% vs 23%; HR 0.79, 95% [passage text removed]) and for all-cause death (HR 1.22, 0.59–2.51), but showed fewer unplanned AS-related hospitalizations (HR 0.37, 0.16–0.88) and better NYHA class at 12 months (OR 0.37, 0.20–0.70) ([crf.org EVOLVED]([passage text removed]); [ctsnet.org]([passage text removed])).

## Regulatory and residual uncertainty

On the strength of EARLY TAVR, FDA approved the SAPIEN 3 platform (S3, S3 Ultra, S3 Ultra RESILIA) for asymptomatic severe AS — the first such approval ([medtigo.com]([passage text removed])). Caveats to weigh: the trial was industry-funded ([crf.org]([passage text removed])); >95% of randomized patients were White ([pcronline.com]([passage text removed])); the endpoint definition credited early crossover AVR as an event; and results apply only to patients ≥65 with transfemoral-suitable anatomy and preserved EF. Definitive mortality/HF outcomes await EASY-AS (NCT04204915, ~2,844 patients, results expected 2031) ([[passage text removed])).

**EARLY TAVR (TAVI vs surveillance)**
- 901 asymptomatic patients with severe AS and preserved EF (mean age 75.8 years); over median 3.8 years the primary composite occurred in 26.8% with TAVI vs 45.3% with surveillance ([passage text removed]); death 8.4% vs 9.2%, stroke 4.2% vs 6.7%, cardiovascular hospitalization 20.9% vs 41.7% [S:d5b0390a]. Asymptomatic status was confirmed by exercise testing in 90.6% of patients [S:a02c0bbf].
- The signal was driven by fewer unplanned cardiovascular hospitalizations, with no isolated mortality benefit [S:3f51db95][S:3280a9e3][S:3f4b8e59].
- Crossover was substantial: 87% of the surveillance arm ultimately underwent AVR (median time to conversion 11.1 months) [S:3f4b8e59]; 116 patients (26%) had TAVI within 6 months, and because any AVR within 6 months was counted in the primary endpoint, this accounts for most of the apparent benefit [S:61f7ca51]. Notably, 98% of surveillance patients crossing over within 6 months were symptomatic (NYHA III/IV or HF hospitalization) [S:bbe723ba].

**Symptoms, quality of life, safety**
- KCCQ scores favored early TAVI during the trial — surveillance patients had a transient QoL fall at crossover — but scores were similar between arms at 2 years; LVEF at follow-up was also similar [S:7fd471bf]. Early TAVI was additionally associated with more favorable cardiac remodeling [S:3280a9e3].
- There was no excess of procedural complications in patients treated early compared with those crossing over later [S:d5b0390a], and early TAVI showed no short- or mid-term adverse effect signal; however, long-term data on endocarditis and reintervention are lacking, which matters most for younger patients [S:df2a97a9].

**Where TAVI sits in the wider randomized evidence**
- EVOLVED (early AVR, 25% TAVI, in patients with mid-wall myocardial fibrosis) did not reduce [passage text removed]) [S:b36b66b9], though unplanned AS-related hospitalizations were reduced ([passage text removed]) with stabilization of NYHA class [S:a02c0bbf].

rows.question: How does frailty burden relate to stroke risk in patients with atrial fibrillation and HFpEF?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Greater frailty burden is associated with a substantially higher incidence of stroke than the lowest frailty category; Stroke risk rises in a graded, dose-response fashion as the frailty index increases; Frailer patients already carried higher conventional stroke risk scores at baseline, so part of the excess stroke risk may reflect confounding by these factors. Certainty: The graded link between frailty burden and stroke is a strong but imprecisely estimated association that may be partly confounded by conventional stroke risk factors, not evidence that frailty itself produces the events. Scope: applies to atrial fibrillation coexisting with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction in older adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it directs intensifying or withholding anticoagulation according to frailty category, or states that frailty-guided stroke prevention has been shown to improve outcomes.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

In the only direct evidence base — a post hoc analysis of TOPCAT — frailty burden in patients with coexisting AF and HFpEF shows a graded, near-linear dose–response relationship with stroke, with several-fold higher stroke risk at higher frailty index (FI) values, independent of conventional covariates. Because frailty is nearly universal in this population, the *degree* of frailty rather than a binary frail/non-frail label carries the prognostic signal.

## Direct evidence in AF + HFpEF (TOPCAT post hoc)

- [passage text removed] region of TOPCAT were stratified by a 35-item deficit-accumulation FI (15 KCCQ signs/symptoms plus laboratory abnormalities and self-reported comorbidities; FI >0.21 defined frailty) into [passage text removed]). [PMID 41691162; doi 10.1186/s12872-025-05306-2]
- **97.8% met the frailty threshold**, which the authors give as the explicit rationale for using a continuous/graded index rather than a frail-vs-non-frail dichotomy in this population. [PMID 41691162]
- Over [passage text removed], adjusted stroke HRs versus Group 1 were **[passage text removed])** for Group 2 and **[passage text removed])** for Group 3; the association was robust across three progressively adjusted models (Group 2: 4.00 → 4.14 → 5.01; Group 3: 4.05 → 4.27 → 6.35). Restricted cubic splines showed a **linear dose–response** between FI and stroke risk. [PMC12905932]
- Higher frailty also tracked with cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. For HF hospitalisation the reported overall association was not significant, though the tabulated Group 3 estimate was elevated (model 3 HR 1.79, 95% CI 1.10–2.93) while Group 2 was null (0.96, 0.62–1.50) — i.e. a threshold rather than graded effect for that endpoint. [PMC12905932]
- The authors conclude FI could serve as a routine **supplement to CHA₂DS₂-VASc** in AF+HFpEF, and raise (without testing) whether high-FI patients need intensified stroke prophylaxis. [PMID 41691162; researchsquare rs-7297650/v1]

Context for the frailty scale used: in the parent TOPCAT frailty analysis (1,767 patients), mean baseline FI was 0.37 ± 0.11 and 94% were frail by the FI >0.21 threshold, with outcomes worsening across frailty classes. [profiles.wustl.edu — Sanders et al., [passage text removed]]

## Consistency with the wider AF literature (no HFpEF stratification)

- **ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48** (20,867 patients; cumulative-deficit index): each 0.1 increase in FI (four additional deficits) raised stroke or systemic embolism by **37% (adjusted HR 1.37, [passage text removed]% (1.42, 1.27–1.59)**; 19.6% had frailty. [PMID 33357217; doi 10.1186/s12916-020-01870-w]
- Systematic review/meta-analysis of 20 observational studies (30,883 patients): frailty [passage text removed] stay. [Age Ageing 2019;48(2):196–203, PMID 30445608]
- Meta-analysis of 1,187,651 AF patients: pooled frailty prevalence 39.7%, with frail vs robust ischaemic stroke **OR 1.59 (1.00–2.52)**, death OR 5.56 (3.46–8.94), bleeding OR 1.64 (1.11–2.41). [PMID 35659945]
- Meta-analysis of 23 studies in elderly AF: frail vs non-frail stroke **HR 1.46 (1.08–1.96)**, all-cause mortality HR 2.46 (1.66–3.65), major bleeding HR 1.34 (1.08–1.66); no significant excess in the pre-frail. [PMID 40103904; PMC11911724]
- **Swiss-AF** (2,369 patients; pre-frailty 60.7%, frailty 10.6%): [passage text removed] higher stroke risk, alongside hospitalisation, death and bleeding. [PMID 31977016]
- Nationwide English primary care (536,955 people ≥65): AF prevalence and mean CHA₂DS₂-VASc rose stepwise across eFI categories (fit 2.9%/2.2 → severe 31.5%/5.0); among anticoagulation-eligible women, severe frailty vs fit gave stroke **HR 3.63 (1.10–12.02)**, with death HR 4.09 (3.43–4.89). [PMID 33951158; Age Ageing 2021;50:772–779]

## Counterpoint on the thrombosis–bleeding trade-off

Not all data show frailty tracking stroke as steeply as bleeding: in the Shizuoka cohort of OAC initiators, bleeding risk rose monotonically with eFI (moderate 1.42, 1.24–1.61; severe [passage text removed] with ischaemic stroke/TIA was weaker. [PMID 37168397] So the AF+HFpEF finding should not be read as automatically favouring more intensive anticoagulation.

## Why AF+HFpEF is a high-risk substrate

HFpEF itself amplifies AF-related stroke risk: in Medicare AF patients, HFpEF conferred higher stroke risk than HFrEF at 1, 3 and 5 years (e.g. 5-year HR 1.19, 1.18–1.21 vs 1.12, 1.10–1.13). [PMC13184894] In TOPCAT, a history of AF independently predicted stroke in HFpEF (HR 2.2, 1.6–3.2). [experts.umn.edu] Mechanistically, an inflammatory/fibrotic atrial myopathy shared by HFpEF and AF has been proposed as the thromboembolic substrate, with AF as marker more than sole cause. [[passage text removed]]

## Caveats

The AF+HFpEF-specific finding rests on a **single post hoc analysis of one trial's Americas cohort**, with few stroke events (very wide confidence intervals, upper bound 17.86), a non-standard 35-item index, restriction to trial-eligible HFpEF patients, and no demonstration that adding FI improves discrimination over CHA₂DS₂-VASc — the authors explicitly frame that as future work. [PMID 41691162; PMC12905932] I found no randomised evidence that frailty-guided anticoagulation or left atrial appendage closure changes outcomes in AF+HFpEF; the source raises left atrial appendage closure only as an unanswered question. [researchsquare rs-7297650/v1]
answers.connect:
**Frailty burden grades stroke risk in a dose-dependent way: in patients with coexisting AF and HFpEF, higher deficit-accumulation frailty index (FI) scores were associated with roughly 5- to 6-fold higher adjusted stroke hazards, with a linear FI–stroke relationship.**

**Direct evidence in AF + HFpEF (TOPCAT post hoc analysis)**
- In [passage text removed] arm of TOPCAT, stratified by a deficit-accumulation [passage text removed]), stroke was the primary outcome. Over [passage text removed], adjusted stroke hazard was [passage text removed]) for Group 2 and [passage text removed]) for Group 3 versus Group 1, with a linear dose–response between FI and stroke on restricted cubic splines. Higher frailty also tracked with [passage text removed]:717e94c6-01b0-59e2-9a39-1cf8986b7d4b][S:f7252e52-3701-5f88-938b-41de634c2660].
- Frailty was near-universal in this population: 97.8% met frailty criteria (FI >0.21 threshold), which is why the authors used a continuous/graded FI rather than a frail vs non-frail dichotomy — the latter cannot discriminate stroke risk when almost everyone is "frail" [S:717e94c6-01b0-59e2-9a39-1cf8986b7d4b][S:7e90081d-4ae5-5040-9bf0-a1e79307096b][S:8d451b89-ccb2-55eb-9801-b95857080f06].
- Models were adjusted progressively for age, sex, race, BMI, then additionally systolic BP, prior CAD, hypertension, eGFR, and beta-blocker/CCB/diuretic/antiplatelet use [S:82572a39-96f4-5040-914b-037a98590de4].
- Frailty burden co-varied with conventional risk: mean CHA2DS2-VASc rose across FI strata ([passage text removed], P < 0.001), as did hypertension (77.6% → 89.4% → 95.6%), CAD and BMI, while eGFR fell; baseline anticoagulant use was similar across groups (~81–86%) [S:50de1e44-3a02-5c69-af15-181ab7d9c4cb].

**Important caveats to that finding**
- Stroke events in the BioLINCC TOPCAT dataset were not consistently coded as ischemic vs hemorrhagic, so it is unknown whether the FI–stroke association is thromboembolic, hemorrhagic, or both; time-varying anticoagulant exposure was also unavailable, precluding FI × OAC interaction testing. The cohort was limited to the Americas subgroup [S:50de1e44-3a02-5c69-af15-181ab7d9c4cb][S:63277006-49c7-54b9-95f8-7e7ed5339b45].
- The authors' conclusion is hypothesis-generating: FI may supplement CHA2DS2-VASc, and whether high-FI patients need intensified strategies (e.g. left atrial appendage closure) requires trials [S:50de1e44-3a02-5c69-af15-181ab7d9c4cb][S:63277006-49c7-54b9-95f8-7e7ed5339b45].

**Consistency with the broader AF literature**
- In ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (20,867 participants; 19.6% with frailty), each 0.1 increase in a cumulative-deficit frailty index was associated with a 37% higher risk of stroke or systemic embolism ([passage text removed] 42% higher major bleeding (HR 1.42, 1.27–1.59); edoxaban efficacy was similar to warfarin across frailty strata, with less bleeding except in severe frailty [S:34db5ae8-7f96-5521-8bf1-587e85e05f78].
- A WSO scientific statement reports a pooled relative risk of stroke with frailty of 1.72 generally, and that in [passage text removed] stroke risk [S:0e1456e7-a517-573d-9c85-ba7ab23ea848][S:890f8bd4-1ecb-572b-b8bf-fa9d2fdc7bb0].
- In the ESC-EHRA EORP-AF Long-Term Registry (10,177 patients, 21.3% frail by a 40-item FI), increasing frailty tracked with both higher CHA2DS2-VASc and higher HAS-BLED, plus higher mortality, MACE and major bleeding [S:c0c3f929-4cdd-5710-a363-0bfaf7515863].
- Frailty in AF simultaneously raises bleeding risk, so the risk–benefit calculus is bidirectional; FRAIL-AF found more bleeding when frail elderly patients switched from warfarin to a DOAC, and frailty-specific data to define optimal anticoagulation remain lacking [S:47b03f4b-72cc-5e6e-bc38-2fa232636404][S:806fb643-7013-53fe-922f-994b89a5f728].

**Context for why AF + HFpEF is high-risk at baseline:** concomitant AF and HF carries about a five-fold higher stroke risk than neither condition, and CHA2DS2-VASc discrimination degrades in patients with both, supporting the case for additional stratifiers such as frailty [S:b13ed0ad-047f-5979-98d7-3d8f68fcb1d7].

**Bottom line:** the AF+HFpEF-specific evidence rests essentially on one post hoc TOPCAT analysis — graded frailty burden predicts stroke steeply and linearly there — and this is directionally corroborated by larger AF trial and registry data, but no source I found establishes that adding frailty to CHA2DS2-VASc improves discrimination prospectively, nor that stroke-subtype-specific (ischemic) risk is what frailty is tracking in HFpEF.

rows.question: How does the timing of anticoagulation initiation after atrial fibrillation-related acute ischemic stroke relate to clinical outcomes?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Starting anticoagulation early after an atrial fibrillation-related ischemic stroke is associated with fewer recurrent ischemic strokes than later initiation, with odds roughly a quarter lower; Safety and mortality outcomes, namely intracranial hemorrhage, other bleeding, death, transient ischemic attack and thrombosis, showed no detectable difference between early and later initiation; The comparison rests mostly on non-randomised studies in which timing was chosen by clinicians rather than assigned. Certainty: The recurrence finding points in a consistent direction across the available evidence, but that evidence comes largely from comparisons in which timing was not assigned, early and late were defined differently from study to study, and the pooled estimates were notably heterogeneous, leaving a moderately supported association rather than a demonstrated effect. Scope: applies to acute ischemic stroke associated with atrial fibrillation in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents a specific severity-independent starting day as established for all patients, including those with large or severe infarcts, or recommends that timing protocol on this basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: across four randomized trials and their pooled individual-participant analysis, starting a DOAC early (within ~4 days, or within 48 h for minor/moderate strokes) after AF-related ischemic stroke does not increase symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and reduces early recurrent ischemic stroke, so delay is no longer supported for most patients.**

**Randomized trials individually showed non-inferiority, not harm**
- **TIMING** (Swedish registry-based, 888 patients, median NIHSS 4) randomized early (≤4 days) vs delayed (5–10 days) NOAC. The 90-day composite of ischemic stroke, symptomatic ICH, or all-cause death occurred in 6.9% vs 8.7% ([passage text removed]%; p for non-inferiority = 0.004); ischemic stroke 3.11% vs 4.57%, mortality 4.67% vs 5.71%, and **no patient in either arm had symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage** (Oldgren et al., Circulation 2022;146:1056–66; PMC9648987).
- **ELAN** (2,013 patients, timing stratified by imaging infarct size) compared early (<48 h for minor/moderate; day 6–7 for major) vs later (day 3–4 / 6–7 / 12–14) DOAC start. The 30-day composite ([passage text removed] ICH, vascular death) occurred in 29/1,006 (2.9%) vs 41/1,007 (4.1%), [passage text removed]); recurrent ischemic stroke 1.4% vs 2.5% at 30 days and 1.9% vs 3.1% at 90 days; symptomatic ICH [passage text removed]** arms (Fischer et al., NEJM 2023;388:2411–21; [passage text removed]; https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/992411). The trial was designed to estimate, not formally test, treatment effects.
- **OPTIMAS** (3,648 randomized; 3,621 analyzed; UK, stroke severity by NIHSS rather than infarct size) compared ≤4 days vs 7–14 days. The 90-day composite (recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic ICH, unclassifiable stroke, systemic embolism) occurred in 59/1,814 (3.3%) vs 59/1,807 (3.3%); [passage text removed]), p non-inferiority = 0.0003, p superiority = 0.96. Symptomatic ICH occurred in 23/3,621 (0.6%) overall with no difference by timing, and there was no effect modification by stroke severity, reperfusion treatment, or prior anticoagulation (Werring et al., Lancet 2024;404:1731–41; [passage text removed]).
- **START** (200 patients, Texas, Bayesian response-adaptive design comparing day 3–4 vs 6 vs 10 vs 14) found the day 3–4 group had the highest posterior probability of being optimal (0.41 vs 0.26, 0.17, 0.15), with no ischemic events in the day 3–4 group; an exploratory analysis gave a posterior probability >0.99 that starting on day 3–4 was superior for preventing ischemic events by day 30 (Warach et al., JAMA Neurol 2025;82:470–6; https://www.hmpgloballearningnetwork.com/site/neuro/news/after-stroke-atrial-fibrillation-earlier-oral-anticoagulant-initiation-appears).

**Pooled data show a net benefit of early initiation**
The prospective individual-participant meta-analysis (**CATALYST**, pooling TIMING, ELAN, OPTIMAS, START; 5,441 participants, mean age 77.7 years, median NIHSS 5 [IQR 3–10]) compared DOAC start ≤4 days vs ≥5 days. The 30-day [passage text removed] occurred in 57/2,683 (2.1%) early vs 83/2,746 (3.0%) [passage text removed]), driven by fewer recurrent ischemic strokes (45 [1.7%] vs 70 [[passage text removed]), with identical symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage rates (10 [0.4%] vs 10 [0.4%]; OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.43–2.46, p=0.96) and no difference in major extracranial bleeding. No interaction was detected with stroke severity, prior anticoagulation, or reperfusion treatment, and 1,326/5,441 (24.4%) had NIHSS >10 (Dehbi et al., Lancet 2025; PMID 40570866; [passage text removed]; ACC summary reports a number needed to treat of 108). The benefit was concentrated in the first 30 days; the difference was no longer statistically significant at 90 days, consistent with the acute phase being the highest-risk window ([passage text removed]).

**Where caution still applies**
- In an ELAN subanalysis by infarct size, all size strata had numerically fewer primary events with early treatment, and the effect was not modified by infarct size, including major stroke (Goeldlin et al., JAMA Neurol 2024; PMC11134281; unadjusted risk differences −0.33% minor, −0.73% moderate, −3.34% major).
- The ELAN hemorrhagic-transformation subanalysis found low symptomatic ICH risk with early treatment overall, but a higher risk of poor 90-day functional outcome among participants with **parenchymal hemorrhage** who started early (Rohner et al., Circulation 2024; [passage text removed]; PMID 38753452) — ELAN excluded confluent parenchymal hematoma within the infarct and OPTIMAS excluded parenchymal hematoma type 2, so these patients remain under-represented.
- Very severe strokes are sparsely represented (~3% of OPTIMAS had NIHSS >21), and OPTIMAS/ELAN did not test superiority successfully on their own ([passage text removed]).
- One observational/mixed meta-analysis found no significant difference between early and delayed DOAC initiation for composite or secondary endpoints, with a non-significant ICH signal in patients with NIHSS ≥5, concluding early initiation is safe but not clearly protective against early recurrence (J Stroke Cerebrovasc Dis 2025; [passage text removed]).

**Practice implications**
A GRADE-based expert recommendation now advises early DOAC initiation within 4 days for minor-to-moderate stroke and states early over delayed initiation is indicated in severe acute ischemic stroke (PMID 41591595; PMC13146428). The OPTIMAS investigators similarly concluded [passage text removed]," moving practice away from the older 1-3-6-12-day delay heuristic ([passage text removed]). Note all of this evidence concerns DOACs; randomized data on vitamin K antagonist timing in this acute setting were not identified in my searches.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Across four randomized trials and their pooled individual-participant meta-analysis, starting a DOAC early (within ~4 days) after AF-related acute ischemic stroke is at least as safe as waiting 7–14 days, and modestly reduces early recurrent stroke — so timing matters mainly in that delay appears to forfeit benefit rather than to protect against hemorrhage. [S:183c2384-3825-50fd-a8c8-61fc571b0d3a][S:76436b6f-c5ab-53d0-99ad-3b4e00d8d1ae]

## Randomized trial evidence

- **TIMING** (n=888, registry-based, Swedish): early (≤4 days) vs delayed (5–10 days) DOAC; 90-day [passage text removed] death occurred in 6.89% vs 8.68% ([passage text removed]%, p-noninferiority = 0.004), with no symptomatic ICH observed. [S:f50693bc-a53f-5761-aca0-7062c95eb157]
- **ELAN** (imaging-stratified: early ≤48 h for minor/moderate, days 6–7 for major stroke, vs later days 3–4 to 12–14): the 30-day composite [passage text removed] ICH, or vascular death was estimated 1.2% lower with early treatment (range 2.8% lower to 0.5% higher) — no formal hypothesis test. [S:7929d67d-d972-5163-a9e7-d49f6b4f7ad4] Recurrent ischemic stroke by 30 days: 14 (1.4%) early vs 25 (2.5%) later ([passage text removed] ICH occurred in 2 patients (0.2%) in each group. [S:2f0dce40-6e44-5652-a79b-6fa7ed5a1e48]
- **OPTIMAS** (n=3621, 100 UK hospitals, early ≤4 days vs delayed 7–14 days): the 90-day composite (recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic ICH, unclassifiable stroke, systemic embolism) met non-inferiority ([passage text removed]; p-noninferiority = 0.0003) with no superiority (p=0.96); symptomatic ICH 0.6% early vs 0.7% delayed. [S:e47c42c1-9df6-539c-b09c-b0b1f2f4c2c4][S:ca3d53ea-96b7-5bfb-872b-5336a21fd2e5]

## Pooled evidence

**CATALYST**, a prospective individual-participant-data meta-analysis of TIMING, ELAN, OPTIMAS and START (5411 patients), found early initiation (≤4 days) superior to later (≥5 days) for the 30-day [passage text removed] unclassified stroke: [passage text removed] symptomatic ICH low and similar (0.45% vs 0.40%). [S:76436b6f-c5ab-53d0-99ad-3b4e00d8d1ae] Importantly, **the benefit was concentrated early**: at 90 days the difference was numerically favorable but not statistically significant. [S:76436b6f-c5ab-53d0-99ad-3b4e00d8d1ae][S:96b30383-0595-5d49-b2bb-de0b147362fd]

A conventional meta-analysis of 17 studies (RCTs plus observational, 17,380 patients) similarly found lower recurrent ischemic stroke with early [passage text removed]) and no difference in ICH (OR 0.74, 0.41–1.33), major bleeding (OR 1.48, 0.51–4.30), systemic embolism, or all-cause mortality (OR 1.00, 0.72–1.39). [S:35574e4a-8b87-5096-aa6d-7207e1d4acc5]

A post hoc weighted net-clinical-benefit analysis of ELAN (1966 participants) estimated ~1.7 weighted events prevented per 100 persons at 30 days (NNT 58) and ~2.1 at 90 days (NNT 47), though confidence intervals did not exclude no benefit or small net harm. [S:aa558b7b-70c9-5c7f-b97e-e34ef58d5d82][S:59423a62-f916-5311-b686-2c3c31d11e18]

## Subgroups and longer term

- **Infarct size/location did not modify the effect** in a prespecified OPTIMAS analysis; among large infarcts (>25 mL) symptomatic ICH was 3/238 (1.3%) early vs 5/239 (2.1%) delayed, and no interaction was seen by ELAN visual classification (p=0.603) or arterial territory (p=0.575). The authors concluded there is no evidence to delay [passage text removed]. [S:3aab72fa-5590-5836-ac49-ea1a0fa4307d][S:f74503e9-419e-54c9-a25d-023dca8c2545][S:3177501a-3da0-528d-afd8-96a9ea408c55]
- **Chronic kidney disease** did not modify the effect in OPTIMAS (3601 patients; OR 1.01 [0.67–1.51] normal kidney function vs 0.90 [0.36–2.25] CKD, p-interaction 0.822). [S:30b30c51-8bcc-55dc-8db7-7e83e7adf545]
- **At 1 year**, TIMING showed a 365-day composite (ischemic stroke, symptomatic ICH, or death) of 14.2% early vs 15.1% delayed (HR [passage text removed]); the concurrent Swedish registry cohort (n=8951) favored early initiation (18.4% vs 22.4%; adjusted HR 0.80, 0.69–0.91), with no excess symptomatic ICH. [S:8fac16d6-297f-534f-a442-46f5f64d6c6d]

## Caveats

The [passage text removed] hematoma) and very severe deficits (e.g., NIHSS >20), so conclusions apply mainly to minor-to-moderate stroke and to severe stroke without radiographic hemorrhagic transformation; a GRADE-based meta-analysis issued a strong recommendation for early DOAC in minor-to-moderate stroke but only a weak one for severe stroke. [S:e348770d-0d52-5fca-b1a0-da1358759d54] Post-thrombectomy patients remain less well characterized: one prospective registry of 234 AF patients treated with EVT reported that *earlier* time from EVT to anticoagulation was an independent risk factor for symptomatic ICH (p=0.043), any [passage text removed]), while longer delay was associated with unfavorable functional outcome (p=0.033), suggesting an optimal window around 4.5 days in that setting. [S:2bd4e936-24a8-506b-b384-b704ed5c04d0] Older guidelines recommending graded delays (e.g., 1-3-6-12 or 7–14 days) predate these trials. [S:cdeda8a9-d65b-546f-a1e2-220b006d7678][S:aef22585-bb8c-5012-b068-2a069582f12e]

rows.question: How do different preservation strategies in donation after circulatory death heart transplantation relate to post-transplant graft outcomes?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: In-situ normothermic regional perfusion recovery of donation after circulatory death hearts was accompanied by acceptable short- and mid-term post-transplant survival; Longer durations of ex-vivo perfusion are associated with worse post-transplant survival after donation after circulatory death heart transplantation; Beating-heart transplantation, an approach that limits ischaemic exposure, was accompanied by preserved early graft function in uncontrolled observational experience. Certainty: Support comes from uncontrolled clinical experience without comparator groups and from an association described without accompanying effect estimates, so links between preservation approach and graft outcome remain provisional and hypothesis-generating. Scope: applies to heart transplantation using donation after circulatory death donors in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents in-situ normothermic regional perfusion as demonstrated to give better graft outcomes than direct procurement, or recommends it as the standard preservation strategy on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Across current evidence, no preservation strategy has been shown to compromise medium-term survival relative to donation after brain death (DBD), and differences between the two dominant donation-after-circulatory-death (DCD) strategies — direct procurement with ex situ machine perfusion (DPP) versus in situ thoracoabdominal normothermic regional perfusion (TA-NRP, usually followed by cold storage) — are concentrated in **early graft dysfunction and early mortality**, not late graft survival; ischemic-interval duration and center experience appear to matter at least as much as the modality itself.

## Survival: broadly equivalent, with an early-phase signal favoring NRP

- Registry analyses defining strategy by death-to-cross-clamp interval find equivalence: in OPTN data (792 DCD of 11,625 transplants), adjusted 1-year and 3-year survival were similar for DBD vs [passage text removed]), with similar stroke, dialysis, rejection and PGD rates ([[passage text removed]]). An SRTR cohort of 13,558 transplants (474 TA-NRP, 899 DPP, 12,185 DBD) found no difference in 2-year graft loss (aHR 0.98 TA-NRP vs DBD; 1.04 TA-NRP vs DPP; 0.94 DPP vs DBD) and unadjusted graft/patient survival curves that did not separate (p=0.47 and p=0.49) ([[passage text removed]]). A propensity-matched two-center comparison of 318 DCD transplants showed 1-year survival 93.1% (NRP) vs 91.1% (DPP), p=0.79 ([[passage text removed]]).
- Other UNOS analyses favor NRP early. In 918 DCD recipients (296 NRP, 622 DPP), NRP was independently associated with better [passage text removed]; 30-day 98.6% vs 96.0%; 1-year 95.2% vs 90.1%), with a lower discard rate (1.4% vs 9.6%) ([S:https://scholars.duke.edu/individual/pub1640574], [[passage text removed]]). The largest contemporary matched analysis (2,831 DCD recipients; 939 matched pairs) found lower survival after DPP [passage text removed]%), 1 year (90% vs 92%) [passage text removed]%) — but survival *conditional on surviving the first month* was identical (94.0% at 1 year in both), localizing the penalty to the perioperative period ([S:https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42595217]).
- A meta-analysis of 10 studies found pooled 30-day survival essentially identical (NRP 96.9% vs [passage text removed]]).

## Primary graft dysfunction: the main discriminating outcome

- DCD in general carries more early dysfunction than DBD: in the randomized OCS DCD trial, severe ISHLT PGD was 15% with circulatory-death hearts vs 5% with brain-death hearts, despite noninferior risk-adjusted 6-month survival ([S:https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2212438], [[passage text removed]]). UNOS data show severe LV/biventricular PGD at 24 h of 9.5% (DCD) vs 5.1% (DBD), converging by 72 h ([[passage text removed]]).
- Between strategies the evidence conflicts. The largest international multicenter series (504 DCD transplants, 20 centers) reported markedly less severe PGD with taNRP ([passage text removed]) and less biopsy-proven acute cellular rejection at 1 year (13% vs 25%, p<0.001), with similar 1-year survival (91% vs 88%, p=0.100); functional *total* ischemic time was much shorter with taNRP (median 15 vs 39 min), and taNRP was associated with less post-transplant mechanical support ([passage text removed]) ([S:https://www.jacc.org/[passage text removed]]).
- US registry data do not reproduce this: severe PGD at 24 h was 9.4% (DPP) vs 9.7% (NRP), p=0.93 ([[passage text removed]]); a larger UNOS series (839 NRP, 1,867 DPP) likewise found no PGD difference (10.1% vs 10.3%) or dialysis difference, yet lower in-hospital (2.4% vs 5.4%) and 30-day mortality (1.7% vs 3.4%) with NRP ([[passage text removed]]). Pooled weighted PGD estimates were 20.5% (DPP) vs 14.4% (NRP), but too few comparative studies existed to meta-analyze ([[passage text removed]]). A single-center study found NRP allografts carried higher adjusted PGD risk than DBD (22% vs 13% unadjusted; [passage text removed]), while 30-day/1-year/3-year mortality, LVEF and renal outcomes were no different ([[passage text removed]]).

## Ischemic intervals and adjunct preservation modify outcomes within a strategy

- Within NRP programs, warm ischemic interval — not the modality label — predicts dysfunction: >23 minutes of functional warm ischemia (oxygen-saturation-based) was associated with increased [passage text removed]]).
- NRP followed by controlled hypothermic cold storage (rather than ex situ normothermic perfusion) appears feasible: 27 GUARDIAN-registry DCD cases with average total ischemic time 3.6 h had severe PGD in 2 recipients (7.4%) and 100% in-hospital survival — small, uncontrolled numbers ([[passage text removed]]).
- Hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (HOPE) is emerging for both DPP and post-NRP preservation. In a porcine DCD transplant model, HOPE after either NRP or direct procurement gave better biventricular contractility, lower inotrope requirement and less troponin release than NRP + [passage text removed]]). Clinical experience is still first-in-series: five DPP-HOPE transplants in the first North American report, with "acceptable" early outcomes ([[passage text removed]]).
- Independent of technique, cumulative DCD program volume predicted 1-year survival (89.0% low-volume vs 92.9% high-volume, p=0.025; plateau after ~20 cases), and NRP vs DPP survival was statistically similar within every volume stratum ([[passage text removed]]).

## Interpretive caveats

Nearly all comparative data are retrospective. US registry studies infer strategy from death-to-cross-clamp intervals with inconsistent cutoffs (≤20, ≤30, or <30 vs >40 min), which misclassifies cases ([[passage text removed]], [S:https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42595217], [[passage text removed]]); donor and recipient selection differs systematically by strategy (e.g., TA-NRP recipients were less often status 1 and less often on inotropes) ([[passage text removed]]). The Louca investigators themselves state a randomized trial is needed to definitively compare taNRP and [passage text removed]]). I found no head-to-head randomized data on NRP vs DPP, nor clinical outcome data comparing 10 °C storage or "reanimation-less" preservation against standard DCD strategies beyond case reports ([[passage text removed]/S1053249825022764]).
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Across strategies, recipient survival after DCD heart transplantation is broadly equivalent to donation after brain death (DBD), so the main measurable differences between preservation approaches lie in early graft function — primary graft dysfunction (PGD), mechanical support need — and in how much ischemic/perfusion time is accrued, rather than in mid-term survival [S:dbf475fb-1073-56ac-b5a0-07bafeb2f71c].

## The strategies being compared

Three clinical pathways dominate: direct procurement followed by ex-situ normothermic machine perfusion (DP-NMP), thoracoabdominal normothermic regional perfusion followed by NMP (NRP-NMP), and NRP followed by static cold storage (NRP-SCS) [S:9d56d30b-f5ae-56f1-ac0e-188a8ca561b0]. Direct procurement forgoes in-situ functional assessment and relies on the ex-vivo platform; NRP reanimates and evaluates the heart in situ before cardiectomy [S:ce0c5d55-f4d8-558d-a4c1-42fbb3220b3c][S:e1656ab7-0b8c-54a0-99c7-d1c9f2adf0c0].

## NRP versus direct procurement

- **Largely equivalent survival.** A systematic review/meta-analysis of 10 studies (923 DCD, 7,236 DBD recipients) found 30-day survival similar between NRP (96.9%) and [passage text removed]), with 12-month survival 93% for DCD vs 91% for DBD and comparable acute rejection (15% vs 19%) [S:6fa3756b-4309-5803-b108-8e7df030163b]. A UNOS analysis reported similar severe PGD rates between TA-NRP and DPP (9.4% vs 9.7%) [S:56d5b426-9e0c-502e-9d64-df04b7ca6235]. In pediatric UNOS data, 1-year survival did not differ (NRP 87.0% vs DPP 78.0%, P=0.40; [passage text removed]) [S:ab1ea15b-d5aa-5594-a7f5-58cbfb7c5a2c].
- **Signals favoring NRP early.** A UNOS study of 842 adult DCD transplants found NRP associated with [passage text removed] donors ≥40 y; 2.3% vs 6.8% in donors <40 y; overall P=0.004) and lower 1-year mortality (P=0.042), without a significant overall-survival difference [S:b795415b-6f28-5cbe-961d-70b9fe5c6fe4][S:e47270e2-1b6e-5d15-9e0f-93d7b6e5f61a]. The authors attribute this to in-situ recovery avoiding ex-vivo circuit-related inflammation and senescence signaling, while cautioning that no head-to-head mechanistic comparison exists [S:beeef5b3-acc1-5eb9-8646-285fa58a46a3]. Other registry work (Ran et al.) found equivalent 1-year survival, whereas Benkert et al. reported improved survival with NRP ([passage text removed]) — i.e., the literature is genuinely discordant [S:98183d93-d462-5fd8-8b67-6c63e3a221c4][S:6ab6a6df-cf4c-5787-ba8d-40d25cb67ff6].
- **NRP + SCS performs well.** In a 15-centre international series of 157 taNRP DCD hearts (mostly cold-stored), transplant activity rose 23% and survival was similar to 673 DBD controls: 30-day 96.8%, 1-year 93.2%, 5-year 84.3% [S:36992553-b5c6-5882-822c-d1984478169b]. Functional assessment during NRP shows LVEF is not significantly degraded by the warm ischemic interval [S:5574dfe0-4f86-5fec-ab31-18bafa38a050].

## Ex-vivo perfusion: dose of perfusion matters

- **PGD is the strategy-sensitive outcome, and it is modifiable by experience.** The Sydney DP-NMP program's initial cohort had 35% severe PGD requiring mechanical support, falling to 8% in a contemporary cohort and 7% since 2021, with no significant difference in 8-year survival versus DBD [S:282e1614-05eb-5507-86f8-b6f6cb4d3b0c][S:56d5b426-9e0c-502e-9d64-df04b7ca6235].
- **Longer perfusion is worse.** Registry analyses link extended ex-vivo perfusion duration in DCD hearts to worse post-transplant survival, while OCS registry data show normothermic pulsatile perfusion is safe within appropriate ischemic limits [S:6108b3b6-26e1-51af-b2b4-aa2445d5ca59]. Perfusion beyond roughly 8 hours (>90th percentile) has been associated with higher mortality, declining contractility, and more renal failure/dialysis [S:26cbdafa-9bdb-5cff-a095-1b53bff181ac].
- **Machine perfusion is not a rescue once PGD occurs.** In a UNOS PGD analysis, ex-vivo machine perfusion conferred no survival benefit over cold static storage among DCD [passage text removed].622) or 72 h (P=0.851), and NRP+machine perfusion was not protective (24-h HR 1.87, P=0.569) [S:673dc982-3a55-56ed-966e-3038b4cdbc12][S:25b4b181-9566-579f-8128-b3390bef099a]. Overall DCD and DBD survival was comparable at 30 days and 1 year, though DCD recipients more often required ECMO and IABP at 72 h [S:0af537ec-10e2-50b2-868a-49fee7ec1c6a].

## Warm and cold ischemia

Functional warm ischemic time is the dominant injury variable; injury scales with its duration and exceeding ~30 minutes is reported to raise severe PGD and early graft failure risk [S:a3e57eb3-b216-570c-9a07-075c0ddc4e2f]. Techniques have evolved to reduce cold ischemic exposure of directly procured hearts, though controlled cold ischemia appears tolerable [S:dbf475fb-1073-56ac-b5a0-07bafeb2f71c].

## Emerging strategies

- **Hypothermic machine perfusion (HMP).** In BDD hearts, a European RCT showed HMP reduces PGD versus SCS, and an Australian unit reported mean preservation >6 h with 5% severe PGD [S:2aa1c79a-f0f8-59cf-869f-15ddb623181a]; a single-centre comparison found moderate-to-severe PGD in 33% with X-Vivo vs 79% with cold storage (P=0.02) and severe PGD 17% vs 64% (P=0.014) [S:ef9e88e0-b976-5953-a494-69c269d26fcc]. Extending HMP to DCD is considered feasible after NRP (viability already established) but of less certain role after direct procurement [S:2aa1c79a-f0f8-59cf-869f-15ddb623181a]. In a mixed Australian cohort, DCD-NMP, BDD-HMP and BDD-SCS had comparable 30-day/1-/2-year survival (P=0.9) [S:71c8b1fe-1653-5a2c-8b7a-6d62ceaf234f].
- **Beating-heart / ischemia-free implantation.** A series of 10 consecutive DCD beating-heart transplants reported 100% survival with no postoperative ECMO or other mechanical support, attributed to eliminating the second ischemia-reperfusion insult [S:63df6af0-4f2b-5424-bb9e-c4916a87c74f][S:d53cb6f2-be97-5a5c-81df-60be6143d65d].

## Trade-offs beyond the heart

NRP gave the lowest liver discard rate versus DP-MP (7.4% vs 18.5%) in simultaneous thoracoabdominal DCD donors, with equivalent patient and superior graft survival versus abdominal-only DCD [S:b0950902-f27c-5712-b284-3165ff121c79]. Direct costs were numerically lower for TA-NRP than DP-NMP ($155,955 vs $223,399; P=0.21), partly reflecting longer DP-NMP length of stay [S:f2edff02-fede-5399-80a3-f1f5bf5ab88c][S:f07d4f18-50e8-50e0-ac35-5bbfc09227ca]. NRP remains ethically contested over possible cerebral perfusion [S:3a0ec834-6e42-53fa-96ab-c8adaaecde0c][S:56d5b426-9e0c-502e-9d64-df04b7ca6235].

## Caveat

Nearly all NRP-versus-DPP comparisons are retrospective/registry-based with confounding by donor selection and centre practice, and protocols vary widely (warm ischemia limits, perfusion-time thresholds), so standardization — not a definitive winner — is the current state of evidence [S:6108b3b6-26e1-51af-b2b4-aa2445d5ca59][S:beeef5b3-acc1-5eb9-8646-285fa58a46a3]. I found no randomized trial directly comparing NRP with direct procurement.
