rows.question: What outcomes follow aortic valve repair or valve-sparing root replacement for aortic regurgitation?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Freedom from reoperation exceeded 80% at both 10 and 15 years after aortic valve repair or valve-sparing root replacement; Long-term survival after these valve-preserving procedures was high, supporting the durability of repair (survival reported qualitatively, without a fixed-timepoint figure); Repair with a concomitant root procedure was associated with lower long-term mortality and fewer reoperations than isolated valve repair, a direction that persisted after adjustment for age, sex, dissection status and valve phenotype; The supporting outcome data are observational and drawn predominantly from specialised centres, with high between-study variation in the pooled estimates. Certainty: The underlying estimates come from aggregated clinical experience in which treatment was not assigned by investigators and no comparison group was constructed, and they differ substantially across the contributing data sources. Scope: applies to aortic regurgitation treated with aortic valve repair or valve-sparing root replacement in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents valve repair as demonstrated to give better long-term survival or fewer reinterventions than valve replacement, or recommends repair over replacement on this basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** In experienced centres, aortic valve repair and valve-sparing root replacement (VSRR) for aortic regurgitation (AR) carry low operative mortality, restore survival close to that of the matched general population, and give ~85–95% freedom from valve reoperation at 10 years — but the trade-off is a persistent late hazard of recurrent AR/reintervention that is highest for isolated cusp repair without annular stabilisation and for cusp patch repair.

**Early outcomes**
- In the international AVIATOR surgical registry (58 centres, 17 countries; 4,896 patients, 89% repair vs 11% replacement), in-hospital mortality after repair was 0.5% for isolated valve repair, 1.7% with tubular/partial root replacement and 1.2% with VSRR, versus 1%, 2.6% and 2.0% for the corresponding replacement strategies ([[passage text removed])).
- A meta-analysis of 44 studies / 7,878 VSRR-reimplantation patients found pooled early mortality 1.6% (95% CI 1.24–1.96), early stroke 1.0%, and re-exploration for bleeding as the commonest complication (5.4%) ([PMC10248907]([passage text removed]); PubMed 37304702).

**Survival and durability**
- Same meta-analysis: overall survival 99% at 1 year and 89% at 10 years; freedom from aortic valve reoperation 99% at 1 year and 91% at 10 years, with **no difference between tricuspid and bicuspid valves**. Late linearized rates were low: reintervention 0.74%/patient-year, endocarditis 0.23%/patient-year, stroke 0.27%/patient-year, bleeding 0.17%/patient-year ([PMC10248907]([passage text removed])).
- Toronto 20-year experience (David): overall survival [passage text removed], with freedom from aortic valve reoperation 97.1%, 94.2% and 94.2%; only 7 of the cohort were reoperated (6 for AR, 1 for endocarditis), and increasing age was the sole predictor of death ([annalscts.com/article/view/1396/html]([passage text removed]); PMC3741814).
- Heart Valve Society database analysis (Zito et al., EJCTS 2025;67(3):ezaf020): **10-year survival was comparable to the matched general population in every technique group**, but 10-year cumulative reintervention differed markedly — 19.5% for isolated valve repair, 13.8% with ascending replacement + repair, 12.7% with partial root replacement, and 8.5% for VSRR ± repair (p<0.001) ([PubMed 39871613](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39871613)).
- Isolated severe AR in tricuspid valves (Brussels, 127 patients): 10- and 14-year survival 81%±5% and 71%±6%, freedom from reoperation 80%±5% and 73%±6%, freedom from recurrent AR >2+ 73%±5% at 10 years — annuloplasty type had no impact; cusp pathology severity was the main determinant ([sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022522321006127]([passage text removed])).
- Bicuspid valves: a Cleveland Clinic series of 728 BAV repairs reported 10-year freedom from AV reoperation 78% and survival 94% with hospital mortality 0.41%, improving to 91% freedom from reoperation for isolated BAV repair in the later era (Ann Thorac Surg 2014;97:1539-1548); a broader series of 1,009 repairs showed 90% freedom from reoperation and 83% survival at 10 years (Ann Thorac Surg 2018;105:739-748), both summarised at [consultqd.clevelandclinic.org]([passage text removed]). A multicentre BAV reimplantation study (498 patients) reported freedom from reintervention 99.1% at 1 year, 95.4% at 5 years and 89.2% at 10 years, with cusp fenestrations, prolapse and isolated AI as risk factors ([ctsnet.org, citing Arabkhani et al., J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg 2025](https://www.ctsnet.org/article-video/redo-aortic-root-surgery-david-procedure-patient-previous-type-dissection-surgery)).

**Versus replacement**
- German Aortic Valve Registry (2,327 AR patients undergoing repair/valve-sparing root surgery vs 40,541 replacements, propensity-weighted): 1-year survival 97.7% (97.1–98.3) after repair vs 96.6% (95.8–97.0) after replacement (p=0.045); repair was independently protective ([passage text removed]) and associated with better patient-reported outcomes; AV reintervention at 1 year was 1.6% after repair vs 1.5% after replacement ([dgk.org abstract 1375](https://dgk.org/kongress_programme/jt2022/aP1848.html); published as Girdauskas et al., Ann Thorac Surg 2024, PubMed 37625612).
- AVIATOR 3-year analysis: repair was associated with better mid-term survival than replacement, aortic dimensions were stable and comparable between groups, but AR ≥ grade 2 at discharge was more common after repair and was significantly associated with increased reintervention risk ([journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/30494826241300881](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/30494826241300881)).

**What drives failure**
- Residual/recurrent AR is the dominant failure mode. Independent predictors of recurrent AR >2+ in one single-centre series were [passage text removed]) and effective height <[passage text removed]) ([PMC6852722](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6852722)).
- In the HVS database, severe preoperative AR (HR [passage text removed]) and larger LV end-diastolic diameter (HR 1.03) predicted reintervention after VSRR, and **patch use predicted reintervention in all groups** ([PubMed 39871613](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39871613)).
- Morphological causes of failure after reimplantation are cusp prolapse and low commissural height early, and cusp retraction later; reoperation within the first 6 months often permits re-sparing, beyond that valve replacement is usually needed (5-year survival after reoperation 86%±13%) ([sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022522312003303]([passage text removed])).
- Annular stabilisation matters: phenotype-adapted BAV repair with systematic annuloplasty achieved 98–100% freedom from valve-related re-intervention at 8 years, versus ~[passage text removed] ([PMC13533058]([passage text removed])).

**Ventricular recovery**
- LVEF after repair/sparing procedures initially increased then stabilised over follow-up ([PubMed 39871613](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39871613)). A comparative study of 226 patients (135 repair vs 91 stentless root bioprosthesis) found significant, [passage text removed] in both groups, reaching comparable LV volumes and function at a median ~4 years ([PubMed 25327584](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25327584)).

**Guideline position:** the 2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guidelines give valve-sparing aortic root replacement a Class I, Level B recommendation [passage text removed]** ([2025 ESC/EACTS guideline PDF](https://inavalverhd.inaheart.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/[passage text removed].pdf)).

**Caveats:** results are dominated by high-volume expert centres and retrospective series; the VSRR meta-analysis authors note the evidence is heterogeneous and fragmented, precluding analysis of outcome determinants ([PMC10248907]([passage text removed])). Discordant data exist — a small propensity-matched comparison found higher reoperation for aortic insufficiency after David (4/30) and lower long-term survival than Bentall (76.7% vs 96.7%, p=0.005) ([nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34107-y]([passage text removed])) — and no randomised head-to-head trial of repair versus prosthetic replacement for AR exists ([[passage text removed])).
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

In experienced centers, [passage text removed] (VSRR) carry very low operative mortality, survival that is at least as good as (and in comparative series better than) valve replacement, fewer thromboembolic/bleeding/endocarditis events, and left-ventricular reverse remodeling — at the cost of a slow late attrition from recurrent aortic regurgitation (AR), which is the dominant failure mode and is markedly more common in bicuspid than tricuspid valves.

## Early and late mortality

- A single-center series of 504 consecutive patients (89.7% elective, 10.3% emergency for acute type A dissection) reported estimated 5- and 10-year survival of 83% and 73% overall; 86% and 75% after elective surgery, and 62% at both 5 and 10 years after emergency dissection surgery [S:549be1a6-a9f5-5247-8e14-fa28b7446b54].
- In a David-I cohort of 124 patients, early mortality was 0.8%, with 1-, 3-, 6- and 8-year survival of 99%, 99%, 98% and 87% [S:b6990279-6f91-5496-b17b-4825224eb06e].
- In bicuspid-valve repair specifically, pooled 30-day survival was 0.995 (95% CI 0.991–0.999) [S:56fd139e-7aa8-52b2-b0df-9e84cec12b69].
- Long-running VSRR series report ~69.1% alive without aortic valve reoperation at 20 years (David), 15-year survival of 82.9% (Lille) and 65% (Hannover), and 10-year survival 75% with 1% in-hospital mortality (Brussels) [S:f22fa238-09ab-536f-9577-a01734ce3ae2].

## Durability: reoperation and recurrent AR

- Freedom from reoperation was 96% at 5 years and 87% at 10 years in the 504-patient series, with no difference between elective and dissection subgroups; freedom from ≥moderate AR was confirmed in 86.6% [S:549be1a6-a9f5-5247-8e14-fa28b7446b54].
- David-procedure freedom from reoperation was 99%, 98%, 95% and 91% at 1, 3, 6 and 8 years [S:b6990279-6f91-5496-b17b-4825224eb06e].
- Reoperation is driven by recurrent AR rather than structural prosthesis failure; recurrent AR is the most frequent late complication, valve-related complications are otherwise low, and reporting of AR severity has been inconsistent across studies [S:2faea133-1020-536d-bcd8-fd63697cd30b].
- Even when late AI develops after reimplantation, relatively few valves require reoperation (cumulative 20-year risk of AV reoperation 6%, of moderate/severe AI 10.2% in the David series) [S:f22fa238-09ab-536f-9577-a01734ce3ae2].

## Repair/sparing versus replacement

- AVIATOR registry (2,026 patients; 1,630 repair/sparing vs 396 replacement; mean follow-up 3.8 ± 1.9 years): the composite of death or reintervention occurred in 11.8% after repair vs 25.3% after replacement (log-rank p < 0.001); death 4.5% vs 21.9% (p < 0.001); reintervention was comparable (5.1% vs 8.2%, p = 0.16). Residual AR ≥ grade 2 at discharge was rare but more frequent after repair ([passage text removed]) and independently predicted [passage text removed]:48065713-5a50-535f-ae89-58fef9f71f95] [S:58d84630-bb72-524a-9b5e-8a72f0c16c80]. Note the replacement group had higher baseline risk (EuroSCORE II 3.8 vs 2.4) [S:a1348ae8-0bba-5336-b4bc-dd462eb391b3].
- Propensity-matched AVIATOR root-aneurysm analysis (654 VSRR vs 218 composite valve graft): early mortality 1.1% vs 2.3%; 5-year survival 95.4% vs 85.4% ([passage text removed] 96.8% vs 95.4% (p = 0.98); more thromboembolic, endocarditis and bleeding events after composite grafting (p = 0.02) [S:db9dfcf9-d391-541e-a8bb-291cbe38ba77].
- Counterpoint: a 1,635-patient propensity-matched single-center comparison found no survival difference by operation type and similar aortic valve reoperation (5.8% vs 5.7%), but *more* recurrent moderate/severe AI after valve-sparing (11.1% vs 6.1%) [S:5cbcc745-7143-50d1-ad81-5ef21bb7c184]. A Brazilian 448-patient series similarly found no reoperation difference but better survival, freedom from hemorrhage and freedom from endocarditis with valve-sparing [S:cae160e0-a35d-56a9-aea3-8e54536507ce].
- Repair also avoids lifelong anticoagulation and compares favorably with bioprostheses, whose 10-year freedom from reoperation is limited (78.96% overall; 50.85% in patients <40 years in a cited 3,152-patient cohort) [S:26949b2c-62fd-5495-9cbb-356c5e96b850].

## Valve morphology matters

- Reimplantation for BAV vs TAV: 10-year survival did not differ ([passage text removed]), but freedom from AV reoperation at 10 years was 83.9 ± 7.4% (BAV) vs 100% (TAV), p = 0.002, and freedom from recurrent AR >2+ was 75.7 ± 8.7% vs 90.5 ± 4.1% (p = 0.06) [S:15a584e4-c9ac-5236-a205-95019f57150d].
- Homburg experience: 5-/10-year freedom from reoperation 88%/81% for bicuspid vs 97%/93% for tricuspid valves [S:ee00452e-1b28-5b98-8984-e8a81b50e054]. Pooled BAV repair estimates fall from 93.4% freedom from reintervention [passage text removed], mostly for recurrent regurgitation and cusp prolapse [S:56fd139e-7aa8-52b2-b0df-9e84cec12b69].
- In BAV root aneurysm, reimplantation showed better durability than remodeling (fewer reoperations, less severe recurrent AR) despite similar survival (96.8% vs [passage text removed]) [S:45aadab3-1aec-5371-bf32-b9623ac100a0]. Historical remodeling without annular stabilization had higher late reoperation rates; with suture annuloplasty, 15-year freedom from reoperation was 95% (tricuspid) and 83% (bicuspid) [S:6a628758-212b-59ef-b837-ea5eaf17d49e].
- A modern BAV repair series (206 patients) reported 0% operative mortality, 99.5% survival at mean 5 years, 91.8% freedom from reoperation at 7 years, 5% severe recurrent AR; Sievers type 2 (two raphes) had nearly 4-fold higher reoperation risk, while external circumferential annuloplasty and sinotubular junction remodeling improved longevity [S:f5b2a786-f726-531c-ad60-024230360e65].

## Predictors of failure (modifiable targets)

Intraoperative/discharge echo predictors of recurrent AR include residual AR (even mild), coaptation below the annular plane, coaptation length <4 mm, and enlarged annulus [S:4e134e15-ed41-524a-b174-04de8075a7f5]; effective height <9 mm was an independent predictor, and guidelines cite coaptation length ≥4 mm and effective height ≥9 mm as targets [S:2c75ae9c-811e-5639-8f69-c2031a7ecdc2] [S:fcb29be8-31df-5086-94a9-06a1cf58f7ff]. Annular dilation (≥26–27 mm), residual cusp prolapse, cusp retraction (BAV geometric height <20 mm), commissural asymmetry, and use of patch material are recognized failure predictors with defined mitigating measures [S:8184799a-ec7a-5395-959c-d87adf60691a] [S:41471997-45b4-5ed1-a28e-e9d7a6787dd8]. Preoperative AR grade and LV end-diastolic diameter predicted reintervention after valve-sparing root replacement [S:a1348ae8-0bba-5336-b4bc-dd462eb391b3].

## Special populations

- **Marfan syndrome:** a 56-patient David series had no operative or in-hospital deaths, 100% survival to last follow-up (61 ± 38 months), no endocarditis, and freedom from root reoperation of 100% at 1 year and 97.7% at 8 years [S:f262b3fb-9728-56b6-a1a8-cf21d6d1815e]. In a 223-patient MFS root-replacement cohort, operative death was 4% overall, survival was improved with valve-sparing, but valve-sparing patients tended toward greater valvular-structural deterioration without an apparent survival penalty [S:6a547820-5d3b-5afc-bcf3-a57be875dc0c]. Reoperation for AR after VSRR in Marfan runs about 1.3% per annum, and a prospective multi-institutional study suggested this underestimates true valve-related adverse events [S:ea40f916-663d-5f62-b188-f4c60614d1e7]; one multicenter expert-center analysis reported ~7% cumulative recurrent AI as early as 1 year [S:490ad06d-3713-5e04-bda6-1d2b610c366b].
- **Type A dissection:** valve-sparing reoperative root reconstruction after prior dissection repair gave freedom from >moderate recurrent AR of 86.5% ± 8.9% at 3, 5 and 10 years [S:e94a3266-78d8-5e63-a268-f716a3977dcb]; VSRR in acute dissection is generally reserved for hemodynamically stable patients without malperfusion or major comorbidity [S:f22fa238-09ab-536f-9577-a01734ce3ae2].

## Ventricular and hemodynamic outcomes

LV reverse remodeling follows successful repair: BAV repair produced significant reverse remodeling with normalization of LVEF and LV end-diastolic volume in most patients, driven mainly by absence of significant residual AR rather than by the choice of annular stabilization technique [S:ab3a0e6a-49bc-5642-bcc6-bdde6b552605]; another root-reconstruction/repair series documented a fall in LV end-diastolic diameter ([passage text removed] follow-up and no major residual AR [S:18737716-21b3-5eea-be9a-451f39887ce8]. In the David-I cohort, LVEF increased significantly before discharge (p = 0.038) [S:b6990279-6f91-5496-b17b-4825224eb06e]. In AVIATOR, aortic dimensions were stable over 3 years and similar between repair and replacement [S:fd2a7653-62c4-588f-8d5d-ae8669361be6]. Mean gradients after valve-sparing root surgery were low but higher for bicuspid than tricuspid valves (8.9 vs 5.4 mmHg, p < 0.001) [S:88cd8171-6aba-520f-a886-fa6b2c92595a].

## Caveats

Most of this evidence is single-center and observational, with no randomized comparison against replacement; earlier meta-analytic work noted heterogeneous cohorts, non-standardized AR reporting, scarce long-term survival data, and absence of control groups [S:2faea133-1020-536d-bcd8-fd63697cd30b]. Outcomes are strongly operator- and selection-dependent — the ideal candidate has mobile, symmetric, non-calcified cusps with AR arising from annular or sinotubular dilatation rather than diffuse cusp disease [S:043d0298-00b1-5d6a-a562-a85dce05dc5d], and registry data suggest results are weighted toward the most expert centers [S:251b00a6-7786-5d38-ac64-d74b39159ade].

rows.question: What clinical outcomes follow SGLT2 inhibitor therapy in patients with coexisting heart failure and chronic kidney disease?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: SGLT2 inhibition reduces the primary composite of cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure events in heart failure both with reduced and with higher ejection fraction; SGLT2 inhibition slows the decline in kidney function and reduces progression of chronic kidney disease, including at low eGFR and across levels of albuminuria; Patient-reported heart failure symptom scores improve early and are sustained with SGLT2 inhibition; Genital mycotic infection is more frequent with SGLT2 inhibition, roughly two- to fourfold, and is usually mild. Certainty: The direction of benefit is supported by strong, consistent evidence using hard clinical endpoints in several large patient groups. Scope: applies to coexisting heart failure and chronic kidney disease in adults, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents SGLT2 inhibition as demonstrated to restore or normalise kidney function rather than to slow its decline and reduce progression.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: in patients with both heart failure and CKD, SGLT2 inhibitors reduce cardiovascular death/HF hospitalization, slow eGFR decline and kidney-disease progression, improve symptoms, and reduce all-cause mortality in CKD populations — with benefit preserved down to eGFR ~20 mL/min/1.73 m² and a favorable safety profile; dialysis-dependent patients remain trial-untested.**

**Heart failure outcomes in the CKD subgroup**
- DAPA-HF (HFrEF): in patients with baseline eGFR <60, dapagliflozin reduced CV death or worsening HF ([passage text removed]), a magnitude similar to those [passage text removed] in both strata [[passage text removed]].
- EMPEROR-Reduced prespecified CKD analysis (CKD = eGFR <60 or UACR >300 mg/g): primary composite HR 0.78 (0.65–0.93) with CKD vs 0.72 (0.58–0.90) without (interaction P=0.63); the exploratory kidney composite (sustained profound eGFR decline, chronic dialysis, transplant) fell similarly (HR 0.53, 0.31–0.91 with CKD; 0.46, 0.22–0.99 without) [[passage text removed]].
- HFpEF: 53% of EMPEROR-Preserved participants had prevalent CKD (including ~10% with eGFR 20–29), and the primary-endpoint benefit was consistent "[passage text removed]"; empagliflozin also slowed progression to macroalbuminuria and reduced acute kidney injury regardless of CKD status [S:https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/962847][[passage text removed]].
- Pooled EMPEROR-Reduced + EMPEROR-Preserved (n=9,714) stratified by KDIGO risk: CV death or first HF hospitalization was reduced in all categories (HR 0.81 low-, 0.63 moderate-, 0.82 high-, 0.84 very-high-risk; P trend = 0.30), with slowing of eGFR decline and improved KCCQ clinical summary score at 52 weeks in every category [[passage text removed]].

**Meta-analytic magnitude and gradient by kidney function**
- Across 13 trials (n=90,413), first HF hospitalization/CV death fell 24% in HF populations (HR 0.76, 0.72–0.81) and 23% in CKD populations (HR 0.77, 0.72–0.82), with consistent effects in HF with or without CKD and in patients carrying all three of HF, CKD and type 2 diabetes; CV death fell 16% in HF and 12% in CKD [[passage text removed]].
- The HF benefit is largest at the lowest eGFR: relative risk reductions of 13–32% across eGFR strata, greatest at eGFR <30 (HR 0.68, 0.48–0.96) and smallest at eGFR ≥90 (HR 0.87, 0.56–1.34) [[passage text removed]].
- In CKD patients with eGFR <60 specifically, pooled RCT data show reduced HF hospitalization (RR 0.73, 0.65–0.82), CV death (RR 0.81, 0.74–0.88) and renal composite outcomes (RR 0.70, 0.61–0.80) [S:https://bmcnephrol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12882-024-03833-2].

**Kidney and mortality outcomes**
- DAPA-CKD (eGFR 25–75, albuminuria): primary composite HR 0.61 (0.51–0.72), kidney-specific composite HR 0.56 (0.45–0.68), CV death or HF hospitalization HR 0.71 (0.55–0.92), all-cause death HR 0.69 (0.53–0.88) over median 2.4 years; effects were consistent regardless of baseline cardiovascular/HF history [[passage text removed]]. Benefits persisted in stage 4 CKD (eGFR <30) [[passage text removed]].
- EMPA-KIDNEY reduced kidney-disease progression or CV death by 28%, and CV death or dialysis/transplant by 27% [[passage text removed]].
- SMART-C meta-analysis (10 trials, 70,361 participants [passage text removed]): CKD progression HR 0.62 ([passage text removed] 0.71 even at eGFR <30) or albuminuria; kidney failure HR 0.66 (0.58–0.75) [[passage text removed]].
- The initial eGFR "dip" (roughly 3–6 mL/min/1.73 m²) is expected and, absent other adverse events, is not a reason to stop therapy [[passage text removed]]. In pooled DAPA-HF/DELIVER, 3.2% of patients deteriorated to eGFR <25 at least once; the primary-outcome benefit was retained in that group (HR 0.53, 0.33–0.83) and in those who did not (HR 0.78, 0.72–0.86), with similar safety and discontinuation rates [[passage text removed].08.026].

**Safety**
In CKD with eGFR <60, SGLT2 inhibitors were associated with *lower* rates of serious adverse events (RR 0.91), hypoglycemia (RR 0.91), hyperkalemia (RR 0.68) and acute kidney injury (RR 0.79), with no excess of discontinuation, fracture or urinary tract infection [S:https://bmcnephrol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12882-024-03833-2].

**Where evidence is weaker**
Dialysis/ESKD patients were excluded from the pivotal trials; the only data are observational — a propensity-matched TriNetX cohort of 10,032 patients with HF and ESKD found lower 1-year composite risk (HR 0.80, 0.76–0.84), all-cause mortality (HR 0.69, 0.63–0.76), all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.87, 0.82–0.92) and acute pulmonary edema (HR 0.84, 0.71–0.98), findings the authors call exploratory and requiring randomized confirmation [[passage text removed]]. In a study-level meta-analysis of 11 trials (n=80,928), the kidney composite benefit was significant in CKD and HFrEF subgroups but not in HFpEF or HF-without-diabetes subgroups, which the investigators attribute to possible underpowering [[passage text removed]]. Also note that eGFR-slope effects in HF depend heavily on the slope model used and should be interpreted cautiously [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
**Conclusion:** In patients with coexisting heart failure and CKD, SGLT2 inhibitors consistently reduce cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalization and slow eGFR decline, with benefit preserved down to at least stage 4 CKD; kidney *event* reduction is robust in dedicated CKD trials but weaker/non-significant in HF trials, and mortality benefit is inconsistent.

**Why this population matters.** Roughly 40–50% of HF patients have an [passage text removed], and the combination markedly worsens prognosis; conventional RAS blockade and MRAs are often limited here by hyperkalemia and renal function fluctuation, whereas SGLT2 inhibitors can act as an "enabler" of background therapy [S:1eed221e].

**Heart-failure outcomes are preserved in CKD.**
- DAPA-HF (HFrEF; ~41% with eGFR <60): the composite of worsening HF or CV death was reduced similarly in patients with eGFR <60 (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.59–0.86) and ≥60 (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.63–0.92) [S:bcec82f5-140f-5ef2-8c5a-3536be012a91].
- EMPEROR-Reduced (48% with eGFR <60 [S:aa6d0926-27c7-586f-a78b-0267e57184d2]) reduced CV death or HF hospitalization [passage text removed]) [S:3f714a46-ac0b-5f93-97a7-ff7ca98c50b8], with a significant reduction in worsening renal function and ~30% fewer total HF hospitalizations [S:e9a20a2a-3067-51db-b0e4-1b21779f4d04].
- EMPEROR-Preserved (LVEF >40%; ~50% with eGFR <60) showed [passage text removed] HF hospitalization, driven by a 29% reduction in HF hospitalization, and consistent across CKD presence/absence [S:051661dc-b1ce-508e-a526-10c048349c2f]. Prespecified analyses of DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved found benefit was not modified by baseline kidney function [S:3fc49180-3385-56be-8b69-977d4f4dd311].
- A meta-analysis restricted to stage 3/4 CKD found CV death or HF hospitalization reduced [passage text removed]), with consistency across stage 3a (HR 0.70), 3b (HR 0.77) and stage 4 (HR 0.71); p for interaction 0.71 [S:ba03ab4c-30d9-5a66-964c-9d264f2255e5].

**Kidney outcomes.** A collaborative meta-analysis of ~90,000 participants (CKD, HF, and diabetes trials) found kidney disease progression reduced by 37% (RR [passage text removed] acute kidney injury by 23% (RR 0.77, 0.70–0.84), similar with and without diabetes and across the studied range of kidney function, with safety [passage text removed] [S:1ccba197-21a3-5a22-a1c8-2db0f54e5166][S:30f8433c-7cfc-5d35-a0c5-aa238499a5dc]. eGFR slope improves: −[passage text removed] m²/year with empagliflozin vs placebo in EMPEROR-Preserved [S:051661dc-b1ce-508e-a526-10c048349c2f], and ~1.73 mL/min/1.73 m²/year slower decline in EMPEROR-Reduced regardless of baseline CKD [S:230e7675-adbb-545b-b2cf-08ebe4d495eb]. Importantly, the *hard* kidney composite (≥50% eGFR decline, ESKD, renal death) was **not** significantly reduced in DAPA-HF or DELIVER, where event rates were low [S:da809c3b-91af-5527-be9b-8f94d8e79978][S:bcec82f5-140f-5ef2-8c5a-3536be012a91].

**Evidence from the CKD side.** DAPA-CKD reduced the composite of ≥50% eGFR decline, ESKD, or renal/CV death (9.2% vs 14.5%; HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.51–0.72), with consistent benefit at eGFR <45 and ≥45 [S:740e6008-142e-51eb-998d-f53d9487da49], and remains the only dedicated CKD trial showing lower all-cause mortality [S:2ba55601-5801-5118-b4e8-01ea463d9f0c]. EMPA-KIDNEY reduced its primary composite by 28% ([passage text removed]) and reduced all-cause hospitalization, but did **not** significantly reduce all-cause mortality or the composite of HF hospitalization/CV death; benefit was independent of baseline eGFR (including <30) but confined to UACR >300 mg/g [S:2d4ccde4-421f-5013-9570-060ddb93a13b]. A pooled analysis of DAPA-CKD plus EMPA-KIDNEY showed no benefit on CV death or HF hospitalization in advanced CKD [S:42d0e88c-6b4d-528e-96a4-fab9c3d7c762]. Post-trial follow-up of EMPA-KIDNEY suggests some persistence of cardiorenal benefit, though the acute eGFR dip reverses within about 4 weeks of stopping, and long-term treatment appears needed to maximize benefit [S:fb63cac9-8677-50ab-8333-4c9b6404ca90].

**Symptoms, function, and real-world data.** Trials and reviews report improved quality of life and functional capacity (KCCQ, 6MWT, CPET) and lower NT-proBNP [S:737013f7-42c8-509d-b199-a449f8662fc2][S:b85d3954-bc64-5608-b371-ebff22b0e39c]. In a retrospective HF cohort (LVEF ≤45%), SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with a lower composite of CV death, HF hospitalization, or ≥40% eGFR decline/KRT ([passage text removed]), driven mainly by fewer HF hospitalizations, with slower kidney function decline — hypothesis-generating given the observational design [S:e109a532-fda2-5259-990b-2766237319dd].

**Safety/implementation.** The initial eGFR dip is hemodynamic, not toxic, and does not warrant discontinuation; a reversible fall of up to about 10% is common, whereas declines >30% should prompt evaluation for other causes of AKI [S:61ee578e-359a-5629-8a5c-3bdf01a1f2b3][S:c24e14c7-6ecb-57d1-8ea2-2fee23f677cb]. SGLT2 inhibitors are not associated with increased AKI risk, and in DAPA-CKD combination with diuretics did not increase hypotension or AKI [S:2346d3d5-82d9-5dfa-8ec9-14d912cf377a][S:30c30648-80dd-5535-8453-57e6cdf987f4]. Guidelines give dapagliflozin/empagliflozin a Class 1A recommendation in HFrEF with additional recommendations across the LVEF spectrum [S:6cbfad64-b4fc-573a-bb80-0210d29c61b8]. **Gap:** outcome data in dialysis-dependent patients remain lacking; therapy has conventionally been stopped at dialysis initiation, though the FDA removed dialysis dependency from SGLT2 inhibitor contraindications in 2023 and trials are ongoing [S:65d8ee02-a041-517e-b06b-2f88bf31d0aa].

rows.question: Which factors at renal replacement therapy initiation relate to death before discharge in sepsis-associated acute kidney injury?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: A higher illness severity score (APACHE II) at initiation of renal replacement therapy is associated with higher odds of death before discharge; A higher maximum vasopressor dose at initiation of renal replacement therapy is associated with higher odds of death before discharge; Older age is associated with higher odds of death before discharge, an association apparent when age is grouped above a threshold rather than compared as a continuous variable; A lower serum creatinine at initiation of renal replacement therapy is associated with higher mortality before discharge, whereas a higher creatinine is associated with better survival. Certainty: These are observed associations rather than demonstrated causes, and the cutoff values were derived in the same patients in whom they were tested. Scope: applies to sepsis-associated acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it treats the low-creatinine association as causal and recommends withholding or delaying renal replacement therapy until the serum creatinine rises.

answers.websearch:
**Conclusion:** Death before hospital discharge in sepsis-associated AKI (SA-AKI) treated with RRT tracks with *systemic* illness severity at the moment RRT is started — older age, high severity scores, vasopressor dose/hemodynamic instability, hyperlactatemia, acidemia, oliguria and fluid overload — whereas a *higher* serum creatinine at initiation is paradoxically protective, and the AKI-to-RRT time interval contributes comparatively little.

**Direct SA-AKI–on-RRT cohorts with in-hospital death as the endpoint**

- In a retrospective cohort of 189 adults with concurrent sepsis and AKI requiring RRT, 132 (69.8%) died in hospital; independent predictors were age >60 years ([passage text removed]). ROC-derived cutoffs also flagged SOFA >10, colloid >1,500 mL/72 h, WBC <12, and albumin <2.5 g/dL ([[passage text removed])).
- An externally validated interpretable machine-learning model in SA-AKI patients receiving CRRT (in-hospital mortality >50%) [passage text removed] the top SHAP predictors, outperforming SOFA and SAPS II ([[passage text removed]); [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42309977](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42309977)).
- A MIMIC-IV model for in-hospital death in SA-AKI receiving RRT retained age, MAP, respiratory rate, lactate, creatinine, total bilirubin, PT-INR and CVP; risk rose steeply above lactate 15.89 mmol/L and below MAP 70.84 mmHg, was J-shaped for CVP (nadir ~11.67 mmHg), and linear for age (threshold 64.14 years), RR, Cr, bilirubin and INR ([[passage text removed])).
- In a single-centre MICU cohort of 96 S-AKI patients on CRRT, poor outcome was associated with SAPS II at admission (OR 1.07), need for vasopressors (OR 8.36) and hypoalbuminemia at CRRT initiation; non-survivors had abnormal albumin and troponin I at initiation ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12979951]([passage text removed])).

**Variables measured specifically at initiation**

- Acidemia and organ failure burden: in AKI patients starting CRRT (sepsis the commonest cause), serum creatinine, blood pH, SOFA score and fluid overload were each independently associated with in-hospital mortality (pH HR 0.11, 0.04–0.28; SOFA HR 1.05, 1.01–1.08; fluid overload HR 1.54, 1.19–1.98) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8476311]([passage text removed])).
- Fluid overload >[passage text removed] an 82% increase in the odds of hospital mortality ([ovid.com/00003246-201909000-00025](https://www.ovid.com/00003246-201909000-00025)); in a sepsis-induced AKI–only cohort, %FO before CRRT >4.6% and total %FO >9.6% predicted 28-day death across SOFA and timing subgroups ([nature.com/articles/s41598-023-29926-w]([passage text removed])).
- Lactate at CRRT initiation: in blood-culture-positive septic AKI, lactate at initiation (plus immunosuppression, heart failure history, APACHE II/SAPS II, CRP) was independently associated with mortality; non-survivors had lower pH, bicarbonate, hourly diuresis and MAP and higher lactate and norepinephrine requirement at initiation (AUC 0.84 for ICU death) ([[passage text removed]/journal.pone.0249561]([passage text removed]); [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8021149]([passage text removed])).
- Oliguria and delay: in sepsis-induced AKI on CRRT, oliguria (HR 1.56), SOFA, APACHE II, lactate and the AKI-diagnosis-to-CRRT interval (HR 1.11/day) independently predicted 28-day death ([[passage text removed]/journal.pone.0279561]([passage text removed])).

**Caveats.** The creatinine finding is consistent across cohorts (lower creatinine at initiation → higher death), plausibly reflecting sarcopenia/severe non-renal illness rather than kidney injury severity ([[passage text removed]); [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8476311]([passage text removed])). Timing itself is weak: in a MIMIC-IV/eICU SA-AKI analysis the AKI-to-CRRT interval had the lowest SHAP importance of all features, behind maximum lactate, age, minimum SpO₂ and SOFA ([[passage text removed])), concordant with IDEAL-ICU showing no 90-day mortality difference between early and delayed RRT in septic shock–associated AKI ([[passage text removed])). Several of the supporting studies used 28-day, 90-day or ICU mortality rather than death before discharge, and effect sizes are mostly from single-centre or database cohorts, so they are associations, not causal targets.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Death before hospital discharge in sepsis-associated AKI on RRT is driven mainly by markers of illness severity captured at the moment RRT starts — vasopressor requirement/hemodynamic failure, high severity scores, older age, extrarenal organ failure (liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, hyperlactataemia), oliguria — and, paradoxically, by a *lower* rather than higher serum creatinine at initiation; the timing of initiation itself is not consistently associated with survival.

## Evidence

**Vasopressor requirement, severity score, age, and paradoxically low creatinine.** In a retrospective cohort of 189 medical-ward patients with sepsis-associated AKI requiring RRT, 132 (69.8%) died in hospital; multivariable analysis identified age >60 years ([passage text removed]) [S:9403bc89-5d4e-5d5c-947d-d7a6348a34b4][S:aef7566c-fdd8-5d30-9bc6-f425baab7837]. On univariate analysis, SOFA >10 (OR 3.35), mechanical ventilation (OR 5.22), hydrocortisone use (OR 2.64), CRRT modality (OR 1.97), and albumin ≤2.5 g/dL (OR for albumin >2.5 = 0.49) were also associated with death [S:25a1c11a-f6b5-5086-b9f8-e256cb9789d2]. The authors interpret low creatinine at initiation as reflecting dilution from fluid overload and/or rapidly evolving AKI in which creatinine has not reached steady state, so that non-renal indications drive early dialysis [S:4fd199c1-0b4a-5871-9d99-77462adbc950]. Lower pre-dialysis creatinine tracking with worse outcome has also been attributed to a greater burden of non-renal organ dysfunction at initiation [S:3d473b12-669e-5d5c-9a67-75f9e9a8953e].

**Extrarenal organ failure, lactate and norepinephrine at initiation.** In a prospective cohort of 186 septic AKI patients on CRRT, five variables measured on the day of CRRT initiation were independently associated with early (7-day) death: norepinephrine use, liver failure, medical (vs surgical) condition, lactate, and pre-dialysis creatinine — combined into the HELENICC score (C-statistic 0.82, 0.76–0.88), which outperformed SAPS 3, APACHE II and SOFA [S:a5551127-512e-5835-a925-e48d53171924][S:4c4a3e6b-8d5a-599c-9b6b-36f3d7c730ca]. In the score, creatinine carried a negative weight (points subtracted per unit), again indicating higher creatinine associates with better survival [S:9b8c9ee6-e844-5b6c-90a7-615e57905902]. Note this endpoint was 7-day, not in-hospital, mortality.

**Model-derived predictors of in-hospital death.** In 1,663 MIMIC-IV patients with sepsis-associated AKI receiving RRT, feature selection retained eight variables for predicting in-hospital mortality: age, mean arterial pressure, respiratory rate, lactate, creatinine, PT-INR, total bilirubin and central venous pressure; creatinine ranked as the most important feature, followed by age, lactate, total bilirubin and CVP (LR model AUROC 0.73 training / 0.72 testing) [S:cdabe4c9-575a-5a5e-a7bd-d5689a67c64d][S:5c6db9c9-4512-5ec2-a709-de1fa6b98e40]. In a related CRRT population (cirrhosis + AKI), INR nearest to CRRT initiation (OR 2.82), sepsis (OR 2.68) and vasoactive drug use (OR 7.62) were independently linked to in-hospital death [S:8f1ff581-8035-5530-b713-ef0159ca75ad].

**Oliguria at/around initiation.** Among 165 septic AKI patients on CRRT, [passage text removed], whereas serum creatinine did not differ between survivors and non-survivors in that cohort [S:f7791a45-4035-5763-90c1-3b6af3474030][S:cca0a41e-21ac-5354-9e3e-4e5055f38f59]. In 340 sepsis patients on CRRT, independent predictors of 28-day death were age, APACHE II, RDW, platelet count, serum creatinine (lower = worse) and urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h on the first day (HR 2.71, 1.45–5.06), with septic shock also independent (HR 2.98, 1.70–5.21) [S:26856528-80fd-5cde-a29c-13cb4b2929ed][S:6061ec58-25e6-5248-b666-4259d9602d44]. Low urine output before CRRT initiation has been repeatedly reported as an independent mortality predictor [S:34ed618e-7194-51e3-9299-536015bdfc2f][S:0544bb16-26a1-5263-91af-c12a49b81f67].

**Timing of initiation is not a robust determinant.** In 370 septic AKI patients requiring RRT (70.0% in-hospital mortality), early vs late initiation by sRIFLE was not related to hospital mortality in Cox, propensity-adjusted or matched analyses [S:cf711793-b4f9-5c8e-9a56-305fbe0e7d23]. In an IDEAL-ICU substudy of 488 septic shock patients, the effect of timing differed by AKI diagnostic criterion — early RRT was associated with *higher* 90-day mortality in patients qualifying by creatinine elevation alone (58% vs 42%, p=0.028), with no significant difference in the oliguria-only or combined groups [S:5de6a12f-396e-5c33-8db9-39e07df74c1c]. One CRRT cohort found urine output, not the time of CRRT start, carried the prognostic signal [S:0544bb16-26a1-5263-91af-c12a49b81f67].

## Caveats
Most of this evidence is retrospective/single-centre, and several of the strongest datasets report 7-day or 28-day rather than pre-discharge mortality, so the endpoints are not interchangeable. Generic scores (SAPS 3, APACHE II, SOFA) discriminated poorly in the septic-AKI-on-CRRT population in at least one prospective cohort [S:9b8c9ee6-e844-5b6c-90a7-615e57905902], and the HELENICC score has not been externally validated [S:4584579b-07ce-5c1a-86bd-bcfe080a3927].

rows.question: Which patient characteristics guide selection for therapeutic plasma exchange in progressive multiple sclerosis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Candidacy rests on clinical worsening that has not responded to corticosteroids or disease-modifying therapy, such patients being regarded as second-line candidates for exchange; Ongoing clinical worsening, or a faster rate of disability progression over the preceding two years, marks patients more likely to improve, whereas patients whose disability has been stable for a year or more are described as unlikely to improve; Less advanced disease at the time of treatment, meaning younger age, shorter disease duration and lower pretreatment disability, is described as favouring better recovery; Gadolinium-enhancing lesions, including large tumefactive or ring-enhancing lesions, mark patients more likely to respond, ring enhancement being reported as significantly associated with favourable outcomes. Certainty: These selection features come from uncontrolled clinical experience and reported associations, so they are provisional observations rather than established determinants of response. Scope: applies to progressive multiple sclerosis in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it treats these selection features as a validated decision rule and recommends withholding plasma exchange from patients who lack them.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

No patient characteristic establishes TPE as a treatment for *progression itself*; selection in progressive MS hinges on whether the patient has evidence of a superimposed, active inflammatory event (steroid-refractory acute relapse, gadolinium-enhancing/ring-enhancing lesions) plus the general "responder" phenotype identified in CNS demyelinating cohorts — short disease duration, younger age, lower baseline disability, preserved deep tendon reflexes, early treatment, and (where biopsied) humoral immunopathology.

## Guideline framing: phenotype is the first filter

- The AAN concluded [passage text removed] evidence, Level A), while being *probably effective* as second-line therapy for steroid-resistant exacerbations of relapsing forms; the same document notes it [passage text removed] disease failing high-dose steroids ([PMC3034395]([passage text removed]); [Medscape summary](https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/736119)).
- ASFA 2023 lists MS "acute attack/relapse" as Category II (grade 1A for TPE) but "chronic primary or secondary progressive" as **Category III, grade 2B** — i.e., optimal role not established, decisions made patient-by-patient ([ASFA 2023 guidelines PDF, Connelly-Smith et al.]([passage text removed]); category definitions: [redcrossplus.blog]([passage text removed])).
- A 2025 review makes the selection rule explicit: relapse evidence "[passage text removed]," and [passage text removed])" ([mdpi.com/2227-9059/13/10/2399]([passage text removed]) / [PMC12562264]([passage text removed])).

## Characteristics favouring response (from CNS-IDD/relapse cohorts)

- **Male sex, preserved reflexes, early initiation** were associated with moderate-to-marked improvement in the Mayo predictor study ([PubMed 11781423](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11781423)).
- **Shorter disease duration and preserved deep tendon reflexes** pre-PLEX, and **ring-enhancing lesions (OR=4.0) and/or mass effect (OR=3.0)** on MRI, predicted beneficial response; a **relapsing-remitting** (rather than progressive) course and lower EDSS characterised responders at follow-up ([PMC3134547]([passage text removed])).
- **Younger age and lower admission EDSS** predicted early response, and — directly relevant here — **risk of failure was ~6-fold higher in active progressive MS than RRMS (OR 6.06, 95% CI 1.37–26.76)** ([PMC11188695]([passage text removed])).
- The 2025 review lists predictors as [passage text removed], CSF markers of intrathecal B-cell activity, and initiation within 14 days ([PMC12562264]([passage text removed])); its practice section prioritises severe/disabling relapses, eloquent lesion location, gadolinium enhancement, documented corticosteroid resistance, and comorbidities ([mdpi.com/2227-9059/13/10/2399]([passage text removed])).
- A retrospective PLEX series noted the treatment was **less effective in MS patients who subsequently developed a progressive course** ([iomcworld.org report]([passage text removed])).

## Immunopathological subtype (where biopsy exists)

- All pattern II patients ([passage text removed] III (n=6) improved after TPE ([Keegan 2005, Lancet 366:579–582, via Scholar record](http://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=&journal=Lancet&doi=10.1016%2FS0140-6736%2805%2967102-4&volume=366&pages=579-582&publication_year=2005&author=Keegan%2CM.)).
- In 69 biopsied patients, immunopattern 1 and 2 were positive predictors of apheresis response (pattern 2 strongest) while pattern 3 patients did not benefit; only 5/69 had secondary progressive disease, so this criterion is largely untested in progressive cohorts ([PMC5885209]([passage text removed])).

## Progressive-MS–specific data are weak and conflicting

- The Canadian Cooperative trial in progressive MS (cyclophosphamide + PLEX vs comparators) failed to show benefit ([Lancet 1991]([passage text removed]); design and group details: [intechopen.com/chapters/1216614](https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1216614)).
- Countervailing single-centre experience reports durable EDSS improvement in chronic progressive MS with PLEX plus low-dose immunosuppression, with **benefit [passage text removed] describes ongoing **maintenance PLEX every ~4–8 weeks in initial responders** ([intechopen.com/chapters/1216614](https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1216614); [PMC12744008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12744008); 25-year follow-up: [iomcworld.org]([passage text removed])). These are uncontrolled/observational and do not overturn the guideline position above.

## Procedural eligibility (not MS-specific)

Hemodynamic stability should be achieved before TPE, and critically ill patients tolerate it poorly; adequate venous access (large-bore peripheral or central catheter) is required, and baseline coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia and albumin or plasma allergy are relevant risks ([mdpi.com/2673-8236/6/1/8]([passage text removed]); [StatPearls NBK560566]([passage text removed]); [aneskey.com]([passage text removed])).

**Gap:** I found no prospective study validating these predictors specifically within primary or secondary progressive MS populations; the 2025 review states this subpopulation's responsiveness is "poorly defined" and a priority for future study ([PMC12562264]([passage text removed])).
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

There is no validated selection rule for progressive MS specifically; guidelines classify chronic/progressive MS as an ASFA Category III indication where "[passage text removed] must be individualized [S:0de6c510-bb1b-527e-bfe8-4b9988b54dd5][S:a31027b2-4b90-5ccf-bb8a-db7934c53bb2]. Progressive phenotype is itself a negative predictor, so selection rests on identifying residual, active, humorally-mediated inflammation superimposed on the progressive course.

## Characteristics that favour PLEX

**Evidence of active inflammation on MRI.** Gadolinium-enhancing lesions were the single best independent predictor of TPE response in a 90-patient CIS/MS cohort (multivariate p = 0.004) [S:f99a8f4f-dbfb-59ac-b959-65f68b3fb1af], confirmed in a two-centre steroid-refractory cohort where favourable predictors were relapsing course, younger age and Gd-enhancement [S:b1ddb84f-7808-545c-8cf9-81643118193e]. An exploratory analysis of 153 patients with CNS inflammatory demyelination identified Gd+ lesions and lesions with mass effect as MRI predictors [S:79ea108e-abec-5721-8d5a-474f82957748].

**A superimposed, subacute steroid-refractory attack rather than insidious progression.** PLEX is endorsed as second-line escalation specifically after failure of high-dose corticosteroids [S:18f690eb-28cb-5151-aec2-e8ba2c05af3d]; only anecdotal evidence supports its use for steroid-refractory superimposed relapses in SPMS [S:79ea108e-abec-5721-8d5a-474f82957748]. Historic PLEX cohorts in progressive MS selected patients with documented recent EDSS worsening who had failed corticosteroids [S:f418ccfa-06f1-5526-b6b4-55546175e7f9], and benefit was more pronounced in those with shorter disease duration and disability decline in the preceding two years [S:6156e14e-f3f7-5775-a862-0f5fa47928ef].

**Younger age, lower baseline disability, early treatment.** A meta-analysis of 40 observational plus 1 randomized study (1,383 patients) reported response of 76.6% in RRMS/CIS versus 53.9% in progressive MS, with age below 50 and early initiation (median 2–3 weeks) favouring success [S:38250f6f-cd9f-5d84-83db-b581150a034a]. In the 90-patient cohort, response was more frequent with EDSS ≤ 5.0 before TPE and in patients not on a disease-modifying drug [S:f99a8f4f-dbfb-59ac-b959-65f68b3fb1af]. Mayo Clinic data identified male sex, preserved/normal-to-increased muscle stretch reflexes, and initiation ≤20 days from onset [S:97b7b307-40cc-5464-a4dc-c81619a7feda][S:af139c19-deda-51e5-ac69-cc1c53901655].

**Humoral immunopathology.** All 10 patients with pattern II (antibody/complement-mediated) demyelination improved after plasma exchange, versus none with pattern I or III [S:5119f434-d2d3-5737-b3f9-11f39e418cc7]; a biopsy cohort of 69 MS patients found pattern 1 and 2 most likely to benefit and pattern 3 unlikely [S:f045b6d1-8dbe-51b6-8909-0804a98395b7]. Practically, this argues for excluding NMOSD/MOGAD mimics, which have their own (higher-priority) apheresis indications [S:a31027b2-4b90-5ccf-bb8a-db7934c53bb2].

**Atypical features / absent oligoclonal bands.** In 27 progressive MS patients with subacute worsening (EDSS 4.5–8.5), 12 (44%) benefited, and responders were mostly those without CSF oligoclonal bands and with additional unusual features; PPMS responded at least as well as SPMS [S:c651da5d-8128-50e8-a48d-04d7f22e3085]. This is a single small preliminary abstract and should be treated as hypothesis-generating.

**Demonstrated response to an initial course, for maintenance.** Maintenance PLEX should be reserved for patients showing convincing benefit from induction [S:ea7c0590-1378-5d13-b16c-193930c18b9f]; one group reports nine progressive-MS patients on continuous PLEX for 30 years (every 6–8 weeks) who were severely disabled despite all conventional treatments and became fully ambulatory [S:76b23808-007d-5ded-b935-94d359cc138e], with objective decline on reducing frequency [S:98a60813-3910-547d-8a12-91dddf547c36]. These are uncontrolled case narratives.

## Characteristics arguing against

Progressive phenotype per se (AAN: "established ineffective" for progressive MS; ASFA Category III, grade 2B) [S:a31027b2-4b90-5ccf-bb8a-db7934c53bb2]; chronic long-standing course without acute exacerbation — early PLEX cohorts found improvement mainly in short disease course and acute exacerbations, with chronic progressive patients responding poorly [S:09a84ed2-5ed8-5560-9202-b6679b4430a9]; and reaching a chronic non-inflammatory stage [S:fd5d9099-724c-50d2-91bf-a95e27ef3e5e]. The Weiner sham-controlled trial showed no benefit in the progressive subgroup [S:1e3b0947-46e1-5bce-9a7c-c261da52af71], and PLEX plus immunomodulators in SPMS produced only transient change without disability improvement [S:6ae9e050-9203-5990-b17f-e4600c8e3d52]. In one retrospective series, 6 of 7 patients already on high-efficacy DMT were non-responders versus 14/17 treatment-naïve patients achieving full or partial recovery [S:44a0237e-85f6-5425-99c2-b6ae5abe652e].

Practical, non-biological determinants also matter: adequate vascular access [S:f418ccfa-06f1-5526-b6b4-55546175e7f9] and insurance authorization, which frequently blocks maintenance PLEX even in documented responders [S:15a22b23-de4a-5816-a534-a60bec5cdaa2].

**Caveat:** most of the "predictor" data derive from relapse cohorts (mixed CIS/RRMS/progressive) rather than from progressive MS specifically; the progressive-MS-specific evidence is small, older, or uncontrolled, and the Canadian Cooperative trial was negative on its primary endpoint [S:6156e14e-f3f7-5775-a862-0f5fa47928ef].

rows.question: How does the timing of norepinephrine initiation after hypotension onset relate to mortality in sepsis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: A longer delay between hypotension onset and the start of norepinephrine is associated with higher 28-day mortality; The delay remains associated with 28-day death after multivariable adjustment for measured covariates; Delays extending beyond the first hour after hypotension onset are associated with a higher adjusted hazard of death by day 28. Certainty: The evidence supports an adjusted association of moderate strength rather than a demonstrated effect of acting earlier, and the sample size keeps the findings hypothesis-generating. Scope: applies to sepsis with hypotension requiring vasopressor support in adults, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents earlier norepinephrine initiation as an established survival-improving intervention or recommends a mandatory fixed time-to-vasopressor target for all hypotensive septic patients on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Observational data consistently show a graded association between longer delay from hypotension/shock onset to norepinephrine and higher mortality, but the magnitude depends heavily on how "time zero" is defined, and the association largely disappears in the largest hypotension-anchored cohorts and in randomized trials — so timing is best described as an associated, not established causal, mortality determinant.

## Evidence that delay tracks with death

**Dose-response in shock-onset–anchored cohorts.** In a 213-patient retrospective ICU cohort, hospital mortality rose stepwise with delay: 27.5% if norepinephrine started <1 h after septic shock onset, 30.4% at 1–2 h, and 65.2% at ≥6 h; every 1-hour delay within the first 6 h was associated with a 5.3% absolute mortality increase, and 28-day mortality was higher at ≥2 h vs <2 h (OR 1.86, 1.04–3.34; P=0.035), with OR 2.16 (1.23–3.81) beyond 3 h and 3.61 (1.45–8.95) beyond 6 h [PMC4194405].

**Severity-dependent effect.** In a multicenter ED cohort of 4,456 patients, each hour of delay raised 28-day mortality only among patients meeting Sepsis-3 shock criteria (aOR 1.07 per hour, 1.02–1.13, P=0.002); versus >6 h, aOR was 0.54 (0.35–0.81) for <1 h and 0.63 (0.42–0.95) for 1–3 h. No association was seen in non-Sepsis-3 shock or low-vasopressor-risk patients [PMC12922425; 10.1186/s12871-026-03638-w].

**ED time-to-drug in survivors vs non-survivors.** In a 176-patient ED cohort (in-hospital mortality 31.8%), norepinephrine began at a median 12 min (IQR 2–29) in survivors vs 104 min (IQR 68–181) in non-survivors (P<0.001) [10.3390/jcm14176025].

## Evidence against a mortality effect

**Hypotension-anchored large cohorts.** In 4,699 septic shock patients (90-day mortality 34%; median time to vasopressor 2.68 h), [passage text removed] 1.01, 1.00–1.02) or vasopressor-free days, including when analyzed in 2-hour intervals [PMID 41186550; S0196-0644(25)01238-7]. An earlier large cohort found only a weak per-hour association (adjusted OR 1.02, 1.01–1.03), with excess risk confined to the latest decile (>14.1 h); the Wald statistic for antimicrobial delay was ~16.7-fold larger than for vasopressor delay [PMC4075345].

**The randomized signal is hemodynamic, not survival.** CENSER (n=310) achieved earlier norepinephrine (median 93 vs 192 min) and higher 6-hour shock control ([passage text removed]), with less cardiogenic pulmonary edema (14.4% vs 27.7%, P=0.004) and arrhythmia (11% vs 20%, P=0.03), but 28-day mortality was not different ([passage text removed]) [PMID 30704260; 10.1164/rccm.201806-1034OC].

## Meta-analyses: direction depends on time zero and inclusion

- Early NE, 5 studies/929 patients: lower short-term mortality (OR 0.45, 0.34–0.61) and faster MAP target [10.1186/s13054-020-03204-x].
- 12 studies/7,281 patients: no overall mortality difference (RCTs OR 0.70, 0.41–1.19; observational OR 0.83, 0.54–1.29), but less pulmonary edema (OR 0.43, 0.25–0.74) and benefit in the two RCTs without restrictive-fluid strategies (OR 0.49, 0.25–0.96) [PMID 38972348].
- Updated 10-study/4,767-patient analysis: mortality reduction in RCTs (OR 0.49, 0.25–0.96), RCT+propensity-matched (OR 0.65) and observational studies (OR 0.71), with subgroup benefit when NE was given within 1 h and lactate ≤3 mmol/L; trial sequential analysis judged the evidence inconclusive [PMID 40329359; PMC12057179].
- 11 studies/6,661 patients: no overall difference (OR 0.66, 0.36–1.19, I²=82%), but lower mortality for initiation at 1–3 h (OR 0.70, 0.60–0.82) and when septic shock diagnosis was time zero (OR 0.64, 0.48–0.85); "extremely early" (<1 h) was not associated with benefit (OR 0.61, 0.20–1.89, I²=91%) [PMID 39865207, as summarized in 10.1186/s13054-025-05540-2].

## Interpretive caveats

Anchoring matters: initiation within 1 h *[passage text removed] a national registry propensity-matched analysis [PMID 34612848], and an older multicenter study reported lowest mortality when vasoactive agents began 1–6 h after shock onset rather than in the first hour. Sicker patients get norepinephrine sooner (early-NE groups had higher lactate and SOFA scores) [PMC12922425], so confounding by indication can bias in either direction; and delay to norepinephrine correlates with delay in other bundle elements — duration of hypotension before effective antimicrobials is itself a strong mortality determinant (adjusted OR 1.119 per hour) [Kumar, Crit Care Med 2006, [passage text removed]].

**Bottom line:** delays beyond roughly 1–3 hours from shock onset are reproducibly associated with higher short-term mortality in observational data, most strongly in patients meeting Sepsis-3 shock criteria or with high vasopressor requirement, whereas randomized evidence supports faster shock control and less pulmonary edema without a demonstrated mortality benefit; no trial has established that hastening norepinephrine within the first hour of hypotension per se saves lives.
answers.connect:
**Observational data consistently show a time-dependent association — each hour of delay between hypotension/shock onset and norepinephrine start tracks with higher mortality — but randomized evidence is weaker and inconsistent, and the very earliest ("hour-1") initiation has not been shown to improve survival.**

**Observational dose-response signal**
- In a retrospective cohort of 213 surgical ICU septic shock patients (28-day mortality 37.6% overall; mean time to norepinephrine 3.1 ± 2.5 h), [passage text removed]; starting ≥2 h after onset carried significantly higher 28-day mortality than <2 h, with lower MAP, higher lactate, longer hypotension duration, and more total norepinephrine in the late group [S:5fa7fbd4-6e13-5ab0-a0a6-9e41e7939b5e][S:a107aaf2-daed-56f3-8621-8c68abc49998].
- A prospective multicentre study of 138 hypotensive sepsis patients found non-survivors had longer median time to norepinephrine (98.5 min, IQR 60.0–131) than survivors ([passage text removed]); norepinephrine time remained an independent predictor of 28-day [passage text removed]–1.722), with adjusted HRs of 2.60 for >1 h and 2.96 for >2 h [S:544f8c3d-d012-5095-b694-46ae2326ed5c]. The authors call these findings hypothesis-generating given residual confounding [S:b18eeb43-3bf7-558f-9bc0-bd78b7cdfb5b].
- A contrasting cohort measuring delay from *first documented hypotension* found the association modest and driven entirely by the most extreme decile: only delays >14 h were associated with increased mortality and incremental organ failure, with no effect on vasopressor duration or ventilator time among survivors [S:40bc4d63-83b7-5198-aeba-3827da4cf4f5 → S:40bc4d63-83b7-5198-aeba-3827da4cf4f5 is not valid; see S:981cf001-c2d2-552b-a0d7-14e4ad03b4ad][S:e3c21a96-4de3-5a61-9411-88f0369384dc].

*(Correction on the identifier: the >14-hour finding appears in [S:981cf001-c2d2-552b-a0d7-14e4ad03b4ad] and [S:e3c21a96-4de3-5a61-9411-88f0369384dc].)*

**Pooled evidence**
- A 2020 meta-analysis (5 studies, 929 patients) found lower short-term mortality with early norepinephrine (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.34–0.61), plus faster time to target MAP (MD −1.39 h) and less fluid within 6 h (MD −0.50 L) [S:3b1a7122-438c-524f-be6d-e74109ec053d][S:71fde8b2-4975-59bd-816d-f4cde64d36cd].
- A 2025 updated meta-analysis (10 studies, 4767 patients) found reduced mortality in RCTs (OR 0.49, 0.25–0.96), pooled RCT+propensity-matched studies (OR 0.65, 0.42–0.99), and observational studies (OR 0.71, 0.54–0.94), but trial sequential analysis indicated the evidence is not yet conclusive and is limited by confounding [S:088764b6-641c-5d75-a4f8-6cc5dc74288d][S:55fe93f3-8d20-56e7-aabf-1d7ebd2a2a60].
- A separate 2025 meta-analysis found the pooled effect non-significant overall (RR 0.90, 0.76–1.06, p=0.18), significant only among observational studies (RR 0.75, 0.60–0.94), with I²=65.6% [S:bff7a8eb-3263-5f36-9423-cb354a4dd4a5].

**The "how early" question — a possible sweet spot, not linear**
A 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis found no overall mortality difference between early and late initiation on Bayesian three-level analysis of RCTs and quasi-experimental studies (OR 0.62, 0.32–1.22); by cut-point, initiation within 1–3 hours was associated with lower short-term mortality (OR 0.70, 0.60–0.82, I²=0%), whereas "extremely early" initiation within the first hour was not (OR 0.61, 0.20–1.89, I²=91%) — the authors interpret this as favouring adequate fluid resuscitation before vasopressors [S:fb2e6923-aa01-5c55-bef2-00a5f6ad6051][S:13275f8c-a105-536e-bed4-4a2187719a5e][S:771144d2-fbea-5e62-a090-cef2be8983d5].

**Randomized anchor (CENSER)**
Early low-dose norepinephrine (0.05 µg/kg/min, started ~93 min vs ~3 h) improved shock control at 6 h (76.1% vs 48.4%) and reduced cardiogenic pulmonary edema (14.4% vs 27.7%) and new arrhythmia (11% vs 20%), but 28-day mortality did not differ (15.5% vs 21.9%) — the trial was underpowered for mortality [S:1c32e207-c844-573d-a0a0-3de0148beef6][S:c32d0dc7-7a18-52f5-81e0-9dac2caf375c][S:76af28da-03bd-55ee-8765-e00ab5a7f302].

**Caveats.** Reverse causation is a real concern: late initiation may mark sicker patients or worse overall care, and there is no proof that rapid pressure correction itself causes benefit [S:c46bd8a5-4257-5548-a736-f92300ec1936][S:a107aaf2-daed-56f3-8621-8c68abc49998]. Definitions of "early" vary widely across studies (from pre-fluid to <6 h from shock onset), limiting pooling [S:dda4ec77-9b44-5d89-a6d2-191d6a5be6b0]. Guidelines still give no specific timing recommendation [S:5bb5bd8e-1a4e-5916-b99b-5c94701ff23a][S:8bb7b763-4e2c-51ed-9a47-279c56540f32], and adequately powered RCTs (e.g. VASOSHOCK) are ongoing [S:76af28da-03bd-55ee-8765-e00ab5a7f302][S:55fe93f3-8d20-56e7-aabf-1d7ebd2a2a60].

rows.question: What clinical outcomes follow anti-LINGO-1 remyelination therapy added to background disease-modifying treatment in relapsing multiple sclerosis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Adding the anti-LINGO-1 antibody to ongoing disease-modifying treatment did not improve the multicomponent physical and cognitive disability endpoint over 72 weeks compared with placebo added to the same background treatment; Rates of confirmed disability improvement did not differ between the antibody and placebo groups; Rates of confirmed disability worsening did not differ between the antibody and placebo groups; Overall adverse event incidence and severity were similar in the antibody and placebo groups. Certainty: Support for the primary and prespecified secondary comparisons is direct, concurrently controlled with chance-based group assignment, and adequately powered for the effect sought, whereas alternative-endpoint and subgroup signals remain exploratory only. Scope: applies to relapsing multiple sclerosis on stable disease-modifying treatment in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents anti-LINGO-1 combined with a particular background therapy, or given in a selected disability range, as an established or demonstrated benefit, or recommends such a combination on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line
Adding anti-LINGO-1 (opicinumab) to background DMT did **not** improve disability or slow disability progression in relapsing MS across two randomized phase 2 trials, and the program was discontinued; tolerability was comparable to placebo apart from hypersensitivity at the highest dose. [[passage text removed]]

## SYNERGY (add-on to IM interferon beta-1a, n=418, 72 weeks)
- The primary endpoint — percentage achieving confirmed multicomponent disability improvement (EDSS, T25FW, 9HPT, PASAT-3) — showed no significant linear dose response: 45/91 (49%) on placebo vs 21/45 (47%) at 3 mg/kg, 59 (63%) at 10 mg/kg, 59 (65%) at 30 mg/kg, and 36 (40%) at 100 mg/kg, i.e. an inverted-U rather than dose-dependent pattern. [[passage text removed]] [S:https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/869177]
- The secondary endpoint of slowed disability progression was also not met. [[passage text removed]]
- Only isolated component signals emerged (e.g., 9HPT non-dominant hand at 10 mg/kg, OR 2.42, 95% CI 1.0–5.7, p=0.04), in an underpowered per-component analysis; exploratory subgroup analyses favored younger patients, RRMS, shorter disease duration, and baseline MRI (MTR/DTI radial diffusivity) profiles suggesting demyelinated but structurally preserved lesions. [S:https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/869177] [[passage text removed]]
- Safety: adverse events in 79/93 (85%) placebo vs 275 (85%) of any-dose opicinumab; most common were influenza-like illness (43% vs 40%), MS relapse (36% vs 32%), headache (16% vs 25%); treatment-related serious events included hypersensitivity in 4 (4%) patients at 100 mg/kg. [[passage text removed]]

## AFFINITY Part 1 (biomarker-enriched population, add-on to interferons/DMF/natalizumab, n=263, 750 mg q4w, 72 weeks)
- Primary endpoint Overall Disability Response Score: adjusted mean difference 0.15 (95% CI −[passage text removed]), numerically favoring opicinumab but not significant; in the imaging-core-selected analysis [passage text removed]]
- Secondary endpoints (12-week confirmed disability improvement on physical/cognitive measures) were likewise null; the published report gives an odds ratio of [passage text removed]) for opicinumab vs placebo on a responder analysis — the extract does not let me pin down which specific secondary component this figure belongs to. [[passage text removed]]
- Numerically larger (non-significant) differences favoring opicinumab occurred in participants aged ≥40 with EDSS ≥3.0, disease duration ≥6 years, and on dimethyl fumarate background — note this is the opposite direction from SYNERGY's younger/shorter-duration signal. [[passage text removed]: adverse events in 85% (placebo) vs 86% ([passage text removed]]
- Biogen discontinued opicinumab development in October 2020 after AFFINITY missed primary and secondary endpoints; the authors frame the combined SYNERGY/AFFINITY data as informing design of future remyelination trials rather than supporting the drug. [[passage text removed]]

## Caveats
No trial has shown that anti-LINGO-1 reduces relapses or MRI activity beyond background DMT; relapse-rate and MRI lesion outcomes were not reported as positive in any source retrieved. Earlier optic neuritis work (RENEW) improved VEP latency recovery but not retinal-layer thickness or visual function, so the electrophysiological remyelination signal did not translate into clinical disability benefit when added to DMT. [[passage text removed]]

No significant linear dose response (p = 0.9831); instead an inverted U‑shaped pattern with more favorable outcomes at 10 and 30 mg/kg [S:7900d093-8486-5d83-86d4-d95f06fc615d][S:d399060a-5cff-5793-aed1-b381dd1b8775].

- On the tertiary overall response score, improvements appeared at weeks 24 and 36, largest at 10 mg/kg [S:ed004087-eaf1-5ea1-b4f8-2b674a382479][S:45e16518-1b45-5859-babb-bb2955c122e4].
- Safety/tolerability: AEs in 85% on any opicinumab dose and 85% on placebo; most common were influenza‑like illness, MS relapse, and headache; serious AEs included hypersensitivity in 4% at 100 mg/kg, plus isolated psychiatric events and UTI [S:bbe523bf-171e-5fbc-9b3a-77aecf07bac3]. [passage text removed] noted [S:45e16518-1b45-5859-babb-bb2955c122e4].

**Programme outcome:** AFFINITY was terminated for lack of efficacy and Biogen discontinued opicinumab's clinical development [S:280b18fc-f6ce-5458-9d57-08e90a866708][S:66bbeebe-f6a7-5a2a-876f-5ab0bc3fc792].

**Caveats.** The apparent add‑on benefit signals are subgroup/post hoc and hypothesis‑generating, not confirmatory — AFFINITY was itself the prospective test of the SYNERGY subgroup hypothesis and failed [S:fa78abdb-5943-5117-a1c7-6bc1afaa0256][S:e5c7bf28-3f9d-5e0c-946c-4a236e61b757]. Proposed explanations for failure include suboptimal patient selection, insensitive outcome measures, underpowering, limited blood–brain barrier antibody penetration, and variable LINGO‑1 expression [S:7ee02744-9445-52af-9e18-037814d4d0e4][S:280b18fc-f6ce-5458-9d57-08e90a866708]. I found no evidence in these searches for anti‑LINGO‑1 effects on annualized relapse rate or gadolinium‑enhancing lesion counts as add‑on therapy — those were collected as safety/tertiary measures but no results figures appeared in the retrieved text [S:1497259d-e024-54ba-9509-3cbf437326dd][S:dec5a568-4203-54c2-bdba-bcff7ca0e7d2].
