rows.question: Which laboratory indices of nutrition and systemic inflammation present on admission relate to ICU-acquired weakness in sepsis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: The systemic immune-inflammation index calculated from the admission blood count is associated with higher risk of ICU-acquired weakness in sepsis and remained associated after multivariable adjustment; The admission prognostic nutritional index showed only a non-significant protective trend, with no clear association with ICU-acquired weakness in the adjusted analysis; Taken alone, the admission systemic immune-inflammation index discriminated ICU-acquired weakness only moderately, ranking among the better single markers but far short of a standalone test. Certainty: The reported links describe associations between admission index values and later weakness rather than demonstrated causal effects, rest on evidence drawn from a single patient population checked only against itself, and involve an inflammation index whose discrimination on its own is no better than moderate. Scope: applies to sepsis requiring intensive care for at least two days in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents nutritional supplementation or anti-inflammatory treatment guided by these admission indices as demonstrated to prevent ICU-acquired weakness, or recommends such treatment on this basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** The admission-time laboratory signals most consistently linked to ICU-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) in sepsis are low serum albumin (and albumin-based composite nutritional–inflammatory indices such as the PNI) plus markers of systemic inflammation — CRP/hs-CRP, IL-6, and other cytokines (IL-1β, IL-10) — together with metabolic markers lactate and glucose; however, several well-conducted sepsis cohorts found none of these to be *independent* predictors once severity and treatment exposures were included, so the evidence is inconsistent.

**Nutritional indices**
- In a pilot ICU study, first-day albumin significantly discriminated ICUAW (ROC AUC 0.688, 95% CI 0.550–0.827), as did hs-CRP (AUC 0.669) and serum gelsolin (AUC 0.711); combining gelsolin with albumin improved discrimination (AUC 0.750), while APACHE II gave no significant predictive value for ICUAW in that cohort ([PMC12984354]([passage text removed])). Gelsolin correlated positively with albumin (ρ = 0.514) and inversely with hs-CRP (ρ = −0.523).
- An early prediction study in sepsis explicitly tested the albumin+lymphocyte–based Prognostic Nutritional Index and the platelet×neutrophil/lymphocyte Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index within 24 h of ICU admission (425 patients; ICU-AW incidence 40.8%; final model included APACHE II, SOFA and septic shock). The authors concluded the nomogram may identify high-risk septic patients within 24 h and that "SII appeared to improve prediction, whereas PNI…" — i.e. SII added value while PNI's contribution was weaker (10.1177/03913988261456928; [read.qxmd 42396697]([passage text removed]); [ResearchGate 408420739](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/408420739)). I could not retrieve the effect estimates for PNI/SII, so I cannot quantify them.
- In severe acute pancreatitis (not sepsis per se), formally assessed nutritional risk was an independent ICU-AW risk factor ([passage text removed]), alongside [passage text removed]) ([PubMed 41867460](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41867460); [PMC13003820]([passage text removed])).

**Inflammatory indices**
- In a prospective multicentre sepsis cohort (116 patients), IL-6 and CRP differed significantly between ICUAW and non-ICUAW groups and entered a nomogram with muscle ultrasound measures ([passage text removed]), AUC [passage text removed]), sensitivity 88%, specificity 95.8% ([passage text removed], 10.1186/s12871-025-02911-8; [full text](https://d-nb.info/136313972X/34)). The authors framed this as evidence that inflammation drives muscle atrophy in critical illness.
- A machine-learning ICU-AW model selected by LASSO retained sepsis itself, albumin, lactate, glucose, IL-1β, IL-6 and IL-10 (albumin with a negative coefficient, i.e. protective) alongside APACHE II, ICU stay, glucocorticoids and neuromuscular blockers; the logistic model including cytokines reached test-set AUC 82.1%, and the authors concluded [passage text removed] ([PMC11658462]([passage text removed]); 10.1186/s12883-024-03981-w).
- In postoperative ICU patients, IL-6 and sepsis were retained as the "inflammatory core" of ICU-AW risk alongside SOFA, delirium and Barthel index ([PMC13507378]([passage text removed])).
- Analogous admission biology outside sepsis: in cardiogenic shock on mechanical support, ICU-AW patients had significantly lower admission albumin and haemoglobin and higher IL-15, creatine kinase and troponin T, with IL-15 inversely correlated with albumin (r = −0.55) and with initial MRC score ([Sci Rep s41598-025-87381-1]([passage text removed])).

**Important negative evidence (why this remains unsettled)**
- In a prospective sepsis cohort that measured CRP, procalcitonin, albumin and NRS-2002 on admission, none differed significantly [passage text removed] (CRP p = 0.171; PCT p = 0.306; albumin p = 0.074; NRS-2002 p = 0.714), and the final nomogram contained only age, MODS, NMBA use, ventilation duration, sedation duration and APACHE II ([PMC13092445]([passage text removed])).
- Among 264 septic patients where lactate, glucose, calcium, PCT and albumin were all assessed, only lactate survived multivariable analysis (independent risk factor; cut-off 2.12 mmol/L, AUC 0.812) with APACHE II, ventilation time and protective restraint ([PMC11168428]([passage text removed]); Heliyon 2024;10(11):e32253).
- In 149 septic patients with PCT, CRP, LDH, lactate, haemoglobin, creatinine, albumin and platelets collected, the only independent factors were sex and ICU length of stay ([PMC12505916]([passage text removed]); Pak J Med Sci).
- In a MIMIC-IV plus external-cohort machine-learning study of 3,842 septic patients, albumin, lactate and glucose were candidate variables but glucose was the metabolic marker retained; dominant SHAP predictors were early antibiotic use, early mechanical ventilation, SOFA and age (random forest AUC 0.772 validation / 0.753 external) ([besjournal 10.3967/bes2026.063]([passage text removed]); [PubMed 42559880](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42559880)).

**Interpretation:** admission hypoalbuminaemia and a high inflammatory burden (CRP/hs-CRP, IL-6, IL-1β, IL-10; SII) plus lactate and glucose are the recurring candidate indices, and albumin-containing composite scores (PNI, gelsolin+albumin) perform better than single markers. But their independent contribution is modest and frequently disappears after adjustment for illness severity, ventilation, sedation and NMBA exposure; the strongest-performing sepsis models add these labs to muscle ultrasound or severity scores rather than using them alone. No source I found reported prealbumin, transferrin or CONUT specifically against ICU-AW in sepsis.
answers.connect:
## Answer

**Bottom line:** In sepsis, the admission indices with the most direct evidence are inflammatory rather than nutritional — the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), procalcitonin, and lactate are independently associated with ICU-acquired weakness (ICU-AW), whereas composite nutrition indices (prognostic nutritional index, PNI) and albumin show only weak or non-independent associations. Early cytokine levels ([passage text removed]) are the best-supported "systemic inflammation" signal.

### Inflammation indices measured on admission

- In a single-centre retrospective cohort of 425 septic ICU patients (ICU stay ≥48 h, labs within 24 h of admission; ICU-AW by MRC sum score <48; overall incidence 40.8%), multivariable logistic regression identified **SII/100 (OR 1.12, 95% CI 1.06–1.19, p<0.001)** and **procalcitonin (OR 1.02, 95% CI 1.00–1.03, p=0.021)** as independent predictors, alongside APACHE II, SOFA, septic shock, intubation, vasoactive agents and DIC [S:fbdb6dd2-ee7c-5608-913c-5df849ca65f5]. On single-variable discrimination, APACHE II, SII/100 and septic shock performed best (AUCs ≈0.72–0.75), while PNI/10, procalcitonin and the other predictors were only modest (AUCs ≈0.58–0.68) [S:fbdb6dd2-ee7c-5608-913c-5df849ca65f5]. Adding PNI and SII to the model improved discrimination only modestly (AUC 0.872/0.851 vs 0.846/0.824 in training/validation) [S:5d5ca7c6-185b-5a43-b11f-1cfe2958d85b], and the authors attribute the small gain mainly to SII, concluding [passage text removed]" [S:df7f9a03-caf2-51d5-bff9-d5523227f094].
- **Early cytokine profile:** in 204 mechanically ventilated ICU patients (99 developed [passage text removed] those who developed ICU-AW; after principal-component reduction and adjustment for age, sex, BMI, **sepsis**, SOFA, APACHE IV, immune insufficiency and corticosteroids, PC1 (loaded mainly by IL-6, IL-8, IL-10) OR 1.27 (95% CI 1.02–1.60) and PC4 (sP-selectin) OR 1.55 (1.06–2.27) remained significant — i.e. [passage text removed] admission [S:169e4233-aacb-5494-a97b-3da04093e4a9][S:186da881-e17c-5c68-8208-9b75e4dd9d21].
- A LASSO/machine-learning ICU-AW model built from admission-time laboratory data retained **albumin, lactate, glucose, IL-1β, IL-6 and IL-10** (plus sepsis, glucocorticoids, NMBAs, ICU stay, APACHE II); the logistic model including inflammatory factors reached AUC 82.1% on the test set, and the authors concluded [passage text removed]:74a13fde-6d35-5a25-80b1-c3c004387acc][S:87e67a2e-c28b-5b2b-a936-c7ad2b4d7020].
- **Lactate:** in 264 septic patients (ICU-AW incidence 43.2%), lactic acid was an independent risk factor alongside APACHE II, mechanical ventilation duration and protective restraint, with an optimal cut-off of 2.12 mmol/L [S:e6a3848d-cff6-5876-aa5b-5204b1a95a2a][S:bcd74da4-833c-5375-9027-7895a2b0935c].

### Nutrition indices

- **PNI (albumin + lymphocyte count)** was retained by feature selection and showed a protective trend but did not reach independent significance after adjustment (PNI/10 OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.79–1.03, p=0.118) [S:fbdb6dd2-ee7c-5608-913c-5df849ca65f5][S:2e5a1ab8-8002-57f1-9d16-626841fdf758].
- **Albumin** appears mainly as a candidate/probable rather than established factor: reviews list hypoalbuminemia among the commonest risk factors for ICU-AW [S:2f0a32e3-5d9b-595e-a0c4-422e26cf9669], and a clinical review lists "[passage text removed]" as uncertain risk factors, in contrast to persistent SIRS/sepsis, immobility and hyperglycaemia [S:5042c5be-8e18-567b-9994-f09035aff32a]. Hypoalbuminaemia is near-universal in this population (87.2% of sepsis survivors in one cross-sectional study), which limits its discriminative value [S:0fc88f2f-a8c3-50c7-b3e6-010f15100115].
- In a 149-patient septic cohort (ICU-AW 43.6%), nutrition-related variables that differed on univariate analysis were **timing of initiation and route of nutritional support**, not laboratory nutrition markers; only sex and ICU length of stay remained independent [S:9d69521d-f6e4-5acd-bfad-a568b8c12860][S:7fc2c80e-4546-583e-917f-1a6f1f0e112c].

### Important caveats

- [passage text removed]: in sepsis their hepatic synthesis falls while acute-phase protein synthesis rises, so they conflate inflammation with nutrition [S:1e6c822c-c07e-5173-9d15-118863d82754].
- Mechanistically, the inflammation signal is plausible: septic systemic cytokine release amplifies intramuscular pro-inflammatory cytokines, suppresses muscle protein synthesis and accelerates ubiquitin-proteasome/autophagy-lysosome proteolysis [S:bcd74da4-833c-5375-9027-7895a2b0935c][S:aded059b-e285-58fd-bbf0-a8834d7845f1].
- **No evidence found** in my searches linking ICU-AW in sepsis specifically to the CRP/albumin ratio, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, neutrophil-percentage-to-albumin ratio, CALLY index or lactate-albumin ratio; those indices have been studied for sepsis **mortality** and other complications (e.g. NLR/BAR for mortality [S:03a1910d-8750-5d73-9b9c-a824377f0c8f]; NPAR for all-cause mortality [S:5c771d29-6825-542f-b898-1e34b39af8e3]; PNI/SII/LAR-based nomogram for 28-day mortality in sepsis-ARDS [S:3bf65b47-37ac-5995-ade4-ee3a393bfc77]), not for ICU-AW. All ICU-AW-specific evidence above is single-centre and retrospective, and requires external validation [S:df7f9a03-caf2-51d5-bff9-d5523227f094][S:be021b38-117c-5187-a9dc-19fc51fb8ec1].

rows.question: Which immunological mechanisms have been proposed to link Epstein-Barr virus infection with multiple sclerosis pathogenesis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Molecular mimicry is a leading proposed mechanism, with EBNA1 expressed during latent infection carrying peptide sequences that mimic epitopes of the glial adhesion molecule GlialCAM; Cross-reactivity supporting this mimicry has been observed in individual immunological studies, where clonally expanded cerebrospinal fluid B cells bound both EBNA1 and GlialCAM and EBNA1-reactive T cells recognised myelin protein peptides; Latent EBV infection of B lymphocytes, which sustains their survival and proliferation, is proposed to seed clonally expanded B cells in cerebrospinal fluid and meningeal ectopic lymphoid follicles lying next to areas of cortical demyelination; More efficient presentation of EBNA1-derived peptides by HLA-DRB1*15:01, alongside the increased frequencies of EBNA1-reactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells seen in patients, is proposed to link genetic susceptibility with activation of autoreactive T cells. Certainty: Support comes from converging immunological and post-mortem observations that make these mechanisms plausible rather than from evidence capable of establishing causation. Scope: applies to multiple sclerosis in adults, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents EBV-directed immunotherapy or vaccination as demonstrated to prevent or modify multiple sclerosis, or recommends such treatment on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Six broad mechanistic families have been proposed, and they are not mutually exclusive: (1) molecular mimicry/cross-reactivity, (2) EBV-driven rescue and reprogramming of autoreactive B cells, (3) altered antigen presentation by infected B cells, (4) bystander/hit-and-run activation, (5) defective immune control of EBV with virus-driven immunopathology in the CNS, and (6) EBV-induced trafficking of B cells into the CNS. A review of the field explicitly frames the candidate mechanisms as [passage text removed], while noting that the exact explanation remains speculative ([Frontiers in Immunology 10.3389/fimmu.2024.1466339]([passage text removed].1466339/full)).

## 1. Molecular mimicry (antibody-mediated)

The best-characterised example is EBNA1–GlialCAM: single-cell sequencing of paired-chain B cell repertoires from MS blood and CSF identified a cross-reactive antibody binding both EBNA1 and the CNS protein GlialCAM, supported by the crystal structure of the EBNA1 peptide–Fab complex; [passage text removed] immunisation exacerbated disease in a mouse MS model, and anti-EBNA1/anti-GlialCAM antibodies are prevalent in MS ([PMID 35073561](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35073561); [Nature s41586-022-04432-7]([passage text removed])). The relevant core epitopes are EBNA1 AA393–398 and GlialCAM AA376–382, and preincubation with EBNA1 AA386–405 blocks antibody binding to GlialCAM AA370–389, with phosphorylation of serine 376 enhancing the cross-binding ([PNAS 10.1073/pnas.2424986122]([passage text removed])). Additional mimicked self-antigens are anoctamin-2 ([Tengvall 2019, PMC6708327]([passage text removed])) and alpha-B crystallin ([Thomas 2023, PMID 37196088](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37196088)). An important caveat: cross-reactive EBNA1–GlialCAM antibodies are found in only about a quarter of MS patients, and demonstrating mimicry is not itself proof of pathogenicity ([PMC9057594]([passage text removed])).

## 2. Molecular mimicry (T cell–mediated)

[passage text removed] and cross-recognise myelin antigens more often than non-MS-associated autoantigens, producing IFN-γ and IL-2 ([Lünemann 2008, PMC2525578]([passage text removed])). Cross-reactive T cell immunity has also been shown for CRYAB: CD4+ T cells from EBNA1-immunised mice responded to full-length CRYAB, and vice versa, but not to CMV pp65 or other MS autoantigens ([PMC10191428]([passage text removed])). Most recently, ANO2-specific CD4+ T cells were shown to be more frequent in MS, to cross-react with EBNA1 in humans and mice, to share TCR repertoire overlap, and ANO2 immunisation or ANO2-specific T cell transfer worsened EAE ([Cell S0092-8674(25)01481-3]([passage text removed])).

## 3. EBV rescue/reprogramming of autoreactive B cells

Pender's hypothesis proposes that EBV infects autoreactive B cells, which become latently infected memory B cells resistant to apoptosis via virus-encoded anti-apoptotic molecules, then lodge in the CNS where they produce [passage text removed] ([Trends Immunol S1471490603002874]([passage text removed]); [PMC3764840]([passage text removed])). Mechanistically, latency proteins mimic B cell activation signals: LMP2A modifies activation and survival of host B cells and could mimic a BCR signal, stimulate autoantibody production and enhance antigen presentation by autoreactive B cells ([PMC11076709]([passage text removed])). A 2026 study reports that [passage text removed] LMP1 leads to demyelinating lesion formation ([Kim et al., Cell S0092-8674(25)01480-1]([passage text removed])); LMP1 is described as mimicking CD40L so that infected myelin-reactive B cells no longer need T cell help to escape activation-induced cell death after entering the CNS ([ECTRIMS spotlight]([passage text removed])).

## 4. Altered antigen presentation and B–T cell autoproliferation

EBV infection reprograms the transcriptome and HLA-DR15 immunopeptidome of infected B cells, and identical MBP peptides were found [passage text removed] or thymus; peripheral and CSF CD4+ T cells of HLA-DR15+ patients responded to MBP(78–90)/MBP(83–90) ([Cell S0092867425014953]([passage text removed])). Independently, memory B cells drive HLA-DR-dependent "autoproliferation" of brain-homing Th1 CD4+ T cells in HLA-DR15+ patients, with RASGRP2 identified as a target autoantigen expressed in B cells and brain ([Jelcic, Cell PMC6191934]([passage text removed])); a T cell clone recognising RASGRP2 also reacted to EBV and *Akkermansia*, with EBV peptides deriving from the lytic products BHRF1 and BPLF1 ([PMC7707104]([passage text removed])).

## 5. Bystander activation ("hit-and-run")

[passage text removed] infectious mononucleosis could generate pathogenic autoreactive T cells, a mechanism contrasted with the "driver" model in which EBV reactivation in latently infected B cells drives EBV-specific T cell activation and CNS pathology ([Neurology NXI 10.1212/NXI.0000000000200460]([passage text removed])).

## 6. Defective immune control, immune evasion, and virus-driven immunopathology

MS patients show [passage text removed] from onset onward, progressive decline of EBV-specific CD4+/CD8+ T cells consistent with exhaustion, and an inverse correlation between anti-EBNA1 IgG titre and EBV-specific CD8+ T cell frequency — interpreted as defective CD8+ control permitting expansion [passage text removed] ([PMID 28197337](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28197337)). On the NK/innate side, cytotoxic NKG2C+ and NKG2D+ NK cells plus [passage text removed], and EBV-variant–specific upregulation of HLA-E mediates immune evasion of these autoreactive cells ([Vietzen, Cell S0092-8674(23)01232-1]([passage text removed])). In situ, EBV-specific CD8+ T cells selectively infiltrate the MS brain and interact locally with infected cells, proposed as a virus-driven immunopathological mechanism ([PMC6880158]([passage text removed])); infected B cells in meningeal follicles express PD-L1 adjacent to PD-1+ CD8+ T cells, suggesting local immune evasion sustaining EBV persistence and immunopathology ([PMID 38422689](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38422689)). Aloisi and colleagues have gone further and proposed EBV as the "gluten of MS" — a driver of disease without invoking autoimmunity at all ([PMID 35908445](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35908445)).

## 7. EBV-induced CNS homing of B cells

In humanised mice, [passage text removed]; effector memory CD8+, CD4+ TH1 and TH17 cells co-migrate to the brain, these B cells colonise submeningeal regions even without other lymphocytes and attract T cells, and rituximab or CXCR3 blockade reduces lymphocyte infiltration ([Läderach, Nature; PMID 40770101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40770101); [research.ucc.ie record]([passage text removed])).

## Less-developed strands

Innate/myeloid mechanisms are explicitly flagged as understudied: primary EBV infection alters host cytokine responses, potentially compromising the blood–brain barrier and priming monocytes/macrophages ([Frontiers 10.3389/fimmu.2024.1466339]([passage text removed].1466339/full)). EBV transactivation of HERV-K18 env, a superantigen activating TCRVB13+ T cells, has been proposed as a further route, but the biological relevance of the related HERV-W/MOG cross-reactivity "[passage text removed]" ([Frontiers 10.3389/fimmu.2023.1304281]([passage text removed])).
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

At least six non-exclusive immunological mechanisms have been proposed, with molecular mimicry (EBNA1 ↔ CNS autoantigens) the best-supported, alongside EBV-infected autoreactive B cells, defective CD8⁺ T-cell control of EBV, bystander damage from anti-EBV responses in the CNS, innate immune activation by viral products/endogenous retroviruses, and EBV-driven reprogramming of B-cell antigen presentation in the context of HLA-DR15.

**Background — why a mechanism is needed.** Bjornevik et al.'s nested case-control study of active-duty US military personnel found MS risk markedly elevated after EBV seroconversion (reported as a 32-fold increase), with seroconversion preceding clinical onset by a median of 7.5 years and preceding the rise in serum neurofilament light; no comparable association was seen for CMV or >200 other viruses screened [S:a4cd0fb6-2512-51ab-91cd-f508e1056b70][S:20143047-08ea-5eee-b7e5-e5cdeb9fc29e][S:fbc13a73-0410-5fce-a1f6-1fb6de7456fc].

**1. Molecular mimicry (antibody-mediated).** Lanz et al. showed clonally expanded CSF plasmablasts in MS — the source of oligoclonal bands — encode antibodies binding a specific EBNA1 region that mimics GlialCAM, an astrocyte/oligodendrocyte adhesion molecule; cross-reactivity was confirmed by affinity measurement and by the crystal structure of the EBNA1 epitope–Fab complex, [passage text removed], and EBNA1 immunisation worsened EAE with stronger CD4⁺ T-cell and cytokine responses and more severe demyelination [S:bc9b8173-c8af-508a-a4c8-a45cbde0646b][S:8711672b-4fd2-5f27-a5cf-f1465fcdf028]. The mimicry "hotspot" sits in EBNA1 aa~360–450, the region whose antibodies carry the greatest MS risk, and shows homology to GlialCAM and anoctamin-2 [S:3f6cc33c-c155-5da1-b7a2-4f37b7d0ab70]. Additional cross-reactive targets include αB-crystallin (CRYAB): antibody reactivity to CRYAB aa7–16 was associated with MS, blocking experiments demonstrated EBNA1–CRYAB antibody cross-reactivity, and evidence of T-cell cross-reactivity was also obtained [S:675e69a8-297b-58a9-8215-b900976438ee]. Summary tabulations list EBNA1 mimicry of GlialCAM, CRYAB and ANO2 [S:9b1bf24f-60a3-59da-92d9-45f0cf3d6c97][S:5455f034-f3cc-5c5a-bddd-b431aac802f1].

**2. Molecular mimicry (T-cell-mediated).** The DRB5*0101–EBV peptide complex structurally mimics DRB1*1501-restricted MBP and both are recognised by a patient-derived autoreactive TCR; CSF CD4⁺ T cells specific for EBV DNA polymerase peptide 627–641 cross-recognise the immunodominant MBP 85–99 peptide; and lytic proteins BHRF1/BPLF1 cross-react with the brain- and B-cell-expressed self-protein RASGRP2 targeted by autoreactive CD4⁺ T cells [S:13bf8a18-5e12-5628-b388-0e43c292d018][S:77621bfd-c54e-57fa-a0e9-e4aa64292ef1]. In humanised mice, HLA-DR15⁺ engraftment gave higher EBV loads and EBV-reactive CD4⁺ T cells showed MBP reactivity, supporting a gene–environment interaction [S:5e4627b2-9347-54fe-8ba9-986f302a565f].

**3. EBV-infected autoreactive B cells (Pender hypothesis).** EBV infects autoreactive naive B cells, drives them through germinal centres into latently infected memory B cells that seed the CNS, produce oligoclonal IgG and pathogenic autoantibodies, and act as antigen-presenting cells supplying co-stimulatory (B7/CD28) survival signals that rescue autoreactive T cells from activation-induced apoptosis [S:fdd527b3-2f16-50bc-a35d-ecc701d9a18d][S:babb20a3-3c11-540a-9717-21e655fe827a][S:13065fc5-d5d3-5233-9167-937d0827a956]. LMP1 and LMP2A mimic CD40 and BCR signalling respectively, bypassing tolerance checkpoints, and BHRF1 (a bcl-2 homologue) confers apoptosis resistance [S:13bf8a18-5e12-5628-b388-0e43c292d018][S:8d301e3f-fe39-5c60-a412-2bc9cdde76a3]. A proposed vicious cycle has CNS autoimmunity releasing antigen and CD4⁺ help that in turn sustains infected autoreactive B cells [S:90e7b21e-3724-56d5-bfef-b3eebdf600ef].

**4. Defective CD8⁺ T-cell control of EBV.** MS patients show reduced frequencies [passage text removed], a reduced overall CD8⁺ proportion that declines with age, and a deficiency of effector-memory (EM/EMRA) CD8⁺ T cells present at onset and persisting — proposed to permit [passage text removed] [S:b3cfa4d2-f045-5e00-bcbb-7af8dbdb09ad][S:6be32df5-6b87-53cf-88cd-1de9f787ca2b]. This rationale underpinned autologous EBV-specific CD8⁺ T-cell adoptive immunotherapy in progressive MS [S:2111f068-0b21-543d-afb0-09d43bde2822][S:075956b5-3a57-50d5-879f-46b6f493e634].

**5. Bystander damage / direct latent–lytic drive.** The bystander hypothesis holds that the CNS immune attack is primarily EBV-directed (especially at lytic antigens), with collateral tissue injury; supporting observations include CD8⁺ T cells adjacent to lytically infected plasma cells in brain and expanded lytic-antigen-specific CD8⁺ T cells during active relapsing–remitting disease [S:03ddf6c7-bb74-58f0-bee2-4a00b19a54ff]. Transcriptional profiling of laser-cut brain infiltrates from progressive MS found in-situ EBV deregulation with local antiviral gene programmes, consistent with EBV-induced immunopathology [S:5455034 — corrected: S:5a32f6d9-5b4f-5f6a-9d74-dd8bd673912f]. Critics note this does not explain primary autoimmunity, nor why an EBV-directed response sufficient to damage CNS fails to clear infected B cells [S:90e7b21e-3724-56d5-bfef-b3eebdf600ef]. A current review frames latent–lytic cycling within CNS or periphery as an alternative to mimicry and the basis for anti-EBV therapeutic trials [S:3e0125c6-1986-597a-8176-9410cdb1eb61].

**6. Innate immune activation and endogenous retrovirus induction.** EBER small RNAs released by infected B cells are proposed to stimulate TLR3 on macrophages and microglia, creating an antiviral inflammatory state in the CNS [S:c910deac-b513-5b1e-bf8a-5ad521f11c5d]; EBER-containing exosomes activate TLR3/RIG-I with type I IFN and inflammatory cytokine output and promote dendritic-cell maturation [S:5037839b-4869-5899-ac82-2656913c64b3]. Separately, EBV (including its gp350 envelope protein) activates HERV-W/MSRV/syncytin-1 in blood- and brain-derived cells in vitro, and HERV-W activation is higher during infectious mononucleosis and in people with high anti-EBNA1 IgG — the "dual virus" hypothesis, with HERV-K18/-W products also acting as superantigens [S:ae6b5c65-9377-5f34-9f75-e3f748a84972][S:e0b0e233-ef03-55aa-8d5d-acf8990d4a63][S:db07a86c-7c34-5b8a-8a4c-9f458e0f689d].

**7. Altered antigen presentation / "mistaken self" and immune dysregulation.** EBV reprograms the transcriptome and HLA-DR15 immunopeptidome of infected B cells, activating autoreactive CD4⁺ T cells [S:5455f034-f3cc-5c5a-bddd-b431aac802f1]; memory B cells from HLA-DR15⁺ patients activate CD4⁺ T cells via RASGRP2 and DR2a/DR2b-derived self-peptides, with CSF CD4⁺ T cells cross-reactive to RASGRP2, MBP, EBV and a gut commensal peptide [S:bbd518b9-be71-55cb-860b-24957b67792b]. The αB-crystallin "mistaken self" model posits EBV-induced αB-crystallin expression in B cells, HLA-DR-restricted presentation, and a CD4⁺ Th1 attack on oligodendrocyte αB-crystallin — a mechanism that explains propagation rather than initiation [S:c910deac-b513-5b1e-bf8a-5ad521f11c5d][S:43da5fc5-6221-5745-8b5b-fcb5047b83f9]. EBV's viral IL-10 homologue has been proposed to subvert IL-10-mediated immune regulation [S:2ce7817b-297a-5dc4-9981-322d508c1466][S:a04d3e4e-d3af-5042-b42f-da6f4630d9ea]. A broader framing contrasts two mechanistic families: amplification over years of immune responses primed during symptomatic primary infection (infectious mononucleosis) versus failure to control EBV-infected B cells in genetically predisposed hosts — hypotheses that imply opposite therapeutic directions [S:f04efb64-9c13-5822-b73e-6bfad4876e24].

**Caveats.** Several mechanisms remain contested: whether EBV-infected B cells are reliably present in MS brain has yielded conflicting findings [S:13065fc5-d5d3-5233-9167-937d0827a956][S:ae6b5c65-9377-5f34-9f75-e3f748a84972], and T-cell cross-reactivity and bystander damage have both been argued to be contributory rather than primary [S:03ddf6c7-bb74-58f0-bee2-4a00b19a54ff].

rows.question: After initial resuscitation in septic shock, what outcomes follow a restrictive fluid strategy versus fluid guided by dynamic responsiveness testing?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: In-hospital mortality did not differ between a restrictive fluid strategy and fluid guided by dynamic responsiveness testing after initial resuscitation; The restrictive protocol delivered substantially less total fluid than dynamic responsiveness-guided care; Dialysis and mechanical ventilation were used more often in the restrictive arm, an observed excess in patients who began sicker rather than a demonstrated harm of restriction; Duration of intensive care stay and of ventilator support was similar under both fluid strategies. Certainty: Because the mortality and organ-support comparisons rest on small numbers of patients from one hospital whose groups differed at the outset, the similar outcomes are best read as an early signal rather than settled evidence, while the smaller volume delivered follows directly from the restrictive strategy itself. Scope: applies to septic shock after initial fluid resuscitation in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the similar outcomes as established equivalence or non-inferiority of restrictive fluid administration, or recommends abandoning dynamic responsiveness testing on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

No adequately powered trial has directly compared a restrictive strategy against a dynamic-responsiveness-guided strategy; the two literatures run in parallel. Restrictive strategies reliably cut fluid exposure but have consistently shown **no mortality benefit** in large trials, while responsiveness-guided strategies (smaller trials, higher risk of bias) show lower fluid balance with **signals of organ-support and mortality benefit** of low-to-moderate certainty. The only head-to-head comparison is a single small pilot showing essentially similar outcomes.

## Restrictive fluid after initial resuscitation: neutral

- **[passage text removed] of fluid (median ~3 L pre-randomisation) to restrictive vs standard IV fluid. Despite clear separation (median ICU IV fluid 1798 mL vs 3811 mL), 90-day mortality was 42.3% vs 42.1% ([passage text removed]). Serious adverse events (29.4% vs 30.8%), [passage text removed] out of hospital did not differ [PMID 35709019; NCT03668236]. Prespecified 1-year follow-up found similar survival, health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L, EQ-VAS) and cognitive function (Mini-MoCA), though clinically important differences could not be excluded (99% CI for mortality −4.8 to 7.8) [doi:10.1007/s00134-023-07114-8].
- **CLOVERS** tested the earlier, ED-phase version (restrictive + early vasopressors vs liberal, for 24 h after 1–3 L). It was stopped for futility at 1563 patients: death before discharge home by day 90 was 14.0% vs 14.9% (difference −0.9 [passage text removed]), despite a median 24-h fluid difference of −2134 mL (95% CI −2318 to −1949) and earlier/longer vasopressor use in the restrictive arm [PMID 36688507; NCT03434028]. Secondary organ-support, ventilator-free, RRT-free and ICU-free days at 28 days were similar.
- Pooled evidence agrees: a Bayesian meta-analysis of restrictive vs standard IV fluid in ICU sepsis found a 90-day mortality risk difference of 0.2 percentage [passage text removed]; RR 1.00, 95% CrI 0.89–1.14) [doi:10.1111/aas.14345]. Other syntheses report no mortality difference with possible reductions in AKI/ARDS and mechanical-ventilation dependence [PMID 41953594; PMID 40739606].

## Dynamic responsiveness–guided fluid: signals of benefit, weaker evidence

- **FRESH** (n=124 septic shock, 13 US/UK hospitals) used passive leg raise–induced stroke volume change before each clinically driven bolus or vasopressor increase. In the modified ITT population, 72-h/ICU-discharge fluid balance was lower (0.65 ± 2.85 L vs 2.02 ± 3.44 L; difference −1.37 L; P=.021), with fewer patients requiring [passage text removed]), and more discharged home alive (63.9% vs 43.9%); no safety differences in the all-randomised population [PMID 32353418; NCT02837731].
- A 2025 systematic review (9 RCTs, n=698) found dynamic-responsiveness-guided fluid **[passage text removed] AKI** (RR 0.66; 0.44–0.98, low certainty) and day-3 cumulative fluid balance (MD −1.57 L; −2.44 to −0.69, low certainty), with **uncertain** effects on ICU mortality, ICU/hospital length of stay, need for or duration of ventilation, RRT, and vasopressor use. The authors flag high risk of bias from deviations in intended interventions and heterogeneous definitions of responsiveness [PMID 40953281; doi:10.1097/CCE.0000000000001303].
- Countervailing evidence: an earlier meta-analysis (4 studies, n=365) found no mortality benefit (pooled OR [passage text removed]) [doi:10.1097/CCE.0000000000000015], and a 2025 network meta-analysis of non-invasive strategies (20 RCTs, 2435 patients) found passive leg raise + stroke volume versus usual care did not reduce short-term mortality ([passage text removed]), with no strategy superior to usual care [doi:10.1007/s11739-025-04179-9].

## The one direct comparison

A single-centre pilot RCT at Cairo University randomised 80 septic shock patients after early resuscitation to a fixed restrictive rate (1 mL/kg/h) vs dynamic testing–guided fluid. Total fluid volume and vasopressor days were lower with restriction, whereas need for mechanical ventilation (P=0.050) and dialysis (P=0.004) were higher; ICU length of stay, ventilator days and in-hospital mortality did not differ. Crucially, baseline APACHE II, SOFA, lactate and creatinine were significantly *higher* and MAP/oxygenation lower in the restrictive arm, and the authors list small size, single centre, no blinding and no 90-day mortality as limitations — so the organ-support difference cannot be attributed to strategy [doi:10.1007/s44349-026-00042-8].

## Interpretation for practice

Guidelines reflect this asymmetry: Surviving Sepsis suggests dynamic measures over physical examination or static parameters alone (conditional/weak recommendation, low-to-very-low certainty), while stating there was **insufficient evidence** to recommend restrictive versus liberal strategies in the first 24 h [doi:10.1007/s00134-021-06506-y; sccm.org guidelines]. Practically, restriction after initial resuscitation is *safe but not superior*, and its main proven effect is reduced fluid exposure; responsiveness testing may achieve similar fluid limitation while individualising who still benefits from a bolus, but the outcome evidence rests on small trials at high risk of bias and has not been tested against a protocolised restrictive strategy in an adequately powered trial. Related work also shows that restrictive protocols can be hard to implement — CLASSIC had non-trivial protocol violations, and a French pilot targeting non-resuscitative fluids failed to reduce day-5 cumulative fluid balance [criticalcarereviews.com/foundational-trials/classic; doi:10.1186/s13054-025-05624-z summary of Boulet et al.].
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Head-to-head evidence is limited to one small randomized trial, and it found the two strategies essentially equivalent: no difference in adjusted in-hospital mortality, dialysis, mechanical ventilation, or ICU length of stay. Everything beyond that is indirect (each strategy vs. usual care), and equally null for mortality.

## Direct comparison

A single-centre RCT at Cairo University randomized 80 septic shock patients 1:1, after initial resuscitation per Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines (30 mL/kg crystalloid), to either a restrictive protocol (fixed 1 mL/kg/h) or a dynamic-testing protocol using passive leg raising with a ≥10% rise in cardiac output defining responsiveness [S:1a262f96][S:19e25ed1]. Adjusted in-hospital mortality did not differ ([passage text removed], 95% CI 0.212–3.935), and [passage text removed], mechanical ventilation, or ICU length of stay [S:b19c50a9][S:19e25ed1].

Two caveats from the authors themselves:
- In unadjusted comparison, mechanical ventilation and dialysis were *more* frequent in the restrictive arm (P = 0.050 and 0.004), but severity scores and baseline creatinine were higher in that arm at randomization; the authors attribute this to selection bias, and logistic regression adjusting for baseline creatinine abolished the difference [S:9d3f3dda][S:066e474d].
- Restrictive management did not worsen kidney function, and 3-hour lactate did not differ between arms [S:9d3f3dda][S:19e25ed1]. Restrictively managed patients had lower baseline P/F ratios that then improved significantly, whereas change in the dynamic arm was not significant [S:9d3f3dda].

## Indirect evidence for each arm

**Restrictive vs. usual/liberal care.** CLASSIC (1554 patients, 31 European ICUs, all receiving ≥1 L before randomization) showed no difference in 90-day mortality or secondary outcomes, and no increase in serious adverse events [S:bb223ccf][S:3970b6ed]. CLOVERS (1563 patients, 60 US centres) likewise found no mortality difference (14.0% restrictive vs 14.9% liberal, [passage text removed]%) despite clear volume separation (median 1267 mL vs 3400 mL over 24 h) [S:f5fae4a3]. The earlier CLASSIC pilot (151 patients) reduced 5-day resuscitation fluid (−1.2 L) with less [passage text removed] a non-significant mortality point estimate favouring restriction [S:f56929d4][S:896310a3]. A post hoc CLASSIC analysis found no difference in time to resolution of hyperlactatemia [S:d16472ae][S:3e409719].

**Dynamic responsiveness-guided fluid vs. comparators.** A randomized trial of dynamic IVC- vs static CVP-guided resuscitation (124 septic patients) found no 30-day mortality difference ([passage text removed]; RR [passage text removed]) but shorter shock duration (0.8 vs 1.5 days, p=0.001) and lower cumulative norepinephrine dose (6.8 vs 16.1 mg, p=0.008) [S:7326b445][S:d5283fa5]. A meta-analysis of PLR-guided resuscitation trials found no mortality benefit, echoing a prior analysis of 365 patients across 4 trials [S:09506775]. The FRESH trial (83 intervention, 41 usual care) reported less fluid over 72 h (3354 ± 2180 vs 4721 ± 3319 mL, p=0.007) [S:23a9ffa4], with lower fluid balance (0.65 ± 2.85 vs 2.02 ± 3.44 L, p=0.021) and fewer patients requiring [passage text removed]) as reported in a review of that trial [S:edaf6d23]. An ANDROMEDA-SHOCK secondary analysis found fluid boluses could be stopped in non-responders without negative impact on clinically relevant outcomes [S:7b5e6dd5].

## Interpretation

No adequately powered trial has compared these two strategies against each other; the one that exists is a single-centre pilot of 80 patients with baseline imbalance, and dynamic-guided trials generally are small, unblinded, and at high risk of bias, with mortality never the primary endpoint [S:09506775]. Practical differences may matter more than outcomes: dynamic testing requires echocardiography, bioreactance or pulse-contour devices that may be infeasible in low-resource settings, whereas a fixed-rate restrictive protocol does not [S:9ca9c3a6].

rows.question: Which factors relate to the duration of mechanical ventilation in patients with myasthenic crisis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Maintenance steroid-sparing immunosuppression already in place at crisis onset is associated with faster extubation, an association clearest in the analysis that adjusts for other predictors; Sepsis arising during the crisis is associated with longer ventilation, roughly a threefold lower rate of extubation at any given time; Older age is associated with a slower rate of extubation and therefore a longer time on the ventilator. Certainty: The findings describe associations noted alongside outcomes rather than established causal effects, and the small number of patients leaves substantial uncertainty around each estimate. Scope: applies to myasthenic crisis requiring ventilatory support in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents lowering the prednisone dose during intensive care as a demonstrated way to shorten mechanical ventilation, or as established practice for cutting ventilator days.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Duration of mechanical ventilation (MV) in myasthenic crisis (MC) is driven by three clusters of factors: **host/baseline factors (older age, multiple comorbidities, late-onset MG, MuSK antibodies, thymoma, high pre-crisis MGFA class), acquired complications (pneumonia, atelectasis, SIRS/sepsis, resuscitation), and management factors (initial NIV trial, first-line plasma exchange/immunoadsorption vs IVIG, pre-existing immunosuppression, timing of tracheostomy and of the first extubation attempt).** Respiratory physiology (vital capacity, maximal inspiratory pressure) contributes but is less consistently reproduced.

## Evidence

**Baseline/host factors.** In the largest multicentre cohort (250 MC episodes, 12 German centres; median MV [passage text removed] MG, high MGFA [passage text removed]); early-onset MG (OR 0.21) and thymic hyperplasia predicted ventilation ≤15 days [[passage text removed]]. A machine-learning model (POLAR) built on the same cohort (195 invasively ventilated patients, MV >15 days as outcome) selected age, ≥3 chronic comorbidities affecting different organ systems, late-onset MG, high pre-crisis MGFA class (IVb), and delirium, pneumonia or cardiopulmonary resuscitation during MC as markers of prolonged MV; first manifestation of MG as MC, low pre-crisis MGFA class and pre-crisis independence predicted shorter MV, whereas smoking and sepsis were not retained [[passage text removed]].

**Antibody status.** MuSK-antibody MC had markedly longer MV than AChR-MC ([passage text removed] days, p < 0.0001), with correspondingly longer ICU and hospital stay; the effect was driven by MuSK-only patients, and MuSK patients more often had ≥3 chronic diseases (OR 4.87) [[passage text removed]].

**Thymoma and pre-admission immunosuppression.** In a single-centre neuro-ICU cohort of 81 MC patients classified by WEAN SAFE criteria (median MV 20 days [11–38]; 55% prolonged wean), [passage text removed], while age was not [[passage text removed]].

**Respiratory/metabolic parameters.** The classic series identified three independent predictors of prolonged intubation: pre-intubation serum bicarbonate ≥30 mg/dL (relative hazard 4.5), peak vital capacity on days 1–6 post-intubation <25 mL/kg (relative hazard 2.9), and age >50 y (relative hazard 2.4); the proportion intubated >2 weeks rose from 0% with no risk factors to 88% with all three [[passage text removed]]. In a protocolised weaning cohort (126 MC episodes, median MV 14 days), each additional day of MV before weaning increased prolonged-weaning risk [passage text removed]%), higher MIP reduced it (3.4% per cmH₂O), and an infectious/identified trigger also related to weaning outcome; pulmonary function tests did not identify extubation failure — the authors explicitly did not reproduce the earlier association with lower forced VC [[passage text removed]].

**Infectious/inflammatory complications.** In a Chinese MC cohort, the short-weaning group had markedly shorter ventilation than the difficult/prolonged-weaning group ([passage text removed]] days, p < 0.001), and multivariate analysis identified pneumonia and [passage text removed] of difficult/prolonged weaning; lowest haemoglobin and lowest serum albumin were also lower in the prolonged group [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35148922]. In a 2025 cohort of 57 MCs, sepsis independently predicted longer [passage text removed]) and longer ICU stay, whereas maintenance immunosuppression at MC onset predicted faster extubation (HR [passage text removed]); age >50 y (OR 7.74) and prednisone ≥60 mg/day in ICU (OR 13.07) predicted sepsis development [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40698586]. Earlier work found atelectasis, transfusion-treated anaemia, *C. difficile* infection and congestive heart failure associated with prolonged intubation [[passage text removed]].

**Weaning/extubation course and airway management.** Weaning failure occurred in 64.2% of MC episodes and was associated with older age, ≥3 comorbidities (OR 4.04), late-onset MG (OR 2.84), atelectasis (OR 3.40), pneumonia (OR 3.45), CPR (OR 5.00) and sepsis (OR 2.57); extubation failure (43% of first attempts) was associated with prolonged MV, ICU and hospital stay, and extubation success was most likely between day 7 and 12 after intubation [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37923937]. Tracheostomy was performed in 107/215 MC (49.8%) and tracheostomised patients had much longer MV (34.4 ± 27.7 vs 7.9 ± 7.8 days); among those tracheostomised, early tracheostomy (≤day 10) correlated with shorter ICU MV (26.2 ± 18.1 vs 42.0 ± 33.1 days, p = 0.006) and shorter ICU stay [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33233998].

**Immunotherapy and ventilation strategy.** NIV sufficed in 38% of 92 crises and was accompanied by shorter ventilation (mean 6.7 [passage text removed] ICU stay; patients receiving [passage text removed]), and sequential combination of IVIG with PE/IA became more likely as MV and ICU stay lengthened [[passage text removed]]. Weaning failure was more frequent with IVIG (OR 2.53) than with first-line PE/immunoadsorption [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37923937]. In MuSK-MC, first-line PE/IA tended to shorten MV versus IVIG, but the difference was not significant ([passage text removed] days, p = 0.36) [[passage text removed]]. A separate cohort found plasma exchange during MC associated with early extubation, and older age, atelectasis and ventilator-associated pneumonia associated with prolonged ventilation [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27856933].

**Post-thymectomy MC (distinct setting).** In 70 patients with post-thymectomy MC, alcohol abuse and higher MGFA and Clavien-Dindo classification scores delayed early extubation [[passage text removed]]. Note these post-surgical predictors should not be generalised to spontaneous MC.

## Caveats
Nearly all evidence is retrospective and single- or multi-centre observational, so associations (especially for immunotherapy choice and tracheostomy timing) are confounded by severity; the German multicentre cohort underlies several of the analyses cited above (250-case cohort, POLAR, tracheostomy and weaning-failure papers), so those findings are not statistically independent [[passage text removed]; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33233998; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37923937]. Age and vital capacity are inconsistent across cohorts (age not predictive of prolonged weaning in the WEAN SAFE cohort; VC not reproduced in the protocolised-weaning cohort) [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Duration of mechanical ventilation in myasthenic crisis (MC) is driven by four clusters of factors: **patient/host characteristics (older age, comorbidity burden, late-onset MG), pre-crisis MG severity and thymoma, in-ICU complications (pneumonia/VAP, atelectasis, sepsis, delirium, resuscitation), and management choices (ventilation mode, immunotherapy, timing of tracheostomy).**

### Patient and disease characteristics
- Age >50 years is a recurrent independent predictor of prolonged intubation (>14 days), alongside [passage text removed]–6 and serum bicarbonate ≥30 mmol/L; patients with none of these were all intubated <2 weeks, whereas 88–90% with all three had prolonged intubation, and prolonged intubation carried ~3× longer hospitalisation and less functional independence at discharge [S:a0f5bf8a][S:f994e3b5][S:f26461f1].
- In a 33-patient extubation-outcome cohort, male sex, age >50 years, atelectasis and VAP were significantly more frequent among those ventilated >15 days; AChR-antibody status and the identifiable cause of MC were not associated [S:a45b8b69][S:8d0d505b].
- A single-centre Chinese series found age, infectious precipitant, atelectasis, pneumonia and bacteraemia significant on univariate analysis, with age, atelectasis and pneumonia retained on multivariate analysis [S:ab7f1cb2].
- In the largest cohort (250 MC cases), [passage text removed] >3 comorbidities [S:9679b26b][S:5e8f1f33].
- The derived POLAR prediction model (AUC 0.78) uses six factors raising risk of MV >15 days — age, ≥3 chronic comorbidities affecting different organ systems, late-onset MG, high pre-crisis MGFA class (IVb), and delirium, pneumonia or cardiopulmonary resuscitation during MC — and three protective factors: MC as first manifestation, low pre-crisis MGFA class, and pre-crisis independence; smoking and sepsis did not contribute meaningfully in that model [S:bc59b357][S:e859d5da]. The authors note the score is more reliable at ICU days 5–6 than in the first 48 h, since complications accrue early [S:695f6a17].
- Other cited series identified pre-intubation PaCO₂ and higher MG-ADL, [passage text removed] as predictors of ventilation duration/ICU stay [S:5e8f1f33].
- In a recent WEAN-Safe–classified cohort (81 patients; median MV 20 days), only **[passage text removed] — age alone was not, and no difference was seen between early/late-onset and [passage text removed] older group [S:a7319a03][S:77e0d446][S:ac29187d]. Candidate variables tested there (from prior literature) included cardiovascular comorbidity, hypercapnic respiratory failure, infectious cause and VAP before the first separation attempt [S:f74647d8].

### Complications and weaning-related factors
- Sepsis independently prolonged [passage text removed]) and ICU stay; sepsis itself was predicted by age >50 (OR 7.74) and prednisone ≥60 mg/day in ICU (OR 13.07). Conversely, maintenance steroid-sparing immunosuppression at MC onset predicted faster extubation (HR [passage text removed]) [S:3a4242ab].
- Atelectasis is the dominant risk factor for extubation failure (present in all reintubated patients in two retrospective studies), with older age, pneumonia, acidosis, decreased vital capacity and need for NIV also predicting reintubation; reintubation in turn lengthens ICU and hospital stay and increases VAP [S:09bfe137][S:a0f5bf8a]. Predictors of extubation failure also include prior MC history and long intubation duration; clinical bulbar/neck-flexor assessment matters because respiratory indices can be falsely reassuring [S:a19c5c04].
- Weaning failure has been reported in a majority of MG patients, with advanced age, hypertension/diabetes/cardiac disease, atelectasis, pneumonia, cardiopulmonary resuscitation and sepsis as risk factors, and plasmapheresis associated with lower risk than IVIg [S:214bb6ed]. In one series, early plasma exchange was associated with early extubation (≤7 days) [S:a45b8b69]. Neurogenic dysphagia has also been flagged as a factor associated with prolonged ventilation and prolonged tracheostomy need in neuromuscular disease [S:d834096d].

### Management factors
- Initial NIV rather than intubation was associated with shorter ventilatory support (median 4 vs 9 days) and about one-third less ICU and hospital time; NIV success predictors were bicarbonate <30 mmol/L and APACHE II <6, failure predictor hypercapnia (PCO₂ >45 mmHg) [S:d4982ca4].
- Timing of tracheostomy matters: in a 12-centre German analysis, tracheostomy was performed in 107/215 crises; tracheostomised patients had far longer MV (34.4 ± 27.7 vs 7.9 ± 7.8 days) and ICU stay, and tracheostomy within 10 days versus later was associated with shorter MV (26.2 ± 18.1 vs 42.0 ± 33.1 days, p = 0.006) and ICU stay (26.2 ± 14.6 vs 42.3 ± 33.0 days, p = 0.003), with the two groups otherwise comparable [S:f785fae5][S:210f8259][S:22a72267].

### Caveats
Evidence is almost entirely retrospective and single- or few-centre; POLAR has not been prospectively validated [S:695f6a17]. Findings conflict on age and thymoma (independent in some cohorts, not in the WEAN-Safe cohort [S:a7319a03]), and centre-specific weaning practice strongly shapes measured duration [S:863c666e][S:ac29187d]. In post-thymectomy MG (a distinct setting), duration of MG and pyridostigmine dose were not associated with prolonged MV, whereas higher Osserman class, prior MC, AChR seropositivity, low preoperative vital capacity and thymoma were [S:0ca827da].

rows.question: Which imaging measures relate to disability progression that occurs independently of relapses in multiple sclerosis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Measures of cortical damage are central to predicting progression of disability that occurs without relapses; Spinal cord degeneration also carries prognostic relevance for disability progression in multiple sclerosis; Cortical thickness in the temporal lobe emerged as the strongest imaging predictor of time to relapse-independent progression. Certainty: Links between these imaging measures and later relapse-independent progression are observed associations rather than demonstrated causes, and the ranking of predictors rests on few progression events. Scope: applies to multiple sclerosis in adults under regular clinical evaluation, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents cortical or spinal cord degeneration as a demonstrated cause of relapse-independent progression or recommends treatment escalation targeted at it on that basis.

answers.websearch:
**Conclusion:** PIRA is most consistently linked to imaging markers of chronic, "smouldering" inflammation and neurodegeneration rather than new lesion counts — specifically cervical spinal cord atrophy, whole-brain/cortical grey-matter atrophy and cortical thinning, paramagnetic rim lesions (PRLs), slowly expanding lesions (SELs), cortical lesions, deep grey-matter (thalamic) volume, choroid plexus enlargement, and retinal layer thinning on OCT.

**Spinal cord and brain atrophy.** In the Swiss MS Cohort, patients with PIRA had faster cervical cord atrophy than clinically stable patients (mean difference in annual percentage change −[passage text removed].0008), holding also when restricted to RRMS (−[passage text removed]); baseline C2–C3 cross-sectional area (HR [passage text removed]), brain parenchymal fraction (HR 0.59) and cortical fraction (HR 0.68) predicted time to PIRA, while thalamic fraction did not, and cord area plus cortical fraction remained independent of T2 lesion volume ([PMC10834139](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10834139); [Neurology 2024;102:e207768]([passage text removed])). Earlier work from the same group showed PIRA was associated with accelerated loss of total brain volume (MD-APC −0.36), total and cortical grey matter (−0.59 and −0.71), faster ventricular enlargement (+1.50), and cortical thinning in temporal, frontal, parietal, insular and cingulate cortex ([PMC9112138]([passage text removed])). Cervical cord atrophy has separately been identified as the strongest predictor of "silent progression" and SPMS conversion in relapsing MS ([Ann Neurol 2022;91:268-281, via]([passage text removed])).

**Chronic active lesions (PRLs, SELs).** In the same Swiss cohort, PRL burden was higher in patients with PIRA than in those without disability accumulation ([passage text removed]) ([PMC10834139](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10834139)). A systematic review/meta-analysis of five studies (744 patients) found PRL presence associated with higher PIRA risk (OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.17–4.29), stronger in studies with ≤4 years follow-up (OR 2.84) ([Zarco 2025, PMID 41205558]([passage text removed])). A large single-centre 5-year cohort reported PRL presence roughly doubled PIRA risk (adjusted HR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1–2.8) and correlated with future brain atrophy rates ([news.medxy.ai summary of the Neurology cohort]([passage text removed])). SELs are the longitudinal counterpart; their diffusion signature (lower fractional anisotropy in lesion core/perilesional tissue) was associated with PIRA ([JNNP 2026;97:405-412]([passage text removed])), and SELs and PRLs co-occur, with joint presence linked to greater EDSS increase (beta = 0.15/year, 95% CI 0.04–0.27) ([Mult Scler 2023;29:352-362, via MAGNIMS]([passage text removed])).

**Cortical lesions and deep grey matter.** In early MS, baseline thalamic volume (HR 0.98), cortical thickness [passage text removed]) and cortical lesion number (HR 1.15) were independent predictors of PIRA after adjustment for age and sex ([NXI 10.1212/NXI.0000000000200399](https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/NXI.0000000000200399)).

**Choroid plexus.** On 7T/3T imaging, choroid plexus ratio correlated with PRL and cortical lesion volume (r = 0.35) and was a key predictor of PIRA in a gradient-boosting model [passage text removed] ([PMID 40854683](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40854683)); in another cohort high choroid plexus volume conferred a 2.7-fold increased PIRA risk ([Cell Rep Med, PMC12923943]([passage text removed])). Baseline PRLs and choroid plexus volume were also associated with *cognitive* PIRMA in early RRMS ([PMC13394531]([passage text removed])).

**OCT (retinal imaging).** Retinal thinning tracks PIRA: each PIRA event per decade corresponded to −2.28 µm pRNFL (95% CI −4.32 to −0.24) and −1.70 µm mGCIPL (95% CI −2.97 to −0.42), with all three measures including inner nuclear layer associated with PIRMA ([J Neurol 2025, 10.1007/s00415-025-13185-y, summarised]([passage text removed])); the original observation that retinal layer thinning reflects PIRA is in [PMC7604994]([passage text removed]), and Austrian consensus recommendations note pRNFL/[passage text removed] PIRA and PIRMA ([PMC12701873]([passage text removed])).

**Conventional-MRI/composite prediction.** A machine-learning model using routine features found baseline disability and MRI predicted 24-month PIRA (AUC 0.73), improving at 36 months (AUC 0.83) when brain volume change, new cervical cord lesions and connectivity (ChaCo) features were added ([S0022510X26001280]([passage text removed])).

**Important caveat.** Part of what is labelled PIRA is accompanied by focal inflammatory activity: in one cohort 30.8% of PIRA events occurred with concurrent MRI activity, and adding new T2/Gd lesions to the definition (PIRMA) halved event numbers (from 47.9% to 23.4%); asymptomatic spinal cord lesions occur in 15%–25% of relapse-free RRMS patients, so brain-only MRI underestimates activity ([Neurology 2024;103:e209444]([passage text removed]); [MAGNIMS commentary PDF]([passage text removed])). MAGNIMS therefore proposes "advanced-PIRMA," incorporating cord lesions, PRLs, SELs, brain and cord atrophy, OCT and fluid biomarkers ([Neurology 2024;103:e209444]([passage text removed])).
answers.connect:
**Conclusion:** Progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) is most consistently linked to imaging markers of neurodegeneration and chronic/compartmentalised inflammation rather than to new lesion formation — above all spinal cord atrophy, cortical and deep grey matter atrophy/ventricular enlargement, chronic active lesions (paramagnetic rim lesions and slowly expanding lesions), cortical lesion burden, choroid plexus enlargement, and retinal inner-layer thinning on OCT.

**1. Spinal cord atrophy — the most robust single predictor.** In a machine-learning feature-selection study across two cohorts, [passage text removed] also predicted PIRA; selected predictors of time to PIRA included C3 and C4 cross-sectional area (CSA) in cohort 1 and CSA at C1–C3 in cohort 2, with C3 CSA the strongest predictor in the relapsing–remitting subgroup, and effects independent of spinal cord lesion burden [S:fb4105ad-9d53-5ba8-8e12-593cb6668cf5][S:bc79e41a-423c-5ed4-879a-d11045a894b8][S:43e0d8fb-6bb6-5351-9b12-6d545672318a][S:fb237fe0-0461-5e0a-957e-7ab3322286d1]. A review of spinal cord imaging states [passage text removed] worsening, "particularly for PIRA," citing faster C1-level atrophy predicting SPMS conversion >4 years in advance and also predicting relapse-free worsening, and C1–C3 atrophy predicting shorter time to PIRA in the Swiss MS Cohort [S:e8d7fcc6-99e8-5b4b-ade4-95af1b774c55]. In a 12-year single-centre study of silent (relapse-independent) progression, spinal cord atrophy was the strongest predictor: a 1% faster cord atrophy rate was associated with 69% shorter time to silent progression [S:0ce9a141-fac7-525a-a5dd-6e87ec02254f]. Reported cord atrophy rates were −1.1%/year in silent progressors versus −0.72%/year in clinically stable patients [S:22434ccd-078d-5419-bda9-a3d0175f9d4d]. Spinal cord *lesion* number has also been identified as the only baseline predictor distinguishing PIRA from relapse-associated worsening in a newly diagnosed cohort [S:3162edaf-69dd-5798-9c9a-6b80929ad657].

**2. Grey matter atrophy and ventricular enlargement.** In the Italian Neuroimaging Network cohort, patients with progression free of both clinical *and* MRI activity (PIRMA) had greater baseline WM lesion volume, GM atrophy and functional connectivity alterations; regression identified higher EDSS, age, cortical atrophy and FC alterations as predictors [S:ddcbd474-416a-5c47-8241-300546ff8258][S:22f61082-1c6f-5cb3-b077-034b544433e7]. In the MSBase registry (n=1598 RRMS), baseline lateral ventricular volume significantly predicted [passage text removed]) whereas whole brain and grey matter volume predicted other disability outcomes but not PIRA specifically [S:d3dd7bec-9e8c-5f47-97b8-fd1bf1a56079][S:f0287c18-7fbf-5c3c-b241-cde7cf49ccd2]. Ventricular enlargement was also the strongest *brain* predictor of silent progression (each 1% enlargement → 16% shorter time to silent progression, p=0.007) [S:0ce9a141-fac7-525a-a5dd-6e87ec02254f]. Regional measures selected for time to PIRA included temporal-lobe cortical thickness, ventricular, caudate, deep grey matter and thalamic volumes; temporal cortical thickness was the only predictor retained in the RRMS subgroup [S:bc79e41a-423c-5ed4-879a-d11045a894b8]. Independently, whole brain volume loss has been prospectively studied as a biomarker of PIRA in relapse-activity-free patients [S:c7b75df2-f496-50c9-a2be-6bba5ced9c64].

**3. Chronic active lesions (PRLs and SELs).** PRLs are described as [passage text removed] and of a more aggressive motor/cognitive course [S:56313a01-2422-59e1-bead-891a69bf880d]. A 10-year study found PRL presence associated with greater EDSS change and greater relapse rates, and PRL *number* with greater odds of PIRA — an effect the authors interpret as relapse-independent, driven by gradual tissue destruction from chronic active inflammation [S:a5bbb076-f0ac-581b-bdd1-012a44b17053][S:67028be0-c9fa-5be1-940c-b2eda6b449ab]. A biomarker-validation table reports greater PRL number associated with higher odds of ≥1 PIRA episode (exp(β)=1.17, p=0.009) and higher PRL burden linked with PIRA in a multicentre cohort ([passage text removed]) [S:2bfc2a0d-1526-5ced-9d8b-ef8e0a9f0c84]. Note contrary evidence: one 10-year analysis concluded baseline PRL presence did *not* predict disability progression [S:b573dcd4-6792-515c-9098-79157201f05f]. For SELs, diffusion metrics matter: lower mean fractional anisotropy in the core of [passage text removed]–0.12, p=0.001) and faster time to PIRA (core HR 0.03, 95% CI 0–0.49, p=0.015; perilesional HR 0.11, 95% CI 0.01–0.95, p=0.045), whereas baseline SEL volume was not predictive [S:baf4b5b7-aef4-57ed-8e28-5f1ea9c021f6][S:9a0ad69b-4cd9-52a6-83ed-fa06ba3c7aa8].

**4. Cortical lesions.** In an 18-year cohort, patients with PIRA had markedly higher cortical lesion number and volume at diagnosis; multivariate models confirmed cortical lesion number (HR 1.15) and volume as predictive of PIRA, with ≥3 cortical lesions the optimal cut-off (HR 12.2, 95% [passage text removed]:53d42d64-c722-5a82-a226-f189bea9de8b].

**5. Choroid plexus volume.** In a prospective multicentre study (891 people with MS screened, 434 analysed), high CP volume conferred a 2.7-fold increased risk of PIRA ([passage text removed]) versus 1.8-fold for EDSS worsening generally, and remained significant after adjusting for sNfL (HR [passage text removed]); CP volume was *not* associated with relapse-associated worsening [S:d158561e-5d39-5616-a43a-cd456ef882f9][S:cb3ef282-9188-5608-ac75-d7a209e1f750]. Mechanistically, CP volume tracks chronic lesion expansion and brain atrophy [S:96374ee9-6c4a-5e09-9b28-2ee4000391fd][S:ea784d77-0cc3-5760-b283-4122d1b0df0d].

**6. OCT retinal layers.** In a 4-year prospective study of 171 relapsing MS patients, each PIRA event was associated with additional loss of macular [passage text removed]), while relapses without EDSS worsening did not influence retinal thinning [S:43971182-e259-56e4-845f-48de83ec3679][S:834f1c50-6e0f-588d-b1f0-7b915e22e5fa]. A longer-observation cohort likewise related pRNFL and mGCIPL to PIRA risk, favouring these over the inner nuclear layer [S:7a638797-8570-5d09-81b9-44c0bd20f3b8][S:bc02a63c-4ee0-5c87-90fe-6fbd60289d5a].

**Caveats.** A dedicated review of PIRA biomarkers notes that MRI and OCT metrics "often reflect both inflammatory and neurodegenerative processes," that current biomarkers do not cleanly separate PIRA from relapse-associated activity, and distinguishes *predicting* PIRA from *measuring* it in real time [S:5c0a1619-64e4-5511-a993-81ae41469936]. Also, excluding new T2 lesions (PIRMA) roughly halves event counts, implying a substantial share of nominal "PIRA" is attributable to subclinical lesion activity [S:6b3fa932-0bc1-5d53-b92e-5afe9ba59ece].

rows.question: In people with relapsing multiple sclerosis, what disease activity outcomes follow treatment with cladribine tablets?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Relapse activity was substantially lower during cladribine tablet treatment than in the year before starting; Most treated patients remained free of relapses, disability progression and new lesions, with residual activity more often radiological than clinical; Treatment-naive patients and those switching from platform therapies showed better clinical and radiological response than patients switching from highly effective therapies. Certainty: The evidence derives from extensive real-world clinical practice data, yet rests on comparisons within the same patients and between groups defined by prior therapy rather than by allocation, so it supports association rather than demonstrated causal benefit. Scope: applies to relapsing multiple sclerosis treated with cladribine tablets in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the observed reduction in disease activity as demonstrating that cladribine tablets are more effective than other disease-modifying therapies, or recommends them in preference to those therapies on this basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** Cladribine tablets 3.5 mg/kg produce a roughly 55–58% reduction in annualized relapse rate versus placebo, ~73–86% suppression of MRI lesion activity, reduced disability-progression risk, and a 2.5–4-fold higher chance of being free of all disease activity (NEDA/NEDA-3) — with benefits appearing within 1–2 months of dosing and persisting for years after the two short treatment courses stop.

**Relapse outcomes (pivotal trial).** In CLARITY (NCT00213135; n=1326), ARR over 96 weeks was 0.14 with cladribine 3.5 mg/kg vs 0.33 with placebo (57.6% relative reduction, p<0.001; 0.15 with 5.25 mg/kg, 54.5% reduction), and 79.7% vs 60.9% of patients remained relapse-free (OR 2.53, p<0.001) [medscape.com/viewarticle/702193; NEJM Giovannoni 2010, PMID 20089960]. Reductions in ARR were consistent across subgroups defined by sex, age, disease duration, prior DMT use, prior relapse count, baseline EDSS, T1 Gd+ lesions and T2 lesion volume (all p≤0.05) [hero.epa.gov/reference/3054292]. Relapses requiring steroids or hospitalisation were also reduced by over half [[passage text removed]].

**MRI activity.** In CLARITY, relative reductions versus placebo were 85.7% for T1 Gd+ lesions, 73.4% for new/enlarging T2 lesions and 74.4% for combined unique active (CUA) lesions [PMC10980660]. In MAGNIFY-MS (NCT03364036; n=270 highly active RMS), mean CUA lesion counts fell significantly versus the baseline period early after starting treatment (mean differences −1.193 for months 1–6, −1.500 for months 2–6, −1.692 for months 3–6; all p<0.0001), indicating an early onset of action [PMC9197134; PMID 35701185].

**Disability.** Confirmed disability progression risk was reduced (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48–0.93, p=0.018 for 3.5 mg/kg) [medscape.com/viewarticle/702193]. In a post hoc analysis, 6-month-confirmed EDSS worsening risk fell 47% overall (HR 0.53, 95% [passage text removed]), and by 82% in high-relapse-activity and [passage text removed] subgroups (vs 19% and 18% in the corresponding non-HDA subgroups) [PMC6460686; PMID 29716436].

**Composite disease-activity freedom (NEDA).** Over 96 weeks, 44% (178/402) of the cladribine 3.5 [passage text removed] vs 16% (60/379) on placebo (OR 4.28, 95% CI 3.05–6.02, p<0.0001); corresponding figures were 67% vs 39% at 24 weeks and 54% vs 24% at 48 weeks [PMID 21397565]. Using 6-month confirmed progression for the disability component, 2-year NEDA was 47% vs 17% ([passage text removed]].

**Durability after stopping treatment.** In CLARITY Extension, patients who switched from cladribine to placebo (CP3.5, n=98) had 2-year NEDA-3 of 29.6% vs 32.8% in those given two further courses (CC7.0, n=186), with no benefit from additional dosing [PMID 34634968; PMC9189728]; ARR was [passage text removed]) in the switch group vs 0.10 (0.06–0.13) with continued treatment, and relapse-free proportions were similar between groups [[passage text removed]]. In the MAGNIFY-MS extension (n=219), Kaplan–Meier NEDA-3 [passage text removed]) in year 3 and [passage text removed]) for years 3–4 combined (relapse-free 80.8%, free of 6-month confirmed disability progression 84.5%, MRI-activity-free 53.0%) [hcp.merckgroup.com/.../DED589.PDF; [passage text removed]]. Some patients with a prolonged treatment gap showed a slight rise in T1 Gd+ activity without loss of clinical benefit [PMC5788142].

**Real-world data are concordant.** A Danish nationwide cohort (n=268, median follow-up 34.7 months) found ARR fell from [passage text removed]) pre-treatment to 0.11 (0.08–0.15) after a 3-month re-baseline, an 84.8% reduction [sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211034822009956]. A Polish real-world cohort reported NEDA-3 in 42.7% at year 1 and 66.7% at year 2 [journals.viamedica.pl/.../PJNNS.a2023.0050], and a Norwegian hospital series reported NEDA-3 of 40% at 2 years [frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fneur.2025.1698334].

**Caveats:** NEDA-3 estimates vary widely across cohorts (roughly 30% to ~86% at 1–2 years depending on definition, re-baselining, MRI frequency and population) [frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fneur.2025.1698334; mdpi.com/2077-0383/15/13/5121], and the HDA-subgroup and NEDA analyses of CLARITY are post hoc rather than pre-specified [PMID 29716436; PMID 21397565].
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Cladribine tablets 3.5 mg/kg over 2 years substantially reduce clinical and radiological disease activity in relapsing MS — roughly halving relapse rates, sharply reducing MRI lesion activity, and roughly tripling-to-quadrupling the odds of NEDA — with benefit that persists for at least 2 further years without redosing, though a minority of patients still show breakthrough activity.

## Relapse outcomes (pivotal trial)

In CLARITY (1326 patients with RRMS, 96 weeks), annualised relapse rate was 0.14 with cladribine tablets 3.5 mg/kg vs 0.33 with placebo (57.6% relative reduction, p < 0.001), and 0.15 with 5.25 mg/kg (54.5% reduction) [S:2143c977-5b11-5d69-b749-2cc52d86ec6b][S:d34e22c2-53e6-5395-ad9b-47bbf7c81b7b]. Relapse-free proportions were [passage text removed]% for placebo (OR 2.53 and 2.43, p < 0.001), time to first relapse was prolonged (15th percentile 13.4 vs 4.6 months; HR 0.44), and fewer patients needed rescue interferon therapy (2.5% vs 6.2%) [S:2143c977-5b11-5d69-b749-2cc52d86ec6b][S:ce0ecd01-ec65-5b9d-934e-8ee796f284e7]. Separation from placebo appeared early — significantly lower relapse rates by 16 weeks [S:ce0ecd01-ec65-5b9d-934e-8ee796f284e7]. A post hoc analysis found significantly lower risk of qualifying/all relapses [passage text removed] (all p < 0.0001) **and** of severe relapses (all p < 0.005), sustained in CLARITY Extension without further treatment [S:c9f5ed56-aa0f-5d61-afb1-f44405b0fb25].

## MRI activity

At 2 years, mean T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesions per patient per scan fell 85.7% (0.12 vs 0.91), active T2 lesions 73.4% (0.38 vs 1.43), and combined unique lesions were similarly reduced (all p < 0.001) [S:2143c977-5b11-5d69-b749-2cc52d86ec6b]. Lesion-free proportions: 87.2% free of new T1 Gd+ lesions vs 47.4% placebo (OR 8.14), 61.8% free of active T2 lesions vs 27.6% (OR 5.34), and 60% free of any MRI lesion activity vs 25.5% (OR 5.52; all p < 0.0001) [S:2143c977-5b11-5d69-b749-2cc52d86ec6b]. Reductions in combined unique lesions were consistent across baseline strata of relapse count and baseline Gd+ lesion status (approximately 73–90% relative reductions, all p < 0.001) [S:0aa6ef83-301d-5a80-9b49-6d69bca907a1].

## NEDA / disease-activity-free status

NEDA (no relapse, [passage text removed] T1 Gd+ or active T2 lesions) was achieved by 67%, 54% and 44% of the 3.5 mg/kg group [passage text removed], vs 39%, 24% and 16% on placebo (p < 0.0001 at each timepoint); using 6-month CDP, 47% vs 17% at 2 years (OR 4.25) [S:e272c0c4-f317-5b45-ae66-6139a9bfb8c2][S:071343c6-9e76-5186-bd63-aff4b6a9739c]. Pooled CLARITY+ONWARD data gave an OR for NEDA of 3.95 (95% CI 2.90–5.37) overall, with consistent benefit across subgroups [S:8c0b8b2f-bb5f-5479-9c63-0721f84c9fae]. In a NICE appraisal review, NEDA-3 favoured cladribine significantly in the ITT population and in all subgroups, including a suboptimally-treated subgroup where most other individual outcomes were not significant [S:9f37cffe-069a-5f7e-9dc9-2513c8043411].

## Disability

Risk of 3-month confirmed disability progression was reduced (HR [passage text removed]; 85.7% vs 79.4% without progression) [S:2143c977-5b11-5d69-b749-2cc52d86ec6b]. In the overall CLARITY population, 6-month confirmed EDSS worsening was reduced by 47% (HR 0.53, 95% [passage text removed]) [S:66d58ba6-8ed3-5833-af00-b56b4efd2d99].

## High disease activity subgroups

Effects were at least as large in patients with high relapse activity (HRA) or HRA plus on-treatment disease activity: 76–77% relapse-free and 84% free of T1 Gd+ lesions (vs 49% and 31% on placebo), NEDA ORs of [passage text removed]) and 7.82 (4.03–15.19), both p < 0.0001, and an 82% reduction in risk of 6-month confirmed EDSS worsening (interaction p = 0.0036 and 0.0037 vs non-HDA) [S:aec67023-7166-5249-ab0a-7ab11e31a859][S:3ff3fc0a-a9f9-5d80-8c4e-b61a8eeff940][S:66d58ba6-8ed3-5833-af00-b56b4efd2d99].

## Durability without redosing

In CLARITY Extension, ARR in patients re-randomised to placebo ([passage text removed]) was not significantly different from those continuing cladribine ([passage text removed]) [S:53c6eb29-5387-5bf6-8e9d-e6e6406e1724]; about 75% of those switched [passage text removed] [S:04fcec4a-6659-5f72-a89c-4652983fda1c]. MRI benefit was likewise durable in most patients, but a small proportion re-randomised to placebo showed increased MRI activity, associated with a longer treatment gap between studies [S:aee433b6-bcd7-5948-9e89-3f8626f06ff1]. NEDA-3 benefits were sustained up to ~6 years from CLARITY baseline, and EDSS remained stable for up to 5 years in over half of treated patients [S:7022b26b-ba80-5581-9692-65c87d561417]. In CLASSIC-MS (median 10.9 years since last parent-study dose), EDSS remained relatively stable; cladribine-exposed patients had a smaller median EDSS increase (1.0 point) than never-exposed patients (1.5 points), and 55.8% of those exposed required no further DMT [S:3d491d1f-9676-548e-89e8-61b8cc85d19e][S:24fcab5d-a089-5f96-b372-a0c1fffa0b33].

## Real-world data

MSBase registry (633 cladribine-treated pwMS, propensity-matched): significantly longer time to first relapse and lower ARR than fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate or teriflunomide cohorts, plus far greater persistence (adjusted HRs for switching 4.00, 7.04, 6.52 respectively) [S:7d812ba1-e324-5974-bd2e-fbf0585476b7]; an MSBase report gave on-treatment ARR [passage text removed]) vs 0.41 pre-cladribine [S:59ce126a-9899-509d-a62e-0d934ce2ab4f]. Real-world NEDA-3 varies widely with population and prior treatment — e.g. 74.9% at 2 years in an Italian cohort (90.9% relapse-free, 76.7% MRI-activity-free) but only 24% at 24 months in a Danish cohort [S:09ade601-3589-5268-80b7-cbcab16e0923]. In a 4-year multicentre cohort of advanced RRMS, ARR fell from 1.42 at baseline to 0.26 (year 1) and 0.22 (year 2), with patients showing active MRI lesions falling from 90.4% to 36.3% and 25.2%, and NEDA-3 of 47.4%/51.0%/40.4%/71.4% across years 1–4 [S:5a7f52ad-0259-5149-850f-562a9f550667].

## Caveats

Not all patients respond: higher baseline Gd+ lesion counts predicted first relapse and MRI activity in an Italian cohort [S:b641d7ec-abea-5de7-aea2-4df863efb409], and a target-trial-emulation study reported higher risk of MRI disease activity and 4-year relapse with cladribine than with rituximab, with the difference emerging within the first 6 months, suggesting a delayed onset of effect [S:7c549537-f93e-542e-945b-e548ef667b50]. In indirect comparisons, cladribine achieved NEDA-3 more often than dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide but not significantly differently from fingolimod [S:9f6328ba-c745-582b-909c-6a55836a4a9d].
