rows.question: Which CSF kappa free light chain index thresholds distinguish multiple sclerosis from other inflammatory demyelinating disorders?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: When the non-multiple-sclerosis comparator group is dominated by aquaporin-4 and MOG antibody-associated disease, the best-separating CSF kappa free light chain index cutoff lies well above the widely cited value of about 6, at approximately 12.6; At that higher cutoff sensitivity stayed high (around 84%) while specificity against these antibody-mediated mimics was only moderate (around 72-74%); At the widely cited cutoff near 6, roughly half of aquaporin-4-positive and MOG antibody-positive patients tested positive, so specificity was poor while sensitivity remained high; Removing antibody-mediated mimics from the comparator group lowered the best-performing cutoff back towards about 7 with sensitivity and specificity preserved. Certainty: The cutoff values and their accuracy estimates should be treated as provisional, since they were both derived and evaluated within the same sample set at one site rather than validated in a separate, independent group of patients. Scope: applies to suspected inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system undergoing CSF analysis in settings where antibody-mediated mimics make up a large share of the comparator group, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents an elevated kappa free light chain index at any threshold as establishing multiple sclerosis or as excluding antibody-mediated mimics, or recommends deferring aquaporin-4 and MOG antibody testing on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

There is no single validated threshold: the discriminating κ‑FLC index cut-off rises substantially when the comparator group is other inflammatory demyelinating disease rather than non-inflammatory controls — roughly **~6 for MS vs. MOGAD/mixed controls, but ~12–19 for MS vs. AQP4‑NMOSD or pooled inflammatory mimics.**

## The reference threshold (mixed/non-inflammatory controls)

The 2024 McDonald criteria adopt a κFLC index cut-off of **6.1** as a positive CSF result [practicalneurology.com/…/54598], derived from a systematic review and meta-analysis of 32 studies in which κ‑FLC index sensitivity ranged 52–100% (weighted average 88%) and specificity 69–100% (89%), with no significant accuracy difference from OCB [[passage text removed]; sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352396425003494]. Reviews note that reported cut-offs span roughly **2.4–10.6**, explicitly "[passage text removed]; PMC12457562].

## Disease-specific thresholds against demyelinating mimics

**MOGAD vs. MS.** In a multicentre study of 303 patients (140 MOGAD, 37 AQP4‑NMOSD, 126 MS), median KFLC-index was lowest in MOGAD (0.60, IQR 0.33–2.09; 71% with undetectable CSF KFLC), intermediate in NMOSD (8.85, 3.04–16.78), highest in MS (49.90, 16.31–113.39). Optimal threshold for MOGAD vs. MS [passage text removed]), sensitivity 0.89, specificity 0.89, AUC 0.93 [neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000214806].

**AQP4‑NMOSD vs. MS.** In the same cohort the optimal threshold was more than double: **[passage text removed]), sensitivity 0.70, specificity 0.75, AUC 0.82 — and 2.3 separated NMOSD from MOGAD [neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000214806].

**Chinese cohort (n=428).** Optimal cut-offs were **8.3** for MS vs. non-selective controls, **18.5** for MS vs. MOGAD, and **12.1** for MS vs. AQP4+NMOSD, with accuracy comparable to OCB [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40645758; PMC12961222].

**Korean cohort (n=103 MS vs. 105 non-MS enriched for NMOSD/MOGAD).** Optimal threshold **≥12.6**, sensitivity 83.5%, specificity 74.3%, accuracy 78.8%; the authors note that a cut-off of 6.1 yielded specificity of only 50% for MS/CIS vs. NMOSD in prior work [[passage text removed]; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41454730].

**Pooled other inflammatory neurological disease (Argentine pilot, 49 MS/CIS vs. 48 OIND).** Optimal cut-off **14.6** (sensitivity 73.5%, specificity 68.1%); the 6.1 threshold gave sensitivity 85.7% but specificity only 35.4%, and Reiber's κ‑FLC diagram gave the highest sensitivity (91.8%) with specificity 45.8% [PMC13259835; [passage text removed]].

**Inaugural optic neuritis (n=210).** ≥**6.7** separated MS/CIS-with-conversion from all other diagnoses (sensitivity 95%, specificity 86%, AUC 0.94); <**4.9** identified MOGAD vs. MS/CISwc (sensitivity 92%, specificity 96%, AUC 0.97). The [passage text removed] [PMC11913550; [passage text removed]].

## Very high values

In a 371-patient differential-diagnosis cohort, mean K‑FLC index was 90.9±134.2 in MS vs. 18.0±15.1 in NMOSD and 12.6±24.4 in other immune-mediated CNS disorders; values **>100** occurred almost exclusively in MS and were therefore strongly predictive [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31837636].

## Caveats

Thresholds are assay-dependent (nephelometry vs. turbidimetry, differing lower detection limits) and depend on how undetectable CSF κFLC values are handled [[passage text removed]]. Elevated intrathecal κ‑FLC is not MS-specific and occurs in NMOSD, MOGAD and autoimmune encephalitis [PMC13259835]. Sex-specific thresholds have been proposed but I did not retrieve the specific values [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41454730]. Note one internal inconsistency in the NOMADMUS report: the results state 13.2 for NMOSD vs. MS while the discussion states 13.7 [neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000214806].
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

There is no single validated threshold: κFLC index cut-offs that separate MS from *other inflammatory* demyelinating disorders are consistently **higher (~11–19)** than the cut-offs (~4–8) derived against mixed or non-inflammatory control groups, and all are assay- and population-dependent [S:bb167cdc-9ce6-59ff-99b4-8715352f8da6][S:c849870b-f564-5b41-a258-608615c0fe60][S:696fde50-1933-5a3a-8b94-6eb618b74efa].

## Disease-specific thresholds

**MS vs other inflammatory neurological disease (OIND) generally.** In a large multicentre cohort (675 MS, 90 CIS, 297 OIND, 559 NIND), the optimal κFLC index cut-off was 8.92 against all controls, 8.39 against non-inflammatory disease, but rose to **11.56** when MS was compared specifically with OIND (κFLC index AUC 0.896) [S:bb167cdc-9ce6-59ff-99b4-8715352f8da6].

**MS vs MOGAD and AQP4+NMOSD.** In a Chinese cohort (130 MS, 41 MOGAD, 25 AQP4+NMOSD, 123 OIND, 109 NIND), median κFLC index was 20.1 in MS vs 4.8 in MOGAD (p=0.003) and 4.5 in NMOSD (p=0.011). The overall cut-off vs non-selective controls was 8.3 (sens 0.69, spec 0.85, AUC 0.84), but the optimal thresholds were **≥18.5 for MS vs MOGAD** (sens 0.55, spec 0.91, AUC 0.77 — specificity superior to [passage text removed]) and **≥12.1 for MS vs AQP4+NMOSD** (sens 0.63, spec 0.94, AUC 0.76) [S:c849870b-f564-5b41-a258-608615c0fe60][S:1435395b-b0f5-5037-a2cd-14a5553ad713][S:63d9df3c-dfc6-5645-abd2-2fc44a6eff30]. Notably three MS patients with low-titre MOG-IgG (1:10) had κFLC indices [passage text removed], supporting the index in resolving that ambiguity [S:ebb3710f-2ca0-5512-a92b-b77300e7d3dd].

A French multicentre study (140 MOGAD, 37 NMOSD, 126 MS) found median κFLC index 49.90 (MS), 8.85 (NMOSD), 0.60 (MOGAD), with an optimal **MOGAD-vs-MS threshold of 5.7** (AUC 0.93; sens 0.89, spec 0.89) and weaker separation of NMOSD from MS (AUC 0.82) — i.e. a much lower threshold than the Chinese cohort, illustrating assay/population dependence [S:74237344-9216-5d00-959b-303f3e50ffbb].

**Where mimics are common.** In a Korean cohort (103 MS vs 105 non-MS, including 64 NMOSD and 14 MOGAD), the widely cited 6.1 threshold gave sensitivity 92.2% but specificity only 55.2%; [passage text removed] it. The optimal threshold was **≥12.6** (sens 84%, spec 74%, accuracy 79%), retaining sens 84.5%/spec 71.8% in the restricted MS-vs-NMOSD/MOGAD comparison, whereas against OIND/NIND *without* NMOSD/MOGAD the optimum fell to 6.9 (sens 92.2%, spec 81.5%). Thresholds of 4.2 (sens 95.1%, NPV 88.9%) and 35 (spec 90.5%, PPV 86.1%) served as rule-out and rule-in values, and sex-specific cut-offs (**≥22.8 female, ≥7.0 male**) improved accuracy [S:696fde50-1933-5a3a-8b94-6eb618b74efa][S:a5b442a5-f4f9-5755-b867-14e9eccee043][S:595f1c03-a923-542e-8447-fc9eee328959][S:560e8282-81a4-5650-a852-9f671d49fb29][S:9d50e939-f0a0-5518-a3fc-cb0965facc43].

**Myelitis.** Using intrathecal fraction rather than the index, an **FLC-κ IF >78%** separated MS myelitis from NMOSD myelitis with sensitivity 88.5% and specificity 88.9%; intrathecal FLC-κ synthesis was present in 96% of MS myelitis vs 55.6% of NMOSD and 14.3% of non-inflammatory myelopathy [S:c12da859-cccc-58fe-b5ee-0e9b070c9c84][S:e798beb7-ddb5-5dbb-b696-3875463497d4].

## Caveats

- The 2024 McDonald revisions make the κFLC index interchangeable with OCB, but absolute κFLC values differ between platforms, so cut-offs are method-specific [S:a830f58a-1b95-5b32-8f52-372856766bbd]. Paired-sample comparison of two assays gave optimal index cut-offs of 7.7 (Freelite-Optilite) vs 4.71 (N Latex-BNII) in the same cohort [S:6928293e-b08b-5308-9190-7034d6fb5acc].
- Reported cut-offs against general controls span roughly 3–12 (e.g. 3.045 and 6.6 [S:19a785c0-bce5-5093-8f8a-810b612d82b8]; 5 [S:ddd69bba-6853-513e-8ea9-0f5daae4f73e]; 5.9 [S:ee3b933d-6889-5c50-aea2-a3982387d007]; 10.62 in CIS [S:2d34db76-ee0c-58a4-9630-ec20dc360b02]; 12.0 [S:c13d40c6-e4d0-5104-aedc-98f95fce7d8b]), with the increase driven by including other inflammatory disorders as controls [S:08f8d9d5-9034-5bec-a5a9-e2fd1ca204ac].
- A consensus grey zone of **2.4–20.0** has been proposed within which additional OCB testing is recommended; in a two-centre prospective study no tested cut-off within that zone outperformed 6.1, and κFLC index specificity was lower than OCB (67.4% vs 78.6%) in a cohort where 24.6% had other inflammatory conditions [S:35c6749b-076e-57c3-bf8d-3cc3741631d2][S:33f28d7b-f80a-5e0b-94cc-cc6e7fea92c0].
- Authors of the Korean study state explicitly that the κFLC [passage text removed] only add incremental value in differential diagnosis [S:a5b442a5-f4f9-5755-b867-14e9eccee043], and combining the index with OCB improves specificity over either alone [S:c849870b-f564-5b41-a258-608615c0fe60][S:560e8282-81a4-5650-a852-9f671d49fb29].

rows.question: What is known about the effects of anti-CD20 therapies on soluble immune mediators in multiple sclerosis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: B cell depletion with anti-CD20 antibodies is accompanied by lower levels of several pro-inflammatory soluble mediators, including spinal fluid interleukin-15 and the B cell-attracting chemokines CXCL13 and CCL19; Interleukin-10 responses to anti-CD20 treatment point in different directions across treated groups, with reductions, an early post-infusion peak, rises after B cell reconstitution and unchanged levels all described; B cell activating factor moves inconsistently after anti-CD20 treatment: serum levels rose in one ocrelizumab-treated group and fell in another, while intrathecal rituximab raised serum but lowered spinal fluid levels; Not every measured mediator shifts: in small primary progressive groups treated with ocrelizumab, interleukin-2 and interleukin-12 levels showed no change. Certainty: The evidence is early and drawn from small treated groups with differing measurement methods and routes of administration, and for some mediators the reported directions disagree. Scope: applies to multiple sclerosis treated with anti-CD20 antibodies in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents soluble mediator measurement as an established biomarker of anti-CD20 treatment response or infection risk, or recommends monitoring, redosing or drug selection on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Anti-CD20 therapies produce a consistent, reproducible reduction in a narrow set of soluble mediators — chiefly the B-cell/lymphoid chemokines CXCL13 and CCL19, the Th1-recruiting chemokine CXCL10, soluble TNF-receptor-family decoys, and axonal-injury markers (NfL) — while paradoxically **raising** BAFF, and leaving intrathecal immunoglobulin output and most astrocytic/glial markers largely untouched. Evidence for effects on canonical pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNFα, IFNγ, IL-17) in body fluids is fragmented and inconsistent. [PMC13172085; PMID 41820782]

## Chemokines: the most robust signal

- **CXCL13 and CCL19.** In a phase II add-on rituximab study in relapsing MS, both CXCL13 and CCL19 fell significantly in post-treatment CSF (P = 0.002 and P = 0.03), whereas CCL4 was unchanged. [PMC13172085; [passage text removed]] In a post hoc analysis of 30 relapsing MS patients on add-on rituximab, CSF CXCL13 fell from 17.5 [passage text removed]) and serum CXCL13 from 79.0 [passage text removed]), with the intrathecal-production "CXCL13 index" also falling (0.036 → 0.026, P = 0.042); higher baseline CXCL13 index predicted achieving NEDA. [PMC5433328]
- **CXCL10/IP-10.** In a prospective study of 70 clinically stable RRMS patients switched to rituximab and profiled by multiplex electrochemiluminescence against 55 healthy controls, IP-10 (CXCL10) and IL-12/23p40 showed the largest changes, moving toward normalisation and persisting over two years. [[passage text removed]; PMC5805315; PMID 29420590] The authors interpreted this as B-cell depletion indirectly affecting Th1 function via the CXCR3 axis. [[passage text removed]]
- **Ocrelizumab (OBOE study).** At week 52, CSF CXCL13 fell 63.2% and CXCL10 22.8% in relapsing MS. [[passage text removed]; PMID 38466277] The narrative review reports the same magnitudes (CXCL13 −63%, CXCL10 −23%) in a cohort of 101 RRMS patients. [PMC13172085]

Mechanistically, CXCL13 reduction is thought to be indirect — B cells themselves do not produce CXCL13; depletion is presumed to act via follicular dendritic cell support, which also explains the parallel drop in CSF T cells. [[passage text removed]]

## Soluble TNF-superfamily receptors and BAFF: a divergent, paradoxical pattern

- **BAFF rises in serum.** Ocrelizumab increased serum BAFF and decreased soluble TACI, while APRIL and sBCMA did not change; sTACI–BAFF complexes rose and correlated positively with BAFF. The proposed explanation is reduced BAFF consumption, since [passage text removed]] Rituximab likewise raised CSF BAFF (107.1 → [passage text removed] serum BAFF (1116.3 → 2549.8, P < 0.001), with the BAFF *index* falling — i.e. the rise is peripherally driven. [PMC5433328] The same directionality is seen across autoimmune disease and in ME/CFS trials, supporting a depletion-intrinsic feedback effect rather than a disease-specific one. [PMC1794511; [passage text removed]; PMID 17040963]
- **Conflicting BAFF data exist.** *Intrathecal* rituximab in nine MS patients produced a sustained serum BAFF rise but *decreased* CSF BAFF. [PMC13172085; PMID 25175066] Another study of 19 patients found BAFF increased in both serum and CSF at 12–19 months. The review explicitly tabulates BAFF under both "increased" and "decreased." [PMC13172085]
- **Soluble activation markers fall.** OBOE reported week-52 reductions in [passage text removed] (−33.6%; −21.3%) and sTACI (−47.6%; −27.8%). [[passage text removed]] Ocrelizumab also reduces serum kappa free light chain concentration, though this did not track disease activity. [PMC12372195]

## Pro-inflammatory cytokines: weak and contradictory

The narrative review's summary table lists IL-6, TNFα, IFNγ, IL-1β, IL-12, IL-17 and IL-23 as each appearing in the "increased," "decreased," and/or "unchanged" columns depending on the study, and concludes that evidence for these mediators is fragmented. [PMC13172085] Cellular work is more consistent than fluid-phase work: rituximab-treated patients' T cells show reduced proliferation and reduced IFN-γ/IL-17 production, attributed partly to B-cell lymphotoxin and TNFα [[passage text removed]; PMC10076836]; repopulating B cells secrete less GM-CSF and more IL-10, essentially normalising the GM-CSF/IL-10 ratio, with persisting reduction in myeloid pro-inflammatory responses [[passage text removed]]. Notably, one study found repopulating B cells secreted *more* IL-6 than pre-treatment, a finding commentators flagged as unexplained. [[passage text removed]]

## Neuroaxonal and glial markers

- **NfL falls consistently.** OBOE reported a 30.8% sNfL reduction at 12 months [[passage text removed]]; OPERA showed 43% reduction from baseline to week 96 with ocrelizumab vs 31% with interferon beta-1a (p<0.001) [[passage text removed]]. CSF NfL reduction was a met primary endpoint of OBOE and persisted over 5 years. [[passage text removed]] Ofatumumab reduced sNfL vs teriflunomide by 8.7% [passage text removed] all). [[passage text removed].852563/full; PMC9009385]
- **Glial markers are resistant.** In OBOE, [passage text removed]%), TREM2 (−12.1%) and NfH (−19.6%) showed only modest reductions [[passage text removed]], and ocrelizumab did not affect GFAP at week 52 [[passage text removed]]. CHIT1 fell (median −41% in RMS) but SERPINA3 was unaltered. [[passage text removed]] Real-world data are mixed: one cohort found sGFAP fell at 12 months in NEDA-3 and inflammatory-activity groups but not in PIRA patients. [PMC11600310]

## What does *not* change

Oligoclonal bands and the IgG index are unchanged despite CSF B-cell depletion [[passage text removed]; PMC5433328; PMC9208251], and serum/CSF IgG remain largely unchanged early on — a key argument that anti-CD20 efficacy is antibody-independent. [PMC4705194] Adhesion molecules (sICAM-1, sVCAM-1, ALCAM) were addressed by only a single study in the review, so no conclusion can be drawn. [PMC13172085]

## Caveat

The only dedicated synthesis I found on precisely this question concludes that the literature is limited [passage text removed] populations, and that anti-CD20 agents [passage text removed]" — a hypothesis, not an established mechanism. [PMID 41820782; PMC13172085] Head-to-head comparisons of rituximab vs ocrelizumab vs ofatumumab vs ublituximab on soluble mediator profiles were not identified in my searches.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Anti-CD20 therapies clearly shift the soluble immune milieu toward a less inflammatory profile — most reproducibly by lowering B-cell-associated chemokines (CXCL13, CCL19, CXCL10) and immunoglobulin/intrathecal inflammation markers — but the cytokine data are fragmented and **no single soluble mediator has been shown to change consistently** across studies [S:5c39dad3][S:da2e8a91].

## Chemokines — the strongest signal

- A structured review of 39 studies concluded that evidence on chemokine modulation is limited but suggests a suppressive effect: a phase II rituximab trial in 30 RRMS patients showed significant reductions in CXCL13 and CCL19 (with no change in CCL4) in serum and CSF at 6 months, alongside lower relapse rates and less MRI activity; in a prospective cohort of 101 RRMS patients on ocrelizumab, CSF CXCL13 fell 63% and CXCL10 fell 23% by week 52; and in 70 RRMS patients on rituximab, CSF CXCL10 and CXCL8 fell toward near-normal levels [S:53fb3fc8].
- Independent confirmation: in the OBOE study (ocrelizumab) and a rituximab add-on trial, marked reductions in CSF CXCL13 accompanied >95% CSF B-cell depletion and ~50% CSF T-cell reduction, with reduced IgG index and CSF kappa free light chains at 52 weeks in both relapsing and primary progressive MS [S:679d6427].
- In [passage text removed] given add-on rituximab, treatment reduced the CSF CXCL13 index (p=0.042) as well as myelin basic protein (p=0.046) and neurofilament light (p<0.001) [S:64757942][S:1fda37d7].
- Compartment matters: intrathecal rituximab in RRMS/SPMS produced no change in serum or CSF CXCL13 [S:faf7b8b2], and in the RIVITALISE trial only B-cell-related CSF biomarkers (sCD21, BAFF) changed, sCD27 fell slightly (−10.97%, p=0.0005), and neurofilament light did not change, because CNS-tissue B cells were depleted only ~10–20% [S:01ea058f]. The EFFRITE trial of intrathecal rituximab in progressive MS found CSF osteopontin stable, with only a slight NfL decrease (−[passage text removed]) [S:1fc1af81].

## Pro-inflammatory cytokines — reductions reported but inconsistent

- Some studies report anti-CD20-induced reductions in [passage text removed]; transient post-infusion rises in IL-6 and TNFα are attributed to cytokine release after profound B-cell depletion [S:5c39dad3].
- IFNγ effects are heterogeneous: only one identified study showed decreased soluble IFNγ, most showed no change or even transient increases, though reductions in IFNγ-producing T cells are described [S:5c39dad3].
- Cell-intrinsic evidence is stronger than soluble-protein evidence. In 53 PPMS patients, ocrelizumab reduced numbers of [passage text removed] (p<0.0001 for all), yet the *proportions* of GM-CSF- and TNFα-producing B cells rose, and these changes accompanied a fall in serum NfL (p=0.008) [S:488e8345][S:cfa37df8]. Similarly, GM-CSF-producing B cells are elevated in untreated MS and decrease after anti-CD20 therapy [S:7012abdd][S:70be4c6b], and elevated IL-6 normalizes in blood after rituximab [S:347ff8a3].
- IL-17: no significant IL-17A decline over 24 months in 22 PPMS patients on ocrelizumab, whereas ofatumumab-treated PBMCs produced less IL-17 on stimulation and rituximab progressively lowered serum IL-17 in rheumatoid arthritis [S:0bb9d13a].
- BAFF is bidirectional: intrathecal rituximab raised serum but lowered CSF BAFF in 9 MS patients; ocrelizumab increased BAFF in both serum and CSF in 19 patients at 12–19 months, while another 24-patient ocrelizumab cohort showed decreased serum BAFF and IL-20. IL-2 was unchanged at 12 months in 22 PPMS patients [S:9af1c727].

## Anti-inflammatory cytokines

Evidence points both directions: anti-CD20 therapy can raise or lower IL-10 depending on immune milieu, timing and disease stage, and the inconsistency [passage text removed] [S:13490bbe][S:da2e8a91]. IL-4 was unchanged after 12 months of ocrelizumab in PPMS; IL-35 data come from non-MS disease (rituximab in type 1 diabetes) [S:93825879]. A conference report described increased IL-10, IL-35 and TGFβ-1 production by naive B cells over 6 months of ocrelizumab [S:18d9b073].

## Adhesion molecules — sparse

Only one study in the review reported change: in 70 RRMS patients on rituximab, CSF sVCAM-1 and sICAM-1 fell significantly toward healthy-control levels; because this is a single study, no definitive conclusion can be drawn [S:1cf837a0][S:da2e8a91][S:30e93c14].

## Immunoglobulins

Serum Ig declines with prolonged exposure — IgM more than IgG/IgA across rituximab, ocrelizumab and ofatumumab trials, with reduced IgG more strongly associated with serious infections over 5.5 years of ocrelizumab follow-up [S:0bc5594c]. A meta-analysis of 39 articles (20,501 patients) found an overall hypogammaglobulinemia prevalence of 11% (95% CI 0.08–0.15), highest with rituximab (18%), and a significant post-treatment decrease in mean IgG (mean difference 0.57, 95% CI 0.22–0.93) [S:4b4d24d1]. Notably, early trials found serum and CSF IgG largely unchanged despite >90% B-cell depletion, which is why antibody-independent mechanisms are invoked [S:c72c8e25].

## Gaps

The main limitations flagged in the literature are scarce longitudinal sampling, heterogeneous compartments (serum vs CSF) and time points, and reliance on non-MS diseases or animal models for several mediators (IL-23, IL-35, TGFβ) [S:9af1c727][S:5c39dad3][S:13490bbe].

rows.question: Which immunotherapy approaches are used for antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis presenting during pregnancy?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange are the immunomodulatory treatments most often given when antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis presents in pregnancy, with corticosteroids used most frequently; Escalation to second-line rituximab is described in only a minority of these pregnancies, and cyclophosphamide in exceptional single cases; Second-line treatment is reserved for patients showing no improvement on optimised first-line therapy, with rituximab generally preferred over cyclophosphamide. Certainty: The pregnancy evidence is a small pooled description of individual reported experiences, enough to show what is usually given but not to compare regimens or establish safety. Scope: applies to antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis, most often NMDA receptor antibody encephalitis in pregnant women, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents an immunotherapy sequence for pregnancy as an established, guideline-backed protocol or as demonstrated superior to the alternatives.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Management follows the standard stepwise autoimmune-encephalitis (AE) paradigm, adapted for gestation: corticosteroids, IVIg and plasma exchange as first line (all regarded as acceptable in pregnancy), tumour resection when an ovarian teratoma is present, and escalation to rituximab or cyclophosphamide in refractory cases, with mycophenolate avoided. Evidence is entirely from case reports/series and pooled systematic reviews — no trials.

## Evidence

**Framework and observed practice.** The largest pooled analysis (49 pregnant AE patients; anti-NMDAR most frequent, onset mostly in the first two trimesters) reports first line as corticosteroids, IVIg, or plasmapheresis alone or in combination, with second line (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, rituximab) considered when response is inadequate. Actual use: corticosteroids 40/49 (81.6%), IVIg 28 (57.1%), plasmapheresis 23 (46.9%), rituximab 10 (20.4%), cyclophosphamide 5 (10.2%), azathioprine 3 (6.1%), no immunosuppression 5 (10.2%); 13 (26.5%) had a surgical procedure and 51% required ICU admission ([PMC10690706]([passage text removed]); PMID [37562964](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37562964)).

**Anti-NMDAR case series.** In Joubert et al., immunotherapy was given during pregnancy in 7/11 (64%) of their own patients and 18/21 (86%) previously [passage text removed] ([NXI e668]([passage text removed]); PMID [31948997](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31948997)). A recent review pooling these 32 patients records 25 treated with: 21 corticosteroids, 15 IVIg, 10 PLEX, 4 rituximab (started in the first or second trimester, median 21 weeks' gestation), and 1 cyclophosphamide (6 weeks before delivery), with no adverse effects reported in mothers or infants ([10.1007/s12325-026-03513-7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12325-026-03513-7)).

**Tumour-directed therapy.** For teratoma-associated disease, identification and resection of the ovarian teratoma is treated as part of first-line therapy, including during pregnancy — e.g. right salpingo-oophorectomy plus corticosteroids, IVIg [passage text removed]" ([PMC11826843]([passage text removed])); a pregnancy case report likewise emphasises prompt immunotherapy plus timely teratoma removal ([frph.2026.1895027]([passage text removed])).

**Refractory disease / second line.** A documented case escalated from 11–15 weeks' gestation through steroids, plasma exchange, IVIg and rituximab with no response, then received cyclophosphamide at 16 weeks with improvement after 4 weeks and a healthy term delivery ([NXI 10.1212/NXI.0000000000200007]([passage text removed]); PMID [35728968](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35728968)). Another case used plasma exchange plus rituximab at 27 weeks after relapse, further immunotherapy for a postpartum relapse, and maintenance rituximab ([AAN abstract 53895]([passage text removed])). Authors of that report note rituximab has been used in only "a handful" of such patients and cyclophosphamide in one.

**Agent-specific caveats in pregnancy.**
- Rituximab crosses the placenta and [passage text removed] reduced gamma globulins; in one pooled analysis rituximab exposure was not associated with significantly increased spontaneous pregnancy loss ([10.1007/s10072-024-07448-1]([passage text removed]); [PMC11306544]([passage text removed])). It is described as potentially [passage text removed] in the first trimester ([frph.2026.1895027]([passage text removed])).
- Mycophenolate mofetil is contraindicated in pregnancy (major congenital malformations, pregnancy loss); azathioprine has been used with good outcomes in some AE reports though one study suggested [passage text removed] ([10.1007/s12325-026-03513-7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12325-026-03513-7)); a related review calls azathioprine "relatively safe" and flags mycophenolate/methotrexate as high risk ([fneur.2022.1048502]([passage text removed])).
- Plasma exchange may precipitate maternal hypotension which, combined with dysautonomia, risks uteroplacental malperfusion ([PMC11826843]([passage text removed])).

**Non-NMDAR antibodies.** Reports are sparse; one anti-GABA-B receptor encephalitis in pregnancy responded to corticosteroids plus intravenous immunoglobulin ([PMC11635330]([passage text removed])).

**Outcomes context.** A 2025 systematic review of 66 pregnancies in 61 women found [passage text removed], though neonatal outcome reporting was frequently incomplete ([PMC11877225]([passage text removed]); PMID [40041614](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40041614)).

## Gaps
I found no pregnancy-specific evidence for third-line agents (tocilizumab, bortezomib, daratumumab, intrathecal methotrexate, FcRn antagonists); these are described only in general refractory-AE literature without gestational data ([PMC9477937]([passage text removed])). No consensus guideline dedicated to AE in pregnancy exists; experts agree only that prompt treatment including tumour resection and immunotherapy is warranted ([fneur.2022.1048502]([passage text removed])).
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** Management mirrors non‑pregnant autoimmune encephalitis — prompt first‑line immunotherapy (corticosteroids, IVIG, plasma exchange), escalation to second‑line B‑cell/cytotoxic therapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide) in refractory cases, plus tumour resection when a teratoma is found — with drug choice individualised for fetal risk; there are no guidelines, and evidence is limited to case reports and small series, overwhelmingly in anti‑NMDAR encephalitis. [S:756d8098-c661-5fc3-adc0-411fe04c76d2][S:98c26248-1850-541d-96b9-4e2cd11c5332][S:3dc85325-cfe5-52eb-bcfe-9406a9f2ec31]

**First-line (generally considered acceptable in pregnancy)**
- Corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone/oral prednisolone), IVIG [passage text removed] acute therapies and may reduce circulating antibodies in mother and fetus. [S:756d8098-c661-5fc3-adc0-411fe04c76d2][S:98c26248-1850-541d-96b9-4e2cd11c5332]
- Non‑fluorinated steroids (prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone) carry low fetal risk after the first trimester, milk levels are low, and delaying breastfeeding several hours after high‑dose methylprednisolone is advised; PLEX has been used in other antibody‑mediated pregnancy conditions without evidence of increased harm. [S:413503e0-37c6-5b4a-b16d-cca16ebea028] Methylprednisolone/prednisolone are preferred over dexamethasone because of limited placental penetration, and IVIG is regarded as safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding. [S:4f0b2c69-3bf5-50d3-bc52-83d2058eb03f][S:842865f4-9a4b-5af5-af28-56399571c3ef]
- Reported pregnancy cases have mostly used pulsed IV [passage text removed] added PLEX and/or IVIG; steroid‑unresponsive cases have been salvaged with plasmapheresis alone with good maternal outcome. [S:f180965e-304c-5372-89f1-3e26ad7d7e6a]
- Beyond NMDAR: a pregnant woman with anti‑GABA‑B receptor encephalitis was treated with IV methylprednisolone and IVIG (with bilateral ovarian wedge resection and emergency caesarean), becoming seizure‑free though with residual cognitive/psychiatric deficits. [S:5b1fbf87-4129-5154-9706-37f9d490f431][S:5d9f3045-bbde-5901-8089-01f93e945da4]

**Second-line / escalation**
- Rituximab and cyclophosphamide are the standard escalation options and can give good responses; cyclophosphamide is generally avoided once the fetus is viable because of teratogenicity, and rituximab is not routinely recommended but has low first‑trimester transplacental transfer and has been used peri‑conceptually and antenatally in autoimmune disease. [S:98c26248-1850-541d-96b9-4e2cd11c5332] Azathioprine and rituximab have both been used, with residual teratogenicity/preterm‑delivery concerns weighed against maternal benefit. [S:756d8098-c661-5fc3-adc0-411fe04c76d2]
- In refractory disease, escalation has succeeded: a patient treated from 11–15 weeks' gestation with steroids, PLEX, IVIG and rituximab without response improved four weeks after receiving cyclophosphamide at 16 weeks and delivered a healthy term infant — the authors stress this remains an individualised risk–benefit decision. [S:7637c563-de1e-55af-82a7-4cbb0394b122][S:2815affa-192c-565f-ac56-df20c85376b1]
- Conversely, some centres have withheld PLEX and rituximab because of limited safety data, illustrating practice variability. [S:82e95101-a58d-5f3f-b6ef-f7ad78052a11]
- Published pregnancy case tables show the actual mix used: corticosteroids alone, IVIG alone, IVIG + methylprednisolone, PLEX, rituximab, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, with or without teratoma resection. [S:6ff4e07b-2861-564f-8808-7cf9f8ee6ba6][S:928defed-7509-5f80-8959-913ac84a7f0f]

**Adjunctive and non‑immunotherapy elements of care**
- Tumour treatment is integral: laparoscopic resection is the treatment of choice for teratoma and is not associated with fetal complications, with close fetal monitoring; teratoma detection may need MRI or reduced‑dose CT in mid‑to‑late pregnancy. [S:756d8098-c661-5fc3-adc0-411fe04c76d2] Early excision plus immunotherapy is linked to rapid recovery and good prognosis, and in one case obviated second‑line therapy. [S:98c26248-1850-541d-96b9-4e2cd11c5332][S:1aff8e1f-bfd7-5006-9920-0db0ae6d026a] Cases combining salpingo‑oophorectomy/teratoma resection with immunotherapy and ICU care have delivered healthy infants. [S:4f919aff-b9fe-57bc-b268-762b5b4f8e5f]
- Symptomatic treatment: psychotropics (haloperidol, olanzapine, lithium, lorazepam) and antiseizure drugs are used, though seizures are more responsive to immunotherapy. [S:756d8098-c661-5fc3-adc0-411fe04c76d2]
- Obstetric decisions (elective preterm delivery vs termination) are debated: older literature suggested termination hastens recovery, while more recent analysis suggests [passage text removed]. [S:98c26248-1850-541d-96b9-4e2cd11c5332] Recurrence has been reported in successive pregnancies with improvement after termination. [S:0d06e62a-d111-5b18-a845-87cfcc26f27f]

**Pre‑conception and maintenance**
- Best outcomes appear linked to achieving and maintaining antibody‑negative status before conception and through pregnancy, with immunotherapy as needed; teratoma surveillance is advised. [S:1aff8e1f-bfd7-5006-9920-0db0ae6d026a]
- Mycophenolate is contraindicated in pregnancy; one GAD65 limbic encephalitis patient was switched from mycophenolate to hydroxychloroquine specifically for family planning after withdrawal of rituximab, IVIG and mycophenolate. [S:e0833bb6-bd76-519c-bd73-a214a5eb2dc7]

**Caveats:** No consensus treatment strategy for autoimmune encephalitis in pregnancy exists; randomised [passage text removed], literature is largely anti‑NMDAR case reports, and multicentre studies with child follow‑up are needed. [S:756d8098-c661-5fc3-adc0-411fe04c76d2][S:3dc85325-cfe5-52eb-bcfe-9406a9f2ec31][S:2815affa-192c-565f-ac56-df20c85376b1] Third‑line agents used in refractory non‑pregnant autoimmune encephalitis (bortezomib, tocilizumab, and others) are documented in general AE literature [S:4b674b40-e09c-5e13-9e68-d39a603e3774][S:2e012192-b7c8-5d32-9cef-ca81c8a63ec8]; I found no source reporting their use for autoimmune encephalitis during pregnancy — tocilizumab pregnancy experience cited in the antibody‑mediated CNS disorder review comes from NMOSD, not encephalitis. [S:dee2d4c8-2878-5a56-877e-b7377f883ca9]

rows.question: Which patient characteristics identify those in whom earlier antibiotic administration is associated with mortality in sepsis without shock?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Advanced age, greater comorbidity burden, higher acute physiology scores and acute liver dysfunction marked the patients with the greatest estimated mortality benefit from earlier antibiotic administration; In the oldest patients earlier antibiotic administration was associated with lower 28-day mortality than in younger patients, a direction opposite to earlier emergency department work in which younger patients appeared to gain more; Across unselected patients, earlier antibiotic administration compared with later administration within the first twelve hours was not associated with 28-day mortality. Certainty: Because timing was not assigned and the characteristic profiles were derived within the same patients used to build the heterogeneity models without separate validation, these patterns are exploratory associations rather than established effects. Scope: applies to sepsis without shock in adults receiving intensive care, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it recommends deferring or withholding antibiotics in patients outside the identified higher-benefit profiles on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

In sepsis **without** shock, earlier antibiotics show no mortality benefit on average; benefit is concentrated in patients who are older, more comorbid, more physiologically deranged, or have specific acute organ dysfunctions (notably liver and haematologic) and metastatic cancer — plus, at the population level, only delays beyond roughly 5–6 hours matter.

## Evidence

**Overall neutral effect in non-shock sepsis.** In a Bayesian analysis of 8,400 ICU patients meeting Sepsis-3 criteria without shock who received antibiotics within 0–12 h, time-to-antibiotics ≤3 h was not associated with 28-day mortality overall (posterior median OR 0.92; 95% CrI 0.79–1.06) [PMID 41714565; PMC13043842]. Similarly, in a 5-hospital cohort of 23,619 patients with sepsis without shock, each hour of delay (≤6 h) was not associated with mortality (aOR 1.03; 95% CI 0.98–1.09), whereas it was for septic shock (aOR 1.07; 1.04–1.11); modelling each hour separately showed only delays >6 h raised mortality in non-shock sepsis [PMID 37531612; PMC10686960]. A nationwide cohort of 3,035 patients found antibiotics within 1 h benefited septic shock (adjusted OR [passage text removed]) but not sepsis without shock (OR 0.85; 0.64–1.15) [PMC8756674].

**Characteristics identifying benefit within non-shock sepsis.** In the ICU cohort above, three concordant analytic strategies (conventional subgroup, risk-based stratification, causal forest) identified **advanced age** (≥78 years: [passage text removed]**, and **acute liver dysfunction** as the most robust markers of greater benefit from shorter time-to-antibiotics; [passage text removed] showed the most favourable estimate ([passage text removed]) [PMID 41714565; PMC13043842].

**Corroborating heterogeneity from a large community-onset sepsis cohort** (273,255 patients, 173 hospitals; not restricted to non-shock): shorter (≤3 h vs >3–12 h) time-to-antibiotics conferred greater absolute 30-day mortality reduction with **metastatic cancer** (5.0%, 95% [passage text removed]%, 0.2–0.6 without cancer; P<0.001), **acute liver dysfunction** (7.1%, 5.8–8.3 vs 2.5%, 2.0–3.1; P<0.001), **acute haematologic dysfunction** (7.0%, 5.9–8.0 vs 2.7%, 2.0–3.3; P<0.001), and **≥3 acute organ dysfunctions** (4.8%, 3.9–5.6 vs 0.5%, [passage text removed]); effects also differed by temperature and age. Notably, patients *without* shock still showed a 2.9% (2.2–3.5) absolute reduction, versus 7.0% (5.9–8.2) with shock (P=0.005 for interaction). Causal forest highlighted metastatic cancer and shock [PMID 38261986; PMC10995570; [passage text removed]].

**Characteristics that do *not* identify benefit.** Immunosuppression does not: in 39,842 suspected-sepsis hospitalisations, antibiotics at 1–3 h vs 0–1 h raised mortality only in septic shock ([passage text removed]; immunocompromised OR 1.21, 1.002–1.47), with no association in sepsis without shock in either group (OR 1.22, 0.93–1.60 and 0.94, 0.76–1.16), nor for 3–6 h vs ≤3 h [PMID 42456126; [passage text removed]].

## Caveats

All of this is observational and, for the non-shock subgroup analyses, explicitly exploratory/hypothesis-generating requiring prospective validation [PMID 41714565; PMID 38261986]. Meta-analytic estimates in non-shock sepsis are unstable and based on few studies — one pooled analysis found ORs of 1.05 (0.66–1.68) at ≤1 h, 1.27 (1.05–1.53) at ≤3 h, and 0.53 (0.38–0.74) at ≤6 h, drawn from only 3, 4, and 2 papers respectively [ejinme.com/article/S0953-6205(24)00262-0/fulltext]. Current guidance recommends rapid assessment and antimicrobials within 3 h for possible sepsis without shock (very low quality evidence), with deferral reasonable when infection likelihood is low [[passage text removed]; PMC8486643]. The two heterogeneity studies diverge on age direction (advanced age favoured in the ICU cohort; the community-onset cohort's authors illustrated benefit with a *younger* patient with metastatic cancer and liver dysfunction [[passage text removed]]), so age should be treated as unresolved.
answers.connect:

**1. The population-average effect in non-shock sepsis is weak.** In a prospective nationwide Sepsis-3 cohort, [passage text removed] septic shock (adjusted OR [passage text removed]) but not in sepsis without shock (OR [passage text removed]); spline models showed rising mortality per hour of delay only in the shock group [S:6f107761-f8db-5bbe-984d-5adc66c830f5][S:966d8ff4-e8a6-5cb1-bb41-a4c3b18dcc2b]. A meta-analysis of door-to-antibiotic time found no benefit at 1 h in non-shock patients (pooled OR 1.05, 0.66–1.68) [S:8db8b8f7-0b89-52f8-860d-29a199617da7]. In an ICU cohort of 8,400 non-shock Sepsis-3 patients, time-to-antibiotics ≤3 h was not associated with 28-day mortality overall (posterior median OR 0.92, 95% CrI 0.79–1.06) [S:9cd3427c-86d3-5096-a218-993d1f8eeebf].

**2. Characteristics marking benefit — acute organ dysfunction burden and cancer.** In 273,255 patients with community-onset sepsis at 173 VA/Kaiser hospitals, absolute 30-day mortality reduction with ≤3 h vs >3–12 h antibiotics was larger with metastatic cancer (5.0%, 95% [passage text removed]%, 0.2–0.6 without cancer, P<0.001) and with ≥3 acute organ dysfunctions (4.8%, 3.9–5.6 vs 0.5%, [passage text removed]]. Two dysfunction types were themselves strong modifiers: acute hematologic dysfunction (7.0% vs 2.7% absolute reduction, P<0.001 for interaction) and acute liver dysfunction (7.1% vs 2.5%, P<0.001), with modification also seen by temperature and age [[passage text removed]]. Applied specifically to non-shock patients, that cohort showed shorter time-to-antibiotics lowered 30-day mortality mainly [passage text removed], while other non-shock patients had no meaningful survival gain [S:c47631e8-b3b2-5da7-ac6d-9792f4d5336e].

**3. In ICU non-shock sepsis: age, comorbidity, physiologic severity, liver dysfunction.** Using subgroup, risk-based, and causal-forest analyses, greater benefit from ≤3 h antibiotics was seen with advanced age, [passage text removed], and acute liver dysfunction [S:4b7f98f6-246d-5906-b312-2ead877ceee1][S:75fd6811-9c08-5d78-8916-eb5094c4b355]. Conventional subgroups showed a distinct effect at age ≥78 years ([passage text removed]), and risk-stratified analysis favoured the third quartile of baseline mortality risk ([passage text removed]) [S:9cd3427c-86d3-5096-a218-993d1f8eeebf]. Effects also differed by [passage text removed]), peripheral vascular disease (0.49 vs 0.97), and prior myocardial infarction (0.56 vs 0.96) [[passage text removed]]. Notably, benefit rose from low to moderate severity but attenuated at the highest APS III values, i.e. the sickest patients did not gain most [S:aff9085e-1ff9-5dfa-9b79-98cd0d8fc9a1]. Supporting the age finding, a MIMIC-IV study of 12,425 elderly septic patients found delayed antibiotics increased 28-day mortality specifically in non-shock patients, with no significant association in shock patients [S:82669396-bfb2-5d5d-baf7-db90c5d628eb][S:1e0d6114-6fd5-5756-8e94-16847f10a496].

**4. Direction of the age effect is setting-dependent — an important caveat.** ED-based community-onset cohorts have found greater benefit in *younger* patients (e.g. antibiotics within 1 h reduced mortality in those <75 years, OR 0.63, 0.44–0.91, and in those without prior antibiotics in 90 days, non-pulmonary infection, and ICU admission) [S:966d8ff4-e8a6-5cb1-bb41-a4c3b18dcc2b]; a prehospital-trial reanalysis likewise reported a significant age–benefit interaction (P = .03) favouring younger patients [S:cad2015e-d885-5f0b-bfb9-609a68fde746]. The ICU authors attribute the discrepancy to differing physiologic reserve and community- vs hospital-onset case mix [S:a73f3dbc-0293-594a-9c85-a4419915b952].

**5. Characteristics marking *absence* of benefit.** Patients without shock and with low likelihood of progressing to shock had similar mortality whether antibiotics came before or after the recommended threshold, supporting deferral for further work-up [S:7179cb5e-c62d-5bcb-b70f-48422342cb92][S:775a3335-b210-5a61-9275-1f0430f6ed20]; in a 166,559-patient ED cohort, non-shock groups had median times to antibiotics of 3.2 h (probable infection) and 5.5 h (possible infection) with mortality of 3% and 2% respectively [S:6b6ad34d-5fbd-5570-8a26-0b868b12fd45].

**Caveats:** all of these modifiers come from observational data subject to confounding by indication, are explicitly labelled exploratory/hypothesis-generating by the authors, and await prospective validation [S:4b7f98f6-246d-5906-b312-2ead877ceee1][S:492e6c98-4fe5-5994-afe5-ff5eff2a26d5]. One cluster-randomised trial secondary analysis dissents, reporting similar per-hour effects in patients with and without shock ([passage text removed]) [S:9da2ef64-3812-56c5-a347-2193c796ffcb]. I found no evidence identifying infection source, sex, or biomarker thresholds as validated modifiers within the non-shock population specifically.

rows.question: What outcomes follow adjunctive Xuebijing injection added to standard care in patients with sepsis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Adding Xuebijing injection to conventional treatment reduces 28-day mortality compared with conventional treatment alone; Mortality during the treatment period is also lower with added Xuebijing injection than with conventional treatment alone; The APACHE II severity-score benefit is less secure than the mortality benefit: estimates range from a clear improvement to no clear difference; Adverse event rates did not differ between conventional treatment with and without added Xuebijing injection. Certainty: The two mortality reductions rest on reasonably strong evidence combining allocation-controlled comparisons across multiple patient groups, whereas the APACHE II severity benefit is less secure, and the safety finding reflects only an absence of detected differences in harms rather than demonstrated equivalence. Scope: applies to sepsis, including severe sepsis and septic shock in adults receiving standard care, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents an optimal Xuebijing injection dose as established or recommends a particular dosing regimen on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Adjunctive Xuebijing injection (XBJ, 100 mL IV every 12 h for 5 days) added to standard care reduces 28-day mortality in sepsis by roughly 7 absolute percentage points, with signals of improved organ dysfunction and fewer ICU/ventilator days; the safety profile in trials was comparable to placebo, though evidence is dominated by trials conducted in China and post-marketing reports flag rare anaphylaxis.

## Mortality (primary evidence)

**EXIT-SEP** (multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 45 ICUs in China, Oct 2017–Jun 2019; 1817 randomized adults aged 18–75 with Sepsis-3 present <48 h and SOFA 2–13) randomized patients 1:1 to XBJ 100 mL vs volume-matched saline every 12 h for 5 days on top of standard care. 28-day mortality was 165/878 (18.8%) with XBJ vs 230/882 (26.1%) with placebo, absolute risk difference [passage text removed]<.001 [PMC10152378; jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/article-abstract/2804120]. Benefit was seen in both ICU and general-ward strata [medpagetoday.com/hospitalbasedmedicine/infectioncontrol/104283].

An earlier placebo-controlled trial in **severe community-acquired pneumonia** found 28-day mortality 15.87% with XBJ vs 24.63% with control (difference 8.8%, 95% CI 2.4–15.2; P=0.006) [[passage text removed]].

A **pooled patient-level reanalysis of EXIT-SEP plus XBJ-SCAP restricted to septic shock** found 28-day mortality 99/427 (23.2%) with XBJ vs 132/434 (30.4%) with placebo, absolute risk reduction [passage text removed]; PMC12502413].

## Secondary/organ outcomes

- **EXIT-SEP:** ICU mortality 14.2% vs 20.[passage text removed]; P=.001) and hospital mortality 17.0% vs 22.8% ([passage text removed]; P=.002), plus differences in ICU-free days and 28-day mechanical ventilation–free days — but the authors state these secondary results were **exploratory only** and did not control type I error [PMC10152378; medpagetoday.com/...104283].
- **Septic shock pooled cohort:** [passage text removed]), and greater day-6 SOFA improvement (−[passage text removed] change did not differ significantly [[passage text removed]].
- **In a smaller RCT of sepsis-related myocardial injury**, XBJ improved cTnI, NT-proBNP and PCT trajectories at days 3/7/10 and shortened ICU stay (11.5 vs 13.8 days; P<0.001), but 28-day mortality was not significantly different (14.7% vs 22.9%; P=0.39) — i.e., single small trials are underpowered for mortality [PMC7147202].
- **Sepsis-associated AKI meta-analysis:** XBJ as adjuvant therapy reduced 28-day mortality and improved kidney function, immune parameters, APACHE II scores, and inflammatory cytokines; subgroup analysis suggested 200 mL/day suppressed TNF-α more than 100 mL/day (MD −1.48 vs −0.71 ng/mL; interaction p=0.03) [PMC12583064].

## Subgroups / heterogeneity of effect

- **Diabetes subgroup of EXIT-SEP:** 28-day mortality 29/173 (16.8%) with XBJ vs 56/198 (28.3%) placebo (difference 11.5, 95% CI 3.1–19.9; p=0.01), with lower ICU (14.5% vs 23.2%; p=0.03) and hospital mortality (16.2% vs 24.8%; p=0.04); length of stay, ventilator-free days, SOFA and APACHE II changes were not significantly different [PMC11905295 / [passage text removed]].
- **Phenotype post hoc analysis (n=1760):** benefit concentrated in SENECA-like phenotypes [passage text removed]), though the treatment-by-phenotype interaction was not significant; phenotype δ (acidosis, coagulopathy, shock) had the highest 28-day mortality (32.5%) and showed more ventilator-free and ICU-free days with XBJ (p for interaction <0.001) [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40666169; PMC12257024].

## Meta-analytic and dosing evidence (weaker)

Multiple meta-analyses of XBJ + routine treatment vs routine treatment report reduced 28-day mortality (e.g., [passage text removed] across 13 trials; RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.44–0.59 across 32 trials/2315 patients; OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.56–0.97) plus improved APACHE II, WBC, PCT, CRP and coagulation indices — but GRADE certainty was rated only **low to moderate**, with serious risk of bias and inconsistency, and one review found benefit at 100 mL/d but not 200 mL/d (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.00–1.54) [lcm.amegroups.org/article/view/7467/html; sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378874118303003]. A network meta-analysis concluded 100 mL/day best improved APTT and CRP, ~150 mL/day was best for 28-day mortality, and 300 mL/day best for APACHE II, recommending total daily dose between 100 and 300 mL — with explicit caution that SUCRA rankings should not be generalized [PMC12137327; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40475962].

## Safety

In EXIT-SEP, adverse events occurred in 200/872 (22.9%) with XBJ vs 222/878 (25.3%) with placebo; the commonest with XBJ were raised ALT (5.8%), raised AST (4.4%), and high leukocyte count (4.1%), with no treatment-related severe AEs or discontinuations for toxicity [PMC10152378; [passage text removed]]. However, a correspondence piece notes that a systematic review in sepsis-associated AKI [passage text removed] after IV XBJ in septic patients, and that pharmacovigilance data list unpredictable anaphylactic/anaphylactoid reactions as the most frequently reported serious adverse events [[passage text removed], citing Crit Care 2025;29:522].

## Caveats

Evidence rests essentially on one large efficacy trial conducted entirely in China; commentary in the same journal noted the single efficacy study, non-US setting, and unusual infection-site distribution (lung 45%, intra-abdominal 32%) as limits on generalizability, calling for an international trial [[passage text removed]]. Other stated limitations include loss to follow-up, pre-allocation antimicrobials in ~95% of patients, exclusion of the most severe patients, and no long-term survival data [infectiousdiseaseadvisor.com/...]. A retrospective comparative-effectiveness/trial-emulation study using EXIT-SEP XBJ recipients (n=911) against MIMIC-IV external controls (n=8,764) showed crude 28-day mortality that was actually *higher* in XBJ patients (18.1% vs 15.5%) yet, after overlap weighting, an HR of [passage text removed]) — illustrating how strongly these external-control estimates depend on adjustment [[passage text removed]]. A real-world confirmatory study (EXIT-SEP REAL, 5,400 participants) is under way [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** Adjunctive Xuebijing injection (XBJ) added to standard sepsis care has been associated with lower 28-day mortality — roughly a 7-percentage-point absolute reduction in the pivotal placebo-controlled trial — plus signals of reduced ICU mortality and more ventilator-/ICU-free days, without an excess of adverse events; but the supporting evidence is almost entirely from China and the non-mortality outcomes are exploratory or of low certainty.

**Pivotal RCT (EXIT-SEP)**
- Design: multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled; 1817 patients randomized across 45 ICUs in 22 Chinese provinces to [passage text removed]); antibiotics, resuscitation/vasopressors and source control followed guideline care in both arms [S:793cf88a][S:10f97a8c][S:2f7f62ed].
- Primary outcome: 28-day mortality was 18.8% with XBJ vs 26.1% with placebo [S:fcbfa01c], described by the investigators as a 7.3-percentage-point reduction, exceeding the 6-point difference the trial was powered for [S:f810b170].
- Secondary outcomes: XBJ reduced ICU mortality and was associated with more [passage text removed]; the authors caution these are exploratory, since 10 secondary outcomes were analysed without adjustment for multiple comparisons [S:f810b170][S:793cf88a].
- Safety: no statistically significant between-group difference in adverse events, and no treatment discontinuations attributed to drug toxicity [S:f810b170].

**Subgroup / pooled trial data**
- In a post hoc pooled analysis of EXIT-SEP and XBJ-SAP restricted to 378 septic patients with diabetes, 28-day mortality was 16.8% (29/173) with XBJ vs 28.3% (56/198) with placebo (risk difference [passage text removed]; P=0.01), with lower ICU (14.5% vs 23.2%) and hospital (16.2% vs 24.8%) mortality [S:fb982e0a][S:94eeac37]. In this subgroup, however, ICU-free days, ventilator-free days, and SOFA/APACHE II score changes did not differ significantly, and adverse events were comparable (24.4% vs 27.7%) [S:94eeac37][S:fb982e0a].
- In severe community-acquired pneumonia (a related XBJ trial of 710 patients), adding XBJ reduced 28-day mortality from 24.6% to 15.9% and improved pneumonia severity index, SOFA and APACHE II scores [S:0547a0f7]; post hoc analysis found the survival benefit was significant only in non-overweight and non-hyperglycaemic patients, with no significant difference in adverse events [S:546655a2][S:435e3541].

**Meta-analytic evidence**
- An updated meta-analysis of RCTs totalling 3007 septic patients (1551 XBJ + conventional treatment vs 1456 conventional treatment alone) reported reduced 28-day mortality (RR 0.69, 0.60–0.78), reduced mortality during treatment (RR 0.74, 0.62–0.88), lower APACHE II score (MD 3.91, 2.45–5.38) and lower body temperature (MD 0.43, 0.31–0.55), with no significant difference in adverse events (RR 0.91, 0.77–1.07) [S:aa450154][S:668559a6].
- In sepsis-associated AKI, 18 RCTs (1650 patients) found reduced 28-day mortality (RR 0.82, 0.69–0.98), improved renal function (serum creatinine MD −17.55 µmol/L; BUN MD −1.58 mmol/L), lower TNF-α and IL-6, improved T-cell subsets, and lower APACHE II score (MD −3.12); reported adverse reactions were all mild, but [passage text removed], and the authors call for large double-blind RCTs [S:e2165e05][S:bd18ae44][S:22b2814d].

**Caveats**
- An overview of 13 systematic reviews of XBJ for sepsis rated all as critically low methodological quality on AMSTAR-2, concluding the apparent synergy with Western medicine should be interpreted cautiously [S:e1eea673].
- Earlier trials were small and methodologically limited, which the EXIT-SEP authors cite as the reason a large trial was needed [S:e05af476][S:3d819dd1]. Because the evidence is China-based, commentary notes that regulatory approval elsewhere would typically require two independent adequate and well-controlled trials plus demonstrated applicability to other populations [S:fcbfa01c].

rows.question: In children with sepsis in emergency departments, how does time to antibiotic administration relate to mortality?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Pediatric evidence on antibiotic timing and mortality is inconsistent: a large multicenter collaborative found longer times to antibiotics associated with lower rather than higher 30-day mortality, while other pediatric reports tie higher mortality only to delays of several hours, so the direction of the timing-mortality relationship is unsettled; Antibiotic timing was not associated with 3-day mortality, either as a continuous measure or across the 60-minute threshold; The inverse timing-mortality association is open to confounding by indication, because illness severity was not recorded and children who received vasoactive agents were more often treated within 60 minutes. Certainty: The evidence is an association drawn from routinely collected care records with no measure of how sick each child was, and it points opposite to other pediatric reports, so the relationship should be treated as unsettled rather than established. Scope: applies to sepsis in children and adolescents, emergency department settings. An answer is wrong if it treats later antibiotic administration as protective or advises deferring antibiotics in children with suspected sepsis on the basis of these findings.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Longer time to antibiotics is associated with higher mortality in children with sepsis presenting to the ED, but the association is strongest for substantial delays (roughly >3–5.5 h) rather than for missing a 1-hour target, and antibiotic timing in isolation is a weaker predictor than completion of a full sepsis bundle.

## Evidence

**Largest ED-based study (inflection point ~330 min).** In a retrospective cohort of 19,515 children (ages 29 days to <18 years) with [passage text removed] at [passage text removed] (IPSO) collaborative, median time to antibiotics was 69 minutes (IQR 47–116). Piecewise regression identified 330 minutes from ED arrival as the point at which 3-day sepsis-attributable mortality began to increase. Children treated before 330 minutes (n=19,164) had [passage text removed]); those treated at ≥330 minutes (n=351) had 1.2% (4 patients) and 2.0% (7 patients), with adjusted [passage text removed]) at 3 days [passage text removed]) at 30 days. Beyond the inflection point, each additional 30 minutes carried [passage text removed]). Notably, ICU admission, vasoactive use, and ventilation did not differ significantly across the 330-minute threshold (JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(6):e2413955 — [passage text removed]).

**Bacteremia subgroup.** Among 2,054 patients with bacteremia who received antibiotics within 180 minutes, the estimated inflection point was 90 minutes — but this was not statistically significant; the authors flag bacteremic children as the group most likely to benefit from truly early antibiotics and a priority for future study (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2819560; [passage text removed]).

**Earlier single-centre PICU data support an ~3-hour threshold.** In children treated for severe sepsis/septic shock, [passage text removed] was 140 min (IQR 74–277). Mortality risk escalated with each hour of delay but only became significant beyond [passage text removed] >3-h delay to initial antimicrobial [passage text removed]) to first *appropriate* antimicrobial; after severity adjustment these rose to 4.84 (1.45–16.2) and 4.92 (1.30–18.58). Delay >3 h also meant fewer organ-failure-free days (16 vs 20; P=.04) ([passage text removed]).

**Antibiotic timing alone vs. bundle.** Following the New York State sepsis mandate, among 1,179 children (≈69% with septic shock), completing the whole 1-hour bundle within 1 hour lowered risk-adjusted [passage text removed]; P=.02), whereas antibiotics alone within 1 hour did not reach significance ([passage text removed]; P=.18), nor did blood cultures (0.73) or fluid bolus (0.88) individually (JAMA 2018;320(4):358–367 — [passage text removed]). In IPSO (37,339 episodes, ~34% "critical sepsis"), a *time-liberalized* bundle (fluid bolus <60 min, antibiotics <180 min) was associated with greater mortality reduction than the original stricter bundle, cutting 30-day sepsis-attributable [passage text removed]) in the critical-sepsis group (Pediatrics 2023;152(2):e2022059938 — [passage text removed]; https://www.khaquality.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Improving-Pediatric-Sepsis-Outcomes-Change-Package.pdf).

**Discordant/null pediatric findings.** A single-centre retrospective study [passage text removed] ED (2007–2015) found no significant association between target time to antibiotic administration and mortality, PICU admission, length of stay, or organ dysfunction resolution (Hosp Pediatr 2020;10(4):311–317 — https://publications.aap.org/hospitalpediatrics/article/10/4/311/26065/Antibiotic-Timing-in-Pediatric-Septic-Shock). Conversely, in 441 Indian children, delay beyond 1 hour from recognition was associated with increased [passage text removed]), significant only in the septic shock stratum (77% of the cohort) (reviewed in J Pediatric Infect Dis Soc 2024;13(11):608–615 — [passage text removed]).

## Caveats

- The authoritative pediatric review concludes that while the literature supports an association between antibiotic timing and outcomes, **a specific threshold at which mortality increases remains undefined**, attributing this to cohort heterogeneity, non-randomized designs with residual confounding, and low short-term sepsis-attributable mortality in children that limits power (PMC11599145).
- The 330-minute inflection point is *longer* than the guideline targets and differs from prior studies; the study authors caution that low overall mortality and few very-late-treated patients may have influenced where the inflection fell (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2819560).
- Adult meta-analytic data show the same pattern of a weak 1-hour signal and clearer benefit at longer windows: OR 0.83 (95% CI 0.67–1.04) for ≤1 h vs >1 h, but 0.80 (0.68–0.94) for ≤3 h and 0.57 (0.39–0.82) for ≤6 h across 42 studies/190,896 patients — adults only, so not directly generalizable to children ([passage text removed]).
- Current guidance (2020 Pediatric Surviving Sepsis Campaign) remains antibiotics [passage text removed]-associated organ dysfunction without shock (PMC11599145).

**Not supported by retrieved evidence:** I found no randomized trial in children comparing antibiotic timing strategies, and no pediatric-specific meta-analysis pooling time-to-antibiotic effects on mortality.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line: observational evidence shows that *long* delays are associated with higher mortality, but the pediatric data do not support a sharp mortality penalty at the guideline-recommended 1-hour mark — and studies using very short thresholds paradoxically show higher mortality in the fastest-treated children, most plausibly confounding by indication.**

**Long delays are harmful.** The largest study (multicenter retrospective cohort, 51 US hospitals in the Improving Pediatric Sepsis Outcomes collaborative, 19,515 children aged 29 days to <18 years [passage text removed]) identified an inflection point at 330 minutes from ED arrival, beyond which [passage text removed] rose [S:c2ffb292, S:ee5b782c, S:730e7e79]. Sepsis-attributable mortality was 0.5% (3-day) and 0.9% (30-day) among the 19,164 treated within 330 minutes versus 1.2% and 2.0% among the 351 treated at ≥330 minutes [S:94c2e418]; adjusted odds were 3.44 (3-day) and 3.63 (30-day), with an OR of 2.44 per additional 30 minutes beyond the cut-point; median time to antibiotics overall was 69 minutes [S:49e1b94a, S:dc774e3b]. Notably, ICU admission, vasoactive use, and ventilation did not differ across the inflection point [S:730e7e79], and inflection points were similar in the critical-sepsis and high-risk-condition subgroups [S:12733bab].

**The 1-hour threshold itself is not well supported in children.** A separate multicenter cohort (6,153 patients, 19 pediatric EDs, 2013–2016) found that *[passage text removed] all-cause mortality — both as a continuous variable and dichotomized at ≤60 vs >60 minutes — with no association with 3-day mortality, vasoactive use, or ICU/hospital length of stay, and results unchanged after adjusting for fluid bolus timing [S:cf857087, S:3fb5055e, S:ad56d6a1]. In the IPSO cohort, children given antibiotics within the first 29 minutes had higher mortality (1.3%) than those treated at 30–329 minutes (0.4%) [S:730e7e79]; post hoc analysis showed this group was sicker and enriched for malignancy and fever-and-neutropenia protocol patients, i.e. rapid treatment marked severity rather than causing harm [S:12733bab]. Authors of the smaller cohort attribute the inverse association to the same confounding by indication, which they could not fully adjust for absent consistent severity data [S:1e55def2].

**Earlier pediatric studies, mostly single-center, are heterogeneous.** Weiss et al. (PICU patients with severe sepsis/septic shock) found escalating mortality risk per hour of delay, statistically significant only beyond [passage text removed]; 4.84, 95% CI 1.45–16.2 after severity adjustment) [S:730e7e79, S:16be1be9, S:94e29102]. Sankar et al. reported higher mortality odds ([passage text removed]) with antibiotics after 1 hour from recognition in ED sepsis/septic shock, though no difference when dichotomized at 2 hours [S:730e7e79, S:3fb5055e].

**Mechanistic/contextual caveats.** Guidelines recommend antibiotics within 1 hour of septic shock recognition and within 3 hours for sepsis-associated organ dysfunction without shock [S:ee5b782c]. Evidence suggests the *whole bundle* rather than antibiotic timing alone drives benefit: in a 1-hour bundle mandate analysis, full bundle completion [passage text removed] antibiotics alone [passage text removed]) [S:a88031b8]. An accompanying editorial notes that randomized trials are precluded by practical and ethical constraints, that observational data consistently favor early antibiotics in septic shock specifically, and that nonspecific presentations and predominant viral illness in pediatric EDs complicate universal time targets [S:70e9d553]. All the pediatric evidence here is retrospective and subject to residual confounding by illness severity — the IPSO authors used only surrogates (high-risk conditions, dichotomized lactate) as severity proxies and call for prospective study [S:699ceb5c].
