rows.question: What can peripheral blood DNA methylation profiles indicate about Alzheimer's disease risk in adults with periodontitis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Peripheral blood DNA methylation at selected loci is reported to associate with incident Alzheimer's disease risk and with measures of disease progression; Peripheral blood DNA methylation profiles are reported to correlate with cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers of amyloid, tau, neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration; Blood DNA methylation findings in Alzheimer's disease are enriched for immune and inflammatory pathways that overlap with the pro-inflammatory axes altered in periodontitis, with reported convergence in genes of immune regulation and protein processing; Blood-to-brain correspondence is reported at some loci such as APOE, while DNA methylation is described as highly tissue specific and blood is used as a surrogate tissue rather than a faithful copy of cerebral change. Certainty: The evidence is a narrative synthesis without effect estimates, so these are reported associations rather than causal or clinically validated links, and blood-to-brain correspondence holds only at selected loci. Scope: applies to periodontitis and Alzheimer's disease in adults, population-based settings. An answer is wrong if it presents blood DNA methylation testing as an established way to determine which people with periodontal disease will develop Alzheimer's disease, or recommends clinical action on such a result.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

No study has yet measured blood DNA methylation in a periodontitis cohort and followed those adults for incident Alzheimer's disease, so peripheral methylation profiles cannot currently be said to *indicate* AD risk in this population. What exists is indirect and hypothesis-generating: partially overlapping methylation signatures (notably HOX-cluster and imprinting-regulator loci) and shared epigenetic-ageing signals, set against Mendelian randomization evidence that argues against a causal periodontitis→AD pathway.

## What blood methylation shows in periodontitis

An Illumina EPIC pilot in peripheral leukocytes (8 periodontitis cases, 8 age- and sex-matched periodontally healthy controls) found 81 hypermethylated and 21 hypomethylated genes, with *ZNF718* and *HOXA4* hypermethylated and *ZFP57* hypomethylated in the intersection of position- and region-level analyses; enrichment was immune-related ("detection of bacterium", "antigen processing and presentation"), and the authors framed leukocyte methylome profiling as a window onto *systemic* immune-related epigenetic patterns in periodontitis ([J Periodontal Res 2021;56:710–725]([passage text removed])).

The largest clinically-examined replication, in 1077 African American and 457 European American ARIC participants, confirmed a *ZFP57* region (6p22.1) significantly hypomethylated in severe versus [passage text removed], plus a Chr10 region (*ENSG00000231601*) differing in African American participants with edentulism ([PMC10528731](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10528731); [preprint]([passage text removed])).

## Where these signals touch AD

- **HOX-cluster convergence.** Blood EWAS in Add-NeuroMed (284 individuals: 89 controls, 86 AD, 109 MCI including 38 who progressed within 1 year) identified robust *HOXB6* hypermethylation in AD ([Maastricht record]([passage text removed])); a blood-based diagnostic panel found *HOXA3* methylation the strongest predictor alongside *NXN*, *TREML2*, *ABCA7*, adding value to a plasma pTau181 model ([Neurology 10.1212/WNL.0000000000207865]([passage text removed])); and a leukocyte AD study reported differentially methylated *HOXA-AS3* and *HOXA6* among top genes ([10.1177/25424823251341176]([passage text removed])). This makes HOX loci a plausible but unproven shared axis with the periodontitis *HOXA4* finding.
- **The only review addressing the intersection directly** concludes that aberrant methylation [passage text removed] suggests converging molecular pathways, and evaluates blood-based epigenetic biomarkers as a *potential* — not established — tool ([J Alzheimers Dis 2025;109(2):499–525](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41295894)).
- **Epigenetic ageing links both ends but in the opposite direction.** MR found GrimAge acceleration increased periodontitis risk ([passage text removed] in FinnGen; [passage text removed] in GLIDE), with *HOXB7* a shared gene across periodontitis and all age-acceleration measures ([PMC12619391](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12619391); [PMC12599416]([passage text removed])). Separately, DNAmPhenoAge and DNAmGrimAge predicted progression from normal cognition to MCI/AD and cortical thinning ([npj Dement 2025;1(1):7]([passage text removed])). So accelerated epigenetic age is a candidate *shared upstream* driver rather than evidence that periodontitis-related methylation causes AD.

## Key caveats

- Bidirectional MR studies find no convincing genetic causal link from periodontal disease to AD ([PMC11034860](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11034860); [PLOS One 10.1371/journal.pone.0228206]([passage text removed])), and none [passage text removed] ([BMC Oral Health 10.1186/s12903-024-04367-7]([passage text removed])) — even though observational meta-analysis links periodontitis to dementia (OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.65–3.09) ([umbrella review]([passage text removed])).
- Blood methylation marks in AD may be consequences, not predictors: in AD-discordant twins, an identified mark was *not* predictive and became differentially methylated only after disease onset ([Clin Epigenetics 2019;11:130]([passage text removed])).
- Overlapping loci are not disease-specific: the *ZFP57* region is also implicated in autistic traits ([PMID 40819066](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40819066)) and *HOXA3/HOXA4* in lung cancer risk ([PMC8993104]([passage text removed])), so shared hits likely reflect generic inflammatory/ageing programmes.
- The periodontitis discovery study had 16 subjects total; effect sizes for epigenetic clocks against AD biomarkers are described as modest with limited predictive power ([PMC12315259]([passage text removed])).

**Practical read:** peripheral methylation is a legitimate, non-invasive readout of the systemic immune dysregulation and biological ageing that both conditions share, but as of now it supports mechanistic hypothesis-generation — not AD risk stratification — in adults with periodontitis. The missing study is a periodontitis cohort with baseline methylomes and prospective AD ascertainment.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

At present, peripheral blood DNA methylation in adults with periodontitis is a **plausible but unvalidated** indicator of Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk: blood methylation signatures exist independently for periodontitis and for AD, and they converge on inflammatory/immune pathways, but no study has yet shown that a blood methylation profile measured in periodontitis patients predicts incident AD. The most directly relevant synthesis is explicitly hypothesis-generating and does not establish causality [S:c154b18b-029f-5039-8919-f4f5c50987ab].

## What the evidence actually supports

**1. Both diseases leave detectable blood methylation marks, and blood is a defensible proxy tissue.**
Blood-based epigenetic measures are attractive because collection is minimally invasive, allows longitudinal monitoring, and captures immune/inflammatory signals implicated in neurodegeneration [S:41124658-aca5-591d-aa62-58f933b2288f]. Peripheral blood [passage text removed], with differential patterns in AD patients versus healthy individuals suggesting a [passage text removed] [S:d6195bf1-301d-5170-be4c-4296c7e1703c]. [passage text removed] for co-expressed, heritably variable genes, and blood methylation has been correlated with CSF biomarkers, implying CSF-level pathology is partly reflected in the blood epigenome [S:3b22fcca-2387-5d2f-bf26-b240371e24d3]. An independent blood-leukocyte AD study found enrichment of immune and intracellular signalling processes and identified brain-surrogate CpGs in PCDHGB1-3/PCDHGA1-6 [S:f20bbe37-180a-54f4-a089-deee6b087d13][S:7c32cc83-1f3b-5d2e-ba4b-9fe82768a108].

**2. Periodontitis itself has reproducible blood methylation signatures — but they are periodontitis loci, not AD loci.**
A well-powered EWAS in ARIC (1077 African American and 457 European American adults with clinical dental examination) replicated a hypomethylated ZFP57 region in severe periodontal disease in European Americans and found four HOXA4 CpGs hypermethylated in severe disease in African Americans (ORs per 1 SD ranging ~1.24–1.30) [S:10962f19-f657-5240-aeb3-8f50e345a593]; the ZFP57 region overlapped a 21-CpG region previously reported hypomethylated in a small clinically diagnosed periodontitis cohort [S:9f10ee53-b334-5bf1-a462-50466d39895b][S:e662080d-b4dd-5892-9196-3a3494217ed9]. A UK twin EWAS found cg21245277 (ZNF804A) associated with gingival bleeding and 58 sites with tooth mobility (top signals IQCE, XKR6), plus enrichment at candidate inflammatory loci including VDR, IL6ST, IL1RN, CD44, IL1B and CXCL1 [S:9a31629c-c819-507d-9660-c04736f06227][S:2493ac4c-82b8-5ceb-b275-940dd6bdc7b1]. None of these loci has been linked to AD outcomes.

**3. The mechanistic rationale is inflammatory convergence, not a shared methylation signature.**
Chronic periodontal inflammation is proposed to trigger systemic responses that compromise blood–brain barrier integrity, facilitating amyloid-β and hyperphosphorylated tau accumulation, with aberrant methylation in immune-regulation and protein-processing genes suggesting convergent pathways [S:c154b18b-029f-5039-8919-f4f5c50987ab][S:cefff91b-39a7-543d-9043-957db59c8d86]. Transcriptomic crosstalk analysis nominated 48 genes, three transcription factors (FOS, MEF2C, USF2), pathways (JAK-STAT, MAPK, NF-κB, NK-cell cytotoxicity) and core shared genes C4A, C4B, CXCL12, FCGR3A, IL1B, MMP3 [S:f8ade185-35cc-5b46-a4d8-6f282edde423][S:d6195bf1-301d-5170-be4c-4296c7e1703c]. Experimentally, *P. gingivalis* gingipains induce CpG hypomethylation of the TREM1 promoter in neutrophils, proposed to reduce Aβ phagocytosis/clearance, and LPS-driven promoter hypermethylation in hippocampus can amplify neuroinflammation [S:2ce36778-90e5-576f-92ac-3fe5d8719d40]. A murine methylome-wide study of microbial-induced periodontal disease found more differentially methylated genes in blood than in maxilla, supporting a systemic methylation footprint of periodontal infection [S:81b0892a-267b-517f-af50-71cfc172f48f].

**4. Where blood methylation does carry AD-risk information (in general populations).**
Peripheral blood studies report APOE 5′UTR hypomethylation with concordant brain patterns in AD cases, and population analyses associate blood methylation at selected loci with incident AD risk and longitudinal progression — the basis for claimed preclinical risk-stratification potential [S:f94d66e3-554b-5f95-b647-4e190984355b]. A blood meta-analysis nominated five CpGs (SPIDR, CDH6, intergenic) as candidate AD diagnostic markers [S:3b22fcca-2387-5d2f-bf26-b240371e24d3]. Replication across studies is limited and effect directions conflict (hyper- vs hypomethylation), and blood findings are hard to interpret given tissue specificity [S:55091f7e-6ade-5045-b33b-e4e24767f66a].

**5. Epigenetic-clock evidence is indirect and partly discordant.**
Mendelian randomization linked GrimAge acceleration to increased periodontitis risk ([passage text removed] in FinnGen; [passage text removed] in GLIDE) [S:96e904be-efac-5b74-9e61-d275b6626bd2] — i.e. faster biological ageing predicting periodontitis, the reverse of the direction needed. Clock-based dementia prediction is inconsistent: the Lothian Birth Cohort 1921 found no consistent association between four age-acceleration measures and incident dementia in those over 79 [S:abe06b4e-482b-5dda-ae0a-e70e23841fa4], and a systematic review notes mixed results [S:39808557-d247-5fb8-91ff-55c2b7fbc937], though DunedinPACE and PhenoAge/GrimAge have been associated with cognitive decline and MCI/AD progression in other cohorts [S:243dfc92-eb11-5977-a960-43ef7a1e81f0].

## Key caveats

- **No direct evidence.** I found no study measuring blood methylation in periodontitis patients and following them for AD incidence; the review that raises the idea recommends that future randomized periodontal-therapy trials prospectively add blood methylation endpoints ([passage text removed], methylation risk scores) to permit mediation analysis [S:f94d66e3-554b-5f95-b647-4e190984355b].
- **Confounding is substantial.** Smoking is a shared driver — the ARIC EWAS had to adjust for self-reported smoking, pack-years and methylation-predicted pack-years plus leukocyte composition [S:0cd2f9f8-d7d9-53c3-be9d-a180a3d692be] — and in AD twin work, methylation at a candidate mark was influenced by sex, age, zygosity, APOE genotype and smoking, and became differentially methylated only *after* disease onset, i.e. it was not predictive [S:478e1809-e28e-5e96-859a-4ae609654a41].
- **Cell-composition and tissue-specificity artefacts** limit inference from leukocyte DNA to brain [S:746680c9-6386-5ad7-a9d3-86c2c407e103][S:55091f7e-6ade-5045-b33b-e4e24767f66a].
- Even the upstream clinical premise (periodontitis → dementia) is not fully established; cohort studies of tooth loss and dementia have yielded conflicting results, and causality has not been confirmed [S:e2eec60b-5cc5-572d-902a-4a8ebc646226][S:68ac6fa0-a05a-52ec-93c0-2f1fdc1bc2c5].

**Practical read:** blood methylation profiling in periodontitis patients is currently a research tool for hypothesis testing — useful for characterising systemic inflammatory burden and for nominating shared immune/complement loci — not a validated AD risk test.

rows.question: What visual outcomes follow a first episode of optic neuritis in children presenting without prior demyelinating disease?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Decreased visual acuity at presentation is nearly universal and often severe; Acuity improves substantially thereafter, with more than half of children recovering full vision from the first episode; A substantial minority nevertheless remain legally blind in the worse-seeing eye at last examination; In this small series, children with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder had the poorest visual outcomes. Certainty: The evidence rests on descriptive patterns from a small group of children tracked over several years, sufficient to characterise the spread of visual outcomes but with too few children in each diagnostic category to resolve differences between phenotypes. Scope: applies to first episode of optic neuritis without prior demyelinating disease in children and adolescents, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents high-efficacy long-term immunotherapy as demonstrated to prevent further relapses after a first optic neuritis episode in children, or recommends it as established on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Most children with a first episode of optic neuritis (ON) and no prior demyelinating diagnosis recover good high-contrast visual acuity by 3–6 months and hold it for at least 2 years, despite often severe acuity loss at presentation — but low-contrast acuity and structural recovery are incomplete, and a minority (roughly one in five) are left below age-normal vision.

## Prospective evidence (PON1)

The Pediatric Optic Neuritis Prospective Outcomes Study enrolled 44 children aged 3–15 years presenting with a first episode of ON in previously unaffected eye(s) within 2 weeks of symptom onset, at 23 US/Canadian pediatric ophthalmology or neuro-ophthalmology clinics ([PMID 33057592](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33057592); [PMC10357378]([passage text removed])).

- **6 months:** mean high-contrast VA improved from 0.95 logMAR (20/200) at baseline to 0.12 logMAR (20/25); mean distance low-contrast VA improved from 1.49 logMAR (20/640) to 0.73 logMAR (20/100) ([PMID 33057592](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33057592)).
- **2 years (28/44, 64%, completed):** high-contrast VA was 0.12 logMAR (~20/25⁻²) at 1 year and 0.11 logMAR at 2 years; 24 participants (79%) had age-normal VA and 21 (66%) had 20/20 or better. Low-contrast VA plateaued at ~0.68 logMAR (~20/100), i.e. persistently subnormal ([PMC10357378]([passage text removed]); [Ophthalmology 2022, Pineles et al.]([passage text removed] 6 children *without* age-normal VA at 2 years had final diagnoses of NMOSD (n=2), MS (n=2), and isolated ON (n=2) ([PMC10357378]([passage text removed])).
- Further ON episodes occurred in 5 (18%) participants (3 relapses, 2 new episodes), and children whose ON remained clinically isolated were less likely to relapse or develop an associated neurologic condition ([Mayo Clinic record of Pineles et al. 2022]([passage text removed]-); [AAO summary]([passage text removed]-)).

## Retrospective confirmation and timing of recovery

In 59 children with first-episode ON at a tertiary pediatric hospital (mean age 12.6 years, 72% female, 41% bilateral), 81% were ≥20/20 and 89% ≥20/40 at 1 year; at 3 months 67% were ≥20/20 and 89% ≥20/40 ([PMID 24907434](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24907434); tabulated data at [entokey extract]([passage text removed])). Mean time to recovery of normal acuity was 61 days, but 97 days for those presenting at counting fingers or worse versus 35 days for better presenting acuity ([AAO summary](https://www.aao.org/editors-choice/characteristics-visual-outcomes-of-pediatric-optic)). The only predictor of poor 1-year outcome (<20/40) was VA <[passage text removed], OR 13); presenting acuity, sex, bilaterality, disc edema, treatment and underlying diagnosis were not predictive ([entokey extract of Wan et al.]([passage text removed])).

A prospective Indian cohort of 45 children (77 eyes) with ON — 67% of eyes worse than 6/60 at presentation — found median VA improved from a nadir of 2.1 logMAR to 0 logMAR, with 83% of eyes recovering; at median 35 months, 10 children (22%) had ≥1 relapse, and relapsing ON was the significant risk factor for poor recovery ([Eur J Paediatr Neurol, doi:10.1016/j.ejpn.2024.01.003]([passage text removed])).

## Underlying diagnosis matters

Roughly half of children presenting with a first ON episode prove to have or develop an associated neuroimmune disorder. In PON1, 6-month diagnoses were isolated ON 48%, MOG-associated ON 18%, ADEM 16%, MS 11%, NMOSD 7% ([summarized from PON1 in this review]([passage text removed])); at 2 years, isolated 40%, MOGAD 29%, MS 14%, NMOSD 11%, ADEM 7% ([AAO summary]([passage text removed]-)). In PON1, baseline high-contrast VA was worse in children under 10, in those with associated neurologic autoimmune diagnoses, in those with white matter lesions, and in non-White/non-Hispanic participants ([PMID 33057592](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33057592)).

Prognosis diverges by antibody status: a systematic review identified three pediatric studies in which the risk of [passage text removed] than [passage text removed]–84.34), though the authors flag small sample sizes ([Front Neurol 2020, doi:10.3389/fneur.2020.540156]([passage text removed])).

## Caveats

- PON1's 2-year figures rest on 28 completers of 44 enrolled, so attrition may bias outcomes ([PMC10357378]([passage text removed])).
- Structural injury persists even with good acuity: RNFL thinning after ON is well documented in children ([J Optom review](https://www.journalofoptometry.org/en-optic-neuritis-in-pediatric-population-articulo-S1888429613000897)), and RNFL thinning correlates with worse visual outcome — but that study (Eyre et al., [passage text removed]) was in children with a *relapsing* demyelinating syndrome, and its cited figure of long-term visual impairment in 40% therefore does not apply to a first, isolated episode ([abstract]([passage text removed]); [PMID 29637998](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29637998)).
- I found no trial-quality evidence in these searches on whether corticosteroids alter the final visual outcome of pediatric first-episode ON; PON1 treated participants at investigator discretion and was not randomized ([Pineles et al. 2022]([passage text removed]-)), and commentary on the retrospective cohort noted the absence of evidence-based treatment data ([AAO]([passage text removed])).
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** Children presenting with a first, "sentinel" episode of optic neuritis (ON) typically have severe acuity loss at nadir but good recovery — most reach ≥20/40 (0.3 logMAR) within 3–6 months — yet a substantial minority (roughly a quarter in long-follow-up cohorts) have incomplete recovery, and outcome is heavily driven by the underlying phenotype that declares itself later, with AQP4-seropositive NMOSD faring worst.

**Severity at presentation.** Pediatric ON is more severe and more often bilateral than adult ON: about 50% of children present at 1.00 logMAR or worse versus ~36% of adults [S:30631a20]. In a three-centre UK series of 44 children with first-episode ON, maximal deficit was <6/60 in 77%, and involvement was bilateral in 57% [S:dc716ec1]. In a 50-child single-centre cohort [passage text removed], median nadir acuity in the worst eye was 2.4 logMAR (hand motion) with nearly 80% at 1.0 logMAR or worse, and >1/3 were bilateral [S:6192d379].

**Recovery.** Full visual recovery (to 6/9 or better) occurred in 70% of eyes in the UK first-episode series [S:dc716ec1]. A French multicentre study of 102 children with a first ON episode found complete acuity recovery in 57% at 6 months and 71% at 1 and 2 years [S:25c3e7de]. In the prospective PON1 study (children 3–<16 years), mean presenting high-contrast acuity [passage text removed] and remaining essentially unchanged at 1 and 2 years [[passage text removed]]; a UK 10-year review reported 86% achieving ≤0.3 logMAR finally, with most gain by 3 months but clinically meaningful further improvement possible out to 1 year [S:2db670a3].

**Incomplete recovery is not rare.** In the 50-child first-event cohort, more than half had full recovery but about a quarter were legally blind in the worst eye at both the second and final examinations (28% overall at final exam) [S:0f022175][S:d2aa63dc]. A Chinese cohort of 76 children with first-episode ON was less favourable: 48.7% presented <20/200, and at final visit 53.9% reached ≥20/40 while 46.1% remained worse than 20/40 [S:a6c97afa].

**Predictors.** Younger age is favourable: children ≤10 years had better predicted outcomes than older children (OR 2.73, 95% CI 1.05–7.07, P=0.039) [S:a6c97afa]. Age ≥10 years, optic disc pallor on funduscopy, and an MS diagnosis were the principal factors for poor recovery in the French series, where MS patients recovered fully in only 27% at 1 year [S:25c3e7de]. [passage text removed] predicted poor vision at 6 months in a Turkish cohort (1- and 6-month acuities were highly correlated, r=0.98, p=0.001) [S:af78125e][S:3937e3e8]. Presenting acuity, laterality, sex, disc oedema, MRI findings and AQP4 status were not significantly associated with final acuity in the Chinese cohort [S:a6c97afa].

**Phenotype matters more than the index attack.** 50–60% of children with ON are ultimately diagnosed with an underlying demyelinating disease — MS (14–39%), MOGAD (29–36%), AQP4+ NMOSD (11–33%), MOG-seronegative ADEM (7–13%) [S:9fa86645]; PON1's 2-year diagnoses were isolated ON 40%, MOG-associated 29%, MS 14%, NMOSD 11%, ADEM 7% [[passage text removed]]. NMOSD children had the highest relapse rates and worst vision (mean logMAR 1.9 then 2.3; 83% legally blind in the worst eye at last follow-up; all four bilaterally blind patients had NMOSD) [S:0f022175][S:d2aa63dc]. MOGAD-ON in children generally recovers well despite severe onset (89–98% [passage text removed] one review) [S:0eea7de9]. In the UK review, final outcomes did not differ significantly between MOG-positive, MS-associated and isolated ON groups [S:30631a20].

**Recurrence.** Estimates vary by cohort and follow-up: 7% had recurrent ON among PON1 2-year completers (5/28, 18%, when counting all recurrent-ON events reported over 2 years) [[passage text removed]-]; no recurrences occurred in the small UK series [S:eeb6b502]; whereas half of the 50-child first-event cohort relapsed (most often ON, 19/25, or longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, 9/25), leading those authors to conclude pediatric ON is less often monophasic than presumed [S:9fa86645][S:61924e8e]. Relapsing ON strongly predicted subsequent MS or NMO diagnosis (log-rank p<0.001), with a 2-year cumulative probability of MS/NMO of 0.45 (95% CI 0.25–0.65) [S:dc716ec1].

**Caveat:** measures beyond high-contrast acuity are less well characterised in children; in adults after a single demyelinating ON episode, contrast sensitivity remained [passage text removed] 6 months despite complete high-contrast recovery [S:a656462b] — I found no pediatric-specific quantitative data on residual low-contrast/colour deficits in first-episode cohorts.

rows.question: What is known about quality of life in children with myasthenia during the COVID-19 pandemic?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Quality-of-life scores in children with myasthenia showed no statistically significant difference between prepandemic and pandemic-era assessments; Daily-activity scores likewise showed no statistically significant difference between the two assessments; Both sets of scores shifted in the direction of greater disease burden, a trend falling short of significance rather than a demonstrated worsening. Certainty: The evidence is weak and early, drawn from very few children at a single center, with numbers far too small for the absence of a significant difference to settle whether these measures truly changed. Scope: applies to myasthenia gravis or congenital myasthenic syndrome in children and adolescents, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it concludes that pandemic conditions had no effect on quality of life in children with myasthenia and advises reducing quality-of-life monitoring on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

The evidence base is very thin: exactly one study has directly measured quality of life (QOL) in children with myasthenia during the COVID-19 pandemic, and it found **no statistically significant change**, only a non-significant trend toward worse QOL. Everything else must be extrapolated from adults with myasthenia gravis (MG) or from children with neuromuscular disease generally.

## The one pediatric-specific study

A single-center retrospective review at Children's Hospital Los Angeles (Sosa, Pascual, Paquin, Dawoud, David, Santoro, Tiongson, Ramos-Platt) compared MG-QOL15r and MG-ADL scores recorded between March 2020 and December 2021 against at least one pre-pandemic score from January 2019–February 2020, in children with congenital or acquired myasthenia; the authors explicitly note that no such evaluation had previously been performed in pediatric populations ([PMID 40856578](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40856578); [doi:10.1177/08830738251366857]([passage text removed])).

Key findings, as reported in the abstract:
- Of 35 individuals with myasthenia screened, only 8 (23%) met inclusion criteria — a very small paired sample.
- Paired *t*-tests showed no significant difference in MG-QOL15r (*t* = 2.31, *P* = .054), MG-ADL (*[passage text removed]).
- MG-QOL15r scores nonetheless "trended upward" (i.e., worse QOL) at visits from March 2020 onward; the authors conclude QOL "was [passage text removed]" ([PMID 40856578](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40856578)).

Interpretive caveat worth stating plainly: with n = 8 and *P* values of .054 and .08, this study is underpowered, so "no impact" is better read as "no impact detectable." A further methodological limitation is that MG-QOL15r and MG-ADL are validated in adults, not children; a pediatric-specific instrument (PM-QOL15) exists and has been correlated with the MG Composite in a juvenile MG cohort, but pediatric validation work is ongoing ([[passage text removed]); [PMID 33604899](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33604899)).

## Indirect evidence: adults with MG

The rationale for expecting an effect comes from adult data, where pandemic-era QOL decline is better documented:
- In an Indian MG cohort, MGQOL15 (median 6.5 → 7.5; *P* = .036), MG-ADL (median 0.5 → 1; *P* < .001), sleep quality (PSQI; *P* < .001) and HADS-depression (*P* < .001) all worsened after COVID-19 onset ([PMC7803624]([passage text removed])).
- A Serbian study using a self-designed questionnaire plus MGQOL15r and SF-36 concluded there was significant pandemic impact on psychological status and especially sleep quality in MG patients ([PMID 33223669](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33223669)).
- Compared with healthy controls, adults with MG reported worse HRQoL on SF-36, more severe anxious-depressive symptoms (*P* = .[passage text removed]* < .001) ([PMID 37287657](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37287657)).
- In an Australian self-reported survey, most patients said the pandemic had no impact on [passage text removed]%), with the authors emphasising psychosocial rather than disease-control effects ([PMID 39730952](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39730952)).
- In MG, anxiety and loneliness were independent correlates of MG-specific QOL during the pandemic, with the regression model explaining 52.9% of variance (*p* < .001) ([PMID 37851275](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37851275)).

## Indirect evidence: children with neuromuscular disease

- A Danish national survey (811 adults, 67 parents of children with neuromuscular disease) found 46.6% of parents reported anxiety and 27.6% depressive symptoms, with the pandemic contributing [passage text removed] school and reduced QOL — particularly among those perceiving high risk of severe illness ([doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0253715](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0253715); [PMID 34191825](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34191825)).
- A Latin American study using PedsQL found a mean total score of 55.85 (SD 22.05) in children/adolescents with neuromuscular disease during the pandemic, with physical health most affected (mean 41.67, SD 33.25) ([PMC10036245]([passage text removed])). Note: the reported diagnoses were Charcot-Marie-Tooth, Duchenne, SMA and "other," so myasthenia is not identifiable in this sample.

## Plausible mechanisms and context (not QOL outcomes per se)

Pediatric review literature notes that COVID-19 poses a risk of worsening respiratory muscle function in myasthenia gravis and congenital myasthenic syndromes, and that chronic immunosuppression may raise infection risk ([PMC8876161]([passage text removed])). Care patterns also shifted: IVIG became a treatment of choice for refractory pediatric generalized MG during the pandemic partly because home infusion avoids immunosuppression, and clinicians were advised to probe school and social history, including remote-class performance and PE/homework fatigue ([[passage text removed])).

## What is not known

I found no source addressing: pandemic-era QOL in juvenile MG measured with a pediatric-validated instrument (e.g., PM-QOL15 or PedsQL) in a myasthenia-specific sample; caregiver/parent-proxy QOL specifically in pediatric myasthenia; long-COVID effects on QOL in this group; or any multi-center or longitudinal replication of the CHLA finding. These are genuine evidence gaps, not omissions.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** Only one study appears to have directly examined this, and it found no statistically significant change in quality of life among children with myasthenia between pre-pandemic and pandemic assessments — though scores trended toward worsening in a very small cohort [S:4f3c9d9a-3dc7-5296-a413-d05663d7a1db][S:25aa7a28-a77a-501c-a772-8de73b64cbe5].

**The single direct study** (single-center retrospective review at Children's Hospital Los Angeles/USC, *Journal of Child Neurology* 2025) included patients under 21 years with juvenile myasthenia gravis or congenital myasthenic syndrome who had an MG-QOL15r or MG-ADL score documented March 2020–December 2021 plus at least one prior score from January 2019–February 2020; comparisons used paired *t* tests [S:0cb7119f-9664-56e4-b494-f0987308c591][S:9290663c-d57c-5331-a8cf-b7c4e799737a].

- MG-QOL15r (n = 8): mean 7.38 ± 6.14 pre-pandemic vs 9.25 ± 7.50 during, mean difference 1.88 ± 2.15, *t* = 2.31, *P* = .054 [S:942e51a5-0d74-5240-bc9f-ae9121e89706].
- MG-ADL (n = 7): mean 2.39 ± 3.45 vs 4.25 ± 4.13, mean difference 1.57 ± 1.99, *t* = 2.09, *P* = .08 [S:942e51a5-0d74-5240-bc9f-ae9121e89706].
- Motor measures were unchanged: [passage text removed]; tip pinch *t* = 1.20, *P* = .30 [S:25aa7a28-a77a-501c-a772-8de73b64cbe5].
- Interpretation by the authors: no significant change in QOL or strength, but MG-QOL15r trended upward (worse) and MG-ADL similarly but less markedly, suggesting an effect that a larger cohort might detect; they emphasize children faced distinct stressors such as school closures [S:25aa7a28-a77a-501c-a772-8de73b64cbe5][S:c8a9808f-cf54-5cca-897d-8e9d25870081].

**Important caveats stated in the paper:** underpowered, single-center, patients aged ≤5 years excluded because they could not complete the instruments at baseline; only total scores were usually available so domain-level analysis was impossible; quaternary-center severity/ascertainment bias; reduced physical activity during quarantine could have artificially lowered fatigue-driven MG-ADL items; and fatigue measures and social determinants of health were not collected [S:410b81aa-604a-58cc-a5a6-a2d63be9a51d]. The authors note that larger samples would require pooling across multiple pediatric myasthenia centers, and that MG-QOL15r/MG-ADL are not yet validated in this population (no validated outcome measures exist for congenital myasthenic syndrome) [S:96a25438-8060-5a2d-9981-3484e7d1f8c4][S:4f3c9d9a-3dc7-5296-a413-d05663d7a1db].

**Context from adults, and a discrepancy worth flagging.** The pediatric authors explicitly state that before their work there were no studies of pandemic effects on QOL in pediatric myasthenia gravis or congenital myasthenic syndrome, and they cite two adult studies (Stojanov; Kalita) reporting worsened QOL, with Kalita also reporting worsened sleep quality [S:eaf77a6e-bc2b-5763-9014-2db617a9db8c]. However, a Stojanov et al. one-year follow-up abstract of 57 adult MG patients reassessed in April–May 2021 versus April 2020 reported MGQOL15r scores that were *significantly better* in 2021, with some SF-36 subscales ([passage text removed]) also improved; higher Hamilton depression scores independently predicted worse QOL [S:58c42caf-0e52-584e-ae3d-ee93fb384010]. So the adult trajectory is not uniformly one of decline, and depression appears to be an important driver of QOL scores independent of disease activity [S:eaf77a6e-bc2b-5763-9014-2db617a9db8c].

**Related but not QOL-specific:** a review of neuromuscular disorders in children during COVID-19 notes little pediatric-specific guidance for myasthenic syndromes, that COVID-19 poses a risk of respiratory worsening, and describes telemedicine adaptations such as the MG Core Exam [S:1d1512ee-b910-5300-82aa-b88ea57773ac]. Pediatric-validated instruments (PM-QOL15, alongside MGC/QMG) exist and correlate with disease severity, but the validation work was not pandemic-focused [S:b81c7416-76f1-5da5-b126-6286ac9cf1ba][S:ce274ea3-d540-5909-a7df-0342a7ec6b61].

I found no evidence on pandemic-era QOL in younger children with myasthenia (≤5 years), no multicenter pediatric data, and no data on caregiver/parent-proxy QOL in this population.

rows.question: How do COVID-19 vaccine antibody responses relate to breakthrough infection and severe COVID-19 outcomes in people with MS on disease-modifying therapies?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody and sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator therapy are associated with impaired vaccine antibody responses, with seroconversion frequently incomplete despite repeated doses; Antibody responses on other disease-modifying therapies are broadly comparable with those of healthy comparison participants; Seroconversion is associated with lower odds of breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection in multivariable adjusted analysis; Severe COVID-19 outcomes, including hospitalisation, ventilatory support and death, are rare in this vaccinated population despite impaired antibody responses. Certainty: The antibody findings rest on a large body of consistent observed comparisons, while the link between antibody status and clinical outcome is associative and the severe-outcome picture rests on very few events. Scope: applies to COVID-19 vaccination in multiple sclerosis treated with disease-modifying therapy in adults sampled through a national registry-linked serology study, population-based settings. An answer is wrong if it presents antibody seroconversion as an established determinant of protection against severe disease, or recommends post-vaccination antibody testing to decide who needs additional vaccine doses or shielding.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Vaccine-induced antibody titre is a reasonably consistent correlate of protection against **breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection** in people with MS, but it is a poor and inconsistent correlate of **severity**: most low- or non-seroconverting patients (typically on anti-CD20 or S1P modulators) still have mild breakthrough disease, and where severity is elevated it tracks with anti-CD20 exposure at the time of infection rather than with the postvaccination antibody level itself.

## 1. Which DMTs blunt the antibody response

A meta-analysis of 48 studies (6,860 pwMS) found attenuated serologic response after full vaccination [passage text removed] S1P receptor modulators ([passage text removed]) versus no DMT, with no significant effect for IFN-β, glatiramer, dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide, natalizumab, cladribine or alemtuzumab; vaccination within six months of the last anti-CD20 dose predicted blunted response (p = 0.001). Importantly, T-cell responses were preserved on anti-CD20 but significantly reduced on S1P modulators ([PMC9230320]([passage text removed])). Depth of response scales with B-cell reconstitution: longer anti-CD20 duration and lower CD20 counts predicted blunted response, with CD20 reconstitution >0.1% "necessary but not always sufficient" ([PMC9330583](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9330583)); a threshold of 20 CD19+ B cells/µL [passage text removed] ([research-collection.ethz.ch, Disanto et al., *Neurol Neuroimmunol Neuroinflamm* 2023;10:e200043]([passage text removed])).

## 2. Antibody level predicts breakthrough infection

- **CovaXiMS (Italy, 1,705 pwMS):** probability of Delta-wave infection was associated with anti-SARS-CoV-2 level 4 weeks after dose 2 (HR = 0.57, p < 0.001), preserved over [passage text removed]), but with significant attenuation for Omicron cases ([passage text removed]); a third dose reduced Omicron-wave risk ([passage text removed]) ([PubMed 35526306](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35526306)). In the same cohort antibody level was the only significant multivariable predictor (HR = [passage text removed] per 10-fold increase), with a best discriminating cutoff of log 2.82 (659 BAU/mL; AUC = 0.71, sensitivity 85%, specificity 58%) ([PMC9069178]([passage text removed])). Antibody levels were 201-fold lower on ocrelizumab and 26-fold lower on fingolimod ([ResearchGate 360398780](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/360398780_Breakthrough_SARS-CoV-2_infections_after_COVID-19_mRNA_vaccination_in_MS_patients_on_disease_modifying_therapies_during_the_Delta_and_the_Omicron_waves_in_Italy)).
- **Longitudinal Swiss cohort (120 pwMS, 392 samples):** the last measured anti-S IgG titre predicted infection risk ([passage text removed]), independent of age, sex, dose number and DMT; median anti-S IgG before infection was 324.6 AU/mL vs 676.0 AU/mL in remaining samples. Specific memory B-cell positivity was not significantly protective ([passage text removed]) ([PMC9747147]([passage text removed])).
- **Ocrelizumab, 3 doses (Denmark/UCSF):** breakthrough rate 59%; uninfected participants had higher mean antibody levels than infected (54.3 [passage text removed]), while spike-specific CD4+/CD8+ T-cell reactivity did not differ ([jnnp.bmj.com preprint PDF](https://jnnp.bmj.com/content/jnnp/early/2023/04/24/jnnp-2022-330757.full.pdf); [PubMed 37185261](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37185261)).
- **Population-level corroboration (England):** after mass vaccination, infection IRR versus the general population rose for ocrelizumab (1.13 → 1.79) — attributed by the investigators to reduced vaccine response ([AJMC summary of Garjani et al., *Mult Scler Relat Disord* 2021;57:103458]([passage text removed])).

## 3. Antibody level does *not* cleanly predict severity

- **NYCNIC-2 (209 patients, 211 breakthrough infections):** anti-CD20 use *at time of infection* was associated with greater severity during Omicron (OR = 5.923, 95% CI 1.021–34.373, p = 0.0474; total cohort p = 0.0553), but **neither anti-CD20 use at [passage text removed]**. The authors concluded the attenuated humoral response "may not drive increased infection severity" ([PMC10333977](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10333977)). Of 22 hospitalizations, 17 (77%) were on anti-CD20 and all three critical/fatal cases occurred on anti-CD20 ([PMC10333980]([passage text removed])).
- **Seronegativity without severe disease:** in 111 vaccinated rituximab-treated pwMS, 34.2% had no detectable spike IgG, 72.1% no RBD antibody and 88.2% no HAT titre, yet only 7 (6.3%) were hospitalized over 22 months, none in ICU, no deaths — though hospitalization did correlate with absence of spike IgG ([ScienceDirect S221103482400347X, *Mult Scler Relat Disord* 2024;89:105770]([passage text removed])). Similarly, all 59% of ocrelizumab-treated breakthrough cases had mild courses without hospitalization ([jnnp PDF](https://jnnp.bmj.com/content/jnnp/early/2023/04/24/jnnp-2022-330757.full.pdf)).
- **Anti-CD20 severity persists despite vaccination in some cohorts:** in the Italian breakthrough analysis, ocrelizumab hospitalization was 16.7% vs 19.4% pre-vaccination (RR = 0.86, p = 0.74), versus 3.9% on all other DMTs ([journals.sagepub.com 10.1177/13524585221102918](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/13524585221102918); [PMC9422340]([passage text removed])). Among 3,974 vaccinated pwMS, rituximab-treated patients were more likely to be hospitalized than those on no/other DMT (aOR [passage text removed]), with no deaths in either group; mRNA vaccine (aOR 0.36) and booster receipt ([passage text removed]) independently reduced hospitalization risk ([PDF of JAMA analysis of rituximab use and timing]([passage text removed])).
- Case-level evidence shows severe breakthrough COVID-19 is possible in an ocrelizumab-treated patient who failed to seroconvert after three doses and after infection ([PMC8801059]([passage text removed])).

## 4. Interpretation and caveats

The prevailing mechanistic reading is that **humoral response mediates protection from infection, whereas preserved cellular immunity limits severity** — consistent with anti-CD20 patients having near-absent antibodies but intact T-cell responses ([PMC9422340]([passage text removed]); [PMC9230320]([passage text removed])). Practical corollaries supported by the evidence: time vaccination relative to anti-CD20 dosing/B-cell reconstitution ([PMC9330583](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9330583)) and boost ([PubMed 35526306](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35526306)).

Limitations: these are observational cohorts with modest event numbers, heterogeneous antibody assays and units (BAU/mL vs AU/mL, so thresholds are not transferable), confounding by age/disability/comorbidity in anti-CD20-treated groups, and variant-era shifts that weakened the titre–protection relationship for Omicron ([PubMed 35526306](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35526306)). No validated protective antibody threshold for pwMS has been established — the CovaXiMS cutoff had only moderate discrimination ([PMC9069178]([passage text removed])) — and I found no source establishing a causal antibody-severity link in this population.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** Vaccine antibody titres in people with MS (pwMS) track fairly consistently with the *risk of breakthrough infection* — lower/absent anti-spike IgG (mostly in those on anti-CD20 agents and S1P modulators) predicts more infections — but the link to *severe* COVID-19 is much weaker and inconsistent: breakthrough infections in this population are overwhelmingly mild, and the residual excess of hospitalisation is driven mainly by anti-CD20 exposure itself rather than by a measurable antibody threshold, with preserved T-cell responses the likely explanation.

**1. Which DMTs blunt the antibody response.** Seroconversion after primary vaccination differs sharply by DMT: in a 757-patient two-centre cohort, seropositivity was lowest with anti-CD20 antibodies (23.2%) and S1P modulators (30.8%), and anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG declined significantly by six months [S:8e0c20fd-b78b-5b19-871e-9aa31634244d]. A large real-world registry found reactive IgG in 40% of anti-CD20-treated and 41% of S1PRM-treated patients versus 100% for all other DMT classes and no-DMT [S:947844bc-e80a-5b4a-aea7-a6a20ff1b38a]. Longitudinally, anti-CD20 (β = −2.07) and S1P modulators (β = −2.02) were associated with lower anti-spike IgG versus untreated patients, while teriflunomide and cladribine were not, and titres fell with time since vaccination regardless of therapy; boosting produced only a mild rise on anti-CD20/S1P [S:0c701089-8978-552a-80d5-059671865085]. Fumarates do not appear to blunt humoral responses [S:1cd5d855-2ef1-545d-a585-2b1cacb8f38e].

**2. Antibody level and breakthrough infection risk — generally predictive.**
- In the Italian 27-centre study of 19,641 vaccinated pwMS, breakthrough infection rates were higher on ocrelizumab (2.00% vs 0.57%, RR = 3.55) and fingolimod (1.62% vs 0.58%, RR = 2.65), with no significant difference for other DMTs — the authors interpret this as antibodies playing a dominant role in preventing infection [S:8773726e-f695-5df6-b560-e775da478380][S:5efe3045-18e4-5f1e-9982-30f98fbd2d5f]. Notably, protection waned with time only in the other-DMT group (0.14% → 0.32% at 4–8 months, OR = 2.32), whereas rates on ocrelizumab/fingolimod were already high and time-invariant [S:ca21dbec-cbaf-5ee7-90b7-0b5726ee2fe7].
- In a prospective 120-patient cohort, the last measured anti-spike IgG titre before infection predicted COVID-19 risk ([passage text removed]), independent of age, sex, dose number and DMT; spike-specific memory B-cell positivity did not reach significance ([passage text removed]) [S:f7ef3d4e-48bd-5b8c-809d-9803cf79dfb6].
- In a UK multicentre cohort of 647 pwMS, seronegativity after dose 2 conferred higher odds of subsequent infection (OR 2.35, 95% CI 1.34–4.12), but seronegativity after dose 3 did [passage text removed]) [S:71ee1935-e9e2-5bc6-9875-9e62e1df035a].
- In the Swiss MS Cohort (242 pwMS), antibody levels >150 U/ml after dose 2 were associated with a 64% lower risk of Omicron breakthrough versus <0.7 U/ml ([passage text removed]), persisting after adjustment for DMT and time since vaccination — a contrast with general populations where antibody level poorly predicted Omicron infection [S:db261ef7-aa22-5b56-a9ae-35925e777c6c][S:2d85f5de-ac1d-5960-a1fd-39296748eeae].
- A Dutch prospective cohort found Omicron breakthroughs more frequent on anti-CD20 and S1PR modulators, in [passage text removed] in those without prior infection [S:934b5da4-0cbd-5631-8a85-25768b2ed3b5].

**3. Severity — the link to antibodies largely breaks down.**
- Breakthrough disease is usually mild: 105/110 (96%) Omicron breakthroughs were mild in the Dutch cohort, with the single moderate case being an anti-CD20 patient who never seroconverted [S:5e86ec80-7472-5c80-b6d2-ab4537c8b06f][S:934b5da4-0cbd-5631-8a85-25768b2ed3b5]. In the UK cohort only 5/647 (0.8%) had severe COVID-19 — but all five were seronegative after their most recent dose (four on ocrelizumab, one on alemtuzumab) [S:71ee1935-e9e2-5bc6-9875-9e62e1df035a][S:f984c030-fea0-5913-9a92-dd1d66504b2e]. Similarly, of 39 breakthrough infections in a US cohort, only two hospitalisations occurred, both in seronegative patients [S:8e0c20fd-b78b-5b19-871e-9aa31634244d].
- However, when formally modelled, antibody status did not predict hospitalisation. In NYCNIC-2 (211 breakthrough infections), "abnormally low" pre-infection antibody levels were not associated with hospitalisation in the whole cohort (OR 3.34, 95% CI 0.71–15.75, p = 0.127), nor in the anti-CD20/S1P subset (p = 0.500) or anti-CD20 alone (p = 0.645); all 8 hospitalisations among those with antibody data were on anti-CD20, 6 with low antibodies [S:f581e6d5-2662-596a-9da0-b0e2b5dc0de0]. The authors concluded attenuated antibody production may not itself drive severity, and that intact T-cell function may confer protection against severe disease — while reduced vaccine response may still drive higher breakthrough *frequency* [S:8aa425b9-4f9e-53d1-b4f7-4b39afe72928].
- Anti-CD20/S1P *drug exposure* did predict severity in that cohort: use during infection raised the odds of hospitalisation or worse ([passage text removed]), and anti-CD20 use at vaccination did so within the Omicron subgroup ([passage text removed]:6e45eb22-ce38-5745-915a-276a460e034a]. In the Italian cohort, vaccination reduced hospitalisation by 67% among other DMTs (3.9% vs 11.9% pre-vaccination, RR 0.33, p = 0.02) but not on ocrelizumab (16.7% vs 19.4%, RR 0.86, p = 0.74) — though the authors caution about admission bias and small numbers [S:ca21dbec-cbaf-5ee7-90b7-0b5726ee2fe7][S:d43b10f3-bfb3-57e6-b58b-b853d6327109]. Vaccination still clearly helps anti-CD20 patients: unvaccinated rituximab-treated pwMS had markedly higher hospitalisation odds than vaccinated ones (AOR 5.56, p < 0.0001), and first dose >6 months after the last infusion lowered risk ([passage text removed]) [S:29890124-9aa8-543b-ac6f-27dad937397b].

**4. Why antibodies are an imperfect surrogate.** Anti-CD20-treated pwMS retain substantial cellular immunity — in one series 26/30 (86.7%) seronegative ocrelizumab patients had measurable T-cell responses after dose 3, and none of the four who got infected required hospitalisation [S:fe3c309a-d13c-5693-b413-670a36096296]. Conversely, T-cell measures alone do not predict breakthrough: in a prospective study of 31 pwMS, spike-specific Th1 responses (IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF-α, IP-10) were not associated with protection against breakthrough infection (which occurred in 38.7%, predominantly mild), while male sex (IRR 4.05) and primary progressive MS (IRR 3.65) were [S:ebe0f665-fdc8-5228-89a1-3e3da4404298]. Higher anti-RBD titres (≥809 BAU/mL) and an IFN-γ response were, however, associated with faster swab reversion, i.e. shorter infection duration [S:05af485e-7e0e-5fea-a6a3-587bf6702428].

**Caveats:** several of the severity analyses are underpowered (few hospitalisations, wide confidence intervals), assays and thresholds are not harmonised across studies, and hospitalisation of anti-CD20 patients may be inflated by clinician caution [S:d43b10f3-bfb3-57e6-b58b-b853d6327109][S:f581e6d5-2662-596a-9da0-b0e2b5dc0de0]. Data are also mostly from the Delta/early-Omicron era, so extrapolation to current variants is uncertain.

rows.question: What have immunomodulator treatments shown in children with severe infection-related inflammatory syndromes?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: In children with sepsis-induced multiorgan dysfunction and immunoparalysis, randomised granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor treatment was stopped early because of a safety trend and low probability of efficacy; In children with septic shock, granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor was not associated with any reduction in 28-day mortality; In children hospitalised with the hyperinflammatory syndrome following SARS-CoV-2, methylprednisolone and, where inflammation was refractory, tocilizumab were associated with shorter hospital stay; In that same syndrome, neither intravenous immunoglobulin nor anakinra was associated with a shorter duration of hospital stay. Certainty: Evidence strength is uneven: the hyperinflammatory-syndrome effects come from controlled comparison of concurrently allocated treatment groups, whereas the colony-stimulating factor signals rest on a single uncontrolled clinical dataset and an investigation halted early whose findings remain unpublished. Scope: applies to sepsis-induced multiorgan dysfunction and post-infectious hyperinflammatory syndrome in children, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents corticosteroids as proven to reduce mortality in children with septic shock or recommends steroids for every child with a hyperinflammatory phenotype on that basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** Across paediatric infection-related hyperinflammatory syndromes, immunomodulators have shown clear benefit in some settings (adding glucocorticoids to IVIG in MIS-C; corticosteroids/IL-6 blockade in severe COVID-19 extrapolated from adult trials), no benefit in others (IVIG in neonatal sepsis and streptococcal toxic shock in children), and only uncontrolled/observational signals for IL-1 blockade in sepsis-associated MAS/HLH — with a conspicuous absence of randomised paediatric trials.

**MIS-C: IVIG + glucocorticoids vs IVIG alone**
- In the CDC-funded Overcoming COVID-19 surveillance cohort (518 children at 58 US hospitals), propensity-score matching of 103 pairs found new or persistent cardiovascular dysfunction on/after day 2 in 17% with IVIG plus glucocorticoids vs 31% with IVIG alone (risk ratio 0.56); left ventricular dysfunction 8% vs 17%, vasopressor-requiring shock 13% vs 24%, and adjunctive therapy 34% vs 70% [NEJM Son et al., [passage text removed]/NEJMoa2102968 as reported in [passage text removed]].
- The contemporaneous international BATS observational cohort (614 children with suspected MIS-C; 246 IVIG alone, 208 IVIG+glucocorticoids, 99 glucocorticoids alone) found **no** significant difference in adjusted odds of inotropic/ventilatory support or death, though escalation of immunomodulators was significantly less common with IVIG+glucocorticoids [McArdle et al., [passage text removed]/NEJMoa2102968; https://europepmc.org/article/pmc/8220965; [passage text removed]]. An expanded BATS analysis of 2,009 children again showed no significant difference in the primary outcome for glucocorticoids alone or combination vs IVIG alone [Channon-Wells [passage text removed]-2, via [passage text removed]].
- Pooling individual patient data from BATS, Overcoming COVID-19 and Pandor (~958–1,000 children) reconciled these: IVIG+glucocorticoids improved cardiovascular dysfunction vs IVIG alone (OR 0.62, 0.42–0.91), whereas glucocorticoids alone did not differ from IVIG alone (OR 0.57, 0.31–1.05) or from combination therapy (OR 0.67, 0.24–1.86) [Ouldali et al., Pediatrics 152(1):e2022061173, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37376963; [passage text removed]].
- An earlier study-level meta-analysis (3 studies, 756 patients) found combination therapy reduced treatment failure (OR 0.57, 0.42–0.79) and need for adjunctive immunomodulation (OR 0.27, 0.20–0.37), but not LV dysfunction (OR 0.79, 0.34–1.87) or inotrope need (OR 0.83, 0.35–1.99) [[passage text removed]].

**Biologics in MIS-C**
- Single-centre data: initial IVIG plus infliximab vs IVIG alone was associated with less need for additional therapy, better cardiac outcomes and faster CRP decline [Pediatrics 148(6):e2021052702, [passage text removed]].
- Anakinra evidence is inconsistent: uncontrolled series report rapid reversal of heart failure/MAS (e.g., 18 refractory French patients, LVEF normalisation >55% within 48 h with falling NT-proBNP, troponin and CRP, all surviving without sequelae) and Italian data that early anakinra is "safe and very effective" in severe MIS-C [[passage text removed]; Taddio et al., Rheumatology 63:366–375, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37647645]. However, a propensity-score-matched cohort of moderate/severe MIS-C found anakinra added to IVIG plus steroids did **not** improve outcomes and was associated with longer hospital stay [[passage text removed]], and a systematic review concluded the evidence base (observational, no RCTs) is insufficient for clinical recommendation [BMC Infect Dis 24:847, [passage text removed]].

**Sepsis-associated MAS/HLH (infection-triggered)**
- The definitive adult sepsis RCTs of anakinra were negative overall, but a reanalysis of 763 patients identified 43 with hyperinflammation (hepatobiliary dysfunction + DIC) in whom anakinra improved 28-day survival (65.4% vs 35.3%; HR [passage text removed]) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26584195]. Paediatric evidence is retrospective only — small series of children with sepsis/MODS meeting HLH criteria treated with anakinra reported ~89% survival against historical ~50% [Rajasekaran et al., Pediatr Crit Care Med 2014;15:401–8, via [passage text removed]]; IV anakinra in 19 children with MAS/sHLH was tolerated with essentially one case of transaminitis, and some patients improved on Ravelli MAS parameters yet still died [[passage text removed]].
- For corticosteroids in paediatric septic shock, the adequately powered SHIPSS RCT (target ~1,032 children, primary outcome new/progressive MODS to day 28) is still ongoing — i.e., no definitive paediatric answer yet [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41504575; [passage text removed]-].

**Where immunomodulation failed**
- Neonatal sepsis: INIS randomised 3,493 infants with suspected/proven sepsis to IVIG or placebo and found no effect on outcomes, overturning earlier small trials; the Cochrane review (n=3,973) confirmed no mortality reduction [https://www.nature.com/articles/pr2010349; [passage text removed]].
- Paediatric streptococcal toxic shock: in the largest cohort (192 children, 36 hospitals), propensity-matched analysis showed IVIG increased costs without reducing mortality or length of stay [Shah et al., Clin Infect Dis 2009;49:1369–76, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2761980]. Adult-weighted meta-analysis suggests a mortality benefit in clindamycin-treated STSS (30-day mortality 15.7% vs 33.7%), and UK paediatric surveillance reported 8 deaths among 29 children with all IVIG recipients surviving — but that study was underpowered and questionnaire-based [Parks et al. 2018, [passage text removed]].

**Severe paediatric COVID-19 (as distinct from MIS-C):** paediatric recommendations for dexamethasone and tocilizumab are extrapolated from adult RECOVERY data (dexamethasone 28-day mortality 22.9% vs 25.7%, RR 0.83; tocilizumab 29% vs 33%, RR 0.86), because RECOVERY included only a small number of children and no paediatric RCT or cohort establishes tocilizumab efficacy/safety in this group [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9281416; [passage text removed]].

**Caveat:** almost all paediatric evidence above is observational and propensity-adjusted, not randomised; discordance between the Overcoming COVID-19 and BATS cohorts illustrates residual confounding by illness severity and treatment-selection bias, and biologics were generally excluded from the main MIS-C comparisons [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
**Bottom line: results are context-dependent — clearly beneficial in MIS-C (where any of IVIG, glucocorticoids, or their combination works and no regimen is convincingly superior), promising but unproven in hyperinflammatory sepsis/MAS phenotypes, largely negative in neonatal sepsis and unselected pediatric septic shock, and narrowly beneficial (hearing, not mortality) in childhood bacterial meningitis.**

**MIS-C: consistent clinical response, no clear winner among first-line agents**
- Immunomodulation is the core of MIS-C treatment, with IVIG and glucocorticoids as first-tier therapy and escalation to anakinra, tocilizumab, or infliximab in refractory disease [S:fced4ffa-fe83-5e98-8f29-b8f12ff45ec0]. Response is typically rapid — fever resolution, improved organ function, and falling CRP within about 24 hours; failure to respond signals refractory disease requiring escalation [S:5f314acf-6930-5e9c-a0c4-d7a1bd07cda4].
- The largest comparative dataset (BATS; 2,101 patients enrolled from 39 countries, 2,009 analysed, median age 8·0 years) found that after propensity weighting, glucocorticoids alone or IVIG plus glucocorticoids did not differ significantly from IVIG alone for the composite of inotropic/ventilatory support from day 2 or death, or for time to improvement on an ordinal severity scale; coronary artery aneurysm occurrence and resolution were similar across groups, with most aneurysms resolving [S:f16b634b-619f-5d63-b7dc-e921ee96a605][S:eed68379-8c0b-5e4a-bb78-58ad9c3a0157][S:3e5ef2e0-1102-54d0-88fe-7ec7fbac5a65]. Combined therapy showed a small time-to-improvement advantage over glucocorticoid monotherapy, apparently confined to children not needing intensive support at baseline, plus faster fever resolution and less treatment escalation [S:eed68379-8c0b-5e4a-bb78-58ad9c3a0157]. The authors concluded initial glucocorticoid monotherapy is an acceptable alternative given IVIG cost and scarcity [S:8b7c95e0-a771-5cfd-82fe-72e665b9dda1].
- Earlier and smaller comparisons favoured combination therapy: a meta-analysis of three studies found IVIG plus glucocorticoids lowered [passage text removed]) and need for adjunctive immunomodulation ([passage text removed]), without significant reduction in left ventricular dysfunction or inotrope need [S:94608c0b-bd82-509e-bdee-5275446e058a].
- A propensity-matched Vietnamese cohort (391 patients; 41 per matched group) found methylprednisolone monotherapy non-inferior to IVIG plus methylprednisolone, with no significant differences in left ventricular dysfunction, coronary dilation/aneurysm, or PICU and hospital length of stay [S:748d45cf-3313-55a4-ad11-b7a65f68dee4][S:a799425f-a80b-5e6f-852f-0cbc7d502403].
- Importantly, all of this remains observational: no randomised trials comparing MIS-C treatments have been published, and systematic reviewers grade the evidence as low quality [S:fdc3229a-adaa-50b7-9364-1eb61ba0d466][S:f58ffa16-63c5-51a3-ac54-25ecff5b2080].
- Biologics: anakinra plus IVIG was associated with fever resolution and improved LVEF in severe MIS-C, but confounding by concurrent steroids and lack of a comparator preclude direct efficacy claims [S:df340f67-b455-5502-b282-b24c2c7f83cf]; systematic review supports anti-IL-1, anti-IL-6, and anti-TNF as second-line options with anakinra the best-supported [S:c9245941-ab44-55df-a5bc-802617a1ee52].

**Sepsis-associated hyperinflammation / MAS-HLH: signal in selected phenotypes**
- The rationale rests on a reanalysis of an adult phase III anakinra trial restricted to patients with hepatobiliary dysfunction and DIC, where anakinra improved 28-day survival (HR 0.28, p=0.0071), whereas the original trial showed no overall benefit [S:03b7ccd7-9f60-5cd6-a466-33876afaee67].
- In children, evidence is small-scale: a retrospective pediatric cohort with sepsis and ferritin >800 ng/mL treated with anakinra reported 30% overall mortality — lower than previously reported figures for hyperinflammatory sepsis — with no serious adverse events, including at high doses and by the intravenous route [S:aa175f8e-4f6e-5794-aa3a-37fb9d2d0c60][S:00e1b61d-f61c-59e5-b1b9-946e7745bbcc]. Pediatric MAS case series describe rapid remission with anakinra, including steroid/ciclosporin-refractory cases, and consensus documents now list it as preferred second-line for HLH/MAS [S:b7d02aae-d52f-5a16-aee2-66db9352d4a7]. A review of five anakinra studies in children with secondary HLH (72 with concomitant sepsis) was inconclusive, and RCTs are needed [S:03b7ccd7-9f60-5cd6-a466-33876afaee67]. Definitive pediatric data are pending from biomarker-stratified platform trials (PRECISE/TRIPS testing anakinra in hyperinflammatory sepsis-induced MODS, target 500 children; GRACE-2 testing GM-CSF for immunoparalysis) [S:91e05d6e-2718-586e-a8c2-1c4393a973f5].

**Unselected pediatric septic shock: no demonstrated benefit, possible harm**
- In a multicentre cohort of 496 children stratified by a biomarker tool, corticosteroids were associated with increased [passage text removed]) and [passage text removed]) overall, and no benefit within any mortality-risk stratum — consistent with prior meta-analysis and registry data [S:3f15941f-30f7-5a3f-8ba7-a7733bd11911][S:d4068dc0-dd99-548d-ba3b-9b29b1dfe04b].
- Hydrocortisone was associated with longer duration of MODS specifically in septic children with immunoparalysis, supporting immunophenotype-guided trials; pediatric RCTs are lacking and Surviving Sepsis guidance recommends neither for nor against hydrocortisone [S:cd46d297-3678-559c-943c-2aff79fc9321]. Overall, interventional pediatric immunomodulation evidence is described as limited [S:399de134-0f4a-5250-b889-1ae12ce7898f].

**Neonatal sepsis: negative for polyclonal IVIG**
- The International Neonatal Immunotherapy Study found no difference in death or major disability at 2 years between IVIG and placebo in infants with suspected sepsis, nor in the culture-positive subgroup, with no subgroup showing advantage [S:1f4bd9a8-acec-53eb-acd0-ab4309186454]. A small double-blind RCT of IVIG in an LMIC NICU found no shortening of hospital stay [S:39d84333-0cf6-5953-a4cb-2f9918e343eb], and reviews conclude IVIG is not recommended for suspected or proven neonatal sepsis [S:076f1fa9-89ee-5d1e-99ee-0fc4d932a4a0]. IgM-enriched IVIG may benefit defined hyperinflammatory or refractory-shock phenotypes, but on heterogeneous evidence [S:91e05d6e-2718-586e-a8c2-1c4393a973f5].

**CNS infections: organ-specific rather than survival benefit in children**
- In childhood bacterial meningitis, adjunctive dexamethasone reduced hearing loss ([passage text removed]) with no effect on other neurological complications or mortality; the effect was strongest in *H. influenzae* meningitis ([passage text removed]) and in high-income settings (RR 0.32), with no benefit demonstrated in low-income settings [S:ed6f3366-6249-502c-a47a-a67aba17ddb9][S:01fce025-0b76-5eb5-a843-6f3f926f9b39]. An individual-patient-data meta-analysis of five major trials concluded benefit for any subgroup remains unproven [S:682a3610-2394-5f20-b2cd-631e70cf78b5], and controversy persists for pneumococcal disease in children [S:2e1770b5-9683-535c-8b16-c1e82c0db73a].
- In tuberculous meningitis, meta-analysed corticosteroid data show reduced death (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67–0.91) and death-or-disability (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.70–0.97), with subgroup analyses suggesting benefit specifically in children [S:199e970a-6661-5ce1-82a8-6bfb95d0d1c1].

**Not supported by retrieved evidence:** I found no trial data on immunomodulators in children with dengue-associated hyperinflammation — only a protocol for a biomarker-enriched randomised anakinra trial [S:61fb528e-0b4b-5d87-a033-6af74cf6e105].

rows.question: What is the spectrum and timing of psychiatric comorbidity relative to neurological onset in MOGAD?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Depression, anxiety and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder are the psychiatric diagnoses most often documented in patients with MOGAD; A substantial share of patients acquire a new psychiatric diagnosis after neurological onset, although smaller published series have reported none; New psychiatric diagnoses in MOGAD cluster shortly after the first neurological attack, whereas in age-matched and sex-matched relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis they more often begin years before neurological onset. Certainty: Because the compared groups were matched rather than assigned and the diagnoses were drawn from clinical records compiled after the fact, the findings support temporal associations and documented patterns rather than causal effects, and smaller published accounts disagree on how often psychiatric illness is recorded. Scope: applies to MOG antibody-associated disease in children and adults under specialist care, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the post-onset clustering of psychiatric diagnoses as demonstrating MOG-IgG-mediated inflammation of limbic circuits or as a basis for escalating immunotherapy to treat mood symptoms.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Psychiatric comorbidity in MOGAD is common (~half of patients) and dominated by anxiety, depression and ADHD, with a temporal signature that is the mirror image of MS: symptoms cluster in the months-to-first-year **after** neurological onset rather than preceding it by years.

## Spectrum

In the largest dedicated cohort (388 MOGAD patients, Mayo Clinic 1991–2025, with a complementary NeuroBlu real-world EHR analysis), 54.8% had ≥1 psychiatric disorder — anxiety 47.7%, depression 36.6%, ADHD 9% ([PMID 41956817](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41956817); [PMC13439468]([passage text removed]); [JNNP 97(9):817-826]([passage text removed])).

Age-stratified patterning: depression frequency rose with [passage text removed] at 51–70 years (44.7%); ADHD (15.4%) and suicidal ideation/[passage text removed] aged 18–30, and 13.1% of children/adolescents combined had ADHD. PTSD, bipolar disorder, substance use disorder, schizophrenia/other psychotic disorders, insomnia and eating disorder were each rare (<5%) ([PMC13439468]([passage text removed])).

Beyond chronic comorbidity, acute psychiatric/behavioural presentations occur as part of encephalitic MOGAD attacks — reported features include hallucinations, psychosis, anxiety, paranoia, insomnia, agitation, memory difficulty and suicidal ideation, sometimes reversing with steroids or plasma exchange ([PMID 31980213](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31980213); [Turk J Neurol case report/review](https://www.tjn.org.tr/full-text/2147/eng); [Acta Neuropsychiatr, anti-MOG schizophreniform psychosis]([passage text removed])). MOG-IgG in isolated psychosis appears uncommon and of unclear significance — 1.5% of 262 patients with a psychotic episode were seropositive, and the authors explicitly did not claim a causative role ([PMC12316182]([passage text removed])).

## Timing relative to neurological onset

- [passage text removed], most often within the first year; 69.1% of all psychiatric disorders with a known onset date occurred at or after the first MOGAD attack, and histograms peaked within the first 6 months post-onset. Overall 28.4% developed depression or anxiety after the first attack ([PMC13439468]([passage text removed]); [PMID 41956817](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41956817)).
- By contrast, [passage text removed] ([JNNP 97(9):817-826]([passage text removed])). A companion ACTRIMS 2026 analysis quantified both directions: >5 years pre-onset, depression/anxiety onset was more common in RRMS than [passage text removed]), whereas in the first post-onset year MOGAD predominated (23.1% vs 8.6%, P<.001) ([Niederschweiberer et al., ACTRIMS Forum 2026, P346, reported via NeurologyLive]([passage text removed])).

## Cross-disease comparison and correlates

MOGAD had similar anxiety (46.3% vs 48.6% RRMS; 41.4% NMOSD) and ADHD rates but lower depression than MS ([passage text removed]) ([PMC13439468]([passage text removed]); [NeurologyLive]([passage text removed])).

New psychiatric comorbidity did **not** track with attack phenotype (optic neuritis, myelitis, or brain involvement), but was associated with relapsing course, higher attack number, and higher EDSS at last visit; on multivariable adjustment only attack number remained independently associated ([PMC13439468]([passage text removed])).

## Caveats

A smaller Singapore cohort restricted to *psychiatrist-diagnosed* disorders found essentially no psychiatric burden in MOGAD either before (0/48) or after (0/48) neurological diagnosis, versus 5.2% and 12.2% in MS — so absolute prevalence is highly ascertainment-dependent, though the direction (low pre-onset burden in MOGAD vs MS) is concordant ([Tan et al., Mult Scler Relat Disord 2024;89:105775]([passage text removed] Mayo study is retrospective, without longitudinal symptom tracking, reliant on clinician documentation, and did not adjust for chronic pain or socioeconomic status ([Medscape summary of the JNNP paper]([passage text removed])). Whether MOG-IgG–mediated demyelination itself drives psychiatric vulnerability, versus reactive/steroid-related mechanisms, remains unresolved by the authors' own statement ([PMID 41956817](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41956817)).
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Psychiatric comorbidity in MOGAD is common (~55% of patients) and dominated by anxiety, depression and ADHD rather than psychosis, and — unlike MS — it clusters in the months just *after* the first neurological attack rather than preceding onset by years.

## Spectrum

In a large tertiary cohort of 388 MOGAD patients, [passage text removed] ADHD (9%) [S:6c155de3-767d-517e-aeb2-e342d1957bff]. In the matched comparison (n=257 each), anxiety was equally frequent in MOGAD, RRMS and NMOSD (46.3% vs 48.6% vs 41.4%), [passage text removed]) and similar to NMOSD, ADHD did not differ (8.9% vs 10.1% vs 5.2%), and [passage text removed]); suicidality was recorded in 7.4% [S:5517b6eb-506d-5bb0-b882-99d121bb2d3f]. PTSD, bipolar disorder, substance use disorder, schizophrenia/other psychotic disorders, insomnia and eating disorder were each rare (<5%) [S:d50b9b8e-59cd-52d5-b9c4-752e2d380aa8] — schizophrenia/psychotic disorder was documented in only 1/257 (0.4%) [S:5517b6eb-506d-5bb0-b882-99d121bb2d3f]. On patient-reported measures, 48% of MOGAD patients had moderate-to-severe anxiety symptoms and 19.6% moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms, not significantly different from RRMS or NMOSD [S:2998131d-a83b-5e4f-a574-14c960cce0c9]. An independent Mayo Clinic cohort of 394 MOGAD patients gave concordant figures (depression 37.6%, anxiety 47.5%, ADHD 10.2%, ≥1 condition 54.8%), with ADHD notably enriched in adolescents (27.3%) and young adults aged 18–30 (20.6%) [S:0140654c-e9a5-5f58-b2e6-7f74eb90e377].

## Timing relative to neurological onset

- Onset histograms for depression, anxiety and ADHD cluster immediately after MOGAD onset, with a peak within the first 6 months; 69.1% of psychiatric disorders with a known onset date began at or after the first attack, and 30% of those within 1 year of it. New (post-onset) psychiatric comorbidity affected 31.4% of all MOGAD patients, and 28.4% developed depression or anxiety after the first attack [S:d50b9b8e-59cd-52d5-b9c4-752e2d380aa8]. Overall, 33.3% developed a new psychiatric disorder after the first attack, often within the first year [S:6c155de3-767d-517e-aeb2-e342d1957bff].
- Direct contrast with MS: in the window within 1 year after onset, MOGAD patients were more likely than matched RRMS patients to acquire a new psychiatric diagnosis ([passage text removed]–6.59, p=0.003), whereas 5–10 years *before* onset MOGAD patients were less likely ([passage text removed]–0.90, p=0.028); RRMS onsets were spread more evenly across time [S:2998131d-a83b-5e4f-a574-14c960cce0c9]. The corresponding conference report of this cohort found >5 years pre-onset depression/anxiety in 27.2% of RRMS vs 17.6% of MOGAD (p=0.037), and within the first year post-onset in 23.1% of MOGAD vs 8.6% of RRMS (p<0.001) [S:048866b5-2934-5888-bd35-00e6713492af].

## Correlates and caveats

New psychiatric comorbidity was not predicted by the attack phenotype (optic neuritis, myelitis or brain involvement) but was associated with a relapsing course and a higher number of attacks, with attack number remaining independently associated on multivariable analysis; cumulative oral prednisone exposure did not differ between those with and without new psychiatric comorbidity (median 2 vs 1.5 months, p=0.239) [S:12b9b71c-10c2-5136-82e8-24125d62ec86]. In the Mayo cohort, adults >30 years with a relapsing course had higher odds of depression/anxiety/ADHD than monophasic patients (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.22–3.29, p=0.004) [S:0140654c-e9a5-5f58-b2e6-7f74eb90e377]. Findings are subject to ascertainment/referral bias, and heterogeneity exists across cohorts — one 48-patient Singapore cohort reported no psychiatric disorders, plausibly due to shorter follow-up, while a 259-patient quality-of-life study reported [passage text removed] comorbidity in 44% [S:22c3905f-a070-52b1-8274-f1aebd9d1fbd].

## Psychiatric symptoms *as* the neurological presentation (distinct from comorbidity)

Acute neuropsychiatric features can be part of the presenting attack itself: MOG-IgG-positive encephalitis in children included abnormal behaviour in 50% alongside impaired consciousness and seizures [S:109ea9f6-3b51-5bbb-ac3b-8a3932148bd6], cortical encephalitis phenotypes include mental disturbance and memory impairment [S:89e54d04-a69b-51a7-ab2f-d9712f26fc29], and MOGAD has been reported to present as new-onset psychosis leading to behavioural-health admission and diagnostic delay, or as insidious flat affect [S:ad79fe86-c584-5813-9b41-4a3705c272da]. Conversely, MOG-IgG is only rarely found in primary psychosis: systematic screening of 262 patients with ≥1 psychotic episode found MOG-IgG in 1.5% versus 0.6% of 166 controls (3 of 4 seropositive patients had visual hallucinations), with clinical relevance unresolved [S:253485c8-28b8-5e63-b63e-aef44706fd28]; the only detailed reported psychosis cases with MOG antibodies did not meet criteria for MOG encephalomyelitis or definite autoimmune psychosis [S:dcdc711c-814f-5969-b832-f3c41d843a79].

**Practical implication supported by the evidence:** routine psychiatric screening in the first year after MOGAD onset, particularly in relapsing patients [S:d68dccba-b077-5bb9-a5f2-7875f9af8fe7]. No source I found addresses whether treating MOGAD relapses alters psychiatric outcomes, so that remains unsupported.
