rows.question: What is known about sex-related differences in efgartigimod efficacy in AChR-antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Responder proportions on the daily-living and quantitative myasthenia scales with efgartigimod versus placebo showed no significant difference between female and male patients; Quality-of-life improvement and attainment of minimal symptom expression favoured efgartigimod over placebo in both female and male patients; Mean total immunoglobulin G reduction was greater with efgartigimod than with placebo in both female and male patients. Certainty: The sex comparison rests on a small, post hoc subgroup split, so similar efficacy in women and men is suggestive rather than firmly established. Scope: applies to acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents similar efgartigimod efficacy in women and men as demonstrated equivalence, or uses it to rule out sex differences in response.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: the available evidence — a prespecified-endpoint post hoc sex-specific analysis of the phase 3 ADAPT trial — shows no meaningful sex difference in efgartigimod efficacy in AChR-Ab+ gMG, with similar responder rates, quality-of-life gains, IgG reduction and safety in females and males.**

**Primary evidence (ADAPT post hoc, SAGER-guided)**
- The analysis covered the 129 AChR-Ab+ participants (86 female, 43 male) randomized to efgartigimod 10 mg/kg weekly per cycle or placebo; endpoints were assessed by sex at birth ([PMC12969971]([passage text removed]); trial NCT03669588).
- Baseline sexes differed clinically: females were younger (mean 42.9 vs 54.8 years), had lower weight/BMI, were more often post-[passage text removed] (16.3 vs 14.3) ([PMC12969971]([passage text removed])).
- Primary endpoint (Cycle 1 MG-ADL responders): 67.4% (31/46) of efgartigimod-treated females vs 32.5% (13/40) placebo ([passage text removed]); 68.4% (13/19) of males vs 25.0% (6/24) placebo ([passage text removed]). Test for homogeneity of the between-sex treatment effect: p = 0.7014 ([PMC12969971]([passage text removed])).
- QMG responders: 56.5% (26/46) female vs 17.5% placebo ([passage text removed]); 78.9% (15/19) male vs 8.3% placebo ([passage text removed]); homogeneity p = 0.1595. Early Cycle-1 MG-ADL responder homogeneity p = 1.00 ([PMC12969971]([passage text removed])).
- Deeper-response thresholds at Week 4 of Cycle 1 also favored efgartigimod in both sexes: ≥3-point MG-ADL improvement in 73.3% (33/45) of females and 72.2% (13/18) of males (vs 36.8% and 36.4% on placebo); ≥3-point QMG improvement in 65.9% (29/44) of females and 94.4% (17/18) of males (vs 31.6% and 15%) ([PMC12969971]([passage text removed])).
- Pharmacodynamics were comparable: maximum mean total IgG reduction 61.8% (female) vs 60.0% (male) at Week 4 of Cycle 1; quality-of-life improvements and minimal symptom expression rates were greater with efgartigimod than placebo in both sexes, and safety profiles were similar across sexes ([PMC12969971]([passage text removed])).

**Nuances and caveats**
- A separate ADAPT subgroup publication notes that although females clearly benefited (MG-ADL difference [passage text removed]; QMG difference [passage text removed] vs placebo), their absolute responder rates were *numerically* lower than males' on QMG (56.6% vs 78.9%), i.e., a directional but not statistically supported difference ([PMC13233976]([passage text removed])).
- The male subgroup was small (n = 19 efgartigimod / 24 placebo), so the analysis is underpowered to exclude modest sex differences; it is post hoc, and hierarchical testing had already stopped before the "early MG-ADL responder" endpoint in the parent trial ([PMC12969971]([passage text removed])).
- Context motivating the question: the authors note females more often have early-onset MG, thymic hyperplasia, exacerbations and worse QoL, and that a phase 3 nipocalimab study reported females improving less than males on both objective and patient-reported outcomes — making efgartigimod's sex-homogeneous effect a contrast worth noting ([PMC12969971]([passage text removed])). I did not independently verify that nipocalimab sex-specific finding in the Vivacity-MG3 reports retrieved.

**Real-world data**
- Sex was not a predictor of response in an Italian multicenter cohort of 13 IVIg-refractory/intolerant AChR+ gMG patients: MG-ADL reduction was unrelated to sex (p = 0.76), as was QMG reduction (p = 0.079) ([Neurology and Therapy, doi 10.1007/s40120-026-00923-1]([passage text removed])).
- A Chinese retrospective analysis of first-cycle non-responders found a non-significant excess of females among non-responders (80% [8/10] vs 44% [11/25] of responders, p = 0.071) — hypothesis-generating only ([Front Neurol 2025;1715486]([passage text removed])).
- A 46-patient Israeli multicenter cohort found heterogeneous responses with no clear predictors of success identified (late-onset MG tended toward greater efficacy); sex was not reported as a predictor ([PMID 41582064](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582064)).

Overall: sex-stratified efficacy data exist mainly from one adequately described ADAPT post hoc analysis, which found homogeneity; larger prospective sex-stratified real-world data are not available in the sources retrieved.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

The only dedicated dataset — a post hoc, SAGER-guideline-based sex subgroup analysis of the Phase 3 ADAPT trial — found **no significant sex-related differences in efgartigimod efficacy, pharmacodynamics, or safety in AChR-Ab+ gMG**, in contrast to the female disadvantage reported with conventional therapy and with at least one other FcRn blocker [S:0d6e488b-6d73-55b1-afd9-6b5f0c0c494a][S:ed60601c-2fb9-556e-ab0f-cd46ca87edb2].

## Evidence from ADAPT (post hoc, AChR-Ab+ only)

**Baseline asymmetries.** Females were younger (mean 42.9 vs 54.8 years), more often had prior [passage text removed]); baseline MG-ADL, MGC, and MG-QoL15r did not differ significantly by sex [S:0d6e488b-6d73-55b1-afd9-6b5f0c0c494a][S:ed60601c-2fb9-556e-ab0f-cd46ca87edb2].

**Efficacy was homogeneous across sexes.** Tests for between-sex heterogeneity of treatment effect were non-significant for the primary endpoint (MG-ADL responders, Cycle 1: p = 0.7014), early MG-ADL responders (p = 1.0000), percentage of time with clinically meaningful MG-ADL improvement (p = 0.6801), and QMG responders (p = 0.1595). Cycle 1 MG-ADL responder rates on efgartigimod were 67.4% (31/46) in females vs 32.5% (13/40) placebo ([passage text removed]) and 68.4% (13/19) in males vs 25.0% (6/24) placebo ([passage text removed]) [S:1f2c601c-426f-5185-8c2c-dc0997a26f58].

**Where a numerical gap appeared.** The QMG-responder odds ratio was much larger in males ([passage text removed]) than females ([passage text removed]), but this did not reach significance and MMRM analysis of change from baseline over the first 8 weeks showed no sex-specific treatment effect; the authors attribute the apparent gap to very small male cell counts (only 2 male placebo responders and 4 male efgartigimod non-responders) [S:1f2c601c-426f-5185-8c2c-dc0997a26f58][S:8e0ce2e1-74ce-5e17-a2cb-e5fcbb62d042].

**Pharmacodynamics and safety.** Maximum mean total IgG reduction at Week 4 of Cycle 1 was 61.8% in females vs 60.0% in males [S:3af70e1e-4d3a-544a-a260-39b57b1b9961]. Safety profiles were comparable between sexes, though the low frequency of individual adverse-event types precluded formal statistical comparison [S:68392f5e-084f-5e21-8847-a435488ac944]. MSE rates and QoL improvements favoured efgartigimod over placebo in both sexes [S:0d6e488b-6d73-55b1-afd9-6b5f0c0c494a][S:8e0ce2e1-74ce-5e17-a2cb-e5fcbb62d042]. Sensitivity analyses adjusting for age showed no significant treatment-by-sex interaction [S:1f2c601c-426f-5185-8c2c-dc0997a26f58].

## Why this is notable

Females with MG generally improve *less* than males on conventional care: in a prospective cohort of 107 patients, females improved less on [passage text removed] confounders [S:57bfe6bf-8e31-5cfb-99d3-d0272c92e0fb]. The ADAPT authors also cite a Phase 3 nipocalimab study in which females improved less than males despite comparable dosing [S:8d4926ac-4c05-5d8b-9923-e7ba4e02270a]. They hypothesise — without testing it — that efgartigimod's strictly weight-based dosing (10 mg/kg, with few deviations) may explain the sex-consistent response, and flag weight-based dosing across subgroups as an open question [S:8e0ce2e1-74ce-5e17-a2cb-e5fcbb62d042].

## Real-world signal in the opposite direction

In a prospective 15-centre Chinese AChR-gMG cohort (n = 116), male sex was a *significant univariate* predictor of MSE response (male 37.1% of responders vs 18.5% of non-responders; OR 2.60, 95% CI 1.07–6.35, p = 0.034), but sex lost significance in multivariate analysis (OR 2.51, 95% CI 0.92–6.95, p = 0.073); only baseline MG-ADL remained an independent predictor (p < 0.001) [S:4a37db03-02af-5db7-a79c-b662113bc1a8][S:081b7124-e0b3-5b9e-973f-52f36e71fe96]. A separate single-centre non-responder analysis identified comorbidities (thymoma, other tumours, thyroid and other autoimmune disease) rather than sex as predictors of poor first-cycle response [S:868759dc-3f7a-5dd2-ab26-6b39c85b1f51].

## Caveats

The ADAPT sex analysis is post hoc and underpowered — only 43 male AChR-Ab+ participants (19 efgartigimod, 24 placebo) — so homogeneity tests cannot exclude modest true differences; sex was self-reported binary "sex at birth," and some participants may have reported gender identity instead [S:68392f5e-084f-5e21-8847-a435488ac944][S:be874c1e-d46c-5ef7-af02-0612a028f7ed]. It was funded by Argenx, with the funder involved in design, analysis, and manuscript preparation [S:6f64b64b-cb49-5b56-9f5e-4e7799626440]. Earlier drug-profile literature had already reported efgartigimod benefit "regardless of ... gender" in exploratory/post hoc ADAPT analyses, consistent with this finding [S:9c19240b-67cd-51aa-8923-94048fb706f2]. I found no sex-stratified data for subcutaneous efgartigimod (ADAPT-SC/SC+) or for AChR-Ab-negative populations.

rows.question: How does disease-modifying therapy efficacy class relate to progression independent of relapse and MRI activity in RRMS?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Exposure to low-/moderate-efficacy disease-modifying therapy is associated with a several-fold higher hazard of progression independent of relapse and MRI activity than exposure to high-efficacy therapy; This pattern suggests that early progression independent of relapse and MRI activity remains at least partly sensitive to treatment efficacy rather than being a purely degenerative process; Qualifying progression events were few and the hazard estimate spans a very wide confidence interval, so the size of any advantage of higher-efficacy treatment is uncertain. Certainty: The evidence is early and imprecise, resting on very few qualifying progression events in a single referral population, so the direction of the relationship is better supported than its size. Scope: applies to relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis in adults receiving disease-modifying therapy, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents higher-efficacy treatment as proven to prevent relapse-independent progression or recommends universal early escalation on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

DMT efficacy class shows a clear dose–response for relapse-driven disability (relapses, relapse-associated worsening) but little to no consistent effect on relapse-independent progression — and the residual signal largely disappears once asymptomatic MRI activity is also excluded (PIRMA). The evidence base is, however, methodologically fragile in a way that biases against detecting a high-efficacy benefit.

## Evidence by strand

**1. Within-class RCT signal exists but is much weaker for PIRA than RAW.** In pooled OPERA I/II (n=1656), ocrelizumab vs interferon β-1a reduced 12-week [passage text removed]), but the split was asymmetric: RAW HR 0.47 (0.29–0.78) versus PIRA HR 0.78 (0.63–0.98); at 24 weeks PIRA HR was 0.78 (0.61–1.00). PIRA accounted for 78.0% of CDA on interferon and 88.0% on ocrelizumab — i.e. more effective therapy shifts the *composition* of worsening toward PIRA ([PMC7281382]([passage text removed]); PMID 32511687).

**2. Real-world efficacy-class comparisons mostly show null PIRA effects.** In 2563 DMT-naïve relapsing-onset patients in the Swedish MS registry, initial high-efficacy vs platform DMT gave RAW HR 0.60 (0.38–0.92) and EDSS-3 HR 0.26 ([passage text removed] (0.18–0.54), but PIRA HR 1.05 (0.79–1.39) ([PMC13043616](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13043616); PMID 41920324). The Danish nationwide comparison of early high-efficacy (n=594) vs escalation from moderate-efficacy (n=2722), median follow-up 7.4 years, found time to first PIRA HR 0.89 (0.59–1.36, p=0.60) alongside a 40% ARR reduction (IRR 0.60, 0.46–0.77) and [passage text removed] ([PMC13475077]([passage text removed]); PMID 42602817). Head-to-head *within* the high-efficacy class (MSBase/OFSEP/Danish registries; ocrelizumab vs fingolimod, natalizumab, alemtuzumab) showed ocrelizumab superiority on relapses and RAW but "[passage text removed]" ([jnnp.bmj.com/content/97/9/763]([passage text removed])).

**3. Adding the MRI criterion (PIRMA) largely abolishes the efficacy-class gradient.** In the French MS registry (2666 HET vs 7833 moderate-efficacy, mean follow-up 3.7 years, propensity-score framework), restricted mean survival time to first PIRMA was *slightly shorter* with HET (8.7 vs 8.9 years, p=0.017), while time to first RAW and to MRI-associated worsening both favoured HET (p<0.001 each); the authors conclude [passage text removed]" (PMID 41689266; Brain 2026;149(6):2022–2031). A small Canadian cohort (n=823) using a still stricter criterion found rates essentially flat across drugs — 3.75% dimethyl fumarate, 3.67% fingolimod, 3.82% ocrelizumab, 3.52% minocycline ([Front Neurol 10.3389/fneur.2025.1595929]([passage text removed])).

**4. A dissenting result, but fragile.** An Argentine cohort reported low-/moderate-efficacy exposure associated with higher PIRMA risk ([passage text removed]) — based on only 26 PIRMA events over a median 7 years, hence the very wide interval (PMID 42057337; doi 10.1177/13524585261442036). A Swedish registry ECTRIMS 2024 abstract (N=4358) reported statistically higher unadjusted CDW in the low-to-medium group (9.98 vs 9.19 per 100 person-years, p=0.0439) and RAW (1.21 vs 0.89, p=0.0141) — a very small absolute CDW gap given RAW was only 9.7%/12.1% of events ([practicalneurology.com]([passage text removed])); this is conference-level evidence only.

**5. Two caveats that cut in opposite directions.**
- *Bias toward the null:* because effective therapy suppresses relapses, standard PIRA definitions detect PIRA differentially between arms. In OPERA I/II, the estimated effect ranged from a non-significant HR 0.83 (0.66–1.04) to HR 0.73 (0.59–0.90) purely by definition; simulations showed underestimation of the true effect that grew as the relapse effect grew ([PMC12219353]([passage text removed]), eBioMedicine 2025;117:105802).
- *Bias toward inflation:* adding brain T2/Gd activity roughly halves PIRA events (reported as 47.9% → 23.4%), meaning part of any apparent PIRA benefit of potent DMTs is actually suppression of asymptomatic focal inflammation ([Neurology 10.1212/WNL.0000000000209444]([passage text removed])).

**6. Where high-efficacy therapy does appear to touch relapse-independent progression:** among 4713 MSBase patients who had already had a PIRA event, high-efficacy DMT use at the event predicted *non-persistent* (reversible) PIRA (adjusted HR 1.22, 1.08–1.38, p=0.0015), as did younger age (HR 0.84 per 10 years) and lower baseline EDSS ([PMC12405762]([passage text removed])). One Italian analysis of 466 patients starting high-efficacy therapy found 70 (15.0%) developed PIRA, predicted by older onset age (HR 1.07 per year) and longer onset-to-treatment delay (HR 1.10), while pre-treatment relapse rate predicted RAW but not PIRA (PMID 42688020).

## Bottom line for interpretation

Efficacy class maps onto the inflammatory/relapsing axis, not the relapse-independent axis. The Danish authors' framing is the consensus reading: relapses and [passage text removed]" ([PMC13475077]([passage text removed])); MSBase investigators state flatly that "treatment of PIRA remains an unmet need" ([jnnp.bmj.com/content/97/9/763]([passage text removed])). Two unresolved points I found no adequate evidence for: whether *timing* of high-efficacy initiation (as opposed to class) modifies PIRMA specifically, since only the underpowered Argentine study addressed this directly; and whether any efficacy-class gradient on PIRMA emerges over follow-up longer than the ~3.7-year mean in the French registry.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Higher-efficacy DMT classes clearly reduce relapses, relapse-associated worsening and MRI activity, but their effect on progression independent of relapse (and MRI) activity is inconsistent across studies — some real-world cohorts show a substantially lower PIRA/PIRMA hazard with high-efficacy therapy, while several registry and matched analyses find no difference at all. Part of this discrepancy is methodological, because standard PIRA definitions systematically underestimate treatment effect precisely when relapse suppression is strong.

## Evidence that efficacy class matters

- In an Argentine RRMS cohort using the stricter PIRMA phenotype (progression with neither relapses nor MRI activity), a marginal structural Cox model with overlap weighting found exposure to low-/moderate-efficacy DMT carried a markedly higher PIRMA hazard than high-efficacy exposure ([passage text removed]; 26 PIRMA events over a median 7 years' follow-up), with model-based cumulative risk curves diverging in mid-to-late follow-up [S:a0c8e902-6f1c-5f7a-aa3e-5fa2ef4f4b85][S:e2d81fc2-f1cb-5a02-bf5a-8de27aac9e4b]. Note the very wide confidence interval and the fact that fingolimod was classed as moderate-efficacy here [S:f2d77067-9979-59dd-820e-430b28d198ac].
- A prospective Argentine tertiary-centre cohort (conference abstract) similarly reported high-efficacy DMTs associated with significantly reduced PIRA risk, with moderate-/low-efficacy exposure conferring [passage text removed]) and initial-treatment failure requiring a switch HR 2.56 (1.5–4.3, p<0.001) [S:5aaaf5eb-3211-5e43-bb69-152434431537][S:3f3b5dff-16c8-5b6a-8361-166e58469d5c].
- In MSBase, high-efficacy DMT use at baseline was associated with *non-persistent* (regressing) PIRA (HR 1.22, 95% CI 1.08–1.38, p=0.0015), and non-persistent PIRA carried far lower risk of EDSS 6 (HR 0.19) and SPMS (HR 0.18) — i.e. efficacy class may influence PIRA reversibility rather than only its occurrence [S:9942e1b4-2bb8-5a42-afda-ed213d407ba8]. That paper also notes prior work linking high-efficacy DMT to lower PIRA risk, implying some PIRA events are inflammation-driven [S:d7fee554-82ad-5700-a99b-1bd60b0a90e1].
- Older Swiss work found fingolimod superior to interferon-beta/glatiramer acetate for disability progression in relapse-free RRMS [S:7508ee8d-29d4-500f-9c01-0a50c5c41eb7], though a related prospective cohort saw only a non-significant PIRA trend ([passage text removed]) that vanished when treatment was modelled time-dependently (HR 0.8, 0.4–1.4) [S:31431017-0321-5133-868c-01613c39af61].

## Evidence that efficacy class does not matter for PIRA

- Danish nationwide registry (3316 treatment-naïve patients; 594 high-efficacy vs 2722 moderate-efficacy; median 7.4 years): no difference in time to first PIRA (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.59–1.36, p=0.60), despite a 40% ARR reduction (IRR 0.60, 0.46–0.77) and a 75% reduction in RAW hazard (HR 0.25, 0.12–0.53) with early high-efficacy therapy — a clean dissociation between relapse-driven and relapse-independent disability [S:f93a1d39-2e0d-5c18-8ac9-df8e0d29ebe7][S:1999c3a0-a769-5fe5-98cc-9f0b7eb24c9e].
- A real-world cohort (conference abstract) found identical PIRA risk for high- vs low-efficacy early therapy (adjusted HR 0.99, p=0.95) but lower RAW (HR 0.48, p=0.015); sub-stratifying into high vs very-high efficacy did not change PIRA risk [S:15f7a957-dfb5-5570-9478-ffb30e5f7d14].
- In late-onset MS, moderate–high-efficacy DMT reduced relapse risk but showed no difference in PIRA, and CDP was driven by PIRA [S:840c5024-7342-5abd-be73-15133ffb71f4][S:c8fad63c-3f54-5482-89c8-0644a38e58ca].
- A German 1:1 propensity-matched cohort found large reductions with high-efficacy DMT in relapse hazard (0.41), MRI activity (0.37) and NEDA-3 loss (0.47), but no difference in 3-month confirmed disability progression (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.45–1.30, p=0.3) [S:0aa26020-eec9-5750-8f99-3abe84357041][S:9c4bac29-4ba3-5dbf-bedf-2f3919041cc7].
- A Polish PIRMA analysis found the proportion progressing rose with time on treatment but with no significant variation by drug choice (p=0.625) or treatment line (p=0.315) [S:b0d8795c-2f7d-5120-9649-cf678b7f3138]. A Calgary cohort applying a stricter "PIRB" criterion found it rare and essentially constant across dimethyl fumarate, fingolimod, ocrelizumab and minocycline despite differing overall progression rates [S:feb59a85-5905-505d-8840-3152f207d760].

## Why the two literatures conflict

1. **Unmasking / denominator shift.** Because high-efficacy DMTs abolish relapse-related events, the remaining accrual is reclassified as PIRA; a systematic review of 48 studies found the PIRA-versus-RAW proportion rose with age, longer disease duration and potent relapse suppression by high-efficacy DMT, even though absolute event numbers were lower [S:3b315a63-e8f1-5c52-bf09-3d0eb029bed6]. Reviews describe this explicitly as an "unmasking" phenomenon [S:feea39cd-1e28-5ca6-a33e-582f5d89346e].
2. **Definitional bias.** Simulation work shows standard PIRA definitions progressively underestimate true treatment effect as relapse reduction increases — with a 50% relapse reduction, standard methods failed to detect a genuine PIRA effect (e.g. [passage text removed] against a true HR of 0.75), with bias up to 0.28 at 80% relapse reduction; relapse-independent-censoring and Bayesian methods reduced or removed the bias [S:b11dab05-e6d0-5376-b049-65818722771a][S:2a3d817c-0953-5592-950b-e8820bef5598]. Roving versus fixed baseline and whether the confirmation visit must be relapse-free also change event counts substantially [S:451b4708-643e-5390-ac85-9a00f732b6c5].
3. **Mechanism.** PIRA is attributed to smouldering/compartmentalised processes — microglial activation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, slow axonal loss — poorly reached by peripherally acting immunotherapies [S:4d4a8e79-e789-5c0b-a273-e93e769d4cd5][S:db742281-387b-5fd8-b1bc-0ca2de552103], and current DMTs differ only slightly in preventing it [S:90a3bb8c-927c-5740-a8ec-140f445a2f2b][S:d50c9098-8481-56fa-8127-fa5bde1cb764].

## Caveats

Several supporting datapoints come from conference abstracts (limited peer review, interim analyses) [S:5aaaf5eb-3211-5e43-bb69-152434431537][S:15f7a957-dfb5-5570-9478-ffb30e5f7d14]; efficacy-class definitions are not standardised (e.g. fingolimod is classed high-efficacy in some studies [S:36843e74-d1a6-53db-bb63-8a2fda843895][S:92c3a2c4-30b4-5a70-9e63-3e61613e847b] and moderate in others [S:f2d77067-9979-59dd-820e-430b28d198ac]); and I found no randomised head-to-head trial evidence in these results directly answering whether efficacy class modifies PIRA — the pragmatic trials DELIVER-MS and TREAT-MS were still ongoing as described [S:a3d217ec-980b-5b30-a993-2ab837b416b4].

rows.question: What outcomes are observed in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis who receive ocrelizumab?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Relapse activity declines during ocrelizumab treatment, with fewer patients relapsing and the median annualised relapse rate falling; Median disability scores on the Expanded Disability Status Scale improve from their pre-treatment values over the treatment year; Walking, hand-dexterity and processing-speed components of the multiple sclerosis functional composite improve from their pre-treatment values; Gadolinium-enhancing lesions become less frequent during treatment, with no enhancement detected at one year. Certainty: The evidence rests on early within-patient comparisons in a small group of patients over about a year of treatment, so it describes change during treatment rather than a demonstrated treatment effect. Scope: applies to relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis treated with ocrelizumab in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it claims a reduction in overall brain and spinal cord lesion burden rather than in enhancing lesions alone.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: in RRMS/relapsing MS, ocrelizumab produces large reductions in relapses and MRI lesion activity, less disability progression and more disability improvement than interferon beta-1a, high rates of "no evidence of disease activity," and these benefits persist for up to ~9–10 years — at the cost of frequent infusion-related reactions and a modest infection/hypogammaglobulinemia signal.**

**Relapses (pivotal trials).** In the identically designed phase 3 OPERA I and OPERA II trials (n = 821 and 835; ages 18–55, EDSS 0–5.5), annualized relapse rate was 0.156 vs 0.292 (OPERA I) and 0.155 vs 0.290 (OPERA II) for ocrelizumab vs subcutaneous interferon beta-1a, corresponding to rate ratios of 0.536 and 0.532 (~46–47% relative reduction, p < 0.001) [[passage text removed]].

**MRI activity.** Gadolinium-enhancing T1 lesions were reduced by 94% and 95% (0.02 vs 0.29 and 0.02 vs 0.42 mean lesions), and new/enlarging T2 lesions by 77% and 83% [[passage text removed]].

**Disability.** Pooled 12-week confirmed disability progression occurred in [passage text removed]–0.81; p < 0.001), and confirmed disability *improvement* at 12 weeks was more common with ocrelizumab ([passage text removed]].

**NEDA.** By week 96, 47.9% (OPERA I) and 47.5% (OPERA II) of ocrelizumab patients had no evidence of disease activity vs 29.2% and 25.1% with interferon (exploratory endpoint, non-confirmatory because of the hierarchical testing failure) [S:https://dialogoroche.com.ar/content/dam/roche-dialogo/dialogo-argentina-assets/downloadable-assets/digital-events/ovrevus/opera_1_y_2.pdf].

**Long-term extension.** In the 5-year OLE interim analysis, low disease activity was sustained from years 3–5 in continuers, while switchers from interferon showed rapid decline in relapses and near-complete MRI suppression; at year 5 the proportion with confirmed disability progression was lower in those originally randomized to [passage text removed]]. In a 9-year OLE analysis of 757 treatment-naive early-RMS patients (505/757, 66.7% completed), NEDA favored continuous ocrelizumab at week 96 (72.5% vs 43.8%; OR [passage text removed]) and at 9 years (48.2% vs 25.7%; OR [passage text removed]); 78.7% of ocrelizumab-treated patients had no 24-week CDP over 9 years, and brain volume loss was numerically greater in later starters (p = 0.09) [[passage text removed]]. Sponsor-reported 10-year OLE data indicate 77% of RMS patients were free of 48-week CDP and 92% still walked unaided, with earlier initiation associated with lower disability risk — note these come from a press release and conference posters, not a peer-reviewed paper [[passage text removed]].

**Real-world outcomes.** In the MSBase MSOCR-R prospective cohort (1011 patients, 18.1% first-line, median 3.4 years on drug, median baseline EDSS 3.0), ARR fell [passage text removed]) pre-treatment to 0.05 (0.04–0.06) after initiation; [passage text removed] confirmed disability worsening and PIRA were 25.2% and 21.9%; NEDA-3 probability at 4 years was 39.7% (36.0–43.5); persistence was 88.0% at 4 years. Treatment-naive patients fared better than previously treated ones (4-year CDW 6.0% vs 16.6%; PIRA 14.8% vs 23.3%), and MRI activity fell from 20.4% pre-treatment to 2.2% at the first post-rebaseline scan [[passage text removed]; S:https://www.neurologyadvisor.com?p=163653]. Real-world data also indicate PIRA rather than relapse-associated worsening is the main driver of residual disability accumulation on ocrelizumab [[passage text removed]].

**Safety/tolerability.** Infusion-related reactions were the commonest adverse event: 34.3% with ocrelizumab vs 9.7% with interferon in pooled OPERA, mostly mild–moderate (92.6%), most frequent with the first infusion (27.5% at the first 300 mg dose, falling to 4.7% at the day-15 dose), severe in 2.4%, with IRR-related withdrawal in 1.3% [S:https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30844611; [passage text removed]]. Serious adverse events were 6.9%/7.0% (ocrelizumab) vs 7.8%/9.6% (interferon), and serious infection occurred in 1.3% of ocrelizumab patients [[passage text removed]]. In the pooled all-exposure analysis (5,680 MS patients, 18,218 patient-years), rates per 100 patient-years were 7.3 for serious AEs, 25.9 for IRRs, 76.2 for infections, 2.01 for serious infections and 0.46 for malignancies, consistent with the controlled period; IgG below the lower limit of normal rose from 1.5% at week 96 to 7.7% at week 312 in ocrelizumab-randomized OPERA patients [[passage text removed]].

**Caveat:** the OPERA trials enrolled relapsing MS broadly (RRMS plus some SPMS with relapses), so RRMS-specific effect sizes come mostly from subgroup/naive-cohort analyses; the 10-year figures above are conference/press-release grade evidence.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Ocrelizumab in RRMS consistently produces marked reductions in relapses and MRI inflammatory activity, modest but significant slowing of disability progression, high rates of "no evidence of disease activity" (NEDA), and some improvement in patient-reported quality of life — at the cost of infusion-related reactions, increased infections, and progressive hypogammaglobulinemia.

### Relapses
In the pivotal OPERA I/II trials (600 mg IV every 24 weeks vs. subcutaneous interferon beta-[passage text removed] 0.16 with ocrelizumab vs. 0.29 with interferon (rate ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.43–0.66; p<0.001) — roughly one relapse every 6.5 years vs. every 3.5 years [S:7fa5d144-abf3-541e-b5d2-618d1866c1d2]. This corresponded to a 46% (OPERA I) and 47% (OPERA II) ARR reduction [S:34dbb1b8-becb-5926-8053-7c48e4c9e639]. Suppression is rapid: ARR and time-to-first-relapse already favored ocrelizumab within the first 8 weeks, and over 96 weeks time to first relapse was reduced by 46% ([passage text removed]) [S:23527d73-f519-5c05-880c-d28b6c895e18][S:e1909259-5ead-5979-b6ef-4006afda2810].

### Disability
Confirmed disability progression was lower with ocrelizumab [passage text removed]%; HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.45–0.81) [passage text removed]) [S:7fa5d144-abf3-541e-b5d2-618d1866c1d2]. A pooled OPERA analysis showed superiority over interferon for both components of disability accumulation — relapse-associated worsening and progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) — including in the subgroup at higher risk of SPMS [S:9eaf54b2-6c97-588b-a854-1470331fd56d]. In the open-label extension through 6 study years, patients who started ocrelizumab earlier retained lower CDP24 rates than interferon-to-ocrelizumab switchers (19.2% vs. 23.7% at OLE year 4) and a 44% lower risk of requiring a walking aid (p=0.004); switchers' ARR fell from 0.2 pre-switch to 0.04 [S:f3e4e99f-7959-5790-bd72-604cfc8e62ba].

### MRI and brain volume
Gadolinium-enhancing T1 lesions were reduced by 94% (OPERA I) and 95% (OPERA II), and new/enlarging T2 lesions by 77% and 83% [S:f77d40f5-506f-5984-ab0b-219d6fa648ce]. Effects on new T1-enhancing lesions were detectable by week 4 versus placebo and by week 8 versus interferon [S:23527d73-f519-5c05-880c-d28b6c895e18]. Among patients achieving NEDA, ocrelizumab-treated patients had significantly less whole-brain (32% reduction), white-matter (34%), and cortical grey-matter (30%) volume loss than interferon-treated patients [S:f2312872-6a99-5eee-959e-007e3f666c6a].

### NEDA
Over 96 weeks in OPERA, 48% of ocrelizumab patients achieved NEDA versus 27% on interferon (p<0.001) [S:f2312872-6a99-5eee-959e-007e3f666c6a]; another report gives 47.9% vs. 29.2% (OPERA I) and 47.5% vs. 25.1% (OPERA II), though these were formally non-confirmatory because of hierarchical testing failure [S:34dbb1b8-becb-5926-8053-7c48e4c9e639]. In a real-world single-center cohort, 62.1% of RRMS patients reached NEDA-3 at 2 years, 90.5% were free of disability worsening, 95.1% were relapse-free, and 67.1% were free of MRI activity; better outcomes occurred in treatment-naïve patients and those with lower baseline EDSS [S:fe314d12-e665-59a8-b751-026b3197045a][S:b8c80f3a-5e9d-5c81-b640-341e3f4cf0ba].

### Quality of life and cognition
In a 130-patient PRO study, HRQOL rose over 12 months [passage text removed] the Mental Component Summary, and on Neuro-QoL Positive Affect, Anxiety, Emotional/Behavioral Dyscontrol and Fatigue [S:28da5cc9-59d1-5f4c-bbf9-db256ccde47f]. A 93-patient RRMS observational study reported EDSS falling [passage text removed]), MOCA rising [passage text removed]), BDI falling [passage text removed]), and expansive lesions dropping [passage text removed]) [S:cfb859ae-7206-55aa-b281-68b8dc8a2f4b]. A separate two-year prospective cohort found mean EDSS decreasing [passage text removed] (p=0.032), the proportion relapsing falling [passage text removed]), and new/[passage text removed]) [S:b14930df-387a-50e6-a56a-e1ee320a0c52]. Note these single-center observational designs lack a control arm, so regression to the mean and expectation effects cannot be excluded.

### Comparative effectiveness
In MSBase registry data, ocrelizumab gave superior relapse control versus interferon-beta and fingolimod, and relapse outcomes similar to natalizumab ([passage text removed]; HR 0.77, 0.45–1.33) [S:2fadad01-a66a-5f91-921e-a0b5f94be753][S:35420cb5-97dd-5f31-9bad-f73d16050b70]. In people over 60, ocrelizumab lowered ARR versus interferon/glatiramer (0.01 vs. 0.08; ratio 0.15, 95% CI 0.06–0.33) but the groups did not differ in confirmed disability progression or improvement over 3.57 years [S:382a44d5-1727-5f12-bce0-6d2520a0abd3]. One EHR-based analysis found lower 2-year risk of moderate/severe disability with ocrelizumab than natalizumab ([passage text removed]) [S:8fa05f1c-e709-570e-ae4b-641407c574a0].

### Harms
Infusion-related reactions are the most common adverse event — 34.3% with ocrelizumab vs. 9.7% with interferon in OPERA I/II — mostly mild-to-moderate (pruritus, rash, throat irritation, flushing) and most frequent with the first infusion [S:7cedeb67-5176-555a-ab15-945cc0f0b650][S:422b1fab-d118-5586-b473-d8f4d8435612]. Infections (predominantly upper respiratory and urinary tract) reached an overall rate of 84.5% up to 8 years, with serious infections in 1.3% (vs. 2.9% on interferon); approximately 30% develop hypogammaglobulinemia [S:422b1fab-d118-5586-b473-d8f4d8435612]. A 7-year safety report gave rates per 100 patient-years of 7.3 for serious adverse events, 25.9 for infusion reactions and 76.2 for infections, without excess malignancy [S:4e06cd54-2b7c-5cb7-b58e-14550de6ed59]. In a real-world cohort (87% RRMS), IgM hypogammaglobulinemia occurred in 32.8% after 6 infusions but was not associated with serious infection [S:8fb832af-75d7-5609-ba3c-44dd4502a42c]. Rare events include late-onset severe neutropenia [S:42d824ca-6ab6-5c90-86c1-da30d3af380a]; PML cases have been reported, mostly attributed to prior natalizumab or fingolimod exposure [S:422b1fab-d118-5586-b473-d8f4d8435612]. In one observational cohort, 3.9% discontinued for severe adverse events [S:fe314d12-e665-59a8-b751-026b3197045a].

rows.question: What is known about corticosteroid prescribing for surgical intensive care patients with septic shock?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Nearly all corticosteroid-treated patients received hydrocortisone; Fludrocortisone was added for only a small minority of treated patients; Among treated patients, initiation was divided close to evenly either side of 24 hours; Corticosteroids were dispensed to a minority of the surgical patients identified with septic shock. Certainty: These are descriptive prescribing counts from record data, and the matched mortality and complication comparisons carry no effect estimates in this material, so no statement about benefit is supported. Scope: applies to septic shock in adults managed in surgical intensive care, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents earlier corticosteroid initiation as causally improving survival in these patients, or mandates a fixed initiation deadline on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

For surgical ICU patients with septic shock, guideline-concordant practice is low-dose IV hydrocortisone once vasopressor requirement is ongoing, but the direct surgical-specific evidence is almost entirely observational: it suggests benefit only when steroids are given early (≤24 h), possible harm when started late, and no consistent excess of surgical/infectious complications — while real-world prescribing is highly variable and applied to only about a quarter of eligible patients.

## Guideline position (not surgery-specific)

The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign makes a weak recommendation, moderate-quality evidence, for IV corticosteroids in adults with septic shock and ongoing vasopressor requirement, defined as [passage text removed], typically hydrocortisone 200 mg/day as 50 mg q6h or continuous infusion ([Evans et al., Intensive Care Med / SSC 2021]([passage text removed]); [SCCM guideline page](https://www.sccm.org/clinical-resources/guidelines/guidelines/surviving-sepsis-guidelines-2021)). This replaced the 2016 stance of suggesting against hydrocortisone when fluids and vasopressors restored stability; the change was driven by trials showing shortened shock duration with unclear mortality effect ([PMC10246868]([passage text removed])). A 45-RCT meta-analysis found corticosteroids probably reduce short-term mortality ([passage text removed]) and increase 7-day shock reversal (RR 1.24, 1.11–1.38), with increased hyperglycemia (RR 1.13), hypernatremia (RR 1.64) and possibly neuromuscular weakness (RR 1.21), optimal dose ~260 mg/d hydrocortisone equivalent ([PMC10798738]([passage text removed])).

## What is known specifically in surgical patients

- **Trial data are diluted, not surgery-specific.** ADRENAL enrolled in medical-surgical ICUs with ~31% surgical admissions (31.2% vs 31.8% by arm), randomization stratified by medical/surgical admission type; the primary site of infection was predominantly abdominal among surgical admissions ([ADRENAL, NEJM 2018 full text]([passage text removed])). Overall 90-day mortality was [passage text removed], 0.82–1.10) with faster shock resolution (median 3 vs 4 days), and no differences were found across the six prespecified subgroups including medical vs surgical admission ([wikijournalclub/ADRENAL](https://www.wikijournalclub.org/wiki/ADRENAL); [criticalcarereviews/ADRENAL](https://criticalcarereviews.com/foundational-trials/adrenal)). Notably, ADRENAL's tallied serious adverse events included one ischaemic bowel event (hydrocortisone) and one abdominal-wound dehiscence (placebo) — surgically relevant but uninformative numerically ([thebottomline/ADRENAL]([passage text removed])).
- **The largest dedicated surgical analysis is a TriNetX cohort of 13,512 surgical patients with septic shock** (no steroids n=8,180; any steroid n=5,332; early ≤24 h n=2,911; late >24 h n=2,421). Early steroids were associated with lower 90-day mortality vs no steroids (31.5% vs 33.3%; HR 0.74, [passage text removed] was associated [passage text removed]* surgical site infection ([passage text removed] pneumonia (RR 1.22), myopathy (RR 2.25) and bowel ischemia (RR 2.29) ([PMID 41924889]([passage text removed]), Surgical Infections). The authors frame timing as a possible explanation for conflicting results from mixed medical-surgical trials.
- **An earlier abstract of the same program reached a weaker conclusion**, finding no survival difference for early corticosteroids vs no corticosteroids (6,494 matched pairs; [passage text removed]) while confirming an early-vs-late survival advantage (1,103 pairs; [passage text removed]), with early steroids showing higher wound dehiscence risk (OR 1.8) — the opposite direction to the published paper ([Surgical Infection Society abstract]([passage text removed])). This inconsistency across analyses of the same database is a reason for caution.
- **Historical surgical trials used high-dose steroids and are not applicable.** Schumer's 1976 study in adult surgical patients with septic shock reported mortality of 11.6% (methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg) and 9.3% (dexamethasone 3 mg/kg) vs 38.4% for placebo, driving 1970s–80s practice; subsequent trials (Sprung 1984, VA 1987, Bone 1987) showed no survival benefit from high-dose steroids ([The Bottom Line, Steroids in Sepsis]([passage text removed])).
- **Stated barrier to use in surgery** is concern about postoperative and infectious complications limiting surgeon uptake ([SIS abstract]([passage text removed])). Biologically, this concern derives from chronic/high-dose steroid literature — e.g., preoperative prednisone-equivalents >20 mg/day are associated with increased postoperative infectious complications and anastomotic leak/pelvic sepsis risk in colorectal surgery ([ASCRS ulcerative colitis guideline 2021]([passage text removed])) — not from short-course stress-dose hydrocortisone in shock.

## Prescribing behaviour

Uptake is low and variable: among 5,322 patients with vasopressor-dependent septic shock, only 24.3% received corticosteroids within 2 days of vasopressor initiation; ICU-level median use was 21.8% (IQR 18.5–25.7%) and physician-level 22.0% (IQR 11.9–32.7%), with 16.5% of variation attributable to ICU and 10.1% to physician. Patients receiving and not receiving early corticosteroids were similar in ICU admission source and **surgical status**; those treated were sicker (SOFA 7.3 vs 6.1) ([Soni et al., Crit Care Explor 2025;7(3):e1196, PMC11845208]([passage text removed])). Across 26 ICUs, use ranged 9.5%–46.2%; among physicians with >10 patients, 2.9%–83.3% ([MedPage Today coverage](https://www.medpagetoday.com/meetingcoverage/sccm/114404)). An international survey of 861 critical care practitioners found 39% always/almost always prescribe [passage text removed]% always/almost always co-prescribe fludrocortisone, with 76% [passage text removed]–0.25 μg/kg/min ([CHEST Critical Care survey]([passage text removed])).

## Caveats

- No randomized trial has been powered specifically in a surgical ICU/postoperative septic shock population; the surgical evidence is retrospective EHR-based and vulnerable to indication bias and residual confounding (the sisna/Surgical Infections discrepancy illustrates this).
- I found no source addressing hydrocortisone in postoperative septic shock stratified by anastomosis presence, nor surgery-specific fludrocortisone data; APROCCHSS-derived fludrocortisone benefit ([passage text removed], 0.78–0.99) comes from a general ICU septic shock population ([APROCCHSS summary](https://criticalcarereviews.com/foundational-trials/aprocchss)).
- One retrospective ICU sepsis cohort reported corticosteroid use associated with *worse* 30-day ICU mortality, longer LOS, more new infection and hyperglycemia, underscoring that observational signals in either direction are confounded ([AJPPS retrospective cohort](https://ajpps.org/[passage text removed]-critically-ill-patients-with-sepsis-treated-with-corticosteroids-a-retrospective-cohort-study)).
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Evidence specific to surgical ICU (SICU) patients with septic shock is thin and observational: the landmark trials were run in mixed medical–surgical units, so surgical patients are effectively extrapolated to; the available surgical-specific data suggest that *timing* matters (early administration associated with lower mortality, late with higher), that fludrocortisone is almost never co-prescribed despite being the component tied to trial mortality benefit, and that steroids carry a mixed rather than uniformly harmful post-surgical complication profile.

## The generalizability gap

Guidelines conditionally recommend corticosteroids for adults with septic shock (and against them in sepsis without shock) on low-certainty evidence, with ADRENAL showing no 90-day mortality difference for hydrocortisone versus placebo and APROCCHSS showing benefit when fludrocortisone was added [S:8e5e2c85-997f-59bb-807a-8db4b19c2907]. The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommendation is 200 mg/day hydrocortisone (50 mg IV q6h or [passage text removed] [S:1ab6dd8e-02da-5cd2-bfaf-2d2d836a8686]. Because these trials were predominantly conducted in mixed medical–surgical ICUs, and because they did not report surgically specific harms such as [passage text removed], or DVT, extrapolation to surgical cohorts is uncertain; an observational report cited in that work found 23.7% of [passage text removed] h — outside the intervention windows used in ADRENAL and APROCCHSS [S:8e5e2c85-997f-59bb-807a-8db4b19c2907]. Notably, CORTICUS enrolled a large proportion of intra-abdominal sepsis patients (reported as 48%) versus the earlier French trial, and it has been argued that source control rather than adjunctive therapy dominates outcome in intra-abdominal sepsis [S:750e36bb-f385-5bc2-9e67-a81de8d3b460].

## Surgical-specific data

**Timing (largest surgical dataset).** A target-trial-emulation retrospective cohort of 13,512 surgical septic shock patients in TriNetX (no steroids n=8,180; any steroid n=5,332; early ≤24 h n=2,911; late >24 h n=2,421) found early administration associated with lower 90-day mortality versus no steroids (31.5% vs 33.3%; HR 0.74, 95% [passage text removed]), while late administration was associated [passage text removed]) [S:ac8a1bef-4f58-512f-b509-233bf1100272]. Complications were mixed: lower SSI ([passage text removed]]. Early versus late also had lower hyperglycemia rates ([passage text removed] — as reported) [S:06000b36-862a-5883-b366-e1ff76d15a8a]. The authors emphasize that fludrocortisone — the agent in the only trial showing survival benefit — was prescribed in only 6% of their cases, and they call for post-hoc SICU analyses of ADRENAL and APROCCHSS [S:06000b36-862a-5883-b366-e1ff76d15a8a][S:75b5a3e0-8093-54d5-bf9c-d89e278793ae].

**Abdominal source / emergency laparotomy.** A Japanese nationwide database study of 2,164 [passage text removed] lower intestinal perforation (155 corticosteroid, 2,009 control) found no unadjusted mortality difference (19.4% vs 25.1%; difference −5.7%, 95% CI −12.8 to 1.3) but a significant reduction in propensity-score-weighted analysis (17.6% vs 25.0%; [passage text removed]) and in instrumental variable analysis (−[passage text removed]) [S:476f0f56-47af-577a-a094-94fcaf507e0a]; corticosteroid use was also [passage text removed] [S:400548bf-e6e5-57ea-8e34-9ac3bc97f602].

**Postoperative steroids after GI perforation.** A single-center propensity-matched cohort of 354 ICU patients operated for gastrointestinal perforation (2013–2023) found postoperative systemic corticosteroids independently associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation without adverse effect on mortality or overall morbidity; cumulative hydrocortisone-equivalent dose was the strongest predictor of prolonged ventilation in a random-forest model, though no steroid variable reached significance in regression [S:6904064b-f7b8-50b8-80d7-d3094af7355a][S:0a61e9b1-45af-5264-a01b-494ba1db0a8d]. The authors conclude that in selected cases (progressive ARDS, refractory septic shock) postoperative steroids may not substantially increase anastomotic leakage, pneumonia, or SSI risk, while noting conflicting leak evidence [S:d06e3aaa-e1b0-51bd-8ef4-dc1047b0ff1f].

## Prescribing practice is heterogeneous

Real-world use varies widely and is heavily confounded by indication: in a 3,411-patient septic shock cohort at one academic center, 1,593 (47%) received hydrocortisone; those patients were sicker ([passage text removed]; APACHE III 104.1 vs 91.0, both P<.01) and had higher crude hospital mortality (52% vs 38%), but after multivariable adjustment no association with [passage text removed]) [S:05584ecc-72eb-5a1e-8184-49fb34e97bd0]. Surveys show near-universal but unprotocolized use — among 65 UK intensivists, [passage text removed], and none gave fludrocortisone routinely [S:0482adc4-9a66-5958-bb94-764b038aacac]; internationally, 79% of clinicians reported not prescribing fludrocortisone [S:7e2e1056-5925-578b-a98a-25664fa92df1].

## Caveats

All surgical-specific evidence above is retrospective/observational and susceptible to confounding by indication and immortal-time bias, which is precisely why the "late steroids → worse mortality" signal should be read as hypothesis-generating rather than causal — the authors themselves frame it as generating hypotheses about timing [S:06000b36-862a-5883-b366-e1ff76d15a8a]. I found no randomized trial conducted exclusively in surgical ICU patients with septic shock, and no surgical-population dosing or fludrocortisone recommendation, in the sources retrieved.

rows.question: How does oral corticosteroid dose change during complement C5 inhibitor compared with FcRn antagonist treatment in generalized myasthenia gravis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Over twelve months of continued therapy, oral corticosteroid average daily dose falls more with complement C5 inhibitor treatment than with FcRn antagonist treatment; Fewer patients remain on high daily corticosteroid doses at one year with complement C5 inhibition than with FcRn antagonist treatment; Because treatment was not assigned and the groups differed beforehand in immunoglobulin use and in how many stayed on uninterrupted therapy, the dose difference reflects unmatched patient groups rather than a controlled comparison of the two mechanisms. Certainty: The evidence is an observed difference between treatment groups that were not assigned, with a small comparison group, so it supports an association rather than a demonstrated advantage. Scope: applies to generalized myasthenia gravis treated with an approved targeted biologic in insured adults taking oral corticosteroids, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the greater corticosteroid dose reduction as a demonstrated causal advantage of complement C5 inhibition over FcRn antagonism, or recommends selecting one mechanism over the other on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Both drug classes reduce oral corticosteroid (OCS) dose, but the observational evidence is discordant: US claims and Italian cohort studies show substantially **larger and faster steroid tapering with C5 inhibitors (eculizumab/ravulizumab) than with efgartigimod**, whereas a propensity-score-matched German real-world study found **comparable** prednisolone reductions between classes. No randomised head-to-head trial exists.

## Evidence favouring greater OCS reduction with C5 inhibitors

**US claims analysis (IQVIA PharMetrics Plus; ravulizumab/eculizumab vs efgartigimod).** Baseline OCS average daily dose (ADD) was similar between cohorts (C5IT 22.5 ± 14.7 mg/day; efgartigimod 20.7 ± 14.5 mg/day). By 3–6 months the change was −7.5 ± 15.1 vs −2.8 ± 16.8 mg/day, and by 9–12 months the reduction was significantly greater with C5 inhibition (−11.2 ± 18.0 vs −3.6 ± 21.0 mg/day; P = 0.034), corresponding to a 49.9% vs 17.5% relative decrease (P = 0.056). Fewer C5IT patients remained on >30 mg/day (7.5% vs 22.2%); in the efgartigimod cohort the proportion on >30 mg/day actually rose [passage text removed]%. OCS discontinuation was numerically higher with C5IT (32.8% vs 24.4%), and dose decreases ≥5 mg/day occurred in 59.7% vs 40.0% (P = 0.056). Nonsteroidal immunosuppressant claims fell (55.2%→39.6%) with C5IT but were unchanged with efgartigimod (48.9%→48.9%) [PMC12804516; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41389129; [passage text removed]].

**Italian prospective real-life cohort (n = 63; 32 eculizumab, 31 efgartigimod).** Prednisone fell from 20.3 ± 18.7 to 3.7 ± 5.7 mg/day with eculizumab (−16.7 mg; CI −10.8 to −22.5; p < 0.001) versus 12.4 ± 16.4 to 7.1 ± 11.5 mg/day with efgartigimod (−5.2 mg; CI −1.9 to −8.6; p = 0.003); the between-treatment effect favoured eculizumab (−11.5 mg/day; F = 11.728; p = 0.001), also in the AChR-Ab+ subgroup (F = 9.035; p = 0.004). Percentage drop was −79.12% vs −38.23%, and tapering speed −13.1 vs −3.2 mg/day per month of follow-up (p = 0.001). Two efgartigimod patients increased from 0 to 25 and 50 mg/day. The authors attribute the difference to eculizumab's greater disease-modifying effect and to the cyclical, worsening-triggered efgartigimod schedule [PMC11377599; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39080054].

**US chart review (ravulizumab vs efgartigimod).** Among patients on OCS at initiation, 17/19 (89.5%) on ravulizumab vs 33/46 (71.7%) on efgartigimod reduced their dose; no ravulizumab patient increased, while 3/46 (6.5%) efgartigimod patients escalated to >20 mg/day [[passage text removed].0000000000208765].

## Evidence for equivalence

A German multicentre propensity-score-matched study (eculizumab/ravulizumab vs efgartigimod; 40 per group after matching) found both strategies produced rapid clinical improvement and "substantial reductions in prednisolone doses," with comparable MG-ADL change (primary endpoint) and similar secondary outcomes including steroid dose change — explicitly contrasting with indirect trial comparisons [PMC12015038; [passage text removed]].

## Within-class context (single-arm)

Efgartigimod alone does taper steroids: US claims data show glucocorticoid ADD falling from 17.2 mg/day (95% CI 15.1–19.3) at baseline to 10.2 mg/day (8.3–12.0) at month 12, with 54.9% tapering ≥5 mg/day and 26.2% reaching 0 mg/day — but 12.2% increased by ≥5 mg/day [https://argenxmedical.com/.../[passage text removed]]. Eculizumab cohorts show comparable within-class tapering (e.g., Chinese multicentre cohort: prednisone 21.21 ± 13.68 → 13.32 ± 10.42 mg/day, p < 0.0001) [[passage text removed]].

## Caveats

- All comparative data are observational; the claims study is limited by prescription-based ADD estimation and open-claims incompleteness, and channelling bias (which patients get which drug) cannot be excluded [PMC12804516].
- Efgartigimod's intermittent cycling with retreatment triggered by MG-ADL worsening may mechanically impede protocolised tapering, independent of efficacy [PMC11377599]. A prospective single-arm trial of fixed-interval efgartigimod for tapering prednisolone to ≤5 mg/day is only now underway, and its protocol states no prior prospective trial has tested this [PMC13396050].
- I found no comparative OCS-dose data for zilucoplan, rozanolixizumab, or nipocalimab versus each other or versus C5 inhibitors; the German study explicitly excluded zilucoplan and rozanolixizumab for lack of real-world data [PMC12015038].
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

In the only direct, propensity-matched head-to-head comparison available, oral corticosteroid dose fell to a **similar degree** with C5 inhibition and with FcRn antagonism — there is no evidence that one class spares steroids better than the other. Both classes reduce oral steroid dose by roughly 5–7 mg/day of prednisolone equivalent over ~6 months, and by larger amounts over 1–2 years.

## Direct comparative evidence

In a German real-world study of AChR-antibody-positive gMG comparing ravulizumab with efgartigimod as add-on therapy, reductions in daily prednisolone dose were comparable: 5.3 ± 8.2 mg/day with ravulizumab versus 6.7 ± 11.5 mg/day with efgartigimod (p = 0.525), as were pyridostigmine reductions [S:c4201cba]. Primary and secondary efficacy endpoints (MG-ADL, QMG, MG-QoL15, PASS, MSE) were likewise indistinguishable between the two mechanisms [S:ac966578][S:425d4c6a]. An accompanying editorial confirms this was the design's intent and notes no clear efficacy or safety separation between efgartigimod and ravulizumab, or between ravulizumab and eculizumab [S:9f7d4569].

A second German multicenter cohort (153 patients on eculizumab, ravulizumab, or efgartigimod) tracked daily corticosteroid dose to 6 months but stratified by **timing** of escalation rather than by drug class; prednisone declined more steeply when add-on therapy was started within 24 months of diagnosis (p = 0.001) [S:3a8eb7cf][S:10bb6460]. This suggests treatment timing may matter more than which class is chosen.

## Class-specific magnitudes (indirect, non-comparable cohorts)

**C5 inhibitors:**
- CHAMPION MG open-label extension (ravulizumab, mean ~2 years' exposure; steroid changes were prohibited during the 26-week blinded period and only permitted in the OLE): mean corticosteroid dose fell from 17.5 (SD 11.9) to 11.7 (10.9) mg/day; the proportion on >10 mg/day fell from 58% to 37%, 31% reached ≤5 mg/day, and 12% discontinued steroids [S:0ca1f20d][S:506b33fa].
- ELEVATE (eculizumab, US chart review, n = 119): 64% of patients on prednisone reduced their dose and 13% discontinued it by 24 months [S:89f81c30].
- Single-centre eculizumab series: mean daily prednisone fell [passage text removed] years [S:27c8e9e7].
- Real-world ravulizumab: 11/14 (78.5%) on prednisone reduced dose; in complement-naïve patients mean dose fell from 20.44 (±11.69) to 15.55 (±17.21) mg/day over ~4.7 months [S:f143bd73][S:84cbe811].
- A target-trial-emulation cohort found complement inhibitors produced significantly greater steroid tapering than mycophenolate (3, 6, 9 months) and than azathioprine (6 months) [S:368aed3f][S:c6bdfdd3].

**FcRn antagonists:**
- US claims analysis of 169 gMG patients on chronic oral corticosteroids continuing efgartigimod ≥12 months: mean average daily dose fell from 17.2 (13.7) mg/day at baseline to 13.2 (13.9) at 6 months and 10.2 (12.1) at 12 months (both p < 0.001); 18% and 27% were off steroids at 6 and 12 months respectively [S:7e04bde3].
- Single-centre individualized-dosing series (n = 19): mean daily prednisone fell from 20.0 (20.7) to 3.1 (5.2) mg/day; 9 of 11 baseline prednisone users discontinued, though 2 patients newly started low-dose prednisone [S:d16a2d9c].
- Two-centre Greek/Cypriot cohort: tapering achieved in most patients, with ~50% overall reduction from baseline; the authors note European and US real-world data showing 50–70% of patients reduce or discontinue steroids [S:4c1ec23a].
- An earlier single-institution series found all continuing patients reduced prednisone, but the reduction was "relatively modest," with mean daily dose still above 10 mg/day after 6 months [S:af75f4a0].

## Caveats

No randomized head-to-head trial has compared steroid dose change between the classes; the pivotal RCTs prohibited corticosteroid adjustment during their blinded periods, so all steroid-sparing data come from open-label extensions or observational cohorts [S:506b33fa]. Indirect trial comparisons that do exist address MG-ADL/QMG/QoL, not steroid dose, and give mixed results (some favouring efgartigimod on QMG/QoL, others showing no difference) [S:0a5c731e][S:d1b695bf]. Published rozanolixizumab and zilucoplan steroid-dose data did not surface in my searches, so the comparison rests essentially on eculizumab/ravulizumab versus efgartigimod. Finally, one commentator argues the effect of both classes plateaus and does not remove the need for medium- to long-term immunosuppression [S:9f7d4569].

rows.question: Which serum or cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers indicate dysregulation of the oxidative stress–neurosteroid axis in multiple sclerosis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Proposed indicators of dysregulation along the oxidative–neurosteroid axis include 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine, the serum allopregnanolone-to-DHEA ratio and 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase enzymatic activity; These indicators are put forward as candidate markers of dysregulation rather than as measures with demonstrated clinical performance; Oxidative markers such as malondialdehyde, 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine and nitrite are reported at higher levels in the serum and cerebrospinal fluid of people with multiple sclerosis; These higher oxidative marker levels track with greater disease severity and progression. Certainty: The paired oxidative–neurosteroid indicators are candidate measures supported so far by mechanistic reasoning and animal work, while the higher oxidative marker levels rest on comparisons with unaffected people and remain associations. Scope: applies to multiple sclerosis in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it recommends antioxidant plus neurosteroid treatment selected or monitored by these marker levels, whose supporting benefit data come from animal models.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

No single validated "oxidative stress–neurosteroid axis" biomarker exists; the axis is inferred from two separate, individually measurable marker sets in the same fluids — lipid-peroxidation/redox markers (chiefly MDA, plus isoprostanes, 4-HNE, 3-nitrotyrosine, NO metabolites, thiols/TAC, SOD/catalase/glutathione-reductase, 8-OHdG, oxysterols) and neuroactive steroid profiles (allopregnanolone/tetrahydroprogesterone, 5α-dihydroprogesterone, pregnenolone, DHEA, isopregnanolone, dihydrotestosterone). A 2026 narrative review is explicit that the interplay of the two pathways remains poorly understood and that biomarkers able to reflect oxidative stress *and* neurosteroid function simultaneously are still needed [PMID 41490296; [passage text removed]].

## Oxidative-stress arm

- **MDA (lipid peroxidation) is the most reproducible marker in both compartments.** A meta-analysis of 31 studies (2,001 MS patients, 2,212 controls) found significantly increased blood [passage text removed] chemiluminescence (CL-LOOH; [passage text removed]), decreased albumin (g −1.036), and elevated CSF MDA; blood GSH, SOD, TAS, TOS, uric acid and AOPP did not differ significantly [[passage text removed]]. A later narrative review concurs that a CSF meta-analysis confirmed only MDA, while serum/plasma studies most often show raised MDA and lowered TAS/TAC and thiol (–SH) groups with raised TOS and oxidative stress index [[passage text removed]; PMID 38927996].
- **Other CSF markers:** increased hydroxyalkenals, diene conjugates, 4-hydroxynonenal, oxidised phosphatidylcholine and isoprostanes; iNOS in CSF is associated with CSF protein nitrotyrosine, S-nitrosothiols and altered glutathione [[passage text removed]]. A review proposed serum nitrite, CSF/serum SOD, CSF/plasma catalase, serum and leucocyte 3-nitrotyrosine, CSF isoprostanes and serum MDA as candidate surrogates of activity, progression or treatment response [[passage text removed]].
- **Redox-active cholesterol oxidation products (mechanistic bridge to steroidogenesis):** serum 24-hydroxycholesterol, 27-HC and 7α-HC were significantly lower in MS than controls (p = 0.015, 0.004, <0.001), with 7-ketocholesterol higher in progressive than relapsing MS [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5581166]. In CSF, RRMS showed increased (25R)26-HC and the bile-acid precursors 7αH,3O-CA and 3β-HCA versus control patients [[passage text removed]].
- Correlational data: 8-OHdG [passage text removed]) in MS, and was higher in those with a relapse in the prior year (p = 0.023) [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12215555]; higher serum ferritin was associated with higher AOPP and lower NOx and TRAP [[passage text removed]].

## Neurosteroid arm

- **CSF and plasma progesterone/testosterone metabolites are the key readouts.** In male RRMS, LC-MS/MS showed increased CSF pregnenolone and isopregnanolone with decreased dihydroprogesterone and tetrahydroprogesterone (allopregnanolone), increased 5α-androstane-3α,17β-diol and 17β-estradiol with decreased dihydrotestosterone; in plasma, increased pregnenolone, progesterone and DHT with decreased dihydroprogesterone and tetrahydroprogesterone [PMID 24766130; https://www.academia.edu/129793816/].
- **Phase- and sex-dependence makes these candidate activity markers.** CSF pregnenolone and DHEA were increased in male and female RRMS versus two control groups; ALLO was lower in female than male RRMS and than female non-neurological controls; during relapse female patients showed increased pregnenolone and lower ALLO than males; patients with gadolinium-enhancing lesions had higher ALLO than same-sex patients without enhancement — the authors propose these steroids as prognostic factors and markers of MS activity such as relapse [PMID 26892094].
- **Tissue corroboration of a biosynthetic block:** allopregnanolone and related molecules were suppressed in MS white matter (P < 0.05) alongside downregulated 5α-reductase 1 and AKR1C2 transcripts and reduced 3α-HSD protein, with pregnenolone unaltered [PMID 21908875; [passage text removed]]. Lesion-level GC/MS work found the opposite direction in female lesions (ALLO higher, p = 0.0002; 20α-DHPREG markedly reduced in females, p = 1×10⁻⁵), interpreted as a compensatory response — so direction of change depends on sex and compartment [https://inserm.hal.science/inserm-05354135/].

## Caveats

- Plasma ALLO was reported unchanged versus controls in a mixed-sex study, and female MS plasma ALLO has not been reported separately [https://inserm.hal.science/inserm-05354135/].
- I found no study measuring neurosteroids and oxidative-stress markers in the same MS serum/CSF cohort and reporting their correlation; the cortisol/DHEA-S ratio is linked to oxidative stress in non-MS populations only [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12745230], so its use as an MS axis marker is unsupported by the sources retrieved. Mechanistic linkage (ALLO/DHEA/progesterone raising SOD and GSH and scavenging ROS) is described in review-level, largely preclinical terms [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

No single validated "oxidative stress–neurosteroid axis" biomarker panel exists; the composite indicators explicitly proposed for this axis are **8-OHdG (oxidative DNA damage), [passage text removed]**, put forward in a narrative review rather than validated prospectively [S:d3f872e2-64ef-5c2d-ae97-3d5700b8b3ec]. The individual halves of the axis, however, are supported by primary measurement data.

## The oxidative-stress arm (best-supported markers)

- **Malondialdehyde (MDA)** is the most reproducible marker in both compartments. A meta-analysis found MDA significantly elevated in MS versus healthy controls in both CSF (4 studies, Hedges' g 3.275, 95% CI 0.859–5.691, p = 0.008) and blood (9 studies, g 2.252, 95% CI 1.080–3.424, p < 0.001), alongside elevated lipid hydroperoxide by chemiluminescence (CL-LOOH; g 0.383, p = 0.018) and lower albumin (g −1.036, p = 0.002); GSH, SOD, total antioxidant status, total oxidant status, CRP, copper, cholesterol, uric acid and AOPP did **not** differ significantly [S:f50c7716-7eff-57db-9188-937fbd8e2253]. A narrative review likewise concluded that CSF and serum/plasma malonyl-dialdehyde are "the most reliable markers" [S:7b4431bd-cbd6-5844-b779-103170df5619].
- **F2-isoprostanes (8-iso-PGF2α)** in CSF. All 24 normal controls and all 16 patients with other neurological disease had CSF 8-iso-PGF2α below 20 pg/mL, whereas MS patients (n = 231) had significantly elevated mean levels; the elevation was CNS-specific (no CSF–serum correlation in 39 paired samples), was present in treatment-naive patients, and was higher in patients with recent relapse, EDSS change or new MRI lesions — but 57% of RRMS, 30% of SPMS and 35.8% of PPMS patients had "normal" values, so oxidative stress is not universal in MS [S:71209adb-2c14-5f70-9836-0ef40fc23c94, S:813bd552-f96a-548b-8220-ca3b29d4d433]. Plasma 8,12-iso-iPF2α-VI was raised in relapsing MS but was **not** predictive of 2-year progression [S:73157250-f6f0-5318-9158-aecdd67e4dd7].
- **Nitric oxide metabolites and glutathione peroxidase.** Serum nitrates/nitrites, MDA plus 4-hydroxyalkenals, and GPx activity were all significantly increased in RRMS [S:c1dd1011-a31e-511a-9692-7aa2b3959e44]. Note discordance: another cohort found *lower* plasma NOx together with higher lipid hydroperoxide and protein carbonyls and reduced TRAP and sulfhydryl groups [S:2853a7cc-ae33-51d1-b217-e9df12567408].
- **8-OHdG/8-oxodG.** Elevated 8-OH2dG has been reported in blood of RRMS patients and DNA oxidation products proposed as diagnostic markers [S:d4c52082-af98-5a9d-9649-fc3bbc1e5aad]; 8-oxodG is described as a systemic oxidative-stress biomarker of potential significance in MS pathology [S:8bc4d7f2-ab49-59c3-a1dc-a0301bf6c7b6].

## The neurosteroid arm

- **CSF steroidome.** In untreated female MS patients, unconjugated steroids showed a strong trend to lower levels (12 lower, 6 unchanged, 1 higher, p = 0.002) while conjugated steroids were unchanged, implying increased sulfotransferase (SULT2A1) activity; serum and CSF steroids correlated strongly, indicating peripheral steroidogenesis contributes to CNS levels. Reduced [passage text removed] were found, and MS severity was inversely associated with pregnenolone and its sulfate, DHEA and its sulfate, and androstenediol; impaired cortisol synthesis (reduced CYP17A1 and CYP11B1 function) tracked with more severe disease [S:8711c4e6-d8c2-5142-aa1c-2e422d9f5a66, S:70de9964-139b-5992-b9c6-e6bef37fbfc1, S:825a0b03-910a-596c-8f3a-19a5fe7502b2].
- **Direction of change is inconsistent across studies.** CSF of male RRMS patients showed *increased* pregnenolone and isopregnanolone with *decreased* dihydroprogesterone, allopregnanolone, 5α-DHT and estradiol; CSF pregnenolone and DHEA have also been reported as increased versus controls, while DHEA and allopregnanolone are decreased in MS white matter, and female patients have shown *higher* circulating pregnenolone, progesterone and allopregnanolone [S:a6df9977-754c-5bd0-b049-81a1a5b3f1ad, S:05184d16-cbfd-5040-b173-a2c84ec1b4ac, S:fbeb4e9a-ce82-565c-9418-225802a6d084]. Serum DHEAS findings are frankly contradictory (two studies lower, one higher, one no difference) [S:fbeb4e9a-ce82-565c-9418-225802a6d084].
- **DHEA/DHEAS and fatigue** is the most consistent peripheral signal: in primary progressive MS, [passage text removed] fatigued versus non-fatigued patients over 24 months, with an inverse correlation to Fatigue Severity Scale scores and no such correlation for cortisol, IL-1ra or sTNFRII [S:20c7c5f0-f15a-5747-95e1-9d3743b2c12b, S:628ee85c-9c48-54bf-8af6-f13b138b954a].

## Mechanistic rationale linking the two

The proposed axis holds that chronic ROS production suppresses steroidogenic enzymes CYP17A1 and 3β-HSD and the nuclear receptors PPARγ and Nrf2, lowering allopregnanolone and DHEA and weakening neuroprotection, while those neurosteroids in turn suppress NF-κB and induce antioxidant genes — a bidirectional redox–steroidogenic loop [S:cb5d5870-badb-529b-a55f-318e4a32f942, S:7acf95f2-f4c7-5fc3-b139-dc88d06f4a1d]. Experimentally, oxidative injury is not uniformly suppressive: rotenone-treated human microglia *increased* allopregnanolone synthesis while other neurosteroids fell, and oxidative agents can trigger a CYP17A1-independent route to DHEA — suggesting compensatory steroidogenesis [S:58896e93-1282-55af-ad29-1768146e49e6].

## Caveats

The axis-specific triad (8-OHdG + allopregnanolone/DHEA ratio + 3β-HSD activity) is a review proposal, not a validated panel, and the same review notes no new data were generated [S:d3f872e2-64ef-5c2d-ae97-3d5700b8b3ec, S:8a4919c2-5ae4-5a49-bad2-fc5127ab573e]. Oxidative-stress meta-analytic estimates carry very high heterogeneity (I² ≈ 97% for MDA) [S:f50c7716-7eff-57db-9188-937fbd8e2253], neurosteroid directionality varies by sex, menstrual phase, compartment and MS subtype, and prior work has failed to find a relationship between peripheral and central neurosteroid levels in MS [S:bef215e7-27f9-5a41-89ad-ebe2066b00cb]. I found no study that measured oxidative and neurosteroid markers in the same MS cohort and correlated them directly.
