rows.question: How does azathioprine compare with mycophenolate mofetil for reaching minimal manifestation status in acetylcholine receptor-positive generalized myasthenia gravis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Similar proportions of patients reach minimal manifestation status on azathioprine and on mycophenolate mofetil; Minimal manifestation status is reached sooner with mycophenolate mofetil than with azathioprine; On either drug, minimal manifestation status is typically reached only after many months of treatment. Certainty: The evidence is a statistically balanced comparison of treatment as chosen in ordinary care, so the earlier attainment with mycophenolate mofetil is a reasonably supported association rather than an established superiority. Scope: applies to acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents mycophenolate mofetil as an established superior or better-tolerated option than azathioprine, or recommends switching or preferential prescribing on that basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: no head-to-head randomised trial exists, but the two available comparative-effectiveness studies in AChR-antibody-positive generalized MG agree that the *proportion* of patients reaching MGFA post-intervention status of minimal manifestations (MM) or better is essentially the same with azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) — roughly half to two-thirds of patients — while MMF appears to get patients there faster.**

**Prospective cohort (PROMISE-MG).** In this 19-centre prospective study in Canada and the USA (NCT03490539) of immunosuppressant-naive patients, one co-primary outcome was a composite of MGFA-PIS MM-or-better plus low adverse-event burden (CTCAE grade ≤1). It was met by 22/47 (47.7%) on MMF vs 9/31 (28.1%) on [passage text removed]), i.e. not statistically significant; the patient-reported co-primary outcome (MG-QOL15r change) also did not differ ([passage text removed]) ([PMID 38365379](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38365379)). Adverse events occurred in 11/34 (32%) azathioprine vs 9/48 (19%) MMF patients, the commonest being hepatotoxicity with azathioprine (5/34, 15%) and gastrointestinal upset with MMF (7/48, 15%); the authors judged azathioprine's events "potentially more serious" ([PMID 38365379](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38365379); [scholars.duke.edu/publication/1619135](https://scholars.duke.edu/publication/1619135)). A caveat reported for this cohort: [passage text removed] below those recommended for immunosuppression, whereas most MMF patients were dosed conventionally ([[passage text removed])).

**Retrospective cohort restricted to AChR-positive gMG (Duke MG Registry III).** Among 320 AChR-positive gMG patients receiving recommended doses for ≥90 days (177 azathioprine, 143 MMF), the treatment goal of MGFA-PIS MM or better was achieved by 66.1% on azathioprine (median 17.5 months) and 68.5% on MMF (median 10.5 months), with the time difference significant (p=0.0004). Concomitant prednisone — taken by two-thirds — increased the proportion reaching the goal with either drug (p<0.0001), and longer disease duration before starting the drug correlated with longer time to goal ([passage text removed]⁻⁶) ([PMID 41700316](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41700316), Muscle & Nerve 73(5):851–857). The faster MMF effect held both with prednisone (15.5 vs 25.8 months) and without it (21.1 vs 40.4 months) ([[passage text removed])).

**Randomised-trial context (indirect only).** In the international phase III trial confined to AChR-antibody-positive MGFA class II–IVa patients on corticosteroids, the primary endpoint was exactly MM or pharmacologic remission with scheduled steroid reduction: 44% with MMF 2 g/day (n=88) vs 39% with placebo (n=88), p=0.541 ([PMID 18434638](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18434638)); the companion Muscle Study Group trial of MMF 2.5 g/day plus prednisone 20 mg/day in AChR-positive generalized MG also showed no QMG benefit over prednisone alone at 12 weeks (p=0.71) ([scholars.duke.edu/publication/796930](https://scholars.duke.edu/publication/796930)) — both plausibly confounded by prednisone efficacy and short duration ([PMC12998209](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12998209)). Azathioprine, by contrast, has positive randomised data as a steroid adjunct: added to prednisolone it lowered the maintenance dose and produced [passage text removed] effects ([PMID 9633727](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9633727)), and versus prednisone alone treatment failure occurred in 5 vs 12 of 41 patients (p=0.02) ([PMID 8229026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8229026)).

**Supporting single-arm data.** In AChR-positive MG on MMF, 77.4% attained PIS of MM or better during months 19–24 ([Hehir et al., Muscle Nerve 2010; [passage text removed]); [PMID 20405499](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20405499)). In a retrospective AChR-positive gMG series of 105 patients on prednisolone plus azathioprine, MGFA-PIS was MM-1 in 10.5%, MM-2 in 30.4% and MM-3 in 48.6% (plus 7.6% complete stable remission, 2.9% pharmacologic remission); the 10 patients switched to MMF for intolerance or non-response had better PIS after switching ([neurology-asia.org PDF, Neurology Asia 2025;30(1):141]([passage text removed])).

**Practical reading:** choose between them on tolerability and speed rather than expected MM rate — comparable MM attainment, faster onset and fewer/less serious adverse events favouring MMF in observational data, with concomitant prednisone and early initiation being stronger determinants of reaching MM than drug choice ([PMID 41700316](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41700316); [PMID 38365379](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38365379)). Both comparative studies were non-randomised and modest in size, so a true efficacy difference cannot be excluded or confirmed.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line: the two drugs get similar *proportions* of AChR‑antibody–positive generalized MG patients to minimal manifestation status (MMS) — about two‑thirds with either — but MMF gets them there faster.**

**Direct comparative evidence (Duke MG Clinic Registry III).** In a retrospective comparative‑effectiveness study of 320 AChR‑positive gMG patients receiving recommended doses of azathioprine (AZA, n = 177) or mycophenolate mofetil (MMF, n = 143) for ≥90 days, with the treatment goal (TG) defined as MGFA Post‑Intervention Status Minimal Manifestations, TG was reached by 66.1% on AZA (median 17.5 months) and 68.5% on MMF (median 10.5 months, p = 0.0004) [S:09438b1b-cc94-5274-bafa-aba17a426cef]. The proportion achieving TG did not differ significantly between drugs in any stratum — without prednisone 42/60 (70%) AZA vs 33/57 (58%) MMF (p = 0.1837); with prednisone 74/117 (63.2%) vs 65/86 (75.6%) (p = 0.0680); overall 116/177 (65.5%) vs 98/143 (68.5%) (p = 0.6331) — but mean treatment duration before TG was shorter with MMF both without prednisone (40.4 ± 37.6 vs 21.1 ± 28.6 months, p = 0.0136) and with prednisone (25.8 ± 29.6 vs 15.5 ± 16.7 months, p = 0.0115) [S:23e22f2a-475f-5acb-b12b-7d1d50d06d30]. After inverse‑probability‑of‑treatment weighting (covariate balance SMD < 0.1) [S:13b12f89-8368-5d4f-8236-57669ee9d6f5], a Cox model including patients who never reached [passage text removed] (HR = 0.67, 95% [passage text removed]), with no sex difference in time to TG [S:23e22f2a-475f-5acb-b12b-7d1d50d06d30].

**Modifiers that mattered more than drug choice.** Concomitant prednisone (taken by two‑thirds of patients) increased the proportion reaching TG with either agent (p < 0.0001), and longer disease duration at drug initiation correlated with longer time to TG ([passage text removed]) [S:09438b1b-cc94-5274-bafa-aba17a426cef].

**Consistency with prospective data.** An accompanying commentary notes these findings confirm PROMISE‑MG, the prospective observational comparative‑effectiveness study of AZA vs MMF, which likewise found MMF reached TG sooner, and interprets the pattern as explaining why the two large MMF randomized trials — of inadequate duration — failed [S:b728f6de-d145-53af-b115-03a7e1ac259b]. PROMISE‑MG itself found no clinically meaningful difference between AZA and MMF in its two primary outcomes while showing clinically meaningful improvement in over two‑thirds of patients; its gMG sample was small, limiting subgroup analysis [S:be906d80-5dc9-564e-8365-2ff1f0fd0154]. A separate review of PROMISE‑MG reports no difference in clinical outcomes between groups, but more potentially serious adverse effects with azathioprine over 20–25 months of follow‑up, while noting AZA's advantage of lacking teratogenicity [S:9217c1d1-4f23-5be2-b1d9-bab6ec598f2b].

**Supporting non‑comparative data.** In 102 [passage text removed], the proportion [passage text removed] <4 or MGFA‑PIS minimal manifestations or better) began rising after 6 months and reached 80% among those followed >24 months — class IV evidence that MMF's benefit emerges after about 6 months [S:78f7139c-d127-530d-93a3-6853afd519be].

**Caveats.** The head‑to‑head MMS comparison rests on a single‑center retrospective registry cohort with propensity weighting, not randomization [S:09438b1b-cc94-5274-bafa-aba17a426cef]; in the Duke Registry, side effects were not consistently recorded and so are not reported [S:60e9bc24-c34c-5785-ac9c-9b89a4770dc8]. I found no randomized trial directly comparing AZA and MMF using MMS as the endpoint.

rows.question: How do nerve ultrasound and nerve conduction features differ among typical, motor-predominant and pure motor CIDP?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Upper limb nerve, cervical root and brachial plexus cross-sectional areas are larger in motor-predominant than in pure motor CIDP; Significant nerve enlargement was most frequent in typical CIDP, less frequent in motor-predominant disease and was observed in none of the few pure motor patients examined; Demyelinating features on nerve conduction, namely distal motor latency prolongation and motor conduction slowing, are least marked in pure motor, intermediate in motor-predominant and most marked in typical CIDP; Objective thresholds for nerve enlargement in CIDP still require validation before ultrasound is used to assign an individual patient's subtype. Certainty: The graded pattern is an early observation from very small motor-variant groups with widely overlapping nerve sizes rather than an established distinction. Scope: applies to chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy including motor-predominant and pure motor variants in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it asserts that nerve cross-sectional areas are significantly larger in typical than in motor-predominant CIDP, or that ultrasound reliably separates these two subtypes by nerve size.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Across these variants the findings form a graded spectrum rather than discrete categories: nerve cross-sectional area (CSA) enlargement is greatest in typical CIDP, intermediate in motor-predominant CIDP, smaller in pure motor CIDP, and least in MMN — while motor conduction velocity moves in the opposite direction (fastest in MMN, slowest in typical CIDP). Motor variants are instead distinguished by proximally-weighted enlargement and a high burden of conduction block.

## Ultrasound

**Magnitude of enlargement is graded.** In a study of 19 MMN, 15 motor CIDP and 117 typical CIDP patients (bilateral median/ulnar nerves and brachial plexus), [passage text removed]" ([PMID 40485489](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40485489); Canadian Journal of Neurological Sciences). A separate cohort of 206 CIDP patients (145 typical, 10 motor-predominant, 8 motor) found CSAs at most upper-limb nerve sites [passage text removed], and the authors explicitly framed this as "[passage text removed]" (Niu et al., Muscle & Nerve, [doi:10.1002/mus.70242]([passage text removed])).

**Distribution of enlargement differs.** In typical CIDP and MMN, enlargement was distributed roughly evenly along the limb — typical CIDP: brachial plexus 78%, arm 76.8%, forearm 79.4%; MMN: 45.7%, 42.9%, 42.9%. In motor CIDP, by contrast, enlargement was disproportionately proximal (brachial plexus 74.1% vs. arm 65.5% vs. forearm 58.6%) ([PMID 40485489](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40485489)). This proximal weighting is the ultrasound signature that separates motor CIDP from both typical CIDP (diffuse) and MMN (mild, multifocal, with greater side-to-side intranerve variability and lower CSAs than CIDP — [PMC4903137]([passage text removed])).

## Nerve conduction

**Conduction velocity is the mirror image of CSA.** [passage text removed]" ([PMID 40485489](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40485489)) — i.e. pure motor CIDP shows the least demyelinating slowing among the CIDP forms. Concordantly, upper-limb MCVs were slower in motor-predominant than in motor CIDP, and slower in distal segments in typical CIDP than in motor-predominant CIDP ([doi:10.1002/mus.70242]([passage text removed])). The distal predominance of demyelination is a recognised hallmark of typical CIDP ([PMID 25424435](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25424435)).

**Proximal conduction block distinguishes motor CIDP from MMN.** The CMAP<sub>Erb</sub>/CMAP<sub>axilla</sub> ratio was significantly higher in MMN than [passage text removed] vs. 0.60 ± 0.37, P = 0.017), indicating more proximal block in motor CIDP — matching its proximally-accentuated ultrasound enlargement ([PMID 40485489](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40485489)).

**Conduction block and F-wave abnormalities dominate the motor variants.** In 17 motor CIDP patients (2% of 700 CIDP; 7 pure motor, 10 motor-predominant), the most frequent abnormalities were conduction blocks (82%) and F-wave abnormalities (88%) ([PMID 32364302](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32364302)). Conduction block is likewise described as the most common electrophysiological finding in pure motor CIDP ([Frontiers in Neurology, 10.3389/fneur.2021.653734]([passage text removed].2021.653734/full)).

**Sensory conduction is the defining boundary.** By EAN/PNS criteria, ≥2 motor nerves must meet motor conduction criteria with normal sensory conduction in median, ulnar, radial and sural nerves for pure motor CIDP; sensory abnormality in one nerve reclassifies it as motor-predominant CIDP ([rarediseaseadvisor summary of the 2021 guideline]([passage text removed]); [Practical Neurology]([passage text removed])). This boundary is not static: 4 of 10 motor-predominant patients developed sensory symptoms on follow-up while none of the pure motor patients did ([PMID 32364302](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32364302)).

## Clinical corollary

The gradient tracks treatment response: pure motor CIDP had worse outcome than motor-predominant CIDP ([PMID 32364302](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32364302)), and motor CIDP patients did not improve after steroids whereas motor-predominant patients did ([doi:10.1002/mus.70242]([passage text removed])).

## Caveats

Every study addressing the pure motor / motor-predominant split is small (8–10 motor-predominant and 6–8 pure motor patients in the largest series), so the ordinal CSA and MCV gradients should be read as trends, not validated thresholds. I found no source giving discriminative cut-offs (sensitivity/specificity) for separating motor-predominant from pure motor CIDP by ultrasound or NCS.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

The three phenotypes form a graded spectrum: moving from typical → motor-predominant → pure motor CIDP, nerve cross-sectional area (CSA) enlargement on ultrasound progressively diminishes, distal motor latency (DML) prolongation and motor conduction velocity (MCV) slowing become less pronounced, while conduction block (CB) becomes relatively more prominent [S:32af7acf-b470-53a3-b8fa-e8a57a3e6734][S:c3f73761-0125-5c83-8338-03268c47f05a]. Most of the direct comparative evidence comes from a single prospective Chinese cohort of 206 patients meeting 2021 EAN/PNS criteria (145 typical, 10 motor-predominant, 8 motor CIDP) [S:32af7acf-b470-53a3-b8fa-e8a57a3e6734].

## Ultrasound

- **Frequency of significant enlargement** declined across subtypes: 34/145 (23.4%) typical, 1/10 (10%) motor-predominant, and none of the motor CIDP patients [S:32af7acf-b470-53a3-b8fa-e8a57a3e6734].
- **Motor-predominant vs pure motor**: CSA was significantly larger in motor-predominant CIDP at multiple median nerve sites (e.g., A1 8.5 ± 2.1 vs 7.1 ± 1.0 mm², p = 0.021; A3 9.5 ± 2.9 vs 6.6 ± 1.1, p = 0.005), at most ulnar sites (A1 5.0 ± 1.4 vs 3.7 ± 1.1, p = 0.007; A10 9.6 ± 2.4 vs 6.3 ± 1.9, p = 0.001), at the C5 and C6 roots, and at all three brachial plexus trunks (e.g., lower trunk 20.0 ± 5.3 vs 11.9 ± 3.8, p = 0.001) [S:b0c7ce28-4bb7-52c7-80f6-e122a0198bc8].
- **Typical vs motor-predominant**: CSAs were largely similar, with almost no significant differences across median, ulnar, root and trunk sites (only ulnar A10 differed, p = 0.042) — i.e., motor-predominant CIDP sonographically resembles typical CIDP, whereas pure motor CIDP stands apart [S:b0c7ce28-4bb7-52c7-80f6-e122a0198bc8].
- The authors attribute the milder enlargement in motor phenotypes to the fact that [passage text removed], so predominantly motor-fibre pathology produces less bulk enlargement — and note this makes ultrasound-supported diagnosis of motor CIDP harder [S:c3f73761-0125-5c83-8338-03268c47f05a]. Consistent with this, other work shows CSA in CIDP is greatest in segments with predominantly demyelinating rather than axonal features [S:66a99e84-dad3-568b-92d1-2ff39f25bd43].

## Nerve conduction

- **DML**: median DML was longer in motor-predominant than pure motor CIDP (4.5 ± 1.1 vs 3.7 ± 1.3 ms, p = 0.031), and longer still in typical CIDP (6.5 ± 4.9 ms, p = 0.027 vs motor-predominant); the same gradient held for the ulnar nerve [S:e61611d0-f161-564f-aff6-391a7918f56b].
- **MCV**: median forearm MCV was 33.7 ± 11.8 m/s in typical, 39.2 ± 9.1 in motor-predominant (p = 0.046) and 51.5 ± 7.8 m/s in pure motor CIDP (p < 0.001 vs motor-predominant); axilla–elbow MCV showed the same ordering ([passage text removed] / 57.5 ± 7.2 m/s) [S:e61611d0-f161-564f-aff6-391a7918f56b]. Pure motor CIDP thus had near-normal-range velocities.
- **CMAP amplitude / TLI**: distal CMAP amplitudes were numerically higher and TLI similar in pure motor CIDP, without statistically significant differences [S:e61611d0-f161-564f-aff6-391a7918f56b].
- **Conduction block**: CB or probable CB was present in 66/100 (66%) typical CIDP patients, 7/10 (70%) motor-predominant, and 8/8 (100%) pure motor patients; at the nerve level 46.1% (183/397) typical, 55.3% (21/38) motor-predominant, 62.5% (20/32) motor CIDP. The motor-predominant vs motor comparisons did not reach significance (p = 0.130 nerve level, p = 0.136 patient level), so the CB gradient is a trend rather than a proven difference [S:8b3e1a2c-93fb-57fb-91c8-d2d0d13aad1b].
- The authors interpret the pure motor pattern — CB-predominant with little uniform slowing — as possibly reflecting nodal/paranodal dysfunction rather than severe demyelination, a hypothesis they explicitly flag as pathologically unvalidated [S:c3f73761-0125-5c83-8338-03268c47f05a].

## Corroborating and contextual literature

- Independent sources agree that motor conduction block is the most characteristic electrophysiological finding in pure motor CIDP, often with absent sensory conduction abnormalities, making it hard to separate from multifocal motor neuropathy [S:ad8bd4b6-0356-50ea-b44b-1eb3e7d2dc79]; and that CBs [passage text removed] in pure motor CIDP compared with typical CIDP [S:db0f65d7-97fd-5e1f-bf0b-5dc932dc68a6]. Earlier reports also describe more frequent F-wave abnormalities and less frequent DML prolongation/MCV reduction in motor CIDP than typical CIDP [S:c3f73761-0125-5c83-8338-03268c47f05a].
- In pathology-based series, pure motor CIDP was too rare (n = 4 of 106) for separate electrophysiological characterisation, while typical CIDP showed markedly prolonged DMLs and F-wave latencies [S:5f3d03ac-0f31-50f8-82c4-2281ac23f2c6].

## Clinical corollary

Steroid responsiveness declined in parallel: 93.8% (106/113) typical, 85.7% (6/7) motor-predominant, 50% (3/6) motor CIDP [S:32af7acf-b470-53a3-b8fa-e8a57a3e6734], consistent with guideline preference for IVIg first-line in motor CIDP, although reported steroid response rates in motor CIDP vary widely (25–80%) [S:fc339615-fdd9-54b9-a682-7afa0f606b69][S:ad8bd4b6-0356-50ea-b44b-1eb3e7d2dc79].

**Caveats:** the head-to-head ultrasound + NCS comparison rests on very small variant groups (10 and 8 patients) from one centre; the authors themselves call for multicentre studies with standardised quantitative ultrasound protocols and validated enlargement thresholds [S:23b26437-3199-5a81-a3d4-a0b6581391ca]. Studies comparing enlargement *sites* across variants have generally examined typical, multifocal and distal CIDP plus MMN rather than motor CIDP [S:6d261571-d51e-5fab-b4fd-26ed8bd2de6d], so site-specific ultrasound patterns in motor phenotypes remain poorly characterised, and I found no lower-limb or longitudinal ultrasound data specific to these three subtypes.

rows.question: Which blood transcriptomic markers linked to lipopolysaccharide signaling distinguish septic patients from healthy controls?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: A lipopolysaccharide-responsive blood gene signature comprising S100A9, S100A12, IL1R2, GSTO1, UQCRH, LBH and SYNE2 separated septic patients from healthy controls with high reported accuracy across several expression datasets; S100A9 and S100A12 were markedly higher in septic blood, with IL1R2, GSTO1 and UQCRH also higher than in control blood, as a preliminary observation on targeted measurement in a small confirmatory sample; LBH and SYNE2 were expressed at lower levels in septic blood than in control blood in the same small confirmatory measurement. Certainty: The evidence is preliminary and associative, since the reported separation of septic from healthy blood depends on previously archived public gene-expression data, and the direction of the expression differences was verified in only a very small number of participants. Scope: applies to sepsis in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents this gene panel as an established or clinically ready test for separating sepsis from other causes of critical illness, or recommends using it to make that distinction at the bedside.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Several LPS/TLR4-axis transcripts are reproducibly elevated in septic patients' blood versus healthy controls — most consistently the LPS co-receptor **LY96 (MD-2)**, the endotoxin-tolerance regulator **IRAK3 (IRAK-M)**, the receptors **TLR2/TLR4/TLR5**, and LPS-inducible effector genes **IL10, STAT3, MMP9, MMP8, S100A8/A9/A12, ARG1, LTF, CD177, ELANE** — accompanied by downregulation of adaptive/T-cell transcripts. No single "LPS signature" is established; the individual gene panels differ by study.

## Evidence by marker set

**Curated LPS-related gene panels selected by machine learning**
- In three pediatric septic shock cohorts (GSE26440, GSE9692, GSE13904), DEGs intersected with database-curated LPS-related genes yielded four feature genes — **IL10, MMP9, S100A12, STAT3** — all **upregulated**, each with AUC >0.7 in training and validation, and a combined StepGLM+LASSO model with mean AUC 0.994; larger LASSO/SVM-RFE candidate sets also contained **TLR1, TLR2, IL1B, CXCL1, NFKBIA, SOCS3, ITGAM, CD163, CYBB, HCK, JAK2, IL1R1, FCER1G, SPI1, CCR1** ([10.3389/fbinf.2026.1729982]([passage text removed]); PMID 42292668; PMC13261020).
- A separate integration of bulk microarray plus scRNA-seq identified **seven key LPS-related genes** with diagnostic AUCs >0.89 across validation cohorts and cell-type-specific expression in myeloid populations, but the gene names were not visible in the retrieved text, so I cannot list them (PMID 41649833; 10.1002/ddr.70241).

**LY96/MD-2 — the direct LPS-binding co-receptor**
- **LY96, HPGD and OLAH were upregulated in sepsis patients relative to healthy volunteers** and to non-septic surgical controls, while **ABLIM1 was decreased**; the four-gene risk score gave a diagnostic AUC of 0.99–1.00 (E-MTAB-1548, E-MTAB-5273, E-GEOD-28750 discovery/validation) (PMC11613189; PMID 39628572; iScience 27:111277).

**IRAK3 — negative regulator of LPS/TLR signaling**
- IRAK3 transcript [passage text removed]," correlates with severity and mortality, and is higher in non-survivors (10.1371/journal.pone.0263968).
- Independent GEO-based analysis with RT-qPCR confirmed **IRAK3, ADM, ALOX5, MMP9 and S100A8 significantly upregulated** in sepsis blood versus healthy controls (ENTPD1 was not different) (PMC5783525).

**LPS receptors themselves**
- Monocyte **TLR-2 mRNA and protein and TLR-4 mRNA were increased in sepsis versus healthy and non-septic ICU controls**; notably, TLR-4 mRNA in sepsis monocytes was refractory to further in vitro LPS or IL-10 modulation, unlike healthy monocytes — consistent with LPS tolerance (PMC1809013).
- **TLR4 and TLR2** appeared among the top ten upregulated hub genes (with GAPDH, TNF, IL-10, IL-1β, MAPK3, MAPK14, PIK3CB, EGF) in whole blood from 98 pediatric septic shock versus 32 control samples (GSE26440) (PMC6098424).
- **TLR5** was upregulated in septic patients in a five-gene panel (with HMGB2 and C19orf59 up; TXK and DGKA down) validated in GSE236713 and GSE185263 (PMC13421852), and was one of four genes up in all six datasets of a whole-blood meta-analysis (10.1186/s43042-025-00640-8).

**Downstream LPS-responsive innate effector programme (and reciprocal T-cell suppression)**
- Meta-analysis of six whole-blood datasets: up — **[passage text removed], S100A9, MMP9, ELANE** (LTF explicitly linked to TLR4 signaling); down — **FCER1A, IL7R, CCR7, CX3CR1, CD3G, CD40LG, CD247, CD3E, GZMK** (10.1186/s43042-025-00640-8).
- CD14+ monocyte scRNA-seq showed **TNFAIP6 and PLSCR1** higher in sepsis than healthy controls, and both were **significantly upregulated by ex vivo LPS stimulation** of PBMCs — a direct link between the sepsis marker and LPS responsiveness (10.1186/s10020-025-01350-y).

## Caveats

- The blood coding-RNA changes of sepsis are broadly **recapitulated by controlled LPS administration to healthy volunteers (human endotoxemia)**, which supports LPS signaling as a driver but also means these markers are not pathogen- or endotoxin-specific (eLife 58597; PMC7775110).
- Much of the whole-blood signal reflects neutrophil/monocyte expansion and activation plus lymphocyte suppression rather than LPS pathway activity per se (PMC12294327; 10.1186/s43042-025-00640-8), and several of the "LPS-related gene" panels above are database-curated gene lists rather than experimentally defined endotoxin-response modules.
- Panels are largely from retrospective GEO reanalyses with small qRT-PCR validation cohorts; the pediatric septic shock panel used septic shock versus control, not sepsis broadly.
answers.connect:
## Answer

The best-characterized panel is a seven-gene lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-related signature — **S100A9, S100A12, IL1R2, GSTO1, UQCRH (up in sepsis) and LBH, SYNE2 (down in sepsis)** — supplemented by consistent evidence for upregulated proximal LPS-sensing/signaling transcripts (**TLR4, TLR2, IRAK3/IRAK-M**) and LPS-inducible effector genes (**hepcidin/HAMP, METTL7B**) in septic versus healthy blood.

### 1. A seven-gene LPS-related diagnostic signature

An integrated study combined seven bulk microarray cohorts (including GSE95233: 102 sepsis, 22 controls; GSE65682: 760 sepsis, 42 controls) with whole-blood scRNA-seq (GSE175453: 5 healthy controls, 4 sepsis donors), intersecting sepsis DEGs with 6,571 LPS-related genes curated from the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database [S:7c439531]. Differential analysis of GSE95233 yielded 1,024 DEGs (556 up, 468 down), of which 47 overlapped with single-cell DEGs [S:4251c63b].

LASSO, SVM-RFE and XGBoost converged on seven signature genes — **S100A9, S100A12, IL1R2, GSTO1, UQCRH, LBH, SYNE2** — with training-set AUCs of 0.995–1.000, and AUCs above 0.90 for most genes across five independent external GEO datasets; the majority were significantly upregulated in sepsis versus controls [S:7d146682], with overall diagnostic performance reported as AUC > 0.89 across validation cohorts [S:3fa3481c].

Direction of change was confirmed by qRT-PCR in [passage text removed] patients, while LBH and SYNE2 were significantly higher in controls** [S:0268489c]. Within [passage text removed] higher in the high-risk group, and elevated IL1R2 and UQCRH tracked with poorer survival [S:3ca8b8dc]. The authors interpret the panel as capturing neutrophil/calgranulin activity (S100A8/A9/A12), excess [passage text removed] loss of homeostatic regulators (LBH, SYNE2) [S:a065f4c5].

Mechanistically, AUCell scoring of 109 sepsis-associated LPS-related genes showed macrophages with the highest enrichment; high-score cells were enriched for oxidative phosphorylation, fatty acid metabolism and coagulation, and showed increased cell–cell communication with MDSCs as hubs [S:55020017]. Signature expression localized predominantly to myeloid populations (monocytes, macrophages, MDSCs), including an HLA-DR-low, S100A9/S100A12/IL1R2 co-expressing monocyte subset [S:8699190b].

Independent corroboration: **GSTO1 and S100A9** also emerged (with IRAK3 and TXN) as RT-PCR-validated genes elevated in sepsis patients' peripheral blood versus normal controls, while NFATC2 was decreased [S:d405496a, S:bf4ccdfc].

### 2. Proximal LPS receptor and signaling transcripts

- **TLR4/TLR2:** In sorted blood monocytes from 10 sepsis patients versus 6 normal controls, TLR4 mRNA and cell-surface TLR4 were significantly increased, as was surface TLR2; [passage text removed] were not significantly changed [S:4cda4e64]. Bioinformatic analysis of pediatric and adult sepsis datasets likewise found TLR2 and TLR4 transcripts significantly upregulated in PBMC/blood of sepsis patients versus healthy controls, correlating with IL1B [S:1cb84000]. A pediatric sepsis screen found TLR4 among nine genes with higher mRNA than healthy controls in GSE95233 and confirmed TLR4, LTF, ELANE, DEFA4 and PRTN3 upregulation by qRT-PCR [S:52d13de1].
- **IRAK3 (IRAK-M):** transcript expression is markedly induced in septic patients relative to healthy subjects and correlates with severity and mortality, with non-survivors showing higher IRAK3 mRNA than survivors — a marker of endotoxin tolerance [S:91395af3].
- **Negative regulators of LPS signaling:** IRAK-M, ABIN-3 and LY64 mRNA (alongside TNF-α, IL-10, HLA-DRA, CIITA) were used as a qRT-PCR panel documenting the immunosuppressed/endotoxin-tolerant state in septic shock whole blood [S:7dabf864].

### 3. LPS-inducible downstream transcripts

- **Hepcidin:** peripheral blood leukocyte hepcidin mRNA was significantly higher in severe sepsis (n = 14) than healthy controls (n = 16), and was inducible ex vivo by LPS via an NF-κB-dependent, TNF-α-mediated route [S:ac57f00c].
- **METTL7B:** upregulated in blood and PBMCs of septic patients versus healthy controls with significant diagnostic potential, and induced by LPS in a time- and dose-dependent manner in macrophages [S:d6c75c2b].
- **HSP90AA1:** elevated in platelets from sepsis patients versus healthy donors, with TLR4-dependence demonstrated in TLR4⁻/⁻ septic mice [S:5fae6363].

### Caveats

Some transcripts move in the opposite direction to a naive "LPS activation" model, reflecting concurrent immunoparalysis: monocyte membrane CD14 expression is reduced in septic states [S:99f08787], and monocytes from infected patients show decreased SITPEC, TAK1 and MEKK mRNA with elevated IRAK-M [S:19117691]. Broader whole-blood sepsis signatures are dominated by neutrophil degranulation/innate signaling upregulation with translation and ribosomal pathway suppression rather than by LPS-pathway genes per se [S:14a25cd2, S:8a1d6411]. Note also an internal inconsistency in the seven-gene paper: one panel describes GSTO1 as "downregulated in control" and SYNE2 as "upregulated" in a prognostic-cohort comparison [S:3ca8b8dc], which reads ambiguously against the qRT-PCR result [S:0268489c] — treat SYNE2's direction with caution. Finally, most of the LPS-related-gene work is retrospective GEO reanalysis with modest qRT-PCR cohorts; no prospective clinical validation was found in these sources.

rows.question: What factors are associated with death in immunocompromised patients with opportunistic pulmonary infections?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Admission lymphopenia, seen as a lower lymphocyte count and a higher neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, is associated with death within 28 days; A higher C-reactive protein at admission is associated with death within 28 days; Growth of multidrug-resistant bacteria is more frequent among patients who die than among those who survive; Septic shock during the hospitalization is associated with higher 28-day mortality. Certainty: The supporting evidence establishes association rather than causation, and residual confounding may remain despite multivariable adjustment. Scope: applies to opportunistic pulmonary infection during immunosuppressive therapy in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents a high admission neutrophil count, lactate dehydrogenase or procalcitonin as an established predictor of death in these patients.

answers.websearch:
**Death in immunocompromised patients with opportunistic pulmonary infection is driven less by the type of immunosuppression than by illness severity at presentation, organ failure, delayed or failed respiratory support, failure to identify the causative pathogen, and specific high-lethality etiologies (invasive fungal disease, CMV).**

## Severity and organ dysfunction at presentation
In the Efraim multinational prospective cohort of 1611 immunocompromised patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (ICU/hospital/day-90 mortality 32.4%/44.1%/56.4%), independent predictors of hospital death were older age (OR 1.18/year, 1.09–1.27), day-1 SOFA excluding respiratory score (OR 1.12/point, 1.08–1.16), PaO₂/FiO₂ <100 (OR [passage text removed] (OR 1.43, 1.04–1.97); direct ICU admission was protective (OR 0.69, 0.54–0.87) [Azoulay et al., Intensive Care Med 2017;43:1808–1819, doi:10.1007/s00134-017-4947-1]. In the larger Efraim III study (9854 patients, 103 ICUs, 26 countries; 30-day mortality 47.3%), predictors of death were older age, higher Charlson Comorbidity Index (HR [passage text removed]) and [passage text removed]) [PMID 41856149].

## Timing of intubation / failure of non-invasive support
In a pooled individual-patient-data meta-analysis of immunocompromised patients ultimately intubated, [passage text removed] raised mortality ([passage text removed] protective (OR 0.83, 0.72–0.96), and propensity-matched delayed intubation carried OR 1.56 (1.44–1.70) [PMID 33751920]. In Efraim, mortality odds rose progressively with the mode of intubation failure, from first-line IMV (2.55) through NIV failure (3.65), standard-oxygen failure (4.16) and HFNC failure (5.54) [doi:10.1007/s00134-017-4947-1]. No validated tool (ROX, HACOR) reliably predicts non-invasive support failure in this population [doi:10.1007/s00134-026-08554-8].

## Failure to establish a diagnosis
Undetermined etiology is consistently associated with excess death across cohorts [doi:10.1007/s00134-026-08554-8]; in Efraim III unidentified cause of ARF carried HR 2.16 (1.74–2.68) [PMID 41856149]. A trial protocol describing Efraim 1 reports that undetermined etiology overall carried [passage text removed] [NCT04680884 listing]. Delayed recognition and inappropriate empiric antimicrobial selection are recognised contributors to worse outcome in immunocompromised pneumonia [StatPearls, NBK557843].

## Causative pathogen
Mortality is highest with invasive fungal infection and with no identified cause, and lowest with cardiogenic pulmonary oedema [Azoulay et al., Lancet Respir Med 2019; PMID 30529232]. Efraim III found invasive fungal infection as cause of ARF (HR 1.82, 1.45–2.28) and [passage text removed]) predicted death, whereas solid organ transplant (0.62) and vasculitis/connective tissue disease (0.61) were protective [PMID 41856149].

- **Pneumocystis (non-HIV):** a meta-analysis identified age, concomitant other pulmonary disease at diagnosis, solid tumour, [passage text removed] hospitalisation, and pneumothorax as mortality risk factors [PMC8244732].
- **Invasive aspergillosis:** predictors of increased overall mortality included allogeneic HSCT [passage text removed], corticosteroid therapy, renal impairment, low monocyte count, disseminated disease, diffuse pulmonary lesions and pleural effusion; neutropenia predicted attributable mortality [Clin Infect Dis 2008;47:1176–1184]. In hematologic malignancy, persistent neutropenia (OR 2.0), ICU admission (OR 6.6) increased IA-attributable death while antimould azole therapy reduced it [PMC3228136]. In solid tumours, steroids within 30 days (HR 2.2) and chest radiotherapy (HR 2.6) predicted 12-week mortality [PMID 30230385]. Bacterial/fungal co-infection, age, absence of remission and nodule number were independent predictors of in-hospital death in bronchoscoped hematology patients [doi:10.1007/s11046-025-01005-w].
- **CMV:** delayed-onset CMV pneumonitis independently predicted death in lung transplant recipients (HR 1.63, 1.09–2.46), alongside bacterial (2.80), fungal (1.80) and viral (1.49) pneumonia [PMC4534357]. In a retrospective CMV respiratory infection cohort, interstitial lung disease and respiratory failure predicted 30-day, 1-year and 5-year death [PMC12107962]; in AIDS patients, BALF CMV DNA >10,000 copies/mL independently predicted 90-day death (aOR 3.78, 1.12–12.71) [doi.org/10.3390/pathogens15040377 record, mdpi.com/2076-0817/15/4/377].
- **HIV/TB:** older age, CD4 <200 cells/mm³ and thrombocytopenia were independent mortality predictors in HIV-TB co-infection [PLOS One, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0329267]; lower CD4, hypoalbuminemia and lower haemoglobin were associated with death among pulmonary complications in people with HIV [doi:10.1186/s12879-026-13438-9].

## Caveat
The characteristics of the underlying immunosuppressive condition are often *not* independently associated with hospital mortality once ICU-admitted, though this varies with admission and do-not-intubate policies; performance status and comorbidity burden are consistent predictors [PMID 30529232]. Several figures above come from single-centre retrospective studies or meta-analyses of heterogeneous cohorts, so effect sizes should not be treated as interchangeable across populations.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Death in immunocompromised patients with opportunistic pulmonary infections is driven by three broad domains: **host/underlying-immunosuppression factors** (age, comorbid lung disease, solid tumour, type of immunosuppression, profound T-cell/lymphocyte depletion), **severity and complications of the acute episode** (need for or escalation to invasive mechanical ventilation, ARDS, septic shock, pneumothorax, refractory hypoxaemia, high LDH), and **process-of-care factors** (delay from symptom onset to pathogen-targeted therapy, delayed diagnosis or undetermined aetiology, high cumulative corticosteroid dose after admission).

### Host and underlying-disease factors
- In a meta-analysis of 19 studies (1,310 non-HIV PcP patients; 485 non-survivors), older age (mean difference 6.61 years, 95% CI 4.48–8.74, p<0.00001), concomitant other pulmonary disease at diagnosis (OR 3.42, 95% CI 1.96–5.96), and solid tumour (OR 2.06, 95% CI 1.32–3.21) were associated with death, whereas sex, albumin, PcP prophylaxis, corticosteroid use after admission, and time from symptom onset to treatment were not [S:14c06e73-0587-5889-ab7a-4ea13b0c4cd8][S:b5526e06-d464-51c9-b372-91bc5d4e0ed6][S:7e1619d4-e826-5381-86be-4661413ef8a6][S:6bb1caff-abe8-5107-83e6-17ab82937731]. The authors hypothesise chronic lung disease destroys lung architecture, facilitating progression [S:13f7a1a2-bb5d-573d-a260-93791665dab8].
- In a post-hoc analysis of a 29-centre randomised trial of immunocompromised patients with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, factors associated with in-ICU death related to the cause of immunosuppression, acute disease severity, and response to non-invasive respiratory support; solid cancer and increased patient discomfort after starting non-invasive support were independently associated with ICU mortality, and solid cancer also predicted death/poor performance status at 6 months. Pre-ICU performance status was not a good predictor of ICU mortality but drove longer-term outcome [S:b37577c9-e324-595f-9437-12642dcf4fd1][S:37d65f0c-62c7-54c3-ba28-7ee24dac962f][S:96b41f46-7a6c-55e7-9973-471ac8caf1b2].
- Depth of cellular immunosuppression matters: [passage text removed] and <75 cells/mm³) were associated with early mortality (log-rank p<0.001), with AUCs of 0.82–0.94 for predicting [passage text removed]].
- For invasive mould disease in haematologic malignancy, frequently reported risk factors for death include severity and duration of neutropenia, type/duration of cytotoxic therapy, amphotericin B (vs voriconazole) therapy, allogeneic HCT, and GVHD; most IA-attributable deaths occur within six weeks of diagnosis [S:c87b395a-7ffb-5a2c-9ab0-b71d75ca123d].

### Acute severity and complications
- Invasive ventilation during hospitalisation was the strongest pooled predictor of PcP death (OR 29.24, 95% CI 13.09–65.33), along with pneumothorax (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.13–5.77), CMV co-infection (OR 3.59, 95% CI 1.91–6.75), higher LDH (mean difference 91.12, p=0.05) and lymphocyte count [S:6bb1caff-abe8-5107-83e6-17ab82937731][S:7e1619d4-e826-5381-86be-4661413ef8a6][S:14c06e73-0587-5889-ab7a-4ea13b0c4cd8].
- A multicentre Chinese study of 127 non-AIDS, non-solid-tumour immunocompromised patients with opportunistic pulmonary infection found septic shock during hospitalisation ([passage text removed]) and escalation to endotracheal intubation with invasive ventilation ([passage text removed]) to [passage text removed]; septic shock was the strongest contributor in the derived nomogram (C-index [passage text removed]) [S:671f9fab-9f2b-5009-9bde-bfefcd318e50][S:2f262573-852b-5cbf-a078-d78471a6ac80][S:7147549b-8d37-5345-9aef-b5f291a62455]. The authors note concordance with prior work showing IMV need at admission and escalation to IMV — rather than initial oxygenation — predict in-hospital death [S:e1dac91c-6c19-51ad-9530-47e2aaa0db8b].
- In an ICU cohort of severe non-HIV PJP (n=82, hospital mortality 75.6%), age (OR 1.051), lower white blood cell count (OR 0.802) and pneumomediastinum (OR 16.514) were independently associated with hospital death; non-survivors also had higher APACHE II scores, less fever and more hypotension [S:4e5aff0f-5f70-5943-8d45-d0e2bff35e8e].
- In critically ill immunosuppressed patients with influenza, [passage text removed] were independent risk factors for death, with mortality approaching 100% when these occurred alongside co-infection; severe hypoxaemia and diagnostic delay were also flagged as mortality risks [S:be53635e-aa78-5d08-9557-5d1d3a465bd6].
- Other prognostic signals in non-HIV PcP include lower albumin, higher corticosteroid dose at PcP onset, wider A–a oxygen gradient, higher A-DROP score, LDH, BUN and BUN/albumin ratio in non-survivors [S:268b2012-2115-5b87-9ab5-b62b206240d4]; and, in a mNGS-based cohort, mixed infection and elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio were independent predictors of poor outcome [S:0fcdfc73-a259-5e41-9487-c1907bc1b3c6]. Higher CMV DNA load in BAL fluid was positively associated with mortality in PJP patients (p=0.012) [S:97f3ad4f-9be1-541a-81c9-d0ac8622f3f3].

### Treatment and process-of-care factors
- [passage text removed] per unit, 95% CI 1.004–1.091) and greater cumulative glucocorticoid dose in the first hospital week ([passage text removed]) independently increased 28-day mortality, while [passage text removed] was protective ([passage text removed]) [S:671f9fab-9f2b-5009-9bde-bfefcd318e50]. The authors conclude that early recognition, timely targeted antimicrobials and minimised glucocorticoid exposure can prevent escalation to intubation and septic shock [S:f6a6bcd2-3758-5e00-a603-603bb85227bc].
- For invasive aspergillosis, delayed treatment is lethal: one study cited reported ~90% mortality when treatment began more than 10 days after pneumonia onset versus ~40% when started within 10 days [S:441b6576-0729-56d8-8266-4ea562b8f1e3]; delayed amphotericin B-based frontline therapy likewise increases mortality in haematologic-malignancy zygomycosis [S:ce52ff23-63ac-5f6b-ba36-2f11d33337ce].
- Synthesised ICU/oncology data indicate mortality rises when IMV is required, when the aetiology remains undetermined, [passage text removed] — supporting standardised early diagnostic work-up [S:60fb8abe-5d1c-5558-b5e2-bf2928473fe8]. Older prognostic literature in HIV-negative immunocompromised patients with pulmonary infiltrates similarly names need for mechanical ventilation and diagnostic delay [S:2489310b-29d1-5625-aa35-639f4caa6dcc].

### Caveats
Findings are inconsistent across cohorts: neutrophil count and LDH were independent predictors in some studies but not in the multicentre opportunistic-infection cohort, attributed to heterogeneity of pathogens and immunosuppression types [S:9e9f9ef5-e875-58a6-8293-d394678727b5][S:e1dac91c-6c19-51ad-9530-47e2aaa0db8b]. CMV co-infection's independent effect is disputed — some studies found no mortality difference by CMV status, and one PJP cohort found no significant mortality difference between CMV-positive and CMV-negative groups (p=0.15) [S:ba67367a-69d8-5f84-9451-a8a1416d38c3][S:97f3ad4f-9be1-541a-81c9-d0ac8622f3f3]. Also note the largest multivariate study of opportunistic pulmonary infections specifically excluded HIV-positive patients and those treated for solid tumours, and was retrospective with only 127 patients [S:7147549b-8d37-5345-9aef-b5f291a62455].

rows.question: Which imaging features distinguish multiple sclerosis from AQP4-antibody NMOSD and MOGAD in suspected demyelinating syndromes?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Brain lesion patterns typical of multiple sclerosis, such as lesions in the inferior temporal lobe and beside the lateral ventricle, Dawson's fingers, or U- or S-shaped juxtacortical lesions, favour established relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis over AQP4-antibody NMOSD and MOGAD with high reported sensitivity and specificity; The central vein sign and the paramagnetic rim sign are reported as highly specific for multiple sclerosis rather than AQP4-antibody NMOSD or MOGAD; Imaging during remission shows the lowest lesion burden in MOGAD, an intermediate burden in AQP4-antibody NMOSD and the highest in multiple sclerosis; Discrimination by these multiple sclerosis-typical patterns is weaker in very early disease, including clinically isolated syndrome and pediatric-onset presentations. Certainty: The supporting evidence consists of descriptive imaging comparisons across antibody-defined patient groups, so these features shift diagnostic probability rather than confirm a diagnosis. Scope: applies to suspected central nervous system demyelinating syndrome in adults and children, specialist neurology settings. An answer is wrong if it presents these imaging features as sufficient to establish or exclude MOGAD or AQP4-antibody NMOSD, or recommends forgoing antibody testing when the scan looks typical.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

No single MRI feature is diagnostic, but the combination of lesion **shape/perivenular topography and cortical involvement** favours MS, **AQP4-rich periependymal/area postrema sites plus central longitudinally extensive myelitis** favours AQP4-NMOSD, and **fluffy, ill-defined lesions with perineural optic nerve enhancement, conus/central-grey myelitis and near-complete lesion resolution** favours MOGAD. [S:10.1212/WNL.0000000000201465] [S:10.1007/s00415-025-13303-w]

## Brain parenchyma

**MS-specific:** [passage text removed]) are the highest-performing discriminators. In a prospective 3-group cohort (31 RRMS, 30 AQP4-NMOSD, 30 MOGAD), the proportion of CVS-positive lesions was 84% in RRMS vs 33% in AQP4-NMOSD (accuracy/specificity/sensitivity 91/88/93%), and cortical lesions gave 84/90/77%; combining CVS + cortical lesions + optic nerve magnetisation transfer ratio reached 95/92/97% for RRMS vs AQP4-NMOSD [S:10.1212/WNL.0000000000201465]. Notably, CVS was present in 78% of MOGAD lesions — twice the AQP4 rate — so CVS does **not** separate MOGAD from AQP4-NMOSD, and pathologically MOGAD plaques may form around multiple small vessels [S:10.1212/WNL.0000000000201465]. In a broader MS-mimic cohort, a single cortical lesion carried ~94% specificity for MS/CIS but only 59% sensitivity, while the 40% CVS rule gave 78.7% sensitivity/86.0% specificity; combining both improved AUC to 0.92 [S:PMC10714285]. CVS and paramagnetic rim lesions are now incorporated in the 2024 McDonald revision as optional highly specific tools, with Select-6 positivity supporting MS [S:[passage text removed]].

**Lesion burden:** Brain white matter lesions were seen in 100% of RRMS, 83% of AQP4-NMOSD and only 27% of MOGAD; lesion number/volume were higher in RRMS than either antibody-mediated disease, and lesion number was the single most accurate marker separating RRMS from MOGAD [S:10.1212/WNL.0000000000201465]. A 66-study meta-analysis (2933 MS, 3296 AQP4-NMOSD, 1559 MOGAD) associated periventricular, subcortical, Dawson's finger, U-fibre, inferior temporal, cortical T2 lesions, T1 "black holes" and brain gadolinium enhancement with MS [S:10.1007/s00415-025-13303-w]. A first-imaging study found ovoid lesions (OR 0.029), Dawson's fingers (0.031), pyramidal corpus callosum (0.058), periventricular (0.136), temporal lobe (0.137) and T1 black holes (0.154) all favoured MS over NMOSD [S:PMC8458658].

**AQP4-NMOSD-specific:** Lesions cluster in AQP4-rich regions — dorsal medulla/area postrema, periependymal brainstem and diencephalon (third/fourth ventricle lining, hypothalamus, thalamus), long corticospinal tract and extensive corpus callosal lesions [S:PMC6223278] [S:[passage text removed]]. Area postrema and hypothalamic T2 lesions were meta-analytically associated with AQP4-NMOSD [S:10.1007/s00415-025-13303-w], [passage text removed] (16.8) and hypothalamic (7.2) lesions predicted NMOSD [S:PMC8458658]. Periventricular lesions in AQP4 disease tend to be linear periependymal or focal nodular rather than large [S:PMC7363520].

**MOGAD-specific:** Lesions are large, bilateral, poorly marginated ("fluffy"), often brainstem (pons, midbrain, middle cerebellar peduncle) and deep grey/thalamic, with ADEM-like and cortical-encephalitis-with-seizures phenotypes essentially confined to MOGAD [S:[passage text removed]] [S:PMC9247462]. Cortical/juxtacortical lesions favoured MOGAD over AQP4-NMOSD, in which they were absent in one comparative series [S:PMC7363520]. Fluffy lesions and peri-ependymal third/fourth ventricle T2 lesions were meta-analytically associated with MOGAD [S:10.1007/s00415-025-13303-w].

## Optic nerve

MS-related optic neuritis is typically unilateral, short-segment (<50% of nerve length), retrobulbar, with mild enhancement; AQP4-NMOSD favours bilateral, long-segment, **posterior** nerve/chiasmal involvement; MOGAD favours bilateral, long anterior-segment lesions with **perineural (optic nerve sheath/orbital fat) enhancement** and optic disc oedema, with chiasm involvement rare [S:[passage text removed]] [S:PMC9247462]. Bilateral optic nerve involvement at first presentation occurred in 84% of MOGAD and 82% of AQP4-NMOSD vs 23% of MS optic neuritis; perioptic sheath/orbital fat enhancement is reported in 50–80% of MOGAD [S:[passage text removed]]. Meta-analysis linked optic chiasm and optic tract T2 lesions to AQP4-NMOSD, unilateral optic nerve T2 to MS, and perineural enhancement to MOGAD [S:10.1007/s00415-025-13303-w].

## Spinal cord

- **MS:** multiple short (<2 segments), well-demarcated, peripheral lesions occupying <half the cross-section, favouring dorsal/lateral columns; posterior column and peripheral cord T2 lesions were MS-associated (posterior column PPV 0.994 in Western populations) [S:[passage text removed]] [S:10.1007/s00415-025-13303-w].
- **AQP4-NMOSD:** LETM ≥3 segments, usually a single lesion, central/whole-cord on axial images with swelling, T1-hypointense core, elongated ring or patchy enhancement, plus **bright spotty lesions** and later cord atrophy; ORs for NMOSD vs MS were LETM 203, bright spotty 93.8, whole-axial 57.8, Gd-enhancing cord 28.6 [S:PMC8458658] [S:PMC9247462] [S:10.1007/s00415-025-13303-w]. Short myelitis can nonetheless be the presenting lesion [S:practicalneurology.com/.../54601].
- **MOGAD:** LETM (~60%) but often with >1 lesion, **conus medullaris involvement**, central grey-matter-restricted T2 forming the axial **"H sign"** (reported in ~30–50% of MOGAD, much less in AQP4-NMOSD, absent in MS), frequently non-enhancing or with only faint/patchy or leptomeningeal enhancement, and sometimes cauda equina root enhancement [S:PMC12394311] [S:PMC9247462] [S:[passage text removed]]. The H sign and conus lesion are formal supportive MRI features in the 2023 international MOGAD criteria [S:10.3389/fped.2024.1451688].
- Cervical cord lesion presence was the only measure separating AQP4-NMOSD from MOGAD (OR 30.36, accuracy 71%), and ≥1 cervical lesion occurred in 55% RRMS, 40% AQP4-NMOSD, 4% MOGAD [S:PMC9869760] [S:10.1212/WNL.0000000000201465].

## Temporal dynamics (highly useful when serology is ambiguous)

Follow-up imaging is discriminating. Index T2-lesion resolution was far commoner in MOGAD than AQP4-NMOSD or MS (paediatric cohort: brain 60% vs 25% vs 0%; spine 67% vs 0% vs 8%, p<0.01) [S:PMC10626581]. Complete resolution of cord T2 lesions is reported in 62–79% of MOGAD myelitis but is uncommon in MS and AQP4-NMOSD; residual cord T1 hypointensity was seen in 3/34 AQP4-NMOSD, 1/29 MS and 0/28 MOGAD [S:10.3389/fneur.2022.1011579]. Conversely, **asymptomatic/silent new lesions** are a hallmark of MS and rare in the antibody-mediated diseases — new remission lesions occurred in 5/167 (3.0%) MOGAD remission MRI sessions, and in AQP4-NMOSD in 6/136 patients (4.4%) across 7/269 (2.6%) remission scans [S:[passage text removed]] [S:jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2786936]. Cord atrophy is greater in AQP4-NMOSD than RRMS and absent in MOGAD; grey matter atrophy occurs in MS but not NMOSD [S:10.1212/WNL.0000000000201465].

## Caveats

Locations overlap substantially, and brainstem lesion appearance alone does not reliably separate MOGAD from AQP4-NMOSD [S:PMC11108817]. MOGAD-typical features are often absent outside the acute phase, and no standardised algorithm combining these features exists [S:10.1212/WNL.0000000000201465]. Thalamic lesions, traditionally ascribed to AQP4-NMOSD, were in meta-analysis more suggestive of MS or MOGAD [S:10.1007/s00415-025-13303-w]. Antibody assays remain central to diagnosis [S:[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** MS is identified by perivenular, chronically evolving, tract- and periventricular-patterned lesions (central vein sign, paramagnetic rim lesions, Dawson's fingers, U-fibre and inferior temporal lesions, T1 "black holes", short peripheral cord lesions, short unilateral anterior optic neuritis), whereas AQP4-NMOSD favours AQP4-rich periependymal/diencephalic/area postrema sites with longitudinally extensive central cord lesions and posterior/chiasmal optic neuritis, and MOGAD favours ill-defined "fluffy" lesions, grey-matter-restricted cord involvement, conus involvement, bilateral anterior optic neuritis with perineural enhancement, and near-complete lesion resolution on follow-up. Details below.

**1. Susceptibility-based markers (most discriminating for MS)**
- In a prospective study of 31 RRMS, 30 AQP4-NMOSD and 30 MOGAD patients, the proportion of lesions showing the central vein sign was the single most accurate discriminator of RRMS from AQP4-NMOSD ([passage text removed]%), and combining CVS proportion, cortical lesion count and optic nerve magnetisation transfer ratio reached 95/92/97% [S:36f80806-da27-5749-a4d4-e09137e48a73]. For RRMS vs MOGAD, white matter lesion count ([passage text removed]; 94/94/93%) and cortical lesions (84/97/71%) were most accurate [S:3aa70231-b735-5608-b4b1-213b0955c64a].
- Another 3T study reported CVS in 32% of AQP4+ NMOSD brain lesions versus 80% of MS lesions [S:e734aa1d-160f-5a4f-983d-74f2702992b7].
- Paramagnetic rim lesions (chronic active lesions) appear essentially MS-restricted: in a matched adult cohort, no MOGAD patient had PRLs versus 52% of MS, and CVS positivity was 36% vs 100% (median perivenular lesion proportion 80% MS vs 62% MOGAD) [S:149af21b-6ffa-5cad-8949-8f5078267a23]; in paediatric cohorts PRLs were detectable only in paediatric-onset MS, and CVS-positive rate separated MOGAD from POMS with ROC = 1 [S:aec5e3f9-0174-5820-86b4-0069157a3181]. Pathologically, chronic active/iron-rim lesions are absent in MOGAD but present in MS [S:02f246b8-c1de-5ae4-aaf2-d5abcccd6035]. Quantitative susceptibility mapping likewise supports paramagnetic rims as an MS-specific marker versus NMOSD [S:0802e91a-1d9a-506c-a8d0-4f191d834dba].

**2. Brain lesion topography and morphology**
- Meta-analysis (66 studies; 2933 MS, 3296 AQP4-NMOSD, 1559 MOGAD) found MS-associated features: periventricular, subcortical white matter, Dawson's finger, U-fibre, inferior temporal, cortical T2 lesions, T1 hypointensities (black holes), pontine and enhancing lesions; AQP4-associated: optic chiasm T2, LETM, bright spotty cord lesions, area postrema, hypothalamic T2, cord atrophy, optic tract lesions; MOGAD-associated: conus medullaris, "fluffy", perineural enhancement, periependymal third- and fourth-ventricle lesions [S:ccde303b-2668-59dd-b53f-887d4f206264]. Strongest odds ratios: Dawson's fingers (OR 34.11), subcortical WM (12.16) and U-fibre lesions (11.44) for MS; LETM (11.38), chiasm (5.95), hypothalamic (5.65) for AQP4-NMOSD; fluffy T2 (18.78) and conus lesions (14.50) for MOGAD [S:7a1b4ac5-c0c8-5982-a290-c9915d5c4189]. Dawson's fingers had specificity 0.958 and cortical T2 lesions 0.881 for MS; area postrema 0.945 and bright spotty cord lesions 0.988 for NMOSD [S:821dee5d-87e7-566f-b1e6-c2c3c562b334].
- AQP4-NMOSD lesions cluster in AQP4-rich regions — diencephalon around the third ventricle/aqueduct, dorsal brainstem adjacent to the fourth ventricle (area postrema), periependymal lateral-ventricular/callosal regions ("arch bridge" splenial lesions), corticospinal tracts, and tumefactive hemispheric lesions — with poorly marginated "cloud-like" enhancement rather than MS's ovoid/ring enhancement; cortical lesions are characteristically absent [S:5e14965a-7513-5f40-bfcc-d5c54dda140f][S:0fae0dd0-1ce1-53cb-9e4c-6ccfa75aaa7d].
- MOGAD brain lesions are ADEM-like/fluffy, ill-defined, often bilateral, involving deep grey nuclei, pons and middle cerebellar peduncles, with juxtacortical U-fibre sparing and absent Dawson's fingers; area postrema lesions are comparatively rare; cortical FLAIR-hyperintense encephalitis (FLAMES) with overlying leptomeningeal enhancement is a distinctive phenotype [S:a21ead70-fa00-5e83-a198-4393266fe2dd][S:e734aa1d-160f-5a4f-983d-74f2702992b7][S:5d21c31a-98cc-598e-ba4b-a4836ebf2dca].

**3. Spinal cord**
- MS cord lesions rarely exceed 2 vertebral segments, are "cigar"/wedge-shaped, occupy lateral and posterior columns, and seldom involve >half the cross-section; AQP4-NMOSD and MOGAD lesions typically span ≥3 contiguous segments, are centrally located and occupy much of the cross-section [S:95009b8b-4070-56ba-ae03-7f78ff2b6f6f]. The same source's comparative table lists bright spotty lesions as frequent only in AQP4-NMOSD, grey-matter-restricted H-sign as frequent only in MOGAD, conus involvement as frequent in both antibody diseases, nerve-root enhancement in MOGAD, cavitation only in AQP4-NMOSD, and lesion resolution as very frequent in MOGAD [S:95009b8b-4070-56ba-ae03-7f78ff2b6f6f].
- The "ventral sagittal line" and axial H-sign are the most characteristic MOGAD myelitis signs, reported in 30–60% of MOGAD myelitis versus 33% in AQP4-NMOSD and exceptionally rare in MS; up to ~10% of MOGAD myelitis has an initially normal cord MRI, with abnormalities appearing on repeat scans [S:1cebf400-e1d2-5e7e-bdcb-927150cb1faa]. Whole-cord inflammation is largely restricted to AQP4-NMOSD and is not seen in MS; short lesions occur in up to ~50% of MOGAD cases at some point versus 10–15% in NMOSD [S:e4506ff5-8f89-5793-9b97-bf208ec5a5d8]. Brighter spotty lesions on acute axial T2 help separate AQP4-NMOSD from MOGAD [S:b56f6451-66c6-5863-8861-85602f4f866f]. In paediatric cohorts, MOGAD shows an additional "snake-eyes" anterior-column pattern, while POMS myelitis is short-segment and peripheral (lateral/dorsal columns), which can falsely appear longitudinally extensive when confluent [S:d1dc2b76-900f-5cd7-9b57-892ec899f32f].

**4. Optic nerve**
- MS: unilateral (bilateral <5%), short, anterior (intraorbital/intracanalicular), perineuritis and disc enhancement extremely rare. AQP4-NMOSD: bilateral in 13–37%, longitudinally extensive (>50% of nerve length), posterior/intracranial predilection, chiasm ~20% usually in isolation. MOGAD: bilateral 31–58%, longitudinally extensive, anterior with perineuritis and orbital fat stranding in ~50%, disc swelling/enhancement in 20–50%, chiasm ~16% usually as extension of a long nerve lesion [S:6870140c-0b9e-5f27-8033-4225864f5aa7]. Longitudinally extensive enhancement (>17.6 mm) favours NMOSD/MOGAD over MS but does not separate the two; chiasmal involvement with a long lesion favours AQP4, and perineural enhancement (up to 50%) favours MOG [S:df0c0e02-a6b7-5550-a140-46810089c287]. In one cohort, chiasmal involvement arising from an orbit-to-chiasm longitudinally extensive lesion occurred in 54% of MOG-ON versus 7% of AQP4-ON [S:a4cd918b-84e4-5db7-982c-80086a7df530].

**5. Longitudinal behaviour (an underused discriminator)**
Paired attack/remission MRI showed T2 lesion resolution far more often in MOGAD than MS (median 4 vs 0 resolved lesions); remission MRI was normal in 32% of MOGAD brains and 78% of MOGAD spines versus 0% and 19% in MS; resolution of ≥1 T2 lesion at 1 year gave sensitivity 95% and specificity 95% for MOGAD, and ≥2 resolved lesions was 100% specific; T1 hypointensity (11% vs 67%) and ovoid periventricular lesions (0% vs 77%) remained MS-typical, and no MOGAD patient developed new asymptomatic lesions [S:750a8909-adcc-58b5-be6e-0c96fe595a3a][S:457aea00-b6fa-5e18-8607-3942aadb2d63]. New asymptomatic brain lesions on follow-up occurred in 8% of NMOSD versus 54% of MS and 4% of MOGAD [S:d4f2aafc-d8ff-53be-9d61-95b46d1c3d29]. MOGAD rarely causes cord atrophy or persistent T1 hypointensity, unlike AQP4-NMOSD [S:a5f95ab6-edff-5d64-9720-0bf7425759c7].

**6. Validated lesion-distribution algorithms and caveats**
Matthews-type criteria (lesion adjacent to lateral ventricle body plus inferior temporal lobe lesion, or U-fibre lesion, or Dawson's finger) separate RRMS from NMOSD/MOGAD with >90% sensitivity and 87–95% specificity; Cacciaguerra (≥2/5 brain+cord features) and the 3-item "MS lesion checklist" are alternatives [S:ddec8363-75f0-5038-976d-3081a897417e][S:eae972f7-257a-5504-a7b3-b2cbd6f1701c]. Important limitations: sensitivity falls in very early MS, CIS and paediatric-onset MS [S:eae972f7-257a-5504-a7b3-b2cbd6f1701c]; ~33% of MOGAD and 16% of NMOSD patients can meet MS dissemination-in-space criteria [S:1bf66d32-338c-5f08-bac8-669b5cd5f990]; and conventional-MRI algorithms and PCA consistently fail to separate MOGAD from AQP4-NMOSD [S:8ebefd4f-d84d-505d-86ee-c1bc40182a80][S:eae972f7-257a-5504-a7b3-b2cbd6f1701c]. In one MOGAD-vs-MS/AQP4 cohort, LETM, conus and central cord involvement did not discriminate MOGAD from AQP4-NMOSD [S:9f20e7dc-51d4-5b0f-9a66-34d64be5bf96]. Brain MRI is normal in roughly half of MOGAD optic neuritis presentations, and both antibody diseases rarely show MS-typical lesions [S:6870140c-0b9e-5f27-8033-4225864f5aa7][S:05eebe34-3272-53b7-973e-1bf7dbc68317]. Imaging is therefore supportive rather than a substitute for cell-based AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG serology [S:cefdffc9-f7ba-53c0-bc22-cf097cdbe52f].

rows.question: What is known about blood transcriptomic markers that separate adults with sepsis from healthy controls?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Machine-learning feature selection on blood transcriptomic data identified TLR5, HMGB2 and C19orf59 as a candidate sepsis signature; Blood transcript levels of these three markers are higher in septic patients than in healthy controls; TLR5 and HMGB2 separate septic patients from controls best in those with the greatest organ dysfunction; C19orf59 separates septic patients from controls to a similar degree across all severity strata. Certainty: The evidence is early, resting mainly on previously collected public expression measurements alongside very small confirmatory experiments, so this marker panel is a promising lead rather than a demonstrated diagnostic test. Scope: applies to sepsis in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents this three-gene panel as a validated bedside test that can be used to diagnose sepsis or grade its severity.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Separating adults with sepsis from healthy controls is the *easy* transcriptomic problem: it is highly reproducible, driven by a stereotyped "innate-up / adaptive-down" whole-blood program, and achieves near-ceiling discrimination — which is precisely why it is a weak benchmark for clinical utility.

## Discrimination performance

In a systematic review of 117 studies (n = 17,469; 132 datasets), pooled AUC for transcriptomic diagnosis of adult sepsis [passage text removed]); the healthy-control subgroup gave [passage text removed]) versus 0.84 (0.78–0.90) against non-infectious SIRS controls, with pooled sensitivity 0.82 (0.79–0.85). Notably, 71 of 132 datasets used healthy controls, which the authors judged less valuable because the clinical challenge is sepsis versus mimics ([PMC11789890]([passage text removed]); [PMID 39888601](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39888601)). A dedicated benchmarking study across 26 healthy-vs-infection datasets (2,417 samples) found [passage text removed] for the 11-gene Sepsis MetaScore and 0.94 ± 0.09 for the *FAIM3:PLAC8* ratio, but only 0.71 ± 0.20 for Septicyte Lab — i.e. signatures optimised against *sterile inflammation* can perform poorly against healthy controls, and vice versa ([PMC5518756](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5518756)).

## The recurring gene-level signature

A whole-blood meta-analysis of six GEO datasets yielded 233 consistent DEGs (146 up, 87 down) and 20 hub genes. Up: *[passage text removed], S100A9, MMP9, ELANE* (innate immunity, neutrophil activity). Down: *FCER1A, IL7R, CCR7, CX3CR1, CD3G, CD40LG, CD247, CD3E, GZMK* (T-cell function, antigen processing/presentation). Only four genes (*HK3, TLR5, MPO, ITGA2B*) were shared across all six datasets, underlining cross-study heterogeneity ([10.1186/s43042-025-00640-8]([passage text removed])). Independent cohorts recapitulate this: *CD177, ARG1, FAM20A, PCOLCE2, SLC51A, MMP9* were the most upregulated versus healthy controls at ICU day 1, with *FAM20A+OLAH* alone separating health from SIRS/sepsis at AUC 0.9906–1.0 ([10.3389/fimmu.2023.1308530]([passage text removed])). The 11-gene Sepsis MetaScore comprises six over-expressed (*CEACAM1, ZDHHC19, C9orf95, GNA15, BATF, C3AR1*) and five under-expressed genes, biologically linked to immature neutrophils and downregulated adaptive immunity ([PMC5954302]([passage text removed]); [medRxiv 2022.10.05.22280692]([passage text removed])).

Effect size is large but the reported DEG count is method-dependent: 454 DEGs (361 up) in one RNA-seq study of 23 patients vs 10 controls ([s41598-022-09175-z]([passage text removed])), 1,639 DEGs in PBMCs (24 vs 20, 78% up) ([medsci.org/v17p2077](https://www.medsci.org/v17p2077.htm)), and 3,677 across 5 days in another microarray cohort ([PMID 23807251](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23807251)). Unsupervised PCA typically separates the groups cleanly, with control samples tightly clustered at one pole and septic shock at the other ([PMC13335145]([passage text removed])).

## Cellular basis

Single-cell work localises the signal. Reyes et al. profiled 29 people with sepsis against 36 controls and identified a CD14+ monocyte state (MS1) expanded in sepsis, validated as discriminating sepsis from controls across 18 cohorts (n = 1,467) ([Nature Medicine 26:333–340, dspace.mit.edu record]([passage text removed])). MS1 is characterised by high *RETN, ALOX5AP, IL1R2* and reduced MHC class II, and was described as virtually absent in healthy controls ([PMC10953179]([passage text removed]); [10.1186/s40635-021-00383-x]([passage text removed])). Longitudinal single-cell/proteomic profiling of 98 adults with sepsis or sterile inflammation plus 12 healthy controls confirmed early MS1 expansion with HLA-DR downregulation and alarmin (*S100A8/S100A9*), resistin and clusterin upregulation, alongside sustained CD8+ naive and CD4+ memory T-cell depletion ([medRxiv 2025.05.17.25327533]([passage text removed])). Deconvolution of bulk sepsis data recovers *IL1R2*+ immature neutrophil and cycling neutrophil progenitor expansion with mononuclear-cell depletion, and reduced *HLA-DRA/HLA-DRB1* in classical monocytes versus healthy volunteers ([medRxiv 2022.03.22.22272723]([passage text removed].03.22.22272723.full)).

## Important caveats

1. **Specificity.** "[passage text removed]" ([10.3389/fmed.2026.1844619]([passage text removed])). Consistently, MS1 proportions were elevated in both septic and non-infected critically ill patients relative to 42 healthy controls, with no significant difference between the two patient groups ([10.1186/s13054-024-04868-5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13054-024-04868-5)).
2. **Cell composition, not per-cell transcription.** Because circulating leukocyte subsets carry highly distinct transcriptomes, any shift in the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio produces near-genome-wide changes in whole-blood signal even absent true per-cell transcriptional change — and violates common RNA-seq normalisation assumptions ([s41598-023-41443-4]([passage text removed])).
3. **Sepsis is not one state.** A consensus framework across >1,800 patients defined three transcriptomic subtypes — CTS1 (immature neutrophils, inflammatory/endothelial), CTS2 (heme metabolism, coagulation, platelets/eosinophils), CTS3 (interferon signalling, lymphocytes, nonclassical monocytes) — so a single sepsis-vs-health contrast averages over distinct biology ([PMID 41028542](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41028542); [s41591-025-03964-5]([passage text removed] companion SUBSPACE analysis of >7,000 samples from 37 cohorts found the same myeloid and lymphoid dysregulation axes recur in ARDS, trauma and burns, not just sepsis ([s41591-025-03956-5]([passage text removed])).
4. **Time and severity dependence.** Signal magnitude tracks severity and evolves over days 1–7, so single-timepoint case–control contrasts are not stable estimates ([PMC13335145]([passage text removed])).
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

The blood transcriptome separates adults with sepsis from healthy controls very reliably — near-perfectly in most datasets — via a highly reproducible two-part signature: upregulation of innate/neutrophil-granule and pro-inflammatory programs with concurrent downregulation of adaptive/T-cell and translational programs. The critical caveat is that this healthy-control contrast is the *easy* comparison and substantially overstates clinical utility, because much of the signal reflects leukocyte composition shifts and non-specific systemic inflammation rather than infection per se.

## The consensus biological signature

Meta-analyses across independent cohorts converge on the same axes. Rank-aggregation of six GEO datasets covering 232 septic patients and 116 healthy volunteers found 1,487 upregulated and 1,276 downregulated genes; neutrophil degranulation was activated while adaptive-immune pathways (CD28 co-stimulation, T-cell receptor signalling, Th1/Th2/Th17 differentiation) were inhibited [S:83af8b38][S:9f9ce2fe]. A separate whole-blood meta-analysis of six datasets reported 233 DEGs (146 up, 87 down) with 20 hub genes: upregulated **[passage text removed], S100A9, MMP9, ELANE** (innate/neutrophil activity) and downregulated **FCER1A, IL7R, CCR7, CX3CR1, CD3G, CD40LG, CD247, CD3E, GZMK** (T-cell function, antigen presentation) [S:99367ccc][S:69749c1c]. Network-based meta-analysis independently nominated IL1R2 and ARG1 as highest-degree hubs with ELANE, MMP9, FCGR1A and MPO also prominent, validated by semiquantitative PCR [S:931b4cf4].

Primary case–control studies reproduce this. Whole-blood arrays in 20 early-stage sepsis patients versus 9 age- and sex-matched healthy controls showed clear MDS separation, with innate immune/neutrophil degranulation/cytokine signalling activated and lymphocyte differentiation, antigen presentation, translation and metabolism suppressed; notably the reported DEG split (344 up, 9,703 down) is extreme relative to other studies and illustrates how platform and pipeline choices affect counts [S:04b31a14][S:01861dc9][S:cdaeb760]. RNA-seq of 22 sepsis patients versus 10 healthy volunteers found 4,681 DEGs, with overlapping proteomic changes enriched in leukocyte/neutrophil and inflammatory responses [S:42651935]. RNA-seq in 23 adult septic patients versus 10 healthy individuals yielded 454 DEGs and hub genes TLR5, FCGR1A, ELANE, GNLY, IL2RB, TGFBR3, localised by single-cell data to macrophages (TLR5, FCGR1A, ELANE) versus T/NK cells (GNLY, IL2RB, TGFBR3) [S:2e68c060]. Non-coding species also differ: lncRNA profiles in sepsis peripheral blood differ from healthy volunteers, with ENST00000452391.1, uc001vji.1 and uc021zxw.1 validated by qRT-PCR in 22 patients versus 22 controls [S:324d6837][S:333e0212].

Other candidate panels derived against healthy controls include CECR1, ANXA2, ELANE, CTSG, AZU1, PRTN3, LYZ, DEFA4 from time-series co-expression modelling [S:b8653aab]; CLEC4D, GPR84, S100A12, HK3 [S:cb2867f4]; and a three-gene TLR5/HMGB2/C19orf59 signature trained on GSE134347 (83 healthy, 156 sepsis) with external validation in GSE236713 and GSE185263 [S:424305c9][S:ea5c3721].

## Discrimination against healthy controls is close to trivial

An early classifier separated healthy controls [passage text removed]%, and was explicitly described as a "quality step" rather than the clinically meaningful task [S:adf9e8cd]. The same gap appears with published scores: the Sepsis MetaScore and the FAIM3:PLAC8 ratio reached AUCs of 0.97 (0.85–1.0) and 0.94 (0.65–1.0) for septic patients versus healthy controls, but only [passage text removed]) against non-infectious inflammation [S:9a6659ef]. Likewise, a candidate signature achieved AUC >0.94 for septic shock versus healthy controls but fell to >0.72 for septic versus non-septic shock, and dropped further for uncomplicated infection [S:cf6597e8]. Accordingly, the FDA-cleared assays were built and validated on the harder contrast: SeptiCyte LAB uses PLAC8, PLA2G7, LAMP1 and CEACAM4 to separate sepsis from infection-negative systemic inflammation with AUC 0.82–0.89, robust across sex, race, age and independent of APACHE IV/SOFA severity [S:f9dc85b7][S:cca1bdaf][S:9eca8f80]; SeptiCyte RAPID (PLAC8, PLA2G7) reached AUC 0.81–0.84 in a full retrospective+prospective cohort [S:b5ac7874].

## Why the healthy-control signature is not infection-specific

- **Shared with sterile inflammation.** ELANE, MPO, CD177, OLFM4 and OLAH — among the highest-expressed genes in sepsis whole-blood meta-analyses — were comparably upregulated in sepsis and sterile inflammation, indicating a generic neutrophil response to bacterial infection *or* tissue injury [S:0e2cbf07]. Marker genes of early terminal granulocytic differentiation (emergency granulopoiesis) recur in ARDS and non-resolving multiple organ dysfunction signatures, so it is unclear how much of a sepsis signature is attributable to infection versus ensuing tissue damage [S:13f119c9].
- **Cell-composition confounding.** Neutrophil and lymphocyte transcriptomes differ substantially, and in 138 emergency-department patients the genome-wide distribution of whole-blood transcript abundance tracked donor neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, with high-NLR specimens resembling isolated neutrophils and low-NLR specimens resembling lymphocytes [S:b245f2b2]. Since sepsis raises NLR, much of the "sepsis signature" is partly a composition readout. Cell-sorted designs make this explicit: CST7 was upregulated in purified sepsis neutrophils versus healthy-control neutrophils (effect size 2.3) while CTSC, CTSG, PRTN3 and ELANE were unchanged in that compartment [S:c706c410].
- **Poor specificity against other severe illness.** In a common benchmark across seven studies (1,661 sepsis patients, 3,407 patients with other severe diseases), published signatures reached 65–84% AUC for sepsis but ~48–58% against comparator severe diseases — i.e. the best tests largely or completely failed to distinguish sepsis from [passage text removed]:b34dfac7][S:05a8ac9d].
- **Case-mix caveat.** Some authors argue healthy donors are the wrong reference altogether; one NK-cell transcriptomic study used presurgical patients instead, calling this "[passage text removed]:88e4cc73][S:ef9cb0aa].

## Heterogeneity within "sepsis"

A single sepsis-versus-healthy contrast averages over distinct endotypes. Whole-blood transcriptomics in pneumonia-derived sepsis defined SRS1 (immunosuppressed: HLA class II downregulation, endotoxin tolerance, T-cell exhaustion, higher mortality) and SRS2 (relatively immunocompetent), assignable from seven genes (DYRK2, CCNB1IP1, TDRD9, ZAP70, ARL14EP, MDC1, ADGRE3) [S:7a6713e5][S:d173e7de][S:4d106e7a]; SRS accounted for more transcriptional variation than the anatomical source of infection [S:8b0305ed]. Independent groups reported Mars1–4 and inflammopathic/adaptive/coagulopathic subgroups [S:7a6713e5][S:4d106e7a]. Sepsis samples also show markedly greater transcriptional dispersion than the tightly clustered healthy controls [S:01861dc9].

## Bottom line

Well-replicated: an innate-up/adaptive-down whole-blood signature with a stable recurring gene set (S100A8/A9/A12, CD177, MMP8/MMP9, ELANE, ARG1, IL1R2, RETN, LTF up; CD3E/CD3G/CD247, IL7R, CCR7, CX3CR1, FCER1A, GZMK down) [S:99367ccc][S:931b4cf4][S:83af8b38]. Not established: that any of these markers is specific to infection, transportable across severe illnesses, or clinically useful for the decision that actually matters — sepsis versus non-infectious systemic inflammation [S:0e2cbf07][S:b34dfac7][S:9a6659ef]. I found no source addressing whether the healthy-control-derived gene sets outperform the SIRS-derived ones prospectively.
