rows.question: Which host blood gene expression signatures distinguish patients with sepsis from non-septic controls?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: In datasets not used for gene selection, a compact panel of immune-related blood genes including the calgranulins S100A8, S100A9 and S100A12 together with CD177, ARG1, GATA3 and SOCS3 separated sepsis samples from non-septic control samples with high discrimination; Classifiers built from the neutrophil-driven calgranulin gene cluster discriminated sepsis samples at least as well as the other immune gene clusters tested; Pathway enrichment of this refined gene set is concentrated in pathogen sensing, innate immune amplification and immune regulation. Certainty: The supporting evidence is preliminary and computationally derived from archived blood expression datasets, holding consistently across several separately analysed sample sets but not tested during clinical care. Scope: applies to sepsis in adults and children sampled during acute illness alongside healthy or non-infected comparison groups, mixed settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the gene panel as a clinically validated diagnostic test, recommends it in place of existing sepsis diagnostics, or uses it to justify withholding antimicrobial treatment.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Several reproducible whole-blood host-response signatures separate sepsis from non-septic controls, but their difficulty depends entirely on the comparator: discriminating sepsis from **healthy** controls is near-trivial (AUCs ~0.94–0.97), whereas discriminating sepsis from **non-infectious systemic inflammation (SIRS/sterile inflammation)** yields AUCs of roughly 0.73–0.89 for the best-validated classifiers. [PMC5518756]

## The main validated signatures

**SeptiCyte (4 genes → 2 genes).** SeptiCyte LAB quantifies whole-blood expression of *CEACAM4, LAMP1, PLAC8, PLA2G7* by RT-qPCR; the score is computed as (PLAC8 + LAMP1) − (PLA2G7 + CEACAM4), with PLAC8 and LAMP1 predominantly upregulated and PLA2G7 and CEACAM4 predominantly downregulated in sepsis. [PMC4672921; journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.1001916; PMC5518756] It was discovered in 74 sepsis vs 31 post-surgical infection-negative patients with an overall AUC of 0.88 across five validation cohorts [PMC4672921], and in a 447-patient multicohort validation gave AUC 0.82–0.89 for sepsis vs non-infectious systemic inflammation, adding only marginally to clinical variables including procalcitonin; it is FDA-cleared (K163260). [PMC6835074] SeptiCyte RAPID reduces this to two transcripts (*PLA2G7*, *PLAC8*), with reported AUCs of 0.82–0.85 [septicyte.com/references] and [passage text removed]) in a prospective Sepsis-3 ICU-admission study. [[passage text removed]] Pediatric validation gave AUC >0.9 (0.954 by RT-qPCR) for severe sepsis vs infection-negative systemic inflammation. [[passage text removed]]

**Sepsis MetaScore (11 genes).** A time-course-matched multicohort meta-analysis of 27 datasets (5 discovery datasets, n = 663) identified 11 genes (FDR ≤1%, heterogeneity P > 0.01, effect size >1.5-fold) with mean discovery AUC 0.87 (range 0.70–0.98), validated in 15 independent cohorts; adding the gene set to SIRS criteria improved infection prediction (continuous net reclassification index 0.90). [PMC4734362; pubmed 25972003] The genes are *CEACAM1, ZDHHC19, C9orf95, GNA15, BATF, C3AR1* (infection-up) and *KIAA1370, TGFBI, MTCH1, RPGRIP1, HLA-DPB1* (infection-down) [dx.doi.org/10.3390/jpm10040266; patents.google.com/patent/US20180291449A1]; the signature was enriched in band cells and myeloid lineage. [PMC4734362] It also validated for neonatal sepsis. [pubmed 28419265]

**FAIM3:PLAC8 ratio (2 genes).** Derived from a 78-gene CAP signature in ICU patients, with AUC 0.845 (discovery) and 0.784 (validation), outperforming procalcitonin, IL-6 and IL-8. [PMC4731623; [passage text removed]] Its authors caution it was validated only for CAP vs non-infectious respiratory distress at ICU admission, not for generic sepsis-vs-SIRS discrimination. [[passage text removed]]

**Head-to-head benchmark.** Across public datasets, mean validation AUCs for sepsis vs non-infectious inflammation were 0.82 (0.73–0.89) for the Sepsis MetaScore, 0.78 (0.49–0.96) for FAIM3:PLAC8, and 0.73 (0.44–0.90) for SeptiCyte LAB; for infected vs healthy controls they were 0.97, 0.94 and 0.71 respectively. Differences in overall sepsis-vs-SIRS performance were not statistically significant, and *CEACAM4* was found to be down-regulated only in its discovery cohort. [PMC5518756; journals.lww.com/ccmjournal 00003246-201701000-00001]

**29-mRNA panel (InSep/TriVerity).** A 29-gene panel organised into modules ([passage text removed]*; plus bacterial–viral and severity modules) [dx.doi.org/10.3390/jpm10040266] gave AUROC 0.94 for bacterial vs viral/non-infected and 0.90 for viral vs bacterial/non-infected in emergency department patients, versus 0.88 for procalcitonin, 0.80 for CRP and 0.78 for WBC. [link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40635-021-00394-8; medrxiv 2020.12.01.20242321] It was FDA-cleared in January 2025 and clinically validated in *Nat Med* 31:4044–4054 (2025). [sepsis.gr/.../HISS_29-mRNA...pdf; 10.1038/s41591-025-03933-y]

**Other signatures.** A 5-gene panel *CMTM5/CETP/PLA2G7/MIA/MPP3* discriminated sepsis from SIRS with AUC 0.9758 in a two-tier scheme (a separate 5-marker "I°I" signature first identifies systemic inflammation vs healthy). [pubmed 38332914; PMC10850284] A 53-gene RNA-seq signature separated blood-culture-positive sepsis from aseptic inflammation in antibiotic-treated ICU patients ([passage text removed]), outperforming CRP (0.72) and SeptiCyte LAB (0.80) but comparable to procalcitonin (0.96). [sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0883944123000357; pubmed 36965223]

## The consistent underlying biology

Versus healthy controls, sepsis blood shows upregulation of innate/neutrophil programmes (neutrophil activation and degranulation, NET formation, IL-17 and TNF signalling; hub [passage text removed], S100A9, MMP9, ELANE*) with coordinate downregulation of adaptive/T-cell and antigen-presentation programmes (*FCER1A, IL7R, CCR7, CX3CR1, CD3G, CD40LG, CD247, CD3E, GZMK*). [jmhg.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s43042-025-00640-8] Independent RNA-seq work reports the same pattern — [passage text removed] signalling with suppression of lymphocyte differentiation and antigen presentation. [PMC12294327]

## Caveats

- Signatures that perform well against healthy controls may reflect generic systemic inflammation rather than infection; the clinically hard task is sepsis vs sterile SIRS, where performance drops and in some datasets falls below AUC 0.7. [PMC5518756]
- Context-specificity matters: a signature derived for one comparator (e.g. CAP vs non-CAP at ICU admission) should not be assumed transferable to trauma, post-operative or paediatric mimics. [[passage text removed]]
- Diagnostic signatures are distinct from the sepsis *subtype* signatures (CTS1–3, derived from 2,142 samples across four cohorts) that stratify already-diagnosed patients rather than establishing the diagnosis. [inflammatix.com/inflammatix-announces-three-landmark-publications...; nature.com/articles/s41591-025-03964-5]
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Sepsis is distinguished from non-septic controls by a reproducible two-part whole-blood transcriptional pattern — upregulated innate/neutrophil-granule programmes with concomitant suppression of adaptive-immune, T-cell and translational/ribosomal programmes — and this pattern has been distilled into several small, clinically validated mRNA classifiers (SeptiCyte LAB/RAPID, the 11-gene Sepsis MetaScore, the FAIM3:PLAC8 ratio, and the 29-mRNA InSep/TriVerity panel). Performance is good but not perfect, and signatures transfer inconsistently across cohorts.

## The underlying biology of the signature

In RNA-seq of whole blood from critically ill adults, patients with microbiologically confirmed sepsis differed from patients with non-infectious critical illness across thousands of genes, with gene-set enrichment showing upregulation of neutrophil degranulation and innate immune signalling and downregulation of translation and rRNA processing [S:14a25cd2-21d4-563a-835a-a6eb8e9bf5c1]. The same directionality emerges in meta-analyses versus healthy controls: neutrophil degranulation, neutrophil migration/chemotaxis, IL-17 and TNF signalling activated, while CD28 co-stimulation, T-cell receptor signalling and Th1/Th2/Th17 differentiation are inhibited [S:83af8b38-8699-54ca-b290-c8ebe23b730f]. Microarray work describes the same "two-hit" structure — innate genes (CD14, TLR1/2/4/5/8, complement, MMPs, neutrophil elastase, defensins) up, MHC, TCR, CD3, CD8, granzyme/perforin and B-cell signalling genes down [S:e089830d-62e1-55c4-aa5c-a9526983151c]. Recurrent individual marker genes include elevated CD177, MMP8, HP, ARG1, ANXA3 and suppressed FCER1A, LRRN3 [S:cc96e51c-e7ad-54cf-80d6-965ba5666e5e], elevated CD177 with suppressed HLA-DRA in plasma RNA [S:5a629ffa-6437-54e7-8b49-6e9be99df81b], and OLFM4/S100A12 up with HLA-DRA down in early sepsis [S:567d7a08-cdb2-549f-bf51-9277c4269875].

## Named, validated signatures

**SeptiCyte LAB (4 genes) / SeptiCyte RAPID (2 genes).** Derived by greedy search over >30,000 transcripts, the classifier combines the expression ratios PLA2G7/PLAC8 and CEACAM4/LAMP1; PLAC8 and LAMP1 contribute positively and PLA2G7 and CEACAM4 negatively [S:0890d96b-7f82-5ae5-b4aa-ec8a9d4afb4d][S:0da36f30-6e4b-582a-bb8f-efc9775d9a24]. RAPID reduces this to PLA2G7 and PLAC8 measured by RT-qPCR with ~1 h turnaround, reported as a SeptiScore of 0–15 [S:85ae67cd-b83d-5a7b-a9a2-d874959cbc25][S:f63a4db0-8195-5c5e-943d-6c6b40f4b4e3]. In a combined retrospective (N = 356) and prospective (N = 63) ICU cohort adjudicated by three blinded physicians, AUCs were 0.82–0.85, with NPV 0.91 (sensitivity 0.94) in the lowest band and PPV 0.81 (specificity 0.90) in the highest band; SeptiScore was the most important variable in multivariable analysis with up to 14 clinical variables [S:81fbe3b6-023b-5e54-adbd-88a5cd2d8ab3][S:3fbfc936-4930-587e-be99-d407a44ad4f1]. Performance was consistent (AUC 0.81–0.93) across demographic, microbiological and interventional strata [S:5dbde499-9b4e-5ae3-a4a5-97568cdac3c9], and higher for blood-culture-positive sepsis vs SIRS (AUC 0.91) than culture-negative sepsis vs SIRS (AUC 0.80) [S:37b09a72-0d99-591b-90ad-d60a7dca62ee]. Mechanistically the four genes map to granulocyte granule-biogenesis pathways: LAMP1/PLAC8 are promyelocyte-restricted azurophilic-granule genes, CEACAM4/PLA2G7 are PMN-restricted cell-membrane genes [S:77a5f8c4-1728-515d-a5c4-5f0788aa0d69].

**Sepsis MetaScore (11 genes).** Developed by multi-cohort meta-analysis to separate infection from non-infectious inflammation, validated in adult, paediatric and neonatal transcriptomic cohorts [S:0ac703f6-c23a-52cc-8e7c-e4262dfabda7][S:c0aba61a-fb3b-529b-b1d1-2d27ee5f33d0]. In a prospective ICU validation, AUROC for sepsis vs [passage text removed] SeptiCyte LAB [S:22aa6eb9-5943-5293-b9bb-efcc15e4c5ec]. It was also the best-performing published signature when external signatures were tested in an infant sepsis dataset [S:57542ba8-57c8-5b1d-851c-7a671ed3ba7d].

**FAIM3:PLAC8 ratio.** A two-gene ratio originally derived to distinguish confirmed community-acquired pneumonia from non-infectious mimics at ICU admission, with AUC 0.845 (95% CI 0.764–0.917), outperforming procalcitonin, IL-6 and IL-8 [S:57cc1f77-e0d4-5a66-838c-c50b89a20bb2]; MMP8 was the most overexpressed single gene in confirmed CAP versus non-infectious differential diagnoses in the same cohort [S:f381aca7-5fb2-572c-84a6-d72e118a0b3f].

**29-mRNA InSep / TriVerity.** A whole-blood panel producing three scores (bacterial likelihood, viral likelihood, illness severity) [S:891bb876-6def-5c06-95e4-ed6af3718962]. In the prospective PROMPT ED trial (397 patients), AUROCs were [passage text removed]) for bacterial vs viral/non-infected [passage text removed]) for viral, exceeding PCT (0.88), CRP (0.80) and WBC (0.78) [S:888fc81c-f86b-5b7d-8172-e74efc7b99e6]. It runs in ~30 min by RT-LAMP [S:7d32ccd5-9440-5056-8ee6-9aaafde0f19d] and has been FDA-cleared, with a reported AUC of 0.83 as a bacterial-sepsis predictor [S:4b25c820-5b47-5c17-ae91-c46b1c846771][S:1693f8c6-38d7-5006-93bc-45bbab58beed].

**Other signatures.** SeptiCyte TRIAGE sums [passage text removed]), discriminating bacterial infection from viral infection and healthy controls with ROC AUC 0.77–1 in discovery sets after explicitly filtering out ratios that also separated non-infective diseases from their controls [S:81439a4c-e695-557d-8c65-763cf42b66b6]. A UK multicentre ICU study (abdominal/pulmonary sepsis vs out-of-hospital-cardiac-arrest SIRS vs healthy controls) identified 19 "indicators of inflammation" including CD177, FAM20A and OLAH (FAM20A/OLAH giving AUC >0.99 for severe systemic inflammation vs control) and a separate best sepsis-vs-SIRS signature [passage text removed]) [S:eb5a910d-11c9-54c8-975d-406c6c7fce9f]. A machine-learning classifier trained on whole-blood expression separated sepsis from non-infectious systemic inflammation with AUC 0.81 (training) and 0.82 (held-out validation); plasma cell-free RNA gave AUC 0.97 training / 0.77 validation, and an integrated host-plus-pathogen model captured 99% of microbiologically confirmed sepsis with 78% specificity in the no-sepsis group — versus a best clinical-variable model AUC of 0.62 and qSOFA 0.48 [S:e237abfb-2dd9-57d1-84ca-9510f64ba3e4][S:64065579-a305-58d5-a253-2c0b998a5eec][S:269a7e21-a086-5f3c-a9fa-7e07c0127eae]. In children with suspected sepsis, a 10-gene severity signature predicted organ dysfunction within 24 h with AUC 82.2% (95% CI 76.3–88.1) [S:e3e298dc-92ca-5917-bb90-0b872b43376b].

## Important caveats

- **Signatures do not replicate reliably.** Of five published sepsis-vs-SIRS signatures tested in one independent ICU cohort, only two discriminated significantly (SeptiCyte LAB AUC 0.8377; Bauer [passage text removed] AUC 0.7877) [S:f0160433-a298-5b7d-828f-eac6a4727899]. A head-to-head comparison found no significant difference in overall sepsis-vs-SIRS discrimination between the Sepsis MetaScore, FAIM3:PLAC8 and SeptiCyte LAB [S:cc96e51c-e7ad-54cf-80d6-965ba5666e5e], and reviews note inconsistent terminology, poor reproducibility and weak alignment with clinical endpoints across transcriptomic sepsis studies [S:1c6177e7-cb6d-513b-a1c4-999e861d8f3e]. Predictive gene sets overlap little between studies, plausibly because of differing populations, infection types and control groups [S:4b25c820-5b47-5c17-ae91-c46b1c846771].
- **Specificity for infection versus severity is unresolved.** Sepsis gene signatures correlate with severity and mortality, which can also arise from sterile tissue damage; several feature markers of emergency granulopoiesis shared with ARDS and non-resolving organ dysfunction, so it is unclear how much of the signal reflects infection per se [S:13f119c9-41ab-5181-8df1-205fee92bd59]. Indeed, acute traumatic spinal cord injury produces the same up-neutrophil/down-CD28-T-cell pattern versus uninjured controls [S:5b18c5d7-f917-5f39-a626-5095813db762].
- **The reference standard is itself imperfect** — three expert clinicians failed to reach unanimous or consensus diagnosis in 41/419 (9.8%) patients, capping measurable test performance [S:3fbfc936-4930-587e-be99-d407a44ad4f1].
- **The signature is not monolithic.** Host response varies by infection source, pathogen and host factors; in critically ill patients with bacterial bloodstream infection the cultured pathogen explained 42% of blood transcriptomic variance [S:fba63e8a-98ab-588c-ac92-402e774f93d9].

rows.question: How does time from emergency presentation to nephrostomy drainage relate to infectious outcomes in infected obstructing ureteral stones?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Among patients drained soonest after arrival, the proportion with sepsis fell after nephrostomy insertion; The proportion in septic shock rose after insertion in the later-drained groups, whereas it was unchanged in the soonest-drained group; Patients drained soonest arrived with the most deranged physiology and the highest proportion of septic shock at presentation; Septic shock at arrival was associated with lower odds of non-immediate drainage. Certainty: The evidence supports associations only: the infectious rates before and after drainage were compared within each timing group without a comparison group, and the soonest-drained patients were the sickest on arrival. Scope: applies to obstructing ureteral stone with urinary tract infection drained by percutaneous nephrostomy in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents prompt drainage as demonstrated to cause the better outcomes, to prevent septic shock or to reduce mortality, or treats a fixed hour-based door-to-drainage threshold as an established standard on this basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: shorter presentation‑to‑drainage intervals are consistently associated with better infectious outcomes — but the strength of the signal depends on how "delay" is defined, and studies using narrow windows (e.g. <12 h vs 12–48 h) find little difference, so the evidence supports "hours matter in the septic patient" rather than a single validated cut‑off.**

**Direct evidence for nephrostomy specifically (ED arrival as time zero).** The only study that explicitly anchors timing to emergency department arrival and restricts to PCN is a retrospective review of 744 patients with ureteral stones and UTI (2011–2023), stratified as immediate <6 h (n = 241), early 6–24 h (n = 232), and delayed >24 h (n = 271). Only the immediate group showed a fall in sepsis after drainage ([passage text removed]), with septic shock [passage text removed] 6–24 h group sepsis was unchanged (59.1% vs 59.5%) while septic shock rose (12.9% vs 31%, p < 0.001), and in the >24 h group sepsis was unchanged (38.7% vs 36.9%) while septic shock rose (7% vs 15.5%, p = 0.001). Immediate drainage was also [passage text removed] definitive stone treatment (all p < 0.001). Non‑immediate drainage was predicted by night‑shift arrival (OR 4.846), female sex (OR 1.917), elevated creatinine (OR 1.262), and older age (OR 1.009) — i.e. logistical, not just clinical, drivers ([PubMed 41468118](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41468118); [cris.tau.ac.il record]([passage text removed])). Note the immediate group was the sickest at baseline, so this is a within‑group before/after comparison, not a randomised contrast.

**Day‑scale delay and mortality (mixed PCN/stent).** In the National Inpatient Sample 2010–2015 (n = 311,100 with UTI plus ureteral stone or stone with hydronephrosis), decompression ≥2 days after admission independently increased odds of in‑hospital [passage text removed]), with delay more likely on weekend admissions (OR 1.22), in non‑white patients (OR 1.34), and in the lowest income quartile (OR 1.25) (Haas et al., J Urol 2020;204:1256–62, [PubMed 32501124](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32501124)); a commentary on the same dataset reports mean time to decompression of 0.42 vs 3.08 days and roughly 7% increased odds of death per day of delay ([urologynews.uk.com]([passage text removed])). A newer NIS analysis (2016–2022, n = 9,172 with sepsis/septic shock and obstructing ureteral stones) found same‑day decompression favourable ([passage text removed] decompression >24 h associated with higher [passage text removed]) plus more AKI, mechanical ventilation, and dialysis ([BMC Urology, doi 10.1186/s12894-026-02119-z]([passage text removed])).

**Systematic synthesis.** A PRISMA‑registered review of ten studies concluded that [passage text removed]: ≥2 days delay OR 1.29; >48 h a larger mortality signal (OR 2.33); ≤48 h vs delayed mortality 0.16% vs 0.47% (derived OR 0.43, p = 0.044); and no decompression at all the worst ([passage text removed]). An ED cohort in that review showed earlier stenting shortened stay (≤6 h: 35.6 [passage text removed] vs 82.4 h, p = 0.04). Septic shock remained common despite low crude mortality (20.8% and 33.3% in two series), and post‑decompression urosepsis occurred in 18.7%, associated with pyonephrosis and higher procalcitonin ([PMC12693273]([passage text removed]); [J Clin Med 14:8546]([passage text removed])). Higher ICU use [passage text removed]) is attributed to confounding by indication, not modality harm.

**Contrary / null evidence — important caveat.** A multicentre propensity‑score‑matched study of 240 patients with stone‑related obstructive pyelonephritis comparing emergency drainage (<12 h from admission) with delayed drainage (12–48 h) found only time from admission to temperature normalisation differed ([passage text removed]), with no difference in post‑drainage course; high pretreatment CRP predicted emergency drainage ([Kayano et al., World J Urol, PubMed 38478082](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38478082)). Similarly, a study explicitly examining symptom‑onset‑to‑presentation and presentation‑to‑decompression intervals concluded that neither interval was associated with higher post‑decompression sepsis rates, while clinical and laboratory parameters were ([Silvani et al., World J Urol, doi 10.1007/s00345-023-04513-w]([passage text removed]-023-04513-w)).

**Process‑of‑care corroboration.** A hospital‑wide obstructive‑pyelonephritis‑with‑sepsis protocol reduced time to decompression, with dramatic improvement in time to PCN, and quicker decompression was linked to shorter length of stay ([PubMed 32668984](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32668984)); the presented data showed median urology‑consult‑to‑PCN time falling from 7.3 h to 4.3 h ([UroToday WCE 2019]([passage text removed])). Consistent with this, an ICU urosepsis cohort found [passage text removed] associated with lower 28‑day mortality, though the authors caution that few outcome events and wide confidence intervals leave the effect size uncertain ([Eur J Med Res, doi 10.1186/s40001-026-04679-0](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40001-026-04679-0)).

**Interpretation.** All timing evidence is observational and subject to confounding in both directions — sicker patients are drained faster (biasing against early drainage) while socioeconomic and after‑hours factors drive delay (biasing toward it). The reproducible finding is that day‑scale delay (≥24–48 h) or omission of drainage tracks with mortality, AKI and organ support, and that ultra‑early PCN (<6 h) tracks with sepsis resolution, fewer ICU admissions and shorter stay; within the first 12 h the marginal benefit is less clear. No randomised trial of presentation‑to‑nephrostomy timing appeared in my searches.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Shorter time from ED arrival to nephrostomy drainage is associated with better infectious trajectories — resolution rather than progression of sepsis, fewer ICU transfers, less antibiotic escalation, and shorter stay — with the sharpest inflection at roughly 6 hours; mortality differences by timing appear only in large administrative cohorts using coarse (≥2-day) delay thresholds, and some smaller series find no timing–sepsis relationship at all.

## Evidence specific to nephrostomy timing

**The largest dedicated PCN-timing study** (744 patients with obstructing ureteral stones plus UTI, 2011–2023, grouped by time from ED arrival: <6 h n=241, 6–24 h n=232, >24 h n=271) found that only the immediate group's infectious status improved after drainage: sepsis fell from 61.4% pre-PCN to 45.2% post-PCN (p=0.03) with unchanged septic shock ([passage text removed] 6–24 h group sepsis was static (59.1% → 59.5%) while septic shock rose from 12.9% to 31% (p<0.001), and in the >24 h group sepsis was static (38.7% → 36.9%) while septic shock rose from 7% to 15.5% (p=0.001) [S:8cee2b2b-01d9-5f36-8dd1-22a57ee393bc][S:22354f95-062c-509a-bfe7-b5867a85d51b]. Downstream infectious/utilisation outcomes graded the same way: length of stay 5 vs 7 vs 8 days, transfer to a monitored unit [passage text removed]%, and need for antibiotic upgrade 11.6% vs 29.7% vs 33.9% (all p≤0.001) [S:22354f95-062c-509a-bfe7-b5867a85d51b]. Mortality did not differ significantly between groups (in-hospital 1.6%, 30-day post-discharge 2.7% overall) [S:21d8d0d9-ac0a-53c5-b150-35cf239e5629]. Independent predictors of *not* achieving <6 h drainage were night-shift arrival (OR 4.846), female sex (OR 1.917), elevated creatinine (OR 1.262) and older age (OR 1.009) [S:8cee2b2b-01d9-5f36-8dd1-22a57ee393bc].

Important confounder: the <6 h group was physiologically the sickest at the time of drainage (systolic BP <90 in 46.9% vs 13.4% vs 7.7%; septic shock 23.7% vs 12.9% vs 7%), i.e. triage acuity drove speed — so the comparison is not of like with like, and the authors frame results as associations [S:b81bc998-90b5-514b-88a2-3b1cd253a48b].

**A smaller PCN cohort** (107 patients, urosepsis from upper ureteral stones) found emergent PCN ≤24 h led to earlier definitive ureteroscopic lithotripsy and shorter hospital stay than delayed PCN; post-URSL fever (32%) was predicted by antibiotic duration and the PCN-to-URSL interval, not by PCN timing itself [S:3f8837b5-4ee2-566b-b552-0e08a60a50aa][S:f426143c-ca9b-5bf0-888a-c9d70468e30b].

**A qSOFA-stratified PCN series** (96 ED patients, mean time to PCN 229 minutes) found no LOS–timing correlation in qSOFA <2, but significantly shorter hospitalisation when PCN preceded 4 hours in patients with qSOFA ≥2 — i.e. the timing benefit concentrated in the sickest [S:9cd65887-eac3-56c2-9a24-080ab8d6870d].

## Wider time-to-decompression context (mostly stent-based)

A 2025 systematic review of ten studies concluded that timeliness, not device choice, dominated early outcomes: delay ≥2 days raised in-hospital mortality ([passage text removed] AKI (aOR 1.12, 1.03–1.22); mortality was [passage text removed]; no decompression at all carried [passage text removed], 1.9–3.7). Apparent PCN-associated ICU excess (OR 3.23, 1.24–8.41) reflected confounding by indication, since PCN patients had higher APACHE II (15 vs 11) and larger stones (10 vs 7 mm) [S:39e907d1-fcac-58fb-bc86-86c38777dae4][S:1f564c6f-d406-5a50-adad-a08bd79ad7a9][S:54c07ae0-5d5b-5909-8826-ed13d6693320]. In an ED stent cohort, decompression within 6 h and 10 h shortened LOS (35.6 vs 71.6 h, p=0.01; 45.7 vs 82.4 h, p=0.04) without a difference in ICU admission [S:d9a6f987-c306-5130-9788-5f8549a4ae52]. A hospital-wide obstructive-pyelonephritis-with-sepsis protocol reduced time to decompression — with the most dramatic improvement in time to PCN — and faster decompression was independently associated with lower odds of prolonged stay [S:ebcf18d3-2888-5f3e-94f1-13ce38d82f13].

## Discordant evidence

- A 62-patient stent series (median time to decompression 25.0 h) found no significant difference in post-decompression sepsis across <24 h, 24–48 h and >48 h groups; only LOS was longer with >48 h delay (p=0.027), and both <24 h and >48 h had more intraoperative hypotension (p=0.029). The authors argued for a 24–48 h window allowing resuscitation [S:a3807ddb-3c4f-5c34-9e25-1670dfbb65a1].
- A prospective analysis of septic shock after decompression found no significant relation between decompression delay and septic shock (leukocytosis was the risk factor) [S:38b2af51-c85a-50c5-9a05-b033ef3cb564].
- Post-decompression urosepsis still occurred in 18.7% in a randomised emergency-drainage trial despite most patients being drained within 48 h, driven by pyonephrosis and higher procalcitonin rather than timing — meaning early drainage reduces but does not abolish infectious deterioration [S:e19714ed-986f-55db-b475-4199055791e5][S:d7d5b84b-2303-5f8c-8ae5-c7feb2473483].

## Bottom line for practice

Guidelines mandate urgent decompression by either PCN or stent without specifying an hour threshold [S:e1c2033e-1641-5d56-8896-c6c9400e26e3], and no consensus optimal PCN timing exists [S:059bb020-7559-523b-9f6a-d47b46cbdad9]. The best available PCN-specific data support targeting drainage within ~6 hours of ED arrival for improved infectious and clinical outcomes [S:059bb020-7559-523b-9f6a-d47b46cbdad9], while acknowledging that all supporting studies are observational and vulnerable to acuity-driven confounding; no randomised trial of PCN timing thresholds appeared in these searches.

rows.question: Which bedside scores stratify in-hospital mortality risk among emergency department patients with suspected sepsis receiving intravenous antibiotics?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Scores that combine vital signs with routine admission blood results, the REDS score and its shortened qREDS variant, discriminated in-hospital mortality better than NEWS2 in adults given intravenous antibiotics for a suspected infection; At the upper score bands, specificity for in-hospital death was high for the REDS and qREDS scores and low for NEWS2; In the upper bands of the REDS and qREDS scores seven-day survival was lower than in the population overall, whereas a high NEWS2 band marked patients whose short-term survival matched the population average. Certainty: The evidence rests on previously recorded data from a single hospital comparing bedside scores, so it can rank mortality risk but cannot show that acting on a score changes outcome. Scope: applies to suspected sepsis treated with intravenous antibiotics in adults, emergency department settings. An answer is wrong if it presents these scores as validated decision rules for triage or for withholding, delaying or de-escalating acute sepsis care in patients who score below a cut-off.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** In ED cohorts defined by receipt of IV antibiotics for suspected sepsis, the REDS score (and its electronically extractable variant qREDS) is the tool most directly derived and validated for in-hospital mortality stratification, outperforming SIRS and NEWS2; qSOFA, NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS, SOFA and MEDS also stratify risk but with well-characterised sensitivity–specificity trade-offs.

**Scores derived in exactly this population (IV antibiotics for suspected sepsis)**

- **REDS** (qSOFA + simplified-MISSED + lactate + refractory hypotension, range 0–12) was derived and validated in adults aged ≥18 who met two SIRS or one Red Flag criterion, received IV antibiotics in the ED and were admitted: 2115 patients, 282 (13.3%) in-hospital deaths; AUROC 0.78 (0.75–0.80) in derivation and 0.74 (0.71–0.76) in validation, cut-off ≥3, sensitivity 85.0% and 84.5% respectively. Specificity for scores ≥3, ≥5, ≥7 was 54.8%, 88.8%, 96.9% with corresponding mortality 21.8%, 36.0%, 49.1%; a score of 0–2 carried 2.6% mortality when all variables were measured [BMJ Open 2019;9:e030922; PMC6720479].
- **Head-to-head comparison** in 2594 such patients (332 deaths, 12.8%): REDS AUROC 0.73 ([passage text removed] SIRS 0.51 (p<0.0001) and NEWS2 0.69 (p=0.005), and similar to CURB65, SOFA, MEDS and PIRO; REDS had the highest sensitivity for mortality (80.1%) at its cut-off. Graded mortality by REDS band 0–2/3–4/5–6/≥7 was 5%, 16.1%, 25.6%, 54.3% [PMC8547872].
- **qREDS** (REDS minus refractory hypotension, suited to electronic extraction) in 3202 patients (433 in-hospital deaths): REDS 0.74 (0.72–0.75) and qREDS 0.73 (0.71–[passage text removed] (0.65–0.68), p<0.0001; cut-offs ≥3, ≥3 and ≥6; specificity at ≥5 was 89.2%, 90.6% vs 43.9% for NEWS2. Performance of REDS/qREDS was better in patients without specified comorbidities (dementia, malignancy, frailty, LTOT, prior DNAR), whereas NEWS2 did not differ [BMJ Open Quality 2025;15:e004168].
- Beyond discharge, in 1057 ED patients admitted after IV antibiotics (146, 13.8%, died in hospital), REDS ([passage text removed]) outperformed Red-flag, NICE high-risk and NEWS2 for 180-day survival; SIRS did not discriminate (log-rank p=0.98) [Front Med 2023, 10.3389/fmed.2023.985444; openaccess.sgul.ac.uk/id/eprint/115338].

**Generic bedside scores (suspected infection/sepsis ED populations)**

- **qSOFA vs SIRS** meta-analysis of 16 prospective ED studies (35,756 patients, 2,285 deaths): qSOFA pooled sensitivity 0.43 (0.32–0.54), specificity 0.89 (0.84–0.93), summary AUC 0.76 (0.72–0.80); SIRS sensitivity 0.80 (0.73–0.86), specificity 0.39 (0.30–0.50), AUC 0.67 (0.62–0.72) — i.e. qSOFA rules in, SIRS rules out [PMC9098353; PMID 35572161]. The Sepsis-3 ED validation similarly found greater prognostic accuracy for in-hospital mortality with qSOFA [jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2598268], with Freund et al. reporting AUROC 0.80 (0.74–0.85) for qSOFA vs 0.65 (0.59–0.70) for SIRS in 879 ED patients [as reported in PMC9098353].
- **NEWS/NEWS2/MEWS** also stratify, and discrimination depends on infection focus: in the Acutelines ED cohort, NEWS and NEWS-2 reached AUC 0.86 (0.76–0.95) for in-hospital mortality in abdominal infection but only ~0.65–0.68 with an undefined source; qSOFA ranged from 0.83 in "other" infections to 0.57 in skin/soft-tissue infection, and qSOFA calibration was poor in several subgroups [Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis, 10.1007/s10096-024-04961-1].
- A prospective ED triage study of suspected infection found qSOFA (AUROC 0.79) and NEWS2 (0.77) both significantly better than SIRS (0.66) and MEWS (0.69) for 28-day in-hospital mortality, with the qSOFA–NEWS2 difference not significant [PMID 41504404; preprints.org/manuscript/202505.0682].
- **MEDS**, a laboratory-inclusive ED sepsis score, gave AUC 0.87 (0.82–0.93) for 30-day in-hospital mortality in 249 SIRS-positive ED patients (46 deaths, 18.5%), outperforming APACHE II (0.77) and SOFA (0.78) [PMC6716723].

**Caveats.** The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends against qSOFA as a *single* screening tool versus SIRS/NEWS/MEWS [ctv.veeva.com study record]; REDS/qREDS remain single-centre and explicitly await external validation [BMJ Open Quality 2025;15:e004168]. Also note that a large cohort defining suspected sepsis by IV antibiotics and/or cultures (8204 patients) compared qSOFA, SIRS and NEWS against 10- and 30-day rather than in-hospital mortality, so it is only indirectly applicable [10.1371/journal.pone.0211133].
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** In ED cohorts defined by receipt of intravenous antibiotics for suspected sepsis, several bedside/near-bedside scores stratify in-hospital mortality — the REDS score and its simplified qREDS variant perform best in head-to-head comparisons, while qSOFA, NEWS/NEWS2, SOFA, MEDS, PIRO and CURB65 all discriminate to a moderate degree and SIRS essentially does not.

**Scores developed in exactly this population (IV antibiotics for suspected sepsis)**
- **REDS** combines six dichotomous items (RR ≥22, [passage text removed], albumin ≤27 g/L, INR ≥1.3) with stratified refractory hypotension and lactate, range 0–12 [S:6398ed5c]. In derivation/validation among 2,115 admitted ED patients given IV antibiotics (282 deaths, 13.3%), AUROC was 0.78 (0.75–0.80) and 0.74 (0.71–0.76), cut-off ≥3, sensitivity 85.0% and 84.5%; specificity at ≥3/≥5/≥7 was 54.8%/88.8%/96.9% with corresponding mortality 21.8%/36.0%/49.1%, versus 2.6% for scores 0–2 [S:75f20156][S:5ffa3999]. REDS outperformed each of its components, including qSOFA (AUROC 0.70) and lactate alone (0.60) [S:5ffa3999].
- **Comparative cohort (2,594 patients admitted after IV antibiotics for suspected sepsis; 332 deaths, 12.8%):** REDS AUROC 0.73 (0.72–0.75) was greater than SIRS 0.51 (p<.0001) and NEWS2 0.69 (p=.005), and similar to CURB65, SOFA, MEDS and PIRO; sensitivity at identified cut-offs ([passage text removed], PIRO ≥10) was highest for REDS at 80.1% [S:31754156]. Graded mortality by REDS band was [passage text removed]% for [passage text removed] [S:8e3ea040]. A ΔSOFA ≥2 gave sensitivity 63% [S:31754156]. NEWS2 ≥3 was highly sensitive (97.6%) but almost non-specific (5.8%), suiting it to screening rather than stratification [S:31dc0868][S:6ef16764].
- **qREDS** (REDS minus refractory hypotension, electronically extractable) in 3,202 ED patients admitted after IV antibiotics (433 in-hospital deaths): AUROC REDS 0.74 (0.72–0.75), qREDS 0.73 (0.71–0.75), both > NEWS2 0.66 (0.65–0.68), p<0.0001; cut-offs ≥3, ≥3 and ≥6; specificity at ≥5 was 89.2%, 90.6% vs 43.9% for NEWS2, and 168-hour survival probability at ≥5 points was 78.3%, 78.0% vs 90.6% [S:c892bd04][S:0f97ae8e]. At clinically used thresholds, NEWS2 ≥5 gave sensitivity 78% vs 76% for REDS/qREDS ≥3, but lower specificity (44% vs 57%); qREDS/REDS ≥5 gave sensitivity 35–40%, specificity 90% and a 37% mortality rate, with median time to death 131.6 h at ≥5 [S:78b34556].

**Physiological scores in ED "treated as sepsis" populations**
- In emergency admissions treated as sepsis, for in-hospital death qSOFA ≥2 was most specific (79%) but least sensitive (37%); SIRS ≥2 most sensitive (80%) and least specific (21%); NEWS ≥5 intermediate (74%/43%). AUROCs: NEWS 0.65, qSOFA 0.62, SIRS 0.49 [S:eb226527].
- In ED patients with suspected infection, qSOFA modestly outperformed SIRS for in-hospital mortality (AUROC 0.64 vs 0.52; sensitivity/specificity 0.55/0.65 vs 0.88/0.14) [S:84f3d30b]; a smaller prospective cohort found SIRS, qSOFA and NEWS statistically indistinguishable (AUROC 0.659, 0.711, 0.711), with mortality 38% at qSOFA ≥2 vs 3.5% at qSOFA <2 [S:10e08a14]. A prospective multicentre ED validation is reported to have shown in-hospital mortality of 3% with qSOFA <2 versus 24% with qSOFA ≥2 (AUROC 0.80 vs 0.65 for SIRS) [S:308fbd84][S:c54c775c].
- In a mixed non-ICU/ICU suspected-infection cohort, SOFA outperformed qSOFA, SIRS and NEWS for hospital mortality, and NEWS discriminated better than qSOFA — arguing qSOFA should not replace early-warning scores where full data are available, though it remains useful where complex scores are impractical [S:6a1b97b2].

**Sepsis-specific mortality scores**
- **MEDS** (nine items, 0–27, five risk strata) had pooled AUC 0.83 with sensitivity 79% and specificity 74% for short-term mortality in ED patients with suspected infection [S:be8eae83][S:fcd7b367]; an ED validation reported MEDS AUROC 0.857 with cut-off ≥10 (sensitivity 71.9%, specificity 84.1%) [S:205ee5d2].
- **PIRO, SOFA, MEDS** all discriminated one-month mortality in ED sepsis (AUROC 0.83, 0.87, 0.94 respectively) [S:921309f6]; **SPEED** predicted 28-day mortality with AUROC 0.81 in derivation and validation, outperforming MEDS in that cohort [S:d3349f62]; **abbMEDS and CURB-65** stratify ED sepsis risk categories and relate to management decisions [S:ea2ce471]; **simplified MISSED** (age >65, albumin <27 g/L, INR >1.3) identifies high-risk ED sepsis patients and is a REDS component [S:08479b81][S:6398ed5c].

**Caveats:** these are single-centre or heterogeneous cohorts; the REDS score requires bloods and assessment of blood-pressure response to fluid, so it cannot be computed immediately at triage [S:6398ed5c], and outcome definitions and "suspected infection" definitions vary widely across studies [S:f02872c6]. Surviving Sepsis guidance advises against qSOFA as a single screening tool versus SIRS, NEWS or MEWS [S:b6a4e161]. I found no evidence on which of these scores improves outcomes when implemented, only on discrimination [S:b6a4e161].

rows.question: What phenotype characterizes patients with coexisting MOG antibody and anti-NMDAR antibody positivity?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: At onset these patients present with an encephalitis-spectrum picture in which fever, headache, altered consciousness, neuropsychiatric disturbance and seizures are the common features; Brain MRI is abnormal in roughly two thirds of patients, with supratentorial cortical and subcortical lesions predominating over spinal cord involvement; Neuropsychiatric and behavioural disturbance was more frequent in the overlap group than in the MOG antibody-associated disease comparison group; In the same series, cortical/subcortical lesions and gadolinium enhancement were less frequent in the overlap group than in MOG antibody-associated disease. Certainty: The evidence is preliminary, resting on only a handful of dual-antibody-positive patients, so the phenotype should be regarded as an early description and the apparent differences from MOG antibody-associated disease as associations rather than established facts. Scope: applies to coexisting MOG antibody and anti-NMDAR antibody positivity (antibody overlap syndrome) in children and adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the fall in disability scores after acute immunotherapy as demonstrating treatment efficacy, or as showing that antibody overlap responds better to steroids plus immunoglobulin than single-antibody disease.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

Coexisting MOG-IgG and NMDAR-IgG ([passage text removed]) produces an **encephalitis-dominant phenotype resembling anti-NMDAR encephalitis clinically, but carrying MOGAD-type demyelinating imaging features and a markedly high relapse rate** — psychiatric/behavioural disturbance and seizures at onset, superimposed on cortical/subcortical, brainstem, cerebellar or spinal demyelinating lesions, in young, male-predominant, tumour-free patients.

## Supporting evidence

**Encephalitic rather than demyelinating symptomatology.** In a systematic review of 35 publications, [passage text removed]]. A meta-analysis of 58 dual-positive cases (median age 21.0 years, 58.6% male) found prominent symptoms were seizures (56.9%) and abnormal behaviour (51.7%) rather than demyelinating features such as speech disorder (34.5%) or optic neuritis (27.6%); its authors concluded "[passage text removed]].

**Demographics.** A pooled review of 49 MNOS patients found young males (male:female 31:18), median onset age 23 years (range 4–54), no tumours or associated autoimmune disease, and prodromal fever (20.4%) or headache (34.7%); manifestations were psychiatric symptoms 71.4%, seizures 51.0%, sleep disorders 36.7%, movement disorders 30.6%, cognitive impairment 30.6%, speech disorder 24.5%, limb weakness 24.5%, ataxia 18.4%, visual impairment 16.3%, autonomic dysfunction 12.2% [[passage text removed]]. The absence of tumour and male skew distinguishes MNOS from classic ovarian-teratoma–associated NMDARE [[passage text removed]].

**Imaging.** In the 49-patient series only 12.2% had normal brain MRI; commonest structures were [passage text removed]), with T2 hyperintensity and sometimes parenchymal or meningeal enhancement — whereas pure NMDARE more often had negative MRI or cortex/medial temporal involvement [[passage text removed]]. The meta-analysis reported cortical/subcortical changes in 70.7% and brainstem in 31.0%, with 31.3% showing unilateral cortical encephalitis with epilepsy and 12.5% bilateral frontal cortical [passage text removed]].

**Position between the two mono-antibody phenotypes.** Versus MOG-IgG+/NMDAR-IgG− patients, dual-positive patients had more mental/behavioural change, involuntary movement, sleep disorder and leptomeningeal lesions, and *less* optic neuritis; versus NMDAR-IgG+/MOG-IgG−, they had more relapse, more preceding infection, and more subcortical, basal ganglia, brainstem and spinal cord lesions [[passage text removed]]. The same pattern was reproduced in Chinese paediatric MNOS: lower psycho-behavioural abnormality and involuntary movements than NMDAR-only patients, but higher sleep disorders, seizures and psycho-behavioural abnormalities than MOG-only patients, with consciousness disturbance, seizures, visual disturbance, psycho-behavioural abnormality and cognitive/memory impairment as common MNOS manifestations [[passage text removed]]. In a paediatric MOG-Ab encephalitis cohort, the two NMDAR-Ab co-positive children "[passage text removed]].

**Relapsing but generally steroid/immunotherapy-responsive course.** Relapse occurred in 63.4% of dual-positive patients (50.0% relapsing with encephalitic and 53.8% with demyelinating manifestations), a rate far above NMDAR-IgG+/MOG-IgG− patients, yet functional outcome was usually favourable [[passage text removed]]. Most of the 49 pooled patients responded to immunotherapy with good long-term prognosis [[passage text removed]]. Attacks may be simultaneous or sequential, with NMDARE preceding demyelination or vice versa [[passage text removed]].

**Caveats / heterogeneity.** A 2025 single-centre cohort of 13 dual-positive patients found *fewer* psychiatric/behavioural disturbances (38.5% vs 83.3%, P = 0.010) and less epilepsy (23.1% vs 62.5%, P = 0.038) than pure anti-NMDAR encephalitis, greater brachium pontis involvement (P = 0.037), a relapse rate of 38.5%, and no significant relapse-rate difference on Kaplan-Meier analysis; the authors interpreted the lower pre-treatment mRS as supporting *milder* disease than pure NMDARE [[passage text removed]]. A 23-patient adult cohort likewise reported sleep disorder as most common (69.57%), then psychiatric/cognitive (65.22%), consciousness disturbance (60.87%) and seizures (56.52%), with relapse in 26.09% [[passage text removed]]. So relapse frequency and severity relative to isolated NMDARE remain unsettled across small retrospective cohorts. A broader review of overlapping NMDARE and demyelinating disease (256 patients, 94.5% MOGAD) also stresses that MOG-IgG must be confirmed by cell-based assay to avoid false positives [[passage text removed]].

**Practical implication:** test for MOG-IgG when NMDARE patients develop optic neuritis, myelitis or demyelinating MRI lesions, and test for NMDAR-IgG when MOGAD patients develop psychosis, seizures, sleep disturbance or memory loss [[passage text removed]].
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Coexisting MOG‑IgG and NMDAR‑IgG ("MNOS," MOGAD–anti‑NMDAR encephalitis overlap syndrome) produces an **encephalitis‑dominant phenotype grafted onto demyelinating features**: psychiatric/behavioural symptoms, seizures, sleep and speech disturbance resembling anti‑NMDAR encephalitis, combined with optic neuritis, myelitis, brainstem or cortical/ADEM‑type demyelination — typically in a younger, male‑predominant, non‑paraneoplastic patient with a relapsing course but generally good treatment response.

## Clinical features

**Symptom spectrum is NMDAR‑encephalitis‑like with superimposed demyelination.** In a systematic review of 70 dual‑positive patients (104 episodes), dual‑positive episodes were dominated by [passage text removed] and movement disorders (both 11/47, 23.40%), while a substantial minority had [passage text removed]%) [S:3217eade]. The authors concluded the dual‑positive clinical spectrum, though approximating the sum of both single‑antibody syndromes, "[passage text removed]:3217eade], and that encephalitis is the predominant phenotype when MOG‑IgG coexists [passage text removed]" [S:83989f94]. Encephalitis being the predominant phenotype — with convulsions, abnormal psychiatric behaviour, sleep and memory disturbance as first symptoms — is echoed elsewhere [S:de027d93].

In a 23‑patient adult cohort, sleep disorder was most common (69.57%), then [passage text removed] and headache (both 39.13%) [S:cc161bc5]. Among the 13 who met MOGAD criteria, cortical encephalitis was the commonest demyelinating presentation (6/13, 46.15%), then optic neuritis and ADEM (2/13 each) [S:8266309f]. In a Mayo-type dual‑positive series, features of both diseases co‑occurred (encephalopathy, seizures, myelitis, optic neuritis), and 10 dual‑positive patients met criteria for **both** ADEM and anti‑NMDAR encephalitis simultaneously [S:5c2b6970]. Rarer cortical variants such as FLAMES overlapping NMDARE are described [S:48608226], as is isolated seizure presentation with unilateral thalamic change [S:a76b5f60].

**Demographics: younger, male‑shifted, tumour‑free, infection‑triggered.** Median onset age 21 years (range 2–63) with only 40.28% female in the pooled review [S:e984237d]. In the adult cohort, 20/23 (86.96%) were male, mean onset 36.17 ± 11.21 years, with the male proportion significantly higher than in either anti‑NMDARE or MOGAD controls [S:cc161bc5][S:0f2fecf9]. Compared with overlapping NMOSD+NMDARE, MOG+NMDARE overlap had a [passage text removed]) and younger onset (19.8 vs 32.4 years, P=0.025) [S:4183a1cb]. No tumours were found in the adult cohort [S:8266309f], and dual‑positive patients lacked [passage text removed]" [S:9fb737fd]; prodromal infection occurred in 9/23 (39.13%) [S:cc161bc5].

**Imaging: more extensive and atypical than NMDARE alone.** Dual positivity [passage text removed] ± cortical enhancement than MOGAD without NMDAR‑IgG [S:5c2b6970]. Beyond the frontotemporal cortex typical of NMDARE, dual‑positive episodes involved infratentorial regions, subcortex and basal ganglia [S:e3f3e757]; NMDARE patients with additional MOG‑IgG more often had atypical brainstem/cerebellar features and lesions in subcortical white matter, infratentorial regions or spinal cord, sometimes with basal ganglia, cortical or meningeal enhancement [S:486213dd]. Pediatric MNOS patients had significantly more MRI abnormalities than NMDAR‑only patients [S:ff0a3dbf].

**Severity relative to single‑antibody disease.** Dual‑positive patients had milder disease than typical anti‑NMDAR encephalitis [passage text removed] [S:e3f3e757]; overlap has been described as having milder manifestations than NMDARE alone [S:0c2559fa]. In children, MNOS patients had less psycho‑behavioural abnormality and fewer involuntary movements than NMDAR‑only patients, but more sleep disorders, seizures and psycho‑behavioural abnormality than MOG‑only patients; NMDAR‑only patients had higher ICU admission rates, longer stays and more second‑line escalation [S:ff0a3dbf].

**Course and outcome: relapse‑prone but usually favourable.** 45/70 (64.29%) had a relapsing–remitting course and 26/28 (92.86%) scored mRS ≤2 at last follow‑up [S:e984237d]. In an 18‑patient review, 13 (72.2%) relapsed at a median interval of 12.25 months with no deaths [S:b992e58c], and the recurrence rate tracked MOGAD (60–90%) rather than NMDARE (4–26%), implicating MOG‑IgG in relapse risk [S:a373edaa]; another report cites a 63.4% recurrence rate with relapses as encephalitis (50.0%) or demyelinating events (53.8%) [S:84e1be2b]. In the adult cohort all received first‑line immunotherapy, 16/23 (69.57%) needed second‑line/long‑term therapy, median mRS improved from 3 (IQR 3,4) to 1 (IQR 0,1), and 6/23 (26.09%) relapsed [S:cc161bc5]. Prognosis was better than in NMOSD+NMDARE overlap (mRS 0–2 in 86% vs 41%, P<0.01) [S:4183a1cb].

**One caveat — the literature is not unanimous on prognosis.** One review argues [passage text removed]:2ec11fab], and a tumefactive‑lesion study found coexisting MOG and NMDAR antibodies did not significantly influence overall prognosis, though MNOS+ patients more often had cerebellar/brainstem syndromes [S:a078ff23].

MOG–NMDAR is the most frequent neural‑antibody overlap (68.14% of MOG‑IgG coexistence cases) [S:83989f94], and antibodies may appear simultaneously or sequentially in either order [S:36bf82f1][S:e984237d]. Accordingly, test both antibodies in serum **and** CSF when a MOGAD patient develops psychiatric/cognitive symptoms, or when an NMDARE patient shows demyelinating or atypical infratentorial imaging findings [S:4183a1cb][S:e3f3e757][S:c88d40b8].

rows.question: What is known about starting cladribine tablets soon after natalizumab discontinuation in relapsing multiple sclerosis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Cladribine tablets started within about a month of the last natalizumab infusion were followed by relapse rates and MRI lesion activity that stayed as low as before the switch in uncontrolled observation; No new safety signals were reported after this rapid start in the small group observed; The switches observed were prompted mainly by JC virus risk rather than by breakthrough disease activity on natalizumab. Certainty: The switch observations are early and uncontrolled, drawn from a small low-activity group reported in abstract form without a comparison group, so they support feasibility rather than protection against rebound. Scope: applies to relapsing multiple sclerosis treated with natalizumab in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the short interval to the first cladribine course as an established means of preventing rebound activity, or recommends it on that basis for patients with breakthrough disease activity while on natalizumab.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** The only prospective, purpose-designed evidence — the small phase 4 CLADRINA study — suggests that starting cladribine tablets within ~2–4 weeks of the last natalizumab infusion is feasible, well tolerated, and associated with maintained disease stability without PML or rebound, whereas essentially all reports of disease reactivation after this switch involve substantially longer washouts (~2–4 months). Evidence remains low-grade (single-arm, n=40, low-activity population), and formal guideline-level recommendation is still lacking.

**Why the timing question matters.** Natalizumab withdrawal carries a predictable return of activity: in pooled AFFIRM/SENTINEL/GLANCE analyses, ARR and gadolinium-enhancing lesions rose after [passage text removed], irrespective of prior exposure duration or whether another approved DMT was started ([PMC10996356]([passage text removed])). Expert opinion holds that rebound after withdrawal of anti-trafficking agents (S1P modulators, natalizumab) generally occurs within 3 months, so a rapid-onset successor and a minimised washout are advised ([Chan et al., Neurology and Therapy; PubMed 41854800](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41854800)); the same reasoning underlies advice to make the gap short or absent when leaving natalizumab ([Cleveland Clinic switching fact sheet]([passage text removed])).

**CLADRINA (NCT04178005).** Open-label, single-arm, multicentre phase 4 study in 40 patients with RRMS or active SPMS, with cladribine tablets 3.5 mg/kg started ~14 days after the last natalizumab infusion (maximum permitted washout 4 weeks); primary endpoints were lymphocyte/myeloid subsets and serum neurofilament light, with ARR secondary ([Sguigna et al., Ther Adv Neurol Disord 2024;17:17562864241233858](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38585373); [PMC10996356]([passage text removed])). At 24 months (ACTRIMS 2025 abstract P147): mean transition time [passage text removed]); ARR [passage text removed] versus [passage text removed]) at 12 months, sustained at 24 months; median EDSS 2.3 (0.0–5.5) → 2.0 (0.0–6.0); 100% [passage text removed] new/enlarging T2 lesions at 24 months; MSDA scores unchanged or improved; no PML and no rebound ([Neurology Advisor conference report]([passage text removed]); [ACTRIMS poster]([passage text removed])). Safety in the poster: [passage text removed]. A treatment-free extension reported stability of ARR, EDSS and MRI through 36 months with no PML or rebound ([ECTRIMS 2025 CLADRINA extension poster]([passage text removed])).

**Contrast: longer washouts and worse outcomes.**
- Pfeuffer et al. (Mult Scler 2022;28(2):257–268): among 23 natalizumab-pretreated patients (median washout 66 days, IQR 49–81), 18/23 developed disease activity after cladribine induction, 12 of these within 6 months — activity the authors note could reflect natalizumab-cessation rebound ([PMC8795224](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8795224)).
- Zanghì et al. (Neurotherapeutics 2021;18:1166–1174): in 120 JCV-high-risk patients switching from natalizumab (ocrelizumab 64, rituximab 36, cladribine 20), IPTW propensity-adjusted models favoured ocrelizumab over cladribine for ARR ([passage text removed], p=0.020) and [passage text removed] PML occurred and safety was similar ([PMC8423885]([passage text removed])).
- MSBase (Zhong et al., Mult Scler 2023;29:119–129): of 513 patients switching to cladribine, [passage text removed] the first year; relapse hazard on cladribine was predicted by prior-year relapse ([passage text removed]), gap relapse (HR 6.18, 95% CI 2.65–14.41), switching from natalizumab (HR 4.08 vs injectables, 95% CI 1.35–12.33) and younger age ([PubMed 35894247](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35894247)).
- Möhn et al. (Ther Adv Neurol Disord 2019): 17 patients switched for high JCV index with a mean gap of 16 weeks (range 9–23) had no clinical relapses, though new T2 lesions were described ([msard-journal expert opinion]([passage text removed]); [Zhong et al.]([passage text removed])).
- In a Finnish cohort, subsequent DMTs often failed to prevent reactivation after natalizumab, with longer washout linked to higher 6-month reactivation risk and a suggested cap of 3 months — though no patient there received cladribine ([Mustonen et al., Mult Scler Relat Disord 2020;38:101498, as summarised in PMC10996356]([passage text removed])).

**Important caveats.** CLADRINA participants were largely clinically stable patients switching because of JCV-antibody positivity, with very low baseline activity (ARR 0.10; 97.5% free of T1 [passage text removed]), and the study was single-arm and hypothesis-generating by design ([poster]([passage text removed]); [PMC10996356]([passage text removed])) — so absence of rebound cannot be attributed to rapid sequencing alone. The most recent international expert opinion explicitly states that anti-CD20 switching is the rational choice when natalizumab is stopped in the setting of moderate/severe activity, that restoration of control with cladribine tablets may be possible for some patients, and that additional data are needed before a clear recommendation can be made ([PubMed 41854800](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41854800)). I found no randomised comparison of short versus long washout for this specific switch, and no published peer-reviewed full paper of the CLADRINA efficacy results (only the rationale/design paper plus congress abstracts).
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** The evidence — one small prospective phase IV trial plus real-world cohorts and expert consensus — indicates that a *short* interval (ideally ≤2–4 weeks) between the last natalizumab infusion and the first cladribine dose is key: rapid switching in patients who are *stable* on natalizumab (typically switching for JCV/PML risk) has looked safe and effective, whereas long washouts (~2–3 months) and switching because of breakthrough activity are associated with substantial early relapse/MRI activity.

**Rationale.** Natalizumab withdrawal carries a risk of disease reactivation/rebound, generally within ~3 months [S:10960611][S:48ec89a8]. Because natalizumab sequesters lymphocytes in the periphery in a more inflammatory [passage text removed] was hypothesised to make the cladribine lymphocyte nadir coincide with the rebound window and to normalise PML risk [S:b2b54afd][S:2c868bf7].

**Prospective trial data (CLADRINA).** Open-label, single-arm, multicentre US phase IV study in 40 patients with relapsing MS after ≥12 months of natalizumab; cladribine started ~14 days after the last infusion, maximum 4 weeks, with baseline MRI as PML screening; primary endpoints were lymphocyte/myeloid subsets and blood neurofilament light, with ARR secondary [S:76cf383c][S:2bd3f1fa]. In the 12-month interim analysis (39 completers), mean [passage text removed]) pre-switch and [passage text removed]; mean baseline EDSS 2.46 remained stable; Gd+-lesion-free rose from 95% to 100% and freedom from new/enlarging T2 lesions from 87.5% to 97%; no PML and no rebound reported [S:0e3da63f]. Two-year data (abstract) reported ARR 0.10 at baseline and 0.03 at both years 1 and 2, no Gd+ T1 lesions, 86.5% free of new/enlarging T2 lesions at 2 years, and no new safety signals; notably only 2.5–12.5% had disease activity in the year before switching — the main driver was JCV status, so this cohort was largely stable disease [S:66a7da1b].

**Supporting real-world/safety series.** In 20 UK patients switched for JCV positivity, treatment was well tolerated with no severe opportunistic infections and no PML [S:c53d1a6c]; 46 German/Austrian patients followed 6–12 months likewise showed no PML [S:3243fc0d]. A Barts audit of 6 patients with a mean switching interval of 4.8 weeks (range 2–8) and median 29.5 months' follow-up reported no relapses, EDSS worsening, MRI activity or PML, and the authors recommended [passage text removed] [S:c03faa9f].

**Counter-evidence — long washouts perform poorly.** In Pfeuffer et al., patients switching from natalizumab showed persistent activity mainly within 6 months of cladribine initiation (median washout 66 days, IQR 49–81), likely rebound, though they also had higher baseline T2 lesion loads [S:b47d7aa1][S:5ba91b0a]; Zanghì et al. found higher ARR with an extended washout [S:5ba91b0a]. An Italian cohort switching off natalizumab with a cladribine washout of 6 ± 2.9 weeks estimated ARR 0.5 versus 0.001 for ocrelizumab [S:a521f7b8]. A 12-centre Russian real-world analysis found relapses between cladribine courses in 77.3% of natalizumab switchers, concluding this switch was not optimal compared with switching from first-line drugs [S:26b8fbf1][S:f737347d]; a Moscow cohort attributed an early rise in ARR to patients starting cladribine no earlier than ~12 weeks after the last natalizumab infusion, with clinical and MRI activity falling thereafter [S:0e1d7afa]. An MSBase-based analysis identified prior natalizumab as the strongest predictor of relapse in the first year on cladribine (HR 4.08 vs first-line injectables) [S:27792859].

**Current guidance.** International expert opinion: start cladribine [passage text removed] to minimise rebound [S:41f769c7]; French expert opinion: washout up to 1 month, with MRI to exclude asymptomatic PML [S:74fdce40]; Gulf-region recommendations: 4 weeks, with prompt initiation taking precedence over waiting for lymphocyte-count recovery [S:1edfb772]; an earlier Delphi consensus gave 4–8 weeks plus PML exclusion (MRI ± CSF JCV-PCR in JCV+ patients treated >12 months) [S:c9cde550]. A narrative review frames the window as at least 4 weeks to avoid additive immunosuppression but under 12 weeks to limit rebound [S:40e2ad23]. Importantly, the same expert panel does *not* generally recommend switching from natalizumab to cladribine because of breakthrough disease activity (reserving it for stable disease/safety-driven switches, de-escalation in older patients, or selected subgroups such as neutralising anti-natalizumab antibodies), and notes that additional data are needed before a firm recommendation [S:4a24cb73][S:90740846][S:c06fe43a].

**Caveats.** CLADRINA is single-arm, open-label, n=40, with immunological rather than clinical primary endpoints, and its 2-year outcomes are so far reported in abstract form [S:76cf383c][S:66a7da1b]; carry-over PML in the first months after natalizumab remains a theoretical concern requiring baseline MRI [S:3243fc0d]. No randomised comparison of natalizumab-to-cladribine versus other post-natalizumab strategies appeared in my searches.

rows.question: How does lactated Ringer's exposure before sepsis diagnosis relate to mortality in critically ill adults?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Lactated Ringer's exposure before sepsis diagnosis is associated with lower 28-day mortality than no exposure; In-hospital mortality is also lower with pre-diagnosis lactated Ringer's exposure than without exposure; The lower-mortality association persists after adjustment for elective surgery and total recorded fluid volume; Weighting-based sensitivity analysis reproduces the lower mortality seen in the exposed group. Certainty: The strength of this evidence supports an association only, because the mortality difference may reflect earlier recognition and resuscitation practice rather than the fluid itself. Scope: applies to sepsis meeting Sepsis-3 criteria in critically ill adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it recommends pre-emptive lactated Ringer's infusion in patients not yet suspected of sepsis, or presents earlier fluid exposure as established grounds for changing resuscitation practice.

answers.websearch:
## Conclusion

In the one study that directly addresses this timing question, lactated Ringer's (LR) started in the [passage text removed] — but the authors explicitly frame this as hypothesis-generating and warn it does not justify pre-emptive LR administration.

## The timing-specific evidence

A retrospective MIMIC-IV propensity-score-matched cohort stratified patients by when LR was first given [passage text removed] (≤24 h after onset), Group B (≤24 h before onset), Group C ([passage text removed] (no LR exposure during ICU admission) ([doi.org/10.1177/20503121261481481](https://doi.org/10.1177/20503121261481481)). Of the eligible cohort of 32,316 patients, group sizes were 2,303 (A), 1,939 (B), 587 (C), and 27,487 (D) ([PMC13535053](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13535053)).

Key results as reported in the full text ([PMC13535053](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13535053)):
- [passage text removed] showed significantly better survival in the **pre-diagnosis** group (B) versus no-LR (D), log-rank P<0.001.
- Groups A and C (post-diagnosis initiation) showed **smaller** survival benefits — i.e., the signal was concentrated in the pre-onset window, which is what prompted the authors to run a targeted 1:1 match of B vs D (1,938 vs 1,938).
- Robustness was tested with IPTW in Groups B and D, achieving [passage text removed] confirming result stability.

I was unable to retrieve the matched-cohort adjusted hazard ratio itself from the accessible text, so I am not stating an effect size.

## Important caveat the authors themselves raise

The published conclusion states that [passage text removed]" ([PMC13535053](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13535053); [PubMed 42688428](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42688428)). This is the crux: patients who receive LR *before* meeting Sepsis-3 criteria are, by construction, patients already under active clinical attention and being resuscitated — an exposure definition vulnerable to confounding by indication and to the timing artifacts inherent in defining onset by a SOFA increase. A separate MIMIC-IV analysis illustrates the same measurement problem, noting [passage text removed] SOFA score, which is why it used a symmetric 12-h pre/post-onset window, and that precise fluid volumes in that window could not be measured due to fluid-balance recording limitations ([nature.com/articles/s41598-025-03141-1]([passage text removed])).

## How this fits the broader LR-vs-saline literature

The direction is consistent with fluid-choice evidence, though none of the following tested *pre-diagnosis* timing:
- **CLOVERS secondary analysis:** among 1,563 patients with sepsis-induced hypotension, [passage text removed]/622 (12.2%) with LR vs 110/690 (15.9%) with 0.9% saline (adjusted [passage text removed]); this covered fluid given *before* randomization, i.e. initial resuscitation ([PMC12047640]([passage text removed])).
- **SMART sepsis subgroup:** 30-day in-hospital mortality 217/… (26.3%) with balanced crystalloids vs 255 (31.2%) with saline ([passage text removed]) among 1,641 medical-ICU patients with sepsis ([PMC6909845](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6909845)).
- **Meta-analysis (15 studies, 20,329 adults with sepsis):** balanced crystalloids associated with lower overall mortality (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81–0.96) and 28/30-day mortality (RR 0.87, 0.79–0.95), but **no** difference in 90-day mortality (RR 0.96, 0.90–1.03), and the RCT-only subgroup for overall mortality was null (RR 0.92, 0.82–1.02) ([mdpi.com/2077-0383/11/7/1971]([passage text removed])).
- **Countervailing data:** a propensity-matched analysis found in-patient mortality similar after matching (8.5% LR vs 8.0% NS), despite a large unmatched difference (10.9% vs 6.4%) driven by LR patients being sicker (19.0% vs 6.7% septic shock) — a direct demonstration of how severity confounds LR exposure ([frontiersin.org 10.3389/fmed.2023.1071741]([passage text removed]/full)).

## Bottom line

Pre-sepsis-diagnosis LR exposure is associated with lower 28-day mortality, and the association appears stronger than for LR started after onset ([PMC13535053](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13535053)). Given that only a single retrospective single-database study addresses this timing question, that the 90-day mortality signal for balanced crystalloids is null in pooled RCT data ([mdpi.com/2077-0383/11/7/1971]([passage text removed])), and that at least one matched cohort nulls out entirely after adjusting for severity ([frontiersin.org 10.3389/fmed.2023.1071741]([passage text removed]/full)), this should be read as an association generated by observational data rather than a reason to give LR before sepsis is diagnosed.
