rows.question: How do ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, and zanubrutinib compare for atrial fibrillation risk in mantle cell lymphoma?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Newly recorded atrial fibrillation or flutter is less frequent with acalabrutinib than with ibrutinib, on the order of a third as frequent; Newly recorded atrial fibrillation or flutter is likewise less frequent with zanubrutinib than with ibrutinib; Atrial fibrillation or flutter frequency is similar between acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib, with no clear separation between the two second-generation agents. Certainty: The claims rest on consistently observed associations rather than demonstrated causal effects, and residual confounding by baseline disease risk, line of therapy and treatment era leaves the magnitude of each difference uncertain. Scope: applies to mantle cell lymphoma treated with a covalent Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it treats the lower atrial fibrillation frequency with second-generation agents as proof that ibrutinib causes atrial fibrillation or as grounds for switching every ibrutinib-treated patient.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Ibrutinib carries roughly a 2–3-fold higher atrial fibrillation/flutter risk than either acalabrutinib or zanubrutinib in MCL, while acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib appear equivalent to each other. There is **no head-to-head randomized trial in MCL** — "[passage text removed]" ([targetedonc.com]([passage text removed])) — so the comparison rests on single-arm registration trials, MCL real-world matched cohorts, and extrapolation from randomized CLL/WM trials.

## MCL-specific comparative evidence (propensity-matched, TriNetX)

The only direct three-way MCL comparison is a retrospective propensity score–matched TriNetX study (Homeniuk et al., *Cancer Med* 2026;15(8):e72111; [PMC13429935]([passage text removed])). Over 365 days of newly recorded AF/flutter:

- **Acalabrutinib vs ibrutinib:** 28/629 (4.5%) vs 77/641 (12.0%); RR [passage text removed]), HR 0.387 (0.251–0.596) ([PMC13429935]([passage text removed])).
- **Zanubrutinib vs ibrutinib:** 22/438 (5.0%) vs 54/439 (12.3%); RR 0.408 (0.253–0.658), HR 0.421 (0.256–0.690).
- **Acalabrutinib vs zanubrutinib:** 18/449 (4.0%) vs 25/439 (5.7%); RR 0.704 (0.390–1.272) — **not significant**. At 180 days the two were nearly identical (3.3% vs 3.4%; RR 0.978).

The signal appeared within the first 6 months and persisted to 365 days. Heart failure did not differ meaningfully across any pairing (e.g., zanubrutinib 4.3% vs ibrutinib 4.5%, RR 0.956, CI crossing 1). GI bleeding favored the second-generation agents but is labelled exploratory and incomplete ([PMC13429935]([passage text removed]); [ajmc.com]([passage text removed])).

## Single-arm MCL trial rates (cross-trial, not comparative)

The ACE-LY-004 final report explicitly juxtaposes the three MCL datasets ([haematol.2023 final results PDF]([passage text removed]); Haematologica 2024;109(1):343-350):

| Agent | MCL AF/flutter |
|---|---|
| Ibrutinib (pooled R/R MCL) | any-grade 11.4%, grade ≥3 6.5% |
| Acalabrutinib (ACE-LY-004, median 38.1 mo) | [passage text removed]% |
| Zanubrutinib (pooled) | any-grade 1.8%, grade ≥3 0.89% |

The authors caution these are "limited [passage text removed]." Corroborating primary sources: ACE-LY-004 at 15.2 months reported **no cases of atrial fibrillation** in 124 patients ([Lancet 2018;391:659-667]([passage text removed]-)); BGB-3111-206 at median 35.3 months follow-up reported **no cases of AF/flutter or grade ≥3 cardiac AEs** ([Blood 2022;139(21):3148-3158 / PMC9136878]([passage text removed])); the two-trial zanubrutinib R/R MCL pool (n=112) reported AF/flutter of 1.8% ([PMC8518153](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8518153)). For ibrutinib, the 370-patient R/R MCL pooled analysis at median 41 months listed grade ≥3 atrial fibrillation at 5.9% among the commonest severe TEAEs ([jhoponline.com]([passage text removed]), from *Br J Haematol* 2017;179(3):430-438).

## Randomized head-to-head data (CLL/WM) that anchors the class inference

- **ELEVATE-RR** (n=533, median 40.9 mo): any-grade AF/flutter 9.4% vs 16.0% with ibrutinib, p=0.02; de novo AF in patients without prior AF 6.2% vs 14.9%; median time to onset 28.8 vs 16.0 months; 0 vs 7 discontinuations for AF; exposure-adjusted AF incidence rate 2.0-fold higher with ibrutinib ([Blood 2023;142(8):687]([passage text removed])).
- **ALPINE final analysis** (n=652, median 42.5 mo): AF/flutter 7.1% vs 17.0%; overall cardiac events 25.9% vs 35.5%; **0 cardiac deaths with zanubrutinib vs 6 with ibrutinib** ([PMID 39316666](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39316666)). Across ASPEN cohort 1 and ALPINE, treatment-emergent AF was ~4-fold lower with zanubrutinib, with significantly lower exposure-adjusted incidence rates (ASPEN p=0.0010; ALPINE p=0.0003) ([onclive.com]([passage text removed])).

Mechanistically, ibrutinib's excess arrhythmia is attributed to off-target inhibition — preclinical rodent work implicates PI3K-Akt and C-terminal Src kinase; ibrutinib inhibited Lck/Src downstream of CSK in patient samples whereas acalabrutinib showed minimal inhibition ([PMC10644206]([passage text removed])).

## Acalabrutinib vs zanubrutinib: unresolved

The MCL matched analysis found no difference. However, a conflicting TriNetX analysis across B-cell malignancies (CLL, MCL, WM, small B-cell lymphoma) reported AF/flutter of 5.70% with zanubrutinib vs 8.61% with acalabrutinib ([passage text removed] with no difference in event-free survival by Kaplan-Meier (p=0.286) — this is a *Circulation* supplement **abstract**, not MCL-restricted ([circ.152.suppl_3.4366329]([passage text removed])). Clinicians in the field state there is "no way to comment" on choosing between the two ([targetedonc.com]([passage text removed])).

## Practice context

NCCN guidelines now recommend acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib as **preferred** agents for R/R MCL over ibrutinib plus rituximab, based on the more favorable toxicity profile in head-to-head trials in other histologies; ibrutinib's MCL indication was voluntarily withdrawn after SHINE ([PMC11898374]([passage text removed])). The MCL matched-cohort authors suggest their data "[passage text removed]," while stressing these are observational associations, not causal effects ([ajmc.com]([passage text removed]); [PMC13429935]([passage text removed])).

**Caveats:** the MCL three-way comparison is retrospective claims/EHR-based with code-defined outcomes and shorter follow-up (365 days) than the AF risk window in trials; the randomized AF data come from CLL and WM, not MCL; and the single-arm MCL rates differ in follow-up duration, ascertainment intensity, and population, so the apparent zanubrutinib-vs-acalabrutinib gap in those tables should not be read as a real difference.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line: ibrutinib carries a roughly 2.5-fold higher risk of atrial fibrillation/flutter than either second-generation agent in MCL, while acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib appear equivalent to each other. There is no head-to-head randomized trial in MCL; the best MCL-specific comparative evidence is a propensity-matched real-world cohort plus an indirect comparison.**

**MCL-specific real-world comparison (strongest direct evidence).** A retrospective propensity score–matched TriNetX cohort of MCL patients on a single covalent BTK inhibitor compared newly recorded AF/flutter over 365 days [S:abfb870a-1e13-595c-a1ef-f1e5ffc43e93]. Matching was 1:1 greedy nearest-neighbor (caliper 0.10 SD) on age, sex, race/ethnicity, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, COPD, chronic ischemic heart disease, [passage text removed], and anticoagulant/antiplatelet use [S:3cc39516-59d1-5167-aab1-da436ffbd21d].

- **Acalabrutinib vs ibrutinib:** 28/629 (4.5%) vs 77/641 (12.0%); risk difference −7.6 points, RR [passage text removed]), HR 0.387 (0.251–0.596) [S:a04a0dc9-1fe8-53ce-b9dd-18d7baa22b26].
- **Zanubrutinib vs ibrutinib:** 22/438 (5.0%) vs 54/439 (12.3%); risk difference −7.3 points, RR 0.408 (0.253–0.658), HR 0.421 (0.256–0.690) [S:32d73f3f-cec0-5bbf-838c-a694be906291].
- **Acalabrutinib vs zanubrutinib:** 18/449 (4.0%) vs 25/439 (5.7%); RR 0.704 (0.390–1.272), HR 0.714 (0.390–1.309) — not statistically distinguishable [S:32d73f3f-cec0-5bbf-838c-a694be906291].

The signal appeared early and persisted: at 180 days, acalabrutinib 3.5% vs ibrutinib 7.8% (RR 0.448, 0.275–0.731), zanubrutinib 3.4% vs ibrutinib 8.7% (RR 0.396, 0.221–0.709), and acalabrutinib vs zanubrutinib essentially identical at 3.3% vs 3.4% (RR 0.978, 0.484–1.976) [S:8c4f2346-5c32-53bd-bf96-0dd9f156fe2d].

**Other outcomes did not separate the drugs cleanly.** Heart failure showed no significant difference in any pairwise comparison (e.g., acalabrutinib 5.4% vs ibrutinib 6.1%, RR 0.893, 0.575–1.387) [S:a04a0dc9-1fe8-53ce-b9dd-18d7baa22b26]. GI bleeding was higher with ibrutinib vs acalabrutinib (4.3% vs 2.2%, RR 1.985) and numerically higher vs zanubrutinib (4.7% vs 3.3%, RR 1.443, not significant), with acalabrutinib-vs-zanubrutinib output unavailable — the authors label bleeding results exploratory and incomplete [S:1e793067-1017-50d8-ab46-fbdda6051a0d].

**Supporting MCL trial-level and indirect data.** In the pivotal ACE-LY-004 phase 2 acalabrutinib trial (n=124 relapsed MCL), any-grade AF was 2.4% [S:32b3839d-ecde-5ef3-9324-44d9547c710a]; a pooled zanubrutinib MCL safety analysis reported AF of 1.8% (0.9% grade ≥3) [S:3c847cbe-d2e4-5e20-a9e8-191ac40aefd2]. Across trials, AF has been reported at 10–17% all-grade with ibrutinib versus 0–5% with zanubrutinib and 1–7% with acalabrutinib [S:80aa5cae-9a03-57d4-8817-ec39cc6ae6e3]. A matching-adjusted indirect comparison in R/R MCL (122 acalabrutinib patients weighted to pooled ibrutinib trials) found significantly lower grade ≥3 AF with acalabrutinib, with no significant PFS or OS difference [S:c6bdf0fd-92ce-5781-abd0-e9e3dc66678c].

**Extrapolation from CLL is consistent but imperfect.** ELEVATE-RR showed all-grade AF 9.4% with acalabrutinib vs 16.0% with ibrutinib (p=0.02), and ALPINE 2.5% vs 10.1% (p=0.0014) [S:b866de99-dc4e-598e-82f9-612b3e02e2f1]. A CLL network meta-analysis found AF more common with ibrutinib than [passage text removed]), with no difference between the two second-generation agents; in sensitivity analysis the ibrutinib–acalabrutinib difference lost significance, and grade ≥3 AF was similar across all BTKi monotherapies [S:6d2be086-cbcd-5421-972b-8074f5d4070b]. The MCL authors caution that CLL data may not fully generalize given differences in disease biology, treatment sequence, aggressiveness, and competing risks [S:a93c7dec-3fc2-527a-89d2-2a68d1a961fa].

**Mechanism.** The AF liability appears off-target rather than BTK-mediated: patients with inactivating BTK mutations (XLA) do not develop AF, and in mouse models ibrutinib but not acalabrutinib induced AF, with CSK inhibition implicated [S:f886955f-87df-5d63-8abf-958bfb6b4b34].

**Caveats.** The MCL cohort study is observational; residual confounding is likely, and line of therapy, MIPI, TP53 status, treatment duration, dose intensity, and prior transplant/CAR-T could not be matched on [S:e522210a-75cd-5cc6-bb5c-2ff29bb9e8d0]. Outcomes were "newly recorded" rather than confirmed new-onset [S:3cc39516-59d1-5167-aab1-da436ffbd21d], and the authors explicitly state the findings should not be read as a definitive three-way safety hierarchy [S:6984b372-bfe1-5d9d-acc2-d08531958c1d]. Also note that acalabrutinib is not AF-free: a CLL meta-analysis of RCTs found a trend toward increased any-grade AF with acalabrutinib (RR 2.56, p=0.05) without increased high-grade events [S:5dc6196f-7ae3-5252-94ad-9c8b93d10a31]. I found no evidence of a randomized head-to-head acalabrutinib-versus-zanubrutinib trial in MCL.

rows.question: What psychological factors relate to distress in adults with autoimmune inflammatory rheumatic diseases?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Higher ruminative thinking is associated with greater psychological distress; Greater perceived compassion from others is associated with lower psychological distress independently of the other psychological, clinical and demographic factors examined; Self-compassion's association with lower distress appears weaker than that of perceived compassion from others. Certainty: The evidence is preliminary and correlational, drawn from a small, narrowly recruited group of participants, so the direction of influence cannot be established, and whether self-compassion carries less weight than compassion received from others remains unresolved. Scope: applies to autoimmune inflammatory rheumatic diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis) in adults, predominantly women in middle age, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents compassion-focused or rumination-targeted therapy as demonstrated to reduce anxiety and depression in inflammatory rheumatic disease, or recommends it on that basis as established care.

## Conclusion

Distress in adults with autoimmune inflammatory rheumatic diseases (AIRDs) is driven less by objective disease activity than by modifiable cognitive–emotional and interpersonal factors — chiefly rumination, helplessness, negative illness perceptions, experiential avoidance/maladaptive coping, and illness-related uncertainty — with self-efficacy, resilience, cognitive reappraisal, and compassionate social support acting protectively.

## Cognitive-emotional processes

**Rumination and pain-related cognition.** In 105 patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), psoriatic arthritis, or axial spondyloarthritis, hierarchical regression identified rumination as the strongest predictor of psychological distress (anxiety/depression), followed by pain intensity [S:63601215-4d97-57f3-9ff3-dd56d83dc85e]. The authors note this is among the first work on *general* ruminative thinking (not pain-focused rumination) in AIRDs [S:9d1f6903-e9ca-554b-a1e4-6ec96d16d4a6].

**Helplessness.** In SLE, helplessness (Arthritis Helplessness Index) *fully* mediated the relationship between pain and anxiety, depression, and perceived stress — pain itself no longer contributed once helplessness was accounted for [S:d2a173b8-844e-5c0e-ad41-2640e2f177ce, S:deef66bc-8b88-5ea2-81e8-a138abb8c07d]. A separate SLE outpatient study found learned helplessness correlated with depression (r = 0.588) and anxiety (r = 0.472), and with illness perception dimensions (consequences, identity, concern, emotional response), but not with disease activity, duration, age, gender, education, or employment [S:a9d29105-69fd-5ac1-a6de-62b1b782197f].

**Experiential avoidance vs. cognitive reappraisal.** In 97 AIRD patients, experiential avoidance explained how severe pain was linked to lowered euthymia; this indirect effect [passage text removed] reappraisal is protective [S:fea1fdbe-7b19-5b7f-a66b-d50f47855b58].

**Illness perceptions and coping.** Perceived consequences, identity, and emotional response were mediators between depression and pain in RA [S:3d23f22b-a14d-5ce6-a37a-95b1c36c2c25] and were negatively associated with HRQoL domains, while [passage text removed] [S:762a2b03-343e-54bf-be26-1a3d8a105612, S:edc639d0-9aeb-50cb-a3c8-84e8b10eba1e]. In 210 hospitalized RA patients, dysfunctional coping mediated the link between illness beliefs ([passage text removed] depression [S:3ce38e2c-3cdb-5981-bda6-cae5360b1f70]. In SLE, [passage text removed], whereas disease activity and organ damage showed no association with illness perception [S:8910eb85-5177-55c2-9853-ee6e6e0274be]; negative illness perception clustered with anxiety, depression, pain, fatigue, and poor sleep [S:d364aea9-905a-5233-8e89-98c9826c16fa].

**Uncertainty.** Illness-related uncertainty is prevalent in systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases and associated with poor emotional well-being [S:684a3c4c-fe8a-53ac-88eb-6832dd81aa38]. A newly validated brief measure (developed in IgG4-related disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, systemic sclerosis; confirmed in vasculitis) captured *ambiguity* and *unpredictability* and showed small-to-moderate associations with anxiety, depression, and sickness impact after adjusting for age and sex [S:8a8dfb7a-f362-5722-a921-4b3b313a65cd, S:3853f53d-ac58-54e8-87da-ec8e780c4a60, S:9139fbcc-c9e3-5456-be6e-881ab89499a9].

Recent stressful life events predicted perceived stress in SLE, but significantly only among those with prior trauma or ≥2 adverse childhood experiences [S:821329fd-e082-5ee3-9e1b-1943806e512c]; those with trauma history [passage text removed]]. In early arthritis, [passage text removed] were associated with disease presence [S:80a2cf04-7b67-589c-9c1c-7be98d71629b]. rows.question: What is known about which patient characteristics accompany the choice of JAK inhibitors, IL-6 inhibitors or CTLA4-Ig in rheumatoid arthritis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: JAK inhibitors are more often started in patients who lack features that would make them ineligible for the pivotal trials; IL-6 inhibitors and CTLA4-Ig are more often selected for patients with anaemia or organ dysfunction; Trial-ineligibility features are unevenly distributed across the biologic and targeted synthetic DMARD classes; This allocation is described as deliberate safety-driven prescribing, that is channelling of higher-risk patients towards particular classes. Certainty: The evidence is descriptive rather than comparative, drawn from prescribing as it occurred across several Japanese treatment sites, so it indicates how clinicians distribute patients across drug classes rather than how those classes perform in such patients, and allocation habits in other settings may differ. Scope: applies to rheumatoid arthritis requiring biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD therapy in adults treated in Japanese specialist practice, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents IL-6 inhibitors or CTLA4-Ig as demonstrated to be more effective or safer than other classes in patients with anaemia or organ dysfunction, or recommends class selection on that basis as established.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Choice among JAK inhibitors, IL‑6 inhibitors and abatacept (CTLA4‑Ig) is strongly channelled: all three are used predominantly in later treatment lines than TNF inhibitors, abatacept is channelled toward older and more comorbid patients, IL‑6 inhibitors toward older, longer‑duration, higher‑disease‑activity and methotrexate‑intolerant patients, and JAK inhibitors toward heavily pre‑treated patients — with a documented shift after 2021–22 safety warnings toward younger patients with fewer cardiovascular risk factors.

## Line of therapy and co-medication (common to all three)

In a nationwide Swedish register cohort of RA patients starting TNFi (n=6,422), JAKi (n=1,827), IL‑6 inhibitors ([passage text removed]–2019, TNFi and rituximab were used mainly in earlier lines while abatacept, IL‑6 inhibitors and JAKi were more often later lines; TNFi starters had slightly lower disease activity and more frequent csDMARD co-treatment, and confounder adjustment required demographics, comorbidities, treatment line, glucocorticoid/NSAID co-treatment and RA characteristics (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11865685; summarised at [passage text removed]

- **Heavily pre-treated, active disease, less MTX/steroid co-therapy:** In a US rheumatology EMR registry (22,929 initiators/switchers; 13% JAKi), JAKi recipients had more prior regimens, less methotrexate and glucocorticoid use, more commercial insurance, and moderate/high disease activity and higher number of prior regimens independently predicted JAKi over biologics; non-commercial payer predicted against JAKi ([passage text removed]).
- **Older, longer disease duration, more comorbidity when used first-line:** In the CorEvitas RA Registry, first-line JAKi initiators were older with longer disease duration than etanercept or adalimumab initiators, less often on combination csDMARD therapy, and had higher prevalence of cardiovascular disease and malignancies ([passage text removed]).
- **Within-class channelling:** In a French single-centre cohort of 120 first JAKi initiations, baricitinib went to older, more comorbid patients with the most erosive disease and most prior neoplasia, upadacitinib to younger patients with the highest joint counts, and filgotinib exclusively to women in line with reproductive-safety advice ([passage text removed]).
- **Post-warning shift:** A Finnish nationwide register time-series found that after the safety alerts, JAKi initiation declined and shifted toward younger patients with fewer atherosclerotic risk factors (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42156017; [passage text removed]); a multi-registry analysis found [passage text removed] (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41722160). Regulators explicitly direct prescribers to age ≥65, smoking, cardiovascular and malignancy risk and VTE risk factors when choosing JAKi ([passage text removed]). Applying these criteria, an Italian cohort classified over half of 194 patients as JAKi-"ineligible", mainly for MACE risk, then age >65, smoking, VTE and malignancy ([passage text removed]). Note one earlier French study found VTE risk-factor profiles of baricitinib/tofacitinib starters did not differ significantly before vs after the EMA warning ([passage text removed]).

## IL‑6 inhibitors

- **Older, longer-standing, more active, later-line disease:** In CorEvitas, IL‑6Ri monotherapy initiators were older, had longer RA history and higher baseline CDAI than TNFi monotherapy initiators and were more often third-line; IL‑6Ri combination initiators also had higher CDAI and were more often third-line (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37060528). In a separate CorEvitas analysis, IL‑6Ri initiators had the highest mean baseline CDAI and HAQ, longer mean RA duration than TNFi initiators, and were mostly third-or-higher-line ([passage text removed]-022-02955-y).
- **Monotherapy channelling (methotrexate-inappropriate patients):** In the French ACT‑SOLO study (n=577), independent predictors of tocilizumab monotherapy were age ≥65 years (OR 1.56) and no methotrexate in the previous 2 years (OR 5.74); monotherapy patients were slightly older, more comorbid and had higher baseline DAS28‑ESR ([passage text removed]).
- **Inflammatory-phenotype signals:** IL‑6R inhibition produced greater haemoglobin rise and CRP fall than TNFi or JAKi in CorEvitas ([passage text removed]-022-02955-y), and registry work has proposed anaemia and high CRP as markers favouring IL‑6 blockade (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37354495; [passage text removed]). Higher comorbidity burden among tocilizumab initiators was also seen in US claims (mean Elixhauser score highest for tocilizumab vs abatacept/TNFi) ([passage text removed]).

## Abatacept (CTLA4-Ig)

- **Age, comorbidity count, infection/TB risk, prior adverse events, monotherapy preference:** In the Italian LORHEN registry (1,910 patients), age was higher in abatacept and tocilizumab than TNFi starters; ≥2 comorbidities was significantly associated with abatacept over both tocilizumab and TNFi; positive latent TB screening, dyslipidaemia and hypertension featured in the abatacept group; discontinuation of a prior bDMARD for adverse events pushed choice toward abatacept, while high DAS28, latent-TB positivity and pulmonary/cardiovascular comorbidity favoured second-line tocilizumab. The authors concluded age, infection risk, number/type of comorbidities and preference for monotherapy were the main drivers ([passage text removed]).
- **US claims confirm the same gradient:** Abatacept initiators were older, more often women, and had more comorbidities (e.g. hypertension 32.5% vs 26.3%, type 2 diabetes 13.6% vs 11.0%, COPD 6.8% vs 5.3%, CKD 2.2% vs 1.7%) and less baseline methotrexate/NSAID use than other bDMARD initiators; the authors noted patients receiving abatacept "[passage text removed]). In an ACPA+/RF+ real-world cohort, abatacept was more likely than first-line TNFi with delayed [passage text removed] and older age, with numerically higher Charlson index ([passage text removed]). Clinic-based data likewise show abatacept starters older (67.0 vs 60.3 years) with more pre-index hospitalisations than TNFi starters ([passage text removed]).
- **Seropositivity as a selection factor:** Abatacept is preferentially studied/used in ACPA/RF-positive patients, and higher baseline anti‑CCP2 titres were associated with greater improvement with abatacept but not TNFi ([passage text removed]).

## Why this matters

These characteristics are the classic source of channelling bias. In a US claims cohort of 25,305 RA patients, rituximab, abatacept and JAKi showed higher 2-year incident cancer rates than TNFi (rituximab [passage text removed]; JAKi [passage text removed]), and commentators attributed much of this to channelling rather than drug effect (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39565623; [passage text removed]). In a Spanish registry of patients with prior malignancy, IL‑6Ri and abatacept carried the numerically highest cancer IRRs while JAKi and rituximab were lowest — but follow-up was longest for IL‑6Ri/abatacept and shortest for JAKi/rituximab, again indicating differential channelling ([passage text removed]).

**Caveats:** most of these data are observational registry/claims analyses from Europe, the US and Japan; few directly model three-way choice between JAKi, IL‑6i and abatacept (most compare each against TNFi), and I found no source quantifying head-to-head determinants of choosing IL‑6 inhibition versus JAK inhibition versus CTLA4‑Ig in the same model. Some studies report only minor profile differences between biologic and JAKi recipients (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40004820), so the magnitude of channelling varies by health system and era.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Choice among these three classes is strongly non-random: across registries and claims databases, **IL-6 inhibitors and CTLA4-Ig are channelled toward older, frailer, more comorbid patients (anaemia, low eGFR, high glucocorticoid dose, no methotrexate), whereas JAK inhibitors are given to comparatively "cleaner," younger, trial-eligible patients, more often at second or later line** — with country-level exceptions and a further shift away from JAKi after the ORAL Surveillance/PRAC safety warnings.

## Evidence by characteristic

**Organ function, haematology and trial-eligibility.** In the Japanese FIRST registry (5462 b/tsDMARD initiations, 2003–2023), the proportion of patients who would have met at least one phase III RCT exclusion criterion was highest for IL-[passage text removed] for JAK inhibitors (31.0%) [S:0ad26298][S:770c50b8]. Item-level differences: haemoglobin <10 g/dL in 20.5% of IL-6 inhibitor and 17.9% of CTLA4-Ig starters versus 8.7% of JAKi starters; eGFR <40 in 10.9% and 9.2% versus 4.1%; prednisolone ≥10 mg in 11.9% and 8.3% versus 6.0%; lymphocyte count <800/µL was most frequent with CTLA4-Ig (18.5%) [S:770c50b8]. The authors interpret this as JAK inhibitors being preferentially prescribed to patients without trial-ineligibility features, while IL-6 inhibitors and CTLA4-Ig are [passage text removed], reflecting safety concerns in higher-risk patients plus the anaemia-correcting and monotherapy-capable profile of IL-6 blockade [S:8bd63095].

**Age, renal function and methotrexate co-therapy.** A 20-year, 5130-case FIRST registry follow-up found [passage text removed] with lower eGFR and lower concomitant MTX use, while TNFi went to younger patients with higher eGFR and higher MTX use [S:4d809c3e][S:5f6b9c40]. In the KURAMA cohort, concomitant MTX in b/tsDMARD-naïve patients was 74.5% for TNFi but 40.7% for IL-6Ri, 47.3% for CTLA4-Ig and 62.0% for JAKi [S:0620ece9]. EULAR guidance explicitly names IL-6 pathway inhibition as a preferred option when MTX is inappropriate or contraindicated, which underpins this pattern [S:dd775f52][S:1ddb4f61].

**Age, sex and comorbidity burden as formal determinants.** In a Japanese MDV claims cohort (2008–2020), age 61–75 [passage text removed] TNFi (OR 0.72; OR 0.55) and IL-6i (OR 0.80; OR 0.53) but strong *positive* determinants of first-line CTLA4-Ig (OR 2.23; OR 4.31). Female sex favoured TNFi (OR 1.11) and disfavoured IL-6i (OR 0.86) and JAKi (OR 0.76) [S:aabb81a4]. Higher Charlson comorbidity scores were negative determinants of TNFi use (OR 0.68 for CCI 3–5; 0.51 for CCI >5) [S:aabb81a4]. The authors attribute the age-related shift to serious-infection risk with TNFi/IL-6i in elderly Japanese patients, ACR guidance favouring abatacept after prior serious infection, and lower risk of worsening pre-existing ILD with CTLA4-Ig [S:78dc29f4]. The same study found non-TNFi classes (IL-6i, CTLA4-Ig, JAKi) were more often given as monotherapy, and JAKi were more frequently prescribed second- or third-line than first-line [S:237c2518].

**Line of therapy and refractoriness.** In a head-to-head Japanese comparison, among previous-bDMARD-failure patients, tofacitinib recipients were older (66.7 vs 61.6 years), had longer disease duration (13.9 vs 11.2 years), and less often used concomitant MTX (54.5% vs 69.5%) and prednisolone (27.3% vs 46.3%) than tocilizumab recipients [S:ac1dffbd]. A FIRST-registry machine-learning analysis found patients with higher predicted difficult-to-treat risk [passage text removed] (mean score 0.94 vs 0.65 for JAKi), though [passage text removed]) [S:63e1b48d]. In low-inflammatory difficult-to-treat RA, JAKi were the most frequently chosen post-switch agent [S:234cba3d].

**Cardiovascular/malignancy risk and regulatory pressure.** EULAR/PRAC guidance directs clinicians to assess age >65, smoking, prior thromboembolism and malignancy history before starting a JAK inhibitor [S:bded7c84]. A survey of 21 Italian centres (4421 pre-PRAC vs 4376 post-PRAC RA patients) documented a 4.9% absolute fall in JAKi use (p=0.0003; baricitinib −3.0%, filgotinib −1.5%, tofacitinib −1.4%, upadacitinib non-significant −0.3%) with a concurrent rise in IL-6 receptor inhibitor prescriptions from 10.7% to 17%, while abatacept use remained stable — though mean patient age and comorbidity prevalence did not differ significantly between periods [S:878525c8][S:a6a15cd0]. A systematic review of difficult-to-treat RA similarly concluded JAKi improved disease activity but require [passage text removed] comorbidity, whereas abatacept was effective and safe in RA-ILD [S:9d87b014].

**Serology.** Prescribing may also be influenced by autoantibody status: an abatacept observational study explicitly flagged selection bias from serological status, since ACPA positivity predicts better response to abatacept [S:cffc70f4]; pooled European register data show the seropositive-versus-seronegative remission advantage is larger for abatacept (+1.5%) and rituximab (+5.9%) than for tocilizumab (+0.9%) or TNFi (−0.1%) [S:c0f5ef3d]. I found no study directly demonstrating that rheumatologists select CTLA4-Ig over JAKi *because of* serostatus.

## Caveats

Direction is not uniform across health systems: in Brazilian DATASUS claims, age >50 years was associated with *greater* likelihood of initiating a JAK inhibitor (OR 1.78) and with switching from bDMARD to JAKi (HR 1.08), alongside non-clinical determinants such as distance from the treating centre [S:f527851b]. In a Korean claims cohort, JAKi initiators were older than bDMARD initiators before matching (55.4 vs 50.6 years) [S:206e3417]. Most of the class-level channelling evidence above is Japanese, so generalisability is limited, and all of it is observational — comparative-effectiveness authors consistently identify this channelling as the principal source of confounding [S:86205f7d][S:63e1b48d].

rows.question: Which ocular manifestations occur in children with juvenile systemic lupus erythematosus on ophthalmologic screening?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Dry eye abnormalities are the predominant finding on ophthalmologic examination, with a short tear film break-up time in most children and positive fluorescein staining in nearly half; Only a small minority of these children report dry eye symptoms, so the abnormalities are picked up on examination rather than from complaints; Fundus examination and optical coherence tomography showed no retinal structural change attributable to hydroxychloroquine in children whose cumulative dose and duration of use were low; Inflammatory, glaucomatous and vaso-occlusive ocular lesions such as retinitis, optic neuritis, scleritis and glaucoma were not found on examination. Certainty: These are single-examination observations from a small group of children without a comparison group, and the proportion classified as having dry eye depends on the criteria applied, so they should be treated as provisional. Scope: applies to juvenile systemic lupus erythematosus in children and adolescents, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents these tear film and staining abnormalities as establishing secondary Sjögren's syndrome in most affected children or recommends starting treatment for that diagnosis on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

On systematic ophthalmologic screening, most children with juvenile SLE (JSLE) have **ocular surface/dry eye disease — often asymptomatic — while sight-threatening findings (uveitis, vaso-occlusive retinopathy, optic neuropathy) are uncommon**; a substantial share of detectable ocular damage is drug-induced (corticosteroid cataract/glaucoma, hydroxychloroquine retinopathy) rather than inflammatory.

## Overall burden

A systematic review of 42 studies found that across 9 cohort studies (2,696 JSLE patients), 212 (7.8%) reported ocular manifestations, whereas in 4 cross-sectional studies (210 patients) 155 had ocular findings — a gap that reflects active screening versus routine care. Retinal involvement was the most frequently reported category; the review's headline manifestations were [passage text removed] cataract. Of 34 patients in case reports/series, 15 (44%) had the ocular finding as the inaugural manifestation of JSLE ([Nikolaidou et al., Eye 2025, doi:10.1038/s41433-025-03664-x]([passage text removed]); [PMC11978895]([passage text removed])).

## 1. Ocular surface / dry eye disease — the dominant screening finding

- In a Brazilian cross-sectional study of 46 JSLE [passage text removed] dry eye disease criteria, with tear break-up time <5 s in 76%, abnormal fluorescein staining in 45.65%, and Schirmer <10 mm in 21.7% — yet **only 8.7% reported dry eye symptoms**. Mycophenolate use was associated with DED (p = .041) ([Lupus 35(2):182–188, doi:10.1177/09612033251408937]([passage text removed]); [PMID 41529287](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41529287)).
- In 40 Egyptian children with JSLE (mean age 13 ± 2.8 y; mean SLEDAI-2K [passage text removed] (40%); photophobia was the presenting symptom in 24 (60%), with ocular hyperaemia in 4 and periorbital oedema in 1 (Gawdat et al., Semin Ophthalmol 2018;33:[passage text removed] — [abstract]([passage text removed]); patient-level detail in [PMC11978895]([passage text removed])).
- A prospective controlled study of 34 children with SLE found higher corneal fluorescein scores than [passage text removed]) and more abnormal corneal fluorescein scores ([passage text removed]) (Ong Tone et al., Cornea 2019;38:581–586, as summarised in [PMC11978895]([passage text removed]) and cited by [AAO]([passage text removed])).
- Al-Mayouf et al. found abnormal Schirmer testing in 7 of 52 JSLE patients (2 bilateral), without associated Sjögren's syndrome, and noted keratoconjunctivitis sicca may co-occur [passage text removed] ([PMC11978895]([passage text removed])).

## 2. Anterior segment and cornea

Episcleritis and corticosteroid-induced cataract were each seen in 1 patient in a Turkish cohort of 42; corneal vortex keratopathy was reported in a Brazilian series of 76 patients; bilateral iridocyclitis coinciding with a systemic flare was described by Al-Mayouf; periorbital oedema and ecchymosis were the commonest orbital findings ([PMC11978895]([passage text removed]), [Eye 2025]([passage text removed])).

## 3. Uveitis

In a retrospective multicentre survey of 852 childhood-onset SLE patients, 7 (0.8%) had uveitis — 4 posterior, 1 panuveitis — with average onset age 10 years (range 8–14); uveitis was present at JSLE diagnosis in 4 (57%). Uveitis patients had higher disease activity (SLEDAI-2K 19 vs 6; p < 0.01), and one developed retinal ischaemia with neovascularisation and unilateral blindness; four choroidal haemorrhages were also observed (Kahwage et al., Clin Rheumatol 2017;36:[passage text removed], as detailed in [Eye 2025]([passage text removed])).

## 4. Retina and choroid

- **Hypertensive/vascular retinopathy:** 7 of 40 children had retinal vascular changes (arteriovenous crossing in 2, arterial attenuation in 3, congested tortuous veins in 2); all had systemic hypertension, and changes correlated with hypertension rather than disease activity or duration. Fraga et al. reported cotton wool spots and papilloedema in 3 (25%) of 12 hypertensive JSLE patients ([Eye 2025]([passage text removed])).
- **Severe vaso-occlusive retinopathy** is rare but devastating: reported cases include bilateral vaso-occlusive retinopathy with a macular "cherry-red spot", [passage text removed] progressing to tractional retinal detachment, and combined central retinal artery and vein occlusion with subsequent vitreous haemorrhage despite steroids, anticoagulation, immunosuppression and panretinal photocoagulation ([Eye 2025]([passage text removed])).
- **Choroid:** OCT-measured choroidal thickness and total subfoveal choroidal, luminal and stromal areas were significantly greater in JSLE patients than controls ([Eye 2025]([passage text removed])).

## 5. Neuro-ophthalmic

The review's cohort data include unilateral optic neuropathy in 3 patients and visual field defects in 11 (4 bilateral, 7 unilateral), and it lists optic atrophy among reported findings ([PMC11978895]([passage text removed])).

## 6. Treatment-related (a major yield of screening)

- In a Malaysian cohort of 141 JSLE children (median age 10.8 y), [passage text removed] at 29.7% (42 patients) and was predominantly corticosteroid-related (93%): cataract in 29/42 and glaucoma in 10/42 ([PMC11978895]([passage text removed])).
- Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy is listed as a recognised medication adverse event in JSLE ([Eye 2025]([passage text removed])), though in the 46-patient Brazilian cohort **no SD-OCT abnormalities attributable to HCQ toxicity were found** (median cumulative dose 204 g, median duration 2 years) ([doi:10.1177/09612033251408937]([passage text removed])). Microperimetry has been proposed for detecting early HCQ retinal toxicity in JSLE children (Youssef et al., Ophthalmologica 2017;237:180–184, as referenced in [MDPI J Clin Med 13:1047]([passage text removed])) — I did not retrieve that paper's results directly.

## 7. Subclinical findings detectable only with imaging

OCT-angiography detected reduced deep capillary plexus vessel density in JSLE patients with an otherwise normal ocular examination (Yılmaz Tuğan et al., Ocul Immunol Inflamm 2023;[passage text removed] — [summary]([passage text removed] macular vessel density alterations were also reported (Xu & Zhang, Lupus 2023;32:1619–1624) and meibomian gland changes in JSLE patients without dry eye symptoms or [passage text removed]) — both identified via reference lists ([maxapress OCTA review]([passage text removed]); [MDPI 13:1047]([passage text removed])).

## Screening implications

No established guidelines exist for routine ophthalmologic evaluation in JSLE; the systematic review recommends a comprehensive baseline examination at diagnosis, routine follow-up **every 6 months regardless of symptoms**, more frequent assessment in severe or active disease, and prompt evaluation for any visual change, pain, redness, photophobia or floaters ([Eye 2025]([passage text removed])). The high rate of asymptomatic dry eye disease and of subclinical microvascular change supports this.

**Caveats:** Much of the evidence is case reports/series and small single-centre cross-sectional studies with heterogeneous definitions; prevalence figures above are therefore study-specific, not pooled estimates.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** On systematic ophthalmologic screening, children with juvenile SLE (JSLE) most often show subclinical ocular-surface disease (dry eye/keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and treatment-related changes (corticosteroid cataract/glaucoma, fundus changes), while sight-threatening disease — retinal vaso-occlusion/vasculitis, uveitis, choroidopathy and optic neuropathy — is uncommon but the main cause of visual loss.

## Overall frequency and spectrum
A systematic review of 42 studies found that among 9 cohort studies (2696 patients), 212 (7.8%) reported ocular manifestations, whereas in 4 cross-sectional screening studies 155 of 210 patients had ocular findings; retinal involvement was the most frequently reported, and the notable manifestations were [passage text removed] cataract [S:2600e2fd]. Findings are grouped as external/adnexal, anterior segment, posterior segment, neuro-ophthalmic, and drug-induced [S:2600e2fd], with ocular symptoms sometimes being the first indication of disease onset [S:4f37a6da].

## Ocular surface / dry eye (the dominant screening finding, usually asymptomatic)
- In a Brazilian cross-sectional study of 46 JSLE patients <18 years (median age 10 years, 84.8% female) undergoing BCVA, BUT, Schirmer, fluorescein staining with van Bijsterveld scoring, tonometry, fundoscopy and SD-OCT [S:e7550571][S:02b43780], 76.1% met 2006 Japanese Dry Eye Society criteria for dry eye disease but only 8.7% reported symptoms; BUT <5 s in 76%, abnormal fluorescein staining in 45.65%, van Bijsterveld ≥4 in 23.9%, Schirmer <5 mm/5 min in 21.75%, and 32.6% met ocular Sjögren's criteria [S:f3e1fc8f][S:9dee5316]. Dry eye was associated with mycophenolate use (p = .041) but not with antibody or complement levels, corticosteroid use, SLEDAI or SLICC damage scores [S:bb197a74][S:f3e1fc8f].
- Other screening cohorts: abnormal Schirmer test in 16/40 patients (40%), with photophobia reported as the first symptom by 60%; abnormal Schirmer in 7/52 patients in another series; and children with SLE had higher corneal fluorescein staining scores than healthy children [S:654de6bb]. Keratoconjunctivitis sicca in JSLE may coexist [passage text removed] [S:654de6bb].

## Eyelid / external and anterior segment
Reported eyelid findings include diffuse lid redness, darkened skin, discoid eruptions, and bilateral eyelid oedema (the latter in the context of iridocyclitis or with renal involvement) [S:bdf4b934]. Episcleritis was found in 1 of 21 screened patients in one cross-sectional study and in 1 of 40 in another (sectoral); diffuse scleritis with anterior uveitis, choroidal and RPE detachment has been described [S:d474fc9a][S:0b0e7a39]. Corneal involvement with peripheral scarring/stromal inflammation has also been reported [S:d474fc9a].

## Posterior segment
- Fundoscopic abnormalities on screening include cotton-wool spots, papilledema and macular changes, often associated with systemic hypertension and/or antimalarial use [S:d391bc4c].
- Vaso-occlusive retinopathy and retinal vasculitis: branch and central retinal artery/vein occlusion, macular ischaemia, intraretinal haemorrhage, cotton-wool spots, retinal neovascularization, vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment, and Purtscher-like retinopathy, frequently as the inaugural manifestation of JSLE [S:5e05acf5][S:71170848][S:356822a7][S:83adf8d0]. Retinal findings are attributed to antiphospholipid antibodies/immune-complex vasculopathy, active vasculitis and thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, hypertension and infection risk from immunosuppression [S:8e06be2c].
- Irreversible bilateral blindness from retinal vasculitis and/or severe uveitis occurred in 2 of 263 JSLE patients (0.8%) in a single-centre series, associated with disease activity and viral infection [S:a9d6a124]; one case had severe iridocyclitis with retinal vasculitis and haemorrhage [S:980632a0]. Chorioretinal scars attributed to prior chorioretinitis with neurological JSLE have also been reported [S:7f6e7d96].
- In the Brazilian screening cohort, SD-OCT (32 patients) showed only one abnormality — an 18-year-old with JSLE and common variable immunodeficiency who had asymptomatic granulomatous uveitis (granulomatous keratic precipitates, iris nodules, mild disc hyperemia, 1+ vitritis, snowballs) with angiographically confirmed active retinal vasculitis; no acute retinitis, optic neuritis, scleritis, glaucoma, drusen or vascular-occlusion sequelae were found [S:02b43780][S:f3e1fc8f].

## Neuro-ophthalmic
Fourteen studies in the systematic review reported optic nerve involvement — optic neuritis/neuropathy, optic atrophy and papilledema — all in teenage females; unilateral disease is attributed to focal thrombosis and bilateral disease to systemic vasculitis, while papilledema usually accompanies retinal changes in intracranial hypertension [S:7f6e7d96].

## Drug-related findings
- Corticosteroid-induced cataract and glaucoma are the most prevalent medication-related findings [S:d391bc4c]. In 117 JSLE patients, 24 (20.5%) had ocular changes: 16 with abnormal fundoscopy linked to hypertension and/or chloroquine, 4 cataract, 2 glaucoma, 2 both; patients with ocular changes had received higher and longer glucocorticoid pulse therapy [S:ec8bcb88]. In a 12-year cohort of [passage text removed]%) and 93% of findings were corticosteroid-related (29 cataracts, 10 glaucoma) [S:d391bc4c]. Posterior subcapsular cataract occurred in 4/52 patients in another series, and single cases of steroid cataract were found in 1/21 and 1/40 screened patients [S:d391bc4c][S:0b0e7a39].
- Hydroxychloroquine maculopathy is the key screening concern but was not detected in the Brazilian cohort (median cumulative HCQ dose 204 g, median 2 years of use), consistent with low exposure; the authors note adult-based AAO screening guidelines still need validation in children [S:9dee5316][S:fc174746][S:02b43780]. Likewise, no retinal pigmentation or visual-field defects were seen despite hydroxychloroquine in a 21-patient cohort [S:8d29929e].

## Subclinical imaging abnormalities in eyes that look normal
Screening with OCT/OCTA detects changes before clinical retinopathy: choroidal thickness was significantly greater at all five measured points in 21 jSLE patients versus controls, with normal peripapillary RNFL and no intraretinal/subretinal fluid [S:17614b62][S:0b0e7a39]; and macular vessel density was reduced in all retinal layers and in the choriocapillaris in JSLE patients without ocular involvement, prompting the authors to recommend early screening and close follow-up [S:9d37787d][S:1d2551f3].

## Practical implication
Because most findings (especially dry eye and early cataract) are asymptomatic, multiple authors conclude routine/regular ophthalmologic examination of all JSLE children — including asymptomatic ones — is warranted [S:ec8bcb88][S:bb197a74][S:87b0ef48]. Pathophysiology in children remains inadequately characterised, and pediatric-specific diagnostic thresholds for dry eye and HCQ screening are not yet validated [S:4f37a6da][S:30a8d4f7].

rows.question: What outcomes follow allogeneic stem cell transplantation in high-risk chronic lymphocytic leukaemia?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Most patients are alive and free of progression two years after transplantation; Survival free of graft-versus-host disease and relapse is clearly lower than overall survival; Acute and chronic graft-versus-host disease each develop in a substantial proportion of transplanted patients; Late relapses after transplantation continue to be observed. Certainty: The supporting evidence comes from one small, mixed group of transplant recipients that also encompassed Richter transformation, so the outcome estimates should be treated as provisional rather than established. Scope: applies to high-risk or heavily pretreated chronic lymphocytic leukaemia treated with allogeneic stem cell transplantation in adults, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents post-transplant cyclophosphamide or post-transplant ibrutinib as an established means of reducing graft-versus-host disease, or recommends either on that basis.

[S:https://www.nature.com/articles/bmt2016282]
- Prospective trial with 10-year follow-up (GCLLSG CLL3X, RIC): OS 51%, PFS 34%, relapse 46%, NRM 20%, with long-lasting remissions in about one-third. [[passage text removed]]
- CIBMTR RIC cohort (606 patients, 2008–2014): 4-year OS 56%, PFS 41%. A meta-analysis of 1,903 patients gave pooled OS 51–60%, PFS 41–46%, NRM 23–32% (RIC vs MAC: PFS 46% vs 41%, OS 60% vs 51%, NRM 23% vs 32%). [[passage text removed]]

**TP53-aberrant / adverse-cytogenetic disease**
A prospective EBMT observational study of 39 patients with del(17p)/*TP53*-mutant CLL reported 5-year OS 49%, RFS 29%, cumulative relapse 42% and NRM 29%; 11 of 39 died without relapse, GVHD-related in 7. [[passage text removed]] Across studies, durable remissions still occur in a subset with high-risk cytogenetics (reported OS 44–60%, PFS 29–43%), though evidence on whether del(17p)/complex karyotype worsens post-transplant PFS is conflicting. [[passage text removed]]

**GVHD and toxicity**
Grade II–IV acute GVHD ~46% and chronic GVHD ~55–59% in the meta-analysis. [[passage text removed]] In the TP53 study acute grade II–IV GVHD was 36% and 1-year chronic GVHD 63%. [[passage text removed]] In an EBMT idelalisib-exposed cohort, acute GVHD grades II–IV 51% (III–IV 24%), 1-year chronic GVHD 39%, and 2-year NRM 31%, with infection (n=8) and GVHD (n=7) the leading causes of non-relapse death. [[passage text removed]]

**Prognostic determinants**
Outcome is strongly risk-stratified: a RIC prognostic model gave 5-year PFS of 83%, 63%, 24% and 6% for scores 0, 1, 2 and ≥3. [[passage text removed]] Refractory/bulky disease pre-transplant predicts progression, and post-transplant MRD status drives relapse risk; in a prospective MRD-driven immune-intervention trial, achieving MRD negativity at any time point was associated with less [passage text removed]) and better PFS (HR 0.18) and OS (HR 0.18). [S:https://haematologica.org/article/view/9779]

**After BTK/BCL2 inhibitor exposure (contemporary era)**
Outcomes remain favourable: 30 patients previously given a BTK and/or BCL2 inhibitor had 3-year OS 87% and PFS 72%; a second series of 65 heavily pretreated patients had 2-year OS 81% and PFS 63%, irrespective of number or class of prior novel agent. [[passage text removed]] An EBMT registry analysis of double-exposed patients (n=105, median age 59) reported 3-year GRFS 30%, PFS 48%, OS 56%, relapse 30%, NRM 21%; triple-exposed patients (n=22) had 3-year GRFS 20%, PFS 36%, OS 56%, relapse 34%, NRM 30%, with most relapse and NRM events in the first 6 months. Disease responsiveness at transplant mattered (3-year PFS 51% double-exposed responsive), and the del(17p)/*TP53* subgroup (n=38) had 3-year PFS 42%, OS 49%, NRM 22%, relapse 35%. [[passage text removed]] A single-centre intent-to-treat application of the ERIC/EBMT algorithm transplanted 16 patients with 2-year PFS 71% and OS 88% and no non-relapse mortality, including after failure of a first pathway inhibitor. [S:https://haematologica.org/article/view/8986]

**Relapse after transplant is salvageable**
Options include immunosuppression withdrawal, DLI, and BTK/BCL2 inhibitors; DLI results are inconsistent (complete responses in 20/43 patients in one report vs sustained remission in only 2/13 in another) and carry a 38–48% risk of clinically significant GVHD. [[passage text removed]]

**Current positioning**
The 2025 ASTCT recommendations place CAR-T for patients progressing after ≥2 lines including a covalent BTKi and a BCL2 inhibitor, recommend CAR-T for relapse after allo-HCT, and recommend allo-HCT for disease relapsed/refractory to CAR-T provided an objective response is demonstrated pre-transplant, plus for clonally related Richter transformation in objective response. [S:https://digitalcommons.providence.org/publications/10627][[passage text removed]] The EBMT Handbook likewise treats allo-HCT [passage text removed] failing at least two pathway-inhibitor classes. [[passage text removed]]

**Caveat:** none of these outcome estimates come from randomised comparisons; the comparative studies favouring transplant were largely pre-BTK/BCL2-inhibitor era and are subject to selection bias, so whether allo-HCT outperforms modern alternatives remains unresolved. [[passage text removed]]

## Bottom line

Allogeneic HCT is the only therapy with proven curative potential in high-risk CLL, delivering durable MRD-negative remission in roughly a third of patients long-term, but at the cost of substantial GVHD, non-relapse mortality (NRM), and a continuing relapse risk [S:3e6a32af][S:615109e1].

## Long-term survival and cure fraction

- [passage text removed] of RIC allo-HCT for poor-risk CLL, 10-year OS was [passage text removed]%; EBMT registry data gave [passage text removed] at 10 years [S:615109e1].
- CLL3X at 6 years showed [passage text removed] poor-risk mutations [S:1d3020d2]; the 4-year OS was 65% for the whole cohort, with overall response 94% [S:f7d7a4c0].
- Later events do occur: relapse ultimately affects more than 30% of patients, late relapses have been reported beyond 20 years, and survivors carry persistently elevated late NRM and secondary-malignancy risk, so survivorship care is needed [S:33916317][S:615109e1].

## Effect of conditioning intensity

Myeloablative conditioning was historically limited by transplant-related mortality of 38–50% [S:dd584972]. RIC reduced NRM (to as low as ~15% in some series) while preserving the graft-versus-leukaemia (GVL) effect [S:b7c4fa9b]. Across four classic RIC/nonmyeloablative series (n = 76–90), 4–5-year PFS was 36–43%, OS 50–70%, NRM 16–23%, and 100-day mortality ≤10% [S:b7c4fa9b]. A Dana-Farber comparison found similar 3-year OS for RIC vs myeloablative (65% vs 50%) but lower NRM with RIC (15% vs 54%) offset by higher relapse (30% vs 8%) [S:7bb2abf1].

## Does transplant overcome adverse biology?

Largely yes, though not uniformly. Phase II and registry data show long-term disease control in 30–45% of patients with del(17p)/TP53 mutation, and purine-analogue refractoriness did not independently worsen PFS in CLL3X or the Seattle series (5-year PFS 39% despite 87% fludarabine-refractory) [S:531bf5d5]. An EBMT analysis of 44 del(17p) patients showed 3-year PFS 37% with no event beyond 3.5 years [S:531bf5d5]; in CLL3X, 7 of 13 del(17p) recipients remained in CR at median 43 months, 6 of 7 MRD-negative with full donor chimerism [S:f7d7a4c0]. CLL3X also showed benefit independent of NOTCH1, SF3B1 and TP53 mutation [S:309d5eb1]. Evidence on del(17p) and complex karyotype is conflicting, but durable remissions still occur, [passage text removed]% in high-risk cytogenetic subsets [S:abf9830a].

## GVL, MRD and immune intervention

GVL underpins efficacy — falling relapse rates over time, lower relapse with chronic GVHD, higher relapse with T-cell depletion, and responses to DLI [S:22c92231]. MRD negativity at 1 year post-transplant is durable in >90% and highly predictive of freedom from relapse [S:22c92231][S:33916317]. Using high-throughput IGH sequencing in 40 RIC allo-HCT patients, among those in remission at 12 months, disease-free survival was 86% with MRD <10⁻⁴ versus 20% with MRD ≥10⁻⁴ (relapse HR 9.0, 95% CI 2.5–32) [S:6de0eeb4]. A phase II trial of 42 patients using MRD-guided immunosuppression withdrawal ± DLI achieved MRD negativity in 64% at 12 months, with 3-year OS 87% and PFS 63% [S:33916317]. Notably, DLI given at frank clinical relapse is often of limited benefit [S:478ec79f]; in one series of 46 patients, no response was seen to DLI given for haematological relapse [S:b5639a26].

## Toxicity

GVHD, infection, organ failure and resulting NRM remain the limiting toxicities [S:db3a0263]. In 46 transplanted CLL patients, grade II–IV acute GVHD was 43%, 2-year extensive chronic GVHD 51%, 3-year transplant-related mortality 24% (9 of 16 deaths from toxicity), with 3- and 5-year OS 65% and 57% [S:b5639a26]. In a 30-patient high-risk cohort (3-year OS 78%, PFS 71%, relapse 10%, NRM 16%), acute GVHD was associated with significantly higher NRM and chronic GVHD with worse PFS [S:97c136af]. Reported allo-HCT OS declines over time (62% at 2 years to 35% at 10 years) as NRM rises to 40% at 10 years [S:a44b8a1f].

## Modern era (post-BTK/BCL2 inhibitor)

Outcomes appear better with contemporary practice. Among 108 CLL patients transplanted since 2010, 3-year OS was 73%, PFS 61%, NRM 14%, relapse 24% [S:615109e1]. In 30 high-risk patients [passage text removed], 3-year OS was 87% and PFS 72%; in a separate 65-patient cohort, 2-year OS was 81% and PFS 63%, with TRM of 7% and 13% respectively and outcomes similar irrespective of number or class of prior novel agent [S:abf9830a]. A 44-patient single-centre series (2006–2023, including Richter's transformation) reported PFS [passage text removed], OS 81.4% and 74%, and GVHD-relapse-free survival 57% [S:08df54e0][S:4ea5861a]. In real-world "double-exposed" (BTKi- and venetoclax-treated) CLL, median PFS by next line was 11 months for allo-HCT versus 5 months for PI3K inhibitors, 4 months for CAR-T and 3 months for chemoimmunotherapy [S:61ac990c].

## Richter's transformation

In the largest series (CIBMTR, 118 patients), 4-year OS was 52%, PFS 43%, relapse 30% and NRM 27%; being in complete or partial response at transplant predicted superior outcome, whereas del(17p), conditioning intensity and prior BTK/BCL2 inhibitor exposure did not affect prognosis [S:ae8ec73c]. Allo-HCT is therefore the preferred consolidation for eligible high-risk Richter's transformation [S:ae8ec73c], and patients refractory to induction derive no benefit [S:2575693b].

## Current positioning

Current EBMT-aligned guidance requires high-risk disease (refractoriness/early relapse or TP53 aberration) plus failure of at least one pathway inhibitor before referral, with individualised timing weighed against sequential targeted therapy, using HCT-CI/EBMT/PAM scores to estimate NRM [S:3e6a32af]. Outcomes are best when transplant is performed while disease is still controlled, since disease status predicts relapse risk [S:39b60b5a], and are significantly impaired once disease is completely unresponsive [S:7bb2abf1].

Caveat: none of these cohorts had a concurrent control arm, so it remains unclear whether allo-HCT outcomes exceed those of other modalities in the current era [S:615109e1].

rows.question: How well do clinical screening criteria detect interstitial lung disease in rheumatoid arthritis?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Criteria combining risk factors, persistent respiratory symptoms and auscultation behave as a rule-out rather than a confirmatory test, with high sensitivity and negative predictive value but low specificity and positive predictive value, so a positive screen needs imaging confirmation; Items based only on respiratory symptoms and auscultation have low sensitivity, because most disease found by systematic imaging is subclinical; The risk-factor score used on its own identifies most cases but is also positive in many patients without lung disease; Velcro-like crackles raise the probability of interstitial lung disease enough to prioritise which patients undergo chest imaging. Certainty: The evidence is a descriptive single-visit account of how the screening criteria behave against chest imaging in routine specialist practice, adequate for ruling disease out but not for showing that the rule anticipates disease appearing later, and component-level performance rests on few disease cases. Scope: applies to rheumatoid arthritis without previously diagnosed interstitial lung disease in adults in routine specialist care, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents longer disease duration, diagnostic delay or higher inflammatory activity as established characteristics that should drive screening decisions on this evidence.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line: symptom- and exam-based screening alone misses most RA-ILD; composite risk-factor criteria (SER/SEPAR, ACR–CHEST, ANCHOR-RA) achieve high sensitivity and negative predictive value but at the cost of specificity so low that they flag most of the clinic for HRCT — they triage rather than detect.**

**Clinical assessment alone performs poorly.** In a prospective case-control screening study using low-dose photon-counting CT as reference, [passage text removed]%, and combining the two gave a sensitivity of only 12% (specificity 87%); of 171 patients with interstitial involvement on CT, only 12% had basal crackles, 18% dry cough and 27% dyspnoea, and 15% had abnormal PFTs (NCT05391100, PMC12593899). In the SER/SEPAR validation cohort (270 RA patients, 21.5% with ILD on HRCT), individual items were weak: "Velcro-type" crackles sensitivity 39.7%/specificity 92.9%, cough and/or dyspnoea >3 months 32.8%/84.9%, chest X-ray 47.5%/85.8%, FVC <80% 32.1%, DLCO <80% 52.9%; sensitivity of radiography and PFTs stayed ≤50% even among symptomatic patients ([S:[passage text removed]]).

**Composite criteria: sensitive, not specific.** The same validation found the full SER/SEPAR algorithm had sensitivity 96.5%, specificity 25%, PPV 27.2%, NPV 96.1% — but recommended [passage text removed]% (same source). The multicentre VAR-EPIDSER study (424 evaluable HRCTs, ILD prevalence 13.0%, of which 63.6% subclinical) reported AR-EPIDSER sensitivity 0.93 (95% CI 0.82–0.98), specificity 0.36, PPV 0.18, NPV 0.97, with 68.2% screening positive (RMD Open 2026;12:e006934). In early RA (146 patients, 19.1% ILD), the criteria gave sensitivity 92.86% and specificity 45.76%; the risk-factor score ≥5 alone was 72.73%/49.54%, and lowering to ≥4 raised sensitivity to 90.91% but dropped specificity to 23.85% ([S:[passage text removed]...]; see also Aguilar-Coll & Narváez, PMID 40334368).

**Head-to-head external validation shows criteria-dependent extremes.** In the prospective SAIL-RA cohort (172 early RA patients, 19 [11%] with ILD on HRCT), sensitivity [passage text removed]; ANCHOR-RA and ACR–CHEST at a one-factor cutoff), and specificity from 0.11 to 0.97; number needed to screen per ILD case was 3.6–7.7 (PMID 41106411, PMC12758494). The four-factor score five-point cutoff, SER-SEPAR seven-point cutoff and Paulin criteria all had low sensitivity with high specificity.

**Derivation-stage scores look better than they validate.** Reported development performance includes 75%/85% (sex, age at RA onset, DAS28-ESR, MUC5B; PMC9828082, where subclinical ILD prevalence was 19.0% and 16.9% in discovery/replication), 86%/58% for a four-variable model, and 90.4%/63.6% (two-point) vs 51.9%/90.9% (four-point) for a five-risk-factor case-control score ([S:[passage text removed]]; [S:archbronconeumol.org/...S0300289626001225]). Independently, one study found risk scores had almost no discriminating value compared with lung ultrasound (Spanish consensus ≥5: +LR 0.97; Juge ≥25: +LR 1.45), whereas LUS reached 95.5% sensitivity/77.8% specificity in asymptomatic patients ([S:arprheumatology.com/files/article/diagnostic_performance_of_lung_ultrasoun...]).

**Practical implication.** Adjunct physiological/imaging tools outperform clinical criteria: LUS+PFT screening gave 93% sensitivity, 72% specificity, NPV 95% ([S:[passage text removed]]), and electronic-stethoscope breath sounds 93.2%/76.9%, superior to symptoms, examination, chest X-ray and PFTs ([S:archbronconeumol.org/...S0300289626001225]). Risk-factor screening does enrich yield — in ANCHOR-RA, 9.1% of 1169 at-risk patients screened had previously undiagnosed ILD ([S:[passage text removed]]) — consistent with the 2023 ACR/CHEST conditional recommendation to screen risk-factor-positive RA patients with PFTs and HRCT, and against chest radiography ([S:jrheum.org/content/53/4/362]).

**Caveats:** most evidence is cross-sectional and single- or few-centre, with heterogeneous ILD definitions and HRCT reference standards; a systematic review of RA-ILD diagnostic methods judged risk of bias low in 20 of 36 studies and unclear in 15 ([S:[passage text removed]]). HRCT itself is imperfect against histology for UIP pattern (sensitivity 45%, specificity 96%, AUC 0.708 in 69 patients), so "missed" cases partly reflect reference-standard limits (same review).
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

Clinical screening criteria for RA-ILD behave as **rule-out, not rule-in, tools**: composite risk-factor–based criteria achieve sensitivity >90% with negative predictive value ~96–97%, but specificity is only ~25–46%, so most positives are false positives; symptom-based criteria alone miss the majority of cases because most detected RA-ILD is subclinical.

## Composite criteria validated against HRCT

The multicentre Spanish VAR-EPIDSER study applied the SER/SEPAR AR-EPIDSER criteria at a rheumatology visit and gave **every** patient HRCT with centralised reading as reference standard [S:62126195-d2de-5c86-8f5a-cd012b44aa67]. In 424 evaluable patients, 51/55 ILD cases screened positive but so did 238/369 patients without ILD [S:fd9393ed-6022-5f87-812b-3a3b5f2069b7]. This gave sensitivity 93% and NPV 97%, against specificity 36% and PPV 18% — "the expected profile of a screening tool... useful [passage text removed]" [S:d9757170-4e98-569a-8c5f-e911d8478cac]. ILD prevalence was 13% (95% CI 9.9–16.6%), with subclinical disease in 8.3% (95% CI 5.7–11.1%) [S:7c243d76-7c4c-5937-baad-1d97331add6f].

An external validation in early RA (146 patients, 28 with HRCT-confirmed ILD) reported sensitivity 92.8% and specificity 45.7%; excluding cases where ILD preceded joint symptoms, sensitivity fell to 87.5%. Lowering the threshold from ≥5 to ≥4 raised sensitivity to 90.91% but dropped specificity to 23.8% [S:1a0eb4bf-2614-54ec-914d-b94058ddbaeb].

## Which components carry the signal

Within VAR-EPIDSER, individual components diverged sharply [S:fd9393ed-6022-5f87-812b-3a3b5f2069b7]:
- Cough and dyspnoea >3 months: sensitivity **16% each**, specificity 92%
- "Velcro" crackles: sensitivity 18%, specificity 96%, PPV 40% (highest PPV of any criterion)
- Any respiratory symptom/sign combined: sensitivity 36%, specificity 85%, NPV 90%
- Risk-factor score ≥5: sensitivity 86%, NPV 95%, but specificity 39%

The authors conclude sensitivity is driven almost entirely by the risk-factor score, while crackles are useful for *prioritising* HRCT [S:d9757170-4e98-569a-8c5f-e911d8478cac].

## Symptoms and physiology perform poorly as standalone screens

In 116 RA patients all receiving HRCT, symptom instruments were near-uninformative: AUROC 0.603 for mMRC dyspnoea and 0.637 for VAS cough for clinical ILD, versus 0.936 for lung-ultrasound B-lines and 0.942 for DLCO%predicted; B-lines significantly outperformed mMRC and VAS cough (both p<0.001) and FVC (p=0.007) [S:e23a73d5-16a0-5ba3-9c71-136ef8f0d5ad][S:10bd1551-d4c8-5b5f-9d3c-d623aa1c722b]. Similarly, in the VECTOR validation cohort (137 RA patients, 43.1% with ILD), clinician-elicited findings were weak: dyspnoea sensitivity 41.2%, dry cough 15.1%, chest X-ray 57.8%, DLCO<47% 30.8%, and rheumatologist-auscultated Velcro crackles 69.1%; the digital crackle algorithm reached 93.2% sensitivity, 76.9% specificity, 83.9% accuracy [S:9b957369-8773-535b-a6af-90022335367a][S:a2c55788-5491-582e-a2f8-898664467281]. Older HRCT-based series make the same point: all subclinical RA-ILD cases had HRCT abnormalities despite normal chest examination, yet only 26.7% had abnormal PFTs and 20% abnormal chest radiography [S:85fd261d-f84f-52b1-955a-0afb8d7230be].

## Multivariable risk scores: modest discrimination, unstable calibration

The four-factor score (age, ACPA, RF, smoking) had AUC 0.76 (95% CI 0.71–0.82) with sensitivity 86% and specificity 58% at a cut-off of 5 [S:48d15817-c42a-50b9-af02-fd7ebbc34a63]. In an independent Swedish cohort of 54 RA patients, three published scores performed comparably — Juge AUC 0.71, Wheeler 0.75, Koduri 0.70, differences not statistically significant — but the Juge score's operating characteristics shifted dramatically, with sensitivity 100% and specificity only 10% (versus 75%/85% in development), ruling out just 7.4% (n=4) as low risk [S:893f50d8-517e-55bd-9f60-4d59151c7626][S:4e07f88a-0a71-5d17-9092-fa5e689557ff]. A machine-learning model on 1,156 RA patients dropped from AUC 0.773 (random forest, derivation) to 0.713 on external validation [S:a8da00ce-122f-5204-9fd8-9c7893e704ac].

## Interpretation

The 2023 ACR/CHEST guideline recommends risk-factor–targeted rather than universal screening, using HRCT plus spirometry with lung volumes and DLCO [S:4339d080-0e4d-5dab-bca1-2d09b8b9db2d][S:300c4340-fbf8-5749-a5ee-ea97d98e43c6]. The evidence supports criteria as a **first step in a stepwise strategy**, with HRCT reserved for screen-positives — especially those with persistent symptoms or Velcro crackles [S:90450448-7369-5d93-8559-0985959a9b0e]. Caveats: VAR-EPIDSER excluded ~10% of recruits for lack of evaluable HRCT, a possible selection bias [S:90450448-7369-5d93-8559-0985959a9b0e]; the VECTOR study was retrospective, which may explain some false positives [S:9b957369-8773-535b-a6af-90022335367a]; and the risk-score validation cohort was small (n=54) [S:893f50d8-517e-55bd-9f60-4d59151c7626]. I found no evidence on whether criteria-based screening improves clinical outcomes (mortality, lung-function preservation) rather than merely case detection.

rows.question: Which neuroimaging patterns are described in patients with neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Microhaemorrhage was the most commonly recorded brain parenchymal abnormality; Haemorrhagic and ischaemic infarcts were each recorded in fewer patients than microhaemorrhage; Arterial imaging showed a beaded appearance of the middle cerebral artery or its branches in a minority of patients; Venous imaging showed filling defect, narrowing and irregularity of the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses in a smaller minority of patients. Certainty: Because the supporting evidence comes from a small, uncontrolled group of hospitalised patients with no comparison group, the reported patterns should be read as illustrative of what may occur rather than as established frequencies. Scope: applies to neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus in young adults, predominantly women, inpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents a beaded angiographic appearance as an established or specific diagnostic marker of cerebral vasculitis in lupus, or recommends withholding immunosuppressive treatment when angiography appears normal.
