**Conclusion:** NPSLE has no single diagnostic signature — roughly half of patients have normal or non‑specific conventional MRI, and the described patterns fall into (i) focal structural/vascular lesions (white‑matter hyperintensities, small‑vessel disease, infarcts, atrophy), (ii) recognisable pathophysiology‑defined syndromes (vasculitis/vasculopathy, antiphospholipid‑related thrombosis, PRES, demyelinating/encephalitic patterns, longitudinally extensive myelitis), and (iii) abnormalities visible only on advanced/quantitative imaging (microstructural, perfusion, BBB, metabolic, network, and PET changes).

**1. Conventional MRI: frequent but non‑specific**
Around 50% of NPSLE patients have a normal MRI, particularly [passage text removed]; in the remainder the commonest findings are multiple small white‑matter lesions (reported 30–75%) and cortical atrophy (15–20%) [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4505788]. Hyperintense WM lesions on T2/FLAIR, brain atrophy, infarctions and enlarged ventricles are the classically described repertoire [[passage text removed]]. A structural‑MRI meta‑analysis reported pooled prevalences of white‑matter hyperintensities 34.1%, grey‑matter hyperintensities 22.9%, cerebral atrophy 16.9%, parenchymal defects 6.5% and small‑vessel disease 48.6%, with the pattern varying by syndrome — e.g. small‑vessel disease and WMH dominating cerebrovascular disease and cognitive dysfunction, WMH plus cerebral atrophy in seizures, and normal MRI in up to 90% of anxiety cases [[passage text removed]].

Crucially, these lesions do not separate NPSLE from SLE without neuropsychiatric disease: SLE patients have larger WM lesion volume than healthy controls and lesion volume correlates with cognitive dysfunction (verbal memory), but no differences emerged between NPSLE and non‑NPSLE subgroups under any attribution model [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29523054]. A review of [passage text removed] attributed lesions (WMH, ischaemic, inflammatory‑like, atrophy) to inflammatory NPSLE in 24%, ischaemic NPSLE in 13.2% and non‑NPSLE causes in 62.8%, with lupus anticoagulant significantly associated with ischaemic lesions and cerebral atrophy [[passage text removed]].

**2. Mechanism‑based patterns**
A radiology review classifies NPSLE imaging by underlying pathophysiology: vasculitis and vasculopathy, antiphospholipid syndrome, demyelinating syndrome, and autoimmune antibody‑mediated encephalitis [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34990324]. PRES is a distinct, characteristically posterior/occipital reversible vasogenic‑oedema pattern in SLE, associated with hypertension, nephritis, immunosuppressive drugs and antiphospholipid antibodies, resolving clinically and radiologically over weeks [[passage text removed]; https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1146456-clinical]. Dural sinus thrombosis with associated oedema or haemorrhagic infarction, and large‑vessel occlusions or multifocal beaded narrowing suggesting vasculitis, are described in the antiphospholipid/vasculopathy group [https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1146456-overview]. Suggested (though non‑diagnostic) "lupus‑leaning" patterns include stroke in a young patient, more than one infarct, coexisting [passage text removed] [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4505788].

**3. Spinal cord**
Lupus myelitis lesions are usually longitudinally extensive, typically spanning three or more vertebral levels [[passage text removed]]; the typical appearance is a central T2/STIR‑hyperintense lesion with or without cord swelling/oedema, often contrast‑enhancing, with cervical and mid‑thoracic (T5–T8) segments most affected and normal cord imaging possible early in the course [[passage text removed]]. In one small series all five patients had abnormal spinal MRI, three longitudinally extensive, with essentially unremarkable brain MRI [[passage text removed]].

**4. Volumetric / morphometric patterns**
Cortical thinning plus reduced subcortical grey matter volume in thalamus, caudate and putamen has been reported in NPSLE [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2844408]. VBM studies describe grey‑matter reduction in limbic (including posterior cingulate), frontal, temporal and occipital regions and right thalamus in NPSLE versus non‑NPSLE and controls [https://www.nature.com/articles/srep19026]. Hippocampal atrophy occurs even in SLE patients without major neuropsychiatric manifestations [[passage text removed]], and a meta‑analysis of structural MRI found lower bilateral hippocampal volume, corpus callosum cross‑sectional area and total grey matter in SLE versus controls [[passage text removed]].

**5. Microstructural imaging (DTI, magnetisation transfer)**
DTI shows reduced fractional anisotropy and increased mean diffusivity across multiple WM tracts, interpreted as vasogenic oedema, expanded extracellular space, network disruption or reactive gliosis [[passage text removed]], with regional specificity able to distinguish acute NPSLE from SLE in one study [[passage text removed]]. Magnetisation transfer imaging in patients with unremarkable 3T MRI showed significantly lower white‑matter MTR histogram peak height specifically in inflammatory NPSLE compared with healthy controls, SLE patients and non‑SLE‑related neuropsychiatric disease, with change over follow‑up tracking clinical course [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26894522; https://scholarlypublications.universiteitleiden.nl/access/item%3A2870025/download].

**6. Perfusion and blood–brain barrier**
Primary NPSLE was characterised by significant hypoperfusion — lower cerebral blood flow and blood [passage text removed] [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29259047]. A systematic review/meta‑analysis of perfusion‑weighted MRI found reduced CBF in NPSLE versus non‑NPSLE (SMD −[passage text removed], I²=94%), particularly frontal and temporal lobes, though not significantly different from healthy individuals [[passage text removed]; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39230717]. Results are inconsistent: a DSC‑MRI cohort found perfusion differences from controls (hypothalamus, putamen, thalamus, insula, pons, corpus callosum) in SLE irrespective of NP attribution, no NPSLE/non‑NPSLE difference, and increased CBF/CBV/MTT and leakage parameter K2 within WMHs versus normal‑appearing WM, suggesting BBB dysfunction [[passage text removed]], while an older DSC study found no group differences at all [https://nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/node/6384]. DCE‑MRI demonstrates increased BBB permeability [[passage text removed]], which has been linked to altered resting‑state connectivity and cognitive impairment [[passage text removed]].

**7. Functional / network imaging**
Resting‑state fMRI shows altered functional connectivity within and between the default‑mode network and central executive network, plus salience and working‑memory networks, and abnormal degree centrality, including in patients without overt NP symptoms [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29498293; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8333697]. Task fMRI has shown greater frontoparietal activation during memory tasks in NPSLE, and cortical reorganisation with sensorimotor, putamen and dentate activation [https://achaiki-iatriki.gr?p=545]. Abnormalities cluster in limbic system, hippocampus, and frontal, parietal and temporal cortex, some correlating with cognition, mood, autoantibodies or inflammatory proteins, with longitudinal progression [[passage text removed]].

**8. MR spectroscopy**
Reduced NAA/Cr and increased Cho/Cr are described, particularly in active disease, reflecting neuro‑axonal dysfunction and membrane turnover/myelin breakdown; changes tend to normalise with disease control and may precede visible lesions [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43045-023-00303-7]. Multivoxel work reports increased Cho/Cr in internal capsule and increased Cho/NAA in left posterior insula and posterior grey matter in NPSLE [[passage text removed]], and reduced NAA and total creatine in posterior cingulate/lenticular regions [https://www.nature.com/articles/srep19026].

**9. Nuclear medicine**
In adults, FDG‑PET classically shows cortical hypometabolism with parieto‑occipital predominance, often when MRI is normal: hypometabolism in ≥1 region occurred [passage text removed] versus 40% of those without, parieto‑occipital regions affected in 96%, while MRI was abnormal in only 11/22 symptomatic patients, and follow‑up PET tracked symptom course [[passage text removed]]. A controlled PET study found significantly reduced bilateral parieto‑occipital glucose metabolic index in mainly MRI‑negative neuropsychiatric SLE [[passage text removed]]. By contrast, juvenile NPSLE showed an extensive bilateral cortico‑subcortical *hyper*metabolic pattern (occipital, temporal, frontal cortex, thalamus, basal ganglia, cerebellum) with no significant hypometabolic area, consistent with mixed hypo/hypermetabolism in autoimmune encephalitis [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10987444]. Perfusion SPECT shows diffuse patchy or focal hypoperfusion, most often parietal, then temporal and occipital [[passage text removed]].

**Caveat:** studies grouping all NPSLE syndromes together cannot differentiate NPSLE from non‑NPSLE, and no MRI finding confirms or excludes the diagnosis — imaging largely serves to exclude alternatives and, increasingly, to define mechanism (inflammatory vs ischaemic) [[passage text removed]; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4505788].
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

NPSLE has no pathognomonic imaging signature; instead the literature describes a set of recurring patterns — normal-appearing scans in roughly half of patients, small- and large-vessel ischaemic changes, inflammatory-like lesions, atrophy, and specific syndromic patterns such as PRES — supplemented by microstructural, perfusion, metabolic and functional abnormalities detectable only with advanced techniques.

## Conventional MRI

**Normal or non-specific scans.** Up to about half of NPSLE patients have no apparent conventional MRI abnormality, particularly [passage text removed] [S:18c4f160][S:76384ebc]. A meta-analysis of 21 studies (818 participants, 1064 NP episodes) found normal MRI was significantly associated with anxiety disorder, whereas abnormal MRI was most strongly linked to cerebrovascular disease and demyelination [S:f931d4dc].

**Small-vessel disease.** The most commonly reported lesions are white matter hyperintensities (frontal, parieto-occipital, temporal, basal ganglia, infratentorial), lacunes, recent small subcortical infarcts and microbleeds [S:18c4f160][S:88c36024]. WMH are reported in roughly 30–75% of patients [S:76384ebc]; lesions are typically small, discrete, subcortical or periventricular and non-specific [S:8571f696].

**Large-vessel disease.** Wedge-shaped, vascular-territory infarcts involving grey and white matter, predominantly in the middle cerebral artery territory, occur in 10–15% of patients, with a tendency to multiplicity and recurrence, and have been associated with antiphospholipid antibodies [S:18c4f160].

**Inflammatory-like lesions.** Multifocal grey matter lesions, contrast enhancement and diffusion restriction form a distinct category in proposed NPSLE MRI classifications [S:18c4f160][S:88c36024]. T2 hyperintensity in deep/subcortical white matter not conforming to a vascular distribution can mimic multiple sclerosis, and lesions may regress after immunosuppression [S:c664ff6b].

**Atrophy and volume loss.** Atrophy is reported in roughly 15–20% of patients [S:76384ebc], with cortical atrophy, ventricular dilation and hippocampal atrophy described [S:c664ff6b][S:88c36024]. Volumetric work shows grey matter atrophy in both NPSLE and non-NPSLE patients [S:76384ebc]; NPSLE patients showed overt subcortical grey matter atrophy [S:ce7ceca7], and structural atrophy can precede overt neuropsychiatric signs [S:b4f961b3]. A case with seizures and psychiatric symptoms showed stable bilateral periventricular/deep white matter FLAIR hyperintensities with diffuse cortical volume loss and enlarged ventricles disproportionate to age [S:44e9fd6d].

**Phenotype-specific volumetric patterns.** Comparing 38 NPSLE with 117 non-NPSLE patients, NPSLE showed higher WMH volume; the *inflammatory* phenotype showed lower total brain and white matter volume plus higher WMH volume than non-NPSLE, and lower white matter and total brain volume than the *ischaemic* phenotype [S:5bb320b4].

**Syndrome-specific patterns.** PRES is well documented in SLE: posterior white matter vasogenic oedema in parietal, temporal and occipital lobes, conspicuous on T2/FLAIR, typically without matching DWI restriction but with increased ADC, and resolving clinically and radiographically within about 1–4 weeks [S:3ecc8fe7][S:30d472e5]. Variants include frontal, basal ganglia, brainstem, cerebellar and spinal cord involvement, and associated microhaemorrhages on SWI [S:828b7256][S:b6eb360b]. Symmetric bilateral globus pallidus T2 hyperintensity without diffusion restriction has been reported in NPSLE mimicking serotonin syndrome [S:a1124301]. Vasculitic presentations with large-artery stenoses, sulcal hyperintensities and multiple foci of diffusion restriction are also described [S:c60e90ca].

**Paediatric series.** In 28 children with neuropsychiatric lupus, 24 had abnormal MRI, with T2/FLAIR signal change in supratentorial white matter (n=17), brainstem, basal ganglia, cortical grey matter and cerebellum, and atrophy in 11 [S:72377ab0]. A systematic review of 120 case reports found neuroimaging abnormalities in over 80% of imaged patients, commonly white matter lesions, cortical atrophy and focal grey matter involvement [S:b250f603].

## Advanced MRI

- **DTI:** decreased fractional anisotropy and increased mean/axial diffusivity in frontal white matter, corpus callosum and thalamus, plus limbic system, internal capsule and corona radiata [S:76384ebc][S:bbce0ab2]. In 64 SLE patients, FA was reduced in the right rostral cingulum, mid-sagittal and forceps minor of the corpus callosum, and MD increased in the left hippocampal cingulum, with no significant NPSLE vs non-NPSLE difference [S:f4f1c640].
- **MRS:** reduced NAA/Cr in focal lesions *and* in normal-appearing white matter, with elevated choline, suggesting diffuse neuronal/axonal damage; reduced NAA with hypoperfusion in NAWM has been associated with atrophy [S:c664ff6b][S:8571f696].
- **Magnetization transfer imaging:** reduced MTR indicating global/microscopic brain involvement in NPSLE patients without explanatory conventional MRI abnormalities [S:dea95e59][S:8571f696].
- **Perfusion:** perfusion-weighted/DSC-MRI abnormalities in normal-appearing white and deep grey matter [S:59175643]; quantitative susceptibility mapping shows increased oxygen extraction fraction, interpreted as vasculitis-related ischaemia/"misery perfusion" [S:cb17d7e5][S:da7068d6].
- **Resting-state fMRI:** reduced connectivity within the default mode and central executive networks and between them, with increased sensorimotor network connectivity; hypoconnectivity was more pronounced in patients with neuropsychiatric complaints [S:94708598]. NPSLE patients showed weakened default mode and salience network function, altered cerebellar posterior lobe activity and connectivity, correlated with disease burden and antiphospholipid antibodies [S:ce7ceca7]. Abnormalities also occur in non-NPSLE patients (e.g. increased degree centrality in bilateral hippocampi and right insula) [S:61ea9406].
- **Synthetic MRI:** NPSLE showed more extensive increases in grey matter T1 and T2 relaxation times than non-NPSLE, with reduced grey matter volume in SLE overall [S:510abd62].
- **High-resolution vessel wall imaging:** across 10 studies (69 patients), about 46% had white matter lesions and 77% had normal MR angiography; HRVWI detected vessel wall inflammation despite normal 3D TOF angiography, with most findings resolving on immunosuppression [S:cc75c714][S:601b0d99].

## Nuclear medicine

FDG-PET in 46 NPSLE patients identified two clusters; one showed [passage text removed], insulae and cerebellum with relative hypometabolism in frontal, parietal, occipital and lateral temporal cortex, and higher SLEDAI-2K scores — a pattern resembling autoimmune encephalitis [S:e7d22425][S:e473fd50]. Cortical hypometabolism (most often frontal and parietal) is the better-established finding, with hypermetabolism most commonly in basal ganglia [S:e473fd50]. In 19 juvenile NPSLE PET-MRI exams without significant MRI lesions, voxel-based analysis showed a bilateral cortico-subcortical *hyper*metabolic pattern (thalamus, subthalamic brainstem, cerebellum, basal ganglia, visual/temporal/frontal cortices) with no hypometabolic areas on group analysis [S:85bac55c]. Older PET and SPECT literature reports grey matter hypometabolism and hypoperfusion in NPSLE [S:cb17d7e5].

## Caveat

Many of these abnormalities — DTI changes, atrophy, connectivity alterations — are also found in SLE patients *without* neuropsychiatric manifestations, so their specificity for NPSLE is doubtful [S:bbce0ab2][S:f4f1c640][S:0e8339f2], and no MRI abnormality is pathognomonic [S:88c36024].

rows.question: What is known about emerging treatments for systemic disease activity in Sjögren's disease?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Dual BAFF/APRIL blockade with telitacicept reduced systemic disease activity scores compared with placebo in randomised trials conducted in China; FcRn-directed IgG lowering with nipocalimab or efgartigimod met its primary endpoint in early randomised testing; Patient-reported dryness, fatigue and pain improved only numerically or not at all with FcRn-directed treatment; Inhibition of JAK-1, SYK or BTK signalling did not separate from placebo on primary or secondary endpoints. Certainty: Support is firmest for dual BAFF/APRIL blockade, yet it rests entirely on evidence gathered within a single country, whereas the other agents have been assessed only at a preliminary stage, where disease heterogeneity, small participant numbers and sizeable placebo responses constrain interpretation. Scope: applies to primary Sjögren's disease with systemic disease activity in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents any of these targeted agents as established or approved therapy for systemic Sjögren's disease, or recommends adopting one in routine care or for preventing long-term organ damage on this basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Sjögren's disease is on the verge of having its first approved systemic disease‑modifying therapies: B‑cell/BAFF–APRIL‑directed agents (ianalumab, telitacicept), FcRn blockers (nipocalimab, efgartigimod), co‑stimulation blockade (dazodalibep) and BTK inhibition (remibrutinib) have all reduced ESSDAI versus placebo, and ianalumab and telitacicept have now succeeded in phase III — though symptom endpoints (ESSPRI) have improved far less consistently than systemic activity [[passage text removed]].

## Agents with the strongest evidence

**Ianalumab (anti‑BAFF‑R, B‑cell depleting + BAFF‑R blocking).** The phase 2b dose‑finding trial randomised 190 anti‑Ro–positive patients (ESSDAI ≥6, ESSPRI ≥5) to subcutaneous 5, 50 or 300 mg or placebo and met its primary objective of a dose‑related ESSDAI decrease at week 24; stimulated whole salivary flow improved with 300 mg (placebo‑adjusted change 0.20 mL/min, P=0.037), with leukopenia and injection‑site reactions but no excess serious adverse events [S:https://acrabstracts.org/abstract/ianalumab-vay736-safety-and-efficacy-in-patients-with-sjogrens-syndrome-[passage text removed]-trial][[passage text removed]]. Two global phase III trials — [passage text removed]), enrolling patients with ESSDAI ≥5 and allowing background immunosuppressants — both met the primary endpoint of change in ESSDAI at week 48 [[passage text removed]]. FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation was granted and global submissions were planned from early 2026 [[passage text removed]].

**Telitacicept (TACI‑Fc, dual BAFF/APRIL inhibition).** In a Chinese phase III trial (NCT05673993; 381 anti‑SSA‑positive patients, ESSDAI ≥5, 79 centres), week‑24 LS mean ESSDAI change was −4.4 (160 mg) and −3.0 (80 mg) versus −0.6 for placebo (P<.0001 both), sustained at week 48; ≥3‑point ESSDAI response at week 24 was 71.8% and 47.1% versus 19.3%, and ESSPRI also improved significantly (week‑48 LS mean −2.56 and −1.74 vs −0.41) [[passage text removed]]. Treatment‑related adverse events were more frequent than placebo (74.9% vs 50%), including upper‑respiratory infection, reduced IgG/IgM and injection‑site reactions [[passage text removed]]. A global phase III (UPSTREAM SjD) is recruiting [S:https://www.centerwatch.com/clinical-trials/listings/NCT07404865/[passage text removed]-sjogrens-disease].

**FcRn blockade — a validated new mechanism.** In DAHLIAS (NCT04968912; 163 patients, anti‑Ro60/Ro52‑positive, ClinESSDAI ≥6), nipocalimab 15 mg/kg q2w met the primary endpoint (LS mean ClinESSDAI −6.40 vs −3.74 placebo; [passage text removed]), with concordant gains in PhGA, ESSDAI, STAR and CRESS, a median 61% predose reduction in total IgG at week 24, and falls in anti‑Ro60/Ro52/La, rheumatoid factor and circulating immune complexes; patient‑reported outcomes improved only numerically and the 5 mg/kg dose behaved like placebo [[passage text removed]]. Results were published in The Lancet, nipocalimab holds Breakthrough Therapy designation, and phase III DAFFODIL is enrolling [[passage text removed]]. Efgartigimod replicated the mechanism in the small phase 2 RHO study (NCT05817669; 34 randomised 2:1): CRESS response at week 24 was 45.5% vs 11.1% placebo, cSTAR 54.5% vs 33.3%, median ClinESSDAI change −7.0 vs −4.0, with ~58–60% IgG reduction and ~57–64% falls in anti‑Ro52; ESSPRI did not change meaningfully and all adverse events were grade 1–2 [[passage text removed]]. Phase III UNITY (NCT06684847) is testing subcutaneous dosing in patients with ClinESSDAI ≥6, [passage text removed]].

**Dazodalibep (CD40L antagonist Tn3 fusion protein).** In a phase 2 crossover trial, population 1 (74 patients, ESSDAI ≥5) met its primary endpoint: ESSDAI change −6.3 ± 0.6 vs −4.1 ± 0.6 for placebo (difference −2.2 ± 0.9, P=0.0167), with benefit similar in patients with concomitant RA or SLE; no symptom score improved significantly in this population, whereas in population 2 (109 patients, ESSPRI ≥5 with ESSDAI <5) fatigue, dryness and pain improved significantly [S:https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-03009-3][S:https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/993026][[passage text removed]]. Serum proteomics showed reduction of a core set of 29 B‑, T‑ and dendritic‑cell activation proteins in both populations [[passage text removed]]. A phase III programme was announced [[passage text removed]].

**Intracellular signalling.** Remibrutinib, a selective oral BTK inhibitor, [passage text removed] LOUiSSE trial (NCT04035668; 73 patients with ESSDAI ≥5 and ESSPRI ≥5): ΔESSDAI −2.86 (p=0.003) for pooled 100 mg qd/bid versus placebo, with a trend to improved unstimulated salivary flow, reduced CXCL13 (~50%) and immunoglobulins, and adverse‑event rates similar to placebo — but no ESSPRI effect (ΔESSPRI 0.17, p=0.663) [[passage text removed]]. Deucravacitinib and tofacitinib remain in active development per the RMD Open review [[passage text removed]]; tofacitinib data so far are from uncontrolled/retrospective work (112 patients treated 5 mg twice daily for 6 months), not randomised trials [[passage text removed]].

**Repurposing.** Leflunomide plus hydroxychloroquine improved ESSDAI in the small RepurpSS‑I phase IIA trial (29 patients; ESSDAI improvement of 4.35 vs placebo, no ESSPRI benefit), and a phase IIb repurposing trial confirmed significant ESSDAI reduction plus improvements in IgG, rheumatoid factor and C4 and higher STAR/CRESS response rates, again without ESSPRI or objective dryness benefit [[passage text removed]].

## Setbacks and cautions

- **Iscalimab (anti‑CD40)** showed clinically important ESSDAI improvement over placebo in both TWINSS cohorts (N=273) and was well tolerated, yet development for Sjögren's was discontinued by the manufacturer on benefit–risk grounds [S:https://acrabstracts.org/abstract/iscalimab-cfz533-in-patients-with-sjogrens-disease-week-24-efficacy-and-safety-results-of-[passage text removed]].
- **Older biologics largely failed on ESSDAI**: rituximab in TEARS and TRACTISS, abatacept in ASAP‑III and in a phase III trial (ESSDAI change −3.2 vs −3.7, p=0.442), and tocilizumab [[passage text removed]].
- **Endpoint problems are a major confounder**: large placebo responses and substantial natural fluctuation of ESSDAI have been documented, with ESSDAI varying widely within individual patients over 5 years in a standard‑of‑care cohort, motivating composite measures (CRESS, STAR, cSTAR) and ClinESSDAI [[passage text removed]].
- A recurring pattern is dissociation between systemic activity and symptoms: agents may improve ESSDAI without improving fatigue, pain or dryness, which limits perceived value [[passage text removed]].

## Earlier-stage / exploratory

Low‑dose IL‑2 expanded regulatory T and B cells and was reported to improve [passage text removed]]. CD19‑ and CD19/BCMA‑directed CAR‑T approaches are being explored for refractory disease (e.g., NCT05085431; sequential BCMA/CD19 CAR‑T in relapsed/refractory autoimmune disease including Sjögren's), with evidence so far limited to case reports and early trials [[passage text removed]]. Other mechanisms listed as in or entering development include sibreprenlimab and HZN‑1116, alongside [passage text removed]]. Baricitinib has preclinical support from a Treg/interferon mouse model but I found no randomised Sjögren's trial evidence for it [[passage text removed]].

**Limitation:** head‑to‑head comparisons between these agents do not exist in the sources retrieved, and several key datasets (NEPTUNUS, telitacicept phase III) are so far available only as conference abstracts or press releases rather than peer‑reviewed full publications.
answers.connect:
**Bottom line:** After a long run of failed trials, several targeted agents have now met ESSDAI-based primary endpoints for systemic disease activity in Sjögren's disease (SjD) — most notably the anti-BAFF-receptor antibody ianalumab (two phase 3 trials), the dual BAFF/APRIL inhibitor telitacicept (phase 3), the FcRn blocker nipocalimab (phase 2), and the CD40/CD40L-pathway agents dazodalibep and iscalimab (phase 2) — though no disease-modifying therapy is yet approved and placebo responses remain a major interpretive problem. [S:3da16202-ec93-5b3b-b40d-4081e1cb3216][S:7656040e-2a26-5804-b887-14e4178af63e]

**Context:** SjD has systemic manifestations (joints, skin, lungs, kidneys, peripheral and central nervous system) in a substantial minority of patients, and management still relies largely on symptomatic measures plus corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine, conventional immunosuppressants, and off-label rituximab for severe disease or cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis. [S:7656040e-2a26-5804-b887-14e4178af63e][S:baaee219-52aa-5f8c-bed1-8fead06b4418]

**B-cell / BAFF-APRIL axis (most advanced)**
- **Ianalumab (anti-BAFF-R; ADCC + BAFF-R signalling blockade):** a phase 2b dose-finding trial in 190 adults with moderate-to-severe disease showed a dose-response in ESSDAI improvement at week 24, supporting subcutaneous 300 mg every 4 weeks, with efficacy sustained to week 52. The phase 3 NEPTUNUS programme (NEPTUNUS-1, n=275; NEPTUNUS-2, n=504) met its primary endpoint with monthly dosing — statistically significant ESSDAI improvement versus placebo at week 48 — with adverse and serious adverse event rates comparable to placebo. [S:a1558130-9338-506e-8414-17117912092d][S:7937d933-8f92-5253-a139-4e373e9b3cbf] Caveats: phase 3 results so far exist mainly in abstract form, the placebo-adjusted ESSDAI effect is described as modest against high placebo response, and phase 2b showed no significant improvement in patient-reported outcomes despite gains in physician global assessment and stimulated salivary flow. [S:da4b605a-81eb-59b4-b117-3c59164ae0fc]
- **Telitacicept (TACI-Fc, dual BAFF/APRIL):** phase 2 in China showed significant ESSDAI/ClinESSDAI improvement with 160 mg as early as week 12 in a small completer population; a phase 3 trial of 381 patients confirmed significant ESSDAI reduction at week 24 for both 160 mg and 80 mg, with consistent secondary-endpoint gains including ESSPRI and STAR response, and mainly mild-to-moderate adverse events. Notably, the detectable effect was helped by an unusually low placebo response, so multinational replication is needed. [S:49b19b49-1737-50da-8b8c-55c89e884328]
- **Sibeprenlimab (APRIL-only neutralisation)** is in an ongoing phase 2 trial in SjD. [S:49b19b49-1737-50da-8b8c-55c89e884328]
- **Rituximab** failed its original endpoints, but reanalysis using the newer STAR and CRESS composites indicated modulation of peripheral and salivary gland inflammation and prevention of exocrine deterioration, reviving B-cell depletion as a viable strategy and highlighting endpoint choice as a key issue. [S:3da16202-ec93-5b3b-b40d-4081e1cb3216] Rituximab plus belimumab was well tolerated and improved ESSDAI in a randomised trial. [S:81ddbd13-9516-5e3a-a749-6472afca8ea5]

**Autoantibody/IgG-directed (FcRn blockade)**
- **Nipocalimab:** the phase 2 DAHLIAS trial in moderate-to-severe anti-Ro-positive SjD (5 or 15 mg/kg IV every 2 weeks) met its primary endpoint at week 24 with the 15 mg/kg dose (least-squares mean ClinESSDAI difference −2.65; p=0.002); [passage text removed]. There were dose-dependent falls in total IgG and anti-Ro60/Ro52/La, similar serious adverse event rates across groups, no severe hypogammaglobulinaemia, and numerical improvements in saliva flow and symptom scores. Nipocalimab received FDA Breakthrough Therapy and Fast Track designations, and phase 3 (DAFFODIL) is ongoing. [S:cbe32a7e-d2d8-5d73-9a58-88a4827f9847][S:71efc651-c4c4-52a1-926a-cec3b2e74609]
- **Efgartigimod:** a phase 2 proof-of-concept trial in systemic SjD (ESSDAI ≥5) met a CRESS-based primary endpoint (45.5% responders vs 11.1% placebo) with ~60% mean total IgG reduction and good tolerability, but no ESSPRI effect; a phase 3 study in moderate-to-severe systemic SjD (clinESSDAI ≥6) is ongoing, plus a separate phase 2 (OASIS) in the dryness-dominant/low-systemic-activity population. [S:aaacf7a2-bb51-50e0-9927-87e86bdbcf42][S:7d6a53a2-dc0f-5404-acc9-9cdc7778ea3b][S:71efc651-c4c4-52a1-926a-cec3b2e74609]

**Co-stimulation blockade**
- **Dazodalibep (CD40L antagonist):** phase 2 crossover trial in two populations met both primary endpoints — ESSDAI change at day 169 in the moderate-to-severe systemic cohort (n=74; DAZ −6.3±0.6 vs placebo −[passage text removed] ESSPRI change in the high-symptom/low-systemic cohort (n=109; −1.8±0.2 vs −0.5±0.2, p=0.0002), generally safe and well tolerated; phase 3 (NCT06104124) followed. [S:1e43388e-0fa6-5461-b330-b24925959217][S:dcaa7b0b-74f8-5f97-9fd5-cffae12efe72]
- **Iscalimab (anti-CD40):** phase 2a and the phase 2b TWINSS study met endpoints, with the intravenous route reducing ESSDAI, physician global assessment and CXCL13; however development was discontinued on the manufacturer's benefit-risk assessment. [S:258f1ad1-34d7-572f-bad3-b2ba28d5c41e][S:dcaa7b0b-74f8-5f97-9fd5-cffae12efe72]
- **Failures in this class:** abatacept (CD28-CD80/86) did not meet ESSDAI endpoints in phase 3; anti-ICOS-L (MEDI5872/AMG557) showed no meaningful benefit; frexalimab (anti-CD40L) was discontinued for insufficient efficacy. [S:258f1ad1-34d7-572f-bad3-b2ba28d5c41e]

**Intracellular signalling (oral agents)**
- **Remibrutinib (BTK inhibitor), phase 2 LOUiSSE (n=73):** significantly improved ESSDAI versus placebo with favourable safety, ~50% reduction in CXCL13, falls in IgM/IgG and anti-SSA/SSB titres, and a trend to increased salivary flow — but no PRO benefit, small sample, short duration, and no phase 3 planned. [S:6f678585-83d6-540c-83b7-437ee3dd8877][S:c1f7a515-4c34-50fc-9cdf-e741a55c6dac]
- **Filgotinib (JAK1), lanraplenib (SYK), tirabrutinib (BTK):** a phase 2 trial using a CRP+PRO composite primary endpoint was negative for all three, though filgotinib showed ESSDAI trends particularly in those with high baseline activity, with pharmacodynamic evidence of target engagement. [S:fbcdb2e7-c667-5140-ad45-5027b5867cfd][S:c1f7a515-4c34-50fc-9cdf-e741a55c6dac]
- **Seletalisib (PI3Kδ)** was terminated early/underpowered with trends to improvement but more drug-related adverse events. **Deucravacitinib (TYK2)** is in the ongoing phase 3 POETYK SjS-1 trial (ESSDAI ≥6; ESSDAI change at week 52). [S:c1f7a515-4c34-50fc-9cdf-e741a55c6dac][S:9be20b72-27cb-54a0-aa00-673254861115] Tofacitinib data in SjD come only from an uncontrolled cohort and should be interpreted cautiously given large placebo-arm responses. [S:fbcdb2e7-c667-5140-ad45-5027b5867cfd]

**Earlier-stage / experimental**
- **Type I interferon and pDC targeting:** an interferon signature is present in most patients and associates with higher systemic disease activity, providing rationale; RNase-Fc (RSLV-132) has been reported to improve the interferon score in SjD, and anifrolumab is listed as having a phase 2 trial ongoing in SjD. Clinical experience with pDC-directed agents in SjD remains early-stage. [S:fe842477-2bc0-5dbb-8068-16485880ab6f][S:524950f5-f460-5ba9-9a38-130a9d5355c5][S:b67293d1-4be3-5d7b-87c1-7096ab9f557d][S:c1f7a515-4c34-50fc-9cdf-e741a55c6dac]
- **Deep immune reset:** CD19- or BCMA-directed CAR-T and T-cell engager basket trials are registered, including one dedicated SjD study (NCT07041099). [S:49b19b49-1737-50da-8b8c-55c89e884328] Human SjD data are currently limited to case reports — e.g. a patient with lymphoma and 10-year SjD whose ESSDAI fell from 5 to 2 with seroconversion after anti-CD19 CAR-T, accompanied by [passage text removed]. [S:ced62b22-6059-5c18-babf-0cd3b9a68e4a]
- **Other agents meeting ESSDAI endpoints historically:** leflunomide plus hydroxychloroquine and low-dose interleukin-2. [S:81ddbd13-9516-5e3a-a749-6472afca8ea5] **Iguratimod** was compared head-to-head with hydroxychloroquine in a multicentre randomised trial using SSRI-30 response at week 24 as the primary endpoint, with STAR/ESSDAI/ESSPRI as secondary outcomes. [S:71d9dd94-8958-5cfd-9e9d-1aec2f3b5d19]

**Cross-cutting caveats.** Interpretation is limited by disease heterogeneity, small samples, and substantial placebo responses — in some trials exceeding [passage text removed] of ≥3 points, partly because several ESSDAI domains rely on patient/physician interpretation and partly through regression to the mean when high activity is an entry criterion. [S:71efc651-c4c4-52a1-926a-cec3b2e74609][S:25623cbe-dfbe-5833-92ed-e99b4d6c851d] A recurring pattern is that systemic activity improves while PROs do not. [S:da4b605a-81eb-59b4-b117-3c59164ae0fc][S:6f678585-83d6-540c-83b7-437ee3dd8877] Responses to this include new composite endpoints (STAR, CRESS, NECESSITY), dual-cohort designs separating high-systemic from high-symptom/low-systemic patients, and reduced exclusion of seronegative or longer-duration patients. [S:02dc026b-cffd-5a66-8ed1-c3226b760e7a][S:3da16202-ec93-5b3b-b40d-4081e1cb3216] Symptom-based stratification into four endotypes showed differential treatment effects — hydroxychloroquine in the high-symptom-burden subgroup and rituximab (on salivary flow) in the dryness-dominant-with-fatigue subgroup — though these reanalyses were not powered for stratification and need validation. [S:8ce457de-3f02-5201-b5fb-bd24571413c8][S:0c01f0ae-961e-5f69-a32c-d828097ed5a8] Trial populations also remain racially and ethnically narrow, with inconsistent biomarker reporting. [S:91fad7f7-b2cd-5d04-8162-1416010ae28f]

rows.question: Which quality-of-life domains remain impaired in Hodgkin lymphoma survivors compared with the general population?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Overall and physical health-related quality of life is lower in people treated for Hodgkin lymphoma than in age- and sex-matched general-population comparators, by margins that are modest in size yet clinically important; Fatigue and dyspnea are the symptom domains that differ most from comparators; The lower quality of life is still evident more than ten years after diagnosis, with the relative difference narrowing as time since diagnosis increases; Mental and emotional functioning also scored lower than in comparators in this comparison, but this domain is contested, as earlier survivor reports describe emotional and mental health as comparable to or even better than the general population. Certainty: The pattern is consistent across several validated measures in a large matched comparison, but it reflects associations measured at a single point in time rather than demonstrated causes of the impairment, and modest, unbalanced survey response leaves room for residual confounding. Scope: applies to Hodgkin lymphoma after completion of treatment in adults across a wide age range, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents treatment-related cardiopulmonary toxicity as the demonstrated cause of the reduced quality of life, or recommends routine cardiac and pulmonary surveillance of all survivors on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

The domains that most consistently remain worse than general-population norms in Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) survivors are **fatigue/vitality, cognitive functioning, role functioning, social functioning, and "symptom-burden" domains (dyspnoea, sleep problems, financial difficulties)**, plus **sexual functioning**; general health and physical health are impaired in some cohorts but not others, and emotional/mental health findings are mixed — several large series find mental HRQoL essentially normalises.

## Evidence by domain

**Fatigue — the most robust and reproducible deficit.** In a Dutch population-based comparison with an age- and sex-matched norm cohort, the QLQ-C30 fatigue subscale identified fatigue in 43% of HL survivors vs 28% of the norm population (P=0.002), and the Fatigue Assessment Scale gave 41% vs 23% (P<0.001) [PMC3929869]. In a Norwegian cohort, chronic fatigue prevalence was ~3-fold higher than in matched controls ([passage text removed]% after HDT-ASCT, vs 14.9% and 10.6% in controls, P<0.001) [[passage text removed]]. Fatigue remains frequent even after contemporary risk-adapted regimens with limited radiotherapy (42% of responders), without association with stage, chemotherapy or RT, and is linked to worse work ability and unemployment [actaorthop.org/actaoncologica/article/view/35007].

**Cognitive functioning.** HL survivors had significantly and clinically relevantly lower cognitive functioning (concentration/memory) than the norm population, closely tied to fatigue [PMC3929869]. In the German Hodgkin Study Group longitudinal analysis of HD13/HD14/HD15, cognitive function was one of the domains that failed to recover — notably, cognitive function and motivation were the domains that did *not* improve in the H8 trial follow-up either [[passage text removed]; PMC4966803].

**Role, social, emotional functioning and symptom scales — persistent deviation from reference values.** In the GHSG analysis, "[passage text removed]" in the fifth year after therapy, with deviations from reference values of 14–23 points (12–29 points from year 2 onward, against a ~10-point clinical-relevance margin); by contrast, **no** deficits were seen for physical functioning, pain, nausea, appetite, diarrhoea or constipation [[passage text removed] systematic review of HL/NHL survivors similarly concluded the most affected domains with clinically important differences [passage text removed], with social functioning worse in 5 of 8 comparative studies [PMC3150657].

**Financial/socioeconomic domain.** Financial difficulties recur as an impaired domain both in the GHSG trials (most affected domain in the first follow-up year) [ascopost.com/...] and in registry reviews [PMC3150657]. In adolescent/young-adult lymphoma survivors from the PROFILES registry, seven domains were significantly and clinically relevantly poorer than in a matched normative population: physical, role, cognitive, emotional and social functioning, fatigue, and financial difficulties [medicaljournalssweden.se/actaoncologica/article/view/24917].

**General health / physical health.** The classic Norwegian SF-36 study found HL survivors scored lower than [passage text removed], sex and education, concluding poorer HRQoL "primarily in physical health" [[passage text removed]; PMC3150657]. A later Norwegian cohort also found worse bodily pain, general health, (role) physical and social functioning [PMC3150657]. However, the same review found physical functioning deficits in only 4 of 10 comparative studies [PMC3150657].

**Sexual functioning.** A systematic review of male lymphoma survivors concluded [passage text removed] [eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/152450]. In a long-term HL survivor cohort with matched controls, erectile dysfunction was more prevalent (18.89% vs 6.67%, p=.0239) and female sexual dysfunction markedly so (46.88% vs 15.22%, p<.0001), including loss of desire (38.04% vs 23.26%, p=.0361) [PMC11695136]. The GHSG longitudinal sexual-QoL analysis found scores recovered to the reference line in early stages but remained below it in advanced stages [nature.com/articles/bjc2012550]. Note a discordant smaller study: male HL survivors' IIEF scores were comparable to matched controls overall, with problems concentrated after BEACOPP [PMC7471085].

**Mental/emotional health — inconsistent.** A methodological review of lymphoma survivorship concluded survivors experience "[passage text removed]" [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20218810], and the HL/NHL review found no clinically important differences in mental health [PMC3150657]. Against this, depressive symptoms were more prevalent than in matched controls in a Norwegian survivor cohort (10.5% vs 6.1%, p=0.03 after conventional therapy; 20.0% vs 5.1% after HDT-ASCT, p<0.01), though all effect sizes were small [[passage text removed]], and anxiety/depression symptom levels were higher than norms in the Dutch cohort (23% and 18% vs 13% and 12%) [PMC3929869]. A survey of older HL survivors found emotional functioning and worries similar to controls, with only fatigue and mobility reaching moderate clinical significance [[passage text removed]].

## Important caveat

Not all datasets show persistent impairment. The EORTC reference-value analysis of 5-year HL survivors from four randomised trials concluded that "[passage text removed]," suggesting scores may normalise over long-term survival [[passage text removed]], and a Dutch long-term survivor study found SF-36 PCS/MCS medians close to 50 (the Dutch population average) and EQ-5D-5L index scores very similar to population values [pure.eur.nl/.../205102748]. A population-based study also reported better HRQoL in 10–15-year than in 5–9-year survivors [repository.tilburguniversity.edu/.../607a7a96]. Differences across studies are partly attributable to instrument choice (SF-36 vs QLQ-C30), era of treatment, and survivorship duration [PMC3150657], and women and survivors with comorbidities or late effects consistently fare worse [PMC3150657; medicaljournalssweden.se/actaoncologica/article/view/24917].
answers.connect:
**Answer:** Across studies, the domains that most consistently remain worse in Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) survivors than in the general population are physical functioning and role/physical role functioning, fatigue/vitality, dyspnoea, social and cognitive functioning, and general/global health, with financial difficulties and (in some cohorts) emotional/mental functioning affected earlier in survivorship; evidence is not unanimous, and some cohorts report near-normalisation at long follow-up.

**Largest matched comparison (Danish nationwide, 1777 HL vs 6166 matched comparators; HeartQoL, QLQ-C30, SF-36, EQ-5D).** HL respondents scored consistently and significantly lower than comparators at [passage text removed], with differences that remained clinically important even beyond 10 years [S:c2ff2167-8bd6-5729-b86e-123dd773a975]. On the QLQ-C30 functional scales, [passage text removed] were significantly and clinically importantly lower in all follow-up strata; emotional functioning was clinically meaningfully lower only in the short and medium strata (adjusted MD −6.2 and −6.1 points) and no longer met the MCID beyond 10 years (MD −4.0) [S:cbbeb934-2b39-57a0-a8ac-ca92c6b5f948]. Symptoms: fatigue, dyspnoea and insomnia were elevated across all follow-up groups; fatigue was the most pronounced overall (adjusted MD 13.6, 12.9 and 9.1 points for short, medium and long follow-up), while dyspnoea showed its largest difference in the long-term group (MD 10.0 points). Pain, appetite loss and financial difficulties were worse only in the short/medium strata (financial difficulties MD 5.6 and 9.0 points) [S:d7addedc-4b99-501f-bffc-9ea6938dddc5]. On the SF-36, both component summaries were statistically lower but below the 5-point MCID; the largest domain-level gaps were [passage text removed] in all follow-up groups, with general health the one domain whose relative difference did not attenuate over time [S:e6efa077-9f7e-5cb0-8dd5-65b4e6cf8322]. EQ-5D index differences were statistically significant but sub-MCID [S:5e5a348a-ef4a-537a-8d75-e39101e047ea]; HeartQoL global, physical and emotional subscales were clinically importantly impaired in all strata [S:55b001a5-9c57-531a-9242-f5e300c9f6f6]. The authors note earlier French and Spanish matched studies similarly found lower physical, cognitive and social functioning plus more dyspnoea, fatigue and financial difficulties, whereas mental/emotional deficits were generally not detected in those smaller cohorts [S:cb2b5e7c-764c-5a24-910a-d175dba01803].

**Systematic review evidence.** A systematic review of HL and NHL survivors concluded [passage text removed] [S:c66f21c8-498f-55b0-a244-bbfbf381e79c].

**Younger survivors.** In AYA lymphoma survivors (PROFILES registry), significantly and clinically relevant poorer scores were seen in seven domains — physical, role, cognitive, emotional and social functioning, fatigue and financial difficulties — with the largest gaps [passage text removed]; global quality of life and psychological distress did not differ [S:fd9c3ed6-b051-5393-a9a6-898eddf1ce3e][S:b2131e10-b383-54bc-83f7-fd647d4ef1b8].

**Fatigue specifically.** Chronic fatigue prevalence is higher in HL survivors than in the general population, and HL survivors report decreased physical functioning relative to the general population [S:4e5a5c8b-e09a-53d9-8a8e-97bbb3a2dfd7]. A review of haematological cancers likewise reported fatigue levels in HL survivors exceeding healthy controls years after treatment [S:3fa2d2c6-f549-5ad4-8375-2f13a736e0ba].

**Counter-evidence / caveats.** EORTC reference-value work found 5-year HL survivors' HRQoL comparable to the general population, suggesting scores may normalise over long-term survival [S:d4f1666b-ff16-598b-8c4f-6257f4fbad2f]. In the Dutch BETER/INSIGHT cohort (median ~25 years since diagnosis, SF-36 and EQ-5D-5L), overall HRQoL matched Dutch general-population levels [S:461d0510-fd30-5b87-81ba-2e07d924d17d]. A German long-term survivor survey found all SF-36 subscale means below the norm mean of 50 but within one SD, interpreted as not substantially reduced [S:7f8dd8fc-4d43-5a06-81c2-fb45a54b9e6b]. Discrepancies plausibly reflect sample size/power, era of treatment and instrument choice — the largest study explicitly attributes its detection of emotional-domain deficits to greater power [S:cb2b5e7c-764c-5a24-910a-d175dba01803].

**Domains flagged clinically but not quantified against population norms in the sources retrieved:** sexual function, fertility, employment/insurance and memory–concentration problems are described as common psychosocial late effects reducing survivors' quality of life, but these passages do not provide a general-population comparison [S:fb81bfd6-485f-5a10-a452-34b7e1f88e22].

rows.question: What is known about immunosuppressive management of shrinking lung syndrome in systemic lupus erythematosus?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Reported management pairs corticosteroids with a steroid-sparing immunosuppressive agent, most often rituximab; A substantial share of reported patients received high-dose corticosteroid monotherapy instead of a steroid-sparing agent; Pulmonary function improved in roughly half of the patients who were treated; In a small single-centre series, most patients given rituximab with corticosteroids had no residual respiratory symptoms. Certainty: The supporting evidence comes from a handful of individually described patients treated without any comparison group or head-to-head comparison of agents, with heterogeneous and often incomplete follow-up, so the findings describe observed patterns of care and recovery rather than established treatment effects. Scope: applies to shrinking lung syndrome complicating systemic lupus erythematosus in adults, predominantly women, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents rituximab, or any other agent, as an established first-line therapy of proven superiority, or prescribes a standardised regimen on this basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** There are no controlled trials or guidelines; glucocorticoids are the near-universal first-line therapy, added immunosuppressants (azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, mycophenolate) have no proven efficacy beyond steroids, and rituximab is the best-supported option for corticosteroid-refractory disease — with most patients improving symptomatically but a minority regaining normal lung function.

**Level of evidence and first-line therapy.** There are no evidence-based guidelines; [passage text removed]," usually 0.5–1 mg/kg prednisolone daily, optionally preceded by short-course IV methylprednisolone depending on severity, and corticosteroids are typically successful as monotherapy ([StatPearls NBK568683]([passage text removed])). Two 2026 systematic reviews confirm glucocorticoids as the mainstay in 95–96% of reported patients, with rituximab emerging as the effective primary biologic for refractory cases ([PMID 42301754](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42301754); doi 10.1177/09612033261461973).

**What the largest pooled series show.** Duron et al., combining 15 new cases with 155 literature cases, concluded that steroids and analgesics [passage text removed], that [passage text removed]," and that [passage text removed]" ([PMID 27481038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27481038)). In their review, [passage text removed]%) and, when given first-line, were always combined with corticosteroids; [passage text removed], and rituximab in 7 cases — improvement was reported both as first-line with corticosteroids and after corticosteroid failure, including one patient who responded after low-dose steroids and beta-mimetics failed ([hal-01397175]([passage text removed])). Outcomes: clinical improvement in 48/52 (94%) and PFT improvement in 36/47, with worsening in 4 ([PMID 27481038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27481038)); a review reported clinical improvement in 94% and functional improvement in 77% of cases ([Smyth, QJM 2018]([passage text removed])).

**Incomplete functional recovery is the rule.** Despite treatment, most patients do not normalise PFTs: only about 20% regained normal lung function in one review of 35 cases with paired PFTs, Duron reported chronic persistent hemidiaphragm elevation in 42.9%, and an 20-case single-centre report found 86.7% with continued restriction ([PMC7789161]([passage text removed])).

**Steroid-sparing strategies (newest data).** A 2026 systematic review of 52 cases (44 literature + 8 single-centre) found immunosuppressive therapy used as a corticosteroid-sparing strategy in all of their own cohort versus 52.2% of published cases, with rituximab the most commonly used agent; pulmonary function improved in 62.5% of their patients and 50% of reported patients, stabilised in roughly a quarter, with [passage text removed] ([PMID 41823883](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41823883?fc=None&ff=20260315133251&v=2.19.0.post6+133c1fe); doi 10.1177/09612033261435924). Those authors argue that early diagnosis and timely initiation of immunosuppression *beyond* corticosteroids is critical, and report that early rituximab and mycophenolate mofetil as steroid-sparing agents gave good symptom control with improved or stabilised function ([10.1177/09612033261435924]([passage text removed])).

**Agent-specific signals.** A pooled analysis of 49 patients (corticosteroids, azathioprine, hydroxychloroquine, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, MMF, rituximab) found symptomatic improvement in 92% but functional improvement in only 61%, relapse/progression in 12%, and mortality 2%; high ANA titre (>[passage text removed] positivity (OR 6.75, p=0.036) predicted poor outcomes and those patients additionally required rituximab, whereas azathioprine correlated with delayed symptomatic recovery ([ACR abstract, Gupta & Raman]([passage text removed])).

**Rituximab-based salvage.** Individual reports document response after failure of conventional therapy: a patient unresponsive to glucocorticoids plus azathioprine/mycophenolate improved symptomatically and functionally on rituximab 1 g ×2 repeated 6-monthly, allowing prednisone taper to 5 mg/day ([Reumatol Clin S2173574314000239]([passage text removed])); a 14-year-old achieved full recovery of lung function with rituximab plus HCQ/MMF and steroid withdrawal, returning to competitive sport ([PMC7789161]([passage text removed])); and a 28-year-old with SLE/Sjögren overlap who developed severe SLS *while on* corticosteroids and azathioprine had dramatic improvement with rituximab plus cyclophosphamide, one of the largest vital-capacity gains among 35 published cases ([Respiration 84:144]([passage text removed])). A recent case also reported sustained response to combined cyclophosphamide and rituximab ([PMC12643461]([passage text removed])).

**Belimumab and breakthrough on therapy.** Evidence is limited to case reports, and SLS can arise during immunosuppression: one patient developed SLS while receiving belimumab and improved after switching to mycophenolate plus prednisone ([institutional report]([passage text removed])), while another report describes improvement in symptoms and lung volumes with belimumab ([Chest 2016;150:300A, cited in Borrell reference list](https://www.academia.edu/85093691/Shrinking_Lung_Syndrome_And_Systemic_Lupus_Erythematosus_A_Case_Series_Literature_Review)).

**Adjuncts.** Non-immunosuppressive measures are used alongside: [passage text removed] ([StatPearls NBK568683]([passage text removed])); theophylline 750 mg daily improved dyspnoea and PFTs in the first such report ([PMID 8124905](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8124905)); beta-agonist use was associated with clinical and functional improvement in the pooled analysis, though not at conventional significance (OR 10.02, p=0.052) ([ACR abstract]([passage text removed])).

**Key gap:** published series do not specify steroid dose, sequencing, duration or tapering, so dosing is at the treating physician's discretion and standardised recommendations are lacking ([Rheumatology Advisor feature]([passage text removed])). No randomised trial data exist for any agent in SLS.
answers.connect:
## Bottom line

There is no guideline-backed or trial-tested regimen for shrinking lung syndrome (SLS) in SLE; all evidence is from case reports, small series, and pooled reviews. Practice converges on moderate-to-high-dose glucocorticoids as first-line, with a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant added early (increasingly rituximab), which reliably relieves symptoms but rarely normalizes lung function.

## Evidence base and its limits

[passage text removed]," and evidence for refractory disease is "purely empirical" without standardized protocols [S:61cd878b]. Available data are "[passage text removed]," and heterogeneity in treatment and reporting precluded quantitative synthesis/meta-analysis [S:0c4a0a45][S:2d5867ec]. The updated review also flags likely publication bias overstating efficacy of both steroids and rituximab, since clinical improvement is reported in 75–95% of published cases [S:0aff3f69].

## First-line: glucocorticoids

Glucocorticoids were first-line in 95–96% of pooled cases [S:0aff3f69]. In a recent case series, patients with more severe presentations (including hypoxemia) received IV methylprednisolone pulses followed by oral prednisone 0.3–0.5 mg/kg combined with an immunosuppressant, explicitly to shorten corticosteroid exposure [S:a7706aa7]. Still, 39% of reported patients in the past decade were treated with high-dose prednisone monotherapy [S:0c4a0a45].

## Conventional steroid-sparing agents

In the Toronto Lupus Clinic cohort (SLS prevalence 1.53%), regimens combined corticosteroids and antimalarials with azathioprine, methotrexate, or mycophenolate mofetil; clinical improvement occurred in 19/20 (95%) after a mean 2.8 months, and spirometric improvement in 15/16 (93.8%), but was partial — 13/15 (86.7%) responders retained a restrictive defect despite increased volumes [S:8c75823d]. One patient improved on methotrexate monotherapy; one failed corticosteroids plus azathioprine; two relapsers (at 2 and 9 years) were re-treated with glucocorticoids plus cyclophosphamide pulses (500 mg every two weeks, six doses) [S:8c75823d]. Cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, MMF, and rituximab have been used after azathioprine failure or intolerance [S:0c4a0a45].

## Rituximab

Rituximab is now the most frequently used immunosuppressant in the recent literature [S:93554005], used at some point in 75% of one case series versus 18.1% of reviewed literature cases, dosed 1 g on days 1 and 15 repeated every 6 months [S:6cf0fbcd][S:a7706aa7]. It "[passage text removed]," and worked both as targeted SLS rescue and when given for a concomitant systemic flare such as nephritis; symptomatic relief typically appears within ~2 months, but PFT stabilization takes 6–12 months [S:0aff3f69]. Supporting case-level data: a pooled review found 15 adult and 2 pediatric rituximab reports, with all 4 adults having well-documented post-treatment PFTs achieving normal or near-normal values and the remaining 11 improved or stabilized [S:a0b54ceb]; another literature review reported improvement in 11, stabilization in 3, and deterioration in 1 [S:3e728b3c]. A 14-year-old with FEV1 27%/FVC 29%/TLC 43% treated with rituximab plus methylprednisolone reached FVC 83% and TLC 94% at 4 years [S:97d9602d]. Steroid-refractory cases responding to rituximab (sometimes with cyclophosphamide) are also reported in adults [S:dcea334f][S:d82eb407].

## Outcomes and de-escalation

Symptomatic resolution occurs in 75–95%, but complete PFT normalization in only 20–23%, with ~80% retaining chronic restriction; SLS-attributed mortality is low (2–5.5%) [S:61cd878b]. Immunosuppression could be stopped in 3/8 patients after a mean 5.5 ± 2 years of sustained pulmonary remission [S:a7706aa7]. One narrative source argues SLS "usually" does not need long-term immunosuppression, distinguishing it from diaphragmatic palsy due to inflammatory myopathy or myasthenia — and reported a steroid-refractory patient who responded to two 1 g rituximab doses two weeks apart [S:67cb73b6].

## Adjuncts (non-immunosuppressive)

Recommended alongside drug therapy: non-invasive ventilation, inspiratory muscle training, and respiratory rehabilitation as adjuvants in refractory disease [S:2d5867ec], with a case of substantial functional improvement over six months using nocturnal NIV plus structured rehabilitation [S:6602fbbd]. Theophylline and beta-[passage text removed], with efficacy described as controversial [S:3967cbd1] or effective in a minority of patients [S:7232b15f].

## Gaps

No randomized comparisons of agents exist; head-to-head efficacy of azathioprine vs MMF vs rituximab, optimal steroid dose/taper, and treatment duration are unresolved, and prospective multicenter standardization is called for [S:2d5867ec][S:0c4a0a45]. I found no evidence in these searches for newer SLE biologics (e.g., belimumab, anifrolumab) as SLS-directed therapy beyond a single pediatric-onset case in which lung function improved on belimumab [[passage text removed]/PMC7789161].

rows.question: How do multiple chronic conditions relate to health outcomes in adults with autoimmune and inflammatory rheumatic diseases?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: A greater burden of coexisting chronic conditions is associated with increased all-cause mortality and shorter survival; A greater burden of coexisting chronic conditions is associated with worsening disability, poorer functional status and lower health-related quality of life; A greater burden of coexisting chronic conditions is associated with more healthcare utilisation and higher healthcare costs; The mortality signal is not uniform: excess all-cause mortality accompanies multimorbidity in rheumatoid arthritis and in condition clusters involving cancer or cardiorespiratory disease, whereas lower mortality has been reported in polymyalgia rheumatica and attributed to closer medical follow-up. Certainty: The direction of the outcome associations holds across most of the diseases considered, yet the supporting evidence establishes association rather than demonstrated causation, the mortality pattern is not uniform, and the survival and disability models leave their sample size and specific disease population unstated. Scope: applies to autoimmune and inflammatory rheumatic diseases in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents multidisciplinary, deprescribing or self-management programmes as demonstrated to improve survival, function or quality of life in adults with these diseases and multiple chronic conditions, or recommends them on that basis.

answers.websearch:
## Bottom line

Across autoimmune and inflammatory rheumatic diseases (AIIRDs), multiple chronic conditions (MCCs/multimorbidity) are both more common than in matched non-disease populations and independently predict worse outcomes — higher mortality, less remission and more flare, worse physical function and quality of life, and greater treatment/healthcare complexity. A recent narrative review of the field frames the risk as arising [passage text removed] from the comedications they require, concluding that [passage text removed]" [journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1759720X261462685].

## Mortality

- A systematic review of 19 longitudinal studies in RA (Canning et al., *Arthritis Care & Research* 74(9):1500–1512) found multimorbidity significantly associated with higher all-cause mortality in 9 of 10 studies reporting mortality [PMC11475560; eprints.gla.ac.uk/235733].
- In the Nurses' Health Study matched cohort (1,007 incident RA vs 10,070 comparators, 61 conditions in the Multimorbidity-Weighted Index), morbidity accrued faster after RA onset and the MWI "[passage text removed]" (adjusted HR 1.25, 95% CI 1.13–1.40) [PMC7275877; [passage text removed]].
- In SLE, a systematic review/meta-analysis of Charlson Comorbidity Index studies reported a pooled OR for all-cause mortality of [passage text removed]) in patients with high comorbidity burden, with no heterogeneity (I²=0%) [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41008417].

## Disease activity, remission and flare

- In a population-based incident RA cohort (median follow-up 10.3 years; 55 chronic conditions), multimorbidity (MM2+) predicted higher odds of flare visits (OR 1.29, 1.04–1.59) and lower odds of remission visits (OR 0.66, 0.49–0.90); substantial multimorbidity (MM5+) showed similar effects (flare OR 1.26; remission OR 0.67, 0.51–0.90), with reduced remission odds in women but not men (interaction p=0.046) [PMC12336466; [passage text removed]]. In the earlier abstract of this work, [passage text removed]].
- Patterns matter more than counts: mental health/[passage text removed] were associated with higher DAS28 and MDHAQ, whereas the metabolic pattern was not; only chronic pain remained associated longitudinally, and scores rose with the number of patterns present (highest with all 4: DAS28 β 0.59, 0.36–0.83) [[passage text removed]; PMC10758525].
- Treatment response: using a counted multimorbidity index in the BRASS cohort, each additional morbidity carried OR 0.72 ([passage text removed] (0.70–0.94) for low disease activity [PMC6348828]; a review summarises that [passage text removed]% and that patients with comorbidities often receive less aggressive RA treatment despite higher disease activity [[passage text removed]].

## Function, quality of life, patient-reported outcomes

- In RA, all 10 studies examining function/QoL found multimorbidity predicted reduced functional status, with independent contribution to functional decline over time; somatic comorbidity and depression were particularly detrimental, and the 3 QoL studies showed significantly lower QoL [PMC11475560].
- In axSpA, a nationwide population-based study (1,776 patients) found each additional comorbidity associated with BASDAI +0.17 (0.09–0.24) and BASFI +0.24 (0.15–0.32), independent of treatment; depression and chronic pulmonary disease drove much of the effect [[passage text removed] Ankylosing Spondylitis Registry of Ireland cohort similarly linked multimorbidity to worse BASDAI, worse physical function and increased disability [jrheum.org/content/47/2/218; ankylosingspondylitisnews.com/2019/06/17].
- A single-centre axSpA cohort found extended multimorbidity [passage text removed] — but, notably, with *better* mental health and vitality domain scores, illustrating domain-specific effects [PMC12141145].
- In PsA, patients with multimorbidity had worse SF-36 bodily pain (34.7 vs 47.5), physical functioning (52.1 vs 63.1) [passage text removed] vs 42.8; all p<0.01) [[passage text removed]].

## Why the burden accumulates

- Multimorbidity is more prevalent at diagnosis and accrues faster afterwards. In population-based RA, cumulative incidence of multimorbidity at 10 years was 56.5% in RA vs 47.9% in non-RA (adjusted HR 1.39, 1.14–1.69), though substantial multimorbidity incidence was not clearly increased (HR 1.17, 0.93–1.47) [[passage text removed]].
- In SLE (Lupus Midwest Network, 57 conditions), 81.5% of established cases had multimorbidity vs 61.6% of comparators (OR 2.98, 2.18–4.11) and substantial multimorbidity 52.8% vs 27.6% (OR 3.35, 2.50–4.53); excess burden was evident even before SLE incidence and was initially driven by conditions unrelated to the lupus damage index [PMC11534092]. After SLE classification the risk of developing ≥2 conditions was 2.5-fold higher (HR 2.46, 1.84–3.29) [[passage text removed]...].
- Contributing mechanisms include systemic inflammation, treatment toxicity, care fragmentation across providers, and exclusion of comorbid patients from trials [rmdopen.bmj.com/content/8/1/e002022]; polypharmacy is a linked risk, with BSRBR-RA data showing that the likelihood of clinically meaningful improvement fell and serious adverse events rose with each additional non-rheumatic medication [[passage text removed]].
- Frailty commonly overlaps: a systematic review of 19 studies across RA, SSc, SLE, vasculitis and PsA found frailty prevalent [passage text removed]; Lieber et al., thelancet.com/journals/lanrhe/article/PIIS2665-9913(24)00191-7].

## Caveats

Evidence quality is limited by inconsistent terminology and measurement (comorbidity vs multimorbidity; CCI, RDCI, MMI, MWI capture different conditions), few QoL-focused studies, under-capture of mental health conditions, English-language restriction, and scarce data in younger, ethnic-minority and lower-socioeconomic populations [PMC11475560; journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1759720X261462685]. Findings are not uniform: one study of patients starting a first biologic DMARD found no remission difference between multimorbid and non-multimorbid groups [[passage text removed]], and Busby et al. found baseline RDCI did not predict worse HAQ at 5 or 10 years [PMC11463754]. Most data are observational, so causal direction (multimorbidity → worse control vs worse control → multimorbidity) is not established.
answers.connect:
## Conclusion

Multiple chronic conditions (MCCs/[passage text removed] are consistently associated with worse outcomes across the board: higher all-cause mortality, poorer physical function and accelerated disability, lower health-related quality of life, worse disease control, and greater healthcare utilization and cost.

## Prevalence and patterns

MCCs are ubiquitous across AIIRDs and often exceed rates in age-matched general populations, with reported [passage text removed] (RA) and 81.5% in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) cohorts; cardiopulmonary and mental health disorders are frequently observed patterns [S:32ff72be-b30f-5600-96b4-228b297716d2]. Machine-learning analyses of US claims and Veterans Affairs records identified cardiopulmonary, cardiometabolic, and mental health/chronic pain clusters, all overrepresented in RA versus non-RA [S:783a7418-72aa-5e9f-8893-f1e6756a868b]. Population-based work confirms higher multimorbidity prevalence in RA than non-RA and expands the condition list beyond the standard 44 morbidities (e.g., organic sleep disorders, vitamin D deficiency, foot ulcers) [S:357e89aa-ef41-5ce0-863b-0bda7f7a0659]. In axSpA, multimorbidity and extended multimorbidity were present in 63.8% and 38.7% of a real-world cohort [S:9b712b9c-448b-5102-9f22-22d7b581c9e7]; in idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM), 35% had basic and 14% complex multimorbidity [S:783a7418-72aa-5e9f-8893-f1e6756a868b].

## Mortality and function

A systematic review of 19 studies found multimorbidity [passage text removed] RA [S:eeffe4cf-1dcb-5623-a767-6f5f53fdc584][S:38e904ab-3593-5df7-8643-2f17668f5fcc]; nine of the 19 showed increased mortality and ten showed impaired functional status [S:98a5273d-77c9-5a59-9d1a-cc4ae5536cd1]. Specific quantitative signals include worse survival with multimorbidity ([passage text removed]), worsening HAQ-DI disability (+[passage text removed]), and greater odds of a high-increasing disability trajectory over 10 years ([passage text removed]); in ANCA-associated vasculitis, 3+ morbidities were associated with a 3.89-fold increase in healthcare costs [S:38e904ab-3593-5df7-8643-2f17668f5fcc]. In UK Biobank RA participants, specific condition clusters (e.g., cancer, or asthma/COPD/heart disease combinations) carried significantly increased risks of mortality, major adverse cardiac events, and emergency hospitalization [S:38e904ab-3593-5df7-8643-2f17668f5fcc]. Beyond RA, systemic sclerosis with high comorbidity index scores was linked to worse survival and poorer physical function, and multimorbidity in AAV to increased costs and mortality [S:4dc9bd2e-e2ff-54e6-95a8-d9a296973a80]. Notably, a "mortality gap" persists in rheumatic conditions despite biologic therapy, and concomitant conditions have been reported as the strongest predictor of mortality [S:fdb1ef1a-d028-5caf-9ae7-46d0502d3518]. Reduced mortality reported in some polymyalgia rheumatica studies was attributed to possible surveillance bias from regular follow-up [S:38e904ab-3593-5df7-8643-2f17668f5fcc].

## Disease control and patient-reported outcomes

MCCs impair achievement of treatment targets. In a population-based incident RA cohort (659 patients), [passage text removed]–1.53) higher odds of flare, and [passage text removed]–0.90) lower odds of remission [S:03af7cc6-0c6d-5ced-a7b4-37facc160e53]; effects were modified by sex and social vulnerability [S:2e8ab8de-2966-5765-9e22-5d3d4173fa4f][S:c1c41a44-63c2-58bd-ac5f-845f101e479b]. Earlier work found the odds of remission decreased by 28% per additional morbidity one year after DMARD initiation, with patient global assessment rising almost linearly with morbidity count independent of RA disease activity [S:9dd8f4d3-04d6-5a4d-81b1-0d02ea16e541]. Functional ability deteriorates with increasing number of comorbidities independent of disease activity, and comorbid patients are less likely to reach remission [S:457f05b6-8c9f-5e17-8214-f4fbd6cdc179]. In axSpA, extended multimorbidity was associated with higher (worse) HAQ and MDHAQ scores and higher BASDAI in those with ≥3 comorbidities — though, unexpectedly, comorbidity count correlated with better SF-36 mental health and vitality domain scores [S:9b712b9c-448b-5102-9f22-22d7b581c9e7]; a nationwide axSpA study likewise linked overall comorbidity burden to disease activity and functional impairment [S:31ebf31e-3ab3-53e9-abfd-294e0fd23568]. In IIM (COVAD-2, n=1558), patients had higher odds of comorbidity, basic and complex multimorbidity, and mental health disorders than other AIIRDs and healthy controls, with correspondingly worse PROMIS global physical/mental health, physical function, and fatigue scores (all p<0.001) [S:991707aa-d4ae-56a3-961d-1a807b39a693][S:38e904ab-3593-5df7-8643-2f17668f5fcc]. In PsA, comorbidities are associated with greater pain, functional limitation and poorer quality of life [S:4dc9bd2e-e2ff-54e6-95a8-d9a296973a80].

## Mechanisms and care implications

The MCC burden is attributed to chronic inflammation, cumulative organ damage, lifestyle factors, and treatment effects (e.g., glucocorticoids); MCCs can obscure AIIRD symptoms, delay diagnosis, necessitate complex polypharmacy with drug–drug interaction risk, and limit treatment options [S:65060aa2-eb9d-5120-b103-8b62d3b3eeb1][S:b04c011d-a2c4-5c45-bd97-3fe77a118ebf]. Multimorbid patients are also systematically excluded from randomized trials, limiting the evidence base and generalizability of single-disease guidelines [S:457f05b6-8c9f-5e17-8214-f4fbd6cdc179][S:9dd8f4d3-04d6-5a4d-81b1-0d02ea16e541]. Authors therefore advocate a holistic, person-centered framework using multidisciplinary teams and [passage text removed] [S:32ff72be-b30f-5600-96b4-228b297716d2].

## Caveats

Definitions of multimorbidity vary widely (condition counts, weighted indices such as Charlson or the Rheumatic Disease Comorbidity Index, machine-learning clusters), which hampers cross-cohort comparison [S:a7948948-85e6-5f3b-b365-1a5788383493][S:357e89aa-ef41-5ce0-863b-0bda7f7a0659]. Evidence is heavily RA-weighted, with data sparser in SLE, systemic sclerosis, vasculitis and myositis, and the impact of concurrent mental health conditions remains understudied [S:eeffe4cf-1dcb-5623-a767-6f5f53fdc584][S:98a5273d-77c9-5a59-9d1a-cc4ae5536cd1]. Much of the evidence is observational, so directionality (inflammation driving comorbidity vs. comorbidity worsening disease control) cannot be firmly established from the sources retrieved.

rows.question: What is the treatment outcome for combining duvelisib and oral azacitidine in patients with relapsed or refractory mature T-cell lymphoma?
rows.gold: A strong answer conveys: Duvelisib combined with oral azacitidine produced objective responses in roughly half of evaluable patients, most of those responses being complete; Complete responses were enriched in the T-follicular-helper phenotype, a preliminary observation resting on very few such patients; Median progression-free survival in the overall treated group was short; Median duration of response was not reached because responders left treatment for allogeneic transplant rather than for progression. Certainty: The evidence is early, uncontrolled and rests on very few treated patients with heavily censored time-to-event data, so it points to encouraging activity rather than established benefit. Scope: applies to relapsed or refractory mature T-cell lymphoma in adults, outpatient settings. An answer is wrong if it presents the combination as demonstrated to be superior to single-agent therapy or recommends it as standard treatment or a routine bridge to transplant on this basis.

answers.websearch:
**Bottom line:** In the only trial of this combination — a phase 1, open-label 3+3 dose-escalation study at Moffitt (NCT05065866, N=14) — duvelisib plus oral azacitidine (BMS-986345) produced an overall response rate of 46% with a 31% complete response rate, a manageable safety profile, and a striking but very small subgroup signal in nodal T-follicular-helper (TFH) lymphoma; median PFS was short (2.2 months) while median duration of response was not reached ([PMC13431344]([passage text removed]); [PubMed 42545812](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42545812)).

**Efficacy**
- Of 13 efficacy-evaluable patients: ORR 46% (n=6), CR 31% (n=4), PR 15% (n=2), 1 unevaluable. Median PFS [passage text removed]) ([PMC13431344]([passage text removed])).
- All 4 evaluable nodal TFH-lineage patients achieved CR; the authors explicitly label this 100% CR rate hypothesis-generating given the denominator of four, and recommend prioritizing/restricting further development to the nodal TFH subtype ([PMC13431344]([passage text removed])).
- Median DOR was not reached. Only 1 responder (PTCL-NOS, PR) progressed, at 2.5 months; three were censored at allogeneic transplant (1.3, 3.4, 3.7 months while in response) and two remained in ongoing CR off therapy (one ~[passage text removed] ~9.9 months). The authors state the short median PFS understates durability in responders because responders were censored for transplant or toxicity discontinuation rather than progression ([PMC13431344]([passage text removed])).

**Dose and safety (N=14 treated)**
- MTD = duvelisib 50 mg BID for the first two cycles then 25 mg BID, with oral azacitidine 100 mg daily [passage text removed]. Escalation stopped at dose level 3 after two DLTs of grade 3 transaminitis, establishing dose level 2 as MTD; both DLTs were reversible with drug interruption ([PMC13431344]([passage text removed]); [cancernetwork.com]([passage text removed])).
- Grade ≥3 events: [passage text removed]%, leukocytosis 14%. Most any-grade toxicity (nausea 71%, vomiting 43%, cytopenias) was grade 1–2 and manageable ([PMC13431344]([passage text removed])). Discontinuations: 2 for grade 3 transaminitis at cohort 3, 1 for rash after 19 cycles ([cancernetwork.com]([passage text removed])).

**Mechanistic correlate:** on-treatment suppression of AKT phosphorylation in peripheral CD3+ T cells was greater [passage text removed] lead-in ([PMC13431344]([passage text removed]); [cancernetwork.com]([passage text removed])).

**Context/caveats:** These numbers are not clearly superior to single-agent duvelisib in the phase 2 PRIMO-EP population (ORR 48.0%, CR 33.3%, median PFS 3.4 months, median OS 12.4 months, n=123), where the AITL subgroup also outperformed (ORR 62.2%, CR 51.4%) ([securabio.com press release]([passage text removed]); [hematologyadvisor.com](https://www.hematologyadvisor.com/news/duvelisib-primo-trial-ptcl-lymphoma-demonstrates-activity-treatment)) — so no cross-trial claim of added benefit is supported. The trial authors themselves cite small sample size, phase 1 selection bias, short follow-up, and absence of global DNA-methylation pharmacodynamics as limitations, and call the combination worthy of further study rather than established ([PMC13431344]([passage text removed])). No randomized data on this doublet in relapsed/refractory disease were found; a separate randomized phase 2 (Alliance A059102/A051902) tests duvelisib or oral azacitidine added to CHO(E)P in *untreated* CD30-negative PTCL ([onclive.com]([passage text removed])).
